name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars
detailed_description: Voice of Cards Trilogy + DLC set A set containing the Voice of Cards Trilogy that brings together all 3 titles from the Voice of Cards series and all the DLC items for each title. Voice of Cards Trilogy The Voice of Cards Trilogy bundles together all three titles from the series; Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars, Voice of Cards: The Forsaken Maiden and Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden. DOWNLOAD THE DEMO! This prologue episode reveals what happened on the day before the events of Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars, following the Ivory Order as they search for a stolen royal treasure. Enjoy an all new, yet appealingly nostalgic gaming experience from YOKO TARO, Keiichi Okabe, Kimihiko Fujisaka. Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars ＋DLC set This product is a set containing 7 DLC items for Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars, that can change the design of in-game components such as cards and avatars to be styled after other YOKO TARO titles as well as an item that can change the appearance of all characters and enemies to a pixel art style. Reviews & Accolades “Excellently crafted” - 8/10 GameSpew “A welcoming turn-based RPG” - 8/10 Noisy Pixel About the Game Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is an RPG set in a world of swords and sorcery, told entirely through the medium of cards. The story follows a self proclaimed hero as they set off to slay a recently awakened dragon, presented in the manner of a tabletop RPG and playing out through narration from the gamesmaster. Enjoy an all new, yet appealingly nostalgic gaming experience from YOKO TARO (Creative Director), Keiichi Okabe (Music), Kimihiko Fujisaka (Character Design.) * Please be aware that parts of the game which require an internet connection may cease to be supported at any point.

_childDocuments_.review: **Don't be confused. This is not a card game. Do not expect a card game. This is a JRPG using a DM and cards as a medium to tell it's story. Play the demo first.My steam hours are off compared to my in-game time and I have finished the game at 18 hours. This included trying to do all the optional content and find all the gear. The combat is disappointingly easy and simple - though I’m still liking it, it feels like a missed opportunity. There was a total of one fight that posed a threat to my party, and I finished the game with zero game overs. Random encounters are very common too, which wouldn't be a problem, but the game is agonizingly slow. Any turbo function would be a huge boon. The combat is your standard turn-based combat with turn order based on speed, enemies have resistances and weaknesses. I'm sure the person reading this has played a game with such a system ten times over. The minor differences seem to be: 1. Mana Generation - every turn you generate a mana crystal which is a resource in using certain skills.2. You can only have up to 4 skills equipped. 3. Dice rolls affecting the dmg/outcome of the skill cardAs a whole, it feels limited and I wish it had more depth.The standout is the presentation of the game. It's set up as a DM guiding you through an adventure with gorgeous card art and beautiful music (although there seems to be a small amount of tracks). The story has been a very standard "Go kill the dragon" so far, however; there have been some nice expected "Yoko Taro Moments" but nothing as impactful in his other works. The charming interactions between the characters make it feel like a light-hearted romp with a good group of friends. The character moments are easily the highlight of the narrative and the most memorable parts. Overall, the narrative is the equivalent of some good comfort food. The random events that can happen while travelling around can be quite amusing, but there aren't a whole lot so you will see lots of repeats. I enjoyed my time with the game, but it's not some great new must-have.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is basically a D&D session summarized with charming aesthetics and presentation. It honestly felt like they had a D&D session and made it into a game. It works. I don't know if it's worth the price tag but maybe these small bullet points can help you decide. I suggest playing the demo before the full game though since they add context to characters.One thing I like is that New Game + keeps everything.Story-specific stuff:◆ There's a total of 5 playable characters. One is misgendered for some reason.◆ Don't expect "Yoko Taro deepness." It's very predictable.◆ The flip side descriptions are either dark, hilarious or creepy. You unlock them by either repeated encounters, talking to every "clone" of them in all towns you visit, etc. Just remember to go back to towns or NPCs after an event.◆ The "banter" can be fun. Although the MC / Ash being a random jerk on some innocent choices is weird. Expect things like these: ◆ There are some hard choices (whether or not it actually matters, I haven't had the time to check).◆ There is no skip cutscene, only mash the confirm key.◆ You might want to talk to NPCs again after certain events.◆ The presentation is very fun but slow. If you are one brave/cheeky adventurer, you can plug a speedhack x2 ~ x3 just to make it more tolerable for you.The gameplay only looks like a card game on surface level but it's more like your typical JRPG. It has the following mechanics:◆ Global Mana / Energy Pool. ◆ You can only equip 4 skills at once. Characters gain 3 passives max as they level up. The Max Level is 30.◆ There are dice rolls to determine success of a status effect or for damage multiplier.◆ Happenstances. They normally contain Random Buffs/Debuffs, Elemental/Status Effects, EXP or Gold Up.◆ Even if you put a character on reserve, they will still level up. So don't be afraid to mix up your party now and then. Don't be too invested in just one character and try to learn their skillsets to be flexible when the story throws a wrench at you once in a while.◆ There's an inventory limit (not per item) of 30.◆ You cannot use your healing spells outside of battle. Inns are always free.There are also some cute mechanics on the overworld map. Random events happen and here are some versions of them:◆ Hidden Merchants without any indication that gives you either a sale or rare items.◆ Stocking up on items and giving it to random events net you a reward while you are exploring.◆ On specific maps, you get 'traps' or 'calamities' that may or may not give you some rewards for properly tackling them.◆ You get random treasure maps or eavesdrop on bandits. Those items are usually the best in the game so keep an eye out!And here are some spoilers I guess:◆ MC / Ash is all rounder but has the strongest single target heal (+30). He takes a while to get good.◆ Mar is the party tank but also the slowest. Her ultimate gear is found in the Mausoleum.◆ Melanie is the mage. Her ultimate weapon is found in the Mausoleum. Her ultimate armor is a treasure around the area.◆ Ridis is the rogue / bard. Secretly insanely strong once you get her weapon. Has an OK AOE heal (+10).◆ Bruno is a mix between a buffer and a fighter. Has a good AOE heal (+20).◆ That 20,000 weapon is legit and easy to obtain. You should have enough money by Chapter 4 (without spending) to 6 (if you bought starter gear) without grinding (just don't escape fights). You also get a ton of cash once you reach the Isle of Blight.◆ This game is not hard at all. Status Effects are nice in this game especially Freeze. Once you get Zero Elements + Triblade/Deadly Mirage, you pretty much win the game.◆ Sometimes, you have to get out of a dungeon and find that there's some secrets unlocked. The easiest one to miss is the superboss.◆ There is no skip cutscene, only mash the confirm key. It gets really annoying when you're trying to get all 4 endings (that I know of) and have a long boss fight in between that. You can fast forward or skip credits though.◆ If you are a huge fan of the RPG Maker series, MC / Ash having the same skillset as the Actor 1 heroes is hilarious.That's all! I'll update if I find out more.

_childDocuments_.review: IMPORTANT FOR FIRST TIME PLAYERS:Do yourself a favor and play the demo first, rush through it until you reach the end (Data doesn't carry over and for good reason.). The Demo's introduction puts you in the shoes of the Ivory Order and how they ended up in the cave to look for the medicine. You get a small glimpse of what the group is all about. Without this bit of information, the sudden twist the actual game presents to you at the beginning doesn't quite hit as hard. It adds a little flavor to that beginning scene.REVIEW:First thoughts,I spent a good time grinding because I'm a junkie for numbers and min-maxing. But despite all of the grinding and preparation, the game is definitely not an 80+ hour journey as you can see from my 21 hour playtime. The level cap is 30 if you're curious and you eventually stagnate with how strong you become because of this. It is a rather short game with not a lot of side quests to keep you busy aside from finding treasure chests. Some world events while cute at first become repetitive as you learn the right solutions to them.STORY:It's really well narrated and if you have a good imagination you can paint yourself a good picture with how things are said and described, very D&D-like. I had a good laugh from time to time and if you're invested in the characters you will too. Not for the impatient though. Let the voice carry you, not so much your eyes. The story has it's twists and turns, and there are decisions to be made, although most fall flat as opposed to being impactful. There's only ONE choice in the game that really matters. You'll know which one it is because you'll gouge your eyes out deciding considering everything that transpired before it.MUSIC:Beautiful compositions. But not varied enough. Boss battles get their own jingle, but its the same one each time. Normal battles get nothing, the overworld music's what you'll get, and you better be prepared to hear the same slow-relaxing tune over and over. It'll drive you nuts if you're grinding, I had to turn the music off when I did this and just jam to my own playlist.There's an alternate album you can purchase but I didn't invest in it. Not that I should to be honest.PROGRESSION:As mentioned before, the progression is really linear. Go here, buy new armor, fight monsters, get stronger, fight a boss, end of chapter. Each chapter is tied to a new area, and unless you're exploring and trying to get stronger the chapters are rather short. Don't expect a lot of variation from that gameplay loop. Your characters have 4 skills they can equip, and as they level they gain a handful more. You choose what fits your needs. Its a pretty basic RPG, no blacksmiths to upgrade your current gear or customize effects. You get what you pay for and you just have to replace it when something better comes along.FRUSTRATIONS:The most frustrating part of the game was the inventory management. You have 30 slots, and if you find an item in the open world that doesn't fit, the clunky card-like menu prompts you to discard something you have. It's so tediously time consuming, I wish they could just offer you the option to discard the item you got from the chest right then and there, or at least give you 100 slots so you don't think about it for a while. DIFFICULTY:The game's not difficult if you prepare. Once you find your preferred synergy of skills/characters you can take down monsters easily, just make sure to upgrade your equipment if you reach a new area and take it easy on later bosses so you don't die from being too bloodthirsty trying to kill them fast. A few mistakes is all it takes to mess up your rhythm, just as any good RPG.NEW GAME PLUS:There's a "new game plus" where you get to start the game with the progression you had when you beat it. Which does satisfy the curiosity I had about a certain event in the beginning, but nothing to write home about. I don't think they added anything in new game plus, and if they did the replayability of the game is too low to merit a second playthrough as the narration and exploration at this point are a drag. My wishes for the new gameplus would have been to raise the level cap further so I can at least feel justified playing it again. But none of that occurs. FINAL THOUGHTS:Good experience, different for sure. I enjoyed it as much as I would enjoy any other RPG of it's linear, simplistic nature. You play, enjoy the story, and beat it. That's that.  Is it worth 30 bucks? Nah... It's 15-20 at best. You're paying and extra 10 for the excellent narrator. But for that price tag I would have hoped for more content, more customization on my team set-up, etc.I recommend it, if only for the niche experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I was so psyched about this game when I heard about it, but it ended up being really lackluster IMO. - For one, it's incredibly easy, and so far none of my decisions really matter. Because of this, it basically feels like you're just clicking through a story rather than actually playing a game.- The card aesthetic is just that: an aesthetic. It has absolutely no impact on gameplay and doesn't really add anything. Especially since the UI is also all cards, it makes navigating menus extremely tedious. They could have done the UI better even with the cards to make it easier to navigate, but they didn't.- The narrator's voice sounds really good at first, but after a while you realize he's fairly monotone, even in more tense/emotional/exciting moments, which really detracts from the story being told. I really realyl wish the characters had their own voice acting.+ The music and graphics are beautiful. If they put the same effort they put in the art and music into the gameplay itself, this would be a much better game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an extremely basic JRPG wrapped in the skin of a card game. If you're looking for an old-school JRPG this one has all the hits:-random enemy encounters-using the same 1-2 spells for every fight in the game-not being able to save or heal through the multi-phase end boss-random rolls for the majority of ability effects-dialog "choices" that don't actually do anythingAside from all that the game feels like it's got too few of everything: enemies, party members, skills, etc. Every single aspect of this game could have used more variety because most of it gets old very quickly.Honestly I wish Steam didn't just give me Yes/No options for this review because while I wouldn't recommend it I also wouldn't tell you to avoid it either. This game probably would have been a sick game like 10-20 years ago but these days it's just meh.

_childDocuments_.review: I tend not to write reviews for games I absolutely love, nor ones that make me hate them. Instead it's the ones that leave me conflicted or frustrated that make me most want to write a review about them. To preface. I loved this game and thoroughly enjoyed it. But I think there's a certain kind of person you need to be, and the right mindset you need to have to properly enjoy this game.To get to the main point of my thoughts, this game is what might best be described as a 'fast food' sort of game. This comparison isn't perfect, so bear with me. There's a lot of different fast food restaurants, some worse for you than others. If Call of Duty could be considered the McDonald's of video games (quick, easy, doesn't take too much thinking to digest or enjoy), then this game could perhaps be compared to a Wendy's meal (or some other fast food you find agreeable). Not really spectacular, but pretty good when you have that craving.Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars, a game with a terrible-but-fun name, is a generic fantasy JRPG with not much in the way of gameplay twists for the genre, and a story that's not amazing with some twists that are interesting to think about for a few minutes. This game is not a huge 60 hour completionist JRPG. It's not even 30 hours. My first playthrough ended at about 14 hours. One thing that might have helped my expectations is that I played a JRPG recently called Radiant Historia. That is a DS (or 3DS Remake) game that is also a generic fantasy RPG, with an interesting twist on combat mechanics and a story about time travel, self-sacrifice and there's also a thing about royalty being bad maybe? Clocking in at 30 hours, it was as long as it needed to be and I was satisfied when it was done. For clarity, I *am* a completionist sort of person.I'd use similar wording to describe Voice of Cards. It's as long as it wants to be and doesn't overstay its welcome. I try not to claim I know developer intentions, but as a writer I experience burnout after working on long projects and want smaller things to work on while being creative. This game comes across as someone who gets tired of working on huge games and wanted something that would be easy to make and play, so one can still be creative without pushing themselves to the limit. That isn't an excuse for any flaws that might exist, and they do exist, but it is a good reason to explain why the game is the way it is.Let's get the cardboard elephant out of the way. The advertising and theming is very confusing because the game does not involve card play in any capacity. There's no drawing cards, no deckbuilding, no true card games save for an optional minigame. There's no functional reason for the game to have this card theming. And I love it. I love the card theming and the dice hitting the battle board, the sounds of what seem to be plastic crystals falling into a box, the sound of my game piece clattering along the map. I like the transition to the battleboard and the sounds of swishing cards. The game sticks to the theme of a tabletop game in aesthetics and doesn't let up, even for the final boss which has a cute visual of being made of 20 or so cards to for their full picture, to express how huge and imposing they are. All of this comes with a mature sounding man narrating, acting as the 'game master'.This entire thing works for me probably because I host regular Dungeons and Dragons games. I must do so online, but there's something fun about making a small world for players to play in. One that isn't massive or has deep lore, one that just has some dungeons to explore and a story with some not-very-deep twists, but are just fun to play with. Aesthetically, this game captures that feeling perfectly. There's no denying, though, the way the game presents itself in promotional material doesn't make this clear. I don't blame anyone who goes into this disappointed.I think the biggest thing that works against the game is the narrator. A game like this lives or dies on charm. Unfortunately, the English narrator they got isn't bringing their best to this mock tabletop. There are moments where he expresses himself and gets good and deep into character. These moments are far between, though not few. Most of the time he's droning and not exactly into it. One of his intro dialogues for fights is "Aaaaaaand... Fight!" You'd expect something like that to be full of energy to get you pumped, at least a little bit. But nope. His read of the line is so bad and it's a crying shame. When he does his best, his best is really good. But he either wasn't trying too hard or, more importantly, the director of the English translation didn't care enough.Past the aesthetics of a tabletop game, voice of cards relies on a humorous story, charm and quick, easy combat to entertain. There's a sort of mindless zen one can get into with random monster encounters. Hit the monsters, get the XP, get the gold, level up, do it some more until you've hit the final boss to 0 HP. If the combat could be compared to anything, it would be Earthbound with slightly more production value. The cards move in flashy, occasionally amusing ways to representing hitting each other. The most interesting thing about the system is that instead of traditional mana, you instead gain a plastic crystal on each of your character's turns. Basic attacks cost no crystals, stronger attacks do, ranging from 1-5 crystals (the max you can be holding at once is 10, a tricky thing to do). Meanwhile, character's attack and defense values are located on their cards, so there's no question why you took X damage and why enemies are taking Y.The mechanics are so simple that they're easy to pick up and even easier to master. This would make an excellent introduction to RPGs, I feel, with easy to understand mechanics that are fairly self-explanatory. With that said, there's no challenge to be found in this game unless one goes hunting for an optional boss that's not available until after you've beaten the game and made your way back to the final island (a thing made easier with an item that allows you to ignore monster encounters). There's not much to sink your teeth into aside from the final boss, which feels almost built around your party being max level, and the secret boss, which requires a good amount of preparation and planning after understanding it's mechanics (likely after dying).If Voice of cards suffers from something, it's nitpicks that become big issues in the void of not having overly fancy graphics to distract. For example, if you're a completionist it's painfully easy to outlevel the two party members you get later, making it hard to want to use them.  While there's an elemental weakness system in the game, it's sometimes hard to make use of it, and by the end of the game it's not worthwhile to engage with it. There's a decent amount of depth to the combat system that goes underutilized because of how you equip attacks and how it's easier to just do a lot of damage with big swinging attacks. It's easy to out level the bosses you're heading for, with only a misunderstanding of how to prepare yourself being a threat.Despite all those flaws, I love this game and would give a recommendation. I think it's worth 30 dollars (the cosmetic DLC is not worth factoring in), but you have to accept you're paying for the experience of a tabletop game more than you're paying for a truly engaging JRPG. There's enough here to be fun, and as someone whose favorite genre is RPGs (JRPG or otherwise), it was nice to play one that didn't consume so much of my time and was just relaxing. I do wish the game was better, better balanced and paced, but ultimately I regret neither my time nor my money.

_childDocuments_.review: Very neat idea with very poor balance and execution.  (and this game has nothing to do with deck building or card battling). It's just a grid-based RPG, and a very easy one at that.  Even on the hardest difficulty, I find myself beating most battles just pressing "A" over and over.  I actually was wishing I could find some reason to use the different abilities from a strategy perspective, but couldn't. The cards are simply an aesthetic (albeit a very pleasing one at first)--that help hide the fact this is a grid-based RPG and that the character UI and customization options are extremely bare.  You will have very limited  number of skills and equipment upgrades are railroaded and feel unoriginal. After a while of exploring, however, the card aesthetic begins to drag on. I simply wanted to get to the next part of the quest.  Or I just wanted to finish and explore. The one interesting part is an exploration mini-game where you find "treasure map" clues and have to decipher them, usually by identifying the zoomed in location on the map. That was probably the funnest part of the game, but those are very few and far between. Overall, this game (which is incredibly short and easily beat if not 100% within 20 hours) is not worth the price tag.  You won't feel challenged, the story is cookie-cutter RPG, and while the card aesthetic feels very novel (and pleasing soundtrack) it drags on. Pros: Neat exploration mini-game on occasionUnique aestheticCons:Very, very easy combat Card aesthetic hides overly simplified character UI (almost no skills and/or equipment)Grid-based movementCookie-cutter storyPrice not worth the amount of time it will take to quickly beat the game (which was minimal replay value).
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I got deceived from the promise of the game, from the trailer, from the artistic design of the gameplay, but I find myself regretting having bought this game. I saw the game and thought it was a card game/deckbuilding mixed with RPG, but it isn't the case. The game is just a plain jrpg but with an art design that presents the game with cards. This choice is interesting and enjoyable, until you see that the cards on your screen make the UI a little bit too slow, even with the patch that updates the speed. You might not find the indivitual clicks or UI actions slow, but when summed up you can feel that the game itself is too slow overall. The idea is nice, but brought into the gameplay you understand that maybe the price to pay to have the game played like if it were cards is not worth.The dialogues are the same old JRPG copy-paste script brought in a DnD world. A quest, some enemies, some challanges, some predictable unsurprising conversation. Also they have you make choices during the dialogues, choices that are completely ignored and it feels like they don't influence in any way. For example you heal your friend with a potion and you have to show your happiness with: "hug your friend" or "scream of happiness". The difficulty brings no challanges, and the grindey aspect of playing a jrpg gets even more tedious by the slow UI. The combat system makes you think that it would be a deck building game but it's just a plain jrpg where you choose 4 abilities and always spam the highest damage that you have available. Some positive points are: the art of the cards, the voiced texts.Well, if you want to play Final fantasy 1 with an updated graphics this is the game for you, otherwise it's not worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: I desperately wanted this game to be good. I loved SE and I loved card games and RPGs. The game is just way too shallow when is comes to gameplay. Lots of people will be baited by the visuals and audio, which is understandable. I would recommend avoiding this title, it's just not worth the effort or the cash. 30 bucks is too much for what this game is and people quoting 15h are wrong. Even with collecting everything needed for the "perfect ending" I finished at 11.7h. There is an option piece to go back in for, but I can't imagine why anyone would bother. People are describing this as "like a D&D session" because it's an rpg with a DM. But it's not, your choices don't matter and the story is thin. This is a shallow RPG with a gorgeous coat of paint.

_childDocuments_.review: I really do enjoy the game and would recommend it. I loved overly everything ; out of the slow pace menu and the lack of real multiplayer ; they could have really done something huge along the JRPG style, they already have the cards anyway...But ; It's not for everyone, unlike Nier and Drakenguard which are both more polished in term of gameplay and all, Voice of Cards is more of a looking-like small indie company first game (but with a huge name on it). I guess people are expecting so much about this game. It's not a card game and it's not as spectacular as alot of actual JRPG. It have cards skin ; telling a small story that is pretty easy to guess i'd say, knowing Yoko Taro's usuals.If you really wish to play this game, try first the demo (it tells a bit of the story that is not inside the actual game) and maybe take it in sales if you value alot more the price/hours than the rest.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this based on how I felt about the demo version. I liked the idea that the whole game is simulation of a TRPG while actual mechanism is a turn based JRPG. I even thought it was brilliant.But that only extends to the demo version.While I still enjoyed the game fully, I think Yoko Taro should've listen to Saito P and abandoned this project. This game feels like it should have been released for free if this game was really Yoko Taro's experiment. But then I guess the cost of using AAA developer's manpower couldn't have been ignored.Good storytelling. Kinda obvious plot line though.Good art style. Wish it extended to UI designs.Good idea/try on overall game mechanics. But not polished at all.Bad price. the volume of the game and the extent of replayability does not warrant $30 price tag. Bad UI. Clunky, slow, laggy inputs (for K/M, works fine on gamepads), and confusingOverall, this game is Yoko Taro's experiment like all of his games pretty much, but the worst one of all. At least his Nier and Drakengard series had great storytelling that is worth enduring through unpolished game mechanics, this game has neither story or polished game mechanics.Interesting idea of bringing TRPG playing experience to his audiences in a video game format was pretty much the only positive part that I can think of this game. I guess I should've stopped after playing demo.

_childDocuments_.review: Play the demo first. Yoko Taro is too much of a troll to not say that the demo was the real prologue. It's still a pretty good experience, a fun one. So far, this game is pretty much just a visual novel with gameplay and open-world adventure board-game style (not that I've played those).  Since I believe this is pretty much just a visual novel with twist, I'll be focusing on prose (so far). These damn letters man... They are such a roll to read. Yoko Taro is a God.EDIT: 2 hrs in and finished my first real main-quest. I'm already in tears. Yoko Taro's way of narrative is just unique, which is to say, despite the early noticeable cliches of these story, a gradual shift would immerse the reader instantly. I've seen a lot of reviewers complain about the storyteller's indifferent tone, but I fully disagree to their criticism of his performance. My take is that the storyteller is just our voice when reading this game. Since I think this game is basically just a book with a bit of chill and easy gameplay to immerse people who does not fully like playing games merely for the story, that might be the reason for why characters are not voiced.Anyhow, I would recommend this game if you love reading and of course fans of Yoko Taro games. Ost and Writing are the main reason why you should buy this game. Other stuff are kind of mixed but I don't think they are bad per se, maybe just not unique.

_childDocuments_.review: i get the ideai don't get it's executionis it good on the merits of beeing an "oldschool jrpg"?...hell no. you got 3 gear slots (weapon, armor, trinket), your characters get new skills trough leveling up...that's it. mix in some items and you've seen it all.this is even more basic as some rpg-maker games that try to include atleast some complexety. job-system? skill-tree? anything? zilch.mechanicaly this game is bereft of anything and pretty much plays itself. it's not neccessarly bad, but ungodly boring.how basic the game is will become pretty clear once you take a glance at the "collection". there ain't much space there. then there's the presentation. the idea was presenting an oldschool jrpg completly in card-form. in the very first "real" story-room you enter npc-cards already repeat. it's a 2D artwork, a tiny one at that...and just crossing the 1st settlement you get bombarded with repeats. then there's the "gameworld". whereas character art is pretty darn good, the world-art is horrendous. calling it basic is an understatement. i could paint that...and i can't paint. furthermore there's nothing to ad to the 2D art. some spells, abilities and co. have (pretty bad) 3Dish effects when used...but that's it. 10 Dollar roguelites spend more effort on their art and visual presentation.the UI and the menus are just horrid. it's like someone went out of their way to create to most annoin menu-system humanly possible...including input lag. then there's playing the actual game. most if not nearly all dialogue is presented in the same card-form as the rest of the game. which means what dialogue there is is short, tiny. yeah, there are grains of witiness and some of Yoko's charm here and there, but neither the characters nor the "plot" get much exposure. which mixed with the minimal presentation kills whatever immersion or entertainment (j)rpgs usualy try to invoke. to ad insult to injure there's a card mini-game in this card-looking-barebones-jrpg, which is more fun, interesting and entertaining than playing the actual game.get it on a high discount. it's not the worst game ever, but for 30 bucks (average) you can far, far, far better jrpgs.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards is a deliberately slower paced RPG, presented in a way that fosters the imagination. It has a very specific style of writing that is refreshingly literary, and all of it is voiced by a narrator with a gravelly voice, creating the illusion of playing a board game in the company of a talented gamemaster, while also feeling like a fantasy novel being read in front of a cozy fireplace. In this regard, Voice of Cards radiates with soul and distinct purpose.Much of this soul lies within the small details of the presentation, which never betrays the game's premise. Whether it be during combat or dialogue, the way the cards are animated manages to convey each character's actions perfectly. The fact that you can "see" Ridis performing a quick roll (or a backflip, if you're extra imaginative) before firing two more poisoned arrows, just from how her card moves when she gets a critical hit, is incredible.There's a lot of appeal to be found there. Whenever an image is forming in your head while playing a game, that is the ultimate form of suspension of disbelief. It means that the game has successfully immersed you, because that thought came from your own subconscious.~ ~ ~An unforgettable facet of this game's beauty is the heavenly music composed by Keiichi Okabe. Enchanting melodies, able to soothe and revitalize the most aching of hearts and dispel cynicism through pleasant chills of warmth.~ ~ ~ On a more technical standpoint, one greatly appreciated detail about the music is that it knows when to play and when to stop. For instance, when it's deemed more fitting, the dungeon music will continue playing during battle instead of the regular combat music. In other words, the battles are not detached from their context, and the intended mood is retained at all times. This might seem trivial, but it's extremely beneficial to the atmosphere of a game when the combat encounters throughout feel like a genuine part of the journey. It can't be overstated how important and valuable good music and sound design is to the medium of video games. On a related note, the narrator also knows when to keep quiet and lets important battles speak for themselves. He never comes across as annoying, which is an impressive feat in a game where one person does all the talking.~ ~ ~There may not be a ton of depth to the combat, but the simplicity works in favor of the sublime presentation, and from a roleplaying perspective, what's there is well designed. You don't play Voice of Cards to beat your head against a wall with numbers, you play it to have an immersive pen-and-paper-like RPG experience, complete with cards and dice rolls. While the pacing of each action is intentionally slowed down to preserve the realistic look and feel of the presentation, the pacing of the overall game is designed in a way that respects the player's time. In blunt gaming terms, there is no grinding needed, no avalanche of side-quests that you feel forced to do just for the EXP or anything of the sort. In essence, it's just you and your merry band of adventurers, setting out on a quest to take down a dragon, with narrated eventful incidents happening along the way.~ ~ ~If you'd like to increase both the challenge and your own immersion, you can skip buying new equipment at Armorers until it becomes too dangerous to keep venturing forth in your old gear. Your party may come close to being wiped out on multiple occasions, which is always exciting. Remember, you can run from battle if it feels like you've got no chance to make it out alive.Playing this way, each character should have a more specific role in battle; for example, your would-be-hero could be the dedicated healer, keeping a taunting Mar alive while Ridis poisons the monsters. There are other strategies, but the idea is that a character who spends his turns healing others doesn't need to spend gold on a strong weapon, while one acting as a protector only needs good defense, and the priority for one dealing damage is to simply carry a powerful weapon.The reason playing this way is immersive is that the protagonist is canonically strapped for cash and doesn't like splitting rewards. Of course, he's not so bad that he would let his companions get hurt, so it makes sense to spend some money on consumable items as they're cheaper than equipment. They make battles more interesting too, when you use them in an emergency against formidable foes. Sell the Revive items though, they're worth a lot.~ ~ ~Due to its intentionally slow burn nature, some may find Voice of Cards not very fun to play. That, however, takes absolutely nothing away from its qualities.There is one particular thing that feels out of place in this game, and it has to do with a handful of characters sporting bulging muscles. More specifically, it's their attire... or lack thereof. A bit of comic relief is all well and good, but here it comes at a cost, as those character designs just don't quite fit with the mystical fantasy ambience of the game. What is unfortunate though, is that this game has a niche appeal to begin with, and those few questionably revealing character designs (the rest are excellent) only restrict that appeal even further, by making it needlessly awkward to recommend this game to children or anyone who might find those designs off-putting. Regardless, that's the only eyebrow-raising design decision in the game, which is impressive for such an original concept. It's a well conceived execution of a great idea that sticks to its ambitions. Voice of Cards has something to say and delivers it without compromise.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is a beautiful crafted world with gorgeous artwork. I can see the inspirations this game is created from. I get old school Final Fantasy vibes while playing it (for those of you who remember roaming around the map and bumping into enemies every few steps and then you take turns attacking each other). But instead of walking around you leap around a map made of cards as a token piece or avatar. The game play, npc's, story and awards are all represented by playing cards & your actions are boosted in combat by dice rolls. The artwork for me was the deciding factor to buy this game and I did play the demo beforehand. The presentation is extremely strong and tries to push the rpg gaming experience to be something different. However some things do fall short. A lot of the npc's you meet are the same artwork from town to town which is sad. The artwork is so beautiful they should have really put more effort into varying the characters you meet. The narrator I honestly love at times with his dry humor and dislike at times for being too monotone in his reading of cards and events that come up. I strongly urge anyone interested to try the demo first. It gives you a good sample of what to expect as far as game play and basic mechanics.  I do recommend this game and I did purchase it at full price, but honestly it could be a tad cheaper so if your on the fence I would wait for a sale. But play the demo and get a feeling for this game as it best experienced than just read about before purchasing.  ✨

_childDocuments_.review: I went back and forth alot on if I should recommend or not, ultimately I decided on no. While the game is very pretty and genuinely made me laugh afew times in the story its ultimately has some major downfalls that makes it impossible for me to recommend it. So let me start by saying for a jrpg this game is very short, 8 to 10 hours even taking your time then post game content is basically non existent, one single boss that you can beat easily by setting up your team right. The game gives you the ability to explore the entire area but almost no reason to do so, you cant find any dungeons or caves that dont exist for story reasons, exploring ahead is just a waste of time. The characters are barely given any depth, infact you can easily forget they exist if you dont have them in your party. Ultimately it is a very interesting concept that just wasn't given what it needed to grow, it rarely uses the cards in an intresting way and barely does anything intresting as a jrpg. The coolest thing the game does imo is at the start you run into a merchant who is selling you a legendary weapon, giving a goal very early on that encourages you to be risky to make money that gives you a connection to your main character making it very interesting to get his legendary weapon. Every other legendary weapon in the game however is just laying around on the ground basically. the games "side quest" more often then not are give man medicine congrats you did it, and while that fits the themes its also very basic. Lastly there is the amount of reused card art, almost every villager shares a card art outside of one per town basically, there is a very limited amount of unique enemy cards and after the half way point your mostly gonna see variants only. it just really feels like they had the artist for a week and really drags you out of the game. I am just disappointed, i get that this game is half the price of a triple A game but this is so much less then half the scale, it is basically like a triple A game jam and if you compare this game to bravely default a 3ds game worth 40$ more work went into the art of one town then this entire game and that game is 50 hours long with near infinite depth to the the combat

_childDocuments_.review: When I picked this game up I was expecting another wild ride from Yoko-taro; This is not that. I am fairly certain that Square Enix just slapped his name all over the marketing for this game as a marketing ploy, and it sure got me.However, it is a nice experience in it's own right. Maybe not worth 30 dollars/euro/whatever, but servicable for what it is. I found myself having a good time, enjoying the gameplay and characters. The game shines in characters and their dynamics together. The mix of main characters make up a fairly unique roster, from the money-driven self proclaimed "hero" to the muscle-man nutritionist, you'll be hard pressed to find a character you don't like. The character writing at work here is definitely up to square enix standards!The gameplay is pretty standard as far as turn based rpg's go. There's not a lot of flashy animations though, given how all the characters are, well, cards. Still, they do what they can with the format and if you fill in the missing spaces with your imagination then you'll find it servicable. A problem I had was that it at times felt really slow, but that feeling started disappearing in the later stages of the game.Overall, I really enjoyed this game and I hope to see more of these characters in the future somehow. I might have been lured in under false pretenses but I don't mind that at all anymore. I am actually happy for it, since otherwise I might not have given this hidden gem of a game a try.This game is a fun little rpg experience with charming characters which will last you about 12-15 hours, 20-25 depending on if you are a completionist. Buy at a discount if you can, but I can certainly reccomend it at full price as well.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have mentioned, this is not really a card game but rather a JRPG with a card based aesthetic. Being a Yoko Taro game - story is probably a big attraction for many people coming into this. It's a fairly simple but enjoyable story, with a few twists and turns along the way, as well as multiple endings as per usual with Yoko Taro games.The combat is a hard thing to judge. The majority of the games combat massively suffers from difficulty. Like many Yoko Taro games it really suffers from being too easy - and unfortunately this time there is no difficulty setting either. There's only a couple bosses in the entire game where it feels like the combat really starts to stretch its legs, with one of these two bosses making me go and look at my skill and equipment setup, at which point the game really does start to get much better, it's just a real shame there's not much of it.I'd probably wait for a sale on this one unless you're really a big Yoko Taro fan. I'd highly recommend checking out the demo - the story in the demo is unique to it and serves as a prologue to the game, and serves as a really good way to know if it's something for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked up this game for about $10-$15 on a sale, and I will say that is about how much it is worth to play.Please note that this is NOT a card-based game. Think of your standard turn-based RPG, but if the same mechanics were portrayed as cards and dice. That is what this game is--it is a turn-based RPG just with the flair of a TTRPG with cards.The story is on the basic side, but the characters are fairly interesting. The queen of a country has issued a decree stating that she will handsomely reward adventurers who successfully take care of a dragon that has been terrorizing them recently. You are Ash, an gold-digging adventurer who jumps onto this opportunity for the sole purpose of getting rich. You, your beloved partner and mascot Mar, and a strange magician girl who agrees to join you set off to find this dragon. You visit various villages, deal with the incidents in each of these villages, pick up some new party members on the way, and search for this dragon while accidentally falling into a mystery that surrounds this same dragon.The story is a bit bare-bones and after like 3hrs, you can see the same story formulas over and over again. The combat is fun, but can get very repetitive and frankly very very easy (until the final boss, then the difficulty level randomly spikes up out of no way). The main party has some fun banter and makes them memorable (especially Bruno--Bruno Best Boy).What makes this game charming for me and frankly is what keeps the game engaging is the Game Master. Imagine you are a sole player in a TTRPG, with the GM handling everything down to the storytelling. The GM is the only voice actor in this whole game, reading everything from flavor text to dialogue. It really drills into you that in this game, you are a TTRPG player who is playing this story and world that the GM has created for you. He even has some funny quips every now and then that has made me  chuckle. The fact that this game is designed this way makes it stand out, and really added to my experienceI beat this game in about 10hrs and felt like I did maybe like 80% of the whole game. I say this game is worth like $10, not really $20, and definitely not full-priced.  However, I will not be playing the other three games in the series (btw the second game is not included in the Trilogy bundle, no idea why). It does make me a bit sad because I've read that the story in The Forgotten Maiden is the most interesting but its the very same mechanics as Isle Dragon Roars and thus really boring and tedious to play through since they do nothing to change it up. But still, I am glad I checked out Isle Dragon Roars.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I don't recommend this game due to poor storytelling and just general blandness. At least at full price. I would recommend you buy it at maybe at least 50% off.Thoughts on Gameplay:⚫ It's not a real card battler / deckbuilder, I'd say. It really is just more of a typical turn-based JRPG, just that instead of 3D models for characters, you get cards. That's not bad, just a headsup. Lol⚫ Gameplay is straightforward and easy to understand, and it's engaging enough to be fun I guess, but it's really nothing special, and mechanics are actually VERY simple. The max level you achieve is lv30, I think. "I think" because I saw that there was no more "next level" requirement once my characters hit 30, but I didn't bother double checking.⚫ That's all there is to say really, the gameplay isn't complicated.Thoughts on the world:⚫ Like imagine your DM only had two biome decks and had to reuse those for every area you went to. A lot of the areas feel the same and villages and towns are ridiculously small. I honestly don't feel like there was a lot of thought put into it.⚫ Most of the enemies are just reskins of each other with different elements for abilities, but they're all essentially the same thing. I mean, I know that's a common thing, but for a game that barely had any different biomes or even pretty villages to begin with, you'd think they'd have it in their budget to at least draw different monsters.⚫ Again, that's all I have to comment on, because there's not much to talk about.Thoughts on Story:⚫ The storytelling is awful. The way they tell it isn't very immersive. Like instead of a dialogue between characters, it's more like they just summarized what this character said in one paragraph. Takes away any kind of immersion whatsoever, making it hard to get invested in the story. It doesn't help that the beginning of each chapter even has minor spoilers for you.⚫ And no, just because it's meant to feel like a tabletop game doesn't mean they should have done it this way. Whenever I play DND with my friends, my DMs would play as the NPC and talk to us as the characters rather than summarize what the NPC said.⚫ Speaking of characters, the way other party members joined your party was just so... idk what's the word for it. Fake? Forced? Something along those lines. Character interactions were also very few. Like you'd beat a mini boss, and there's ZERO dialogue between your characters afterwards. Like "Okay? We just beat something, aren't you guys gonna say something?"⚫ The backstories on the character cards also make zero sense. Like they reuse the NPC cards for different NPCs, what was the point of giving the NPC card one specific background lore?⚫ Spoiler about getting the best ending ahoy. ⚫ Overall I didn't enjoy the story at all for this game due to the storytelling, which is sad because this is where they should have focused on more given that everything else is so simple. ⚫ I read that there was more to discover in new game+. Well, I'm new-game+-ing but I'm not seeing anything new? But honestly the first run just left such a bland impression that I'm not at all interested in playing through that whole game again.Overall thoughts:⚫ Bland story, bland world, super simple gameplay, can be finished in under 15 hours, with not much going for replayability. At least in my opinion. If you want a game where you can just chill out, honestly, find a different JRPG. If you really wanna try this one out, I'd recommend to not buy it at full price. Wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: if you're looking for a fun RPG game with elements of card games, you won't find it here. i made it through the first chapter and most of the second, and couldn't get myself to play any further. sorry if i'm missing some taro-brained gigatwist in the last chapter, but i just can't do it. TL;DR: cards are just aesthetic, and saying it's a mid-tier RPG at best still feels overly charitable. go play inscryption if you want an actual card RPG game with a cool story. or if you want it JRPG flavored, try the Baten Kaitos games. if you're 50/50 on cards and an RPG with board game elements is what you want and don't mind roguelikes, try For The King. ______________________________________________________________-the cards are just an aesthetic. there is no real collecting or deckbuilding, beyond swapping out your weak old skill cards for new ones. the game is just a super basic turn based JRPG with less options or depth than OG final fantasy games. the addition of dice rolling and your gem "mana" resource just adds to the board game facade without making the gameplay any more interesting. -everything, and when i say everything i mean EVERYTHING, is painfully slow. there is always a lengthy animation to wait through. you have to click twice to confirm just about every action you take, including yes/no interactions. just moving around involves waiting a second or two for your 'board piece' to do its little animation. anytime you get into combat, you have to wait through the "battle start!" warning, wait for the table to be set up, wait for the cards to be doled out, and then once the battle is over, wait for it to be swapped back out again so you can continue. even on the newly added fast game speed setting, which is basically a requirement to play the game in spite of what the options menu says, the game will often force a pause between clicking through dialogue boxes, etc- especially because everything requires a card animation to play.-credit to the narrator(s) for dedicating to an entire game's worth of content, i hope they were paid well for their work! it was not executed well at all. whoever instructed the narrators to have a boring mid-tone description of literally everything, including dialogue, was out of their mind. there is no emphasis, no feeling, no character voices, just the 'hey isnt this funny that im just one guy narrating everything, kind of like a tabletop game? haha. sometimes i'll make a little comment on the side or clear my throat.' i think anyone who's spent any time playing or watching tabletop games (especially now with how popular live play shows are) knows that this doesn't make for interesting storytelling. even barring that, if you've ever listened to a narrated e-book or something- there's just a huge dip in quality. every character sounds the same, and even when in the text something is described as being whispered or shouted, the narration doesn't change. at most the line might be a few decibels louder or quieter.at the start i tried to listen to lines in their entirety, but by the first hour in, i was skipping through them once i finished reading- by then it was just noise. again, it's something i doubt the voice actors had a say in, considering that both ENG and JP had the same problem- i expect it was just the direction they were given. it's unfortunate, and throws out a large part of the sell for this game, especially when the voice talent (Todd Haberkorn and Hiroki Yasumoto for ENG and JP respectively) are absolutely incredible at their jobs. it feels like a waste.-writing is completely forgettable. in the beginning, even Final Fantasy 1 led you in with the prophecy of the warriors of light and decaying world. in here we just get "hey there was a dragon. then there wasn't. now there is again, do something about it" with some emotional music over it, and after the intro a smattering of "maybe the Good Guys in White... aren't actually very Good??????" there's nothing interesting about the game's world, nothing interesting to explore, nothing interesting to learn beyond the """lore""" about nameless NPCs that exists just to fill the "oh wow this is such a yoko taro game look at how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up this random old lady's life is" slot. the main characters so far have said less than five lines each in a few hours of play, barely interact with each other beyond making an offhand comment or joke, and exist as suggestions of archetypes, let alone archetypes themselves. they'd be better off as pretty JPEGs that you project personalities onto yourself. ______________________________________________________________in the end, it's a pretty milquetoast game that i doubt many people will remember, and IMO it only glides by with its shiny coat of yoko taro and co. paint. i tried my best to enjoy it, but all that effort was wasted. maybe wait for the next one. thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like the game but I just can't. The visuals are great but there isn't much else.It's a JRPG that's styled around cards. This is not a deck builder or has any gameplay mechanics around cards, they are just for visuals and the general stylistic vibe of the game. It feels somewhat like a DND tabletop session.Pros:+ Cards look beautifulCons:- Boring and extremely plain story- Dull gameplayThe first town is called "Nexton" and the one after that "Thriceton".. man. Everything is as plain as these town names.The main character doesn't really have any character.The story kept me very bored, it's the most plain fantasy story I have ever seen. Not every story has to be the most innovative, like I like various Isekai stories even if they follow the same structure. But the story of this game just felt boring to me. Even in the grand opening of the game you are supposed to talk to various NPC characters, no one ever says anything interesting or entertaining. There is no world building or build-up to anything interesting.The game is very linear. This doesn't have to be bad, but it is when the story is this bad.The game also doesn't save itself with its gameplay elements, combat is dull and other than that it's a clicking through text simulator.The cards look gorgeous though, the visual design of the cards is great. But that's it.The game is voiced in a way like a DnD master is talking to you, it's always the same somewhat monotone voice for everything.The sound design and music are both good.I tried to like the game. The majority of the aesthetics are great. Love the core idea of doing more with cards. But otherwise it fails at everything else, it's not awful but it's just not good.Since everything is so simple I would have loved to try some language practice with it, sadly there's no Korean option, not even for text.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth while on a sale. The game is about ~15 hrs for a $30 price tag, and even then it does feel unnecessary dragged out arbitrary. The final boss in chapter 7 is the most challenging part of the game, but if you are not too underleveled and have the legendary equipment it's not too much of a challenge. If you want the true ending please collect all 10 mysterious cards, look it up beforehand on steam or google, it really easy to get them.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting looking game, but the user tags are a bit misleading. It's been tagged "card-battler", but the cards are just visual, mechanically they don't work or play like cards at all. What this game IS, is a nostalgic turn-based JRPG presented with some pretty card art. Every single line of text or action is displayed on its own card, and cards individually animate in and out every time. It's so tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be deceived by the card-like look this game has. It is just an RPG. Not even a good RPG, mind you. The story is extremely bland, cliche, and poorly written. The characters were written 30 years ago and are STILL boring. Combat involves pressing your highest damage ability you can afford on all 3 characters, then all the enemies are dead, or you maybe take a few points of damage. Characters only have 4 stats (health, attack, defense, speed), which ultimately amount to level-ups feeling worthless. There are technically elements in the game, but they don't really add or subtract in any way to the playstyle. Consumable items are restricted to 30 TOTAL items, across the like 25 different types of consumables. It's just not a good game. Spend your time playing FF 1-6 (the originals), because those 30-year-old games are significantly better than this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea why this game is so highly rated. I keep buying games from Square Enix and I keep getting more and more disappointed in how little thought they put into the gameplay. Note: I'm a completionist, but completing pieces of this game got very tedious, very fast.The good parts of the game:-VERY casual. It's a nice and simple game to casually play in between doing other things.-decent narration. Provides a few humorous moments-pleasant soundtrackThe bad parts...:-plays agonizingly slowly-every character has extremely similar skills (e.g., hit one enemy, hit every enemy, hit an enemy with a specific elemental damage type, cause a status effect)-every enemy is extremely similar to the other enemies in their area, and most enemies are just a palette-swapped version of an earlier enemy-fights are ridiculously easy. There are no real tactics needed-Abilities (passives) require no management and merely provide a boring buff (e.g., +5 resistance to a certain elemental damage type). Each character gets 3 of these. You probably won't notice them and they provide no strategic depth whatsoever.-Skills (active abilities): you'll have all of the skills your characters will ever get about halfway through the game. You probably won't swap them out much, although you can use 4 and will end up with about 8. They don't vary much. Some hit for more damage or cause a certain elemental damage type.-massive plot holes: several plot elements not only fail to make sense, but are actively stupid even if you buy into them. At one point, *mild spoiler* a terrible threat is revealed and a party member is wounded. Your party promptly abandons that member in the exact area that it was just attacked with the perpetrator left to their own devices. This works out for some reason.  -odd quality of life issues: high-speed play is available, but it turns off after closing the game. every time. Options for going to the title screen or exiting the game is hidden under sub-menus as "other." There's a data page used for saving/loading, but it took me a couple minutes just to hunt down how to exit the game. Weird. Item menus and such require scrolling to the side, which works incredibly unreliably. Camera controls are locked to arrow keys for some reason, which is still preferable to playing with a controller.Overall: this game is way too boring and lacks interesting gameplay mechanics. The writing is uncompelling and would probably appeal most to a middle-school aged child. I bought it on sale because I wanted a casual game to play in-between other tasks. It was definitely a casual game, but it very easily could have been more enjoyable. It just comes off as lazy and trite.

Someone pops a cap in your friend the literal instant you turn the corner on the street, so you choose "No way in hell am I going to let you join me"? Sorry but she said she'd work for free, so all grudges forgiven even though she also never apologies. Choose to help the old lady to the doctor? Well, you can't princess carry her so you drop her back on the ground and give up, and then the game makes a point three times in the next five messages about how you chose not to help in the slightest. Don't give us dialog options if you're pulling the old Fallout 4 style of "Three options to say yes, and then an fourth option to say no but yes."Exiting the game is a joke. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Very unique premise, the game is set up to be like a Tabletop RPG. The entire game is narrated by a game master and he also does all the voices. Your characters and the world are all cards sprawled across a table.-The story is really solid. Nothing groundbreaking but if you're a fan of past Yoko Taro games there is a lot to like here.Cons:-First play through took about 14 hours and there isn't a whole lot of replay incentive even with New Game Plus.- The style of the game though charming at first can start to feel like it's a little daunting and dry once it's kind of ran it's course. I took a few breaks from playing this over a few months for this exact reason.-If you're a seasoned player of JRPG's this game is not very challenging and is downright too easy at times.Overall if you're a fan of Yoko Taro's work, this is another unique game by him with a very solid fantasy RPG story. _childDocuments_.review: It's a neat little turn based RPG and not really a card battler with deck building elements as you might think.It is very reminiscent of a fully guided "on-rails" type of D&D campaign. I can say if you're not really into reading and kinda just want to listen to a story and cruise through a turn based RPG that isn't particularly difficult, you absolutely can and you'll probably enjoy the game for what it is. There are definitely some issues though. I give it a 6.5-7/10That was is the tl;dr of the review. Read on if you want more context for the score.I'll go ahead and do a "Pros and cons" type deal because I'm lazy and it keeps my peace of mind.PROS:- The narrator has a good voice and everything is voice acted, so you really don't have to read if you don't want to.- The "events" range from kinda funny to interesting concepts and have a decent variety to keep you going.- There's no reason to grind if you don't want to. You keep your levels, items, gold, and equipment for NG+ and characters level up without being in the immediate party. - A good amount of humor was put in to keep you from getting too bored and to keep the game from treating itself too seriously.- The visuals and aesthetics of the game are very unique, in a good way.CONS:- Choices are an illusion that mean nothing. Seriously they mean nothing. You can only "fail" at maybe two things, but it will still end up at the same conclusions. - The main character is a piece of sh*t and no, none of your decisions will make him better. He started off a tw*t and ends as a tw*t. You can't change his twattery to play either the "good" or "worse than he already is" character.- It is a MAJOR slog to get through all the endings.- The encounter rate is pretty high in some areas and it will likely piss you off since there's no item to help you avoid enemies until NG+ and running is for chumps.- If you want to see all of the different "Event" endings, you'll have to waste a lot of time to make that happen. There should have been an item that increased event chances for NG+ or event chances should have just been increased for NG+- The game's world feels really empty if you did everything on the first play through. If you already did everything the only thing to look forward to is slight dialogue variations.NEUTRAL:- The game is pretty easy. The only things that could really be considered hard is the end boss and the NG+ boss. Depending on your preference, this can be good or bad.- Your inventory for items is kinda small or at least it will feel that way after a while.- You'll need to talk to nearly every "NPC" and kill at least 5-6 monsters of each type to get the flip stories to get the achievements. It can definitely feel like a waste of time if you dislike that type of thing.- The game isn't particularly long. I spent 35 hours to get all the achievements but I also wasted a LOT of time and even left the game running for a bit. Getting everything should reasonably take about 20-30 hours.- You will never get "one shot the final boss" powerful even with max level and the best equipment. The unskippable battles later on still take a chunk of time.- It's less a "card battler" than it is a turn based RPG. Cards are just the main premise. There's not really a luck or deck building element to go off of here as you might be lead to think.I could probably come up with more pros/cons/neutrals but that's good enough. Anywho, I liked it for the most part. I'd say it's a slightly above average RPG at a solid 6.5-7/10 in my eyes. I'd recommend it if the cons and neutrals don't sound like they'd bug you too much.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has literally every element that should make it a smash hit with me. I'm a huge Yoko Taro fan, I love board games and card games, I think the art style, interface, and music are incredible. I'm never turned off by a lack of flashy cutscenes as long as the game is fun. Yet for some reason it just kinda fell flat with me. I think that part of the reason is that, unlike games like Slay the Spire or Steamworld Quest, this isn't actually a true card game, just a bog-standard JRPG that uses a board game motif. The card thing is more of a novelty than a mechanic.While admittedly pretty, it just doesn't innovate enough using the cards to make it better than a game where you simply run around beating up monsters, with all character art being static pictures on cards. I respect the effort to experiment, but even if I do eventually beat it, I think there's a pretty low chance I'd be interested in the sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards was a game I was either grinning at or holding back tears with. All your party members are, as the narrator puts it, colorful characters, and they get to express their personalities frequently through the random events you bump into while traveling. Who will you choose to break down this door? The big muscle guy is the obvious choice, but maybe you should ask the magician... basically, it's fun to pick the wrong answer, and you're never really punished for it. Much!Gameplay is a lot more straightforward than you might think, with the tabletop/card aesthetic the game has going on. Anyone familiar with typical turn-based RPGs will be fine, and it's not a terribly difficult game to begin with. This is your cue to pick your favorites and just do whatever!The game is slightly clunky in the sense that moving/menus/choices all feel like they take a liiiiittle too long to happen, but it's nothing I wouldn't recommend the game over. It's a rather short game, by the way, so take your time!Overall, highly recommended for people who like: JRPGS, card-shaped things, himbos, cute monsters, and Yoko Taro making them cry.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a while to settle into the aesthetic -- especially how much it slows things down -- but once I slowed down along with it, I found Voice of Cards to be a relaxing game with an interesting story and a soothing grind. I also had to get over how "everyone is awful" but it's just part of the tongue-and-cheek weirdness of this game. Recommended to RPG fans who want a relaxing game with a light story and light grind on top of it, and who can (or can bring themselves to) appreciate a different aesthetic. Oh, and I could have done without the "no ♥♥♥♥" moments, but at least it's better than the outright mockery we used to get out of Japan. I mean, one of your companions is a walruspottamus but the man in the loincloth is "terrifying." Sure, guys.

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant little RPG adventure. Music is wonderful, and the game has the pleasant essence and flavor of Yoko Taro's team throughout which put a smile on my face. I can easily recommend this game as a light RPG game, either to be enjoyed in one or two long sittings, or casually picked at in-between other games as a cool down or palette cleanser.Though be aware: if you expect a typical JRPG's mechanical depth and length, you will not get that. This is a a tabletop adventure game led by a narrator, with light RPG elements (leveling, character growth, combat, etc.). My completion time on 1st playthrough (roughly 12 hours) included uncovering all map cards and finding the secrets for the best ending, through natural play, without stopping to read any guides or any miscellaneous pauses or stepping away that might have fluffed up play time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some pretty major flaws that I can't believe weren't ironed out before release. Biggest one is some cards say they roll dice to add to damage, but they don't tell you how many faces those dice have. So it can be a six sided die or a 12 sided and it doesn't tell you before you roll. Besides that just be aware there is only one voice actor and he doesn't emote or change his voice for any of the characters in the story so it's really hard to feel like anyone is different at all. I honestly can't believe they didn't have the main party voice their own lines at the VERY least. Another note is the fact it is all cards doesn't matter AT ALL besides just being visual dressing.

_childDocuments_.review: **Not worth $30 USD. This game should be $20 and even then I would recommend not buying unless it was ≤ $15. This is not worth half the price of day one Nier: Replicant ver 1.22etc or Automata. And I'm not the one making that comparison, Sqeenix is by throwing Yoko Taro's name around to advertise this game.6/10 game with 7/10 writing.TL:DR- surface level aesthetic with lukewarm story and a cozy atmosphere.For fans of Taro's other work, this game does not scratch the itch. It only reminds you that the itch is still there. Feels like a really watered down version of Taro from a mechanics and story standpoint.~~Card Aesthetic and Single Narrator - Nothing below the surface:~~It's a novel idea, and I was excited to see what tricks they were going to pull with this unique design choice. The answer is... nothing. It's just a rpg with static character art and zero character animations. It's exactly that and nothing more. The narrator (aka Game Master) has an alright voice and only breaks the fourth wall 2-3 times, exclusively for humor. There is one boss fight that uses cards in a mildly cool visual way, but that is spoiled by the trailer for the game. There are exactly 3 cards that have animations on the card face. XP and Gold numbers count up after battle, and the saving card has a jumping monster in it. And these just felt distracting in how they broke the established aesthetic.~~Gameplay:~~Extremely simplified turn based rpg gameplay. The only interesting mechanic in battles is each turn generates a gem that can be used as mana or saved up. Spells and powerful attacks cost gems and that's it. World navigation is the most interesting bit. As you explore the world one tile (card) at a time, the next ones flip over until you obsessively go in to every corner and edge to flip over every single wall tile because, 'what if?' It's an interesting idea that could have been explored more or be used to create surprising moments that shake up the status quo. But it isn't and it doesn't.The encounter rate is way too high, leading to an over-leved party, and even if the rate was lowered the game would be extremely easy. That's fine, but when you have to wait for the battle board to be put down and all the enemy cards to enter so many times, just to finish off the battle with negligible resistance, even running away takes too long. It's not game-breakingly annoying, but it certainly is closer to detracting than adding to the experience. It's the same gameplay loop and animations from the first hour to the fifteenth with zero variability.~~Story:~~We like Taro games, that's why we are here. We can trudge through mediocre-to-bad gameplay if the story holds up well enough. Answer? It's just good. Not really good. Not bad. Not great. It's good. None of the twists are new or particularly unique for Taro games. There is no big twist moment, there is no meta narrative, there is not Taro surprise in this game. There might be some very mild ones depending on how you gauge things, but certainly nothing like you might be expecting or hoping for.~~Overall:~~A solid meh/10. It's not bad, but the design choice is paper thin with nothing underneath. The writing is better than the gameplay and design, but by a small margin. It's a decent enough way to unwind at the end of the day and it is undeniably cozy. But, there is no big hook at any point either in the design, the story, or the gameplay. It's all just alright. It's probably not worth developing your own opinion on this work by playing it for yourself if it doesn't appear to be immediately interesting without Taro's name attached.

_childDocuments_.review: It's so close to being something good, here. There are a lot of concepts in this card-based RPG that are compelling, but where the game fails is they're all shallow and watered down. The item cards, the equipment cards, the skill cards, the enemy cards, the terrain cards, the NPC cards...all conceptually great, but are hampered by incredibly limited diversity and design. It's almost a proof of concept more than a deep compelling game experience. You can further see this in the tone of the story and the quality of the narration. They're both lifeless. Even the generic art is lifeless in that it does not tie together a vision at all. All of the peripheral elements, such as the art, the music, the story, the narration are just totally on an island of their own, and could be swapped out with something entirely different, as they add nothing to the cohesion of the game's elements. The game also suffers from far too many combat encounters that just make the game feel like a slog as you move through the chapters/dungeons. Despite some good ideas in the gameplay department, I can not recommend this game as anything more than a 5 dollar proof-of-concept experience and a reflection on potential and missed potential.

_childDocuments_.review: While yes, the voice of the Gamemaster is extremely monotone, it leaves me speculating about them: Like what happened to them, and who are they? Also, this game is supposed to make us submerge ourselves in the story: If you played any other Yoko Taro game, its really philosophical and sad as we the player are a 3rd party/acknowledged as a 'fourth wall breaker'. We can imagine everything up to us, and how everything plays out. they don't specify specific ways actions are taken, only the tone of the story and how it 'should be' imagined.That's why I really enjoy playing this game as of right now (I haven't beaten it entirely but its what I expected from Yoko Taro) I feel like everything Yoko Taro chooses is intentional because of NieR: Automata and NieR: Replicant. He considers that the player varies based on themselves, and it leaves us as the major concept that brings the story to life.
