_childDocuments_.review: What an interesting experiment this game is. I will separate this review in three parts to better explain it: reviewing the game as an RPG, reviewing it as a Yoko Taro directed game, and reviewing the experience as a whole.The RPG part.This game is a pure classic RPG, it has almost no card game element and the cards are only visuals.The party setup is the usual JRPG 3 characters (with more in reserve). But the base 3 characters are so good I ended up never swapping them.It is an extremely simple RPG recommended for beginners, with a level cap of 30 which you will reach by the end. The one superboss in the game also isn't that hard to beat. If you are looking for a challenge this will not be the game for you.Here is a list of interesting mechanics that this game tries to work with:-limited party wide heals. You don't get a ton of party wide heals, making attacks that hit your entire party extremely effective, and putting you in situations where you have to choose who gets the heal and who can stay at low health, making for some tense late game encounters.-no healing out of combat except items. If you are not using items the only for you to heal is to find someone to fight, this is interesting because you will have moments where you want to delay the end of a fight or the phase of a boss in order to heal before proceeding.-random events. some fights will have random events happen and they usually affect both the enemies and your own party. These are truly random so restarting a boss fight will put you in a different situation depending on the event card drawn.-visible stats. The game shows you precisely the attack/defense/hp of everyone, enemy included. Due to some weird maths the numbers aren't 100% correct but you can still use them for quick calculations.-tile jumping. You can move to any tile you have encountered with some very specific exceptions in like 5 rooms in the entire game. Meaning you can skip every encounter from Overworld to Dungeon by jumping to the exit tile, this weirdly invalidates an item in the game that allows you to escape dungeons.-gem system. This RPG completely removes mana points and replaces everything with a gem system, at the end of a character's turn, you get a gem, some skills require multiple gems to activate. This gives you some simple strategies where you save gems for a big heal or a strong AOE.-completely free inns. Not only are the inns free they also all have different reasons for being free in every town, be sure to check them out!-elemental weaknesses. The most used trope in RPG games, they are here to stay. Sadly even though you have a monster compendium you can't see enemy weaknesses anywhere in the game, you have to remember yourself which element they are weak to, hard for players with a poor memory like me.tl;dr Short RPG (12 hours to beat, even faster if you turn on fast animations), extremely simple mechanics but enough to keep you engaged.The Yoko Taro partHow does this compare to Yoko Taro's other works?Well in the first 30 minutes of the game, you encounter an old lady on the road and help her. Not even 2 minutes go by and you discover she was actually abused by her husband and she cut him up and ate him.This might seem shocking to most players but honestly after what he wrote in his other stories this seems a bit too predictable at this point. I can't say the game really surprised me in big ways. It's missing a lot of 4th wall breaking moments (there is only one that happens in a conversation with an NPC).I accidentally got the true ending on my first playthrough and damn this is the happiest ending Yoko Taro has ever shown us I have to say it's a wild departure from his other games.There is no NG+ that dramatically changes the game, the only way to get the endings is to redo the final boss. NG+ should have been used to either add on top of the story or remix encounters.tl;dr if you want more of small scale yoko taro (the one you get in the weapon stories), you'll get exactly this. But don't expect some mind bending 4th wall break.The ExperienceOverall it's a solid experience, the art on the card is absolutely stunning, and the pixel art DLC changes the cards of every NPC, every main character and every monster in the game including bosses (only things unchanged are the items and skills).The mood is there, the narrator is great, the soundtrack isn't oppressive and lends itself to a small tabletop adventure like this one. You sadly don't get a lot of unique mechanics tied to the entire game being a board, with the exception of the final boss visual, looks really cool.In conclusion, the experience of the game is really good, not perfect, not the level of NieR. But it's a cozy game with great visuals, great mood. It is very short however, 12 hours to finish (with normal animations), and got the full achievements at 17 hours (with fast animations on this time). So you might want to get it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards isn't a card battler, it's a poorly disguised JRPG.  It's a pretty game, it has a great theme and sticks to it...annoyingly.  The story isn't bad, but it's very short, and unfortunately shallow due to the format.Everything, including menus, is cards, which is thematically cool but completely obnoxious if you want to...yknow...change a setting and you have to sit there waiting on card animations to flip through whatever.  I got aggravated just trying to find the exit game button (which is about 8 menus deep) and just ALT+F4'd the first time.  The narrator sounds fine at first but quickly turns into a drone with very little inflection, as if you're telling a boring story over a campfire. Combat drags slower than my great-grandfather's rotting corpse in North Africa.  Even though the first 3/4ths of the game have enemies that can each be killed by one card play, it still takes forever to end each combat because of the animation systems.  They did add an increase in card speed, which helps and you should turn that on immediately but even then there are so many things that have animations that take forever: the board and table setup, putting cards down, swapping between skill and item decks etc.Difficulty is laughable until about 75%, at which point it just gets a little slower and you may need to heal once.  You get a random encounter every 1-7 moves, averaging for me around 3ish.  Each character only has about 5-6 skills max.  The moves are not unique or interesting (wind damage +1d6, or fire damage +4 WHAT RIVETING CHOICES), they don't combo, the "powerful" spells that require gems have no useful interactions with each other.  Progression is relatively meaningless because of how easy the whole thing is, and even after progression, fights take longer at the end regardless of what you do.  Honestly, the most irritating thing is that it could've been great, if it'd been tuned better.  Spells/skills could've been interesting.  Armor and weapons could've been meaningful choices.  Builds could've been a thing.  This may as well have been a movie for the amount of brainpower needed.  If the characters had more story and could be invested in, it'd be better.  This could be a decent prologue/introduction if they made the rest of the game that got much deeper into mechanics.  But instead it's none of these things.  Just a short, unmemorable blob of a game with some pretty art.Ugh, man.  C'mon.  Looks pretty, but so do a lot of things with no substance.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A good game with great music, fun characters but mediocre gameplay.Pros:- Story: A great simple story carries this game. The writing of characters is fun (if not a little tropey) and the central plot while nothing mind blowing had enough twist and turns to keep me playing.- Art style: The card style for this game works surprisingly well. As someone who generally doesn’t like deck building games I thought this might throw me off but far from it. The cards are animated in certain cutscenes and its almost surprising how between the animation and the narrator how “alive” individual cards can feel- Music/sound: Great music throughout. Perhaps needing one or two more tracks just to fill out the roster but still very strong. The Narrator is also very well done.- Gameplay: There are elements of the gameplay in this game I quiet enjoy. The turn based system is simple but with the added combination of Gems it gains a little bit of complexity.Neutral:-Length: This game might be a little short for some people. It took about 11 hours for me to complete (and that was with completing many but not all of the side quests).  Cons:- Speed of Gameplay: The biggest issue this game has is that combat goes way too slow. It feels as though animations are playing only at ½ speed. This effects every encounter and drags the game down a bit in my estimationConclusionThis is a fun game with exciting characters, great music and a fantastic art style but be warned that battles can drag on. ALSO if your are planning on buying this game play the demo first. The Demo acts as a prologue for the main game and gives a very good taste for how the whole game will play.

_childDocuments_.review: There are many RPG games out there that can range from simple and fun, to complex and challenging, this one falls into the former, however the direction of the game, while its mostly card based, is very much like a single players DnD game *Dungeons and Dragons*.As your playing the game you have a "Game Master" urging you on as you progress through your story, occasionally giving small hints or backtalk at times. Most of the game you'll be exploring the map, which will mostly be blank until you walk around the area, uncovering the map which is all card related, or you'll be in random encounters of battles, which i liked in some aspects.Battle order is based off speed, and your attack stat is very important versus enemies with high defense, unless you are able to apply a ailment, otherwise you'll just be doing at best 1 damage. While your basic attack can be used as much as you want, other skills you have will cost "Gems", which you earn a single gem per character turn and you start each combat with two. What brings in the DnD aspect of the game in battle also comes from your moves, some moves may require you to roll a 6 faced or 10 faced dice to either determine damage or if you apply a ailment on a foe.Aside from battles theres also a fun and interesting minigame should you wish to divert from the story and have a bit of fun, winning once on each of the difficulties will even unlock cosmetic styles on your dice, table board and even your card designs.If i had to say if this would be a good choice for new people starting RPG games to try out, i would say yes, but if your looking for a game that will last you days upon weeks of playtime, then you might be better looking at something else. The gameplay and combat sounds intriguing at first, but once you fully understand its way of play, the game then just feels really easy, albeit with the random RNG chance with the dice rolls. That combined with how quickly story chapters go, and even the end level cap, if you really pushed yourself, you could maybe speedrun a normal clear *not the good ending clear* in a hour or two.So yes, if your new to the RPG genre, this is a good stepping stone into the genre, but if your a person with a fair bit of experience and wanting a longer game time, then it might be worth passing on.I however had alot of fun playing this, ergo why i approve of this style of RPG game~

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not usually the type to leave reviews, but after seeing so many that talk only about what this game is not, rather than what it is, I felt the need to weigh in.I'm a huge fan of tabletop roleplaying games, and few other games have captured their spirit like Voice of Cards. The constant presence of the game master is a unique and compelling element, with his voice guiding you along your adventure, not just describing and narrating but also commenting on your actions and even adding human touches, like fumbling an NPC's name or gently pushing you back onto the intended path.Alongside that is gorgeous music, as usual from a Keiichi Okabe production, Yoko Taro's twisted sense of humour and adroit narrative pacing, and a surprising depth and complexity from the card based aesthetic, initially seeming simple, but using the medium for unique animations and effects to convey the events of the battles and the story. It's not the longest game, but it doesn't need to be, not overstaying its welcome and giving you an enjoyable ride from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Short and basic RPG. Buy on sale for $10 or so.If you enjoy very old school classic rpgs like Final Fantasy 1 or Dragon Quest 1 then you'll like Voice of Cards. It's a VERY basic rpg. The cards are really just used as tile sets like rpgs used in NES games or in RPG Maker style games. Though it's not a bad thing in my opinion. The game is really short and incredibly easy. If you just play the game and uncover the map you will never have to worry about being under leveled. Money comes easy so buying the newest equipment is easy as is getting healing items which I never used in my playthrough. The game also has multiple party members but it suffers because you'll basically be using the same 3 party members through out the whole game after getting your third (or technically 4th) member. I think a big drawback to the game is the narrator, though he can be funny at times he is the ONLY voice in the game reading every bit of new dialogue. If he was the narrator and there was more voice acting for the small cast of characters it'd be more bearable. The gameplay also wears itself thin pretty fast being speed turn based with attacks being chosen by cards of certain costs with some cards rolling dice to decide if effects are placed or increase damage.There's also this optional mini-game where you and the CPU  or Online Friends play a card game where you match 2 or 3 cards with various additions that add to the game's difficulty. I can see it being fun with friends but against the CPU if you don't get to go first or second in the harder games you're out of luck.It's only really a 10-12 hour game so if you're looking to kill time and be told a alright story with nice artwork I guess go for it if it's on sale for at least 50% or higher. I don't hate the game but I wouldn't fully recommend it either.

_childDocuments_.review: Basic premise/StoryFrom developer studio Alim and directed by Maasa Mimura with creative director Yoko Taro. With the main composer being Oliver Good. A new tabletop jrpg emerges into the scene. Where you control a small band of adventurers as they hunt for the dragon who has threatened the safety of the realm.  Unique GameplayGameplay in Voice of Cards. Is simple. You control three characters with each character taking an action like attacking or using a gem spell which is located to the top left of the screen. As you level up you will earn more spells/abilities which will consume more crystals. You can buy and find equipment out in the world. With random encounters in the overworld. You can flee battles as long as you attain the required dice roll number. Although this can vary depending on how weak or strong your enemies are. Each character has a health bar and you can use consumables while fighting in battles. Be careful, if all your party members are wiped out, you will need to reload your last save. Thankfully, the autosave saves periodically. As you travel in the overworld you may come across random events from helping a monster, to finding hidden clues to treasures. The exploration of the world isn’t that large, however, players may feel fatigued from traveling three steps then immediately going into a battle. Or six steps or more than a random encounter battle. This ruins the pacing a bit since I constantly wanted to move onto the next bit of the story only to become impeded by random encounters every time. However, it should be noted there is a ‘jump’ action for players whenever they mouse onto a card tile that the party has already uncovered in the overworld. Allowing players to jump far. This will save some time. Final thoughts/RuminationsThroughout my 13 hour playthrough, I was enthralled in the beginning how simple and classic the story is. Hunt the dragon with your party members. And while you do gain more party members of which you can change whenever you’re out of combat. The game performs under a rinse and repeats formula, as you traverse through the overworld. Travel to battle, travel then battle, moving to the next main story event. Travel then battle. Dungeon then battle. Then countless battles later you face off a story boss. Then the cycle repeats. There just isn’t enough to keep the player engaged in a level to hook players continuously. And while I will admit during the last legs of the journey I raised my score quite a bit for going into areas I didn’t expect in a classic story. The game just doesn’t do enough to raise the game into a higher tier. From developer studio Alim and directed by Maasa Mimura with creative director Yoko Taro. Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is a simple if not classic game from Square Enix. The game feels more like an experimental indie title looking to transform the mobile developer into a console/pc platform. And I for one welcome such a change. This is why it’s all the more painful to say, the game doesn’t blow you away to leave a lasting impression. The story is classic through and through, and while I did have moments that raised my eyebrow quite a bit. There wasn’t enough here to be memorable enough, since the trailers attached the notable Yoko Taro director of Nier/Drakengard fame. Music is splendid. Oliver Good does a decent job getting the soundtrack to be powerful in key moments. Gameplay is pretty simple and doesn’t require much thought. I do think there needs to be a no-encounters button to alleviate the boredom of battles constantly. It’s a short game. I would wait for a sale since the price is a bit too high for what players are getting. Would only recommend this game for Nier fans only and the lowest expectation possible. To be fair, i still enjoyed my time with the game. A classic story is not inherently bad, and Voice of Cards creates a simple if not decently classic story through and through. Total Times Beaten: 1Score: 7/10 Date Finished: 11/1/21Date Reviewed: 11/2/21Hours Played: 13+

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very simple but charming little game. If you're a fan of the kinds of stories told in Yoko Taro's games (NieR, Drakengard), then you'll really like this one. The card-based tabletop RPG-styled presentation is excellently done, and is a great way to make a game with a small budget. The art on the cards is wonderful and the character designs are pretty fun, and the way the cards are animated adds a lot to the immersion. The solo narrator, while a bit repetitive at times, does a great job telling the story and voicing all the characters, and the occasional fourth-wall breaks are a good touch. The game has turn-based RPG combat that is very basic and easy to understand, but pretty satisfying thanks to the wonderful card animation and sound design. If you're up for a casual RPG experience that is short and sweet, you really can't go wrong with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The fact that you have to click the next button to do anything makes the game slow and boring. Heard a line of dialogue, click for the next one. Attacked by a monster, click to go to the battle. Won a battle, click to find out what you got for winning and through all the new skills. Want to play a mini-game, click to chose the rules, click to hear the rules, click to draw cards, click to listen to more rules, click to make a set, click to listen to even more rules, click to discard cards, click to end your turn; then watch the AI opponents be told all the rules every turn.The developer needs to cut out all the pointless clicking and let the player play the game, instead of having to alternate between playing and clicking go to the next thing.Other problems with this game are that it's clear the volcano wasn't balanced in any way, which is why they had to include a rest area in it but not the final area.The plot doesn't make any sense. All the dragon was doing was scaring away fish; yet for some reason the queen asks everyone to kill it, even though she has an entire order dedicated to fixing problems. After you beat the dragon it flies to the one island it should have no reason to ever go to. Then a guy kills the dragon, it's corpse falls into a volcano, and the volcano erupts. Then you have to stop that guy using a magic spell on an altar, even though you have no reason to save this altar and could easily grab the item you need while he's casting his spell. Finally if you drop a dragon's tear into the volcano near where a dragons corpse fell in, melted to nothing, and was blown into the sky by the eruption it will cause that dragon to come back to life and jump out of the lava with it's body fully restored because all the tears it had in its body weren't enough to save it. However if you don't have 10 special cards he won't help you.Overall the game is too slow and the plot doesn't make sense.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is in part on addressing the surface 'No Recommendation' reviews of the game. My review 'so far' at the end.I don't think a lot of the reviews knew VoC was announced through the Nintendo Direct 3rd Quarter video release. Later, was offered for PC purchase before the official release. I was fully aware this game may not look the best on PC being placed at 1080p - 60 fps. I'm usually on my PC more than I am on my Switch, hence this purchase and this review. I'm not sure why anyone is expecting top notch work for this game, it's not one of Square Enix's bigger franchises. Also, just because we have game releases of multiple choices does NOT equate to story shift. To be honest, this feels like a game that is in release to test the waters on how else to view RPGs and a tie over for other Square Enix major releases.--My take on the game so far, it's a really pretty game and immersive for me, the background music and narrator is really warming and cozy to go through the game straight through. YES, THERE IS A LOT OF RANDOM ASS ENCOUNTERS. To reiterate this game feels to be an homage to old school RPGs that's random encounters, grinding, and rerunning monsters or encounters to collect things. The main character is a money grubby person. A set personality isn't the norm, but it's a change of pace from the blank slate. You're given 2-3 line options to respond for voice.As for game mechanics, there isn't any room to tell you anything about dice rolls, but put 2 and 2 together. They're usually rolls to 1) add on to a base damage 2) be the set damage or 3) the success of an effect. Otherwise, it's your average turn base game.-- I do hope to revisit the review for an endgame recap.

_childDocuments_.review: This game starts out as a fun little card battler, with a halfway decent story, and good mechanics.  It's fatal flaw unfortunately does not manifest until late in the game after you're invested in it.The game requires grinding to complete.  There is a substantial rise in difficulty between story line bosses and the final encounter, so much that you must grind for a lengthy period of time via random encounters to gain sufficient level to beat the final boss.This isn't interesting grinding either, you will have explored the entire map by this time and still need 5-10 levels for each of your characters to beat the final boss if you are going with anything other than a tightly optimized build.  This means that you must either min-max your party for that encounter that you are yet unaware of (while you are doing the story) or grind.  Grinding in a game is lazy design.The other major annoyance this game has is the UI.  To exit out of the game you have to go deep in the menu, rather than it being an easily available option.  It's buried under Other and I had to poke around for five minutes before I found it.  You cannot exit while a battle is ongoing so if something comes up, you'll have to force close the game.Overall interesting concept and like 95% of the game is great, but the 5% that is bad, really ruins the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't feel like Yoko Taro's new baby. It's rough around the edges to say the least, lacking the polish that one would expect from such a simple game. Because yeah, it's pretty much an RPG Maker template game, with a "cards" visual makeover.I did enjoy the character art and the music, as well as the over-world exploration which has a nice feel to it and some simple puzzles. But the list of positives ends here. My mains issues:- The flow of the game is so awkward. There are uncomfortable delays between literally every other thing, *pop-up* tutorials and tips all the time, and navigating menus and confirming any basic decision takes more clicks than it should. Targeting in combat *requires* you to drag and drop. Some controls are unresponsive. You'll be very frustrated if you're used to the "Hearthstone" level of responsiveness and quality. I'm a Mouse + Keyboard user, and it feels like this might've been designed with controller-users in mind first.- I haven't completed the game or anything, but gameplay-wise nothing has hooked my interest so far. It plays like the most basic of RPGs and nothing stands after 2 whole chapters. I've made 0 decisions so far, so it's not exactly emulating the "tabletop" feel I've seen people mention in reviews either. It's insanely easy, due to how little strategical depth there is. Sadly, lsooking at other reviews, the whole game just seems to be like that.- That may be up to taste, but I found the scenario and characters to be quite simply bland. At best, it can be silly at times, like that time I got hit in a nut and lost 5 HP while exploring, three times in a row. Most frustrating of all is that I *wasn't* the character I played. The game pretends to give you (already very restrictive) dialogue options, but then twists the meaning of the words you picked or makes you fail spectacularly without checks, in order to stick to the main character's insufferable personality.- There's this big emphasis on the card arts, you're supposed to "contemplate" them in your collection and whatnot. Except the in-game viewer toasts the pictures' quality, and if you look at the cards any closer than they're shown in the base game, you'll have to deal with crispy JPG compression artifacts. Also it's only character art, nothing most people would be head over heels about. I personally don't see the point of this feature when the rest of the game is already lackluster.- There's a huge framework for customization and collecting "extra stuff" like card arts and weirdly cryptic lore about NPCs you don't care about, but none of that is really interesting.- The narrator really aces the "grizzly old man" voice. However, not a single character he voices is a grizzly old man. Young boys and elven women all share that voice and it's silly at first, but it disconnects you from characters after a while.I was hyped for this game, but I can't recommend paying 30€ for what seems to be a low-effort money-sink.

_childDocuments_.review: At first, Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is another generic story about heroes on a quest to defeat a dragon, but what made this game stand out is the tabletop presentation. Knowing myself, I'm a sucker for this sort of dungeon-like style or anything with to do with dice or cards used as a mechanic and this game delivers by incorporating them to tell a simple story. In this case, the cards are used to covey a lot of emotion and events like getting ruined when the character is wet, cards tackling each other when characters fight, flipped face-down when a location or enemies are hidden, or even when they are sliced in half if they gotten stabbed. The animation doesn't stop there as they are also used in combat, for instance, the cards spin around when they are attacked with a wind ability or are used to display different stats buff and debuff like being frozen or covered in green goop when you're characters are poisoned.Voice of Cards is mainly RNG, with a lot of skills requiring you to roll a higher number off the dice to get more benefit out of the ability and a lot of 'good' abilities cost a lot of gems and need you to roll a high number, so there is some risk factor in play. Either way, this game is generous with save points, and much like Child of Light the battle is simple enough to get by as your character is mostly stronger than the enemies in most cases, but that's where I have some issues with this game. The difficulty mode is generally easy with no hard mode, so there's no challenge in this game, by the time I made it 3/4 of the way through combat it became too boring that I ended up increasing the speed of the animation to skip past the filler content and to finish this game as quickly as possible. At least the final boss fight toward the end was a challenge in comparison, I love how supreme it looks with all the card layers around it to make it as gigantic as it is on the table. I would have liked this game more if there was an option to increase the difficulty and more challenging battle encounters.My nitpicks I need to mention about this game were the narrator calling anything non-human 'monster', it gets annoying after a while, lacking any vocal variation. Other than that, this was a fine game on its own in being able to tell a simple story (with a nice twist) by presenting them with cards literally coming to life and I adore it for that. I can't get over the fact of how polished they look and the medievally stylized that fit the theme of this game. Where can I get a physical copy of these cards?

_childDocuments_.review: I would highly suggest giving this experimental title from Yoko Taro's team at least one play through. I'm going to leave my review as clear cut without any spoilers. Pros: The game is short enough to dive into and complete in just a few sittings. Perfect if you're waiting for other titles to release or you have too busy of a life style to dive into JRPGs regularly. The battle system while it is bare bones for most JRPG veterans there won't be many challenges, but again Yoko Taro games are meant to be easily accessible and this will be a big big pro if you're not a big JRPG enthusiast. The music: even though it is a very short track list (I believe there are only ten songs without counting variations) Oliver Goode does a damn good job making the music fit what is to be expected from this dev team if you're familiar with them. The plot: While most of it was easy to guess, some plot twists still took me out. You'll get many if not ALL of your questions answered. Cons: The game is short. If you're big into JRPGs you will be disappointed in the length.The characters, some of them are a bit flat. The battle system and boss fights are not challenging if you're a JRPG veteran. You'll probably get super bored if you're really big into them like I am. (Though I still had tons of fun going through this game)The plot is pretty linear you won't find yourself doubling back very often. There is little reason to revisit the game once you've beaten it and obtained the true ending, which is easily done your first go through. For my closing statements: Pretty much go for it especially if it's on sale and you want a little game to tide you over. I understand holding back on a title like this especially since it was probably a hard pitch and you never know how the consumers are going to feel about an experimental title done in such a unique style. I adored the board game feeling, as it made me feel like I was having a cozy night in playing board games back when I was younger. I really hope this series takes off, as I would love to visit this world more.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing for 10 hours (12 Steam hours because I stream and sometimes leave games on to set up), I've completed the True Ending, so here's my review.:- Music is incredible. Wow.- Art and visuals? All great. Made me really feel like sitting down at a table, and that comes from a DM of nearly two decades.- English narration was very good, really brought out the "just sitting at a table with your DM" feel.- Gameplay is solid and simple; at no point was I really confused as to how the game worked.- :- The story was kind of average, a very run-of-the-mill fantasy romp like you've seen before. Again, there's more to it, but the real story is mostly just in the character cards: side text is not my favorite way to get lore.- Game is pretty short. If you're looking for an RPG because RPGs go for length? This is not that. 10 hours to get the true ending. Would be another 4 to finish all the remaining achievements, if I wanted to.- :- Menuing controls in this game are absolutely abysmal on mouse and keyboard. The overworld? Fine. Most of combat? Also fine. You try to use an item in battle? Now you have to, unprompted, use the arrow keys to shuffle through all of your inevitably full inventory because there's no way to scroll through items with the mouse. The pause menu was similar; at times felt very clunky and frustrating, I kept closing out of the menu entirely on accident because the keyboard is only necessary for menuing, and even then only for certain commands.Despite the scathing criticisms I have, I hope we get a sequel. I hope we get something, because this game was great despite its flaws, and it could be so much more -- more stories could be told with this system and I would be absolutely fine with that. Here's hoping. Thanks, Yoko Taro.

_childDocuments_.review: This plays like a good game of DD with an invested/over-invested dungeon master that is doing everything to make the players have a good time. The characters and story are top notch, and the mechanics are diverse enough to remain fun throughout the game. I have seen the following 3 arguments against the game: Its not a card game, Its $30, and Its not hard enough.1. This is not supposed to be a card game. The cards act as a medium and work to represent characters as well as define the world. They're board game figures except they're well drawn and have enough detail to keep them fun to look at as the game progresses.2. The game is costly at $30, but it pales in comparison to what trying to make this game in real life would cost. Voice of Cards has a DM that not only bought the book but also took the time to craft out your characters and each chapter with love. The ability to play the game without having to get a large group of friends together is also a bonus in its favor. The game design can feel minimal for what other games cost, and the price being at half that of a big square title invites this type of response from the community, but the $30 is way under what would be expected to compensate someone in person for making a game that shows an unrealistic amount of time and effort to craft and set up.3. Being well balanced is not a bad thing. The game is at a difficulty that is enjoyable to me. There's a mix of having fun characters that feel strong to use while always having the threat of damage/death. Random encounters are designed to be fun and not annoying where they usually result in a 1-2 characters taking damage, and the goal for each area is to minimize this damage in a way that allows the player to progress to the boss. Bosses are big enough to incite the player to unload their strong attacks that they've been learning while inviting the threat of death to the party. The difficulty also allows for flexibility in the party being used. Each of the characters have different and strong strategies for dealing damage/surviving, and being able to use a party that consists of your favorite combination of 3/5 for most of the game is part of the appeal, but the game does get more difficult at times where it expects you to use other combos which gives the player the want and ability to craft new set ups for each area.-Whoever made the minigame should be fired though. Advice is to skip the game parlor until you have gotten sufficient enjoyment out of the main game.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is a particularly ambitious JRPG that takes on a card based format while taking an innovative departure from the classic JRPG format to better fit the genre of a tabletop RPG with engine building mechanics. Voice of Cards as a whole is fairly enjoyable game, with amazing presentation and story telling, but unfortunately runs into some pitfalls in the form of imbalanced team building mechanics, lackluster item progression and lack of replayability. Voice of Cards for me excelled in its playful way of story telling. The narrator always kept me engaged with the story, as the way the cards danced on the screen allowed me to fully visualize each individual scene. Pair that with the game's amazing sound track I wouldn't be hesitant to call this one of my favorite games of this year, but only from a visual stand point.Personally Voice of Cards ends up lacking of the game play department. I find many people call this a spin on the classic JRPG genre. Which I guess that's true to some extent, but this game has the soul of a tabletop engine builder when it comes to setting up your skills and resource management with your gems. Finding the most optimal rotations to defeat your opponent. Instead of going too deep onto each and every issue with the game play I would rather make short bullet points.1. Gear is lacking. Gear in the game are basically stat sticks and don't have any unique or interesting effects.The only important stats being ATK, DEF, and SPD. Speed only being used to manipulate turn order between your characters for rotations. The only really important rings in the game are the frost ring and the seal ring, and these status effects only really come up often on the final boss.2. Melanie is too good, and Mar is too weak. Without going terribly deep into this Melanie as a whole isn't strong, but their ability charge is too good not to implement into any party. I found it hard to play without it once I started to use and abuse it. Mar on the other hand doesn't offer anything significant to the party. Their damage isn't amazing and their tanking skills are pretty bad too.3. Navigating shops suck. Even though beyond buying equipment I didn't need to buy items often for my playthroughs of the game. Navigating the item shop is a chore, buying more than one item at a time is insufferable at best.4. Too many random encounters.5. Repetitive and Badly Design Random Events. The first time you get random events through the game they feel pretty cool and organic through the first play through of the game, but in the second area of the game, The Bewildering Wood, you get to really see how repetitive these events can be. The Bewildering Wood alone only 2 events that can be cycled repetitively as you venture through the game on your first play through. The second event I think is terrible, is the drop the armor in the hole event. I never completed this event since I never had just random armor sitting in my inventory, and even if i had the armor on one of my characters the event wouldn't give me the option to drop the armor i was wearing into the hole. 6. Buffs and debuffs don't overlap..? This was a weird one for me. This made making skill sets harder since not just debuffs, but buffs weren't stackable. Not even if you tried an attack buff and a defense buff together. This really made me had to try to see what was more attack or defense. (I think defense is better)7, AoEs are useless. The game is designed to have a max of 3 on 3 fights. Unfortunately this makes all the AoEs in this game borderline useless. It tends to be more efficient to take out one enemy, to mitigate one attack rather than AoE all of your enemies just to not kill any of them and take 3 attacks to the face. Since AoEs in this game tend to either cost 4+ resources or if they're less than that only do slightly more than your character's base damage.Lastly I'd like to address the game's replayability, or it's new game plus. Honestly, It's unnecessary. New game plus is so devoid of new content, you might as well just stop playing after the first play through. Choices you make in the game are rather linear, and only make a difference after the last boss fight. The only thing you get out of new game plus is a new set of dialogue from the white order trio after defeating them. Access to the Secret Boss, and one more hidden boss to get finish your equipment collection. Beyond that, there isn't much else besides the four different endings you can choose at the end. Despite my critiques of the game I found Voice of Cards as a pretty enjoyable experience as a tabletop fan and a JRPG fan. I more critical in this post mostly because I wish the game can improve and for these kinks to be ironed out if Yoko Taro wishes to venture into this style of game once again, because I think stylized take on the JRPG genre should not be slept on.I give this game a 7/10 and i'd reccomend it at it's current price point. I'd reccomend it even further once the price drops.

_childDocuments_.review: Just started chapter 2.Amazing, I really hope Square make more of these or make it a franchise.The voice-over, music, art style are top tier.It plays like an old turn based FF RPG but as cards.Moving through the over-world, has cards flipped to represent fog-of-war, wade your way through plains/forests/deserts (more terrain types later I assume) to find towns and caves. Enter into these and the terrain swaps to a town with citizens and shops to visit and buy equipment, seek information and pick up quests.Combat is as you'd expect from an older JRPG, turn based, abilities, equipment, status effects. All good stuff.Top tier RPG/Table top RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: artwork is good, music is good, overall presentation is excellentgameplay is decent: gem regeneration gives you options for every turn and basic skills can serve you well for the entire game; however battles become much more tedious toward the endgame due to enemies with high hp and more debuffing skillsdifficulty is not very hard: the game is very forgiving and in general weighed in your favour; random happenstance cards during event battles tend to benefit you rather than hinder you and even the "harmful" ones harm the enemy too; the game gives you plenty of healing and revival items so youre rarely in danger of a game overstory and characters are alright: the game makes it obvious that there is more going on beneath the surface plot and keeps it engaging with the character interactions and the dry narration; the game gives each character life and personality of their own, through their story moments and dialogue and even the movements of their cards during battlebad things: item inventory is locked to 30 slots and the game is sometimes too generous with handing you items, many of them are completely useless until the final dungeon as they cure statuses which only appear there; equipment management is clunky as you cannot swap equipped items between party members which forces you to unequip and then reequip; menus in general are a bit slow and occasionally unresponsive due to the slow card animationsconclusion: jrpg with strong and unorthodox presentation, engaging writing and battle system, only real faults are the somewhat slow pace and clunky inventory management; Recommend if you are a fan of jrpgs

_childDocuments_.review: Let me get some misconceptions, I keep seeing around, out of the way first. This is not by any means a card game, or ever aimed to be one. It is not some in depth turn based jrpg with wild mechanics. This is an interactive fairy tale told through well, cards, and it uses this medium and jrpg paint coat to do so.The story is honestly great, it has that Yoko Taro charm of fairytale gone dark. Simple premises give way to darker stories and bigger stakes as the story progresses and it is all done in Taro's masterful way of easing you in for that gut punch time and time again. While not connected with the Dragonsphere universe at first glance, veterans will see some parallels with Drakengard. Is it Fujisaka's superb artwork? Is it nostalgia for the good old Drakengard series? Is it some foreplay for a new Drakengard game? (PLEASE YES BTW) I dont know but this feels pretty stand alone, but also not.Music is once again done by Keichi Okabe and is an instant classic, with vocals done by Emi Evans for the main theme and I dont need to say more at this point.Gameplay takes the form of a very simple turn based jrpg akin to the first FInal Fantasy. I think this is intended, both game, world and story structure have a very early FF or DQ era game. Simple spells, quests and enemies that get more wraped and twisted as the narrative goes on. The only issue I had was that I wanted something more challenging to await at some point but I feel that was never the point.It is easy to reccomend this honestly. Price is just right imho and multiple endings paired with a fun card mini game are more than enough meat to chew with the asking price. And hell Fujisaka and Taro working together again is reason enough for the price alone. A very fresh take that is honestly worth every second.Fingers crossed for a new Drakengard game now...

_childDocuments_.review: This review does not contain spoilers.Cleared the game in 14 hours, and Full Clear in 17, Score: 5/10.Remarkables:-Rich Art on most of the Cards, and there are lots.-Enjoyable Fantasy music towards the end of the game and in the intermissions.-Provides a Fast Mode.Could be fixed:-Multiple Damage instances do not provide a Total Damage at the end.-Inventory limit is unnecesary, or at least too small, discarding excessive items is a really cumbersome process.-Skill Card picking in battles with mouse on PC could be more precise and fluid, as you will sometimes pick wrong skill cards mid fight.-Camera Movement with mouse is choppy and cumbersome, directional buttons work better.-Accept/Cancel buttons cannot be customized to any key, have to stick with mouse or enter/backspace.-Shops should show the amount of items you posess in inventory without having to select the item first.-The Fast Mode enabling shortcut, "R" key on keyboard doesn't work mid-fight.Lastly, English narrator or GM has an emotionless tone of voice, breaking immersion in many scenarios, Japanese narrator is better in my honest opinion.Story 5.0/10Gameplay 5.0/10Music 6.0/10Difficulty 4.0/10 (This constitutes how challenging is the game, low challenge equals a low score.)

_childDocuments_.review: Having completed this game to 100%, I can safely say it was a thoroughly enjoyable time, which I would definitely recommend to anyone who enjoys turn-based combat or JRPGs. The game itself isn't too long, easily completed within 10 - 12 hours, with anything beyond being the player going into the Gambling minigames, or trying for the 100% completion.The game itself is a fresh, standalone entry from the mastermind behind the NieR and Drakengard series, YOKO TARO. Seemingly the only ties this has to any of his other games is that the vocals used in the music (which is amazing by the way) sound like they also use the language of the ancients from NieR. The story features a cast of flawed characters which I enjoy, as they all feel a bit more relatable with their own selfish ambitions.Honestly, just play it for yourself, and lose yourself in the music and aesthetic. This game was an absolute gem from beginning to end, and I found it very relaxing to play something that was both this engaging and humorous after a day at work. The animations really help to convey the narrative, despite everything being represented in the card format, and it really plays into using your imagination to fill in the details.I'd recommend it at full price, the DLCs are just nice extras, nothing more, no need to grab them if you don't want them. If it's on sale, then definitely grab this game, it's a real treasure.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sad to say I have to give this game a thumbs-down; while there's some good stuff here, it's overall mediocre.Story: Nothing happens plot-wise until the final two chapters, when all the world's secrets are revealed at once. There's some stuff hinting at it beforehand, but it feels like a huge chunk of the game is just an extended sidequest. Those last two chapters /are/ good from a story perspective, at least.Characters: The main party ranges from 'fine' to 'why do I care about this character again?'. Only the first three party members really have an impact on the plot, and one of those three is more of a plot device than an actual character.Combat: It doesn't get repetitive as quickly as JRPG combat often does, but it /does/ get repetitive eventually. I appreciate that the gems system means that you're not just spamming attack during non-boss-fights, but at the same time, once you've determined a strategy, you just keep using that same strategy in basically every battle. Towards the end, I was basically running away from battles every time, just because they were a pain and the rewards weren't worth the time.Aesthetic: This is where the game gets a lot of points for me. The card-based aesthetic is controversial, but they pull it off well, and it means that every asset can have a lot of care put into its artwork.Atmosphere: Separately from aesthetic... the world's atmosphere is basically 'generic fantasy'. Nothing that really makes it stand out all that much. It's not bad, but it's not good either.Music: The music is nice; it's not my favorite video game OST, but it's well-made and helps set the atmosphere.Other good: The ability to 'jump' around the map makes exploring easier, and the fact that your backline party members still get full EXP is pretty nice.Other bad: Random encounter rate is way too high. Barely any character customization. Equipment is just piles of stats with no interesting effects. The game gives you choices and then makes them do nothing whatsoever (the most egregious was the first time this happened, when you have a choice to try and help an old lady to the apothecary. If you chose to help, you're too weak to lift her... and then the party just, acts like you refused to help her). Most battles are pretty trivial once you unlock some status effects, until the bosses start being status-immune like in most JRPGs, which makes status effects useless again. Animations are painfully slow, and there's no way to skip them.Overall, it's got some good concepts, but there's just not enough there by basically any metric. I'm basically neutral on it, leaning slightly negative... I'll say it's a 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Short review: a fun, light-hearted table-top RPG with a beautiful soundtrack, minor exploration, and an evolving story. Travel with a band of humorous misfits and slay the Dragon! Long review:1) Story: The story begins with the Queen of the land calling for champions to slay the evil Dragon. As a money-hungry adventurer with a silent monster companion, you sign up to slay the Dragon to get the riches the Queen promises. Overtime, you meet more companions that make your adventure grander and hilarious.2) Gameplay: It’s a turn-based table-top RPG where you make use of cards and dices to defeat enemies. Characters gain experience and learn new skills and passive abilities. The entire game, including the larger world and towns, are all completely made up of cards—very unique. The default gameplay is a bit slow but can be sped up with the “high speed” option. Various aspects of the game can also be customized such as the table, dice, and cards that are played with. All in all, the gameplay is not very complex and doesn’t require deep strategies to win. The difficulty cannot be changed but is fairly easy for the most part until you get to the final area, which can be an issue or blessing to some. There is no voice acting except for the “game master” that narrates the entire story and all dialogue (in English or Japanese). Honestly, it would’ve been a lot better if the party had their own voice actors. 3) Visuals: good use of color but can be a bit dark and dull. Has a medieval-inspired art style that works well. Animation is simple and not too flashy. 4) Music: a mix of beautiful emotional tracks (especially the title screen) and upbeat tracks that make you feel like you’re on an adventure. The music is very fitting in each area. 5) Performance: depends on your PC but it ran flawless on mines (I have a Lenovo RTX 2060) with fullscreen 1920x1080. I played the entire game on the “high speed” option without any issues. 6) Overall: 8 out of 10. If you like a slower-paced, narrative table-top game that isn’t difficult, this is your game. Expect to spend around 10-15 hours on the story, light grinding, and some exploration. 20-25 hours for full completion and achievements. Pretty easy to 100% on Steam. Definitely give the demo a try.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is a short JRPG whose strong points are its soundtrack and its visual presentation. It's a solid game but honestly somewhat overpriced for its depth and length, so I would recommend picking up this game on sale if at all.STORY: The story is not particularly standout, with perhaps the most interesting part of it being its framing device, that is, narrated by a GM. While the illustrations for the characters are beautiful none of them are particularly interesting or deep. There's perhaps some humor in the storyline, although it wasn't for me personally. Ultimately, a lackluster effort. 4/10GAMEPLAY: The game presents itself as a card battler but is really a very straightforward party-based JRPG. As far as JRPGs go, it's an easy one. Only the last battles in the game present anything close to a challenge. The rest of the game is spent talking to NPCs and wandering dungeons/the overworld, which are spiced up compared to other JRPGs by including random events such as encountering wandering merchants in addition to the standard random encounters. The encounter rate is fairly high and there is no way to reduce it on your first playthrough, but the game reduces forced grinding by allowing you to basically teleport to any previously seen square on the map. Ultimately, the battle system is not very compelling, there's little to no exploration, and there's basically only the main quest to do. 7/10LOOKS: The game has a unique presentation through cards (all beautifully illustrated) and a narrator with 3D rendered dice clearly meant to evoke tabletop RPGs like Dungeons and Dragons. The aesthetic is very interesting and there's certainly no other games I can think of with a similar look. However, beyond the initial novelty, little is done with the card/tabletop game look. 9/10VALUE: The game is very short and there is little reason to play it again on NG+ unless you are a completionist who wants all the achievements, and even in that case you only have to simply start a NG+, not play the game through again to the end. Purchased at full price, $30, I don't believe this game is worth it. There is a multiplayer component where the in-game card game can be played, but this card game is heavily luck based, so it doesn't strike me as particularly deep. 4/10OTHER NOTABLES: The soundtrack is pretty good.OVERALL: 24/40. If you want to play an interesting RPG with a dragon antagonist, play Dragon's Dogma instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars comes from the imaginative mind of Yoko Taro of NieR and Drakengard fame. Acting as Creative Director, the game contains many of Yoko Taro's signature styles. The game is a casual card-based RPG reminiscent of tabletop games in terms of story, combat, and pacing. Don't walk into this game expecting a complex story or in-depth characters. The game is a relaxing role-playing experience that lasts for about 15 hours.Taking on the role of a hero, you will be accompanied by the adorable Mar, your companion, throughout the game. Your main objective is to kill a dragon sentenced to death by the kingdom's queen. The gold reward for taking down the dragon pushes you onward, meeting a rambunctious cast of characters. Along this dangerous journey, your party will be filled with various characters, each with a unique back story explaining why they are joining you. However, most of the game is light on character development and depth. Combat is tragically simple but maintains its freshness for the game's length. Accompanied by a limited but strong soundtrack, it helps bolster the world and adds tension to each battle. The artwork is easily one of the most impressive aspects of the game. It provides unique monster designs, beautifully intricate artwork for the main characters, and a fresh world compared to other games. One of the glaring downsides is the repeated use of character art for the limited cast of NPCs in the game. You'll see the same old man, young kid, and woman in each town you visit. A sin that many games make, but with such a small amount of NPCs, it is glaringly apparent. In my opinion, a lot could've been improved without much effort.Initially, the game didn't click with me. After giving it a second chance, I enjoyed it for what it was. I feel like setting the right kind of expectations is critical to helping others enjoy this game. It's a short casual role-playing experience with enough to love about its world and characters to push you forward to complete the game. There were a lot of witty gags or bits that I found clever or even had me laughing out loud. The price for this game is reasonable for the amount of time it asks of you and the content it delivers. It helps that 100% completing the game doesn't ask much more of you outside of what completing the game will net you. Overall, you'll complete most of the game by playing through it normally, with the cleanup for remaining achievements only taking an extra couple of hours. I'm not sure I would be compelled to continue the series and play the other Voice of Card games, but I did enjoy my time and recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: For me this game was a very disappointing experience. I sat through double of what I have here as steam deck hours do not show up and I kind of kept waiting to have fun in this game.The UI must have been designed by a 2 year old but that is obvious from most other reviews as well.The gameplay is your bog standard turn based RPG with very watered down mechanics. This game is about as deep as pokemon games are which in itself reveals to me that this was meant to be a mobile experience as Yoko Taro has been pretty much farming Ls after Automata and Replicant with predatory mobile games.Artwork is extremely mid tier and they did not even bother avoiding the same avatars in the same village for different NPCs. Story is also very average especially if you played/read/saw anything from Yoko Taro previously. The card medium and lack of a proper voice over (yes I know the excuse here is that the game is "run" by a DM who btw sounds like he does not want to be there) make it hard to immerse oneself in the story. With his enthusiasm of a dead rat, the voice over guy reminded me of the times when I experienced Polish TV (if you know, you know), no offense to Polish TV enjoyers.I really tried liking this game but the incredibly sluggish (yes I changed the speed) gameplay and incredibly frustrating enemy spawns just strangled any possibility of fun as every 1-3 steps you get an encounter which made me audibly groan every time after about 2 hrs when I "mastered" the games mechanics. The dungeons are very long and the insane enemy encounter rates make it a massive chore to get through as I found myself destroying my left click just to skip any possible animation so I can press the same 3 spells in the exact same order every single encounter to win.One thing I didn't mention is the stories on the cards which you can "flip" after certain conditions. These are pretty much the same as weapon descriptions in Automata but once you read one you pretty much read them all. It all boils down to normal NPC is very normal, flip card, but they do bad stuff in secret/and/or they are sad, hehe bet you never expected this for the 17th time.Still I did enjoy some of the writing and I chuckled a single time when swole Melanie took the stage. _childDocuments_.review: The presentation of this game is phenomenal. The music and art is excellent, and I loved the use of cards to serve as the interface for the game. Presentation is by far this game's strongest suit. Beyond this, the game play and mechanics are unfortunately quite shallow. While the combat system in the game has some great ideas, it gets stale after so many fights. The game is far to simplistic in its exploration as well. I found that searching dungeons and exploring the map was uninteresting and tedious. Character progression, similarly, didn't have much to offer. Equipment loadouts didn't have much choice, just items with increasingly larger numbers the further you get. Managing what characters to use and their skills is the aspect of the game which requires the most thought, but most of the game is easy enough that there isn't much challenge involved.Overall, the game is maybe a good intro to JRPGs due to its simplicity, excellent presentation, and streamlined design. But I found it to be somewhat tedious and boring after awhile. I think many of the concepts in the game just needed fleshed out a bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: I *really* wanted to like it.Yoko Taro's deconstructive storytelling, the gorgeous art, the incredible soundtrack, and the world-made-of-cards gimmick and combine into a really neat sensory presentation, but beyond that... I've played for three hours, and most of that playtime has been the blandest random battles I could imagine, over and over again, with the faintest scraps of narrative in between.I like jrpgs. I like card games. I like tabletop rpgs.And this does all of those things aesthetically, but I couldn't find any substance beneath.I like Griftlands, Hand Of Fate, and other stuff in this genre. And I do plan to try the other two Voice Of The Cards games since I've heard they're mechanically different.But if you're looking for a crunchy card game or an immersive rpg, this is probably not either of those things. Pick it up if you want something simple and vibesy and very, very repetitive.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the worst game I've played in a long while, far worse than any number of free games on steam or elsewhere.  I mistakenly bought it out of respect for Square Enix.  From the presentation of it here, this game could very easily fool you into thinking it plays like some kind of card game, which it doesn't.  Steer well clear of this ripoff, especially if you're looking for a card game!Story: 2/10 Our crude vagabond hero has a heart of gold, while the sanctimonious powers-that-be are corrupt.  Now save the world!  Nothing here except a parade of boring tropes you've been subjected to a million times already.Characters: 3/10 They're kind of nice visually, but there's almost no dialogue in this entire game.  Instead, most events consist of you listening to a narrator monotonously reading words off a card onscreen painfully slowly.Mechanics: 1/10  ...The game doesn't break, so I figure that's gotta be worth at least 1, but the 'mechanics,' such as they are, are completely braindead and offer the player zero things to think about.  Attack with BIG number!  Restore HPs.  Have a stock of 30 combat items that serve no purpose at all (No, no one is ever going to inflict that status ailment on you, and if they did, it would be a waste of a turn to remove it). Shockingly, there is NOTHING CARD-RELATED in this game's mechanics!!!  Why?  Cards make for amazing game mechanics.  This game actively forgoes that option, and instead its combat is markedly less interesting or strategic than, say, Dragon Quest (1986).Sound: 5/10Some of the music is sorta nice, but most of the sound design is grating and even volume controls are weird and clumsy.  Graphics: 4/10The character drawings are interesting if you enjoy the style, and I do, but the card art gimmick gets completely out of hand when every single movement tile in the game is its own ugly card and moving between them jolts your characters around as opposed to moving smoothly.

_childDocuments_.review: A turn based RPG built around having a card and tabletop roleplaying aesthetic for visuals and narrative, neither of which it takes advantage of. Leaving it a short, overpriced, mostly mediocre RPG.The visuals of the game are based around cards, this includes the menus, the characters and enemies, the map and dungeons you move around on are cards that flip over to reveal terrain as you move, during battles your equipped skills show up as cards with art and their description on them. As a game styled around a tabletop RPG, the story, events, character dialogue, and sometimes just descriptions or hints as you explore are narrated by an out of sight game master.At a glance I would have assumed I would have enjoyed the game quite a bit because of how much I like those two things but it ended up being a fairly dull playthrough that takes advantage of neither of the elements the game is built around. With the fairly ridiculously high price of the game (as well as needless cosmetic DLC), especially with all the indies that have done much more interesting GM and/or card focused RPG games, they could certainly have gone further at making the card aesthetic a lot more visually interesting with less generic tiles you move on, the monsters you fight and your character skills could have had cool looking detailed artwork like you would get out of something like Magic/Lord of the Rings LCG/Netrunner/etc instead of just a generic small variety of monsters just drawn in a rectangle or weapon and element symbol with text of what skills do, the characters could have been drawn onto cards in different ways or on not just generic blank backgrounds to show emotion and be more visually interesting. What could have been a much more interesting world to explore ends up being fairly generic. The style actually lead them to having some other issues. Everything is a bit slower than it should be and the odd card style of the menus make them slow and more of a chore to navigate than they should be, even lacking basic functions like cycling through characters with the shoulder or trigger buttons when you are swapping out equipment (it all functions even worse with a mouse and keyboard). I used no combat items in the game until the final battle but for some odd reason instead of limiting the max number of certain kinds of items you can hold they give you an inventory limit of 30 total items. This lead to a lot moments in the last 1/3 of the game where I would find a chest and be given a useless item or finish a battle and be rewarded with a useless item that would then slowly bring up a text about having too many items before slowly taking me to a screen where I can slowly choose one item to throw away before being allowed to move on.The GM narration focus is also a thing that really doesn't go anywhere. He's just kind of there to only need to pay one voice actor and for some reason to give away any hints when a dungeon does anything different (dungeon has walls that turn into doors when you move onto them, "Why don't you try moving there"). The entire Game Master thing is never really used to add anything to the world and ends up just taking away from it, even more so because the added assumption of having a GM would be that the characters would have their own players but it's just the GM narrating what few inner thoughts or actions they take.What you end up being left with is a short, overpriced, and mostly mediocre RPG. What little story there is can have a few moments of humor but doesn't offer much for world or character building. Every town will have the same shops and a couple people to talk to, you can explore three larger landmasses near towns to find the dungeons or other towns you need to go to or to run into often repeating random events. There is never really anything interesting to the design of dungeons, the biggest thing they do is put some spikes in some tiles right before you reach the end boss that you just don't want to step on to avoid taking any damage (these spikes are clearly visible, though one of the character's best weapons does require you to just walk through a couple spikes to reveal a chest a few spaces in). There are no route deviations or big side quests as it is a primarily linear game, you can get four choices for your ending that will amount to a few lines before the credits roll.Most of your time playing will be taking a few steps, getting into a random battle, and completely destroying those enemies (over and over and over again because the low enemy variety doesn't help things). If you remember to upgrade your equipment at new shops, 80% of battles will be over before enemies can even get an attack off. With an ice attack spell that can freeze enemies permanently and causes you to break them out of the ice but do double damage when you hit them, even the first couple bosses didn't get to attack me. You start off with a party of three characters and get two more characters to join you over time, one coming fairly late but you have a limitation I've never been a fan of of only being able to use three characters at once but then two of the characters seem more focused on buffing or having some defensive skills and this is a game where healing and buffing has no use 99% of the time. At least this is one of the games that doesn't make the mistake of older titles and the characters in reserve still gain full XP from battles. As characters level up and change their equipment they can add to their health, attack (which influences all skills be they melee, ranged, or magic), defense, and speed and gain access to a few passive skills they always have (mostly element or status effect resistance), and active skills of which they can equip four of. In battle your skills are powered by crystals, you start a battle with one and gain another at the start of every character's turn. A basic attack costs nothing but using more powerful or status effecting skills can cost between 1-4, so you will want use your heavier hitting skills or skills that enemies are weak to while focusing on basic attacks or turn passive to help prepare stronger attacks.While the battle system works and can be simple and enjoyable at times, the AI is terrible. In addition to all those times where enemies just couldn't do anything there will be so many times where when they do get to act they will try to do something like buff itself as it is near death and all of your characters move next. You will frequently see an enemy use a turn to slightly debuff one characters defense or elemental defense, often to a degree less than what their hit damage would have done only to then have their other allies attack other non debuffed characters. One positive here is that even with the battles taking place with the card visual style the attack animations do have varied effects for every type of skill and additional critical hit they can do while moving the cards around, making it a bit more visually interesting than the what you would get with the old first person kind of Dragon Quest/Wizardry battles that the animations would resemble otherwise.It's a simple and fairly quick play (taking me about 9 hours) with a few funny moments but with all the good ideas aesthetically and mechanically or ideas that can be used in a much more interesting way it doesn't take advantage of anything and when it is selling for $30-$40+ there are a lot of other games with some similar themes that are worth more, cost less, and support an indie studio.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: Had this as recommend but after finishing it I came back and changed it. I don't really want to recommend this game or say I don't recommend this game -- it's a shame Steam doesn't allow other options.Game is too easy and lacks depth. I just have to assume that somewhere along the line it was rushed out; it's missing a few rounds of balancing which leads to the game being too slow and fall flat. With all love intended I hope that whomever's decision it was to push out this project as it currently is and not let it get a few more rounds of changes loses their job and never works in the video game industry again because this could have been a masterpiece.Like... it's really easy. If you keep your equipment up to date; the combats (and boss combats) are kind of a joke. There are multiple enemies who I don't even know what moves they have because despite hitting them every 4 squares they have never taken a turn. To put it another way, game was so easy I stopped saving. In my playthrough a character was knocked out twice. I had to revive only TWO times the entire game. Once from being one shot from a freeze/double attack combo and once during the final boss -- imagine playing a JRPG where there was only two times in your playthrough a party member dropped to 0 hitpoints. The game's difficulty is designed for 15 year olds whom have never played a JRPG before and don't update their gear. It's as if they expect you to not equip heal abilities and keep your party topped up as you play.EDIT: The issue isn't really that it's easy but that the combat isn't varied. A script could solve ALL combats "if not full HP, use heal skill. If full HP and < 2 gems, use basic attack. If >2 gems and no status effect, use status effect ability. If > 2 gems and status effect, use heavy attack." There isn't a reason to vary from this pattern at any point. Heal up the party, use a status effect focusing an enemy. When the majority of the game is combat you need the combat to have more variety. For example; the game has elemental weaknesses (a basic rather boring mechanic) but you can ignore these - at least in something like Octopath or Persona you have to at least pay attention to the enemies weaknesses.  Everything is voiced but it's one VA.Looks great. Story is cliche yet the writing is good, I chuckled a few times.I returned the game... and then bought it back a few days later because despite its shortcomings the concept is great and it's a pretty chill playthrough. Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't realize I played this for 11.3 hours straight...So from the top, the visuals are incredible illustration wise. That's what drew me to the game and what got me to purchase it. However, I don't really have anything else to praise about the game. The game play is okay. The story is okay. Nothing really stands out to me except the aesthetic.Most of the characters don't feel memorable particularly, except for one; the son of the nutritionist who has insane muscles. If you play, you'll find out why.I do like that combat in this game is on the simpler side. There's flexibility to each of the characters' roles, and they all get experience whether they were in combat or not. The downside is if you overlevel before you get a character, they'll be behind.I'm not sure how else to express it, but this game feels like a test dummy for a larger, more ambitious project, and the company is just testing the current reception.Combat animations are lackluster--about the same effort as current Pokémon animations, and nothing seems like it was made to leave lasting impressions.I think this game is suited for playing if you like looking at pretty art and enjoy simple things. Elsewise, there's a high chance it could feel like a waste of money.

_childDocuments_.review: Yoko Taro + Keiichi Okabe = . Great story and amazing soundtrack with some excellent NieR-esque tracks.Actual gameplay isn't great. It's way to easy most of the time and random encounters just become an annoyance when you can one shot everything. Bosses are actually fun because they are more challenging but then the final boss is ridiculously hard compared to the rest of the game to the point where I'm just annoyed and not having fun. It probably wouldn't even be that bad if the rest of the game was well balanced but you just have this huge leap in difficulty out of nowhere. As much as I love Yoko Taro games, I really hate how he has to make the endings as inaccessible as possible(see Ending E for Replicant and DoD3). It feels like he actually hates his fans sometimes with some of his game design choices and he'd probably have way more fans if not for this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.There's a card game you can play in towns that's a lot of fun but it's just a side-thing with no real effect on the rest of the game. If they could have incorporated a simpler/faster and less random version of that game into the combat system it would have been way more interesting imo.As you'd expect, the story is great but it takes a while to get there. When it finally does it really delivers; definitely nothing on the level of NieR or Drakengard but it's got a similar feel and it  even take place in that connected multiverse(I've seen people mention this but I haven't noticed any of the connections myself yet). I found it somewhat similar to Drakengard 3 in terms of the absurd and wacky(but much less depraved) characters you meet. I'd definitely recommend this to Yoko Taro fans but probably not to anyone else just because the gameplay itself is so bad. From being so easy that its boring, to being so difficult that you stop having fun, it just sucks all-around. Kind of a shame but I'm hoping it's improved in the next two games.So yeah, I wouldn't recommend this to the average gamer but I'm giving it a thumbs up anyway because Yoko Taro is amazing(and the worst), and there's enough interesting elements of the game that I'm enjoying it despite the terrible gameplay. The soundtrack, characters and story(eventually) are the games strongest points and if you can get past the ass gameplay then you'll definitely enjoy this.
