_childDocuments_.review: A solid "meh" out of 10 Lack depths in the gameplay, and length in the content to make it a 30e game.I paid the full price and it took me 12h to finish the game. Even if the story was nice and the drawings splendid, the overall feeling of the game is grindy and a money-grabber. The general rule for me is that if the game can't offer at least as much hours to play as euros I pay, then it's not worth it. If it was for less than 12e than I would recommend it. The good: the story is great, the characters are funny and the design is gorgeous!With just cards and the storyteller voice the world is nicely fleshed out and it feels great discovering it.The bad: RPG and tactic elements are almost non-existent. Making the game repetitive and grindy.The RPG part follow this formula: get into town, buy equipment, go kill monsters, get enough gold, and... go to the next town, buy the next best equipment, etc.Tactic is about finding the best 2 cards of each party member and spamming them. For example, the mage has 6 spells overall, about one per elements. I played the same 2 over the full game, because the others suck.A free mobile app has more layers than this game.The weird: - Some story arcs are quite "off" when comparing it to the rest of the game. Overall the game has a lively and not-to-serious approach to the story. Which I found refreshing. But then, at random, you get yourself into children cannibalism (the words of one of the NPC were something like "we didn't realize he was eating our children", talking about their mayor (???))... - You can't speed the animations. For a game where you'll play the same cards over and over, being able to speed animations would be nice. Even if they are nice to see.- The menu feels heavy and slow to use. A lot of click is needed just to change one equipment. And the first time I played, I Alt+F4 to quit the game because I was in a hurry and I couldn't intuitively find the button to exit. Turns out that from the in-game menu, you need 4 different steps to quit the game. 4 steps are 3 steps too much. I ve never seen this kind of UI in a game before.So overall, I feel that a part of the devs were really into providing a great game, and another were taking themselves very seriously about making money with the least amount of commitment towards the gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: A good warrior wastes no time on this game-Story is absolutely worthless, generic, forgettable trash. Yoko Taro's worst directorial work I've played, Drakengard 3 included.-Keiichi Okabe's music is toothless, largely what feels like milquetoast rehashings of his previous soundtracks. Admittedly the last dungeon track is pretty alright-Gameplay is trivially easy, many of the bosses can thoughtlessly be beaten by spamming the same attacks disregarding buffs, ailmlents, and heals so long as you try to explore the world-A world that is bereft of character, life, and interest that has so shockingly little to offer that when the twist came that the "Isle of Bliss" was the "Isle of Blight", I was mostly confused as I still hadn't heard anyone mention the said island at all.-Combat is a meandering bore that takes minutes at a time to expel even the weakest sets of foes, of which there is an abominable number. Encounters every 5-10 steps.-This happens despite the visuals of the game having nothing to offer in combat, cards just flop at each other with the pace of molasses as you wish you were doing anything else. It probably didn't help that I played Inscryption, a very snappy and tactile card game 2 weeks ago.-2 of the 4 final bosses I dispatched in 2 party-turns. Characters died twice, once in a random encounter where I didn't want to bother healing, another time when I forgot about the curse ailment and killed myself. I never experienced a party wipeAnd on top of all of this they have the audacity to take Muscle Melanie away from me.Looking forward to washing this awful taste out of my mouth with SMT5 in a week

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo a while ago and thought that this was an interesting game, especially by the time I saw the fisherman's appearance and had a good laugh. However, by the time the game actually was released I found myself incredibly frustrated with the controls and ui in general. Here's my experience's listed and if the rant doesn't interest, feel free to skip to the end.- For one thing, you aren't allowed to bring up the pause menu during combat or dialogue. Like wtf? But okay, try to move on. - Attempt to select a skill to use and you need to select a target and you'll quickly find that the skill is covering up the enemy's card making it difficult to see their health stats and other stuff. Alright, fine, go back and look at the stats before selecting a skill. - The tutorial will teach you that if you hold a key while hovering the mouse over an option, you can get a small glimpse of the text that option has. Granted I only played for like 30 minutes before getting fed up and refunding this game, but there was at least 5+ choices during that time, none of which remotely used this mechanic. You'd think if it was only applicable to certain things they would let you know but no. Whatever, just ignore that whole part then I guess.- There's no easy way to select a card or option other than clicking over and over. It gets bad sitting through a long playthrough when you need to click to progress the dialogue, double click to confirm your choices, click on every skill and actually double click to confirm the target you want to use said skill on. Of course the first thing I do is try to rush over to the options to address this because you'd think they include an option to change the controls right? Well yes, your options is space bar and enter key. That's it. One is confirm the other is cancel. The enter key? Are you friggin kidding me, Im forced to use the opposite side of my keyboard? (Like for real, just let me use "e" to confirm like literally every other game that exists.) - Lastly I try to explore the third option listed there, some azerty layout to see if it includes some hidden option to manually set control actions. Immediately the menu closes and now whenever I use the menu it closes the instant I try to go to any page at all. Want to change a setting? Nope. Closed. Want to look at your character's stats/skills/equip or items? Nope. Closed. At this point i'm just done, I may be desperate to kill time but even i'm not willing to put up with this much nonsense.On the bright side, the game does offer a simple rpg, even if it doesn't explain why your characters will sometimes get extra hits you didn't expect. Seemed like it would've been an easy enough rpg given my experience in the demo at least, so I guess if you don't mind the game just expecting you to know why you get extra hits due to a crit probably or other weird stuff then it's still playable in that sense. The story is probably generic but I guess I won't be finding out. The card art is quite lovely as well, no complaints there.Short story long, my experience was not an enjoyable one. Perhaps I will be willing to give this game another shot if square enix addresses these issues and changes all the characters and monsters card art to the  fisherman in the demo.

_childDocuments_.review: As other reviews have stated, this is not a card game; it is a JRPG with card game aesthetics. In other words, it's awful. This was like a performance piece in how to make a game with only one positive quality, the artwork, to see if that would make a game successful.JRPGs tend to be very story-centric for a reason. Their combat and game mechanics are typically a means to an end to deliver story and dialogue. This mirrors card games, which tend to be very mechanic-centric. So they took the two worst parts of two different genres to support a game with terrible writing and intentionally annoying humor.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this because I'm a huge fan of Nier and Yoko Taro. the art is great and they use the same music composer and vocalist from the Nier games. The influence of Yoko taro's fun weirdness on the story and world is noticeable, mainly in the flip-side stories for the character cards, so it's full of charm. That being said, though, this game is really boring. While the entire game world being presented as cards is unique, it also limits what you can do to make the visuals interesting. The combat has the potential to be fun and complicated, but the fights are so easy they just become tedious. It's so easy to get strong that there's no challenge, yet every fight takes a full minute to win. I cannot say the music is bad, it actually fits the idea of this being a game played in a tavern, but the vibe is TOO chill. When combined with the narrator's monotone voice, I was practically dosing off. Part of me wishes the narrator put more effort into doing voices for the different characters. Speaking of characters, the story isn't particularly interesting, at least at the point where I stopped. I didn't even finish it. It has fun moments and dark comedic moments and genuine emotional moments, but man, it just doesn't come together. I understand that not every game made by Yoko Taro or Square-enix is going to be an award winning success, maybe the sequels to this one do a good job improving on what they set up here.

_childDocuments_.review: For experienced jrpg players, this game edges toward being an idle game in its simplicity (though I'm still at the start of the game. I may update my review after a while). I've muted the narrator's voice, as I found it too slow for my reading pace, and I enjoy voice acting to myself anyway. Lovely illustrations, though I felt they could do with much more variety. It seems like the team was trying to squeeze into every and any budget restraint possible by removing animations, mob and card variations, and multiple voice actors from the mix, which almost makes the title feel like a misnomer. I expected...I don't know, multiple voices of cards? While the soundtrack is gorgeous, I was disappointed to find that right away, two dungeon areas with different landscapes (cave and woods) had the same songs. The same npc character cards appear everywhere with no look variation. The things they say feel similar to an amateurish RPGMaker game. HOWEVER, I am enjoying the relaxed atmosphere, with simple clicking and WASD movement around a gameboard, some fantasy D&D reading and light humor (sometimes juvenile). I hope to have an update after progressing that shows a lot of expansion in the card playing aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line, up front, I would recommend the game.I do however, think it is important to understand that this is more a story than a game.  The game initially feels like it is going to be deeper than it is.  It is quite linear, the choices you make don't have a significant change on the outcome.  The game is not very hard (there is a fair amount of hand holding), I think the only fight that I felt really frustrated in was the final boss.  The above being said, I still don't think the game is bad, if you are coming in thinking this will be a deck building card game like M:TG, Hearthstone, Ascension, or even Gwent, you will be disappointed with those expectations.  This is a story told using cards as an artistic medium, and not an actual mechanic of play.I took my time with my first play through, which took closer to 20 hours, not 6.5 that steam indicates, I will probably come back at some point to 100% it.

_childDocuments_.review: A game I fully respect, not in spite of its lack of ambition, but because of it. There is nothing groundbreaking about its simplistic story and repetitive gameplay mechanics, but with all the attention to detail in presenting this budget turn-based RPG with a wonderful soundtrack, sardonic voice acting and clever card motifs, it evolves into something much more interesting and charming. We need more games like Voice of Cards to keep the industry alive, as they can give much more variety to a market that is oversaturated with mediocre, overly expensive blockbusters.

_childDocuments_.review: The Chinese-Japanese puppet fantasy-drama Thunderbolt Fantasy has been described as a dramatization of a D&D session as DM'ed by Gen "The Urobucher" Urobuchi, writer and creator of beloved stories from Madoka Magica to Fate/Zero to Psycho-Pass to Black Lagoon. The Voice of Cards series answers the question: what if you could have a similar experience but with beloved storyteller Yoko Taro at the helm? Not quite your bog-standard sword-and-board heroes and hardly the most qualified group attempting the feat, the main characters of The Isle Dragon Roars ventures across the realm to slay a dragon in the name of riches. However, nothing about this mission, from the dragon to the kingdom to your avatar character themselves, is exactly what it seems.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence about this game, but have to give it a thumbs down in the end. Let's start of with the positives: The game has a very charming aesthetic, the soundtrack is great (if not quite small) and it's a very chill experience.While the game is almost fully voice-acted, it's only voiced by the narrator and his monotone voice. In a way it gives this audio book feel, but at the same time it is a lot less engaging and emotional this way. There are audio books like graphic audio that have individual voice acting for each character + the narrator, so a 30€ game lacking it feels cheap.The game is also way too easy besides the final boss and a one or two side-challenges. The combat also lacks depth and choice where some skills and combos are just way better than others, but perhaps that was only my experience.The game is also quite short, doesn't offer much in terms of side-content, is very linear and your choices don't matter except for the very last choice that affects the ending. The story itself was...fine. It wasn't anything special, but had it's moments all the same.Presentation-wise while the aesthetic is charming the game really doesn't do much with it's format to impress and generally cut scenes are very dry visually. There are no animations, splash arts/CGs and backgrounds are reused and limited. This game screams budget.In conclusion:+ Charming aesthetic+ Good music+ Chill and laid back game.~ Combat is hit or miss, personally it lacked choice as some skills were just plainly better to use~ Story was mostly mediocre- Too short and content bare for 30€, if interested get it during a sale- Lacks character voice acting, diminishes the emotional moments and overall engagement- Lackluster presentation, seems very budget constrainedI don't necessarily regret playing it, as I got it on a sale, but I got the trilogy bundle and kind of regret getting all three now. I feel like playing one was enough, but I might revisit the other two VOC-games someday when I want something chill to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, I love Yoko Taro's work and many Taro-isms are in this game as you'd expect. It has multiple endings that are gut-punches, really random humor at times, banger character designs, and beautiful music. But even Yoko Taro's usual charm can't hold up this game. The game is based off of tabletop games, and the entire world space is quite literally made of cards, true to the game's name. There's no voice acting in this game besides a narrator, true to the tabletop vibe. Unfortunately the game is painfully easy as well. I assumed since it was a JRPG, I'd grind a bit before the first dungeon, reaching Level 11 when the recommended Level was 3. And although the levels normalized, I went through the game deathless until the final boss, which I beat on my second try. Really disappointing game, which hurts me to say as a fan of Yoko Taro. And Emi Evans too, she's great in the music of this as well. But unfortunately, it's just a middling RPG that's held up by some lovable charm.Score: 73

_childDocuments_.review: This game is enjoyable, but not risky at all. Yoko Taro does crazy stuff with storytelling in some of his games that make them amazing, but hard to recommend or review. This game is the opposite, try the demo and you will easily know if this game is for you. The card aesthetic is nice, but not a lot is done with the world all being cards. The combat is  simple. The characters are charming, while the story is pretty alright.The game is good for what it is. A digestible little JRPG with its own aesthetic defined by everything being cards and a game master voicing everything. The game is enjoyable as it is. As a big fan of Yoko Taro I was hoping for something a lot more risky, but that's not what this is. This is just a humble little JRPG. Sadly, that means its competing with a bunch of other RPGs/JRPGs and this one doesn't stick out in any way besides its art and music. So while this game is good, being just "good" isn't really enough these days when there are so many good choices. This game scrapes into a positive for me, the music really hauling it over the line. However, don't go into this game expecting something that it isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: This was not a difficult game, but that also wasn't the point. This was a whimsical, short story where you get to be a hero in a foreign land. The card mechanics are relatively basic, but it's not offensive given the length of the game. Overall, it reminded me of reading a children's book and the narrator does a decent enough job of keeping things rolling. Provided I purchased this on a pretty heavy discount, I only have good things to say for the experience as a whole. I would definitely urge others not to purchase the DLC unless they're dead set on a few very specific party card designs. They only change three out of the five character party which I found sort of silly. There's also a few additional changes such as the dice, game board and background music, but I found that I enjoyed the default options for all of those choices more. The last bit of advice I'd add to those like myself who have a desire to overpower your party... in this game, don't. The story will pump you full of experience points at specific moments rendering any additional grinding time completely unnecessary. As I mentioned in the first line, this is not a difficult game. Just go along for the ride.

_childDocuments_.review: A highly creative blend of the card game and rpg genres The Isle Dragon Roars is a game that relies on keeping things peaceful and simple.  Combat is normally kept fairly short and is a very easy concept to grasp only lasting about 2 full rounds on average depending on the playstyle so it can feel a little monotonous as you reach the end of the story.  And there is a good deal of combat as is normally the case with this style of rpg games so you do want to make sure you have a couple hours if you're going to open up this game if you actually want to progress, but combat isn't the main focus of this game and it's not where this game shines.  The Isle Dragon Roars tells a tale of sacrifice and growth through loss.  It is a beautifully narrated story that kept me engaged anytime I had the time to open it back up.

_childDocuments_.review: Very classic Turn-based RPG, but with the unique spin of presenting the entire game through cards. Pretty fun overall, but has a few flaws. Will see if the format holds up over the next two games.- : Like I said in the beginning, it's a very classic turn-based RPG. It's got all the standard things - stronger and stronger gear that upgrades your stats, elemental weaknesses and resistances, status effects, and energy-requiring skills. - : While the card aesthetic of the game effectively rules out rating the game on a traditional 'graphics' sense (although the card parts of the game are very clean), all the artwork presented is just incredible. Every named character has an incredibly unique design and looks great, and there's even a decent amount of detail put into the standard townspeople and shopkeepers.- : On the surface, you're just dropped into the beginning of this classic 'Hero slays the Dragon' plot, but as the story continues, more truths about the world you've been put into are revealed, and there's a decent amount of plot twists, however unimpactful they may be to the individual's experience.- : Most of the game is quite easy, save for a few minibosses and the final and post-game boss.- : The $30 price tag is a little steep for the amount of time you get out of the game, I'd reccommend either waiting for a sale or buying the Trilogy (which effectively cuts the price of each game in half), or both if you want.- : There's a side activity in every town called the Game Parlor, and beyond the first game mode (Simple), all the other ones are entirely RNG-dependant, and the NPCs don't even try to hide that they're hardcoded to target you except for if another NPC is winning by a large margin. And wouldn't you guess, there's an achievement for winning a game in each of these modes.- : There is in fact a NG+ mode unlocked when you beat the story, but there's really no reason to play it besides unlocking the exclusive NG+ ring for starting it, as besides seeing the outcomes of a few different stories, which usually have no larger impact, nothing is really changed.

_childDocuments_.review: General Summary: 8.5/10 (-1 for the UI design alone)The game's philosophy carries it from beginning to end. On the surface it is a gentle and childlike wonder of adventure and riches and fame. Yet, below the surface it turns into a horrid world of misery and decay with lies and deception at every corner and the suffering of many forgotten in the bliss of the golden age. Rather fittingly the game will only get hard when the curtain is pulled back and the "Isle of Bliss" shows its true face. Everything up to Chapter 5 will carry the mask of innocence until tested, but the last two chapters make no effort to hide the truth of the world. This game is not for small children without parental guidance as it tries to compete with Drakengard in dystopian facades. A facade that begins to distort the lively and upbeat melody of the intro over time.The facade is a young adventurer from poor background out for the big reward of slaying a tyrannical dragon that came to terrorize the Isle of Bliss and the kingdom which is supported by the Ivory Order keeping it safe. A boy and their little buddy monster now set out to save the kingdom to gain fame and riches. Along the travel they will meet three unlikely allies and come face to face with the dirty secret keeping everything running. Always accompanied by the great soundtrack and ambience of the game, with beautiful battle animations, this story is well-told and mantled by a good English and a good Japanese narrator, the choice being yours. They both carry entirely different atmosphere. Neither of them fulfills it to the levels of a Theodore in Thea or the master of narrative Valenos of Hand of Fate, but below these tremendous talents, they do their job to the fullest expectation.Further pushed by the unique and nice exploration of a map made out of playing cards, the game shows its full artistic sellingpoint from A to Z. It is debateable if the offset grid on the world map helps navigation or not, but due to the jump feature it works either way.Despite all these great things, Voice of Cards, the Isle of Dragon Roars will test the patience of the modern audiences of fast-pace gameplay and limited time in their lives. It suffers heavily from consoleritis and even beats them by selling things one at a time or asking for "one more" per click and navigation. It also hides important things like the exit button in a sub-submenue of the submenue (open menue, switch to options with the top button, go to other, go to exit game). Thus some people to this day believe the game has to be exited by hard-crashing it or with the Steam stop button. Let's hope the UI designer of this game has gone on to learn their craft, because this ain't it chief.

The text can be VERY slow, even on the fast setting, and it's impossible to skip entire conversations - even ones you are seeing for a second time playing in Game+, which leads to just spamming the "next" button ad infinitum (yes, you are forced to unlock every. single. part. of. the. story. again.  FFS. - and, of course, you can't get certain achievements until the end of the second playthrough, so, you're going to waste an unbelievable amount of time if you're a completionist).Overall, the art, music, gameplay, and story are all at least decent, if not good, but those menus, and the text speed, along with not being able to easily skip some of the more tedious portions can make the game drag on unnecessarily.

_childDocuments_.review: IT's.... DIFFERENT.  IN a reductive sense, its Classic JRPG but WITH A YOKO TARO TWIST.The median, is cards as art, told entirely thru cards.  It's unique.  It has a GM, with their smooth voice, could put you to sleep, but still carries that oomph, The artwork is by the Artist who did work for Mistwalker on Terra Battle, 1 and 2, and Sino-Alice.  Love The artwork.The BGM is fantastic and helps to carry the tale. As an experienced player, one could just churn this out under 10 hours if you turned on the game speed to high speed, but you're not here for that.If you want a return to old-school JRPG told thru a table-top median and wonderful story-telling with a smooth GM, Artwork;  Come to this, it won't disappoint.If you want a progressive JRPG that's gonna turn it's formula, have diverse voice acting, or flashing scenes, avoid this as it may not be your cup of tea.  I'd recommend taking this in brief stints. Don't expect a HEAVY depth to this. Just enjoy it for what it is.Also, The random encounters in this are cranked which perverses the genre with dungeons and bloating the time to completion.  The Random EVENT though, 1000% bangers, absolutely fun to watch the party interactions with it and hope to see more in the next VoC.All in All,  would like more of the Voice of Cards series but at a cheaper price.  Buy at discount if you can, I'll update this once I finish Forsaken maiden

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of review that if Steam allowed for a "maybe? perhaps?" recommendation, it would apply to Voice of cards: The Isle Dragon Roars. If you are a fan of turn-based RPGs, you will come out with mixed feelings as some aspects of what make RPGs great are present, but in a very shallow form. If you are not a fan of RPGs, you will wonder why people like that genre.First and foremost, the game is very short. And I'm talking really short. Took less than 25 hours to 100% all achievements, which for a RPG, this feels like blinking your eyes twice. The difficulty is also cakewalk easy. I only had 2 KOs on the post-game optional boss and barely used any items throughout the game. Of course, I'm not new to RPGs, so at a glance I knew what to guess for monsters elemental weaknesses (like forest creature = weak to fire). Expect maybe 2-3 fights that will make use of the game's mechanics fully. There are no model animations and only a single narrator for the whole game. Speaking of the latter, he does a very good job at it, but there is so much immersion a single narrator can provide, especially one that doesn't change his voice whenever a companion speaks to add a little flair to party dialogues. The world exploration will be hampered by a lot (really A LOT!) of random encounters; I suggest playing the game on 'High speed' and ALWAYS use the teleport mechanic (once you have a tile explored, you can teleport to it at no cost) to minimise random encounters. The game doesn't display any puzzles or convoluted secrets; it is very linear/easy to 100% without a guide.For the positive: the music is really great. With the game length being as it is, they don't get to become repetitive. I really like the card artistic design. I wished you could have a few more cards for your party (say to reflect change in equipment, etc.), but the game is pretty bare-bone. The price for this game is also a positive: sure, my review sounds overall negative, but the game provide some entertainment for a low price. If it's on sale and know that it is a short easy story RPG, you'll get decent fun per $ invested. The combat mechanic in itself was something I really like. Basically you generate resources and get to spend them on either weak spells or hoard a bit and unleash a bigger one, but allowing the enemy to take a full turn. It makes mages not reliant on mana which usually lead them to be dead weight in random encounters while they save their mana for the upcoming boss fight. The game is simply too easy to really make use of that system, since 90% of encounters are dead on round 1, 99% dead on round 2, with the exception of boss fights.I'd give Voice of cards: The isle dragon roars a 6/10.TL;DR: Cheap game, good base concept, but very short, shallow and bare bone.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn’t go into this game expecting it to be extremely advanced, because frankly, at this price point, you’re paying to experience something a bit more basic and fun but was created with decent budget. And that’s exactly what I got. This isn’t an overly complex game that has a story that keeps you on the edge of your seat. It’s more like a comfy book you sit down and read casually. The story is your bread-and-butter hero “saves” the world while encountering casual plot-twists that make you learn more about your journey and role. The music is stunning, the character cast is lovable and diverse, and the art is easy on the eyes. What more could you want for a basic RPG?I feel like people will state that this game being basic is an issue, but I feel that it’s actually its strength instead. You don’t need an overly complex game to craft an enjoyable experience for every gamer. Most modern games try to distinguish itself so hard that sometimes it falls through instead. This game was executed as it was intended to.1.	Fun, basic but still engaging story. The narrator you get indirectly points out that it’s going to be a short story from the beginning. It’s going to be stereotypical, but that doesn’t detract from the enjoyment you can get from it. Unless you just prefer something that’s super deep of course.2.	Combat is simple, but fun. The different party members you can use allow you to strategize differently and use your resources differently as well. The battle system utilizes a “mana” system in which certain skills cost you points to execute them. It relies on you to decide how you want to manage your mana throughout the fight. Will you just use up all your mana on one character? Will you spread it out to allow all of your frontline characters fight? Or could you focus on mana economy? It’s entirely up to you. You don’t need to overthink anything as the game does not intend to punish you. The game literally lets you play however you want.3.	The art is charming and fun. The premise of the game is based on cards so you’re usually limited to portraits, but the portraits, especially for the characters, have personality and reflect who they are. The monster art is also nice in its own right. Cute monsters have cute portraits, and strong monsters look their part.4.	The music is amazing. It would not be an overstatement to say that this game boasts a good soundtrack even though this isn’t a mainstream game. As much as I would love to say I love this game, I do think there are a few things to be addressed as they could have been improved or implemented differently.1.	The difficulty scaling doesn’t seem to exist for nearly 2/3 of the game. A lot of the core gameplay seems repetitive and way too easy for the most part, and normally this would be a major issue, but you also have to remember that it’s standard for RPG’s that if you grow stronger, you’ll obviously curbstomp most of the enemy encounters.2.	The characters in your parties are not customizable in terms of their skill sets. Meaning, if I want to turn my support character into the meanest damage machine, it would be nice to have some sort of outlet to do so, but no, there isn’t an option. All of them were crafted with a very specific role in battle, and that’s fine! It’s not wrong at all, because then you know exactly how to use them, but it would have been nice to have access to more skills whether through more events or possibly a skill tutor in the cities. This would not only make exploration more exciting, but also give the towns you visit more purpose which leads me into my next point.3.	The towns feel extremely lackluster. I understand that you’re not meant to be staying for long in the town when you’re on a quest to hunt a bounty, but they ultimately end up being stale because you only ever visit them to talk to a few NPC’s for story progression and the occasional rest/healing. They serve as nothing more than convenient rest stops even though the town NPC’s are fun to talk to.Here’s where I think they just had horrible administrative calls on the design of this game.1.	Resources are either too easy to abuse or have almost no purpose in the game. It doesn’t really help that you barely have anything else to use your resources like gold on other than just buying new gear per town/chapter. I forgot I even had gold at points in the game until I started fighting enemies whose stats jumped up which meant I either needed to gain a few levels or grab new gear. 2.	The maps feel lackluster in design. They could have easily added more puzzles no matter how simple they may be just to add a bit of spice and exploration. Especially for dungeon maps. Overworld exploration is cool because you get to explore all the tiles to see what events pop up, but in dungeons it just feels like you have to go from point A to point B and that’s it. There could have been more puzzles, or more discover-ables but no.3.	Game feels way too short and rushed at times. I think they could have extended it to a total of 10 chapters even if the last few chapters aren’t part of the main story. I feel like they added so much color to your characters that it would have been fun if you could have side quests for your characters’ back story. Despite the flaws this game has, I don’t regret a single minute spent on this. It was one of the few games where I actually felt like I wanted to 100% it. It was fun, the character cast was charming, the battle system can be both simple and complex depending on how you approach each battle, the music was constantly keeping me engaged, and the story made me have a good time with some of its plot twists. Highly recommend this game if you like RPG’s.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually beat this game first on the Nintendo Switch before playing it on Steam (will post the link to my full review down at the end). This game is extremely charming and not at all what you would expect. Though the game is made up of cards, this is not like any other card game as it actually just plays like old-school RPGs. The story for The Isle Dragon Roars starts out slow and seems more like some weird slap-stick-comedy meets dark humor, but the more you get into it, the better that it gets. I will admit that the first VOC game had places in the narrative where there are some gaps...but even then, the tale that this game weaves is exciting and emotional. The game has a weird difficulty spike, especially once you reach the final areas and so it's very easy to get "too comfortable" only to then get bulldozed by the final boss. The mechanics are pretty simple and the grinding is not horrible. I think this would be a good RPG for a first-timer. If anyone knows how Yoko Taro games go, things might seem really nice on the surface, but there are horrible things laying underneath which is why collecting the various cards is so exciting. I like that there are some side-quests and love the fact that there are multiple endings. The added "bonus" dungeon gives the game some replay-ability but not a lot. It's a shorter experience being only 15-20 hours if you're not going for all the achievements. I do like both the Nintendo Switch version and the Steam version...but I will say that I seemed to run into more bugs in the Steam version (though this only happened a couple of times thus far in my playthrough). There is one mini-game for those that want to take a break from the story. It's not bad but i hear that in the harder modes, RNGesus is not on your side.So yes. Great game, absolutely recommend. _childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards was a short but sweet experience that takes inspiration from NES-era RPGs as well as tabletop role playing. The game very much commits to the tabletop aesthetic, with nearly everything in the game being represented by cards, even the settings menu! It then mixes in a few other tabletop conventions, a few tokens, and occasional *literal* dice rolls during combat. The experience is tied together by an ever-present narrator, a la Bastion, who does all the voice acting for every character, and describes what happens. The cards themselves have stunning artwork and memorable character designs. Rather than have the actual artwork be animated, the game animates the cards. For example, two cards might start bumping into each other to illustrate a tussle between two characters, or one card might turn on its side during a story moment when a character faints. These simple animations imbue an unexpected amount of life into these characters. The fantastic narrator also works to help paint a mental picture of the game's world. It is on the short side, but this is probably for the best as it helps prevent the presentation from wearing out its welcome, and turns it into what is, for an RPG, a bite-sized morsel to be savored.

Honestly I found that refreshing about it, and I could go back and get the other endings and collect everything to get a few more hours from it. I personally think full price is a bit high and I would wait for a sale, but definitely pick it up if you're looking for a chill, melancholy mini-RPG to experience during some downtime <3
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: This game art is really gorgeous and the musing is amazing. This is more of a standard jrpg than a card game, the card are used more for the style and effect but it's really well made. Also the naration of the game is done in a way that remind when you're playing D&D and the dungeon master speech of what you see and what is happenning and I think they suceed in that too. My only negative point about the game is that is not long enough, I've really took my time to complete the game and it took only 14 hours, you can probably finish it 2-3 hours faster so is really not long enough I found, but aside of that the game is wonderful and you really feel you are part of the game since the music is so nice and the naration is very good. I think it worth it if you can get it at discount, since the game is so well made, but at full price I would have like to get a little more time to complete the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the thought of an JRPG taking place as a card game and like stories that take different turns than expected this game is for you! I just have to tell you, that this game is not as deep gameplay-wise as other card games. I don't feel the big impact of the weaknesses taking place and when you get into the new game+ and just want to hunt for the final achievements (which I don't encourage to get them all), missing the option to skip story parts fast enough, was exhausting.The characters are once again well written as one is used to the works Yoko Taro. Story is great with some twists that were unexpected. In conclusion I would say that I recommend this very short game for people that Enjoy the idea and like pen and paper like games as these, but don't expect it to be full of action or a deep strategy inside it's gameplay with the cards.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: If you're expecting something as crazy as nier or drakengard, you'll be disappointed, expect a indie jrpg with some unique combat mechanics and a good story, and you should be happy, the game's two biggest weaknesses are it's slow combat and it's terrible balancing, since this RPG is half the length of a normal one even if you 100% it you'd think they'd balance it around you going off the beaten path, but no, in my experience most of my characters were max level before I reached the final boss the first time, and to experience all ending you have to kill a multi-phase boss for every ending, which isn't helped by the slow combat. If you enjoyed the demo you should enjoy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: A game that uses cards to express everything about the world. I mean it. Characters are cards, the map is cards, the equipment are cards, and even the menu is cards. It's a neat idea and I think that it could have been a great way to structure a game along the thought process of Final Fantasy + Kingdom Hearts:COM + Dragon's Crown Art style and humor = my fantasy dream game. Sadly that's not quite what we get here. The story is the classic fantasy affair with a few twists and turns here and there but nothing stellar. The combat is actually just a standard turn based system like most RPGs but with the added function of essentially a group shared mp pool that goes up by 1 every time you do an action. Skills require these points to use higher tier attacks. The problem really comes down to the game is too easy. For the majority of the game you can stick to the starting party for mob wipes and only switch out for one boss killer when needed. I only lost one fight and that was a supposed to lose fight. The game is also painfully slow. Thankfully they added the option to drastically speed it up and that's the way you should probably play it. If I have this many problems why is it still going to get a recommendation? Because in this game there is a party style card game that's like UNO, Yatzee, and the Monopoly Chance chest had a freak baby. It is more entertaining then it has any right to be and I can't really explain why. I spent probably 8 hours on that alone. For the game that's here I would say that $10 is what I would recommend for it. I don't think most people will get a lot of mileage out of it but it has a certain charm that I would say is worth a look and I hope a better sequel comes out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been the most relaxing and enjoyable RPG I have played this year. Have there been better? Without a doubt. But none have captured me quite like this one. From the artwork and music, to the characters and story lines, it's an all around lovable game.EDIT:It's sad to see this game have negative reviews. This was never meant to be the next Nier series nor final fantasy. It's supposed to be a charming DnD like adventure with Yoko Taro as your DM. It did everything it was supposed to do and did it well. To those complaining of the simplicity and ease of the game, I beg you to stop reviewing similar games. Sorry it's not Dark Souls I guess /:
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fun, unique experience into a roleplaying-esque world filled with fantastic artwork and amazing music. The story, whilst not groundbreaking, is engaging and gets its hooks into you with ease. The combat mechanics are well thought out and interesting, and overworld exploration is cleverly manipulated to keep you on your toes whilst not being a pain to play!All in all would recommend this game for anyone looking for a fun little exploration into a fantasy world filled with magic.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards is a fantastic game created by the NieR team, YokoTaro, Yosuke Saito and the composer Keiichi Okabe. The story started with a very basic beginning, set out to kill the dragon, but if you know anything about yokotaro and his games you would know there is SO much more under the surface, moments that had me spiraling as i come to realization as events came to be. The Characters where all lovable and unique with moments that had me dying of laughter or in tears. The music alone is worth the price, i wouldn't say its NieR tier but its still worth the listen. All in all i had an amazing experience that lasted 13 hours of completion, for $30 its something you shouldn't pass over especially for those who love Turn Base Strategy. Factoring the story, music and the price alone i have to give this 9/10. Keep in mind there is only one voice and thats the game master and he does an amazing job.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: The story is not amazing but it is not bad either, so if you don't have super high standards for storytelling you'll be satisfied. The turn-based combat was neat since it was a bit different than the typical turn-based combat. I enjoyed managing gems (the sort of mp of this game) to make sure I had enough for skills to beat the enemies. The art for both characters and monsters looked nice. As for the narrator, he may not have the most expressive voice, but I still enjoyed listening to him tell the story as it played out.If you are still not certain if you want the game, play the demo. What's great is the demo is set right before the base game's story so you don't have to worry about going through the beginning of the story twice. It also can't hurt to wait for a sale since I myself got it 20% off on the Christmas sale. If you do wind up getting it, I hope you enjoy playing it.  ^^
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10. Solid JRPG for people who like minimalist JRPGs. The music and art are pretty fantastic. It has a DnD feel, but doesn't succumb to the need for wild RNG swings. _childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Good soundtrack and history. - Different game presentation in a card-based scenario and good card illustration.Cons:- Simple gameplay that makes the game too easy.- Battles are not a chanllenge.- Short game.Conclusion:Good game for people who like RPG Card-Game, but I think it's overpriced  due to its short play.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Very beautiful game and the soundtrack is great too. This isn't a card collecting/gatcha game. It's an rpg through and through, just instead of "normal graphics" the game is presented through the cards and a narrator. Your moves are cards and as you level up you'll get new cards. I will say you don't get a ton of move cards, but you get a pretty good variety. (Think pokemon, but instead of only getting four moves, you get around ten moves, but can only have 4 of them active at any one time.)  There's not that many character to choose from either (5 total as far as I can tell). However, the character's roles are each different and it's fun to create a team strategy choosing your moves and characters to see which have the best synergy. The battles aren't very difficult at all. I think I only died once the entire game. However, currently I'm stuck at the final boss which is kicking my ass unlike anything else I've passed by in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Very good old school tabletop RPG.I can wholeheartedly recommend it, you definitely feel the Yoko Taro in it's charm.Music is good as always, the art and style of the game absolutely gorgeous.Did 100% it and loved every second. It's a bit short, but the price is only 30 bucks, so i think that's okay too.You don't need to get the DLC's but it was a nice homage to the OG Nier.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Just a heads up, this game is a traditional RPG. If you were expecting something different because of the visuals, check out some videos of the combat to get an idea.Cool visual aesthetic and great music. Character designs are interesting. Dialogue is humorous. The game runs really well and the controller support is great. Farming endings is kind of annoying in this one, and so is having to speed through the game in NG+, all the way towards the end, to get to some very minor additional content. I'm happy it's there, but I would have liked to see it implemented in a more convenient way. Overall, I liked the characters and the story quite a bit and I recommend the game for the $30 price tag it's listed at.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, would recommend to most people. Not all that challenging if you take the time to explore the areas and don't run from random encounters, but really good soundtrack and a pretty good story. Just a great game to play through when you want to relax and listen to chill music and let the narrator present the story to you as you continue on.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Be aware that this is a budget title. It isn't very difficult and you can probably beat it in under 7 hours if you rush through. I thought the story was very interesting but it is nothing ground breaking. The music is good but I feel like it could do with a few more tracks. _childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: When D&D meets early final fantasy and meets cards. I was surprised to see D&D dice being used here, I haven't seen those since I was a teenager. The gameplay is good with a decent story and the maps are literally turning over cards as you explore the land and dungeons. I like that idea. The music is switchable depending if you have the DLC or not. I have all the DLCs. The combat system is what you would expect with RPG card games like this, but you can buy weapon, armor, and item cards, and as you level up, you get new spells, buffs, or passive ablities. All in all it's pretty solid and is one of those games that kind of pulls you in. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: I've never finished a JRPG in my life until this one. If you're looking for a super deep game with hundreds of hours of story this isn't for you, but if you're looking for a fun and sometimes heart breaking story with a simple combat system, and very loveable character this is a perfect choice! The "Voice of Cards" is utterly charming and even though he doesn't do voices for each character he somehow still gives them more personality than the text alone could do. There isn't a lot of side stuff to do but there is enough to stop the game feeling totally linear, and doing this stuff will reward you with some of the best gear (and the best ending).As I said at the start, this is the first JRPG I've ever completed (and i even did the ending 3 times to get different endings AND did the New Game+ boss) and I really really hope we see more in this setting in the future!PS. The music is amazing and the DLC is utterly unimportant unless you're a Neir Turbo Fan or something! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards first and foremost is just a very pleasant game to play. The art, animations, writing, narration, and most especially music are all incredible. Like others have said, this is not a card game or deckbuilder like Slay The Spire or anything, the gameplay is pure JRPG, and a fairly simple and easy one at that. The gameplay is held up massively by the art, animations, and music, and only in a couple if even that many places did I really have to think about what I was doing instead of "hit guy, heal when I get hit."  It is certainly a Yoko Taro game, and the writing and some of the subplots really show it, but the overarching story is pretty pedestrian. It wasn't so predictable as to make me lose interest, but it also isn't going to give anyone an existential crisis or the impetus to watch a YouTube video explaining the complexities like his other wild rides might.Overall, every bit of time I spent playing the game, I was enjoying what was being presented to me. It is a little short, I clocked just about 12 hours to get my first playthrough done (though in true Taro fashion there is a 'true ending' that I missed, so I'll be trying NG+ out) but even then, I feel like my money and time were well spent, and would wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys short, highly polished, self contained JRPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved the concept of the game, hiding an RPG behind mechanics of a card game. It was fun, the music is awsome the art of the cards are amazing too. Perhaps the only problem i got with the game was the fact that i was constantly discarding items because you can only have 30, and the fact that the game is small (2 playthroughs were about 20h or 25h or so). Besides that, a really good game in my perspective.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pleasant little JRPG that has a unique visual style, a sharply written script, and some good plot twists.  It's a little on the short side, but the gameplay is simple enough that it'd wear out its welcome if it took too much longer.  I'd give it a solid recommendation if you find the aesthetics appealing and are in the mood for an oldschool JRPG.The one caveat I'll give is that it *is* an oldschool JRPG, not a card game.  If you're here for deckbuilding mechanics or shuffling cards, you're going to be disappointed; the cards, dice, and other accoutrements are purely for style.  The exploration and combat systems have more in common with Dragon Quest than any card game you've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Short game but Pretty good overall only real problem is that everything is really slow really hope they give it an update to make combat faster and that the final boss is the only really challenging fight otherwise its a very linear game with only a few hidden collectibles and paths that really do help out in the endgame or finding all ten mysterious cards to get the best ending in the game. Not much reason to replay after you beat it unless you want to clean up achievements or replay for the story which was nice. 8/10 !
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest here.. and I am sure a lot of 'Drakengard' fans thought this too when they say it.I was expecting maybe a cameo or perhaps DLC that would tie this in with Drakengard 3 somehow but sadly that is not the case.This is a completely NEW IP from Toko Taro and it's... well, while I would say I loved it I would also say it wasn't as strong as of an impact to me compared to Drakengard and Nier.Give it a try, but don't come in expecting cameos from his past games.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time with this game. Although it is flawed, it is decent in everything it does. The only thing that annoyed me was the UI because of how slow it is.The story is simple and engaging until the end, but the last scene is kind of disappointing and all four endings are straight up bad. And don't bother with elemental weaknesses or resistances, just paralyze everyone and freeze those who cannot be paralyzed.I would have appreciated the game to be more difficult as enemies take several turns to kill me when I could end them in a couple. The most fun battle was the secret one but it is such a chore to unlock it .
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Love the concept and wish there were more of its kind. There is about 12-14hrs of gameplay not including new-game plus. As someone who is not into jrpg's, this is pretty good for casuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: I would very much you play this game. It's one of the better examples of insanely good jrpg writing, and the aesthetic adds so much to the experience. The only regret is that it's *very* short of an rpg (about 12-15 hours having done all side content.) I'll definitely be playing again, and definitely be waiting for a sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: is a turn-based RPG fantasy game with a unique form of storytelling and different kinds of characters that project unusual/quirky personalities. The story follows you as a bounty hunter, the main protagonist along with your partner , searching for the dragon to collect the bounty. Along the journey, you meet a witch named  who yearns for revenge on the dragon. Together they form a party that leads to an extraordinary journey that had never been felt before. is similar to the usual types of jrpg where every enemy has a certain weakness for a certain elemental attack. There’s also different types of ailments such as poison that can be combo to a certain character. There’s no mana or MP rather there’s a gem that can be used to use a powerful move. The gem increases with each character turn. There are many spells or skills the further you level up the character.  is unique and fun where you traverse across the board and suddenly an event happens. Events are useful and resourceful. There are also hidden treasures that can be gold or legendary equipment.   is made by none other than the renowned  for its symphony and euphony songs of the . The music is soothing and fitting for the world of swords and sorcery. It makes the journey more enjoyable and sorrowful at the same time during a certain scene.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Jrpg with an unique visuals where the game mechanics are based on board games and dnd. I really enjoyed playing through this. The story lacks a bit compared to the previous Taro games (I described it as a Yoko Taro game for teenagers while discussing it with friends) but I think it's really worth a try if you like his production. I still haven't gone through the flipside stories of the cards I've collected so far but I'm sure there will be more interesting details to the story.If you want to have smooth sailing and complete the game in one try, make sure to collect all of the mysterious cards.Oh yeah, and pick the JP narrator. I think it made the feeling of the game better for me and also added some fun parts of the game that were lost in translation.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: With the probably only real issue being rather short, this JRPG with some table-top elements is pretty good.It seems like SquareEnix had some in-house game jam or competition lately for different talents to work on small games, which is also the case of Dungeon Encounters.The story... it's pretty short, decent, some funny dialogs but could use more backstory explanation for each character. Like the protagonist after their incident, waifu mage's indepth background etc.The music 10/10 pogThe Card game is pretty cool, but not a must for your progression ( kind of a shame )Battle strategies can be a tad-bit shallow, in both ways.- Battle can be won as long you have the higher stat, pretty old school JRPG trashmob philosophy, higher level means you'll win regardless of what you do if your party stay alive except for the fact that this can be applied to  bosses as well in this game.- Enemies are pretty simple, no real challenge on this. The difficulty on the mobs ( including bosses ) are very sub-par.The above points could easily be fixed if they included way more negative effects, such as deducting your gemstones, force 0 on dices, Doom debuff, blind (misses all), seal gemstone regeneration, etc.Overall experience for $30 is good although as mentioned, pretty short.PS, why not add the ability to skip dialogs in new game+?
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

All the art on the cards look insanely good, like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, especially the cheeks ;)The music had me boppin on every enemy/boss encounter!!! Definitely get this and take your time playing it. _childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars is the first card based game I have played in a long time and it was definitely worth the time and effort I invested in to it. Story:The story is rather simplistic and straightforward but does have quite a few twists and turns that keeps you interested and engaged for the entirety of it. If you just go through the main story without grinding for levels (which you don't really need to do since most of the game is pretty easy until the end of the game) then you can probably beat the game within 10-15 hours. While it doesn't have has many crazy twists and turns as a typical Yoko Taro game, the story was still very enjoyable overall and I really liked the length of it. Gameplay:The gameplay of the game is rather simple, picking cards which have physical attacks, spells, to use on enemies to picking cards which gives buffs to the party. There is a decent variety of cards for each character which gives each character their own role within the fight. Music:The team at studio Monaca did an amazing job with the soundtrack of the game. While the game doesn't feature as many tracks as other games they worked on (such as NieR) it still is very well composed and fits the theme of the game perfectly.Art:With being a card game, one of the best things about it should be the card artwork and artwork overall, right? In this case, Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars exceeded my expectations. The artwork on every single card looks amazing, from simple things like items to important things like characters and monsters, each one is done exceptionally well.Overall:I don't really play card games all too often but I thoroughly enjoyed playing this game from start to finish. 10/10. Especially for the price that they're asking for, I'd say it's definitely more than worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Though the game is rather short, I really enjoyed the world and characters, as well as the presentation.Combat system is simplistic, and feels like some kind of prototype for a sequel. In the end, the final boss is the only time I felt truly challenged and really enjoyed the combat, but some simple improvements like more slots for allies and enemies in battle, maybe a back and front row like there is in many other jrpgs and deeper deck building options could go a long way.A piece of advice: make sure to do all the side quests and gather all misterious cards, it's worth it if you're invested in the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards is a simple, easy-going, and short rpg experience with all the aesthetic than comes with Yoko Taro's touch.  I've seen some general complaint about length and lack of depth, which is valid, but comes more from expecting this to either be a deck-building card battler or long, complex turn-based rpg.  It's neither, and you should temper expectations before buying.  If you're looking for Heathstone meets SMT, keep looking, this isnt it.Also to Yoko Taro fans, we know why you're here, same reason I'm here, so let me stop you before you dive in.  Yes, funny skull man's name is on the box.  Yes, all the dlc is Nier skins.  Yes, it's about a dragon.  But no, this game has absolutely nothing to do with Drakenier.  If you were hoping this would answer or raise questions about Accord, or YoRHa, or Lunar Tears, or anything Drakenier, I'm sorry to say there's nothing.So, lets get to the, ya know, game.  First, Steam should probably take off Card Battler from the tags.  The cards here are purely aesthetic, which is disappointing.  I'm not sure how well the type of randomness inherit to card games would mix with a turn-based rpg, but I'm sad there's no attempt at any experiment there.  Battles play out like any classic jrpg: monster show up, turn order is determined, everyone goes around casting spells and swinging swords until one side's health is 0, nothing new.  The only moderately unique thing in the battles, other than aesthetic, is the Gem system, which is effectively mana, where you generate one at the start of each turn, and can spend it one increasingly powerful abilities.  This *does* add some strategy to fights, were you might opt to have one character use just a basic attack and save your Gems, so the next person in order can spend them all for a powerful attack.  Its nothing super in depth, but its something.  There's some minor gripes with how long some animations go (yes I know its all cards, but theres some flashy animations for everything), some UI annoyances like not being able to check what powers your other characters have on any given turn, and frankly annoying random encounter rates in dungeons.There is also the topic of the voice actor.  Yes, -The- voice actor.  There's only one, a faceless voice only known as Game Master, who narrates all the dialogue and story.  and Todd Haberkorn does an excellent job, carrying this wizened gravitas of some grandpa, who's been playing these D&D games since the original back in '74 and is totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ into it still, and delivers it all like a wizard reading you a bedtime story.  But if the prospect annoys you, yeah, it probably will annoy you.So, its a short and standard jrpg with some minor annoyances and a neat aesthetic and simple story.  Does it have anything else going on?  Well, the art's really good, there's a hot himbo, and the soundtrack is by Okabe, who is the Danny Elfman to Taro's Tim Burton at this point.  But other than that?  No, not really,  It's nice and inoffensive.  Hell, the only thing it does wrong is arguably the price, 30 dollars feels like a lot for the package, even if it was enjoyable.So why the hell do I recommend it?  Well other than just genuinely enjoying my time with it, my main takeaway from this game was that it was a short, fun pet project for Taro and his team, something they could knock out in a short development cycle between larger projects.  And I think it's incredibly important for gamedevs to be able to do that, to make games with relatively low ambition and scope.  It's important for devs to be able to make games that wont be life or death for their studios, where every increasing entry in the series needs to sell 5 million more unit than the last.  Not every game should be a 60 dollar, Triple A, mind-blowing, game of the year contending experience.  Game should be allowed to be humble, little things if that's what the developer wants to make, If we reject this game for everything it isn't, then all we might ever get from Taro will be incredibly long, ambitious projects, which *sounds* great, but we need to remember series like Dead Space or the Tomb Raider reboots, where ambitions and expectations were beyond anything realistic, and killed their studios as a result.  Voice of Cards needs to walk so that future Nier games can keep running.Pleading heart aside, in the end, Voice of Cards is short, simple, and sweat.  It entertained me for a few nights.  That's all it ever set out to do, and it did it well.  If you're looking for a time-killer to last a few week nights and like the look of it, especially if it's on sale, go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Near "must-play" status for JRPG fans, Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars has most everything I'm looking for in a JRPG: Great music, great art, side quests, secret legendary treasures, colorful characters, surprise twists, and killing god, all with Yoko Taro's wonderfully bizarre sense of humor and tone.Despite the card game aesthetic, the mechanics are fairly standard turn-based JRPG, just with the math tuned down to "board game" levels, and the inclusion of actual die rolls as parts of mechanics. This simplification and streamlining of the JRPG experience applies to other areas to: there's a world map and dungeons to explore, but you can teleport to any space you've already been making backtracking painless. Your towns have all the standard shops you've come to expect, but the inns are always free. Some twists and extensions of the JRPG formula I also thought were cool ideas: while fights are the most common thing you'll hit in the overworld, the game has a handful of non-combat events as well to mix things up. The game also generally respects your status effects as well which is always appreciated. As a fan of tabletop rpgs I also really liked the approach of having the story narrated by a game master.The game is not flawless though. For one, the obsession with having everything displayed via cards leads to some UI being a bit confusing, and feeling a little clunky at times. This is especially strange considering that none of the actual game mechanics really rely on things being cards. Sure it calls your stuff a "deck" and your available cards your "hand" but there's no randomization, drawing etc, it's just an aesthetic choice. The non-combat event idea was cool, but there were far too few events considering how simple they were. There were a lot of repetitions, and while getting the same combat multiple times is just par for the course, getting the same "the wind picks up and begins pelting the party with nuts from nearby trees" multiple times per chapter was strange. The inclusion of puzzles was cool, but having nearly identical puzzle event setups and similar solutions also felt strange, and damaged my suspension of disbelief. Lastly, the gamemaster idea was cool, but he didn't really change his voice at all for different characters, and some of his speaking intonation on longer sections could get a bit stilted. Lastly, while I don't regret buying this game full price - I did manage a true ending on my first play through in under 20 hours of play. You are not getting a good "bargain" here on entertainment hours if that's important to you. But the game is a rare one these days from a major company - a single player game, that once you're in, you won't get a single prompt for DLC, and isn't bloated with "daily quests" or events. If you are looking for a modern polished JRPG experience, with some fun new ideas, that you can beat over a weekend or 2, and don't mind the price, I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say it's about a 7.5/10 overall.I don't normally give reviews, but seeing how there's not a lot of them at the moment I felt the need to add my two-cents.I enjoyed it for what it was. _childDocuments_.review: I'm NOT RECOMMENDING this game but giving this game a thumbs down feels deeply unfair since it's technically better than 75% of the game that I thumbsed up on Steam.TLDR: This game is very pretty and technically competent, but not what you're looking for.If you're interested in this game you're most likely expecting two things: A Yoko Taro-ish metatextual twist that change the context of things you've seen earlier in the game, and/or an interesting use of the card game mechanic. This game delivers neither. It's just an ordinary, short JRPG (you can 100% this game in 15 hours or so), with admittedly very beautiful card game aesthetics The story is as straightforwardly JRPG as you can expect from a JRPG, there are some JRPG-ish twist that you've seen before, the characters are amusing and banter off each others in a way you've seen before, and the gameplay is almost as straightforwardly JRPG as you can get, though with some interesting shallow card game-based twists. In a way I guess this game deliver the two expected things I mentioned earlier, but very shallowly and sadly underdeveloped.So to sum, what you get:-A very beautiful, almost twee, board game aesthetic. I'm not kidding, the illustrations are very beautiful, it uses cards in very pleasing way, the story and narrator feels very simple and personal like this is just your friend playing game with you (you don't expect your friend to deliver some award winning story, don't you?), or a melancholic fairytale you read from a richly illustrated book.-Really good soundtrack as you expect from MONACA, though somewhat limited in number of songs.-Ordinary JRPG story and characters and gameplay that you've seen somewhere else (don't take me wrong, once again, this game is competently made)-Short playtime.Get this if you're die hard Yoko Taro fan that have to play everything he directed, are interested in the twee aesthetic and melancholic story I mentioned, or it's discounted heavily.

_childDocuments_.review: Voice of Cards is a fairly unique concept - it is a tabletop RPG... video game. Its world is made up entirely made up of cards, including the characters, the monsters, your spells, the NPCs, the dialogue, etc. The story and everything that happens is narrated by the game master, just like in a real world Dungeons & Dragons campaign. It is made by Yoko Taro, the director of Nier: Automata, a hugely popular 2017 game.I found it very immersive, with likeable chararacters and light-hearted humour. The combat was fun, and generally not restrictive, as the characters aren't pigeon-holed to any one role - I had my main character switch from damage dealer to healer constantly during my playthrough. The story was interesting though not super deep.On the downsides, the game is a bit too easy throughout, I stomped my way up to the last dungeon. The  only real challenge was a post-game boss fight. Also, it's a bit too short for an RPG, at 10-15 hours, which is a shame because I really enjoyed my time playing it, kept wanting more afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great Yoko Taro-lite game. I mean that in both the good ways and the bad. For those who have played a game by Yoko Taro, you probably have a pretty good idea of what I mean, but I'll clarify a bit.The story of the game is the real star. It starts deceptively simple but adds layers of complexity as time goes on. There are little to no side quests that add to the story, giving an opportunity for a clear-cut experience. However, to get the "true ending," you'll need to a handful of side activities. Most of these activities I accidentally stumbled across and fulfilled without really trying. The twists and turns of the story are, for the most part, satisfying in a very Yoko Taro way.Where the game falters a bit is in the gameplay. It isn't bad. It just isn't great. The card battle system works well. It starts very easy, and by the end, boss battles require planning and strategy to win. The final boss was especially fulfilling, but I wish they developers played with the concept as much as they did on that boss. Most of the time, battles become monotonous. As you approach the end of the game and dungeons get longer, regular get downright boring. There are also a handful of quirks with the battle system. Damage isn't calculated by the exact numbers listed on the cards, and it is possible to miss attacks while having no accuracy stat to work off of, basically just going by random chance. None of these things were bad enough to make me stop playing the game, but they did get in the way of fully enjoying it.Overall, I think if you go into the game understanding all of this, most people will find an enjoyable indie-sized experience, full of gorgeous music and art, along with a story that makes you think by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: This is a mostly positive game. The core systems are all very well designed, the story is engaging and the characters are interesting. I would say that, if this were on sale, it is an easy recommendation. At the price point of 40 CDN, that's a bit much however.However, there are a few parts that really drag the game down, if these are show stoppers for you then you should not purchase this.1 - The game is slow. I don't mean the pacing of the story, I mean the UI, battles, animations, etc. If the pace of these things were closer to most other games, you'd likely cut hours off the game time.2 - It's a Yoko Taro game (creative director), but it never goes full Yoko Taro.3 - It's a bit content light, especially for the price point.Even given these points, I found myself wanting more at the end of it, and had enjoyed my time with it. I hope Square Enix returns to this product and fleshes it out in a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. It looks like a card game, but it really is a traditional JRPG like the old Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest games. The story is pretty simple, but the presentation is fantastic. There are plenty of memorable or hilarious moments, enough that I am happy with the purchase of this game. The entire game is voiced by the same person who takes a "game master" role, and the aesthetic and storyline is a tabletop game feel. And it does mostly achieve this with it's simple math-light battle system, random encounters that are not always battles, and of course the fact the whole game is told using cards on a table. I adore the voice actor for the game master. I feel like he is pouring himself another glass of bourbon while giving you a wry remark. Overall, it makes for an atmospheric and relaxing game.There are some other things that I like about this game in no particular order:It is worth mentioning that there is a card-game within this game that is a minigame. I love the idea of being a card, walking up to a card npc, and playing cards with them, but It is not good: you end up not having any real choices the entire time you are doing the mini game. Complete luck. This minigame is completely optional, with only cosmetic unlocks, but this is just my biggest disappointment so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars

_childDocuments_.review: Game is a very nice change of pace from every other JRPG out there. The simulated TRPG aspect is definitely not something I've ever played before, and it was quite fun. Game is fairly short, which isn't a bad thing. Not every game needs to be 100+ hours filled with meaningless bloat. Everything about this games story is nice and to the point. Only downside is its a little slower paced and menus are a little more convoluted than need be. Overall, a good JRPG to spend a weekend on.
_childDocuments_.name: Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars
