_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - initially enjoyable, but upon closer inspection found game with little to no actual depth, and a ui that is straining for the modern day game. while the playthrough initially was quite enjoyable, i have since reviewed my stance on this game. while at first it is fun because the grittieness of the game a lot of the story makes little sense, or your actions in the game are simply pointless. PROS-the music is top notch- The musical score of this game rivals some of the best OST's out there, you can tell an OST is good if i listen to it on it's own-characters are well written and likeable even though some of them (aselia) are token cardbord cutouts of tropes and whatnot. -the art is prettyCONS-No real sense of sovreignty, instead of being a king your character is basically a lord in comparison to the kings around you. -No real managment- Instead of managing the resources of a kingdom, or dealing with the internal politics of your court, you are limited to managing very few resources. 1. your gold2. your "supplies"3. and your agents each of these resources are incredibly shallow in there implementation and management. the gold is just gold, the "supplies" are just "supplies" and your agents work for you regardless of the state the kingdom is in. you don't have to work to keep them happy, you don't have to secure their loyalty, they just appear. -multiple playthroughs are pointless - unless you are achievement hunting, then there is little to no reason to play through this game multiple times, from the tests I've done the petitioners come in predictably based on the turn counter. the core events / acts are the same regardless of your choices / competence there are two main paths to take and once you see them for what they are the seemingly deep game reveals itself to be quite shallow. multiple playthroughs are also a chore as there is no skip function for dialogue you've already seen. as this game plays like a visual novel that's another QOL feature that should be in the game. -Game plays like a glorified visual novel- considering how the mechanics are already pretty lame in the visual department / don't strain anything, this game could very well just be a visual novel yet it doesn't have the literary depth a typical visual novel has.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished a first run in 15 ish hours. MOstly 1 day, ending at 2:30 am. It was really good, like a great combination of visual novels with some light gameplay interaction. Like visual novels, you have a set number of tasks and actions you can do per day, and it ramps up in difficulty as the plot progresses. You also talk to characters and important people, like your daughters and wife, as the plot proceeds. The plot is very good too, a lot of surprises, although some were predicted by me.There is no voice acting per say, but there are interesting voiced responses. They sound like the voice sounds of Danganronpa when you click on a character. Or sims talk. Some of it is very funny and musical. The tone of their voice really gives emotional depth and tone to the text and plot. It fits very well, and makes it like you are hearing a foreign language. DAA Urraaw.It's a foreign language, like Japanese, I don't expect to understand it but the emotions come through very well.I recommend it for people who like visual novel gameplay, who want a good story, and who want to do a little kingdom building/management. The Kingdom simulation elements are mostly centered around helping people as the king, it isn't city skylines or Per Aspera. Overall, I would put this in the 90%+ group in terms of quality, out of 100%. There are slightly different endings depending on good your gameplay/memorization is, but this is not a reflex combat game. The mood and atmosphere it gives is very close to fighting wars by commanding armies though.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game via the sequel demo during the pixel art steam sale. It looked super cool, but I realized 5 minutes into playing, that that game was a sequel and found the original here. I played it... and played it.. and played it until I realized I was about to be late to work. Spent the whole day thinking of this game, only to come back and finish the next day. Worth every penny I spent on the game. The game has fantastic management and decisions to make. I had to make choices on who to save, who to let go, who to kill, and this extended from peasents to merchants to lords and even my own royal family. So many great decisions and I am inching to try this again with different choices in mind. The heart felt moments in the middle and end of the game really hit you because you made the choices that got you this far. It is absolutely brilliant game design and I highly recommend this game for anyone who is interested in story and/or management games.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: Its a great story about family and responsibility. There is also a good dose of slavic folklore. Its not very long, thou its long enough for its genre. As for possible story options, we do have a lots of choices, but most of them are trivial, and only apply their effect in short term, that is on quest rewards. There are some important chocies in the game, so I guess you can have at least one additional playthrough. howerev, I belive that Papers Please for example, did it much better.Game lacks in actual gameplay perspective. Gameplay is linked to chocies, some of them are time based, so we have for example battles, where we have to decide what to do at any given time, but possibilities are quite limited really, and its not very engaging.Yes, Your Grace has some nice pixel art graphic, there are many details, some cool animations, and every model seems to be unique in some way. If Graphics are good, then soundtrack is great. It has a great choice of music, that suits the climate we are facing on the screen, and its also great to just sit in the main menu and listen to beautifull vocals.All in all I recomend this game to anyone who is interested in good story with some chocies. However, if you want some engaging gameplay, then you may chose Papers, Please instead. For more choices, you can check Suzerein for example. This game lies somewhere in between the other two, but its distinct in its unique way, and definitly worth trying ouy.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it! Games with this much reading rarely hold my attention all the way through anymore, but this one did. Really enjoyed the gameplay; may be a bit too repetetive for some, but optimizing resource management + an engaging story hit the spot for me here. I got real anxiety over some decisions and found myself unable to make decisions that would benefit me politically but I couldn't agree with morally or emotionally. That's good writing. Also not too long, played all the way through in a single 4 to 5 hours sitting.Small caveat: The German translation is comically bad. I played in English, so whatever, but it really takes away from the experience when a game depends so heavily on immersion - and when the writing itself is this good when not ruined by a bad translation, it's a shame all the more! Spend a few bucks on a new translation, please. I'd be happy to do it!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun.I liked the characters, the story is not all that surprising, but the overall looks, soundtrack and gimmicks of the game are really enjoyable.The pixel art looks amazing at times, specially on battles, and I like the little voices they made for the characters.There is a lot of replay value if you want a perfect run or something like that, but the game, although not forgiving, is not really difficult to beat with the good ending, if you pay attention to what the people say and need, that is.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: This game goes too far with certain events, to the extent that I wasn’t enjoying the game anymore.  You begin the game in a poverty stricken castle, going into a war you both caused and can’t avoid, with no military at all.  You then have no choice over how the game moves forward, and the competent king comes and just demands whatever he wants to make your problems go away.Next you prepare for war by trying to barter deals with the lords of the land, and this is actually the best section of the game.  It has an interesting secondary story too as you play detective in your spare time.  Unfortunately that plot loses a lot of points because it isn’t actually solvable.After the midpoint, the fun drops drastically.  You no longer deal with lords and instead call civilians in one by one week after week to beg for their support as you try to remember who’s who from the first half of the game, meanwhile the antagonist commits atrocities against you that are downright upsetting, to the point where I was no longer enjoying the game.I enjoy games were decisions have consequences, but here it feels like these decisions were already made long before you took control.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: This game was everything I expected and more. I expected tough choices, and hard tradeoffs. I expected a mixture of silly and serious little plot lines. But what I didn't expect was just how emotionally connected I would feel to the characters. The strength of the main plot caught me off guard. By the end I was shedding tears over the tragedies, and cheering for the successes.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: I really really enjoyed this game, it's short but it nails the immersion, sometimes during conversations with certain people you hear music you only hear with them and I would just sit back and let it play sometimes there are absolute slammers in this soundtrack.There are highs and there are lows, it's filled with an emotionally impactful story, and the resource management game is fun if not particularly toughGet this game if you like a good story and playing as a King hearing out petitioners
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: Game is pretty short and as long as one does not missmanage priorities, decently simple.I noted no real random factors, so I do not feel there is any replayability for someone like me outside of a desire to gather achivements.Even so, the story told in itself was told with a great job on the the characters and that makes it a real must-play experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought it thinking it was a "Kingdom" clone. What I got was a medieval 2D adventure! Ok, you're right, if you rise the theatrical curtains you'll see your decisions make little to no difference, a little polishing is missing, the preparations for the war are only a nice excuse for the resourses managment and the story has one and only final. But! The good scripting, how the story unfolds, the family dramas, and, last but not least, being a King and making Decisions (nor good nor bad, but you'll have to cope with their conseguences) will keep you hooked until the end (6 to 7 hours). Of course, no replay value.Was it good? Yes, it was.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic! Everything from the visuals to the story itself is great. The story is liner in nature with choices along the way. Their are also major choices to make through the game as you play and the game gives you plenty of warning of those choices. The choices you make can mean life or death for a variety of characters. The music is also well done and helps to immerse you in this world. I love the characters in this story and I love that everything is connected in some way. The only reason you would not like this game is if you do not like reading a lot. I'd give this game a 9/10. The only reason it's not a 10/10 is because of some grammar mistakes that can easily be fixed, but also to account for all the people who do not like to read. Voice acting of the lines will fix this, but it might ruin the feeling of the game by removing our imagination of the characters personality; In my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I very much enjoyed my time playing the game. Took about 5 hours to finish my first run through. Might go back to try some other routes or achievements. There are a few things that stood out to me while playingoverall score 4.5/5 excellent game that i'd recommend to friends.The Bad:- I disliked that there was often times not an option to do something that seemed like an obvious option.- Some of the choices aren't clear what they mean. I have selected an option or two that came out much different than I intended. It usually wasn't terrible but given that the whole game is built on these choices it was a bit annoying.- The order you talk to people matters a lot more than i'd want it to. Make sure to talk to your agents before talking to the peasants even though you start in the throne room. Also do your best to figure out who you most think you'll need to help. you can't tell someone to wait till you've heard other people. - Battles were awkward and felt pointless. I will avoid spoilers on anything, but there are times in battle where you are told to go talk to archers and then they fire and they seem to have negligible effect. It also just feels a bit weird given the rest of the game.- you can't back out of conversations once you started them since most of the time your conversations with people one and done. The Good:- Surprisingly amazing music. Like i normally play games on silent or low volume because it's not that important to me, but man is this music killer. I am currently rocking to it as I type. It added a lot to the game and i highly recommend keeping your volume on during your play through.- surprisingly good story. I wasn't expecting that much honestly but i enjoyed it thoroughly. There were some obvious twists that i'm a bit annoyed that I couldn't call out in character, but alas a king can only do so much.- The resource management was very simple but felt meaningful and impact at all times.- I think they did a great job at getting you to become invested in the characters. i'd give examples but it would be difficult to do so without spoilers. but lets just say smudge the real MVP.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is reminiscent of some favorites of mine from the 1990s. It's hard to pin down its clear antecedents, though there are elements that reminded of Castles 2 and Princess Maker 2. It's the sort of game I'm always excited to play, a narrative based simulation with ethical choices made by the player that lead to different outcomes. I also love the artstyle and the characters are also well developed for a game with such a short playtime.On the negative, I did feel the game was a bit too forgiving, and I was able to make some very risky, empathetic choices without significant consequences for doing so, and on the other hand I also thought the rewards you reap later on for having made good choices were not particularly significant. So I would say that the game is probably more appealing to someone interested in the narrative than someone wanting a game of making the best possible decisions.For people who enjoy this game, I would also highly recommend Suzerain.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough (about 5-6 hours) and was compelled the entire game. Yes, Your Grace manages to convey that "one more turn" feeling from beginning to end, as you struggle to balance kingdom resources, opinions of nobles, and prepare for the next major challenge. All that challenging decision making is bound up in the story of a father deciding the best course for his three daughters, with all the frustration, adoration, and heartbreak that can bring. I figure that my second playthrough may have a slightly better ending than my first, and by the third run I can probably be happy with my choices. Altogether that will probably be about 15 hours of gameplay spent with some very endearing characters in a beautifully illustrated setting.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a little bit of a struggle to get into at first, but man, this game really takes off.  A nice smooth tutorial phase that feels very motivated by the narrative -- and then, there's these profound modulations of the game and the concept.  I loved it.  I started playing, did about an hour, took a break.  Came back to it today, and just hammered through it in one play-through.   One of my favorite things was how subtly the "choices matter" things happened!  Looking at notes from other people's playthroughs, I'm seeing how mine /could/ have gone... but it had felt super inevitable!  That's a really rare feeling for a game in this genre, and it really blew me away.There's a nice balance of resource-management and narrative RPG happening here.A nice way to spend five hours.

_childDocuments_.review: This was part of the July 2022 Humble Choice (i.e. monthly sub) bundle.The game is mainly about managing gold/supplies & listening to requests from your subjects.You progressively get more "agents" to send out and take care of business around your kingdom and the ability to contact 1 other lord/king to ask them to join your cause (for a predetermined amount of soldiers/supplies/gold).There's two main consecutive story lines, but I don't want to spoil anything  There's also side-stories involving your family, and mini-quests involving the foreign lords/kings that arrive at your request.I finished my first play-through in about 8 hours of gameplay.It saves every week so if you forget something you can reload to a previous week to try again.Try to figure things out without a guide at first; failing never feels great but if you learn and succeed afterwards it feels more rewarding. There are guides that tell you how to achieve certain alternate endings, but one is enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, Your Grace is basically what would happen if a foreign devteam tried to re-create The Banner Saga without knowing anything about what made The Banner Saga work while also getting rid of that game's primary weakness - that being the combat system. The problem is that again, I don't think the devs entirely understood what it is that made The Banner Saga work.At the start of the game, you play as a king with three daughters who is really more akin to a count of some sort since you don't have any vassals (or at least none are ever shown) who suddenly comes under attack by a band of barbarians who definitely do not at all share a color scheme with the Dredge from Banner Saga (they absolutely do). The barbarians give you an ultimatum: give their leader one of your daughters as a wife, or fight them head-on. With just a few months to prepare, you have to (theoretically) carefully manage supplies to win the war.The game itself is divided into two parts. The first is handling your audience chamber - peasants will come in asking you for things, and you can decide whether to give them anything or not. Most of the time, they'll want things that are mutually exclusive: you'll have three people all coming in wanting your general at the same time. The good news there is that your choices ultimately don't matter. The bad news is that your choices ultimately don't matter!While I totally understand what the developers were going for - they didn't want to put in a fail state where it'd be impossible to finish the game - it kind of makes everything meaningless. Ultimately, you can ignore every peasant in the game (well, not EVERY peasant as just like in Banner Saga, Morale is a stat and goes down when you ignore them but you get the idea) and still get the best ending. I really wish that instead of having a bunch of choices, you got fewer but they had more of an impact. In fact, this actually leads to kind of a problem when later on you have to re-visit the people you helped, most of whom are marked only by a vague description and some of which have a description that's virtually the same.Apart from this being a game where most of your choices don't matter, Yes Your Grace is at least a better Banner Saga clone than Ash of Gods Redemption was. The pixel art is quite well-done and the sound design is also quite good, and even though this isn't a game that's nearly as deep as Banner Saga, it's at least playable to the finish without being bad enough that you'll want to drop it.Really, all I wish is that the choice system was a little deeper, and also maybe that there was some more stuff to do. For the last probably half of the game, once I knew I'd secured everything I needed to win, I basically just went on auto-pilot until the game ended.  It's still worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only recommending this game because it's cheap, got pretty artstyle, and the music works well enough. The storytelling and dialogue that's supposed to be the main course of the game is honestly underwhelming. It has a lot of things that takes you out of the immersion, and reminds you these aren't believable characters you should care about (admittedly, when the dialogue fits the situation, it's well-written). I'm pissed because with a few more writing passes, this game would've been awesome, but if these issues arent fixed by now, it never will.Examples below, spoiler free:- At some point in the story the queen will ask for some items for a ritual. Even if you've gathered all the items, she'll end every conversation with "just go and gather all the things"- Same goes for the dungeon guard when he's proposing castle upgrades. I've bought all the upgrades, you can stop trying to convince me, please.- Oh yeah, the dungeon roof. Even if you pay for the dungeon/pantry repair, that roof will still visually leak to the end of the game. The game does mechanically recognize the fix and removes the malus you get if you dont fix it though. Hurray. Somehow, fixing the castle wall and gate does bring about visual change.- To King Talys in the council room, you can only end convos with "We can proceed with the marriage". This is very jarring if your previous convo with him in the throne room is "I'll think about it/I'll ask my family first". I know the game will force me to accept the marriage anyway, but please recognize that I havent made a decision yet, cmon.- The amount of lese-majeste in this game is atrocious. No, stupid peasant, I don't care that you have diarrhea. Come back when the situation is more dire, like the whole village having it or something. And I heard you insulting my throne farts, only reason I'm not beheading you is because the game won't let me.- I can't hear all the audience of the day before deciding who to send people/resources to? Am I not the king you can wait 10 minutes for? Now I cant prevent a drought because I just sent the royal witch to cure someone's flea problem.- And no, I cant send the hunter to kill this monster because he's off dealing with a R.....abbit infestation.- Who let this drunken old fisherman in to beg me for booze money? Which guard allowed this?- WHO LET THE DRUNK GUY IN FOR THE SECOND TIME TO ASK FOR BOOZE MONEY?These are only the examples I can remember off the top of my head.All this makes the arc words of this game, "Yes, Your Grace" fall flat. This game suffers heavily from the trope "Dude, Where's My Respect"? You're not the king, you're everyone's errand boy because the game mechanics demand so.Compared this with Suzerain, a game with similar mechanics but less graphics. It's 150% the price of this game, but it does what it advertises (reactive dialogues and story branches) well with no loopholes like above.

_childDocuments_.review: Very excellent and engaging game, worth a replay. I beat it in two days of playing. I love the gameplay, I've been wanting a game for while that would let me respond to everyday events as the monarch of the kingdom instead of going out to fight battles everyday. This is exactly that. Graphics are charming. Soundtrack and the little "voices" of the characters are quite excellent. If outcomes of your gameplay really matter to you, USE A GUIDE. I restarted four weeks in because I was dissatisfied about an earlier choice I made that I thought affected a later event (it didn't, I was tricked, lol. But reading the guide helped me avoid a lot of mistakes that would have seriously annoyed me, like missing items I needs, having fewer resources than I need, and failing to save characters). There are multiple endings and outcomes to the game. One thing that slightly bothered me, probably because I'm female, is there is a bit of the fridging trope in here. It's not terrible, like it doesn't happen right at the beginning and it isn't really "used" as a major motivation for characters, but there's nothing you can do to stop it - it's part of the main story. There's also another event that's part of the main story that you can't stop, even though it seems like you can (the reason I restarted my game, because I thought I could prevent it). Another charming thing about the game is that it drops a couple of Witcher references that I thought were nice. One is a major plot point of the first half of the game. The other is just a little thing but it was nice all the same. Definitely looking forward to the sequel. 9/10 game.
_childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: A short but sweat decision and resource management game. Good story with dialog that's not too wordy, while still being colorful. Simple and elegant with a few twists. The game really makes you feel like your decisions matter in a way that impacts both your resources, success, and the outcomes of fake digital characters that the writing has you emotionally invested in.Honestly expected this game to be a boring "art game", but it was far from that. My only complaint is that there isn't a (longer) sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's the thing with Yes, Your Grace:The Primary Gameplay Loop is "decision making"By that, I mean, where most games use something like violence/action as the second-to-second gameplay, Y,YG has you making choices about your kingdom as the main way you interact with the game's world. Much like most games, the primary gameplay loop doesn't really affect anything. In Zelda, it doesn't matter if you kill every enemy in a dungeon or completely ignore the primary gameplay loop and just run to the end and kill the bosses. You're gonna get the same story, no matter how many enemies you kill, and the only thing that affects you getting to new plot points is your performance in those final tests, like puzzles or boss fights.But because "Making choices" feels like it should affect the story in a significant way (see games like The Walking Dead or Life is Strange) this can sometimes feel like your choices don't have any impact on the story.That's true, but killing Deku Scrubs in Zelda has no impact on the story. It's just a fun way to pass the time until the next plot point. And with that in mind, the primary gameplay loop of Yes, Your Grace is fun, and interesting, and the story is full of dynamic and rounded characters and is well told. I recommend it, and I hope this Review helps you figure out if it's right for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I enjoyed the nearly five hours I spent with this game (in one sitting, with a few breaks), I expected much, much more out of it, especially considering the price tag. The game doesn't give a clear indication of its length, either, to the point where halfway through I expected a reveal that I had only been playing some form of prologue tutorial. As it stands, although I enjoyed my time with it, this was mostly because of the assumption that there was much more to come. I can't say that I recommend it--which is disappointing, because there are the glimmers of a fantastic gem here that was clearly inspired by other pocket RPGs and could have set a new standard for indie story-based games. Yes, Your Grace has all the markings of what was seemingly meant to be an intricate, highly replayable experience. This was trimmed down--significantly--to a linear tale with the mere illusion of repercussions. You can even see glimpses of what might have been in the finished product; unresolved plot threads involving witchcraft, more recruitable agents, more opportunities for accumulating resources, and potential paths that might have actually changed the course of the game. Yes, Your Grace instead drip-feeds you the few gameplay mechanics that were finished and then abruptly concludes. This is Chapter One of a saga that will never be finished. It does an incredible job of developing its characters and the overall tone, with some genuinely shocking twists. But those characters are railroaded along a choose-your-own-adventure story where your actions as king don't ultimately matter at all, in a world with mere hints of richness and no means of exploring it. And it's a damn shame, because the developers obviously saw it as a labor of love and put a lot of thought into it. I can imagine their vision for this game. Unfortunately, it is not the game I played.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, Your GraceA pretty short, but pleasant game about managing a kingdom whilst under threat of an incoming invasion. It's quite pleasant. The sprites and artstyle are very well-done, and the music is usually well-suited for whatever it tries to accomplish.All-in-all, the game took me 5.5 hours to beat, and that seems to be a tiny bit faster than the average. I did not 100% it, but I managed to get what I'm sure most people would consider the "Good" or "Best" ending. Up to you whether this game is worth it's price for a roughly 6~ hour little indie game.In essence, the game is divided into roughly two-ish loops. The start of the week, where you take petitioners and resolve their problems, the solution to almost all of them is usually "Give them Gold, Supplies, or send one of your Agents", barring I think two petitioners who had unique resolves, and then you distribute your remaining agents (If any) to visit towns and villages to resolve their problems there. For a time, you also send messenger pigeons out to other lords, though that system is dropped roughly halfway through, and is mostly pointless for the rest of the game. The other "gameplay" loop involves you wandering around your own castle talking to NPCs (mostly your own family), and occasionally picking items up and using them in a classic adventure game style.The game isn't particularly difficult, especially once you figure out the trick to it. It's more-or-less just about trying to manage your limited resources as best you can. Some options are better than others and all that. There's only a few 'timed' choice, though the timer seems to be pretty lenient.My two complaints are that most of the petitioners problems really only being resolved by "spend X resources", rather trying to come up with creative solutions, or what-have-you. That, and at the end of the game, a minor plot thread has a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ twist ending to it. It's not a major plot thread (by that point in the game), but it is just annoying how the twist was more-or-less ham-fisted in and serves basically no purpose, when the story would have been better-served by getting rid of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review originally written for . The full article can be found . Feel free to take a look at the Opium Pulse Steam Curation page  as well.Yes, Your Grace is the brainchild of developer Brave at Night. Releasing in March of 2020, it's been out for a fair amount of time. However, with the up and coming release of the sequel, Yes, Your Grace: Snowfall, it's a game well worth experiencing before the Quarter 1 release. A mixture of Point and Click with Kingdom Management, it's an absolutely unique title. Each of your choices matter as you weigh the needs of your kingdom as a whole, your people, and your own family. Not everything is as black and white as it appears, and some of the consequences of your actions are much more far-reaching than they may initially appear. With easy to understand controls, gorgeous pixel graphics, a fantastically deep story and an outstanding musical score, while somewhat short, there is so much here to love.Step into the shoes of King  Eryk of  Davern, and bear the responsibility of the crown. Surrounded by your loved ones; Queen Aurelea, as well as Princesses Lorsulia, Asalia, and Cedani, there is often a lot going on not only within your kingdom, but withing the structure of your family. Beyond your immediate familial ties, you also have members of your court to direct, as well as managing military power, your gold income, and your supplies. To add to your list of Kingly duties, invite neighboring Lords to your castle, make alliances, and gain additional troops and resources. However, aide is never free. Weigh your options carefully. Assisting one Lord may alienate you from another, perhaps in more ways than one.While management plays a large part in Yes, Your Grace, one of the two strongest elements of the game is it's storyline. While at first the story may seem deceptively simple, straight forward, and just about as par the course as one would come to expect from a medieval-dated RPG, players will quickly come to the realization it is the absolute farthest thing from. While the marriage of your eldest daughter, Princess Lorsulia, may just seem like another day in the Kingdom of Davern, this singular event is absolutely pivotal. Prepare for a most lavish event, making sure each and every detail is in place. You've planned accordingly. Clearly nothing could go wrong... could it?Part of what helps draw players into the beautifully crafted narrative, is the skillfully crafted soundtrack. While most of the vibrant and rich melodies are composed by Carlos Filipe Alves, the eerie and beautiful vocals are provided by the Polish metal-folk band Merkfolk. I sincerely cannot overstate enough that this game is worth playing for the music alone. Both forces are masters at their craft, bringing life and raw emotion to the world of Yes, Your Grace. Players will all too easily find themselves humming haunting tunes when they least expect it. It is an absolutely perfect marriage of talent that Brave at Night has arranged, and I cannot praise them nearly enough for it.Yes, Your Grace is a wonderful tale, with multiple endings. Depending on your choices throughout the game, you can have a whole plethora of outcomes. Some are more positive, while others may leave you contemplating your life choices. Post game, you get an overview of how you shaped the lives of those around you- and you could be in for some post credits guilt (though achievement hunters may just have to grin and bear it). With Yes, Your Grace: Snowfall rapidly approaching, it has yet to be seen what may or may not fall into "cannon" lore, but there is sure to be some based on the trailer. So while you may have chosen poorly in your own run, know that, perhaps, not all is lost. It is still up in the air as to whether prior decisions will impact the plot of the sequel, though for simplicity sake, it perhaps appears they may choose to go with a more established timeline.In short, Yes, Your Grace is an absolutely unique masterpiece. It weaves together fantastic storytelling, music, and kingdom management in a way that is not too overwhelming or overbearing, keeping itself open to a broad player base. Easy navigation and user interface are a boon, and it's easy to find yourself caught in a loop of "Just One More Day". Characters are a sheer delight, each being very unique, making them fun to learn about and how they fit into the world. Brave at Night has done a beautiful job in bringing together some of the best elements of a whole array of genres, that is well worth looking into. In doing so, they've truly created something wonderful and unique that is well worth the price tag, and time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to sound odd, but this game needs more choices. Funny, right, from a game that's literally based on the choices you make? But you're railroaded by a story that doesn't allow you to actually make any real difference. You're forced to complete quests for your family, with no way to actually say no. Trying to end the day gives a line such as "I need to talk to X." Why won't it let me marry my daughter off to a king? Oh, only the right king that the game says is okay? Is it because if I decided to, I don't know, instead of having a big stupid battle, meet with the 'barbarians' and discuss peace? But the game doesn't let you do that. It's a game that's too focused on telling its own narrative to let you actually do what you want to do. Is it a *good* game? It's ok. It's well-written, the music is lovely, and despite the simplistic art style, it is quite pretty. But you're railroaded into a storyline that could very easily be subverted by making better decisions than the game allows. It's honestly like a graphic novel with a little resource management sim attached, not fully fledged choices and decisions. Also the whole Maya somehow living right in the capital since almost the beginning just doesn't make sense. The entire plot surrounding her and her family has a million holes despite the railroad they want to send you down.Spoilers: You can't save your daughterYou can't save King TalysIvo is a prick.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to be able to recommend this game, but for most folks, I can't. The good: WONDERFUL soundtrack, beautiful art design. It's really what got me to buy the game in the first place. The storytelling was well done and even evoked some genuinely emotional moments. The core resource management system is fun, though not terribly challenging. The bad: A bit short - I won the game in under 9 hours. The game is definitely on rails and you definitely feel it. I haven't done a second play through yet, but based on what I've seen from others, your decisions only really result in some flavor differences or a fail state. It is not a kingdom management game like I had hoped. Also, the choice to play as either a male of female ruler would have been nice. Gender roles are very prominent in this game where they don't need to be. The one same sex relationship represented in the game is depicted as exceptional - again, unnecessary. Its a fantasy world with made up places, people, magic, etc, but for some reason we still need traditional gender/sexual orientation rules for it to make sense? I think the developers had good intentions and did not mean to alienate anyone. I think we just need to understand that recreating a society with built in gender bias without addressing those issues from multiple perspectives can be alienating. We ask ourselves why more women aren't playing our games while continuing to make games that glorify men. That said, I think the developers show a lot of promise. I personally don't regret buying the game at full price because I feel like it will help fund future projects that realize the vision they had. Otherwise, I would wait until this goes on sale and pick it up for closer to $10.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful little game with a healthy balance between story and having to manage your resources as well as your 3 daughters, wife, and advisors for the coming wars. Managed to play through it all in around 4 hours and it left me a little emotional at the end, especially as I was fully invested in the fates of my family. Can't wait to see what they bring in the sequel, this game is a must play for anyone who loves a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: A resource management game with a great story? Sign me up!Well, I am quite late to the party when it comes to this game. With me only being able to learn about this game when it got recommended to me on Steam. And I must say 15 bux well spent! I loved playing through this game. With me being able to use my visual novel choice experience to get the best ending on my first try! I loved the story very much, had a lot of fun with the characters, and was able to use in-game hints and my writing experience to figure out certain character moments and plot twists, Overal a great experience to play through! _childDocuments_.name: Yes, Your Grace

_childDocuments_.review: This little game is a masterpiece!From the gorgeous pixel art to the sublime soundtrack, from the well written plot to all the little choices left to the player, from the humour of some dialogues to the dire atmosphere of the war accurately represented. Everything was absolutely brilliant and masterfully crafted.The one aspect that falls a bit flat compared to the others is the replay value. Choices you make in this game either makes you lose (easy to avoid) or don't drastically change the outcome of the playthrough. The main story will basically be the same, no matter what you decide to do. This is not apparent in the first run, as the game deceives you and makes you think that every decision counts.Despite the limited replay value, I found the first run to be filled with joy and decisions to make and stuff to do and things to watch. Consider it a beautiful 7 hour-ish game. I just finished it and I really wish there was a sequel available right now!  Great work to the development team, eagerly looking forward future games!

_childDocuments_.review: To preface this, I had long been interested in this game after seeing some youtubers play it, and I, being the medieval nut I am, decided to pick this up. I'm glad I did.To begin, the pixel art was most excellent; the animations felt fluid, and I personally liked the realistic and yet distinctly fantasy art direction. The castle was easy to understand the layout of, though I would have liked to see a bit more direction on how to advance the weeks along, as it was not immediately obvious. Perhaps I missed a brief explanation, but even a small popup when all the activities available during the first week ended would be harder to potentially miss.On the note of the story, I very much liked it. I binged the story for nearly seven hours nonstop. That being said, the story is compact; not in a bad way, mind, as there are a lot of choices, but I did find a few loose ends to the plot I would have liked to see explored more thoroughly. Spoilers will be marked at the end, if I mention any. Regardless, I found the characters and their plight to be very interesting and thought-provoking, albeit difficult to work through at times. On a larger scale, though, I find the plot to be rushed in sections, namely in world building. I had a hard time figuring out where nobles were and their relationships with one another, as there is no marker on the map to show any interior borders amongst the fiefdoms. Some borders and possibly a portrait or name tag of the lord governing said territory would go a long way towards making the first part easier to approach intuitively. I personally felt that many of the lords and other kings were merely a means to an end, rather than living entities in this world, which is a shame, because the mythological elements were very enjoyable. This could simply be a case of nitpicking things I like, but I felt like more could have been done.On that subject, the lords all had the start of character and placement in the world, but after the first part they ceased to hold much importance. What began as a game of juggling politics, resource management, and population happiness, devolved into a mildly diverting game of, 'collect the resources'. With nobles 'locking' into their opinion of you very quickly, and no means of swaying them in either direction later on except for one case, I felt that a big opportunity to flesh out the nobles you chose was left on the table. I genuinely wanted to know more about the nobles and how they would react to various things happening in the plot, either for or against you, and influenced by your decisions. There was one moment when I thought that was going to happen, and one of my lords was going to betray me and turn their soldiers over to the other side, but after a single scene, it was never brought up again.Even if that was not implemented, I felt that a bit more could also have been done with the micromanagement. I frequently came across cases where I wished to be able to hire more agents. While only one of each type is sufficient for the game balance, my adviser spoke a few times on hiring more agents, and I wanted to make use of that, but could not. If that is not an intended feature, that bit of dialogue confused me greatly, and I wasted time trying to figure out how to hire more agents that, to my knowledge, could not be obtained. Granted, the agents are good enough as-is, but rewarding players who master the resources quickly with a bonus agent would certainly not go awry, either. The drains on resources that are already in place would be more than sufficient to prevent, say, two generals from being overpowered in my mind. On another, related tack, while the peasant management was very nice overall, I would have loved to see a bit more in the way of consequences for your choices. Perhaps a population stat that allows some events to reduce population and others to increase it would have added some more complexity.On the subject of the resource management, I personally found it a small challenge to get right, but lacking in some respects in regards to depth. I would have liked the bank to increase the due payment after giving out the chosen resource every time you used that same resource, making using the bank as a crutch not very viable. Moving on to characters: I really liked the royal family for the most part. I felt that some of the decisions and reasoning skills were a bit beyond the ages involved, but I can suspend my judgement in that sense because it was reasonable enough considering their wealth and higher education. I would have liked to see more personality in my agents and seeing more of their personalities would have been quite interesting beyond the final stages of the game alone.Finally, I was confused about the mythology; is this a case similar to Poland and Lithuania in the medieval period when they're neighbors but one is monotheistic and the other is polytheistic, or is it a case where both are pagan in nature but distinctions are important? The game does not answer this, and that somewhat disappoints me, because I was genuinely curious about a lot of aspects of the world that the king should probably know at least a bit about, but never go explained.In conclusion, I recommend this game if you like pixel art, excellent music, and decisions that can legitimately have you stand up from your seat and pace around wile agonizing over the decisions available to you. The art direction is fantastic for this game, and I absolutely love it. The plot, while short, is compelling and has a good punch to it for its length. At the current sale price, I would say it's worth it. I got seven hours out of it for less than what I'd pay to see a move less than half the length in a theater, and it's worth it to see the plot unfold in my opinion. I only hope the developers add to it in future, as this world has a lot of untapped potential.*Spoilers Below*As for cons, I did run into a couple of bugs while playing. The first one was with the Dragonslayer and the Captain; when the captain is killed, I got to trigger forgiving his killer twice as opposed to once, giving me another set of his forces and possibly a boost to his per-week resource bonuses as well, though I did not check this carefully.The second is a minor bug which left the conversation crystals lingering over buildings I had already spoken with, leaving me wondering if I had made a mistake in the dialogue tree somewhere. Eventually I gave up and continued the story, as there were no more dialogue options, simply a small glitch.*End Spoilers*

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR +++ immersive story+ bit of plot twists never hurt anybody+++ lovable characters+++ stays true to it's time period+ inclusion of minority characters+ Fantastic soundtrack+ Nice graphics, color palette doesn't hurt eyes (also great art)+ bit challenging+ the way characters talk (full voice acting might've made this less interesting)+ Cedani, my 'lil pumpkin- might be a bit linear for some- At times you might be a bit unsure what exactly you need to do ie. click- the scarf (oh god, please no)'Yes, Your Grace' is a great game for you if you like choice-based and management games. The game stays true to history and doesn't shy away from very real things like war and child-marriages but it does have some fantasy elements, which is done in a believable way by mixing it with folklore. Many games have a problem with creating characters the player actually cares about, 'Yes, your Grace' does this well. Right off the bat you're thrown into the chaotic duty of being a ruler in a kingdom amidst war, helping or dismissing peasants and finding allies while keeping an eye on your resources. Desperate for help, some come to you with bigger problems - others because their potatoes keep on vanishing. You have to keep in mind though, that some of your petitioners might be lying and it will cost you a lot. If this isn't enough, you have another duty of keeping your family afloat as the father of three smart daughters- all the while trying to secure an heir with your Queen. The story will pull you in and you're going to have a hard time making choices, for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: While somewhat engaging and with pleasing visuals, Yes Your Grace falls short both mechanically and as a story. It features opaque decisions that render choice largely irrelevant. This is reinforced mechanically by the agent and petitioner system. Petitioners are presented linearly and choices about their requests must be made immediately, meaning that you never know even the immediate context of the choice, or what you might be giving up by making it. If you promise one of your few agents to a petitioner and the very next petitioner also requires their services, the choice to not help has already been made for you. It is a shame that it is not possible to hear multiple petitions before making any decision, which would lead to potentially more interesting choices between two comparable options. Instead you are almost always forced to either act or not act, where acting means that any subsequent decisions are often rendered pointless - not in my opinion an interesting dynamic.All of the above leads the player down a pretty narrow path in terms of mechanical impact, and sadly this lack of depth carries over to the story. We gain no real sense of who important characters are, and even when time is spent with them they lack depth and development. Aurelia - arguably the person with the most important relationship the players character - is reduced to an anxious mother the majority of the game and has little to discuss with her partner. The daughters, while often charming, are similarly one note. All of the agents lack any story dialogue of any kind, despite being the characters we interact with most mechanically.It is possible I was so disappointed with Yes, Your Grace because I have just come from playing two similar games that excelled both mechanically and as stories - Roadwarden and Return of the Obra-Dinn - so if you have been enjoying Yes, Your Grace or are looking for something in a similar style with more emphasis on complex choices, deduction, and depth of characters, I would strongly recommend both.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game that does what it claims with surprisingly distinguishable and likeable characters. Throughout the game a quite predictable but relateable story unfolds that makes the approximately 8 hours of playtime fly by fast. Overall, it is more a storytelling game than a strategy one and you will sometimes feel that you would either like to decide some things that you already forsee a bit earlier or that you would like to decide things just a tad later. Unfortunately it isn't possible to hear all people first and decide then.Storytelling and character-depth wise it reminded me of The Banner Saga. Although you can decide upon a lot of things, sometimes it seems the story processes the quite same, one way or the other, which is my biggest critique. Also the feminism lurking here and there feels kind of displaced in a more or less medieval story. One more slight critique is the pricing. Though the game clearly has a lot of charme and details, the full price feels a bit much for 8 hours of gameplay in a - yet very beautifully done - pixel graphic.  I still highly recommend it as an interactive and entertaining novel, with a clear risk of failure.

name: The Almost Gone
detailed_description: Poised between life and death, isolated and alone, you must unravel the poignant truths that led to your fate. Dig beneath the beautifully rendered façades and interiors of an ordinary suburban lifestyle to discover a contemporary tale crafted by an award-winning author. Piece together this compelling story by revealing objects and memories, and decipher these clues to reveal more of the story and its secrets. From your own home to eerily deserted streets, beautiful apartment blocks to abandoned hospitals, you must search forensically for clues and the path forwards . Each new revelation takes you that one step closer to understanding, and to the people and places that surrounded you, in your all too short life. Why are you here? Why are you trapped? Will you ever get home? Experience an emotional and immersive story written by award-winning author Joost Vandecasteele Explore every nook and cranny of each beautifully rendered diorama Play through five compelling chapters , with each revealing more secrets and twists that will lead you to the truth From an unassuming sitting room, to a tent in a forest, from a police car in a tree to an abandoned hospital, a hauntingly different suburbia is yours to discover

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is I would actually give the game a  if I could. Nevertheless, I decided to give it a positive rating with a few less stars because I really liked the game and the puzzles. However, I would still recommend you, if you are interested in the game at all, to read through a few of the other reviews, explicitly the negative reviews, because I believe that the game is only suitable for real point & click fans who also like puzzles that require a lot of thinking and the story can also be of secondary importance.Or you can just try the demo version where you can play the first chapter.If you can get involved with the game and the reduced design, you can expect a tragic and graphically reduced life story of a girl in five chapters.At the beginning you explore the house where the girl grew up. The pink rooms, which are small dioramas, can be rotated in all directions. An essential function of the game, since the different perspectives only reveal further small details or puzzles that are relevant for progress. Even though the controls of the game are relatively simple, I had a lot of fun figuring out how to get to the next room. The environmental puzzles used for this are very well coordinated and intertwine with the story.The pastel pink tones at the beginning become increasingly dark and threatening as the game progresses and you only gradually learn something about the tragic events of the family. The story is, I personally would have found it much more interesting without the sometimes cryptic fragments of history, exciting and leaves a lot of room for interpretation.However, that's my subjective opinion and as far as the story goes, they differ quite a bit.The further the story progresses, the more often you have to cross the sometimes barren rooms and repeat certain things several times in order to progress, and the circumstances of the protagonist are consequently connected with the environment and the puzzles. Sometimes it can be really lengthy and annoying to be sent through the same rooms over and over again until you finally find or combine the right item to progress. But as long as you remain curious and can absorb the increasingly dense atmosphere of the game, it makes up for it all the more.And in case you really get stuck, you can use the walkthrough linked in the game that is available for each act or this .In addition to the music and effect settings, the menu also offers the option of changing the rotation at the push of a button and adjusting the in-game text size from 100% to 125% and 150%.The achievements work flawlessly and most of them are obtained in-game. Unfortunately, there are one or the other pointless achievement that you can still do without much effort. Check out the achievements beforehand.There are currently no trading cards.Review date: September 12, 2022✅ Simple art design✅ exciting story✅ good game mechanics✅ interesting puzzles❌ too much backtracking❌ partly fiddly controls

_childDocuments_.review: This is a positive review in name only. If this is on sale, and you're a real point-and-click fan, then sure. For everyone else, stay away.The puzzles on display aren't particularly inventive. The visuals are functional, but not particularly evocative. The story touches on some very serious subjects, but does nothing with these issues aside from referencing them. This kind of makes the story feel... cheap? If that makes sense? It's emotional, without real depth.  Sound design works, without being top shelf.This isn't bad, but  exists in the same space and price range, and that's a bloody masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: is an interesting mystery set in a minimalist design. You view portions of a room, get to rotate it to look at it from each angle, and discover how to advance through the five acts by interacting with the rooms in each act. It's to the game's merit how they manage to keep the puzzles as varied as they did. Sure, there seems to always be a "find the key to unlock this door" mechanic but thanks to the other puzzles and the varied settings throughout the acts, with different color palettes, you don't feel you're doing the same thing over and over again.You might be wondering by now why I don't recommend this game. I think a game is only as good as its story and  not only fails with its ending, but falters throughout the acts with its silent protagonist. There are heavy (and some heavily implied) themes of death and abuse starting from the get-go which never fully develop. The protagonist sees every innocuous object as negative. An example, a teddy bear turns into a teddy bear the protagonist couldn't name herself because it had a name already. The laptop she received from her family wasn't something she asked for. Every object turns into an object of oppression or emotional pain. By act five, I can't say I learned as much as I wanted to about the protagonist's family all the while being annoyed at the person I was playing as. Maybe it's kept obtuse to make it more generally relatable. More importantly, there's no personal growth in the protagonist, so by the time act five just ups and leaves and the protagonist reaches her conclusion, I felt it came out of  and was entirely unearned. I felt like I earned it more than the protagonist did by solving puzzle after puzzle, especially act four's visuospatial maze (okay, it's not that bad, but I suck at direction). An ending may be anti-climactic, but an ending should never feel unearned. I felt like  was trying to be that typical indie game with heavy themes, but it didn't know what to do with itself. It's a shame because the graphic design and puzzle execution are lovely, but at full price, I can't justify the 2-3 hour game length, unless you don't really care about story or character. Maybe get it at a heavy discount.

_childDocuments_.review: The very first moment I looked at the screenshots of The Almost Gone, I thought it must be a great game. It looked nice, even lovely, and I was convinced by the number of positive reviews. Moreover, for the game like this one, there are already many good examples. Too many trust credits to give, probably, but what can go wrong with a little puzzle game? I'm not going to question the idea of it – actually, it's kinda good – but the implementation is the thing which leaves a lot to be desired. There are, of course, many good puzzles. However, I can say absolutely the same thing about the bad ones, too. And what makes me especially sick of this game is the amount of empty rooms. There are SO many places that are filled with the dialogs which are useless both for solving the puzzles and the story itself as well as the rooms which you just have to pass by because there is nothing to do at all. Considering the fact that there is already too much backtracking here.Vice versa, in some rooms, there are round boxes appear to interact with. Or, to be more clear, the player may think it's implied to be interacted with since the game gives some experience of successful interaction and combining items in these boxes. Nothing happens, though, when you try to interact with them. At best, you'll just see another popup dialog.As for me, I see no good in the concept of developing two different types of interactions with items, both of which end up with just a dialog box. While the first one doesn't confuse the player, another one forces the player, left without ideas of what to do next, to run around empty rooms and look for clues to solve the thing which doesn't even require solving.The second thing is the speed of animation – if you ask me, it's too slow. I'd even say it's extremely slow for the game with the rotation set up as the major mechanic. What you can see on the gifs in the description of the game is about twice or even triple multiplied speed of what we actually have in-game. But it's not only about rotation, since the game requires a lot of movement between the rooms. The animation speed of passing by through the rooms is not any faster. No matter what you do and where you are, in fact, all the animations are slow and a bit fiddly. The person who is able to bear more than 30-40 minutes in a game session without a break is a real hero for me, since I myself couldn't stand it. Oh, and as for the time... The Almost Gone has 3 time-related achievements, but it takes no time to start hating them right away. It would be too easy to minimize the game's window and do something else instead, so, of course, you can't do this, since when you come back, you'll see that the game is paused. You see, it actually gets paused any time you click somewhere else but the game's window. And to get the achievements, you need to play, not to stay idling in the pause menu. The next thing is the plot itself. All in all, it becomes almost impossible to understand the story in the situation like that when there are too much things of no sense. It's clear that something bad has happened, but there are too many unnecessary details that are randomly scattered around the map. It's not surprising that all together it becomes a real chaos that the player is unlikely to be able to solve. All the mystery around the story is superfluous when the game cannot tell the story. It would be better if there were no mysticism, but smoother storytelling and controls as well as less rooms and more connected puzzles. I genuinely wanted to like this game. The way it looks is just awesome. However, the way of its implementation is so awful that I can say nothing good about the game overall except – once again – the visual part of it. Some good puzzles with the pipes in the hospital weren't worth it since it's not even the major part of the game. Even if you are able to get used to slow animations, there is no way one can get used to endless clicking and the wild guesses. Once I've got so confused that I started to think maybe it's something about me, maybe it's just me who doesn't like the genre. And yet no, there are so many great point-and-click games out there and so many games I enjoyed. The Almost Gone, however, feels like there are just clicks, and no point.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: I have a problem with that game. I went through the story, took care of the puzzle, didn't try to find the hidden achievements etc. And while it's a pretty game, it fits better as a $4.99 mobile game than a $16 Steam game.There is a story, but it's really short and doesn't go into details, there are puzzles, but you just have to spend 5mn checking the items you gathered or the room itself to find the answer, there are pretty rooms, but so little that you will be done checking them all within an hour if you don't AFK every now and then as I did. So yeah, this game just lacks of content and story while the price is really high and I got to the end wondering what will the next chapter be about rather than feeling it really was the end of it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is a fairly simple puzzle game with in depth storytelling hidden in plain sight. The details of the story can be easily missed but a more observant and curious player will discover a beautiful and somber tale about life, death, and loneliness. And you'll soon find yourself emotionally connected with characters who you'll never see nor meet.The isometric design coupled with large blank backdrops and small scaled environments creates a sense of loneliness in a clever way. The delicate color scheme masks the dark undertones of the narrative. And the lack of music, with the exception of low ambient background noise and the occasional haunting melody, adds to the atmosphere by making it feel almost too quiet.A short but enjoyable game to pass the time on a quiet starry evening by yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the idea of piecing together a story through dioramas as though I'm peering into a dollhouse, however, no matter how hard I looked, there was only ever the vague outline of a story that emerged. Allowing for speculation and leaving room for interpretation are one thing, but The Almost Gone manages to give scattered snippets of detail amidst puzzles that feel very disjointed and boring; it gives the impression that Joost Vandecasteele doesn't know the story either and never bothered to actually flesh it out himself. 2.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: A not-entirely-unfun game, but the gameplay mechanics are pretty infuriating. The environment with which you interact is shockingly small, even in full screen, so changing perspective and clicking on items can involve guesswork and precision. It's hard to see what's even available to click, much less actually finding the right object. I had to look up the developer's own walkthrough a couple times I got stuck, only to learn that something I thought I had already clicked or wasn't even clickable was the reason I got stonewalled. If the square of space you're looking at was twice as big (which would absolutely be possible, as it takes up just the center of the screen), it would be far easier to orient yourself.Most of the puzzles were pretty cool, none of them being too difficult, but challenging enough that you feel good about yourself for figuring it out. And the loose narrative thread throughout the game was good, too. It's pretty much all below the surface of the gameplay, but you don't need to be a genius to follow it.As far as indie games go, it's above average. $10 isn't unreasonable to charge for the length of the game, especially considering its short-ish length and clear level of effort put into it by the devs, but I bought this when it was only $1.99, and I got exactly that price's worth of enjoyment from it. Other players might enjoy it more than I did, though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: it's not a bad game , but still maybe not worth your money and timei would leave a neutral review if i could but the achievements tip the balance in the favor of a negative one , so that's what you get .wait in a room for 30 minutes ?? and one for just having the game open for 5 hours ...i guess they wanted to artificially inflate the play-time the game actually takes like 2,5 hours to complete some of the puzzles were pretty good , but nothing groundbreakingit was more difficult to figure out what things are clickable than to solve any actual puzzlesif you think the game looks nice , try the free demo ! then you can make your own decisions whether to buy ityou probably should know that the ending is kind of ?? weak ?? as well , maybe i missed something crucial , but it sure feels like the developers just couldn't figure out how to end the game and just gave up

_childDocuments_.review: Another game where I wish there was a middle option to choose when writing a review. This game was okay. The art style is cool, the puzzles interesting and the music is appropriately haunting - the story is where I have a problem. The game tries to take on some really heavy themes, but it just falls flat for the most part. If it's on sale, go for it. If not, I wouldn't bother.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game until the ending - or mostly lack of it. It ended up being heavy and emotionally exhausting without any sort of release. Generally I really love games that give you hints of the full story here and there along the game, and then in the end you can see if you guessed correctly. It would've made up for the backtracking, going back and forth between rooms and even trying to memorize the traumatic hints. But no when there was no ending, no closure, not even a diary entry, it was not worth the time and heavy feeling on my chest.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: There's just something not quite right with this game. I like the interactive block rooms you can spin them round to find little hidden secrets and clues.As point and click puzzles go it's good. I always have a soft spot for them since I grew up with games like Discworld.Near the end I think act four was a lot of literally going round in circles.
