Instead I got end credits and I still don't really know what happened.I don't know about other players but it's just left me really disappointed if anyone can explain to me the actual story that would be great.So would not recommend it builds interest and leaves you disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me unbelievably angry. It is a story driven point&click puzzle game that severely lacks in both story and puzzle aspects. On top of that gameplay length is synthetically prolonged by maze like levels and tediously searching for easy to miss items.If it had anything decent enough going for it apart from its beautiful presentation, i would at least count The Almost Gone as an average game but alas, it doesn't.Not worth your time or money.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are so-so. Nothing revolutionary. It's just hard to invest myself because of that and because of the lackluster "story" that's more just randomly depressing while trying to be deep. On top of that, the achievements are ridiculous. Normally short games like this use achievements to add a little spice, but these are blatant attempts to keep you playing longer than you need to for no real reason.Example (these are literally most of the not story-auto achievements):Stare into the telescope for two minutes.Play the game twice.Spend five hours in the game (Why?? Just leave it running in the background, I guess. So fun).Spend more than 30 minutes in Emily's room (again, what fun leaving the game running in the background for no reason other than to get an achievement).It is a creative concept, but I wouldn't recommend this even on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I'd quickly recommend something like this, a light point-and-click puzzle storytelling affair with a simple style and smooth gameplay. But after playing it - twice - there are a number of elements that bother me enough to ruin any enjoyment of the story. 1. I completed the entire game in just over an hour and a half, and that includes some fruitless clicking around the first level for ten minutes because I was overthinking the first puzzle. However there's an achievement for playing the game again (despite there being no additional content) and one for simply having the game running for 5 hours. I really can't think of any reason for such achievements except to blatantly pad out users' total Steam playtime for statistics sake. It's deeply irritating. 2. While some of the environmental storytelling is beautiful, the effect is spoiled quickly by most of the other attempts at environmental (and more direct) storytelling that are about as subtle as Sharknado. There's an excuse to be made that the levels are supposed to be emotional rather than physical landscapes, projections of more subtle feelings, but that gets muddled because sometimes the narration suggests that some of the extreme elements are real. "Muddled" is a good word for the storytelling overall. We're not given many answers (at least as far as I can tell, and I'm usually fairly generous with interpreting vague hints) and that makes the use of highly disturbing content feel more like shock value than storytelling. The levels open with an indication of where we are in the timeline, but sometimes those statements just seem wrong; in particular the apartment level, which says "30 years ago" even though it initially reflects the house contemporary to what the young narrator remembers recently and then flashes back to memories that seem much older than 30 years. These kinds of issues stand out even more on the second achievement-demanded runthrough. Overall I don't know what I'm supposed to take from this game's story other than "sometimes people are just terrible and they make everyone around them suffer," and I don't think that's the intended message. 3. There's a deliberate low-detail high-contrast art style at work, and while I appreciate the dramatic effect and emotional suggestions - the living spaces being washed out and colorless, then suddenly being plunged into shadow - it makes the game VERY frustrating to play in places. There were spots where I really wasn't sure what I was looking at or what I was trying to click. A game like this desperately needs a brightness or contrast slider to help make sure players are experiencing the most atmosphere they can while still being able to see the game. TL;dr, skip this game. Either go play a point-and-click that gets the story right, like Last Day of June, or an actual puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful art and sound for a two or three hours tale about a girl that is remembering her own past.This is sad story that shows us how some tragedies of your relatives could affect your life. Developers seem to left the meaning of the tree house up to you, so I don't understand very well the end. However, if it's true what i undestood, that end is a litlle bit dreadful.The game is a point-n-click adventure where you have to rotate the stages to find ítems and clues to solve all coherent and logical puzzles. The game has achivements but not trading cards.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: Mehh. While I didn't expect much I am still disappointed by this. I am not a huge fan of point& click games so I expected not to be a huge fan of the gameplay/ puzzles but was very excited for the story...The puzzles are mediocre and very unintuitive ones at that. A lot of going back and forth to solve some of them. Many objects blend in with the other things you cannot interact with, which ends up in a random clicking until you eventually find something. The controlls in general are iffy and feel more like a mobile game. Navigating the maps is annoying and even though there is a "map" i never had a sense of where i was or where i wanted to go. The maps/rooms do look very pretty though and the music was quite nice as well to be fair.But the story... you get random snippits when clicking around a room and i am guessing that you can miss a good bit of it. You kinda jump around in the timeline (between 30 years in the past and some years into the future), which makes it even more confusing. I ended up playing the story twice and after that i was still non the wiser as to what the story was effectively.And after all of that mediocre content there are the achievements, the biggest disappointment of all. I quite like trying to get them as often they make you try different things or try to explore everything. And then there are those that are just trying to unneccessarily expand the playtime. The Almost Gone sadly belongs to the latter. There are 3 or 4 achievements that just need you to idle at certain points in the game (between 2 and 30 minutes!). You are also required to play for 5 hours. If there was enough content that wouldn't be too bad but I finsished 2 playthroughs in 2,5 hours.I got this game in a bundle so I'm not too mad but it's definitely not worth the full price (or anything that is not a heavy discount).
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: This is yet another situation where I wish I could give a rating that wasn't positive or negative; however, I have decided to go with a thumbs-down approach this time around. The primary reasoning behind my choice is threefold: 1) the achievement that requires simply letting the game idle for thirty minutes in the opening room, 2) the achievement that requires simply letting the game idle for FIVE HOURS, and 3) the achievement that requires replaying the game a second time when there is absolutely no replay value and the story isn't going to get any better on a second run. Furthermore, the game takes approximately two hours to beat on a first run, less on a replay if you remember the solutions and skip unnecessary puzzles, so you quite literally have no choice but run the game (and you can't shrink it or click off the window) for at least two more hours after completing a second run. Any modicum of positive emotions I had from playing were immediately nullified by this choice. Okay, I actually have more substantive reasons to give a negative rating, but I'm still pretty incensed about those ridiculous achievements.Now, for a critique of the game itself: The story is "okay" at best, plodding at worst. The real tragedy is that it seemed to have great potential that was then deflated with the sad whimper of a balloon by the fifth chapter. While I have my own ideas about what happened and can admire using understatement and environmental storytelling, I do not think simply ending the game without any kind of narrative resolutions is good writing. The story didn't really do anything compelling with its subject matter either. Yes, it's dark and disturbing. We've got generational trauma, substance abuse, dead animals, possibly murdered humans, suicide, mental disorders, child abuse, etc. You know what else, unfortunately, has some, if not all, of these things? Most people lives. Simply having distressing material chockablock in your story doesn't make it good, even if it is realistic as in real to life. Our singular protagonist, Emily, has no development. I know almost nothing about her except that she was abused and possibly murdered, and that's just disgusting to be honest. No victim of abuse wants their entire personality to be summed up as "abused person," just as someone who was murdered deserves to be known for more than being a murder victim. If this is supposed to be her reexamining her life post-death, then...where is the introspection? Where is the meaningful reflection as she is coming to terms with her death and the events surrounding it? It's cheap to be like, "Hey, guys, guess what? She was actually dead the whole time~!" Yet, Emily herself never seems to gain clarity on what happened to her either. I've read some really interesting fan theories about what actually happened, and some are wildly imaginative and actually good enough to make me like the plot. However, I still think extending chapter five even a little bit or providing an ending cutscene--even with just words--was warranted.Despite my issues with the plot, I thought the art style was utterly lovely and I enjoyed the mechanics of exploring the dioramas. (This was actually what drew me to the game in the first place.) I will say I loathed navigating them after a while--for the love of all things holy, let me turn the room and move between rooms with my keyboard--but it was a neat and clever idea. The music was fine, though nothing to write home about, EXCEPT the music in chapter three, which I absolutely loved. The puzzles were enjoyable. I can't say I would have wanted to deal with them for several more hours, especially after the headache of chapter four, but the novelty didn't really wear off before I finished the game, so that was good. All in all, it's not a horrible game, but it's not a great game either.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: The clicking around part really turns me off, as much as I enjoy the beautiful cube-shaped room designs, clicking back and forth with half a second in between just pains me to death. It's one of those games where I feel like I  a lot but didn't  much. I do appreciate the method of storytelling: the cute design and the depressing plot create a compelling contrast, the indirect telling of the story through objects and places makes the otherwise flat story a bit more interesting to unfold. I think the most memorable part of the game is its visual design, then the storytelling method. But other aspects do fall short for me personally. I do see someone really enjoy this game though, it's just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: I thought it was meh. It's not terrible, but I can't say I liked it. There's no "neutral" rating so I went with "not recommended." The graphics are nice. The puzzles weren't hard, but the backtracking was tedious.  You examine the scenes to find stuff that you will use for puzzles.  You may have to rotate it to find everything.  For navigation, there's a sort of mini grid-type map which indicates your current location, as well as the explored and unexplored areas.  It does not indicate the areas with unsolved puzzles or "landmarks" so you have to note down the square where you're supposed to go back to, or do what I did... go through everything until you find the specific location. I have a terrible sense of direction so I kinda got lost in the bigger maps. Going through everything to look for a specific location became boring after a while (I was literally falling asleep).  About the story, well... uh... some terrible stuff happened, and the story ends. For achievements, they're not hard to get, but this game has those annoying "spend x minutes/hours doing this thing" achievements.  On the positive side, the worst was the one where you have to play the game for 5 hours.  At least it's not one of those obnoxious "play this 2-hour game without any replay value for 40 hours" achievements. My first playthrough took more than 3 hours, and the second one (using a walkthrough) took around 20 minutes.  To unlock that last achievement, I just let the game run (making sure that it's the active window and not paused) while I did some chores.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: The minimalist art style, and atmosphere are nice enough.But the HYPER cynical protagonist drove me nuts. Is it really necessary to look for the worst side in every detail and memory?? I realise they are dealing with some stuff, but it's very 1-dimensional.The puzzles were ok, but varied wildly in their difficulty and level of abstractness. It doesn't help that it took 15 minutes just to find out I had a hidden off-screen inventory. That would have been helpful to know!! Navigating the house, and spinning things around was more often a hurdle rather than a cool mechanic. That part wasn't so bad. But I was already frustrated by other elements - so that contributed to my overall declining enjoyment.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is a smart. well made and surprisingly dark, for a puzzle game. It has some mysterious elements and as I venture on, I got to know more about the character's past and family. With 5 chapters, the game is relatively short and can be completed in one sitting. The graphics is beautiful and the controls are smooth too, which is great as you will be rotating the room scenes throughout the game. Definitely a fun puzzle game, recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I found it a fun game but pretty short.Gameplay: I tried controller but mouse felt more comfortable for me. The controls are pretty simple. Rotate by Left click and dragging left/right. Left most to select. Right click for inventory. Left click and drag items to combine.Puzzles: Mostly straight forward. Only a few had me stumped where I just kinda brute forced it with guesses.Story: This game is not one I'd recommend for everyone as it deals with some heavy themes of family abuse. It this is a triggering topic for you. Then avoid this game as it the theme grows stronger throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: While a point and click puzzler isn't anything new, there is something quite charming about how it's delivered, using tiny dioramas that need to be twisted and turned.That does lead to suboptimal pathfinding and orientation, but the puzzles are good enough to overcome that.Keep in mind that the subject matter, some sort of family mental health dream-like drama, isn't for everyone. If it triggers you, stay away. I just found it a bit heavy-handed and nonsensical, it's not really for me, but the game was good enough that I plowed through the narrative.It's a short one at 2.5 hours, but if the subject matter and point and click puzzle games interest you, go ahead.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: I played the game for the puzzle aspect in which it was rather enjoyable, however, the actual story and such of the game was not as much so. The game attempts to dive into the topic of exploring troubled parents with a very dark tone throughout. A lot of the atmosphere created bordered the line of horror which was quite interesting to me. All of this was alright until the game proceeded to lack in any resolution. Additionally, having 100% the game, I would say the animations and loading transitions become extremely tediously long to move between areas. The achievements are odd in that the hardest one to complete is in fact just leaving the game open for a total of 5 hours. Entered the game with enthusiasm, definitely did not leave with the same level of it.TL;DR: Alright puzzle, bleh story, and tedious to 100%
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice little puzzle game with a pretty sad story. It ended pretty abruptly, leaving you with quite a few questions. I did like the game mechanics and it looks very pretty. The achievements are a bit dumb tho; you need to play it twice (so you can just breeze through it since you can remember all the solutions to the puzzles and skip about 70% of the game) and there's an achievement to spend 5 hours in a game which takes 3 hours for the first playthrough.Overall definitely worth the 5 bucks for an evening or two of relaxed puzzling.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: Around 50% of the puzzles are sensible, but the half that are not, and spoils a otherwise brilliant plot. I kept wanting to unpack more of the story as I went.I could write up more detail about what the game is like, but ultimately it was not my cup of tea. Not a place I'm likely to dwell long. It felt very limiting and hemmed in. A lack of soundscape is the other big thing that killed this title. All really a pity since the level design and game concept are great, the puzzles and their clues just lacked progression, I felt the whole way, "how much further to go?". Very flat.For more like it see
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoyed the visuals of the game and found the puzzles to be very approachable, I finished the game feeling confused and unsatisfied by the ending of the story. I'm personally not opposed to including dark topics in a game as long as they're handled well and contribute to a larger narrative. However, it felt like dark topics like alcoholism, abuse, parental issues, psychiatric mistreatment, etc. were included to "make" a story that wasn't there. Given the lack of resolution to tie all the pieces together, I ended the game feeling like I had to hear about these emotional subjects for the entire game for seemingly no reason and I won't be recommending to others despite finishing the game myself.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: While the puzzle mechanics were interesting and varied, it sucked that you couldn't zoom in (leaving it hard to find some clues) and the ending feels far too ambiguous - what should've been open-ended felt more like they didn't have a good way to wrap up the "story," and you're ultimately left unsatisfied.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting concepts, really bad game. It entices you to engage in a pointless story about important issues in life.Story reminds me of Gone Home, except that this one does not resolve. The whole game introduces the characters and then ends. I understand that this character is suffering, but nothing done is of any consequence. Nothing revealed is of any consequence. Some good mechanics are developed and an engaging world is established and then it ends.Especially frustrating is the looming darkness and encroaching tree, which is actually just a mechanic, not actually a character nor antagonist.There is a mysterious final place the character seeks, and it is never tied back to the original references in any way. It remains unclear whether anything actually exists, who actually guides the protagonist, and whether the sanctuary you seek is the same sanctuary as the ones referenced by the other characters. If the sanctuary is a metaphor, there isn't even an attempt to relate it to other concepts.This is clearly a game about depression and mental illness, but at least in other games, like Senua's Sacrifice, the ending gives the actions purpose. At least in other games, like Spiritfarer, the characters resolve. This is a great idea, half-baked.This game tries to make a story, but it's just a series of snapshots of different struggles of a rough childhood. The game should have ditched the story and made it a set of struggle puzzles. [spoilers] I think the character was actually the developers and they just wanted to stop developing the game, which is essentially what the ending was.[/spoilers]This game is better as a puzzle game engine for other developers to use to make games that are worth your time, let alone money.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is pretty and the story topic about generational mental health and how it affects their children is great.The gameplay is simple point and click, most of it isnt too bad, its good that its a short experience, I think first playthrough was about 2 hours.The storytelling is spotty though, hard to keep track of what matters and why the environments look like they do. The ending is terrible as the conclusion is nonsensical.I personally like to get all achievements in these smaller games and for this game, most are easy, but three are only there for game "metrics":Spend 2 minutes looking in a looking glass, spend 30 minutes in the first area, spend 5 hours in the game, but not in a menu, paused or tabbed out. Just to farm "Engagement Time"?It would have been a weak recommendation without the bad achievements. But until they are changed this is a hard no.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: it's good to see more games trying to tackle tough subject matters, but this one didn't work for me.if you want a *well-written* puzzle game about abuse, with a protagonist you can sympathize with instead of be irritated at, I recommend Papo & Yo; that game's incredible.The Almost Gone's visuals and UX are great, and fun, and compelling... but for a story + puzzle game, it had two big issues:* the writing was very quickly irritating. the protagonist comes off as whiny, repetitive, and in many moments actually stupid. this game is trying to talk about very-real and very-important topics, so it's doubly-important that the writing not make the reader want to throttle the protagonist.* the puzzles weren't puzzles: half the time they were too obvious to be puzzling, and the other half of the time they were "keep clicking on stuff until you find the mcguffin"... and failing to find the mcguffin causes you to revisit old interactables, for which you're punished with repeated exposure to the bad writing...I wanted to like this game: I like the visuals, the unique way of exploring the world, and that it's trying to tackle an important subject. but I found the writing and puzzling completely disappointing, with no signs of them getting better. after 1.4 hours (according to Steam) of trying, I stopped. there are many better games out there to play.better, similar-ish games:* Papo & Yo: puzzles, parental abuse, third-person* Firewatch: walking sim, relationship & mid-life crisis, first-person* Sayonara Wild Hearts: action & music, relationships & depression, third-person
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wanted to like this game, I can't say I recommend it.  The puzzles are not super difficult, the aesthetic is very nice, but the story simply doesn't exist.  I have ZERO idea as to what this story is supposed to be about.  The achievements for this game are relatively pointless.  There is one that is achieved by spending 5 hours in the game.  This isn't that long of a game.  To have to sit here with the game idling, wasting time and energy, just to 100% the game is pretty stupid.  Total game play of my first run through was around 2 hours, give or take.  In order to complete achievements, I now need to complete the game again (which is absolutely stupid, as there is NO NEED for a second playthrough. _childDocuments_.review: I wish there was something between thumbs up and down.  I had just recently finished a playthrough of it, and I have mixed feelings.  Conceptually, the game is a unique puzzler as a mechanic and the story always hints at darker things underneath.  I feel like that is where my mixed feelings come in, because much of the darker elements are hidden.  Don't get me wrong, the metaphors and hinted meanings convey a powerful story, it's just that I felt i missed portions of that story during my playthrough.  I read through discussion boards after, and there was a lot of pieces that I clearly missed.  On one occasion, I brute forced a puzzle (which was something you can do, and ended up getting an achievement for guessing). I think for me while I do enjoy puzzle games, I also missed out on a story details that were important for understanding the entire background plot.  By the end, I honestly wasn't sure what I had ultimately experienced.  So it's very hard to recommend this game, because I think this will appeal to a certain high brow audience that will appreciate it's subtle story telling.  But for a general or casual crowd, they may leave the same way I did.  It was different, and unique, but not sure it was worth it.  It's not something I will play again, and I will likely forget it's in my collection.

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone tells the story of a young girl floating between life and death, learning more about herself, her parents and her family. You do this by examining her house, street and other buildings. It reminded me of Gone Home a bit in that sense, because you learn more about people by investigating how they live... without actually seeing those people, ever. In that sense the developers rely on your imagination quite a bit. You have to fill in the blanks and nothing is really spelled out. Gameplay-wise this is a short puzzle game that's light on challenge, but that's the intention since it's more focused on narrative. You get an isometric view of a bunch of diorama's and learn more about the characters by exploring floors and rooms. The subject matter can get a bit intense and heavy, just so you know. The only issue I had was with the ending, it's very abrupt and it didn't feel like I actually finished the game for some reason. But otherwise this is an interesting character-driven game that gives the player a lot of agency in figuring stuff out.

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is a short, artful puzzle game that covers some dark themes, including mental illness, generational trauma, and death. It also does not have a happy ending (at least in my interpretation). So consider that a content warning.The Gameplay: You navigate a series of isometric dioramas, solving puzzles as you explore the protagonist's mental state and family history. The puzzles were not too difficult, but you still need to pay attention, as navigating the dioramas can be disorientating. The achievements are a bit of a negative mark, as a number of them are literal wastes of time: there's no reason to spend 30 minutes in the starting room, for example. I finished the game in 4 hours without rushing or using a walkthrough.The Story: I've noticed that the story is getting mixed reviews from other users, particularly the ending, which many found abrupt and unsatisfying. I didn't feel that way. That's because (spoiler and dark):  The ending does happen abruptly and without any followup, but, as I saw it, the game was clearly leading towards that conclusion.Overall I'd give it maybe a 6-7 out of 10. The gameplay is solid, but could be smoother, the art is pretty but not outstanding, and the intriguing themes never really coalesce beyond vague (though haunting) impressions.
_childDocuments_.name: The Almost Gone

_childDocuments_.review: I wish the recommendation system wasn't so binary because while I'm erring on the side of "don't recommend" I can see that there's a lot of talent and passion behind this project and I'm interested in what Happy Volcano does next. My main complaint about this game is that this felt way more like a proof of concept than a fully fleshed out game. I hate saying that because there's some really great potential with elements of the story and there's real interesting mechanics like traveling through time and going inside smaller and smaller models of one house; but what cool elements there are aren't nearly fleshed out enough and the ending is ultimately unsatisfying in that there's no culmination of anything the story touches on. It felt like a waste of the otherwise really interesting artstyle and novel mechanics. I hope Happy Volcano gets to expand on this subject more and I sincerely hope they improve!

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Being alive is an amazing journey, from the day we’re born to the day of our death. And we each have our own path. The truth is that our paths are heavily influenced, especially in the early stages of our life, by our family and the circumstances that come with each of the individuals in the family unit, from parents to grandparents and sometimes even beyond.  Some will experience sheer happiness, while others will face fear and sadness. The reality is, it’s a bit of both for most of us. In some cases, if the family unit is very dysfunctional, it might take a lifetime for an individual to put the pieces together, just like in The Almost Gone! The Almost Gone is story-rich, point and click puzzle game developed by Happy Volcano and published by Playdigious and X.D. Network Inc. on Steam platform on the 25th of June 2020. The game is also available on Nintendo Switch, the App Store and Google Play.The game consists of five chapters in five different locations, of which you, the narrator, have memories. They are your house, the streets, the apartment (grandparents), the psychiatric hospital and the treehouse.Each of the chapters is made up of a certain number of diorama scenes. The first four chapters are the largest ones, while the last chapter is pretty much the conclusion of the story. As you start the game, you’ll see the first diorama in the middle of your screen, with the content on the floor and the wall in front of you. By clicking and holding on the left button of your mouse while moving it from right to left or vice versa, you’ll be able to see the other sides on the room, as well as items that might have been hidden from the previous angle. By hovering around with your mouse cursor, you’ll be able to interact/search on particular objects when your cursor becomes an eye icon. You’ll know straight away which items you can pick up, and retrieving them from your inventory is very easy. The puzzles are not too difficult and are well-designed. But bear in mind that you need to thoroughly scan each of the rooms as some of the clues/items are well hidden (especially the ones that involve numbers and shapes to open locks). Each diorama will have arrows at the end of some walls, which will indicate to you in which direction you can move to the next room. There is no map indicator in this game, and you will find yourself going around in circles a few times per chapter before having a good grasp of the full area. It would have been nice to have a map in order to see where you are, but to be honest, it’s really not needed. I really enjoyed exploring and rotating each of the rooms and finding clues and objects. And I like the specific colour patterns of each of the chapters, making each of them unique. In terms of gameplay, it will take you around three hours to complete the game.Outstanding graphics and the puzzles are well-designed. The story is pretty good but the game fairly short. In terms of controls, you play the entire game with the mouse. I think the price on Steam is too high for the length of the game; you might play it through a second time to complete all achievements, but apart from that, there is not much replayability.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Great artwork+	Well-designed levels and puzzles+	Interesting story+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	No trading card as yet-	The asking price is a bit high on SteamThe Almost Gone: beautifully presented with well-designed puzzles and a touching story!7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: (Potential light spoilers)This game is very emotional and the backstories of Emily's parents are really heartbreaking, especially seeing what happens to her Mother. The puzzles are actually so well made and thought out, they were extremely fun to work out! Lots of great subtle foreshadowing and little details in the game that reference the story/characters that would be otherwise missed if you don't pay attention. The little quotes that pop up when clicking on items really makes this game immersive and helps the player empathise with Emily. The UX is a bit stiff? I feel like clicking on arrows to other rooms, clicking on objects and the like takes a little while longer to execute than most games. It feels just a bit slower like I'm waiting for things to load fully/ animations to stop before I can click. (Soft spoiler?) There also wasn't much of an ending I was pretty disappointed having gone through 2 acts of intense puzzles only to not really get a solid answer to the stories you've been trying to work out. Maybe that's part of the creators idea as death doesn't ever make any sense. I like to have solid answers and lore to things and this game lets you come up with many different stories of your own as to what happened but some answers from the creator if there are any would be nice :)Regardless, for $13 this game is worth it in my opinion! It's like a dark, intense, advanced version of a point and click puzzle game ;3

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this isn't brilliant, but it is fairly fun and some of the puzzles are quite clever, so it is overall an enjoyable game.-Positives-Gameplay:  Some of the scene rotations can be a little janky (I use a keyboard and mouse), and it's not always 100% clear what you're looking at due to the stylized graphics, but taken as a whole the puzzles are intuitive and straightforward, and absolutely don't all into "galaxy brain" territory, i.e. it all makes sense, and you'll feel pretty clever when you finally figure out the solutions.Graphics:  They're not bad, and I enjoy the low-poly look, especially the highly stylized colour scheme used.  They're not going to win any awards, but they service the story and the atmosphere.But, there is one critical flaw to the game... ....-Negatives-Story/Dialogue:  Maybe this made more sense in the original language, but I doubt it.  Here's the thing, they try so hard to weave this tale of a child from a highly dysfunctional family trying to explore their memories and come to terms with their family's troubles, troubles so bad that at least one of the parents is heavily drugged up and indeed is committed at some point in our narrator's past.  Oh, and there's a creepy black ooze that keeps intruding on things that no doubt represents either the horror of depression (not likely) or the trauma of exploring and uncovering a traumatic past that should remain buried (more likely).       But NONE of it works (well, it does at first before it becomes too bogged down in its elliptical, stylized way of trying to craft a narrative) because the dialogue is so ham-fisted and clumsy and it all becomes just so melodramatic and not realistically framed in the slightest, and by the WTF ending you won't care one wit about the narrator's tragic upbringing.    So.   The game part of this title is fine and can be recommended, but the storyline is pretty poorly written and very little of the "heavy" material actually hits with any emotional impact because of how clumsily and even surrealistically it is presented.  I can ultimately recommend the game, but purely for the puzzles and graphical style.....the less said about the "story" the better.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting narrative puzzle game with a beautiful art style wrapped around a dark story. You navigate through a series of detailed dioramas to find clues, solve puzzles and advance the story of a young girl trapped between life and death. While not always matching the tone of the story, puzzles walk a fine line between too obtuse and too easy. Some more complex ones will definitely induce that trademark “genius” feeling when solved. Depending on how much of the narrative you explore and how smart you are about puzzles, the game’s runtime will be somewhere between 3 and 4 hours. That’s perhaps a bit too short to stomach all the trauma heading your way (the story handles heavy themes such as child abuse, substance abuse, mental illness, quite gracefully), but at the same time the game never outstays its welcome. In the end, it’s an experience well worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: I struggled with whether or not I should give this game a positive or negative review, but ultimately settled on a positive one.  Where the game succeeds, it definitely succeeds.  The atmosphere it creates with its visuals and music is perfect, and while the style of the game makes it pleasing to look at, the game is also effective at making the player feel varying degrees of discomfort, at least in my experience, which was definitely intentional.  The game is able to discuss mature and dark topics without showing you anything particularly disturbing, and I commend it for that.I have two main issues with the game.  The first is that I didn't find the puzzles particularly challenging.  There were a few points where I felt stuck, but it was only because I didn't realize I could open a certain container or interact with a certain object.  There were some unique puzzles throughout the game that I found interesting, but everything else was pretty standard for this genre.  Because of this, it only took me 3 hours to beat the game, and it's not as if I was rushing through it.  My other issue is with the game's ending, Overall, the game is still worth playing if you are looking for a good puzzle game to spend an afternoon on.

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is a minimalist point and click puzzle game which deals with a family’s history and some very heavy issues.The gameplay loop of Almost Gone is pretty simple. You examine a room to look for clues and progress to the next area. There are visual hints and the puzzles aren’t brain wracking. For the most part the game is happy to let you progress while telling its story. Speaking of the story, it is not wise to give spoilers considering any thing I will tell you might ruin the experience, but it deals with heavy subject matters. The length of the story is around 2 hours and might extend if you take your time solving the puzzles. One thing that disappointed me a little about the game’s story was that it never went deep into its subject matter. Something like Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice which dove headfirst into the issues would have been more appreciated. The game almost feels like it is afraid of its own subject matters. It also feels a little rushed and considering the wide range of topics it wants to deal with, the story is given a very short length. The subject matters are spread too thin and that is what makes it lose its focus.Very Crisp and soothing, The Almost Gone is a very nice visual pallete. There is a minimalist tone to the graphics and every room is presented in a very clean way. The visual hints are a very important part of the game and it would have been a car crash if the visuals were messy or crammed. There is a certain charm to this game’s visuals and it might remind you of other such games like monument valley. Overall, Visuals are a big selling point here. Just like the visual fidelity, the sound design of The Almost Gone is wonderfully designed. The score goes from soothing to creepy very subtly and you wouldn’t notice how it got there. It compliments the visual design impeccably and is a soundtrack you will remember for some time. Along with the visuals, the overall sound design of The Almost Gone is another big selling pointBrilliant visuals and an excellent soundtrack takes a game that would have been average at best to above average. It’s short length and heavy subject matter might put off some buyers but the game is very good for a one time experience. The story could have been a little less rushed and I wish it would have delved in the subjects more but as it stands, this is a perfectly solid game that is a treat for your eyes and ears.This Review was brought to you by  ''If you liked this review and you want to get in touch with us, mail to contact@dnbmedia.co to get your game reviewed or promoted''

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from a questionable split-second graphic telling you how to access the inventory, the real sinker of The Almost Gone is the writing. In the first few minutes of the game the protagonist's thoughts move at so fast a clip that she's jumping to spurious conclusions as to what's 'going on' before there's any legitimate evidence towards any of it, and then devolves into utterly obnoxious world building writing as her life is revealed. The complicated, knotty subject of dysfunctional families is portrayed in the most banally miserable, overwrought, and unrelenting manner possible, and for a game that's based around exploring the idea of place there is nothing about the world that has a semblance of any realness or life.The puzzles and goals are decently serviceable, if seemingly arbitrary, but even the best puzzles in the world could not save this game from the sheer insufferability of the story that's supposed to be the hook for solving said puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: I seem to always find myself playing these minimalist puzzle games. Something about the laid-back nature of their gameplay, their light aesthetic, and nice music always keep me on the lookout for new ones. So here we have one that seems to fit all of that and tell an actual story in the process — I had to check it out.If you're familiar with game The Room and its sequels, this game plays very similarly. You're given this puzzle that involves a bunch of smaller steps to complete and moving around the puzzle will slowly reveal bits and pieces to help you put together a solution. This can be anything from an object that needs to be picked up and placed elsewhere to an electrical panel that needs to be tinkered with to unlock the next area. This is also where the game's puzzle design shines, as, just like The Room, these seemingly small puzzles add up to something much more and it's cool to have this sense of progression while playing.What makes it even better is that the game actually manages to tell a decent story through these puzzles. A lot of the objects you pick up will oftentimes be accompanied with a short description of the character's thoughts on it, which in turn reveals details about the overall story. These can be small details like trash bags in the corner of the room to major ones like legal documents.Of course, this is on top of game's puzzles actually taking place in areas relevant to the story, the game really thrives on environmental storytelling. The story is rather depressing, but it was at least told in a very cool manner.As for the difficulty, I wouldn't say it's too difficult a game, but when you have a bunch of these little things to do, the complexity can quickly stack up and I would be lying if I said I wasn't stuck at least a couple times during my playthrough. There are some puzzles that span upwards of ten or so rooms, so there's definitely a lot of ground to cover.The downside to this is that, while the puzzle design itself is generally pretty good, it does rely a bit on pixel hunting. By that, I mean that there are items and such that need to be clicked on that are so small that it's very easy to miss them. That or they blend in perfectly with the environment, leading to situations where I began spam clicking certain areas hoping to find the object that I need to progress. It isn't every puzzle that was like this, but enough so that it needs to be mentioned.My main complaint is actually with the game's UI. This is a game developed for mobile devices first and it shows in just about every aspect of its design. From the awkward mouse controls that are obviously adapted from touch controls to the the large amounts of wasted screen space, it's very obvious that this is a mobile game port.In fact, part of the reason why the pixel hunting segments stood out to me was simply because everything, not just those specific objects, is so small in comparison to the amount of screen space used. I ran the game at 1440p, and while the game does work properly at that resolution, the gameplay almost entirely takes place in the very center of it, leaving a ton of blank space around it. You're unable to zoom in or out of that space, so it can definitely make certain areas of the game harder to see.Altogether though, I would say that The Almost Gone is deserving of a light recommendation. It has some good puzzle design going for it, an interesting story to match, and an aesthetic that I can definitely get behind. However, the game does suffer from its reliance on pixel hunting and its lackluster UI, which do bring down the experience a bit. It's still a decent enough game, but it might be worth waiting for a sale first.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is a perspective based puzzle game.  Each room one goes into can be turned to view it in 4 directions, with answers & items being hidden in places a single angle couldn't find.  It does this quite well, on top of the puzzle design that never strays into moon logic.  The puzzles all have solutions that can be found by tracking down hints scattered through each area.  Story-wise, this title takes a slightly more abstract approach, very similar to Braid.  It leaves multiple clues for the player, but never says anything outright, allowing for a different interpretation for different players.  The visuals match the simplistic design the game is going for, with enough detail to bring a point across, & the soundtrack flits between soothing & eerie, coming across like a horror game at times. Unfortunately, the puzzles don't change between different playthroughs.  This is great for speedrunning or hunting down specific achievements, but for anyone looking to re-experience this title, one can mostly skip entire beats of the 5 acts to solve the game in under 30 minutes.  The only other thing that comes to find factors into the story.  It's vagueness can be a little exhausting for those who want to understand what exactly is going on.  Though this does open the game up to discussion, the lacking of a direct narrative other than the figurative gestures of death & mental health.  This is without going into spoilers, & it is minor, so this may not resonate as a problem for everyone. A simple list involving plenty of tedious waiting.  Completing the game twice through isn't that bad, as nothing changes for a second playthough, & one achievement must be obtained through a missable action.  The remaining 3 achievements are all time based, doing certain actions for 2 & 30 minutes, & then having the game running in game for 5 hours.  That must be specified because time doesn't count in menus.  Get the 2 minute one, then leave the game running while stepping out or going to bed for the remaining ones. The Almost Gone is a well designed, vaguely told puzzle game that hits all the high notes of what one could want out of a puzzle game of this style.  Though the story is vague & the puzzles are unchanging, it's still a memorable experience thanks to the well designed puzzles.  Easily worth a purchase, even more if a player is a fan of stories that leave the player to decide the meaning.

_childDocuments_.review: I should preface this with the fact that I do relatively enjoy point-and-click adventures/puzzles, which leans this game towards being far more positive than it might be for some people. The Almost Gone is a game that attempts to use its puzzles/exploration as environmental storytelling. It covers heavy topics like childhood abuse, grief, and trauma, and the settings and puzzle designs chosen to progress the story are relatively well-chosen and not at all out of place. However, like many others have already pointed out, the ending is left relatively ambiguous and a number of questions are left unresolved.The gameplay itself is nothing dreadfully innovative, but each chapter has its own interesting core puzzle gimmick that ties the entire level together, and it doesn't feel like it's roughly thrown. The puzzles are well-thought out, but there is a decent amount of backtracking which can be frustrating, especially in a couple levels where the puzzle requires links that are less intuitive. I had a reasonable amount of fun, and I could see where the the story was trying to go, but it could have done with better execution. 6.5-7/10. Pros: - Clean, pretty art no clipping or other issues- Some attempt at integrating story + level design - Relatively interesting puzzles - Sound design was decent. Cons:- Storytelling merely invites you to uncover a story but doesn't make any sort of point with it- Less than satisfying ending which  It would have been better if we got some kind of ending that gave more closure considering Overall if you're not looking for deep, moving writing, but just a decently made game, this one sort of works, would recommend getting it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone feels like a game that ran out of something. Maybe it was time, money or just the will to continue. But let’s back up a bit.Gameplaywise The Almost Gone is a classic point-and-click adventure game. That means you’re scouring the levels for items to solve a variety of puzzles while a lot of the story is told through monologues by the main character. Crucially though for a point-and-click adventure, she’s never actually on screen. This is where the main visual draw of the game comes into play. The levels are all rendered in this cute isometric diorama aesthetic. All of the rooms are broken down into little cube sections that you can freely rotate and explore. This obviously implies that perspective plays a crucial part in the game, which is certainly the case. A few of the puzzles require you to use multiple chunks of the levels to solve, which sometimes require spatial awareness. However, these puzzles are in a clear minority over those that can be solved with traditional inventory items.I have to say that, while I like the puzzles that require you to rotate the dioramas to figure out solutions to the puzzles, it carries with it the downside that you have to rotate each room repeatedly to make sure you’ve found everything. And since a majority of segments don’t benefit at all from this rotation, I can at best attest mild praise for the mechanic. Given that the levels are divided into these cubic chunks, you’ll end up traversing all these segments multiple times, especially whenever you’ve missed a detail and are stuck with a puzzle.But adventure games are always part puzzle and part story. And I have to say, the story of The Almost Gone is what absolutely drew me in and also ultimately made me question whether I should recommend it at all. The story is told in five chapters in non-chronological order. The implication, I think, is that our protagonist Emily isn’t really exploring these spaces. It’s heavily implied that something bad has happened to her and that what we’re seeing is some kind of glimpse into the afterlife, given that one of the chapters takes place in the future while others happen decades earlier. The narrative touches upon a lot of themes surrounding familial troubles and in general revolves around Emily trying to make sense of these troubles to overcome some trauma. Emily tells of frequent fights, of being reprimanded by her parents and of substance abuse. Her mother suffered from depression and is later revealed to have been institutionalized. Meanwhile, her father seems to be a victim of his own parents’ shortcomings when raising him, while said grandparents had to fight with their own demons and failures in life. It’s all fairly heavy stuff and I generally like the juxtaposition of the early, pastel-colored levels that sink into ever increasing darkness as the backstory unfolds. There’s some pretty fascinating and effective character building going on, even though our Emily’s monologue is supremely cynical, which can be a tough pill to swallow for some people.But then, the game just kind of stops. It’s not even that the game has a downer ending or anything, it just seems, as I mentioned at the start, that the game reaches the final rooms you get to explore, and then the designers stopped making the game. There doesn’t seem to be a thesis statement that would attempt to try and tie the narrative together, to put all these topics I’ve mentioned into proper context. There are plenty of hints that point towards a bigger picture, but overall, it’s a bit insubstantial.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a basis here for an agreeable experience that could have been, with definitely a lot of work needed still to make it cohesive and whole.The narrative gravitates around a dysfunctional family and its confused narrator's attempt to make sense of curious events and memories. Intriguing elements include Emily's inability to remember consuming food or being thirsty, tree roots inexplicably overtaking the landscape, flashbacks to different times, and the presence of some mysterious black goo, but that's about how deep these mysteries are explored. As a whole it feels like a work in progress, a rough draft of key beats that remain superficial up to the very abrupt ending.Awkward controls quickly drain the fun out of every move. Attributable in part to an uneven mobile port, but mostly it's as though the developers ignored decades of point-and-click refinement and common convenience features.Nothing differentiates interactive elements; simply click on everything. Some drawers open, some don't. The useless map doesn't inform which room is where and makes navigation a pain. Sometimes its icon is even missing from the UI in certain scenes. I repeatedly wished for a more polished interface to let me enjoy the few well-designed puzzles on offer.With the highest price point of all platforms on Steam and probably the least enjoyable adaptation of this title, it's best to look elsewhere, or wait for a huge discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I was  to review The Almost Gone positively,  its problems, but then the achievements pissed me off. As such, it can go ♥♥♥♥ itself. A pretentious and shallow point and click that mocks and degrades serious and emotional topics by lacking any kind of conclusion, depth, or nuance. TAG actually starts out positively, successfully creating the bones and layout of an emotional experience, generating mystery, and hinting at trauma, dysfunction, and the effects thereof. But then these things are trivialised, demonised, and just not explored in an interesting or deep way by a character that offers no insights and yoyos in their perception of events. Finally, and sorry to spoil it, it ends on nothing. All the work that’s gone in unravelling like the toilet roll you dropped, and used in the same way. If you’re only interested in the puzzles, and the little % achievements complete means nothing to you, then this is a simple point and click with simple puzzles that’ll keep you busy for about half an evening.If you’re a point and click lover, this might entertain you briefly.If you’re a story lover, this has literally nothing to offer. I personally, am too incensed by needing to leave a game running for an additional hour and a half, for no reason, while I can’t do anything else with it, to get the recognition for finishing it all the way, to give it a thumbs up. It can piss off.

_childDocuments_.review: This review contains minor spoilers.At turns spooky, somber, horrifying and incredibly sad, The Almost Gone delivers an excellent puzzle experience with beautifully understated graphics and a painful mystery at its heart. In the same vein as Gone Home, you explore your house (and eventually multiple other environments with significance to the player character's family history), unraveling the tragedy that brought you to this moment in your life. The story is left ambiguous, told through visual metaphor and text-based narration. An excellent game, and one I'd wholeheartedly recommend to anyone looking for a narrative puzzle game with a lot of emotional depth.My one gripe with the experience is that it would have been ideal for me to play using a controller, but it's a minor nitpick. Some players may also feel let down by the game's somewhat open-ended conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not often that games leave me at a loss of words. Most of the time, they are easily dissected; writing, music, gameplay, flaws and virtues. Sometimes I'm instead driven to write from my personal perspective, what a game does or doesn't do for me, how it can differ from other people. Very rarely, however, I come across a game that defies that kind of framing. a game where the seams are almost invisible, a game that leaves an impression that is difficult to quantify. If you haven't already guessed, The Almost Gone is one of those games.It is a sign of a skilled storyteller when the story is vague enough that you can't quite wrap your head around all of the details of the plot, but then the emotional quality is striking and undeniable. That is what open-ended stories often aim to do, I think, creating a contrast where what is felt becomes so much clearer due to the opaqueness of what is seen. The Almost Gone is no different, and while I would have difficulty describing what events it depicts, I have no such trouble saying that no other game has given me such a feeling of  throughout its runtime. Every part of this game, from visual design to music and sound to puzzle construction work together to create a feeling of an unavoidable, terrible fate, something that there is no escape from. Howling winds, dissonant strings, the black sludge that follows you and the  that is slamming the inside of a fridge, trying to get out – all of it keeps you on edge, unrelaxed and anxious, searching for an end where the tension finally will resolve and the truth will appear. That is an end that never comes, and it is up to yourself to try to find the answer among the clues the game leaves you. An answer you can never get fully confirmed.Thus, the tension never leaves, only ever Almost Gone. The darkness never quite left me after playing this game, like I had been splattered with some of that black goo myself, a feeling I can't help but think that the developers intended. This is something as rare as a true thriller game, sharing more of a DNA with the unspeakable horror of Lovecraft than the cozy puzzle-solving of titles like Monument Valley, which the visuals might remind of. But unlike Lovecraft, there is a personal edge here, a broken home that never gets fixed. It is tragic and dark and frightening, all at once, which only works to its credit.I think The Almost Gone is a great game. It effortlessly does what it sets out to do, creating an oppressing experience of tension, trauma and sadness. What makes it terrifying is that it also rings true with a clarity that few other games manage. I can only wish for the well-being of the developers, and give this game my highest recommendation. If you can and feel able, you should play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The usage of a diorama to tell the story of a person's life was certainly a neat take for a puzzle game. But what had me intrigued was the story:First time playing the game something felt off, every chapter had me taking small notes, jotting down every clue i came across until the end of the game. Afterwards i tried to put everything together and come up with some kind of explanation to it all, but I didn't feel like i had solved the case that maybe, just maybe there was more that i may have missed. So i played it again. I would say that my answer stayed the same, what with all the clues i jotted down, but that would be a lie. In all honesty the conclusion to this tale came off a lot darker than I had imagined it to be and I can't even say that i'm right about my answer. My hats off to you game! I would gladly play it a third time, but i don't think i could get a better answer than what i have now, but what a great story. The puzzles in Almost Gone were very enjoyable. Nothing to difficult to solve, except for one i won't spoil, but lets just say i wandered around for 10 minutes overlooking a specific object.The rooms; each room was unique in terms of what it meant to the story or puzzle. My only note and this was a like/dislike; more rooms meant more puzzles and that was exciting, but the downside was i got lost trying to find my way back to rooms i had previously been in and would sometimes do a loop back to the same rooms. Also would not recommend playing this in the dark, its not scary or anything, but there were some moments i felt like i got hit by a flash bang from transitions to new rooms. Could of just been a mistake on my end, but fair warning to those with sensitive eyes. Aside from that minor problem everything else was great.I found this game by complete accident while searching for a game that I never found. And yet I am still glad i picked this up. I would highly recommend this game to anyone, whether it be on sale or not.  8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a slight positive for me. Clearly, this game was influenced by The Room series of games from the eerie music, astrological and astronomical themes, and the ever present blackness that ends each chapter. The art was nice, and the theme was interesting (albeit dark and depressing). My main issues were the map and some of the puzzles. In many of the puzzles, it was cumbersome to get to a desired map square after finding a clue piece on another square as the game only provides a basic layout and cardinal directions to move from your square without any indication of the surrounding options. A few of the puzzles were also hidden within the map, requiring an attention to detail and/or backtracking rather than actual deduction.Lastly, the ending felt a bit disappointing and failed to explain/address many of the issues of trauma brought up in the game,Ultimately, this was a short, relatively simple puzzle game (it took me 3 hours with an hour of AFK time for New Years to complete. There is a achievement for spending 5 hours in the game too.) I would recommend it, but advise getting it on sale as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Game is a short puzzle game that takes you on a journey through your families past as you discover the dark secrets and stories that have been hidden away to be forgotten. You slowly peel back the layers of the generations of your family and the story starts to slowly unfold and by the end of the game you really do feel for this family, and the character you play as. You never see any of the family members, or yourself but you get to know each one a little bit and everything starts to make sense. If your a fan of stories, especially ones that focus on darker subjects and explore themes like mental health then this is a solid one that  you will enjoy. It doesn't quite take that final step into greatness I think, but it's a very solid story and it kept me engaged during the 2ish hours I spent on my first play through despite the The Puzzles themselves were well done, and fun to figure out. There wasn't anything crazy interesting about them, and only 1 or 2 really stick out to me after finishing but there is enough variety that I didn't get bored playing through them. They're well thought out and nicely executed and fit the story telling nicely. My biggest issue with the game however has to do with the main "gimmick" if you want to call it that, being the way the world is laid out. To travel throughout the world, you go from each little section to the next. Often time these will resemble different rooms and when used for smaller areas it works nicely and I don't have any complaints. However, when you're put into larger areas with 8 or 9 sections, it can quickly become frustrating trying to figure out where you are at times. It was never too much of an issue but it did get annoying at times. The soundtrack is also kind of annoying after a while. There's very little actual music and it's mostly just these atmospheric noises and they all kind of have the same ominous sound and it can get a little irritating, but again this was a very minor issue and is more a nit pick than anything. I also want to quickly mention some achievements for the completionists out there because this game is a bore to complete for no reason. There are some absolutely stupid achievements that exist for no other reason than padding out the time spent playing the game. There's achievements that require you to sit in the same room for 30 minutes, completing the game two times when there's no different paths or changes, and to play the game for 5 hours. I was done with all the other achievements within 3 hours so I had to sit there with the game open for 2 hours. These don't change my thoughts on the game itself, just annoying for completing it.Overall, if you're a fan of shorter puzzle games that focus on a darker story with themes of mental health, I think you'll enjoy it, and if you can get it for 5 dollars or less than pick it up. _childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is a point and click mystery puzzle game that tells us the story about the difficulties of life alongside how our paths in life can influence how we are as human beings, from what I interpreted from the story. When you first start this game, the story raises many questions about the protagonist, regarding what happened to them that made them go on this journey and find out more about their family. This is a solid short game that I would recommend if you manage to get it on sale. $10 is a bit too much for how long this game truly is, where I would say $5 is the most I would really pay. In terms of expectations of the gameplay, it’s what you would typically expect out of a point and click game, needing the player to connect the dots and use the gathered clues along each of the 5 worlds to build up the narrative that the game is trying to tell us. I would rate this game around a 7/10, for its simplicity and a story that makes you asks questions as to why the characters and world are as it is shown in this game. This game is of course, not perfect, but something to look into you can manage to find sales or deals on it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this even though I have barely played the game.  I think an important tip was missed in the tutorial.  To access your inventory on PC, use the right mouse button.  Your inventory should appear along the bottom of the screen.  In general, I would say the controls on the PC could be more intuitive and less fussy, some puzzles take way longer to complete because you have to sit there and fiddle with it for way longer than necessary.  Some of the puzzles are designed for a touch screen as this game is available on the switch and on mobile. The recommendation for headphones isn’t quite necessary, it is really there to facilitate jump scare noises.  To be blunt, the music lends to the atmosphere of the game but it is very unpleasant to listen to for any length of time. I have completed the game and like many players I did find the ending abrupt and the story full of holes.  I suppose it is part of the charm in this game, a realistic facet of life.  I can see the logic of it, no human truly knows anything and all you are really experiencing in this game is the main character’s narration.  However, it left me feeling empty and a bit sad.  It isn’t a game to create hope or to give you freedom like so many other games. I find myself feeling very neutral towards this game.  I won’t give it a negative review (in spite of my frustration with the controls), I will say expect grief and sadness from this game but don’t expect it to lift you from that state like Gris and When the Past Was Around do. There are no cats in this game and the dog does die.

_childDocuments_.review: A dark isometric escape room type puzzler made up of five chapters which sees you trying to piece together your rather upsetting family history and what's happened to you, the narrator. Each chapter is a different location - your house, a hospital, a treehouse - with many rooms to explore. You view each room as a cut away diorama which you can spin and rotate with the mouse to reveal new doors and sometimes puzzle elements, which appear as close ups in the room. Each room is beautifully detailed and you'll have to search high and low through every minute element to move on to the next stage.The puzzles are intuitive and great fun to solve, the right side of clever but not too taxing. They normally consist of you unlocking new parts of the area you're in by finding codes or combination locks through interacting with objects and the room you're in or using things you pick up in your inventory. I had a lot of fun figuring things out, people who have played puzzle games such as The Room or Rusty Lake games will enjoy the puzzles in this one too.The game tells you to use headphones if you can and it's certainly an experience, in fitting with the dark tone of the story it can often feel like the developers are trying to unsettle you with the loud, sometimes grating accompaniments. As for the story, it is not a light hearted jaunt! There's explorations of animal abuse, depression, and drug addiction. The narrator can be very judgemental and bitter (perhaps unsurprisingly) and is hard to warm to throughout the journey. Sometimes the dialogue, written as text from the perspective of the narrator, is a little stilted (perhaps because it is not the developer's first language), which makes the narrator feel less believable. It also has an abrupt end, which left me with more questions than answers. Each area has a lot of rooms to explore which can get a little bit confusing, but that's part of the puzzle. It took me about three and a half hours to finish which I think was paced very well. I was given a steam key for this game - and I'd suggest trying to get it during its current or a future promotion price as its original price feels just a little steep. That said I had great fun exploring The Almost Gone's five chapters, each one has its own style and sense of place, with plenty of  trinkets and rooms to unlock and explore with some really well designed puzzles. TLDR: Good PointsIntuitive and inventive puzzles to solveEach chapter feels unique and had its own styleEach room is beautifully detailed and fun to exploreBad PointsStory ends abruptly, is a little confusing in partsYou can find yourself backtracking through rooms a lot, can get frustrating as most areas aren't signpostedDialogue can at times feel a little stilted and impersonal

_childDocuments_.review: The Almost Gone is visually gorgeous, with a mysterious narrative, clever puzzles, and an eerie atmosphere. I enjoyed the puzzles and the narrative a lot. However, the game was too short to be worth its asking price ($14.99 for ~3 hrs of gameplay), and the ending left me wanting a lot more, especially since there was no conclusion or even climax in the narrative.Would I recommend this game? Yes, but NOT for $15. It was enjoyable, but it leaves a lot of room for improvement. If there were more chapters, or more of a resolution or culmination in the storyline, it would be more worth the money (and time) it takes to invest in the game and the story.

_childDocuments_.review: (Narrative Platformer): This game is a narrative experience, and the gameplay reflects that.  There is NO precision platforming nor impossible-to-figure-out puzzles along the way.Options include volume controls for Master, Music, SFX and Voices; Brightness, Resolution (for me the default was 1536 x 864), Controller or Keyboard (re-mappable), and choice of Language.:The store page expresses the gist of the game and story well, but in my own words, this is about a girl struggling to face life and pain, darkness and light, yin and yang.We journey as two parts of the whole...  Part of us depends on the light, traveling through the shadows upon flat surfaces, whilst the other part is afraid of the light, and moves about in 2.5D world... It's not quite 3D, but it still *feels* 3-dimensional.Each character is controlled separately, and you can switch back and forth at will.  You will have to cooperate with your shadow in order to progress, the goal being to get you both to the marked checkpoint.  These are pretty close together, and you may be blocked off from the last segment once you both hit the save point.Why is this important?  Because there are , and finding them can add just the slightest bit more to the tale.You can see how many you've collected in the top right corner of the screen, but more helpful is the '' section of the Menu, which will show you how many you've collected (and missed) per chapter.  You can, I assume, replay a chapter at any time and not lose your progress.There are no HINTS available, but in general, you won't need them.  The puzzles tend to be on the easy-to-figure-out side, as the driving force behind this game is learning the story.  Gathering the birds can be a little trickier, but it's obvious that the devs WANT you to complete the game, and rage-quitting doesn't exactly make one want to keep playing non-stop. XDAlthough not super-challenging, the mechanics do evolve and become more complex as you progress, making things even more interesting, and blending beautifully with where we are in the story.A lot of things come to mind as I think about the game.  Whimsy.  Fear.  Sorrow.  Beauty.  Strength.  The devs managed to convey these feelings in a manner that is both fluid and poignant, enhancing their tale in a variety of ways.  There are elements of the known: A sprinkle of the shadow-play from , visible word play and environmental unlocks like in , 2.5D gameplay reminiscent of ... and yet as a whole  is nothing like other games I've played. :Shady Part of Me is a little slow to start off, but quickly becomes hard to pull yourself away from.  I found myself completely engaged, and absolutely recommend the game to anyone who enjoys a good narrative.  Quick reflexes are not required!

_childDocuments_.review: is a beautiful puzzle platformer with stellar art design, excellent soundtrack that mellows you out, many creative puzzles and well executed gameplay mechanics. The "shadow" part of you navigates through a 2D environment while the "child" is navigated through a 3D environment bound by avoiding light. You have the ability to seamlessly switch between the two in order to work together with "yourself" to overcome any obstacles. The light and shadow mechanic is executed flawlessly and surpasses both  and  in terms of mechanic use (Both are good games regardless). For those that want an additional challenge, there are 98 origami birds hidden in puzzles that are sometimes harder to collect than to reach the exit to continue the story. The rewind feature is perfect since it keeps the flow going non-stop without you ever restarting from the beginning of the area. The game can be completed between 5-8 hrs. If you want to play an unique and enjoyable puzzle platformer, than give this game a try. [10/10]
