Resource gathering (which is the central point and challenge of the game) is frustrating and confusing because many buildings have unintuitive dependencies -- I expect mastery of the game relies on just knowing that in order to create a level 2 herder's hut, you need a supply of wheat and stone, but that's difficult to remember, as there's no way to know until you build a herder's hut and it doesn't really make any sense. You need to direct your people on what to do, which is complicated by the fact that they are basically indistinguishable from one another, and hard to see on the hexes, so even if you're clicking on the correct one, it's difficult to tell. Then, because the frustrations of the game design aren't enough, we have every modern game's friend: procedurally generated maps and random events. It's not uncommon to arrive in a new area and find it's completely unsuitable for the tasks that are required to advance to the next by dint of the terrain being more than 50% unusable mountain, ruins, and lakes. Should you manage to thrive, there are no shortage of random events, all of which are negative, that will damage your buildings and hurt your villagers, seemingly without rhyme or reason. Occasionally, a friendly caravan will happen by, at which point they will offer you a completely random assortment of trades with no regard for whether or not it's even possible for you to complete what's on offer (for instance, offering you 200 meat in exchange for 50 wool... on a map where you have not been collecting wool and therefore have 0). I enjoy the premise of this game, but in practice it's an exercise in frustration and playing it doesn't really feel meaningful. I'd recommend sticking to more polished 4X games over this mess.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Originally, I left a negative review for this game, because the "campaign" made it seem like there is no save option (not for one halt/level, not even for the entire run), nor a "reset turn" function, which is also mentioned in some negative reviews.  Upon completing the "campaign", however, I ventured into the "play" section of the game. What I found was that, first, this part of the game does indeed have both a save function, and a reset turn function. Second, the "play" section is, in fact, the campaign of this game. What is designated as "campaign" is nothing more than a dressed-down version of the full game, or rather a tutorial. This is a pretty serious oversight, as most people consider the campaign section of a game to be most representative of the full game. That is to say, most people know that the tutorial is not representative of the full game, and will thus push through the tutorial, into the campaign section, before leaving a review of the game. The fact that this game does not properly distinguish between tutorial and campaign may actually be the cause of a significant portion of negative reviews. It pains me to think that the solution to this would be as easy as changing the text of two of the buttons in the main menu. Because this game is actually pretty great. It feels a lot like Frostpunk on iron man mode.There were a few other complaints in the negative reviews that I find to be fair, but, in the end, most of those you can control for, once you're aware of them.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of promise. The only thing holding it back are random events called "Vagaries". They're intended to make the game more difficult but what it really does is make the game unfun. They're too random and punishing. Getting hit with two "all bulidings lose 50% hp" events in a row kills your run.Also theres no real way to heal your people or buildings. The time is so constrained that you have to focus on gathering very specific resources on each map. These resources usually don't line up with what you need to heal or repair. Meaning any damage you sustain is usually permanent.All in all I wish I could recommend this game but I just can't
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: It's an okay little strategy game; manage a small tribe of people as they make their way across the lands, assign them gathering and production tasks and build buildings to get them through the hardships and costs of traveling.My recommendation is half-hearted because it's a bit of a mess. It wants to be zen, but it also wants you to struggle. It wants to be stylish, and prefers stylish over clarity. The tutorial tells you things that are thematic, and which contradict the actual game play. There's a decent strategy game in there if you want to search for it, but you're going to wrestle with the visuals and the UI to get the information you need to make it through.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Best target audience of this game is someone who is patient, likes cutesie art and gets attached to characters he himself can rename and shape throughout a journey. Turn-based resource management and task-based progression of your tribe in games that range from half an hour to about an hour and a half are on the menu. You have the option to save your game and resume later but if you're like me you'll forget your setup by then. The tiny animal characters are very cute indeed and the music is relaxingly inoffensive. The game appears to sell a min/max experience, but going for such tactics will likely leave you frustrated. You're best off making most of your cast a diverse jack-of-all-trades, which is what this game probably went for. If that's the type of experience you want you will probably like this game.Biggest critique of the game is its unpredictability that is easy to miss. The game has mechanics such as sudden events that are supposed to tweak the gameplay but oftentimes feel like a nuisance or straight up unfair "you lose lol". It doesn't happen too seldom that you skip a few turns in a row because all your workers are busy doing something, but in doing so you might stumble on without noticing events and ask yourself "why do I suddenly need wheat to progress?". If you are impatient the game punishes you with moments of frustration, and it does not do a good job of explaining this in the beginning.Second critique would be the abundance of resource types coupled with unpredictable needs clashing with a game-to-game diverse experience. Resource harvest is done by specialized workers that progressively get more efficient, and oftentimes you will suddenly be asked for a resource you don't have a specialized worker for later on within a margin that seems quite unfair. This circumstance would want you to collect almost everything, but the game actively discourages that by not telling you what you need later and limiting the resources you can take with you from point to point. At the same time the later perks of a dedicated worker are shimmering in front of you. Sometimes the game hints at subtle differences between specializations, but if you play as if you potentially need everything you might very well miss out on these gameplay changes as the lower progression is limited to "more efficiency". It feels discouraging to try out a new "build" as the environment in general rarely seems to allow for you to mix up your game, and although the different resources hint at a distinction from one another these only become apparent later on.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Hard as nails, brutal, unforgiving, oppressive even at times, but also cute, fun and deep. As it is a turn based recource management game, it requires you to keep a very close eye on your recources at all times and gives you a lot of other things to watch too. Actually requires more attention than most games on the market which is also the source of most of the negative reviews so don't pay too much attention to reviews which complain about difficulty. The game is just not for them. If you want a game that plays itself and holds your hand all the way to the bitter end:better move on because this isn't that game. If you don't back away from a challenge on the other hand: go right ahead. Easy to learn, hard to master. 8/10(minor glitches)recommended for fans of the genre
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: After I played through the campaign (which was basically an extended tutorial) I found this game to be a joyous and very positive experience. I was really looking forward to playing the main game. Imagine my massive disappointment then when the actual sandbox game experience proved to be anything but joyous. It was horrible. The game has serious balance and "fun" issues. It's all down to a mechanic called the "Vagaries". Completely absent from the campaign, these are random negative effects that occur if your "Harmony" (a stat that is hidden from you!!) on a given map gets too low. So while the game strongly encourages you extract as much resource and experience for your workers as possible from each map you halt at, it punishes you very hard for trying to do so. Vagaries come thick and fast after a while, with the next one arriving while you are still coming to terms with the last. Literally only two or three turns apart! This is not fun at all, and ruins the game by putting a massive hidden clock on everything you do (over and above the actual visible clock of the incoming flood). These random effects are never fun to deal with and are simply frustrating and annoying at best, or run-ending at worst. Very bad game design here.The game does allow custom setups for your runs, but as far as the Vagaries go, the choice is either on or off. Turn them off and the game becomes pointlessly easy, but turn them on and it becomes frustratingly unplayable. There is no happy medium where you can simply turn them down a bit. The game desperately needs that.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: As Far As The Eye is very medium, so there's some good and some bad, but I think fundamentally I won't be recommending it to anyone.Pros: The art is very stylized and looks good, even if it can be hard to visually distinguish between different thing. The leveling system with the different animal hats is really interesting and cool.Cons: The biggest problem is that the game just should not be a roguelike. A single run takes FAR too long since everything is so slow, and every run feels like you're doing the exact same tasks with barely any variation. Adding onto that, the game doesn't feel difficult at all except for some spikes that result in annoyance more than anything else. There's just no way I will ever do run after run with this game when I'm already feeling really tired of it after the third one.I genuinely think As Far As The Eye has some really good material, but it needed more time in the oven and perhaps an overhaul to better take advantage of what it has going for it while stepping away from the roguelike genre.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not really one for writing reviews but I saw this game has mixed reviews recently and thought I should help improve that metric.The tutorial is not a fully scripted walkthrough, and the game does allow you to fail.  Failure is an important part of this game.  One the surface, it's a cute 3-X game (there aren't really enemies to exterminate, so I can't justify calling it a 4-X game) as described in the game's own description.But beneath that surface is an incredibly challenging resource management game that rewards thinking several moves ahead and exploring the options the game offers but doesn't explicitly tell you to explore.  It will be frustrating, there will be a lot of failure, and sometimes you'll hit dead ends mid way through a run that felt really solid.  If you want to be able to win every rogue-like run you start, this is not the game for you.  If you enjoy working out strategies over multiple iterations, you may enjoy this game.In fairness, I think my biggest pet peeve with the game is the trait system.  When you start each run your characters are given X number of random traits.  Some of the negative traits are truly debilitating to the point where I will immediately abandon a run and start a new one if a character receives any of a few particularly nasty ones.  The idea is to be able to adapt and accommodate those negative traits, but some of them present what amount to insurmountable challenges, especially at the start of a run.  Thankfully the game doesn't really punish you for just restarting, and you can play custom games where you can remove negative traits altogether if they become too annoying.Beyond the gameplay, I personally found the theme and conceit of the game to be really great.  The "campaign" (tutorial) provides just enough background on this little world you're playing in to allow you some attachment to the success of your characters.  The lore of this game, while limited, is actually really neat, and fits quite seamlessly with the actual gameplay mechanics.  I'm also a big fan of the fact that excess resources gathered and left behind count against your final score.Also, for anyone who enjoys this game and is reading this for some reason, check out Slipstream, another rogue-like resource management game I've really enjoyed.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but there are several flaws that make the game not enjoyable. The pawns have to be micromanaged between buildings to gather resources. The buildings are not labeled on the map and can be difficult to see with all the bright colors. The RNG from events can end a game quickly because of the limited time and resources.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: After many hours of enjoyable gameplay, "roguelike turn-based resource-management game" is definitely an accurate description. However, there's a lot to break down there. In the abstract, you control workers — called Pupils — to exploit resources while progressing through sections — called halts — to ultimately reach a finish line, called The Eye. Each halt requires a variable amount of resources to be gathered within a time frame. The challenge lies in optimizing decisions while random events — called vagaries — can throw a wrench in your plans. Planning ahead is key, which takes gaining familiarity with the many available options.As expected in a roguelike, elements of randomness and uncertainty are present. These primarily come in the form of required resources to move past a halt, random vagaries and the halt's layout. Gathering a required resource is trivial earlier in a run, but your decisions at the start can greatly affect your ability to handle other challenges closer to the end.A strategy will always be built — at least partially — around survival because Pupils require food upkeep. It's great you got that iron ore (or whatever resource) you needed, but it's not so great when you realize everyone is going to starve. Unfortunately, a run that's about to fail will likely be unavoidable unless you have a lot of things already in place to recover. This often led me to prematurely end a run. There isn't a "push your luck" factor because there is minimal permanent progression. Aside from the tutorial campaign, there are eight scenarios to unlock with minor variations. Completing a scenario also unlocks traits for Pupils.In a single run, progression comes in the form of upgrades and skill trees. Pupils can work any role, but the more they do in a given field, the more proficient they become. For example, a gatherer can become a woodcutter who will gather wood more efficiently than a Pupil that has no experience in gathering. Specializing Pupils is a very satisfying part of the strategy and synergy.A complaint I've seen in other reviews is that a resource will appear to be inadequately available on a halt. I have learned about ways to mitigate this the more I've played. The council building has upgrades that allow you to block negative effects from vagaries and plan further ahead for each halt. This information could greatly alter which path to take and which resources to focus on. There is also the market building which allows for trading one resource for another at a loss.Overall, I found the learning curve and difficulty to be reasonable for anyone familiar strategy and resource management. The game does fall short as there is no way to plan ahead certain building upgrades without already knowing what they are and their cost. For example, if you build a mine, you will know what its possible upgrades and associated costs are only after it's built. As far as I can tell, there is no in-game method to open a UI to look ahead at a building's possible upgrades (i.e. Civilopedia in Civ). It is slightly frustrating needing to remember info — that's readily available in many other games — in a game where planning ahead is really important.The UI can also be a little frustrating at times. Giving Pupils orders as it cycles through them can often lead to accidentally assigning an already-assigned Pupil. Additionally, it's hard to know a Pupil's specialty at a glance without opening a separate information panel or hovering over icons. These images are arbitrary and will only be recognized after lots of runs. Even after my playtime, I am not always sure which icon is which at first glance. Resources can also be hard to spot on the map. You can always check via tooltip by hovering over a hex, but I found myself overlooking resources, such as stone on a mountain. As far as I know, there is no way to simplify the map view so that resources are easier to spot (i.e. strategic view in Civ).The art style is very pleasing, and it's one of the factors that immediately drew me in to learn more about the game. Like with the resources, it visually can be hard to separate certain things at glance. The music is very relaxing. Even though it's a game about survival, the soundtrack is very calming and fits nicely with the game's aesthetics.Strategy-game fans who decide to pick up As Far As The Eye are likely to be thoroughly entertained.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a challenge, this game is for you.  It's a turned based survival simulator that doesn't hold your and and will let you fall flat on your face if you aren't paying attention.  The UI is sleek, if a bit hard to get used to at first.  Tips:- I like to rename the characters based on the jobs I assign them.  - The bow tie color on the pupils can be changed- Clicking on the resource in the upper left shows all resources on the map- The campaign is a tutorial for the game
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful, the sound is relaxing, the act of balancing short and long term harvesting feels like a worthwhile endeavour. You feel in control.But then you get hit by a random vagary. You get some warning - 4 or 5 turns - to be prepared. You take a pupil off harvesting wood because the trees are going to be hit by lightning. You don't have enough wood now to run your bakery, the line is so thin.The lightning hits, you go back to harvesting wood while you reassign your baker to pick up pepkins (a basic food resource) that are less effective than baking, but you need to feed your guys. Another random vagary is projected. Rats are going to eat your pepkins. You reassign your guys to baker and woodcutter (your ration stocks dwindling...) and they take damage because yes, you're out of food.To heal them? A pupil must build a dispensary to harvest spice and concoct potions. You can't reassign your baker and woodcutter, so you pull the miner who was gathering stone to get you to the next map (or what is referred to as a 'halt') but you nearly have enough.The wave is coming soon. 30 turns left. It's enough to heal up, get your food and mine that last 40 stone you need.Another vagary.Oh... you just lost 20 turns. Can't make it anymore. End run.The other reviewers aren't people who are 'bad' at roguelites. This is a beautiful game where the only enemy is RNG and he is an unreasonable, malevolent enemy with no balance or respect for your time.It's not fun to lose this way, I really, really wanted to like this game but couldn't get there. A tweak to the random system and I might re-evaluate, but this game trivialises your investment too quickly. Don't buy yet.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, As Far as The Eye looks like it is a cozy game, but it's not. It's quite a challenge, and therefore if you're looking for something that seems chill, this likely wouldn't be your cup of tea. As a whole, I enjoy this game for the turn-based challenges as each turn counts, and it is not at all forgiving. Take note that save points don't exist, and you'll likely die more often than you succeed. Making each stage a reward for those who seek the challenge. Safe travels!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: In summary; A game with beautiful lore, artwork and music, terrible balance. As Far As The Eye is a gorgeous game set in a beautiful world full of music and myth. The Aesthetics of the game are really soothing, friendly, warm and misleading. There is a real tragedy felt when playing this game, because you see a wonderful world filled with elegant and memorable characters and designs, being killed mercilessly through every play through.You can be doing everything right, with ample food, resources and storage for taking it all with you, and then the wrong combination of circumstances will destroy the game.For Example;I had extra storage sorted at the start of my game. Ample cooked meat from my game hunter and chef. Everyone was at full health. Enough wood, stone and ore without being too greedy, just enough to pass the level and enough to start me on the next.Then, catastrophe. Fog appeared, and covered the map so I couldn't see anything. Then, mosquitos in the jungle began making my people ill. 50% of my halt was jungle, so navigating around them in the fog was unavoidable. I couldn't move on, and there weren't any spices for medicine. My people died. The game will punish you relentlessly, and with each failure you have learnt little to nothing. The music lures you into a false sense of tranquility, before tearing your progress from you.All this game needs, is a little balance patch.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but it is so so difficult. This game sat on my wishlist for a long time. I held off on buying it because of the "Mixed Reviews", until I received it via the Humble Monthly Bundle.The art, setting and music are incredibly charming. Particularly the lore around the "Pupils" travelling to the Eye each year before a great flood arrives, and the way the Pupils take on different forms for the jobs they do. The "Campaign" (actually the tutorial) is also quite well-written and well-constructed in how it introduces some (but not all) of the mechanics.However, once you start the game proper, the resource management is incredibly unforgiving. The starting tribe, the West Tribe, starts with a lot of rations, but even then you should immediately start working toward a Bakery or Cookhouse (which in turn need stone or ore) to produce more rations.Once you have more than three Pupils, it's impossible to produce enough food each turn without having a Bakery or Cookhouse. Because of the incredibly tight tech dependencies and resources, it's easy to underestimate how many steps are needed to setup a Bakery/Cookhouse until your Pupils are starving to death. And unless you get very lucky at your first halt and create a mobile Bakery/Cookhouse, you'll need to repeat this again at your second halt.This means although you may have an obvious goal of gathering certain resources to make it to the next halt, that will actually take a backseat for several turns until you've just managed to save your tribe from starving to death.Adding to this, there are some UX problems which make it very easy to make mistakes and waste a turn. The main one is that after you end a turn, the game may randomly change your selection to a different unit. So if you're watching a specific unit so you can give them an order on the next turn, you may accidentally give that order to a different unit instead, wasting multiple turns. This problem seems to be caused by the game focusing units which move on each turn. You can make the selection change more obvious by disabling the "simultaneous movement" option under Settings > Gameplay, but you can't disable it completely.Issues like these wouldn't be quite as frustrating, except the game has a huge focus on optimising time and resource management. And lot of the tools the game gives you to help with this, e.g. Pupils learning skills, the knowledge tree upgrades, mobile buildings, etc aren't helpful because it's a struggle just to keep a game going long enough to unlock any of these things.The game could be improved with some UI fixes and easing the difficulty curve, but from all indications the developers have stopped working on the game, so I would not expect these things to be fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I feel compelled to leave a public review of this game because of all the misleading and disparaging comments. This game is unique. It is hard. It will throw you off. You make a plan, and it falls apart. Failure is to be expected. You will not unlock everything each run. You need to focus and plan 2-3 nodes out. You need to learn the effects of catastrophes. You need to learn how to optimize build orders and adjust based on the size/type of node you are on. Despite the cutesy art style, this is a complex strategy game. Respect it as such. Yes, there are some bugs. The UI is not perfect. And the performance can fall out at times. But all of those things are to be overlooked for anyone that is looking for a new school game that is on par with greats like FTL and Into The Breach.  If the flavor and style of this game even remotely appeals to you, get it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, but as said, the RNG is brutal. And it feels like it ramps up at the end of every run. Lightening strikes 6 turns after Bog Mosquitoes, 10 turns after a fire, and then 4 forest tiles in and I need to have 1200 Wood while also using cooking for food and repairing structures during a hailstorm, but a caravan up ahead just told my tribe that there was an earthquake and we need 1800 more wood than before. Seems a bit much.The game is fun, the graphics are beautiful, and the Devs are working on balance issues, but for now, I'd say put it on your wishlist and grab the game when you see negative reviews turning back to positive. Don't let the small issues keep you away forever or risk burning you out. The core of the game is solid, just needs a few tweaks.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The bad reviews I saw for this almost turned me away, but having now completed a few runs, I am extremely glad I thought better of it. As an avid fan of both 4x/city builders and roguelike/lite games, AFATE manages to strike a very pleasing balance that doesn't compromise on any of the qualities of either genre that make them two of my favorites. If I had to draw a direct comparison, it's very reminiscent of how fresh the changes made to city planning in Civilization 6 felt when it first released, with the importance of careful planning and consideration for both nearby valuable resources and foresight for expansion dictating where to park your caravan at each stage of your journey. However, since this is something you do at each location you arrive at, rather than being something only done at the very start of the game, you get to spend more time really optimizing your placements and getting a good idea of how best to utilize each map. Perhaps a bit hyper-specific, but it's a gameplay loop I am incredibly fond of and am very glad to see it here.As for the roguelite aspects, it's very much in the realm of your FTL-likes, where you find yourself journeying from node to node across a world map, making your way to higher ground as an oncoming flood threatens to drown all the little critters you are responsible for guiding. Each stop tasks you with reaching certain milestones, either in the form of a resource quota, or by training up your tribe into various specialized jobs, and you have a limited number of turns to perform this task before the waters come to claim you. The timer tends to be pretty forgiving, but what makes it interesting is the various hazards and unfortunate events that can befall you, complicating the act of simply sending your "pupils" out to gather resources.Looking at the negative reviews, the complaints I am repeatedly seeing all boil down to the old adage of RTFM. The chief complaint is that the game has brutal RNG, but this is only true if you engage with none of the systems it provides to give you the opportunity to survive any of the catastrophic random events that are thrown at you. Train one of your pupils to be a druid and they can forewarn you about what the effects of exploring a ruin will be, and at higher levels even allow you to turn ones with negative outcomes into positive ones. Investing in upgrading your caravan with a Council allows you to conduct rituals to mitigate, or even sometimes outright eliminate, impending bad events. These are not deeply hidden or cryptic mechanics, and playing through the tutorial campaign will quickly and clearly acquaint you with them, as well as the charming lore of the cozy little world this game takes place in. Suffice to say, play the tutorial, learn the mechanics, and save yourself the frustration of trying to play a hybrid of two already complex genres without actually knowing how (not to mention the embarrassment of leaving a scathing review that indicates as much.) All-in-all, this is definitely one of the more forgiving entries in either of its composite genres, but it still offers a nice challenge and level of depth to be entertaining for a few runs at a time. As you complete runs you unlock more advanced tribes which offer an array of modifiers which will likely push the game's brutality factor up considerably, but for now I've just been enjoying getting acquainted with all the ways a standard run can go and piecing together the lore and mythology that all this is grounded in. If you like the idea of a slower more methodical FTL crossed with a cozier, more small scale 4x experience, it's a lovely way to spend an afternoon.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like it's still in the early stages of early access.  If you look at the achievements, only 1/3rd of people who play the game even finish the tutorials.  I understand why: I had to restart two tutorials because of very specific requirements that were unclear.  It's not like they're complicated; just unclear... and they lock you if you don't do it exactly right.  In general, the writing is barely comprehensible and needs to be scaled back a few notches.  The UI is absolutely horrid: tiny buttons with lots of submenus everywhere.  Lots of things look the same and your guys change appearance if they do a different job and there's no way to keep track of them.  There's no summary of what people are working on and where.  Everything's super bright so you can't make out individual things.  So much mis-clicking because you can't see.  ...and the gameplay boils down to hitting 'next turn' a BUNCH and praying that the place you're at has enough food and resources to get to the next place.Was excited for this one, but the devs really need to do a QoL pass or three.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend this game with a strong caveat. You should only play it if you enjoy stressful and harsh resource management. This game is ALL about optimal resource gathering in a time limit. If that weren't enough, gathering  comes with a penalty. Not to mention there's a food upkeep, health and various other things to consider. There's a lot going on, and frankly its a little too much for me to play a lot of it but I enjoyed it for the 5 hours I put in.I found the visuals to be extremely cute and generally pleasing, the sound design was interesting without being annoying, the gameplay was deep and fun (though stressful), I had no problems with the UI, and the lore/setting was fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game with the caveat that what everyone is saying about this game being difficult is correct and also an understatement. The game isn't just difficult. The game regularly generates scenarios that are outright impossible to complete. It generated a game level for me where I had to collect 500 ore, and the map it generated had 0 ore on it. Ok, that's fine. You can just trade for ore, right? Wrong, because the trading ratio for ore was 1/20, and there physically weren't enough combined resources on the map to trade for 500 ore. Very frustrating. It was the last level generated for my migration, so it's not like I could just take a different path. I had no choice but to go there, and they generated an impossible scenario. I wasn't even on the hardest difficulty level.So, that's what people are saying when they say the game is difficult. It's not difficult; it's downright impossible at times. All that being said, I recommend the game because it's really cute, and I love the gameplay mechanics. If they would tweak the map generator so that it stops generating impossible scenarios, this would be an awesome game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone that doesn't enjoy micromanagement, hyper-efficiency, and sheer-random luck in your game draw. This game is like a mesh of Stellaris (without the automation for resources), FTL (random survival journey to get to the end of the line), and Binding of Isaac (random starts, paths, traits, and misfortunes). The only downfall is it doesn't have the one thing that makes those games a reward to play: planning for the downfall you know is coming. The basic game is starting a path with 3 Pupils that have random positive and negative traits that can help or hinder your progress. That's fine. What the real kicker is the resource management. Naturally, one knows that not every resource is going to be available all the time, and you're given things like building a Market or Council to help with resources or with avoiding some of the harsher misfortunes (or Vagaries) that will hit your tribe. And they WILL hit. You up your chances for misfortunes or negative effects when you deplete too many resources (or "more than you need" according to the game), but you need those resources to either build your buildings EACH time you make a stop at a new location (because Mobile buildings are expensive, but worth it if you put the time into it), or because you need to sell/trade those resources when you're at a stop that doesn't have things like stone or ore, or in one instance, trees for wood (I immediately reset that game, wasn't even worth trying when it's the FIRST stop and you NEED wood to build anything). After that, the things like auras and ritual sites or "remains" and some such, hit you more often with negative effects than helpful ones. Things like: you start a game and its requirement is 2 Pupils, but you searched a ruin without first analyzing it, so you didn't know it was going to take 1 Pupil from you. Welp. You can suffer through that, but I don't, and reset. Ruins and Auras are more trouble than fun to interact with, as unless you have an Expert Druid (which you won't have until 3-4 stops in, IF you dedicated 1 Pupil to soothing auras and harvesting medicine extremely early on, which, why would you, that's expensive), and that Expert takes 2 turns to sooth it, UNLESS you remembered to take the trait to permanently sooth auras late in their tree.Granted, the game does have some enjoyment, but again, that's mostly when you get lucky, don't have 6 misfortunes 10 turns each apart, and remembered to focus your Pupils to their dedicated trades (and not accidentally mix them up because there is NO automation for resource gathering) and remember to check on them so you don't forget to assign them jobs when they run out of resources (because pressing the spacebar to finish a turn doesn't trigger the same warning box as clicking the turn button does to tell you that a Pupil isn't working). Finally, I think my last dislike of the game is the fact that, for some reason, after assigning Pupils build requests or movement requests, or any request to do something, sometimes they just... won't? They'll stop halfway through their action and sit, pondering why life is so hard, and unless you check on them because you're accustomed to the spacebar tactic, then... well. Good luck?The graphics are pretty, the sound effects and music are interesting and do help with setting up an atmosphere whlie you're playing. Ultimately, the frustration of trying to get to the end, only to have a misfortune tell you "well, all your mobile buildings take 80 damage" and there's not enough resources in your storage OR on the tiles you're on to fix it -- kills it for me. By all means, give the game a chance. I bought it while it was on sale, and I would recommend you do the same.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun enough game so far, however if you are an impatient sort of person maybe not the game for you. I wish there was a "maybe" recommendation because whilst I've hit the checkmark in the "yes" box I shall now proceed to complain about the game.I've failed to get through the second portion one of the tutorial levels a few times now, and there is no saving so each time I fail I have to go through the first part before I can try the second part again. This seems like a flawed design.However, what irritates me most about this game is the English. It is either poorly written or poorly translated from another language. I do have a sense that it is probably poorly translated based on the sorts of grammatical errors as well as inconsistencies between English and American spellings - pick one or the other and stick with it. It is a great shame to be let down on the writing so badly when the world building relies so heavily on said writing. It is tiring to figure out what they meant to say. There has clearly been a lot of love and care put into this game, and so why they wouldn't simply have a native English speaker proof-read all of the dialogue and instructions before release is beyond me.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game, as a premise, is sound - travel, manage your supplies, and make it to the Eye. It's a premise that we've had since some of the earliest days of gaming. It's something we go back to frequently. And it works. And boy does AFATE fail at it. In a way that makes me wish I hadn't sunk as much time in as I did, and instead refunded it when I had the chance. See, the game tells you to take your time, to optimize, to plan and make the best use of your villagers. But it woefully lacks any sense of control or agency over your travelers that would enable to you to correctly plan. The system has depth, but lacks meaningful choices - there is often a singular best choice, and that is to make Food. See, the game starts you off with a decent supply of Cooked Meals to get you going. These meals are consumed every turn by your travelers, and you very easily start to see that they begin to dwindle away at a rapid speed, increasing for every additional villager you require. But in order to replenish your stores, you need *three* of your villagers producing food. One to gather wood, one to gather a foodstuff (of which there are three, and the mysterious *spices* that can't be eaten on their own, but can be used in recipes) and one to actually cook the goods. Now, that sounds fine in principle. The problem is that you have three villagers. Meaning to prevent your travelers from starving, you need to be constantly producing food using them; which puts you behind in gathering the spices, the wool, or stone you might need to actually progress. And because each villager consumes six food per turn, even if they can't work, you end up having to either continually produce food, or you'll find yourself starving very quickly; switching jobs takes precious time that your travelers could be using to gather resources or cook food, so you're suffering additional losses of productivity that you so desperately need. If you want to use more than three travelers, you'll need to improve your capacity which requires resources, and travelers use food even if they can't work because you lack the capacity on your caravan. Gods help you if your travelers end up with traits that make them take up 2 capacity, or always take one capacity even when not working. So you *barely* begin to eek out an existence when using more than 3 travelers, but it is extremely expensive to the point where nearly 80% of all the cool upgrades you could get are ignored in favor of simply spent getting more travelers going. And on the hardest clan your travelers require wool in addition to food, making them even more costly to survive. The fundamentals of a good game are here. But the sheer base system of the game forces you into a specific decision that means as you play and unlock more traits for travelers to have, that are potentially extremely crippling, half your runs may be dead at the start. You generally know if a run is dead a handful of turns in; and every run that lives past the first halt ends up having very similar gameplay: set up your food, use your one or two other travelers to gather whatever you need, and hope that the random events don't smite your run without any way for you to really recover. You barely get to touch on the good stuff in the game such as healing potions and druids, explorations and sacrifices, or the Council Tech system because you're so focused on barely eeking out an existence even with optimal play so your travelers don't die of starvation. It's not fun, it's not engaging, and it's just too frustrating. This game really, completely, is not worth it, even for rogue like fans.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most frustrating games I've ever played. It feels almost impossible to actually win. You do your best, gather resources, keep them safe and bam! The game adds an extra resource that has to be gathered in order to move on, like ore, or stone, and often is a resource you don't have on that halt, or don't have enough of it. Ok, that's fine you say, I'll use the market. The thing is... there's nothing to trade! I need stone to trade for the ore, but I need all the stone on the halt to move to the next one. I could trade wood, but it's 14 to 1, so no way in hell I will ever be able to gather enough wood for 300 ore. I really love this game, but there was always something that ruins my experience: vagary that kills the little guys, something ruining my buildings, or just no food on the halt. And I did try it before buying! And it was way easier and much enjoyable, one of the earliest releases. But no, they had to ruin it with updates that make it unwinnable. Such a pity...
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: As Far As The Eye is a beautiful turn-based strategy game. You have to build up a village. Each resident has his own personality. You can level each one up individually and let them learn different skills on a skill tree. The goal is to survive to get into the centre of the world - The Eye. On your way, you have to get different resources to get to the next map. You can't take everything with you to the next one, since there is an inventory and you have to manually stack resources or buildings in it. The counter tells you when the wave arrives. Each turn lets the timer count down. If you don't have the resources to travel 'til it reaches zero, the game is over. The campaign works as a tutorial. There are 5 missions which will teach you how the game works. Aside from that you can set up your own session with your own rules OR just play in sandbox mode where you have to unlock each tribe. A session is different thanks to procedural events, skill trees and negative or positive traits for each resident.  It is somewhat comparable to games like civ even through there are no battles in it. Tbh, civ and the likes are to complicated for me. There is so much detail, you have the feeling you need to study before you can enjoy it. With As Far As The Eye it's not like that. The game starts out pretty simple which is a good thing since you have fun from the start. The longer the game goes, the more complicated it gets. You're learning while playing. There are many little details in the game. It's not like its to easy. It's more accessible.  The game just looks so beautiful. The music is atmospheric. It's easy to learn and hard to master. I didn't thought i'll have that much fun while playing a tutorial. It's much more accessible than civ or other games in the genre. I would have liked more missions in the campaign. Aside from that even sandbox sessions are fun since there comes always a story with it (somewhat like in frostpunk). It's different than other games in the genre. Everyone who is into city building sims should get this game. It's definitely worth it! If you like my review and are into strategy games please consider following my curator page:
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The game is nice and challenging. Haven't yet finished any expert scenarios yet, only all of the basic ones with all the tribes and of course the "campaign" (actually, it is just a tutorial). The tutorial does not explain all of the mechanics, but you will learn most of them. The rest have to be explored by paying attention to the interface (click on all buttons and read all tooltips on them, buildings especially), the council stuff and caravan upgrades especially, which is fine, and reading random tips on the global map, which is a weird place to learn things that can be important, but whatever. Despite what some of the reviews say, in my opinion, the GUI is good and easy to use. There are enough tooltips that explain what everything does, selecting what you want is most of the time easy and to highlight resources you can leftclick on them in your storage (top left). But there doesn't seem to be a way to highlight all of them and quickly finding sacred sights and remains is hard since those can not be highlighted. But these are mostly minor problems.Again, despite what many reviews say, the council building (and its upgrades) have not been necessary for me to finish most of the basic scenarios. Many vagaries (random bad events) can be safely ignored or their effects circumvented. There is a way to play by highly relying on the council building, but it is not the only one. The harmony score that can be seen at the end of a scenario seems to reflect how much resources you have gathered and wasted (symbolizing taking what is not necessary for survival and completion of the journey) and probably increases the frequency of vagaries. So if you are mostly working directly for the objective (which you should anyway, since the game is about optimization) you will not have to worry much about the harmony score and face less bad random stuff. Probably.Random generation could be improved, since some things just don't make sense (auras that protect ore in an area when there is none or vagaries that affect jungles that may not be on the map at all).All in all, game is nice, clean, cozy (despite the challenging nature), allows for multiple strategies to achieve objectives, presents challenges that require adaptation (depending on the difficulty of the scenario) to win and has random generation for maps, scenarios and other things which provide replayability. A fresh idea and good execution.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is bizarre. I held off writing a review for a long time, because this is one of those games that I would give a sideways thumb or a neutral review if I could. It has a lot of aspects I like, but also a considerable amount I don't, but in the end I gave it a recommendation because I think it's a great game for a specific subset of people -- the game has plenty of polish, and some of the aspects that I would take the most points away for are also some of the ones with the greatest overall subjectivity.As Far As The Eye does provide a roguelike experience, but the challenges are centered around route planning and gathering cycle optimization. A lot of the game involves repetitively having your followers complete the same set of actions over and over again with the goal of attempting to acquire specific combinations of resources needed to move onto the next area. Unfortunately, as you get into the longer journeys, you can't see the entire map (and the resource types and quantities needed to complete your journey) from the beginning. Since the combinations of resources are random and not every type of area has the same resources (or a guarantee that there's a meaningful amount of the types it does have), this means that you may end up in a section of the map where the only paths available to you don't provide even a chance of successfully completing your journey. With that said, many reasonable assumptions can be made about the likely resources available and resources acquired, making that situation unlikely if you know what you're doing. It could be compared to similar situations in roguelikes such as FTL in which you end up at the end of the game in an unwinnable fight -- it's possible that your run simply had no possible path to victory, but more likely a more experienced player would have been able to identify play and pathing errors that could have given you a better chance if corrected. Since there isn't a direct opposition or any type of combat in AFATE, though, losing to the situation of "none of the resources you need are available" could end up feeling impersonal and frustrating.Aside from weirdness on the direct gameplay loop, AFATE also has a progression I'm not particularly fond of -- unlocking penalties. As you play the game, you unlock different traits that are rolled on each character. Both negative and positive traits are unlocked, and while overall you gain more than you lose, it's possible that early on a player might actually put themselves in a worse position by accidentally unlocking some very poor traits while failing to unlock any particularly good ones. Finally, I just don't like the game's color palette very much. It does stand out from the crowd, but I find that it grates on me as I actually play the game. I can definitely see this as being a positive for some people though, which is why I save it for last -- it's a big deal for me, but anyone that the color palette or aesthetic doesn't appeal to can already see that from the screenshots or trailer; they don't need me to point it out.Anyway, hope this helps someone in coming to a bit of a better understanding about the nature of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game and I feel like I should put in a positive review for it because I see a lot of negative reviews talking about things that were pretty contrary to my experience with it. I think the game may have been updated or changed because most of the negative reviews focus on how punishing the RNG is and how there's no way to counteract it and your runs will be ruined purely by a negative event. Some of the negative events are pretty harsh but you almost always have advance notice that they're coming, and you can usually plan around them. You can also build a special building that lets you predict them further out or even cancel them a limited number of times. Now, this building is never mentioned in the tutorials so I'm not surprised people don't really notice it, but it's there.Overall I really enjoy this game, it's a fun balance between relaxing worker management and tense moments of crisis management. Beautiful aesthetic and sounds really add to the experience. I'd say the major shortfall of this game is that some of the mechanics are poorly explained, like the aforementioned council building or how harmony works (look it up on google and you'll find a fairly detailed wiki page). It is definitely a roguelike so be prepared for the procedural generation to give you a pretty nasty situation, and try to plan ahead as much as possible. You can see the next path so you can start saving up resourced for your next path before you reach it! The council can even let you see further down the path.If you like resource/worker management games and you don't mind losing a few times then I recommend checking out this game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game initially but got sick of it fast.  The randomness of the bad effects frequently generate unwinable situations and there is no way to save your progress in the game.  Its very frustrating to invest so much time and then have it randomly kill you off.  It has become a chore to play so I really cannot recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: RNG dictates your runs way too much in this. Suddenly, half of your buildings get wrecked or one of your starters can't gain any type of specialization due to a negative trait. The negative traits outweigh the positive ones greatly in my opinion. One cook I got from a caravan had a negative trait I couldn't see prior to getting him that literally made him unable to generate food.... as a cook. I typically really enjoy survival and resource management games, but this one feels really bad when you can have one of your three units on gathering food 100% of the time and still end up starving.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Really nice idea and cute graphics, but REALLY bad execution. I've played 11 hours and never managed to win once. Even in your best run you get unwinnable halts (including the last one, where there were something like 8-9 Aura tiles on all the main resources I needed to harvest. I even managed to harvest the other 2 needed resources, but due to all the turns wasted sooting auras I just couldn't harvest enough pumpkins to feed my tribe and clear the requirement). The game should at least allow you to restart an individual halt instead of the whole game, because no matter how good you are, you could just be unlucky in your last halt and everything's lost. I might try to at least play some custom games instead of abandoning it completely, but knowing you can't see 90% of the game (the other tribes unlock only after you win with the first) really make you lose interest. I could have loved this game, but ended up feeling like I wasted my time :(
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, unique gameplay but lacks polish and replayability. Know what you are getting into before purchasing.AFATE does a great job in what it sets out to be. You get that feeling that you are barely making it throughout most of a game session, the same feeling as playing FTL. The resource management is strong and punishing, if you focus on food production, all of a sudden the big wave is coming soon and you didn't harvest what you needed to advance. Or focus on advancing and lack food and watch your pupils starve in a few turns.The problem with AFATE is the UI and some of the programming. There is no overlay to see all the resources like in Civ or any other 4X game and it's annoying. There also needs to be a short overview of what all of your pupils are up to and make it obvious when a pupil is idle. Missing tooltips, pathfinding issues, hard to select pupils over the tile they are on. I also would like to know more information about future stops, yes it is a medium marsh zone but what the heck is in there?> How about a ballpark. The most hilarious part is that there is no warning if you end your turn when the big wave hits and you get a game over. I've lost a few games completely focused on something else and you go through turns very quickly and boom gameover, no going back, gg. But how is the RNG? The RNG is strong and at sometimes unfair. There's a building to stop an RNG event before it hits but that building is cost intensive and takes a long time to build, so you are mostly stuck eating whatever comes at you. The events are either bad, very bad or nothing. For example, you have the 1,000 stone needed to advance, but boom rats are coming to eat half of your stone and now there isn't enough stone left on the amp to advance, game over. Or you are cooking meat to food and boom now pupils cooking get sick. Etc, etc. It's a *roguelike* and you need to be prepared for the game to just screw you over.I am recommending this game because when it comes down to it, I got the feeling of "Grrrr, gotta play again, gotta win" and it consumed a few weekends. I look back and feel is was better than average, frustration level at a 7/10. I don't prefer RNG that completely wrecks your run but when it does I always think "if I just did this I could have continued" and that pushes this game into an upvote.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the story very much, the graphics a little and some of the mechanics mostly.  However, there are too many random game ending events which no amount of preparation can ward against.  Whilst I may still try to finished the remaining scenarios, it has quickly become repetitive and I am not really having much fun.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Conceptually, this is excellent, and I wanted to like it. However, the UI is quite clunky, and the settings are not optimised for 1440x900 resolution - in fact, I couldn't progress past the second sentence of the tutorial, since the "continue" arrow was off the screen. As far as I can tell, the devs are not supporting the game any more, and several people commented in the discussion forum about this, to no apparent resolution. Sadly refunding.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, this game looks like it could have been made for me. It's a rogue-ish game with procedurally generated "halts" (hex maps) that you travel between FTL-style to reach a final halt. But instead of slaying every foe on your way, you explore, gather, and build. It's such a beautiful little game that should, by all rights, be a relaxing experience, but the mechanics just don't line up with the feel it gives off at all. In a game that's thematically about rebirth and cycles, you keep failing for arbitrary reasons that you had no way to prepare for. I'm fine with learning by dying, but if the death doesn't bring any new knowledge...Please bear in mind that I am not one of those people who complain about randomness in every punishing game out there. I loved Darkest Dungeon, which is very punishing, but in DD and many other games like it that I have defended against the "fake difficulty" mobs, the randomness can be . The negative effects can be mitigated by hedging your bets, withdrawing when things are rough, etc.In As Far As The Eye, you can't do anything except hope you don't get certain vagaries (random negative events that happen every now and again) that are nearly guaranteed to ruin you. The "rodents" vagary has single-handed ended three runs in a row for me now. Rats keep eating whatever resource I happen to need the most at the moment, leaving my pupils dying for hungry or straight out blocking me from moving on. I gave up when not only did they eat all the meat I had hunted, but directly after another vagary stopped my trappers from working.So despite some good ideas and a beautiful theme, I can't recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting concept based on 4X games, where you have to gather different resources to move to the next level. But instead of fighting enemies to create a challenge, the game throws random negative perks at you that often ruin the plans you have in mind. Things like suddenly losing 500 skill points without any means to prevent this felt unfair to me and became even frustrating in the longer runs. Not my cup of tea.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to make sure I had a decent amount of time invested in it prior to writing a review.  At the time of writing this review, I have approximately 38 hours of gameplay in this game and I have completed the main campaign along with 3 of the 8 scenarios, along with many attempts to complete the remaining 5.  So yes, I do have a lot more to do in this game.  Things that I liked:At the end of completing a scenario, you receive new perks for your pupils.  I was particularly excited about obtaining one that allowed one of my pupils to walk on water.I love the art and the music.  It is really relaxing and unique.  The design of the game is different from anything else I have played.I like that the game is challenging.  It requires you to use your brain and think.  You cant just blast through a halt without planning.  In order to do well, you have to have your pupils specialize and pay attention to what you are having them do.What I did not like:I did not like the inventory management system when traveling between halts.  I like that there is a puzzle in what you can bring, but it is difficult to move things around in the box and arrange.  I know that this is probably designed this way to make it more difficult, but I feel like it could have been better executed.Some mechanics can be a little confusing.  The RNG of vagaries can get very frustrating.  For example, when  a wave is about ready to hit and you need wood to move on…. Yet you get hit with a vagry that makes workers in forests sick… it has the potential to break your game if you are not prepared.  All in all, this game has way more positive aspects than negative ones.  I enjoy the challenging aspects of the game and I even enjoy the RNG (even when it causes me to fail).  I like that you need to take time to learn the game, and I feel like completing a scenario does reward you and give you a sense of accomplishment.  I encourage everyone who enjoys turn based strategy games to give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: A neat concept, it's like Civilization except a rogue like. You get a few buddies and try to reach the end by completing a handful of stages. In each stage there is challenges to overcome as well as opportunities for you to explore, gather resources, and improve your buddies. I don't particularly like strategy or civ games but this provides it in a sort of bite sized format. You can finish a full run in an afternoon.I'd love if there were a form of progression that persisted through runs, but other than that my only complaint is that the tutorial is a bit long.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great little resource gathering and management game with adorable style. It is also deceptively difficult. Don't load this up, listening to the calm music and whispered ASMR gibberish of the creatures, thinking you're going to have a relaxing time. You're often going to be painstakingly plotting each turn and fighting to survive.High Point: The wonderful design and smooth experience. I love the little world they created in this game. It's colorful and vibrant and really feels alive. The randomness of each time you load up a new game (between the map layouts, character traits, resource requirements, pathing, etc) keeps things from getting overly procedural. Low Point: I would honestly say that the food requirements for the "pupils" you lead are...perhaps a bit too demanding. There are so many potential things available in the game to focus on, but I felt for a lot of my runs, I spent so much time trying to keep my little peeps fed that I couldn't enjoy expanding them out into all the varied classes and traits. I literally just finished getting the 100% for achievements (which are annoyingly not detailed), so I think I'm about to hang this up for good. Over time, you do figure out the tricks and it gets more intuitive. Just be prepared for a steep learning curve. For anyone just starting out and struggling, I'll just say: Don't sleep on pepkins. Harvest Hut + Fruit Gatherer will get you to the end most runs. And the Council building will be your best friend, don't put off building one. ;P Good luck, and see you at the Eye!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really, REALLY want to like this game. I love the concept and the "idea" of the basic gameplay loop. Interesting setting and lore. Graphics are fun and pretty enough for me.I am going to continue playing it so I may in fact update my review to positive if something clicks and I start to enjoy it more. BUT...The main hurdle you're faced with is just random punishments that pop up with a few turns warning. Generally not enough time to actually take any action to meaningfully mitigate the bad thing that is gonna happen.How to recover from this? Spend resources. Which you get by gathering resources. Which you get by spending resources. Also you need to save up resources that you get to eventually move on to the next level. But also you get TONS of random events that cost resources, which you probably don't have because this game is a vacuum of RNG without any consideration of what's available to you or what you likely already have had a chance to get by a given point in the game.I so far don't really have the time and resources necessary to build the infrastructure to gather a large variety of... other resources. IDK, maybe more skilled players can, but I am not able to do so with the very first tutorial campaign. And it just feels like a micromanagement warehouse game rather than an epic journey of your tribe's migration and survival.And the random punishments generally just cause damage to your buildings. Or a penalty to what resources you can gather in an area. And to repair those damaged buildings, you just need to spend resources. Don't have any of that particular resource b/c it's not on the map and/or not a goal that you're stockpiling towards? (Or you don't have any more and HAVE to keep that stockpile or else it's an instant game over at the end of this level's timer?) Then you cannot repair it. Once a building gets to zero HP, it's gone and the invested resources lost forever. Random events range from cause 50% to 90% damage to a building in my experience, and you can repair 10% a turn. Does that sound fun to you? It doesn't feel fun to play, for me. Oh, and one of the bad events is literally just "your workers forgot what they were doing" and you have to just click all the workers and reassign the tasks they were already doing. What a challenge! Totally not unnecessary busy-work that's as fun as hitting your head on a wall.The gameplay simply isn't interesting. Gather basic resources to spend on buildings to gather advanced resources to use to repair buildings that were randomly damaged and stockpile for the goal of the level, then play a tetris minigame where you try to bring as many resources with you to the next level but invariably leave a TON of stuff behind. All while dealing with random penalties totally tied to RNG and not at all taking into account your goals and what's available on the level you're on.On first impression I thought this was gonna be a super fun game that was right up my alley, but instead I am experiencing frustration and an unsatisfying gameplay loop. The challenge of the random setbacks just feels too random, too arbitrary, and not in any way fun to deal with.There's ALMOST a really fun and enjoyable game here, but something went wrong with execution and it leans far too much into RNG and/or boring stuff for "challenge". If you're gonna do that, you gotta give the player permanent advantages like a rogue-like so that eventually they can beat the unlucky RNG situations through sheer accumulation of advantages, but doesn't seem to happen in this game.Sadly, I cannot recommend this game despite really wanting to like it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game if you don't mind suffering, you become obsessed with winning and you have a lot of time to sink into realizing the universe is out to kill your pupils.I really enjoy resource and strategy games like this. The concept is fantastic, it's complex and each campaign is unique. My complaint is that it may be a little too hard. The amount of times I've become attached to my pupils just to watch them perish literally a few resources away from the eye was very heartbreaking. I was definitely obsessed for a bit there and may have screwed over my sleep cycle to suffer just a little longer.In other news, thanks to all the beautiful strategy experience in this game, I was finally able to beat the New Home campaign in Frostpunk so I can't be too mad.All in all, this game is really hard. Don't expect to win the first, fifth or twentieth campaign you play. Honestly, don't expect to win at all and then maybe you'll be surprised! Happy gaming y'all.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I've never written a review before, despite having thousands of hours on steam (like a degenerate). I feel like I need to counter out all of the negative reviews.First of all, I do not even love this game. I like it, but thats it. I'm writing this because I am a guy who cruises through the negative reviews on every game I'm interested in before I buy it. So many people were saying this game is impossible and that they've never completed a run after [so many hours]. I really don't know what to say about that... This game is hard as hell, you need to think out everything you're doing, and its unforgiving (these are all qualities that I like). ----but It is not impossible.I read like 20 reviews by people who could not complete a single run, but I just beat the game on my first try. I beat it on my first try, and honest to God, I'm a complete idiot. I like to get ♥♥♥♥-faced drunk (I'm hammered now, forgive any grammar issues), and play video games. I beat this on like 16 beers. It is not impossible.If you're interested in worker-management games, and you want to play against a difficult rule-set, this game is pretty solid. If you can't afford to drop $20-30 bucks or whatever, don't go for it. If you're like me, and you like difficult games, and make more than minimum wage, buy it. Its pretty solid; you'll have some fun with it (I only have like 5 -6 hours prolly at the time of writing this, so I don't know about replayability). Biggest cons? For you 'negative review' guys out there? The art (though I do like it) makes it difficult to understand whats going on without paying close attention. Second, all of the characters are explicitly genderless. Draw your own conclusions from that. I have a friend named George who is gay. I would not recommend this to him, or any of his Gay friends (this is not a judgement of homosexuals generally).
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The game is adorable, and really calming to play, but the difficulty is scaled just a tiny bit too high for my taste.  I wish there was an option to restart from the beginning of a halt, without the rogue-like aspect of "Oh hey, you played this round one turn too long, BACK TO THE BEGINNING".Luckily, there's custom games, which might be a little more my speed, but the food requirements are just a touch too punishing for me.  I've lost several games where a Pupil has been harvesting pepkins from the first turn, only to starve to death by the second halt.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but I really like this game conceptually and would like to advocate for an improvement to the vagaries system. There are several Vagaries that makes the game feel more frustrating than fun. Not because they are random or difficult, but because you can receive a mix of them within a few turn span that will end your game. That is, there is a chance that your game can just end.For example, I can be 2/3 through a level with 40 turns remaining and receive two vagaries that reduce the turns on the level by 20. You can also receive vagaries that increase the resource requirements to leave the stage beyond the resource availability on the stage.There are ways to mitigate these issues by trading for resources, etc., but often times the game strikes a careful balance between resource consumption and production and you can be put in a position that is mathematically impossible to recover from. I think a simple change that prevents receiving a few of the vagaries more than once per stage could go a long way.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Concept behind this game is flawed. On one hand, you're forced to think ahead, on the other hand, your plan may or may not be totally undermined by factors completely outside your control. You may think that the solution is adaptability and flexibility, like it usually is in roguelikes. Not here - most of the time the game punishes you for flexibility. It's like the core mechanic of the game was supposed to be planning and careful management, but then the designers decided to make it roguelike without adjusting the core or giving us tools to deal with the randomness appropriately. It's simply not enjoyable. Pity, because the sounds are amazing and it looks pretty.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The RNG events in this game make this unplayable. You might say, ah you are just unlucky or that I should plan better, but you can literally be hit with 2 events in a row that completely wipe you out. It happens far too often (6 attempts in a row). I played CK II and EU4 for along time, so I am used to being screwed over by RNG, but this is on a whole nother level. I would highly suggest to anyone wanting to purchase this to wait to see if they fix any of the RNG issues currently being experienced.I really hope they do fix those issues, because this game is beautiful and well made other than that one game breaking issue.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the weirdest and most heartbreaking thumbs down I've ever given. I love everything about the game....Except the visuals. And I don't mean the graphics, I mean the screen is so incredibly dense with visual information that I becomes incredibly taxing for me to process all of it. A single hex might have 3 different resources (visualized as multiple 3D objects, a worker (called Pupil) with a distinct model that informs you of it's function, multiple balloons (that acts as worker selectors and representations of current stage of work) and some additional status information, or a model of a friendly caravan passing by. And the screen consist 8+ similarly packed hexes. It's just to DENSE. If some of it were less embellished, or there were more empty space between hexes, or some information would be relegated to icons...I'd love it. As it is it's just...exhausting to play.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Without question the most luck orientated game i have ever played, the entire set up of each game is random and more often than not you will come across a map you cannot get past even if you play it perfectly. Such as a map where i need to collect 600 stone to advance + other resources, but there is only 300 stone on the map, even with a fully upgraded market its a 6 -1 ratio to buy stone meaning you need to collect at least 1800 other resources before the time runs and got a random event that shortened the time limit by 20%, and this sort of thing is a pretty common occurrence, If you have played battle brothers and found the RNG too nice and forgiving in that game you might like this otherwise I would avoid.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The game premise is beautiful and I love the intro cinematic. It seems like a rewarding challenge! I wanted to love this game. I took my time with it, I didn't give up like some reviewers did after losing on the first tutorial.I came to prove all the negative reviews wrong.I was wrong.The problem with this game is , possibly even going through Halts (which are NOT checkpoints). By the time you do feel the ramifications, there's NO chance to recover due to the nature of the turn limit and you must just lose/quit. This makes you feel like you are wasting your time. The game is challenging, yes, and planning is required. But after you lose several times in a row without feeling a tangible reason, you start to feel like every move is not enough. You can feel efficient for 30 turns squeezing every bit out of your turns...and suddenly you are starving somehow and everyone will die before you can even react to that. So you adjust and stock a lot of food next play...but now you have none of the actual resources you need to progress, so you adjust again. 10 turns later you are starving again. Some call this "challenging" but really it's more like a huge chore. Alas, even after you finally get the "right solution" to the "puzzle" you don't feel like you solved anything meaningful, just that you got the game to "work" so you might finally begin to play a game that actually isn't there.---P.S. If you going to randomly remove skills from my pupils when they explore ruins, don't explain it to me as "he read some useless info so now he has to forget some of his skills". What a bizarre and lousy reason. How about you actually GIVE him some useless or niche skill, but something that goes with what you told me in the dialogue, not just "he forgot how to do X now from reading something on the wall".
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game so bad. The basic premise of tight resource management and city planning in a rogue like setting really appealed to me. I really enjoyed the process of planning out each halt (map) versus the entire journey. What really stopped me was the fact that so many of the game's mechanics failed or simply served no purpose. Some examples:1.) There are random events that can be discovered. The benefits are often wildly trivial and the consequences often result in a complete run loss. Complete run loss happens often, and you often have very little control over it.2.) ANY loss of the life of a pupil is game over. When your time is limited and skills have to be cultivated over the course of your entire run, you usually get your full group of pupils and stick to them until the end...otherwise you may simply lose because you lack enough specialized skills.
