Couple that with miserable traits like "lose hp every turn" and some runs are a non-starter.3.) Healing is terrible. In a game where it's often tight to get from halt to halt, and in a game where hoarding resources is punished...the fact that it requires upwards of 12 turns to make ONE healing potion that restores a portion of a pupil's hp is downright terrible design. It's better to avoid illness altogether or tank the hp loss and hope your pupils don't die (unless the world's most lucky trader comes by).4.) There's an entire knowledge point system that can go into a few categories of "tech"...but only one of them (the main knowledge tree) seemed useful to me. I toyed with the others for testing, and it came at the cost of my odds of winning.In short, if you want to try a game that's a bit frustrating and fallen short of what it could have been...go ahead and give it a try. Otherwise, I'd recommend looking elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Up Front: Overall its not a bad game, but beyond that, it's not particularly strong. I recommend getting it on sale, but $25 is a bit expensive in my opinion.Long story:Graphics: Pretty simple yet the vibrancy and character make for a unique and fun experience. It's not mind blowing though.What is a bit disappointing is that the campaign lacks integration of animation like it had shown in the trailer. Plot: Whats additionally disappointing is that there is almost no plot aside from some very skeletal text written out in the campaign. There isn't a lot to connect with as the game proceeds as you go from caravan to caravan, and you never connect with any of the characters. There is a clear underlying emphasis on nature, but that too is unexplored. Mechanics: The mechanics are smooth, well balanced, and once you understand them the game is straight forward. In fact I think that it is a bit too easy. Punishments in the terms of vagaries are rather underhanded as I see it. That they are more like random potholes that might blow out your tire rather than plot twists. Finally, it is not unpleasant nor is it overpriced as far the experience goes. It would be unfair to down vote it for its lack of depth over its outward professional quality. It's probably not something I would buy a sequel to unless it was less than $20. I got 45 hours out of it, which is alright.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: ✔️ Creative and interesting game mechanics, compressing a colony management game into a roguelike experience.✔️ Cute and cozy graphics & sound design.❌ The game is just too difficult in my opinion. Its general mood doesn't prepare you at all for how difficult it is to actually complete a run. Not only you have to juggle with tons of resources to build structures, feed your characters, and advance in the game - but the game also punishes you with devastating events for having extra resources. I get the point of only taking what you need to keep going, but the overall complexity of the game is already pretty daunting even without that. At this point it's an actual game design flaw in my opinion.❌ In addition to the crazy difficulty of this game, the randomness can completely mess up your progression, sometimes giving you areas without enough food to advance, or without enough resources to fulfil your travel prerequisites. So not only sometimes you will lose because of poor decisions in an unforgiving game, but also sometimes you will just be destroyed by the game itself without any chance to compensate for the bad luck.Sadly I cannot recommend the game, despite finding it generally interesting and cute, but its challenge level is just too dissonant with its general presentation, and after 7 hours I still haven't completed a single run of the easiest game mode, so I'd rather prevent other people from having a similar experience... I might keep trying to play it, and maybe if I realise at some point that I was approaching it from the wrong angle from the beginning, I could change my review, but that seems unlikely.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: A decent idea poorly implemented. I paid <$7 for this on sale and even at that price I'm kind of irritated with how bad the balance is. Usually these type of games have multiple paths of victory and you must read the map and situation to execute a win. I love difficult games with razor-thin victory margins. But with AFATE, it's always a coin toss; what negative events you get dealt, what negative traits you get dealt. They can end a run early on with no way to adapt. This being a 'roguelike' I thought, "Okay, fail your way to victory. Get better, unlock perks to be able to handle a wider variety of problems that come up." Nope. More randomization that makes it less predictable with less control over your play through. Its lack of rewarding progression and improvement as you learn and unlock things make me want to just go play something else. Back to the drawing board, guys. This needs a major mechanics overhaul. There's room for a decent game here, but it's definitely not one, yet.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is nice, but there's a big issue with the campaign: you can't save! Even if there are no more than 2 jumps in the first 4 chapters, I found it impossible to finish chapter 4!Lack of time, restart the whole chapter! Wrong planning in first run? Restart! Game crash? Restart! And the game did crashed right when I finished chapter 4. I didn't manage to see the ending, nor did I get an achievement.The free play has another design issue: you don't have all the tribes unlocked at first, nor is there a description on the requirements. Besides this, free play has a single save slot. While these mechanics don't bother me in other games, AFATE isn't a rogue-like/lite.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I would really love to recommend this game, but I just can't.It looked so promising in the beginning and I was really looking forward to playing it.After 5h in, I decided to quit.It looks gorgeous and the gameplay with the different skill trees could be so much fun, but the rest of the gameplay is just hindering.It feels like on one hand you need to micromanage every aspect, which I like, but on the other hand, you are not given the tools to do so.For example I did not find a way to have an overview of my eco, how much food do I produce each round, how much do I use, what's the net profit?I did not find a way to stop my pupil from eating the rations, which I specifically produce for the quest and just give them fruits, as soon as they have rations, they chew down on them.I can not set certain paths for the pupils to avoid danger, on the other hand they straigth up walk into infested jungles and die of the illness.TL:DR Wants you to manage, but does not let you manage. Looks nice though.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: As much as me hurts me to do this, I have to give it a negative review for now.The game has great asthetics and the mechanics are interesting. I especially love the ability to specialize each pupil for certain jobs. But that's as much praise I can give it for now.This game has a lot of problems that cumulate to an annoying experience that afterwards made you feel like you wasted your time. A lot of reviews here mention the absurd amount of high impact randomness and they are not wrong, there is a lot of that in this game. However, my biggest issue doesn't lie in the negative traits or bad random events. You can play around these to some extend. Not always, there are some combination of random events are pretty much a game loss but that hasn't happened to me that much. The worst part about all of this is the map generation. Sometimes it presents you with only resource heavy paths of wich barely any of the resource spawnd in the map itself. Maybe there is more to the market but as it stands I was unable to ever compensate that issue with trading let alone you are able to build a market in the first place. The exchange rates are ridiculously high and upgrading it probably costs the resource you need and doesn't improve the exchange rates to be worth it. I've lost several runs I was doing well in because the path forward required me to have 1200 of a resource which wasnt present on the map. You can spend knowledge to see what the future paths cost but you cannot know exactly what is on the next map. Another thing I want to mention is that the balance is insanely harsh. Your production feels very inefficient compared to what is required from you. It's also the reason why a random event hits so hard. You sometimes cannot afford to play around it and in both reagrds it may lead to a loss easily. The upfront cost of aquiring any resource on top of the consumption makes having anything but the bare minimum (sustaining yourself and the cost for the current path forward) almost impossible in later stages (if possible at all due to map generation). The game feels like it requires you to have so many more resources than it let's you produce especially since it only hands out rewards to you if you have this randomly selected obscure resource.And while I like the pupils gaining skill in their job, I also don't like how certain actions are locked behind them. This is mainly a problem because it takes so insanely long for you to unlock these actions. For the first 3 maps you have so many dead tiles on top of already empty tiles because you cannot interact with them. And dealing with multiple auras feels almost impossible without a druid but since he is a higher tier profession you generally don't have access to him until late and he is such a burden to your tribe. All in all, to me, map generation is the most frustrating part of this game. It just feels awful to have a good run and then sit there unable to do anything because only 200 rock spawned but you need 500 to progress. "Welp, guess I die". I want to keep playing this game but everytime I do and it ends like that, it feels like a punch to the face.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I initially enjoyed this game. Civ style strategy games always have a spot in my heart, specially when they do something different like AFATE. I've played it for 4 hours and really liked the narrative, the mechanics and the way you carry items to the next levels with this tetris-style bag management. But then I got annoyed by repetitive tasks and the bad UI. After almost three years I decided to play it again and there's almost no improvements since the first time I played. I really hope this game receives quality of life updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly difficult and unforgiving, brutally punishing, and so satisfying.At first, I thought the game was just unfair because some maps just don't give the resource you need to get to the next. In reality, I needed to be spending knowledge points to see the future & get more cargo space so I could plan ahead by bringing resources I'd need. I needed to use markets to exchange for that last item I couldn't farm. Disasters can be punishing, but you have the ability to cancel a small number of them.As far as the Eye is incredibly rewarding once you realize long term planning is the key to success. When that planning pays off it feels great.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The controls ui and game design for this game is what kills it in my opinion For example the fact that units are selected after some commands but not others makes giving the wrong command to the wrong unit a common occurrence. The amount of times you need to restart because the game changes who you have selected about 5 seconds after a turn has already started...There are countless notifications for everything you are already aware of, but nothing for the things you are not. Like bakeries running out of food. There is also no warning for the flood. so if you click one time too many, you lose and have to start all over again, several hours wasted by one click.There is little to no reward for completing the game or bringing resources to the eye, despite what was hinted at in the campaign. There are no real unlocks, just tribes with different skins, and a few new random traits that don't add much; there is no real progression.There is no real point levelling people up, or collecting copious amounts or resources, exploring ect.The games actually quite easy when you realise you can pretty much just ignore all the mechanics and just make food to win. But this takes out what little fun was actually in the game anyway.Its not fun to play for progressionor achievementsnor is it relaxingor quickI feel like this could be a really great game. But the fact the devs seem to have made these intentional features, and they punish players for no good reason. 2/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. I loved it during the first 5-10 hours I played, completing 2 runs.The art is awesome, the concept of pupils being able to change apearence when they change jobs, and level up those trades to unlock new forms is inovative, as is the permanent and portable building system (but ultimately both are shallow). Then two things happens : (1) it gets repetitive and tedious, as new tribes unlocks basically does not change the gameplay much. It pushes you towards a different strategy, while offering little to no new gameplay features. Every run is : get a food production stream rolling in the 1st/2nd map, then when you are confident with it, focus on caravan/council upgrades and harmony generating schemes. Since portable buildings take up space in the caravan, you will always only get portable building for your main supply chain, which is food (gathering fish, game or wheat + cooking, and maybe a 3rd for spice), reinforcing the repetitiveness of it. Maps are randomly generated, but it does not matter as the gameplay itself isn't really impacted by map layout. You spot ressources available, deploy, exploit as much as you can, then move. Once you are past the 1st/2nd map, your production streams should be well oiled enough that nothing short of an extreme combination of major bad lucks (or player errors) could make you lose. (2) Every game you finish unlocks new pupil traits based on what you did, and roughly half those traits are NEGATIVE AND CANNOT BE DISABLED, meaning your pupils will have chances to have those negative traits at random. The set of negative traits you start the game with are quite manageable, but some of the unlocks are nasty stuff. So, instead of that classic take on roguelikes where, the more you play, the better your team/character/ship/whatever gets at achieving your goal, in As far as the eye, the more you play, the more new ways of getting your run screwed by bad traits you unlock. You can spend a currency to change those traits for a new set of random traits, so this just becomes a currency drain which adds nothing to the fun.There is a good base, and alot of potential, but the game cruelly lacks depth. Give us a currency after each run to spend between runs to increase the probability to get a set of chosen traits and/or decrease the probability to get a set of unwanted ones. Allow us to use that currency to chose some of our starter pupils traits, give them some pre-leveled skills. Let us unlock "tribe perks" that needs to be chosen before the run and that allow us to customize our gameplay. There could also be more scripted interactions, like multi-halt side-quests where you need to bring X ressources to someone on the next halt, or habor a pupil until you reach his destination X halts later. Anything to give a personnality and a sense of uniqueness to the randomly generated maps.There are so many option to add depth to a roguelike like As far as the eye, it feels like a waste not to have any of them.

_childDocuments_.review: I went through the first 3 chapters and never really felt great playing it. If I had to describe in one word, I would use "clunky". There may have been a bit more to keyboard shortcuts, but I just felt like I was playing with one hand the whole time. The mechanics are never felt quite right. For example, one chapter requires using the difference between permanent buildings and mobile buildings. The tutorial often doesn't let you do things until you hit a trigger, but in this case it lets you make a bunch of permanent buildings despite not being able to complete the chapter if you do so. The point of mobile buildings is to be able to use them to more efficiently gather resources, but in that chapter it feels like 2 permanent buildings would probably do the job better. I know its a tutorial trying to teach me things, but it clearly didn't do a great job. There's a ton of text to read and the triggers that allow you to progress are obstructive at times and not often enough in others. Some might say that reading isn't difficult, but I think a game with a good visual representation of mechanics wouldn't need as much text. Another thing that bothered me is that it often felt like I was in a position where I was just mashing the end turn button and waiting. I may have tried more, but I didn't see enough promise to warrant not returning it. I like the presentation, theme, and concept. I just never really felt great playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: The general vibe of the game and the story it is going for does not line up with the actual gameplay. You are actively punished for doing the "right thing" storywise and you soon lose sight of the cute visuals and sounds when you have to concentrate on micromanaging every little detail. I am not sure if there was an intention of making "losing a run" very much part of the story, but you would lose every single run if you do not go for the good old exploitation, dictation and optimization, which strongly conflicts with the expected feeling of the game according to promotional material. I have seriously tried to give this game a chance, but even the nice artstyle and soundtrack can not make up for the contradictory gameplay flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to love here. The gameplay is fun, the graphics, gorgeous, and the worldbuilding, fantastic. I like this type of game and the various genres being mashed together here. But overall, once I got through the Campaign (which is a very challenging tutorial, but also maybe not a tutorial), I kept dying. I spent some time getting better (it is a rogue-like in many aspects) and watching videos of other players to see if I was missing something obvious. I don't think I am. I think the game is simply out of balance. It has maps without the resources you need to collect (and without enough ways to use the market to purchase them nor a way to know you needed to harvest one or two maps prior). It throw very late-game curveballs at you, like adding addition 600 of something to harvest on maps where that would normally be difficult but it only tells you that long after you're locked into your strategy for completing that map. The balance seems to be set up so that only the best players getting the luckiest rolls can possibly have a chance at winning. This is on the first scenario. If the game became more balanced, and gradually worked up to difficulty levels that challenged your skill as opposed to your luck, I'd have easily been hooked for a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The game comes off as the devs didn't know how to make the economy difficult, so they just throw events that take everything away from you so you have to start over repeatedly. You never feel like you lost because you were doing something wrong, as it is simply the game decides when your run is over. Maybe I was just unlucky? but this is my experience in my three runs:In my first run, I saw my path was leading to a section with 700ish rations and 500 knowledge, and the next only one path and it is 900 ore. but in the two sections leading to 900 ore, there were only 3 ore nodes and totaled to <900 so run is over, nothing I can do about it.Next run, last section is small and required 800 rations, some wood, and some ore, not too bad, but there is only 2 fishing spots and 2 fields, but a rodent event on fish, then a damaged path adds stone just as I was finishing collecting rations, when I almost had the stone, another rodent event on rations which made it impossible to beat as there were no more sources of rations.The third and final run crossed the line, as the first section required knowledge for both paths, but had 2 separate amnesia events taking away 500 each.... no coming back from that in the first area.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is addicting and visually well-polished, but feels unfinished in terms of gameplay mechanics and is probably getting in its own way trying to force a message of environmentalism. It needs rebalancing, manual save options, and general bug fixes.  The negative RNG effects are far too strong in the standard play mode and there's often no way to recover if your run doesn't go well consistently. The challenge is nice, but it seems like it would not have been too much to ask for difficulty scaling options. As is, it feels like it's forcing you into one play style so that you're forced to rush to victory. I like to take my time and level up my characters so I created a custom game with negative RNG turned off. After a few hours in the playthru, it started to crash no matter what action I took. There is no way to periodically back up the run so I can go back and try to prevent the situation that was causing crashes; you simply need to start a brand new play-thru and abandon your hours of play.  There's some replay-ability, but sooner or later I'm going to get bored of having to choose between racing the RNG timebomb and playing on easy mode. I get that the message is that you need to respect mother nature and take only what you need or else you'll fail, but limiting play styles limits the appeal of the game as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely graphics and music provide a window into a beautiful world that's plagued by cyclical floods ... and very poor game balance.As Far As The Eye (sic) is a turn-based resource-management game set in a weird sort of fantasy world, from developers, Unexpected. This review is based on a pre-release version from the week before public release. You play The Sigh -- the wind -- and your goal is to save the various tribes from the rising floods that inundate the land on a cyclical basis, by directing them to harvest resources in order to make their way to The Eye: a sort of sanctuary from the encroaching waters.As Far As The Eye has all sorts of unfamiliar words and terms for things that you'll just have to get used to if you want to understand what's going on. Each androgynous person is a "pupil", for example. And the whole idea of playing "The Sigh" is really just a gimmick; you have direct control over each pupil in ways that aren't related to the wind.Relatively frequent grammatical errors and some untranslated French, together with a number of screens where text is simply cut off mid-sentence, confound understanding, which is a bit of a shame given the effort that otherwise seems to have gone into producing the unique game world. I didn't really feel a great sense of immersion, in any case.Pupils have no personality. They're each given a name and one positive and one negative trait. They make no individual responses, react exactly the same to everything, and -- other than their traits -- are each exactly as good as the other at doing everything. To me they just ended up being "the builder", "the food harvester", "the miner", and so on. It seemed like a wasted opportunity.The beautiful watercolour-style graphics of the static title screen, supported by lovely minimalist ambient music that hints at the relaxing adventure that should follow, provide an excellent first impression of As Far As The Eye. (Though the pedant in me demands that the capitalisation is incorrect!) The pleasant graphics and musical style both continue through into the game proper, with a relaxing soundtrack and unique 3D graphics with impressive hand-drawn materials.It's played on a hex grid, with undiscovered hexes being drawn like plain paper. As you uncover these hexes they're populated with terrain types and resources. The pupils are the least engaging of the game's animated models: little non-descript colour-coded humanoids. It's sometimes hard to tell in exactly which hex a pupil is positioned -- a serious issue for a turn-based game in which movement costs are based on hexes moved through.You can zoom and rotate the main view, but I found the rapid change of angle from almost-top-down to almost-side-on rather disconcerting when zooming in close to ground level; this should be adjusted, I think, to not be so sudden. The hexes seem to change shape between full zoom levels, too -- a side effect of the chosen field of view, perhaps? I found it weird, anyway.The game features two game modes: "Campaign" and "Play". To make it even more confusing, "Campaign" is actually the four-mission tutorial -- which, by the way, seems to be broken -- while "Play" is the main game mode -- the campaign, as I would call it. Um ... .Both modes introduce you to the game through dialog boxes explaining the basics, and, while the tutorial limits the effects of some of the game's more evil design decisions, both modes effectively present the same game with the same goals. It's worthwhile playing through the tutorial once, I think, as long as the developers fix it so it's actually able to be completed.The actual campaign mode ("Play", not "Campaign" -- sheesh!) offers a slightly different experience each time you play, through the use of those most common of Rogue-like elements: procedural generation and permadeath. You're given three pupils to lead on their journey to The Eye and your path there is different each game. While the game's store page mentions turn-based resource management, once I started playing the game proper, I most often found the actual resource management aspects of the game being rapidly overwhelmed by RNG factors over which the player has no control.There's no traditional conflict, so you'd be forgiven for thinking that the gameplay would be casual. Instead the challenge is supposed to be in managing your pupils and resources efficiently. Oh, and the food limit! Yes, each pupil consumes six units of food every turn. Go without food for a turn and they get sick and start to lose HP. After a few turns of that, they're dead. Game over.What this means, at least when you're starting out, is that you basically need to discount one pupil entirely from any activity other than food collection. This makes the much-more-generous flood turn limit completely irrelevant, at least early on, since lack of food will kill you long before the halt turn limit expires. Especially if you're lucky enough to get one of the halts with requirements that simply can't be met. Hooray!So the challenge is actually fourfold, and resource management doesn't really figure into it most of the time: 1) impossible progression requirements, 2) halt turn limits, 3) food turn limits, and 4) "vagaries". I'll explain the vagaries next; they're so bad they need their own section.Vagaries are events that occur using the rising waters as a nonsense plot hook. They all seem to be bad, and they're game changing. I'd probably call them game breaking in many cases. The RNG seems to be used vindictively for vagaries, in that every game I played they ramped up so rapidly after I started making any progress that it became a gauntlet run of frequent randomly generated ass-kicking events. To make them even worse still, Vagaries are only announced a turn or two before they come into play, unless you've progressed to the point where you can detect them earlier. And that's typically not enough time to efficiently cope with a vagary's effects.Some vagaries are relatively benign or easily dealt with by simply avoiding them. Others can destroy any progress you've made in a single turn, with absolutely nothing you can do about it. They're completely unbalanced and very poorly thought out, and often seem to be there just to punish you for making progress. I usually love the introduction of Rogue-like elements in games, but when they're this unbalanced and completely unavoidable, they don't add anything to the game.I want to really like As Far As The Eye, but I just don't.While its turn-based nature; lovely, light and frolicky music; pretty, colourful graphics; and lack of combat make me think that it should appeal to a relaxed and casual play style, I find myself getting frustrated with it. I find the Rogue-like aspects unbalanced and poorly implemented. It feels too fiddly and cumbersome to enjoy, and the continual drain on food resources alone is enough to make me quit in frustration. Combine that with the game breaking bugs, unbeatable levels, and reliance on vindictive RNG, and I rage quit almost every time I play.It's beautiful and complex, and I can believe it becomes more enjoyable later -- at least if you're very patient, lucky, or both. But it's not fun to begin with, and, try as I might, I haven't been able to force myself over that first hump. The game has worn out its welcome before it's had a chance to shine.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game BUT:1) The "Campaign" is actually a bunch of tutorials which don't cover all aspects of the game2) Food consumption is ridiculously high, before an earlier patch it was near impossible to prevent your 'pupils' from dying of hunger on one of the TUTORIAL missions3) Each 'Halt' aka map gets smaller and harder the closer you get to the 'Eye' aka the final destination, and there is no way to make it easier, plus the lack of resources on later Halts means you have to gather/hoard as much as possible on the earlier Halts4) Building the Council consumes so much time and resources that its impossible to build on the earlier maps, and by the time you build it on the later maps, the value of half the upgrades are greatly diminished.Overall this game has some nice touches like excellent graphics and good soundtrack, but the overall gameplay is unbalanced and still needs a lot of tweaking. To me this game feels like its an Early Access and not a finished product.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this is like dating a particularly hot therapist/psych student. They know they can do better than you, and they will notice every potentially problematic thing about you - and what's most likely to happen is that eventually they'll dump you, without you truly realising what you even did wrong. But if you have enough patience, knowledge and willingness to learn, you'll be awarded with an incredible experience like no other.In other words, the game is hard; and for all the wrong reasons. I can think of four main issues that scare people off. One - the game's aesthetic makes you think that this is a pleasant, spiritual game. It's not, it's a meticulous and unforgiving marathon where you're always one bad day from defeat. Two - it has different aspects of difficulty which are at odds with each other, and the margin of error you're allowed is rather thin. Three - unless you  know what you're doing, it's very possible to get screwed by the RNG, even pretty late into a run. And four: the game simply doesn't provide enough information. There is a tutorial of sorts, but it's a deluge of info that you'll only pick up bits and pieces from, and there are no reference materials later on.The game's themes and aesthetic... well, you can see what they are. Everybody's supposed to have made this journey multiple times, the tribes know of each other, everybody's happy to see their fellow travellers, and your pupils seem to operate on child-like wonder, curiosity and kindness rather than some grim will for survival.The gameplay, in contrast, feels like some kind of post-apocalyptic journey to some kind of mythical refuge - where you will never have to set foot from; the outside world will be just a bad dream. Many will die, but those who'll survive shall carry their legacy. If this was the theme of the game, I think it would've gotten away with the cruel difficulty it presents.Since spiritual connection to the land is one of the game's themes, the consequences of your actions are following you via an invisible "harmony" score. You want to keep it as high as possible, since the lower it is, the more often you'll fall victim to vagaries - random disasters. Some things you do increase the harmony score, others lower it. In particular, leaving behind harvested resources is counted as wasteful, and is the most common way to lose harmony.So that's all good - nice, environmental message - but in order to have any chance of survival, you'll need your pupils to gather stuff mainly so they can accumulate experience in a given trade, since you're going to need that expertise later (absolutely mandatory). So if you just leave a pupil to harvest something and forget about it, chances are you'll be left with a pile of stuff you won't be able to use. And your carrying capacity is very limited, even if you put lots of work into expanding it!In truth, learning to navigate this conundrum is part of learning the game. But this definitely feels like something that simply shouldn't be an issue - and yet it is, and many players will ditch the game without even realising that there is a way around it.Note: there is a pretty much foolproof way of dealing with this issue. But you won't learn, much less master this method until much later - so it will be an issue for you for quite some time.Every X turns, you'll get a message than in a few turns a vagary is coming. You'll always know exactly what is is beforehand, so you can prepare. There are a lot of possibilities - some of them are very easy to deal with, while some can singlehandedly sink your run. Luckily, most of them are absolutely manageable - and, indeed, even the harder ones can be dealt with. There will be situations, though, where a single vagary can ruin your otherwise successful run. It's what will make you take vagaries and planning ahead a lot more seriously - but the frustration factor can be huge. Again, this can ruin the game for many people.The game contains a tutorial, which is somewhat deceptively named "Campaign". It's not a campaign, you pretty much have your every step guided and your options are severely limited. It provides you with some info as well as some nice exposition detaling the nature of the world, but sadly, it's nowhere near enough to actually get anywhere in the scenarios, or the main game.Harmony, for example, is not very well explained. You wouldn't think that harvesting (or "rescuing") wild animals to be your beasts of burden is a virtuous act, and leaving them is not. There's also the "proximity bonus" - if you have your buildings huddled together, all of them will work more efficiently while consuming the same amount of resources. I don't think I need to explain just how huge of a difference this can make. But how are you supposed to know? You can get it in hints sometimes, and that's about it.The game gives you a lot of different tools to fight back against its difficulty. But, unless you read tooltips, look into menus, try things out, chances are you'll never even know that this or that is possible.All of those complaints probably sound like I hated the game. But no. Once you learn the ropes, you learn how to survive, thrive, manage different challenges... the satisfaction of pulling through a successful run is unreal. It took me many, many tries to get my first win, and then probably just as many to win again. But once I got it... it just kept on rolling, each win just as satisfying as the last - if not more.As Far As The Eye is a very unique experience. It requires some patience, sure, and is quite rough around the edges. But I honestly believe that if you can get past its many hurdles, you'll learn to appreciate its unorthodox design. Just don't pick it up if you expect something nice and slow.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Overtuned. Badly.The core gameplay loop is fun, but gains are small and the Vagaries (bad things that happen randomly) are both entirely too frequent and often border on crippling. Additionally, the "balanced" starting Halt is often anything but, and frequently spawns with only one or two tiles with a given resource available at all, which makes the Market more necessary which in turn makes the Vagaries that damage buildings even more punishing. I'm enjoying the game, but it's obviously tuned around someone who has 100+ hours and extensive experience to be able to complete a journey to the Eye on the default game mode *sometimes*, which is obscene.Adding to the frustration, the game frequently changes the focused Pupil without reason or warning, and often a Pupil will either ignore a command or accept it and simply not follow through on the next turn. This also applies to the Caravan pre-deployment on a Halt, sometimes the Caravan will just... not move on a Turn. Given the incredibly tight scheduling required to succeed with any consistency, it would be generous not to call these bugs game-breaking. To add insult to injury, completing a Journey To The Eye unlocks new traits, good, bad, and "neutral" (many of the Neutral traits are either nearly useless or more bad than good, absolutely none are generally positive) and as a result, later journeys to the Eye are even less likely to succeed. After two successful Journeys I've found myself rerolling more starts than not due to the punishing bad Traits or simply getting extremely unfavorable Jobs with my opening Pupils.I paid $10 for the game, and I feel like that was fair, but if I had paid full price I'd be livid, especially with the game getting progressively harder and less fun as time goes on. The game is absolutely gorgeous, even on lower settings, but I cannot in good faith recommend that anyone buy it because after a few enjoyable experiences it becomes a repetitive exercise in failure. Again, the core mechanics are good and custom games are still enjoyable, but the developers have a lot of tuning to do before I feel like I'm doing anything but wasting my time managing Pupils into unavoidable death spirals.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I can’t believe how much I am gushing over this game. It looks like a simple and relaxing city builder at its surface, but there is so much more to it. Even with its deep skill trees and challenges, I found the game incredibly relaxing. Listening to the whispers of the wind and the dulcet strumming of an acoustic guitar as I guided my pupils to The Eye was a memorable experience. From the beginning to the end of any given run, the pupils would gain personalities in ways that made them feel more alive. I cared about the pupils in this game, I felt connected to the atmosphere and settlements it offers. This, paired with a great blending of theme and mechanic, make this a truly unique game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game had great ideals but executed poorly on the balancing which made the game not very enjoyable. Most games increases the difficulty of your experience by throw in a bit of random elements but still provides ways to avoid them. That's a very important key concept since that would challenge players' analytical skills and strategy/management mindset. However, this game is the exact opposite of that. It has random elements on the get go which could lose your run right off the bat even without you started to plan for things. This made me restarted so many runs and rerolling for winnable games. Even on some of the good runs i've had, i ended up losing the game due to environmental RNGs giving the worst rolls possible.If you're into management games like me, I don't recommend this game to you at all. Regardless of how hard you try and how precise you planned, things goes wrong easily since the game will just hand you  way too many environmental RNGs than you can handle.With that being said, I've had runs those are as easy as a piece of cake when i didn't even planned that well and some runs were harder than a puberty boy seeing p0rn for the first time. Not that i planned like a genius to make it easy nor that i'm an inexperienced player in my hard games. The experience varies in two extreme opposite.When RNG factor is greater than management, then you'll know it aint a great game after all. If you enjoy RNG to this extend, might as well just go gambling which you'd have a better prediction on the result but the statistics are also better than this. Overall, i'll give it 4/10 in terms of "strategy games"

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, it is very easy to lose but most of the losses are fair. Go as fast as possible, have a lot of food, and be prepared to need extra resources. _childDocuments_.review: This game really teaches you to be patient and strategic with your choices. I am not, and am terrible at this game, but that's not the game's fault. However, I'm the sort of person who is going to keep hitting next turn in rabid succession to get my resources and not pay attention to the world around me, so I don't think I'll be playing this one much longer.

_childDocuments_.review: As Far As The Eye is a hybrid of a strategy game and a roguelike, where players must effectively manage resources to survive on randomly generated terrains.Sounds like something that may be fun, right? In practice, the game is extremely frustrating and simply too hard. Hard difficulty when done right can be satisfying, but in this case, I never felt rewarded.I don't even think that the As Far As The Eye is bad. I like the general idea of it, and the basic mechanics are solid. It's the difficulty level and the lack of a satisfying end goal that makes this game unfun. As much as I would like to, I can't recommend it. In its current form, the game is too irritating - at least it was for me. If you want to try it despite it, wait for a discount. The Campaign contains a small amount of story. Nothing interesting. Just some flavor text to make the tutorials less boring. Did it achieve this goal? Not really.You're thrown into a procedurally generated map. There are usually a few of them linked with each other, and you need to pass them to evacuate. You have limited time to get enough resources and move to another map on the "chain" (you can take limited resources or mobile buildings with you). The main gameplay loop is mainly about optimizing time and resource management. You need to rotate your "villagers" between tasks, build better supply chains (build a bakery or cookhouse) to not starve, and trade in a market/with caravans to get stuff that you're missing. Your "villagers" will gain experience doing tasks, which gives you an option to unlock simple "skills" (like gaining extra resources per turn or using less food). Always make sure that you're using the best workers in proper places to save time and extract more. Someone in the reviews section gave As Far As The Eye a fitting name - a crisis management game. I couldn't agree more. You're constantly barraged with new problems - earthquakes, fires, floods, something eating supplies, sickness, curses, and much more. If you're unlucky and the RNG god hates you, your run will end just because a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ events piled on you. There's also a chance to spawn in an area that is unsuitable for the task that is required to advance.There are 5 chapters in the Campaign. The Campaign is basically a tutorial, that tries to introduce you to the basic mechanics (+ some more advanced stuff). Honestly, it doesn't even do that well. The game starts getting overwhelming after a third chapter.The UX is terrible. Important mechanics are buried under less important stuff and the icons are in idiotic places. Selecting units can be problematic as hell.I like the stylized visuals, even despite the uninspiring color palette (which makes things harder to distinguish). The design of "pupils" aka. "villagers" is charming.The soundtrack is relaxing and fits the art style well. Other sounds are also good quality.Some texts weren't translated. No other problems. Great performance (stable 144 FPS).

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly difficult. It might be more frustrating than fun for some players, but I'm really enjoying it. The beautiful art style helps. You lead your band of transforming people across the landscape along some predetermined routes. You have to collect resources at each stop along the way, and determining the best and most efficient way to do that is the central puzzle of the thing. And you have to get it just right or start over.

_childDocuments_.review: I too believe that this is a nice game if you enjoy roguelike games.When I first saw the list of buildable buildings I was worried the game wouldnt have much depth, as there are exactly 15 buildings which can be built.So .. I was worried I will just figure out how things work and lose interest in the game after a few days, because I found some safe winning strategy.Luckily it was different!The overall difficulty is quite high. After the tutorial campaign you get to play 4 tribes with increasing difficulty (you have to start with the lowest difficulty tribe). However, even that tribe took me quite some effort to win with.There might not be much buildings, but it is quite a tough choice when to build and operate which of them and which ressources to take with you after the mission.It is highly RNG based, so you gotta like to work with randomness and make the best out of things, as a lot is determined by random traits of your characters, the random map layout, random bad events (Vagaries) and random goals you have to achieve to get to a new waypoint.But for people who like the challenge of figuring out a way through a random situation (like me), this game proves to be quite an enjoyable experience.I still think Ill probably lose interest once I played through the fourth tribe.But considering Im only at the second tribe, I figure it will be rather weeks than days that Ill play this game.A lot of reviews mention the Vagary system to be broken, but I believe it is perfectly fine. The Vagaries are negative events which randomly happen to you and add some pressure. To be honest: If it weren't for the Vagaries the game would have little challenge and would be fairly bland once you figured out some working strategy. At least they keep you on your toes and force you to adapt, and the more you learn about the game, the more you will also consider possible Vagaries in your choices.  Yes, they can hit hard if you are unprepared.. but thats part of a roguelike. You lose, you start over, you learned something new and make it better next time.And really, there are numerous ways to counter them. There are game mechanics which allow you to predict them earlier or to manipulate them (slow them down or cancel them out entirely). And in a pinch? Remember that some of your buildings can just be taken out of dangers reach...Anyways, don't get me wrong, Im not giving a "clear thumbs up" here. Its more of a neutral "yeah, its ok and I like it, go for it for a solid experience."-thing, where I would give a neutral review with a slightly tilted thumb upwards if I could. 6/10, I guess.Not the game of the year for me ... but by FAR not as bad as some reviews make it to be.Best decide for yourself if it makes you curious. But bring some patience and tolerance to losing if you do.Edit:I have to add to my above review, that shortly after the launch a patch was published as reaction to the reviews which criticized the balance, vagaries and difficulty.To summarize: They made a lot easier, rebalanced some things to be less punishing and took out some content alltogether. As standart game mode (no option here), so you can't really play the game anymore like it was initialy.I was thinking about downvoting my rating to 5/10 (and by that putting it to not recommended), but considering I didn't feel motivated to try the game with the new patch yet, I believe that wouldn't be fair.So just take my above review with a grain of salt, and keep in mind that it was written before that patch. I don't know how much of a challenge it currently is.

_childDocuments_.review: The tutorial is truly awful. It's very poorly designed. Once you get past the terrible tutorial, the game improves, even though there are plenty of things that are not explained in the tutorial. The learning curve is steep. Expect to fail out of the gate. _childDocuments_.review: I loved this game, and could easily play it for hours despite the fact I'm honestly terrible at it. LOL There is just so much good stuff here with the story, sound, and graphics!But I don't recommend it for one key reason:Each play-through involves clearing several different levels ("halts") before finally reaching the end. It doesn't matter how many halts you have already cleared, if you lose or die on a particular level ALL of your progress is lost. You cannot simply redo a single halt. Games like Civilization or Age of Wonders: Planetfall let you obsessively create save files for every possible outcome, and it would be super awesome if this game let you do the same. The fact that it doesn't is hugely disappointing.And on top of that,  With how easy it is to fail at this game, you'd think you'd at least get some rewards or perks via interesting stats to follow. But sadly that is not the case.If you lose, it's like nothing every happened. You don't get any rewards for what you did complete. You don't even get to look at the stats for all the times you died or at what stage you died. There is a lot of data that could be compiled just so you don't feel like you've wasted hours of your life when you lose. Even the data that is tracked when you do complete a successful game is lacking, IMHO. I'd be really curious to see how many times I gathered certain resources, what resources were the most popular, how many total Ruffalos I saved, what professions I use the most etc.  - The game appears to be designed with competitive gameplay in mind. (I believe there was a , not sure if it's still something they do?) And could use some serious Quality of Life improvements for your average/casual player that just wants to explore and enjoy themselves. Until that happens, I don't feel comfortable recommending the game.(Also - just tossing this out there, but if you are considering getting this game on the Switch DO NOT DO IT. I originally played the Switch port and it's essentially unplayable. Honestly, it's the worst port I think I've ever played. But I liked the concept and the art enough I decided to give it a shot on Steam while it was on sale.)
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: INITIAL RELEASE:The game has a great concept, but it feels like it's in early access.It has serious issues in the rng of events and also traits.The tutorials are good, but it misses the large and important portion on more advanced buildings, upgrades of buildings and the importance of traits (both good and bad).I tried to complete my first game after the tutorials for the next 12 hours.It took me the first two hours to understand the importance of the positive and negative traits (I thought it was just a cute extra fluff). The brutality of those negative traits waaaaaaaay out play the positive ones.First game was a start with 2 pups that refuse to use the caravan to forage, while the 3rd ended up dying because it was clumsy (loses health every turn). Neat...Next game I was about to go into the next halt and an event with rats stole all my resources to get to the next zone.... Okay...Every lightning event take out my population camps, not once randomly. EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.I had all the wood on the map removed at the start of that map in a bad random event. This was the last halt to the Eye, no way to recover, since i need wood to build EVERYTHING. The previous halt had two events to kill off mobile buildings in a row... Great...I tried restarting until I had ok positive and negative traits, but the events that popped up are never good and having a continuous roll on of horrific events didn't help. I had no way of knowing how to prevent or at least stall them. It was brutal.I ended up playing a custom version of this game, no negative traits, no random events and won the game really easily. It showed me how important it was to have advanced professions (there is also a trait that stops those) and how to use the other caravan addons (since lightning took away my house buffalo every other game). I didn't know that the knowledge your pups accumulate was useful. As events constantly took it away most of the time or it was for getting to other halts.TL;DR: It needs to be rebalanced.SINCE  1st UPDATE:A lot of the issues I've had have been addressed or being fixed since the initial review.A lot more of the balance issues with the vulgarities are being fixed, so I'm happy to say my house buffalo are not being imploded with lightning.The shorter games are good additions.Still hate the clumsy negative trait.Happy the devs are going to be adding additional tutorials on upgrades and advanced buildings.Game isn't quite there yet, but its getting close.Not recommend as a complete game.Recommend as early access as there are still a few tweaks needed.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the genre (survival, city builder, strategy...) I think it's worth value purchase it. I won't make spoilers but I like to point a positive / negative thing:Positive:-The tutorial is nice! I love games whos designers invest time in create a usefull and nice tutorial to encourage players to play. And make them easy to do it... I don't want to spend like 3 hours in youtube videos for learning...-Music is nice!-The art is cool!Negative:-Something with the technology tree is wrong: I miss a real campaign were you can use the knowledge you learn (investing points) or at least the possibility to use it more.
