_childDocuments_.review: A pretty game with a brilliant concept hampered by bugs, bad UI/UX, and poor balance.There are some unfortunately severe bugs present given that the last bugfix patch was in Oct 2020. Things I have encountered include the game thinking I don't have enough population slots (if you have 4 workers but 3 slots, only 3 can work. Multiple times I had 4 slots but only 3 workers were allowed to work, which is a massive setback) and sometimes the game flat out loses/deletes resources & units when you load a saved game (in a game where you will regularly only have 3 or 4 units, having 1 disappear is essentially game over).I understand that the game is random and balance is often luck. But there are too many random things that will kill your run if just 1 happens early. Also you might as well restart if you get a bad set of starting units, because the difference between getting a balanced squad and one that has useless skills is huge. Not to mention that some unit traits (i.e. Agile) are game-breaking powerful.The UI/UX is really bad. I had an event that said idle units will get sick, and a unit en route to interact with a Caravan (friendly NPC) was counted as being idle without warning. Sometimes the game notifies me when a unit has no job, sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes I get a bonus at the start of a run due to last run, sometimes I don't, with no indication why. Given the state of the game it's difficult to say if those are bugs or bad UX. In the UI it's too hard to see what unit you have selected (and the game constantly swaps selection on you without warning), it's too hard to see at a glance what units are doing, and since they all look the same it's too hard to remember which unit you want to specialize in which job.The concept of a moving base is brilliant, and the way you have to manage production and unit skills and cargo space is really fun. The bad UI/UX alone could have been tolerable quirks, but the bugs push this review into the negative. Stay away if you don't want to be disappointed by what could have been a fun game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The campaign/tutorial is unnecessarily frustrating. It reminds me of that one DM killing the party because the players decided to bash a door down instead of picking the lock.Think for yourself just once, and it's mission failed for you - not immediately of course, but you can't finish the mission and get drowned. You have to do absolutely nothing until explicitly told to, even/especially if you could. Try something out, be curious, be creative? Hell no, you play this "right" or you're getting killed. They will disable game mechanics you know are there just to cripple you into doing things in the exact order the script prescribes. This goes so far as to not letting you play for an hour but then not letting you leave the map when you fulfill all the prerequisites - because you built something one turn too early so now you "still" have to build it and therefore you can't leave. Please, people. Encourage players to think, don't stifle them! If a mission needs a farm, check for a farm, not for the action of ordering one built. If a mission needs a certain amount of x, check for that amount of x, not for where it came from.I still love the game itself, I just wish it wouldn't go out of its way to appall its players before they can even get started.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: There is a good game in here, with a lot going right.What holds it back are the UI, excessive micro managing, and general lack of Quality of Life features. I don't think the RNG is overly combative, but for an economy focused 4x game, the UI and lack of save creates an issue where it's easy to make a simple mistake that can snowball your whole playthrough attempt into oblivion. The tutorial campaign is charming. I wish there was more story like this in the game. The random generated scenarios are fun, but feel unfulfilling with their lack of story, and frustrating when things, which feel avoidable, are thrust upon you due to poor design.TL;DR - Charming, yet Frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The "Campaign" is just a long tutorial, don't even think to start a normal game without completing it. The game has style, but the UI interaction is just plain bad. No indication if something stopped, no proper overview for anything, and the encounters are way too random. Once I died because there were literally no trees on the stop. No trees, literally. There are hits about the resources of the next top, but they are far from accurate.Also, skipping over stops is not rewarded at all.Losing is 30% player error, 70% random death sentence. Quick, short runs are fine, don't go for long journey. But some massive UI improvements would be needed to better identify units and overview production.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game!I finished all the levels except for the last one involving the long journey with the north tribe. This game is really difficult, but that's a good thing because if I beat all the levels too quickly, it wouldn't really  be fun or challenging, and the game would be over too soon! I lost so many times, however, the soothing soundtrack and beautiful visuals were what got me to come back to play more. Unlike other turn based hex games, or civilization survival games,  each session you play doesn't last forever, making it the perfect activity for a half hour or hour between my meetings.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gorgeous and the concept is great, but the tutorial is lacking and incredibly easy, then the main game is incredibly difficult.Recommendations to the game devs:1. If your pupils aren't doing anything because they're waiting for resources, that would also be a great thing to get notified about. 2. The icons on the side with updates, left click details and right click close? They both close. There's no way to see details.3. I frequently had visitors passing through and no warning about them.4. If the jungle is poison, it'd be nice for the pupils to reroute around the jungles if possible, rather than walking head-first into poison. Am I supposed to manually move my pupils when hexes are poison?5. It'd be great to line up tasks, like finish gathering pepkins then switch to sheep, etc.6. Harmony is so important but barely discussed at all, and I get *frustrated* having too many cells with resources because I can't build anywhere. Shouldn't we be excited by all the resources on the landscape and grateful for the bounty of the earth, and not think "drat to access that field, I have to clear the pepkins on it and to do that, I need to clear 2 forests and some birds to so they have only 1 MP between the harvest hut and the field with pepkins on it.."7. The vagaries are so random - you have to be prepared for anything and 7-10 turns is not enough turns to actually become prepared given that every gathering round takes ~4 turns.I'd recommend it if there was a slower ramp-up in difficulty and fixes to comments above.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't pay attention you'll suffer. Even if you do, you'll still suffer, but not in a good masochistic way. There's a learning curve to games like xcom, darkest dungeon, hades, fighting in tight spaces etc that punish you for mistakes but reward good gameplay. In this game, there's no feeling of achievement, satisfaction, or even purpose.There's a lot of good aspects; the unique character traits, upgrades, classes/specialization, appealing environment/models/soundtrack, solid resource management. The base game is pretty enjoyable, but the purpose is almost absent. It has a tutorial campaign and a rudimentary narrative about migration which is fine, but there's nothing satisfying about clearing a stage. The idea of why you need certain resources in certain amounts is weirdly addressed for like 10 seconds and then never mentioned again. In the tutorial you're crossing a mountain or something so you need wool to stay warm or something like that; its simple, reasonable, and gives you some idea of why. The rest of the game is literally you need X to the go to Y with nothing in between but a line connecting them. I don't need an animation of humanoids using the harvest wood to make a raft to travel downstream between locations, just something. Maybe this sounds minor and insignificant, but when you're getting rolled by what feels like a deliberate anti-success algorithm (same turn I build a structure it catches on fire, the exact tree im actively harvesting gets hit by lightning, etc) you need some kind of substance to warrant the abuse. tl;dr unfair difficulty + no direction
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: + managing proper placement of buildings is quite fun+ progression between levels - you take your stuff from one level to the next with a tetris-like inventory system+/- it's just resource management of ~10 resources (of which you will probably not use all in a single playthrough) - no more no less+/- very difficult, your min-maxing has to be top notch, but it does not seem there is much to discover after a game or two (which you will fail), so it's a matter of repetition until you get good and get good dice rolls- unnecessary micromanagement - e.g. there is a random effect in which a stonecutters will get sick in next turn. So I have to stop harvesting stone for one turn on this one tribesman and restart it on the turn afterwards. Or there is a fire in the forest, but the woodcutter still goes there and loses life.- extreme negative snowball - lost a building or a tribesman? Restart. This is caused by low number of everything - you start with - 3 tribesmen (probably you woul end the game with ~6) and no buildings - creating new ones is very costly, so you cannot lose anything- getting a new tribe members at correct time is essential but also random - pretty much everything that can happen has negative effects - there is nothing to look forward to, everything just gets worse, occasional random effects range between bad and forced-game-restart (e.g. random building destroyed, because it was not at 100%)
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is a Positive review.Pretty cool game, neat gameplay loop and unique idea for a rogue-like, but there are a couple of dumb things that break this game for me.One: It's entirely possible for the requisites to leave a zone (Halt) to not be present within the the one you're in. Twice in 3 runs I had an impossible/no-win scenario where I needed a LOT of Rations and either Pepkins or Cereal to leave to the only connecting zone and then there was only a SINGLE patch of pepkins/cereal. Even with feverishly harvesting everyhting else and trading it all on the market, I could not generate 600 Rations while keeping 450 pepkins/cereal. Literally getting RNG'd out of the game, not fun.Two: Food management is not handled well. I had a scenario where I had 23 Rations, 17 Pepkins (I was one turn from profiting Rations) when a Puny character starved to death when the requirements was 24 Rations. Like, you telling me your system isn't smart enough to mix and match, it HAS to be all of one food type? Alt+F4, bye. MAJOR red flag for the game's systems if this simple concept is absent.Fix these (among other things like the camera functions not working/bugging out, shift-stacking move commands, etc) and it's an easy Recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: is a building simulation game with roguelike elements that will involve a good amount of thinking.There are several game modes available, including a player-custom mode. The campaign mode is actually the tutorial with 5 different campaigns. On the other hand, the actual main game also has a small tutorial. There are 4 different tribes with their unique positive/negative traits.Starting with a caravan and some pupils within, your first task is to find the best place to settle the caravan. After that the pupils can explore, gather resources, build stuff, etc. The game is turn-based with a time limit--a limited number of moves before the flood will arive, so you need to be sure to get to the next level before the time is up.Seemingly easy, the game is complicated by the limited movement points of the pupils and their need for food each turn. If you find extra pupil around the map, you will get an extra hand BUT you will also have an extra mouth to feed.If you die, it's game over. You will have to do it all over and hope to do better.Everything is in pastel colours, it looks great.The music is very relaxing, and the sound effects are pretty good too.This game can be fully played with a mouse is the first roguelike building game that I have played. It's also a relaxing game. Almost everything is explained in the game, and you will have to think a lot about what you are doing. Every action has consequences. You really need to keep in mind that it is a combined roguelike building game. I really enjoyed the combination of both genres. But if you don't like roguelike games, maybe this would not be a good game for you.Score: 7,5/10
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: [24h at the time of writing] As Far As The Eye is an interesting take on the resource optimization genre mixed with Civilization hex optimization and logistics. Challenging and rewarding while learning the game fulfills my personal desires for a video game.Everything is scarce and I managed to fail the easiest journey several times before getting my first victory. However, every run I learnt something interesting and often could only blame myself for the mistakes. Many of the reviews harp on the game being unfair - I do not share this opinion. Like in many deeper resource management games the point of failure is NOT the point of error. Neither should losing count as negative, but as a learning experience. If one attributes a lost game to the last event that tipped you over the edge you fail to improve on what lead you to such a teetering position in the first place. Long term planning and a balance of greed while knowing when its time to run is the key.Each of the offerred tribes come with their unique challenges and I found myself adjusting my strategy heavily from previous run to win with the harder difficulties.If you enjoy resource management / rogue like / city builders the game is well worth the 9.99$ that I paid on sale. Thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The concept for the game is pretty good, but the difficulty is just brutal. You can just have random catastrophes happen one after another, destroying everything you've created. You can also end up on a plot of land, where you need to gather a bunch of wood, and there's almost no trees. Meaning you have to build a Market and trade for it, but it takes like 8 of something else to get 1 wood.Overall the balance just seems wrong. I got it heavily on sale, so I don't feel I got ripped off, but it was disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I keep wanting to like As Far As The Eye, but the game mechanics make it no fun. Early game you spend your time trying to ramp up food production before your pupils starve. Late game you're penalized for having efficient production. It feels bad.A lot of folks seem to be complaining about the RNG. I'd agree, but with a little nuance. You can definitely learn how to get better at the game and that'll increase the number of successful attempts. By the mid and late game you should have the resources to recover from bad RNG.That said, in the early game a single bad event/trait can tank your game. If you make it passed the first 2 halts, you should have the ability to deal with most bad events. Early game though, you have no such wiggle room, and there is little you can do beside abandon the run and start another. Again... it just feels bad.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely incredible 4X, with tight procedural campaigns, each consisting of a string of clear missions.Not only is it pretty and tactical, it's also a lot more goal-oriented than I've grown to expect from 4X games? Most 4Xes are very... number go up, very quadratic score multiplier-y. But here it's all about small turn budgets and getting the 150 metal you need to make it to the next valley, or whatnot. More chess than tetris.A lot of people say the game is really hard, but honestly I don't mind. The game is a roguelike. You're expected to lose a lot of times for every time you win. And the losses don't feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ either - they're always cause I made a critical mistake in my planning somewhere or the other.Love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: It's far too easy for the game to screw you with the RNG and there's just not enough in terms of interest to justify restarting after I got a "broken path" event that took all my wood just before I jumped to the next halt where there was only one forest tile that was immediately struck by lightning. I tried once or twice more after that, but I was completely deflated.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This games looks pretty, but don't let that fool you it is quite punishing. My main critique of the game is that the random events dont align with available resources. I haven't been able to progress through the second level of scenarios, in part due to my own mismanagement, but mainly because the randomly generated issues the game throws in your path are often incompatible with the resources available. I.e. it suddenly asks for 600 stone, but none is on the map and you have absolutely no means of trading enough other resources to gather that many. Given the permadeath and lack of save and reload options this means you instantly lose the game and need to start an entirely new game. This gets incredibly frustrating, especially when you're on your 50th play through of the same level and you've done everything else "right" but then this happens and you lose AGAIN. While I like the game this issue is starting to frustrate me to the point of not wanting to play it anymore and changing my review to a negative one. I'm ok if I lose the game because of my own mismanagement, but not because the game has critical faults.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Very pleasant game, finished the first four maps of the campaign in my current 2h of play time. The missions are not extremely hard but force you to care and understand what you're doing otherwise you'll lose in very few turns! Very soothing atmosphere and the art style is pure eye candy.I do wish that it would be easier to click on your pupil, when they are on busy cells it can get hard to immediately find the correct pupil!EDIT // Five hours in, done with the campaign and started a few "normal games" some of the pupil negative traits really are show stoppers... Still really enjoying the game!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game has impressive art and music but the gameplay destroyed everything.Many ppl only mentioned it's hard, but the reason why it's not fun is the way of 'hard'. The binding of Issac is hard, but it's because you are not familiar with the bosses/items, and you will build confidence while playing since you know what will happen and will plan for it.However AFATE has a totally different feeling of "hard". In the first few patches you are facing totally random events which will ruin the game suddenly - lost ALL of one kind of resource, erase key buildings, reduce the turns, etc. I remember once I got 3 -20 turns in a row and failed the game from winning to game over in 1 min. Those events got nerfed later but as you can see those negative reviews now, they are still unreasonable and full of random jokes.The map is another disaster. Some maps even don't have enough resource to reach the requirement - which means you can restart once you enter the map. In most of the cases it's not controlled by you since you can only see the next few maps but not all the nodes on the path.Those stuff is quite easy to fix tbh, but I just saw almost half of the news are ads about their other games lol. I'm pretty sure the development team is not planning to update this game anymore, so this game is not worth buying.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could put neutral on this, because I think this game has a lot of potential. At the moment though, some of the gameplay elements are frustrating and outright unfun.Firstly, there are some negative traits so overwhelmingly bad that if you find them in the early game, you restart, if you find them later on, said characters are likely to find themselves in 'an unfortunate accident'.Clumsy: Lose 5 hp every harvest cycle. Unless this character is standing still, that practically means that it slowly dies over the course of about 50-100 in-game turns. Which isn't a lot, given that there's about 160-200 turns in a single halt, of which there's approx 5 of in total. Healing this one character becomes so much of a hassle that it literally takes a dedicated druid to keep them alive. That's insanely inefficient.Eternal beginner: Not as damming as the other one, but a lot of the later skills are insanely useful and necessary relatively early on in the game, so I'll usually restart if I see this in my first three characters but I'll live with it if a later character has this trait.Quick term definition: Semi-murder; This doesn't quite kill your character, but one other bad event, and they'll likely be dead.Secondly, there are some vageries (Random negative events) that are a bother:Mosquitoes: Some squares basically semi-murders your characters now, and that means you'll have to micro-manage each and every character to make sure that each and every character traverses only the paths that don't have bugs on them. This takes a long time and can quickly be undone if one of the workers change their pathing due to a resource drying up.Nap: This just cancels what everyone was doing. So that you have to recall and redo each and every command you'd been planning up until then. Just why?Ovework: "everything that works semi-dies", aight then, I guess I have to manually select every character and ensure they don't move the turn before this happens. Starting to see a pattern with the negative vageries?Some folks complained about shake and the other building damaging things, but they weren't a problem for me. Having a dedicated builder usually meant I could pop up stuff wherever in a hurry.Finally, the one thing that annoyed me more than anything else: Accidentially spending vital resources and then losing because I no longer have that vital resource to be able to travel with. I'd love if there was a way to spend these resources prior to moving around so that I don't press a button and accidentially doom hours of gameplay. This accounts for about 50-75% of my losses.All in all, the gameplay has a good foundation as it stand, but it's just too frustrating to be able to fully recommend it as of yet.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The worldbuilding and the artwork are really good. The set of rules for this universe make sense and are quite enchanting. If you enjoy strategy games like CIV, this is kind of in the same vibe but without the fighting. If you like survival games like Don't Starve this could also be for. It's somewhat similar but softer. It is challenging enough an it has a relaxing ambience and I really like the soundscape. Definitely give it a try!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. It's well made, original, with good visuals, sounds, and music. I have not run into any bugs either. However, after completing all the short starts, at the core I just don't feel like its fun.My "x trait" unlocked steam achievments show under 10% of the playerbase have them, so around 90% of people probably never finished a single run, which would take 2-3 hours at most.Since planning ahead is the key to sucess, when you lose, its often hard to figure out what could you have done differently. So after figuring it out everything gets better? Well no.It feels like there is just one strategy, you just play it a bit differently depending on the map. And that is rush Council, bank Knowledge, remove bad RNG. I hoped something would change, and as I unlock new starts something would be different, but it becomes even more true, as events become more frequent.For example, winning a run "earns" you traits. I don't feel like they are very interesting, but some are very annoying, for example losing health constantly. How to deal with it? Get Council, spend Knowledge.Runs snowball however, if you manage a good start. There isn't that much to do at the last stops, unless you barely scraped by until then, but if you have a bad start you probably die at the first or second stop anyway.So getting to the end feels unsatisfying I guess? You get a Score, and some traits. Overall new runs feel like "ok now do the same thing again but this time it will be even more tedious".Maybe you will be in that portion of the 10% who's having fun, but unfortunately I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Kind of puzzled by some of the reviews. This game isn't that unfair or difficult. It's a bit tricky and there's some RNG but with some good planning attention you can mitigate most of that. Are you going to win every run? Probably not, but some of the failure rates mentioned in the other reviews seem unreasonably high.I've been really enjoying this game so far. It's a fun and stylish resource management 4Xish game that provides a decent challenge. If you're a fan of the genre and don't mind a bit of RNG, I'd definitely recommend it. It's kind of like the Slay The Spire of resource management games.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: As Far As The Eye does what all great pieces of art does: it combines elements from other, familiar works and arranges them in a way that feels unique and satisfying. The two biggest influences seem to be FTL (just like most indie games these days) and Civilization, but there's also elements of European board games thrown in there. I find the setting and light storytelling to be quite interesting and calming, which is juxtaposed with a gameplay loop where you doing everything just to survive both the next turn and the 100+ turns after that.There are a lot of choices to be made, and you will find yourself in many dilemmas over high risk/high reward vs low risk/low reward. Sometimes there isn't a clear option to take, and it's up to you to decide what tradeoffs and risks you're willing to take. It is extremely rewarding when you leave a "halt" (maps you progress through) with large surpluses and a healthy tribe.How you play one halt can have drastic effects on all of your future halts, but there's enough random events thrown in to keep you in check in case you happened upon one of those magic RNG seeds where everything just works out (anyone who's played a roguelike has experienced one of those runs). Basically, you're never safe and should always keep an eye out for surprises if things are going _too_ well.From the amount of cons listed above, it might sound like I didn't like this game. Quite the opposite. I pulled the trigger on purchasing it after less than five minutes of watching some gameplay on YouTube. I've been itching for a game like this for a long time, but most strategy games that have come out in the past decade have completely disappointed me. As far as first impressions go, I completely lost track of time in my first sitting and didn't quit until I realized it was past 1AM! It's definitely not a perfect game, but what it gets right it absolutely nails.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Great premise but flawed execution. The art and music are perfect for the style of game, and there are several redeeming factors to this game such as the character progression, tetris-style inventory management, and camp and council upgrade trees, but not enough to overcome the base-level issues.Selecting each unit is a pain, with the only two options being clicking on the balloons/units themselves, or their portrait in the lower left but having to hover over each one to see their names (if you've memorized which one is which since you can't rename them; I had to have a word document open of each unit's name and what they were good at).All points of the game are way too harsh and reliant on RNG. Even on the very easiest mode one turn I got a vagary, then the very next turn I got TWO MORE vagaries... Like chill I'm on the first zone of my first game lets back it up please. Then the second zone was so small there were only 4 places to put buildings at all, and that's after I cleared the pack animal out of one, and from my research there is no other way besides exhausting a resorce to clear a hex for further construction so that's just the end of the run.I love a good difficult roguelike, but this feels more like Russian roulette where your choices do not matter and any preparation you have done does not affect your overall success which all comes down to luck.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest, this is one of my favourite games, and it's really hard to understand why. It's absolutely beautiful, and I love its soundtrack and atmosphere. It has to be one of the chillest death simulators I've ever played. It is, however, difficult, and not necessarily in a satisfying way. Because it's procedurally generated, it's entirely possible to spawn pawns who can't possibly win, or end up on dead-end maps. Victory is as much a luck of the draw as it is actual skill. But there's still just something deeply satisfying about building this little village and doing your best in a world that is absolutely set against you. Much like reality, it's not always winnable, but that doesn't mean the struggle along the way can't be rewarding. I love this game for that, and I'll keep loving it, even as I lose, over and over and over again. If you want to read a more thorough review, check out my reviews here!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend the game, the experience is really enjoyable! The music's great and matches the gameplay quite well, creating a relaxing and casual atmosphere... BUT it's a shame there isn't an easier mode, for players to really get more familiar with the whole thing. At some point, losing repeatedly got annoying and that kind of stopped me from wanting to play more. The whole concept and the aesthetic make it great, it's just too stressful and difficult for now, which is paradoxical when you see the soft and cute character and game design, the pretty pastel colours and the scenario. The story told by the game doesn't lead to understand you'll have a hard time winning!..PS. The tutorial is quite long and messy. Never have I ever restarted one so many times in a row!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice, enjoyable game with relaxing music and cute art style.The gameplay is simple but offers a lot of options for upgrades and specialisation and the rng makes every run unique with different resource requirements and obstacles encountered (including pupil traits) which keeps it interesting.I do see a decent number of people complaining that the game is frustrating and too rng-dependent. While it is true that a lot of things depend on rng and a few unlucky conditions can sometimes ruin a very promising game, most of those can be mitigated/prepared for if you manage your resources properly (which the whole game is about in the end).I have encountered a few instances where I couldn't get past a certain point in the game and got a little frustrated but usually some practice and/or change of strategy is enough to overcome the obstacles, especially if you have a little luck to go with it.All in all, it's a very enjoyable game if you like time and resource management and have a little patience to look at what you have and what you need, and plan ahead. It is not overly complex but provides a decent challenge, especially in longer runs.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: +Visual+Sound+Overall idea is quite unique and interesting-Interface1. Unit picking is tricky. After 15 hours I still misclick 1-2 out of 10 times.2. Objects are hard to distinguish.     a. I have to pick every unit dozens of times every game session to find the one with right specialisation because they only change their appearance according to the current job. Maybe it's better for them to change appearance based on their best skill?    b. Every single event is a torture: locate tile type affected (be sure the forest is tropical, not regular. And do confuse lake with a swamp) and find all the buildings surrounding these tiles. Why is there even the event for units 'forgeting' their tasks??? So I spend 2 more minutes to remember it the turn before and rearrange everything right after... Most events are like 'ok I need to take these guys of out certain job/tile and put them back the next turn' which is damn boring.    c. Locating resources on the map may also be difficult. It's nice I can bring up a pictogram of a single resource for the whole map but it doesn't solve the problem. Why isn't there some kind of "strategic" view??    d. I have to skip 3-4 turns to understand the income-expense balance for a given resource. Thanks god there is a panel with expenes list but the income is dynamic since it depends on amount of units working on the same task, their specialisation and distance between storage and the resource tile for every workerAll in all I liked the game but I can't recomend it since the process become frustrating when you have 5-6 workers and the events frequency rises...
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on recommending this game, but for a lack of neutral recommends, I'll give it a negative one in relation to it's average positive score.Essentially, it's a cross-over between Civilization, a roguelike and a pawn placement game. Combined with a very simple (but fitting!) art style and a likewise very artistic/spiritual theme to it. Sound does it's job and is nothing to write home about, in either direction.Controls are about as fine as they can be for a simple mouse-.controlled game, though I did occasionally run into issues in sending the wrong workers to the wrong task, because the game switched focus from one worker to another in between turns. If you spot that mistake before the next turn, it's fine as the game comes with a 'reset to begin of turn' option.Regarding the gameplay... I'm both intrigued by the detailed mechanics working into each other, and the astounding precision that has gone into balancing the game to be a legitimately difficult logistics puzzle in most of it's levels/halts. I'm just coming off one run where I was exactly one turn from having my entire tribe spiral into doom due to not bringing enough food to set up shop. I specifically had to withdraw two workers from non-critical jobs to basic food gathering, just to squeeze out those 2 extra turns in between starvation until the cooking house was set up. Beautiful!HOWEVER, those moments are regrettably rare, as the game, once you put some thought into it, comes down to a rather simple formula of picking your trades and then executing a "1 guy gathers raw food, 1 guy processes the food, everyone else gathers/builds" kind of blueprint. It took me a couple hours and A LOT of deaths to get to that point, but now that I'm there, the game appears... too easy? There's nothing left to do once you got the optimized formula, as the random events don't tilt it enough to matter, and with a minimum of foreplanning the randomness of the levels and availability of resources isn't an issue either.Essentially, the challenge of the game boils down to learning it's detailled, but otherwise simple system, and then not falling for one of the MANY stupidity pitfalls (such as not repairing, not having medicine stored ahead of time, not investing into mobile buildings, spending that barely-sufficient ressource you need to move, overproducing one resource or not spending knowledge to bypass the actual critical events when you come across them). And that's it.At this point, I'm not sure whether I'll replay the game much more. Sure, there's a couple more traits to unlock, a couple more different (even customizeable) starting setups.. but it's all same-y, and the lack of any real overarching story (beyond the introductionary world building provided by the tutorial) kinda makes me a bit moot about it.Overall, it's not a bad game. But it's also not a great one, and I don't see how I would put many more hours into it... it does have a low 20€ price tag though, so that is kind of a saving grace, I suppose?I'll give it a 6/10. A neutral review, if that option would be there, and a negative one to adequately compensate for the (as of this moment) 70% score.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: There are some interesting concepts in here, but:- Most of your time will be spent hitting End Turn, often ten or twenty times in a row.- The UI is terrible- The tutorial is terrible, long, and overwhelming- The map is cluttered and it can be hard to select your units and understand what anyone is actually doing- The game is unforgiving (yo I got a game over during the third tutorial of five)- The game talks about things that... doesn't exist?  It kept telling me in the tutorial that I had to cross a glacier and I did not see the word "glacier" anywhere in game, nor did I see anything at all icy in gameI failed out of this one in the tutorial.  It was not fun, it was not engaging, I felt like I had no idea what was happening, and then I got a game over.  Would not recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: First, let me say that this game is beautiful and I love the premise. My only issue is with the RNG, I have played over 16 hours and have been unable to win even one game with the very first tribe that starts out unlocked. Most games I have tried don't even have the resources necessary to move forward. Even trying the marketplace and trading doesn't work. The trades are too expensive and you harvest too slowly to be able to trade for a lacking resource before the wave gets to you.You need more hands to do the work, but then you have a food supply issue because all the pupils eat too much unless you are lucky to get one with a special trait. The campaign is easy compared to the rest of the game and is more of a tutorial than a campaign. It doesn't teach you about all the game features at all, but it covers the basics.I would love to be able to recommend the game, but as it is, I can not. However, if you like simple games that are very difficult or maybe nearly impossible to win, then you might enjoy it, like a difficult game of solitaire.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for August 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before September 7th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.This is a rogue-like, turn base, worker placement game.  Players will have a group of characters who are on a trip to the Eye, the only place safe from a coming apocalypse.  Players will have a limited number of turns to gather their supplies for the trip to avoid certain death. Each spot on the larger map will ask for different characters, different resources, and different abilities, and players will have to find the best path from their starting location to the location of the Eye and earn those resources before time runs out.I got through two out of the five tutorials, and the first part of a run.  I expect the game to get decently difficult before long, but overall, it’s a fun and inventive game that will probably take hours to get a handle on, and even longer to master. Pick this up if you enjoy turn-based rogue-lites.  This is a bit slower than what many fans might be used to, but it also has a high level of strategy and pushes the player to avoid hoarding and overconsumption, but rather pushes players to plan.If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Lost interest - the game is a slow turn-based resource management with a barely cobbled together lore and narrative. The world is flooding collect these resources to get to the next area. That's pretty much it - build buildings, harvest and level up. Played through the tutorial and that's really enough for me. Got this in a bundle, can't really recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to get into the game as a more relaxed and slow-paced city/colony management sim but that's not what the game is at all. That's only the surface and once you start playing it's clearly a difficult resource management game that's very prone to RNG and generating scenarios doomed to failure from the start (insufficient resources generated across maps to complete requirements, etc). But then if you treat the game as a challenging city builder or colony sim it falls short because it actually has very little complexity beyond the rpg-driven resource scarcity. Sure, there are many buildings and upgrades, unit classes and specialisations, etc but often those make little difference if there are just not enough resources to progress.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Cute game, but randomisation means you can be screwed and lose through no fault of your own. Choices are consequential, but given the procedural nature you have no way of knowing if you've made the right choice until it ends. Multiple times I got to the end of a zone and realised that by choosing to focus on a particular resource I basically killed myself. Frustrating, but the art style and music are cute and calming
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: How have they not fixed the bugs that make the tutorial unplayable!? I needed to run a non native resolution to be able to interact with the tutorial overlay. And then it just continues being frustatingly annoying, asking you to move the camera while movement is diasabled. And with no UI scaling the UI is bloody massive and intruding.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I can really see how others might like this game. You play scenarios which unlock different scenarios, but what I honestly don't get is there being such a large skill tree, but no time to explore even a quarter of it.The first playthrough is kind of fun. If you really don't mind starting 100% over again and playing a civ-like resource management game then this is for you. For me? Not so much. The long version of the campaign should not have been locked. Feels like it kind of spoiled it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: As Far As The Eye is an atmospheric & charming base building survival game, that does things in an elegant and fun way.  The sounds and animations fit the world they have crafted perfectly. The skill tree the pupils have allows for deep customization and give each one its own unique characteristics. There are 5 campaign missions that show you the ropes, and then you get into the normal play, where you pick from 4 different tribes to start with. Each with its own starting resources and background. Here is what gameplay looks like if you want to see it in action.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game,but be prepared to fail... A LOT. Don't get me wrong, I like the game, but there is a lot of luck involved in whether you succeed or not. It is so easy for one small event to completely ruin that run, you have to really plan to make it through. I recommend looking at tips & guides to help. Also play the campaign first, it is actually a tutorial.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I am not really an active reviewer of games, but I wanted to throw in my opinion on this one as a bit of a corrective to all the harsh reviews.  There IS a lot of frustrating RNG in this game, but much of the problem people are having is that they do not understand the Harmony mechanic.  Now, this is mostly the fault of the long-departed programmers; Harmony should have been FAR better explained.  However, after just a quick look at the boards here or the game Wiki, you can see how this mechanic works which makes the game much less opaque and (critically) much less brutal in the RNG department.  Basically, there is a hidden "play nice with nature, nature plays nice with you" mechanic.  Beyond that, the game is beautiful, fun, and deeply clever.  I have enjoyed it immensely, and I expect it will be on heavy rotation for a while.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks amazing and should feel amazing too but to me it becomes very tiring with a lot of randomization almost forcing me to want to finish the game before it throws me a curveball (or a bug that deletes all my resources which also has happened). I gave it more than a fair share of time but it comes down to a negative which hurts to say. It's the best looking game I've played this year at least.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: As Far as the Eye is a rogue like turn based strategy game that lacks any form of combat. This might be a turn off for some but I think the concept is refreshing. The game revolves around guiding a tribe of animals on a journey to the “Eye” a safe haven that will protect them from an imminent flood. You guide your tribe from one step to the next by gathering the necessary resources to reach the next “halt” on a bite size turn based strategy resource gathering map. You only have so many turns to gather a set number of resources and move to the next step before the waters destroy your tribe.The gameplay at first seems a bit shallow and easy but before long you are balancing the needs of your tribe with the required resources to move forward while random positive and negative events befall your pupils. There are moments when the random nature of the game can feel punishing and a few balance tweaks around healing may be necessary but it generally feels fair.There is a short campaign which is primarily a set of tutorial missions to teach you the mechanics but the main draw of the game is the procedurally generated levels. Each of these games allows you to pick a starting tribe with different numbers of starting pupils, resources and traits. Each of the levels is randomly generated so with the different tribes, biomes and procedurally generated levels the game has a ton of replay value.The graphics are colorful and pleasant with a lot of nice detail, from your pupils changing outfits for each task they perform to the flora and fauna spread across each halt. The music and sound effects are quite good and fits the theme and setting nicely.The story is not very deep but the game has some interesting commentary on your pupils responsibility to the planet and with the main threat of the game being rising flood waters the message seems pretty clear. Overall I have really enjoyed my time with the game and after completing the currently available campaign levels and playing several of the procedurally generated levels I can recommend the game to any fans of the genre.You can see a video review on my channel
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Well well well... well... well...This game is... kind of awesome. While graphically childish with kind of a childish way to tell things, the game mechanics themselves are not childish at all. Very simple to understand, quite hard to master. I currently passed the "campaign" which is the tutorial of the game. Now, I just try to finish the first mission and... that's the third or fourth run I fail while writing this review... And I like it. Why ? Well, because I usually have no problem with managerial games, no problem at all I'd say. Paradox games ? Piece of cake. Sid Meier's ? A joke I love to play since I'm a kid. Age of empires, Settlers, Anno, Simcity, ONI,... ? Let me laugh ! As far as the eye can see ? WUT ?! Why do I keep losing while everything is simple ? Well, because I'm not that good. Let's develop a bit. Again, everything is simple. Very simple. You build to collect ressources for your little nomadic tribe in order to avoid getting caught by the sea. You have a limited number of turns to finish each step. To reach the next step (of your choice) you need to gather a certain amount of ressources of certain type or/and reach some level of experience in some jobs. You may find other people to come to your tribe and gather more ressources more efficiently. Simple, very simple, too simple, too childish. Well, until you understand that Mother Nature wants you to take care of its lands before the sea rises. So you want and need ressources right ? Fine, then collect. Oh, you depleted a hex of wood ? Hmmm... of stone ? Hmmm... Well, whatever you'll deplete, you may see that wasn't a good choice later on as Mother Nature won't reward you, that's quite the opposite, you'll get plenty of events that'll make your task pretty hard. It means, growing in number will make your task harder. But if you stay small, you'll have hard time producing what you need to reach the next step. Not countring the fact that your caravan has a limited amount of space for ressources and the next step may not have the ressource you need to reach the next step (and trading is soooooo expensive you'll have to anger Mother Nature and you'll be soooooo in deep trouble). So choose well as the nomad life is really tough. Oh, yes, there's no going back by saving and reloading. Nice huh ?! See, this is more a roguelike than a proper managerial game. And roguelikes are awesome because they threat you like you deserve when you're not clever enough. That's life, and that's how I like it ! Well, I need to play a simpler game, like a Paradox one, it's better for my current level of intelligence.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I was not a fan of As Far As The Eye. My key problem is the gameplay, more specifically I found the gameplay loop to be annoying. The whole goal of outpacing the water is a pretty good concept, but doing so in the game is less so. In every area you have to gather resources to build items, maintain your units, and then use some resources to move to the next area. See the problem is the resource management, you know, the core gameplay. Gathering resources efficiently requires specific conditions either it needs to be a non-specialized resource with your main base nearby or a specialized resource with a building built for that specific resource nearby. Building these specialized gathering posts takes a bunch of resources even more so if you want the mobile variants if you do not want to rebuild them. Naturally, the mobile option seems like the best choice but the extra resources it takes to build them and the extra space they take in your inventory make this problematic. So I usually ended up just building them on-site, and did so exclusively at the start. But this just became annoying as a base-building game it sure does seem that you spend like 20+ turns each zone setting up just to have it all destroyed once you leave (during your time there if you are unlucky with disasters). Let me offer a personal example of how problematic this can all be.Say perhaps that you have enough resources to get through several turns from your last zone, but pushing it further is going to put you at great risk so you spend the next several turns trying to find a good place to set up shop. You have to settle in a suboptimal spot because you have barely explored the map, but you need to get out there and get food so you really can’t waste the time. So you set up shop and immediately have to gather food which is primarily berries so one person is on that, berries suck so you have the other person set up a kitchen, and the last worker you still need to find stuff so you immediately start exploring (I was always in a bad position/or in a rush when I had opportunities to grab other workers). Turns out that the fish you need for traveling are across the map and you need to then spend the resources to get that and build what is necessary, so get metal as that is one of the resources you need to travel to the next zone. So you head back and have used 10+ just to figure out your start spot was not as centralized as it should be, but you have to deal with it. So then you gather the resources, but guess what RNG hates you and straps you with illness and damages your stuff with enough storms that you have to rebuild them, so the fish get delayed. Once you finally get to the fish you have gone through half of the allotted turns, so you spend the turns getting there and building what you need, you start gathering it. And what a surprise! RNG is going to beat you with a stick again. Somehow you have to get 1000+ fish in a tight timeframe it is doable, but you have run out of accessible berries as all the other stuff took too long to gather so you will never go positive on food without using your fish, so you have to eat and cook that fish as well slowing your progress heavily. You can’t send another person because someone has to cook and the other needs to gather the wood for the stove. So you spend the next 30 turns making no changes (hitting the space bar repeatedly should NOT count as gameplay it is boring and I spent way too much time doing it), but once again get beaten up by RNG once or twice slowing you down but you got this. Turn 11 hits, you are so close to getting what you need less than 30 away then you can leave and take your victory. Ice hits on the next turn. You can no longer fish, you are forced to die with less than 20 left to go; RNG and distance have killed you. The RNG in this game has given me some real terrible maps as resources can be set to be quite far from where you need them to be far and events will beat you in the worst ways, maybe I am just unlucky but my random events were 90% or more negative and the process of doing all of this was monotonous, not fun. And I think that describes my whole experience, just hitting a space bar most of the time and feeling like the game wants you to lose instead of making you feel like you are outsmarting the world.So yeah I disliked the gameplay, but I also did not like how it controlled and the games interface. I would have liked numbered hotkeys for the workers, the ability to adjust your center even when zoomed all the way out, a smaller interface, easier to interact with objects on the board, and more compact menus and fewer of them so that I can more easily navigate them. It was just annoyingThe good news is that is where my negativity ends. I did find the story/tutorial (though somewhat limited) to be fairly interesting. I was not nearly as interested in the characters as I was in the world, so that was a bit of a letdown that it was more about the inhabitant’s stories. Overall though, I think it is really cool: a mysterious reoccurring flood, shapeshifting creatures, their traditions and history… All of it is neat, I would love to read a book about this world or follow an archeologist or scientist who is trying to figure out what is really going on in another game.Graphically I do like this game as well, the style is very bright and colorful, character designs are unique for each role they do, the units feel mobile and the animals being particularly bouncy is a plus as well, the tiles feel lively in their own right, and the drawn art is very well done. I don’t have any complaints.The music is pretty good as well, though I don’t think I can be as positive with the music as I am with the story and the artistic direction. The music is fitting to the game's mood and setting, but it is too basic. It never stood out to me, it was just background noise. Of course, the game is the main portion of the experience (though I have made it clear how I feel about that), but some of the best games I have ever played have had killer soundtracks that stand out with the game. It checks all the boxes that soundtrack should be and as such has a fitting soundtrack, but I would say it does not excel is the only problem. It was too generic, too safe. Despite that, I listened to it the entire time and was not bothered by it, so I think that is a big plus.I wanted to like As Far As The Eye, in fact, in many of the games I play I come in with high hopes. I like to come in with the best attitude as people have put in hard work and skill into something I lack the skill to create. But I try to be honest and fair. I found this game's gameplay, interface, and controls to be less than satisfying. And sadly that is the biggest part of any game. I fully praise the story, art, and music though, and I hope the developers continue to utilize that creativity. From what I see of their titles that are finished or in development it does look like that is the case, and I may go and pick one of those up to review it as well I would love to see what more the developers have to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I love roguelike/x hybrids. In this case, the x is actually 3x (explore, expand, exploit). Behind the calm and peaceful surface appearance lurks a very hard, tightly balanced game, with a small but robust tech tree that provides multiple paths to victory, letting you adapt your strategy to the random world you're given.The game gives the tense feeling of constantly being one mistake away from losing, while being lenient enough to allow a winrate close to 100%. This is not something seen often in roguelikes, but here it is appropriate, given that each run takes several hours to complete. As a result, playing this game will put you in a mood that is a nice mixture of relaxed alertness. The simple but very well made graphics enhance the depth of this experience.There are some minor balance problems in the game: these mostly take the form of flavorful but  underpowered mechanics, which you can mostly ignore. Luckily, this doesn't affect the core game mechanics which are clever and subtle, allowing for different styles of play and making you face a variety of challenges on your path to victory. Overall, the developers really succeeded in breaking new ground and making something unique, interesting, and beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like this is about 80% of the way to being really great. It needs a considerable amount of balancing to smooth out the RNG issues, the techs could be more varied and interesting, and there are some pretty glaring UI flaws.That said, I bought it on sale and easily got my money's worth. It's a challenging and satisfying optimization puzzle that rewards planning and attention to detail, and it's pretty stylish to boot.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: 4/5 stars fun game. Little buggy. Very chill single player game.Gather resources, build buildings, train skills, invite others to join your caravan, it is just a very pleasant strategy game.Notable bug:On occasion units will finish gathering resources, bug out and then immediately start collecting again, losing those resources. Could be game losing if it happened at a bad time. Whenever this happens, the unit has been assigned to two tasks via glitch and you need to reassign them to a task you don't care about to fix their state before reassigning them to what you actually want them to do. Not sure what causes this glitch just yet.I think there may be some glitchiness regarding resources protected by aura, but I honestly just don't understand that mechanic well enough to say.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I would not recommend this game on full price simply because it has several major bugs (especially the building on fire), and the devs have supposedly abandoned the game. The game is a good oregon trail style gameplay where you need to balance your per-turn food (and wool) costs with the cost to leave, on a very tight schedule. All the while you're getting wrecked by acts of god, which can be toothless or completely make it impossible to leave, if you don't foresee them early enough and delete events with a mid-tech building.In short, the game strategy on harder difficulties is demanding and punishing if you just fumble into it. You want to look at the paths you'll take, maybe build a mobile building for wool gathering if you see that two paths ahead require lots of wool to continue. You want to upgrade your scouting so you can check if the halt has enough stone, or you might have to go the other path. You want a cook at the end so you can support 4-5 pupils or more, or else how are you going to harvest 1500 worth of resources within the 80 turns or so. Better start training that cook from day 1. Stuff like that.The UI could use a lot of clarity. A section to show what pupils are assigned what tasks, a way to see what resources the entire halt has without individually scanning each hex. Even the amount of food you will produce from cooking is not shown.Again, I enjoyed it for what it is, but it has a few run-breaking bugs, unforgiving at harder difficulties, and there's no more patches.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This. You were fun, you just didn't do a great job at explaining yourself. What is someone meant to do? Especially when the map tile screws you over and there's not much you actually can do before the wave washes you away and you die. There's some definite unfortunate RNG elements in this game, that can be very punishing. Once you understand it, the game is great. The issue is, do you want to put in 40 hours to work towards understanding? That's what you've gotta think about. The learning experience can be fun, it won't be for a lot of people though I feel. 6/10.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I would recommend this game! This is a lovely puzzle, but pretty challenging at first - very easy to spiral out, but losing a little in the beginning is all part of the fun. I really enjoy the atmosphere of the game as well as the logistic puzzle of trying to get the things you need to get to the next halt. At 12 hours in I've had one win and I think there's much more to learn in this game. I streamed this game close to its launch about a year ago and I've been thinking about it ever since!
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: AFATE is great. It feels like a love child between FTL and Oxygen Not Included, with an absolutely unique aesthetic. The controls are simple, the resources basic, but the ways to play are numerous. It is up to you to play, and fail, and play again, before you start to grasp what you need to focus on from the start.The lore really pushes towards a philosophy of balance, but I as surprised at how the game mechanics naturally push you towards balance as you play. Every decision is a compromise between opposites. Some examples: * some resources now, or more efficient resources later * cheaper buildings vs versatile expensive buildings * Fewer villagers (fewer mouths to feed) or more villagers (can get more done)Every time I play I get absolutely engrossed in the progress of my villagers (called Pupils), trying to determine the most effective tasks to assign them for the long term well being of the caravan. I also get lost in the beautiful art and music, which help to suck me into this enchanting world.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I was surprised at how much I like this game.  It reminds me of kind of a mix between Rimworld, Age of Mythology, and Civ.  It takes some time to get used to the mechanics, but once you do, the game is very enjoyable.You start with a small tribe and you get to decide what they'll work on to guide their career advancement.  Each campaign is a journey to the eye broken down into small halts, or maps.  I really like that you can unlock techs with knowledge, keep your pupil's skills, and build mobile buildings to give yourself a leg up in the later game halts.The major problem I had on my first 2 campaigns is that I would get to the last mission before the eye and deplete all of the resources before I could get to the eye and either my Pupil's would starve, or the flood would come.  I found that the longer campaign feels like you have more control as you have more missions to accumulate techs, buildings, and skills.  I also found it helps to look at the map and highlight the future paths.  I try to start gathering the resources needed for the next round before it even starts. Also the size of each Halt matters.  The larger the Halt the more resources there are.  I try to avoid small maps at all costs.This game is honestly very enjoyable and extremely cute to see your pupil's transform into different animals when they become different professions.  I really like the mystical feel of the game and the ability to improve and build up making future halts easier.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great concept with excellent narrative and art design that needs serious balancing.  Although the challenge of a rogue-like is dealing with adversity, managing limited resources, and accepting the cruelties of fate, the starting conditions and available player choices feel too restrictive to form actual strategy.Player choice is often illusory.  You may have to decide between two paths, but one may require a resource that you cannot acquire with your starting tribe, or lead to a region you can't effectively exploit. Game units feel fragile, dysfunctional, and neurotic, depending on the random traits you are dealt. Many random disasters simply can't be avoided, mitigated, or insured against. If you're 10 turns from the goal on a well-designed resource engine, you could still pull an event that simply adds 20% to your target number, putting it out of reach.The fail state of challenging is frustrating. In the future, I would like to play more scripted campaign or challenge modes, see some of the unit traits balanced, and see more choices on the main map to increase the sense of player agency.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: A weird mix of Slay The Spire's branching map system with the resource gathering systems of a 4x strategy game, As Far As The Eye is a placid caravan sim... until it isn't. You really have to balance how you play incredibly well, and one wrong move or decision can send your caravan into an unstoppable death spiral that only gets worse as the numerous negative events pile on, grinding your poor pupils into dust.It's pretty fun. Just be ready to try and fail, a lot, because As Far As The Eye pulls no punches.I hope they add some difficulty modifiers/turn down the negative events a bit (a lot really), but for now I'd still recommend As Far As The Eye if you're looking for a unique take on roguelike design.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this and I would love to play it more but I cant get past the basic levels after the campaign.  I've killed so many tribes people - Instead of relaxing and playing the game, I'm getting frustrated that I cant accomplish anything - I'm always struggling - AND there is no Easy mode.  I wouldn't recommend this Game - even tho I love the concept, the art, the story etc etc.  I wish it was different
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful, charming, and full of great ideas. I can't recommend buying it unfortunately.I can see these designers embracing mechanics they've developed here to make a truly delightful and rewarding roguelite strategy game, but what they have in this game is a little too dense and unfocused to get there. If they polished the UI a bit to highlight important elements over the course of turns, and tightened up the progression between stages I would probably change my tune, but what's here now is doing too many things at once without highlighting any of them enough.Lovely and frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I'm mixed on the review for this game.  It definitely has potential to be great.  Basically like FTL and Civ combined but with a false relaxing exterior.  Going into this, I was expecting the game to be relaxing.  One you could jump in to to accomplish the task of getting to the end, while taking time and effort, would still be an enjoyable experiece.  But the game is brutal.  Some of the brutality is just how the game is set up and a small part of it are some minor details I'll get into detail below.  Basically you can feel pretty good about how a game is going only for it all to go down the drain in a turn or two.  Definitely a game that makes you wanna rage quit.  It's a very aesthetically pleasing game; but I'm not sure it's the type of game that will make me wanna play it again.  I enjoy games like FTL that are tough to beat, but it doesnt work for this kind of gameplay, imo.  The small details I mentioned above that make it a bit more difficult is just how I find my mind deals with some aspects of the game..  Each run starts out easy enough.  It's basically just resource gathering.  You send a 'pupil' out to gather resources.  You'll need various variety of resources for various reasons.  Because of this, a lot of the game is just waiting for your pupils to collect the resources so you just click to go to the next turn and it starts being automatic for you.  (Space is the hotkey for it so it's super easy to skip to the next turn.) So at the start, when it's easy, it's basically just waiting for your pupils to collect enough wood, food, etc so I just tap Space a bunch.  However I find myself taking this habit into later gameplay when bad events are more prominent.  I end up missing a bunch of notifications for events the turn they happen because 1) I'm in the middle of tapping, and 2) the alert noises/visuals aren't prominent enough to catch my attention.  Another annoying part of the game is that it's easy to mix up villagers and accidently select the wrong one to do a task.  And sometimes I find a villager not doing any work after I skipped to the next turn a bunch.  It'd be nice if the game worked like Civ where if a unit isn't doing anything, you need to give it a command (Even if it's just wait/defend) before going to the next turn.  Another issue I found is that there's no warning when your food starts to run low.  I usually only notice when I'm out of food (after there's a change in rate of food gathering/consumption) when all my villagers start taking damager per turn.  And even if you set all your villagers to switch to gathering food, that can still take a few turns to collect and store so there's a good chance they die.Basically, the aesthetic/ general gameplay of this game doesn't seem to match how difficult it is.  It feels like if Tom Nook killed you if you didn't pay off his loan in enough days.

_childDocuments_.review: In its current state the game has a lot of promise but the UI and controls are frustrating to utilize when trying to do simple tasks like sending 1 character to point A and another to point B. _childDocuments_.review: It's refreshing to find a challenging turn-based resource management game that doesn't involve combat! The game is fairly slow-paced, but there is an underlying tension because the land is going to flood, and you have limited time to prepare your Pupils.Decisions are at the heart of this game.Which path will you take to the Eye? Different paths lead to different lands with differing resources to be gathered. There are also different obstacles to overcome, so some routes might be inherently easier, but you also need to match your route with the skills and strengths of your Pupils.You need to decide how you will feed your Pupils. Maybe raw pepkins are good enough, but you should consider the alternatives of fish, meat or grain. Your choice will depend on the resources available within the Halt, but also the route you will take, and again the skills and strengths of your Pupils.Where will you place buildings? You want them to be close to the resources, but you will also want to cluster them for camp bonuses. Will you build cheaper permanent buildings, or more expensive mobile buildings you can take with you? Mobile are great if you can upgrade them too, but they need more advanced resources to build and also you can't carry too many because that will limit the number of resources you can take with you too. Should you build a market, workshop or council building?There are no right or wrong answers. Much will depend on your play style and there are many viable strategies to follow. Much could depend on the random starting stats of your team. Will you prioritise gaining knowledge or resources? What will you spend your Knowledge points on? How will you balance your team? Will you choose to have a Druid? How will you deal with vagaries?Speaking of vagaries, these are negative events which hamper your progress. Many can be safely ignored, but eventually some will cause you problems. You will always have some time to prepare. Can you adapt? So many choices!I'm only 16 hours in, and haven't faced any of the more difficult challenges yet. So far it's all well within my comfort zone. I will edit this review once I have tried the 2 & 3 star challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: It has gorgeous graphics and a nice gameplay loop. I like the fact that you have to think ahead and plan out your route and plan your resources. But that's about it...The game feels unbalanced. I Could not even finish the campaign without failing many times. I mean gathering food is so slow that if you get 1 more pupil, you are already lacking in food. Even when I had 1 gatherer and 1 baker and a wood gatherer (needed for the bakery) I barely had enough food to keep up the 3 pupils. That was in the campaign.... where you almost have no debuffs. I couldn't even gather all the other resources I needed without the pupils starving to death. Not untill I got the 4th pupil, an expert baker in the campaign, could i finish the first halt. But boy was that the worst decision I could make, cause in the next halt I couldn't get enough food to even maintain the 4 pupils I had. So yea, one could argue that I suck in the game. Or that the game is just unforgiving if I can't even keep 3 pupils alive even if I have put them all on food gathering/creation duty.Also there are a few questionable choices regarding difficulty... Like all pupils above the amount of 3 need a camp or else they won't do anything. And if you come across a halt without a rhino thing, you can't build a camp. This means you have 4 pupils that need food, but 1 pupil that doesn't do anything without a camp. Feels a bit like a forced difficulty. If you need to survive, who cares if you have a camp... You will get one if you contribute, not when everyone is dead because there is no resource to create a camp for you. In the next runs I made sure not to have more than 3 pupils.After this campaign mission, I felt like trying a custom game. When I started noticing the complaints of some people in the other negative reviews, I decided to refund the game and not even go beyond the treshold of no return for refunds. I feel that the learning curve for this game is just way too steep and you need lots of hours and luck to win some runs. So this is definitely a no go for me at least and I won't recommend it to anyone. Just don't underestimate the difficulty of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: So many things to keep in mind at once! I really, really want to enjoy this game, but I just keep loosing in the stupidest ways, because it's so easy to make an irreversible mistake! I forgot to monitor the food - everyone starved. Forgot about the turn limit while exploring artifacts - everyone drowned. Forgot the location of the resource after the fog came - no longer able to continue the journey.  Forgot to upgrade a key building - no longer able to continue. Forgot to leave enough of the already mined resource when upgrading things - no longer able to continue. All while keeping tabs on everyone so no one gets ill and everyone is working according to their skills. And when I really get into the strategy, it's way to easy to forget to keep tabs on the basic things. Add to this the solid chance of random failure, and the game becomes too hard. The interface should be remade to help with prioritizing. Health markers on buildings, notices about depleting certain kinds of resources are not as important. I need an earlier reminder about the hunger and the wave, and the option to "lock away" the resources needed for travel.

_childDocuments_.review: - A turn-based micro-4x roguelike. You progress from zone to zone with your small tribe of multi-purpose builders/gatherers/crafters while gathering resources, building things, developing your units' skills, and progressing through tech trees. - If you don't gather enough specific resources to progress to the next area, a giant wave will wash over the zone and kill everyone. Random events will occur along the way (with a few turns notice) that will jeopardize the health of your tribespeople or structures, or make your mission harder in other ways. You have to manage a Diablo-style inventory between zones to determine what can come with you; no hoarding allowed! - Quite fun and very cute, with a wonderfully relaxing aesthetic and a surprising amount of depth and challenge.
