_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRThe game is beautiful, but a literal RNG Fiesta that wont let you win unless you roll 12+ d20's in a row. The only way to play it without losing your hair is a custom gamemode that disables the 100% RNG Events that will ruin your gameplay. There are NO GOOD EVENTS. They're ALL BAD.The game overall is very well made, it has an interesting story, great music and a fun artstyle, combined with a very unique style of gameplay. Unfortunately, that resource-management aspect is entirely overshadowed by 100% RNG Vagaries, or whatever you want to call them. Personally, I call them ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.There's few vagaries you can even SEE coming, a few examples being the 2-3 odd events related to Auras(AKA The big ♥♥♥♥-off shrines that stop you from gathering efficiently that you need to prostrate yourself in front of to make it stop for about 3-4 turns at best.)  Eclipses, which basically turn ALL of the shrines back on, and OCCASIONALLY, you can see an "Overworking" or "Bored" event coming in.These are the easy ones to deal with. And I use the word easy in a very relative way, compared to the next set of events.Drought, Wildfire, Thunder, Fire, Fire in your buildings, half the maps resources being burnt down, lose 20 turns towards the flood meter and be given only a single day left to gather up the 200+ wood you need to get out, whereas if that didn't happen you'd of survived and actually beaten the game.These "Gameplay mechanics" are only for the most masochistic, self-hating maniac who truly believes skill=RNG. I'm VERY PATIENT with games. And if you don't believe me, check my Achievements in "Getting over it with bennet foddy."I can say without a doubt that the only way to play this game without wanting to CRY at the loss of time and life, as the game calls you a bad planner after you watch all your favorite pupils die of hail/drowning/starvation/malaria/whatever the ♥♥♥♥ else, is to play the Campaign (Which is SHORT, and a glorified tutorial, but that's fine.) And the CUSTOM GAME where you can TURN OFF EVENTS.Seriously. I know the play modes are supposed to be challenging, but it's rediculous the difference between "Challenging." And "Pray you roll 20 twelve times in a row."This game is new, and I'm loving it, but seriously. Change the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ values on these random events, because they're simply not fair. It's not only that, but NONE OF THE EVENTS ARE EVEN GOOD! You'd think in a world like this one, you'd have a nice day where you feel like working a little harder, or that you know, if you DONT that you'll DIE. For ♥♥♥♥♥ sake, they TAKE A NAP as an event. I don't know about you, but if I was in their tiny little ponchos, I'd be a lot happier to work. Make some events that are GOOD. Maybe it'll dilute the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of bad ones, and make the bad ones BEARABLE.Oh, and if anybody wants to laugh and say "Just get good." And/or pull a video of somebody winning, just know that the difference between me and them is the fact that I don't want to wait around for that perfect game. Games are meant to be played, enjoyed, and you're meant to get BETTER at them. Not flounder around until the game lets you win. That's how you win this game, which just destroys all of its amazing qualities.If a game isn't fun, why play it?

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game from Humble Bundle so as the other reviews say I will point out things I agree with along with a small description of gameplay:It's an interesting take on a strategy board game. You are trying to beat the time limit (Tide) and progress through the map through resource collecting, prioritizing task and making the bare minimum to make it to the next stage. Yes, you can build structures to make collecting resources faster though it's not necessary for basic materials. You can also focus skills on specific people to make them masters at the task you give them. The visuals remind me of niche but it definitely isn't. That said I think the game is fun for the few hours i've played it but the thing that hinders me from wanting to play more is that there is no save function to restart a stage if you messed up. Biggest Point: It's unforgiving, this is a very hardcore game and mistakes can throw away hours of work. There is no save function which I find the biggest drawback from getting this game at full price. You should know this before getting the game, this is honestly the only reason I just can't recommend it. I will admit I'm not a perfect person and I like to play strategy games while drunk... when the stages can take up to an hour or more to do and there is no option to restart I tend to rage quit. I really like this game but, because of that lack of a save function I kinda got discouraged at campaign and rage quit. Otherwise it is a very fun game, I hope the devs make it an option to do hardcore instead of forcing it into the main game. The work put into it is very apparent and it really is well done. It's just because of the lack of being able to save I just can't recommend it because it's such a vital thing for a game like this. Hopefully it makes more sense if I play more into it but at a bit more than 2hrs I don't know if I'll be retrying this. TL:DR Imagine playing Civ 5 without a save function and you had to depend on RNG to win. Then do that again several times without a save function through each civ map and that's probably why besides some folks hating the User Interface.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game expecting it would make me feel the same excitement I felt playing XCOM or Frostpunk - feeling tense because I only had limited time and limited resources to get my animal pals to safety.  Or maybe the feeling I got from finally cresting the top of Slay the Spire.But actually playing the game after finishing the tutorial, I just felt...kind of bored.  Not tense, or relaxed, or excited for anything.  There were nothing about the buildings or upgrades that made me feel "oh, I've definitely got to get that."  The skill wheel mostly works itself, offering modest upgrades but not really changing gameplay overmuch.  And the random vagaries, random shrines, random auras, and random villager quirks all felt like they were just in the way - obstacles between me and doing something exciting and meaningful.  And this is outside of that one time I spawned in to a small canyon halt into a space completely surrounded by mountains that my caravan could not cross.I don't want to trash the game - there are some legitimately neat things here to experience.  Like the choice between cheap disposable buildings or expensive ones that travel with you, at the cost of storage.  Or the idea of trying not just to produce lots of goods, but just the right amount.  But there's just none of the fundamental joy here from a city-building game, or a resource-management game, or a rogue-like, as far as I could tell.  It looks and sounds very pretty, but that isn't enough to make me want to actually play it again.  I do hope the developer(s) keep at it with this and other projects.  I feel like they're just on the cusp of something awesome, but not quite there yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd rate this like a 7/10 maybe 6/10 but I gave it extra credit for the beautiful art style and interesting concept. The sound.  It's just not immersive.   I know that it sounds weird to say;  But other games really put quite a bit of energy into sound and storytelling.  This game was a total miss.  Lots of text lots of story; and it's hard to follow along with; and the characters seem a bit lifeless and detached from the narrative.  It's a bummer cause just a small update could fix this pretty quickly.  But as it stands.  I felt really not immersed even though the world would seemingly be very complete judging this book by the cover. Secondly.  It looks sorta like a Civ game or a builder game - I'd say that it's not.  Its a puzzle game that looks like a builder game.   It moves pretty quickly and obviously that's the point.  If you like kinda quick thinking race to the end kinda style games then this is for you.  But for me I like to take it slow and max things out and build stuff and explore and expand.  This game didn't really scratch that itch for me. All in all.  I think I paid something like 25 dollars for this game.  :/ I played it 5 hours.  and lost interest.  I'd say it's an okay value for the money.  Maybe something in the future i'll pick up again.  But i'll say it again.  This is a puzzle game.  If you like puzzles, you'll love this, it's challenging and sometimes frustratingly challenging.  Every stage is slightly different and comes with different art styles as you travel from map to map.  It's very cute, very well designed and very interesting in concept.  It's actually a game that has a lot of potential.The story is interesting in concept.  But it's short.  It feels a bit faceless, especially with no voices or main characters.  I sorta didn't fall in love with my little worker sprites the way I do with other games... so.  It just lacks personality in the places that count.  And unfortunately for me... that's where this game took its greatest hit.

_childDocuments_.review: A good concept, but poorly executed from a gameplay perspective.  The map is very intensely cluttered, to the point that it's difficult to select your units or parse what is going on.  If you zoom out to see the layout of the map, the details of each square are hazy.  If you zoom in to see the details, you can only see one tile in each direction.  There's no comfortable middle ground, it's just "Too far out to see what's going on" or "Too cluttered and myopic to see what's going on."I might be able to get past all the (incredibly frustrating) gameplay hangups that all the bad reviews seem to mention with some practice, but I frankly won't be putting in the time because the UI is so cluttered that figuring out what is happening is a visual chore. _childDocuments_.review: I absolutely would not recommend this game.It's beautiful. It clearly has some artistic vision. However, it's not designed to be intuitive, and the text is quite dense.First, there's a lot of reading. A *lot*. I don't mind reading when it's something fun and interesting...but tutorials have no reason to be walls of text in this day and age. Point to what I'm doing, point to where it needs to go. If you have to explain I'm building a raft therefore I need wood...there's a flaw in the game design. This isn't a text adventure.Second, there are several poor design choices that make it difficult to tell at a glance what's going on. The largest flaw is the choice to make every occupation an animal. I don't care what animal it is. I care what task is being done. But I can't manage my characters easily because every time I reassign work I have to mouse over the stupid bird face to remind myself whatever the hell they do well. Whenever someone new pops up, I have to figure out what the new animal is. Save everyone some time and use universal symbolism. If they build stuff, put a tool on it. They cook, put a dish on it. They gather, put a basket on it. Just let it make sense. Your backstory is not so important it should make the game harder simply by being filled with lore in the most obtuse way possible.Finally, the relaying of the story itself is flawed. The plot is not particularly bad (though it's not really anything to rave about either), rather the issue is that the developers are trying to build this world where none of the things relate to the current world. You want to measure time in blinks? And then each section of the trip is called...a halt? At length I understand this is a thematic attempt because it's a caravan, it's just strange. Call it a campsite or "leg of the trip" just make it plain. Throwing this in the strange story about the storm that isn't well explained at onset (because it cuts in at the start as if you understood the world already). Calling the units pupils...? What are they studying? Ancient Animorph history? Just simplify it.That said, the music is calm, the art is pretty, and the game play is standard. It's not that it's an awful game; it's just really mediocre. There's other games that do this exact same premise, but without all the jargon. It's just a fresh coat of paint, and I don't particularly enjoy the paint that was chosen.I had to quit during the fifth tutorial level. I could no longer stand trying to figure out how to interact with the new buildings, or which characters are skilled in it. No room for trial and error is given... another poor choice, especially for a tutorial level. Check your stats, devs: Only 25% of players are earning the 4th tutorial's completion. 75% are finishing the first. That means you're losing players in there somewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, the game is relatively hard and punitive but is not really unfair and rng-based despite what is said in most negative reviews. Keep in mind that the game has a lot rogue-like mechanics so you will have to die and learn from it. There is also a custom game option if you want your game to be easy.Aside from the difficulty, the game is really beautiful, and has a pleasant, peaceful atmosphere. Some things could be better explained like the fact that the game autosaves every turn (except in campaign) and that's why there is no save button (so you can't cheat è_é). I encountered only a few graphical bugs, nothing game breaking.This game is unique, and great, as long as you take the time to understand it.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics: 10/10Story: 9/10Gameplay: Intermediate/Hard. Stream worthy: NicheAt the time of this review I’ve played nearly six (6) hours of this game. I originally wanted it thinking it was going to be a colony simulator. I was both surprised and disappointed in this assumption. It is enough of a colony simulator to start to scratch around that itch but not enough to fully satisfy it, however, the game has enough to do that you’ll likely not realize it. The game is down right beautiful, down from the character and world design, to sound design and story. Don’t let that fool you. This game is not easy at baseline and I shudder to try and play this on “hard.” Now I’m not going to yank your chain and tell you I’m the best strategist gamer, but I’m not completely stupid either. But this game made me pull my hair out sometimes and the way the story likes to knife you in the feelings when you fail makes you want to try and do better. All in all I liked the game and will be continuing my play.

_childDocuments_.review: For a game about choice optimization why did it feel like there was nothing to choose, and that choices didn’t matter? The failed to accomplish the only gimmick it was going for. In the learning tree, none of the choices are really that appealing, I wasn’t excited that I got any, and because of that I didn’t care what I picked. You have these little meeples that are supposed to get bonuses in whatever specialization or task they do most frequently, but none of the bonuses are interesting or matter. Rougelike doesn’t mean the game should completely fail to explain simple mechanics, so you die for no reason. Once I watched a YouTube pointing out mechanics they fail to address, the game was very winnable, but I didn’t care if I did. How to get to the last node, oh you need a ton of rock from some land with no rock. Well, my only option is to build a trading center and farm wool for 70 boring click as fast as you can turns. There barely any things to choose, the choices don’t matter, and they aren’t interesting. Why would you bother building a worthless workshop? Or taking on extra pupils that are just extra mouths to feed? Why worry about “disasters” that only apply to lake tiles when I’m in the desert?Probably uninstalling, I’m not even waiting for it to be patched. Go play Rimworld, watch for Dwarf Fortress, check out Slay the Spire, or Griftlands.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: It's a captivating premise with truly beautiful lore and music. It's close to being an amazing game; its almost fun, but overall it feels unfinished. Worth if it's on sale though. Apart from is balance system that feels... randomly unfair at times, my biggest gripe is that the game suffers from "tell, don't show" syndrome. It's user interface is not very intuitive, and key mechanics are left to huge blocks of instructional text-- as is our introduction to much of the lore. Most of this could be fixed with more simplified tutorial missions with a storybook narrator, more icons and less text in general, and a more polished menu system. I shouldn't need to reread the bloody wiki to pick this game up a second time. Here are some useful comparisons that succeed imo: Armello, a tabletop RPG game, achieves an effective introduction to its characters and general mythology through it's tutorials, with more detailed explanations available as extra unlockable content. Ex: The spiritual forces of nature are demonstrated with avatar to environment interactions and *brief* blurbs of text through item/event interactions. Frostpunk, a survival city-builder, brings unique elements of storytelling throughout it's entire play-through. The challenges of the city come alive with an amazing intro-cinematic, clearly defined management goals (and suggested solutions), and visual art seamlessly integrated into the UI.I really hope this game gets a major UI overhaul or a sequel because it has a lot of potential.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the most frustrating gaming experiences I´ve ever had. Traditional rougelikes take away control from you; be it by giving you random traits/quirks or randomized enemy spawns, weapons and map layouts every single run. But you always have enough control to give you a feeling of the game being fair. With enough skill, you can definitely win. However, this is not the case with As Far As The Eye.Many aspects of the game are entirely luck-based and sometimes impossible to work around. The layout of the maps, it´s resources and their amounts, the requirements to progress to the next map, your pupils and their traits, as well as possible disasters. On paper this sounds fine, having randomized components keeps every run more or less fresh. But when you run into scenarios that are not beatable, the fun quickyly stops.As Far As The Eye is, without a doubt, a beautiful game. The environment, buildings, animals, action effects, animations - everything looks perfect. On top of that, the sound is more than fitting for the game. All sounds are distinct enough, so I know based on the sound what exactly happened. Only the design of the pupils I don´t quite like. They looks way too simple compared to everything else.Not all pupils are created equal. All of them start your run with a randomized selection of traits, that can both be quite helpful and also make run a living hell.Sometimes you´re blessed by traits like Agile (1 less turn to harvest), Fast (+1 MP) or Ermit (Doesn´t need housing to work); setting you up for an easy beginning.Other times, the RNG curse is screwing you hard. Get Invading (takes 2 housing when working), Puny (-1HP per turn), Slow (-1MP) or Fantasist (warns of Vagaries that will not take place) on your pupil and be prepared to have a hard time. The worst offender of them all is Glutton (+50% food consumptions). Food take quite a while to harvest, especially in the beginning of the game. If, for whatever reason, your food gathering is delayed for a couple turns, a pupil with Glutton will make sure, that all your pupil will die of starvation. You´re better of starting a new run instead of taking such a pupil with you.Sidenote: By unlocking achievements, you´re granted both positive and negative traits associated with the achievement. Time is always limited, and this is especially important when looking at gathering resources. Most of the time, you´re 3 or 5 turns away from failing your run. Vagary has disabled your gathering hut? Depending on the amount of HP lost, it takes multiple rounds to repair it in which you can´t gather food. Forest full of Mosquitos? You have to wait up to 10 turns for them to disappear; if you don´t your pupil will get sick when gathering wood. Heat wave is killing all crops? Better try to gather as much food as possible before everything dies. Rats are coming to eat all your excess food? Either build a storage or be screwed and starve.Vagaries can get not only annoying but run-ending very fast. Take for example a scenario, in which all mobile building are being damages - in our case it´s the mobile gathering hut. So to avoid damage and very costly repair costs, you disassemble it, wait for the disaster to pass and assemble it again. Depending on your perks and skills, this procedure can take 3 - 5 turns. In the turns, your gatherer most likely wasn´t able to gather food, bringing your pupils closer to starvation. That in itself is not a big deal, if it wouldn´t happen multiple times on a map, sometimes even in quick succession. Throughout my playtime, it happened more than a dozens times, that this kind of disaster struck me more than 5 times on a single map. This lead to my pupils starving to death almost every time.Another run-ending vagary is the "Damaged Path" one. This one adds one more resource to your requirments of advancing to the next map. In more than half of my runs, the resource added was not present in the amounts required to advance to the next map. Not a single time I was able to get enough of said resources through the market in that scenario. It always led to me having to abandon the run.Depending on how safe you play, a single map (a short run consists of atleast 3 maps) can take you about 30 minutes. Considering the fact that you can lose at any moment due to a RNG event, spending 1.5h on a run and getting RNG´d at the very is soul-crushing and annoying. This happened quite a few times to me and is one of the main reasons why I´m not fond of this game.Overall, the game is too luck-oriented and quickly and often punishes you for things that are out of your control. No matter how much planning you did, how well you played the entire time: RNG will destroy you and your ambitions.

_childDocuments_.review: A simple yet deep resource management game, where the only conflict comes from the environment. You are never under attack, nor do you ever build weapons or fight. It is simply a struggle to survive as you attempt to travel to the safety of "The Eye". Each run is unique, and part of the fun is trying to figure out how to tailor your play-style to the specific challenges of the game at hand (rather than just doing the exact same thing every time). The game is turn based, and a bit unforgiving, as every choice you make, for better or worse, is permanent (you can save and quit, but not restore old saves). It would be nice if a few of the mechanics were spelled out a little better (like Harmony, which is some hidden score that represents your connection to nature), but all in all a very chill and enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game is cute, really cute. The art design is adorable, Your worker units in this game, called Pupils, have such great character to them, which is only bolstered by the sweet written moments in the campaign. I want every one of their polymorph forms as a plushie. As for the writing, there isn't a lot but what is there paints the deep lore of this game. Gameplay is tight, keeping things engaging although able to be pretty forgiving in the earlier difficulties. This plays like a 4X game with roguelite elements. Namely that there's no going back on your decisions in a  Journey (the in-game name for these "runs") and that death of your Pupils is permanent. Every Journey is a series of individual levels or stages called "Halts" wherein you have to collect the necessary resources to progress to the next stage. These resource requirements tend to be somewhat random, but not impossible. Often this game demands a great deal of optimization and resource management to make it through these challenges. It's as if you were required to play the first 20 turns of Civ or Humankind or Endless Legend, optimizing just those first 20 turns before you start the match all over again on a different map (which lets be honest is how some of those games go). Resources, particular buildings, and Pupils are carried through to the next Halt, enabling large payoffs from good optimization early in a Journey. Personally. I really like this design and I think it's an interesting take on both the rougelite and 4X genre.There are a couple small quality of life changes I'd appreciate, namely in regards to having some sort of shortcut to automatically select the best Pupil for a particular task rather than having to tab through each one to check. Also at least for me, the ASMR whispering voices make me anxious (as does all ASMR in general, so this isn't an issue with the quality of the ASMR in this game). I wish there was an option to disable only those sounds although turning down "Sound Effects" helps. This leaves me feeling that I'm still missing some of the rest of the atmosphere though so I often just suffer through the anxiety.There's often an urge with game journalists and reviewers to call good indie games "indie gems" and I feel as though that term gets used way to often for it to have any meaning. But I'd genuinely consider this game a gem. It's a relatively small game, but leaves me with an incredible impression.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This looks cute. But underneath it is a very frustrating game. I don't recall a game ever making me lose during the damn tutorial simply due to some crappy RNG. Well done.I recommend to avoid this unless suffering due to no reason happens to be your hobby.P.S. If you had long enough patience to hit many bumps on your head and learn, this can bring some satisfaction. If you like a masochistic learning curve, perhaps this is the game for you. All others: stay back.

_childDocuments_.review: To start i have to say if i could give a maybe i wouldve selected that. This game in my opinion has a sharp learning curve and the RNG rolls are stacked against you at pretty much every turn. It is enjoyable (but at times super frustrating) if you like resource management games. I have to say it is pretty hard if you don't play custom games. I will say that it gets a little hard to see whats on the screen as it does get cluttered pretty fast. I have had the game on multiple accounts screw me over at literally the last area/halt where i couldn't do anything at all to fix it within the remaining time. One example is on the last area/halt they had me need 1.2k wood as a requirement to win my run, but didnt give me that amount on the map. Thats fine cause i could use the market, no biggie a little harder but doable by all respects. 20 turns later they throw me a curve ball where lightning strikes random spots on the map, RNGsus did not smile upon me cause of course one of my forests gets burnt to a crisp. Later in the run i get hit with the random event where i now need 600 meat added to my requirements to move to the next area. At this point im thinking i might still be able to win the run but it'll be really close. Finally im starting to build my stores of wood that are needed i get hit with "mice have run through your camp destroying wood leaving little of your camp stores" and my stores of wood drop dramatically. At this point i dont have the needed amount of turns or the resources to build up needed requirements and maintain the cost of my workers.So yeah keep in mind the game will hate you but in my opinion the saving grace is the custom games where you can (in my opinion) at least level the playing field a bit or even stack the odds in your favor.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an odd turn-based strategy game about efficiency. There are a lot of resources to worry about, logistics of moving things around, and random events or prices you need to contend with. I am not a fan, but I also didn't hate this game, it exists in some weird little corner niche of the strategy game genre. In fact, I applaud them for reaching into such a strange place to establish this game. I just wish that the game was actually fun to play.The bright, colorful world, is at first really nice to look at. Especially in the first 2 missions of the tutorial. After that the game sort of turns into a mess of details. Too much of this and that, too much clutter, most things are either shaped similarly or colored similarly. Building are almost impossible to tell apart, resources are often similar in appearance, or worse yet hidden behind or inside of each other. Even the characters, the Pupils, that you need to control are difficult to tell apart or even figure out which hex they are standing on (since they sit on the edge of hexes I was constantly miss-reading their actual locations).The first two missions of the campaign do a good job of teaching some of the basics of controls. I still don't understand the movement system in this game (I swear sometimes the Pupils move through hills and bogs faster than they ought to), but I got most of the basics. After that, oh boy. The other three missions are weird and messy, things aren't really explained to you clearly or at all, and they are long, requiring you to restart them over and over again.The game never really explains the math of the food system which is the most crucial thing that you need to figure out.It's the heart of the game. You need to move Pupils around, gather resources, and travel to the next region. I feel like the game was inspired by the first few turns of a strategy game, where you plan out the whole game and get stuff moving. Since you have to keep moving in this game that's all you do, get started, over and over and over again.Yes the Pupils improve, but mostly in the sense that they can carry +5 of a resources per trip (called cycle), or generate +15 of a secondary Knowledge resource when gathering a specific resource. Mostly you'll just be building things and leaving them behind.Which brings us to the issue of actually moving on and leaving things behind. The game punishes you for harvesting more resources than you need. Leaving stuff behind causes the game to throw more bad events at you. But actually taking stuff is really annoying. When you are prepared to move from one area to another you have a packing minigame, with each 100 of a resource taking a tetris block-like shape that you need to fit on the back of your caravan. While I get the basic idea it's really just annoying to deal with, and the game doesn't give you any warning that you have more stuff than you can carry, this massive, massive problem just gets thrust upon you suddenly with no real good way to handle it.It really is, too. It's absolutely horrible. A single Pupil gathering fruit can barely feed themself plus one more.Pupils eat 6 rations or fruit each turn. It takes between 3 to 4 turns for a Pupil to gather the fruit and return it, carrying 40 per trip. So a net of 22 to 16 fruit per trip (cycle).You aren't really supposed to survive on fruits alone, and you can't while getting other things that you need, so you should be harvesting other things like wheat, spices, fish, or meat and cooking them into rations using wood for fuel. But this doesn't really make it easier, it makes it more complex. The whole game is basically balancing your food industry with other needs. And did I mention the lovely, wonderful, joyous fact that you get to rebuild the whole food industry each level, over and over and over again?! And if you invest in say training a baker and building a portable bakery you may land in a region without wheat. So not only do you need to rebuild your whole food industry in each region you also may find that none of your Pupils have the skills to use the resources in the new region!If you read only one nasty comment about this game then I bet it was this. Randomness is important in games. I actually really like it! I love it! The issue here is that the randomness can swing into completely insane territory. It can require you to have skills that are impossible to get in the current region. Require vast sums of resources that aren't available i the current region. Completely obviate all of your planing and preparation. Random events can strip skills from your Pupils, change or remove resources from the map, destroy buildings. It's just too much.This game isn't horrible. I wanted to like it, I played a bit really trying to find stuff to like or figure out how the pieces fit together. I just don't think that they do. That being said, I bet there are lots of people who like this sort of random onslaught of issues and problems, and trying to fit difficult pieces together to scrape by. I think those people would like this game. Sadly, I'm not among them.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautifully designed game that is surprisingly difficult. You manage a handful of pawns with the goal to help them survive the coming disaster, and as you'd expect survival requires adaptability as well as preparation for the unknown. If you're not into strategy or civilization type resource management games, this one probably isn't for you. There is a lot of random qualities to the game, but once you learn what the random events are you can usually avoid or mitigate most of the negatives of them. That being said, the game is pretty unforgiving if you make a lot of mistakes or don't prepare properly. There is also the occasional nearly impossible scenario, which can be frustrating but I've also learned a lot from those runs. Overall, I love the game. Completing a run successfully is very rewarding, and the game flexes different strategic muscles than I'm used to.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This game actually feels fresh. That's the first thing that came to mind after playing through the tutorial. I am a veteran of countless hours of turn based strategy games, my favorite game series is Civ and everything in this game just came naturally to me - there was no "oh, how does that work?" or "why are they doing it this way now?". It was all intuitive and easy to understand and I felt at home immediately and yet, I was elated. There was so much stuff that I had already seen elsewhere but put together in a shiny new way that just felt right. I think this is the game that Jon Schafer wanted to make when designing "At the Gates", at least that is what I imagined after reading his description.So what does this game right that made me say this? It is a hex grid turned based strategy game with a low number of units that can specialize via a flexible job and experience system but can't be built, minimal but (for a price) mobile bases/districts and various resources that can be combined in production chains... oh and you can explore a fog of war map and some special sites and your enemy is not some other party but time. And in the end, you load what resources and base components you can carry on your animals and take them with you to the next step of your journey.It's awesome so far and I am really looking forward to playing more of it
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played a small amount of this game thus far but I can tell it's going to become a favorite of mine for a long time to come. The art direction is superb: color palettes and balance, animation, character design, environments, etc. Just all to die for. And, along with that, the sound design and music is also top notch. It's a pleasure to experience. Also, the lore of the world is so, hmn, gentle? Not sure how else to describe it. Like, the danger the Pupils face is imminent and defeats can and do happen when the water reaches the caravan or starvation comes upon them or any number of other things. But the heart of their history, their culture, and the way they view and interact with the world has a softness to it that's so calm and pleasant. I only have a few complaints so far. Namely, in the Campaign stages, around and after the stage where farming is introduced, I feel like there needs to be some tweaks made to make it smoother (especially for those playing that are newer to the genre). There's a tightness to the timing that can be off-putting. There's an efficient order of operations that needs to happen, to optimize the potential outcomes and, to a veteran of the genre, it's clear what needs to happen, in what order, to best avoid stagnation that can lead to starvation or other failures. But I don't think that that efficiency will be as obvious as it needs to be, for people coming to the game as people newer to the genre. Like, the Campaign is the tutorial with story laid down over it. It's a beefier tutorial than you might expect for something not titled explicitly as "tutorial". And that hybridization of story mode and tutorial may be muddying things a bit. If it's meant to be a story-driven tutorial, then it definitely needs tweaks to make it gentler for people learning the game. If it's meant to be a Campaign with story, but beyond tutorial, then that steeper jump in difficulty/management makes more sense. But it seems to be aiming to be the former more than the latter, what with how actions are halted with tooltips and the like that walk you through how the game is played. So there's a bit of jank there that probably needs to be addressed a bit better.Anyway. That's really my only complaint with the game thus far. Everything else has been a great experience and I'm very glad I stumbled upon this when looking for games similar to others I have but wasn't in the mood to play. And even with the issue I feel are present in the Campaign mode currently, I definitely recommend picking this title up. It's truly great.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I received a key for this game as I was looking for a slow-burn builder. I fell inlove with the graphics (especially the pupils!) and the entire sound design. Highly recommend if you enjoy games like Civ, Sim City... The randomness of some of the numbers can feel frustrating, but I find myself improving on resource management each go around! The latest patch seems to be more forgiving than first go, so I believe the team is listening to player comments on improving~
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: While I am just getting into this game, I can see what it really can be: a roguelike that will grab your attention, run after run. Like all good rogue-like games, As Far as the Eye is all about making the best out of your situation. Each run presents new challenges and opportunities, and forces the player to adjust. You might spawn with a tribe that is great at gathering, but is weak with medicine or has trouble with Auras. The great part about this game is that it is punishing and fair.Yes, there are random events that can really mess you up, but once again, the game is all about making you adjust and overcome adversity, and it never lets you get too comfortable with your run. There are a variety of unlockable tribes you can acquire by winning runs, so there are hundreds of runs in this game before you can get truly bored.I would highly recommend looking into this game on Twitch or YouTube before purchasing, as the tutorial takes around 2 hours and that will lock you out of a refund, but at $20, you can't really go wrong.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: The game is something new and fresh in the survival-builder genre. You are playing as a small tribe of individuals and gather ressources on a map until you have enough to get to the next map (think: Sectors like in Faster Than Light). Each individual gathers experience points and can specialize, so you will have your Stone cutter, your druid, your gatherer who is also a cook etc.The game is turn based, a map has about 50 - 200 turns. Since you don't have forever on the map, you really have to optimize what your individuals do, where you put your buildings etc.The artstyle, writing and presentation is wonderful. Very cute, with just the right amount of mystical-fantasy stuff that is neither cliché nor "too out there".If you are like me frustrated by the small amount of good survival builder games, I recommend to try this one, since it really goes a different route.On the negative side, the UI could be clearer at some points and I miss some Quality of Life stuff (like keyboard shortcuts), but it doesn't hamper the fun.At first I gave a negative review due to unfair RNG, but the developer reacted immediatly to the criticism and I would expect some more finetuning there, so no worries about that,All in all, a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is very pretty, the gameplay is quite choppy and the UI is very cumbersome.I bought and refunded this game due to how annoying it became to manage things with the current UI.Some examples:- It's difficult to select workers to make them do something.- Major mechanics like building or settings jobs takes a lot of clicks constantly.The tutorial doesn't really explain the game well either.I love many of the genres this game falls into, but the game look and feel is too busy for me to enjoy it.

Feels very cozy.The difficulty is high and is full of unpredictable events, so it's not apt for casual gamers. _childDocuments_.review: It's a short-term city-based hex game that functions in several acts, so you're never one "city" for long.  Combined some of the Civ 5 hex-strategy with a randomness of Slay the Spire, with a Tetris "fill in the boxes using random shapes and sizes" type minigame.  The game does a lot of these things to keep your interest, difficulty curve is very hard, due to randomness, though bugs and issues can catch and blindside you.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very addictive and entertaining rogue-like resource management strategy. It certainly is NOT overwhelmingly difficult like many reviews claim, no more than most other rogue-like games.You play as a group of cute shape-shifting "pupils" who are travelling towards "the Eye" to escape the seasonal flooding of their world. The branching path takes several stopovers and at each stop you get a small map to explore and exploit, where you are required to gather a certain amount of specific resources required to move on to the next stopover. The problem is, at each stop you only get a finite number of turns before the area floods.A major challenge is providing sufficient food for your pupils during the stopover, while also being able to gather other resources. There are several sources of food, including hunting, gathering, fishing and farming, but all of them except gathering require a special building, and all food except gathered fruit called "pepkins" require preparation in one of the two production buildings. Random complications called "vagaries" occur periodically and their impact can be anywhere from completely trivial to utterly devastating, depending on your level of prep. A special building can be built in the game to help you predict vagaries long before they occur, as well as cancel them completely limited number of times.After you have collected and paid the necessary resources to move on, you have to decide what to take with you, because the space on your caravan is limited. You can take some portable buildings as well as resources, and you have to make sure you carry enough food and basic building materials to be able to comfortably set up in the next stopover.The game is clever, but unfortunately the limited tutorial "campaign" doesn't teach you all mechanics, or provides confusing information. For example, the tutorial provides you a trained druid and explains how to soothe auras and create potions, but it doesn't explain how to actually train a druid on your own. It also makes it sound like only druids can soothe auras, while in fact any worker can do it. Tutorial also implies that vagaries are somehow related to your workers exhausting resource hexes, and that you get punished for exhausting. I've seen a few people comment on how frustrating it is to manually try to prevent pupils from exhausting resources (workers pick which hex to harvest automatically based on the closest available), but as far as I can tell from my own game, it is unnecessary because vagaries are completely random and the frequency depends simply on how far into the path you are.Overall, I'm definitely enjoying the hell out of this game. I've finished West and South tribes on short path so far, moving on to East. If you think a rogue-like game based on resources rather than combat is your cup of tea, I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I am very glad I picked this up. It's unlike anything else I've ever played before, drawing elements from a variety of genres with resource-gathering and city-building components without being especially beholden to them. But I think it is a game that really requires you to be in the right mindset to play it, or to have somebody keeping you company while you play, if only because answering their questions will help you more fully process what you're doing.Above all else, As Far As The Eye emphasizes flexibility. You have limited numbers of workers, so even if some of them are specialized, you'll often have to switch their roles. You can place a fixed structure, but invest some extra resources and you'll have one you can reposition when the nearby tiles dry up. Stockpiling certain resources can be wise, but often it's best to grab what you need when you need it, and use what you have as soon as you have it. I like these aspects of the game a lot! It's easy to have the sunk cost fallacy hit hard in city-building games; A FATE seems specifically designed to counter that.There are also decidedly unforgiving aspects to the game. Having to avoid interrupting workers lest you make them drop (and thereby destroy) their resources is just rough. The UI doesn't do a great job communicating... well, most things, to be honest (it's unpolished and a little overwhelming to look at, with lots of tiny tiny type). And it's especially easy to miss when second-tier workers, waiting for materials to process into goods, are standing around doing nothing, because there's no good visual cue for this.And yet, when I reeeeeally slowed down, carefully studied the map and my workers, and played the game in good company, it really started to sing. This is a game that's putting serious thought into how its mechanics ask you to relate to the game world, and if you pick up its train of thought, it really is something special. I just wish it did a better job inviting you aboard.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous game, love the color scheme and the design. It is really unforgiving as others have said but it is also very satisfying when you make it through to the end. There is also luck involved as you never know what type of pupils you get or what natural disasters are coming to get you. The only complain I have is the tutorial is already difficult so it is possible to fail it and have to go through all the dialogues all over again (pretty annoying tbh). I just skipped some of them and went to the campaign to learn through playing instead. If you are the type of person who doesn't mind trial and error then this is a game to pick up. Definitely would recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game so much. The art style is great, the animals are cute, and the use of color is really fun. I mean, look at that skill wheel for abilities, it's great.The game trips over itself with the UI. There's a lot that's left unexplained, I was frequently mousing over things expecting some sort pop-up to expand on the details because I didn't have nearly enough information to make informed decisions. And if you make uninformed decisions your adorable little critters will starve to death over several agonizing turns where there's little you can do.Starvation got me in both games I played. The game tells you how much food each worker consumes as a base, but each one can have individual modifiers, and if there's a way to tell what your overall food consumption per turn without manually calculating it or watching the change between turns (and *then* manually calculating it) then I never found out how, and while a low food warning exists, by the time it pops up it's likely too late.There are technologies that look like they do one thing when you mouse over them (increase volumes per stack or reduce stack sizes in your storage), but only when you click on them do you realize that you must then specify what type of item you want to apply them to. Which is fine, but simply revising the tooltip to "Increases the volume per stack *of a resource of your choosing*" would make it way more transparent.There's a lot of potential here, but if the game is gonna brutalize me with starvation that's inevitable enough that I can't change it but slow enough that I have to click through several turns to actually die then I expect to meet me halfway and not make me run manual calculations and do google searches to understand what's going on.I sincerely hope the devs will make a pass through and just flesh out the UI a bit, because I really do believe there's something good trapped behind it.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Its very cliche for a review to start but I dont understand all the negativity for this game. Its a cute little board game with an interesting alternative to the very Euro-centric heavy genre. Its never gonna compete with CIV with it being a small studio and the price point reflects that. Ive spent a long time playing, usually in small run attempts. You will loose more then you win but thats sort of expected. It also wants you to be planning more of your journey in advance. There is always ways to get some resources even if there isnt the resource on the map point, but you are told to think of the next paths before then.I havent encountered any bugs right now, usually you just dont see an interaction when something goes wrong such as a student skill or aura. So if your looking for an intensive long form game that you will always know how to win,  this isnt for you. If its a simple cute board game like sim that you can dip in and out of without much issue, this is your game.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR is this game should be really fun to play, but a lack of clear information given to the player really hurts its presentation. After an hour with this game I can say I don't really like it and I'm sad to say that. It's FTL meets Civ. However, both of the former games do a much better job respectively. It's difficult to tell where to build in the beginning. There's no notification when a resource runs out. It's hard to tell where your minions are standing. It's unexplained where you can and can't build extra camps. Building zones aren't highlighted in a way that you can understand (it's white bars around a white barred hex map). The terrain looks too samey and it's hard to tell what resources are available where in some instances. Selecting minions is difficult and the game deselects them if you hit the wrong thing. If you have a minion who you've been interacting with, but another minion finishes a task, you'll have that minion selected on the next turn with very little indication as to which minion you're actually interacting with. Minion trait icon are very difficult to understand what information they are relaying. I had to basically always highlight every icon to figure out which minion was best at what job. If they took a little longer to design a clearer to understand game vs a pretty to look at one I think we'd have had some real gold here. As it stands, if you're looking at this and thinking it's your next casual Civ game... I'd say pass on it. Just replay an older Civ. If you're just looking for something new and interesting, this might not be a bad buy. The concepts here are new and the idea and gameplay are certainly something to take note of. However, as an enjoyment aspect, I don't feel like I really got what I wanted.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: This is reviewed after the 1.0.2 balance patch.A resource management game where there are two things ticking down to you doom, the incoming flood, and your dwindling food supply. As a player that tries as much as possible not to be wasteful, I found the RNG events to not be very punishing. Most of the time I simply lost because I didn't keep an eye on my food and everyone just starved.High-tech buildings are nice to have, but feel more like a "win-more" option than a necessity (except in extreme cases). As long as you plan your route and have necessary resources on hand, games won't be lost. Even when I did lose, I did not feel like it was the game's problem, but rather my own carelessness or greediness.The game is easy to grasp at the start, and one can win without heavy optimization. Later levels will need you to optimize to achieve the heavy resource demands (both for the journey and for your large crew).The game provides a good balance of challenge and simplicity. Its great to pick up for veterans and newcomers of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see this having a ton of staying power for the right audience.  By not getting through the "campaign" (Also See: Tutorial) I have proven I am NOT this audience.  Beautiful art design, pleasant tunes, and with overall cool twist to strategy roguelikes, I most certainly can see folks falling in love here.  Not me, sadly....not me.  The learning curve felt overwhelming, as you get fed a ton of gameplay mechanics early on.  Couple that with resource and character management alongside a ticking movement clock where a flood chases you down, and I was hit with more frustration then fun.  Seriously still, those with a slight interest in this genre should have no problem giving it a go.  I'm sure it'll scratch that strategy itch.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: A very tough resource-management rogue-like, which does not correlate with the cutesy visuals and zen lore. I concur with others that it's FTL meets Civ, but doesn't quite hit the mark.I love the idea of a civilization game where your "city" must keep moving, gathering the resources as it goes, else be sweeped up in a tsunami. There are a plethora of resources (pepkins, wood, stone, ore, wool, fish, fine fish, spices), and each worker gains experience in one of the 19 professions depending on what they're collecting or doing. So you're urged to specialise your workers to maximise their resource collection. However, starting with only 3 workers, you frequently need to get your workers to specialise in 2 or 3 professions. And the only way to get more workers is to find them in random events.So the key gameplay is prioritising the resources you NEED. But beware, if you take too much resources (empty a tile, or leave some at a previous node), you anger mother nature, who will cause catastrophic events to occur more frequently.The game could have done with more polish, such as making more defined graphics to more easily see tiles, clarifying a lot of the hover-information, and making a clearer turn synopsis text box.In a "games are art" way, this game can be construed as a commentary on climate change, where it shows just how hard we would have to work to be "one with nature" to reduce carbon emissions.This game did not provide the "just one more turn" kind of gameplay I was after. I guess I'll keep an eye out for a Mortal Engines mod for Civ 6.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Deciding whether or not to recommend this game was very difficult. While the game has many positive qualities and I really appreciate what it is doing, it is also significantly flawed. I would like to imagine that since this game is fairly new, it might be improved down the road since it shows so much promise. So here's how I'd break it down:Pros: Interesting concept, great strategy elements, cute characters, great skill progression systemCons: Random disasters are excessively punishing to the point where I have yet to make it to the eye ONCE after playing for 20 or so hours. You can plan and strategize all you want but you'll get nailed by disasters you could never predict and it feels like the game is largely luck-based. I spent hours thinking that I was missing some major aspect of the game and just wasn't understanding how to play, but it's as simple as it seems, it's just excessively difficult in the wrong ways. It's discouraging to make it all the way to the last stop only to realize that the resource I need to get there isn't even available AT ALL and trading is so uneven, there is absolutely NO way to acquire the needed resource in time. All of my problems with this game are fixable, so I really hope the developers actually listen to some feedback so this game can live up to it's vast potential.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to reluctantly give this game a negative review. It has a lot of charm and potential but ultimately flounders by being rigid and confusing. I think reducing the number of food sources and resources would help immensely to streamline the game. It is a cute little roguelike strategy game but still needs a lot of work and suffers from having way more rules than is fun. Sadly you cannot simply remove the extra rules and resources like you can in Don't Starve or Rimworld

_childDocuments_.review: As Far As The Eye is like a 4x strategy roguelike that is one of the most innovative and fresh ideas for a roguelike I have seen in a long time.One of my favorite things ever is when a game takes a pre-existing genre and then turns it into a roguelike. So Slay the Spire did that for deckbuilders, Spelunky did that for platformers, and now As Far As The Eye is doing that for 4x like turn based resource management games like Civilization. So it is kind of like a roguelike version of Civilization.So in As Far As The Eye, apparently every like hundred years or so the entire earth floods and kind of resets the land and so it's a tradition for all the creatures of the world to migrate to this specific place in the center of the world that is protected from the floods. To do that though you will need resources to make your journey. So you can look at this branching path map similar to the map in Slay the Spire and see where you want to go. Each new area you goes requires a certain amount of resources to get there. So one path might be blocked until you get 200 wood and 100 stone in order to repair a bridge. Or another path might be super cold so you might need like 250 wool and 100 of the default food in order to make it across. So after you settle your caravan you get a couple of pupils that you can tell to do different tasks. You can have them start gathering basic things wood, or basic food like pumpkins and they will continuously gather it and bring it back to the caravan over and over and then you can build more complicated buildings that allow you to do more complicated things.Each of your pupils have a massive skill tree as well that allows them to get new abilities and perks depending on what type of work they are focusing on which is really cool.I absolutely love the concept, the artstyle, and the execution of As Far As The Eye.So if you are a fan of 4x games like CIV and you are a fan of roguelikes this is 100% up your alley and I would recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: A good roguelike with civilization-like management. So far, I found the game to be very engaging, the good UI and charming aesthetic playing a crucial part in that. Still, I can say that I've had runs that felt impossible to win and some that felt way too easy, although both were enjoyable overall because they had little challenges in them that were rewarding to beat.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, the art style is beautiful and I like the zen-ness of it, but the unwinnable scenarios are pretty frustrating. I am really good at these kinds of games too. I played through the tutorials, easy enough. I read a bunch of stuff about people saying how you just need to prepare properly and what not, and that's fine, so I did. I got through all the Vargies that lowered how many turns I had and wrecked all my buildings. Felt pretty confident. My final Halt (The areas you stop and play in) had 10, freaking, 10 Aura's on it. Most of them interlinked with one another. For those of you who don't know an Aura is something you have to send a Druid to calm down so that your other Pupils can harvest resources in that area. The only issue is I have one druid, and by the time I calmed down two Auras in an area and started working on a third aura in the area, the first would kick back up and prevent anything from being harvested. That was just for one small spot of the map, not even mentioning the other seven. There was literally nothing I could do. No amount of preparation of resources could get through this wall. You would need several druids to clear the map, and the game only allows you 3 pupils at start, and two that you can get through other caravans. Even if I had all five pupils from that scenario, I would have had to have them all constantly calming the aura's while having one harvest food, simply so we didn't starve, let alone gather the resources to move on from the flood.Just sort of bad RNG. I feel like if the game had like, a limit to how many auras can spawn on a map or something, and how close to one another, this unbeatable wall would have been unavoidable.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another what in the world is, yet another indie game that was provided by the publishers, and for that I want to thank them. As always, this will not be affecting my opinion on my critique.+Pleasant presentation+Joyful audio design+Unique gameplay+Challenging (Arbitrary)+Custom difficulty mode for casual gameplay-Unexpectedly difficult-Can get repetitiveAs far as the eye is the next game to come from developer Unexpected and published by Goblinz Studio as well as Maple Whispering LTD. You assume responsibility of your pupils, and you are tasked with leading them to safety. Your goal is to reach "The Eye", as far as that might be (get it?) while trying to avoid the big wave consuming everything in its path. Starting off with the gameplay mechanics. Each Pupil (Character) has a set amount of MP. Each MP is consumed to traverse between each hexagon tile. When there are obstacles such as hills, 2 MP is consumed. You must find the perfect balance between gathering resources used to feed your pupils, and gathering resources to build buildings necessary to further progress your story. For example, you need to harvest wood (no building required) to build a mine. Other resources include mineral, wool, flakes, rations, game and so forth. If your pupils run out of food, they will lose 10HP per turn until their ultimate demise.There is a nicely implemented skill tree in the game for each of your pupils. The more they perform each action, the more they gain experience in that skill, making them more efficient. You want to focus on giving your pupils a couple of skills that are unique to those pupils in order to cover most of the skill tree. Eventually the pupils will stop earning XP. When they reach that point they need to perform their actions in accordance to a specific building that will further progress their skills. That is also the point in which you must choose what specialisation your pupil is going to have.Each pupil starts off with up to 6 traits, negative or positive. In the custom game mode you have control of how many traits a pupil will have, and whether or not they are negative or positive.The objective of the game is to collect enough resources in order to keep advancing to the next step. The ultimate step is to reach The Eye, the safe haven that will save your pupils. You start off with a set amount of turns. Each turn is completed when all of your pupils expend all of their MP, or they do not have a task and are sitting idle.One hidden element that the game never quite reveals to you straight forward is the karma. Karma needs to be in your favour in order to avoid catastrophes happening. The more you defile the land by depleting each tile of its resources, the more negative karma you accumulate. Throughout each step, you will find a handful of ancient temples that you need to visit. There you can choose to pray, defile, or give an offering. Each action will affect the balance of karma. Making sure that you keep nature and its temper calm will help keep obstacles away that would otherwise halt or hinder your progress.The campaign does an excellent job of describing the setting of the game, as well as help you understand how to play the game. Be prepared to play the campaign through a number of times. It serves as the tutorial but also as a considerable challenge. Everything besides the campaign is procedurally generated, so your experience will always be unique.One of the things that I would like, that is presently not implemented in the game, is the ability to choose the difficulty of the game in all game modes, not just the custom game mode. Thankfully the developer has implemented that mode for those of us who are not very smart in planning out a strategy good enough to beat the campaign without having to try it over a dozen times. there are 4 different tribes that you can unlock so far. Each tribe will be unlocked once the prior tribe is lead to The Eye safely. This is quite a unique game admittedly. It has a similar idea as FTL. In both games you have an unstoppable force chasing after you. The only way to escape is to keep going forward. The more you advance, the more difficult the game will get. Without a checkpoint system however, each move, each turn, each decision, will potentially play a very important role on whether or not your pupils meet their demise, or they make it out alive!#AsFarAsTheEye#Impressions#Gameplay

_childDocuments_.review: I must say this game does has many interesting concept. It is fun at the start but ruined by too many RNG at the last part. You get to mix and match your "pupils" with different trades where you can plan which of them gather the specific resources better(point for this) but the RNG on the type of hexagonal locations (which indicates the type of resources gathered) is quite messy, sure that makes you have to think hard and make wise decisions on where to settle, until you get tired of thinking, you just park it near the basics resources (that helps you survive mostly) which are all over the freaking place. Other resources are just only for the upgrades(temporary) or for the lulz of completing a stage with different requirements.The gameplay starts easy with requirements, at the mid point, things get challenging and this is where you get the fun out of it. At the near end, all the random disasters become annoying and probably turns the winning condition impossible to win. And it feels more of a chore than fun as it goes on.Once you completed the game, the unlocks are of more disadvantages than advantages, which is ok to give the rogue-like feel. But how are you going to get creative in winning the game when you are struggling only to survive until the end game? This is where the fun part dies off. Well the only way to play that is custom game but you probably lost motivation after doing 1 or 2 runs which is already very long since the gathering of resources already feels too grindy.To be fair, the dev did a good job on this game. Love the artwork and sound effects and concepts, but the core of game was not well done. The game has a lot, and I mean A LOT of potential but some on it are wasted. You know it is there but you cannot see it. I am afraid to say I cannot recommend this game, because what hits me bad is that I don't feel the worth of replayability in this game. Don't buy this game at full price, but maybe at discount price.The dev can do better. At least I bought this game to support them a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: I wholeheartedly recommend this - not just for the game itself, but also for the ideas behind it.At first glance, dealing with random* traits,environments and events might make the game difficulty feel anywhere from very easy to impossible. Know that the devil is in the details - especially when you have a rough time.Don't listen to the haters - in any game where there are casual players that barely beat the tutorial, there's gonna be crybabies.The way you interact with the environment has consequences(which may influence your 'luck'), and yes, sometimes bad things you are unprepared for do happen. You have to lose multiple times in different ways if you want to know what can kill you and when(before it does, that is).The game is far more complex than it seems, especially when you have to min-max everything on a bad start roll just to increase your long winter win streak. Also, the 'meta' is different for each type of tribe - and it really isn't about what to do if things go well, but about how to make use of the unlimited time to make them go well in dire situations.If you are bored of getting good rolls and lucky events by restarting on bad draw, try playing the bad draws the same way one plays chess - as in,take you time, have patience, and try to see as many moves ahead as possible in order to outsmart your 'luck'. Yeah, some balancing might be needed, some bugs need to be fixed.  There is lots of potential in this though.For developers:  I bought your other recent game because I wanted to support the makers of this game. Maybe you don't give up on it? - even Among Us was for years less popular than AFATE is now before it got to shine :)
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

Except to die multiple  the tutorial. Lovely art and soundtrack though! Very calming and relaxing while it gives you lots of time to ponder your mistakes. Decisions you make definitely feel impactful, but connecting the dots can sometimes be a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful graphics, nice and relaxing soundtrack and somewhat of an interesting game play loop. Sadly it just isn't that fun. The entire game revolves around RNG, and even the best thought out approaches will lead to your failure.This definitely is not one of the "relax and chill" city/colony builders that you could find on Steam. If you are looking for that, steer clear of this. If you are looking for a game where you mess up 1 turn and then lose, this is the game for you.The campaign was enjoyable for the most part, sometimes you mess up a few turns and lose the entire level and have to redo it but I guess that is what they were going for. Also, there are no save slots/save games. If you lose in the campaign, you start from the beginning of the chapter.The character progression is interesting, the more your Pupil does in a certain skill the better they become. As they become better, unlock perks and become even better - rinse and repeat.But there really isn't too much depth to the game. Build a base, survive the RNG then pack up and leave. Then do it all again at a new level with new RNG. Your pupils eat a crazy amount of food, and you will run out very quickly unless you always have a dedicated food harvester/baker/etc.So that leaves you with an average 2 more pupils to do everything else, except you're gonna need a builder to build everything... then a miner to mine and so forth. 90% of the game is just feeling as if you don't have enough pupils to do what you really need to.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like early access to me. The game feels like the devs played it for a couiple of hundred hours and forgot to add a good tutorial for the rest of us. Tutorial 2 soft locked twice on me and tutorial three asks me to do stuff that's not even explained. Probably some really good game in there, but if that's the first impression they're willing to leave and give the player that much unnecessary frustration, I'm not gonna recommend it. Multiple restarts in a railway tutorial is just terrible and insults the player's timeEdit: Wow, gets even worse in the third tutorial. Doesn't explain how to level the one guy you need to level to beat the level while simultaniously restricting options for everyone else to make it more difficutl and confusing. What an insulting waste of time. I just spent an hour playing a tutorial and have to restart now. Incompetence in game development on a whole new level I guessEdit2: Having played regular play a bit after; there's also bugs and missing (or incomplete) tooltips. Stuff doesn't work sometimes and the game gives you either no or a completely wrong indication why (like wanting to harvest a field next to the hut that is specifically made for harvesting that field won't work, the game gives a tooltip on the hut telling you there's no field withing range, even though the field is literally adjacent).All in all at the moment the game is very frustrating and a waste of time. It feels more like beta testing or early access than full release. I hope they fix all that stuff in the next couple of months, since the basic gameplay loop looks interesting, but at the moment actually playing it sucks the fun out the possible enjoyment quite badly unfortunately

_childDocuments_.review: I think this takes the idea of "Singleplayer Civilization" to its best extreme. The resource management, balancing whether to spend a few more turns gathering while risking running into disasters or our of food, to build the station you need now or spare just a few more turns to get a mobile version, it's full of difficult choices that I am a massive fan of. Much smaller in map size and building/unit count than most of its contemporaries, but requires WAY more attention to detail. It's everything I never knew I wanted and I thoroughly have enjoyed it - only wish there were more modes, like perhaps an endless mode.
_childDocuments_.name: As Far As The Eye

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to get this game based on other user reviews that the game was 'unfair' and generated impossible scenarios.... I am here to tell you to ignore them! The difficulty of the game seems very well balanced. If, like me, you love little turn based strategy games then this is a must pick. I fully believe that all runs are possible so long as you do a bit of forward planning. Look at the biomes ahead and the resource requirements of each path, then plan accordingly what resources you might need to take into the next halt.You will not find it nearly as challenging as a lot of the negative comments will make you believe. If you are competent at strategy games then you will love As Far As The Eye.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as the Eye is a very unique game. It offers game mechanics from the build-up genre but combines them with many original ideas. The visual design, the little stories, the whole flow of the game offers a lot of creativity, and that makes the game a unique experience.With the professions system, the eternally scarce resources, and a penalty system for overexploitation of nature, the strategy in this game is really demanding and challenging. And it does this without trying to throw the player off track with too mean random events.Technically AFATE works well, the scope of the campaign is a bit tight, I would have wished for more here. But the very well done sandbox mode makes for very high replay value. And maybe the developers will deliver a little more campaign, I have high hopes for that.AFATE offers only a small campaign, but extensive sandbox colony building fun. It has cuddly characters, a lot of original ideas, and offers a lot of strategic depth with scarce resources and an extensive profession system.I would like to assign 85% as a base score here. But for the very short campaign, I would like to deduct 5 % again. I wish that the developers would add a little more here, then they could recapture these percentages. But until then I give a final score of 80 % for this very innovative nomadic-building game.EN DE

_childDocuments_.review: Since the game did interest me enough to go for all the achievements for full completion, I should probably help doing it a little justice by leaving a review.Reading the other reviews, many seems to think that this is a casual & chill game, perhaps due to the cutesy artstyle and the overall theme and design, but was shoved off by the gameplay difficulty. IMO this game have turns limit and it is tough, BUT that so-called difficulty only lasted till you learn and understand those game mechanics presented (and you definitely would not learn it all in mere 2-3 short runs), after that, it is mostly a breeze (except maybe the North Tribe long journey, which probably require some re-roll to get pupils with actual useful traits to counter the pre-fix negative one). As long as you know what you are doing and *IMPORTANT* you do spend time to think and plan your actions ahead, you will make it to the eye for sure and find the gameplay experience rewarding.I would also note that although it is also true that RNG could be harsh at times, but many times too a seemingly hard run could also be "saved" by good RNG (i.e always meet the other tribe passing by to get assistance etc...), so it seems fairly balanced and well-designed to me. All in all my point is this game might seems to have a decently tough learning curve, and that is only due to the lack of hand-holding plus nothing would "warn" you against your mistakes (One mis-click could potentially screw a manageable run really), but it is definitely not too unfair and nowhere near unbeatable.My only serious gripe is the game bugs, sometime a pupil's action does not play out / get cancelled without any reason at all, but other than that it works fine. +1 for recommended!
