_childDocuments_.review: The Xbox underrated classic is back and ready for PC, if you never played Kingdom Under Fire then you are missing out on some of the most fun you will have in a RTS game.  Think Total War gameplay but you get to play your commander within the battle, giving out orders and getting messy with the enemy troops.  There is also RPG elements since there is leveling and equipment with different properties on them.  Now the game's structure is more like a linear campaign with missions that provide you with tasks to complete, from sneaking behind enemy lines to straight up battling it out in a massive battle.  You do get to select what troops you want in a good chuck of the missions but sometimes you are limited to what the game gives you.Now besides the game's campaign being linear, it still provides you a great story and tons of fun encounters to test your mantle.  However I will advise that there are 4 campaigns, ranging from easy to hard (with 2 of them being hard), the easy one is mostly a tutorial and isn't difficult at all.  While it isn't bad that its easy, you don't get to control massive armies until the very end (mostly only one or two troops) and it just there to get you into the game.  Some may find it boring and the pace of it is slow (it still provides a good story tho with it).If you feel like starting from the medium campaign instead, go ahead as it still gives you a quick sum up of the game's controls and what units can do.   You will miss out on some story beats but your get to control your own armies and get into the main core gameplay faster.  Additionally it will give you access to the hard campaigns, which is where most of the biggest battles and tough decision making is at.This is one of my favourite series with how unique the gameplay and how good the story is, personally I do prefer the sequel/prequel that came out a year later.  Kingdom Under Fire Heroes, which provides way more content and unique characters to play as.  Hopefully it will come out soon in a few months as well.

The blend of soft rock/metal and medieval fantasy battle inspires the imagination to conjure up feelings of grit and badassery. If you're anything like me and sucked at this game as a kid, it's particularly satisfying to learn the game and understand it's mechanics and then apply those mechanics successfully.Decent story, solid gameplay, good price for value, 8/10 - hoping for a mod someday that'll extend the render distance.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely unique RTS / RPG. Perfectly melding Hack'n'Slash with tactical army management. It kind of plays like a simplified Total War game where you control the commander in battle yourself. I'm glad I stumbled upon this one.There is very limited 'grand strategy'. You are usually just picking which battlefield to go to next in a fairly linear fashion.A large part of the fun is allocating experience points to units and choosing their skills and jobs. The choices you make will largely effect your ability to progress in the game but there are also many different compositions and play styles you can choose to succeed.The story is engaging, a little dated and in some cases hilariously translated or voice acted. It could be better but it works.The art style and character designs are fantastic.My only frustration with this game, is that for some reason, in the PC port, the word Patriarch or any variation like Patriarchal has been cut from the audio, and it comes up a lot. This can sometimes make following the dialog a bit confusing because it doesn't just blank the word, it's cut and the word is instantly skipped. Also I have no idea why such a word would be cut. _childDocuments_.review: Jumping back into Kingdom Under Fire: The Crusaders on Steam feels like rekindling an old friendship. Originally an OG Xbox classic, this game has made the transition to PC with nearly flawless execution. It's a unique mix of RTS, hack 'n' slash, and RPG elements—a combination that feels rare, even today, two decades later.The story, while limited by the era it was created in, still packs a punch, and the characters are unforgettable. Whether it's the nostalgia or the depth of each protagonist, I found myself genuinely invested in their journeys. With four campaigns spanning about 20 hours, you’ll experience an escalating challenge that really keeps you on your toes. The level progression and ability to power up through items make the grind worthwhile, and it’s super rewarding to feel your units get stronger with each mission.Though the graphics show their age, the gameplay and story still feel relevant—almost timeless. If you’re into RTS and RPGs, Kingdom Under Fire: The Crusaders is a must-play. Its unique blend of genres and immersive campaigns will pull you in and keep you hooked. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: This originally released in 2004 and was ported to the PC with some enhancements. Is this game worth playing, is it worth buying? Okay so, I have not played any of the other games in this franchise, so I’m going into this review unbiased and keeping in mind that this is an older title that was ported to PC. With that being said, what did they do to the port to make this enhanced? Well, They added full controller support, it didn’t work with my PS4 controller but it detected my Xbox controller fine. Though there is a Keyboard and Mouse option they recommend using a gamepad, probably because it was originally released on a console with that control scheme in mind and they’ve updated the resolution to widescreen HD. Right off the bat, I have to say that with my time I spent streaming it, I surprisingly had some fun. There are multiple campaigns to go through with varying difficulties controller different main protagonists. The majority of the gameplay is split into two sections, preparing your units and controlling your armies on the battlefield. Let me explain further, during each campaign you’ll choose stages on a map according to the story, some stages will be replayable for experience and money grinding. On this world screen you’ll have a chance to alter your units in many different ways. First of all you have your hero units and officers. You can upgrade skills such as melee efficiency, learning magic attacks, and special battlefield skills with experience. With money you can purchase new equipment like weapons for increase in damage or elemental effects and armors to increase resistances to arrows and curses. Besides your hero units you can upgrade and change jobs of your infantry that follow you around during battle. Depending on the hero’s skills, they can essentially evolve jobs down different class trees. You can make soldiers into paladins later on, and archers into heavy bowgunners. Same with the hero, you can buy equipment to upgrade their stats. As you obtain more units you’ll have to micromanage which armies are worth upgrading and which jobs to work towards to fit your battle preference. The other part of gameplay is controlling your units on the battleground. Depending on the mission you have have more units to control or more limited units to bring with you. You everything is completely doable using the gamepad. You can move one unit across or control all at the same time, the overhead camera can sometimes be extremely trouble to be precise with movements but you can always bring up the mini map to designate movement. Melee units can change formation to fit the situation, more expanded has less defense but can travel quicker, while more tight knit formations move slower but can defend better against ranged attacks. Archers and other long ranged units can control the spread of location damage to strategize against different groups of enemies. There is an ongoing rock paper scissors struggle between cavalry, pikemen, magic users and so on. Besides the overall strategy of field control and unit type advantages, you can use special skills and control your hero directly in action segments. When your hero army gets in contact with other enemy units it shifts seamlessly into a dynasty warrior esque battle system. You attack using light and heavy strikes, charge attacks, defending/countering, and as you do all of this you gain SP, which can be used to do a huge variety of things. In hero battles you can call support strikes and use hero specific special attacks. You keep SP during the whole mission and can share the use with non hero units to activate field skills such as casting spells like cure. The game surprised me with the depth of customization you can have with your armies and upgrades with money. The combat at first is a bit bland but as you gain stronger characters with more offensive and defensive options it balances out. Other than that this is a solid port, no graphics bugs or fps drops. It’s very smooth and satisfying to play on PC with a gamepad.Check out my full gameplay review video for Kingdom Under Fire: The Crusaders. I go into great depth about the Story, Graphics, Audio, Gameplay, and other noteworthy things I feel needs to be mentioned:  Disclaimer: I received this game for free. I was not paid to promote or write a review. All thoughts are solely my own. Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: An old classic that was amazing on the Xbox and is still amazing on the PC. The game allows you to command up to 6 units max (4 direct combat, 2 support) each with their own level and skills (unit type). You control a hero that can be leveled up in a single skill, but equipment can be bought to upgrade your hero and army for the most part and each of the officer skills can be leveled up with a pool of XP. Gameplay is smooth and simple, I have encountered little to complain about beyond Unit variety and most combat is satisfying with each attack having some form of weight. _childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Under Fire: The Crusaders is the critically acclaimed cult classic sequel to the original Korean RTS Kingdom Under Fire: A War of Heroes by Phantagram and its finally on PC!!! Taking place 50 years since the 2nd War of Heroes, the Ancient Heart a powerful but vile relic that caused the great conflicts in the first place has long since been lost and has brought a time of relative peace with even efforts to keep the thought of the Ancient Heart under wraps from all sides but peace can only last so long as a border town beside the Sacred Lands is destroyed making the Hironeiden Kingdom declare war against Vellond to invade Hexter lands with the assistance of the Ecclesians to protect the Holy Grounds. Here you will see from the perspectives of Gerald of Hironeiden on his crusade, Kendel of Ecclesia assisting the Patriarch, Lucretia of Vellond leading a counter attack & Regnier of Hexter on his conquest of all of Bersia. Each general has their own pair of unique Lieutenants who joins them throughout the story where most of the lore is done through narrated texts/scripted sequences with the occasional in-game rendered cutscenes & the rare pre-rendered CGI cutscenes. You get to learn more about the world, characters and events as you progress through the campaigns and difficulties as all the generals fates intertwine to form this brutal Medieval High-Fantasy war story that has a lot of character, memorable moments, likable cast & epic battles despite its limitations & age. The gameplay is both different & innovative from its predecessor while at its core its still an RTS through and through what makes Kingdom Under Fire: The Crusaders so special is the refined hybrid nature of the RTS formula combined with the Dynasty Warrior style Musou combat mixed alongside Role Playing Game lite features all-in-one that turns Kingdom Under Fire into a large scale hack & slash strategic masterpiece that requires you to not just combo to win but properly and efficiently select, upgrade/equip & command your forces to achieve glorious victory where casualties are not to be taken lightly & timing is key. Upgrading works here by selecting the unit type path by meeting certain skill/s requirement/s for the officer of that said unit using XP & gold to turn your Men-at-Arms into say a Knight or a Sapper and etc. and etc. making each faction different & unique depending on how you arm your forces. When the troops are ready in combat itself you can command up to 3 units individually or same time and 2 support units that act as on-map abilities you can call while in the field. When your general's unit is engaged you will initiate Musou combat with each successful kill or melee strike building SP to use your different officer/lieutenant abilities provided your not in melee combat of course except for the Orks who can heal in a fight for a steep price. A thinking man's Musou that will definitely challenge your tactical and strategic thinking then simply button mashing! There's no multiplayer or custom scenario modes but that's alright as the standalone expansion pack Heroes solves the custom games part but each of the 4 campaign gets progressively more difficult with different situations to keep things fresh and engaging every mission all up to you to decide how to approach the challenge. Graphics for an original Xbox game are very impressive despite its age it still looks great with a lot of care given to both animations and overall art style to give that immersion that your in a different world where you in command. Audio too is superb while sometimes the combat audio sounds messy it still immerses you into the chaos of warfare with the killer soundtrack of Heavy Metal to help make the fights even more epic! Performance wise it seems to work very, very well for a PC port with only some minor bugs here and there regarding mostly unit pathing that can be resolved with commanding to Halt then Move/Attack and rarely visual bugs but overall runs very smooth though i do advise you to play the game and its expansion packs with an Xbox controller cause the PC controls seem a bit janky for camera buttons in particular for when you need to react quickly which is almost all the time. Overall just an amazing RTS hybrid game that does something actually unique for the genre to standout from the competition! If your a fan of Rise & Fall: Ancient Civilizations by Stainless Steel Studios & Savage: Battle for Newerth/Savage 2: Tortured Soul by S2 Games but want a more refined, fantastical and tighter gameplay without the RTS base building being in the way (think Total War but your in command personally) this is the game for you! I simply can't stop praising this game for how innovative it is that i Highly Recommend this to anyone who wants something new cause this is fine example of innovation that the genre desperately needs these days!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so, very happy that the stupid MMO-attempt (that 'should' have been a single player sequel to Crusaders) failed. At the same time, it saddens me to know that we will likely never 'see' that sequel now that the company is in dire straits financially. Nevertheless, this is one of the most innovative (mechanics-wise) games ever made, and the heavy-metal soundtrack makes you feel like bashing fantasy monsters over the head with a mace is a truly 'epic' endeavor. A word of warning: do NOT try and play this with a mouse and keyboard! It's a nightmare, trust me. Just pick up a cheap Xbox 360 controller off of amazon like I did, and it will work just as it was originally intended. I played the hell out of this game back in the early 2000's (the final seven year's of gaming's golden age), and I was excited to see it available on steam after my old Xbox finally gave up the ghost. From what I can tell so far, most if not all of the problems the negative reviewers here were having seem to have been ironed out (I finished Gerald's campaign with zero problems and have moved on to Lucretia's with no noticeable issues yet), but this is by no means a definitive take on the matter. The asking price seems a bit too steep for such an old game, but again: the studio is having serious financial problems now, so that explains it.All in all, this is a 'very' fun game with a steep but fair learning curve, and difficulty that is often brutal but (again) fair. This game expects you to think outside of the box more often than not, and in certain missions, you 'cannot' simply attack the enemy head on, as you will be slaughtered. A few helpful hints before I go:Troop positioning relative to the sun in front of them will drastically reduce your archers aim (and damage) as they cannot see, but will have the same effect on enemy archers as well. Positioning your troops in the woods will significantly reduce arrow damage from enemy archers (the logic being that many of the arrows are embedding themselves in the trees, rather than their targets), but again, will have the same effect on yours as well.Spearmen are a somewhat strangely-designed (mechanically-speaking), but incredibly effective unit to use against enemy cavalry units. The idea is to have said spearmen stand perfectly still so thy can 'brace' against cavalry charges (which they do automatically). the problem is that you'll have to use the 'tighten' formation on your other nearby troops to avoid losing a significant number of them: and said enemy mounted units 'will' target 'those' units, and not your spearmen. Keep them 'very' close to the pointy-boys, and the aforementioned enemy will unintentionally doom themselves trying to get to them.Elemental damage is DEADLY in this game. Say you've class-upped your heavy infantry into being Knights. This gives them a significant armor boost, making them a truly dangerous force on the battlefield against other infantry. Guess what? If one of the enemy troops can cast lightning, your Knights in their heavy steel plate-mail will take a 'very' large number of casualties from this if you don't try and intercept the offending-enemy in time. Dark Elf elemental boost-damage, likewise, has the same effect (but because they're filthy cheaters, it has this effect on 'all' enemy troop-types, and is a timed melee buff). Upgrade one of your supporting troops to use the 'Curatio' (healing) spell as early as you possibly can to help offset that damage.8.5/10 It's not perfect. It has dated graphics and ugly character designs, and the English voice-acting is basically every mediocre to bad Japanese Anime-esque English dub ever (yes: I know this game is Korean, don't bite my head off). But the brutally-appealing heavy metal soundtrack, the incredibly fun (if at times frustrating) gameplay, and the weirdly-awesome Eastern-RPG pseudo-Western Fantasy setting combined with a satisfying troop upgrade and leveling system makes for a memorable and supremely enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this is the most slept on series, i swear to god. Loved it as a kid. A gameplay mix of Total War and Dynasty Warriors, set in a dark fantasy settings. Pretty interesting world with humans who have a "god", except that "god" is an eldritch horror. White elves and dark elves arguing over whose the "high elves", and the one smart ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that noone listens to except the orcs. You play as 4 different characters from a standard guy leading a few men, to an immortal king-guy. Each with their own banterring officers, which you can call-upon to do their own special moves. You'll control up to 5 "units", which can seem a little limiting, but never too much that you're overwhelmed, but never too little that you're just looking at units doing their job, bored. You have standard infantry, archers, cavalry, spearmen, mortars, dragons, undead, tonnes more. It has a standard "rock paper scissors" where infantry beat spears, who beat cav, who beat infantry, but is expanded upon with enough variations where you'll always have to consider which units you send into battle. Something so satisfying about being up against an army and personally being able to hack and slash your a hole through their lines. Those archers been giving you trouble? Walk up them and just bash the ♥♥♥♥ out them. Perfect mix of making you feel powerful, but still needing to think about what you're doing. Even with the 15 years of dating, it's still fairly fun, and although the PC controls are a little janky, still fairly playable. Point is, i would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: It is the bare minimum of a port. It runs in Windows 10, it will run at 16:9 and 16:10 resolutions, and the controls have been remapped to support the Xbox One controller with small UI changes. That is it. This is no remaster or remake, it uses all of the original low-res textures and models. This game was on the original Xbox, and it still looks like it; but without the benefit of a softer and lower screen resolution combined with no longer being viewed through a CRT, so now you can see it in all of its awful glory.The game runs at a capped 30 FPS. Yep. Lower to mid range CPU's with just integrated graphics should have no issue running this game at native resolutions, cause it's not asking much. Which is good, cause outside of the shadow map size and screen resolution, the game otherwise has zero performance options available. While it supports widescreen resolutions, the UI does not scale properly, causing the very low-res UI assets to stretch and look even worse than it already does in 4:3. How little work was put into this port? The UI prompts still have have the original Xbox Type S controller analog sticks, cause they didn't bother to change them; they only switched out the black/white and start/select for the newer menu/view and L/R bumpers. When you go to save your game (which can ONLY be done manually from the world-map screen, regardless of how often the game automatically 'saves' when you are spending skill points and leveling up commanders), it tells you how many free 'blocks' you have left. What are blocks? The made-up storage unit used by the original Xbox, cause megabytes was too hard a concept to handle or something. Does it break anything by being there? No. It is, again, indicative of the bare minimum effort put into this port. While it does have keyboard and mouse support, and they can be remapped, the control structure is so convoluted as to be a quite terrible experience. Like, 'hold L Alt to move the camera' and 'ESC is cancel' and 'HOME is pause/menu' bad. Also, while there is an option to invert the camera's Y-Axis, it does nothing. Pressing up will always look up, no matter how the option is toggled, with either controller or mouse.The game was, and remains, the 'edgier' alternative to Dynasty Warriors. You have more RTS elements, what with actually controlling the positioning of units and using abilities, but then it devolves into a button-mashy and really uninspired hack-n'-slack (that pales in comparison to even other hack-n'-slash games of that era) whenever you actually close with the enemy. The goofy heavy metal soundtrack is still there, and everyone still takes themselves way too seriously (again, this is peak post-Matrix trilogy EDGE, lord only know how close we were to having everyone in leather jackets with sunglasses). Voice acting is deadpan and awful across the board, typical of low-budget titles from the era. Battles mostly amount to 'find and kill the enemy commander to win', but always devolve into a bloody mess cause the dark muddy graphics make it damn near impossible to pick out the one dark elf with a slightly more armored bikini on (cause that's the commander), and kill them. This is exacerbated by the claustrophobically narrow level of FOV; again, designed for playing from a couch on a TV with the performance constraints of the original Xbox in mind.Do not buy this game. Even if you have rose-tinted nostalgia goggles, wait until it is on sale for $10 or less, and even then, only buy this if you both have a controller and are ready for all of the shortcomings of this port. Everyone else not looking for the express nostalgia hit (i.e. people who don't remember enjoying KuF: Crusaders & KuF: Heroes on the Xbox) should keep far away.

_childDocuments_.review: Comments enabled in case you want to yell at me for how wrong I am.I bought this after seeing the vid from mandalore, as I'm sure a lot of people did recently. Somehow the PC port flew under my radar. As someone who grew up just outside of the time range for this game while playing the heck out of things like mount and blade and total war, I can't recommend it. Not because of any aging or technical limitations, but because of the controls and some mechanics.On controls: I will start by saying it is a miracle that they got stuff working as fluently as they did with a game of this genre on console. However, that doesn't stop it from feeling at times like you're trying to play Moonlight Sonata on piano with two wet noodles and your head keeps being randomly twisted left or right and someone keeps lifting you and the piano into the trees and expecting you to keep playing.Mechanics wise: It is extremely hard to understand just what you should be doing with troops when leveling and spending money. You don't know just how much a difference one or two points in a skill will make, and good luck trying to figure it out afterward in combat when the game relies heavily on you controlling the commander and trying to assassinate leaders as quickly as possible. This brings me to the next and probably biggest complaint I have. Staple troop types such as archers and cavalry are not viable (or at least they feel that way). Cavalry, for example, require constant micromangement, to the point where if you want them to be anywhere near as effective as your standard infantry troop, you have to dedicate your attention to them non stop, telling them to charge thru the enemy, widen formation so they can turn around without having to orbit the planet first, and then command them to charge thru again while making sure to tighten their formation at the last second so that you deal damage that is barely significant.Whereas with Archers, they require you to constantly make sure they aren't being flanked by infantry and that you don't end up having to pull out your main force to come save their asses. To utilize them effectively, you have to designate their target area from tighter or broad (don't worry, you aren't insane, this does NOT make sense). And what constitutes the need for wider or smaller target areas is NEVER conveyed well (outside of when enemy troops are not in combat, which will last for about 3 seconds after you start shooting them).Then there's the missions and how tedious, unclear, or straight up boring they can be. This review is already long enough and I don't think any fan of this game will even contest this point so I'll leave it at that.I really tried to like this game and I'm super nostalgic about it from watching my brother play and having to hide it from our mom because of the naughty elf clothing, but I honestly can't make myself keep playing it. The last straw was losing all of my progress on the dark elf campaign because I forgot to save before I returned to the title menu. That was about 7 hours of gameplay lost.To anyone who might say "oh well you didn't stick around for the last two campaigns where things really open up!" or some such, I say I can't be made to care. No one should have to sit thru the 15 hours of monotony I did and then some to get to anything that is really fun. On the up side, this game has given me a new appreciation for modern strategy games and how far the genre has come.

_childDocuments_.review: Reposting my review for Heroes since it applies to both games:Kingdom Under Fire is one of my favorite series of all time. It certainly had some jank, but not as bad as in the ports. The best way to re-correct when the pathing gets bad is to lower the distance of your movements considerably almost as if you are working to turn them first and then when the unit is finally facing the right direction go forward a little bit a few times and then you should be all set for long distance movements again.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't say I played this game as a kid, and I wish I could. I'll make the pros and cons concise but I 100% recommend this game. Pros:- Unique game play mechanics are a stand out. Its a mix of RTS and hack n slash gameplay. You control multiple units per battle, ranging from melee, indirect/direct fire ranged units, aerial, with hybrid units in between. Your character you play as can only be melee, but your other units can be mixed and matched between battles to an insane degree.  the player character fighting is simple, but not boring because your in a giant melee straight out of LOTR or other fantasy scenes. Imagine those big RTS battles but your up front instead of above. Other units are controlled indirectly, and you can assign commands to them like any other RTS. -graphics are extremely early 2000s. The more open the environment is, the bigger the fight will be. the landscape can be kinda bland, but for so many units to be on screen its a good trade off.  As funny as they are, the character models faces are horrifying to look at sometimes. Its got a charm to it so if old school is your thing you'll love the look-Music is the secondary stand out. You have to experience it yourself to know, but its not generic fantasy music. The entire soundtrack, from the most mundane to chaotic sections, is heavy metal. I'm a big metal head, and the OST fills that section of this game completely for me. The music makes some battle feel badass to push through.  Cons: - Camera is a pain in the ass. It has a habit of either being extremely high or extremely low when following units.  You do fight it sometimes, which isn't good when controlling units. -story is dependent on knowing the previous games lore. the main story itself is competent, but until the last 3rd feels like the equivalent of a kid smacking his figures together. I won't spoil to much, but characters can jump from boring to annoying really quickly. Side note: look up the localization of this game from South Korea. Funny story. -Last mission is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slog. I genuinely hated it. Without to many spoilers it becomes a bloody meat grinder that took me hours to finish. I legit almost didn't finish the game after 2 hours of work only to die and start over. Overall: has its fair share of problems, some bigger than others that I probably can't remember. If you play it, have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Having only played Heroes on Xbox and having very fuzzy memories about it at best, I jumped on the opportunity of playing this for the first time without prior knowledge. Well, it's a good game, if you are willing to look past oodles of quirks and jank, things that, in time, have become sought after as they give games like this, with competent gameplay, a unique charm not found anywhere else. Well, the first thing you must know is that BlueSide did their job, but didn't go beyond the call of duty: game's locked at 30 FPS and its visuals were only scaled and stretched to fit HD displays accordingly. Settings don't go past the most basic, but it is in 4K and there are mods that help improve texture quality. There's also no multiplayer suite, which is a big deal in any RTS game. As for gameplay, you could say it is real time strategy in a sense, as you manage multiple units (with basic commands) whilst they engage opposing factions in a sprawling battlefield, but the 3rd person hack-n'-slash-to-thundering-Heavy Metal part is what makes the experience sweet. The game is divided into 4 campaigns, each with its own hero and faction, and you follow them as they take on a series of missions where the objective, ultimately, is to rout the enemy. Each hero has its own combos and story, although they are all intertwined. The overarching plot revolves an ancient fantasy land, where its warring factions dispute their rights over holy land and a sacred treasure called the Ancient Heart. The heart is the representation of an old god thought to be mere legend, but obviously there's more to it than just the myth. Our heroes are: Gerald, an outstanding military captain, honest and brave, representing Hironeiden; Lucretia, a flamboyant dark elf with a short fuse and hatred for all living creatures outside of her own race, representing Vellond; Kendall, a paladin whose deep faith overpowers his own desire to question the pope's ambitions, representing Ecclesia, and Regnier, the coolest of them all, who's an ancient hero who gained immortality through mysterious means, and commands a legion of bloodthirsty orcs ready to die at his whim, coming from Hexter.Gerald and Lucretia are your tutorial campaigns. Sadly, you cannot disable these tutorials, which makes replaying their campaigns a chore, but when you hit Kendall's (the toughest one by far) and Regnier's, the game disables your bike's training wheels and sends you to die against nearly impossible odds right at the beginning. Now, gameplay wise, the game allows you to issue commands to each unit as they move and engage in combat. The hero unit can be commanded directly as it fight enemies in melee, but no other unit can be controlled. You can merely issue basic orders to them, such as attack, move, cast spells/use skills, and so on. Once your hero is in combat, the camera zooms in and you can move him/her around, doing sick combos and issuing skill/spell orders to one of your two subordinates. Units have a set number of soldiers or monsters which represent a piece of the overall unit's HP bar. As soldiers die, segments of the bar disappear and the unit is forfeit once all units are dead, although you can also kill the leader to immediately defeat the unit in combat. This also applies to you, but you can manage by recovering red health spamming healing spells with your supporting ranged units, which should always be behind your hero unit. Each faction (human alliance and dark legion) has its own set of units, like archers, cavalry, paladins, infantry and quite a few less obvious ones, like the colossal swamp mammoths and the speedy storm riders. Each unit has its own set of requirements to meet before turning into it, but they are very easy and cheap to get. To level up your unit, you need to increase its leader's main stats (designated with a smiley face), and there's a lot to choose from, but it's never overwheling. There's also equipment that you can buy to increase their stats. Said equipment is randomized in its availability each time you load the game, so you can save scum to obtain your desired gear.. There's not much to the game other than that. For example, there's no base building or resource management, and your objective is to either kill them all or go to the marked destination on your map. Controls are very clunky as well, and though commands are limited, you might find yourself issuing the wrong orders all the time, a drawback from it being designed for console play only. However, this port features keyboard controls as well, but I never used them myself.As for music, it's guitar driven, head banging Metal. Sound design is decent, although many visual effects you'll see won't be accompanied by a corresponding thud, clank or buzz. Voice acting is a joke, almost Resident Evil 1 for PlayStation level, which is somewhat endearing, but pushing it. No MP means little to no replay value. Worse yet, certain missions require very specific units to triumph and if you don't have the prerrequisites to get them at that point, you could easily get softlocked in that campaign, which is why one must always save before and after every mission. Spending money and XP williy nilly is not advisable.There's more jank that I would like to discuss, but that's a flavor that you either love or hate with no in-between. I find it holds up today, yet you might play it and hate everything about it. Personally, I would've enjoyed this game at a higher framerate, but devs always come up with some BS excuse as to why they couldn't do it. Nevertheless, it was a fun hack and slash romp and would recommend it to people who enjoyed at least Heroes back in the day.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: Cleared this game plenty of times on the original XBOXKUF: Crusaders is a semi-RTS mixed with some hack n slash based in a dark fantasy world. It consists of 4 campaigns and two factions: the humans and the dark legion (dark elves and orcs).Presentation - Not too shabby, especially when there are hundreds of troops on the map at once. Models are nice, with a large variety of human, dark elf and orc troops. You can see some of units raise their weapons when approaching an enemy troop. The maps and environments themselves are... decent; sometimes a map would literally just be a flat desert, though you'll mostly be focusing on fighting anyway.Music - A metallic treat for the ears. Gameplay - Very solid and feels great to play on the PC using a controller (a huge plus since it'd crash a lot on the original XBOX). You engage in skirmishes in a board and control a hero troop, plus any additional troops you wish to bring along. The troops you control are groups of units instead of single units (think of Total War). You control your troops in a semi-RTS mode and go into a Dynasty Warriors-esque style mode when your hero troop is in battle with another troop, and your other troops always stay in RTS mode. The campaigns consist of two factions: humans and the dark legion (dark elves and orcs). Both factions have different unit jobs such as infantry, archers, giant eagles and giant scorpions. Each job has strengths and weaknesses you need to learn in order to crush your enemies (and not get crushed yourself). After each battle you can level up your hero and troops, buy gear and hire mercenaries for more troops.Story - Not too bad. Dialogue can awkward and the voice acting is a little shaky, but personally I find the cheesy quality to be enjoyable. Overall, a great and fun mix of RTS and hack n slash. I give it 8 dark elf butts out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember calling my friends over for a sleep over and showing them this game. We would stay up till 4-5 in the morning playing it. _childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Under Fire: The Crusaders is a fantastic game. Replaying this has been one large nostalgia trip I'm positively elated that it was better than I remembered. If you haven't played it I highly recommend this as it's one of the best mixes of RTS/RPG/Hack and slash/Resource manager. In order to succeed you really need to capitalize on each of this games genre components. Learning how to best use each character can give you a steady stream of "SP" which is used for spells and special moves. Understanding the RTS components such as how to use the terrain to your advantage is important for maintaining an edge on the battlefield. Resource management is paramount in this game as exp and gold are both limited over the course of the campaign so keeping a steady reserve is important in case you reach a mission where you need a unit type that you don't have. Lastly don't forget to invest in items as these can be an incredible boon to the strength of your units.At the end of the day this game can really reward creativity. Trying out different unit combinations, gear pieces and tactics is one of the most enjoyable components of this game. If your struggling try changing things up after all you might find an alternate way of doing things that will lead you through missions without losing a single soldier.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let my time fool you, I've played 6 or 7 playthroughs on original Xbox. This game was way ahead of it's time then and still amazing now. The mix of dynasty warriors hack n' slash and RTS lite means there's never a dull moment. To top it off you get to upgrade your hero AND troops equipment and levels. Oh yea, and dark elves in thongs.

If you have never played these games - it is a mix between an action game and strategy game. You control soldiers on the battlefield, but also control a hero too, as you command 100s of units you will also be slashing through hundreds of foes with your sword - it's pretty cool. _childDocuments_.review: Played this game growing up, loved every bit of it. There is a fine equipment system that you use gold to purchase said equipment. EXP is gained each mission by either killing enemies or completing certain tasks during said mission, it is used to upgrade your units "Skills" such as Melee, Ranged, Mounted, Taming, and several others, which are required to change "Job" assignments such as Heavy Infantry, Archers, Knights, Sappers, Ghouls, Scorpions, and many more.P.S.*I PLAY WITH AN XBOX ONE CONTROLLER* and I highly recommend playing this game with a controller of some sort, just feels nice.

_childDocuments_.review: The mix between RTS-Action gameplay this game provides is so unique that you would truly be missing out on an experience not replicated by any other game (trust me, I have looked for a game like this for YEARS and nothing comes close... not even Dynasty Warriors). You get to choose between 4 heroes, customize their personal armies, purchase equipment for them, and allocate experience between the leader unit, their troops, and their officers. There are 3 difficulties, Easy (1 hero), Medium (1 hero), and Hard (2 heroes). Hard difficulty is where this game truly shines and comes alive because of the freedom you have with your armies.This port to PC is absolutely awful... using a controller is HIGHLY recommended.On a more personal note, the nostalgia kills me! I played this game growing up on repeat. I saw this ported to PC, bought it immediately, and was rapidly reminded why I always thought of this as the greatest game of all-time. There is literally no other game out there like this other than its prequel KuF Heroes (which, I agree with the consensus is way better). Do yourself a favor and drop the $20 on a gameplay experience that hasn't been replicated.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing Kingdom Under Fire: Heroes relentlessly when I was a kid so I suppose it was nostalgia that made me play this. KUF:TC plays in a similar fashion, fairly straightforward RTS with great 3rd person action. Graphics: From a graphics perspective, it's fair to say this looks pretty dated but that was never where the game really shone anyway.Gameplay: Across four campaigns, you control the main player character (who has their own unit of soldiers) as well as other units like archers, mortars, cavalry, sappers etc. It leads to pretty fun gameplay. When the main character's unit attacks an enemy you take control of the main character, however if you want to manage other units then the character automatically fights. Missions occur across different maps and landscapes. When missions are completed you return to a base and get to level up your units and main character. Story: Story is decent. You play as four characters across four campaigns and not always from the 'good' side so you get to see different perspectives which is neat. Pretty sure Kingdom Under Fire was originally translated from Korean. Dialogue is cheesy and sometimes a bit janky, you'll notice that they never say the word 'Patriarch' which comes up often and apparently that's because it was originally voice-recorded as 'Pope' but they removed it without redoing the voice work.Cons: While it's a great game, it leaves you wanting similar titles. Kingdom Under Fire: Heroes hasn't been ported and the story ends quite abruptly. The sequel to this game - Kingdom Under Fire: Circle of Doom completely dropped the RTS format in favour of a hack and slash type game and it left me feeling like the story I played was a bit unfinished.Another issue is that two out of the four campaigns feel quite limited in what units you can level up and deploy. Feels quite 'tutorial-like' while the harder campaigns give you more free-reign.Summary: It's a good game that will absorb a couple of hours per campaign. Quite surprised there isn't a more modern version of games like this.

Some of the conversations in the pub are just...third language level English, someone call the grammar police and they can sort that out. Lastly, the mini-games were cut and are not available, but you can still win them.All in all, a great re-buy.

_childDocuments_.review: My first and, most likely, last review ever!Holy nut-balls it is actually here, in existence! Okay, so I got this game for the original Xbox back in 2006 when it had been out for 2 years. I went to GameStop and turned in some games I did not really enjoy anymore and bought KUF.Purchasing this game is way more of a nostalgic trip for me than any kind of hardcore gaming experience. I'll be honest, I bought the Xbox controller as soon as I got this. The keyboard is wonky. Trying to play this game with a mouse and keyboard is fun, if you like meaningless challenges. I like meaningless challenges because I am slightly unhinged. The controls are simple enough when you get a handle for the game. I would say about 3 or 4 missions into Lucretia, I am getting better at the controls, even after playing all of Gerald's story. The only complaint I have, is very minor bugs like the sudden sound of all the Elves casting boost on themselves, or the sound of the floodgates closing (opening?) during the stealth missions. Also, the introduction of the controls is in reference to the original Xbox controller. I guess they are stuck with this since the game has audio voice overs that refer directly to those buttons. Oh well. All of the original voices are as awkward as they were in the original, no one has had a major make-over in the appearance department- thank god. I was a little worried about that, Ellen is literally naked in the banner art for the game; however, she is her normal pixelated-self covered in chainmail, like the original. I personally think it is worth the money in terms of the nostalgia. It does get a bit repetitive here and there and I need to take a break after about 4 straight hours. Then it is right back into the action. I have also played Circle of Doom which bored me to tears. I guess that may make me less of a KUF fan or something.There are a few major bugs to the game that seem to be spotty from user to user. I was lucky enough to not have any real issues, and it seems like the patches are fairly recent, hopefully development continues. Keep this in mind before you commit your $$$. Hope this helps!
