name: STATIONflow
detailed_description: Have you ever been stuck in a train or subway station, crowded and congested, fighting to get on the escalator? Have you ever wandered around lost, cursing the lack of proper signage? Have you ever thought to yourself “I could design this station better” ? STATION flow is a game about controlling the flow of thousands of passengers by building and managing an efficient underground train station. Manage the flow of thousands of passengers with different needs, stats and targets, simulated in real time. Build complex 3D layouts in a multilayered map. Place and shape corridors and structures freely, without the constraints of a grid. Connect your station with stairs, escalators and elevators as efficiently as you can, but make sure everything is accessible. Keep things functional and efficient: your goal is to avoid congestion and to get passengers to where they want to go as quickly and smoothly as possible. Guide passengers via signage, and watch the flow of passengers change. Manipulate the path people take to avoid crowds—sometimes the shortest route is not the most efficient. Satisfy your passengers’ desires for various services: place vending machines and kiosks, construct bathrooms, restaurants and more. Passengers will expect more than just to find their exit on time. Don’t forget about upkeeps. You’re on a budget, so you'll want to keep your station lean and efficient⁠—but make sure it isn't at the cost of passenger satisfaction! And of course, the higher-ups are always watching. You will receive daily evaluations based on passenger feedback. Do well, and you will be rewarded with an extended budget and additional construction options, but also given increased responsibilities. Do poorly, and you may well be on your way to bankruptcy... Create your own maps and share them through the Steam Workshop, or browse other players' creations for your next playthrough. Adjust the game's difficulty to your liking via multiple settings. Give yourself a relaxed sandbox experience, or something to really test your station-building abilities⁠... Good luck.

Have you ever thought to yourself “I could design this station better” ? STATION flow is a game about controlling the flow of thousands of passengers by building and managing an efficient underground train station. Manage the flow of thousands of passengers with different needs, stats and targets, simulated in real time. Build complex 3D layouts in a multilayered map. Place and shape corridors and structures freely, without the constraints of a grid. Connect your station with stairs, escalators and elevators as efficiently as you can, but make sure everything is accessible. Keep things functional and efficient: your goal is to avoid congestion and to get passengers to where they want to go as quickly and smoothly as possible. Guide passengers via signage, and watch the flow of passengers change. Manipulate the path people take to avoid crowds—sometimes the shortest route is not the most efficient. Satisfy your passengers’ desires for various services: place vending machines and kiosks, construct bathrooms, restaurants and more. Passengers will expect more than just to find their exit on time. Don’t forget about upkeeps. You’re on a budget, so you'll want to keep your station lean and efficient⁠—but make sure it isn't at the cost of passenger satisfaction! And of course, the higher-ups are always watching. You will receive daily evaluations based on passenger feedback. Do well, and you will be rewarded with an extended budget and additional construction options, but also given increased responsibilities. Do poorly, and you may well be on your way to bankruptcy... Create your own maps and share them through the Steam Workshop, or browse other players' creations for your next playthrough. Adjust the game's difficulty to your liking via multiple settings. Give yourself a relaxed sandbox experience, or something to really test your station-building abilities⁠... Good luck.
short_description: STATIONflow is a game about controlling the flow of thousands of passengers by building and managing an efficient underground train station.

_childDocuments_.review: STATIONflow has completely captured my imagination of late. It's interesting in that I almost passed on it due to its spartan presentation. But happening on a Let's Play sold me pretty quick.The game is a logistics sim focused on keeping commuters moving through an increasingly complex metrorail system. The game provides the station entrances & train platforms and your job is to connect them all up in a (hopefully) intelligent fashion so commuters can navigate the corridors with as little friction as possible.You're given all manner of tools, most of which successively unlock after each successful daily operation shift. But beyond the raw basics of corridor/stairs/escalators, your most important tool is the direction sign. This is what your little AI travelers will be counting on to get them from A to B to C. Simple and Streamlined is the rule of the day. You place a sign, chose a direction for the arrow to point, and click on pre-made Point of Interest icons. "Platforms P and Q are THIS WAY"..."You can also access A and B Entrance/Exits in this same direction as well." Easy, right?Well that becomes increasingly difficult as your operations grow more complex from day to day. New entrance clusters open up on the same map, usually in groups of 5 (A1, A2, A3, etc.). Most of the time on multiple floors. Make it through a few days and an entire new rail line will set up shop in the station. I just unlocked platform #3. Amenities are successively introduced. Bathrooms, coffee stands, food stalls, cafes, info booths. ALL of this needs to be telegraphed to passengers though the all-immortal directional signage. Hopefully placed smartly at all entrances and corridor terminates. It adds up to a LOT of direction mapping. Oh, and when you unlock a new platform, entrance cluster or amenity? Yeah, you need to update all your old signs.Sounds daunting (it is) but it's also quick & intuitive. And this unearths the strange dichotomy of the game loop. You're spending a lot of time making Big Plans for corridor layouts and connections. Then you're tasked with fine-tuning & adjusting as you're asked to spin more plates. What sounds laborious on the surface also doubles as the Zen experience zone you'll likely slip into as well. Puzzling over guiding commuters through maze-like hallways and levels, keeping them locationally informed at all times. This actually puts you in their shoes navigating the complex station. Urging you to mentally walk the corridors yourself using spacial awareness to discover optimal paths (in both building and directing). It's an incredible feeling when you get that spark of inspiration resolving a route you thought was logistically impossible.Then a new day brings new challenges by way of the unlocks noted above. It makes you completely reevaluate your station layout. Do you utterly slash & burn a subsection to accommodate new demands, or do you work around it and hope it's not too gangly in the end.In my last session I just unlocked a new rail platform. Cool. But more interesting, I also go a new passenger type...Disabled. To service these customers I now have to integrate elevators into a sprawling 5-level underground station with 20 entrances spread across all floors and corners of the map.Legit 1st reaction: Wut.Legit followup: Okay, let's do this.And ladies & gentlemen, that is the true magic of this game. The way it so naturally inspires creative thinking and problem solving.Quick note on passengers and presentation. Like many genre titles, you can click on any random commuter and pull up a profile panel describing their unique archetype (daily commuter, tourist, elderly, student, etc.), their happiness, base stats (walk speed, vision distance, patience level, etc.), their entrance point & desired destination. You'll also see a dotted line on the map representing where they're looking & how far they can see. It's a real-time tool to show gaps in the system that you may not have considered. Upset commuters will rage with icon bubbles over their heads helping you further with layout diagnostics.What's interesting about the raw nature of these graphics beyond clean readability is when you pull back the camera during am or pm rush hour and see hundreds of these little pegs just flitting & flowing through the map like some crazy-complex ant farm, the feeling of satisfaction of channeling chaos into order is just amazing. My current average is around 700 or so at any one time during rush hour. It's a small marvel to see the streams of people (hopefully) intelligently routing by the hundreds by your hand.Easy recommendation for logistics, building & puzzle fans. I absolutely love it.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - Overall this game has potential. Game focuses on the challenges of building a subway station; building and pathing appropriately linking the various exits with platforms across multiple levels. Efficiency enthusiasts may also get a kick out of this game.NB: Review made while game is in early access.As the name suggests, stationflow focuses on the design and architecture of a subway station. The platforms and exits are decided by the game across different levels and you have to create ways for commuters - at the moment these can be regular commuters, students, tourists and the elderly who all have varying attributes of size; speed; vision and patience. Signs can be placed along corridors and at the top/bottom of stairs/escalators/lifts/etc to help guide your commuters, although being able to make the text/icons for these smaller would be a big help so the screen can get cluttered with sign icons if people are liberally placing signs at nearly every junction like me!Building the station, however, isn't an insta-build dance. Instead, the player has to plan out what they want to build and then wait for it to be built - although this can be a matter of in-game hours so there's not a huge wait time for the player.Difficulty is increased as you level up via people you've shifted from their A to B; difficulty at the moment appears to be ramped up with more things to do (next paragraph covers it), new passenger types and platforms/entrances levelling up; generating more football through those places.In addition to trains, you also have to build other utilities for passengers - drinks machines, info boards, toilets - all these builds have a budgetary expenditure and some will make a profit for you. Signs you place may also point passengers to these places although I feel some (like info boards) are best being placed near entrances so commuters aren't going deep into your labyrinth of a station just to find out they're going the wrong way!Overall, it's a game with potential. The challenge to this game is efficiency both with space and budget along with pathing correctly. Really this game has some similarities to Overcrowd but with the staff aspect taken out which is actually quite nice considering the focus is on the architecture and design of the station, not the micromanagement.Some things I'd like to see:- Random seed generator. Currently, it seems there's only one map to play which limits the replayability of the game. Being able to seed where the exits and the platforms are located/orientated would combat this and people would be able to share seeds and make it challenging.- Stairs, etc expect a straight edge when linking them to corridors and doesn't prompt you if the top/bottom of a stair isn't linked until after the fact. Sometimes this can be a matter of millimetres and commuters won't use them as there's no link there. Would be nice if the gap is too small for the corridor tool that the stair tool fills the gap for you.- Lifts are odd - passengers can only use them from the bottom to the top of the shaft and any floor inbetween the lift appears not to stop at them. Perhaps a balancing issue (as or just a programming thing (they appear to work in the same way stairs do with regard to directing commuters) - while I don't mind either way, I feel the tool should at least make it clear to the player that passengers can only use it to go top or bottom of it.- The Corridor tool - As a professional Design Engineer, I  the corridor tool and kudos to the devs on what is already a fairly solid tool; being able to drag an edge to a diagonally shaped corridor and for it to instantly conform to the edge I'm linking it to is great and saves a lot of time and hassle. Although one thing that would be nice for this tool are dimensions (helps plan out and future proof stairways I plan on making escalators) and also if it's possible for the tool to display a relationship with another line/edge? Basically, something that tells me if the line I'm dragging is running parallel or perpendicular (90 degrees) with an existing corridor edge or previously drawn line? Something akin to the "Precision Engineering" mod for Cities Skylines, I guess? Also, are you guys going to introduce more "rounder" tools (fillet, circle, etc?) squares are nice and all but curvvy architecture can be easier on the eye!

_childDocuments_.review: At full price? Probably not.The gameplay is certainly interesting, but there are lots of issues minor and major:- The UI for updating signs is majorly annoying; you can't group common signs (the elevator and the stairs and the escalators) so you need to make changes by clicking into each sign. You can copy and paste, which makes this slightly less annoying, but by the time you get to the truly massive stations this takes forever and gets exhausting. It also doesn't help that when editing signs next to each other, the UI is very finicky and will often not click the thing you actually want to edit.- Lack of clarity; the game has a minimalist aesthetic going on, but at times it's *too* minimalistic. For example, in one of the progressions you get to build a ticket office instead of a ticket machine and info board separately. But why would you want to do that? Does it have higher capacity? Does it process people faster? Does it cost less? Who knows?! The benefits of anything are not clearly explained. There also isn't a lot of descriptive info once you go back and click on things you've already built.- Lack of data; the game has metrics on things like "people take too much time doing X", but you don't know what exits or platforms these people are using, so good luck trying to figure out the proper place to put something. When problems do occur, little bubbles temporarily pop up, but you won't notice them if you're on a different floor.- Performance: This is the kicker. This game will start choking on higher levels if you are building too much stuff, or if you have too many people trying to navigate through too many combinations of hallways and such.At $18 this is not worth it in its current state. Wait for a sale or something.

_childDocuments_.review: The basic premise is that people enter the station through subway entrances and get to the train they need, or they arrive on a train and need to exit the station at a particular exit or hop on another train. So basically you connect the various entrances / exits to the train platforms and mark the intersections with signs so they can find their way.Now all of these things don’t exist on the same level, so you need to connect the levels with staircases so the people can travel between them. When you service the station well enough you level up and the game throws another wrinkle at you - now the people want a place to buy coffee, and then a place to pee that coffee out, or a board so they can figure out what train they need to catch or exit they need to leave. Then I had to start catering to ‘the elders’ and build elevators because they can’t walk the stairs.I’m level eight, which probably isn’t very far, and it has been mostly easy to meet the new demands. The player is constrained by money, but it hasn’t been too tight as of yet. The biggest challenge is that sometimes the building tools are awkward to work with. Sometimes it’s pretty smooth - hallways snap together, stairway connect to their destinations. Sometimes there is a conflict and I just can’t get things to line up right and I need to fiddle, or delete something and try again. So, the challenges so far haven’t been mental ones but after leveling up some more and needing to retrofit new train lines and exits I can see the complexity rising.Some of the other tasks feel like busywork too, like supplying coffee. That just means I need to go throughout my station and plunk down coffee machines. Same with the food. The other busywork is constantly needing to update signs. A new train line pops up, well now I need to go update all of my signs to people know where to go.It’s an interesting concept, but I think the execution falls short to make me want to put a lot of time into it. Maybe later on more interesting things get added, but for now I find myself spending more time on tedious things than solving interesting problems. Kudos to the devs for trying something a bit different.

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly the kind of game I'm wired to enjoy; route-planning, optimization, and a small sprinkling of tedium. For the first 10 to 15 hours with the game I very much did enjoy it but as some of the issues became really obvious it led me to the conclusion that I cannot give a recommendation to this game in its current form.My first issue is with the amount of content available in the game. As new NPC types are unlocked and develop new needs you will have some difficulty keeping up with it all, but that suddenly drops off after a couple hours of play leaving you with nothing much to do but optimize your network and build out the last couple stations that unlock later. There really needs to be more variety in NPC needs to flush out that mid to late-game. Perhaps more late-game shop types or new transportation methods, but it needs something. As it is there are 4 hours of laying the foundation for your system and expanding, 2 hours of optimizing, then an hour of doing nothing but watching your system operate until you decide to start a new map.Which leads to my next issue which is the maps. Each of the maps included in the base game are unique and provide interesting challenges. The problem is that each map will end up feeling pretty much the same in practice. Connect platform P to the A's. Now connect platform Q and the B's. Now platform R... While they may be placed spacially in completely unique ways, in practice it feels very formulaic. They will always unlock in the exact same order and NPC needs will always develop in the exact same order, at the exact same levels as always.The next issue is with the NPC's and their pathing. Initially NPC's getting lost or frustrated was entirely my fault, for not having proper signage or forgetting to update it as my system grew. In the late-game, once I had fully built out my system to cover all available stations and exits, I spent a good deal of time just tracking NPC's and identifying where things were going wrong in the network. I discovered that many NPC's, often the elderly, were simply ignoring all signs from first entering the system and walking from one end of a hallway to the other repeatedly until they got frustrated. Even after resolving some glitches, such as NPC's commonly losing their way in overly wide hallways and plazas, the problem was still quite apparent with up to a hundred people lost for no reason. This problem persisted across two other maps and just gets worse the larger the system is regardless of layout or the amount and placement of signage.My final issue is that the game in no way encourages creativity, and may even actively discourage it. Could I make sweeping curved hallways, large malls, or a network in the shape of Mario? Yeah, probably. But all any of that does is make my system more difficult for NPC's to navigate, harder for me to sign, and would probably leave me broke and then it's game over.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, but the sign post system is just too awful.Every single intersection needs a signpost or people get lost and complain. This means even if you do your best to limit intersections, dozens of sign posts are required. Any time a new exit or line is added, you have to update every. single. one. It is a tedious nightmare.Your station gets so cluttered with sign post arrows you can't see anything that's going on, and their giant icons cover up each other and anything else you need to click on.And the worst thing is they don't even work. People will walk right under a sign with an arrow specifically for their destination and still turn around and walk the opposite direction. Apparently this problem is reduced by running the game in a slower mode, but since there's nothing to do except wait for people to finish walking that's akin to watching paint dry.Building pathways, adjusting to new station layouts, managing kiosk placement, all of it is excellent and should make for a fun game. Unfortunately you have to spend the vast majority of your time managing a mountain of ugly directional arrows that don't always actually work, which ultimately makes it too frustrating to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this? Only for some players.TLDR:For me the best public transport management strategy, but with poor performance (bad optimisation) and hard achievements even with "cheating" (creating specific maps in the bundled editor).Longer version with few hints:It does lag a lot when the station is larger and there are few thousands of passengers in the station. Then even the slowest speed is lagging. The highest speed is then unplayable and I mean really, because when the game lags a lot and you run it on the full speed, you usually get worse rating and therefore money. I got B on the fastest speed on my own station for the high number of passengers per day, but I got A or A+ when I lowered it to the medium speed. It is also visible that the game time passes more slowly if the game lags. Full speed on some maps can mean full day in 4 min, but 8 on another.There are minor bugs with the building system, but you usually learn what to avoid.The tutorial is not enough, you have to learn it by trials and errors, but I am old-school gamer, so no problem for me.Some achievements can be reached easily by special maps you create or find. But some need really long gameplay. Especially the hidden one to transfer over 13 mil. passengers. I have not reached it yet after 115 hours. I am in the 2/3. Because you have to confirm end of each day so AFK does not work here well, you have to confirm it each few minutes.I would love another game like this and more optimised. I have issues with 1-2 thousands people at the same time at the station to not have annoying lag even on the slowest speed (but well developed station with all exits and platforms) and I have AMD Ryzen 7 3800. It uses most likely only one core.So you can easily reach over 90% achievements, if you help youreself with some dedicatd maps in the editor, but reaching the last 2 achievements is tricky and long-term goal.And don't forget, if you suck, try to slower the speed, maybe you will not bankrupt.

_childDocuments_.review: The developers at DMM GAMES pose a question: “Have you ever been suck in a train or subway station, and thought to yourself—I could have done better?” Honestly, I can’t really say I have. The question has never occurred to me. But it has now, thanks to STATIONflow. STATIONflow is a game developed by DMM GAMES which has you control the flow of thousands of passengers in a station. It is really that simple. You build corridors, stairs, ensure that exits and intersections are clearly labelled for passengers to easily find. As the game progresses, you begin to attend to passengers needs, such as the need for a snack or a coffee. As every day begins, you race against the clock to build items and set up the station to flow smoothly during the day. This is necessary because when it becomes rush hour, the station gets CRAZY! I swear I feel the stress coming through the screen as I saw the little passengers scurry about and get frustrated with the layout of my station. If this stresses you out too much—don’t worry! The clock can be paused, or even sped up multiple times for more of a challenge or to speed through construction.There is a huge amount of strategy at play here. I feel like I certainly lacked the mental skills needed for a game like this, because I was honestly at a loss for what to do to make my station run better. Honestly, this game is DIFFICULT. You really need to think through every corridor, every stairway and intersection, be able to figure out which way is most efficient for everybody. I feel like architects or people really good at managing things would find this game to be extremely fun. Even I, who wasn’t good at this game at all, was very sucked in by the gameplay. In addition to needing to manage the passengers and their needs, additionally the game has a money managing aspect as well. Everything you build costs money; however, you do make money off people using the station every day and any vending machines you may have laying around. Watch your finances though, you can’t just build without abandon! If you become bankrupt, then it is game over for you!The game runs fantastically. At first glance, the game looks incredibly complicated, but through a very in-depth tutorial I was able to have full grasp of the game. The graphics are simple, but sharp and clean. What stands out to me for a mile is the incredible soundtrack! It is like a low fi electronic beat, and I seriously love it. The only downside is that it’s only that one song—I want more of this fantastic music! I would recommend this game to honestly anybody. If you are new to strategy games, while this is definitely a more difficult one, the in-depth tutorial really helps you grow accustomed to how games like this work. If you are a seasoned veteran, then the addicting gameplay is sure to pull you in during this tremulous quarantine season.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game to tickle your micro management planning pickle, this is the game for you. It's been a while that i've played a game which, in this case, starts you off on the tutorial level but once the basics are down, it transitions seamlessly into the rest of the game and 3+ hours later i had more or less grasped the basic mechanics and was very satisfied. I can definitely see myself playing this a lot.Would highly recommend! Well done devs!

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is fun, but flexibility in modding seems a bit too low. The game itself have a number of maps and a number of players-created maps are available on workshop, but the game itself support only up to 6 train lines in each map, and there are only two platform type options available for each train lines: island platform and side platform. Terrain are also limited to river and rock. And then the game have not allowed modding of other non-map elements such as amenities. Hence I think there are some wasted potential in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more a first impression of version 14 for now, I have only played an hour so far.The game has great potential for a lot of playtime, but it lacks a lot of key parts that I expected from a game such as this.The biggest problem is the "New game" button itself, it drops you into the game with nothing else to select or specify. I expect another window with some selection boxes regarding whether I want to play the tutorial or not, if I want all exits unlocked at the start or play a sandbox mode even.This ties into the next big thing, variety. The game lacks variety in the stations, it lacks scenarios to select or unlock, sandbox modes or even an editor. This means you can only really find entertainment replaying the level better, which has very limited replayability.Stairs and escalators do not share the same way of signage which means when you unlock the escalators you find yourself confused as to why the signage won't work. They should all be set to the same way, showing at the bottom on where it leads to and for the stairs where they lead down to, not the other way around.Why are they confused or lost? This is not made clear, if they lack information, say so. If they misunderstand the sign and get conflicting information, say so. One must assume they can't think on their feet because they seem to disregard exits entirely unless they know which one they want. This is a bit odd and needs to be communicated to the player in a better way.Probably the biggest annoyance though is placement of objects. When I zoom in I expect things to scale down so that I have more room between the individual objects to align or rotate them, this is not the case so any tightly placed objects become very hard to setup properly.Snapping to rotate an object is a weird concept, why is there no key to rotate an object? Never mind that, but why is there no key to snap to platforms on different levels? It makes placement of stairs or escalators very difficult if one nicely snaps to the floor and the other ends up ever so slightly outside the corridor because it has to be placed manually without snapping to the lower platform.Last metro station I was in had exactly two toilets, that's it. The fact they can't walk a couple meters without needing another one is a bit overkill. In general it feels as though the difficulty is ramped up simply by making them more stupid than the average person. I got lost in a metro station once as well because the signage was not clear, I get that, but when you have a sign directing you toward the next info panel and you still elect to turn around to go back to the entrance you came from then somethings wrong.All those things would be on my list before I would go around asking for 15 bucks for this game. The concept is novel, sure, but nothing that can't be done in Unity with some basic path finding AI and some basic "how to" tutorials so there needs to be some more stuff to justify that price. I am comparing to something like Overcrowd, which currently offers a bit more variety and replay value. I hope in the coming months this game can embrace some of the suggestions above, then I will recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this to be an extremely interesting and deep station builder. You can't just draw paths from station to station and have it work, you have to really plan how people will move through your station. Minor geometry changes to your station can be the difference between people getting where they need to go, or getting stuck with no hope of survival. However, there are a couple of problems. The main gameplay loop is drawing out new parts of your station while paused, then unpausing and trying to see where the problems are. The heatmaps are not really that useful since the game is all about moving from one point to another, so by the time something shows up on there the person it's highlighting is no where near where the problem was caused. Honestly if I could see the paths people take from a point, or between two points, that would be extremely helpful.Also, as many people point out in their reviews, the commuters are not incredibly bright. This is not completely a problem on it's own, but when I can't figure out why someone who was going from an entrance to the closest platform ended up on the other side of the map, it really exacerbates the issues.A good game though.
_childDocuments_.name: STATIONflow

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: Oh my, this is challenging and fun. I definitely like it more than I expected to!Long version:Deceptively simple at first then gets increasingly more difficult as you progress.I don't usually enjoy games that don't have you working towards a specific, set goal, but this one makes it work by having "unlockables" to strive for, different levels with different challenges to them, and a cash incentive to go along with your score, so if you want to stay afloat, you'd be better off catering to all the possible exits/entrances/lines, which makes it challenging. Plus, while it never flat out FORCES YOU to, it's implied that your "goal" is to serve all possible lines and entrances/exits.Also, ever since visiting London, I've always been impressed with the way underground metro stations are planned out. This was my chance to play with it and REALLY get to appreciate it!Pros:-Fun and challenging!-Different levels with their own challenges-Map editor-I usually get bored of sandbox games having no set goals, but this one keeps me interested at least until I unlock all the possible gates and metro lines, which can take hours for each level.-It's a metro system. I just... I just love those, okay?-You can work with angles! It's not just a grid!-Easy to learn, difficult to master-Fairly priced.-I love that this game takes wheelchair users into consideration. I always tend to build wheelchair-friendly places in games like "Planet Coaster", but it's cool to see a game that actually incorporates it as part of the challenge.-The building system is not without it's flaws, but I do like it.Cons (most of these are minor gripes, almost all of which can be patched if they choose to do so)-Elevators only have two floors for entry/exit. This is maybe the most annoying thing in the game right now. I'm currently playing a very vertical level with lots of floors and it's driving me bonkers trying to figure out how to set this up.-The amount of elevators I've accidently placed with one of their exits facing the wrong way is too damn high, and it's nanoying to have to demolish it and build it over again because of something like that.-A sign can't be edited to show that some destinations are over in a certain direction, but only some of them are elevator accessible, making wheelchair-friendly planning more difficult than it should be.-Minor gripe: Game lags when my station gets REALLY, REALLY big. Even though I have a pretty good (albeit old) computer.-Once your station gets really big, people start getting frustrated and it's not always clear why. You can click them to check, and it usually says they spent too much time in the station, but sometimes it's not clear WHY they spent too much time in the station. There should be an efficient enough route from where they were going to where they were going.Or alternatively: People getting frustrated about spending too much time in your station when their entrance/exit are on OPPOSITE ENDS OF THE MAP and there is litterraly no way you could get their ungrateful butts there any faster if you tried.Moving sidewalk update in the future, maybe?-When you add a new destination, you basically have to make sure all the relevant signs all around the station are up to date, on every set of stairs, elevators, etc. that could possibly be used to go there. This is fine, fun, and part of the challenge when your station is relatively small. But once you have a massive, sprawling station spanning 7 floors and as big as a village, it becomes more of a frustrating headache sometimes. Especially in the vertically-built levels.-Stores/services show their daily cost but not their daily profit. This makes it very difficult to know which stores are making you money and which ones are hemmoraging it.-%99 of the time it's fine, but sometimes a person will be lost even though there are signs/info panels right next to them, making me wonder "okay, but why not just USE THAT SIGN, then?!"Lots of grievances, but they're all minor, whereas the positives are very notable and enjoyable. If this game looks like it might be your cup of tea, I say go for it. Full price or sale price are both worth it imo.
_childDocuments_.name: STATIONflow

_childDocuments_.review: It's EA and there's only one map so far, as their blurb says (but I am assuming they'll add more in some way) but even still THIS GAME IS SUCKING MY BRAINS OUT.It looks daunting from the screenshots, and it kind of is, but the progression eases in nicely as you level up to recomplicate matters with more platforms and station exits that you need to link together. Your first attempts will look a bit weird since the building system takes a little getting used to, but you will come to appreciate its flexibility when optimising the flow and structure of everything. So, basically does everything it says on the can. I gather with the devs being after suggestions:- map generation (random and/or user-made - replicating Bank and Monument maybe?)- a few more construction options that you would see in actual stations, like double-back stairs or ramps.- optimisation at the higher levels (it's pretty good up until the fifth station on the EA scenario, then it gets a little chuggy.)- economy balancing, maybe some difficulty settings for that or for passenger tolerance - money does get easy to come by after a while.- maybe a few more snapping options in the construction tools (45/135 degree corners, snap to level above/below, that sort of thing)The freeform vector-based approach with a focus on traffic flow above all else makes a nice change from the usual orthogonal-based "airport/school/prison/shopping mall/medieval tavern" architect genre AND they've implemented it well which is why I'm so impressed even at this stage.

_childDocuments_.review: 《STATIONflow》 is a simulation business game. In the game, players need to build their own train station as a train station operator. This includes the construction of platforms, stairs, signposts, and public facilities (such as coffee machines).. Train as a public transportation is widely used in the world, I  believe that many people have complained about the shortcomings of local train stations. For example, too narrow aisles, unclear platform signs, no vending machines, etc. And the most interesting point about this game is that players can transform their own train station as a manager for the first time. Players can rebuild the train station according to their own imagination. You can either build a very spacious aisle or reduce the cost of infrastructure to save money. As a hardcore simulation business game, many times how to quickly let players feel the fun of the game is the key to attract players. 《STATIONflow》 did a very good job on this point. The first impression of entering the game for me  is that it has very detailed novice guidance. This helps players quickly adapt to the operation of the game and feel the fun of the game faster. Players will feel that the game is very simple at the beginning-this is facilitated by detailed novice guidance. But as the game progresses further, more platforms appear and more facilities need to be upgraded. How to set up concise and clear aisles and efficiently guide passengers to their destination has become the goal of the game. At the same time, you cannot forget your revenue and costs. Of course, the game is not perfect. For example, some annoying UI systems and some complicated settings. The scarcity of game content also limits the imagination of players to a certain extent.If possible, I hope to open up competitive elements such as we can visit other players ’train stations or compete in operations. I think this will add a lot of fun to the game.As a casual game, I think "STATIONflow" is qualified, although many people will be bored, but if you are interested in running a train station, this will be your piece of cake.1.Very detailed novice guidance.2.Interesting game mode.1.UI systems are not so good.2.Some operations are too cumbersome.（For example, set up signs for each staircase.）3.The game content is not rich enough.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game, starts off simple but it gets very complicated. It helps to plan ahead with elevators and escalators in advance (I found out the hard way). It is incredibly satisfying when you have a A+ station at Rank 20+ and you feel constantly challenged to make more efficient use of space/signs throughout the playthrough.There are a couple of things that I would like to see implemented however: Firstly, a useful tool would be to see a traffic map, made going from green to red in more congested areas. I find it hard to see which escalators/elevators that are always busy when I have five floors to manage. Secondly, the AI does seem to struggle sometimes with finding their destination, even though they are surrounded by signs telling them where to go. Works most of the time, though not flawless.Overall, a satisfying, challenging management game that I hope will be continually updated and improved as I look forward to playing more!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is similar in some ways to games like SimCity but also very different. The game starts out fairly simply, but the difficulty ramps up rapidly and you will find yourself starting over several times as you realize your design isn’t going to work. But it’s a fun challenge and an enjoyable game. My only complaints are that frame rate can drop when a station is crowded even on a relatively powerful PC, which is surprising given that the graphics aren’t that complex. Understanding the source of customer frustration can also be a bit tough, as something as simple as one sign can cause passengers to wander aimlessly.Overall a unique game and one that’s a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever been walking through a large train station, airport or transit hub and thought to yourself "This is poorly designed, I reckon I could do a better job of this".  Well, time to put that thought to the test with STATIONflow.STATIONflow places you in charge of a metro subway station, which starts off small and will slowly expand to become a hub station for a system.  The game gives you station entrances and platforms, and your job is to find a way to connect everything up in a way that all the thousands of passengers, commuters and tourists can navigate the station with no stress or delay.  This is such a unique concept for a game, and one I've always wanted to be explored:  station design.How do you this?  By building hallways, stairs, escalators and signs to get your passengers up, down and around your underground station.  Over time you'll unlock more tools like elevators, signs, bins and amenities like toilets but the basics stay the same throughout.  The most important tool is the direction arrow sign.  This is how the passengers can navigate around the station and what they use to figure how to get from a platform to an exit, or from one exit to another.  They'll use this to navigate through the labryinth that will be your station.  The idea is that you'll send different passengers in different directions, or flows, throughout your stations, controlled with signs.  This concept, while simple at the start, will snowball once more things add onto your station.Every so often, new entrances open up on the map in sets of 5.  You first start with A1, A2, A3, A4 and A5, and the next entrances are B1, B2, etc and they'll usually open on multiple floors.  You'll be only be able to progress if you connect them up and open them to the public.  Make it further than a few days and you'll get a new platform with new train lines, new amenities, new passengers with new needs and all of this is solved with construction, sign placing and planning. It can be a lot to take in but you do figure things out quickly and the game doesn't throw it all at you at once, rather ramping things up gradually.  You have time to get your bearings and figure out a plan but once you get going, things will keep happening in your station.  One minute you're trying to fine tune a design you have and then you have to accommodate a whole new set of hallways and entrances, new platforms, and you have to figure whether to demolish a whole section of station or try and smash something something.   It's amazing fun though, and you get into a good headspace doing it all.  You'll be figuring out how to get passengers across your sprawling station, trying to satisfy their needs and it makes you realise how much they rely on you to get them through this place.  Even once you think you've great plan, it always gets tested by a new development like tourist passengers, a new need for passengers like drinks or food or even a dreaded new platform to work into your design.The game isn't without its issues however, and I think any buyer should consider some of these before purchasing.  Some of these are small, others a bit bigger:First, once your station gets pretty large (15 exits, three platforms or so), you're going to have so many signs all over your station that it gets genuinely hard to see what's going on.  The signs are done with large arrows, which is great for the aesthetic design of the game, but the size of these arrows can't be adjusted.  This looks fine on the pictures in the store page as they have large halls and hallways, but you get a couple of hallways or big intersections together, and it becomes a maze of arrows, looking like a gigantic flow chart and it becomes so hard to read as a player.  The sign icons on the map take up a lot of space and just fill the screen and it would be nice to adjust the size they sit at, or have it so you press a key to reveal all signs.  Further to that, as your station expands you'll need to update every single sign one at a time and this gets incredibly tedious in larger stations.Secondly, and most importantly, the game absolutely chugs at times and seems to have a lot of problems processing all the people in the station past a certain level or certain amount of people in the station.  I don't know if the AI's pathfinding is good or not, as sometimes no matter how clearly I signpost a direction to go, how many maps or information booths I have set or how intuitive I make my designs, there are some passengers who still end up lost in the labyrinth of the station and make me lose ratings.  I guess that's par for the course in real life train stations, but it's still hard to know what is intentional and what is bad pathfinding. Lastly, I want more control over the station design here. I want to be able to put signs on walls instead of in the middle of a hall.  I'd like to be able to control access to hallways, with certain hallways or doors being open at a certain time like in peak hours or days of the week.  I want elevators that use space in a better way and don't just go down a single level (yes, elevators only connect one level to another).  I'd like to be able to update ALL MY SIGNS when a new exit or platform opens up, instead of having to find every single sign and update them one by one.  Going further, the game could have more to do outside of just maximising your station design and throughput.  I'd like there to be events that cause congestion at your station like a concert, a public demonstration or a train stops working and you have to deal with the effects, or maybe have things that affect your station like crime, garbage and similar effects.There's a lot of room for scope with a game like this, especially when the concept of 'train station design games' hasn't been explored at all.  Sadly, I don't know if the game is being actively developed or not.  The studio has not posted an update since May 2020, and the entire game seems abandoned.  Prospective buyers beware, it could be this game has been left to sit stagnant, and that should factor into your decision.  If the game has been abandoned, that's an absolute shame considering the gem of a game we have here, and the ways it could be expanded upon and developed.If you love games like Cities in Motion 2 or OpenTTD, planning and optimising your routes and making a system work at its best, you'll really love STATIONflow.  Get it on sale and I think you'd have a pretty good time!

_childDocuments_.review: Not recommended.Game concept is great.  Much of the implementation is great.  However, elevator implementation is bogus (allows only 2 floors); elevators are not available from the start, violating disability legislation; passenger pathfinding is very buggy; financial model is weak. Not worth paying for a half-finished, buggy, abandoned game.  Sad: it has a lot of potential.  I hope they'll open-source it and let someone else fix it.

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to recommend this game, but flaws, bugs and a developer who has disappeared has made it to difficult to do so.I was offered a key to this game without solicitation and I took it to show on my Twitch stream. I was so looking forward to taking this game forward, but the problems make it difficult. Lifts that can only serve 2 floors, commuters that ignore all the signs, get lost and then complain rather than actually looking at a sign, the fact that people demand things before it is actually possible to supply them. All this and more could have been attended to in order to make the game great, but Marcus has obviously ignored it to do better things.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall pretty decent station management game. The point of the game is to manage an increasingly large metro station with several different entries and platforms while also satisfying commuter needs like food, tickets, etc. I does a pretty good job and gets quite difficult. It's satisfying so see your station handling several thousand commuters at once.However, there are a couple of downsides too:- little explanation on the mechanics (you have to place signs so that commuters know where to go, but some of them are just straight up ignoring them, getting lost instead. Even when standing right in front of one, very frustrating)- default difficulty is no challenge- kinda boring late gameIf you like management simulation games, you'll probably enjoy it. When in doubt, wait for the sale

_childDocuments_.review: so sim city is sort of like this relaxing hand off type game.. where you make zones and the city builds itself.. and its kinda statistical and 'fuzzy'.. u can have a good city but never a perfect one... Factorio or infinfactory are much more direct.. like you directly control everything that happens to every item in your factory, by arranging conveyor bets and whatnot.. Those games have more defined goals and you can have a perfect system (though you could always have a more efficient one)  .. Station flow is interesting cus its somewhere halfway in between those two archetypes.. you dont directly control people with conveyor belts, they are autonomous, but you sorta do, by placing signs and corridors.. So you can have a perfect station where almost everyone is almost perfectly happy... Theres a similar satisfaction as with factorio and infinifactory, but its more hands off / relaxing feel like sim city, as you dont have to guide every person directly. Just place signs and they will guide themselves...Also it has some depth.. The UX is very very simple and intuitive, and hides a lot of info from you (which is good) But you can easily drill down and get a lot more info if you want. For instance you can click on a single person and see their full AI state.. their attributes, desires, what they can see, and what they are currently doing..The game loop has two parts 1. design and build stuff... and then 2. 'debug' you observer passengers using your new facilites and see if they are navigating it ok and having their needs met and make tweaks when things dont work or to optimize it.. Also when a passenger is really unhappy about something (ie. being lost for ages) it will be called to your attention with sound + speech bubble.[11:12 PM]I think the only area where the game doesnt excel is challenge, It feels like a sandbox without much pressure.. Theres is a system of structures costing money to build and upkeep, and getting income from passengers.. but its very very permissive.. It felt very sandboxy and I never erally felt under much pressure to optimise my station... Like, in simcity you pretty much spend all your money because you want your city to grow as fast as possible and have the best facilites you can afford, so you as they player automatically adjust the money pressure.. In factorio you have the big goal of building the spaceship to work towards, and you have the feedback of your factory attracting more and more aggressive aliens... In station-flow as your station levels up you will be required to serve more train platforms and exits, making it bigger and more complex, but aside from that ocassionally happening by itself there is no pressure.Though I am looking forward to playing on different maps, and adjusting the difficulty to make it a challenge, so my criticisms about difficulty are not final, only based on 1ts playthrough of the default level.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm afraid I have to give this game a thumbs down. The main principle is enjoyable and it has much potential. I will gladly change to a positive review if the major issues get adressed in future patches.1) Tourists walking right past information signs. I really tried all I can even made a specific arrow pointing right at the sign so you couldn't miss it.2) People too stupid to see there are several ATM-machines/informations-signs/shops etc. in one area, right next to each other. Instead of going to an empty one right next to the one they're queued in they all line up at only one sign/machine/shop thus getting angry having to wait.... the biggest issue is...3) There is no option having information about different means (stairway/elevator/escalator) on one single arrow. Why can't I tell them there is e. g. an elevator to platform P1 and escalator to Q1+2 and an B6 entrance/exit (accessible for all)? Otherwise why should I care?"Station Flow" already is a decent game but feels more like Early Access at this point. I'm really twisted while playing. _childDocuments_.review: The basic premise of the game is you build up a train station pretty much from scratch, and as your level increases you unlock more in game features.It is a simple premise and one that is the staple of pretty much all sim games of the past, all the way back to Sim City. And although graphics change and things become more detailed, the main premise always remains the same, you build something up, the game throws obstacle in your way and you try to overcome them.STATIONflow visually takes on an almost unique approach, it's minimalistic graphics give a real sense of something unique, and as you build more and more complex 3D layouts for your station, you really need to keep on top of things if you want to keep your passengers happy. All of this along with the usual budget restrictions, management reviewing you every day, progress reports etc, make this a fun game, if a bit frustrating at times.You can play the preset maps, or create your own, and although the preset maps are interesting, the create your own ones are the best, each play through you will realise better and more interesting ways to lay things out, you will probably start (as I did) making everything as easy as possible, but then on the next play through you will find yourself becoming more and more creative, and now that the game is live on STEAM, you can now share and download maps from people all over the world on Steam Workshop.So what's good and what's not so good about the game.Well the good first, it works as a sim game, it had the addictive nature that makes you want to start over, and then over again, as you come up with more creative ideas. The graphics are simple but detailed, and you will find yourself fully immersed in the game.As for the bad, sometimes things can get to "busy" on screen, and I don't mean the passengers, you will find that your view is obstructed by the very thing you are building, the arrow signs are guilty of this, sometimes lining up corridors with other buildings, staircases etc can be a pain, and if you are off by one pixel they wont connect, although the game brags that you are not constrained by grids, in fact a grid system here would probably help. The control system for moving around also seems a bit poorly made, although you do soon get used to it. There should be a way to easily update directional queues like the arrows or tops and bottoms of stairs, instead of having to do each one manually.These are little gripes I had when I first started the game, but I soon got used to them and worked around them, I do think the game makers could improve these things and perhaps they will if enough people are complaining about the same issues. But please do not let these things put you off.This is a fun game, I've spent hours and hours playing it, much more than I needed to play just for the review, I enjoy this game, and perhaps the little issues I have will be fixed and then I will enjoy it even more.I do recommend this game. And I score it 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's a Yes and a No.I like the minimalist look and it allows for some creativity. Mostly all of it comes down to your choice and your constraints are only the tracks and gates placement. This means it is also easy to create maps and there are some available on the workshop. It is cool watching something work out and once you grasp the basic mechanics it is quite simple. Which may be the first issue. Depth increases quickly but stops equally fast. In a sense that's not such a bad thing the game is really a relaxing experience with less challenge and bit more busywork which you can get around. Overcrowded has employee management and mechanics that make it closer to a Theme Hospital type game. StationFlow is mostly a puzzle about making sure people don't get lost and can reach some basic services. It will keep you up for a little while.The bad is that this may not keep you up for that long considering the price tag relative to other products. And the game was pretty much abandoned early on. Now the game works perfectly fine and besides the occasional pedestrian getting lost for no reason which is never game breaking, it is mostly bug free and performance is good. ( entirely CPU dependent, in todays market mostly everyone far exceeds the games needs but i can't speak for mobile devices ). I guess the standard is different today and this game doesn't need further updates but i feel like there is a fair amount of things that could improve the game beyond what it is now.. Such as expanding on services, more varied behaviors to give the people some life, more options for decoration.Things that i will add after playing a while more recently.Performance does get hard to manage. With a 9900KF the game will chug hard when over level 25. Doing any editing during the day requires you pause the game which is fine and the lock seems to run on time unlike Cities Skylines where the clock slows down to match the simulation slowing down progress. In the case of StationFlow this means progress isn't impacted but it does get very laggy looking at your bigger maps. I also suspect this breaks the AI behavior as you'll start noticing a lot of confused bots that seemingly ignore directions around them. It's hard to tell if it's due to actual bad management or bugs to be honest but even after making three complete revisions of the core map and a more streamlined layout there's still a major increase in confusion as the day reaches it's end.This may tie into a problem i've noticed with some specific configuration where almost everyone ignored a specific direction regardless of traffic. Bot types need a re-balance mostly with the low vision bots like gamers or elderly people. This essentially is a bad mechanic because all it does it make you place more signs that shouldn't need to be there increasing workload and clutter.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun - it's worth a few dollars, like 5, but once you've made a great station there's kinda nothing else to do. It just feels shallow right now.Making the layout for a station is cool. Managing signage and directions could definitely be implemented better. All the other features feel pretty shallow.  For instance - you can add cafes, food carts, vending machines etc. but you have no control over what they serve or their pricing. You can add info signs but they apparently don't help with people's ability to navigate your station. I added bathrooms at the end of every platform yet people are apparently constantly soiling themselves in confusion. For some reason there's a massive need for medical facilities in my station - even when I have one at every platform. Adding an office... does nothing? You can add ticket machines... once they're already in the station? There's no turnstiles...The whole thing would make more sense if people had clearly laid out needs, if you could see zones where people are affected, if signage were completely overhauled and made more sense, if there were employees and pricing to manage etc. But as is it just feels kinda empty and half baked at the moment. At the very least I'd love to run around my station from a first person perspective.If you're the type of tedious sim builder nerd who enjoys this game and it's on sale, I'd say grab it for like $5, otherwise bail.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. A masterclass in accessibility, especially. Customers with poor vision or limited mobility will act lost until you realize there's no escalator or elevator for them to get where they're going. Also, construction takes time, so if you want the system to stay up and running while you revamp a bunch of corridors and platforms, you'll need to build side paths and update the signage to match.So. Much. Signage. So you also learn to be more judicious about where you put corridors. And when it's easier for you to change the signs, it tends to also be easier for people to find their way around.A+ for a game that teaches you lessons you didn't expect to learn. Within the course of a game, my station evolved from looking like something a labyrinth of the 1920s to looking like more modern stations, because I learned why things do or don't work. Can be a bit confusing at first to figure out why people are lost or going in circles.

_childDocuments_.review: This initially looks easy, connecting up train platforms and exits with some corridors and then adding in signposts to let your virtual passengers know how to get to where they're going. And it is easy at first.But once you've unlocked another couple of rail lines and a handful more exits, suddenly it's easy to make a real mess of your corridor layout, and forget to update all of your signs. So you have a station full of lost, grumpy tourists. Then add in elderly passengers who cannot use stairs, and wheelchair users who require elevators, and the need for tickets, food, medical assistance, and more. It's quite challenging to come up with an elegant layout which offers passengers what they need with as little walking as possible.I'm enjoying this game a lot, though I would like to see some refinements, such as being able to link signs together so that you don't have to frequently update three signs that need to say the same thing. For example, if you have two escalators and an elevator all going to the same place, it would be nice to be able to tell the game to link the signs for all three together.I'm also wishing for travelators, to help shuttle elderly folk along long corridors when they're not able to walk quickly. (Perhaps if the game developer makes an AIRPORTflow game we'll get this.)Overall, though, very satisfying, and it really makes you appreciate why most metro stations have such odd layouts.

_childDocuments_.review: Management sims are a weird genre. How do you explain to your friends that in your free time you enjoy trying to build, maintain, and optimize a subway system? Well, that's the point I'm currently at. Overall, this game is a fantastic value marred by a few small problems. If you enjoy management sims then buy this game at full price and you will not be disappointed.The main premise is simple enough. You begin your journey with a fairly small metro with a handful of stops, separated by both vertical and horizontal distance. You have the freedom to make connecting the various stops as simple or complex as you want. As the days progress, you have more and more stops to connect to each other. Not only this, but some stops have the additional constraint of being directly next to a train line, meaning you are limited in how you design the entrances and exits to these stops. Additional challenges come from certain metro-goers not being able to take stairs or not having great eyesight and therefore need more stringent direction. As you get more and more stops, the game becomes exponentially more difficult, as adding a new stop is not just a matter of connecting it to the others but making sure that a passenger from any stop can efficiently make it to that stop.In terms of performance, there are unfortunate issues. I believe this game does not correctly utilize multicore CPUs, as when I have a lot of people in my subway and use the fastest time stop I drop into the single digit FPS despite running a 2600x which sits at around 20% utilization and a GTX 1060 that sits even lower. Although the dev seems active in the forums I have yet to get a response to a post I made regarding the issue.There are other QOL improvements that would go a long way. The way certain geometries interact can be a bit odd, and it's annoying having to repick an item from the build menu every time I want to build it. There is no way to have an item selected and be able to place it wherever you want as many times as you want.Complaints aside, I can see myself getting the itch every so often and coming back to this game but this isn't something I can see myself consistently playing. That said, in terms of management sims this is a great one. If you can play those management sims over and over then just grab this. Otherwise the sale price is more than fair.
_childDocuments_.name: STATIONflow

_childDocuments_.review: The perfect game to scratch that subway station planner itch! Now I can finally set up a Shinjuku station with good signage! Controls are simple, though the tutorials are a bit simple as well. Graphics are perfect for this kind of game too - simple yet clear. The soundtrack also has a relaxing vibe to it.
