_childDocuments_.review: Grime is a metroidvania with soulslike influence.Is it a good game ? would i recommend it ? well, its kind of a mixbag.PROTHE ART :First of all, the art direction is fantastic and the idea of the world (visual and lore wise) is simply very nice to look at, sure there is this "dark souls" feeling to it, but the world of GRIME come with new ideas that goes beyond another parody of dark souls, its his own thing and i salute the devs for this because it is clear that there were a lot of thoughs put into it.THE GAMEPLAY : will at first it seems to be your very typical 2D soulslike, it has a few twist on it, you will meet similar mechanics already encounter in many rpg/soulslike, but with a nice twist on it that will bring a feeling of fresh air to the overall experience (non linear skill tree, bonus for defeating ennemies, how the healing is handle, etc etc).THE SOUND : The music is ok, it set up the mood nicely. What i will remember more would be the ambiant sound in the cavern, the sound design can be on top and really differienciate a zone from another. CONLEVEL DESIGN :And now we come to the part where everything goes down, however lets begin with whats good in the level design.the region are nice to look at, there is a good amount of ennemy variety, good amount of secrets and secondary bosses and even after going to the next zone, you will still have a reason to go back to older region, to unlock mini zone or stuff that wasn't accessible before, there is a generous amount of exploration at hand.Now that all of this is said, everything is ruined by the lack of fast travel between "surrogate" (its how fireplace are named), wich is something very bothersome, because it kill all flexibility in exploration."there is this zone that i could explore, but its on the other side of the map ....... im stuck at this secondary boss, i should upgrade my weapon, but it would require me to go to the other side of the map again, so i might as well abandon trying to fight this boss and just continue playing."to be fair, i kinda lied when i said there were no fast travel, there is fast travel but not between surrogate, between checkpoints called "nervepass", those are checkpoints that you can find in (almost) every region, but they are fewer than surrogate and do not cancel the fact that you will have to do massive backtracking when you desire to do anything else than pushing on the main path, it is to the point were little thoughs like "why i am playing this ? why doing another 20 minutes of backtracking when i could do something else" would invade your mind, to the point of just shutting the game off.The worst thing is, it is a very well common critic that has been adressed by ....... adding more nervepass (checkpoints) wich doesn't fix the problem, quite the opposite to be honest, there are been a decade of FROM SOFT and souls-like games and this problem is quite common, this isn't a new level design problem, so i don't know why  we are dealing with this problem here.This isn't fun, this isn't immervise or engaging, its just time wasting/consumming, and in the end it will kill all desire of exploration.The weirdest part is that when you look at the map, the position of all surrogate is extremely well balanced in all region, they aren't many, they aren't place to close to each other, its to the point that im pretty sure that fast travel between surrogate was a thing at some point in developpement, but this is just supposition, the main takeaway is that i personnaly believe that the position of surrogate is well enough balanced to allow complete and free fast travel.CONCLUSIONIn conclusion, i truly think that GRIME is a good game that deserve more succes, but it is brought down by weird idead concerning navigation, completly killing the player desire to explore, go found other bosses/secret, killing the desire to play, the lack of flexibility make everything extremely tedious and turn everything into a chore.But beneath all of this, there is a solid metroidvania with a solid artistic direction, fresh takes on the souls-like genre and an overall fun game, its just a shame to see all of this masked by the level design, i would only recommend it before reading positive and negative reviews on the game.If there is a real solution found concerning fast travel (and not some solution make up like with the nervepass system) then i will consider updating this review and i truly think that this game could be quite accessible, in the meantime, i can only really recommend it to souls-like/metroidvania fans that have played the classics, but still want some more.

_childDocuments_.review: Original review is posted below.After beating the game and all of its achievements... I still can't say I really recommend this? Not at full price. GRIME is, in a word, frustrating. And not the positive sort of frustrating but the frustration from lots of small issues that build and build up over time.Pros:- The combat is good, most of the time. Your weapon hitboxes are fairly accurate, the majority of enemy attacks are readable, if heavily weighted to telegraphing an attack but releasing it after a small but noticeable delay later on to make parrying always  what you first expect.- The atmosphere and story design is fascinating, even if you're stuck in dim dull caves for 2/3 of the story.- The music and sound design is overall good. Not stunning music, but a few tracks are memorable, and it's not offensive. Except the final boss track, sadly; that's just orchestral pompousness.- The platforming is, for the most part, pretty decent.Cons:- The world design is full of gotchas: enemies that attack you from beyond range, enemies that leap out of hidden alcoves to attack you, enemies positioned right on the edge of ledges you need to jump to, enemies that explode as soon as you land on them, explosives positioned right there, etc. Enjoy the fact that the number of projectiles an enemy needs thrown back will increase over the game, but there's only one two ways to increase the damage (a trait which needs high ardour to work, and one that does NOTHING ELSE)- The map. Or rather, the lack of one; in far too many of the game's areas the Beacon to reveal the map is after you're halfway through it. It's more of an item-collection completionist aid than a functional exploration tool. Hell, there's one area that you can't unlock the beacon until after the boss.- Fall damage. Not just the you-fell-way-too-far-break-and-reform to stop sequence breaking or getting trapped, the "you skipped one platform on the way down, stun and take damage". It's annoying.- Combine all the above, and you have the usual "backtrack to find your Vessel and recover ardour" thing. At least you don't lose XP (Mass), but a lot of the level designs and some of the more involved platforming sequences are of the "redo it all once you fail", provided you remember the exact path you took (because you have no map, and you fell down something).- When the platforming doesn't work, you'll clip into walls, struggle to pull up ledges, fight with the ladders... or keep climbing through the platforms the game doesn't tell you can have a slingshot effect. Which nothing about the game or world design indicates is possible.- Traits. They're interesting, but let's say you want to respec. Okay, that's one of (limited resource) per --and at a certain point in the game, there's no more general enemies, so traits which aren't useful for the remaining bosses are dead weight. Minor, but also...- Ending fatigue. After one area, there's no more enemies, only two boss fights. And several pure platforming areas between them. JUST platforming. There are several weapons that are only obtained just before this last enemy-bearing area, if you backtrack to the right place to gather them.- And speaking of backtracking for items... 95% of exploration rewards are crap. You'll get a ton of low-tier upgrade materials even after you've fully upgraded whatever weapons you've chosen to use. Consumable after consumable which has to be assigned to a key to use, most of which are useless: next hit has increased breath absorption? Nonscaling throwing weapons? Armour?- Armour. It's purely cosmetic. Okay, that could be fine, sure. But... over half the sets are palette swaps of one outfit! There's about four  for armour total, and the most common one is just "your skin is a different colour", and most of those are shades of pink-purple. - The one good consumable restores your healing. Note, not health: HEALING; so it's not even a good emergency use. It's also impossible to farm or buy more of, so if you're someone that hoards rare resources...It's not like these can't be fixed, but the overall experience is one of exploring a world that only opens up for substantially easier exploration after the penultimate boss fight (at last, double jump), which is full of rewards that just . ====I agree with a lot of the comments--the game has promise in the mechanics section, but the developers need to make up their mind what they  it to be. Is this a soulslike with risky combat, limited levelling, and an emphasis on parrying? Then it needs to dial back the endless offscreen/secret cave enemies right after platforming sections.Is this a metroidvania where you should backtrack and use your newly acquired abilities to explore? Then fast travelling and map revealing shouldn't be so , to the point you don't want to do either because the exploration has minimal rewards and it takes forever to move anywhere.Is this a platformer? Then the ledge grabbing needs to be less wonky, and the platforming needs less enemy hordes waiting.The game is, right now, a confused mess where you can die too easily from all of the above things and then spend five minutes having to platform back to the exact same point  with nothing to show for it.Take the Nerve...something, whatever this area is called. You just finally unlocked the weapon upgrade hub, and to get to this area it's right a screen, down several screens, left several more, then there's some twisty platforming sections, and finally we're at the area enemies. Ah, but we also have timed electricity gates (which damage you), and a non-respawning enemy secreted somewhere away that causes unblockable attacks to come at you from below. Got hit by these more than your slowly-replenishing pool of healing will allow? Enjoy your five minute walk.If there were more checkpoints (not even necessarily ones you can level at!), and those were themselves fast travel hubs or unlocked as such...  it would be a much less frustrating experience. And if the map worked like a normal game map, and not a blank void until you find the beacon after finding everything else in your effort to find the beacon.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fan-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-tastic. I've played a lot of metroidvanias in my time, some of them great, some forgettable.  But this one is extremely memorable and an amazing effort that stands toe-to-toe with kings like Hollow Knight. It oozes atmosphere and unique graphics, and the ending sequence is really something that is going to stick with you for awhileOne of the most important things for Metroidvanias to get right is: a) make swinging sword fun, b) make jumping not suck. It nails both these, platforming feels fluid, forgiving, and not hard., Swinging swords feels meaty and packs punches. Unfortunately a lot of games fail at either A) and/or B) but this one doesn't. Did I mention it looks great? Because yeah, it looks great.There are some minor glitches but it doesn't detract from an extremely unique experience. Any metroidvania fan really needs to check this out because it's truly an unique experience with a very carefully crafted world and really unique plot.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried this game once before and bounced off, I came back to try it again because of the great support and additions it seems to get from the devs, bit I just can't get into it.I could probably finish the game but it's so slowgoing for me that I feel like it'd be a better use of my time to just play other games. It feels slow, the progression is slow, the mechanics, while interesting, are relied a bit too heavily on like absorbing foes, and ardor. Especially with the healing being tied to not just parrying, but absorbing. You can parry all you want but you don't get healing resource back unless you actually absorb the enemies.If you regularly have low ardor then it just snowballs into dying a lot because you're underleveled, so your ardor always stays low. And while the idea is you get double the exp/money with max ardor, it really ends up feeling like you just get half of what you need if you aren't great at the game.On that note, levels feel too hard earned, and not very impactful when you finally struggle your way into enough resources to gain one. The movement speed ends up feeling tedious when you've died a long way down a path you were exploring and have to track aaaaall the way back there through all the same enemies again, just to probably die and get sent back to the start of your trek again.Enemy hitboxes can be funky in that they can stand inside you, hit behind them despite the animation going in front of them, the attacks can sometimes be hard to parse in terms of parry timings, from a combination of speed and blending into the background a little. You can get stunlocked to death because enemies don't care what you're doing they'll just continue with their animations, especially if you miss a parry with multiple enemies around. Sometimes enemies will just stand there doing nothing when you're standing around waiting for an attack to parry.It seems like a great game overall, the aesthetic is interesting, the ideas are cool, but there are just too many little things that stack up into too much of a wall for me to push through when I could just be doing something else instead.I can see plenty of people enjoy the game, and for good reason, but I can't personally recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is a gorgeous compelling, and challenging game. It has excellent platforming, and combat. The world is loaded with secrets, secret bosses, secret weapons, secret areas. Like any metrodvania, the first few zones are slow, giving your character minimal abilities which results in less ways to solve problems. Grime is hard; probably harder than Hollow Knight, and this first salvo demands that you get comfortable with the parry mechanic or perish. With this introduction being the weakest point of the game, it is no surprise a lot of people leave early.I would say if you are not having fun by the time you encounter the boss of the third major zone, Lithic, you can probably call it quits. Otherwise, I'd stack it up there with any other platformer.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great Soulslike Metroidvania. If you enjoyed the likes of Salt and Sanctuary, Hollow Knight, Ender Lilies, or even just regular Metroidvanias like Bloodstained, Symphony of the Night, and so on, this one is a no brainer.The aesthetic is top notch. I love the weird deformed creatures that you fight. The enemies are varied and interesting, there are rewarding secrets all over the map, and each boss fight is highly distinct and memorable. The controls are smooth and responsive and once you get used to it, the absorb mechanic (think parries from Sekiro) is rewarding and intuitive. At the time of writing there are a few frustrations. Fast travel is clunky with too few warp points, and some of the bosses and environmental hazards have a few nearly instant kill gimmicks that can be frustrating. Overall, however, this is a fantastic effort that is well worth any Fromsoft and/or Metroidvania fan's time.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is a 2D Metroidvania set in an extremely interesting world. There is a lot to unravel as you make your way through numerous enemies and challenging bosses, acquiring mass, new armour and new weapons.The art direction is excellent, from the characters, to the bosses to some amazing vistas. For me, this was the highlight. The gameplay is very tight and what you'd expect from the genre. What sets it apart is the parry mechanic and its importance in dealing with enemies. It gave me some real Soul Reaver vibes. Bosses are challenging, yet I kept coming back to try again. Learning the patterns and skills required was enjoyable. This, along with the aforementioned style, sets Grime apart from its ilk.With a number of playstyles (thanks to the weapons and traits you earn) and customisation available, as well as a Developer that seems keen to keep refining the game, Grime is a great pick up. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've played that I'd describe as a Hollow Knight-like, caked in grime and sporting a few cracks, but fundamentally nailing its premise.What really struck me about Grime was just how unique and interesting the setting was. In a world where every soulslike seems bafflingly bound to retread the same story, Grime stands out as its own thing. The world full of cute little rock people, sinister plants, creepy body horror, and cultish societies is incredibly unique and engrossing, coaxing you in with exactly the sort of environmental storytelling this genre excels at. The story lands a little too far on the ambiguous end of the spectrum when all's said and done, but the originality helps make up for it. With a slightly clearer thrust to the central narrative, this could've blown most other soulslike stories out of the water.Gameplay-wise, Grime has some of the best metroidvania combat I've ever seen. It sports a great parry system combined with an invulnerable dash and a magnetic grab that can yank enemies into a vulnerable state. Individually these mechanics are all fun and satisfying, but combine them together and you get combat that sometimes borders on the stylish flow of character action. This shines strongest during the boss fights, some of which challenge you to repeatedly chain all of these mechanics together while working in hits to deal damage. Tough combat can get tiresome when the mechanics are basic and the challenge boils down to harsh punishment for slow reactions, but Grime never feels like that. The tools in your arsenal mean that there's always an obvious way to optimise your strategy, making repeat attempts on bosses thrilling rather than frustrating. Enemy attacks are telegraphed beautifully, patterns are varied and interesting, and platforming mechanics are integrated in an elegant way that makes it feel like you're bringing your full toolkit to bear.Speaking of platforming, that's the second main component of the gameplay, and unfortunately it doesn't hold up quite as well. It isn't bad by any means, but it lacks that tight responsiveness that always makes you certain of your next input. The 2.5D engine results in some occasional glitches with collision, mostly harmless, but occasionally offputting. While one platforming mechanic in particular is very fresh and interesting, the basic functions of jumping, grabbing, and dashing can sometimes be a little finicky. This all results in platforming that's very functional, but doesn't always feel particularly satisfying in the moment-to-moment. When I got to the end of Grime and started tearing around the world searching for all the secrets I'd missed, I eventually began to lose interest, not because I'd run out of things to do (quite the opposite!) but because I wasn't having all that much fun platforming. Again, it's not bad, but the endgame exploration really underlined for me that this isn't a game I would've stuck with if it were about the platforming alone.Speaking of exploration, that's the final part of the metroidvania formula, and fortunately Grime does it very well. Ever since the recent DLC, which expands and improves on the core game across the board, there are a lot of optional paths to take and rewarding secrets to uncover, including unique abilities that come from defeating side bosses. I had a blast getting lost in the midgame going through side zones and taking on harder challenges for greater rewards. There are tons of little secrets to uncover, items to find, and unique areas to progress through. No two zones feel alike, with different layouts, enemies, and environmental challenges keeping things fresh from start to finish. My only mild criticisms would be that the endgame leans a little too heavily on setpiece areas rather than playing to the strengths of the core gameplay, and there are just -so many- secrets that some feel a little underwhelming.Overall though, Grime has way too many strengths for me to get hung up on the weaknesses. This is a 9 that would be an easy 10 if it were tightened up in just a few areas. If you liked Hollow Knight, this is the closest thing to it on the market. In terms of combat and bosses, it might just be the current pinnacle of the genre. It's also got a chunky playtime of 15+ hours, with lots of optional content and alternate playstyles to extend that dramatically. There's an ambitious NG+ DLC coming soon that looks set to make replays a blast.Give this one a shot. It's one of the best in the genre, and definitely deserving of more recognition than it currently has.

_childDocuments_.review: Arbitrary system of positive/negative reviews aside, this game is more of an "eh" than an unworthy product. However, I can't recommend this.I actually tried to think hard about anything positive this game did, besides doing an impressively creative world building of earth creatures, toothy caverns, and still being an action-y platformer with the embraced metroidvania elements.Unfortunately, the rock formations are but one of the cornerstones of why this game is feeling like it doesn't leave a noticeable scratch:The story/lore isn't quite enticing, the characters only cause feelings of indifference, and overall the game just feels like it's designed with levels just sort of existing for the sake of being in places and to have some strange monstrosities to fight against. Which, again, do look quite unique.I still hold my respect for the devs however, because it is a nice looking indie game, from not just the levels but also in how professional the UI seems to be crafted. It's just that I feel no real emotion out of this experience, and why I cannot recommend such a game when there are plenty enough of metroidvanias on the market that have also done their own thing be it by gameplay or  design choices.If you like metroidvanias, I guess I'd recommend buying this on a sale at least, but I feel like the general experience was just not worth the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece, and I almost didn't play it. As I was in between games, trying to look at whatever I had in my Steam library, Grime was suggested to me. I actually already had it; I guess I got it from Humble Bundle.Anyway, the art and the trailers didn't really captivate me, as they weren't attracting me, and the gameplay looked slow. Eventually, I tried it, and I got hooked on it.Here's what you need to know: The game is a metroidvania-soul-like, like Hollow Knight and Blasphemous, for example, and it's heavily focused on parry. If that's not your thing, don't worry: you can use skill points to increase the parry window, making it easier to parry. Also, the game is not as punishing as some other soul-like games; it allows you to keep your soul's currency if you die.Hands on, and after getting used to the game, I don't find it as slow as it looks in the trailers, and now I find the artwork quite good. I loved all of the bosses! I think the battles are just fantastic, and the music is on point. The choreography was insane, and the bosses are very fair and pleaseant to fight.After I beat it for the first time, I couldn't wait to start NG+ and get all the achievements. In this mode, pretty much all enemies, especially bosses, have some new moves, and there are also some new goodies for you to get.It's been a while since I wrote a review. I just had to do it for Grime.Ending the review with the following comparison: I loved both Hollow Knight and Grime, but I have no doubt I had more fun playing the latter. I can't wait for the second game!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that positions itself squarely in Dark Souls' shadow. The art and atmosphere are great, reminiscent of both Dark Souls and Blasphemous, but despite its best efforts, the game doesn't have the polish needed to reach its lofty aspirations.Though none of the bugs are game-breaking (so far), they can be quite frustrating, and many aspects of the game just feel too rough around the edges. The key word is inconsistency. Attack and parry timing, animations, ledge grabbing, platforming, and boss fights can all vary wildly from area to area and even moment to moment. These are at their worst when the game tries to crank up the difficulty. For a game so obviously trying to be Dark Souls, that's a big problem.The Shapely Fidus boss fight is a good example. I'm sure some will hail it as genius design because a lot of effort obviously went into it, but it's ruined by poor telegraphs leading into stunlocks and one shots. There's little difference between a bare minimum success and utter perfection, making it feel like a final boss that drags on too long in an NES game, only with less consistency.I want to enjoy this game, but it's not easy for a small dev team to accomplish the same thing as a large studio, and this is one case where trying too hard leads to a worse result than just accepting your limitations. Even From Software can't always hit the same level of polish, with DS2 being a bit of a weak entry compared to any of the other three (Demon's Souls included). But difficulty without polish isn't fun or unique - anybody can make a game impossible. It's making it feel tough but fair that's the real challenge, and I think GRIME misses that mark.Ultimately, if this review makes you want to say "git gud" then get this game. If that phrase makes you roll your eyes, then it's probably not the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Metroidvania games are primarily about exploration, and GRIME offers the player a truly compelling and alien world to explore. Gameplay ranges from occasionally frustrating through functional to at times fantastic, but to me that's besides the point. The environments and enemies in which the gameplay takes place are genuinely unique and beautifully realised with A+ art, direction and sound design. Even if the game played terribly (which it doesn't by any means) I would recommend on the basis of artistic merit alone.

_childDocuments_.review: GRIME is a deliciously good game, incorporating elements from many successful games to create one wonderful hybrid experience. If I had to describe it in a sentence, it's Hollow Knight meets Dark Souls (again) meets Kirby.Just like in Hollow Knight, you explore a vast and richly detailed world, encountering lots of enemies, healing yourself by fighting and not getting hit. Just like Dark Souls, it has RPG mechanics, a stamina meter, and is truly brutally difficult. Kirby comes into play via the enemies - you can directly steal the power of enemies to use against them later on, which adds a really unique and fresh element to this mix.The combat is satisfying, with many playstyles to mix and match, and the gameplay heavily rewards skill. The design is eerie, dark and mysterious, and the world is filled with secrets to find. It's a solid metroidvania with lots to deliver, even if the animation is less than stellar and the difficulty a bit too much in my opinion.If you liked Hollow Knight or Dark Souls, this game is absolutely right up your alley. Likewise, if you like action-RPGs, metroidvanias, or very difficult games, this game will speak to you.This is not a game for people who want to breeze through it, or those seeking a complex narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never felt compelled to write a review as much as I do for this game, because it pains me how close to gold this game could be. It plays somewhere close to a metroid-vania that employs "dark souls" elements(gaining "mass" to spend on stat increases, stamina based action economy etc.). Starting off with what I liked, the world and the environment in this game is fantastic. Its a bleak and surreal world filled with its own fitting and unique creatures to the environments. None of your typical skeleton and zombie basic enemies, then armored skeletons, then etc. etc..., the enemies are very interesting and fit well with the world. So far, there seems to be an interesting amount of weapons, tools, and traits that you can employ to change up how you fight, giving a potential for multiple playthrus. Finally, it seems the bosses are pretty much the tailored focus of this game, having pretty interesting movesets build on exposing them thru the absorb/parry mechanic. Its an interesting world out of a surrealist painting, theres unique enemies that don't follow the typical script, and fun boss fighting.Unfortunately, this is not enough to carry the game. The issue I have stems from a very fundamental problem that cannot be fixed without taking apart the game from the ground up, the dark souls mechanics. The first issue is the stamina system does not at all fit the metroidvania genre, and this my primary issue with the game. Most actions are tied to stamina, but there really isn't enough stamina to do anything with. Heavy weapons get about 3 solid swings, but don't really interrupt enemies, so you will have to dodge, swing, then wait for you stamina to recover. Since this is a 2D game, its easy to just walk away and ignore the enemy for this time, no threat. There are even enemies where you can just jump on a higher platform and wait for it to recharge, then jump back down. Along with this, you also want to dodge foward to speed up exploration, which eats stamina, then being out of stamina and having to wait to take slow chops at a breakable wall is.... a minor grievance, but not fun. Stamina in this game doesn't act like a fun and intuitive combat resource, but more of a restriction to make sure you just don't dunk on enemies.The next problem is the absorb/parry mechanic. An interesting concept that doesn't gel very well in this combat environment. Combat generally goes like this...1. Wear down enemy shields2. Wait for them to throw an attack you can parry3. Parry/absorb then they dead.It never feels like a reward in combat for parrying, like it would in Dark souls or Sekiro, like oh we were fighting and I saw him using this move but I was quick enough to interrupt! but more like a "let me abuse this mechanic" kind of chore. Waiting should never be a heavily relied upon game mechanic, and this game relies a LOT on it. You gain more of the mass gaining resource by killing enemies and parrying, you gain charges of your healing ability back by doing this, and also you gain traits from enemies with this mechanic. The bosses I have faced so far do not seem to have an issue with this parrying system, and seem to benefit from it. The real problem is just the rabble enemies that make it unfun and tedious.I really want to love this game, and I am going to keep playing it and watching for updates, but at this time I CANNOT recommend it, as it suffers from such disappointing design flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd never even heard of GRIME until I chanced upon it while browsing the Steam winter sale, but it has quickly become one of my best games of the year. It's in the crowded genre of 2D metroidvanias with Dark Souls-like combat, but rises above its peers.The game's most striking feature, and the thing that first made me pause my Steam scrolling, is its visual aesthetic. Unlike many other Souls clones, GRIME manages to recreate the underlying horror and unease of Dark Souls without copying its rotting medieval aesthetic. Instead, GRIME chooses to creep the player out with uncanny valley and body horror. Everything in the game lies somewhere in the triangle of carved stone, wild vegetation, and too many human body parts in all the wrong places. It's gross and unnerving in the best possible way.On the other hand, GRIME's story is very obviously trying to copy the vibe of Souls games. It covers the main points of a world malformed and decaying, and you the protagonist attempting to shake things up by killing a bunch of grotesque monsters and gods. Overall, the worldbuilding is decent, but not as good as the Souls games. However, something about seeing misshapen rock creatures willing to be cut, carved and crushed to attain perfect human body proportions speaks to body confidence and dysmorphia issues that are haunting at an unconscious and primal level.However, it is the game's combat that is its best feature. It's standard Souls stamina-based combat, but stamina costs and regeneration speeds are much more brutal than Dark Souls. Dodges have good i-frames, but you won't have enough stamina to dodge everything while attacking. What you do have is a parry that costs no stamina, does not interrupt your stamina generation, and will become the key component in the game's combat system. Enemy health bars in this game are divided into red and grey segments. If you parry an enemy while their health is grey, it becomes a Repel and they get interrupted for a short time. But if you parry while their health is red, it becomes an Absorb, which is much more powerful. By Absorbing an enemy, you immediately deplete that entire segment of their health bar, and four successful Absorbs will give you a heal, this game's version of an Estus Flask. Essentially, skilled parrying functions as defense, offense, healing and stamina management all in one. Later on you get a force pull that you can use on enemies after they use attacks that leave them off-balance, stunning them and leaving them open to attacks. There are also unstoppable attacks that cannot be parried at all and must be dodged. This creates an engaging defensive game of parry/pull/dodge, similar to the deflect/mikiri/jumpkick/dodge system that is found in Sekiro. Combat in this game revolves around switching between attacking and absorbing to deal with grey and red health respectively, all while making sure to choose the correct option between parry, pull and dodge to avoid incoming attacks. I cannot stress this enough: this game will feel awful if you try to dodgeroll through everything the moment you feel like you're in danger, you need to recognise what attacks the enemy is using and respond accordingly.Another cool combat feature is the game's weapons. Every weapon archetype has a light attack combo that they all share, but each individual weapon has a their own heavy attack with its own unique mechanic. For example, two scythes in the game might have the same attack pattern for the light attack, but one of them has a heavy attack that reaches out and pulls enemies closer to you, while the other has a heavy attack that is a counter slash that deals bonus damage if you get hit during the windup. This means that choosing between weapons of the same type is more meaningful than just seeing which one has the bigger number, and it really encourages you to try many weapons to see their special gimmick instead of just immediately settling on one thing.The one part of GRIME that is somewhat disappointing is the platforming. It's not bad by any means, but it's a bit stiff and janky, which is a big shame for a platforming metroidvania. Many of the platforming sections require you to keep triggering the ledge-climbing animation, which is slightly too slow for comfort and tends to stop your momentum. One of the major platforming upgrades you get is the ability to dash towards fixed points in the air, which once against pulls you to a location and then kills your momentum. The double jump is also kind of floaty and laggy, kind of like Ness or Lucas in Smash Bros, but it is also slow, so once again you tend to slow down after using it. None of these are deal breakers, but when you traverse through platforming sections that you've gone through before you don't get that feeling like you do in more movement-focused metroidvanias like Ori and Hollow Knight that you can use your knowledge and experience to breeze through the area. I want traversal in a platformer to be fun in and of itself, but in GRIME it ends up being filler content between combat encounters.Still, GRIME is overall a fantastic game, with an engrossing world and challenging, deep, rewarding combat. Additionally, the devs are still actively patching the game, so we can expect to see problems be addressed and content be added in future. It's definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: This review is very outdated, as the devs have made all these changes (and more!) to the game, which is superbI really, REALLY like this game. It's super weird, thanks to its dazzling yet bizarre atmosphere, environments, and enemy designs; the surrealism isn't going to fit everyone's tastes, but it definitely was a highlight for me. The combat is well handled, complimented by excellent sound design that makes it feel that much more crunchy. Once you get a certain ability, the platforming also goes wild, and was another highlight. The bosses were inspired and a delight to fight; I don't think there is a single one I did not love, which is rare for any game to do.All that said, there's also some big downsides. The biggest one, in my opinion, is the fact that fast travel isn't unlocked until the final boss, which is... a BOLD decision, but not exactly one that pays off. Instead, there are a couple warp points and elevators in the game, and... that's it. Which for a game map this big, is not ideal, especially since in Metroidvania style, there are things that are closed off in earlier sections until you get the necessary power ups. My understanding is the devs are actually discussing changing that up, and if they do, then this game would definitely improve.Some tiny parts of the level design were REALLY frustrating, due to traps that were placed in really... mean and annoying places. These were worsened by the respawn mechanic that happens if you make a mistake during certain sections; some were so egregious that it spawned me on top of traps repeatedly and I couldn't do anything except die. The healing is also a bit unbalanced. The premise is, to heal, you have an energy storage that depletes upon healing, similar to Hollow Knight's healing mechanic. You need to PARRY four times to get the healing ability back, which is fine because the parry is generous and easy to learn. However, in the mid and late game, there are many enemies you cannot parry, only deflect, which prevents you from getting the heal; it makes hunt abilities (passive power-ups) like "get energy for the healing meter upon killing an enemy" mandatory to progress. And in a game where hunt abilities are limited, I feel it limits what you can really invest in that much more. There's other tidbits that annoyed me that were of personal taste, but these were more subjective, so I won't mention it. These negatives are things that I hope the devs do address, but they are things that didn't rob me of the strangely fantastic experience they intended to deliver.

I was very VERY pleasantly surprised when the first boss (which I took down in 1 try), kicked my ass multiple times. That more or less counts for every ng+ boss. Some of them ARE going to completely ♥♥♥♥ your ♥♥♥♥ up and others get an extra projectile or something. I didn't fight ng+ Shidra, since I went for the weakness ending and then subsequently unlocked the remaining achievements.The only negative I have about ng+ is the exact thing I was making fun off earlier - the maps, item placements or enemies haven't changed. Enemy patterns (maybe 60% of them) have changed, but the enemies themselves haven't. If you collected the weapons and armor pieces before starting a new cycle, you'll receive upgrade materials instead, which is good if you haven't explored everything beforehand, but personally I had more than enough stored up.Still a 10/10 in my books, even if ng+ turned into a slog where I had to rush the bosses to get to the end quicker. _childDocuments_.review: Grime stands shoulder to shoulder with the best soulsvanias out there. Grime is brilliant.Originally beat it on PS5 as it was added to PS+. Brought it for my Steamdeck this time because it's just such a fantastic game. Grime wears its Fromsoft influences proudly but is very much in it's own lane and doesn't feel derivative at all. Grime has an aesthetic unlike anything i've seen before with some areas and bosses being particularly grotesque (but not in a Blasphemous type of way).Cloverbite absolutely the nail the combat and exploration of Grime, with you needing to move through the game methodically as, being souls inspired, enemies typically hit like trucks. This is where the parry mechanic comes in. This is a parry centric title but the parry window is extremely generous and you can even target traits that give you a 40% longer parry window which, at that point if you're still missing parries, it's definitely you and not the game problem. Also, you can damn near parry everything!Grime is a tough game but it's not unfair. All the moves are well telegraphed and and even coloured coded so you just have to learn the rhythms of battle. Exploration in Grime is also well done, although there is a possibility that you might wander into an area that you don't have the requisite movement abilities to get out of. This happened to me - i wondered into Childbed unaware and couldn't get out the way i came in so had to do a mad dash to the other end of the biome to find my way out. It was tough down there but at the same time i came out the area at a higher level and better at the game for the experience so it's not always a bad thing. By the time you get towards the end of the game you'll have all of the movement abilities which just make traversal that much more satisfying. The weapons and armour diversity is also great. It has your standard strength and dex and then a sort of magic (resonance) - i didn't mess with it too much so i can't comment on it, but the build diversity with armour bonuses synergising with traits (you earn trait points to spend on abilities. this is separate to levelling), is expertly executed. You can get to point where you feel very strong against everything if that's you want to do.The story of Grime is quite cryptic at the start but all becomes clear as you and your little black hole made flesh make your way through the game towards an exhilarating finale. I don't understand why this game is more popular. If you like souls games and you like metroidvanias, then this game is damn near perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: GRIME is easily my favourite game of 2021. Despite my first playthrough being brought to an abrupt halt by a (since patched) game-breaking bug involving the last boss, I didn't think twice about starting a new run and doing it all again.GRIME draws inspiration from multiple genres, borrowing mechanics primarily from Souls-likes and Metroidvanias. You've got your Surrogates (Bonfires), where you respawn on death and level up using Mass (Souls) and Levolam Dust (Homeward Bones) to return to them. There's the usual ability gates to return to later with new upgrades, with the standard double jump and a surprisingly versatile and upgradeable Pull that feels like a fresh and mostly enjoyable twist on Ori's Bash. The game also implements a Trait system that I found rewarding: whittle an enemy's health down and Absorb (Parry) them to death and you'll be rewarded with an upgradeable trait, and each one can mildly or wildly change your playstyle. I started out using heavy weapons but once I absorbed Skewer and Madrock, I became a dodge and parry machine, not using weapons at all, and was immensely pleased this was a viable playstyle. This is because unlike being committed to an action in Dark Souls, dodging interrupts whatever action you're doing and unlike Hollow Knight, you can dodge through enemies and attacks without upgrades. Makes combat feel less Souls-like and more Cells-like despite the Force (Stamina) management.On the metroidvania side, GRIME's world is huge and arrestingly, grotesquely gorgeous. Did you think Hollow Knight's map was big? Did you ever stop to admire the stunning detail and motion in the depths of Ori's backgrounds? Do you like tight platforming, lots of secrets, and exceptionally well-designed boss fights? Ever play GRIS, where every frame was art? It's all here, wrapped in a singular, surreal, visual feast of an art style.My gripes are pretty minor. A few areas overstayed their welcome. Some secrets aren't rewarding and the arduous platforming to get to them feels like an insult to my time. A few complex late-game platforming segments were bugged, requiring a reload to reset individual elements in a chain that were no longer functioning, and Pull's targeting could be flaky. I still haven't unlocked some achievements despite meeting the requirements. I had very few performance problems, even at 4K, but at every resolution I played at I noticed an abundance of flickering lines, what I assume to be either seams between or overlap of structural elements that was impossible to ignore, especially in the city. All of these are easily addressable and probably have been by the time of this review. And that leads into my final point.That final boss bug I mentioned earlier? When I went to report that, not only did I discover the developers were already aware, but the fix was already done and in the next patch. Almost every issue raised in reviews and in the forums has been addressed. Feedback has been taken so seriously that parts of the game world have been rearranged to accommodate traversal and game states altered to avoid missables. Bugged saves have been manually fixed. An option to disable backstep and only dodge forward a la Mothwing Cloak was added on request. The latest patch as of this writing added armour sorting and stats with NG+ and additional story content in the works. Support the developers. They've made a great game, continue to make it better, and they're listening. TL;DR: GRIME is a must-play for any metroidvania fan, mashing together the best of and begging to be compared to its inspirational predecessors and standing tall among them, supported by a developer that gives enough of a sh*t to alter the very structure of the world of their game to implement player feedback.

_childDocuments_.review: I've always loved Metroidvania style games and I played a lot of Dark Souls, so a game that combined elements of both was a mixture I just couldn't refuse. It has a dark, mysterious world I genuinely wanted to explore from top to bottom, tough but fair combat and platforming, and a story told to you in just enough pieces to give you SOME idea of what's going on but still leaves room for your own interpretations. The world you explore is creepy and distorted and there's no telling what's waiting for you around the next corner. I also know not everyone is fond of the Parry mechanic in this game but I thought it added a lot of depth to the combat, giving it a good Risk Vs Reward system. Do you dodge the enemy's attacks and chip away at their health, or risk a parry to get some Breath back and maybe one-shot the guy? There's even times you NEED to parry just to be able to deal real damage to a foe.I found the boss fights to be quite intense and challenging, but also enjoyable. They seem tough at first but you can overcome them if you study their patterns and practice enough. I also liked how every enemy type and boss you defeat gives you a lore entry that sheds some light on the larger plot.Like any good Metroidvania, your curiosity and love of exploration is constantly rewarded, with new weapons and armor sets, items, currency, or even just a secret path that will save you time on return trips. The game is also fairly lengthy too, especially if you're trying to reach that 100 percent completion, which I have not but will likely go back and do so at some point. Overall, had a great time with this game, and if you don't mind your Metroidvania being a bit darker than normal, I highly recommend you add Grime to your collection.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most engrossing metroidvanias I've ever played. I can confidently draw a parallel between my experience with this title and my experience with Souls games, the first one, particularly. When I first played the demo years ago, it felt janky and clunky, just like when I first played DS. Visuals weren't anything special from that first impression, and quickly uninstalled it. Now I decided to give it a second try and I deeply regret not having given it a fair shake then.Some noteworthy pointers for me:- Ambiance: The game wears proudly it's souls influence. There's this sense of complete isolation within a completely hostile and unexplained world that progressively unveils itself with excellently crafted biomes. Story threads can be cryptic, but the more you advance, the more you want to learn about this truly weird and unique world. It's exceptionally immersive.- Controls: Snappy and conductive to some deep skill-based platforming, which the game certainly delivers extensively if you're diligent enough in your exploration to find.-Combat: while relatively simple, remains very deliberate and demands a level of poise and deliberate action, particularly with big slow weapons. It feels really good, and will reward learning how to best use your chosen playstyle while punishing recklessness and button-mashing. - Progression: Rock solid. I truly enjoy the fact you actually have to work your way through gauntlet-styled platforming sections in order to access certain items. The weapon system will feel familiar if you're a fan of souls games, with prerequisite stats and upgrades to improve weapons' power. Some have very unique and interesting implementations, although most are fairly straightforward. What I found the most appealing was the prey system, where you'd have to absorb enemies in order to access different upgrades related to their nature. Some are raw stat increments (+ life, damage, etc.) and some can truly change the way you approach combat itself by opening potentially devastating combos based on pulling enemies, or emphasizing on parrying and even damage reduction when failing to do so. These would be your "skill tree", if that makes sense, and depending on your gear, they can be amplified further through gear pieces properties and completing sets of gear.- Boss design: Fantastic combat mechanics that can be unforgiving, but never unfair or cheap. Everything is telegraphed, and you know every death is your own fault. Most bosses are visually imposing and feel wonderful to conquer, accompanied by epic tracks to highlight their importance. They'll kick your ass, but that only makes them that much more rewarding to fight.- Visuals: Once you understand the overall "greyness" of the underlying themes in the game's story, it successfully delivers some awesome visual design, ranging from interesting enemy design seemingly produced by really creative kit-bashing of claymation models, to really good lighting design to convey different moods across each biome. It's a really unique looking game, despite it's initially unassuming and subdued visual presentation. Sometimes you'll come across unusually colourful areas, which make a nice break.- Sound: Music is great, ranging from alien ambient noise-based tracks to epic boss battle tracks. It's very immersive and complements the bizarre story nicely. some weapons could've used a bit more oomph in the sound department, but it wasn't detracting to the experience, and likely just a nitpick of mine more than anything else.- Map design: Metroidvanias live or die here. Grime's map is MASSIVE, but really well thought out, and doesn't make backtracking needlessly tedious like it happens in so many games in the genre. As I mentioned before, I appreciate the gauntlet platforming sections. In other games you'd just break a wall and stumble on a powerup. In this game breaking the wall is just the door to a challenging section that compels you to step up your game and earn your reward. I wish more games did this. Objectives will be loosely insinuated with a pointer, but the game definitely won't hold your hand, which is a big plus in a metroidvania for me. I HATE the GPS syndrome many of them suffer from, and this one fortunately kept that to a bare minimum.Overall, this is a title every metroidvania fan ought to treat himself with, especially if you love the challenge and value organic exploration and immersion. It'll literally suck you in, pun intended :).

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit skeptical when I saw GRIME's steam page at the indie festival. But there was a demo and I decided to download it... aaand it earned a place in my heart around 20 seconds into the opening cutscene. There are design tropes I hold dear - such as object heads, wax drippings, candles, multiple hands or eyes arranged chaotically - and I haven't seen it done this good before. You'd think you can't have the themes of body horror and space (another one of my favorite themes) in one game - and yet here it is! And all of it is done beautifully, I must add.Gameplay-wise it's exactly what you want from a souls-like game - dynamical and unforgiving. This is actually the reason why I keep saying we don't need more hunt points and the weapon requirement system is fine - Grime is supposed to be hard, it's a damn soulslike, not a match-3! And while I was legitimely angry at some points of the game (burning needle throwers deserve a very special place in rocky hell), I think this is proper level of "hard" and it never felt unfair - to me, at least.Yes, there were bugs and there are bugs, but show me a game where there's none. Then again, it's the team's first game, and even though Yarden prefers the harshest criticism possible, he and his team did an awesome job. I really hope for more Grime later - when everyone had a proper rest from the exhausting release.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is either about a guy with a literal black hole for a head wrecking everyone's day and ending them because he can, or it is a wise critique on nihilism and accepting the end. Overall i had a pretty good time with Grime, and find it well worth the asking price. Playtime is around 12-14 hours if you want either of the endings, and most likely 5 or so hours more if you want full completion.Graphics- 10/10 Sound Design- 10/10Story- 6/10World Design-7.5/10Level Design-6/10Gameplay (Have to split this up to better reflect my thoughts on this):                -Overall 7.5/10                  -Combat 9/10                  -Platforming 3/10                   -Mechanics-6/10Bosses-8/10Overall a solid 7/10, and would recommend to anyone looking for a good metroidvainia. Definitely enjoyable, but with some major issues with design choices, centring around platforming and combat. Full Review:Grime is a superb metroidvainia, but suffers from questionable design choices, mainly indecisive direction with the two main elements of gameplay- combat and platforming.In terms of sound and visual design, Grime is absolutely stunning and perfect- each area reeks with its own atmosphere and charm, with richly detailed backgrounds and sound design- audio immerses you into the world and makes it feel alive (ironically). The soundtrack is definitely a highlight of the game- made by the brilliant alex roe, every track feels perfectly appropriate and helps enrich the game further. Bosses are made so much more intense with his grandiose and bombastic soundtrack centring around strings. The story revolves around you- who i'll call Grime- journeying through a truly terrible and gore filled world, with pained and sad and brutal creatures inhabiting it, to the very apex of it to reunite with your kin. A wonderful premise of course, until you realise you have a blackhole for a head, and forcibly absorb everyone into said black-hole when you kill them. Grime's journey has it meeting many wacky and strange characters, including one who literally makes a cult for you, and eventually ascending to the apex of the world. The actual story itself isnt necessarily a problem- its a simple metroidvainia journey- but instead the finer points that are so astoundingly cryptic that it would make dark souls blush. Lore entries are often very light, and give very little information, so that by the end of the story you have nothing but an illumination of the characters and history of the distorted world. The endings are the complete opposite of this however- a simple cut and dry either you do this or you don't- the choice to make is given right at the final boss. Overall i think it could have used a bit more exposition from characters on the state of the world, but it is usable.World design is fairly good, with several areas wrapping back into eachother, making traversal from objective to objective fairly intuitive. Areas are logically placed, and secret areas are not too difficult to find. Level design is significantly weaker however, mainly stemming from the fact that almost every area is designed as a simple maze of rooms or caves, with no visually distinct traversal style on the map. In addition to this, traversing between areas and through the world is slow, and tedious, with the traditional souls like teleporting only being unlocked after beating the final boss- of all the design decisions i have to say this is the most baffling- there is a alternative fast travel from individual points outside of checkpoints, but this is sparse, and the network only helping navigate from seperate regions of the world, not within areas. Gameplay is uneven in its quality, which is a shame because grime has a lot of potential. I feel that grime is trying to be too much of a jack of all trades, and not actually mastering any in the process. The combat is brilliant, and centres around a parrying mechanic that allows for dynamic responses from enemies, which makes combat encountres, especially boss fights, incredibly fantastic, with responsive gameplay and movement options. Weapon variety is excellent, but some balancing issues are present between different gameplay styles.  Killing certain enemies with a parry enough times allows for traits to be unlocked, which increases the variety of playstyles, but sometimes not having certain traits for certain encounters can make things much more difficult than they should be. Healing deserves its own paragraph. Healing Grime requires filling a "breath" bar, which is only replenished through the absorption of enemies (killing with a parry) While a solid enough premise at first, i feel like the developers began to forget that this healing mechanic existed, and made most enemies in the late game downright unabsorbable. There is a trait to help this, but it requires so much investment that it can screw you over in boss fights. Speaking of which, all late game bosses do not allow in-fight absorption, only parrying. Which makes healing more opportunistic endeavour, needing to conserve it as much as possible. There are ways to help this, by increasing the maximum heals you have (to a max of three). Platforming deserves its own space at this point, by virtue of being the thing that enraged me the most about the gameplay. While not necessarily finnicky or needing too much precision, it was the nature of the platforming that was the most egregious- if you think you're going to have your combat seperated from platforming, think again bucko- long platforming sections have immediate combat sections afterwards. This made everything utterly irritating, having long since used the sparse healing system and opportunities. Ultimately i found most of the platforming ideas not to be novel, just more of a distraction from the combat which i always wanted to get back to, and often for long periods of time i did not get to. This was my point with grime- it was trying to do both excellent combat and platforming- and only succeeding in one meant the overall experience was detracted from. If any expansions are planned, please do not expand on platforming and focus fully on combat, or just choose one or the other. Bosses were the highlight of the game, and used the combat system to its fullest capacity, each steeped in personality and design. Difficulty greatly increased towards the end of the game, giving me some extremely satisfying experiences with bombastic scores to go with it. I think there was only one boss with any mechanical issues, and those were minor. The final boss was a slight dissapointment due to its refusal to use the parrying mechanic for its entire first phase, and that i had managed to completely guess that it would be the final boss- something the game itself even acknowledged. Overall, a very good metroidvaina with stellar combat, that suffers from some disjointed design decisions. Definite recommend for anyone looking for a very beautiful metroidvania with dark souls esque story and sekiro like combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Just in case you need more (but why would you?), here we go...Am I wild about 2D soulslike games?  Blasphemous is the odd exception based on its presentation alone. Am I wild about labelling every other action role-playing game and metroidvania a soulslike?  Stone and sand spring forth with anatomical features of faces, eyes, mouths, and hands. They make up the background, your platforms, and your enemies. In contrast, the protagonist has a black hole where their head should be. I can sympathise. That feels like my head most days. It's a complete testament to its world and how it's presented that what could be considered flirting with boilerplate metroidvania and soulslike design is completely muscle-upped.  This is a game genre for which plot is usually left as environmental frills. Thanks to some really standout moments accenting said story, however, Grime really sets itself aside from the usual Dark Souls copycats. I'd take an actual 3D Souls game based on this world any day. I'd argue that undersells the experience, though. It really is greater than the sum of its parts.  The platforming is as deep and well-executed as its combat. The maps are large, but never labyrinthian and just packed with hidden paths and nooks. Grime is a delight to explore and it truly is huge! This is the paragraph I just effuse over random I liked apparently, but my point is that it's the sheer quality of everything on show that means when the music swells you can't help but smile and reflect on how great a time it's all been. The absorb-parry wherein a timed block sees you damage/absorb an enemy's health has plenty of strategic nuance to it. Different enemies have segments of health bar vulnerable to absorbing, you can absorb sequential hits to build up your attack damage, and absorbing both fills a meter to regain health and increases up to a max figure of 100+ the proportional 'souls-like' currency you gain per enemy and from the environment. It's really solid stuff mechanically and this is echoed in everything combat-wise. You have a generous dash that lets you phase though objects, enemies and through small environmental gaps. You have a backstep and those oh so familiar 'learn the window of opportunity of these' light and strong attacks - all of which drain from stamina (force). Most interestingly, a telekinesis ability you can use on platforms and enemies alike.  Just as challenging and interesting, particularly as the manipulation of platforms is married with portal-esque momentum, double jumps, and double dashes. The one thing I can say is that Grime withholds something as fundamental as a double jump for much MUCH too long. If anything is symptomatic of the inherited formula here, this is by far my least favourite element. And the soulslike combat framework of 'challenge-die-collect your corpse' 'sees a solid recapitulation here for sure. With, however, the very solid change of never seeing you lose your 'souls' with death, but only your souls-multiplier value.  Here the incentive is still there, only you can quite happily completely ignore it if you fancy going a different path and you won't see hours of progress derailed. As ever, the latter two are the stars of the show here, but I think what makes fighting such a good time here is not only the very varied (but always manageable) enemy and attack variety, but the absolute mass of weapons you find with which to show them your variety with. What makes exploration an absolute joy is that every corner seems peppered with surprise weapons with dramatically different playstyles and special attacks.  You're constantly invested in something, be it increasing some stat to use that next weapon, absorbing a number of that new enemy to unlock their red gem passive ability, finding this area's map-granting crystal, and where does this odd passage lead - a whole secret area no less!

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, but barely.Really cool worldbuilding, had me theorizing the whole time, which is sorely missed from games now and days. The aesthetic is pretty interesting in most cases, a little basic in some other areas.I really enjoyed the platforming parts, usually in 2D games i suck at these parts but the Mantling I think really helped. (I just wish the mantling wasn't bugging out half the time)I haven't played Nine sols or w.e yet, but this game felt like 2D Sekiro to me with the Repeling & Absorbing & Pulling, and when it all worked and on some bosses it felt great, You had these moments a lot more then you did in Sekiro (or at least in my playthrough... ugh trauma)Also one really big point of positive feedback this game does right and a lot of other games fail at. It does a great job forcing/teaching players to learn the skills of the game. Be it platforming or enemies that lead up to bosses to help reinforce usage of said skills, to semi prepare you for the boss. This is imo one of the fundamentals of gamedesign especially in RPGs/ Action Games, but always dismissed or ignored, it was really nice seeing this.   - (Tangent of a game that doesn't do this. I didn't master the Parry in Sekiro till 10 hours into the game. That is way too late, and a part of it is, a lot of early games just make you lightly need to use it, you aren't required to use it) While in this game, if an enemy has a shield, you have to parry to remove it, or to heal... etcBut.This game is buried under a lot of issues, that really stick out and make the game frustrating in a bad way and pretty often.- The game is buggy. Just from almost an hour into the game to 19hrs I just kept having bugs. These bugs got me killed a lot.- Almost every shortcut in the game are either pointless or sometimes more obnoxious then the main routes. I felt this from the first 2 or 3 hours to late game.- My god the Parry. The timing window is awkward and weird and inconsistent (You will see this word often, and it's one of the biggest issues of the game) Sometimes you have to actually wait till you are hit before you can parry. Sometimes you have to parry wayyyyy before you are hit. I put 3 or 4 points in the trait that upgrades this and only then did it START to stop feeling awkward and janky (still was tho)- Inconsistent Enemy Patterns & attacks or Similar attacks (Example: Giant with Eyes boss, I found this boss the most in the game probably over 40 times(Mainly because I tried beating him too early) 40 times. On the roughly 38th time he used a lean forward punch that he never used. Like wtf. Over half of my attempts got him to the second phase, so they were pretty long) A lot of enemies have attacks that look the same but have different results, making it hard to learn patterns and react- Inconsistent Hitboxes (Example: Theres an enemy that that jumps and does a flip. You can just stand under him and not move and he will prob jump over you. On a couple occasions his toes hit me resulting in my death. There are dozens of enemies that won't have hitboxes that hurt you sometimes then suddenly do)- Reaction Times are incredibly small, it felt like someone played Sekiro and was like what if i making the timing windows and reaction chances smaller.- Camera gets stuck in certain preferred positions sometimes. Lead to my death a couple of times.- You can get a Breatheart in a normal playthrough (Non-NG+) and you can't use it because it's meant for NG + :upsidedown-smiley:- Inconsistent Art Direction/Design Led me to a lot of deaths, where you would see a glimpse of red  or yellow and be like is that blockable or pullable? Oh well reaction times are too small, so that thought.. you are now dead.- I love Souls-like games, but this game forces you to die multiple times to learn enemy patterns/movesets. Some legit feel like they were meant to kill you until you experienced it 3 to 5 times.- Inputs, something about input queueing feels off or just non-existent (Dodging in wrong direction, you can't dodge and pull... etc)- Worldbuilding is really good but they don't delve deep enough into it in each area imo.- Edit: One last kinda vague but big one: There were a lot of weird design decisions/tuning, i've highlighted some already but here's a couple examples other in other reviews have called out. Beacons: Are pointless because by the time you find one in most cases they are at the end of levels that probably took you 10-15 + attempts to get to, so you have already mentally mapped it out. and theres only 20% left to explore. Nervepasses: were in weird unuseful spots and barely used, then you get the surrogate upgrade at the 95% part of the game, making them just pointless, so teleporting in general is a missed opportunity. Shortcuts & Zone Connectors: There are a couple of extra zones that aren't really cool or have story, or really serve much purpose, besides hunting points. I discovered there were connections to other zones, but finding this at the 80% part and when they connect to the first zone and you never pass through the first zone, this is pointless? Items & Rewards: A lot of rewards/items are overused and don't warrant the hassle it took to get it. In a lot of cases. Overall about halfway through i felt like i had a grasp of the game and was really enjoying the worldbuilding and platforming, if either one of these had just been a little bit weaker, i would have quit the game at the 4 or 5 hr mark and gave it a thumbs down. Because throughout my playthrough i was just being attacked by bugs. Bugs killed me probably around 40% of the time. Which is incredibly high in a game like this.I do look forward to the second one, to see more of this story, and hopefully the bugs have been fixed :)

_childDocuments_.review: Like many of its contemporaries, it struggles a bit with difficulty in the early going. But, once you gain your footing, this title bravely faces its competition and—after much effort—overcomes them. This is one of the greatest titles ever released in a genre packed with masterpieces and it can easily hang on Olympus with the other greats. GRIME is ,as the credits describe, “passionately developed” by Clover Bite, who sent it soaring over the fence in their first plate appearance. Every pixel of this is lavishly detailed, dripping with art and tone, encrusted in a world beyond small understanding. I am willing to stake that it is the best-looking 2.5D game ever made.The same love is applied to the gameplay and especially the BOSSES. The bosses in this thing!!! They will make you try 20 times but never feel frustrated. It is so rewarding to learn a bosses’s tells move by move and to then be able to navigate the fight like a beautiful dance, which becomes humorously literal at one point.Can’t recommend this enough to any metroidvania fans. 2.5D metroidvanias are really having a moment

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favorite games in recent memory. I've long been looking for a game that offers the same joy of exploration that I got from Ori and Hollow Knight. This is that game.There is an incredible density of secrets packed into this game, which is doubly impressive considering the monstrous scale of the world. The story is fascinating and cryptic, told mostly through environmental cues.The combat takes some getting used to - I tend to prefer responsive, platformer-like controls, which this game does not offer. That said, after a couple hours I got the hang of it and I'm *really* digging it. It's satisfying in the same way that combat in Sekiro is satisfying. But hey, if you don't want to parry, then just dash the heck around.At 18 hours into the game, I'm currently sitting at 186 deaths, so needless to say I am very good at this game. The fourth boss killed me a measly 45 times... very embarrassing for him.By the way, this game is a Metroidvania in every sense of the word (I noticed someone with 1 hour of play time claiming otherwise..)

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is an absolute masterpiece, a perfect blend of intense, challenging combat, rewarding exploration, and stunningly unique art design that kept me enthralled from start to finish.The combat is brutal, precise, and incredibly satisfying. The ability to absorb your enemies to grow stronger and even heal yourself is a genius mechanic that adds layers of strategy and depth to every fight.Boss fights are both interesting and demanding, but not impossible. Each boss is a memorable and grotesque work of art, requiring you to master the game's parry and dodge mechanics while adapting quickly to new patterns and surprises.The world of Grime is dark, twisted, and beautifully crafted. The level design is top-notch, with areas full of secrets, hidden paths, and rich lore. Speaking of lore, the story is complex and compelling, delivered through cryptic dialogue, environmental storytelling, and item/enemy descriptions that gradually reveal the history of this strange, sad, sad, SAD world and its inhabitants.Grime also delivers a haunting and immersive soundtrack that perfectly complements the game's dark and mysterious tone, adding another layer of immersion that pulls you further into the world.As a con, I would mention some imbalances between weapons, as well as platforming elements that become quite demanding toward the end of the game—not my cup of tea.Overall, Grime is an absolute must-play. A masterpiece with deep combat systems, intricate level design, unique art style, and rich lore that deserves all the praise it gets. I realy enjoyed this game and I can't recommend it enough. I eagerly await its successor.
