_childDocuments_.review: This was a solid Metroidvania which I nevertheless found more frustrating than fun.  It draws a vast amount of inspiration from Dark Souls, so if that's a thing you like, I think you will like this; however, it relies very aggressively on trial-and-error gameplay with inadequate handholding, and as far as I'm concerned I have better things to do than play a game which forces you to repetitively replay minutes of backtracking because you need to "git gud" at a boss which kills you in 30 seconds -- and on top of that, offers no guidance as to whether you are even appropriately leveled for the boss or not; I spent about two hours beating my head against Misbegotten Amalgam before giving up and checking internet discussions, where it was universally agreed that you should take him out after getting the very-late-game double jump, and then came back after doing so and wiped him in less than half an hour.Compared to Dark Souls, this is actually forgiving.  Dying doesn't cost you currency, only "Ardor" (a multiplier to enemy drops which also scales some of your optional skills), so if you're stuck you can at least always effectively grind.  But a lot of your advancement is gated behind, effectively, luck.  You don't get to see area maps until you have discovered the "beacon" for each zone, and while there are some visual cues when you get close, for the most part you're stumbling about with no map guidance, seeing only a little dot trail you've left behind in the darkness.  (Some zones, like the castle, put the beacon in LITERAL HIDDEN AREAS.)  Why even bother with a map if you don't have it while you need it?  I vastly appreciated Hollow Knight's non-awful take on the same enforced map blindness; in that game, you opened up the map as you explored, but that exploration progress was erased if you died, and maps only became permanent when you bought them from a vendor or made it back to a save point.  That felt like it provided incentive to make incursions into new areas; as long as you could get back the way you came, you could always run into a new zone, map it, go back and save, and then your time spent was meaningful.  Here, the incentive is to YOLO forward blindly and hope that you're not retreading ground you covered long enough ago to expire your trail, and maybe if you're lucky you'll stumble across a new save point or a beacon, and if you're not, well, you're just going to die many minutes' walk away from anything you know how to navigate, and maybe you can try to retrace your steps to find your body and pick up where you left off.  Meanwhile, you're so fragile that you'll be dying repeatedly to minibosses (which blessedly stay dead when you kill them) or just bad combinations of normal enemies (which don't, and screw the Servant's Quarters and those red-hot needle snipers you spend your entire run dodging)."git gud" no, f**k you.  Check my achievements, I ultimately stomped flat the game.  But it was tedious and frustrating, and there are better ways to design an experience that makes it fun to learn the intricacies of the game.  Would it have killed them to make clear that you can grapple enemies, too, when they open themselves up and get a brief yellow aura?  That's another one I learned from internet reading, because if you don't happen to notice that those auras are the same color as the attachment points then you just get to fight enemies the hard way (there are multiple bosses that grapple is an integral part of the recommended strategy, one of the few reliable ways to get good openings).  Meanwhile, you get an absolute ton of weapons and armor, out of which you will use approximately two all game.  Because of the Souls-like heritage, armor just gives you flat percentage boosts to certain stats (and a skill boost if you wear a full set), which means that once you've locked in your build there is only ever incentive to wear the set for that build, and maybe the one which gives you a currency gain boost.  Weapons are all basically balanced against each other with the only difference being attack patterns and speed; but, again, you're punished for not locking in your build early, so you're going to mostly be picking up weapons which require leveling up attributes you don't have, and the respec items are so few and far between that changing builds midstream is a Bad Idea.  The end result is a deep system which you are punished for trying to explore, and that's a Soulslike problem, not a this-game-in-specific problem.So what did I like?  Controls are pretty tight; once I had all the abilities (again, double jump is acquired so late in the game that you only have it for map cleanup and the final boss), the final platforming challenge sections flowed well, certainly more so than the endless boss refights.  The primary "absorb" mechanic (parry melee attacks and do damage in return, as well as learning opponents' powers; deflect many ranged attacks back to their source)  has forgiving timing and always feels fun to pull off.  Once you get used to the slower pace of combat (screw that, I used some of the Very Fast knives and added stamina recharge speed to my DEX build), combat is generally fun, except for the parts where you have hit stun and no invincibility so you can take egregious damage by accidentally taking the first hit of a combo on the chin.  It's a gorgeous game, with vivid ambient sound (especially in the Garden) and several solid battle themes.  Just, I kind of wish it had also been fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is a true masterpiece that has left an indelible mark on my gaming experience. From the very first moment I stepped into its beautifully twisted world, I was captivated by its unique blend of dark aesthetics, deep combat mechanics, and an enthralling narrative that took me on a thrilling journey of self-discovery.Visually, Grime is a work of art. The environments are meticulously crafted, seamlessly merging the grotesque and the beautiful. Each area feels distinct and full of secrets waiting to be unraveled. The attention to detail is astounding, and the haunting soundtrack perfectly complements the eerie atmosphere, immersing me in this otherworldly realm.But it's the combat that truly sets Grime apart. The game introduces a fascinating concept where the protagonist's abilities are shaped by the enemies they defeat. This innovative mechanic added a layer of strategy and depth to every encounter, making each battle feel like a rewarding puzzle waiting to be solved. The fluidity and responsiveness of the controls allowed me to execute precise and satisfying moves, leaving me craving for more intense encounters.One of the aspects I appreciated most about Grime was its narrative. The story is told through subtle environmental storytelling and cryptic dialogue, leaving ample room for interpretation. It's a tale that explores themes of loss, identity, and redemption, woven together in a hauntingly beautiful manner. I found myself pondering the game's deeper meanings long after I had finished playing, a testament to its thought-provoking storytelling.Grime also shines when it comes to its level of challenge. The game strikes a perfect balance between difficulty and satisfaction, challenging me enough to keep me engaged without feeling overwhelming. The sense of accomplishment after defeating a particularly tough boss or overcoming a seemingly insurmountable obstacle is unparalleled, and it left me hungry for more.In addition to the core gameplay, Grime offers a vast array of secrets and hidden areas to discover, rewarding exploration and curiosity. Uncovering these hidden gems felt like finding a piece of the puzzle that enriched the game's lore and expanded the world even further.All in all, Grime is an absolute gem of a game. It pushes the boundaries of what a 2D action-platformer can achieve, delivering a rich and unforgettable experience. Its mesmerizing visuals, deep combat mechanics, immersive storytelling, and challenging gameplay combine to create a truly remarkable journey. If you're a fan of atmospheric games that dare to explore the depths of the human psyche, Grime is an absolute must-play. Prepare to be enthralled and embrace the darkness within.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has by far one of the most (if not THE most) satisfying combat system in the genre.At the very least it has the best implemented parry mechanic. And I mean of course it does, the game is more or less centered around it.It also controls like butter, a bit more clunky than Hollow Knight, which is like the gold standard (except for HK's ♥♥♥♥ doublejump and wall jump), with a few more traversal glitches, but the traversal itself is also very satisfying, and the fact that traversal and combat are so seamlessly intertwined is one of the best aspects of the game.The artstyle isn't anything to brag about, kind of lacking to be honest, but it does the job and suits the lore of the game perfectly.Where this game shines is really the bossfights. Has some of the best bossfights in the genre. All the bosses are pretty much unique and all of them are creative and fun to play.The upgrade system (not that of weapons, but of prey) is a really nice substitute for a "skill" system, I'd only wish it was free to reassign your points.The weapons have weight to them and you can feel the damage that you're doing.All in all a solid 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty fun Hollow Knight type of game. A lot of people draw comparisons to Dark Souls which is kind of true, but it's not really as much like DS as it is HK. There is a stats system that you level with what are basically Souls (called Mass), but you can't actually lose Mass when you die. Leveling isn't super important either beyond reaching the required stats for certain weapons, so you don't have to worry about leveling the wrong stats too much like you would in DS.The story isn't as clear or even really as grand as HK in my opinion, but the atmosphere is absolutely on point. The areas and their inhabitants are fascinating, and the bosses are fun and powerful. The gameplay is pretty smooth, with some pretty neat platforming sections that make great use of the movement abilities you get.Overall, I would say that if you enjoyed Hollow Knight, you will really enjoy this game too. The game is a semi-linear Metroidvania type of thing where you have to fight your way through platforming areas filled with enemies, and eventually take on a difficult boss. There are plenty of secrets and extra bosses that you have to explore to find that you'll love if you play for a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game as a result of being an avid listener of Alex Roe's work. Hearing that he created the soundtrack of a Metroidvania, sold me without needing to even watch any gameplay. You guys could not have made a better choice for your composer. I dearly hope that you consider him for your future work.I must admit that I used only one weapon ever since picking it up. The Yr Twinblade. Exploring the corners of the world and finding more weapons with intriguing descriptions, yet stat requirements beyond my reach was exciting! After beating the "weakness" ending I can hardly wait to make more builds. I will at least need to make a strength and a dexterity build each, however with so many weapons, who knows how many I will make by the end!Each area's distinctive atmosphere and theme made me consistently excited to find the next place to go on an exciting "fetch quest". The lore and story progression is incredible. I loved piecing together the things that were not expressly told to you. I can't help but feel that "Goldhead" is a representation of players like me, who stop at every single drop of plot and think about all the potential implications.Yon is a treasure. His story is one of my favorite parts of Grime and I will be thinking back to it for a long time.The fact that the devs managed to fit humor into such a dark game is beyond me. I am not sure how to feel about the guy who enjoyed watching me crush things. I mean I feel kind of used, but I can't help but agree with him. It is pleasant to crush thingsThe only single criticism I have for this masterpiece is the fact that I felt a powerful desire for more once I completed it. Now I can hardly blame the devs for making me feel like Aklahn. After all it just means I will be waiting to crush whatever they make next!

_childDocuments_.review: Amongst one of the greatest metroidvania games on steam currently. The combat is fun, the world is incredibly bizarre and the game offers a decent amount of challenge combined with an strange eldritch world to explore. The game combines aspects of old-school metroidvania games with souls-lite elements spectacularly. The combat can be both fast-paced and methodical depending on your play style which is reflected in the trait/stat system that pushes you to build around your favored weapons to overcome the challenges that the game presents you with.Clocking in at about 18 hours of gameplay, the game sets it's pace pretty well apart from some QoL issues that the devs have talked about addressing in upcoming patches notably regarding the exploration and backtracking.The boss fights are a blend of pattern recognition and reflexes for the most part and from my experience none of them feel particularly unfair once you memorize their movements and timings, The only outlier being "The Final Performance" in which some attack's hitboxes appeared larger than the weapon being swung in the second part of the fight. The platforming and exploration we're spectacular and the game is very sneaky about hiding some of its secrets for only those with a keen eye and natural perception for games in the genre which made going back and trying to acquire everything a lot more rewarding and finding secret encounters/items earlier on extremely pleasant.Difficulty scaling can sometimes be hit or miss depending on which area you find yourself in and how invested your character is by that point, some attacks/enemies seem like they do absurd amounts of damage but it's hard for me to tell if that was simply my experience or if other players encounter some issues with HP to damage scaling.Visually the game is spectacular. Initially I wasn't sold on the visuals when I booted up the game but very quickly I came to appreciate the mindboggling atmosphere of the game and the strange, almost alien look and feel to the game complimented by a good sound score. The interconnection of anatomy and stone lends for a very surreal eldritch look which lends itself extremely well to this medium. Whatever the devs were on when they created this world I want some too.Overall I would give this game an 8/10 and push it to a 9/10 once the QoL changes have hit the live game.If you're a fan of the genre I strongly recommend picking this game up at full price to support the devs and definitely pick it up on sale if you're still on the fence about it.

_childDocuments_.review: What different feelings this hardcore metroidvania evokes, and even if these emotions are not always positive, in the end you get pure delight. "Grime" not only has a high threshold of entry, it literally requires reconciliation with its own shortcomings, or otherwise you will leave it very quickly. The first hours of being in a unique dark ruthless stone world immediately win you over. Clear routes, a vibrating and tight combat system, which anyone can master, but not everyone can come to ideal skill in it, unusual enemies, competently inscribed in the mythology of the local world. Everything is so perfect that it's hard to believe, but then several hours pass, you reach really large locations and problems begin. It would be more accurate to say - a problem. Moreover, it is connected with the map and navigation through the levels, which is one of the most important pillars for metroidvania.Navigation is bad at the moment. As you research the level, the fog of war does not disappear anywhere from the map, you are constantly groping in the dark, and only a single lighthouse hidden in the location can dispel it. Let me remind you that the levels here are huge. There is no fast movement between lighthouses and surrogates (the local analogue of checkpoints), and there is a huge amount of backtracking, so if you are determined to explore the world as much as possible, you will run around everything in the most inconvenient manner, and if you don’t find a lighthouse yet, the suffering will increase many times over. I love exploration, for me this is almost the most important part of metroidvania, so already at the 8th hour of the game I really wanted to quit it. No, at some point in the game "portals" appear for fast movement, but there are very few of them, they are hidden cunningly and are located in the most inconvenient places. The simplest and most annoying example of the ineffectiveness of this approach is the city of Cenotaph, where you have to face the hardest boss - the Final Performance. You see a complete fiasco with your existing weapon build, you decide to upgrade another one, but bad luck - there are no portals at this level. And for such a simple action as returning to the point of crafring weapons, you will have to: again run through the entire Cenotaph, again run through a very difficult platform level with riddles, again run through the Palace to the portal (if you found it at all), go through it to the point crafting and AGAIN all the way to Cenotaph. What for? And, ironically, after defeating the final boss, we are given the opportunity to move between surrogates, as if the developers themselves realized that the navigation system is ineffective.You need to come to terms with this internally, and if you can do it, as it happened to me, then the game will reward you in full. In all other aspects, it is a real gem of stone. The system of absorbing enemies in battle and then gaining their abilities feels fantastic. In any battle, you can build various strategies, even based on absorbing attacks, even on pure parrying, at least avoiding attacks with the help of dash, and none of the strategies looks the weakest, for each of them there is a competent development. The bosses are honest, fighting each of them is a real war, and understanding their attacks is the key to victory. Each of them is very different, there are no reskins of existing main enemies, every time everything feels unique, and some mini-bosses are hidden so cleverly that you can go through the game without even noticing them. The number of weapons is quite impressive and is suitable for a wide variety of combat types, there are also a lot of different armor sets, but they are purely cosmetic in nature, without giving any characteristics. The plot, as it always happens in soulslikes, seems to exist, but it does not seem to exist, it is not really required here, because the incredible integrity of the world itself tells a story. The music sounds fantastic, beautifully emphasizing the appropriate surroundings. None of the most important components - visuals, combat system, music, falls out of the general range, allowing you to constantly keep interest at a high level.It is rare to find such a unique stone face as "Grime" has. She is not afraid to offer something radically new, with her boldness leveling out even an obvious navigation problem that can be easily fixed. And this is another reminder that how important it is to have your own vision, capable of demolishing any stone walls, that the creators have proven. My compliments, it was an exciting ride.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, but quite challenging. I was enjoying it until I encountered a very difficult boss fight. The game tends to steer you toward this encounter, and it's easy to lose track of other areas you can explore to strengthen your character. After doing this and getting the right traits, the boss fight became much more manageable. Also make sure you have a lot of force (this game name for stamina) as it is very useful.One thing I appreciate is that save spots are placed close to the bosses, which is great because you might die a lot while trying to defeat them. However, I’m not a big fan of many bosses having double health bars. That said, the bosses are well-designed, and some that initially crushed me, I later defeated without taking damage.Exploration is enjoyable, but I wish you didn’t need to reach a beacon to see the map.In summary, this is a good "soulsvania," but I’d only recommend it if you're skilled at games, as it's very difficult—much harder than Blasphemous.

I did all of the main game achievements, include the dang abandoned opus, and will probably 100% it because it's just so fun. A further downside is that the game seems to make many weapons fall off greatly in endgame, with only A-scaled options being really viable.------------------------------------------------------------------------------Atmospheric, complex, soulsy Metroidvania with its own style. I love how unique this game is, I love the weapons, I love how you steal abilities from enemies and I love the parry mechanic, I don't love the sweaty hands platforming. Some sequences are a bit frustrating and some enemies more annoying than fun to fight, but this is really worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very good metroidvania / platformer style of game. If I'd compare this to some other games it would be Ori and the Will of the Wisps with some Dark Souls influenced features. You can go just to the places you have to go or you can go for the "100% explore and collect everything mode" if you like such a thing, which I did. For the achievement hoarders I'm afraid at the moment you cannot get all the achievements because of bugged things(?), prolly will be fixed at some point. If I'd have to say something negative about the game, it might just be me but few secret areas were kinda too hidden and cryptic for me. Without any spoilers fex a secret boss in a secret area behind a random wall behind a random wall behind a random wall (no there is no typo here) you only know to break if you hit every wall on that area, some areas even the ground. And at the moment there is a known bug that this certain boss despawns after you reach a certain point in the game. Yes, there was a way to find these breakable areas easier (I think) but still a bit too hidden for my taste. Found only few non game breaking bugs and hickups here and there, nothing severe. For few months I had no exciting games to play, but this one really did get me back the feeling of wanting to play. Would recommend it to anyone that enjoys these type of games!

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game. What a ride this was! Super slow build up but by the end everything gets so insanely fast! Similar to Hollow Knight. But you know what, Grime is now my #1 favourite Metroidvania. For many reasons as listed below but mainly the tight gameplay/combat and it's one of the VERY FEW games that has so many player-friendly QoL features to make your experience more fun. Kudos to the devs. I still very much dislike how I couldn't change my stats endless times or that I couldn't upgrade all my weapons (without wasting time on grinding) but other than that, this game is a solid 9/10 for me. Just well done!The first time I played this game (on Stadia), I gave up too early before even getting to the first boss. I found the absorb mechanic odd, the gameplay slow and expected the game to be boring. Well, I'm glad I gave it another shot because I was wrong!This is one of the most unique metroidvanias I've ever played! I've really grown to enjoy the creative mechanics this game introduces. It's fresh and unpredictable yet familiar in so many ways. Anyways, Here's a pros and cons list:+ Beautiful and [mostly] well done art style+ Very fluid movement. Crisp animations. Very well done!+ Unique combat system (specially the use of absorb instead of parry)+ Simple, yet well thought-out skills and trait system+ Decent death mechanics! It punishes you with some backtracking and losing your damage modifier but 50% of it can be recovered. You don't lose currency or anything else.+ Unique weapons with different animations, specials and variety even within the same class+ Interesting boss fights. Challenging but fair and satisfying to retry+ Good value for the money!+/- Decent variety of weapons and weapon arts. Better than most Metroidvanias yet limited.+/- Boss rewards can be underwhelming. They don't give enough upgrade points. (Though main issue is that weapons and skills both require the same currency)+/- Some quests, merchants, secrets, bosses etc. are a bit too cryptic. I had to look for a guide now and then+/- The lighting makes the game too dark for my taste. The art looks beautiful but I wish environments were a bit less dark and dungeon-like.+/- story is very confusing- Buying new weapons, upgrades etc. requires grinding for the currency (Also can't increase boss rewards with consumables. This is just bad game design forcing players to grind more).- The game forces you to choose a certain build and doesn't allow you to experiment easily. There are limited number of times you can re-spec. Even then, your weapon upgrades seem to be set in stone and you only get enough materials to maybe max out two weapons by the time you reach late game.- Backtracking is annoying.  - Weapon balancing is off. Some weapons are objectively worse than others and not viable- Did I mention grinding? After almost 30 hours and finishing the game, I could only upgrade 3 weapons to max level. Oh well, at least I chose dex which made an easy job of most bosses.P.S. Glad to be trying this after all the DLC has been released. Apparently a lot of the subtle QoL improvements were introduced after multiple patches. It's good to be a r/patientgamer!

_childDocuments_.review: Full review at: GRIME is a game oozing with as much passion as it does other unidentified fluids. With its body-horror inspired aesthetic it is not a look you will forget any time soon. Unfortunately the game fails to innovate much on genres it takes inspiration from, instead opting to blatantly copy many of their flaws. On the flip-side GRIME knows its niche, and when it does take responsibility it reaches surprising heights. Glued together with excellent sound design across the board, an enthralling story and unique world building GRIME stands as a truly unforgettable experience - even if flawed.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 5ish hours in. I've enjoyed it so far, but that is starting to wane. The tedium of working through the map over and over to get to the next checkpoint is has begun to grate on me. They are just a bit too far apart for my taste.The terrible map system has also been an annoyance from the start. I am genuinely puzzled as to what the developer's thought process was locking the map they way they did.The weapons are nice overall. I opted for a STR build, and then found out that I can't even equip any non-STR weapons to test out the move set. There's no way I'm going to replay this game, so I suppose I'll just never get to interact with that part of the game at all. No enticing me to play again by dangling the carrot of a cool late game dex weapon in front of my face.My fundamental problem with this game, and most others in the 2D souls genre, is this: Most developers played the souls games the way they wanted to, which is good. They picked out the method of approaching the game from the wide variety of options like parrying, dodging, blocking, face-tanking, attacking from afar, hit and run, passive/aggressive, etc and ran with it. They then proceeded to confuse they way that THEY played the games with the way the games should be played. So we get games like GRIME where 100% of the mechanics are based around parrying. It's a cute idea for a bit, but it reduces every encounter down to "how am I going to parry this one?". The constraints that decision put on this game didn't need to be there. It's a perfectly fun game dodging around and killing stuff the old fashioned way.In short: It's been decent, but I'm rapidly losing interest and doubt I'll finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is one of my favourite games. I genuinely love its atmosphere, a compelling obsessing weirdness with a deep sorrow underneath carried by elegant anatomical insanity everywhere and wonderful music. Exploration in Grime is not only gradually acquiring a better understanding of the geometrical reality of the world, knowing better how to go from here to there, and realising there was another secret area in this secret area, it is also getting to experience more of its unique vibe. I don't think everyone will appreciate it, but for me the solemn decay of the world was a driving force for 5 (five) playthroughs. I also really like how the combat feels. You are slow and heavy, everything you do has weight, each action is important and fights feel incredibly tense. That alone would be cool, but as you progress through the game, you get to slip more and more actions in between your actions, while also making individual actions even more significant. Something similar happens with the movement, where you are a litteral rock at the start, and get to juggle so many movement tools by the end that you literally fly. This gives a tremendous feeling of power escalation that not only feels great, but is also very pertinent to what the game is about. To what you are. Can't wait for the sequel. From the trailer it seems like they understood exactly what made their game good and expanded upon it. Plus it's set in a world obsessed with art? Count me in! I'm obsessed with art. This might get personal. AND OH GOD THERE WAS A STORY??!

_childDocuments_.review: I meant to buy this game when it released, since I'd played the demo and really enjoyed it, but I couldn't afford it at the time. Now that I have played it, I can say it was worth the wait (mostly).Grime is a fairly simple, yet grandiose, Metroidvania title that sets itself apart with its interesting main character and gameplay. You're a blackhole, basically, and you gain abilities throughout the game related to you being a blackhole. It's fun and it's interesting.Grime's story isn't one to write home about, it's interesting enough but isn't quite worthy of asking the big questions it does, especially when you can't meaningfully answer them. The characters you meet are probably the best part of the game's story, checking in with them as you progress and learning more about their life under The Broken Sky. It's sobering, especially after long sections of platforming and intense parry-focused combat.In terms of gameplay. combat is good. I found that some bosses and special enemies needed a bit more polish, but for a 7 person dev team this is fantastic. Platforming is the big one. I loved some of it, but it starts to wear out its welcome in the second half of the game, and actually starts to detract from the dramatic weight of the ending as you must carefully platform between the final boss and where the ending cutscene actually takes place. It's frustrating, to say the least, but not so much so that I wouldn't still recommend the game overall.In conclusion, it's a pretty good game, and the devs behind it all seem really nice and down-to-Earth, which is great to see after being a Hollow Knight fan and not hearing anything from Team Cherry for two years. Well worth the asking price and I'll gladly pick up whatever the team makes next

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Grime is an extremely challenging, immersive, souls-like metroidvania.  You are a weapon wielding badass w/ a blackhole for a head that absorbs and smashes everything in it's path.  This is a really ambitious project w/ a very large world to explore, gobs of secrets, really well designed combat, and tons of upgrade options.  If you can overlook the slow movement, and somewhat clunky jumping mechanics, this is one of the very best souls-like metroidvania's available today.What's Good:-Grime has a very unique aesthetic that is unlike any metroidvania available today.  It uses a 2d.5 aesthetic that works really well for most of the game (there are a few issues in the later sections).  Grime is the perfect name for this game b/c everything is very grimey, dirty, but paradoxically beautiful.  You will explore caves, mountains, temples, lush gardens, etc.  As nice as the world looks, I'd argue that the bosses and enemies are some of the most incredible features of this game, and are truly a work of art.  -The absorb mechanic (parry) is the most important part of combat in this game.  For you to have any chance, you must master the absorb mechanic.  Not only is it straight forward in learning to utilize, but it's extremely rewarding.  Due to the nature of this mechanic, you will play a lot more defensively in this game than you typically do in this genre.  It works really well though.  The absorb is used to gain breath (which allows you to heal), not take damage from incoming attacks, and is really powerful (vital against most of the bosses).  I was initially worried I wouldn't like this mechanic, but I really loved it.-The learning curve is steep, but the skill ceiling is so high.  This is an intense, ruthless game that will constantly challenge you.  No matter how many enemies you kill, upgrades you find, or stats that you add to your weapons, you will always feel a sense of stress and tension.  Very few players will ever feel overpowered in this game.  You will master every mechanic and become comfortable facing off against overwhelming odds, but you will always feel challenged.-There are so many different types of enemies, and each enemy has it's own attack and movement patterns.  I was amazed at just how many different enemies were created.  You will run into the occasional reskinned enemy w/ enhanced attack patterns, but that was pretty rare.  I wouldn't be surprised if there were close to a hundred different enemies, mini bosses, and bosses that you can run into along your journey.  -One of my favorite choices that the devs made were to have hunt points that you acquire by finding and defeating specific enemies.  This was a really smart choice, b/c it's completely optional but is vitally important b/c these points allow you to have access to the strongest upgrades.  You must use the absorb mechanic on an enemy 5 times and then you will gain access to a specific ability.  In order to actually utilize this ability, you will need to hunt down stronger enemies and acquire hunt points upon defeating them.  This adds another layer of excitement and wonder to the experience.-Exploration is a major component of Grime and there are secret pathways and treasure scattered everywhere.  Most of the secrets that you find will be consumable weapons, upgrade materials, and cosmetic armor.  The world in Grime is just really fun to explore and get lost in.  I never minded going off of the beaten path, there was always something interesting around the corner.Could Use Some Changes:-You will start off as a very slow, clunky character and you will end the game still feeling pretty slow.  This becomes a pretty big issue late game when you are trying to do about four things at once.  Secret hunting becomes extremely tedious b/c jumping, dashing in mid air, and landing on surfaces never feels as smooth as you'd want it to be.  Carven's Palace was hands down my least favorite area in the game, and the amount of time I spent dying searching for secrets or just trying to survive the platforming sections made me consider quitting a few times.-I really think that the checkpoints could use a bit of tweaking.  The amount of times that I would transition from one biome to another and die before reaching a checkpoint was brutal.  You need to do a decent amount of backtracking as well, which is something to keep in mind.  -I would like to see a couple of changes made to the leveling system of the weapons.  I found about 15 really cool weapons but only got to experience 3-4.  You need to use specific stats just to access the weapons, and then if you want to upgrade them, you will need to find very rare materials.  I maxed out two weapons, but didn't get to try out any other weapons outside of the first two weapons I picked up.  That's a bit of a bummer b/c this greatly limited my playstyle options.-The fall damage is quite an issue in a game w/ this much verticality.  Even if you dash at the last moment, you will still take significant fall damage.  It feels like the distance you are given before taken damage from a drop is really limited.  This is a small nitpick, but still something I found really annoying.Thoughts:-I really loved this first half of my playthrough and then I hit a bit of a wall late game.  I still enjoyed the second half, but I ran into a few frustrations.  Even though there a few issues here and there, Grime is still a really good game, and is a must play for fans of Blasphemous, Salt and Sanctuary, or Hollow Knight.  A few patches could clean up a few of the negatives that I mentioned, but even if nothing changes moving forward, Grime is still a gorgeous, extremely engaging, well rounded souls like metroidvania.Consensus:-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  I was planning on giving this game an excellent score for most of my playthrough, but I ran into some issues late game.  There was nothing game ending on anything like that, but it did lower my overall enjoyment.  Grime is still my favorite metroidvania of 2021 so far and is a game I can easily recommend to fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I start!? MAN! I guess I should start by saying that as of the date writing this review, GRIME is my game of the year and it's not even close. Here are my reasons why.Upon the game allowing you to move freely, everything feels so fluid with some really great animations. At this point I was already pretty sure I was about to have a good time but then the game introduced the parry mechanic (absorb) and I absolutely fell in LOVE. Parry in GRIME is used in a really unique way, you can parry enemies to absorb their skills and eventually be able to unlock a perk associated with that enemy. Parrying is also used as your primary way of healing, so it's reeeaaally important to parry lol.I personally am a HUGE fan of parrying in games, nothing quite feels as satisfying as having an enemy try to hit you and you say "nah" GRIME has managed to make parrying feel AMAZING! It's got a pretty generous parry window but not so much so that you feel like there's no skill involved in parrying, it's really in a perfect sweet spot for a game that relies on parrying so much.Combat also feels amazing with SO MANY different weapons to find throughout the world, each having unique move sets or doing something different to other weapons.The damn VISUALS in this game are also BEAUTIFUL! Everything just looks so freaking good and GRIME doesn't shy away from having "unsettling" imagery in the game which when meshed together with how beautiful the game is....it's truly a gorgeous game to look at.Story telling is also done in an interesting way, things start of very vague and weird and as you play throughout the game, things slowly become more obvious through talking with various characters and hints throughout the environment art.Enemy design is just straight up great, there's also a wide variety of different types of enemies which keeps things fresh. Bosses are SO DANG GOOD, they look great, they offer a fair challenge and are really fun to fight even if you're getting your ass kicked lol.In regards to difficulty, I wouldn't say it's overly difficult but definitely does give you a challenge, especially in the later stages of the game. All bosses are super fair, very readable attacks and I always felt like I was progressing in being able to beat them even if I didn't end up being successful in that run.BONFIRE PLACEMENT! So good, same with shortcuts (I know I'm using a lot of souls analogies but it's probably easier for folks new to the game to understand if I do that lol) I never felt "man I really feel like a bonfire should be here" and this is honestly something that a lot of games that take inspiration from Souls games tend to get wrong.SOUNDTRACK IS AMAZING AS WELLHonestly I'm writing so much about what I like and I could go on forever because to me, this game is  10/10 and has cemented itself as one of my favorite games ever. I love how they use souls elements as well as metroidvania elements.......it's just really well done. Buy the game, play the game, it's freaking, gosh darn doodily amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: It starts off OK, becomes really bad, then from that point onwards it slowly grows to become one of the best metroidvanias I have ever played. This is the best attempt yet at trying to make the next best metroidvania ever via a better hollow knight and if the first third of the game flowed as well as the rest of the game it would have succeeded. I recommend this, but be aware that you'll need to put up with hours of unenjoyable gameplay initially before the good stuff comes. Also, make sure to enable the DISABLE BACKSTEP option otherwise you will have a really awful time with dashing.The games faults are the following:- Hollow Knight's cartographer system- the flying basher enemy in the garden.- backloading of most of the mobility upgrades. Air dash is the only one you get for the entire first half of the game.- the existence of backstep- the binding for hover- the virtual impossibility of finding the boss holding the speed booster without an online guide due to poor location.The updates since the release show that the devs are aware of where they went wrong. As such, I believe Grime 2 is the best chance yet of toppling hollow knight rule over the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime succeeds at capturing the formula of games like Dark Souls, or for a better comparison Salt & Sanctuary and Hollow Knight. The gameplay is incredibly smooth, if not a little slow early on. But as you complete bosses, more abilities for both exploration and combat are unlocked, hence the Metroidvania aspect. The combat is challenging but fair, with dodging, parrying, and each tool at your disposal seamlessly integrated in fights to come. The atmosphere is incredible, with fun and interesting NPC encounters in a Neolithic, Beksinski inspired world. Sometime after the second boss fight, I recognized that this game has the potential to be among the great Metroidvania-Soulslike games.One of my main problems is that while the exploration is fantastic, there aren't many opportunities or draws to go back to earlier levels. I barely did any re-exploration because I simply didn't even think about it with level designs that constantly push you forward. The moment in Hollow Knight where you return to the Forgotten Crossroads and it's infected was a fun bit of world development. And certainly Grime has moments like this; when I returned to an area with stone lifts after a boss fight, I was surprised to find they had ceased working and were replaced by platforming the broken lifts to climb up or down. The issue is that I only stumbled upon it randomly, not because anything drew me back to that area. I just decided "eff it" to check it out. Other areas I never returned to because there's always an encouragement of "up & forward." Another weird issue is that some weapons you can find early on have really high stat requirements, making you either just stare at it in your inventory until near the end of the game or focusing on a single stat, forgoing the others which still takes a long time. Part of what makes Souls games so good is the wide variety of weapons, which Grime has, but most of them I can't even equip to take a look at until well into the game. This could be very easily mitigated with a New Game Plus option, allowing you to start with high enough stats for a whole playthrough with different weapons, but alas as of right now, there seems to be no NG+At the end of the day, I still think Grime is a great game that is worth buying. It has some issues, but I still wanted to continue to see what horror was next and where the game would go. Really glad I gave it a shot and definitely plan on another playthrough or two!Update: Just read a dev update today about how NG+ will indeed be implemented! I think that's the biggest thing holding Grime back right now so that's very exciting!

_childDocuments_.review: For everything this game gets right, it gets part of it wrong. I'd give this game a meh, but steam's binary review system won't let me.An emphasis on parrying is neat...but most of the  enemies have both a "parry immediately or get hit" attack and an "actually this one has a windup long enough that pressing parry right away means you get hit" attack, and the patterns just get harder as you go.Tells for attacks you can't parry are good...but sometimes they only show up at the end of a windup animation after you've already hit parry.Needing to parry to regain healing uses is cool...but most of the enemies arbitrarily don't give you any healing charges, and the trait for improving parry healing starts at 4% per trait point with immediately diminishing returns.The game has a couple other ways to heal...but they're either super expensive (at level 60 a single healing consumable still almost costs 1/2 a level in the shop) or super hard to get (the estus equivalent needs you to find and kill 3 of the crystal lizard equivalent per charge, and you start with 0 charges).The leveling system only has the stats that it actually needs...but a single level of any stat does almost nothing (4 points of health per level when starting health is 100? 2 levels in a damage type to get a single additional point of damage on a B scaling weapon when nothing seems to scale higher than B even 20 hours in?) and you have no way whatsoever to improve your defenses except by extending your health/stamina meters (armor can't be upgraded and doesn't scale with anything).Getting traits from killing enough enemies is cool...but you gain trait points at a glacial pace, the scalings on most traits are terrible, several are noob traps, and you have to spend a very scarce resource to respec.Having to uncover the map as you go is a cool idea...but it's a binary "did you construct the additional pylon or not", the pylon is usually in the middle of nowhere, and it's usually at least 3/4 of the way to either the boss or the exit. The pylons have guide trails leading to them...but they usually lead through hazards, or walls that don't open from this side, or the pylon's on an inaccessible ledge.The trail to show where you've been helps with navigating unmapped areas...but the areas are big enough and the trail fades fast enough that half the time when you respawn the trail's nowhere near you.The setting is really cool and the environments are creative...but they also often become so dark you can't see, with platforms that you have to go to that are offscreen even if you're holding up/down to look farther, and if you miss you take fall damage.There are plenty of things to find in the world...but most of them are consumables you'll never use, with the occasional weapons and armor sets you'll never use because the starting armor's bonuses are better than almost everything else and the only difference between weapons is the stat scaling, attack speed, and maybe the special move if the game's  feeling fancy.New powerups give you things to come back to in old areas...but the world is so big and fast travel points are so sparse that you never want to do that if you can avoid it.The powerups are satisfying to use...but most of them either show up way too late in the game (double jump, better fast travel), are too finicky and/or expensive to reliably use (sprint), or are completely context-sensitive (pull, hookshot).The game has multiple uses for your powerups...but never teaches you about them, so you'll often assume you need a powerup from elsewhere to continue exploring when you've actually got everything you need. (Tips for the reader: A huge yellow bubble around an enemy means you should pull it, teeth can't bite down on pulled out platforms, purple-gummed teeth only bite when touched, blue-gummed teeth only bite after a delay, and you can dodge through the spike walls with the red dots on them.)Bosses are never too far from a checkpoint...but sometimes that's only true if you broke a wall that doesn't open from this side, which you didn't know you needed to do before you stumbled on the boss, which the camera and level design tricked you into not noticing until the fog wall had already spawned.Bosses can be pretty cool to fight...but only after you've learned all of their attacks, because the moment you get hit by any of their attacks at all you tend to get either oneshot or stunlocked to death.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this game and wow, what an experience.I played my share of metroidvanias, and also quite a few with souls-like elements. As far as those games goes, they will always have a different balance between combat and platforming. Like Salt and Sanctuary with more focus on combat, with weapon variety and stats, and Blasphemous with a bit more on platforming, while not many customization options and only your default weapon. Still I really enjoyed both games.Grime is different tho as it seems to strike the perfect balance. Combat and Platforming. We have weapons we can choose, not a great number of em, but they have very unique designs and movesets. A few stats to distribute and make builds. And the platforming can get absolutely insane, with parts that could rival the Path of Pain from Hollow Knight, had they only been just as long.What I really liked it hows with this great balance, the game also allows you to use many of the transversal tools you learn in combat, and in boss fights, making it way more dynamic.The world design is also amazing, very unique and alien, from levels to enemies everything is just so bizarre, in a good way. The story is even weirder and honestly I'm not sure I understand it completely, but it all has a very nice gritty feeling to it. And to complement it all the soundtrack by Alex Roe is simply superb.Overall a 9/10 game in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: Back in 2020, when I had less grey hairs on my chin, one game in particular caught my attention at Gamescom - GRIME. As soon as the teaser/announcement trailer finished, I knew that this game would be something special. How special you ask? Well, special enough to become my favorite metroidvania of them all (yes, even surpassing Hollow Knight -  a hot take for many, I know, and doubly so when one takes into account that I am one of the proud original 2,158 backers that helped HK come to life). And just as I saw the spark of masterpiece in HK, so too do I consider GRIME to be a true masterpiece.The surreal looks of the game gets you first, tugging at your curiosity as to what secrets does this strange world foster. Then comes the combat - fluid, methodical, rewarding patience and learning patterns above anything else. This is enhanced by huge amount of armor sets and weapons, rudimentary RPG system of building your character, and both the atmospheric and orchestral music that plays in the background, creating this sense of utmost euphoria with every hurdle passed and challenge overcome. On top of that, the game doesn't overstay its welcome, and is mysterious & beautiful enough that it warrants multiple playthroughs, just so you can enjoy the marvelous vistas and smashing denizens of this masterfully-crafted world. And if you want to learn more about it, all in-game items and enemy descriptions offer lore bits that shed some light on the state of affairs in these quirky, stoneclad lands.Having beaten the game (twice in a row, which is not something I usually do and which speaks of how great GRIME is), I cannot wait to lay my paws on GRIME II, whenever it releases (and surely sooner than Silksong, at this rate). The way Yarden (head honcho behind GRIME) weaves these worlds with threads of his imagination REALLY makes me want to play each and every one of future installments in the GRIME universe, knowing that I'll be richer by one more unforgettable experience by the time I finish with the game.

Exploration is very rewarding, it feels like every second screen there is a secret passage that will lead you to an item or a whole new area.Highly recommended! I had great time.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start with the positive first. Graphics are spectacular, even with the limitation of designing everything with a rock motif, levels are incredibly varied and beautiful. The game is filled with rocks, sand, debris, gemstones, then later architecture that  mix in all sorts of ways that give flavor to every area in the game.Background/skyboxes are also no slouch with all the equally gorgeous landscapes, often in open areas that add a sense of vastness and scale to this world.Music is also great, the soundtrack has a theatrical feel to it, and it very often nails the vibe of the area it's playing for.Not much to say about sound design, but I think that's a good thing. Sound design, to me atleast, is something that you don't notice when it's done well. When you're taking hits and making contact, when objects slide and click into place, when items are being consumed and thrown, explosions, environmental hazards, enemy grunts when they start and finish their attacks, the clanging of weapons, all have sound that is appropriate and as expected.Now... the combat, , the combat...You're basically playing as a badass rock golem called the Carven... that has a tremendous fear of heights, and the stamina of a bedridden person.Let me explain, I was shocked that a game like this (a platformer!) actually has fall damage. A fall from a somewhat relatively safe height in other games actually hurts your character in this game, which can get annoying at some sections where platforming gauntlets are placed at a height that would hurt you if you missed a jump, limiting the amount of tries you have depending on how short your HP is.Nevermind the pain of just starting over, which is going to be alot, because some platforming sections are big enough that you don't see all it's mechanics and hazards in one go, without trial and error. NOOOoooo, the game has to destroy you for it, and send you back to the last checkpoint (have I mentioned that checkpoints are somewhat scarce in this game considering the size of some areas?).Oh, it also does this thing where if you fall for long enough your character just EXPLODES out of nowhere then resets your location. Like I get it, it prevents sequence breaking and the character will die from that height with fall damage anyway. But aren't there lots of other ways to stop players from exploring places they shouldn't go? And yep, this also deals damage, so don't bother doing leaps of faith in this game when your HP is running low.Next is the stamina system, the stamina existing in this game single-handedly ruined this game for me. Everything you do in this game (with the exception of walking and standing still ) eats at your stamina. Light attacks, heavy attacks, , dashing - doing any these unnecessarily during encounters (to have fun, to style, etc) is sure to screw you over and the game will punish you relentlessly for it.The stamina system forces you to have a safe, conservative, and  playstyle that is pretty much "get as much attacks in as you can", then keep your distance and avoid attacks while your eyes drift to the top left of the screen waiting for the stamina meter to fill back up so you can keep playing the game.The sad part is, it even bleeds into their boss design, the boss were made to either accomodate (very slow attacks) or  (super fast rotations) players with limited stamina builds, resulting in most boss fights being not a moment of spectacle and triumph but of patience and frustration.This also indirectly incentivizes avoiding certain encounters, I once walked into a room that has 4 ground enemies and 3 enemies chucking spears at me, and my gut reaction is to ignore all of it, GTFO, and hurry up into the next room, because I know the stamina system will make sure I won't enjoy that fight, which is a damn shame since I consider myself a player who looks for those moments.I've watched some streamers play this game, and they sure as hell have a hard time making fights look good, even the streamers I know who are into hack-and-slash don't bother to move/dash around much when they don't need to. As designed, I guess.There are abilities that allow you to restore stamina with a well-timed block or dash, but that's a band-aid solution, and at most it only restores 1-3 light attacks worth. So yeah, back to walking and resting. I swear if the guy handling the stamina system is given more development time, he would've required players to sit down, or . Could you tell him I hate him? My final gripe is the restrictions on the customization, I'm not talking about the cosmetics, that's good and all but the fact that the game actually requires resources to tweak your build, what was that about? You'd think in a game like this, you'd be allowed resets as much as you want so as long as you only do it in specific points in the game - so you're encouraged to try different playstyles from checkpoint to checkpoint, as well as make you look forward to what powers you unlock later in the game (because you know trying them out will just be a checkpoint away).But currently? The resources to reset or refund skill points are incredibly scarce, potentially locking you out of weapons that you didn't consider building towards (which is likely if it's your first playthrough). You'd also be scared to spend points on mediocre abilities because you think the next prey with a good ability might appear.It's so weird, it's because of this that I actually groaned when I went through a gauntlet only to find a weapon in the end that I can't use. Metroidvanias should not make me dislike finding stuff. Supposedly, the magic of a system like this (ex: Dark Souls) is it allows you to expand your options and add depth  a particular playstyle, all GRIME does is lock you of it.The last part would probably be me discussing some animation glitches and jank in rebinding the controls, but I won't be too hard on that as the developers seem that they're still working on that, and patches are still rolling in. So there's no doubt in my mind that it will eventually get better.But at the moment, I'll hold on to my opinion that this whole thing is massively hurt by that annoying little meter beneath the HP bar, and the rest of this otherwise pristine gemstone of a game is held back by it.:Alright, I played enough to reach the part where I  and unlocked the  ending, though looking at the comment threads, I clearly missed out on a few other bosses. But I've seen enough to change my mind.Fall damage tolerance appears to have been adjusted. It still annoys me from time to time, but it no longer feels like the floor is a bigger threat than actual enemies.Stamina regen has been buffed just enough that it restricts your movement options, but not enough that it feels you're playing with a straitjacket on. Stamina cost for jumping is also almost negligible now, though you're still required to pay attention to how you use your dash, which I'm fine with.As for the builds: I'll be honest, still not a fan. I sorta gave up on the whole thing - I just picked a weapon that has a light and heavy attack that I like, upgraded it as much as I can and stuck with it, the second weapon slot was practically empty my entire playthrough and I actually forgot the button I use for weapon swaps.One new thing I noticed that grinds my gears: hitbox detection. I can't totally pinpoint what I hate about it, but it feels like the i-frames operate via RNG.I had too many "I swear I dodged that" moments late game... might wanna look into that.Credit where it's due, here's my T-Up.

_childDocuments_.review: GRIME could be best described as a somewhat unsettling, weird and surreal game. While some of its design choices are influenced by Soulsborne games, at its core this is a fully fledged metroidvania title featuring huge interconnected map with plethora of hidden shortcuts, platforming, plenty of ability gating that encourages backtracking for optional content, hidden areas, optional and hidden bosses as well as plenty of loot to reward those who take their time exploring.Character progression works on several fronts: Killing enemies grants you points you can spend to level up a selection of attributes. Weapons are found in the world or obtained from vendors, equipping weapons requires specific attributes and each weapon scales differently based on an attribute or attributes. In addition to that GRIME features a mechanic where you can absorb regular enemies, once you have absorbed a required amount of an enemy type you unlock a perk unique to that enemy: These range from basic passive buffs (+health or +force (stamina), increasing your parry window, improving regeneration etc.) to large variety of more active things such as damage buffs that triggers based on specific conditions, adding different modifiers to your dash, unlocking ability to walk slowly etc.But in order to actually "equip" these perks you need to spend hunt points to equip/level them (some of the perks feature multiple levels that increase the benefits you obtain from the said perk while some are one and done type of deals), these points are obtained from special enemies and by other hidden means. In addition to that main and mini bosses also unlock specific things, be it new traversal mechanics, something required for exploration or other means of making you more powerful.All of this contributes to replayability with different sets of perks, attributes and weapons which is further reinforced by the satisfying combat loop of the game alongside some excellent boss encounters that provided both variety and a decent amount of challenge. Unfortunately where the game falls a little flat is its story which at best is vague and forgettable. Ultimately though that did not matter much for me as the setting itself, world design with its wonderfully bizarre environments, interesting enemies and bosses alongside the overall atmosphere proved to be enough much of a driving force to keep me hooked throughout the game. While the combat is excellent I have to give credit where it is due, art direction, visual and audio design along with the exceptional soundtrack truly made the experience what is was.That being said my relatively thorough playthrough of the game with around 85% of the map explored took me roughly 15 hours and I enjoyed it a lot. While I experienced a few bugs and had some gripes about certain design choices of the game such as some weapons have a little too high attribute requirements, not being able to test weapon movesets without spending attribute points first, fast travel being bit too stingy right until the end of the game - these issues were not critical enough to hamper my enjoyment.All in all, I had a lot of fun and would definitely recommend the game. For those who are on the fence, why not check out the demo that is available as it gives a good overall picture of the core gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Is it a good game, yeah, but would I recommend it to me? No. It is NOT a way to get your Hollow Knight fix. It lacks the polish and fluidity of Hollow Knight. I specify this because it bothers me other people seem to recommend it while we wait for Silksong. It has some themes, but it doesn't deliver near the same experience.I don't know what it is, but something about the general loop within boss fights rubs me the wrong way. The easiest issue for me to accurately pin down is stamina, I think it's crap. I don't care if they scaled bosses to have more health or take less damage, but I HATE getting through a boss's moveset, having them staggered in a damage window, and having to stand there and wait, and wait, and wait, for my stamina to regen. And by the time they are out of the damage window I STILL don't have full stamina. It feels awful, I've streamed it to friends and they agree it is crap to watch me just stand there, and wait, and wait, and wait, and oh wait the boss is using a red attack meaning I HAVE to dodge it, which eats stamina and stops regen.Here's the kicker, when you do the basic heal, it's a health regen that ALSO gives incredible stamina regen. The entire gimic of the game seems to be that it wants you to parry, but as you progress it throws in more and more red attacks, which CAN'T be parried. At to that that the only way to gain the resource to heal is to not only parry, but to parry a boss while they are in a red health bar segment. Early on? I thought it was a great balance. But by the end it seems like you only get the few heal/stamina regen bursts that you spawn with, and good luck getting a boss to give you anymore. Again, the game is balanced with this in mind, but it feels bad. I would rather the game be more generous with this stuff and balance to compensate. Clearly other people like this game, but I think it feels really clunky at the worst times. I would refund it if I could because I feel like it doesn't deliver on the potential shown in the first half of the game. Play Hollow Knight if you haven't, if you had and you want more, this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is a truly amazing experience. For people who are fans of souls games and metroidvanias like Hollow Knight, this should definitely be a no brainer to pickup. All this dose is discourage experimentation and build variety. You find a number of weapons and armor throughout the game, but most of the time you just throw them on to the pile, since there is no real way of trying them out without changing your whole build, since every part of your build will be connected to one another, which basically means, when you change out one part, you're gonna have to probably change all the other parts as well. _childDocuments_.review: Okay I don't really write reviews but I think this game has earned one.I would recommend this game and say it is a 7/10, so I'm going to give you 7 good things and 3 bad thingsGood-1. Concept: So I think the bones of this game are really good. You play a walking, punching blackhole going through a world absorbing things. This feelings pretty well explored in game, and fits very well with the souls feel. Nothing feels forced and events happen logically2. Visual Storytelling- Because this is a souls-like, you get a lot of visual story telling. Pay attention to that opening cinematic and to your actual environment, its very well thought out how everything related to one another. The enemy design also definitely plays to this. There isn't a ton of story here, but there is a lot to piece together and get your head around.3. Atmosphere- Those visuals also help to make the atmosphere pitch perfect. The world feels like a place both lived in and falling apart. So much of it feels unnatural but very alive, its a very different place from our own. Now there are a decent amount of different kinds of feels that you are suppose to have based on the area and event, and I think the game nails making you feel the right things each time. Think like Hollow Knight when you go through Deep Nest.4. Music- Speaking of Hollow Knight, Grime has the same level of music quality. Personally I normally turn off most music and game sounds to opt instead for videos or my own music. Here I didn't wanna do that, and I think that adds a lot to the game, especially on an immersion basis.5. Absorb- Story and gameplay blend very well, but are at there best with the absorb mechanic. It is literally the first thing you learn to do and is remarkably important gameplay wise. You'll learn more about it, but feels very much like a riposte is Dark Souls. It is your block/deflect but can do a lot of damage or outright kill a lot of enemies. You wanna beat the game, master it6. Stickyness- If you have ever played Infamous or had aim assist on, you might understand what I mean when I use the word "Sticky" in referring to how a game plays. The game wants to help you succeed, so there are generous windows for most things. The absorb mechanic, for example, frequently worked when I was either way to late or way to early to handle an attack. Though where this is most important is in the exploration. More than once I look at something like it was the Path of Pain, and instead just breezed right by it because more often than not I was close enough.7. Build Diversity- For being a small game, there are a lot of different ways you can take a character. You have a number of different weapons, points you can put into leveling, but where it gets different is in the Hunt Points. Absorbing creatures nets you new abilities, and you unlock different levels of them using the Hunt points. This takes customization to a new level, because these abilities are generally very powerful, helpful, and interesting.Not so good stuff-1. Exploration- Frankly this is one of the games weakest points for me. To be clean, outside of finding checkpoints and bosses, there is little reason to explore. Most of the consumables in the game I didn't use or thought were a bit useless. There aren't a ton of weapons in the game either and most are pretty similar, so use one you like until you find a better one. Last thing is the armor, it is purely cosmetic and at a later date might change, but presently it seems extremely pointless. The main reason to explore is to find the mini bosses that give you more Hunt Points or increase your ability to heal. So overall this is a pretty big knock for me especially since the game is relatively linear. 2. Completeness- Grime is a finished product no doubt, but it feels like it has some small holes in it. The game is relatively buggy, not game breakingly so but enough that it started to kill my immersion. You will get stuck on stuff all the time, or experience graphical glitches. One of the most beautiful sections of the game had a glitch for me where there would be random flashes of blue light that were clearly not intended. There are however some more basic aspects of the game that need to be addressed, there is no new game plus, the armor is purely cosmetic, there is very limited end game, and honestly feels a little short. Most of this things will be cleared up I imagine but presently they are issues for me.3. Tweaks- Okay so stuff I think should changed about the game. Points can reallocated in the game using these beads, that's fine but is for both Hunt points and your normal leveling making it difficult to try new things or adjust your play. I'd say that they should only be used for leveling and be closer to an Orb of Regret from Path of Exile (1 for 1), and let you swap the Hunt points at checkpoints. Many of the abilities that you would unlock with them are usable in limited circumstance and make it more difficult to balance out what you want and what you can try. I also like that after killing certain bosses, the areas around them are effected. Most become empty though and lose a lot of the life too them, I don't mind this because of how it tracks with the story, but I would massively prefer if the areas instead became more hostile to you and you would have to "clear them". I think this also tracks with the story and would also make for a great end game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game revolves around an incredibly awkward parry-like "absorb" mechanic, which means you'll be doing a lot of waiting around for enemies to use specifics attacks. You need to absorb 4 times to get a one-time gradual heal which is useless in an actual fight.You need to absorb up to 8 times to get new abilities which don't unlock right away.You need to absorb to gain experience at a reasonable rate.Between the trial and error of figuring out when to absorb, what is actually absorb-able and the stamina bar accommodating 3 or 4 dodges in the early game (I really wish developers would stop forcing in stamina bars where they don't belong), you're essentially forced into one very slow style of play, which is a shame because there's some nice variety in the weapons available. I can understand why someone would like it though, it's a good looking game with some neat ideas and good presentation, and while the gameplay is not truly terrible, it's far too restrictive for me to enjoy.I'm also a bit salty that I'm not able to refund this product because I bought it in a bundle with Vigil: The Longest Night, which I just so happened to boot up first, but that's neither here nor there.

_childDocuments_.review: Grime is an action adventure RPG set in a surreal world full of minerals and alien entities. As a humanoid black hole, players need to repel and absorb all kinds of rocky creatures to become more powerful than ever, and ultimately return to its former self. I played the demo during steam indie games festival and I was drawn to its eerie artstyle immediately. The fluent combat and interesting level design were icing on the cake. As a result, I purchase the game and enjoy every moment of it. Even though there are some still bugs and glitches to be fixed, it does not dwindle my favor towards the game. What's more, the devs listen to the feedback of community and are tweaking and ironing out bugs frequently. That's a plus for me. It might turn down some people, but I love the artstyle of Grime. Something about the mixing the bodily horror and grimes really tickle my interest. From the mob design to different biomes, The game just keeps oozing its strange personality. Whenever I visit a new area, I always marvel at how the devs create this kind of setting. Take Unformed Dessert for example. As you first exit the Weeping Cavity, a strong light shed upon your face. Then you see a vast desert area, desolate and barren. Fractured giant faces lay waste among the sand white. Up on the purple velvet sky, something is stirring, devouring like a black hole. This scene never cease to amaze me.Most of the time the abilities you require from or after defeating the bosses serve only as tools for traversing new levels. Grime does this idea differently. Instead of following the traditional way, the game turns these maneuvers into tools of combat, mainly the Pull ability. In middle to late game, enemies often have some powerful attacks. Players have not choice but to either dodge or distance themselves. With Pull, however, players can change these moments to windows of opportunity. Yellow aura will notify the players and they can use Pull to pull down the enemies or stun them, making them open for damage. This interaction helps me neutralize a lot strong foes, and I love the design philosophy behind it.Every item in Grime is useful in all situation, which kind of shocks me. In other games of the same genre, they always have some items that are only viable in one or two situations. Grime does this differently, from the usual throwables and bombs, to items that grant you damage buff, damage reduction, stamina recovery, instant stamina recovery, and breath gain increase(Grime's way of healing). I never thought there will be a day to see my inventory empty, using up every consumables in these kinds of video game.→Interesting NPCs.→Ambiguous but intriguing story.→Secrets hidden all over the places, only for the keenest eyes.→Parry/Repel/Absorb is super easy and forgiving. I like how armor is just purely for pleasing your own eyes. You are not obliged to wear certain gear just because its attribute is higher. Mixing up different parts to create your own style. However, doing so also reduces the factor which can effect damage reduction. Currently in order to have damage reduction, you need to either use consumables or perform certain action. There are no permanent way to gain protection, not even leveling up will help.Unlike the steam page suggests, Grime is sadly not a metroidvania, at least not a quality one. Progress is way more linear than other metroidvania titles. You cannot  choose which main boss to fight first. The only similarity is that with new ability unlocked, you can explore some hidden optional areas. However, each area is only connected with one after another. It's a shame because weapons in Grime are all fun and unique to use. In current state of the game, weapons with slow movesets can hardly survive in later encounters. Enemies are faster than the player, which means less attack and recovery window. Therefore, using stamina-hungry weaponry automatically puts yourself into huge disadvantages. I suggest making heavy weapons take less stamina to use, or making the movesets just a little faster.Here is my take on why Grime needs this. Let's make a comparison. In Hollow Knight, players are also limited to stag station which connects to the set areas. However, because of the character's unlimited and faster movement, players can easily zoom through several rooms in a second, let along the level design connecting each other. In Grime, quite the contrary, the main character's movement is slow and limited to stamina. The general level design does not do it justice either. Nervepasses do alleviate the situation a little, but the tediousness is still apparent.→Some areas are just too dark to navigate, either lighting up these place a bit or giving the player a lantern purely for illumination.→Why do I have to assign items to quick slot before usage? Why can`t I just use the items in the menu?→All weapons should be at least equipable for player to try out the movesets.
