_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I would describe Chicory: A Colorful Tale as a coloring book with a motivational story. If you're comfortable with coloring outside the lines, it’s an easy recommend.You can spend several times the story length just coloring in the world map as you traverse it. Not to mention the many canvases you’ll be creating, optional and story relevant. Puzzles and bosses are prevalent, but aren’t overwhelmingly difficult. Lastly, initial options for coloring are limited which may feel clumsy and off putting for some. However as the story progresses you will gain access to various brush textures, stamps and the option to create your own color palette if you explore the right places. PS: Please put the game on GOG store, Devs. I'll pay for it twice.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this was a fun little game with a cute story. I enjoyed exploring all the regions and colouring stuff in. There are sidequests and lots of characters to talk to. My highlight was the art school where you're given prompts for what to paint. I had a lot of fun doing that. I recommend this game especially if you're a bit of an arty person
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: One really great side effect of playing Chicory was being trained to be more comfortable jumping into creative tasks where the results can not be quantified. I am an engineer professionally and while there is a ton of creativity in my work, the output needs to achieve a result, and I need to both be able to quantify that result and have confidence that I will meet some standard when I am working on a project. I had not realized just how averse I had become to tasks where those things were undefined or undefinable. Minor spoilers: The art class prompts in Chicory were REALLY hard for me to engage with, and I avoided them at first. And the portrait events? Emotionally exhausting. I am very very grateful that the game sprung them on me the way it did, otherwise it might have stalled out avoiding them. But after the first, I was able to go back and do some of the art class prompts, and then I started doing more free form stuff in the overworld. The encouragement from the characters helped. And the desire to see what interactions I could trigger was enough to motivate me to keep going. A couple months later when work offered a painting class as a fun team event I signed up and had a great time; something that absolutely would not have happened had I not played the game. I still use 'just like you' and other music from the game to psych myself up when I want to do a project like this.So yeah. Life changing game. I can't thank you enough for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I sometimes got a bit turned around and the side quests are a bit tedious, the story is a bit meh, would be even more fun if you could modify the area colors more. So i would barely give this a positive review and would have liked to give a neutral one. It was fun playing but there are a lot of flaws. I particularly didn't like the boss fights, it just feels like they could have been more interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A million times yes. This game was amazing. The soundtrack was astounding, the game mechanics were surprisingly clever, and to top it all off, the game is essentially an adult coloring book. In a world of quirky earthbound inspired indie rpgs about depression, this game stands out as a diamond in the rough. I could not recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I have a smile on my face, a whole day after finishing this. And I am broken-hearted, since there is none of it left for me to unravel. My flat our suggestion is that you get. this. game.I'm not artistic, but I was surprised how over time the game drew a bit of creative flair out of me. I started out with monotone zones, not particularly caring about making places look nice. Barely even coloring some places in. Then I started mixing up light and dark hues for elevation and walls. Maybe sprinkle a splash of variety on the trees before filling the floor in. Why not add a texture to the beaten path... The game develops a sort of meta growth, as both you and the protagonist learn to have fun with the experience and trust your judgement when deciding how to color the land and handle the character's struggles. The game goes far into exploring that journey, and the trials taken to accept oneself.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: My favourite things about this game where the music, story and gameplay elements. The mechanics where very inventive and fun to use and it was paced very well. I also really enjoyed the dialogue, each character has a lot of personality and I find it similar to something like Undertale in that way. The feel of the game reminds me a bit of Paper Mario, mainly the looks and animation. Overall very good game, my only minor gripes was probably to do with the actually painting system. I found it annoying that you can only use 4 colours per area and couldn't be very precise with your work, but overall it was still fun and its other applications where great. Overall this game is stellar, highly recommend to anyone interested.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game! The story was great, the gameplay was fun, and the characters were pretty good. I'm not much an artist myself, but coloring in everything was fun. The map was awesome! I love games that make you explore before you find the objectives and that's what Chicory did. Great game! i'd give it a 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game I've played all year.  What started off as a cute coloring book adventure has expanded into a complex narrative about friendship, forgiveness, impostor syndrome and finding your place in the world.  I have been talking everyone's ear off about it and will continue to do so until everyone I know has tried it or someone finally asks me to kindly place duct tape over my mouth.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely amazing to play through, you may think it's an overstatement but it's how I truly experienced it.To start off with, you needn't be a great artist or anything to play this game, there are obvious limitations to the drawing system which I am glad are there, it lets things stay relatively simple and easy accessible for everyone without feeling like an artistic failure.The atmosphere of the game is fantastic, I always went to hear what the NPCs have to say and it really gives the world life. It was actually very suprising what a variety of toppics are talked about, be it humor, serious or both.I played the game while showing a friend, giving the characters voices and while it may sound and feel weird, I suggest you do, too. It was way fun messing around like that.But enough of NPCs for now or almost, that is. First I have to mention the amazing relationship between the name giver Chicory and your player (that I named Lasagna). The interactions they have are strong and were my favorite to read. but now actually what this game is mostly about, the color and drawing.The world feels empty and desolate at first, as it is intended to. One may not want to spend multiple minutes coloring each individual screen nicely and that's absolutely fine, neither did I but I sure as hell enjoyed having done it multiple times and seeing the nice filled pretty screen.Sometimes the area based color restrictions may not suit your color taste but even then, coloring a screen with them may make you come to appreciate them.You also get the ability to use your own colors later on, letting you color whatever you want however you want it which is pretty neat.The areas were well designed with fun puzzles and the mechanics felt great to use.A bit heavier topics are talked about and core theme of the game so beware of that or don't, since taking on those things is also big part of it.Drawing pictures always made me feel like a bad art thief, somewhat messy and silly looking but it still ended up with me being satisfied with the work I have done "Good for the limitations that are present"I like to collect stuff so I went for 100% and as one would expect from a relaxing, comfy game like this, it wasn't all too hard to do so. Going around looking for stuff, it may not be for everyone but I see it as a must, experiencing all the game has to offer.Chicory best bnuy
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Most of the games I hold dear to me have helped me get through some difficult phases in life, or helped me confront and understand the troubles I carried in the past. This was not one of those games. This game brings forth the themes of impostor syndrome and depression not behind the cute and wholesome elements, but alongside it. In addition to the story of confronting your darkest thoughts, the game tells the stories of friendship and support from characters you meet and demonstrates how people in our lives empower us to believe in ourselves and enable us to accomplish what we set out to do. This game did not help me through anything in life because luckily I'm at a point where my demons aren't out to get me. But it did put a smile on my face the whole time and I believe that this game will do the same for many other people. It could be that game that helps people in a tough place much like other games in the past have done for me. This game has reminded me of all the friends and family that I have who helped me overcome a lot of obstacles and bouts of depression that haunted me throughout the years. It is amazing how much I love playing this game, as I dislike coloring. It is a tedious and difficult way for me to express myself. But when I play Chicory I am inspired to bring life to the breathtaking scenes of the world while enjoying the beautiful soundtrack. I'm not the best at it, but the game has so any tools that help you unlock your imagination while not overwhelming you with loads of decisions to make. Throughout the game some characters will stop by areas you have colored and express amazement at the scenes you make which, alongside the smile-inducing dialogues in the game, evoke feelings of joy and satisfaction. I already enjoy conversing with characters in games that I play, but there is something about the interactions in this game that make wholesomeness, that could easily be redundant, exciting and has me eager to meet more animals in the world. To break up these happy moments are intense action sequences that have the players confront the darker thoughts of the world which are highlighted by a hype soundtrack and creative mechanics. The game is super forgiving in these parts yet still has me at the edge of my seat with how intense these parts of the game are. Add in some platforming that utilizes the coloring mechanics in unique ways which probe the puzzle-solving parts of the brain and you have the masterpiece that is Chicory: a truly Colorful Tale.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played. It was a really good experience.A touching and very real-feeling story about the emotional difficulties of the creative process, a cute world and characters that I found myself wanting to care about, a gentle gameplay experience that pushes without straining and one of the best game soundtracks that I've heard in years.I think if you're looking for a more intense gameplay experience you might come out disappointed but I found it very right for how I was feeling at the time I played it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is worth any price. And I desperately hope it'll get the attention it deserves.You don't need to be good at painting. I can just about draw a stickfigure and nothing more.The story and the characters are magical and charming and so full of life with so many layers.It's a story with art at its core, yes. But it is more about selfconfidence, friendship, selfdoubt.Bonuspoints for naming everything after food. Towns, people. It's cute and charming.Packaged with memorable and awesome soundtrack too.The gamemechanics are very well done too. The puzzles feel creative, always new and refreshing and rewarding.You can always just call your parents and have them give you the answer. Your mother will give you a general pointer as to the story, but if you're really stuck then dad can tell you exactly in what screen to find your way and how to overcome puzzles.It's also super fair in telling you things like: Don't swim down that waterfall, you won't get back up. Like the game perfectly knows when something is frustrating and it is one step ahead of you to prevent it.Later on shortcuts naturally unlock if you unlock new powers making it a cakewalk to get to unexplored chests.And if you're totally not up for bossfights and you just want to go for the story, you can increase your health, make urself immortal or skip the bossfights in your options. Or want colours that are easier on your eyes? Yup. It got you covered. Scared to have missed a costume? There's a shop that lets you trade your costumes for whatever is in undiscovered chests. So you can never miss clothes you really want.This game gives you all the tools you would possibly want.Bonuspoints:The german translation is really really good. There's a couple words missing like typo style. But aside from that I felt at home in my native language. And I do say that playing MMOs and most other games in english cuz those translations are usually lacking. So big thumbsup.* * *If I had to name negative things theres only two details that come to mind. The first NPC I encountered was - the only - NPC that speaks in text language "lol". And I was wierded out and scared at first that everyone would talk like this. I would maybe place that NPC a few screens further away.And this one paintbrush style. The paintbucket? I thought I needed something else for the puzzle and straight up skipped the screen. And went on to colour in the entire world without the pain bucket. Yeah. Don't do that. I would have wished that this special tool would be awared for the paint classes or otherwise through the story. Something you can't miss. But that's also just me being dumb. And nitpicky.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Just writing a quick, temporary review to boost the algorithm.I love everything about this game - the premise, gameplay, puzzles, accessibility, and Lena's wonderful soundtrack. These are probably things that everyone's spoken about already, so I'm just going to highlight some features that really make the game shine.- The fact that you can colour in and paint however you want, and the world colours show up on your minimap- The fact that you can slap down furniture anywhere in the world and return later to see other characters show up where you've placed stuff to chill out- The fact that you're allowed to swap clothing items you have for items you've seen but didn't pick up- The fact that the music, in real time, changes (eg. going in and out of a shop, the soundtrack keeps playing but the saxophone (insaneintherain!) drops to a more mellow violin in real time)- Lots of lovely sidequests, and other characters have real personality to them. The game doesn't recognise if you go the extra mile for characters (one wants you to take photos, but I coloured in the scenes before giving them to him) but you really do lose yourself in it and feel really happy helping others out.- Find lost kittens!- Commentary on how letting go of materialism lets art literally fluorish- A wonderful analogy on mental healthWill update the rest of this once I'm done with my playthrough. This game has so much potential and the extras above really make it feel like an indie game made by passionate people. Please buy and support it - I'm actually surprised by the lack of waves this game is making - you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game. I describe it as "weaponized wholesomeness". The most impressive aspect for me is how the game is fantastically written with charming characters. Most side characters that you only interact with in passing aren't very deep, but I'm still excited to talk to them whenever they appear around the world. The characters you do interact regularly are quite complex. The game does a great job of introducing conflict between the characters without shoehorning in contrived reasons to argue or disagree, which is especially impressive for how short the experience is. The sound and visuals are also great! They really take advantage of allowing the player to colour everything. Everything has defined silhouettes that are still identifiable at a glance, and adding your own colours is a simple way to add so much.My only complaint would be the minimal gameplay. The game is mostly carried on simple puzzles and metroidvania-style exploration as you gain new paint-based abilities. You are encouraged to search for objects in each area that you go through, but that is mostly just looking for hidden objects or paths, and the only rewards are cosmetic items and achievements. These aspects have very little depth, and aren't actually that challenging. There are also "fights", but they are also limited in scope. Overall, my complaints are small. I believe that the simple gameplay is probably an attempt of making the game very accessible, which I cannot fault. The game's focus is definitely writing, visuals, and mood. I recommend this game, and think everyone should experience it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: When at about 4 hours in steam asked if i would recommend Chicory, the answer was yes. It was yes to the point that this is my first steam game review ever. However I wanted to finish the game before putting together said review. This game is beautiful. Sitting and coloring the areas was fun and incredibly relaxing. The story was engaging and while relatively simple is still very sweet. Side characters in the world actually had interesting personalities, and seeing and interacting with them outside of their areas when they came out to see how you colored the world. And speaking of coloring, the COLORS! Each area limiting you to a palette of 4 colors was genius and really made the world pop way more than I expected. The art direction of everything in the game is fantastic. My partner is terrified of all things bugs. Spiders, insects, anything, she hates them all. BUT THEY LOVED THE BUGS IN THIS GAME!! If that doesn’t show how fantastic the character design is in this game I don't know what would.In short though, if you’re reading this and you haven’t played chicory yet, just do it. It is genuinely one of the best games i have played in 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an Eya-tier masterpiece of a game, and an experience I enjoyed thoroughly. Gameplay wise the puzzle platforming was very satisfying, and knowing how to get everywhere felt so rewarding. As the game goes on the environment becomes more and more enjoyable to explore, especially exciting was the way and the time the tools needed to do that are introduced to you.I loved the main mechanic of painting everything, it's very therapeutic to draw in this game, especially because it's pretty much impossible for anything you make to look bad. Only nitpick with it is the blank space in the center of 3 or 4 different colors but it was only really a nitpick whenever I drew in the art academy and even then never got in the way.What even is there to say about the soundtrack? Lena Raine. What more could you possibly ask for? The moment I realized Lena played a huge part in this I knew I had to play it immediately.The story is really something beautiful, especially for somebody like me. I'm not going to delve into spoiler territory and im gonna keep it brief, but a lot of things said were things I needed to hear. It's a warm feeling. If only I could just keep talking to all of these people, heheI also LOVE the inclusion of the post-game that gives everyone extra dialogue (and ). _childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I initially picked up this game only because Lena Raine was doing the soundtrack (which is fantastic, by the way). But to my surprise, I really started enjoying this game.The coloring options you get do expand quite a bit and with the coloring book vibe combined with lovable characters (<3 u pickle) and great writing, it starts to feel like a personal project that you've invested a lot of time and love into, especially when you stroll through old regions that you colored in a while ago.This is a pretty different type of game than most people are used to, but if you like chill, atmospheric games, RPGs with great stories, or beautiful soundtracks, this is your game!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game to other players? HECK YEAH I would! Yes, part of makes this game truly unique is that it invites players to draw out their creative side and express it in a meaningful way throughout the game. And it does it so well. But if you don't want to do that, that's alright! You don't have to put a lot of effort into being creative if you don't want to be. That's not all this game has to offer either! For example,Do you like wholesome story-rich games with a lot of heart and inspiring themes? Then play this gameHow about unique characters with lots of personality all around? Play this gameWide adventures through distinct environments filled with puzzles to solve and treasures to find? Play this gameFantastic music that does a great job setting the tone wherever you go? Play this gameOptional collect-a-thons that are fun AND useful rather than over-bearing or pointless? Play this game!The only thing I will say is that if you like combat then there isn't a lot in this game; there's only bosses and, if you don't even want to fight at all, you can disable boss fights altogether. BUT, if anything, I quite like games with interesting and challenging combat, and I did really like the boss fights in this game! They weren't particularly hard, but not WAY too easy either. Controlling Drawdog to dodge while using my mouse or the right joystick to paint-attack was pretty cool to me, the attack patterns were neat, and the way the story meshed into the fights was well done. But yeah, from everything above, to smaller yet thoughtful features like being able to "call home" for help when you're stuck or settings that help its players be as comfortable as possible playing (ie. disabling "wet" sounds that's not your thing)... you can really tell this game has A LOT of love put into bringing its world and gameplay to life. And in turn, this is a game I think players will love back.Edit: ah, on the small chance a dev will see this, one thing I'd  like in the game is to be able to save progress for art pieces and come back to it later ^^; 400 hours but most of it was leaving my game on because I wanted to work on it more but needed a break in-between
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much. The coloring-book-world mechanic is fun artistically, and it features intriguing paint-based puzzles. For the periodic boss battles, you can increase your character's hit-point count (even to invulnerability, as I did) or skip them. After you finish the main plotline, you enter a free-play epilogue, where you can finish up any side quests you didn't do earlier, or just wander around and have fun painting the world. I'm so happy to have the free-play mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is awesome to play as an artist, especially with its amazing stability in the mouse controls. It has adorable yet simple character designs and a well established world. There are some challenging puzzles that can get a bit frustrating, but those are few and far between. Achievement hunting is simple yet rewarding, and dedication really does pay off. A definite must-have for anyone who appreciates art and its creation. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a little hard to talk about. There were moments when I was completely blown away by how on point the writing was, and there were moments when I couldn't bring myself to play for more than 10 minutes at a time because of how horribly boring it was. The short version is that I generally think that Chicory is simply not as good as both devs' previous works (Celeste and Wandersong, respectively). To keep things simple: it's best to think of it as three separate things. Chicory is a story, a game, and a colouring book. The game and colouring book parts are pretty mediocre; enjoyable at times, but generally a slog. But the story is so incredibly good, you keep playing anyway.You walk, you explore, you solve puzzles which involve using your brush in different ways. Later on you learn abilities which make the exploration a bit more interesting... in theory. But in practice everything feels flimsy and there were many times where I wondered "wait, was it supposed to be like that?". Jumping in particular felt just bad.Admittedly, the world of Picnic is rather interesting to explore, but I found it too big and empty. And due to the nature of the game, everything you find will be devoid of colour... unless you paint it yourself, that is. So whenever you're exploring you're faced with a dillema: do I continue exploring, or do I stop and doodle a bit to make this boring cliff a little more appealing?Well, I chose to paint in every single screen that I encountered, and it really ground the pacing to a halt all the time. But at least I was somewhat satisfied with the result.Every area has five (or four?) colours available to use. On one hand, it's an interesting limitation, forcing you to make orange trees and blue grass - fitting for a jungle, I'd say. On the other, it simply prevents you from truly making the world the way you want it to be (until much later, at least).Still, there's the same problem I mentioned before: you have to make a choice of either killing the pacing of your adventure or walking in a boring, colourless world. Admittedly, some areas were more fun to paint than the others, but in general after 2-3 screens of a new area I've had enough already.At some point you unlock the ability to place ornaments. So you can turn this empty meadow into a campsite, perhaps into an outdoor art studio, and NPCs will react to whatever you do! Even sit on chairs that you place. That's nice, but I felt like it doesn't really add much to the game.And here we go, the reason why I'm recommending this in spite of all the complaining.The writing itself is razor-sharp. It just cuts directly to the core; every conversation feels like this super earnest exchange that you have at 2 AM in the kitchen when the party is slowly winding down. I absolutely loved this. I know not everyone is into New Sincerity, so if you're one of those weirdos who still thinks sarcasm and irony are cool, then you'll probably hate this game.And the topic, well: it's a game about imposter syndrome and dealing with trauma. The thing that just makes it is that you're literally an imposter - you're a janitor that happened to pick up the Brush after the previous wielder threw it away after a mental breakdown. And yet here you are, wielding it to the best of your ability. As someone who struggles with imposter syndrome pretty much daily, I'm very grateful for this setup. "You are not an imposter" is cheap, "everyone is an imposter" is unhelpful. But "You absolutely are an imposter, so what?" is a legitimately refreshing and helpful take.It's not just your trauma, either. In fact, your "only" issues are lack of faith in yourself and imposter syndrome. But there are others. There's the eponymous Chicory of course, but also pretty much every single NPC (they're all unique and named, by the way) has something going on in their life. And they'll tell you about it, if you listen. Maybe you'll even be able to help.I mean... the game is just slow and boring for the most part. There, I said it. I didn't really like the painting, either; I guess I'm the kind of artist who only produces art for the result, rather than for the fun of it, which dooms me to life of misery. I guess I need to work on that.But the writing and the story manage to make you care. About the characters, about the world, about Chicory, about your little dog character. Besides, it taught me a lot about myself. So while Chicory may not be a very good game... it is also an excellent game. Maybe. Definitely.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an excellent piece of creative story telling. The game-play and puzzles are so engaging, the art and music is so fun and inspiring, and post-story play-ability in the world is very high for me. The messages of this game has stayed with me and helped me move past things I've always said no to myself about.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I LOOOOOOOVE THIS GAME WAAAnot a very helpful review but ^^^^^^^^ its so good!! i completed it in a couple days not because its short by any means but simply bc i Did Not want to put it down. immediately the presentation pulls you in: the art is gorgeous even before you get to color it in, and the characters are both cute but also bursting with personality. i love the animal choices and how they're drawn its a great style for them. and the story is WONDERFUL: intense, touching, emotional, sweet, funny, and also personally effecting for me as a person who enjoys art and making it but struggles with it for a variety of reasons, largely mental health issues.of course, whats a video game without the game part?? for that chicory absolutely delivers. i already have a bias towards puzzle games, and the core mechanics of the gameplay along with the puzzles are just fun, a joy to figure out and complete and never frustrating! the whole thing is very well paced and knows when to let you take a break but the breaks are always offers instead of forcing you to- you can plow through the main story very fast and not stop! but you'd also be missing so much of the great dialogue so also why would you??? even when i was excited to see what happened next, i also was excited to talk to every person i could find.okay words are quickly failing me so also consider: my gameplay sessions of this were on average 9 hours with no breaks u get SO invested its just so fun and it just made me happy to play. play it *grabs you*
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: At 28.5 hours and 100 % completion I can now verify that Chicory is a pretty good and fun - and somewhat relaxing - Indie game. 8 to 9 range, imo, maybe less or more depending on your patience / appreciation of being encouraged to do art and fill-in-the-blank color books (which you don't have to do, but way to not engage with the premise of the game if ya don't at least try).It scratched some weird itch for me, at least, given that I'm not even an artist, and I think some people might be Into That. Soundtrack's pretty stellar as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like the perfect blend of Animal Crossing, Zelda, and Mario Sunshine/Paper Mario Color Splash. The story is great, the music is amazing, and the gameplay is so refreshingly different. I am so glad games like this exist because they remind me of why I love games so much. Hollow Knight, Celeste, Everhood, Undertale and now Chicory are some the best experiences I have had in my 30 years of gaming. This game randomly was recommended to me on Steam and I gave it a shot and I am so glad I did. I hope this game and the team that made it get all the attention they deserve for this awesome title.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a beautifully written work, very emotional, and full of heart while also having some insightful commentary on the art world, artists and art in general. The game world feels expansive without feeling empty, and the bountiful number of NPCs and sidequests make the world feel alive. The characters are all well-developed and have colorful personalities (pun wholly intended). All of this is supported further by beautifully-crafted graphics and a soundtrack that covers the entire emotional spectrum.On top of encouraging players to be creative in coloring the world around them, the game also has a solid base as a puzzle-platformer. The brush mechanics get used in interesting ways for puzzles and exploration. And there is a large amount of optional content in the game to add depth and character beyond that.If I had to give one criticism, it is that a handful of the boss fights are a bit more frustrating than they should be. And there were certain points where the coloration of NPCs during certain animations don't always 100% match the colors they had just earlier. But those are relatively minor complaints, and in the case of boss fights there are accessibility options that make boss fights easier to deal with (or even let the player skip them entirely).In short, the game is beautiful and I cannot recommend enough that you play it. It is without a doubt my favorite game of 2021, by a wide margin.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: Amazing Game, buy it now!It is a beautiful game, with solid mechanics and made, even a person like me that doesn't like puzzle or exploration games love it!It got a really cute art in general, but also touches some serious topics in it's story and treats them really well.The coloring part is really good, and makes you still try to be creative even if you aren't good at art in general.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A heartwarming story about the expectations and burdens of being an artist, and the struggle to overcome them.Don't be afraid to buy this if you don't know how to draw.  The game expects nothing of you, and the brush is too low resolution to make anything detailed anyway.  Plus you're working with a very limited color palette most of the time.  Just doodle all over the place, use unrealistic colors everywhere, go nuts!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Really good characters, wonderful animations, a compelling story, and enjoyable gameplay! The painting options are just complex enough to have a lot of fun with different styles and colors without getting too bogged down in the details. I enjoyed talking to all the NPCs in the world and the main story was so so good. Easily recommend this to anyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of heart. The puzzles aren't incredibly challenging, but challenging enough to keep you engaged. The story, itself, is amazing. Incredibly fun idea for a game, with an incredibly powerful message. If you've ever suffered from imposter syndrome, this game will really speak to you. The gameplay is just flat out fun, on top of it. HIGHLY recommend. A game that will really stick with you. <3
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Very charming and effective story and characters. I liked the mechanics of the paintbrush, and they used it in really creative ways. I also really loved that it was only 6 or so hours long; any longer and it would have been way too much. However, this kind of aesthetic often makes it difficult to make things out in the environment, so there were several places where I got lost or couldn't see where I was supposed to go next just because it wasn't clear on the screen, which is frustrating. All in all though it was very good.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A very cute, heartfelt and at times heartwrenching game, it hit me hard at times reminding me of times of depression and negativity, but also of kindness and friendliness. Lovely art style, though I might have made the world of Picnic a little worse with some of my horrible painting skills - and yet none of the friendly characters would mind!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: If you like cute indie games, if you like art, if you like a surprisingly good story, this game is for you.If you play video games, then this is a game you should play.It's a world that you can fill in like a colouring book, and it's up to you to roam the land and spread that colour. And that's fun, traversing the Zelda-like map to solve puzzles, paint new things, meet interesting people, all to charming art and perfectly scored music. But man when the story hits. That narrative that make me feel more enriched for having played through it, that I wish some could have seen.It's basically a cake with all the right ingredients and made to pull out each flavour to their strength.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I want to give this game a "Super Yes" It's not enough for me to just "Recommend" this game, I want it to succeed, I want all of my friends to experience it. I will buy it again for that purpose. This game has, and I must point out by the way I am not even finished, moved me in a way I have not been moved by a game in a long long time.The Narrative in this game is crafted to perfection, as someone who has been struggling with their own self-worth, PARTICULARLY as an artist, feelings of inadequacy, having people I look up to who feel are more talented and creative and maybe even "worthy" of being an artist than me. But it goes beyond just that, delving into those people I look up to as well, exposing their personal struggles of dealing with their own self-worth, doubt. This is very personal to me and I find myself in the protagonist in a way I haven't been able to relate to in any other video game character to date.All the little NPC's that comment on my characters art and try to lift me up also remind me of dealing with my own, albeit small following in my art community. I don't know what else to say but that this game is like, an impressionist re-telling of my life throughout my 20's. I don't know what else to say, I am in love with this game.I could say more about it I guess, the Puzzles are genuinley fun and well crafted, some of them I actually got pretty stuck on haha.The games art style and character design is A+material, the characters are so freaking cute.And the soundtrack is beautiful, I saw someone else mention it was the same artist who worked on Celeste? They do good work, that game as well had a great OST and if you enjoyed that one you'll love this games music too.This game has come out at a time when I really think I needed a story like this and a game like this to play. If you are also struggling creatively you'll know what I'm talking about. Please, if you have $20 bucks, I highly recommend this game. It's well worth the $20, and you get a pretty long lasting story too. I've been playing for about 11 hours now and I'm still roughly half way through I believe? Definitely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. Painting the world is fun, the puzzles and mechanics are good, and it has a really good central story. Honestly though, my favorite part was just the personality of the game and how that bled through into everything. Every character is worth talking to, every screen is pretty even before you draw on it, and the music is great too.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A cute, relaxing puzzle game where you can colour in the whole map! There are various puzzles and platforming to solve, and collectables hidden all over. There are also small quests to complete. The art style and music are nice. For a game this relaxing I would have liked a little more direction, so I could focus on the chill, but I had to resort to Google at some points as I was stuck. The phone boxes are good for hints and tips but don't help with specific puzzles. The boss battles were unnecessary and I didn't enjoy them. I didn't feel they added anything to the game apart from RSI, from repeatedly spamming left click. I didn't realise you could turn these off until the end of the game which was a shame as they were the worst bit for me. Overall a great little game. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous and fully realized concept that has a great game to go with the brilliant aesthetic conceit. This is equal parts coloring book and metroidvania, and it is fantastic at being both, all with a stunning soundtrack and a beautiful story about coming to terms with your own doubts.  I can't recommend this highly enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Current playtime: 15 hours. Finished. Loved it. Almost certainly my GOTY. Play it. Love it. And buy the soundtrack, it's fantastic.My god, its fantastic. Music? Fantastic. Celeste composer is top tier, and super diverse in its tracks. Gameplay? Great. You can paint ANYTHING* *: Very very few exceptions. There's puzzles to solve, secrets to find, and even some darker turns iv'e not been expecting. Story? Great so far. It's sprinkled in a lot of foreshadowing, but overall, it's got a lot of heart and I expect a lot of feels, and hard feelings to process. And lastly, since i'm sure this applies to others too, on the creativity standpoint, it's FUN to paint. Wanna paint the entire ground? Hold left mouse. Paint that tree? Tap it once. There's only 4 colors per screen so it limits you in a good way, while still offering a ton of freedom and making it EASY for uncreative people like me, to actually spark a bit of creativity and not freak out about having to paint.It's always possible my feeling will change as I progress, but I expect them to only get more positive, if anything. Highly recommended, and a GOTY candidate.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: It's cool, but I think I'm not the target audience for it. As an artist, I don't want to be doing art on my time off, and as someone with ADHD, it's REALLY hard for me to leave a square unfinished, so playing this feels more like a chore than it ought to. Music is great and characters are cute, though a little boring. I'd say it's a good game for many, just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Look, I must confess that I've never been one for "cozy games". Not that I'm a bitter person, but often a lot of these cute comfort indie games that come out never click with me. That being said, I ADORE this game. Chicory definitely appeals to the crowd that likes cute little indie games, but I was surprised to see how much more this game had to it. For starters, the core concept of making every screen of a game a coloring book page is implemented very well. Coloring feels smooth and the game gives you a lot of stress-free room and prompts starting out to help you open up creativity-wise. I am not an artist and don't really like drawing on command, but I still found myself talking the time to color entire areas in Chicory by the end of the game.What really stands out to me though is the cohesion of the game's story, gameplay, and coloring. To summarize it in a spoiler-free way, the story has your character gain confidence in themselves as an artist throughout the story. Not only does this line up to your ability to color the world in more diverse ways, but I found that I was also gaining confidence in myself to creatively express myself . This type of cohesion led to me getting super invested in the story and I couldn't put the game down. It helps that the game is also pretty funny and has an amazing soundtrack. Easy recommendation for anyone, not just artists.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really good. And really fun.similar to Wandersong, it takes a genre used by many games (in this case, top-down 2D Zelda-esque gameplay) and makes adds a completely new, unique mechanic. (in this case, the painting system.)The story's great as well, and the soundtrack is excellent.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: For a game so indebted to 2-D Zelda for its structure, Chicory is astoundingly unique.Take, for example, the only "weapon" in your character's arsenal: The brush. It does not cut, maim or harm: It paints. And yet, its impact on the game's setting is so much greater than a sword. In most games of this genre, it does not matter how many enemies you kill: They will always respawn. In Chicory, you are using creativity rather than combat to quite literally make your mark on the world... not just physically (solving puzzles, unlocking paths for traversal), but figuratively. Your work gains fans, attracts onlookers, sparks conversation with the game's NPCs.And those conversations can be quite meaningful. Chicory's themes of acceptance (both of others and ourselves), generational baggage, imposter syndrome, fear of failure, the dangers of gatekeeping, and the joy of creativity for its own sake resonated deeply with me. These ideas go so well with the game's painting mechanics that they never feel heavy-handed or dissonant.I did occasionally find it challenging to manage both traversal and painting with a controller, so I eventually switched to painting with the touchscreen on my Steam Deck. But that's my only real quibble, and the game's lack of lives or a health system makes it very forgiving, so it never blocked my progression.Chicory is a brilliantly designed game, and a delight from start to finish. You should play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that I'll update a review but I kind of have to after getting to the credits of Chicory.This game is a wonderful event. You will be smiling the entire time. It is filled with joy, feelings, earnestness, exploration and most of all: Your own art however you wish to express it. The game is a perfect sphere: no 'edge' anywhere. Just earnest joy and the fun of helping others or sticking around to color the world in your own way. Even more: They deal with real issues that face artists, from burnout to imposter syndrome, but balance it with the cuteness of folk so happy to see you making art. You even get a #1 fan who brings you some adorable gifts! Best of all: It sticks the landing. It really does and you're not going to get to the end and go "Wait that's it?" Nope. The devs know how to make a crescendo and a climax. After all: They did Wandersong. They know something about music.After Wandersong and Chicory I can not wait to see where they go next. I'd happily put Chicory up there with a certain other 2d colorful game about talking animals/monsters that we'll leave un-named for now. Thanks for a lovely piece of art, Chicory Team. You made a little dog/raccoon very happy. ---Original Review below---It is the anti-shooter. It is the color that the brown shaded shooters fear.Against all of the brown milsims can conjure,Against all of the edge AAA can churn out,We shall send unto them:A really cute doggy with a coloring paint brush! Bring joy! Bring Color, bring light to the black and white. And above all, have fun doing it. The game is a treat, that'll have you smiling like a goof at how adorable everything is, at how much love is put into the animations, and how many little side quirks there are.Bonus: Make sure to call home and see how mom and dad chat while you're on the phone. What other games have your parents so happy to chat you up over the phone? What other game lets you design a donut? What other game lets you paint the person you're talking to while talking to them?Go, Wielder. The only thing they need, is you.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good. The music is great, the style is charming, and the puzzles are puzzling. I love playing this with my 12-year-old, mostly I run around and talk to NPCs, and she figures out all the puzzles before I can. It's got a little bit of everything, you can pace yourself and just color in a page if you don't feel like rushing off to the next objective. Not for speedrunners, probably, but it's never boring or tedious, there's no grinding or fishing. It's just solving stuff and coloring things. The only criticism I have is that the map can be a little difficult to navigate, sometimes you don't remember where you met an NPC or which tunnel you need to go through to get there. Still fun to wander around, there's always stuff to do and the more you unlock the more things you can uncover in the places you've already explored. I wish more games could take a design note from how they've done the two-player controls. You can play with two people of equal skill, or two people with different, complementary skills, or one person who can play video games and one small child who just wants to splash paint around. All equally enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don’t understand the reviews on this one. There are a few clever and unique mechanics, but the story did not catch us, the gameplay for at least the first hour is mostly confusing and un-fun puzzles, and perhaps most ironically, it is visually very ugly.I’d say don’t believe the reviews and skip unless you’re researching video game mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game wears its premise and gameplay on its sleeve. The world has lost its color and you'll need to take your time and repaint it. Chicory does a great job easing the player in by limiting your pallate and brush at the start of the game.  Chicory rewards exploration and puzzle solving by giving you more creative options and shapes for your brush. The story is also very good and tackles expectation and burnout. Even if, like me, you are not an artist. Chicory is a chill time.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I just love this game. So glad I got 50+ hours out of it until 100%, but there is still more character dialogue I could go through. I also actually think I got better at art while playing? lol and even had a couple random art spurts when i went and painted stuff for a day irl. but yeah, the topics and themes were so beautifully explored and totally relatable for me-- as a musician/creative person, as someone very prone to long mental health dips, and as someone who thinks alot about how to support friends and others going through tough things (not that i do it well).it's also such a cool game in that, besides enjoying the experience of the gameplay and story, you feel like you really contributed to it with your colors/painting/own style, and you get a lot of little awesome showcases and gifty things throughout the game for it -- super fun and you'll feel like a excited kid showing your art to whoever will look. also the soundtrack. Lena Raine blows us away again.  had diff tunes stuck in my head like every waking moment i wasn't playing and was so ok with it. it was like... the game soundtrack because MY soundtrack? actually i just thought of that.. it's kind of like that for any soundtrack that gets stuck in your head. your head replays it in your life as YOUR soundtrack for a while... ANYWAYS. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, wow my first steam review ever! I just had write something about that little game that has become so dear to my heart. I've started it without expectation but was left in tears at the end of it. The characters, style and music has been charming. The story is simply fantastic. It deals with mentall illness and many problems that I'm all too familiar with. I found myself really relating to Chicory and the main character. The colouring makes a lot of fun and gives the game a very individual touch. It has tons of side quests and you can certainly spend more hours in it than the main story. Boss fights have never been too difficult and the game has options to make them easier. All in all it's a marvellous game that certainly deserves more attention!That being said, there are a couple of small things, which bothered me. First of all, it's sometimes very hard to differentiate heights in the game, which make some puzzles seem way more difficult than they are. Second of all, in the swamp the monitor has this weird cloud, grid pattern effect, which made me feel so dizzy. It would have been great to have an option to turn it off. This effect is also on clouds and in other areas but not as prominently featured as there.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it. Loved it loved it loved it. Every single second of this game was spent doing something. I was either working towards completing a chapter, coloring my entire screen, or having a heartwarming conversation with some of the witty characters in the game. The game opens up with an introduction to the mechanics, and then the problem is presented (there's no more color in the world). The intro to the game had me hooked immediately. Normally, it takes a few hours before I can really get into a game. But as soon as I understood how to color, I started loving every second of my playtime. This game surprised me with how long it actually is. There are so many different side-drawings that you can do. And each time you finish one, you're left knowing that you helped someone that day (even if they are just a talking animal in a video game). Once I completed the game, I was left wondering what could have happened if I had explored more, since it was a common occurrence to find a new tool that helps you SO MUCH throughout the game, even though its optional to find it. The story throughout this game was incredible. The story (surprisingly) focuses on some really deep topics like depression, and I always found myself wanting to know what will happen next as if this game was a TV show that I was watching. The puzzles in this game weren't that hard, although I did find myself getting stuck a lot, it was mostly because I didn't know where to go. But there is a really good solution to all of it... Your Dad. Your Dad, (a raccoon) Is my favorite character in the entire game, yes, even though there are many characters with really interesting personalities, he was my favorite because he was a back seat gamer (the type of person who has already played the game that you are playing and constantly tells you the answers to some puzzles, and gives you directions on where to go). I often found myself asking for his help whether I needed it or not. Chicory Is my new favorite game, which is a high bar since I got a lot of games. Whether it is the quirky conversations or the very interesting story, I was always ready for more of this game. P.S. The replay-ability for this game is outstanding. There were so many things that I missed throughout the game, that I'm ready to pick up a new game and find EVERYTHING and eventually become the god of Picnic (the world).Play it. Please.P.P.S. As a side note, the soundtrack is also incredible. The music changes depending on where you are in the world, and I want to go back to some places just to listen to more of those absolute bops.

_childDocuments_.review: It's quite a horror to see your amateurish art when compared to those generated by the game, a real ego blow. But then again what is art and how do we judge on its merit anyway? So despite my pixel monstrosity sitting next to the esteemed masterpieces in the Wielder Tower I still am proud i created something of my own.Chicory the game is an innovative puzzler making the full used of its potential theme and mechanics. In a world where powerful Wielders ensure the world remains vibrantly coloured, you find yourself the accidental hero put to task to correct the events set forth by your master. Can a mere cleaner save the world? I love the creative range it allows, however limited the tools given to do so and the world created and world lore imagined ties in well with interesting locale and characters. The story line is solid despite a cliche good vs evil theme and that of self discovery of ones own weakness as well as ability.The puzzler mechanics are well thought of and intuitive with puzzle locks spacing you to ensure game play progresses smoothly without difficulty spikes. The battles are challenging but fun, this coming from a person who hates bulletime and rougelike combat systems while the puzzles aren't too frustrating and with an intuitive hint system to help assist if you are stuck. Some platforming is needed and did miff me a bit but in the end the challenging and enjoyable game kept me engaged enough to want to wrap up the story and do a completionist run.All in all a solid and well written game with enjoyable game mechanics that will keep you engaged for hours on end.

It's also quite a long game, giving me 40+ hours of playtime to %100 completion (including all achievements). Obviously playing just the story itself and leaving the side stuff would be shorter but my point still stands. All in all, definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, yeah.Subjective things - It's short and casual, a bit little mental-health themed (more than I expected), and while I wouldn't really call it meta you get a vibe like the creators are talking about themselves a bit. The few bad things - The pacing is a little fast. And the beginning of the game kind of goes through some moral choices (albeit light choices) I'm not sure I'd go through. And again, it's super short - probably less than 10 hours if you're not trying for 100%.Not bad things - It seems jankier than it is; it really isn't. Coloring's a bit more simple than you might expect - don't feel pressured to make every screen a masterpiece. You also want to play this game with a keyboard and mouse.  Combat is rare, but hectic and a bit confusing. I've yet to lose it, not even sure it's possible to lose, however.Good things - The puzzles are fun if a bit easy. Think gameboy Zelda-like environmental interactions. Lots of collectibles - you're never punished for exploring. It's a very creative concept for a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes you need a game to give you (figuratively) a warm hug, and sometimes you need a game to give you a slap in the face. Chicory does both, and it does both  well. For any struggling artist, or any person who's ever felt the desire to be creative, or any person that wants a world of adorable animals where everyone is named after their favorite food, or just about anyone who needs a bit of inspiration, Chicory is the game for you. I was hesitant at first to get this game - I do not consider myself an artist, and was put off by the idea of painting as a primary mechanic. But the painting is meditative, silly at times, and brings the world to life (one of the most meaningful parts of the game, for me, was in the end credits: ).This is a puzzle-based exploration game - there is minimal combat, and the gameplay is fun but extremely forgiving. Don't look to Chicory to challenge your dexterity, but do expect to face some serious conversations about depression, self-worth, the meaning and purpose of art, and the toxicity of long-standing institutions. For a game that looks like a coloring book on the surface, it packs a huge narrative punch. With a stunning soundtrack by Lena Raine, customizable outfits and home decor, secrets scattered throughout the world, and a large cast of diverse characters, this is, quite simply, a wonderful game. Might count as art therapy too, who knows.Edit: Wish I could nominate this for multiple Steam awards.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory; A Colorful Tale is a game unlike any I have played before. It's very much like a colouring book transformed into a game with an incredibly introspective narrative and solid characterisation to boot. Coming from the incredibly talented team behind Celeste, this game was a joy to play through. Note, some of the following paragraphs contain some spoilers, so read on at your own discretion.Whereas this team's previous game, Celeste, covered themes of mental health and coming to accept every aspect of yourself, both good and ugly, Chicory delves into a rather different aspect of emotional and personal development, though equally poignant; Chicory's themes tie very closely into it's artistic presentation and core gameplay mechanic of painting the world around you- they focus on the struggles of an artist, in the broad sense of artistry and development of a craft. It covers subjects such as impostor syndrome, perfectionism, and the various struggles that come with being either a sage master or fledgling student of a craft. It also demonstrates the relationship that forms between teacher and student, as well as the impact that bond has on both parties.The gameplay is something incredibly unique, though I mean that in the best sense. The game has you exploring the world of Picnic as a small dog who is canonically named Pizza, though their name is decided based on whatever food you answer the game's intro question of "what is your favourite food?" to. Pizza, the janitor for the current wielder of the brush, Chicory, becomes the new wielder when they take the brush following the loss of colour across Picnic, and upon Chicory's unwillingness to continue on as the current wielder. Using the brush, you travel across Picnic, restoring colour to the land as you go. Each area within the game gives you a colour palette of 4 colours, which you are free to use as you wish. Initially, I felt 4 colours was lackluster variety of colour, and felt like I couldn't paint areas as I would ideally want to. However, the game limits you intentionally to force you to become more creative with how you paint, giving you access to brush strokes that can change the shape of your brush stroke, give you a little motif you can stamp, or allow you to paint textures. Furthermore, the limited colour palette makes every area feel very distinct, as having so few colours allows one area to feel vastly different to another. The game's narrative really pushes that there is no "right" way when it comes to art, and so it not only encourages you, but in some regards makes you take risks with your artwork, and the NPCs throughout the game praise you for it, which is great positive reinforcement both in the game, and as a message to be extrapolated to honing these crafts in real life also. You're free to paint every screen completely, to have every screen use a different design, or even just to paint what you absolutely need to- the game acknowledges all of these and other options as completely valid, and enables you to play the game however *you* want to. And that is fantastic.The story is equally fantastic- to summarise as briefly as I can: Pizza, the main character, massively looks up to Chicory, the current wielder. However, Chicory abandons the brush out of frustration brought on by her obsession with needing everything to be perfect and feeling like nothing she does ever ends up like how she envisions it. Pizza takes the brush, and  with it the mantle of wielder, upon finding it outside Chicory's room. They begin to paint Luncheon, their home town, as it, as well as Picnic as a whole, has lost all of its colour due to Chicory's resolve to abandon her role as wielder. As they begin to paint more, they end up entering the darkness that is spreading through Picnic to try and purge it. This leads them to face a manifestation of their inner insecurities multiple times- the feeling like they aren't good enough to be a wielder and that they can never live up to the example set by Chicory and previous wielders. Chicory similarly confronts her inner insecurities later down the line, following which she helps Pizza complete the wielder trials to become a true wielder and confront the spreading darkness in Picnic. There's much more to the story than that, but I don't have enough space in this review to go in depth into it, so y'know, go play the game if you haven't already? I can't do the character development and interpersonal relationships of the characters justice in a review anyway, so you're best off experiencing it for yourself.As for the music, I will shill this soundtrack to the ends of the earth and back, holey moley, it is absolutely stunning. I would be lying if I said I didn't expect it to be, Lena Raine is one of my favourite composers when it comes to games and naturally went in expecting a standout OST. Lena is so incredibly clever in her use of reoccurring motifs and motivic development, often combining themes in various tracks to have some kind of narrative significance. She is exceptionally talented at complementing and mirroring the narrative in her soundtrack and it is a joy to listen to. Compared to her work on Celeste, a game that had a very synth-heavy soundtrack, Chicory's OST is far more acoustic in nature, with her employing other musicians to record various instruments within the soundtrack, rather than it all being done on sound libraries in Ableton. There are still multiple synth-dominant tracks, but they take on increased narrative significance within Chicory, only being used during the self-confrontation sections within the darkness. It's reminiscent of Badeline being symbolised by the synth lines in Celeste, particularly within the fan-favourite track of Resurrections, but it's more jarring to hear within Chicory given the abundance of acoustic instruments, which allows it greater tonal impact when the tracks occur. Lena has made a blog post on the website 'medium' entitled "Composing for Chicory — Motifs & Memories", which I think is absolutely worth a read, as it covers the significance of many of the themes in respect to narrative as well as theory, and gives greater insight into just how much time, effort, and thought went into composing for this title.One thing I must recommend about playing this game though, is that if you haven't already played it, take it slowly, particularly if you plan on painting the entire map. Painting even one screen can take a long time, and if you try and speedrun through painting every screen, you'll likely burn yourself out very quickly. It's akin to doing an entire colouring book in one sitting. You *could* do it, but why would you? It'll get very repetitive, you won't be performing at your best, and by the time you finish, you'll likely resent having spent so much time on it, nor will you be proud of the work you've done. Short sessions are ideal for this game.In summary, Chicory: A Colorful Tale, is not only a beautifully unique game, but a game that has an incredibly deep story to tell, with lessons that can be learned from it. The messages within this game don't just have to apply to an art form like painting, they can apply to any hobby you may have, and as a result I feel like this game carries with it a message that can resonate with most anyone. It is fundamentally a brilliant experience from start to finish, catering to all demographics and encouraging everyone to take a few steps out of their comfort zone and take a chance on something unfamiliar. In case this ridiculously long review didn't make it apparent, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. Stellar.

_childDocuments_.review: Just beat the game and wow that was an experience. I think there are a quite a few people that would resonate with this game. People who are creative (not me), people who might feel a little directionless in life (me), and people who might be a little too hard on themselves (...). Maybe that got a little dark too fast. So what is Chicory anyway? You're this cute dog who somehow gets this paintbrush to paint in the world however they want. The ultimate coloring book. You get different ways to paint and you get so many opportunities to go nuts with your creativity. And, as a result there's a lot riding on you. Part of the game is managing what creativity leads to and who your art is for.Gameplay-wise, you use your paintbrush to solve puzzles and get through your struggles. There are lots of puzzles and platforming around and although the platforming can be finicky at times, it's all doable. If you are ever stuck, you can even get hints if you need to!The characters are so charming. I spent quite a bit exhausting all the dialogue for everyone and there were even some pleasant surprises in the cast. Music is amazing. I spent some time in one area just listening to the music. I will buy the soundtrack at some point.For the visuals, you're making the color so it's as vibrant as you make it, but aside from that there is some insanely good art. Even for someone who can't really draw worth anything, I spent quite a bit of time just doing my best to make the place as nice as possible. Points to the accessibility options. Makes it friendly for everyone to play. And people should really play this game. Story... It's wholesome and heartfelt. It's an emotional tale and there were a lot of feelings to be had. I'm being vague here because people should go into this one blind. I will say that it knows what it's going for and guns for it as hard as it can. But at the end of it all, it's a kind game. I think this game at the very least helps you recognize who you are and where you are in this point in your life. I'm not going to say the game is magical and will fix all your emotional issues, but it lets you know that you're valid and that it's going to be ok. At the end of the day, it's a cute game where you can go nuts with your imagination. Go color the world to your heart's content. Give your family and friends a hug. It's that kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, now that's what I call a satisfying experience for a game. Just, Mwauh. Y'know? How has no one thought of this kind of concept before? A coloring book as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. Marvelous. This is the single most relaxing game I've ever played, and unlike most games that aim to be relaxing this one is fun too. It also has a great story and characters, I cannot recommend this game enough. It's one of my favorites now.The main draw to game is probably the story and characters. It was pretty clear what the story was for the most part from the start, the main aim of the story is just to send good life messages, and the characters were fully built around those messages, and it's great. I wish we got more with the main two characters because they're so well written and they're definitely my favorite character dynamic in a video game. (I don't play many story games). In most games I try to 100% the game to the best of my ability before going into the ending, but with this game I wasn't able to wait to finish the story and did completion afterwards.  The slight puzzle exploration game play was so much fun and relaxing. Nothing was difficult, the abilities were surprisingly really fun to move around in (I did not think I'd say that when I started the game), the map is honestly one of my favorite maps. There's a bunch of really neat hidden things, 100% completing this was a joy. (Except maybe the art classes, but to be fair I put those off all game and let them build up). I'm very glad the game gave in game hints to basically everything if you needed them. Had to look up a very few minor things though bc I was a little bit blind. Game took 20.8 hours to 100%, and I didn't really do a whole love of coloring besides filling stuff in, but I did take the time to go back and recolor certain areas to look nicer and that took a while. (I still kinda wanna go back and do that even more my map is ugly af rn)Okay. Music. It's Lena Raine, do I need to say more?No I don't but I need to get out that this has some of my favorite area themes in a game, and the musical motifs just conveyed so much. I get sad every time I walk out of certain areas because I'm leaving the music, but I'm almost always going into music that's just as good. The art style in this game very cute, probably what made me decide to get this game. The animations that happen during the  were very satisfying to the eyes.Speaking of those, yeah I gotta say those were  cool thematically, but they weren't fun gameplay wise at all, and they dragged on for so long, and there always in the middle of the important dialogue. Maybe I just didn't get what I was suppose to do but I just spam clicked through them. There is an option to skip them in the settings, but then you wouldn't get the cool music and animations. This is my only real issue with the game and honestly I don't care because everything else was too wonderful. Though I also wasn't thrilled with the "feature" that isn't a bug. (If you know you know.) No undo button was also sad but that wouldn't have made any story sense I suppose.After I fully completed the game I was sad that I didn't have too play the game anymore. Though I can and probably will go back and color stuff to make it look nicer. Thanks to Ech for recommending me this.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey. It's been a while since I've done this, so I'm gonna ramble for a bit. Consider this a charming (if overly verbose and somewhat annoying) anecdote before the recipe and feel free to skim through until you start seeing some words that look vaguely like unbridled praise. The phrase you're looking for is "And then I played Chicory."It's rare that a game comes along in someone's life that feels as if it was completely made for them. Three years ago, when I played Wandersong, I felt for the first time in my life that I had truly been seen. I felt as though the game itself had taken a peek inside of my soul and shown me parts even I had yet to discover. I felt a joy - a sheer, unadulterated, all-consuming happiness - that I truly believed could never be replicated or even approached.Then the world kinda, sorta, maybe ended. Just a bit.That's a bit dramatic considering I'm lucky enough to still be here, but 2019-2021 was nonetheless a pretty rough period for me (as I imagine it was for a lot of folks the world over). A lot has changed since then, both for me personally and for the world we all live in, and despite my generally optimistic outlook on life it's been admittedly difficult to resist growing just a little cynical and apathetic. Games became a passive hobby for me: more of a way to pass the time than a way to genuinely engage with art and entertainment media. I had begun to wonder if maybe games themselves had become jaded, an industry of profit rather than passion.Of course, this was partially my fault. I'd devoted myself rather completely to live-service titles or otherwise endless games. Titles which could theoretically be played forever, but that you only really play until you realize it's more of a routine than a passtime. Whatever feelings of fun that once came with the game are long gone by the time you stop playing it. When you finally do close it for that last time, it's less of a fond farewell and more like dropping off a check to pay an overdue bill. I've been feeling this sort of way about games - a dispassionate melancholy, very rarely spiked with moments of long-gone wonder - for longer than I realized. I haven't even written (or even attempted to write) a review for anything in years now. The last time I did was for Wandersong, that joyful spark I was sure I would never feel again.And then I played Chicory. You know that scene in Ratatouille? THAT one? Of course you do. Chicory was my first bite of that humble, beautiful plate of ratatouille. Within minutes of beginning, I felt a rush of warmth and nostalgia like I had never thought existed. That feeling - that sheer, unadulterated, all-consuming happiness - did not fade for even one moment of my nearly forty hours with this game. Every single second of this game fills the very fibers of my being with the sense that I am home, where I truly belong.The art direction is charming and endlessly inventive. The music is masterful, marvelous, and moving. The writing is clever, sincere, heart-warming, tragic, playful - fun. The gameplay constantly iterates on itself in ways which feel intuitive and ingenious at the same time. Chicory is exceptional in every sense of the word. There is not a single thing which it attempts that it does not earnestly succeed at with flying colors. I would say that the game's only flaw is that there isn't more of it for me to play, but that would be categorically untrue. There is precisely as much Chicory as is necessary and not a single ounce more. Chicory is a bolt of creative lightning that has rocked me to my very core.I can think of no higher praise for the game than to say this: I followed this game religiously when it was first announced. I carefully monitored the Kickstarter, the Twitter pages of the game and the devs, and the Steam page waiting for any and all news I could get about Chicory. I bought the game as soon as I possibly could when it finally released, and then... life happened. I told myself time and time again I would find a chunk of open time to truly enjoy the game to its fullest, and then a year passed. During that span of time, I heard nothing but overwhelming praise for Chicory from every available source, and despite all of that... Chicory still OVERdelivered.I don't know that a perfect game exists, but if it does, that game is Chicory: A Colorful Tale.

_childDocuments_.review: As an artist who recently graduated from college, this game impacted me a lot. _childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've played in recent years. I found Chicory's art style and painting mechanics charming in their own right, but the developers have also built an enormous variety of mechanics and encounters using those tools (painting and movement). The game's progression uses a Metroidvania structure in a large world with seamless traversal (no loading screens). During the playthrough, I interacted with dozens of characters and found the game's writing to be consistently high-quality. Great mix of puzzles that grow in challenge in each zone, along with plenty of side activities (like painting the sky for a couple standing on a rooftop) to add variety (importantly, these side activities are optional, so players can choose to rush the main questline instead). Lena Raine's music is incredible, just like the soundtrack to Celeste (although I prefer Chicory's even more).I had high expectations going into Chicory and after finishing the game, those expectations were exceeded. Highly recommended.
