_childDocuments_.review: I don't think there are enough words to describe just how incredible of an experience this game was. From beginning to end, everything was absolutely incredible. The art, the writing, the music, and everything in between created an experience I truly don't think I'll ever be able to forget.I don't normally go out of my way to try and 100% complete games often (I currently only have two games in my steam library, including this one, 100% completed to prove it), but Chicory had me so obsessed that it felt like the only option I had was to get every single achievement through my constant urge to pick the game back up after finishing the main story. Let me say right now that 100% completion is SO worth it, both for how fun it was to try and hunt for every last item I needed and for the fun extra "gift" of sorts you get for entirely completing everything the game has to offer. Even if you don't go out of the way to complete the game entirely, experiencing and playing through the main story is well worth your time.A lot of what makes this game good is how it approaches the topic of the struggles of being an artist, a topic that I have yet to see another game cover before. Sure, there are plenty of games that have covered mental health in the general sense, but the way that Chicory covers it through the lens of how being an artist can affect one's state of mind was something that is both new and handled incredibly beautifully. As an artist who has been struggling with mental health issues myself, I've seen how both outside pressure and internal struggles can really affect one's creative work. A lot of what was discussed in this game mirrored experiences either I or people I know have gone through, and it's handled incredibly well throughout.When the credits rolled, I audibly kept repeating the words "wow" silently to myself. I was absolutely floored by how good of a game this was, and I am shocked it hasn't blown up in popularity yet. I think I'm going to say it now, this might just be my pick for GOTY.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A colorful tale is a top-down adventure game, where you become The Wielder; a hero whose mission is to stop dark trees corruption and bring back colors to the world that’s lost them with The Brush, a tool that’s also used to manipulate certain objects in the world to make possible traveling where you can’t access by walking.There’s lot of to do and discover in this game in terms of side content. From different clothes to different brush styles to find hidden in world, to meet different NPCs whom have different wishes for you varying from painting area somewhat to style they like, those whom wish you to decorate area and ones whom need you to deliver something to someone with description based text puzzles.Even though I’m not a great painter it didn’t stop me enjoying of painting everything in this game. Only real small frustration on that part was how some objects it would not paint over even if mouse cursor was right pointing at them or above them.And only other smaller issue I can come up with as of writing this review was final boss battle's Either way, Chicory: A colorful tale is a game I didn’t know I would end up loving this much from gameplay to music and other aspects but here we are. If they ever make Chicory 2  I will definitely be looking at it.Ps. What I also want to give game a shout-out to it's great hint system where you can call your character's parents and mom first gives a subtle hint, but if you want dad gives you precise instructions to get forward. And not only does this apply to main story it still gives hints after completing main story in order to find all brush styles and map areas. Unfortunately that doesn’t cover all lost children’s nor litter (for small indie studio limited resources reasons) but apparently Sony did bring them to Playstation version of the game. Either way thanks mom & dad for helping me find all areas of map and all brush styles! <3

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute, relaxing, charming, and emotionally engaging game. I was surprised with how much I particularly loved the art class parts. _childDocuments_.review: Welcome, to scenic Picnic! Come for the novel gameplay, stay for the story! What kind of novel gameplay? Well, that's where it gets tricky to explain. Imagine if Link to the Past and Okami had a baby, but decided it wouldn't have any combat outside of bossfights, and would focus mostly on ability-based puzzles with the brush. That's the unusual mix that makes up Chicory, and it manages to pull it off expertly.Each screen of the game is a simple puzzle that takes only a few seconds to solve, making for a very satisfying pace, especially when paired with the various collectibles sprinkled about to challenge you to go off the beaten path. As you solve them, you put paint onto those screens, coloring them in as if they were pages in a coloring book. This little touch  trivial, but it adds a lot to the visual experience - an unfolding aesthetic rather than static one. One which is backed up by the beautiful tunes of Lena Raine, of Celeste fame, as well as the myriad personalities you meet along the way. As far as the combat goes, you would  that because it's all concentrated in the bossfights, there is no way that it could be satisfying? And yet, despite not doing anything to train you for them in advance, they never feel like they over or underchallenge you, and are fairly memorable in their own right.But as I noted above, the gameplay is only the hook. Chicory's real chops are on display in its story. Because it's one of the very few games that I've seen have the balls to realisticly portray relationships, mental health issues, relationships  people that have mental health issues, and how those issues themselves can be rooted in a relationship. Specifically, we are talking mind traps that artists tend to fall into. (And I can vouch for the realistic part from IRL experience with artist friends that suffered from them.) Heavy topics that scare most devs into not touching them with a 10-foot pole. Yet Chicory manages to not only do them justice, it does so in a way that results in a heartwarming tale, with twists and turns that you don't expect. In an almost Undertale-esque fashion.That said, the game does have its catches that give it a "results may vary" quality. The novelty of the brush mechanics mean that you often lack the precision to do  what you want to do, which can be frustrating. The critical path is quick to complete, but if you're gunning for 100% be ready for the game to ask a  out of you. Including drawing upwards of 20 paintings, scouring every nook and cranny for hidden paths, and talking to every NPC. Often multiple times. Oh, and did I mention, you will also need to paint in  of the map? Yeah, at times it gets laborious.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is an amazing game! It's so good you don't even need to be good at art! I love how this game treats itself like a coloring book, and allows so much creative liberty even when it asks you to draw something specific! The WRITING don't even get me STARTED on the WRITING, it's so good, the writers at Finji really know how to make an immersive story, they built this beautiful narrative when you first pick up the brush (it's the mechanic that allows you to draw all over the game), and every character whether that be someone with one single text-box or a main character you won't forget them. I really liked the part right at the begging when they ask what your favorite food was, it was really sweet how they fit that into the game. Though there was like one or two times where a character dumped their whole life story without any build up, but it's not that big of a deal if you don't mind it. Anyways...  THE SOUNDTRACK! The music in this game is great! It really shows how good Lena Raine is as a musician. If you didn't know she's the person behind the soundtrack of Celeste, and if you don't know Celeste then go treat yourself to her music. Finally the gameplay, not only are you able to color the world around you, it has great exploration with plenty of collectibles for completionists, cosmetics like changing your clothing to different ways to paint the world around you, and the puzzles it gives you are great! The puzzles are so good that the game feels almost like the "Legend of Zelda Paintbrush of Picnic", it even has dungeons where you get a specific ability to progress further and find more secrets, but unlike Zelda I've never had to look up a guide or a walkthrough, not because the puzzles were easy, they were plenty challenging, it didn't require you to get one specific item hidden behind a wall in a dungeon you already completed. I still like the Legend of Zelda though great games. Chicory is such I good game and I hope whoever is reading this they go play it. Chicory was so much fun and an emotional journey, without spoiling anything it talked a lot about creativity and it's problems with it and I felt like it was very inspiring for me since I too want to be an artist of some kind, and like I am now express myself more. Chicory has taught me those things, and that's why I love this game so much, and I hope you can find it as fun as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is a game that matters so much to me. This game is easily one of my favorites (it's a list that grows, but it is still so special). That is partially for personal reasons because, as someone who loves art and was pursuing an artistic major at one point, this game helped change my attitude towards drawing as well as helped me with art burnout. I think the reason why it helped so much is that the painting mechanics are intentionally not precision-based, so it forces you to treat the game as fun rather than pressure you to create something perfect. You are just supposed to be happy and enjoy yourself while playing it, and this game made me very very happy and I really enjoyed myself. I related a lot to both Chicory herself and the POV character. Wanting to make art to bring joy to others is a desire many artists (including myself) face and this game validates that while also saying "It's important to draw/paint for yourself, don't do it just for others." That was something I had forgotten due to the high standards art majors push you to achieve. The story is so, so special to me, I dare not spoil it, but it has beautiful commentary on self-worth, helping others, and paving a path for yourself free of pre-established expectations, and more. On top of that, this game is just technically masterful. I experienced basically no bugs on the PC. Really, just everything, the game mechanics (painting, running, etc.), the soundtrack and sound effects, the animation, the dialogue, the story, the epilogue, the colors, how the chapters are set up, just everything is so so good. This game gives me warm fuzzy feelings and is my comfort game. It is so cute and above all else, fun! It's just a fun game I'd recommend to anyone, including non-artists. I continuously come back to it. I really want to thank the creators for this game because it came into my life at just the right moment and inspired me to get back into drawing. I will always treasure it for that reason. Thank you so much for your work! I will continuously love this game! Please play it, it is a very heartwarming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Wandersong (Greg Lobanov's previous game) was like playing a fantasy webcomic from the late 2000s, and I adored basically every moment of it, so backing Chicory when I first heard about it was a no brainer. I had high hopes for this one.It met them. It's a sweet, gentle, delightful game, with excellent writing, beautiful music and a simple central mechanic that keeps unspooling with new possibilities throughout. You'll be surprised by how much the game remembers your journey, not just in terms of progressing through the story, but also in how you colour, change, and amend the world based on the new brushes you gain and the new things you learn. That is, of course, if you take the time to paint and enjoy the surroundings, soak in the world and make it your own. If you follow the critical path I'd imagine you'd be done in this game in about 5-6 hours, but I easily stretched that out to twice that length, just enjoying the simple delights of making this screen into a smear of colour, that one full of zig zags and dots. Rushing through it would be missing the point!The game plays well on a pad,but I imagine people who're far more artistically apt than me will get even more enjoyment out of this element of the game. But if you don't... just do it. Challenge yourself with the little side-quests and painting challenges. It'll make this game even more special for you.In conclusion, I wish Beans and Pepper were my moms

_childDocuments_.review: is the latest game from the creators of  as well as the composer of , Lena Raine. Its premise is simple: the world has lost all colors. The Wielder of the Brush, an artist who is supposed to help people all over with their troubles, has disappeared. It’s up to you, her janitor, to pick up the Brush and help restore color to the land! It’s like Zelda, but instead of the Hero of Time, you’re a dog with a paintbrush. Lovely, isn’t it?As you can guess, colors are an important part of the game. You can move your character with standard controls as well as use your brush at anytime, anywhere in order to paint the world. Each area of the game gives you a palette of four colors which helps keep things fresh! Coloring stuff can be used in a ton of ways that I won’t spoil because discovery and curiosity are the best points of  – let’s just say that mechanics are introduced very regularly, and puzzles always feel rewarding yet just challenging enough. The world is presented like a classic 2D Zelda world, with a bunch of towns and dungeons you can’t access right away and shortcuts that you’ll be able to take after powering up your brush by beating bosses. You can also just wander about and draw stuff! One town has an art academy that offers around twenty optional classes, in which you have to reproduce classic paintings or draw depending on themes such as “a cute creature” or “fear”. There is a lot of optional content that you don’t want to miss out on!Nevertheless, they’re not all  has to offer. Its world is vibrant and full of wonderful characters who have a lot to say. If most of them just want to speak with you, some will also ask favors. A dog might ask you to paint a mural, a lost mouse might need your help to color in a path in a dark cave and a gardener could need you to make his flowers bloom… The writing is cute and funny, which fits the overall vibe of the game to a T! Or does it?All isn’t always that wonderful in . I don’t want to spoil things, but the main story goes through some dark and relatable stuff, notably imposter’s syndrome and depression. It’s nothing too bad, and there’s a very positive atmosphere that seems to permeate every pore of the world! But it was an unexpected surprise that really elevated the story beyond simply cute. You can’t not mention Lena Raine’s work on the soundtrack – while most themes are cute and bouncy, the ones that correspond to important moments and boss fights can ooze dread and sadness. It’s comparable to her work on , which was already incredible! Overall,  is a wonderful game and a real breath of fresh air for the adventure game genre. A reviewer said that it’s to Zelda what Celeste was to platformers – I think it’s an exaggeration, but I get the idea. The paintbrush mechanic is a great concept that’s used in all sorts of ways throughout the adventure yet manages to never feel old. All throughout its playtime of around 12 hours, it keeps on being wonderful, fun, cute and lovely at the same time. Accessibility options and a low difficulty make it a game that can be enjoyed by everyone regardless of skill level, and at that price, I absolutely recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty great and I'd highly recommend it! The concept of of painting everywhere you go is quite clever and is solidly executed, with a limited color palette that prevents being overwhelmed, and giving areas their own distinct feel. The game has much to do and plenty of colorful characters, with a thoughtful story and a great soundtrack. It does have flaws that are worth mentioning though. I experienced several small glitches throughout the game, especially with a certain ability obtained. The game crashed on me 5 times, mostly toward the latter half of the game. Sometimes you cant easily reach objects on the edges of the screen to paint and there were a few times where objects simply wouldn't stay the color I painted them in. I remember a few conversations between important characters that felt a bit stilted, (this could be intentional due to some of the themes of the game, but it still can be a bit off-putting). It sometimes feels like the developers are speaking directly to you as opposed to characters conversing with one another, which is fine for minor characters, but when story-important characters speak in this fashion it detracts a bit from the themes the game is trying to convey. I love how this game navigates ideas of self-worth, the pressures of upholding a legacy, and responsibility towards oneself and for others. How it only ever asks the player to enjoy their time with the game and demands nothing more than that, its really relaxing. I ended up painting the whole map and completing all the side-quests, but the game never pressures you to do so and instead encourages you to only do as much as you feel you should. This encouragement to play how you want is also seen through its its numerous accommodations. There really is so much to praise, but I would rather not spoil anything, so take this review as a hearty recommendation to play this game all the way through! About 25-30 hours to 100% complete on standard mode for those curious

_childDocuments_.review: Received as a gift, and is the gift I needed more than anything. And will be my game of 2022 without a massive heavy hitter of a game.What seems like just a cute little painting game ends up being so much more. It builds emotionally and gives the painting as mostly a break from the difficulties those emotions bring. And yet one of the paintings the game has you create, was one that made me break down. After all the heaviness and emotion, my body could not handle it for a moment longer. It all came out at once, when I had let my guard down.Thank you, Chicory. Thank you, Spaghetti.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- The devs treat the players with a huge amount of respect with all the content warnings and accessibility options. Like, they actually care how people feel when playing their game.- The story progresses nicely and even tho the highly emotional motifs aren't engaging to me, the general idea of the story (painting and being an artist) and the impact it had on the gameplay was good enough to keep me interested.- There are a lot of optional (sometimes hidden) presents that rewards exploring.- Coloring the map can be a quite relaxing and rewarding thing to do. You don't have to do it, but you really want to.- There are some boss fights and they are really cool, like the dodging phases in Undertale but you can damage the boss at the same time because it's paint vs paint.Neutral:- Almost all collecting revolves around picking up litter and trading it for furniture or other decoration objects, which means the collecting itself is very disconnected from the reward that you might get for using the decorations later on. The other collecible is kittens and they also don't do anything impactful.Negatives:- The paint bucket should have been there from the start because only then is it fun to color the map. Before that I just couln't be bothered to put in the work.- The game is already really really easy and only about exploration and movement though the world, and with every new ability it only gets easier, almost to the point where it's so trivial to do anything the game wants you to do that it becomes plain boring.

_childDocuments_.review: This game beat any expectation I had for it. It's not often I come across a game that manages to touch my heart so deeply, let alone one to write a bit about. I was going through a really rough patch when my friend offered to play a little drawing game with me, with talking animals named after food. I'm Dutch, so of course I had to go with a Dutch dish as my favorite food, Hutspot. The soundtrack picked me up right away, the dialogue was engaging and fun, and the mechanic of being able to color anything and everything was brilliant to me. I'll go into a few spoilers in the next bit, thou hast beeneth warned. The story hit very close to home. Dealing with expectations, the fear of letting someone down you admire, working through the hurt of rejection and giving someone space to breathe... the developing relationship between Chicory and the new Wielder is portrayed so well, I learned from their interactions. From facing the fears in a paranoid mindscape to the journey through the trials. Nothing is rushed, they connect so naturally. Nearing the end, you just want Chicory to be okay. I think this game is exactly what I needed, and I'll thank my friend every day for it. And the developers for the remote play option. I'm going to continue playing with him to finish up the loose ends, before starting my solo game. Thanks for reading to the end, it means a lot to me to share my experience with you. I hope this wonderful game will help many others, the same way it helped me.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a charming game with an excellent mechanic: the coloring (sometimes drawing) gameplay loop.It plays like a classic Zelda game, which is a plus. There’s an overworld, with hidden and blocked paths, sidequests and lots of clothing and paint style collectibles. Only thing is that practically everything is in black & white and it’s up to you to color the world as you see fit (sometimes listening to villagers for guidance/requests). If you’re a creative person this sounds like a dream come true and it actually controls and works very well, but I wasn’t always in the mood to color things (note that this isn’t required to finish the game). Downside to this is that it makes the game feel very, very bleak, I would even go as far as to call it depressing if you play it for longer sessions (there definitely are elements in the story that deal with this issue).I shortly mentioned there’s also a drawing mechanic. Unfortunately this doesn’t work very well, or not as well at least. Problem is that I found the pencil isn’t very accurate for some of the finer details you might want to add when truly drawing something and you’re not just doodling.There are multiple dungeons in the game; these are all puzzle related since there’s no actual combat in the game except for the boss fights which I thought were kind of awful. They have limited feedback, no health bars and you just have to go on until they eventually go down. They’re easily the worst part of the game. It then also becomes obvious you can get hit two times before going down (and somehow you can still continue playing; the game is very forgiving). It made no sense to even have health for this part of the game but I get that it would made these ‘boss fights’ even more useless. I’d rather have seen some sort of (environmental) puzzles for these, like the rest of the dungeons.Finishing the main story with some side quests and collectible finding will take you around 8-9 hours. To grab and do everything it will probably take up to 15-20 hours. So price/quality/quantity wise this is outstanding.Would I recommend this game? Yes, easily. Sure, there are some flaws and weird choices as far as the bosses are concerned, but if you’re looking for a charming Zelda-like adventure look no further.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is an incredible indie adventure that makes its unique concept of having you color in the world come alive. Chicory is a relaxing puzzle game about bringing color back into the world after it disappears and helping out all the people you meet along the way. You explore a wide array of different regions each with a color pallet of four colors to fill everything in with (Except for a few with five colors). Every region has a terrific background song done by the composer from Celeste ranging from catchy tunes like strings and light drums or an upbeat jazz vibe to more meditative or melancholic piano, guitar, and marimba melodies to more mysterious soundscapes. The world of Chicory is full of NPCs to talk to in each region (all animals named after different foods) giving out a wide range of different quests or fun design opportunities. While none of the characters are voiced they are given a fun variety of different personalities through both what they say and the font of their text. In terms of side objectives there were letters to deliver, lost children to find, and art classes to partake in just to name a few. One of my favorite aspects of the game was the reactivity of the world even if it got repetitive. For example when you paint on certain screens, or design new products for stores people will come and comment on it. Another example is when you complete paintings they get placed in several frames across the province. And a final example of the interactivity is how bikers stop for you in the big city when you get in their way. Whether decorating a new item for a shop owner or completing personal quests for the animals you encounter your rewards are often either litter which can be used to buy items in shops like music players or plants; OR gifts which contain either clothes to decorate your character or new brush styles to use on the world. Both of these items can also be found hidden around the world, often in caves or high up where you need to solve puzzles in order to reach them. The game’s story was quite a stark contrast to the game’s otherwise generally cute and relaxing nature. It dealt with depression and the pressure of wielding the brush. In the game, you fight off a growing corruption by going to ‘spooky’ trees and completing well-designed boss battles. The story does a good job of fleshing out its world and building mystery while also making the characters believable people with genuine worries and feelings. A big surprise to me at the beginning of the game was that your character isn't even named Chicory, you get to name them after your favorite food! Now in terms of negatives since I played this on Mac my biggest complaint was that the Devs still haven't patched the bug where you don't unlock any achievements. The only other real complaint I had was a minor annoyance; there was no undo button. So if you accidentally colored in a character that you colored in with the colors of a region A during the only time they were in region A then you wouldn’t be able to restore their old color scheme. Apart from that Chicory was a delightful and creative experience that truly hooked me. It’s an easy recommendation for people who like unique ideas, art, or puzzle-adventure titles in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing game! The story is amazing, with some hard hitting points and very heartwarming. _childDocuments_.review: I initially saw this game as just "Oh it's a cute art game" and  it off for a couple years before finally playing it. BOY WAS I A FOOL! Chicory might honestly be one of the most heartfelt and special games to ever be created.This game has SO MUCH going for it. It's overall cutesy presentation, so many small and neat details, the dialogue between all of the characters is so precious and all of their individual personalities shine through. Lena Raine's music deserves special attention, it is SO FREAKIN' GOOD! From the catchy ambient tunes used as background tracks, to soft heart tugging melodies, to its intense, synth heavy, and groovy Celeste-like boss themes, there are so many hits in there! And that story...  !!! It's so down to earth yet heart tugging, and I'm sure that everyone can at the very least relate to and resonate with something the game touches upon, especially if you like to engage in creative practices. It looks very simple and lighthearted at first, but it's a lot more meaningful with it's emotional and mental themes.As for the actual gameplay itself, think of the game itself like a Zelda-like adventure game, exploring the world and solving puzzles, only that you have a paintbrush to paint the world to interact with it, kinda like Splatoon now that I think about it. The appeal of the gameplay itself is that you can basically draw and color in the world of Picnic Province, the only limit is your color palette and your own creativity. Chicory's not even too bad as an art program! It's super limited sure, but you can really make some really striking art with it, either using the game's environments, or the dedicated canvases in the art academy. The game also saves the entire process and allows you to export almost everything as a Gif just as a nice cherry on top. Design-wise the game is amazingly solid, being fairly linear at the start for the story, but opening more and more things up as you explore and gain new abilities. The world is interconnected so well and gets getting from point a to b very quick and easy, and the hint system is really thorough so you pretty much always have a good idea of what to do! It's a fairly comfortable experience the whole way through!Chicory is a labor of love from those who made it. It's an absolute gem of a game, and absolutely worth sticking with it from beginning to end. Please do yourself a favor and get this game. It is worth far more than its full asking price. It gets my highest recommendation.Chicory: A Colorful Tale truly is a work of art....So uh... Thanks for reading this dumb hecking review.I tried expressing how good Chicory is as a game and as an experience, and it is just that... but for me it's also something a lot more personal, so I'm writing this entirely separate section for those that care enough to read it. Objectivity goes out of the window here so I do apologise haha.I do a fair amount of creative work myself. Despite this though I don't really consider myself an artist. Some of my works I'm decently proud of what I did and was able to produce, but more often than not I find a lot of my creations very lacking or just plain bad. I also have several artist friends and I can't help but find myself comparing my work to theirs often, and feeling incompetent or talent-less in comparison, even when I make something that I put a huge amount of time and effort into, it usually pales in comparison to them. Safe to say that I doubt myself a lot when it comes to my own artistic ability.Then comes along Chicory with it's own story about how the characters deal with their own self doubt, expectations, their need to prove themselves and what they are able to achieve. I found myself relating to a lot to Pizza (or Pancake in my playthrough) and their insecurities. Chicory herself I also saw a lot of my artist friends in, with Pancake being inspired and looking up to them, to how she acts and what she does. With almost every line of dialogue hitting so close to home, and it hit hard, REALLY hard. In a sense the journey felt really personal to me funnily enough, and it was really inspiring to see the character face and overcome their own doubts and hardships. It hit so many of the right notes for me that at the time, I probably really needed to hear, and I can't thank the game or its developers enough for doing just that. It was really something special for me.Again sorry for the whole spiel, but thank you for bearing with me regardless and reading the whole thing haha.Hope you'll have a good rest of your day!

_childDocuments_.review: Review w/o Context: 10/10 MasterpieceThe Context: I struggle with putting myself out there a lot, whether that's streaming, writing, or a DnD campaign. Honestly, I think it's something a lot of people have trouble with but may not talk about for fear of ridicule or disdain. Art is subjective, wildly varied, and above all honest. Not in the Boy Scout way, but in a truer sense, a little slice of whoever created it. It's vulnerable and hard to share at times. Chicory is about all of that. Far more importantly, it's about the acceptance of all that comes with it, and the celebration with each new person convinced to show more of themselves.At the start however, it's just about a dog inheriting a paintbrush tasked with bringing color back to the world. Thankfully the characters you meet are colorful enough (im so sorry). I still remember so many, all with their own quirks and quandaries. Being the new wielder of the brush makes you a priority call whenever a pizza place needs a new logo, or an art class wants to see your technique.Now if you aren't art-inclined, I may have sent you into a cold sweat there. As a non-artist myself, I was the same. The game however, doesn't care how it looks, and neither do the characters. Only that you tried. This attitude of acceptance is perfect to encourage you to personalize everything you come across. That river, that shirt, those walls vandalized with butts. Why not express your style more?This ties directly into the main story, which is full of excellent music and exploration. Each location is a joy to journey through and culminates with engaging boss battles that expand on characters while still providing a challenge. Imposter syndrome, crises of confidence, and the struggle to be noticed all interweave in the tale in a way that exposes and normalizes it. I truly think it speaks to most of us on some level, and is such a unique game because of it. It's ok to be vulnerable! This gem certainly is.

_childDocuments_.review: They did it! Lord almighty, this is a good one, it is! The character design is adorable and the animations are  (especially during some of those boss fights. Man those were epic! I wish they went on a little longer, like if there was an extended re-fight option after you beat the game).AND THE O S T!!Lena Raine is back once more, knocking you off your feet with a beautiful and thrillingly original soundtrack (original with the exception of the Dinner city track of course, which Lena chose to rip directly from Super Mario 64's Bob-omb battlefield. An odd, though artistic inclusion). Lord am I gonna listen the hell out of these songs. Next time I'm out solo-flying over the aleutians, or am vacuuming my driveway or whatever, I know I'll be boppin' along to one of the ost's 60 (60!) brilliant tracks.Let's see, what else. What really sticks with me from this game (and I ain't even finished all of it yet!) is the valuable things it has to say. Don't let the charming dialogue and cute design fool you. This game has things to say about the creative process, self doubt, social interdependence, and art. It brings things to the discussion that I haven't really seen brought before in a videogame. It's a pioneer in this way, I think.Gameplay:Solid. The painting mechanic works really well (and is fun), and I loved gainingmore movement options as I went along - the world just opens up to you.The brush is easy to use (there are a lot of customization options for size and texture, etc), and is fun to mess around with.The bossfights are super cool, but a bit short. Despite not really being difficult, they feel wondrously epic. I ain't great at videogames (hollow knight's mantis lords took me like 35 tries, and I have over 15k deaths on celeste) so I appreciate the fights not being too hard, but I want a chance to listen to that music for longer! And I want more time to take in those slick animations! Maybe a last-as-long-as-you-can arcade mode (containing attack patterns from different bosses) or something could be added.Accessibility:If this game is a pioneer in it's message, it definitely also is one in accessibility. I played this game with about 1.5 hands <broke my arm recently>, and I could easily adjust the settings to suit my limitations. There are so many customization options, and configuring them is quick and intuitive.There is an immense care to detail within the accessibility options, and I think this extends to the gameplay mechanics. There are virtually no annoying features in this game. Every game has something - some enemy that's a pain to fight, some crafting recipe that takes too long, an menu that is too slow to page through, bad dialogue boxes, or something. But not Chicory. This game has no assassin's creed escort missions, no undertale snowball minigame, no finicky puzzles, no weird bothersome stuff you get stuck on, and have to wade through before you can get back to the main storyline. If you ever do get stuck on a puzzle, you can call for vague or precise tips to help you along in game. There are a number of hidden collectables, and certain NPCs can conveniently point you in the direction of what you've missed, so you don't have to go to the wiki if you want to 100% it (and accidentally spoil something major).Though, I do suppose the volcanic gas bubbles are a little annoying. It's kinda difficult for you to move them where you want to (when you push them, they never quite end up in the place you'd like), but they are a pretty small part of the game, so no big deal. Maybe if they could be picked up and carried by pressing some key, or if the movement bubble movement code was a little smarter.And that is one small complaint among so many brilliances! The character customization, and the story, the funny and well written dialogue, the readability, the furniture options, the poses, and the transit ID photobooth, there's so much good stuff in this game. Oh, I almost forget to mention! You ever playing some game, and you're in the cutscene, and some big awful news is dumped on the protagonist? And then the cutscene ends, and the protag's character model still has a big smile plastered to their face (lookin' at you spiritfarer)? In Chicory, not only does the main character's mood last outside of the cutscene, but the music in MULTIPLE areas changes to reflect their mood! Did I say how much I like the music? I really like the music.It's a cute, well made, chill, and interesting game. If that sounds good to you, give it a play some time, eh?

_childDocuments_.review: With its unique focus on artistic freedom, the player can decide just how much or how little they wish to decorate the world, all in their own style. This is further complimented by the story, which begins wholesome and cute, but also delivers an unexpected layer of depth that is emotionally complex and heavy, resulting in a compelling tale throughout the entire adventure. The characters you'll meet are all expressive and have their own personalities, the environments are carried by the simple, fun storybook visual design, and the soundtrack is pleasant and really succeeds in fitting the vibe of each situation/area of the game. In addition to painting, the player will unlock abilities throughout the game, enhancing the way the map is traversed as well as interconnecting areas seamlessly and avoiding potentially tiresome backtracking. Also while exploring the map, plenty of meaningful collectibles and optional activities will be discovered ranging from short character interactions to full on side quests.My only minor critique about the game involves the way certain scenes depicted emotions (spoiler ahead). Specifically,  It's a small nitpick that is probably insignificant in the grand scheme, but I feel it would've left a stronger impression on the player had it been left to us to make sense of. Overall I highly recommend buying this game and taking your time doing as much exploring and painting as you enjoy if the trailers interest you. You'll find there is plenty more in-store for you with its story to add on to the journey. The team behind this game should be extremely proud of what they created, they really crafted a true indie hit.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. I'm no artist, but coloring everything in this world was fun and relaxing. I also enjoyed the characters, and liked talking/helping them. The character design and personalities were great and really helped differentiate each one. The gameplay is definitely not difficult, but the fun comes more in exploring, drawing, and solving puzzles. I also enjoyed the story. It went into mental health and self doubt, which was interesting and relatable. This game was a good length. It took me probably 18-20 hours to beat the game (although that was at 99% completion), and 25 hours to 100% complete the game. I do wish it was a bit longer, but I feel I got what I wanted out of the game. I highly recommend this game!As a side note for those who don't like bugs SPOILERS, there is a bug area that has some large bugs in it, and a bunch of tiny ones. As someone who can get creeped out by insects, especially if they pop out at me, I did wish I knew what to expect before going into the area. Luckily, all of the insects are friendly, and are designed in a way that I got used to pretty quickly. The only two that really freaked me out were: 1) on the surface world there is a cave with a rug before it, and inside is a spider person who looks more realistic than the other insects. The first time I went in there i was not expecting it and I got out quick. Eventually, I went back in and got used to the design (the friendly personality helped), but for people who have more intense arachnophobia than I do, it may be a cave to avoid completely. If you do skip it, though, just know you wont be able to deliver all of the the mail, so you cant 100% the game. 2) The second is the insect queen. She is a giant centipede. The design doesn't freak me out, but the movements (especially when she emerges from the cave) get to me. She is friendly, so you don't have anything to actually worry about, but it can still be unsettling. By the way, the boss for the area is not bug related, so you don't have to worry if you are fine to get past the meeting with the insect queen. Hope this helps.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game. This is a life-changing experience.Chicory's beautiful world and incredible story spoke to me on a deep, emotional level, in a way that almost no other game, no, no other single thing on this planet, ever has before. Its cutesy style and heartwarming vibe gives it a welcoming atmosphere that instantly captivates you, but it isn't afraid to tackle heavy subjects that, while told through the lens of art, will resonate strongly with anyone who struggles with self-doubt, impostor syndrome, pressure to succeed, or even just the stress of adult life in general. Chicory approaches these subjects gently, yet bluntly, a method that ended up really working for me in particular, and managing to unexpectedly teach me a lot about myself.Even if you don't care for the more mental heath-oriented themes, the characters are well-written enough to tell an engaging story all on their own, one with plenty of excitement, wholesomeness, and surprises. It's a well-paced, heartwarming tale with an incredible conclusion that had me crying, sweating, and popping off all at the same time.The game itself is a ton of fun, giving you the freedom to paint the world however you want, and having you unlock new abilities over time to explore the world in ways that are uniquely tailored to the central painting mechanic. Boss fights are surprisingly stressful, yet are always perfectly intuitive and never too difficult. It's extremely satisfying to see the world become more and more colourful as you traverse it, painting each new area you come across however you see fit, And of course, there's plenty of lovingly made side-content to engage with at your leisure, providing plenty of extra hilarious and heartwarming moments for those willing to see them.And of course, all this is topped off by a gorgeous score from the incredibly talented Lena Raine, one of the greatest video game composers to ever grace the industry. She puts her heart and soul into each and every track, and it elevates the emotional moments to heights that few other games can achieve. Chicory's soundtrack is both whimsical and deeply emotional, delivering perfectly on all fronts and making the game all the better experience.This game truly touched me, and genuinely left me a changed person by the end. I regret that it took me this long to play it, but now that it's in my life, I'm a happier man for it.But no matter how much I say, how much praise I drop, words alone could never do this game justice.Play Chicory.You'll thank yourself later.

It's not a particularly gameplay-heavy experience, but that isn't what Chicory is trying to be, which is a game crafted around its story and characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Deciding that it wasn't enough to make one of the best games ever, Greg Lobanov decided to do it again, this time even moreso to me. An experience so moving and comfy to me that the act of finishing and closing the game, leaving my character a chance to finally rest, was all it took for me to start tearing up. So many things in Chicory feel like a continuation of the core elements that caused Wandersong to be one of my favourite games, only this time with everything also appealing more to my proclivities, culminating in one of my favourite experiences I've had in such a long time.The specific brand of softness and kindness in Lobanov's games is something that feels especially appealing to me, especially with the way that it shines through in all facets of them. Most antagonism present in the game still takes place in a far kinder, more understanding world, one where talking things out will solve the majority of problems and being nice to each other and it'll all be met with understanding. The mechanics themselves are playfully implemented and add so much vibrancy to how you interact with the world, with even the most hostile moments still not really attempting to hinder you and even giving you more options to soften them even more. Even something as simple as text options feel just that bit nicer, never really having something that straight up says "no", only things like "that's ok" or "I'm alright" , and it all makes for something profoundly pleasant from start to finish where everything new you find is full of bright-eyed excitement.The concept of artistic expression in itself being beautiful is taken to even greater heights here, being given a set of intentionally limited painting tools (small colour selection, can only solid fill certain surfaces, no ability to use black or white for linearly purposes) and still being told at every turn that you're incredible at what you do in a self-aware enough way to have an entire side quest centred around this. There are also so many ways to add a bit of mechanically pointless flair to the mix that makes the player see the world as something living and breathing that you can play with, whether it's through the way it's entirely up to the player to add colour to the world, or all the decor that you're able to place everywhere if there's something you feel would fit in the scene. It led me to establishing an extraordinarily close connection with my character to be able to have so much self-expression at my fingertips, and the requirement I had to be filling the world with colour also made me feel similarly close with each individual location full of their unique warmth that I was partially responsible for the vibe of.As someone who's repeatedly artistically struggled over the years, a lot of the topics in here also resonated deeply with me, the relationship between the art and the artist, sometimes having that inability to think about things in terms of myself instead of catering to what others want in all situations, those times of it all just feeling too much. Sometimes all you need is time to rest and support in your life, understanding from your peers, the ability to sit and process your feelings instead of having them overwhelm you with nonstop doubts, and this game touches upon all of this in some very powerful ways that have left me thinking for a while.I don't feel capable of articulating a lot about what this game does for me beyond this, it's just a very abstract sense of how it resonates with me, with every facet of its existence being yet another thing that endears me to it. Between this and Wandersong, Greg Lobanov remains undefeated and I am now another person who is indescribably excited for Beastieball to finally release.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: My favourite game so far this year, and it's going to be hard to beat that too. Much like the developer's previous game Wandersong, Chicory is a story-focused adventure game with various light gameplay elements for puzzling, exploration or combat purposes, where said story is very wholesome and sweet, while also getting quite serious and real when it needs to- which makes for a very effective and evocative combination.There is also a massive focus on creativity, painting in particular - pretty much every screen in the game is one you can add colours to in however way you want - or not, if it's not so much your thing, though most gameplay aspects interact with the colour you create, so you'll be painting at least a bit sooner or later. In addition, there are various optional opportunities which allow you to create specific artworks that will then show up somewhere in the world later. Now, I'm a crazy person who would paint literally everything I was allowed to paint, but for others who aren't as dedicated as that, this might be a fairly short game. However, the main story by itself is more than good enough to get the game for, even if you aren't as interested in secrets or side-artwork stuff. The ending in particular was excellent on multiple levels for me! In any case, I do hope you enjoy the game, if you do get it for yourself. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This review will try to tell you if this game is for you or not. Extremely minor spoilers about the type of content the game provides, so be warned if you want your experience to be 100% blind.I will initially say this game is arguably the best game I have played this  year. It is incredible at what it does. It does target specific types of audiences in terms of the type of gameplay experience someone may enjoy, but it does it so well. If you fall into that target audience, you will have an amazing time with this game and it is fully worth the price tag. Chicory is a game that you can finish in less than 20 hours. It can be finished in less than 10 if you don't care too much for all of the things that can sidetrack you, but honestly that's part of what makes the game beautiful. I 100%'d it completely blind in 13.5 hours. The gameplay experience this game provides draws out the maximum, or close to maximum, potential of the simple brush mechanic this game has. It's honestly impressively how deeply it's explored and pushed, and I was always left surprised and pleased with what the game was asking me to do at any point. The world has no combat or anything in it, but lots of hidden secrets for you to explore and find, as well as introducing puzzle mechanics for you to interact with to make it through the game. The ways that you use your painting skills to navigate through the world's puzzles is impressive; the developers really push the simple painting concept to its maximum in exploring different types of puzzles or navigation methods. There are boss fights in this game. They are extremely creative, their atmosphere is done very well. The mechanics in each are fairly unique and for some could be decently challenging. The mechanics, just like the puzzles, push the simple concept of using a brush to its maximum in interesting and engaging ways. They're just flat out super fun. These boss fights can also be skipped if you don't like the intensity of them and want the game to be more laid-back.The world is built marvelously. It has a strong and interesting main story that you can easily understand and get engaged in, but it also has tons of small subplots that build together and add their own spice into it. There's a large focus on what can be relate-able for a lot of people. Nothing feels forced and the pacing, design, everything feels right on point. The world is a bunch of colorless pictures that are styled to be from a children's coloring book. You can take your time to color in each map the way you want, or be more lazy with it. It's entirely up to you. It's a really great and relaxing experience to just have fun coloring the maps in. The world is built with lots of subplots, side characters you can get to learn a lot more about, and a lot of real-life types of things are explored, mostly people outwardly talking about their thoughts from self-reflection. I'm sure that most people who play this game can relate to some of the characters on a very deep or personal level. If you are a very intrapersonal type who likes to self-reflect a lot, this game can stir a lot of thinking in you in a good way. The subplots are charming and interesting, and explores a lot of different fields relate-able to real life. I would say that it's just about the right size for this type of game too and there are no maps/screens that feel like they shouldn't be in the game. It's not too cluttered and not too sparse; it's just right. Lots of interesting different environments are explored. There's also tons of really good humor in it. For people who love hunting for secrets, this game offers a lot of them that you'll catch with your eye if you notice it. None are too frustratingly difficult, and there are lots of tools the game provides you to help track down the last few you might be missing here and there without directly giving you the answer. Tons of sidequests to do, all with their own unique and respective rewards. While I beat the game in 13.5 hours, it did not feel lacking in sidequest content and felt just right. Sidequests are also introduced at a very healthy rate and it never feels like a "I just hit a new area, time to be overwhelmed by 10 sidequest prompts all at once". The game has a strong thematic in its plotline around depression and other negative emotions. However, if you are particularly sensitive to this, you can toggle a setting that warns you about it before it happens and then optionally skip it. The developers really thought of almost everything that's a good gameplay experience for the players. The music is incredible, between the more intense and more relaxed songs, I loved pretty much all of them. They fit perfectly with what's happening in the game at the time, and a lot of scripted sections like some boss fights are timed specifically with the music too to help the immersion, some songs get more intense as you get deeper into an area, etc.The composer is Lena Raine, the same composer for Celeste. You will definitely see similarities, mostly during boss fight music where the instrumentation is almost exactly the same. I haven't heard her other works much outside of Celeste but I was very impressed by the tunes she created. This game is just super good at what it does, I can't really say much more about it. It has its own originality in the painting thematic, and really pushes that idea as its core identity in the most interesting and pleasantly unexpected ways I could think of. Pretty much every new area and experience I had in this game I was not expecting, but I found it super cool and fun. I love to rip apart bad design aspects in games but I legitimately can't find anything wrong with this  one. Game is super worth it and honestly needs more attention

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Gorgeous hand drawn, minimalistic visuals. Its aesthetic simplicity is genius and makes it unique.- A wonderful, fairly big world with lots of locations, small communities, deep lore and complex relationships.- Brilliant concept. It has some ideas that I haven't met before and some really clever gameplay mechanics. Bonding with your paintbrush unlocks new abilities that allow you to travel in whole new ways. Your perspective of the world changes entirely, new places get unlocked gradually and new gameplay elements are added.- Amazing, well written characters. You'll even see many of them evolve as new dialogues and events pop up all the time. Your character is adorable and there are a lot of options to customize its outfit and colors.- Painting is well implemented with nice animations and sounds. It's so relaxing. You'll catch yourself painting things in various screens without a particular goal in mind. Especially when you unlock the bucket tool then the real fun begins. It's also great that it saves every little paint work that you have done in its world and its characters. The map transforms into a huge canvas.- Great story full of emotions and deep thoughts. It's more about psychology, relationships and social structure than heroic actions. A self-discovery journey full of unexpected events.- Amazing, calm music during the exploration. Awesome fast paced music during boss battles that gives you the right tone.- Well designed puzzles. They're fairly easy, but with some interesting ideas.- Boss battles could be more challenging, but they have fantastic rhythm and some nice mechanics.- Great sense of humor. Some parts and dialogues are really inspiring.- All these scattered hidden collectables and secrets give you extra motivation to explore more. All this content is incredible in a small indie game.- Fast travel is a nice addition and gets unlocked at the right time to save you from lots of unnecessary walks.- There is a funny, well designed in-game help system in case you get stuck. Probably you won't need it because the game does a great job in guiding you to the right path.- Creating and saving on your hard drive .gif images of your paintings is a wonderful addition.The bad- Very slow start. In the beginning you only do some random painting and talk to npcs, while your movement is pretty limited. Give it a couple of hours in order to embrace the characters or acquire some skills and then it becomes magical.- I'm not sure if it's still a smooth experience with a controller. With a mouse and a keyboard it works like a charm.- There are tons of meaningful interactions with the npcs, but there are also a few optional errands that seemed to me a bit silly. _childDocuments_.review: It's... fine.Chicory: A Colorful Tale is an interesting game. The main gimmick of the game is simple, yet very clever: You can paint the world and use paint to solve fun puzzles and find secrets. The soundtrack ranges from fine to amazing, Lena Raine is a very talented music composer. At times, the story can actually be engaging and emotionally resonant. For me, that's where the positives end.The concept of painting your surroundings, although original and, at first, quite engaging, quickly ends up being a chore. The world is a blank canvas, meaning that almost all the areas are entirely white when you visit them. Coloring each and every area takes time, especially if you want the places you visit to actually look visually pleasant. You're faced with a choice: You either take your time to paint everything (there is a LOT to paint) to make the game look good, hastily paint every place just so you don't have to stare at a white screen or leave the game mostly white and get an eye strain. Maybe the devs should've implemented an auto-paint mode, although it defeats the entire premise of the game. Point is, the visuals are hard to look at unless you take your time to paint every nook and cranny.Most of the characters are painfully bland and/or superficial. Everyone constantly praises you for everything you do, for everything you paint, even if it's terrible. In this game's world, there's nothing vile, no one with bad intentions, everyone is just painfully bland and have nothing interesting going on for them. The only characters that have the audacity to say something bad about you are put to shame by everyone else, and/or redeemed. The admiration other characters have for you feels incredibly disingenuous, you can literally submit blank canvases of "art" and everyone will insist that your work is unbelievably good. You can smear the same color of paint everywhere and the others will say they love how you painted the place. It's all just fake praises and "wholesomeness" from shallow caricatures of people.What irks me the most about Chicory: A Colorful Tale is the way it portrays mental health problems, particularly that of depression. The level of understanding of such a complex issue that so many people have is almost child-like, although very few games do it right. According this game, it all boils down to having a stressful time and being too hard with yourself, and can be cured simply by taking a break, talking about it to someone and hugging it out. It's a generic, narrowed down approach to an issue that manifests itself very differently for different people. As someone who's been dealing with clinical depression for many years, although I could relate at times, I felt like the oversimplification of this mental illness is almost insulting (particularly, when Chicory is portrayed as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for lashing out at you while having a breakdown). No offense to the developers, I'm sure they had good intentions, but this approach doesn't feel right. Chicory: A Colorful Tale is not, by any means, a bad game. It has its highs and lows and it might be considered amazing by some people. This is just my opinion based on my experience playing this game.I recommend this game if you are:- A kid;- An aspiring artist looking for encouragement (FYI, this game teaches you nothing about drawing and art);- Looking for a relaxing game to wind down;- New to playing video games.Otherwise, I don't recommend this game. Sorry.

Especially the boss fights came out of nowhere with how they're executed and how they engaged me. I did not expect that at all from this little gem. _childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful puzzle platformer with a perfect soundtrack by Lena Raine (who did the soundtrack for Celeste, and the Minecraft nether update!). It's got incredible writing across the board, from the story, to the individual characters, and to the minute dialogues and just how diverse everything is. The topics covered are also incredibly good, to say the least (very introspective, deals with mental illness and a lot of other struggles).The game is very accessible, with robust in-game hints, that let you pick between 'soft' hints and more 'direct' hints. There's content warnings you can enable, and the few 'combat'-y parts have configurable hitpoints (with generous checkpoints; the combat is not at all the primary focus - the story is).Chicory is just easily the most thoughtfully and lovingly crafted game I've ever played. The soundtrack, all of the writing, and the gameplay are just all incredible and it's the most touching game I've had the pleasure of playing.edit: I've seen a couple reviews mention eyestrain; the game has a setting for that! it has three settings (None, Default, and Lots) - I got a migraine playing on the default, but was fine when I set it to Lots (and once I'd colored in most of the game, I was fine switching back to Default) - I think that generally, most accessibility concerns are addressed.(There's also a nice 'click and hold to fill up to the lines' mechanic to make painting in the lines very easy)
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a game that I fell in love with from the first moment I saw it When I saw the trailer and played the demo I just hoped I could get itIt's so nice because it gives you a peace that I haven't felt in any other game. I haven't finished it yet but this is because I want to enjoy even the smallest detail of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't loved a game this much in a while. The freedom you're given to explore and color in the world only gets better as you progress and get more upgrades. I think I've spent hours coloring in rooms and drawing the art class portraits alone. The story is heavily built around art and self-doubt, and having to live up to expectations and tradition, and all of it hits hard for an artist who's had a lot of self-doubts in the past. This kind of personal interest is what got me into the game in the first place, and what kept me going to the end.Chicory herself is an interesting and lovable character, and the game has some great moments where it slows down and lets you talk with her (my favorite being when you ) Many (although not all) other NPCs are charming, and the side quests are excellent ()Not only can you color in basically everything (including the title screen), but this game has a nice amount of other customization features. 120 outfits to wear, hundreds of pieces of furniture and decorations to place wherever you want, and custom color palettes/styles. The puzzles in Chicory are mostly simple, but fun, and the game is always introducing more mechanics involving your paint and movement to keep things fresh.There are a lot of small touches here too, like how the main character's expression changes after certain points in the story, which re-enforces her current state of mind no matter where you go. If you go back to Luncheon at different times during the story,  The whole food naming scheme of the world and characters is dumb, and I love it.Of course it's not perfect - Coloring in every screen on the map is tedious (you don't have to do it, but it's awfully satisfying if you do!) The jumping ability is buggy, and I've heard reports of other, more problematic bugs, especially on consoles. Boss fights don't make use of your abilities and have a much too forgiving punishment for failure.Any negatives were easy for me to overlook, though, when compared to Chicory's overall gameplay, story, and charm. By the end, it hit me in the gut like few other games have. I've loved just about every minute of my time with this one, and I can easily call it my favorite game of 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the game and completing the epilogue, I can safely say that this game was a fantastic, touching, fun, and creative experience, all at the same time. I cried tears of sadness, tears of joy, and overall felt like the game touched on some thoughts and emotions that resonated deeply with me.Gameplay-wise, there's a lot of dialogue, and a lot puzzles. As you progress, you obtain more movement options for platforming sections, unlocking new areas. There are some boss fights that are a little difficult to figure out, but are sparse and forgiving, while still amplifying the story rather than watering it down. There's a lot to collect if that's your thing, at time of writing I have the game about 86% completed. Painting is also nice--I feel like as I got further in the game, I learned more techniques on how to deal with the limited palettes and was more satisfied with my work, using tools the game provides, and skills the game taught me.Definitely do not rush through the story. The more time you spend investing in coloring the world, interacting with the people around you, setting out decorations, etc, the closer you feel to the world and the more touching it makes later moments. I guess what I'm saying is, if you play, take it slow. I played this game during some stressful moments in my life and it helped me decompress and come to terms with myself, whether through art therapy or encouraging dialogue.TL;DR If you like art, animals, and feel sensitive or experience self-doubt in any way, I strongly recommend this game to you. It's made an impact on me, and I think it has good things to say.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had two playthroughs of this... one with an Xbox Game Pass trial and then another on Steam (just finished the Steam one today, huzzah!)Even when I got to play through it once for free during the game pass trial, I still found myself looking back at this game alot.It's generally quite hard for me to actively seek out to finish a game, especially story based games, as I often find myself busy with life a lot of the time.Generally I like the games for the replayability factor, with features such as an in-game editor, a photo mode, or anything to help inspire work, since I like to do a lot of art based stuff myself for my work.(Doesn't mean I'm good at drawing though, lol)So to find a story game with a very unique take on being able to draw the entire world around you... it really caught my eye!Honestly... I had no idea what I was fully getting into... I just like Colorful things, saw the game, read a rough description of the game, and was like "... sweet! :)"...2 playthroughs later though, I can safely say that this game connected with me more than I feel like a game should. Enough to make me purchase the game on Steam DESPITE completing the main story from the Game Pass version already!Like... HOW THE HECK... do you get a game that connected with me this well through it's story, and the main character was a sweeper/janitor/custodian JUST LIKE ME? XDThat was probably a coincidence, but I mean... sure doesn't feel like it when it nailed basically everything that kind of doubts me to do art in the 1st place!And this is all just the story to!In terms of it's signature mechanic, being able to paint the world around you... I aDORE it!It almost feels like therapy to me... sometimes I just need a moment to color things around for fun, and be "expressive"... ya know?This game does a great job at accomplishing it's main goal, while still providing some fun "side experiences" dabbling with interior/exterior design, photography, and dress up (in the which you unlock as the game progresses), while ALSO leveling up your brush abilities!Also not to mention... all the smaller things that just keep the game fresh, such as naming your character based off of your favorite food... or being able to move the text bubbles around! Such things like that really ADD to the experience!My only real "critique" of the game is that on my 1st playthrough, it was a little confusing on knowing which walls I could swim up on. It clicked eventually, but the game didn't really tell me what kind of "walls" I could swim up on.There are also quite a few glitches, heck, I got one by complete accident on my 1st playthrough... but I'm not critiquing that one. I saw a 6 minute speedrun of the game and was immediately flabbergasted, lol....So, this review was kind of long, so for anyone thinking if this game is worth it...Get it... IF you're a creative person.I cannot promise the same experience to the general audience, but for anyone in the creative "niche" (even if you're not actually producing art and just "like the idea of it"), this game will hit you hard with it's cute characters, fantastic writing, creative gameplay, and glorious soundtrack from Lena Raine, all packaged into a wholesome experience... with a story that (at least for me) positively changed my life for the better!...Welp... time to collect some lost children!

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game some time last year and played it mostly on stream.It's an adorable game that takes some rather dark turns. I was originally drawn in by the demo for the game and the unique game play mechanic and character design.I stayed for the story though. A bit of a spoiler here but it's a really refreshing depiction of depression, self esteem issues, and questioning ones worth. The story gets darker and darker and it was an emotional ride while also remaining incredibly cute.So what exactly is this game? You play an adorable little dog who gets given a magic paintbrush that is used to "paint the world with color". The brush wielder is who makes the world bright and colorful and cheerful.The wielder of the brush, Chicory, however has found herself unable to wield it. Giving it instead to the little dog who serves as her janitor. You use your paintbrush to bring color to the world. From coloring the map to make it pretty to using your paintbrush to solve various puzzles and problems to get around.There are mini games as well. Such as the art museum where you will be asked to paint a specific kind of picture and even with a sometimes VERY limited palette you can still make something pretty fun and cool. Just check out the discussions and shared pictures for the game, people have been making some really cool stuff in this game.So don't let the limited colors fool you, you can make neat stuff here. That being said the limited number of colors you can generally use does make the aspect of painting the map seem tedious and boring.The boss fights aren't super hard and they are the only real time you "fight" anything. The fights usually coming down to dodging attacks and attacking what you are fighting with the paintbrush with the power of paint! They do get difficult at times though. Despite only ever dying a few times (looking at you last two fights for most of my deaths) I found the fights fairly satisfying.So all in all this is a great game. I do give warning to anyone who has struggled with depression or self hatred though as this game does touch on the subjects. Under the cute exterior is a darker theme that I want to give the game credit for.On the surface though it is a fun cute game with a fairly unique mechanic that I had a blast playing. The only big complaint I have is that the backtracking you have to do a lot is a bit frustrating and uncovering the entire map for the achievement has been a chore as there are still some areas I haven't completely figured out. This is in large part caused by needing different abilities with your brush unlocked to progress in certain areas (such as the ability to swim in paint AND for water to hold paint to be able to swim in rivers and waterfalls).I bought the game fairly close to release and I rarely do that. That's how much I loved the demo. So check out the game if it sounds up your alley. It's a unique and fun ride.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've beaten this year. First of all, this is pretty much a 2D-Zelda-like game with the same gameplay loop you are familiar with: backtrack with new abilities and explore more of the map, there are also dungeons and bosses! Although, unlike most of the 2D-Zelda-likes, this does NOT copy & paste mechanics like boomerangs, bombs, arrows, or even the aesthetic; Chicory mainly focuses on brush abilities, and has a  distinguishing artstyle.  Chicory has its own identity and it's pretty strong IMHO, its mechanics are not groundbreaking, but they are well polished. It sounds AMAZING, with a great track and amusing tactile sounds that come out in every interaction.  The soundtrack is made by the same person who made Celeste's OST, this alone tells a lot. I feel like this game deserves more attention. In my eyes, it is in the same league as some indie gems such as Celeste, Undertale, Hollow Knight, Shovel Knight,  Steamworld Dig 2. The only shortcoming I can mention is its length (around 12 hours to 100%), but that might be a good thing depending on how long you like your games. 9/10 Masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Before anything I will say I DON'T WRITE REVIEWS, I will usually just recommend games to friends and sing it's praises to the heavens. For Chicory this is a hugely different story, I still did the previously stated things, but I felt the need to actually write a review for once.I was not expecting much from this game, I thought the paint mechanic was unique and interesting, but it wasn't enough to grab my attention. I bought this game mainly because I played Greg's previous game Wandersong and loved it, so I figured I'd give this a go. Needless to say expectations were low....BUT BY GOD WAS I COMPLETELY WRONG. I really shouldn't have placed it as coloring book the game (especially cause I bought this game after the game award where it was nominated for games for impact). I only watched like one trailer for this game, no clips, and didn't even look at the tags. I was thrown for a loop when I got to the first 2 boss fights, they will be in my nightmares (Thanks Greg). The gameplay was fun, but definitely not the most notable thing in this game (which is saying something cause I found it super fun even if I didn't utilize it). The story was amazing I fell in love with this game, and I even ended up liking it more than Wandersong, which was my favorite game I played blind last year until November. It dealt with heavier themes which was surprising, especially because of the game's rating, another reason why I love it, it's accessible to so many ages which is super important. The characters were super relatable, with it dealing with impostor syndrome, guilt, feeling at fault for bad things, and even panic attacks.Please please please don't sleep on this game it is sooooo GOOD! definitely don't underestimate it like I did, twas very idiotic of me.side note the settings on this game are the most considerate I have ever seen in a video game. Don't like paint sounds?that's fine turn them off. Want trigger warnings? activate them. You can turn off the flashing, screen shaking, and play with the eyestrain (which is huge complaint I've seen for this game, literally just fix it in the settings).This game is getting a 100/10 from me. Greg I will be playing any game you make in the future and never doubt your storytelling ever again, Lesson learned. Also steam can we please have a button higher than recommended please? This game deserves it.
