_childDocuments_.review: When I tried the demo last year, I quickly brushed it aside as a gimmicky color-book adventure and ignored it after that. After release a solid number of remarkably high review scores convinced me to give this another shot and oh boy, did I fall in love. Chicory is essentially a 2D Zelda game without combat and a strong focus on metroidvania-style progression, puzzles and exploration. I don't like to play with mouse and keyboard for comfort reasons these days and I was afraid that a game centered around precision painting would fall flat with an analog stick and to be fair, it really isn't the most ideal input device for this mode of gameplay but it works totally fine after getting used to it - and certain optional upgrades will definitely make your life easier as you progress. This is due to the easy going nature of all aspects of the design, while there are some sections that require fast, precise inputs, you aren't punished much for failing, and pretty much every action of yours in the world is reversible.I am not the biggest fan of the 2D Zelda games, so I can confidently say that this is probably my favorite in the genre. The characters and narrative are so full of heart, the puzzles are clever but never overwhelming and the stellar music by Lena Raine adds an incredibly rewarding layer to exploring all the different nooks in the world. The game drove me to spent extra time in it to explore every part of the map and finish even the most (seemingly) mundane side errants just to get the chance for some new character interactions, which is high praise to the charming writing and world design, that allows its characters plenty of room to breathe and surprise you in unexpected places. I really can't emphasize enough how much this game surprised me. It brought me so much joy over the last weeks and actually hit home quite hard with its themes and narrative. I can't recommend Chicory enough, it is so so good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a masterpiece , I already have 18 hours and eager to put many more into it. It is a MUST play if you're an artist or just interested in art overall. It is the best game I've played, and as an artist, queer person, and having depression, it made me feel great about myself, the way those things are portrayed is enough to make anyone that can relate cry out of joy.● First off, LGBTQIA+ inclusion. Besides portraying many scenarios and having lots of queer characters, the game itself does it's best (and succeeds) to make you feel included.● You can literally play it however you want - Do you want a chill only gameplay? Sure, you can skip boss battles and paint peacefully and go through the game (which has as amazing story). Do you want to play for the story and the action? Sure, you don't need to paint every single thing. Do you want both? Just play the game.● Amazing accessibility - You can customize literally everything, up to how many health points you have, disable sounds that could make you uncomfortable, you can even get tips which describe the exact things you need to do in case you're stuck and don't know how to progress.● Really chill and story based gameplay, but the action is TOP TIER when it has to be.● The OST is just... Heavenly, the way it shifts depending on the area you are is so smooth and almost feels like it was made especifically for the moment you're in. The way certain elements get added to the song as you do things in game is GREAT.● It can be short, it can be long, it just depends on how you want to play it. Some gameplays take 2 hours, some 4 while others 8, or in my case, 18.● It really depicts the struggles of being an artist and goes through deep topics such as being depressed and thinking you're not good enough. It also encourages great messages such as the importance of recycling campaigns, and a bunch of psychological advice that might become a spoiler if I talk about them too much.● It makes you feel happy, sad, energetic, curious, fear, anger, surprised and it goes on... It's a rollercoaster of emotions but not in a bad way.● The gameplay is creative and really based off of art and how you color, paint, and see things. It's something I've never seen before in a game and also something I never knew I needed to see (and experience, also).● It can get tiring sometimes, but it's really just because drawing and painting can be a hard task. It's not much of a big deal though, just take a pause, do something else, and you'll be eager to play it again in no time.● Sometimes the hitboxes to paint certain objects are misleading or just a bit bizarre, but it's not something you can't work it out.The game surely pays off for the cons, it's a delightful experience and it its seriously the best game I have ever played. It is worth the value it's priced and honestly much more. Again, it's a must for anyone that likes art. It is the best game I've played, and as an artist, queer person, and having depression, it made me feel great about myself, the way those things are portrayed is enough to make anyone cry out of joy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an incredible emotional journey, with tons of unique, wonderful, fully-realized characters. The comedy writing is great, and the themes of anxiety and uncertainty are approached tactfully from several angles. Chicory's environments and story beats are made all the more vibrant through its exceptional soundtrack, by Lena Raine.The game heavily rewards exploration, communication, and experimentation. The core painting mechanic provides an incredible amount of artistic freedom, and there are sidequests that help draw out the player's creativity. The system of brush patterns and textures is well-implemented, though precision can be tough with the size of the "pixels" that the brush paints. The small colour palettes in each area feel a bit restrictive at first bit I think that helps guide the player to find creative ways of achieving their artistic goals, instead of focusing on what's "right".I found the slurpy sounds a bit unpleasant on the title screen, but the game provides an option to turn them off. Despite my misophonia, I kept them on, but kept the SFX volume low. They never distracted me in-game as much as they did on initial boot-up. There are also accessibility options for trigger warnings and boss fight difficulty. Some of the colours can be hard to differentiate, and I haven't looked into what sort of colourblindness or contrast options are available. I can't speak to everyone's experience, but I think the creators made an effort to ensure the game is an enjoyable experience for everyone.Chicory was an absolute highlight of my year and I am eagerly awaiting whatever this team works on next.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I was given the ability to make a custom brush and immediately made an UwU brush style.This game is adorable, creative, colorful, charming, and the characters genuinely made me tear up at several points. It uses the coloring book aesthetic mechanically in a way that was fun and rewarding for the player, while still serving the story in a naturally organic fashion. It dealt with complex problems like depression and mental health in artists, creatives, and everyone in between while still fitting the themes of the story and gameplay.10/10, need a main character plush. ʕ •ᴥ•ʔ

_childDocuments_.review: This was probably the best game I've played all year. Chicory is fun, sweet, real, and beautiful. It is a wonderful story about mental illness, finding your place in the world, imposter syndrome, and the nature of a legacy. I found myself strongly attached to every main character and almost all of the side characters. The writing is fun and original, and there is always tons of engaging dialogue for every single situation. The music (done by Lena Raine) was phenomenal as always and you can hear her signature style and way of music composition in every track. The progression was fun and intuitive, and I never felt trapped or restricted by the special abilities I had yet to unlock. Not to mention, the painting system is incredibly well done and the way you blend it with your movement abilities is unique and refreshing. Every part of this game is a treat to behold and it has been one of my most enjoyable gaming experiences ever. If you liked indie games like Undertale, Night in the Woods, and Celeste, I am confident you will very much enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely lovely piece of video game. Chicory's constitution resembles a 7 layer rainbow cake covered in a white frosting. As the knife cuts through the cake to take a vertical slice, each of the well baked layers explode color from beneath the frosting. From cake to plate, the entire experience is transformed. On the surface Chicory is a flash painting game about decorating. The world is a black and white coloring book, and your brush has tons of intuitive and fun tools to color it in. It's lovely getting to see the whole world get colored in with your choice of colors. There are empty canvases around the land which gradually fill with your art. It's low stakes in the same way that wine painting is, nobody is there to be amazing, and it's fun to try hard in a no-judgement atmosphere. Chicory is also a puzzle platformer. Certain flora interact with the paint to allow traversal of obstacles. It's not particularly special, but it breaks up the other part of Chicory, the dialogue. Video game writing has a problem with directness. Lots of games (or at least the ones I play) like to get wordy and dance around the things they're trying to get to. Chicory has no time for that. Each little furry friend in game is funny, direct, and heart warming. There are a million loving pep talks in Chicory, each feeling hand written. I'm particularly fond of a vacationing detective who you meet mid-mystery. He refuses to help because it's important to maintain work-life balance. Chicory wants us to linger for a second on the things in life that cause us hurt and ask why we allow those things to hurt us. Chicory's answers to that question are earnest and often times healing. I found much of the dialogue between Chicory and the main character to be exactly what I needed to hear. I wouldn't go as far as to say that Chicory has improved my mental health, but I feel an awareness of my doubts that was not really present before Chicory. It's not worth going over this game's impact on me, as I think everyone who connects to it will take a different lesson away.Oh and this soundtrack ROCKS. Composed by Celeste's Lena Raine, it pumps blood during the intense moments and makes great painting music when you're eating a slice with your sister.

_childDocuments_.review: An outstanding game that's full of heart and creativity.Playing this feels like a warm hug on a winter day while you sit by a fire. With a mug of hot chocolate. Paired with decent puzzles and an excellent story that tackles themes of depression, imposter syndrome, and art in a way that's grounded and feels emotionally mature, I can't recommend this game enough. _childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a beautiful, sweet, heartfelt work of art. It has the same earnest optimism as Wandersong, but is a step up in its cohesive use of themes: rather than a generic adventure, Chicory is about the trials and tribulations of making art, including topics such as the nature of imposter syndrome and burnout. Definitely worth a play, especially if you are into story-driven games.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Charming. Chicory is basically a very laid back, casual (casual in a good way), relaxing Zelda-clone that focuses on exploration, puzzle solving, collecting things and an occasional bossfight. The main gimmick of Chicory is that you are tasked to bring the color back to the world, which means that you can color almost everything you see. This is used to solve minor questlines and progress through ten chapters of the main story.The story is also surprisingly touching and much deeper than I anticipated at first.It is also very accessible and encouraging with myriad of options to make sure that gamers from all skill levels could beat it. This is not to say that Chicory is an easy game. Puzzles require awareness, thought and creativity, while the boss battles need a special sort of coordination, where you have to dodge attacks while "attacking" your brush.Worth picking up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Holy hell, this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ took my heart. Where do I even begin. I'm just gonna list reasons to buy it, I think.1. The game doubles as a coloring book. Almost every screen can be colored in. Honest to god, coloring each screen in is fun enough on its own.2. The game design teaches you art concepts. Each area has a select color palette of 4 colors, so painting in the world as you go teaches you how to work within limited color palettes. Also there's a literal art school in the game, and you can take classes and study existing works and make your own stuff, and they give you feedback. Admittedly because it's a computer program, the feedback is fairly limited to what was pre-written or programmed, but it's still there and it's cool to see.3. The story. Wow. I don't want to go into too much detail, because I think the story's super important to this game, and I feel like you ought to experience it yourself, but I loved the story for this game.4. Accessibility! Chicory has a ton of accessibility options. Colors can be set to be a bit less extremely contrasting to mitigate eye strain, adjust different fonts to be easier to read, customize difficulty, if you can think of it, it's probably something there. 5. Representation! There's so many different kinds of people in this game just hanging out, and vibing. It's really wonderful to see. Even with a cast of animal characters, it feels more reflective of the kinds of people I might see in real life than some games I've played with human characters.6. THE MUSIC, BABEY. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! Lena Raine and co really outdid themselves! Even without taking into account how it relates to the game itself, the soundtrack stands out as some of the best VGM i've heard in my life. It's got a variety of different sounds, all matching the situations you're in perfectly. And then on top of that, the music adapts to your gameplay in very cool ways! Like if you're moving towards a different area, the first screen you go to outside of the area will play the song from last area but a bit quieter, and then if you move further into the area, you see the title card of the area name and the area theme kicks in, but if you head back into the previous area, it just brings the volume back to normal. Wonderfully adaptive music here! Also if you enjoy the use of leitmotifs, this OST has those too. Very fun stuff!7. The writing! Like I was saying earlier, there's so many different kinds of people in this game hanging out and stuff, and they also have a ton to say! The diverse representation comes through super well in the writing, and there's a ton of moments in the game that made me smile or laugh. 8. Not A Hellscape For Completionists! There are NPCs throughout the game that can help point you in the right direction if you don't know what you're missing for 100% completion, at least for collectibles, sidequests are a little harder to track. But you can track them! And if you have the Camera-Map you get fairly early on, you can mark areas you want to return to on the big map, so you can see on the map where you were planning to go back to. Also there's only 33 achievements, and while I haven't gotten all of them yet, it mostly just seems to be 'have you found all the items and done all the sidequests?' type achievements, so nothing too excessive where I end up being like "okay, i may not have the full achievements for the game but i beat the game to my liking and i just don't care about these achievements". Basically i'm saying that I don't 100% every game, but I think I will 100% this one.9. Pacing. This game lends itself super well to just playing it at whatever pace suits you. At any moment, if you want to take a break from puzzles, or exploring, you can just sit down and color in a screen or two. If you want to take things a bit more at a fast pace, you can find a fill bucket type thing, as well as just fill in things all one color by holding down the brush, but if you don't want to do that, you can pretty much take a break wherever.Honestly, I literally only have one complaint with this game that I can think of. One. That's pretty crazy, considering how it's a pretty damn big game with a lot of characters to talk to and items to find. And hell, it's mostly just a symptom of my hardware setup and my desk. This game is great with keyboard and mouse, but seeing as it was an art-focused game, I wanted to play it with my graphics tablet, and for the most part I did and i had fun with it. Unfortunately, I'm left-handed, so the default control scheme wasn't great for that because my right hand would have to go under my left hand moving about on the tablet, and having to set up my own janky left handed setup without necessarily knowing what buttons are important and where they should be off the top of my head isn't the most fun thing. Also I think as far as being used for a game goes, my tablet's a little big, so making big movements across the screen kinda got a little tiring. Literally the entirety of this complaint is just that there isn't a default setup for buttons to be on the right side of the keyboard instead of the left side. This could be solved with a patch, and even if it isn't, controls are still able to be rebound, so if you knew what you were doing, you could probably set up a decent setup for right hand buttons. (My keyboard has a numpad, so I made use of that. I set movement to arrow keys, brush size / color stuff to ' and /, ctrl, enter, and m for menu stuff and the map, brush styles to Numpad1-3 and decimal, shift for [unlockable move 1] and numpad0 for [unlockable move 2]. This worked well enough, but towards the end I mostly used keyboard and mouse anyway. ) It's a shame I didn't fully enjoy using my graphics tablet for the game about art, but keyboard and mouse isn't too bad of an alternative, and I still enjoyed using my tablet sometimes. If you want to play with a graphics tablet and it has function buttons, look into binding those to important game actions. I'd have done that myself but my tablet buttons are also on the left side of the tablet, meaning it wasn't really something I could do with my right hand. I won't hold this against the game though, because if I could move my setup around so that my tablet buttons were on the right side, or move my keyboard to be on the right of my tablet, this wouldn't be a problem for me, and it's hyper specific to my setup anyway. In conclusion, come on you gotta purchase Chicory. Especially if you're an artist, and especially if you have a graphics tablet. But also if you're literally anybody. It's so good. Everything about this game is absolutely wonderful. And it's only 20 dollars. 20 dollars for all this. Check it out!

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for this game last year and honestly walked away unimpressed, feeling like it was too cutesy and one note to be worth my time. The painting mechanic felt gimmicky and uninteresting and over all felt more like a toy for kids than a game worth playing. I cannot emphasize how dead wrong I was about Chicory. Chicory is easily my favorite game I have played that has been released in 2021 so far. When I played the early minutes of the demo I never would have thought the game would turn into a beautiful blend of Zelda, Metroid, Earthbound, and Night in the Woods, exploring issues of depression, self-loathing, and self-doubt deftly and thoughtfully. The game’s cutesy aesthetic hides a level of depth and beauty in the writing and story that is deeply effective. The game is aggressively kind hearted, reminding me, at moments, of the warmth of games like Dropsy, and on top of all of that I found myself actually growing as an artist in the game, with the map and paintings I created becoming a living document of my evolution as a player and artist. The titular character is easily one of my favorite characters in a video game that I have encountered in a long time, while the player character, Pizza (brilliantly named by asking the player to type their favorite food) is a perfect foil and companion to Chicory. A truly stellar game that I am so glad I did not let my first impression prevent me from playing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is it. This is the one.I'm not one for most games. I much prefer playing indie titles, and especially ones that are going to move me; to evoke as much of an emotional response as possible. And Chicory does that like no other indie has. The dialogue writing in this game is a level of touching I have not seen in any video game to date. It explores so many difficult topics with such grace. There's also not an ounce of negativity in what characters can say that I've come across, which makes it all the more able to fit the description of "a warm hug in video game form". I teared up at quite a few exchanges between characters. Every single NPC in this game has enough to say to you that you'll be emotionally attached to each one in some way. There's plenty of comedic relief as well and I loved all of the quirky exchanges just as much as the hard-hitting ones.The music was something I was excited to hear because Lena Raine did such a phenomenal job on Celeste. I can just say that the music of this game breathes so much life into it, I'll be listening to tracks from the OST for a long, long time to come. It's one of, if not  best game soundtrack I've had the pleasure of listening to. It complements the beauty of every other aspect of this game in a way that completely immerses you. So many live instruments to give it a wonderful, organic feel. Fight music in particular does away with most of the comfortable instrumentation in favour of a more intense sound that is really reminiscent of Celeste, which I think fits those sections perfectly.Pacing is on point so that you never feel tired of a section, but that’s not at all to say there’s very little content as a result. Side quests are all over the place and absolutely none of them are too boring to take on. If those aren’t your thing, there’s still a solid 5-10 hours of raw story content. There are plenty of fast travel benches so you can really make a choice between taking the world in on the way to an objective, or getting right to the meat of the story.Puzzles are difficult enough to make you feel totally clever every time you finish one, without being brain-melting. The hint system is something I've never really seen in another game, where your parents can either push you in the right direction, or tell you exactly how to do something if you feel totally lost. There's phone booths thoughtfully dotted around the map in exactly the right locations so that you're always in a few screens' reach of assistance on difficult areas.Boss fights are super unique, and if you're not very good at dodging attacks, the game just kinda helps you out and puts you back on your feet not too far from where you wiped out. If it notices you're having a particularly hard time with a fight, it'll tell you how you can make it easier. It's such a great way of holding your hand when you need it, which this game does a lot of without ever feeling obtrusive to your experience. It’s perfect.In that same vein, it’s worth mentioning the amount of nice accessibility options, like turning off the foley sounds for painting that might offend some ears, tinting the screen a bit yellow so it’s easier on the eyes, optional content warnings, removing some of the text flair… Really almost anybody can get into this.The core mechanic of painting is so fleshed out, adds so much depth, it's really essential to the experience and does not at all feel gimmicky. You don't need to be a creative to enjoy this game; you don't even need to be able to draw very well. If you make a bad drawing and submit it (there aren't too many instances where it's mandatory), your critiques will never have anything bad to say about it, only words of encouragement.I cannot get over how well-crafted every aspect of this game is; from the fantastic story, to the sheer volume of simple yet effective puzzle mechanics, to the beautiful soundtrack. Of course, replayability is at the very top of the list of pros… Because the whole game is a colouring book, not to mention there’s tons of post-game dialogue to go and experience, and all of those fun side-quests to finish.I have nothing bad to say about Chicory. It's probably my game of the decade. I'm excited to see if anything can possibly top the way it's made me feel, and I'm excited to keep colouring in this map.If you’re wondering if this game is for you; if you are even considering this game to play for yourself: you should. No question.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game as a birthday gift for myself after watching Barry Kramer's and Ariana Figueroa's streams, and I immediately, just from the title screen, fell in love with it and all its details.The art, the music and SFX, the concept, the characters' personalities and dialogues, and the surprisingly super deep and relatable story all made this game into one of my top games of all time. It, coincidentally, has helped through two very long and rough moments in my life where I needed exactly the discussions had in the story for my own well-being and introspection. Not to mention how I could just lose myself while painting to soothing music.I look forward to painting again from scratch soon, if only to re-experience the comfort it brought to me. It gave some good 5 cries I needed; I mean, even the 100% event at the end (no spoilers) made me cry.Will strive to follow all the members of the team that worked on this game in their other projects, past and future, because this was one of the most humane pieces of media I've encountered in a long time, and it came at the time we needed something like it the most.Note: I played offline, so my actual playtime was 50 hours (of painting with OCD and sometimes being too tired to solve even the easy puzzles on the get-go, lol), plus 3 extra hours of me just travelling post-ending because I didn't want it to end.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely adorable adventure game that everyone should play. Whether you're an artist or not, the themes here can be applied to just about any hobby, or just life in general. The writing ranges from humorous to tear-jerking, and does so in such a way that feels natural without relying on being super blunt. The art style is very cute, and it can be lots of fun to bring back color to the world. You start off with just a brush and some basic colors, but gain access to more styles / patterns, as well as new colors in each zone to make them more distinct. The game does a good job of throwing new tools to you so that you're always playing around with something new. The puzzles are for the most part very simple, whether you consider that good or bad is a personal preference. Lena Raine, as always, delivers an exceptional soundtrack.Overall, worth it at full price. If you can get it on a sale, all the more so worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this sweet little bundle of love!  It has had me hooked on its enriching story, stunned by its simple yet captivating visuals, and mesmerized by Lena Raine's soft and moody melodies.  The boss battles are difficult by unconventional means (), the sounds of Picnic Providence are as fun as they are wet, and the painting mechanic feels so... so unbelievably smooth!  The dialogue is all shades of cute and gut wrenching, and it has had me in tears more times than I am willing to admit. Chicory is a game of moments...  whether it's sprucing up the landscapes around you, saving the world, or just giving your cool big sister a hug; it's truly the little things that allow this wonderful masterpiece to touch the hearts of many, mine included!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a unique feel-good puzzle platformer about bringing color to a black-and-white world. Playing this game with a controller is a significant handicap, but the overall difficulty is so low it didn't matter. Coloring in the world is immensely satisfying, and almost all of the finicky drawing sections are optional. I do not have the gene for visual art, but the game makes coloring very accessible while still allowing for higher-order art if that's something you enjoy. Unlocking new abilities and exploring the world was great fun, and most of the puzzles were engaging. Boss fights are really creative and visually stunning, although a couple of them are so gruesome and nightmarish that I can't imagine a child playing them. It's a real shame, because otherwise this is very much a sophisticated game for modern children, with a lot of room for player expression and optional secrets. The game is well-written, but I would have liked a few more "quirky" characters (Pickle is the MVP). The message of the game is beautiful and heartwarming, but it misses the mark a bit by over-indulging in dialogue. For a game that is so diagetically unique and compelling, you really don't need to underline every theme over and over again. If a picture is worth a thousand words, you don't also need a thousand words to explain it.

_childDocuments_.review: A short and sweet Zelda-like puzzle adventure game that also manages to be a relaxing art game! All wrapped in lovely music by Lena Raine, absolutely endearing characters, and plenty of plot and side-stories. The paintbrush is both a colourful distraction from the story and an actual game mechanic that gains more depth as one progresses. Screens can sometimes be tricky to read, but funnily enough colouring them in often helps. I also wish there was some kind of endgame content—especially something that could take advantage of the co-op mode. I wouldn't drop full price on this game, but I would definitely grab it during a sale if it sounds like your kind of thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Premise:Play as a doggy in a colouring-book world that you get to paint yourself. The world is full of animal people, all named after food. Stuff to do:-Meet fellow animal people and chat. Some of them have troubles you can solve with your travels or your painting skills.-Every place (and animal) in the world has no colour in it, and can be filled in with your magic paintbrush. Every region of the world has its own palette of 4 colours. You can colour them however you want with plenty of options available to you in how to draw or flood fill.-Puzzles to get from point A to point B, including painting abilities and local flora.-Find collectables like: clothes, brush styles, lost cat kids, and litter. Getting to these involves puzzles that are a little more involved. (These are more "play around until you understand" puzzles than "look and think about it" puzzles.)-Join art classes, where you get a prompt and you paint on a regular canvas. The prompt might be a concept to paint or it might be "copy this picture but in your own style."-There's even a co-op mode where one person controls the main character and both players can colour at once — or one person could colour while the other person reads the dialogs.Story:-The brush is what paints colour in this world. The animal person who uses it is called the Wielder.-The brush is passed down from old Wielder to new Wielder, not based on family but on old Wielder's choice.-The current Wielder, Chicory, is suffering from depression, and no longer has it in her to continue painting.-The dog you play as is Chicory's cleaner, and ends up as the new Wielder just by being the closest available. The doggy has no training, but they look up to Chicory a lot and they rarely say "no" to someone who asks things of them.-Engage more with Chicory and learn about her depression as time goes on-Engage more with all the animal people in this world as you keep exploring
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really pleasant, enjoyable, cute, creative game. The way it helps to prompt your creativity is very welcome. The world that it builds up feels very real and emotive, and the characters are all delightful, if a bit sad at times. The game could have easily leaned too far into the combat sections, but these are rare and self contained, and that makes the game much better.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game that made me actually cry in all the good ways possible.First of all, the gameplay concept is just amazing. It turned the game into a coloring book, that turned the calmer moments into almost meditative sessions, that never felt like busywork, although it took some time for this gameplay mechanic to come to full strength in the 2nd half of the game, when it got at its most effective, while remaining mostly optional the whole time.While the game started out rather innocent and playful, the story got serious very quickly. The presentation is enough for children to grasp concepts like depression or anxiety, but also intimate and respectful enough for those who have dealt with those feelings and mental states. It threads those difficult waters extremely well while being engaging the whole time. But even the Small things stand out like the expressiveness of Lasagna, the pun-loaded place names, a very diverse cast of NPCs that manage to fit into picnic almost natually, the wholesome dialogues with the family and the best end credits I happen to witness (really, after spending a whole day in play hours, this was the most validating experience I ever had in gaming).And I didn't even mention the music, which is varied, immersive, really well done, with the tracks accompanying every place as if they were there since ancient times.Truly a astounding game by a team of 5 people.

_childDocuments_.review: Very few games can genuinely surprise you, especially on a mechanical level. Chicory's painting/drawing mechanic has the power to do this. Even after playing the game for hours, it still surprises with how novel and inventive it is. The story -- about burnout in a micro sense and mental health in the macro -- is cute and didactic. Some people may consider these elements a turn-off. Your mileage may vary, especially if you deal with things like anxiety and depression yourself. Not everyone wants to feel seen by a piece of entertainment that is still ostensibly a toy. Not everyone wants to feel like they are being lectured, either. But I think Chicory largely avoids feeling cloying or arrogant. In many ways this is a Zelda-style adventure game with a pretty wrapper (the music is incredible, too). There are towns, and dungeons, and macguffins and bosses. Some parts feel a little bit rote, especially the bosses. But 90% of the game feels so fresh that the stale bits are largely not noticeable.At times I struggled to find a control scheme that worked, but that may have simply been a matter of me not being a heavy mouse-and-keyboard guy. It makes me long for the days of stylus-based controls -- if Nintendo had published it on the DS or 3DS, it might be one of my favorite games ever. Hell, it still might be anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game does a great job of making you feel so many emotions, and making you feel so immersed. You start off immediately naming your character your favorite food, personally connecting yourself to it. You then get the brush and start shaping the world around you to however you'd like. Everything around you is colored how you like it. Then, you fill a duty as wielder and fight your first corruption (after helping some people, hopefully). You go back to chicory, and "officially" take the place as the wielder. Notice, that the theme of Luncheon seems off in a way, homely, but yet missing something to fulfill it. After the temple, you go back to chicory, and you two draw paintings of each other to help restore some of chicory's spark. You connect with Chicory for a little, but afterwards, you fight a corruption bearing a striking resemblance of her. You talk to her, hoping all the mean things it said arent true, but they turn out to be. Luncheon's theme grows darker, not being as comforting as before. You get cheered up after a while, with some help from your sis. You deal with another corruption, and head back to chicory, to see what you should do next. Chicory is not doing well, and just wants to be forgotten about, but you help her come to her senses. Her battle theme just feels desperate, lonely, and her screams are painful. This game makes you cry, and helps hit in many places. The music is so amazing though, it conveys emotion so well, Lena did a fantastic job with it (as usual, of course). Each song evokes so much emotion, and helps fully immerse you. Every song has a different feel to it, like Appie Foothill's momentum, carrying through the bars, or Elevenses' comfort, almost exactly similar to how a campfire in the woods feels. Potluck feels like home away from home. The wielders temple empty, with one of the instruments being the recorder (how you as a character are represented). Sips river helps capture the blissful serenity of a flowing river surrounded by trees. And as mentioned before, The town of Luncheon being the first iteration of Luncheons theme, sounds like trying to make it home. Seeds of Doubt, the second iteration, sound as if something is wrong, which fits the story. I stayed away from Luncheon as much as i could while this played, simply because it hit that tone so well. Then finally, A Fresh Start. Everything fits together, so, so well. Everything shines through, and you feel as if this is where you're meant to be. The Mountain Top is a glorious credits theme, telling the story of your character. Also, Banquet Rain Forest, having all of the notes be short and sweet, having melodies be scattered around, but having everything still be fine in the end, all reflecting how the rain can be. Even the menu music changes! Blank Canvas, starting off like it needs some filling in, end with This Colorful World, its response, being filled in with many instruments. I could probably ooze about the music more, but I've probably gone on too long. Please, if you haven't already, play this game. Even if you've watched it before, playing it still is amazing (trust me, i watched skurry's playthrough, and while i loved it, making that world mine felt so amazing).Oh and everywhere being a time to eat and everyone being animals being represented by food and plants is so cute. Even existing food is named different things, a pizza is called slice, some fruit being called squeeze, and gumballs being called chew balls, donuts being called holeys, etc. Best game ive played all year, and it barely has even started.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory was very charming and relaxing. I loved getting to explore, meet all the characters, and solve the puzzles. Most of all I loved getting to color EVERYTHING! The storyline also felt a little off for me, I'm still not 100% convinced I understand what they were going for. Despite all that I was never bored and loved the experience from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: Just from the trailer I thought  was a nice little relaxing game centered around a gimmick of interacting with the game world through coloring stuff...No, it was an incredibly heartfelt story that will see the characters work through stuff using the scene this title paints as a takeoff point.An event wiped all world of color, and nobody knows how or why.You are [Insert Your favorite food here] a janitor with big dreams and an even bigger heart who amidst this stumbles upon the only thing that can give back color to the world, and that is...An oversized brush?Travel the relaxed world of Picnic trying to find clues about what happened along fun event and escapades as a side dish.You roam around the overworld stumbling onto puzzles that will leave an invisible breadcrumb trail to the next big story section.There’s some light platforming but the game mainly revolves around using the power to apply colors on this black and white world to solve the many puzzles that are blocking progression to the next area.The color-in mechanic is the main thing on display here, but also serves as a gameplay, story and graphic tool to knit the experience together.Every character and piece of environment has a notebook squiggle vivacity to them, as well as their own personality.Sometimes, very rarely, you’ll be left directionless, especially at the beginning you’ll be given freedom to roam in almost any direction and interact with any characters you’d like multiple times, this creates a little pacing problem where you either talk to everyone taking so much time that it interferes with the pacing of the story or find your way immediately to the next major story point and feel you’ve missed a lot of characters you could’ve talked to.My suggestion is, go with the flow.I started this title as an unwind from other very long titles, fully expecting just a little nice relaxing game, but Chicory is so much more, the kind of game you’ll remember forever.The pricetag is nice and the many discounts even nicer for a game that I wholeheartedly recommend to just about everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: The game's primary mechanic being painting the world sounds like a great idea in theory, but in practice it rapidly becomes an exercise in patience if you're the obsessive type who has to color in everything. The plot's also very paper thin despite having some actually good ideas that sadly go nowhere because the characters aren't strong enough to support it.That's not the primary reason why I'm voting no on recommending though.I played through the whole game waiting patiently for the author to tip their hand as a postmodern communist hippie, I knew it was only a matter of time before they did, because really the painting was already on the wall, who else would make such a meta art game? Big surprise, I was right of course, but they waited longer than I expected to really tip their hand.About halfway through the game two NPCs are discussing economic systems and one proposed capitalism as a better system than the literal communism that exists in-setting. Now, the irony isn't lost on me of a capitalist existing in-setting as basically a communist IRL and being dismantled and dismissed in much the same way, but seeing the author quietly slipping their political narrative into the game directly is displeasing.  It really didn't help either that the plot basically doubled down on exactly the sorts of beats you'd expect from a postmodern communist hippie art game. Maybe it's just me but it's disappointing for a game supposedly all about creativity and individuality to be exactly what you expect it to be. So yeah, don't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: A tentative thumbs up for this niche masterpiece. If you're here because you're following the minds behind Wandersong and Celeste, you won't be disappointed - the presentation and soundtrack are indeed fantastic.The plotline and character development are surprisingly deep. As you progress, you learn about the history of the world the player character's extraordinary situation. You'll also learn about how characters have been impacted by their time as the Wielder, and how being the Wielder now fills you with nothing but questions. The conversations that take place are honestly the best part of the game.As for everything else... ehhh.....Every screen begs for you to stop and color it in. It's cathartic every now and then, but you can only do so much before your brain starts to melt. Eventually you just stop bothering. Outside of conversations, that's literally the whole game - working your way through puzzles til you reach your next destination, praying you don't fall asleep on the way.Puzzles are straightforward and never take long to figure out. They're really just clicking things in a certain order until you get the reward or get to move on. They're not bad, it's just that none of them stand out. There are boss fights, but they're also very ho-hum. You just constantly swipe at them while avoiding their attacks til it's over.Short confession, I personally took every chance to NOT color things in and just move on (unless a character specifically asked for it). Having to wade through simple puzzles and many, MANY screens with nothing in them really bogged down the experience, and I had to force myself to keep playing multiple times.However, I still wholeheartedly recommend it. There's a LOT to love - a sizeable world to color in at your leisure, superb tunes that embed themselves in your ear, and refreshingly sincere conversations with each of its characters. If any of these points interest you in the slightest, even the ones that I didn't particularly enjoy, it's absolutely worth diving into.

_childDocuments_.review: A game with a great story, fun and intuitive mechanics, beautiful music, and charming characters. The art is well done and that is not to mention that you get to do the coloring yourself.  One of the few games that is actually able to draw me into its story and keep me emotionally invested. _childDocuments_.review: If Wandersong was Greg’s riff on the Paper Mario franchise, Chicory is his tribute to the original Legend of Zelda, with a splash of Earthbound thrown in there for good measure. Just like with Wandersong, he’s able to squeeze out an insane amount of gameplay variety from just a single core mechanic. Combat encounters are present, sure, but the focus here is on exploration, creativity, and puzzle-solving with your paintbrush.But what makes these games shine is a balance between that fantastic game design and their pure, empathetic spirit. Like Wandersong, Chicory wears its heart on its sleeve. You get the sense that Lobanov cares deeply about even the smallest of creatures, so much so that “kindness towards bugs” has become a recurring motif in his body of work. His ultimate goal here is to make these games resonate with the player on a raw, personal level. He wants us to empathize with this world and these characters as much as he does by looking inward, reflecting on our own experiences in order to find a deeper emotional connection.Is he successful? Heck yeah he is. Game’s a masterpiece.(Should probably mention that my name’s in the credits. Backer #263 🤙🏻)

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely want to thank the developers for making such a wonderful game.For most games, you would focus a review on maybe graphics? Sounds? Music? Gameplay? Balance? Story? World building?Don't get me wrong, all of the above are solid in Chicory. But that's not why I'm thankful.I'm thankful because this game woke up a love I had long ago for just... drawing to my heart's content without thinking of making it perfect, or thinking of impressing anyone. Just for the sake of art, of expressing myself and making something that just feels neat.This feeling is something I had hardly felt since 5th Cell's  series. I wasn't sure I'd feel this again. So a big thank you to the whole team behind Chicory, for allowing me to find the part of me that just likes to draw whatever feels nice without a care in the world.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is a beautiful adventure game. You become the next wielder and it is your job to bring color back to the world after corruption has taken hold. And a great soundtrack too! Thankfully you have a lot of control over boss fights and can entirely skip them if you wish. Some might desire this as they can be chaotic and to fast paced for those with movement problems in their hands or over stimulated by fast moving streaks and colors.  The only fights in the game are boss fights and the downside if you fight them besides being chaotic is some are a bit long winded. So the fighting parts were my least favourite part of the game and my only dislike. I had no crashes and and it supports wide screen. I played with keyboard or you can use a controller if you wish. And yes you can re-bind the controls!  A really fun game! It is worth all the great reviews it has received and provides hours of fun. _childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough. It's beautiful, it's fun, the story is insanely compelling, and it's so nuanced. I'm in love with it, genuinely. _childDocuments_.review: There is so much about this game I want to talk about. I will try to split this in multiple points in order to explain this as good as I can. Finji games always are worth playing, and Chicory was another gem I am glad I could enjoy!, I spent a little over 30 hours to 100% it, the gameplay is quirky and innovative without getting in the player's way, there is alot to explore and to do, the art style is adorable and the dialogues are simple yet captivating. If you crave for a Zelda-like gameplay, with tons of exploration, power-ups, sidequests and collectibles, this game will keep you going. Long version: let me do this step by step without spoiling too much of the game. painting the world with your mouse while moving with WASD is such a fresh and interesting way to progress through the game! Everything revolves around this mechanic, and it gets more complex the more you explore and discover things. The puzzles are pleasant, hard enough to give a challenge to the player but never harsh to the point to make you want to give up or become frustrating. The amount of collectible stuff is enormous but it can be traced, there is NO missable and the satisfaction it gives to finish each category is HUGE. There also are some secondary things you can do, like art classes where you actually paint, decorate each and every location with stuff you unlock, and there are some mini-games here and there to pepper it up even more. Moving around the areas gets easier and faster the more you progress, too, so backtracking is never too much of a chore. Without spoiling, there are some fights the player has to go through, but there also is an option to make them easier or skip them completely - they are worth doing though, because the mechanics are very interesting. Finally, only found a couple bugs and glitches but nothing game-breaking.  the main story is nothing too fancy, you start a journey from hero wannabe to actual hero, with all the ups and downs this ensues. What I found beautiful are the interactions with the characters, and the way many things are addressed in a way that really strikes home. I am pretty sure that characters like the protagonist (I called them Sushi so I'll call them Sushi from now on), Chicory and many others will resonate with many of the players one way or another. I feel very close to Sushi in the way they don't feel like having a purpose or a proper direction in life, but they are winging it as things happen. There are many positive messages throughout the game and they are worth listening to. I also loved how talking to all critters around the various areas is actually pleasant, many of them can and will reveal more of themselves to you if you want them to, and if you talk to them. I ended up rooting for some of the characters and wanting to know more about them. Simple but beautiful. the music department is simply wonderful, specially for the way the music actually adapts and subtly changes as you move, change area, progress or something happens. Some of the BGMs stuck with me and I found myself humming them while not playing. They really elevate the experience of the game, by setting the mood and the tone. I think the graphics are one of the strongest points of the game. The whole thing is made to look like one of these old coloring books, and allowing you to color each and every part of it, making it also a key element of the gameplay and having the characters actually acknowledging and actively appreciating what you do is simply genius. The simple yet effective style is absolutely adorable and I crave for more! This is the reason why I enjoy playing indie games so much - you can feel the passion and the enthusiasm of who is making them. Chicory is a labor of love, and I waited to write this review until I got to see and collect everything the game had to offer. This game deserves to be played and experienced. I really commend the developers for such a masterpiece. Thank you very much! ♥

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is far and away the best game that has come out this year. I give it my full recommendation to anyone and everyone, please show support to these developers who poured their heart and soul into this masterpiece.I want to gush about some of the particular things that Chicory does so exceptionally well. Obviously there are more great things than what I list here, but these stood out to me above all else.Innovation + Customization: This game's use of painting as it's core mechanic to traverse the landscape, help others, and bring color back to the world is ambitious and sticks the landing flawlessly. It is such a natural desire to bring color back to this world and the homes of these people that live there. All of the work that you do completely pays off, whether it is decorating a self-portrait, painting a mural, or customizing your character. I am a complete sucker for character customization and it is done so incredibly well here by being able to find new clothes wherever you go and change their colors with your brush. It's rare to see a development team push the boundaries of what games can be and actually put effort into innovating the medium. Chicory is a shining example of a coherent vision that these dedicated artists wanted to give to players.Puzzles: Puzzles are one of the games many facets and I did not expect them to pan out as well as they did here. Each area offers new tactics and pieces to work with and comprehend. I was so excited to travel to new areas and discover what cool puzzles there would be to figure out. They have a great blend of accessibility and challenge, which is another reason to recommend this game to everyone, young or old.Character Design: Each character in this world is distinct with different designs, sounds, and personalities. Each of them are interesting to talk to and even give hilarious or touching dialogue at times. Some of my favorite moments in all of gaming have now come from these characters. I won't spoil any here, but do yourself a favor and make sure to talk to all of the NPCs that you find in the world and complete the side quests that they offer.Music: Lena Raine went above and beyond with this soundtrack. I was already enamored with the amazing score from Celeste, which Raine composed as well, but this music amplified the feelings I had when exploring the world. I am hugely into music and soundtracks and among all of the amazing aspects of this game, I had a major appreciation for the beautiful tracks here.Story: At it's core, Chicory is about impostor syndrome and rising to the challenge of new opportunities. Without going into spoilers, this game dives deep into very real mental health issues and presents this in not just the dialogue, but the visuals and gameplay. For those unaware, impostor syndrome occurs when a person feels that they are not deserving of their skills, talents, or accomplishments. The game is written in a way that is very earnest and clearly comes from a place of personal hurt. The feelings of depression and worthlessness are communicated in a way that doesn't bring down the tone of the overall game, but also strikes deeply in the heart of the player. The story does not progress like you think it would either, it can be quite unpredictable at times. The ending is so strong and gives such a great send off to one of the best gaming experiences I have ever had.Player Involvement: I have played games my whole life, and I have played a lot of amazing ones. However, the feeling of player involvement and enrichment has never been stronger than in Chicory. Everything in this game is customizable and you are able to craft an experience that is unique to YOU. It is cutting edge and revolutionary, but it also touches back on one of the games primary themes: individuality. This game made me feel special like no other game has ever been able to do. This is reinforced by the core mechanics, the story, and the cast of characters that relentlessly boost you up and encourage you to express your creativity. At this point, I hope that I've convinced you to show it lots of love and support. Whether or not this game goes down in history as one of the greatest indie games of all time, I'm not sure (though I hope it will). Regardless of that, it will forever hold a place in my heart. Thank you, to everyone that made Chicory possible.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I saw a couple years ago and thought it looked cool so I added it to my wishlist, and a few days ago a friend finally gifted it to me. And, man, it was WAY better than I was anticipating. Probably my 2nd favorite game I've played this year after Persona 3 Reload.This is a top-down game where you explore a world map and use a paint brush to draw on things (controlled by your mouse). And you can draw on EVERYTHING, in different colors and in different ways. As you progress, you get new abilities which unlock more of the world and allow you to traverse old parts more quickly. You also find optional "brush styles" which change your brush stroke. Most are purely aesthetic, but some provide unique affects: A paint bucket tool, a very wide brush, a rainbow brush, and one that lets you choose your own color palette instead of being confined to the area's palette. The paint bucket, in particular, is a huge game changer, allowing you to quickly fill entire screens (and you want your screens filled with paint as it allows you to traverse them quicker).Not only can you paint, but later on you get decorative objects you can place down. I figured these would be confined to pre-set areas like your house, but no. You can place them ANYWHERE. And they're not purely visual, they have collision and functions (like playing music) as well. This makes the world HIGHLY configurable to a very impressive degree. There are also specific areas meant to be decorated, like an NPC who wants to throw a party but has no furniture, so you can set up the party for them. Once you do, random NPCs will come and go from the party and you can talk to them.Along with decor, your world will change as you go around and meet more people. As you make more friends, you get sort of "followers" who you'll run into at random places around the world and comment on how you've painted that screen or the story. And they are truly random, I once had a random NPC spawn inside of a static NPC, which was funny. This also helps to make the world feel more personalized.It's sort of a Zelda-like. You have the top-down world with towns, mountains, and forests, abilities that unlock more of it, and dungeons. There are two main design differences that make it not quite a Zelda-like, though:1) While you do get new abilities from dungeons, you don't get them until after the dungeon is over, so the dungeons are not structured like a Zelda-like.2) There are no enemies outside of the boss fights. Truly, I don't think enemies would work outside of boss fights since you could hit them from anywhere on the screen, and the bosses are full-screen threats.The world is very fun to explore, puzzles abound to be solved, and secrets are hidden to be solved. The main collectables in this game are gifts which give clothes, litter which is like a currency you can use to buy decor, lost cats which contribute to a side quest and also give you decor, and the aforementioned brush styles. Finding them all was pretty fun for the most part, although I have a note about that laterThe boss fights are awesome. They're fun gameplay-wise but nothing special in that department. Visually, they're VERY cool, and the boss's animations and attacks synchronize to the music. The fights also usually relate to some story beat which turns your emotional response to them up even further. Through the whole game, the music and sound effects are very good.The story and characters... I don't even know what to say. They're so well written. You'll end up loving most people you meet, and it's ALWAYS worth it to check up on people as the story progresses to see what new dialogue they have. Along with the main story there are several progressive side stories, such as the "lost kids" storyline and the art academy storyline. I absolutely recommend for you to do everything you can find and experience every bit of writing this game has to offer.After racking my brain, I can only think of 3 complaints, and all but the first are pretty specific:1) Getting the last few gifts and litter sucks. There are 2 NPCs, one for each collectable type, who will tell you the vague area that your missing item is in. But they will only tell you one area at a time, so you have to keep going back and talking to them after every item you find. Not only that, but both of their houses are several screens away from the nearest fast travel point, making it truly a chore. I think this process would be greatly improved if either their houses were next to fast travel points, they told you a list of missing items instead of one at a time, or they were more specific about where the missing item is, or any combination of those 3. Still, in the end this process only took like an hour so I can't say it was too bad.2) Some of the puzzles where you have to push bombs around are annoying. Both because the pushing is kinda janky, and because sometimes you have to carefully paint something near the bomb without touching the bomb itself (as that will cause it to explode) and the hitboxes do not match visually.3) There were 2 characters who REALLY should have had post-game dialogue, but didn't. Those being your sister (who had new dialogue through most of the game, and your other family members did have post-game dialogue, so it's really weird she didn't) and Blueberry (who was VERY plot-relevant and really should have had something to say about the climax. Hell, even the wielder before her did).I have a lot more I could say, but there are some really awesome things in this game I want to leave as surprises. TL;DR: Play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colourful Tale is a beautiful game about artistic burnout, the pressure of expectations and finding creativity in a blank canvas. The game, to me, started slow because before it truly began I found my own art based perfectionism coming into play and finding it hard to put brush to world because I felt paralysed by indecision. That being one of the main themes and conflicts in the story made the process of working past that through gameplay interesting. I soon found myself becoming more comfortable and confident and just splashing colour about randomly and I felt truly connected to Chicory and the player character's plight.There's a lot to love about the game, the characters are all so wholesome and fun, I found the story of Beans and Pepper to be particularly charming. The character design and art style as a whole really added to the living picture book atmosphere, everything in the environment is clear in its design so hunting for collectibles never felt unfair, I never felt like I missed a collectible because it wasn't legible in the environment but rather because I missed a secret path.And having the art school to break up the exploration to play about with the various brush styles and to imitate the master works was a great way to add to the history of the world in a fun way, I would have loved to be able to see the fellow students interpretations alongside my own.Gameplay wise there's a good sense of progression through the story, with you unlocking a new skill and each new environment coming up with a new form of environmental puzzle to figure out. It made exploring feel more worthwhile and enjoyable because the game didn't rely solely on the brush mechanic and the brush itself improved each chapter. There were several boss fights as well, something I was surprised by since combat doesn't exist anywhere else in the game, and they were more spectacle than challenge since there were no real repurcussions for being hit, with there being accessibility options to change how many hits you could take also. Which to me was absolutely fine! I don't play games like Chicory to be challenged, and the spectacle of the boss fights were more than enough. There was a real sense of foreboding and danger through the visuals and soundtrack alone. And speaking of the soundtrack, every single track was fantastic. An eclectic mix of emotional, playful and epic tracks that added to every scene. Her Wretched Utterances being one of my favourites (I might be biased because Queen Drosera had some of my favourite design and dialogue)I'm wrapping up my review here, I feel like I haven't been able to fully express all that I like about Chicory. There's just so much to love about it! So I highly recommend everyone give it a shot, and if you're like me and struggle at the beginning with a sense of perfectionism try to push through because the story is totally worth it and you might end up coming away from the game with the ability to push through that same struggle in your own art.

_childDocuments_.review: On first glance, this is a game of a cute dog with a brush in a black-and-white world where everyone is named after food and you get to color all the environments and characters! Painting aside, this is mostly a zelda-style puzzle adventure with focus on traversal/exploration (and has boss battles haha)The REAL draw of this game though, is how it serves as an experience - as a love letter to creators everywhere. Working in a creative field is rough, and everyone at every level struggles with self-esteem, burnout, imposter syndrome and other hard topics against the love for their craft. This explores a lot of those feelings in its world of lovable characters and has a very satisfying story arc and conclusion.MUST play for any creator.

_childDocuments_.review: I first came across this game when I saw my friend play it a few months back. Upon first glance I had already been intrigued, given the general focus on painting and the seemingly creative gameplay gimmicks that separated it from others of its type. I didn't have the chance to experience the game for myself until about a week or so ago. Other than the brief snippets of the game I had seen from my friend's own indulgence, I had little to no idea what the experience would have to offer from a story perspective. And, to be honest, this is the best way to go about enjoying this game.The story is most definitely the focal point of Chicory, and while this is the case, it doesn't make other aspects, such as the gameplay, characters, side missions, and ESPECIALLY the music any lesser as a result. In fact, it was a delight to observe the characters living their daily lives in this uniqeu world, and the soundtrack is one of the best in a game I have heard in a very long time. There is not a single song that I didn't like, or even love, while going through this game.While the black-and-white aesthetic of the game as a whole put me off at first glance (and by this I mean for about a minute or two), it begins to really separate the game from most others, even those with a monochrome look to them. Since the main gimmick revolves around using color to access areas or collect secrets, I believe that encasing the world in this colorless environment is beyond fitting, and adds an extra depth to the narrative and overall realism of the story. In short, it makes those brief moments of bursting color all the more satisfying, expressive, and indulgent.I feel that this game connects on a deeper level especially to us aspiring artists in the world. Its message is profound in such a way that resonated with me more than some games with similar thematics such as Celeste or OMORI, and I think that's largely due to the fact that it struck some familiar notes for me personally. I believe this gives me a much greater bias towards the game as a result, but nonetheless, I think that anyone, regardless of artistic background or intent, going about playing this game will still have an immaculate experience.As a whole, Chicory: A Colorful Tale is undoubtedly a masterpiece in most every regard. It's unique, enjoyable, and carries morals that'll stick with you for quite a while. Its level of polish is unmatched in my opinion to the majority of AAA games that come out these days; hell, the ONLY mistake I found was a typo which I only really noticed because I tend to read things a bit more in-depth than the average player would. I recommend getting this game, whether at max price or on sale, for an unforgettable experience.tl;dr This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ incredible. Definitely GOTY in my eyes.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give Chicory 9/10 but I am not one to complain about cute indie games to begin with.My partner said "it's like someone made a game with all the things you love: an adventure game with cute characters who have (weird) food names, a bit of Splatoon, general faffing about, and coloring" I agree, overall very wholesome and fun. I got way more out of this game than I was expecting, because I was only expecting to get maybe 10 hours MAX and got easily triple that. I wanted to go everywhere, color every piece, and unlock every item and I don't normally like to achievement hunt, because I find it exhausting. Color me very impressed! (heh.) The puzzles were intriguing and fun to interact with without feeling old, rehashed, or stale. The puzzles were challenging enough to be enjoyable and clever without ever feeling like punishment.  I love puzzle games like The Witness and The Talos Principle, but some solutions in games like that can make you roll your eyes. In Chicory, nothing seemed too hard to get intuitively (or with having to look up a walk-through or guide like some badly-made puzzles might.)The character interactions were cute, the dialogue never dragged on too long, and it covered mature topics such as identity crisis, imposter syndrome, and mental health issues in very approachable ways for such a cute little game. None of it ever felt forced; every struggle shown by a character in Chicory felt relatable and actually thought-through as you get to know the characters.The "combat" (only to "power up" your brush) was easily my least favorite part, even though the game is very forgiving combat-wise. Combat scenes weren't always clear on what you need to do next, nor did the boss have a health bar/an indicator of how long the fight was going to go on for. This is my only complaint.Lastly, my favorite part: getting to download a gif of your progress at the end. It was like a cherry on top!

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much it ended up as my GOTY :)I really like the accessibility it has with the options menu. I see a lot of complaints about the limited color palette but I honestly like that more. It forces you to use the colors wiser in my opinion. I also just adore the art style and the paintings from other characters are so cute. The games characters and soundtrack is amazing. One of the songs actually made it to #1 on my 2021 top 100 songs which I'm really saying something since I listen to music constantly. The characters are written reasonably and I feel like I can really connect with some of them. The game's plot isn't perfect but I don't really think that makes it bad. It's trying to go for a lot of ideas at once which is awesome but there's some very small sections I wish were different. That's truly my only gripe. I'm glad I got the chance to play a game like this. I hope to 100% it soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. This game is incredible. The paint game mechanic is used so well to where you feel more accomplished as you progress in the game. What do I mean by that? At the start, our main character (named after our favorite food) picks up the brush after the world suddenly turns black and white. Why is the brush important? It's the only thing that keeps color in the world and can only be passed down through select people called Wielders. And our character just took it. Oops. The main character uses their dedication to grow stronger and learn more skills, to not only beat the final boss but to defeat their doubts. That is good character development right there.Seriously, Chicory shines with its creative use of puzzles, cute and thought-provoking writing (two characters debate about capitalism vs communism in a charming cartoonish presentation), combat, and secrets/collectibles. That last point is relevant because I am terrible with backtracking as I find it is not worth my time in most games. This game was different as I wanted to explore the world and color in my surroundings. And when I got new powers, I knew where I should go to see brand-new areas/collectibles. It didn't feel like a slog to color in new areas and I also didn't feel overwhelmed by the backtracking that I had to do using my new powers.Lastly, I want to talk about this game's themes. Chicory's main themes deal with imposter syndrome and mental health with creators. It also deals with pressures from pleasing others with your job,  following someone you admire, and stress created by self-doubt. The game also does commentary on topics like grief, workaholism, and sexuality/identity. For example, one of the NPC characters in the game likes manly colors and wants to be portrayed as a masculine man while also struggling with coming out as bisexual. Another NPC tells our character to have a better work-life balance. These NPC hit close to home for me. Overall, I think the world, writing, gameplay, music, and well-thought-out game mechanics make for a game that you must play for yourself.

_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, heartfelt, achingly real game that is, on the surface, about a cartoon dog (named after your favorite food) going on a magical, old-school-Legend-of-Zelda-inspired journey to inherit a magical paintbrush that is the source of all colors in the world.Beneath that surface lies an evocative study of imposter syndrome, the pressure of trying to make everyone around you happy, what it means to be an artist (of any kind, really), and a painfully, cathartically genuine portrait of several distinctly different types of mental illness. You'll cry, but you'll laugh far more often, and if you have even the slightest hint of a creative spirit in your heart, you'll be moved to try and be the best you that you can be, and to reach out as best you can, to help those around you along on the journey up to the metaphorical mountaintop.The gameplay is just as deceptively simple as the overarching themes; what begins as a sort of platforming-by-way-of-coloring-in-the-world-around-you evolves into some of the more technically complex boss fights I've run into, bending and twisting the way you use a controller/mouse, all with a deeply forgiving, customizable level of difficulty that keeps things as fun as they are challenging.With music by the composer behind Celeste's soundtrack, an immense amount of depth and thought put into even the simplest of mechanics, a deeply thoughtful array of options to make the game as user-friendly as possible (ty misophonia filter!!!), Chicory is easily one of the best indie games to come out in recent years, easily and readily comparable to all-time greats like Undertale and Celeste in almost every way. Take the time to play this one, I've no doubt it'll be near the top of all the GOTY lists come December. And if you play it and like it, give the dev's other most recent work, Wandersong, a try as well, it ticks all the same boxes. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: On the instructions it said that this was a coloring book. Instructions were not clear and I got my brush stuck in the sink. The story is nicely narrated and, even if I miss the vocals I enjoyed reading it with all those blubbling sounds the game offers you with every conversation. The game is so much fun to play, it gives color to your grey videogamer life! Pizza is such a nice character and all Pic-nic (the world) is filled with colorful and enjoyable individuals. One thing I really enjoyed was the fact that when you need some help you can call your mom and dad and they give you clues to where to go next! Great music, great art, great game design, nice story and fun gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: This game...  Crap, dude.I don't know how to describe my feelings about it.The characters are fantastic, the premise is wonderful, the world is immersive, the mechanics are fresh and fun, the music is astronomically glorious, the art style is charming and gorgeous, the sound design is spot-on, the pacing is finely tuned, the story is touching and wonderful.  The game hits highs and lows, it knows how to play its cards, it knows what makes a good ending.But Chicory is more than that.  It's truly a masterpiece.  It told me things I didn't know I needed to hear.  It gave me experiences I will continue to hold dear.  It subverted my expectations, but never held that over me.  It made me tear up several times.  Heck, it even brought me out of weeks-long art block with a fun drawing system - enough limitations to stop me from nitpicking every element of my work, enough freedom to make my creations feel mine.But above anything else?Chicory taught me...  About me.It taught me about my friends, my peers, my family.  I feel I am a better, wiser man for playing it.In my eyes, that's what sets a work of art apart.I had very high expectations for this game.  I was worried because I hadn't prepared myself in case it didn't meet them.  I streamed it - if it wasn't what I'd hoped, it would have shown.Well, anyone who watched could tell you - beaming smiles, looks of abject shock, laughs, groans, tears - all of them genuine - marks of this game's tangible impact on me were present from the second I picked up the Brush.I don't want to spoil the game - if you're looking through reviews to decide whether or not to get it, and you've got this far into me waxing lyrical without deciding, I hereby shake you by the shoulders.  GET IT.  Get the game.  It's right after food, water, and shelter on Haywire's hierarchy of needs.  DO IT!  I can guarantee you, if you were interested enough to click on the Steam page, Chicory has something for you.I would call this game the next UNDERTALE...  But, if Chicory taught me anything, it's that that wouldn't be fair.  No, Chicory isn't the next UNDERTALE, it's the first Chicory.  And I hope it gets all the love it deserves....I swear I'm not sponsored.  I'm just some artist, who loves dogs and loves this game.In fact, it's my favourite.Thank you for reading, and may all your Picnics be colourful.
