_childDocuments_.review: Hello,I completely adore this game, and while playing it, it became probably one of my favorite games of all time. While it appears simple on the surface, there is honestly so much to dig into that I don't know if I can talk about it all in a review.The game plays similarly to a top-down Zelda game, where you explore a big world, tackle some dungeon-like zones, defeat the boss at the end and gain a new ability as a result. The painting mechanic is what really sets this game apart, though. You are tasked with coloring in a whole world that has lost its color, using your paint-brush (controlled with your mouse) and stamps, which you will find hidden around the world. I was initially worried that I would tire of this quickly, but I honestly didn't, and by the end I had nearly every screen completely colored in.Equally as colorful as the gameplay, is the story and characters. Everyone in this game is so charming, cute as heck, and full of character. The story is honestly quite dark and serious, and deals a lot with themes of severe depression, feeling impostor syndrome, moral ethics of tradition, and more. One of my favorite aspects of the story has to be how well it marries with the gameplay, too. Initially I think people will feel frustrated with how sortof inaccurate and clumsy the painting can feel. It's nothing like using a drawing tablet. But it fits in perfectly with the fact that the main character is essentially a brand new artist who feels they cant live up to the artistic pressure put upon them. As the game goes on, you feel less afraid to just paint what your heart is telling you and screw it if it doesn't look amazing to others. It's pretty empowering!Special mention has to be given to Lena Raine's (composer for Celeste) soundtrack for the game. It's simply amazing and one of my favorite game osts now, without question.Anyway, I've been wanting to write this review for a long while now and I finally got around to doing it. I love this game and I wish that everyone would buy it.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I think we can all agree that “Zelda, but a coloring book” is a gem of an idea. I don’t mean an actual coloring book, I had that when I was a kid, and I must say I preferred the genuine NES article. No, I mean taking the adventuring, puzzling, and fanciful stylings of Zelda and wrapping them around the ability to paint your surroundings in a game. Chicory pursues this idea with all the light and heart it can muster, giving you not only command of the world’s hues, but also every opportunity to solve puzzles or problems with a stroke of your brush. And if that’s not enough, the story takes on themes more meaningful that I was ever expecting of such an adorable outing.Chicory is the Wielder, the most recent in a long line of artisans who command a magical Brush that can bring color to anything. It’s a big job, maintaining the very appearance of existence, and it becomes dreadfully complicated by a sudden disaster that saps all the colors from the world. You might think that correcting this mishap would fall to Chicory, but it doesn’t! It falls to you, the faithful janitor of the Wielder’s Tower, as you discover the Brush left unattended and set off on a journey of hope and discovery. Along the way, you’ll learn more about the Brush and its many capabilities, meet tons of residents who may help you or require your help in turn, and uncover the source of the strange malaise that has cost the world its colors.I know I mentioned Zelda a lot earlier, but I want to be clear on where the similarities end. Chicory is a top-down adventure game where you travel the world in search of new powers that let you into new areas and so on. Your main method of interacting with the world is the Brush, controlled by either the right stick on your controller or the mouse. With the Brush, you can freely paint any object or surface on your screen, choosing colors from the immediate palette for that region, and laying down strokes in any way you want. Characters will react to your painting, certain objects will change based on their painted state, and as you gain more abilities, you’ll be able to interact with your own paint in new and exciting ways.There’s a lot you can do here, but what you may have noticed I didn’t mention was combat. There’s no fighting in Chicory, no monsters roaming the countryside to dispatch or dungeons to clear of evil. There are… events that occur that I don’t want to spoil, but they provide a welcome and impactful counter to the generally chill and light-hearted exploration that comprises the vast majority of the game. There’s no end of collectibles to find laying about, from garbage to outfits to new Brush styles to use in your work. Side quests abound, ranging from finding lost kittens to taking entire art courses. That last one is particularly illuminating of how detailed this game gets with its immersion, as your teacher and classmates will comment on the exercises you participate in with wonderfully insightful feedback.It’s not just the details that contain such insight, either. What starts out as a quest to save the world from some unknown menace evolves into something far more likely to hit close to home. The themes of this game go into some very personal vulnerabilities, and touch on topics like self-esteem and personal motivation. It can actually get pretty heavy at times, balanced by the charm of the world and the writing but still cutting right to the quick. I wouldn’t warn people away from this one, there’s definitely an overall positive and supportive message to the game, but just be aware that there are very real feels in this one, and they’re not always going to match the adorable atmosphere.Personally I see the depth of Chicory’s message as a huge strength, and it’s just one of many to be found in this wonderful adventure. All of the characters you meet charm with their own distinct voices and engaging writing. Your powers expand far beyond what you might imagine, and enable you to reach some unexpected secrets. And on top of it all, it’s simply a relaxing, pleasant journey. The world of Chicory is serene, beautiful (as much as you make it), and open to all sorts of wanderings and explorations. It’s a fantastic game to just be in, and every part of the design supports that warm, wonderful atmosphere.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a beautiful little game. To mention almost anything about the story would be a spoiler, so let me just say that it has a wonderful story with very well written characters.  It is from the creators of both Wandersong and Celeste and it really shows, especially as it handles genuinely heavy topics in a very positive way. Buyer be warned if you read "Makers of Celeste" and are looking for a white knuckle puzzle platfomer that will test your reaction and gameknowledge, this game barrows much more heavily from Celeste in the themes and story rather than the challenging gameplay. It is not a difficult game, and you shouldn't buy it for that.On the subject of gameplay however, the developers did add the best feature I have ever seen to a metroidvania (if you can call this that) as having every screen start off without color means you can instantly recognize where you have and have not been. Not only did this mean I almost never got lost in the game, but it also rewards the player for doing what the game wants you to do, paint everything.Getting lost and not knowing where to go or where you have and have not explored is the primary reason I give up on some metroidvania style games (the reason I never beat Hollow knight) but not only do they cleverly help the player know where they are going with the paint, it also has a built in hint system in the form of calling your parents and asking for help, which is incredibly sweet.This game took me 10 hours to complete with about 80% completion, I will probably play a little bit more to see the post game. For some people $20 is a bit much for some indie games, but for me, it is absolutely worth the price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Indisputably a game that has struck a chord with me on such a deep, deep level that I never thought possible. It guided me through its storyline gently, allowing me to make my own character, who I named Hot Wings. I went through so much with him, so many ups and downs, so many experiences, so many things to do. It took me 7-8 months to 100% the game because I was taking my time with so much stuff to make it look good. This game strongly encourages creativity and gives you tools to do some rudimentary drawing, but it's enough to allow even me - somebody who didn't feel like he could draw anything to save his life - to feel competent at drawing, for once. And the storyline had me emotionally attached to so many, many of the characters and especially Hot Wings as well. I felt his high moments and his low moments. His joy, and his sadness. When he was energetic, I was energetic. When he was anxious, I was anxious. And after I finished the main storyline, tied up loose ends, and finished off working to that 100% it was only after I was headed to Potluck to let him get a lengthy rest (A la me being finished with the save) that it hit me like a train just how much of an impact this game has had on me for the past 7-8 months. I've always been thinking about Hot Wings, making headcanons for him, imagining scenarios, situations, and all the rest of it. He really feels special to me. The feeling was hugely overwhelming to say the least, about how it felt like the end of an era, something utterly liberating. I was just that emotionally attached to Hot Wings that it was such an overload of emotion to realize that this was finally it. I don't regret a single minute I spent on this game. I relished every last bit of it start to finish, beginning to end, cover to cover. And that will never change. Thank you Hot Wings for existing, and thank you Greg, for such an incredible game. One that was made even better by the small, but dedicated team of Em, Lena, Alexis, and Madeline to help with production of the game. I will never forget this game, and there's clearly a damn good reason that it was my GotY for 2021, without question.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: a Colorful Tale is amazing- I think that it is definitely worth the price. However, before I bought the game I had a few questions about the game that would determine if I would want it, so here are some answers if you have the same questions and are on the fence:-Does coloring get boring after so many screens?   -The coloring was actually really fun! There are three different brush sizes for different precisions, and if you ever want to quickly color something in you can hold down the mouse/painting button to fill in a section. ()-I know the coloring is good on a mouse, but what about a trackpad?   -I thought coloring was still very fun and easy on a trackpad! However, if you don't want to have to hold right-click to erase you can easily change your key binds so you can hold down a key instead. IF you still aren't satisfied with that, you can also connect a controller.-How long is the game?   -The length of Chicory is largely determined on how much you color in the world and how many non-story parts of the game you want to do. Not coloring anything and quickly doing the puzzles, a chapter could take 10 minutes- however, coloring in every screen while going along could take more than an hour. There are about 10 chapters in total, and plenty to do in the postgame. Currently I'm at 22 hours (Steam says 16, its wrong since I accidentally played the game disconnected from Steam) and I still have collectables to find and places I want to color in more.If someone is considering to get the game but still has more questions, post them here and I'll try to answer them!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm happy to report that the moment-to-moment act of painting feels nice. It's easy to do, as you can just tap discrete objects to instantly fill them with color, and you can hold a button down to automatically fill in large spaces. You don't have to worry too much about coloring inside the lines if you want to maintain a clean look with your work. If you make a mistake, you can do the exact same things with the erase button. Each area gives you a different four-color palette, so you're likely to end up with something visually coherent and pleasing even if you don't have any formal knowledge of complementary color schemes.I'm not really a visual arts person, so I didn't get too much use out of the myriad brush customization options I got from doing sidequests. However, I still found it relaxing and satisfying to fully color in screens with the base painting mechanics. There's cleverness to how these painting mechanics translate to actual progression. You have to consider things like what objects to paint, which specific spots to paint, and what to erase. Some light platforming sections also require a bit of timing with using your paintbrush. The puzzles have just the right amount of complexity that I only had to take a beat or two to parse environments and their interactable elements then suss out solutions for most of them. What platforming there is isn't mechanically demanding, and when I made mistakes, I found the level design to be pretty simple and forgiving that I could get back to where I was quickly.I do wish the boss fights were as interesting as the puzzles. While they look cool, with some neat visual and mechanical wrinkles that vary things up, they don't make any use of your abilities. It's all just moving yourself to the right spot to not get hit and clicking on the boss. It can get hectic dodging the escalating attack patterns because you don't have much mobility, but that's the extent of these battles being engaging. There are only two that I remember posing any sort of challenge, one about halfway through and the other being the last boss. There's no hard failure state as well. The default difficulty setting lets you only take two hits, but you just have to restart a phase (i think?) and not the entire battle, so it all felt low-stakes to me.I played on mouse and keyboard, so I can imagine the boss fights would be way harder with a controller and thus feel more involved.The music does so much to elevate these battles. It's unsurprising because the amazing Lena Raine did the soundtrack. Her work on Celeste is maybe my favorite part of that game, and it might be the same for this game.A good mix of electronic and acoustic sounds make up the score, fitting the different vibes of each area and story moment. There's the relaxing gentle strings in the Town of Luncheon, the dark head-bopping synthwave dance beats of Probably Ancient Evil, the beautiful melancholy piano of Simmer Springs, and the bouncy easy listening sax of Dinners, the Big City to highlight a handful. Together with a ton more memorable tracks, this OST helps bring to life a whimsical adventure that delves into some ~real ♥♥♥♥~.Most of the whimsy comes from the optional activities and NPC conversations. The tone can be a tad twee, but there's enough personality and variety in the surprisingly big cast that I  ultimately found doing sidequests and talking to npcs to be a warm respite to the more serious subject matter of the A plot. The overarching narrative tackles themes of self-doubt, creative burnout, and the burdens of tradition. It does so with the right balance of authenticity and empathy, not being afraid of expressing the thoughts and emotions we all have when our self-esteem is at its lowest, while offering sincere affirmations of support. So even within the heroic fantasy wrappings, the two main characters have believable arcs. Granted, that heroic fantasy layer along with where I'm at in terms of personal growth and acceptance kept the story from deeply resonating with me. The more intriguing point the game tries to make is selling the idea that everyone has a creative spark. I don't quite buy it from the in-fiction storytelling. It rejects the Chosen One trope through the explicit writing aspects, but you're still the only person in the world that gets anything done, and everybody praises you constantly, even if you half-ass tasks. It gestures at this concept at the very end, but by then the game is already over, so it's not actually developed.Where it does succeed in this goal is, more importantly, through player interaction. There's no extrinsic reward to coloring everything on a screen, but I did so for about 80% of the map. There's no grading system for achieving an aesthetic, but I still took the time and effort to color spaces in a way that made sense to my untrained eyes. Sure, the looks I went for were basic as hell, but the fact that I ended up caring at all while having no aspirations to paint without the game straining to make that happen made me believe in its core argument: you don't have to be an ~artist~ to express creativity. While I won't be proudly sharing screenshots or gifs of my "artistic" attempts at coloring in the world, I found calming contentment in bringing back color to the charming world of Chicory over the 13 and a half hours I spent with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a powerful game with its playful mechanics. It seems really cheerful, but brings a lot on depression, self-hate, and anxiety. I love the content warning the game includes tbh, I wish other games would include warnings on sensitive tops. The only issue I have is the boss fights, I cannot imagine what it is like on mouse/keyboard if I already have a hard time on controller. Thankfully you cannot die in the game but it just kind of sucks still....The game so far is really good. It makes you reflect on your actions and thoughts based on mental health in the past and I do not think that isn't necessary a bad thing. I do recommend the game to anyone who wants to understand a bit more about mental health and how it can affect those around you and yourself. It is a really cute game with a powerful message.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A heartfelt tale of anxiety, depression, and the journey to self-acceptance. The characters are charming, and the hand-drawn art neatly comes to life by your illustration; Chicory portrays the artist's struggle in a unique way, letting you take the brush and paint the world as you see fit. Lena Raine's scoring is the perfect companion, splashing playfully around the scene and at other times drawing you further into the darkness and through to the other side.The story and exploration are the key drivers of this game. There are lite combat elements, but a convenient difficulty slider allows you to adjust those to your taste. I recommend playing this with a friend or partner - 2p mode allows painting simultaneously (though you may debate about which brushes and colours to use!).
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is an amazing game and I'm so glad I bought it on a whim. It's now one of my favourite games.At first, I was honestly a bit worried about the gameplay and what the point of the game would be, but I wasn't disappointed. Plus, the soundtrack is wonderful, as I would expect from Lena Raine . The dialogues truly hit close to home at times and the characters are diverse, charming and relatable. I loved everything about it.I'm going to miss playing Chicory, but it left a mark in me forever.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Don't feel like you need to be "creative" or "good at art" to play this game. That isn't what it's about anyways. A touching and wholesome experience that explores what it means to be creative, and to live up to expectations. Even if you've never so much as picked up a pencil, there's probably still something here for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I personally LOVED this game.  It's beautifully executed, wonderfully thought through and just so so good.  I'm likely going to go back through and try and get everything (I was SO CLOSE - 95%+) and take my time even more.I highly recommend slowly going through and being mindful throughout this game.  It's well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: To say that this game is an underrated masterpiece is to say nothing. It had taught me a lot of lessons about life which I had to think over a lot, it teaches about mentorship, it teaches about self-esteem, it teaches a lot about understanding other's pain. It may sound a little overused now days in games to talk about morale, but I really, really loved how it was done. And I really want more of it. I absolutely loved this game from the beginning to the end and I want more of it. Thank you so much Unlimited Wishes for gifting a game that changed my life completely.10/10On a side note I do have to say, while it's up to personal preference. I do think, it is better to focus on the story of the game, because the side quests can take up A LOT of time and causes to break the immersion a bit. But it's up to personal preference, still the game can be fun if you're a 100% completionist.-----------Bellow is review before I finished the game-----------I haven't finished the game yet, but it is an absolute masterpiece already. I am not a big fan of RPG games, but this is completely something else. It's story, it's music, it's gameplay. All of it is mixed just perfectly. It takes dedication to get into the game, it might not be for people who prefer it being more fast paced, but I do really think it's an experience absolutely worth getting through and to most people it will be a treat.9.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is about being a lovable pupper, using their magic brush to solve puzzles, help lovable characters or just make a mess of the place. Go on, the game won't judge.It is also an examination of what makes an artist, impostor syndrome, personal versus institutionalised art, burnout and depression. And even when dealing with those heavy subjects, the game handled them masterfully and never failed to bring a smile to my face.One of my absolute favourites and an easy recommend to anyone looking for a charming and chill experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a wonderful experience from start to finish. The music by Lena Raine is amazing, from the lovely overworld backing tracks to the intense boss fights. The story overall is quite compelling, and if you've ever felt doubt about yourself and where you want to be at any stage in your life this game will really resonate with you. I would highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is a very relaxing and engaging story to play through. The puzzles are fun, the mechanics such as the phone booth are great, and every single character has a unique and wonderful personality. Highly recommend this game, it is perfect to pick up and play for a couple of hours and be immersed in a beautiful world. The music and art are both incredible too!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A sweet game that's a lot deeper than the surface description of it.While it is literally about "A Dog and their Magic Paintbrush", it runs much deeper, touching on topics of self-worth, depression, and mental health.Also the fact that you can make gifs of your paintings is just, super cool.You even get one after you beat the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I've tried to write a description for this game about 5 times. It's impossible. Be ready for this game to reach into your heart and make its home there. I would absolutely recommend this to everyone I know and probably a lot of people I don't. If you do pick this up, STICK WITH IT. It's worth seeing through, to the end and past it, 100%.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really pretty game, because it was very light-hearted initially but I had no clue how deep the game's lore would've gotten into. With that said I definitely liked how the option for content/trigger warnings were present in the game when things got tough (and I believe the option to skip boss fights too?). And even to the extent of the other characters you met who felt almost relatable in some sense.I'm no artist in real life so I was terrible at colourising the world, but knowing how the puzzles worked and how certain obstacles interacted with your paint was a nice take. I definitely enjoyed the soundtrack as well which actually had me check out this game. And again, got more than I expected out of this journey.I haven't completed it entirely, but one thing I didn't realise until later on was basically quick travelling around the world because it was so huge; I found myself expecting a particular means to get around and didn't know how to do so past the teleport option (which I used later into the game because the rest was manageable). Getting around otherwise via walking if you were unaware like I was of how to find the travelling mechanic was a little tedious though, but that might've been something I should've kept an eye on at the time.It's definitely a nice wind-down game that touches into real issues, and the game does give you the appropriate heads up when it appears throughout. Give it a shot. And that soundtrack is definitely on my favourites as well that leans on the majorly acoustic but also other genre side of things ^-^
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. The concept, the gameplay, art, OST, story, characters... everything is beautiful. Even not being artsy yourself you'll certainly end up spending more time than you'd expect coloring entire screens, or stop and actively listening to the music, just because it's pretty!The message it conveys are cheerful and relatable.Accessibility wise Chicory is a masterclass: so many studios should take it as an example. There is no place for gameplay frustration!Be warned though - the game is slowpaced. It might not be a game you'll rush over an entire weekend, but taking it slow is delightful. I played it every morning until finished and it was an uplifting experience!Thanks for this gem <3
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I could talk about how it's beautifully charming, well-written and relatable, with enough gameplay depth to keep it consistently engaging over its 10-14 hour runtime, or how seamlessly all the painting mechanics integrate into the natural flow of gameplay, or how it's basically just Okami but 2D (and you're not a god... maybe...) but all I really need to say is.I want to give Chicory a hug.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I HIGHLY recommend this game! It's an adorable art style, music that is both chill and upbeat, very relaxed game play... I love the inclusion of co-op mode if you want to play with a friend! I can picture playing this at the end of the day when you need to just zone out and get the anxiety to calm down. _childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is a phenomenal game full of surprises and touching moments. It allows you to peer into the soul of an artist and experience both the joy and pressure that comes with creating. The core paint mechanic is varied and there are plenty of secrets to uncover using your various brush skills. There are many character interactions that induce smiles and a KILLER soundtrack by Lena Raine adds appropriate emotional magnitude to every scene. It took me about 20 hours to 100% complete, and I loved every minute of it. Thank you to Greg and his team for helping me better understand what it means to be an artist.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I walked in blind, after seeing the trailer at Summer Games Fest(?), and I thought it was going to be a simple small adventure with the gimmick of painting the background.My S.O and I played through up to the end of 2nd Chapter, and I think it's just such a wonderful game, that I wanted to recommend this. Definitely a must play this season, hook up a controller and enjoy it on remote play!Gameplay:The Gameplay is Legend of Zelda top-down kinda RPG, with the usage of the paintbrush and paint mechanic ingeniously implemented throughout the time I've explored so far. I was complaining to my S.O that there wasn't a map system, and voila they give it to you early Chapter 2.VERY simple controls, but very intuitive and wonderfully built. Soundtrack:Okay, I didn't buy the OST+Game bundle, and that was a small regret.GET IT.Lena Raine's work on this sound track is something to behold, and if I ever met them, I just want to shake their hand and truly from the bottom of my heart for such beauty. They captured the nuances of each town, and the vibe you'll get from that area or event.Overall: 10/10Give this game a shot, zero regrets giving it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory is basically an artistic metroidvania. I can't get over how amazingly well-crafted this world is, how much I adore the characters that I meet in this world. It's adorable and every corner I turn I felt excited to see what I was gonna discover. It also is naturally an art game, and every screen is a canvas to paint to your heart's content. The world painting was also really neatly tied into some of the puzzles.Chicory's story deals with topics that anyone who has ever created something is very familiar with. I think the game did such an amazing portrayal of the fear we all feel when we create and know we can be judged, the self-doubts we get, never feeling good enough, just wanting to be wanted. Creation requires you to make yourself vulnerable. It was such a heartfelt tale that I wish I could erase from memory just to experience it all over again cause it's so wonderful.I liked how most screens had some small navigation puzzle integrated into it, using the environmental mechanics to get to hard to reach places, finding optional side-tracks to get some collectibles, it encourages you to keep exploring and revisiting old areas after you've gained new abilities to move around. There were a few screens that had some frustrating puzzles, mostly due to getting stuck on some red herrings, but overall, they could not stop me from enjoying the game.I can't recommend this game enough. It's such a good game!

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a wonderful game. _childDocuments_.review: Chicory will charm your pants and skirts off. Not only that, its story, action, music, and puzzles will also entertain and make you feel warm and fuzzy inside. _childDocuments_.review: You know that one scene in Ratatouille where Anton Ego drops his pen because of how amazing and nostalgic his meal was? That's what this game feels like to me. I haven't had a greater pleasure in playing a game even with all the really good ones that came out through the past few years. This game is so special to me, I don't think I can really state how much I love this game. There's hardly anything that I could critique, and even the minor hiccups are nick-picks compared to the whole picture. It's message, it's themes, it's characters and soundtrack - they will all stick with me for a very long time. When I do art, this game I will heartily say has helped me find my ground and come to terms that it might not always be perfect, but that's okay and doing what's possible to the self is enough. Anyone can be an artist if they're willing to create.I could go on, but... I can just say this; Play this game. I will never not recommend this game. If Steam had more than a "Yes", I would give it the highest rating I possibly could.To Greg Lobanox and gang - thank you. Your game changed my life for the better.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a HUGE fan of Wandersong, so I was super excited when I found out the same devs were making a new game! And boy, it did NOT disappoint! I just finished 100%ing the game and I had an amazing time.The story was really sweet and engaging, and it really resonates, especially if you're an artist/creative type. The gameplay mechanics are really fun, it felt like one big coloring book! The experience of playing this game was just super relaxing. The characters are all ADORABLE and I found myself becoming emotionally attached to like 90% of them. This game also has really good LGBT+ representation, and it fits in well with the game and doesn't feel forced/performative! There are a ton of collectibles, which was great for a completionist like me, and it never felt too tedious. Also, the soundtrack is BRILLIANT, including the sound effects. Playing this game was like one big ASMR session! I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin with this review.  First off, the game is just fun; painting the various environments; talking up the towns folk; exploring every nook and cranny for various clothes, hats, etc. and doodling your own artwork.  The game is just fun to play.  Chicory: A colorful tale is also chill to play.  One can go at their own pace and enjoy the surroundings while tacking the story which, by the way, is great.  The characters feel relatable too.  The main two characters, especially, were fun to spend time with.  Throughout the story they both must battle with feeling unworthy of what they became/ become.  It's a feeling, I think, we all feel at least some point in our life.  Also, a note regarding the game's "bosses;" I fond them super fun with great music and no stress.  They were epic (to me), but it felt nice knowing it wasn't required to get gud in order to beat them.  And really if the bosses were like that, the game wouldn't be chill any more and that would defeat the style of the game now, wouldn't it.  All-in-all Chicory: A colorful tale is a great game with a wonderful message and sometimes that's all you need.  A+ to you, Chicory: A colorful Tale.  I feel like a better human after playing you.  Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: Wandersong is one of my favorite games ever. It felt perfectly tailored to who I am as a person and I still think about the impact it had on me, my confidence, and my self-esteem. As soon as I found out Greg Lobanov was making another game, even when it was just one GIF from a prototype called Project Drawdog, I was instantly sold. I regret not backing the Kickstarter, but I was so excited when launch day finally came. Chicory is now one of my favorite games ever. You can see so much of the heart of Wandersong in it, but it's still something completely new and different. Between the innovative gameplay, the charming world of Picnic, the absolutely stunning soundtrack from Lena Raine, and the challenging moments of introspection you're encouraged to engage with, I wouldn't change a single thing. I keep trying to find the right words for my feelings now that I've finished the main story, but there are none. It sincerely moved me that much.This is not just a Game of the Year contender. It's an Indie Game of a Lifetime.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is long. TL:DR; PLEASE play this game if you are an experienced or aspiring artist/author/creator, or anywhere in-between. This game boasts a gorgeous soundtrack, funny and engaging dialogue/characters, LGBTQ+ rep (HELL yes), tons of optional stuff besides the main story (which is maaaybe ~4-6 hours?) like item hunting and sidequests - besides, you know, just coloring everything. Controls are incredibly responsive and the game itself is somewhere around an average difficulty mechanic-wise; it's like Undertale, but with the only combat being the handful of boss battles that are scaled down a bit compared to the intensity UT's have. Please please please get this game. It is so good.Chicory: A Colorful Tale, or: how a video game helped me cope with the loss of my dog---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Okay. I know that sounds a little bit sad but hear me out.I've never experienced close, personal loss before. Of course, I knew it would happen eventually and with that hindsight, I cried about the reality that one day, my best friend would be gone. I cried years before it actually happened, and I cried the minutes leading up to it. She was 14 when we put her down three weeks ago. I was with her her whole life, and I never wanted to imagine life without her. It just felt wrong picturing it, and so I avoided it in the months and days leading up to the inevitable.I'm emotional. I've got depression & ADHD, and while I have and take meds for them, it still comes with huge highs and huge lows. I can't describe what I felt in the hours after I lost her, my best friend, the only one of my family who never ever made me feel like I wasn't good enough. I don't think I'll ever be able to explain it.I found this game a while afterwards. I've been drawing (with the goal of improving) for about 6 years now give or take, and writing for way longer. Recently, with my job cutting into my free time, I've felt as if I can't draw anymore, or at least I don't have as much of a drive to anymore. And I think a lot of that is because of my perfectionism, of how I want everything to look great and when it ends up not being to my standards I get frustrated. While I played this game and saw a lot of myself reflected in Chicory, I just... I don't know. The more I played the more I let myself go, the more I let myself make mistakes and just scribble instead of making everything look nice.I went from wanting every piece of the scenery and setpiece to have rhyme and rhythm to just doing whatever I felt like in the moment. It was magical - freeing, relaxing, and I don't think I've ever enjoyed a game as much as this one in a long time. 8 hours doesn't seem like a lot to some people, and I don't have every achievement (.......yet lol), but I seriously am confident when I say that this is one of my favorite gaming experiences thus far. It just.. connected with me. In a lot of ways. And reminded me, subconsciously, that it's okay to mess up. It's normal. And it's okay to grieve; to be sad, and accept that I can't improve without trying in the first place.I made the connection between my character (who I named Pizza :] ) and my dog very fast. Their ears were the most notable similarity for me and I eventually colored Pizza to resemble her. The more I played the more I slowly came to terms with what happened, and I don't know if it's because I saw my dog in Pizza or not but I can definitely say it probably helped. That along with the fact that this game just touches on a lot of the problems I face with the whole creation process, it just... It really made me take a step back and realize a lot of stuff. There's a sidequest where you help someone plant a garden for a loved one they recently lost, and I'll admit I cried there, but after completing it I felt calm. Seeing the NPC content and smiling made me do the same (granted... one of us was definitely still not done crying lol).I love games like this. I adore it when you get to color an entire level, map, or area, with whatever colors you're given and can just go ham. De Blob 2 has been a staple "sit back and chill" game for me for the past decade and I can see this one becoming another game to turn to - for a lot of reasons besides the relaxing nature of painting in things. The soundtrack is incredible and really fits well with each area, and invites the opportunity to just let loose and color.This game has everything I enjoy in video games; collectables, sidequests that are funny/simple and sweet, good writing & characters, representation, good music, literally everything about this game is perfect. There are genuinely no complaints from me. Nothing about this game was frustrating or extremely tricky to figure out, every puzzle was simple and I had a lot of "aha!" moments that made me feel good. There's no pressure to do everything in one playthrough; there's a post-game that lets you do free roam the map and finish 100%ing the game. The boss battles (something I was not expecting but were awesome!!!!) weren't too challenging and the music in each of them have no right to go as hard as they do. The art style of the game is simple and it works very well with the gameplay.Without getting into spoilers, I don't know how else I can say I love this game. I guess, just... I'm really grateful I found it. I don't know where I'd be right now without it, but I'd guess I'd probably be a lot like Chicory at the start of the game: curled up underneath my bed's covers and not wanting to do anything. This game (particularly the ending) showed me it's okay for loss to happen, because eventually you'll heal. It's okay to not be perfect or to make something you're not happy with, because you made something that is uniquely yours, and that's something to be freaking proud of.10/10 i will replay this game a ton (and buy it on my switch if it ever releases there wink wink)
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Worth every penny at full price, Chicory is a fun, whimsical experience with a unique spin on the classic top-down RPG/Adventure gaming style. The drawing mechanic is great fun, and being able to see the direct impact I was having on the game's environments had me addicted to giving each area it's own different color scheme. The way it is incorporated into the main character's abilities is executed well. Anyone who has played and enjoyed top-downs before will know what to expect high-level in regards to how the game's world unfolds, and should be delighted to hear that there are a ton of secrets to find along the way. The level of challenge is flexible with the accessibility settings in the Options menu. Boss battles are not designed for the masochistic gamer, but each is unique in their own way and can get somewhat tough if you elect to leave said settings to their default.The game's visual style is very chill, much like a coloring book coming to life. This creates an interesting (in a good way) concoction when adding in the game's story. The story explores a range of themes that interconnect well in it's arch. Friendship, family, self-doubt, impostor syndrome, selflessness, depression and many more are balanced by a good sense of humor and treated in a way that feels very true to life. The writing for the many characters is great overall, each having their own unique personality that allows them stand out even before coloring them in.The sound design and music is spot-on, with many of the games effects adding to the unique feel of the game. Likewise, the soundtrack is great! Many of the game's tracks will certainly be added to my playlist to enjoy on their own.For reals, play Chicory. Good soup!
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I love a lot of things, but very few games (or I guess, medias in general) have made me feel the way this one has. Not exactly sure how to put it into words but my closest approximation: feels like meeting up with an dear friend you haven't seen for years. It's cozy, and meaningful, and honestly? There for you. I knew the game was good but every time I thought it couldn't get better, it did. Usually games that I find I like in style, or story, or just generally the *idea* of end up lacking something in game play. But Chicory really doesn't have any weak points in my opinion, ALL of it is good! It also has a surprising amount of things to say. Really didn't expect some of the commentary it made (but its all the better for it! Very, very well written and really hit home for me as an artist)I don't normally write reviews, but I want this game to do well so I thought I'd try to help in my own way. The amount of love and care put into this game really shows, please try it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: + Wonderfully creative "metroidvania" game.+ At first I was annoyed that I only had access to 4 colors per screen, but then slowed down and started to think about color placement more and more. Does the grass really need to be green, trunks of trees brown, water blue? Yeah, make blue-ish leaves and orange trunks and yellow dirt. Your choices start to look good and make sense as a whole.+ It's about tearing down power structures and how holding on to the past affects our mental health and society.+ Calming and cute.+ Utopia where workers own the means of production.- There's really nothing negative I could say about the game play or story, but graphical options and higher fidelity like anti-aliasing would have been nice. Maybe some more interactive details to the environment like adding gently swaying trees and grass would have added a lot to the environments.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is a lovely little heavily narrative-based puzzle metroidvania game where you color in the world to navigate the environment.You play as Pizza, the Brush Wielder’s janitor. One day, all the color in the world goes away, and strange black trees show up in the nearby forest. With the wielder, Chicory, apparently out of commission, it is up to Pizza to go save the day.The Brush gives you the ability to paint in the coloring-book like world, allowing you to fill in between the lines with colors, and paint the world. This is used to solve various puzzles, from illuminating the environment to allowing you to move through gaps to activate various things in the environment to achieve some end.In terms of core gameplay, the game is fairly simplistic; you start out with nothing special in terms of powers beyond the coloring, but over the course of the first half of the game gain more abilities – almost all movement based – allowing you to jump, to dive through your paint (allowing passage through small gaps), to climb certain walls, and to swim. There is almost no combat to speak of; there aren’t “normal” enemies around in the world, only bosses at the end of a few dungeons, the source of the “corruption” in the world. As such, the vast majority of the game is a series of navigational puzzles, using your paint to activate things in the environment, move around things that allow you to destroy other things, climb up walls and then jump, toggle switches, etc.This is pretty easy, but works well enough; it doesn’t feel overly time consuming to solve these puzzles, and in terms of quality they’re not too bad.There are basically six “dungeons” in the game with bosses at the end of them, plus three other dungeons that have no boss, and one boss without any real dungeon; these dungeons are a series of puzzle with a boss at the end, though a significant portion of most of them take place on the surface. Overall the game is not, in terms of gameplay, all that long – likely only about 8 hours or so.But you are likely to spend much, much longer on it.In addition to the core puzzles, you can also paint the world to make it look beautiful, and are indeed encouraged to do so. The game will even save a record of your world map to show you at the end to show your progress in coloring it in.There are a huge number of collectibles to find – mostly for cosmetic items, though there are also some “brush styles”, which mostly just make stamps but a few of which are things like the fill tool, which are actively useful for gameplay – as well as various sidequests for charters, mostly fetch quests and fedex quests.On top of all that, there are actual painting minigames, where you are given a blank easel and are told to paint something. There’s close to two dozen of these – and not only do all of these show up in the world afterwards, but a few of them have emotional plot significance, as you paint for someone you care about. This added a lot of time to my playthrough, as it can take a while to create these with the crude tools you’re given; this makes sense, however, as Pizza’s lousy paintings perfectly work for someone who isn’t a real artist but who wants to live up to the great artists of yore who wielded the Brush.This segues into the other main attraction of this game – the story.This game has a very cute aesthetic and cute characters. The characters generally cheer each other on in a cute sort of way, or put each other down in a sort of cute sort of way.But there’s a deeper level to this, and the game ends up playing around in the darker spaces of depression and imposter syndrome as the game goes on – and overcoming these issues.The characters are, on the whole, very supportive of the protagonist, but also want the wielder to help them – and unlike most games, the game actually deconstructs the consequences of this, with the previous wielder of the Brush – the titular Chicory – becoming miserable under the pressure of doing everyone’s sidequests for them all the time and not having a moment for herself, to be herself, because anytime she took time for herself she was letting everyone else down.The game basically can be split into two halves – in the first half of the game, Pizza is on their own, going around and fixing the corruption that plagues the world, while Chicory is alone and miserable in her tower. This serves as an introduction to the world and its locations and NPCs, and over the course of this, you end up meeting a bunch of people.However, it is also very low impact; these people play little role in the plot, and only a few of them actually end up mattering all that much outside of a very small section of the plot. As a result, your relationship with these people is very ephemeral – while you briefly interact with them, you don’t really build a relationship with them in any way, and so you don’t really care much. This makes the first half of the game feel kind of weak – while there is an underlying plot, the fact that no one other than Pizza is really seeing it through means it is harder to care.But at the midpoint of the game, things change; events transpire that result in Chicory going around with Pizza for the rest of the game, and so for the last four major areas of the game, plus the final boss, you have a companion with you. This changes things massively, because the game is very much about Pizza’s relationship with Chicory and their relationship with the world at large, and the pressures Chicory was under that Pizza has inherited.This makes the game so much better, and Chicory – who was already the most developed NPC – becomes someone that the player cares about, and wants to see succeed and be happy, reflecting Pizza’s own desires. The player’s perceptions of Chicory evolve with Pizza’s own, and by the end, the relationship between the two is very satisfying, and has moved from idol and janitor to master and student to finally one of friendship and mutual trust and admiration. You do things with Chicory and for Chicory, and she does things for Pizza.This gives the whole second half of the game much more emotional gravitas and makes the harder hitting themes hit home. The second half of the game also isn’t as cutesy, but it doesn’t forget to be cute, and the relationship that grows between Pizza and Chicory has very serious aspects and very cute ones.All in all, by the end of the game, you are pumped and primed to solve the world’s problems – and to make Chicory and Pizza’s lives better in the process. One of the biggest flaws with “save the world” plots is that they often feel impersonal, but because of Chicory’s personal investment in the situation at hand, it becomes much more meaningful and important due to that human connection.There was a moment during the final boss fight that made me laugh with glee, and while I won’t spoil it, it is something that I feel a lot of games really want to do, but which few game manage to earn the emotional investment necessary to pull off. Chicory and Pizza earn their happy ending (though, alas, they do not kiss. Yet, anyway).If the entire game was as good as the second half of the game was, this would be one of the best games of all time.But, alas, it is not.In the end, this is a game that I’d recommend, but it is not without its flaws. In particular, the first half of the game is not as good as the second half, and the game has a bunch of quite time-consuming sidequests that are very much a mixed bag, particularly doing a bunch of painting side-quests that felt increasingly time consuming and repetitive.But the aesthetic is great, the second half of the game is great, and the relationship that Pizza builds with Chicory over the course of the game is one of the best in gaming. By the end, you really WANT to see things get better for them, and you genuinely care about them as people – something very, very few games pull off.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the weaker games that Greg Lobanov and his team have made but I still had a fun time.The storyline is pretty good but I just wasn't motivated to get all the extra stuff like the litter and children meaning that after beating the game there really wasn't much more for me to do.But if you're into good stories and open worlds filled with collectibles, then this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Chicory: A Colorful Tale is a game bursting with charm. The game asks a simple question: what if the player could color the game world? This single question drives the narrative, the puzzles, mechanics, and the world leading to a game that feels shaped by you the player. Chicory is a game probably best described as a metroidvania. While there isn't really any platforming, you progressively unlock abilities that allow you to solve puzzles in the world and allow for deeper exploration as you traverse new areas and double back through old ones. While the story maybe isn't totally new territory, it was gripping and moving as each of the main characters come to terms with growth and how that growth affects you, the other characters, and the game world. There are some combat sections but these occur on major story beats and used to move the plot forward, revealing new information on the world, characters, and The Brush instead of as a way to challenge the player as the combat lacks any meaningful consequences. And this works as the main focus of the game isn't combat but The Brush. The Brush is how the player interacts with the game world. It allows you to color the world and those colors solve puzzles and routes to traverse the world. The Brush is also the focal point of the narrative: every choice a character has made has been a direct result of it. All in all, Chicory: A Colorful Tale is the best game I've played this year and is one of the best games I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful game emotionally and otherwise, which is something I'd normally hesitate to label ANYTHING as but beautiful is something I think this game truly is. The gameplay is simple but solid, coloring is extremely fun and gives you the full freedom to do what you want, the music is absolutely incredible and supports the characters and story magnificently. Overall this game left a profound sense of warmth and meaning with me and while I know my experience is not indicitive of what everyone will get from it I urge you to try this game if you enjoy emotional games. But again my experience is my own, especially because I always take the stuff from things like this to heart which I know many people hesitate to do.Still, I truly think that you should give this game a try and I hope you enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game I'd recommend to anyone, but especially those who are interested in or are a part of any creative hobby or community. This game gets you, and leads you through a creative journey in a supportive and highly engaging way.I'm in the middle of two playthroughs with different friends, I love the co-op and solo equally, I just want to share this game with everyone I know. My friend and I were marvelling at the sound design and soundtrack. We agreed that the sound of characters speaking is just right, not too loud and jarring as some games can be. The music is hard not to hum along to, so many great tunes!If you're looking for a game to practice reading a language in, I highly recommend this one. The text scrolls at proper speeds, and doesn't impatiently continue if you take too long. The only drawback is that this game has only one save file. There's a workaround, thankfully, and while I understand that it's difficult for the programmers to implement (as said in the forums, not my assumption), it's a little bit nerve-wracking to copy files and change names, hoping that nothing will be lost. I just like this game a lot and happen to be playing multiple versions with friends, and I don't want to spoil the story for one of the other.I also own it on the Switch, playing between versions is seamless, and just as rewarding. All in all, 9.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Chicory: A Colorful Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Something terrible happened. Chicory, superstar artist and wielder of the Brush, is missing, and all the color in the land vanished with her. It's up to you, Chicory's number one fan, to pick up the Brush and fill in for her. It's a big job but you're ready for it! Probably! Chicory: A Colorful Tale is a top-down adventure game in a coloring book world where you can draw on anything. Use your painting powers to explore new places, solve puzzles, help your friends, and change the world!

name: Curse of the Dead Gods
detailed_description: LATEST UPDATE The 'Curse of the Dead Cells' Update has been added to the game on April 2021. Major new features include: Dead Cells-themed content New Curse - The Curse of the Headless lets you kill faster with a visual twist 3 New Weapons - Sword of Conjunctivius (based on the Cursed Sword of Dead Cells ) - Crossbow of the Condemned (based on the Explosive Crossbow of Dead Cells ) - Broadsword of the Knight (based on the Broadsword of Dead Cells ) New Challenge Room - Complete the new Cursed Chest challenge to earn rare items Other new features - A new two-handed fighting style: Bombs! - New Curse - New relics and relics icons! - Assist mode - More room variations Check out all the new content in our Curse of the Dead Cells Update patch notes. About the Game You seek untold riches, eternal life, divine powers - it leads to this accursed temple, a seemingly-infinite labyrinth of bottomless pits, deadly traps, and monsters. Collect mystical Relics and an arsenal of weapons to make yourself unstoppable. Battle through hordes of enemies in dark, cavernous passages filled with traps and secrets of all sorts - fire-spewing statues, explosives, hidden spikes, and worse. Corruption builds in you with every step - encourage or ignore it, but each powerful curse can be a double-edged sword. Your greed will lead you to death, but that is not an escape. Rise to fight again. Delve deeper again. Defy the malignant deities that linger in this place. MAIN FEATURES A skill-based roguelike exploring a cruel, dark temple made of endless rooms and corridors Swords, spears, bows, guns - wield these and many more Light and fire will be your best allies to overcome the threats that lie in the shadows Unique curses influence each attempt, putting a twist on every action Dozens of enemies, with powerful champions and deadly bosses to face off against Don’t hesitate to join our official Passtech Games Discord server to share your experience with the Curse of the Dead Gods community!

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeon delving with the risk/reward choices of curses for power.Play as a Darkest Dungeon mod character going forth to have his own game with Aztecs and Devil Bringers. Loot for power, fame and glory through the OSHA violating public bank of the Aztecs.It may be early access at the point of writing this but has a solid foundation for some fun for its current price.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best rogue like out there. It requires some time to master but is highly satisfying once everything comes together : the skills, the build and the curses! Some weapons / trinket / curses combinations will carry you hard if you pay a bit of attention. I find it very polished and the animations are pretty smooth. I did not find the progression too long - many upgrades are actually additional options for your runs. I did the final dungeon without fille unlocking half of them. A must buy for action rogue likes enjoyers imho!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The main suggestion I would make for this game is it should have some kind of unlockable cosmetic items. The current runes that you can unlock with skulls could have a cosmetic component to them eg: hat graphic, cloak graphic, wings etc. This gives a build a visual element which allows players to have a little more customization with their character's look.Overall, good game for being early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Based on the current gameplay and style in the game, I'd highly recommend giving it a go! There's already quite a wide variation of curses, weapons, buffs, playstyles and relics available to choose on your run, adapting as you go with what curses you're given (and you WILL get them, no avoiding!). Combat feels like it has good weight to it, and the risk/reward gameplay of the greed kills (short-time combo kill system) add that extra element to balancing your stamina, combos and dodges. If more content is consistently added by the developers, adding more ways to play than already exist, it has true promise to become a great rogue-like dungeon crawler! Plus, the aesthetic and the sound design are very fun, somewhat similar in style to Darkest Dungeon!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun take on the rogue-like dungeon genre. The art aesthetics are reminiscent of early adventure serializations with a modern update. The attacks have weight to them which allows for interesting combinations to the typical dodge or parry play of other games. And it will beat you up. Avoid the level 5 curse at all costs.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: You liked Darkest Dungeon? Play this game.You liked Hades? Play this game.Really nice mechanics, great garphic, good sound, well balanced difficulty.The only issue I found is a lack of any story: nothing special, but even few hints about your character, his reasons being here, maybe as a notes colletected during the play, it would be enough and would add a depths to the game.In the end I really recommend playing it: good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent combat mechanics, though it's such a demanding game that I find I can only play in short bursts.  It's not a game I play for many hours in a single sitting.If your favorite thing about Hades was the way the story was integrated with the game, you will be disappointed, but otherwise Curse of the Dead Gods delivers the goods.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: A very punishing roguelike game that keeps me locked on the screen playing. I like the concept and the way one has to ponder every choice while pursued by the corruption. Gameplay is nice; atmosphere too. It lacks on some aspects: no secret rooms (as far as i know after 10+hrs); variety of weapons and rooms; a story, or lore at least; NPCs for quests. As of now it is a lovable game that needs to be improved and expanded. Keep going, and good work.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: It's not Hades, don't expect Hades. There's no story. Reminds me of a good 'ole fashioned SNES type "win because you want to". The combat is tight, rewarding, and occasionally infuriating. You must learn to parry.Well worth five or ten bucks, you can bang out a run here and there for 20-30 minutes of Good Times.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks fun and mechanics are fun ,but it is too difficult. Your power is not improving after the first few runs . After that you are stuk playing the same thing and it is just not intersting. The runs are the same and I don't find any difference between the weapons. I don't find anything in a run to make it easyer only harder. No risk reward system ,no case I am so happy that I found this weapon or item everything is bland and uninspired.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a game! Caught me by complete surprise - the art style is fantastic and incredibly well optimised, running at a lovely 250fps on a vega 56. The gameplay is just absolutely brilliant - the combat is fantastic and I love being able to choose my path throughout the dungeons. Love the mechanics added to the game as well.It's just fantastic and well worth the money
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, this is Early Access in its very true form: there is next to no variety which is crucial for Roguelike, troubles with balance: if you get a hammer as a weapon you literally have no need to use anything else ever, it stuns, it deals tons of damage and as far as I know it can also roll with Stamina-on-kill perk which deletes the only flaw this weapon has - stamina consumption on attack, and even further trivialises the gameplay, making it even more of a cakewalk. Plus it has absolutely pathetic amount of content: in 80 minutes I've already seen everything this game has to offer. Sure, devs will make more content and make it better overall as time goes on.But as it stands right now, Curse of the Dead Gods is not worth your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game. the light /dark mechanic is fresh to me. perfect dodge/ parry action feels really good when excecuted. my only complaint is that the weapons are not balanced. to me, the sacrifying knife (the one +3% base damage per point of Perception attribute) takes all the glory and no other weapon can compete with it. Over all good experience. recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: We played this game with three persons, always rotating after each run. It was not only fun to play, but also fun to watch and comment and laugh about the other guys mistakes (only to make the same mistakes in your own run). I really liked this kinda "Couch-Co-Op".The game itself is very nice for the first few hours, but gets very repetitive. At some point you have numerous of skulls and don't know what to do with them. And you don't get any stronger after each run. What this game needs is a skill tree were you can improve your three main stats with skulls. So that you get a little better after a few runs.That's something I always liked about Rogue Legacy or Dead Cells. It kept you motivated.Otherwise it gets very boring after a few hours. I hope they introduce some mechanic in the future. Then I would come back to the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't take the time to review games but i'll do it for this one,First of all, yes i got this game for free, but only after stalking the discord moderators for giving me acces to the Alpha and becoming an alpha tester lol. I really love Hades and when i saw this game i just had to try it. This game is kind of like Hades but the big difference is that this is more difficult, you need more "skill" to beat the gameKind of like how chess is a more hardcore version of checkers and DOTA2 compared to league etc.Don't get me wrong Hades is amazing but if you want the same kind of gameplay but more rewarding towards skill/player ability then this game is for youSo far the game is far from complete obviously because its early acces, but i've played it for 20~+ hours or so and if you can manage to beat the first act in a week of playing i'd be impressedAs i said its not complete yet but all the things that i feel like are missing atm are being worked on by the developers+++++
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Very impressed with this game!- Controls are fluid, easily customized- Elegant design, UI minimalist but well crafted- Art style is pretty dope, stylized graphic performance will never be an issue- Rouge-like, but enough RPG to make the work feel worth itOne of the best games I've gotten this year. Will deffo keep an eye out for DLC!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very polished game with interesting mechanics; however, the sole fact that the dodge and parry are so cumbersome and unresponsive, I wouldn't recommend this game.  There is no dodge cancelling effect (which would benefit this game greatly) as once you attack, you're committed through the rest of the animation even when the enemies aren't telegraphing their attacks.Otherwise decent game.  Just won't play it anymore.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best roguelite action games out there! The combat feels very fast due to smooth animation canceling, which let's you dodge and parry during your own attack animations. I personally love this kind of gameplay because you are constantly engaged with the enemies, with almost no down time during combat.I also love that enemy attacks are clearly indicated with visual and sound effects, making it clear when you can parry them (unlike many other games where you have to watch the attack animation very closely). If you select the perk that replenishes your stamina completely upon a successful parry, the action almost never stops :)There are 3 different biomes you can select at the start of a new run, each with 3 sub-regions and 1 boss/champion for each sub-region. Each run randomizes the layout of the "rooms" and each room has some randomized elements to it, like enemy spawns and loot. I found it easy to put a lot of hours into this game because it was always fresh!The meta-progression might be the only thing that doesn't stand out to me. It's serviceable but ran out of steam for me after around 20 hours. I still played almost 20 hours more after that, so it's fine ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: There have been a lot of great offerings in the roguelike and roguelite action-adventure category in the last few years such as Undermine and Hades. Unfortunately, Curse of the Dead Gods just doesn't rise to the top against such stiff competition.The good: CotDG employs an art style evocative of dark fantasy/horror classics like Darkest Dungeon, which is what attracted me to buy it. The enemies are somewhat varied, and their animations are fluid. The implementation of a progressive curse, influenced by the player's decisions also works well.The bad: The entire narrative of CotDG is implicit. There is, in effect, no story to be told. Combat is repetitive against the same 4 enemy types per area, room after room. Whereas other games in the genre, keep things fresh by employing permutations of weapons and abilities to test against your foes, CotDG only offers a very limited selection of mostly identical weapons, which can be effectively exhausted within one to two hour of gameplay. The gameplay itself is frustrating, requiring the player to employ split second twitch responses in order to evade damage, but also locks the character into full second attack animations. Perhaps it's greatest weakness is that where peers in the genre strive to create an environment where the player can realize an occasional sense of success and progress, CotDG's limited system of steeply priced token-based unlocks just ends up feeling like a grind job.Overall, I got about 4 hours of mediocre-quality entertainment from this offering. I suggest looking at other titles first.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Good game but boring. No story. A small number of different creatures. The only thing about this game that is likely excellent is its weapons. The game requires you to mix a variety of weapons for your ideal playing style. BUT!!! It will be gone after the run is through, exactly like the other game. Because it will only be used for one round, don't anticipate the best build for the game. If you enjoy playing this kind of game, this game will be fairly simple compared to those.  Let's claim that it isn't really difficult.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is an exceptional game that offers a thrilling and engaging experience for players. The storyline is captivating, with an intriguing premise that keeps players on the edge of their seats. The characters are well-designed and feel like they have depth, adding to the overall immersion of the game.The movements and combat mechanics are fluid and responsive, providing players with a satisfying and exciting gameplay experience. The game's graphics are also impressive, with detailed environments and character models that bring the world to life.Overall, Curse of the Dead Gods is a must-play game for anyone who loves action-packed, story-driven adventures. With its excellent storyline, well-crafted characters, and impressive graphics and gameplay mechanics, this game is sure to keep players entertained for hours on end. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic!!!!!I have always known that the traditional point-&-click diablo-like RPG games are going to die and something like this game would eventually be made. It's a hack & slash dungeon RPG game, very much like Hades, but more interesting in my thoughts.Every new start in the game is totally different. You get different weapons. Every weapon even has different stats. Sometimes you have to decide when to counter and when to block an attack. The combat is so challenging and sometimes you can't guess what is going to happen with the environment traps. Just a few that I can say right now. I really hope that developers have more awesome contents for us when the official version comes up.Developers please make an online game with the mechanics of this game and create more appropriate contents for online experiences, I bet you guys will be seriously rich.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game but then I do not. It isn't a fast ARPG. It is a bit slower. The best comparison I could come up with is Hand of Fate. Although even that game is faster than this one. Originally I compared it to Hades which really wasn't fair because Hades just had so much more to it than this game does. What do I mean by that? Well there is a story to Hades and the more you beat the game the more of the story you discover. This game has a very simple story, you are trapped in a crypt and now you have to explore it and/or escape it by going deeper into the crypt all the while being corrupted and gaining favor from the dead gods. I really like the art style and the combat isn't bad either. The progression is a bit harsh but it isn't that bad. The player moves from room to room sort of like those other rogue like games where you choose a certain path but lose access to the paths you decided not to take. The curses are not that harsh from what I have seen, only the last curse on the build up can feel unfair but hopefully by that point the player can manage it. There are mission challenges which are separate from the main part of the game and you can only run them once. I guess you could call them dailies, as you gain one per day. They feel out of place. Almost like they should've been part of the game as a special room that the players can choose or stumble into that completely changes that run. There is one challenge/daily mission that feels like it shouldn't even be in the game. It is encourage the player to speed run the mission. If you are not fast enough at killing the monsters and traversing through the rooms then you die. The rooms tend to be large and there is no real run in this game. That means that the game is not fast paced enough to compensate for the timer. So you are asking a turtle to move through the dungeon at a hare's pace. The only thing I can think of that I may have not seen is a special passive(s) set up that would allow me to move faster. But then that would require a certain build just for that daily. In closing the devs really should've brought a story into the game as it would've added some more depth. Increased the pace of combat on some level. But as it stands this game is a 6/10. It is above average but it isn't comparable/on par to other games that are similar to it. If you are looking for a slower hack and slash game then this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game plays well and the game mechanics are solid. Overall this game is great. One of the best dungeon crawlers you can get. It only suffers from encouraging certain weapon choices in game. The curses and items you can acquire can all greatly benefit your run. And all are very useful, though bonuses to certain damages or weapons are of course situational. And can make a great item mediocre if it simply won't be able to use all the bonuses the item has. You'd think if you're able  to offer dropped items to the gods, and can reroll items or weapon choices  then those gods should also give secondary uses for bonuses that are not applicable to your  current playstyle? Like significantly lower, but extra flat damage instead of damage boost to specific conditions or weapons when those things are not currently equipped?
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Butter smooth combat, difficult but fair, a new experience every run, cool weapons and power ups, and the corruption system is so unique, it makes you strategize.  This game is Dark Souls meets Hades.  The roll/parrying is so well incorporated.  It is good to practice both, but favoring one or the other doesn't affect the gameplay. (Like in games like Sekiro where its parry or die) This game is definitely brutal at times, but there is never a point where the difficulty spikes are unfair.  When you die, it doesn't ever feel cheap.  The mobs and bosses are manageable but they can easily overcome you.  I never thought I would love a roguelite to the degree of Binding of Isaac, but I think this tops it.  Get this game now before lightning whips and hammers get nerfed! 10/10
