_childDocuments_.review: "." —  ☄️🕯️ "." —  🎖️🧩🥀"" (Alexis Carrel). 💔🔨The sacred vibes felt from the creepy isolation offered by the ruined surroundings and hauntingly prayerful background music with deep voices emitting from the bowels of the macabre, seemingly Mayan or Aztec inspired ancient temple sent chills down my spine. This unseemly reason, along with the player character ending up completely barred from the outside world, accompanied by nothing save for his torch, weapons, and spells sets the tone befittingly for a dark fantasy ambience which thus becomes a disturbing reminder that life in this absurd world is indeed a one-way trip. The fact that what the main character seeks is immortality, wealth, and power is something that parallels, in a warped way, to my own greatest wish as well. How can an unloved person, truly lost, possibly attain limitless knowledge without the gift of timelessness granted by the blessing and warmth of eternal life? What foothold can an individual have over people or perhaps even entire civilizations without the boon of riches beyond their wildest dreams? Who would possibly give their heart and soul wholesomely to an entity with little to no significance to them? In other words, what sort of fool would not seek the secrets of power in one way or another; power in all its complex, and sometimes unquantifiable or even indiscernible, forms... the means to all ends conceivable by the feeble mind of mankind or otherwise? Could the punishment of the cruel mistress fate, through her deadly traps and fearsome beasts under the veil of unforgiving gloom, be the sanguinary candles that wallow in the darkness; the shining, bloody tears of martyrdom that guide alight a path for the tormented spirit who pursues his castle in the air; phantom pains that act as an undying memorial of boyhood fantasies that seem about as reachable as the heavenly sparks of the misty twilight skies, locked beyond the jagged prison of this tomb, once belonging to hungry ghosts long forgotten to the twisting corridors of time… forsaken for reasons only the kindest of divinity would bother to get to know? Could the elusive, or perhaps even illusive, answers lie in the nightmarish pain and suffering in and of themselves… the prerequisites of a journey into the endless destructive and creational potential of the abyss; the ideas of all the evils of the world as we understand it? Could it be that the fatally beautiful goddess of death in my mind’s eye is perversely hinting, through her gruesome curses and unholy trials, that she desires and is meant for, with no exception, the eternal bonding to just the most heartiest, cunning, and wicked of men alone? Once you forge the potential to become a being of abject horror, no corrupt soul would even dare to speak ill of or think about laying a finger on you."" — “.” —

_childDocuments_.review: Neutral vote. There's no option sadly.Would I recommend this game to a friend? Sure, with the following in mind:In this game, the weapons you start with make or break your run. (Unless you're very lucky to find a decent weapon in a shop.) Once you find a great weapon from the starting altar, that's it, just keep upgrading that. The meta? You go start with a decent weapon, get money off of greed combos and buy relics asap.Relics? Just reroll to get gleaming sapphires, or onyx shards. Get 10,000 gold. Do damage. The game pushes you to play a fast, hitless, aggressive style, with how greed combos work. Playing the game without the greed combo mechanic in mind feels unrewarding, but I understand the "No risk, no reward" vibe they're going with here.I wish the game didn't "feel" relentlessly punishing. But it really isn't. You can play the "calm, slow, and calculative" type by being defensive. But the music (yes, the music lol), the greed combos, and how powerful the parry system is, really push you the other direction.It "feels" relentlessly punishing/frustrating with how easily your greed combo can be demolished with some unblockable/"Move-the-♥♥♥♥-out-of-the-way" attacks. (I'm looking at you Soul Reliquary. You and your excessively annoying curse attack.)+Also the sound effect the game makes when you get hit sounds frustrating tbh. Loved how it was at first, but then it just became annoying. The game doesn't really reward you for much outside of the runs when you've performed well. -Crystal skulls? Just farm the easier temples. There isn't a lot to unlock anyway, which I hope they update soon.-Colored painting? I mean the art is great... sure. But what if you gave alternate arts at least? The game became a cycle of "Look for Gambit, a good offhand, run the temple... get bored and not even get the motivation to finish the game because you can kinda know what'll happen "plotwise".

_childDocuments_.review: I am absolutely blown away at how atmospheric and immersive this game is. You really do feel like an unwitting explorer uncovering some ancient and horrific place - deadly enemies lurk in the darkness, while every facet of the environment is full of traps bent on killing you, too.The Corruption mechanic in this game is one of the coolest ideas I've ever seen - each new room you enters fills a bit of your Corruption bar, and some enemy attacks do so too; when your bar fills completely, you gain a curse, which imposes some penalties and changes the way you'll have to approach the run. Interestingly, the game tempts your greed, too - don't have enough gold to get an upgrade? Not a problem, just gain some Corruption and get any upgrade or item the room altar offers. It's incredibly tempting, to simply take every new weapon or relic, but there's a catch - incur too many curses, and you'll become afflicted with the deadly final curse, which slowly but surely spells your doom.The Corruption mechanic, in tandem with the light mechanic - enemies and traps hide in the darkness, dealing more damage, with your trusty torch providing you the safety of light - is some of the best execution of combining both themes and gameplay I've seen. Every aspect of the game, from mechanics to sound design, reinforces its atmosphere and aesthetic, leading to an incredibly cool experience - it almost feels like you're playing a horror movie, but it's an action roguelite. Combined with an intricate stamina-based combat-system, this game is sure to keep you on your absolute toes, throwing challenge after challenge.The only downside is that extended play sessions can becoming exhausting, since the game is quite difficult, and the eerie setting adds to the stress. This is a minor issue, though, as all you have to do is take a break should you reach that point. All in all, this game is an absolute gem, with polished combat, routing, and meta-strategy present each run as you plan your path and juggle all of the resources at your disposal, doing your best to get strong enough to handle what's to come. With steady meta-progression and a good variety of weapons, relics, and room layouts, there's plenty of thrills to be had in this game.

This is not very fun, nor challenging, just annoying. Other than the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemies, its a great game, and I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys rogue-like style games.

_childDocuments_.review: If i had played this game before i played Hades i would have given this game a recommendation, its not really bad. Its just too similar and inferior to Hades. The Combat is slow and clunky in comparison.The surroundings are bland, dark and boring in comparison.The weapons you find are boring and similar to one another.The powerups lack that ooomph that certain roguelikes have, the feeling that once you got it, your run became that much more fun, cooler or just a sense of feeling strong - most upgrades here felt like 5health here or 10 damage there.. nothing mindblowing.And the music, once again - compared to Hades, is lackluster and forgetful.This is not a bad game. I sound harsh, but in reality, its worth checking out... Once youre bored to tears with Hades - So odds are its gonna take awhile.----Edit-----So, went back into Dead Gods after both davidbass and Welucchi pointing out in the comments there had been updates and new additions.The curses was the first improvement I noticed, they were indeed not as... crippling as I remember them to be, in fact - now they, instead of mess up your run just change the rules around abit - I like that.However, most of it just served to remind me in detail why i cant stand this game.. The sluggishness.Every enemy get superarmor when they attack, you cannot interupt them so dodging is your only defense -  doing a full attack combo (3 hit combo usually)  consumes your dodge, so occasionally you will get hit because the game punishes you for wanting to get rid of the enemies too quickly. This feels cheap.Now, in games like dark souls, this makes sense - its your stamina, you tire yourself from swinging - this is not a souls game.There is no reason why you would lose one of your 5 evasion dots everytime you finish an attack combo or fire a ranged secondary weapon - it just serves to further slow down the combat.The upgrades you get are still as boring as ever - +15% firedamage, +15% lightning damage, +30% damage if in darkness, etc - Why not 15% chance for your weapon to explode in a fiery nova per hit? Why not every attack launches a chainlightning for 15% of your damage - ANYTHING but generic higher numbers.And something i had completely forgotten about but got reminded hard when i got back, the godamn extra buttonpress to change your current weapon. So for anyone who have yet to play this game, you have your main weapon on X (assuming xbox controller setup), secondary at Y and Torch (which you need to see ♥♥♥♥) on A.Lets pretend youre using your torch and wanna smack an enemy in the face with your main weapon - Click X, right? no. You click X to swap to the weapon, THEN you have to click X again to actually swing it - this is a tiny nitpick, but seeing as the combat is really slow as is, this addition just  further makes the game feel clunky and unresponsiveEverything from swinging your weapon to evading literally takes ages in this game - roguelikes like these (in my opinion) should be fastpaced to keep up the adrenaline and the feeling of having to constantly move - this game's pace is so slow that i literally had to force myself to finish the new temple before turning off the game and reinstalling Hades and Dead Cells - 2 really good examples of good pacing in roguelikes.Frankly, going back to the game when i havent played roguelikes in awhile I thought would be a good idea, my brain wouldnt be so stuck in Hades as I was the first time i played it - and sure, I didnt think as much about how much better Hades did it - now I just focused on how BAD this game does it, period.Ive gone from feeling that I unfairly judged it because of influence from Hades to literally despising this game. This is NOT a game I can say that I enjoy enough to learn every intricate mechanic, this game bores me to tears, they have added some nice permanent upgrades since I last played and the UI looks better... But that doesn't help when the game is dark, slow, gloomy with literally nothing to look forward to other than a new skin to the current thing you are swinging in your 3 hit combo or perhaps a higher number on said swing-stick.The soundtrack is basically ghostly moans and wind going through empty hallways, the monsters are a hassle and a half to fight since they get occasional super-armor and sometimes the game just dont allow you to evade because youve missed that you currently have no dodge.Everytime you get hit you get further cursed, and everytime you reach a threshold - the next door you open will debuff you in some way - admittedly, these debuffs are the most interesting part of this game, precisely because they are not just generic numbers - I just wish the positives were as interesting.All this combined just results to a challenge thats not fun with a reward thats not worth it. To me, there was nothing to look forward to in this game, at any point. I spent a few hours in it, and frankly - looking back, I regret every single minute. I wish i could refund it - but atleast it was better than RAD.

_childDocuments_.review: Reviews asserting that this game is "Hades but worse" or interpret this game through a very strong "Hades" lens are more-or-less signalling that their experience with rougelites are uncritical at best and braindead at worst.  Simply comparing a top-down roguelite to the most recent success within its shared genre is not an equitable judgment as such interpretations overlook the larger history and context of the genre as well as the internal mechanics of the game itself.  Curse of the Dead Gods deserves its own light within the expanse of the rougelite genre, rather than simply viewing it as a placeholder for carrying on the torch of Hades.This is the fundamental crux of any rougelite - the actual gameplay and the repeated loop in which players participate.  This will be by far the largest section.  in Curse of the Dead Gods (henceforth 'CotDG') is weighty and the measured pacing means that all movement requires player intentionality - this is not a button mashing affair.  Your mistakes will be punished fairly.  There is a unique stamina/dodge roll mechanic at work here.  Basic attacks do not drain stamina, but dodging and certain attacks do drain stamina.  This is where one must see the inspiration of the older 'Souls-like' pace of combat - not the hyped speed in DS3 and Bloodborne, but rather the rhythm of Dark Souls 1 and 2 (or Demon's Souls on the original PS3).  You can animation cancel out of most every move into a dodge, which allows for great-on-the-fly changes in plan and the awarding feeling of (1) barely escaping damage and/or (2) mastering the game's pace.  Utilizing the distance between yourself and your enemies is fundamental in order to maximize your stamina while avoiding damage.One fundamental point is that CotDG does not rely on flashiness to indicate strength nor on over-stimulation to indicate difficulty.  What do I mean by this?First, as your character becomes stronger, the animations that come along with new effects/buffs are not awe-inducing.  In games like Risk of Rain 2 or even Dead Cells where there is a particular extravagance to becoming stronger, that is not the case here with CotDG.  However, I find this choice welcome and fitting, as the moderate graphical effects match the pace of the game itself, not averting my eyes away from the combat while still displaying that my weapons have some unique efficacy.Other roguelikes and roguelites have a tendency to make harder encounters overwhelming by filling the screen with a barrage of on-screen enemy cues in order to induce a sense of panic in the player, to the point where the screen is more chaos than gameplay.  This is not the case with CotDG (although some encounters are difficult).  Due to the pace of the game, mentally processing what is occurring on screen is never an issue due to the explicit cues given to the player.  There is not absurd amount of effects emitted on screen so that one 'hopes they survive out of pure luck' - there is no 'what hit me?' moment; combat is comprehensible. will no doubt be the next question that comes up as this is a rougelite game.  This is where one must decide what they are looking for when they want "replayability" because this word is often uncritically tossed around without any designation as to what constitutes a replayable experience.If one is looking for utilizing a large sense of weapon variety and ultimately trying out different weapons for different playthroughs, then this expectation must be tempered for CotDG.  Most main weapons ultimately end up feeling mostly the same with a small, although still noticeable, variation in speed and damage.  Although my preference is for heavier weapons, I did not experience a large discrepancy in my ability or experience when using medium or light weapons as their characteristics were not diversified enough to constitute a change in strategy.  This is a particularly difficult area of criticism due to not having a clear answer for how this can be fixed - but there is a monotony to the weapon feel.  The fact that one has a main, secondary, and a heavy weapon, with the option to parry, play close-range, focus on long-range, or a mixture gives the appearance of variety without any significant delivery.  That isn't to say that the combat itself is not satisfactory.  It's the variety here that is in question for replayability.That being said, the actual replayability granted from level design and boss design here is welcoming, along with the unique challenges and debuffs one incurs from each playthrough.  Here is where I will explicitly refer to Hades: whereas Hades relied on weapon and debuff choices before each run and buffs throughout a given playthrough to give players the strength to overcome their challenges, CotDG is a much more volatile experience, with weapon variety (as slim as it is), buffs, and debuffs all unpredictable factors.  There are limited buffs that one can apply in CotDG, but they are intentionally restricted in order to not let the player go into a run feeling 'overpowered' in the early going.  This is where one can feel the tonal difference between the two games in their core gameplay: whereas Hades seeks to buff the player and have a bit more control of their experience, CotDG seeks to literally 'curse' the player while traversing the unknown.  Some prefer the former, some prefer the latter, some enjoy both.  I personally enjoy both and find the difficulty in the latter refreshing.I will say this: towards the end of my Hades runs, I was averaging 25-30 minutes.  Each of the dungeon runs in CotDG, I am averaging approximately 10-15 minutes per run.  Given that CotDG has more map variety/dungeons than Hades, this is another determining factor in how one measures replayability.Those drawn to stories in video games should be warned - there is little here on the explicit surface.  This game caters to those seeking a gameplay and atmospheric experience rather than an overall "roleplaying" game experience.  I personally have no issues with this type of gameplay presentation - better to have little to no story rather than a badly written one.I enjoy the art direction here - the parallels to Darkest Dungeon mixed with Mayan influence resonate with my own interpretation.  While nothing is particularly outstanding, the art direction is cohesive and consistent even when exploring different areas.Audio cues are clear and the music fits the setting.  Nothing particularly stellar but the music, along with the art direction, presents a complete mood of chaotic, desperate delirium.Given its price point and current state, I recommend CotDG as long as one takes the game for what it is and not for what it is not - a game that attempts to illuminate more possibilities and its own pace within the rougelite genre.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR 5/10 It's not the worst and it's not the best roguelike. The design choices will leave you scratching your head and none of the systems actually work together for a seemless experience. There are glaring balance issues when it comes to ranged vs melee weapons and 95% of the games many, many weapons are forgettable. I can't recommend this as there are so many better options in roguelikes out there. Dead Gods is just mediocre in everything it sets out to do.Long Version: This roguelike looks like a deep experience on the surface but after a few hours, the many, many issues are what end up glaring at you in the end. To start, the core game play has a corruption system, with 5 levels. Every 100 corruption, you gain a negative effect that stays with you through the rest of your run. Every floor you complete, adds 20 corruption. There are ways to reduce the corruption, but once you cross the hundred marks, you cannot reduce beyond that except by defeating a boss. The corruptions themselves are just annoyances and I didn't find any to be run-ending. I never made it to 5 full stacks, but once you unlock the final tier of the dungeon run, I supposed it would be possible. I just didn't find any joy in the system itself and having to manage it each run. It seems counter-intuitive to punish the player for simply playing the game, but maybe that's just me. You also carry a torch and take less damage in well-lit areas and more damage in dark areas. This quickly goes out the window when you enter rooms that do not have sconces to light, the enemies can break said sconces, and you cannot hold the torch and attack at the same time. The player quickly learns to just attack in the dark and forgo this gimmick. The whole light/dark thing makes zero sense and was horribly designed. Speaking of horribly designed, there is a stamina system in the game also. You start with 5 stamina spheres. Completing an attack combo or dodging, uses a sphere. When you run out, you can do neither. It's not a pain until you make it to the Twins boss. Without giving up too much, you need to quickly move around the room to avoid damage and strike in-between. The stamina system makes this one fight such a chore because dodging uses up all your stamina spheres and you cannot attack which just prolongs the fight for zero reason. You also run into this same issue once you are introduced to elite enemies, which are just beefed up health pools of the original enemies. It just doesn't make sense. Next is the weapons. Once you unlock ranged weapons, the game becomes a breeze. You can simply attack from afar and quickly dodge away if enemies get too close or swing at you. They do the same damage combo as a melee weapon with the benefit of not being in enemy attack range. It is horribly balanced in this way. The very first boss attack pattern requires a lot of dodging if you are melee and minimal dodging if you are ranged. Thus, your damage output is much higher when you can just stand out of range and deal out damage faster than a melee approach. There are offhand and power weapons in the game also, but I never use them as there is no point to. You end up spamming your main attack button. In terms of content, the unlockables in the game, come in the form of unlocking more weapons, more passive skills and the ability to reroll them or start with them. Let me just say that because of the balance issues on the range vs melee, 95% of what you can unlock is completely pointless. The passive skills are all forgettable and don't really have an impact on the game, and the currency to unlock everything is such a grind to obtain. There is a daily run system where you can start a run with a predetermined affliction and every room you clear gives you extra currency to unlock things. For comparison, I completed a daily run and had 100+ in currency. I completed a regular run and had 12. The amount of time you need to spend to grind is insane and equates to less and less fun. The story is non-existent too. You know nothing about the protagonist other than he entered the cave of doom. There's zero story behind the corruption system, the boss, nothing. The combat itself lacks a lot. The most glaring issue is that you get locked into animations and cannot attack-cancel. This is the cause for 99% of the damage you take and when combined with the stamina system, is just painful. In the end, this game has a lot of different systems in it that seemed to have been developed by people who never communicated with each other in the design planning of the game. It lacks cohesion. It lacks depth. It lacks a story. And it lacks a polish on everything it sets out to do. So, when you combine them all together, it makes for an experience that isn't fun by design, and is extremely forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely fun rogue light with all that Darkest Dungeon aesthetic but none of the massive stress induced agita brought about by DD's insane micromanagement revolving around stress and mental conditions. The only thing you have to do here is manage your corruption levels and then kick monster asses to buy, equip, upgrade skills, improve stats, rinse and repeat. And just like true roguelight, there's a veritable ton of carry-over progression between runs to keep you playing for an umpteenth amount of hours depending on your resilience against burnout. The weapon design and graphics are nothing state of the art, something more akin to Warcraft 3 Reforged, but the polish is on overdrive and the gameplay loop is brief and fantastic. Despite the corruption micromanagement and boss bullethell tool kits, the game's more of a stress reducer than an inducer. $8 is an excellent price, grab it now.

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is a little grindier than I would like but this is some of the best Isometric Action combat you could experience. Weapons are punchy and responsive, not to mention the snappy parrying and whip cancels. The atmosphere is thick and bleak with a unique theme for each area. Despite the constant darkness, enemy attacks and projectiles are visually clear and well telegraphed. Even without an I-frame mechanic the fights are still challenging but death usually does not feel unfair. This game is about $5 on sale and that is without a doubt worth it.

I really like the setting, the mechanics and ideas however, I think it definitely needs some polishment!In my opinion, it feels not that smooth like Hades or Dead Cells, sometimes even a little bit clunky. _childDocuments_.review: I usually don't write a review for a game unless I 100% it. In this case though, more people should play the game.There 2 words to describe this game. "Meaningful Decisions". Everything you do in this have either a micro or macro decision behind it. What weapon you can in the beginning of the run, what path you will take, do you want to parry or dodge, go the darkness bonus or live in the light, etc. There are various amount of decision that make each run your own. Also, the combat is silky smooth with a deliberate pacing, the difficulty ramps up beautifully, the interface well though out. Also, the Aztec theme is something that haven't been beaten to death yet. The game does kick your tushy at the final tier but my tushy is like a monkey. It needs to be spanked.

_childDocuments_.review: I played more than 100 hours of Hades, and Course of the Dead Gods might be my favorite action roguelike. I don't know if it has enought variety to keep me invested for so long, but it's moment-to-moment gameplay is excellent. So is the Curse mechanic - at first it seems really forboding and punishing, but as soon as you realise that all but the last curse are just gameplay mutatiors, and not debuffs, it becomes a fun game of resource management. And thanks to this system,  this is the only roguelike I know that manages to be hard, withouth being really stingy in healing and starving you out over the run, or letting you heal often, but killing you in 3 hits that can happen in 1 second (I'm looking at you, Dead Cells) which makes the combat SUPER fun, as getting hit is punishing, but not soul-breaking. Highly reccomended.

_childDocuments_.review: A real disappointment.  There are some good elements here, but they're severely undermined by the combat/controls.  The animation locking forces a slower and meticulous gameplay: you can't cancel an attack into a perfect block or parry--and the window is very short (and a few milliseconds too early, IMO0.  Yet, you're 4 or 5 vs one, which demands you use frequent dodging and parrying in between attacks, but then you run out of stamina, so you have to attack, but the animation locking means you can't dodge or parry even if you time it correctly.  It's a vicious circle.In short: the game plays nothing like Hades, which has spoiled me for good controls.It's not all bad, but I can't recommend it.  It's more frustrating than fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a roguelike with dark aztec theme. It has lots of different weapons with different gameplay styles. Also it has variety of upgrades which can be made during runs and between runs. Overall it lets you make different builds that fit you gamestyle.Core gameplay is based on reaction mosly - you will have to dodge and parry a lot. But every dodge and parry is so satysfing, so it motivates you to improve. Also it includes stamina management and some combos but it's not most difficult game part.However game is challenging and at some point becomes repetative. In late game runs become long and exhausting - some boss fights can take up to 20 minutes. Overall game is fun, but maybe it lacks content a bit to be a truly great roguelike.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Quite frankly I bought this just because I liked the art style. Am I irresponsible with my money? Probably. But sometimes it pays off. Turns out it is a hecking good roguelite game. Combat is fluid and action packed. Controls are responsible and I never felt like "oh no I couldn't do anything", so gameplay comes down to your skill. Unlocks let you create builds that will smash your enemies and make you feel good while doing it. Curses are a cool idea to make your current run more varied. Thanks to them you have to adapt to your current curse, making a run never boring. The best part is, curse don't have to be a debuff, you can actually build your character to profit from it.  It makes every run unique. There's also a mechanic where standing in darkness. Light/Dark mechanis are also interesting. Normally in darkness you take more damage from enemies, but what if you build your character to make more damage in darkness. And yeah, the artstyle I bought the game for is also great.tldr; this game is good, and worth your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a fun rogue-like, a blend of Darkest Dungeon + Hades + a little bit of Dark Souls.Manage your stamina carefully, light up the rooms you fight in to take less damage and avoid spamming at all costs while you fight through Aztec temples. A lot of reviews mention issues with stamina or parries, and the parry timing does sometimes feel a bit off, but otherwise the combat is weighty and tactical - slower and more deliberate pace than Hades for example but very satisfying. Plays fine on KB + Mouse even though the game mentions a controller is recomended.Not much of a top-down rogue like action game player, but from the 2 i have played and finished before (Hades and Children of Morta) this still stands out and is a rather unique experience, even if my favorite still remains Hades.Worth the 15 bucks, will be completing it when I get good.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts off very promising but it falls off pretty fast. The longer you play, the clearer will become the flaws of the game. It has no storytelling whatsoever compared to Hades, its basically a carcass of a game. Upgrades are very underwhelming, there are no sort of permanent boosters for consequent runs like in Hades, upgrades require an enormous amount of grinding.Temples become harder and harder, but not due to newer enemies, but due to stronger hp pools on enemies, so the whole thing starts to get dull, boring, repetitive grind. It is a good game for a few hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun game and will probably be up there as one of my favorites in the rogelite genre next to Hades once it's out of EA. I ended up making a playlist on spotify comprised of other games like Hades (which fits really well), Hollow Knight, Dead Cells, etc. Still gets a thumbs up though.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is a great roguelike, the combat feels amazing, if you're a rogue-liker you'll probably enjoy this one, but unfortunately it suffers heavily from being able to tell how strong your run is going to be very early into the run, while simultaneously being able to ruin great runs in the span of seconds.Also it gives me some uncomfortable colonizer vibes
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game so far. im liking it but i do have some little points that are a tad frustrating which also caused me to take 2 days to beat just the first boss.- feels like its not aggressive enough. for some reason i tend to want to jump in but by doing that you reach the boss with barely half health and you get 2 shot from him. These type of games are supposed to be action played more then hit, run, hit, run, hit etc....- stamina feels like there missing 1 point. im always missing that 1 point to dodge or hit one last time to finish a combo.- stamina also feels a tad slow to regen. (feels even slower when you have 7 ennemies behind you)- parry, parry is off. i can barely get it to work let alone twice in a short span. (live streamed my playing if that can help devs and youll notice i try to play like an action game but it ends up bitting me in the butt. You will also notice i parry in time but it doesnt work.) at this point i don't see the point of the parry. -  parry should be only a shield perk and you could switch the parry button by a second attack button. like a heavy attack.- Another point, i don't feel like theres enough healing chances. if the gameplay was faster, more action-y, it wouldn't matter but the game punishes you for trying to go in with a tad more aggression then it likes so more healing elements would be good. For example put some healing things in the pots (not just when you get the curse that changes the gold for healing blood but also curses you), or make enemies drop some form of healing things, even if it's a small amount.-- overall its needs a tad more speed, more aggressivity. Less hit, run/dodge, hit, run/dodge and more like hit, hit, hit, run/dodge to get stamina back, hit hit hit and so forth.A the end of the day its in early access and game feels really smooth and polished so far for an early access game. _childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: A great roguelike that is difficult and rewarding experience. Difficulty is very scalable though, making it customizable. The rewards and pre-expedition bonuses are quite unique and can really modify how you approach each temple. There are three different temples to explore, with 3 lengths on each temple. After you explore each temple fully, you can enable 4 progressively more difficult modifiers on your future each run.Pattern learning is key and veterans of Souls-like games will feel right at home. However, bosses are a bit underwhelming - they tend to spam the room with hazards, then attack quickly. All three I have seen so far have different designs, but their mechanics are too similar. The temple hazards and regular enemies are more of a threat than the bosses however, because they tend to swarm you.If the game had more boss variety, it would be close to perfection. Given that it is in early access, this is an amazing achievement and well-worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone shopping for games, I generally have one pre-requisite.  Especially EA games.  The amount of hours the 'top reviews' have garnered.  If all around they are a couple of hours, I would say do your research before plunging in, even if the overall Steam rating is Very Positive or above.  For myself, I haven't even put in 30 minutes.  It doesn't mean it's bad, but it didn't pull me in enough to keep me playing.  I'm sure I'll return, but right now it feel pretty far from complete.  It's also not quite intuitive, but that's OK.  The Souls games weren't intuitive either.  I'm sure this will have an audience, but I'm don't know if it's worth the full price, TBH.  Watch some videos first, not trailers.  I'd give it a tentative 'recommendation' for now.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. At first you take a lot of damage because you don't know monsters' patterns or how things work exactly.Then you keep fighting and get the hung of it, still being difficult to finish a "Long Temple run".Still there are some minor features that make this game kind of repetitive or too simple:From a point of view, it lacks of weapon mechanics. I think the number of weapons and variety is ok, but it feels almost the same hitting with one or another: you swing it and you use the most powerful, forgetting about which one would be better for "X" scenario.Some weapons strike harder against alone enemies, or bosses, but that's all the thinking you'll do. Most of times I even prefer to just go with one-handed weapons because the stamina loss: 2H weapons consume stamina with each hit and... well, if I'm killing all the monsters at the end of the day, I prefer doing it without losing my health.On the other hand, I'd prefer not getting LOTS of variety because the "relic system" is kind of useless and boring, and you never get some useful build: I find myself getting generic buffs / relics, and going into "Stats rooms" because yeah, Relics and Weapons still drop here and there and going into a room to get nothing at the end is not funny nor rewarding.How about getting something USEFUL when we enter a Weapon or Relic room? Like, the game checks your equipment and past choices and you get useful options. Would be nice.Parrying system is also a bit confusing. You seem to parry things in the very moment the attack would've reached you, but the parry action has some kind of minimum delay time and it's not so easy to parry, and of course it's less responsive and intuitive than just rolling on floor and avoid damage. I guess it's all about learning right...Maybe that's all. The game can be improved, or not. I don't know what developers want this game to be, so I'll just stop here.For the price and the hours it provides I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game if you enjoy playing roguelikes. If you're looking for a full controller support, this is also your game -in fact you play better with a controller-.For 15€ you get lot of hours just to reach the end of the Long Temple, then another bunch of hours refining and learning to play good.At the current state of the game it's almost impossible that it can get worse, so the above reasons are enough to buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Its fun enough in places, but not interesting or engaging enough compared to the sea of other rogue-likes. Stamina feels sluggish or barely an issue depending on the situation, for example its meant to limit bow spam, but if you have enough distance you can just rapid fire and then wait for it to reset without anything posing a real threat, neither of which are fun. The light mechanic feels uninteresting and often just boils down to "switch to fire when exploring."Going through room after room feels so tedious given the rooms are broken up into rooms themselves and explore sections and the bosses I've fought so far don't have enough presence to justify the wait. I understand its meant to be a test of endurance but it tests my patience more and i run out of energy to play after the 5th same-ish room in a row.The art style is nice, but the art design is lacking, uninteresting and using native south american cultures as a "corrupting evil" feels bland at best and exploitative at worst. The dark environments also leave the game feeling relatively the same between floors regardless of the aesthetic (like machinery or wet or whatever). I wish there was a character select or something because the main character isn't so much as a character as a drawing they drew once and thought was cool enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue like elements of progressions are very limited. You are opening weapons - but RND will decide if you get them. There are 3 slots for equiping mechanic/stats changers with you open as well and thats basicly it. You would have to grind also a lot to open better ones.Enemies dont telegraph their intent always well or at least until you learn their attack patterns.Curse system is not that bad - but I would be much happier if attack of enemies didnt add so much of corruption.Traps are punishing and some do way to much damage and have higher reach then you would expect.Game is super dark (as intended and part of game mechanic I didnt enjoy). Overal game look good on papper but gaming expirience is way less appealing and not worth my time.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah it's pretty good, but I think I'm stuck in a love-hate relationship with this game now.It's got a great art style, the combat is SUPER juicy and its got some fun mechanics with light and darkness effects, offering loot for health/stats/gold and the corruption/curse system.Corruption goes up to 100 then you get a curse, walking through a door gives you 20 corruption, beating a boss or sacrificing an item of the highest rarity removes a curse. The 5th curse constantly drains your health and is essentially the end of your run. The curses themselves are also weirdly imbalanced where some of them are actually just buffs and others are going to completely ♥♥♥♥ up your run.Enemies can also do dark damage which gives you corruption and the amount of corruption damage dealt by enemies feels way over tuned and with just a few slip ups you've got another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ run.And in terms of roguelite elements I have a couple nitpicks: the ratio of currency received vs upgrade costs is pretty disheartening and it seems like the only reason to spend money on unlocking new weapons is so you can permanently exclude them from the drop list because there is only a small selection of useful ones.Just getting to the final tier of each level feels like a huge slog and based more on whether I get lucky with weapons and relics rather than my actual skill.I may also just be bad at the game so your mileage may vary.Regardless of all these negative thoughts I have about the game I still have been playing it daily because the core combat loop is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ satisfying, so yeah its probably worth checking out

_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through Hades, Dead Cells, Darkest Dungeon, Slay the Spire, Crypt of the Necrodancer, Against the Storm; I was adequately prepared for Curse of the Dead Gods.I love how the Devs clearly took inspiration from many other Roguelikes, it's refreshing when game makers don't try and reinvent the wheel, but rather expand on what is already tested and true. The animations are clean, though sometimes the game cheats with the hurtbox because I obviously would've never been hit by that attack. Otherwise, the weapons and power-ups picked up during the run feel meaningful with a good amount of synergies and skill expression, especially when it comes to the different possible combos between primary and secondary weapons.Like many of the previous Roguelike listed above, this game greatly rewards careful and calculated moves. Attacks, dodges, parries must be used with precision rather than mashing; this will remind you of a souls-like. Finally, the game does do something different from the rest, and I'm not sure yet how I feel about it. Most of the games listed above require grinding to finish a map. Usually, you'll often die many times for necessary global upgrades to empower your next run. Although these global upgrades are available in Curse of the Dead Gods, they do not feel as impactful. This is because the game re-imagines the entire grind for a different experience. There are "three" dungeons, and each are divided by three levels until the final boss. Each level of each dungeon must be completed to unlock the next level of that dungeon. This means you will have to beat the first boss of the first map, and your run will "end" to unlock the next level. Then you will have to reach the first boss again, to advance to the second floor, to attempt the second boss, and so on for each dungeon. Once you defeat the third boss of all three dungeons, you'll unlock the final boss map. If I could guess the intention of the devs, this is to try and make the runs more rewarding by returning the character to the main screen with each level completion, but in effect it throttles your momentum by forcing you to rerun from step 1 instead of allowing you to attempt progress until the end. I imagine this was done as a way to facilitate balancing and increase game time. With 16 hrs of playtime I have unlocked the final boss map, so this game definitely feels shorter than most. This especially because without a strong storyline like Hades, not much will hold the player to the game other than collectibles, daily runs, and a hard mode. This being said, I would like to remind the reader of my prior "preparation" for this game. I say this, because I am tired of spending $80 on a great game that takes 18 hrs to complete (I'm looking at you Metroid Dread).TLDR: looks good, feels good, is short. Suggestion: buy on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Good game but not for everyone. To me, it's a blend between Hades and Enter the Gungeon, but with a few frustrating gameplay elements added on top. The game feels way too much on the slow side, especially after a lot of Hades and the stamina mechanics obviously doesn't help with that. You're constantly pausing your attacks to regenerate your stamina, but it's a key element to the game so I can understand the decision to create such system. The environment hazards, like traps, feels unnecessary and extremely frustrating. I find myself constantly rolling around when I've cleared a room to move onto the next room because the character is sooooo slow but then I always sooner or later stumble onto a trap and then I obviously don't have enough stamina to dodge it because I'm rolling around all the time which makes me take heavy hits very stupidely. The light/shadow system is a good idea but I've not found it very well exploited (personnaly I don't care at all and it makes no difference). The game may be too easy (14 success clears, 3 fails, 2 being my very first two runs). I've play 7 hours and feel like I've reached my limit. Still a good game and some might love it. Give it a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This is a damn good roguelike. It is worth every penny you'll spend on it and then some.Why?Well, it:*Has an awesome visual style (Darkest dungeon called, it wants the ancestor back)*Is easy to learn, but damn hard to master. Seriously, can anyone parry consistently in this game without a random lurker clapping their cheeks out of the blue every once in a while because they hit a button one milisecond early?*Has a couple very curious mechanics like light/dark and the curse, which actually is a resource you have to manage, rather than something exclusively bad. Hell, some of the curses can even be considered good. Not the one that makes all the chests try to murder you though. I hope the guy who coded it in has to parry every time he tries to unzip his pants.*Has quite a lot of progression and stuff to unlock*Is surprisingly well-balanced. At least i havent find anything op yet.Elemental weapons are a little more powerful than regular ones, but thats about it. ____________Bonus points for running on a potato PC. My laptop's graphics card is well below the minimal system requirements level, but as soon as FXAA and SSAO were turned off steady 60 fps rolled in. And the game still looks amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I'm split. The game is fun, the mechanics are really great, and the atmosphere and little tidbits of story are all a 10/10. However, the game is also dead. No updates planned for the future, which means the mountain of little gripes I'm left with are all that's left to experience. -Many cursed weapons suck. Both shortswords (not counting the dead cells joke weapon), the throwing knives, the bomb (all the bombs suck pretty hard, ngl), and the fists just don't deal enough damage unless you get a perfect storm of secondary effects. In terms of endgame, it's just the final quest. That's pretty much it. You unlock every weapon, get every blessing, and find out that the green blessings are just all better in some fashion or another. No "heat gauge" like Hades, no bonus challenges, and very importantly- no way to convert excess currency into anything else. It feels like they didn't expect you to continue wanting to play a roguelike after you beat the final mission. I recommend this game tenuously. It's sold right up until you want a deeper experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Just awesome! Hard to play, a lot of content and gameplay for the price.  Feels like a mix of diablo with dark souls. _childDocuments_.review: Great game, if you like roguelites. How does it compare to Hades, which is probably the best roguelite of 2020? Well, this game doesn't have nearly as much content as Hades, at least for now (we'll have to see how it compares when COTDG finally releases though). However, the combat in this game is way superior to Hades' in my opinion. It feels great to fight in this game, and you can tell how polished the mechanics are just by watching a couple of minutes of gameplay. There's enough blessing, weapon, and temple variety in this game to keep you entertained for quite a few hours,As far as cons go, I don't think there are many. A few crashes and bugs here and there, mainly (which is to be expected of a game still in early access). And the final boss of the Serpent temple feels cheap as heck. I won't spoil it here, but know that it's basically a DPS race. If you don't have enough damage, you literally can't win, no matter how well you play, cause he's simply gonna outheal every damage point he takes.Summary: Great game, with a lot of content for the stage it's currently in, and with probably the best combat mechanics I've ever seen in a roguelite. Get it if you like what you see, you won't be disappointed
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I'll make it short: the only thing holding this game back from being even better than HADES is that it has basically no story telling or world building elements to it and long term unlocks don't seem to be as meaningful. Otherwise: I feel that gameplay and core mechanics are more punishing but at the same time satisfying than HADES' ultra-super-hyper builds that make the game essentially an effortless stroll in the park. From a standpoint of just picking up ur controller and playing a round or two, this game is probably the superior choice. If u need a longterm (emotional) investment concerning story/setting, I'd skip it.

_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game today. I have not stopped playing this game today. Please, do yourself a favor and give this game a chance . . . today.Why:- Challenging combat that makes you think- Tons of unique enemies that require different approaches- Players are given the choice to direct how they play the game and unlock what they want- The weapons pair together differently and each is satisfying to use- The combat. It deserves mentioning twice- Minimal (nonexistent) story, which for me is a plus. Don't expect Hades level story but do expect Hades level polish- The UI is beautifulUpdate: The early game of Curse of the Dead Gods is amazing, like my original review said, but this changes once you get around 6-10 hours in. At that point the difficulty spikes considerably while your weapons and upgrades remain stale. To unlock the good stuff that will actually enable you to stand a chance will take hours upon hours of grinding. I know I only have 10 hours of play time, but that's because I'm seeing how long it's going to take and it's just not worth it for me. Of course, it is possible to beat some of the harder bosses and dungeons with sheer skill, but some of the enemies are quite ridiculous at higher tiers and attack together. The parry window timer is incredibly short, which wouldn't be a problem if dodging didn't take up precious stamina.It's a shame because the core of this game is sooooo good, but the pacing is way off and kills the fun.TLDR: Originally recommended because the core of the game is fun, innovative, and challenging, but the grindy nature of upgrades, the overwhelming randomness of success, and the huge spike in difficulty after the second tier dungeons just kills the fun for me personally.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game and have been following its development for months. But being difficult is one thing, but joyless and punishing is another. Great combat games make the player feel powerful through mechanics that reward skillful play (build damage multipliers, fill special meters, etc.) and spiral the fun upwards. But CotD uses a fatigue mechanic that punishes the player for missed timing (lose the ability to roll/dodge) and spirals the fun downwards. Add to that a lack of room and monster variety and ultimately I abandoned this for Hades and Dead Cells.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just, UNF *positive grunting*There is no story to speak of, but the setup and setting ooze mystery and are perfectly ludonarratively suited to the game's mechanics. The combat, once you get a hold of it, is tight-butthole precise with a high skill ceiling for such relatively simple movesets for each weapon. It has a flow state unlike any other game of this type that i've played once you invest the time to learn. I will say that there is still some need for tuning of a few oppressive enemy types, and some of the weapons seem much less useful than others, but overall if you like creepy dungeon crawls, roguelikes, and soulslike combat; buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun Roguelite:+ Combat is fantastic, best part of the game: It is slower and more deliberate than other games of the genre like Hades, but also more technical and skill based. The skill ceiling is high, and if mastered you can be an untouchable, non stop dps machine (Parrying succesfully gives back 2 stamina points out of 5, Perfect Dodging through attacks gives 1 ; Since attacking costs stamina this allows you to turn good defense into relentless offense. )+Definetly a hard and challenging game, the parry , dodge and stamina mechanics are reminiscent of the Dark Souls series, as is the weighty, satisfying combat.+ Aesthetic is very cool, reminds me of a slightly less bleak Darkest Dungeon. +Graphics are good and the game runs perfectly, encountered no bugs or crashes so far.+ Decent weapon variety, each weapon type plays pretty differently.= Meta Progression is just ok : You unlock Blessings (Basically perks) , weapon variants and different Altars (Which offer you different starting weapons). It's not bad but you won't keep wanting to play just for the unlocks.= Even though each type of weapon is very different to one another, weapons within the same type all play pretty much the same. What I mean is, there a lot of different kind of Maces, but they all have the same moveset and playstyle ; They just have different passive effects that are normally not that big/build altering (For example, one mace might do extra damage to enemies on fire, another will do more damage when you are out of stamina... things like that). Could be improved by adding more unique effects IMO.- Lacking in enemy variety (You will constantly encounter the same few types of enemies within each different temple).- Runs can feel samey: You will usually not get super interesting builds with crazy synergy. Think more Hades and less The Binding of Isaac.- Not a crazy amount of content.Overall it's worth playing just for the excelent combat, aesthetics and just fun gameplay. It will probably not be a game you play for hundreds of hours,  but I believe it can give you a very fun 40/50 hours of content. It is soon to say though, I might get addicted for a lot longer !

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first serious game(other than mariokart and CoD), it's hard but it is so worth it. The parrying system allows for you to block attacks even when you can't dodge anymore. The scaling of difficulty is exponential and it definitely took me a long time to make it. There is no story but the art and creativity of the bosses is always a treat.The curse mechanic can be a blessing or a curse and it encourages dodging and maintaining a relatively low curse count (unless you want the final curse artifacts). I've played many other games from dungeon trawlers to rpg, this is my favorite and I continue to play just to relax. _childDocuments_.review: Review Update : As of Official Release, I've cleared the hardest dungeon in the game and seen the ending.Curse of the Dead Gods still requires perfection and significant amount of focus, and anyone who isn't adept at action games will face stress and frustration when dying. Compared to EA release, you can now re-roll shop items, and have a chance to receive healing when consuming unwanted loot. I appreciate that developers listened to the feedback and implemented such features, so players who were unlucky to find Healing Relics still have something to hope for.Enemies in each Temple are unique and challenging enough to keep you entertained, but keep in mind that the last three Expeditions feel repetitive. On the contrary to its early release, I actually enjoyed the 1.0 version of the game. That's why I'm changing my review from Negative to Positive. Review Update : As of Update 0.17.2, they increased the overall difficulty by powering up enemies, weakening the player and reducing the effectiveness of healing. Changes have made the game very difficult for new-players and low-skill players.-----After watching a favorite streamer playing this on Twitch, I decided to give this game a try.<Reviewer Progression>Completed "Path to Cruelty", a Hard mode of the previous stage.<Summary>In short, the game's current status aligns with its intended vision which is the dungeon-adventuring experience. But in-game combat system needs to provide a way for comebacks (by consuming player resources), and a few encounters needs tweaking.<Pro>++ Very cheap and acceptable price for what the Early-Access game offers++ Action and controls are surprisingly smooth for a game made by an independent team (doesn't feel floaty)+ Core mechanics, such as content unlocks, weapon system, combat foundation are solid+ Corruptions which confer debuff as the player continues allow players to work around them+ Most encounters feel challenging, but more importantly, fair<Cons>-- Lack of player-comebacks, specifically healing; obtaining certain items (Relics) for free-healing greatly reduces difficulty, and without them the player-pressure is significant. If healing could be directly purchased with Gold, or a portion of player Health was restored after defeating a champion, the game would be friendlier to more audience. Otherwise, players must risk another Corruption to return to their initial state (by interacting with Haven for healing), which causes negative feedback-loop- Could introduce a practice mode where players can hone their abilities against certain enemies, especially champions and bosses on stage 3; players have to spend a lot of time just to get one shot against those, who often use devastating, somewhat unfair attacks to end the fight quickly- Two cons combined, the game is built for perfectionists who can dodge everything and don't drag the fight too longInformally speaking, the game feels more unforgiving, even than Dark Souls franchise, due to the fact that there's almost no healing. And that's coming from someone who has beaten Dark Souls 2 without dying once. If more methods for covering up mistakes are given, then low-skill players will no longer feel that their fate is marked during the middle of the run and lose the will to play. High-skill players won't be affected by the change, since healing is only needed if mistakes are made.Great game for hardcore players, not so much for the general audience.EDIT 03072020 : Added <Reviewer Progression>.EDIT 03082020 : Updated <Reviewer Progression>.

_childDocuments_.review: Thought I would give an updated review on this seeing as I am roughly 45 hours into this game.I have about 10 clears so far on the hardest difficulty and have cleared with just about every weapon at this point. Weapons have their positives and negatives (Two-Handed weapons cc and do heavy damage, but take up a lot of stamina limiting your dodging if you aren't careful. One-Handed weapons don't take much stamina and don't animation lock you, but don't do high damage or cc for the most part, etc.) This game is incredibly punishing in a lot of ways but no where near the hardest game you will ever play. If you lose focus for one second, you could see your health go from 1500 to 400 and pretty much end your run. At first I was not a fan of the parry block, but the more and more I played I quite enjoy it. Dodge rolling is the far safer way to avoid attacks, but it takes 1 stamina while parrying costs none. For that reason, the fact parry has such a tight window makes a lot of sense.The main reason I recommend this game is the developers have been keeping up to date with patches and balancing items/enemies/anything. The +2 dexterity per perfect room blessing was much too strong, so they nerfed it down to +1. The life stealing off summoned monsters was much too strong, so they made it so you cannot leech off of more than one summoned creature. I have noticed a lot of balancing changes like these every week since the game has come out.There are a few things I would like to see in future updates (new curses, new floors/dungeons, new enemies/bosses) but even just as the game currently stands as of the date I am writing this, it is more than worth the $15.If you love roguelites, it would be very strange to not pick this game up for the price, especially if it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up for now, but it will need some more variety and fixes. For starters, even if it is a roguelite, runs hinge far too much on getting specific item loadouts. If, after the first boss, you don't have a HP regenerating weapon/relic, and a corruption depleting weapon/relic, you may as well restart the run. These two things are just borderline mandatory that they make any other options redundant.The combat is actually pretty stellar overall. Weapons need rebalancing a little: Shields do way more damage than they should, making daggers irrelevant, and range weapons lack a sense of typing beyond being a single projectile.The curse system is a neat idea but posseses some that go beyond mere frustration. If you get the invisible enemy curse, hallucinations, or the one that spawns bats, you may as well give up.Obviously needs way more enemies and bosses (The boss for each segment is always the same), but I assume that will come
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't say I'm a Rogue-like veteran but at least half of my favourite games are from the genre so I know my way around them alright.With a grand total of only two hours of gameplay I'm pretty confident in saying the following:The art-style for this game carries the ever-living ♥♥♥♥ out of it, because the gameplay sure as hell doesn't. That certainly isn't to say it's bad, because it's far from it, it's just... "okay" There isn't a massive amount of depth, some features feel a little tacked on; the light mechanic for example just feels like the devs REALLY wanted to complete the whole Darkest Dungeon aesthetic they're clearly going for. Your character is also surprisingly tanky, when fighting the last of the first three bosses I got fed up and just tanked them for the final third of the fight, which worked perfectly fine because: There is literally no reason for this except to artificially extend the game length. It is tedious and insulting, even games like Isaac let you get to the final (Mega Satan) boss on your first run with some knowledge, a pinch of luck and some skill.There's also a lot of permanent upgrades which I assume you're intended to grind for which I personally just dislike.I'll update this review but as it stands I haven't once gotten that "Just one more run" itch, because to be honest playing this game is pretty tedious once you've figured out enemy attack patterns. Again, this game isn't bad. It's just "fine" and not a lot more.

_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent Roguelike. Curse of the Dead Gods entices the player with tight, satisfying combat and the perfect level of challenge. I particularly love the dodge and parry, because parrying at the perfect moment to recharge stamnina and deliver the final blow makes you feel like a god of combat. Fans of Sekiro and Dark Souls will appreciate this! On the level of progression, Curse of the Dead Gods delivers a feeling of learning something every run. Each time you progress further in the temple, each time you avoid curses better, you experience yourself improving and rising up the the challenges ahead. I fully recommend this game! Enemy movement and attack patterns are fairly basic, easy enough to learn and avoid, but I have yet to master this. I think the real kicker here is Corruption: helpful or hurtful?See, I got my hands on a main weapon that increased damage by how cursed I was, and that was extremely beneficial, but the trap curses are a huge pain. It's got good and bad aspects, I suppose. I don't know how Corruption affects the reward for defeating a Champion because I have yet to successfully do that. Perhaps it's just to add a "moral" dimension to the game: defeat the temple as a pure upright human, or spill your blood for the favor of the unpronounceable ancient ones.EDIT: Completed the first expedition, assumed I was rolling with the same gear, went for the next one and promptly got stomped. On defeating the Champion, you are cleared of all Corruption and resulting curses and get transported back the temple entrance with a good amount of crystal skulls for buying upgrades/perks. Figured out how to parry ranged attacks, timing is key! I think shields are the S++ offhand, they seem incredibly overpowered, plus they can have a chance at auto parry. I barely even mess with getting a heavy weapon, I like the spears the best, but they are just not my speed. I'm picking up the basics slower than I'd like but that fault is my own. _childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods has a lot of great elements to it that will keep you coming back for one more run. Combat feels really good and the diversity of weapons and affixes keep runs fresh while allowing you to tailor each game to your preferred style. The curse meter provides a great risk/reward system.That said, the game is not without issues. Unlike Hades, this game provides a bit more 'exploration' in many of its rooms. Along with a slower base movement speed, this can make runs feel a lot longer than they need to be. At the outset the game can feel like a grind as you struggle through runs to acquire enough resources to unlock some of the better mods, and then at higher levels the game can feel like a slog as you spend time running through the same 'exploration' maps over and over. As I said, combat feels really good - but I feel like there is a disconnect between enemy actions and the parrying window which can lead to a lot of frustration. At higher levels this will likely have you watching mouth agape as a masterful run comes crashing down for seemingly no reason. Likewise, due to the slower base movement speed, a lot of enemy attack spam and a slowly regenerating stamina gauge, you can and will find yourself overwhelmed and see your entire life pool lost in moments. While this may be in the spirit of the genre, due to the nature of the tools you are provided, this often times just leaves you feeling robbed.The game is absolutely worth it if you like Hades and want something slightly different. It can take a bit too long to unlock many of the more interesting weapons and mods, exploration is tedious, and combat can be frustrating, but the core of the game is very solid and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I ALMOST want to give this a thumbs up. There is a lot about this game that is really good:  - Good enemy scaling  - Clear visuals for enemy attacks (many isometric games suffer with poor projectile sprites making them difficult to see)  - Great aesthetic  - Interesting game mechanics   - I-Frames hnnngggg  - Curse System that acts as benefits and negatives and is overall an interesting concept  Unfortunately, in regards to the Curse System, there are a few curses that can really cripple your run. Since they are assigned randomly, you can't really do anything about it other than hope there's a boss nearby so you can remove it. For this reason I am giving this game a thumbs down as the curses that nerf your Stamina can end your run. It seems that these curses, especially Dark Swiftness, are VERY common, as I get this curse almost every run. The following curses should be removed or adjusted, in my opinion:  - Dark Swiftness (Perfect Dodges no longer regenerate stamina)  - Deadly Obsession (Maximum Stamina is reduced by one)In more detail:  There is a Stamina System with 5 pips that is shared with your attack and your dodge. Your Stamina is the only thing that allows you to stay alive as simple footwork and positioning is insufficient to dodge enemy attacks in this game. Your Stamina is a limited resource and you need to manage it constantly or take damage.  The amount of pips consumed with your attacks varies with your weapons; sometimes multiple attacks per pip and sometimes 2 pips for a charged attack with the hammer. Dodging costs 1 pip, but with a perfect dodge, you are refunded the Stamina. You can also parry most enemy attacks and that will return 2 Stamina.  Against bosses and large groups of enemies, especially high HP ones, you have to maintain a good rotation of dodging, Stamina regen, and combo. A couple bosses have health regeneration which can be mitigated, but requires DPS in order to stop.   Even removing a single pip of Stamina, your ability to output any significant damage is almost crippled against a Boss. For instance:  When using the spear (objectively the best weapon in the game), your combo requires 3 pips (attack, attack, finisher). Assuming you had to dodge to position yourself or escape damage for your combo you might then use 3 pips to attack, leaving 1 pip to dodge when the Boss wants to attack. If you get perfect dodges, then you have extra Stamina to output damage. Most bosses have multiple attacks and/or come with additional enemies that you also need to dodge, where you may start your attack with even less Stamina.By removing a point of Stamina or your ability to perfect dodge (this is the worst option), your damage output has been almost halved because of the lack of finisher. At the highest temples, where there are more enemies, who hit harder, and have much more HP, the pacing becomes drastically more difficult with less Stamina.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of potential, but the developers took the old route of artificially increasing the difficulty. I am about 90% complete in the game and I have beaten several other rouge-likes/lites. However, it has been a while since I've seen a rogue-like that so blatantly restricts what the player can do to make the game more difficult. Almost every action you take consumes stamina however, the enemies are not so restricted. Indeed often they will attack continuously until you run out of stamina and are forced to take a hit. Further, stamina does not recharge when you are taking hits so it is easy to get locked into place and have half of your health bar wiped out in seconds. And god forbid if the first attack applies a DOT, losing 500+ health to being on fire while you are stun locked by multiple enemies is highly likely; for context you start each run with 1,000 health and on a good run can maybe max out at 3,000. Additionally, enemy hits stun lock you for significantly longer than your hits stun them if they do at all, because sometimes the enemies can just power through you heavy attacks which are supposed to stun them. Enemies can also smoothly transition from attack to defense while you are locked in place after each combo for long enough to take several hits. To be clear when I say they smoothly transition I mean that there is a boss who will doge your attack, move behind you and hit you before you finish swinging your weapon. So, for those who say that parrying is the answer I am interested in how you parry a dodge counter that occurs before you finish swinging. Dodge rolls also have a tendency to move you into attacks regardless of the direction you aim them. And in a similar vein I have noticed that the character's feet seem stuck in mud when trying to move out of an aoe attack. Not that moving out of the attacks area will help you as being near the attack is good enough to take damage in this game.Games like rouge legacy (1&2), Dead Cells, and Skul among others all reward you for getting better. This game doesn't in fact it seems to punish you by making things even more unfair, not harder more unfair. You want to put a half dozen elites in a room fine, but I shouldn't be forced to take crippling damage due to bad mechanics. Other games also encourage multiple play styles through their mechanics while this game seems to be trying to force one play style. All these things combine for a game that feels far more frustrating than fun. I just don't want to drag myself through 20 more hours of trying to get the right combination of items and luck to even have a chance at seeing the final boss. Especially when I consider that, given the mechanics of this game, the last boss fight will likely entail me having a single stamina point and an enemy which moves too fast to see. Because that's how this game increases difficulty by limiting the player and super charging the enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice roguelite, combines mechanics a la Slay the Spire or Hades to choose your next room rewards. Pretty hard to master, parry window for example is super tight but it gives great rewards (weakens, doesn't cost stamina, combos with lots of stuff) while dodging is easier but costs stamina. Emphasis on fast combat to chain kills to regain stamina on kill and keep your greed chain going to maximise gold from kills. You can decide 3 starting relics to plan your build. At the moment, it seems like there's 4 difficulties, 1 level more everytime, 1 more boss everytime. Planning your build ahead and making sure you can survive a lot of different battles (not a whole lot of healing outside of relic combos which are not always available). Curses given every so often are often beneficial and you can use them to your advantage. Some are straight up always bad but working around them is not as hard as it seems. Killing a boss removes a curse also so if you keep your corruption to a minimum and only from room changes (some ennemies give you corruption on hit), you should be fine.Combat is super rewarding, combos are super rewarding. Played with a controller and it was very tight controls, you cannot interrupt some slow attacks with dodges but I'm sure that's wanted behaviour.You should buy this if you like combat like Hades (but slower),  decision making like Slay the Spire or FTL and difficulty of Salt Sanctuary in the combat a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: I find myself playing this game excitedly and walking away with a big "oh, well, I guess that's it", even after a winning run.The game's theme and visuals are like if the surface elements of Darkest Dungeon were used to suck out the joy from Indiana Jones. This game's curses are totally random and often come with upsides and downsides simultaneously. This makes sense for a game with a single player character instead of a party, but none of them are as interesting as the afflictions in Darkest Dungeon which drip in theme and feel like a part of a character's story. Also, there's no narrator and the game's flavorless. I don't know why they cribbed Darkest Dungeon so hard without trying.The action game elements are quite good, however. It's got stamina and dodge rolls and parries, but the attack wind-ups aren't nearly as long or deceitfully animated as other Souls-inspired indie games, so it's tolerable. You've got attacks that pierce, charge ahead, interrupt foes, act as offensive dodges... Surrounded, you can charge an attack from your claws to slide behind the group--the perfect vantage point for a cone of pistol-fire to knock them back and reclaim the advantage...It's a shame the procedural generation doesn't push the combat, however; there are few emergent situations. Pretty much all the equipment in the game deals 1 of 3 statuses or has some special effect boiling down to "do more damage" based on things you would do with any weapon, like performing perfect dodges or collecting relics. Each biome has its own monopoly on enemy types and traps, so the only encounters that stand out are when you get a room of mostly all the same enemy and have to grind down a room littered with AoE circles. Basically, all the rooms are just trap-filled corridors leading to battle arenas, so there aren't any MEMORABLE rooms; it's all a gray sludge. So, why is it a roguelite? Why not just make a beat-em-up with tighter level design and NG+ difficulties?Oh, and that's another thing: this game's hard mode isn't very interesting. Enemies hit harder, elites are slightly faster, and heals are harder to find. It doesn't give enemies new moves or apply sideways conditions like Ascensions or Pacts of Punishment. The final dungeon in each difficulty setting shuffles the biomes and features mini-bosses... but when you clear that, it's back to vanilla dungeons for the next difficulty. Again: why a roguelite? What about this game is meant to unfold as I play?Think of this as a hack-and-slashy beat-em-up with a satisfying moveset and get out after you beat the final temple on default difficulty, because while the core of it is fun to keep playing, it leaves me vaguely unsatisfied.
