_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the dead gods is a game that delivers exactly what it promises at the store page - some of the best top-down brawler style combat i have ever experienced. It feels EXTREMELY good - despite not having a combo system, it nonetheless allows me to pull off combo attacks and fancy footwork that would make any Devil May Cry protagonist green with envy.If i were to compare COTDG with any other games i have played, that would be Hades and Children of Morta. COTDG is much smaller in scale and scope, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing - it's a very quick game that gets straight to the point and respects your time in doing so. "Compact" and "responsive" are the words that immediately come to mind. It looks great, it feels great. My only complaint is that it... Doesn't necessarily sound great. Don't get me wrong, the sound effects are perfect. It's the music that unfortunately pulls it down a little bit - or rather, the lack of it. There IS a soundtrack, but it's so utterly forgettable you hardly even notice it's there most of the time. It works for learning the game and keeping a cool head, but it also leaves something to be desired - especially for boss battles, where a little hype and excitement can only add to the experience.I absolutely recommend this game, but do yourself a favour - mute the in-game music in the settings menu, open up youtube and find the Dead Cells OST or Caveblazers OST when you play. (OST means original soundtrack.)

_childDocuments_.review: I used to like this game. It was difficult. I couldn't get pass the second last trial so I waited for a patch to hopefully make it easier.But nope. They made it harder. In the name of balancing, the cheese regain hp based on % of crit damage dealt relic and gold on combo blessing got nerfed; useless weapons got buffed (but are still useless), more relics got added (decreasing the chance of getting a specific relic).There are already insufficient viable options (which require heavy RNG to get too) for the later trials. The update just made it much worse. The only thing that made the game easier is the Assist mode. Oh and it disables any future achievements on that save slot. A real middle finger for those wanting to get all achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The strongest side of this game is the implementation of the theme. The darkness, the old gods, the traps, the corruption... Everything fits very well with the style and the gameplay.On top of that, the gameplay itself is very solid. It's fast and responsive. Also, looking for the right relics and weapons to make yourself stronger is very fun. Most upgrades are simple but can make a massive difference when used the right way.In my opinion, it's not quite as good as a game like Hades because all the upgrades are simple and don't do anything more than your weapons already did but it's the next best thing. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, visceral, satisfying game. You can see the devs are really working hard with the project. Initially, it seemed like the tiles keep repeating over and over, but it's gotten better and better with every patch, and the variety now is at a pretty good level. I think there still could be a bit more enemy variety (add 2 new mobs per each "biome") instead of just MORE enemies on the screen. But the game is really fun, and the mechanics seem fleshed out. Solid recommendation from me!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, i really do. But as of right now it all feels incredibly shallow.It honestly feels like the devs focused on slapping together a bunch of things already proven to sell well, but forgot to add any REAL depth to it. The difficulty feels arbitrary, the curses only half make sense and the system of "If you reach max curse you just kind of go on a death timer" seems incredibly lazy. The enemies all seem really cool, until you realize that most of them (bosses included) do exactly two things to the most of bland predictability. The combat system itself is well done, even if half the weapons are copy pasted from Hades. The stamina bar seems like a good idea in theory, but heavily punishes animation canceling, which is a very core concept in these types of games. If i attack wind up cancel into a dodge roll animation, i shouldnt suddenly not be able to move for a couple seconds. Again, this is part of arbitary difficulty. The graphics themselves also feel very Stolen, taking heavy inspiration from a genre thats been popping up recently in steam for its artwork. Its quality is fine, but thats it. Just fine. All in all, i really feel like like this game would of been really good if the devs had taken the time and tried to put love and effort into it, and made it more unique. As of right now, it feels like a high quality rip off.Maybe in the future it will be good, but for now 6/10 buy it on a big sale if you need to waste time.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I usually wait until I have more experience with a game before leaving a review, but it's early access so I feel like giving early impressions is fair. CotDG has some of the most satisfying top-down combat I've seen in ages; every kill is so wonderfully cathartic you get lost fulfilling the urge to wail on an enemy until they crumble under the weight of your machete, mace, two-handed spear, bow and arrow...the list of weapons goes on and on, and though they won't necessarily change your play style in the way that Dead Cells would, this game seems happy to let some weapons feel like copies of others given that the stat variations are the core of what you're trying to build on each run. Some weapons might give you a stat boost if they're equipped in the off-hand slot, but only if your primary weapon is a mace, forcing you to narrow your stat construction based on what will give you the most immediate advantage, given that (so far) runs don't seem to last long. Once you get used to the ranges of weapon attacks and lunges, learn to parry (holy S H I T is the parry ever satisfying when you get it right), a certain kind of momentum begins to develop without any sort of "practice" beyond simply playing the game and having fun until it becomes second nature. This game is NOT about grinding, which I support through and through. Each run feels fresh and leaves you wondering what curses you will be stricken with that force you to adapt and overcome the odds. The balance between gold management and curse adoption hasn't shown its true nature, as I haven't progressed into the longer, more challenging tombs, but even in the early game you may spend a few seconds carefully counting your gold, making assumptions about your curse level, hoping those choices benefit you down the line. Some of the curses are overbearing in their difficulty. One particular makes the enemies invisible as long as they're in shadow, which isn't too harsh on its own, but pair it with the purple torch curse (devs, I'm sorry, I promise I'll learn the names soon) which forgoes the comfort of a familiar flame and replaces it with a dim, chilling purple light that does little to nothing to help your vision. Even with these in tandem, my run, however difficult, was more of the more memorable ones I had in my first hour of play. Nothing feels tedious or arduous in its implementation; each mechanic is a piece of a larger puzzle seeking to assist the other pieces in creating one of the most enjoyable, addicting games I have played in the last few months.I almost don't want to mention that it's an early access game, due to it's quality in comparison to a lot of others in its field, but the game itself isn't shy in reminding you. There is a grayed out skills tab before you enter the tombs for a run that is literally labelled "WIP", which I have to assume means "work in progress". The devs aren't trying to hide the lack of polish, and instead invite you to join them in the early stages and watch this wonderful game improve itself in the coming months, or years. Let's hope for the latter!My biggest complaint stems from the lack of graphics options. I generally play AAA games on my PC and use my (admittedly outdated) laptop to play less demanding titles. Even a game like this, where the textures are far from the focus, I found that I had consistent frame drops and tiny little bouts of lag that removed the immersion. While in the heat of combat, however, your focus shifts so wildly form one enemy, to a ranged attack, to a giant swinging hammer rushing in from behind you, that I would sincerely not notice the frame drops. The moments of calm are where they stand out; such as transitioning between doors or approaching an undiscovered catacomb, but again, I am willing to assume that my laptop is the glaring issue here. I would be thrilled if more graphical options existed so I could fine tune my setting to get the maximum frames possible. Whether it's more in-depth AA options (anti-aliasing is either ON or OFF, no gray area), options to downgrade shadows or foliage, or anything in between. I can't wait to get home and see how i runs on my rig, but I can't imagine there will be any issues to speak on. More of a suggestion to mull over for people who may only have laptops such as mine. Only other issue is that there is a clear lean towards controller support. I personally prefer MnK for anything that isn't racing, fighting, or sports based, and this game doesn't seem to adapt as well to MnK. Dodging is ALWAYS a gamble; your brain knows it has moved the cursor to the left, but as long as the character is still in the process of physically turning around, he will roll in the direction HE IS FACING. This is a glaring flaw in a top-down hack n' slash, as this game is fast paced and leaves zero time available to watch your protagonist slowly do a 180 when you're spamming the roll button hoping he gets out in time. Perhaps this is intentional, to force slower, more methodical gameplay, but much like the Estus flask mechanic in DS2 that restricted movement while consuming, it feels out of place with the heart of the game. I would like to be able to roll in any direction, which is clearly possible since, when stationary, the direction you face does not impact the direction of your dodge. Might be intentional, but I see it as a poor mechanic that only serves to agitate the player when ♥♥♥♥ starts hitting the fan. Folks, this game is on for $15.99 right now, and I can't give it anything other than the highest of recommendations. It's easy to pick up, hard to master, and a hell of a lot of fun. Cannot wait to see what comes next, but I know it'll be good.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: CotDG is absolutely amazing. From the constant pressure to make game-altering decisions to the incredibly fluid and fast-paced combat system, you won't find yourself bored at any moment of this game. I've been streaming it for a week straight now and have never felt as though there were moments that dragged on, choices that were inconsequential, or fights that did not require mindfulness. Great job Passtech! 10/10 from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very fun to play. The combat feels very satisfying as you land hits or dodge, there is an emphasis when an enemy dies and it just feels very satisfying. Pay enough attention to the combat and you could potentially make it through the temple without taking any hits, easier said than done. The curse mechanic is fun because it adds strange depths to the temple and the fights.The weapon variety is underwhelming. There are quite a few different weapons, but I found myself favoring just a couple if I could get my hands on them. Not sure if that's a personal bias, or that I just wanted the ones that had consistently more damage/perks than others.That said, it is still early access so there isn't much variety in the enemies and the combat, I do know the devs are still working to expand the game. I have 20 hours played at time of writing this and I've enjoyed every minute, worth the $15 price tag(considering I regularly pay that amount or more for a 2 hour movie theatre experience). And I do plan to come back and play more as new things are added/and opt in for beta.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Very high quality rouge like game. If you draw closes comparison - it would be Hades. Slower paced, more methodical, more cautions Hades. Yet this game still manages to put you on the edge of the seat sometimes (Especially final boss).I love the aesthetics, graphical style and design choises. The game mechanics are well executed and the game itself plays pretty well,Enemy design is nice, but i personally found some absolutely obnoxious god awful enemies for myself, however, their destign still was good. It gets a bit repetitive once you get used to it, and it does not provide an absolute abundance of content, however it will take you around 50 hours to max out all the contents, it took me 17 hours to beat the game to it's logical end, i don't really want to max out all the content.It was well worth it, it was good fun and left very good impression, i recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Unforgiving and difficult action roguelike with both familiar and some unique mechanicsImagine if you played Hades, but instead of greek gods helping and loving you.You're playing as a greedy bastard and aztec gods are dead and curse and hate you.The environments hates you, RNG curses you, everything wants you very dead, as they should cause you're plundering their temples.Now while this game started out pretty fun it became uninteresting and boring pretty fastAfter the intro, no story, no dialogue ever, no characters, you're just a greedy nobody plundering temples.Runs become very samey while heavily relying on RNG to get some good stuffBosses are pretty lackluster and one of the bosses was a lame DPS check.Rogue lite mechanics but pretty limited and a bad boring progression.The temples, monsters, traps and curses become annoying, not difficult. It becomes a slog through the same stuff and gets really old.Lack of variety and viability, most weapons are just kind of bad and useless and force you to only use the 'good' ones, if you can get them.It got some interesting mechanics and pretty satisfying combat going for it, but that's about it too.I don't recommend it over many of the other fantastic rogue-likes/lites, there's way too many better ones out there than this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This would have been a good game if it didn't exist in the same world as Hades - which is too bad, since I think it owes most of its existence to Hades. The Corruption mechanic is pretty fun, I like the different weapon sets you get, but the tedious enemies and the horrendously clunky dodge rolling, especially coming from Hades' quick rapid-fire dashes, work together to sap the joy from the game. The relics you pick up here are less exciting to get than even Hermes' boons in Hades - and Hermes' boons were terrible.If you really like the genre, or if you have some sort of vendetta against Supergiant Games, maybe you'll like this anyways. It does have some cool ideas, it's just that the basics aren't well-done enough to really make it stand out.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: where to start.. this game is the perfect mix of challenging combat and rewarding Gameplay that pushes you to learn from the mistakes you made so that you may triumph in future challenges that this game presents, its an easy 9/10 for me! if you are a glutton for punishment and live for fighting foes much stronger than you then this is the game for you! i cant recommend this enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great and most of the weird or broken issues seem to have disappeared with the patches as they come out. This game is not finished and gets updates very regularly all of which help further the balance and boost the game without wrecking the overall challenge. The mechanics, the atmosphere of the levels, the style, everything here is top notch. The curse system is cool, taking damage or paying for a weapon or stat boost etc incurs corruption (unless you pay in gold gathered along the way). Once the corruption meter fills you gain a curse. Curses change the game or abilities of the Character which in turn affect combat, stats, abilities, or the game world. Some are as much of an obstacle as a they are a helpful tool. An example would be one curse gives you extra damage in the light but if you take damage any light source nearby will be snuffed out, this is a neat double edged sword. Lots of potential here and it has a great mix of style and mechanics, and seems well thought out. looking forward to the addition of the last temple and new weapons. This just keeps getting better and better with time, so pick it up asap.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy this game, the idea is wonderful. What I do not enjoy is the performance. It is laggy sometimes in normal rooms, but certain bosses are just awful. When the witch throws her skulls or the jaguar elementar burns the floor my fps drop low and it feels like a stun, leading to free damage or a lot of corruption. Pls add an option to lower graphics on effects (since these effects seem to be an issue). Games with comparable graphics never caused any issues. With this fixed I´ll change my review to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

It's just code.2 hrs played, refund requested.  Simply wasn't fun.The viewpoint with that control system is just frustrating.There are games that do what this tries to do much better, and yes, they work great with mouse/keys.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game had potential, but bad design choices accumulated as I progressed. Early stages were fun, but the difficulty increased as I hit the progression ceiling outside of runs. Later stages depended on having a god seed, making it frustrating. Runs varied wildly, from quick clears to hour-long slogs. Overall, the game was disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Overall good. Plays relatively tightly, and gives a rewarding feedback loop as you advance. Unfortunately, many mechanics designed to reward skillful play are rendered meaningless when the entire run can be decided in the first three rooms with a simple question.Did you get a Hammer/Titan Slayer from the first weapon room you found?If not, start the run over because you're going nowhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Love it!I'm bad at the game, so the first ~hour was quite frustrating. I don't know what it was, but something made me keep on playing. Once I plugged in a controller and got past the first boss I had a blast.Really curious on what's coming in the future.Also nice to see some balancing patches on weapons and relics. Some were obviously way overperforming while others were landing a little short.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The game play here is fine, it's ok, but it's not good, it over relies on parries to make the game fun because of the stamina system but then goes ahead and make dodges better to use overall so you'll probably end up dodging more and not enjoying the combat as much.  Biggest thing that turns this into a Not Recommend for me is the the light and dark mechanics because if you're playing in places with glare you're kinda screwed because the game doesn't have a Brightness/Contrast/Gamma setting that I could find so I was just out of luck to playing this during daytime since I couldn't see almost anything on screen.  The use of three weapons that can all be melee or ranged feels very weird.  All the weapons are locked into these three slots but the slots don't really make sense when they all can be anything.  The weapons are also really unbalanced, some are just better than others which is not fun.  There is no story, which I guess may be ok for you, but just seems kinda lame here for some reason because this game feels like it could have added something pretty easily.  The items you find kinda suck and the economy to get them doesn't make sense.   In most roguelites like this you want to go to places where you can find new weapons or upgrades, but here you don't want to bother because most of the time they just aren't worth it.  The corruption systems is interesting but occasionally just breaks your run if, let's say, you have a build that works with you abusing Perfect Dodge mechanics but then you get a curse that takes this mechanic away, that's just not fun and this mechanic would benefit from getting curse "options" when you're cursed or easier to get curses but also easier to get rid of them.  Overall if you get this on sale for $5 you'll play it probably 3-4 times and then drop it so if that's worth $5 to you, go for it.  Definitely don't buy it at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the most satisfying combat of any game I've ever played, words won't describe just how impactful and fluid it feels.  This game was actually the first Rogue / Roguelite game I've ever played and it sucked me in.  I started binging so many games, but this one calls me back each night.  I love the visuals, sounds, progression and the greed system.  Having to choose how greedy you want to be, offering blood and gaining corruption for that sweet piece of gear and getting curses.  It's a wonderful system.  The amount of excitement I get when I try new weapon combos just makes me have to play another round.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Yet again another great rogue-like ruined by poor balancing.  This game is decent if I don't compare it to Hades.  I want to like it.  I've invested the time.  Unfortunately, the devs ramped up the later game difficulty arbitrarily in order to pad their content.  Once you hit the third tier, each run is well over 30 minutes.  You cruise along through all the rooms of the first two sections where only 2 to 3 elites spawn.  Learning to deal with that is challenging, and it requires patience and kiting to manage 2 elites.  The amount of kiting and/or parrying required is just borderline enough to keep it fun once you have enough practice.  , once you hit two or three rooms before the third boss, the game spawns practically nothing but elites.  It is an abrupt and major jump in difficulty that becomes a kiting-fest.  I'm sure some people will reply with "get gud."  This isn't Dark Souls.  The game designers did not provide the level of content to  the difficulty ramp that requires this many repeat runs to progress.   There's maybe content for a 20-ish hour game, so I'm guessing this is a case of playtime padding.  Fix the difficulty ramp, and I'll switch to a thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Comparing this game to Hades, it is like heaven and hell, whereby Hades is the heaven. The game fighting mechanic is so clunky and weak comparing to Hades. After just played for 2.6 hours, I kind of lost interest with it already. Every attack feels weak and slow, it is difficult to dodge/parry enemy attacks. Weapons are not very interesting. No storyline at all, and this make me appreciate Hades even more. After you died, you felt exhausted and do not feel like wanting to play one more round.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. A straightforward and streamlined rogue-lite with enough challenge to keep you on your toes for a while.At the ~25 hour mark got to the final temple, at which point all that was left to do was grind some unlockables and achievements.LE: after grinding said unlockables and achievements, I discovered that after defeating the "final temple", you get to unlock a hard mode where you get to do the same thing (3 basic temples and then combined ones with all the bosses) all over again, but with more enemy hp and damage and less heals.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Expect punishment, if you're ok with that then proceed with the purchase. If you don't get frustrated with roguelike and don't mind dying a lot, then the game is for you. It took me a lot to finish the first encounter with the last boss then right after the game unlocked several other levels (supposedly called "hard" mode). As for me the game was enough difficult already and I didn't play these other levels, killing the last boss once was fine for me. The game is all about "git gud", everytime you die is because you did a poor choice or your reflexes failed you.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very 50-50 on this game. I hate I can't post a rating, rather than a limiting yes or no recomendation. Honestly, for a rouglike game this is good and original, but the game has some problems. First the hitboxes are unclear, for both the benefit of the player and the enemies, the hitboxes seem a little larger than the indicators, this is especially seen with the grenade weapons, and on many enemies attacks. Secondly, the RNG aspect. Yes I realise it's a rouglike game. But some situations which happen rather often are plain demoralizing and make you not want to paly the game. Let me give you one example. If you fight the  jaguar god avatar, if the outer part of the arena is on fire and you fight him in melle in the middle of the part not lit by fire, if he uses a self explison attack, if he is in the right spot, he will completely cover the safe part of the arena, making you take a guaranteed HUGE ammount of damage, from either his explosion or the fire on the outer edges of the arena. This is just one example. The imbalance of some curses, with the imbalance of ranged and melle weapons against most enemies. These seems no real incentive for you to use anything other than a bow or a thorwing knife. It's extremely safe and just as damaging. It's a huge differce fighting a boss like the witch on the caverns (the first boss of the toxic area). Every time you hit her, she drops a curse skull that explodes after a very short delay at her feet. Needless to say, this boss is extremely easier to fight with ranged weapons. But despite these issues the game is good. But I feel the team stopped caring for balance at some point. The extreme handicap you give yourself by simply not using a bow or a throwing weapons is probably the largest problem, since melle combat is so cool and well made, but so objectivelly inferiour to using a bow. Apologies for the bad English. I really hope the devs do some tweaks on this game. These shouldn't be difficult tweaks even.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game was incredibly underwhelming and tedious. I Finished the final boss with only having 6 deaths across my entire play through, and completed the final dungeon first try. it took me 10 hours all up but there was really no need for it to be longer than like 5 maybe.There's 3 different dungeon types/environments with their own enemies and boss and traps. however there's also 3 tiers for each dungeon type. When you get to the end of your first dungeon and kill the boss your kicked back to the start but now you've unlocked tier 2, where you have to do all of tier 1 again but now you can go after the second boss. And then would you believe after the second boss you get booted back again but now you've unlocked tier 3 so you now have to do all of tier 1 and 2 AGAIN and then you get to go after the 3rd boss.AND YOU HAVE TO DO THIS FOR EVERY DUNGEON TYPE if you want to have a go at the final "ultimate" dungeon or whatever you want to call it. This is just incredibly tedious when the game is honestly not that difficult and just feels like padding out the game time.The curse mechanic is cool, though i never got to more than 3 curses at a time so I don't even know what the final curse does.I never felt like two handed weapons were worth it as they had long recovery times and the stamina consumption didn't seem great.The light and dark mechanic is cool except lighting torches is such a hassle that I just played the whole game in darkness. the other down side is that Every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dungeon type looks the same except a minor colour change which doesn't matter when its dark the whole time.parrying was never the better option over rolling except maybe in 1 or 2 fights because its not worth taking damage due to how rough healing is (which is a good thing because it encourages you to play better, especially if you in constant darkness where you take 50% more damage)And the final boss was so incredibly anticlimactic. I might have just had a really good build and got lucky but I was super disappointed when I realised that was it.I nearly refunded after my first 2 hours but thought id stick with it after hearing so many good reviews for this but it really didn't live up to the hype at all. Is it a good game? Sure. Is it a must play or really worth your time? I'd honestly say no. Its incredibly repetitive and most of the unique mechanics are easily ignored. There's harder content once the finish the game but none of its new content, just modifiers from the looks of it so I wont be wasting my time with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely not Hades (it set an extremely high bar), but this game's combat is super satisfying!! Very fun moment-to-moment gameplay, and the builds just get wildly creative sometimes, especially late game. This game is also a little bit difficult, and has a small handful of moments where it blatantly feels unfair. Genuinely fun game though!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Conclusion:  Enjoyable game with good atmosphere, but feels like the difficulty progression and elemental powers are imbalanced.  Will be playing for a bit as the pros outweigh the cons.Pros:-Great aesthetic-Controls feel solid-Decent run to run randomization method-Nice weapon variety-Generally funCons:-Too easy for too far into the game including 2nd boss-Final boss is a large jump from rest of the game (but not impossible)-Slogging to practice on the final boss takes a bit too long after the rest of the lead up becomes trivial-Elemental power imbalance, fire far stronger than poison and lightning / Artifacts help fire far more than lightning and poison
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: It's just not for me, the play style, and the Azteca/Mayan look aren't my thing. Also, the whole get the parry down to the .1 second to parry isn't working for me either. I bet it plays better with a gamepad but that's not my style either. I already have many games that are my style I haven't played yet. I'm sure the game will be a success without my money anyway. It is well designed and well polished.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty neat game actually, I love rouge-like games, and this one is pretty good, actually really hard! I am not a fan of daily events, just why tho... Kinda makes you play it almost daily for like an hour, if you are stuck. What I really love, are the curses. They are pretty neat, sometimes they lose you the game, sometimes they are kinda disruptive, and some of them are more like upgrades. Id reccomend this game, it is neat, flavourful and a nice dungeon crawler, what more do you want?
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: It seems as if the animations are way too clunky and there is always a glitchy attack, the enemy slides forward, slides around a wall, my movement staggers, that makes each run not very enjoyable. I am supposed to fight the bad guys, not the client. The combos are not so satisfying either. I love the aesthetics though, this game has a unique atmosphere.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: If we equate making Curse of the Dead Gods to making Voltron:Darkest Dungeon's light vs dark aesthetic, art, and atmosphere would form the head.Dark Souls parry and dodge stamina-based systems would form the arms.Dead Cells' attribute allocations and weapon systems/merchants would form the left leg.Slay the Spire's route map would form the right leg.And the sword would be formed by how awesome it all comes together. Mandatory Stan Lee-esque respect to grand-daddy Diablo for sharing its DNA with all the lions. Extra points for the crisp control scheme, fair mechanics, level of challenge, and the absolute immersion the game draws you into. 9.5/10 would absolutely recommend getting cursed in this temple. Now for more runs...
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Edit ; changed from No to Yes some months later. I'm giving it a try every few patchs. Game still not astounding and most cons remain but improvements are made. It's just that after every run I ask myself "shouldn't I play [random famous roguelite] instead ?" And the answers is always yes. CotDG just isn't for mePros : Very Good DA and Interesting system of ligh and darkness.Cons : gameplay is clunky, dogde and parry windows are fuzzy, AI telepgraph are unreliable, most weapons animation lock you. Combat doesn't feel good for me.Roguelite aspects are meh. _childDocuments_.review: this game just doesn't feel good to play. the bad stuff way outweighs how good any of the items or rewards you get are - it's like the game was originally made by a bunch of trolls who made curses, traps, and debuffs first...then tacked on weapons, relics, and buffs later. seems like way more thought was put into how to screw your character over than was put into how to build your character to confront said challenges. everything hurts you - from using a healing well to opening the very first door to start a run. even the good rooms have items that must be paid for - either by gold or by - you guessed it - hurting yourself. don't get me wrong, i don't dislike this because it makes things more difficult, it's more that it just makes every event in the game stressful - including events that are supposed to be rewarding. every good moment is instead an "oh, right. but there's this too..." and a lot of times the "this too" part is far worse than the benefit is good.let me put it like this: if you're the kinda person who can know your phone is at 5% battery and not be bothered by it throughout the day, you probably won't have the same issues i had with this game. however, if that feeling irks you and makes you think about when you'll have a chance to charge it, when it'll die, if you'll miss that important call you're waiting for, etc...the design concept of this game may just stress you the hell out.

A variety of weapons, maps, enemies and bosses give this game a high replay value. What sets CotDG apart from all other rogue-like games is its moment to moment game play. _childDocuments_.review: I haven't played long but it's a rogue-like so you can tell instantly whether it's going to be good or bad, and I think it's very good. I've read the reviews about there being little content and I can see that, at least in terms of weapons etc. This isn't a game like enter the gungeon or Isaac where there's a million different combinations and weapons coming out your butt, but there's enough. I'm going to compare it to Hades a lot since it's clear that Hades influenced this a lot. If you haven't played Hades it doesn't matter but if you haven't played a roguelike/lite before then you need to know what you're getting into as these are not for everyone. It's a basic loop of run, die repeat. Roguelikes have a fair amount of RNG in them and it's about making what you get work. I like Hades but to me the game had a lack of variety, again, speaking weapon types. Of course in Hades you pick your weapon and get to upgrade it as you progress, whilst I like games that give you some control over what you're going to use, I don't get the same satisfaction as having a run and getting a great combination and having that "just one more run" feel and CotDG's addresses this issue due to the randomness of the weapons. F.Ex there's a few weapon types in Hades I just don't enjoy, so I won't ever be willingly picking them whilst in this, you get forced to make the most of what you're given, which makes it more interesting. Aesthetically, it looks very much like Hades, but in my opinion somewhat better as Hades can get quite "messy" with the amount of stuff on your screen. The art of the enemies, characters and weapons are up there with Hades and I might say even better at times, but it doesn't have the polish that supergiant gives. Rooms tie together nicely and the procedurally generated rooms do look nice, if somewhat repetitive. Sound is fine, there's some nice weapon hits and ambient sounds. No voice that I have heard. Music is, well, there. It's atmospheric and fits the scene but it's nothing to write home about. This is where supergiant shines over Passtech, their music and voice acting is superb and has a lot of impact to their titles. It's certainly not bad here but I think so many developers lack the understanding at just how much sound plays a part in gaming, especially so for roguelikes/lites due to their repetitive nature. Gameplay is good. Weapons have Oomph and impact. Combat is fluid and tight. Hades is decent as well but I think this game outshines it here. I also like the slay the spire/pathway style "choose your path" which Hades has somewhat but this is done much better. Curses are good as well, unlike deadcells where a curse puts you on edge and can screw up your run in a single hit, this is more like "Oh, that ain't so bad" and lets you take risks. I enjoy this game a lot so far and I hope I can have the same longevity with this as I have other Roguelikes

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is a fantastic game, especially if you like banging your head against a wall.One cannot help but notice its similarity with Hades; the two games feel like siblings. A god of the dead who revives you, letting you make yet another run through his domain. Amazing visual design incorporating aesthetics of a long-lost culture, as well as immersive sound design which makes hitting stuff rewarding. Difficulty that cranks up every time you successfully finish a run, but satisfyingly so. The comparison of the two games is overdone, however it is also apt and accurate, and I believe it is a compliment for any game to be compared to arguably one of the best rogue-likes ever, even one of the best games ever.The game incorporates several features, that lend to its style. The explorer accumulates curses that modify the gameplay over the run, there is a darkness/light mechanism that blends the combat an exploration, a lot of weapons to find and switch to, elemental attacks and traps, and so on. None of them are groundbreaking on their own, but there are a lot of ways that these features interact, so that every run retains some spicyness. There are some balance issues, but they do not detract too much from enoying the game.After playing for ~140 hours, I was often excited to enter the temple, sometimes furious after a death, but never too bored to play. Get it, it is a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: I tend to avoid Early Access releases, but this is one I was a bit excited for. It comes from Passtech Games, the same studio that did Masters of Anima a couple years back. I enjoyed my time with that game and gave it a good review, so I was interested in seeing how their newest game would shape up.So right off the bat, Curse of the Dead Gods is already a massive visual improvement over Masters of Anima. It takes the same overhead camera approach, but with much cleaner visuals. There's a nice amount of detail, great coloring, and some excellent use of lighting, which is a definite plus considering that lighting plays a huge role in the gameplay.The gameplay plays pretty much like any other roguelite. You work your way through randomized dungeons, picking up loot and slaying monsters along the way. This is done using a number of different weapons, including swords, guns, hammers, etc. The game has this cool multi-weapon combat mechanic, allowing you to seamlessly string together combos using multiple weapons. You can start by slapping an enemy with a sword a couple times and then finish them off with a blast to the face from your gun, it's a very satisfying mechanic to play around with. You can even throw in a few dodge rolls and parries in the middle of that.In fact, the game encourages this kind of combat, as your stamina decreases with each move, so there will come a point when you have to dodge an attack. It becomes a balancing act of doing as much damage as possible, but keeping enough stamina to dodge attacks. The result is some very satisfying combat, with hits that actually feel impactful, and movement that doesn't feel clunky in the slightest.And on the topic of balancing acts, the game's exploration and loot could also be described as such. Every time you enter a new area, you gain curse points, which (once they reach a certain amount) add a new curse to your playthrough. These can include hallucinations on taking damage, traps that automatically activate, or enemies that spawn additional enemies when killed. Ideally, you want to avoid getting these curses, but you can also pay for weapons and upgrades by cursing yourself instead of paying gold. Again, a balancing act. It's a very cool system and makes for some pretty fun exploration.As for the game's performance, I didn't encounter any major issues there. It looks great and runs fine at 1440p and 155fps. I didn't run into any frame drops, crashes, or even glitches and bugs during my time with the game. Given that many Early Access games release with all sorts of these problems, I have to give the devs some credit here. I was a bit disappointed that the graphical settings are as limited as they are, but hopefully this is something we can see improved with time. Some better anti-aliasing outside of FXAA would be a great start.And when it comes to controls, I also found no problems there. The game offers fully remappable keyboard controls and full controller support. The latter is the recommended option and the one I went with, as it felt better to play with than the keyboard and mouse option.Outside of that, the one major complaint I have with the game would be its lack of content. Of course, this is an Early Access game, so I can't say that I didn't expect it, but it should be noted regardless. Although the weapons, upgrades, and enemies that are there are good, I did grow tired of seeing the same thing over and over after playing the game for a few hours. This even applies to the room layouts, which I started noticing duplicates of not even an hour into the game. Again, these layouts are fine, there just needs to be more of them.With that said, I will be giving Curse of the Dead Gods a light recommendation. It's got some great visuals, fun gameplay, and some nice performance considering it just came out in Early Access. It's definitely a fun game as it is, even if it is a bit light on the content. However, it may be worth waiting for future updates before finally jumping in. The devs have laid out a rather ambitious roadmap for the coming months, so the wait likely won't even be that long.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is an incredibly immersive and entertaining game that kept me engaged for hours on end. The game's unique combination of fast-paced action, challenging gameplay, and stunning visuals makes it a must-play for any fan of the rogue-lite genre.The game's mechanics are well-crafted and intuitive, allowing for seamless gameplay that never feels repetitive. The combat system is particularly satisfying, with a wide variety of weapons and abilities to choose from, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. I found myself constantly experimenting with different strategies and loadouts, which kept the gameplay fresh and exciting.One of the things that sets Curse of the Dead Gods apart from other rogue-lites is the game's emphasis on risk versus reward. Every decision you make in the game has consequences, and it's up to you to decide whether the potential rewards are worth the risks. This adds an extra layer of depth and strategy to the gameplay that I found incredibly engaging.Another standout feature of the game is its stunning visuals. The sound design is also top-notch, with a moody and atmospheric soundtrack that adds to the game's overall sense of tension and unease.In conclusion, Curse of the Dead Gods is an exceptional rogue-lite game that combines challenging gameplay with beautiful visuals and a haunting atmosphere. _childDocuments_.review: (Totally unrelated: I got spoiled rotten by the recently released great early access roguelike games. Hades, Skul Hero Slayer, ScourgeBringer, and now Curse Of The Dead Gods.)Curse Of The Dead Gods is a roguelike dungeon crawler set in ancient Mayan Temples. Players have to battle through hordes of fearsome foes to seek wondrous fortune in the temple of doom, all while avoids getting complete corrupted by the curses lay upon them. The game is only out in early access for a month, but it is surprisingly polished and balanced in terms of development. Even though currently there's only one map to play, I already sink twenty hours and more in this game.This is core feature of the game and it is a ton of fun to play. There are three categories of your weaponry: torch, single-hand weapons and heavy weapons. Torch, is a weapon. Yes, you can finish the game with it if you are feeling extra masochistic and suicidal. Otherwise it's main functions are to illuminate your surrounding, reveal spike traps, and trigger some mechanic for secret chambers. Most of the time you will be using single-hand weapons: swords, clubs, claws in right hand while pistols, shields, daggers in left hand. The aformentioned has its own combo for you to utilize to your advantage. The game also encourages you to combo weapons in both hands to deal critical hits. Three swords slashes with a pistol blast, two hammer smashes with a shield knock-back, claws four scratches with a dagger swipe to distance yourself from foes, and all of this can be mixed up to your own style. Heavy weapons, aka two-hand weapons, are powerful crowd-control tools if used correctly. Their heavy blows disrupt enemies' attack and at the end of combo is a guaranteed critical hit. However, even with all these combos, you are not a tireless killing machine. The game also features stamina system, which does not work as you expect. There are five cubes under you character representing your stamina. It only drains when you dodge, use single-hand weapons combo finishers, and swing the heavy weapons. The system adds another layer to the combat experience. You need to manage your combos as well as learn when to use dodge or outspace enemies for more offensive opportunities.There are two ways to stengthen your characters: blessings and relics. Blessings serve more like situational buff. They reward you with either a permanent buff such as additional health or golds for head-start, or a temporary buff after performing certain actions. I recommend T'amok's Bones, Indomitable, and Divine Perception for beginner. T'amok's Bones gives you additional 250 health to survive longer. Indomitable allows you to take less damage while remaining on the offensive. Divine Perception is great for a better start considering you are more likely to find strong weapons, enabling you to annihilate your foes swiftly. Relics, on the other hands, slightly alter the combat experience and can only be found in the trials: adding additional elemental damage, less gold offering in the shop, or additional points to your Constitution(Health), Dexterity(Weapon damage), Greed(Gold finds), you name it. The most ideal relics to find are "50% to all healing effects" and "Critical hits also heal you 1%". This setup allows you to heal while dispatching foes, considering healing method is quite scarce in this game.Even though you will get cursed no matter what, do not automatically regard this as a bad thing. I serve these curses more like modifiers to your trials. If you can work around them, they can be valuable assets in battles. For example: Dark Swiftness disables your perfect dodge and snuffs out torch effect for a few second, while offering you to destroy enemies' projectiles with dodges. This especially useful for later stages when Sacrificial Virgin fires three shots at a time; Raging Temple activates all the jaguar statues to shoot fire balls. If you can maneuver yourself and the enemies in the correct order, it is possible to complete a room without attacking; Cadaverous Infestation spawns additional enemies when killed. If you have critical-hit-healing relic, this is a good way to replenish your health. There are a handful of curses in the game. They are double-edged swords forced upon you. How you play around these bene-/malediction determines how well you will survive the trials of the dead gods.Healing methods in Curse Of The Dead Gods are scarce and quite situational. Either you defeat a boss to reach healing fountain, get a specific curse that turn gold urns to blood ones, or you are lucky enough to get critical-hit-healing and healing-when-passing-room relics. Now I know the game is quite generous to give you 1000 health as default, 1250 if T'amok's Bones equipped, but at later stages regular mobs hit like a truck, and the golems are more likely to be encountered which are pain in the neck if you do not position yourself correctly. I am proposing to add a mechanic that there`s a chance to drop little health orb when defeating enemies, which heals around 50 or less, neither blessings nor relics. This way can ease the burden for those who are prone to make stupid mistakes(Yes, I am one of those) and those who are poorly equipped at later stages.This is more of a joke than a serious problem. After twenty hours of playing, I am quite tired of this creepy old man's presence.

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods reviewSaw this on sale recently. While not typically interested in roguelikes, the Mesoamerican theming caught my curiosity (more on that in a moment). To call what I found a pleasant surprise would be a massive understatement.Pros: Solid challenging gameplay, stellar level design, creative use of traps, creative weapon/artifact bonuses and synergies, incentivizes tactical thinkingCons: Minor aesthetic details (details below), obnoxious grind for unlockingIf you would, look at my username. I often find myself being approached by other players asking if I play SMITE based on it. While I do have that game in my library, I have never played SMITE (though I may get to it… eventually). No, I have been using this screen name for a long time, long before SMITE was released. This is because I have been fascinated by Mesoamerican cultures since I was a child, have studied them casually and professionally for decades, and have a particular fondness for the Mayan mythical Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque. As someone who has immersed myself in such cultures the way your average weeaboo obsesses about Japan, I have a sharp eye for detail when it comes to such things. (FYI, do NOT get me started on Mel Gibson’s  I could spend hours picking it apart.) Concurrently, I feel that this cultural region is not given the kind of attention/coverage in pop culture and media that it deserves. Usually, when it comes up, it is relegated to a background detail or superficial theme, e.g. temples in the jungle (something I do like on its own, but it could be done better). In particular, one thing that rankles me is the Mayincatec trope (thank you, TVTropes), the all too common conflation of all Central and South American cultures as the same; in actuality, there are worlds of difference between Mesoamerican, Andean (another favorite of mine, but that’s a story for another time…), Amazonian, etc. cultures, and said regions were largely isolated from one another. Consequently, I have a love-hate relationship with the Mayincatec aesthetic.Unfortunately, these issues carry over into games, too. Very few games overtly focus on Mesoamerican themes, and even fewer do it well. A search of the Steam store returned mostly cheap puzzle games with incredibly superficial Mayincatec theming, war strategy games (or Mesoamerican DLC), incredibly basic platformers, lackluster first person shooters, and several unfinished Indie projects too early in production to tell if they really did their homework. Even classic platformers like  and  suffer from this, though at least there the Mayincatec aesthetics make sense because those only cover one of several historical themes of the ruins encountered, and which in La Mulana conspicuously bleed together.Needless to say, my standards going into  were high. I knew that artistic liberties would be taken, and I had little reason to think they would stray beyond mere Mayincatec theming. Imagine my surprise when I found the in-game text consistently speaking in a Mayan dialect. Granted, most of the gods mentioned and their assorted artifacts were fake, but their names followed the linguistic rules of the Maya language families. More than that, the enemy types and bosses fit surprisingly well with themes from Mesoamerican myths and folklore. By and large, the creative choices they made FELT right. It soon became obvious  Words cannot describe how big of a deal that is to me.Theming aside, this game is an absolute blast. As mentioned, I have little experience with roguelikes, so I’m not exactly savvy to the ins and outs of the genre. That said, I’m starting to see the appeal. The constant threat of the curse, the random bonuses of weapons and artifacts, the light and dark mechanics, the pros and cons of sacrificing gold or corruption for that next goody, and solid combat make for a fascinating tactical adventure which is different every run. I haven’t gotten terribly far, but I am having a great time working my way through.In the end, I can only think of a couple extremely minor nitpics. First off, the cost of upgrades is a pain, as grinding for crystal skulls and jade rings is like pulling teeth. Then again, I don’t know enough about roguelikes to compare to other titles, and part of that could just be a consequence of how little I’ve progressed overall in the main game. Second, I have noticed one bit of gratuitous Mayincatec that breaks the otherwise solid Mesoamerican theme:  Specifically, the icon is based on effigies from the art traditions of Peru’s North Coast, and looks specifically Sican or Chimu in style. But, as previously established, I am an autistic pedant about such things, and  in every other detail for me to care much about that.As someone who loves Mesoamerican cultures, the attention to detail of the aesthetics alone would warrant a recommendation from me. The fact it’s an engaging game on its own makes this a must-buy.Buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Imbiamba Jombes had a nightmare!I don't have a ton of experience in the rogue-like genre, and I haven't delved into the rabbit hole that is trying to classify all of the sub-categories of it. To my understanding, this game falls under the "rogue-light" subcategory with other titles such as Hades and Dead Cells. I played and enjoyed Hades and find myself comparing Curse of the Dead Gods (CDG) mostly to that. The main gameplay loop is essentially the same, so if you enjoyed Hades, you're likely to enjoy CDG, much like I did. But there are some significant differences, the most significant one being the story. I didn't realize how much the story of Hades added to my enjoyment of the game until I played CDG. The gameplay of both games is unique and well done, but after just 16 hours of CDG, I find myself losing my motivation to play. There are still higher level zones for me to complete, different weapon combinations to try, and a ton of weapons to unlock. I find myself continuing to improve at the mechanics of the game as well, but none of this seems to resonate with me in the same way as Zagreus wanting to get his pop-pop back together with his dear mummy. If nothing else, I learned something about myself playing CDG!As far as gameplay goes, CDG isn't as fast-paced as Hades. but it has a much higher emphases on timing and resource management. In CDG, you really have to plan your route out and focus on item and weapon synergies, as well as manage your curses and money respectively. The synergies between some of the items and weapons are really interesting and compelling and can make you feel like Sun Tzu himself if you manage to maximize them. Also, a key gameplay element of CDG is the parry. I found myself leaning more towards dodging and kiting, but the benefits of mastering the parry are evident. As far as the general aesthetics go, CDG is very well done for what it is. The lighting effect of your torch is compelling and immersive. Navigating the traps in order to find the gold and artifacts made me feel like Imbiamba himself. The music queues when you hit a trap make me really feel like someone is stabbing me. CDG masterfully captures the theme of delving into ancient temples. I really enjoyed CDG and might play it more in the future. It was definitely worth the money for me, even being someone who values story in single-player games.

_childDocuments_.review: Always a good day when I stumble upon an excellent roguelite that I didn't know I had been missing.Good stuff: *gorgeous cell shaded graphics hum along at 144frames on a decent gaming laptop. *Cool exploration, with a fun light mechanic to twist things up a bit. Dangerous, but rarely annoying, traps (and they can help you out in combat). Secret rooms! Good progression opportunities, on the 'lite' side of roguelite- although it is fairly slow going at first. I've only got a handful of hours in, but it's clear that having all of your boons in place is going to make a hefty difference.*Strategic choices and tradeoffs to be made, both in terms of your path through the dungeon (you've usually got a few choices for what type of room to enter), and in terms of whether to take some corruption damage in trade for an item you don't have quite enough gold for. *Corruption eventually builds into a curse, of which you can have up to 5. These are varied, but often include a positive trade-off along with a penalty, which is a fun twist.*Most importantly, Combat! The arsenal that you might stumble across is highly diverse, and more can be unlocked (think Dead Cells). The combat is fast but methodical- there is a high skill ceiling with the parry and perfect dodge mechanics. Not as treacherous as (lord forgive me for the tired comparison) Souls types of games, in that a single mismanagement of stamina won't leave you dead, but with skillful usage of your combat techniques, you're not at the mercy of the RNG of your build to make a good run. The combo system is really good and deserves a mention- weapons are bound to one of three keys, primary, secondary, and two handed (if you have one) each with a charge attack and a standard combination (there are also secondary revolvers and bows, which have their own interesting mechanics). These attacks can be chained, with a charged finisher thrown in at any time, with a few interesting synergies between certain weapon types. It's very cool, and there is a solid tutorial at the very beginning to ensure you've got your basics down.It does have a Hades-like feel to the combat, which is a high compliment, but there are some important differences between the two games in terms of other mechanical comparisons:Unlike Hades, Binding of Isaac, and some others in the genre, you're not going to end up with ridiculous off-the-wall builds and items that allow you to circumvent the main mechanics in favor of your triple-down bid on lightning chains, or whatever. That's not to say that there isn't good diversity and strategic building- there certainly is, but the game rests on its fundamentals and only gets medium-wonky with items.In my opinion, because these fundamentals are so good, this works very well. RNG matters, but you're never going to end a run and feel that you didn't have a chance because of bad luck. Strategic choices around how you pick your path through the dungeon (a la Slay the Spire, for instance), matter more.Pick it up while the EA price is still here! If you like this genre, this is a no-brainer.

It doesn't have its own energy. It doesn't enhance the game, it's just... there. It is so forgettable.- Having a similar gameplay to Hades, the comparison is inevitable. _childDocuments_.review: Right now I can't recommend it. It's fun for a time, but you start to realize that this isn't a roguelike. Sure, there are upgrades you can buy after you've died, but there's only three slots to put them in. You get weapon upgrades that appear in the run and on pedestals you can choose weapon sets to start with from.The problem with this game is that you can't build an overpowered character. It's mostly a skill based game, and it has similar flaws to Enter The Gungeon. Albeit it is possible to become overpowered in Enter The Gungeon through skill and time, it isn't possible in Curse of the Dead Gods. The relics feel very underpowered and often have uncreative effects. The weapon types seem cool at first, until you realize they're basically the same aside from range and charge attacks.I can't say I didn't enjoy this game for a time. But the flaws have become so large in it, and the difficulty curve too annoying for me to say it's "fun." If you like a punishing souls-like, this may be the game for you. But this game is not a roguelike, despite a surface level appearance of being one.

_childDocuments_.review: Most comparable to Hades, but with more planning and knowledge involved with how you approach enemies as opposed to high-octane energy simulation. Personally, I enjoy Curse of the Dead Gods more, but both are good games with similar control schemes. Both are rogue-lites, but whereas Hades as more direct upgrades to Zagreus, Curse of the Dead Gods lets you better control your run (IE: More rerolls, starting equipment selection).For more specific details, it's a top-down action rogue-lite, where your objective is to clear temples, with their own enemies, champions (2 per temple, minibosses), and the avatar. Later, you unlock the final temple, which mixes them together for you to test your knowledge and intuition in a way that's incredibly satisfying. Your expectations of how you handle a situation are consistently challenged by what truly plays out, and your skill progression is especially apparent during these events.You have a stamina bar that is used for finishing moves (the last move in a combo; it does bonus damage) or rolling. Rolling gives i-frames, and if you were to take damage during it, you get your stamina back. Parrying is a much lower window, but costs 0 stamina, refunds 2, and will break armor and stun during certain parts of an enemies attack, making it a much higher payout, with the risk of taking damage.The blessings you choose at the start of a run fit almost any playstyle you can envision in the game. I run one that's based around perfection; if you take no damage, you get bonus damage. If you kill fast, you get bonus damage. It's a snowballing sensation, but also applies a lot of pressure for not making mistakes, and means parries are even more threatening to mess up. The metagame in what blessings you like to run makes even deeper systems in a game that has a decent amount to figure out. The hub allows you to unlock starting weapons, unlock more blessings, get more rerolls (used mid-run), increase the quality of starting weapons, and once starting weapons are unlocked, you can choose to keep or remove them from your runs altogether. If there is a specific weapon you hate, you can remove it. If there is a specific weapon you love, you can remove any others to get down to it. It's up to you what you think your best experience would be.There is a lot of freedom in CotDG, and it plays in its favor. You choose what temple, what weapons to run, what difficulty, etc. There's special modes on rotation, and those have special conditions, and making a blessing set specifically for them makes the game feel more of a sandbox than I initially realized. A lot of games are scared of giving the player this much freedom, but I am very glad that CotDG does.I'd talk about enemy design, but each temple has a lot that plays into it, and the final temple combining them is too much for a Steam review. I'd summarize that figuring them out is necessary to complete the hard difficulties, and mandatory for when they're combined. Simply playing the game is enough to intuitively understand the enemies, and their designs seem meticulous to me; no enemy feels overloaded, or similar, and while some have greater threats than others, all of them fill a void that would be present if they weren't there.Also, collab with Dead Cells, which is a 10/10, means this has to be a 11/10, right?

_childDocuments_.review: I just got the true ending for the game today, so I feel like I have to leave a review now. Curse of the Dead Gods is a very good action roguelike with tight, deliberate combat and a high degree of polish. All the different weapon types feel distinct and are incredibly satisfying to use, thanks in large part to the sound design. As for how they're balanced, I definitely found myself gravitating towards the faster weapons like claws and daggers more, and found the slower ones like heavy weapons and bombs to be far too dangerous to use in the harder missions where Elite enemies are faster, but that could just be a skill issue on my part. I know a lot of people like the heavy weapons a lot, and they are definitely satisfying to use when you can pull them off. In terms of difficulty, the game starts out a bit slowly but once you unlock the hard versions of the temples it gets brutally difficult at times. I struggles with the penultimate exploration for quite a while, but the final one right after doesn't seem much harder, so the difficulty curve gets a little wonky right at the end.The artstyle is cool and fits the dark themes of the game well, and the enemy designs range from decent to fantastic. The three distinct temples are gorgeous as well, though the Serpent Temple definitely feels less diverse and interesting than the other two, being underground. The Native American setting feels like a breath of fresh since there seem to be endlessly many games with European or East Asian inspired settings. The music is good but not mindblowing. It enhances the experience and is fitting with the oppressive atmosphere - I just wouldn't put it on my playlist.As for story, it's incredibly minimal. There is zero dialogue whatsoever, so the story is told entirely through entries in the bestiary (which is overall well-written but has a few spelling errors), plus a couple of cutscenes right at the end of the harder explorations. This is pretty typical for the genre, but if you come in expecting Hades you will be disappointed in that regard.On the whole, I can strongly recommend Curse of the Dead Gods to anyone who's a fan of action roguelikes, especially if you're looking for something with more deliberate and less "spammy" combat while still being pretty fast. As a product, this game is well worth the price.

They are terrible against groups of elite enemies, which makes them absolutely useless in some of the later levels. Because of this, players are incentivised to use only the weapons that work. I would expect, in a rogue-like game, that I can have a lot of variety in my gameplay styles, but I wasn't really seeing much of that at all. Most builds were not viable in the later stages of the game. I really wanted to use some of the neat-sounding combo effects that some of the other weapons had on them, only to learn that playing that way actually just makes the game unnecessarily difficult, and I could just run one of the good weapons with a terrible passive effect that wins every single time.Essentially, there are many choices but most choices are undesirable - the opposite of what I would expect from a roguelike game. For that reason, I don't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is a thrilling roguelike dungeon crawler that offers an exhilarating blend of fast-paced combat, exploration, and strategic gameplay. The game features a fluid and responsive combat system that allows players to wield a variety of weapons and abilities. The combination of melee and ranged attacks, along with dodge mechanics, keeps the action intense and engaging. Players are immersed in a richly designed world filled with ancient temples and dark gods. The lore adds depth to the gameplay, making exploration feel rewarding as you uncover the mysteries of the environment. Each dungeon is procedurally generated, offering a fresh experience with every run. The diverse biomes and traps challenge players to adapt their strategies and keep the gameplay exciting. The unique curse system introduces an interesting twist to the game, as players must balance the benefits of powerful upgrades with the risks of negative effects. This adds a layer of strategy that encourages thoughtful decision-making. Overall, Curse of the Dead Gods is an engaging and rewarding roguelike experience that combines dynamic combat, intriguing lore, and strategic gameplay. It's a must-play for fans of the genre looking for an adventure filled with challenge and excitement!

_childDocuments_.review: Sighhhh. Well, I was desperately looking for another game very similar to Hades, which is basically a perfect game. This WOULD be a great game but a few things really hold it back unfortunately. For one, the stamina system is just horrible. I just don't really understand why it's needed at all. Add a few more enemies, let me roll around every second or two and leave it at that. Having to worry about rolling OR using my secondary attack is just dumb. The parrying is just so off-cue to me. It signals, then I hit it and maybe parry 1/10th of the time. It takes far too long after the attack signal for them to actually attack me and by the time they actually attack I'm having to worry about some other attack instead. Add that to terrible stamina management and having to choose between rolling and basically attacking sufficiently just ruins it. I think it just needed to be synced up a bit and it would be so much better. Making it more accessible isn't a bad thing. And you could still keep the combat and amount of enemies attacking at a high difficulty while making parrying and stamina way better. I think the combat would flow way better as well. The corruption systems aren't explained overly well and you're kinda just thrown in like yeah here's all these systems to deal with immediately with a quick hint box and no real natural walkthrough. Idk.. it just took me as kind of messy. All in all I think adjusting these things would bring it a lot closer to being almost on par (not surpassing it or being AS good) with Hades. That being said it isn't far off, just certain things that really kill the experience for me that make it very hard to fully appreciate.I'm extremely torn whether I should refund or keep it and just progress a little more so it's a little more fleshed out. Every time I play I just find myself feeling kind of ehh though because no matter what, those systems that suck, primarily the stamina in general, aren't going anywhere and will drag me down every single playthrough.Edit: I read over the other negative reviews and I'm glad (or rather sad?) to say that a ton of other people have very specific complaints like mine about stamina and the insane skill needed for parrying. I've also seen a lot of mention of being thrust into all the systems immediately without much tutorial or explanation of anything besides a brief blurb.   Unfortunately, these are going to be main points it seems everyone will notice when trying this game, and I really hope the devs fix these things. Like I said..  making a game more accessible doesn't mean you need to make it easier in general. You up the enemies difficulty and it literally offsets any weird systems you have for parrying and stamina and makes the game far more playable and enjoyable. The game is close to being pretty good but it's held back very rigidly.Edit again: I refunded :,( oh well.. i'll keep an eye on it and see if anything changes.. I saw someone else mention the game used to be better until the devs got spiteful of people figuring out the game quickly so they actually consciously made the parrying and rolling, along with other things, more difficult. Just ew..

_childDocuments_.review: While I don't recommend this game universally, I think if you're a veteran roguelike/dungeon crawler player, you'll have a decent time with it, but it's not going to blow your mind at every turn like something expertly crafted by veteran devs like Supergiant, Blizzard, Fromsoft, or at this point, Motion Twin.When you make a game that is inspired by so many juggernauts of gaming, in this case, Dark Souls, Dead Cells, a bit of Hades and Darkest Dungeon (tonally at least), the devil is in the details. Getting snagged on little bits of not so obvious geometry, incredibly samey weapons 80% of which aren't really good enough to go the distance, a starting inventory system that in no way compels you to play out a run even when it's not a perfect start, and a parry system that is not rewarding, and even if you're a seasoned soulslike player, feels completely superfluous. These are all things you will likely experience frustration with in CotDGIn Dead Cells, there are certainly weapons that are better or worse, but the vast majority have different feels, hit boxes, and combos. In CotDG you have about 70 weapons, but really you have 12 different move sets. And really, unless you're banking on dumb luck with rolling certain weapon traits, to combo together, there are only a couple late game viable weapons in each category. The slow attacks of two handers are rarely rewarded because you can't dash-exit their attack end animations, so that kind of feels like it narrows the pool even more, but that may just be a preference thing.Enemies have all sorts of different attack timings, and if you dodge the start of the attack, you dodge the whole attack animation (assuming it's not a rapid attack). I like that, it's very soulsy. However, the enemy designs can feel samey early on, and it felt like actually knowing what I'm looking at, even in a well lit room, was a pain. This might again be a personal issue, but it really killed my ability to find the rhythm.The parry system feels pointless. I haven't found anything worth parrying that I could just pay attention and dodge. I guess it makes it easier to stay in the fight and keep the greed meter going, but I haven't felt so punished by things to feel like the parry is a must-master mechanic.The difficulty level of the early game (or rather the spike in the final temple) makes the first 10 hours feel like wasteful bloat. It was really weird to deathlessly steamroll the first 9 temples and then feel this massive spike with all the champions and corruptions in the final temple. I'm thrilled to finally feel properly challenged, but I still feel like at some point I'll RNG my way into a healing build of some kind and just stomp my way through again. I don't know if this is a core design philosophy issue or just a balance issue, but finishing so many runs in a row in a roguelike feels bad. Like I WANT to get stomped early on, that's part of the genre, and it doesn't feel like a twist when that doesn't happen, it just feels like something's wrong. Part of this is that every boss has 3, maybe 4 attacks, all with fairly straight ahead timings and executions, so the learning period is very short. The bosses who have adds don't feel like they incorporate them in some sort of interesting combo or anything either. That all said, this game has beautiful lighting, an excellent art style, and cool sound design. I absolutely adore the curse and greed systems, and uncovering some of the hidden weapon combos and features was pretty neat too. However, I have found my self befuddled by a number of the core design and balance choices, and I'm honestly surprised that some of these things made it through early access. I guess maybe that means that others like it and it's just not quite for me.
