_childDocuments_.review: Just beat the hardest difficulty, play time: 75.6 hours. Bought it on sale for $7, 10 hours of entertainment for every $1 spent is a pretty good ratio. Roguelite ARPG's are one of my favorite gaming genres. This is one of the best I've played, mechanically and visually. The music is pretty basic and sparse, so I typically have it muted and listen to my own. There's little story in it, but I honestly love the gameplay even more than Hades.The gameplay is just mechanically extremely satisfying to me. Everything is "fair", even though towards the end you're basically to the point of close to no-hitting. Attacks are telegraphed with nice visuals and sounds (I make a lot of use of the sound cues). Parrying is fairly lenient, but I rarely bothered with it since dodging is so strong and easy in this. That said, you're getting ganked in every room and many of the enemies have hyper armor, and in hard mode you REALLY don't want to get hit. Ever. We're talking starting with 1k health and regular enemies are chunking you for 250 damage, and there are 5 enemies all throwing ♥♥♥♥ at you or jumping at you or swinging their giant swords around. You CANNOT trade, the goal is always ultimately to never get hit. All that said? I still get hit, but there are also plenty of ways to heal to make up for that if you only get hit a few times. There are plenty of ways the game rewards you for not getting hit as well (greed counter that builds up with kill streaks so enemies drop more gold, reptillian hunger). So, you really don't want to get hit, and you're getting attacked by multiple enemies that often have hyper armor and projectiles in every room, with traps, but it's all very fair and if you git gud, you can consistently avoid taking damage. Mastering the games mechanics has just been so incredibly fun. Dodging, parrying, attacking. Learning every enemy's moveset. A multitude of weapon classes that all feel unique (whip, spear, gun, claw, sword, mace, heavy weapons... all have unique movesets and behave completely differently from one another), with multiple attack options for each but not too many (main attack, off-hand combo, charged attack.Plenty of ways to make yourself OP, or to increase the challenge, depending on what you want. It's pretty bare bones, but the visuals are stunning and as a big roguelite action RPG fan, I have to say it's my favorite one to play so far because of the mechanics. It doesn't have all of the nice polish of Hades in terms of story, but it's just so damn fun to actually play. It's extremely hard, yet also fair at the same time, and greatly rewards skill and mastering the game's mechanics. Managing your health, gold, and curse meters are all important and satisfying. If you learn about the game deeply enough, you can create a wide variety of very OP builds. The game doesn't hold you back if you figure something out that's really powerful. It's just feels fun to play physically, idk how else to describe it really, like a toy. And $7 for over 70 hours of entertainment is a pretty good deal in my book, with probably more hours to come I'm sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Right now, where the game is, it's just not quite what you'd want from it. The game itself has a lot of potential, and I'd be hard pressed to say it's not fun, but a lot of the mechanics are counter-intuitive or are just so poorly explained that you're left guessing or googling. The main mechanics seem to be the emphasis on lighting and curses. Lighting isn't explained in the game, I had no idea what sitting in darkness did for me or what benefit lighting up torches would do other than make it easier to see some enemies. Curses are just oddly brutal, you have a bar that goes from 0 to 100 and when it hits 100, you get a new curse. The problem is that you get 20 points just for entering a room, and some enemies just casually hit you for another 20 no matter what.Combat has a good amount of potential but the stamina system holds it back. Right now it's a lot of rolling in, taking a swipe, and rolling out. There's no real fluidity and far from any worthwhile strategy outside of that. There's very clearly great weapons and bad weapons, and hardly any in between. It doesn't feel like I'd be weighing any options when it's pretty obvious that there's weapons you're going to avoid and then there's a couple you'll always take regardless of the hindrance.Very little enemy variety. Small melee enemies that like to take swipes, ranged enemies that'll occasionally shoot a bullet, and some really beefy enemies that are a step in the right direction for strategy.I think the game has a lot of potential, I don't hate it nor do I blame the devs, because making games isn't easy. I will say, however, that as it stands, it's not worth buying right now. I might return in the future after significant updates or even the full release, but right now I'm inclined to avoid it.

_childDocuments_.review: Game seems decent enough, but devs who can't differentiate between roguelike and roguelite do not deserve positive reviews. Also Focus seems to use copy-paste EULAs, because this does not seem to use EAC.On more serious note, 26 hours later, I think the game is in need of serious rebalancing to be fun for the people who do not enjoy sticking bamboo skewers under their nails on weekly basis.There's 0 character customization, which I think is fine. You get 3 slots for passives that you then unlock and can change between runs as you see fit, this is fine.I quite like the light/dark mechanic, and the idea of the curses is fine. Some of them are fun, but some are absolutely run ruining. And the final one is always damage overtime effect, which does way too much damage way too often.A lot of the weapons are just bad when compared to others of same kind, and the "banish" (does not appear in the temple) clearly does nothing. You can unlock a total of 4 altars that you can choose weapon set from before run, but those weapons you have banished still appear there, too.The cursed weapons should clearly be balanced better, most of them are not great compared to other weapons, and the affixes they can have could make them absolutely worthless.Many enemies and especially bosses will wombo combo the living crap out of you if the hit connects. Have fun dying on the final boss because you miss one roll and then can't get out of the chain of attacks.Also it would be nice if the game explained stuff better, like what different damage types actually do. (I think poison is DoT, lightning randomly zaps enemies, and fire does something other than make light?)It's a strong meh from me, I'm not hardcore enough to have casual fun with the game, but if you hate fun and think souls games are for babies, go for it. Otherwise I'd say you will get more out of Hades.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I also rage about this game a lot. I can not stop playing it.This game has weirdly satisfying mechanical rythm to its attacks, combos and dodges. Once you get a hang of it, you will be attacking and weaving around enemies in a very satisfying combat dance. This game also has that "one more time" quality. Failing to clear the temple will motivate you to get back right away and try harder.There are some frustration as well:1. Game's arsenal is imbalanced -- claws (especially fire) are better than any other one-handed weapons, two-handed weapons in current iteration of the game (The Cursed Temple update) are borderline unusable.2. Curses can at times completely screw you and some curses are just too punishing compared to  rest of them. 3. Object collision is wonky at times -- you will get stuck on braziers or latch into enemies that will push you forward, which often results in you being hit and breaking your combo count.Despite above issues, I thoroughly love the game. I already have 125 hours sunk into it and can not wait for next update and new content.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: If you like anything about rougelikes just buy this, it's a very good game. The only thing I don't like is the music, there's nothing memorable or intense enough here and that's a real shame. Also, as expected, it has no story. The reason that this game is so good is that it has exactly as many mechanics and the difficulty to be engaging, fun and rewarding as it needs to. It runs perfectly on any equipment (Steam Deck is perfect), it has very pleasant graphics and visual effects. Two defensive mechanics - dodge and parry - make this game really accessible to even the worst player, if I was able to what I did in this game, anyone will complete it. Extremely good value for the money
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice so far. Everything seems polished and well-executed. The atmosphere is on point. The only thing holding this game back is a lack of story and other characters, with whom be could bond and get actually emotionally invested (see: Hades. There is no way of not comparing it to Hades, since it's the same formula, just with a removal of storytelling and all its emotional layers)
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine a roguelite with an exploratory reward system like Hades, with the aesthetics and strategic brutality of Darkest Dungeon, and the unforgiving timing-critical combat of dark souls. Nothing is very friendly in this game, every curse that seems alright might be your demise. Sometimes the game makes you regret your past choices, other times it very blatantly spits in your face and says "git gud" or "maybe you were too greedy?". The light mechanic and weapon sets really forces you to evaluate the most optimal way to dish out damage - or avoid it at the very least. Sound design is beautiful, animations are smooth and polished, the parry system is just frustrating enough to make you want to master it, but not discourage you, and man are the combos satisfying. Very much recommend to any dark fantasy roguelite enjoyer.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: For every gold piece Cortés and Pizarro took from the endless troves of the Mesoamerican denizens, a curse left the lips of those suffering under their boot. Therefore, it comes as no surprise that your character in Curse of the Dead Gods, the ruthless & avaricious Sir Henry McAllister, is met with their wrath, dodging traps and dealing with the arisen defenders of towering temples, challenging even Mayan Gods themselves! The superb combat system, plenty of enemies, loot, emphasis on greed, and brutal difficulty make this game something to watch out for, as it has the potential to become one of the defining roguelites on the market.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I would say fairly solid. The game felt like a less polished mix of Hades(Isometric and combat taking place in several rooms) and Dead Cells(with the combat). If you're used to parrying/dodging in Dead Cells, you'll have a comfortable time adjusting to this game.The strongest part of the game IMO is the bosses. All of them are pretty unique and a lot different from each other. Outside of a couple of bosses for certain builds(low dps), most of the bosses felt pretty fair.The main negative to me is that it was overall very repetitive and the different explorations were all pretty much the same thing after a certain point. The amount of content is definitely a lot less than Dead Cells or Hades. The final few explorations are extremely disappointing as well, since they're pretty much more repetition. If you need an action roguelike to play and like games with the dodge/parry mechanic, then this would be a solid buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: As an isometric hack and slash game, Curse of the Dead Gods is fantastic. It just controls super well, and the combat is really fun. I use mouse and keyboard, and I have no complaints, the gameplay is just good. Enemy attacks and traps are all super clear and fair, there is always something you could have done to prevent it, and it allows you to learn and adapt, which is great. I also cannot name a single bug encountered, the game is just super polished and runs great.My only real criticisms are in the rogue-lite elements of the game. For one, the game gates difficulties when you first start, limiting you to only playing miniature versions of the game in order to unlock further levels. I had a run where I got really good gear early on, and tore through the first 2 bosses, but since I had just started playing, I was gated to a medium adventure, and so the run ended and I had to retire my progress entirely. I don't really see why this system is here at all, just give us access to all dungeon lengths and let us die when we die.The other criticism, which hopefully is solved before launch, is a massive lack of gear and weapons. There is very little variety. There is just enough where you can distinguish a good run from a bad run, but in terms of gameplay, there are very few weapon types and combat altering effects. This leaves the combat options you have in each run more or less the same, and really hurts replay value. This is the only reason I could give for waiting for more content, otherwise the game really is already in a great state.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay feels like Hades but the game design is more like Deadcells.  You run around killing things, but you don't carry anything between runs.  There are no stat-boosts to unlock for your character, just new weapons.  If you're into that, you would probably like this game.  My biggest complaint is that the unlock system is incredibly slow.  You can maybe unlock one weapon and one ability per run.   Maybe.  More often than not, it will take you two or more.  Given the number of unlocks and the length of a run, I can only imagine it would take 100+ hours of grinding to unlock everything and without a story to hold the game together, I can't see grinding for that.  Still, pretty fun for a couple of days.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Besides some balancing issues (like enemies lunging at you from outside of visible part of the screen) it has really pleasant dynamic and interesting builds.The biggest con is: the game becomes very grindy towards final boss. I did not manage to reach it after 35 hours of gameplay and I was nowhere close.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the art, theme, and combat system. The ONLY thing missing from this game is more content, considering it took 18 hours of gameplay to beat all 4 paths, but I couldn't stop playing when I picked it up which is a testament to how well polished and fun this game is. Since it is in early access, I'm really excited to see what else this game pulls out and will stay updated so I can run it again and again.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: A Hades clone without the story and voice acting. That being said, the mechanics are interesting. It could have made this game just flatly better than Hades, but unfortunately it's a bit more of a mixed bag. There are some really neat ideas in here. I love the idea of taking corruption to give yourself some advantages. We just need more weapon types, more curses, more enemies, more bosses. It got a bit stale after about 10 hours, and I found myself bored and just wanting to see the final boss.Still, I got my money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: If u like Hades - u will like this.Gameplay and Hit-Feedback is so satisfying. I think what people will miss from Hades ist the Story part. There is no real Story in here. But for people who dont care much about Story , thats even better. And i dont care much about story so this game is a real Gameplay focused Rogue-Like. Time betweens runs are about 5seconds to maybe 30seconds when u wanna choose a upgrade. And boom - back to action. No NPCs with exclamation marks standing around which u need to talk to. Simple Die - Upgrade - Next run.The Darkness / Light Mechanic is a very interesting and sometimes challenging game mechanic - U take 50% inc. Dmg when standing in the Dark. But u have a Torch which u can equip and make an Light Radius. But when u switch to your weapons, the Light from the Torch goes away. But hey, there a things around which u can light up.These are basic mechanics in the game. But this mechanic gets intersting when u:- Notice u can light ab enemies with Torich or Fire Attacks, so they will give a light radius around them. Good for Boss fights where there is nothing to light up. - u can destroy some things in the enviorment with Heavy weapons like a 2-Handed Mace. But be careful not to slam the wrong things, as u can destroy things that u didnt want to destroy too- Bouncing a on Fire set enemie into a Poisen cloud makes a big explosion. So satistying finding that outCorruption is also an interesting system which makes the runs so different. U get 20 Corruption each time u move to the nxt Area. At 100 Corruption u get a Random Curse. These Curses are hell of a fun, but sometimes change the game completly.Also getting hit by Dark Attacks adds corruption. So dodge these Purple attacks (primary from mage enemies)Difficulty curve is also very well done. i am not at endgame. I thought the first Temples of each Type were a bit easy. Managed to clear every1 in first try. but the Second tier with now 2 bosses and elite mobs after the first half did the job.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that takes the best parts of many good roguelikes like hades, gungeon, etc and combines them into a top-down dungeon crawler borrowing visuals and themes from darkest dungeon. The main mechanic of this game is that you consistently accumulate curses as you play the game, that have both negative and positive effects. Greed is neutral in this game, as you can pay for your items and upgrades with gold, or by taking on extra curses, essentially making two fully different playstyles (Slow and safe or fast and risky) that feel both very distinct.The different temples, thematic and art, many weapon combinations that seem not-obvious at first make this game a delight to play, though some clarity on parryable attacks, bomb timers from enemies, etc would be welcome. Also a hint on how to get the boss weapons too.9/10, game's a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times but is still very, very fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I have not played much of this yet but I am already very much into this game. The similarity of style to Darkest Dungeon which is also excellent drew me in and I adore the art and the pace of this game. There is not much of a tutorial but not much is needed (although it did take me a few plays to understand how corruption and curses really worked, might have been me being slow though). This game is a lot of fun and it hooks you and makes you want to get better. The first try at this game I made it to the boss but got destroyed because I let the curse reach the final stage. The first time I beat a boss was about three or four tries in and victory does taste sweet I can tell you. I am curious where this game will go in the future. I'd like maybe to get some infos on the enemys sometimes, not just the "Nemesis" card at the end, maybe a hint or two at their abilities. Otherwise, this game is on a good path. I am bittersweetly reminded of Akaneiro Demon Hunters which I binged for a long time unless it became kind of abandoned and nobody cared anymore. I hope this game will live a long time!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The entire Curse of the Dead Gods experience at launch has a wonderful difficulty ramp only matched by the best in the genre. Combat is smooth and always challenging, but victory is never out of reach. Rooms get more complicated as players move on, but they're welcome obstacles rather than brick walls that kill a run dead. Add in a stylish presentation and a unique theme and it's hard to find much to complain about with this final release. Passtech Games has carved out a new space in roguelikes that should appeal to fans of The Binding of Isaac and Darkest Dungeon alike.Want to know more? My full review is available now on .(Game was reviewed on Xbox and tested on PC)

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay consists of the regular dodge/attack. In this game, you have a number of "stamina" points available. Each one is needed for an attack or a dodge. So you either dodge, or attack. But you cannot cancel attacks, or dodge through enemies. As a gameplay loop, this might work. If there was some kind of reward for doing it. But there is no story, and no real reward for advancing. It is laughably easy to progress. Probably because combat is so punishing and clunky it had to be easy. 4 hours and 7 runs before my first death. In a "roguelike"This will not give you a lot of challenge. It will not give you any story or rewards for progress.If you like it simple and easy, it might be for you. I'd prefer a little something more honestly.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This is the Dark Souls of Top down Dungeon Crawling. Heavy exploration guided by your light. Fight the enemies, conquer the room and progress to the next level. You are intended to get hit by the enemies. The dodge mechanic is required ,you need to assess, hit and run. You get crazier as you progress through ancient tombs. Hardcore Dungeon Crawler, top-down perspective. All about exploration. You are required to use your lantern to light the way as you walk around a room.  It's like the walking dead, and you need to time the enemy attacks to jump out of the way> The more you attact, the more difficult you make it jumping out of their direction attacks. Regular enemies are hardcore. You start on 1000HP and can still be pretty much murdered in the first room you begin in.Die and spawn again. Collect crystal skulls to be able to earn some background upgrades that can compliment your play style. There are different fighting styles, of which i must still unlock.There are multiple dungeon types too. {3} Jaguar, Serpent, and yet to find outThe art style is also driving me to keep playing :) continue no matter how I die. I was one shot away from killing the first boss, and dying didn't even feel frustratingEach run is going to be different.Your weapons/Inventory can consist of:Main weapon-  Swords, maces, Lycan-Blades I see lots of dota2 references, undermine, even nova drift, in the enemy classes. It's Great, it's full of MANY cultures. It's like taking the world as we have now idolized it and turned it into an exploration passage where you are trying to survive.It is super hardcore though. Like the last boss, twice i arrive there, no matter how much HP you have, you get a curse that reduces you to 1 HP. Incredible experience. Can keep you hooked for hours> Perhaps a suggestion for local co-op or some sort of co-op due to how corruption and everything contributes to the game. It's all incredible. Can be more interesting with a friend. Dark souls difficulty level: yesSurvival rate: Minimal Ability to choose Short, Medium, Long and Hardcore adventure lengths. The Map allows you to start anywhere you want when you begin each temple. It does remind me of Slay the Spire, but Dev's say their game was conceptualized before StS, anyway, it's neat and professional.Each Altar of sacrifice can be used with Blood, or gold, or FavourYour options to travel are stats missions,  - Get stats boosting fountains after defeating enemiesRelic levels - maybe multiple relics per level Gold levels, floors filled with gold.Haven: To heal with cursed blood of this temple, and gain curses depending on how many doses of blood you acquireBoss  is at the top of the map, and it's an incredible journey.No play though will ever be the same again.Bug: First 1 hour play through now: I accepted something from the Jaguar shrine: 9% Total HP recovery when going through a door. I passed through several doors {the ones that shut closed as you pass them} , even multiple levels. _childDocuments_.review: Well I was going to explain some misconceptions in a review but their comments are disabled, I feel I have enough experience through playtime and marathon speedruns so here it goes:This review rubs me the wrong way, not only is it inaccurate, it tries to pass off as accurate through hyperbolas using high playtime and experience in other games.Let’s break it down:“I'm talking almost undodgeable attacks that deal 60% of your damage and stunlocks that end you after an otherwise easy run.”Some elites are fast, some attacks come really really fast, but they are all avoidable through positioning, planning and good mechanical skill (parries vs dodge, sometimes you NEED one and not the other to prevent getting hit). If you DO get hit, yes you may get stunlocked, but the 60% damage is coming from all the attacks at once, not just one. The stunlock itself is a result of planning, not RNG.“The worst thing by far is the attack animations and RNG of enemy attack patterns. In normal games, you learn the enemies attack patterns and get better at fighting them over time. In this game, for some reason the developers decided that making attack timings change by small amounts so that your parries fail.”That’s just factually wrong, the attack timings are set in stone, the moment they WANT to attack is RNG (even that can be heavily influenced), but the attack animation IS and always WILL BE the same. The only exception to this rule is ELITES on HARD, where the game tells you IN ADVANCE that elites, and only elites, attack faster (15%). That doesn’t ever budge, it will always be 15% for the difficulty bracket.“Great examples are the tier 2 shock boss who charges at you, but sometimes decides to charge in the direction you are rolling rather than directly at you so you cannot avoid being hit. Or the Poison tier 2 boss whose swings have varying speeds not only based on his poison status, but multiple speed animations without any indication. Or the Fire Tier 3 boss who usually has a "stunned" animation when you hit them, but sometimes will stop this stun animation and prep his 800 damage explosion that covers half the map WHILE you are attacking him.”Tier 2 Eagle (Malok paal): dashes towards the center of the arena, there’s nothing random about itTier 2 Serpent (Ratyapu): they do have varying speed based on poison status, they got that right, but they have individual animation for every attack, they seem to have missed that completely! The speed of their animation is the base animation + a flat % if they are in frenzy. Tier 3 Jaguar: They seem unaware of how the fighting system fundamentally works: the enemy will only retaliate at the end of a combo if they are not in a hitstun or above, and bosses themselves can’t be stunned outright. Once the Jaguar Avatar starts their attack animation you can’t stop them anymore! The jaguar explosion they are referring to have such a big windup you can literally walk out of it from melee range, dodge if you were attacking at the start of the animation.“These things are infuriating and it frequently feels unfair when you die on a run. Whether it's because the RNG gods were not with you and your weapon is crap despite using 10 divine favours at the weapon store to find something even half useable (I locked almost every unlockeable weapon because most are liabilities)”There’s a lot of RNG you could complain about, weapon viability is probably not one of them unless you’re being offered only heavies and bombs. The vast majority of the weapon roster is viable, especially with weapon upgrade rooms. They seem to imply they spend the entirety of their divine favours on weapon rooms, that is not the way: spend them in relic shops THEY scale your character, weapons are secondary, their type itself is mainly flavour, not power.“and you need to hit a boss 800 times to kill them while they have to hit you 3 times with their jittery animations that sometimes go a second faster and thus become undodgeable and unparriable.”Again that seems like a scaling issue where weapon upgrades and relics were not prioritized, stat upgrades are great too but they come second. Bosses are the most reliable fighting condition you’ll get, so they hit HARD, that to be expected. When I say reliable fighting condition, I say their animations are set in stone and their behaviour is both observable and abusable, I’ve never seen a boss, in hundred of hours, have a jittery animation.“It sucks that the developers hate their players so much. I know fans might tell me that I just don't manage stamina perfectly or that I need to git gud. After 100 hours in this game I can tell you that those people are morons.”I think it’s mostly a lack of information. The main problem I see from reading is enemy animation. Their differences, especially on bosses, can be subtle but they ARE there.“I finished Dark Souls. I like hard games, but hard should be about player skill and perseverence, not about RNG and lopsided attack animations that just end you for no fault of your own. I can't recommend this game to anyone. There are MUCH better roguelikes out there that don't make you wanna punch your computer screen.”CotDG is indeed about player skill and perseverance, that’s all that stands between a completely new player and a veterans apart from rapidly unlocking blessings, the level 1 starting weapons you can find better at the first weapon shop and the 10 divine favours that alleviate the real RNG gate (relic shops that may give sub-optimal, but still usable relics), everything else is enemy, tile and combo/weapon knowledge, and you can complete the game with these alone (see speedruns, where players start from a blank save). The way they refer to lopsided attack animations makes me think they haven’t fought DS3 Dancer of the Boreal Valley, because you get a similar experience. Every single death in Curse of the Dead Gods is my own fault, I can see it, I can feel it, I can learn from it. By learning, I can do better next time: if you look at very experienced players, which I am not, you may even see hitless runs at the highest difficulty, that’s not luck.

_childDocuments_.review: It was fun for a bit, but it just doesn't stack up. There are some interesting mechanics with the light and curses you accumulate, but there is very little to encourage you to keep going. Having finished the short and mediums of all 3 temples and with a few attempts on the longs, I'm ready to put it away.There's a few problems. The combat is solid enough, but there is no story whatsoever. Don't play expecting Hades, ready to tease out every nuance interacting with your favourite characters. You just die, and begin anew, and it can be quite a slog to start again because of the lack of variation.Aside from 3 blessings you can equip, there isn't enough to make you feel more powerful and progress. Sure, you can unlock more weapons, and have more options randomized before you depart. But it also just dilutes your pool of weapons, and you can't filter them out later. There isn't an incremental increase in your health, damage, or lives or whatever, so you're at the whim of what you pick up.It's not the dungeons that typically kill you, it's the bosses. Unfortunately, you'll be spending like 95% of your playtime working through trash mobs. It gets very samey samey very quick. So currently I'm "stuck" on the long temples, because I've met them a few times, but they'll completely obliterate you. I know the point is to learn their attacks and develop your strategy, but that's a big ask when I have to spend 30-45 minutes to reach them again, for a brief fight I'll probably lose.Simply put, every time I'm dumped unceremoniously back to the start, I don't feel fulfilled or ready to tackle another run. Once the sheen wears off, I suspect many might feel the same.

_childDocuments_.review: This is amazing gameplay.  If you want extremely fun, challenging, fair, and satisfying gameplay this is the game to deliver it.  It has atmosphere, it looks good, but the game is all about its gameplay, and it knocks that out of the park.  I'll add the meta-progression is also great.  Varied assortment of fun weapons that you can mix and match to fit your needs on every run, gear, buffs, and the curses system adds more variety and unpredictable challenges and systems to balance.Highly recommended if you don't mind a challenge and pure focus on progression and playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods, what's not to love?Straight out of the gate, you're thrown into this amazing, mysterious world with its own unique mechanics, fluid and rewarding combat, and a sense of swagger that separates it apart from all the other roguelike titles out there. It's an amazing cocktail of great game design, and am I damn well pleased to own it.The gameplay loop seemingly never gets stale, with three temples each with their own respective god, mechanics, traps, layouts, enemies, and so forth, I can simply never get bored. If I'm fed up with one, I can just run down another for the proceeding 4 hours of my early morning! (And as a side-note, at the time of writing this I had just finished what I ASSUMED to be the end of the game. I am so happy to be wrong.) In regards to combat every time I've died it's understandably my fault, the game's traps don't seem unfair, and the addition of the progressive growing corruption (and curses, which can be a double-edged sword) as you go through adds extra depth for your decision making in and out of encounters. The fights are quick and the greed meter is a brilliant addition to reward risky plays, but newer players aren't punished for not being able to get a greed combo off, either.There's so much more I could write but I don't want to spoil the surprise, I can't recommend this enough, I've already bought the damn thing three times. Praise Sich'al!

_childDocuments_.review: Because everyone and their dog is comparing this to Hades, I will as well. I might actually like this better than Hades. The combat is a bit more methodical, and does not get to the over-the-top ridiculous level of explosions and bouncing and more explosions that Hades does... which is totally justified for Hades because you're playing an immortal demigod, but is not justified here, because you're playing a dude with some curses. As such, the slow pacing actually feels good. The weapons feel as though they have weight, and the playstyle between the weapons, of which there are many of, is very different. While I do wish there was more metadevelopment besides the simple weapon unlocks and blessings you can buy (IE, I do think Hades' metadevelopment was better with the weapon upgrades, character boons and mirror stuff), I think this is an excellent framework to improve upon, so I really hope this game gets some FLC or even DLC to expand upon what is already here, because it's damn good. I should also point out, I feel as though this game is harder than Hades. Stamina management, and less potentially ridiculous combos make it a more tempered experience, where it is always going to be more about your personal skill than about the boons you can get. Which is, in my opinion, a good thing. Don't get me wrong, I love Hades, but Curse of the Dead Gods might just be better.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: Game saves data in the game install folder, despite decades of that being known bad behavior.  Also, the game reverted my save to an eight-month-old version with no warning or explanation (or dev response), so you'd better find it and back it up yourself, because you've got upgrades each taking a  of runs worth of currency, and a dev that doesn't care about data safety.Curse of the Dead Gods has virtually no story and very tightly focuses on challenging, nicely mindful, skill-based, mechanical fighting.  If someone wants that, it's pretty good (and you don't have many options anyway), but if they don't, they will not have a good time, because fighting is its sole core value and it both very willfully challenges you and gives you very little for an unsuccessful run (while tying a lot to getting clears), leading to runs usually feeling disappointing rather than rewarding, which has very significant effects.  You do have the tools for very developed skill to make you fairly unstoppable, but you have to get there and you won't feel much reward until you do.Main run variation comes conceptually from the curses you get as you go.  This is an interesting idea, banking on assigning you "problems" to deal with to add interest.  These range from "fun" (enemies exploding on kill is always a good time) to just annoying ("Hey, remember how we have that cool torch and lighting mechanic that really adds to the play and may have stuff tied to it in your build? Yeah, that's just not a thing this run.").  Unfortunately, there needed to be more curses, more interesting curses, and fewer curses that just feel bad to play with or cut down the game.  The system already requires significant player buy-in just to tolerate, and it needed to deliver a lot more on its end than it has in order to contribute to the play.Overall, I'd say run variety feels low. You're going to feel like what you are doing in one temple is always pretty similar, even if the low-level fight view stays interesting. On the positive side, you have three temples to pick from when you start a run, but each temple offers only a single run with the same three bosses, giving you three ways to play what feels like less than a third of a game.  These single runs are each presented as three progressively longer runs, but that's just cosmetic to let it pat you on the head and tell you you won (and kick you out of your run) the first time you beat a new boss.  They have some preset variations on the runs that basically bake in some curses or conditions from the outset, to try and cobble together an adventure theme.  I say "try" because it really doesn't work, and they very stingily limited how much you can do these special runs, so they are practically worthless as content.  If you look to exciting unknowns about what's ahead, you always get pretty much what you expect.  There is also the mixed temple, which could have been a fantastic addition that would bring everything together and kick the game up a huge notch, but that's sadly not at all what the devs delivered and they locked it behind so much that many players will never even have access to it to see.  That's this game in a nutshell: some good stuff, but notably underdelivered and blatantly stingy.Metaprogression is present and has some cute mechanics/play changes available, but you are very limited on what you can use at once and what you have available.  Basically, you can get better and options for starting weapons, three passives chosen from a fixed pool, and shop rerolls, so it's far from playtime=power, although there are a few easier-play options in there.  It does take a heavy, fairly unrewarding grind to get everything, though, as costs get very high and many things add little to nothing.As far as the actual play, you have a dodge, a parry, separate main and off-hand weapons, a torch, and a 2-handed weapon.  Weapons have a basic combo, a charge attack, and off-hand weapons will act differently to end a main-hand combo.  Combos have a "finisher" at the end.  You also have five stamina dots, and consume those with charge attacks, finishers, dodges, and 2-handed attacks. Stamina will recover quickly after a short break without using it, so it lends a nice mindful mechanical feel without getting confining.  Parry blocks everything except area of effect attacks and is tight and satisfying to use aggressively.  Parry and dodge can cancel attacks.  Some attacks can also stagger enemies and act as interrupts before an attack comes out.  Torch passively lights the area and can be used to set things on fire.  It's not particularly interesting to use, but both of those do matter as the game tracks light/dark for some things, so that all definitely adds texture.  Charge attacks are under-varied (mainly just spins or a slam), but overall, you can see a solid toolset at your disposal.  Then there are a small variety of environmental hazards which you can and do use against enemies, making positioning more relevant.There are not many enemies per temple, but they generally have some variation in their actions.  Groups will vary, so that's much of the enemy texture you have, and I feel it's less than it should be.  Enemies will generally wait to be triggered--a bit too much, since you can see them just standing there clearly in your light radius and able to see you, which feels annoyingly artificial and makes it too easy to bait smaller enemy groups instead being pushed towards higher intensity fights.  Still, the enemies feel very engaging and actively and tightly involve you in the fight, which is really important and too often missed or underdone is these kinds of games.As an early access buyer, I remain very disappointed with the lack of real improvement during development and depressingly unused feedback.  The initial temple is still the best and most challenging, leaving the two following temples well short of the game's promise, and the release day version actually  fun to a new player than it was at the start of early access, due to all the stingy locking, grind, and just plain having things reduced and removed in the release day update.  In the end, such feelings don't matter to new buyers: only that it does show that the dev did not try to make this the best game they could, and the development so far (and likely limited market) leaves little prospect for real post-release growth. It still comes in pretty good for what it is and has some rare value, but definitely has a quite narrow player market plus high chance of being actively disliked by players not a good fit for its intent.  If you're in the refund window wondering whether there's more to the game than you're seeing, there really is not.  The low-level fight of mindful mechanics vs engaging enemies is where the game shines, and all it really has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game that I bought into right at the start of early access. Updating my review for the 1.0 launch...The core concept to this game is greed: the more enemies you kill in a row, the more gold you get. The more you wanna keep pushing your attack chain, the better you do, until you run out of stamina. The more items you want the more Corruption you can take (and get subsequent curses) to get them instead of using gold.The combat is tactical, impactful, deliberate, and some might say slow (compared to the flashiness of Hades). There's a lot of nailbiting moments when your stamina is low and there are a lot of enemies. Managing your pacing, attack chains (including a TON of variety with alternating main/offhand weapons), and how to approach fights never gets old. The gameplay loop is super satisfying. If you played Spiral Knights (before the twin-stick shooter craze) you'll be right at home here.Meta progression is alright: you can unlock new weapons, a few traits/perks, and more re-rolls for upgrade shops. Level and enemy variety is good. The game is extremely atmospheric and has some of the best sound integration I've ever seen (in terms of audio cues as you do stuff).All in all a great game and a solid addition to the overpopulated genre of twin-stick roguelites. I hope the devs continue support after 1.0!
_childDocuments_.name: Curse of the Dead Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Dead Gods is a fantastic, albeit kinda short, rogue-lite that relies primarily on mechanical skill and knowledge of every facet of how the game functions to do well. There is never a time where I feel like the RNG of the game screws me over too much as nearly every weapon in the game is viable through playing around each weapons' main strengths and properties (all of which are viewable in the hub before you start a run by pressing select). And due to the fact that you can see the entire temple's layout before or during the run you're able to strategically path towards certain rooms that may help you more than the rest, such as going to a gold room when you have none or going to a weapon room if you have mediocre weapons.The enemies are difficult but fair to beat due to having their attacks visually and audibly choreographed but deal a lot of damage and aren't able to be interrupted outside of specific attacks on certain weapons or by being hit by the temple's traps. The bosses are similar, but they can't be interrupted so you are forced to learn their attack patterns and play around them to beat the bosses consistently; luckily you're able to combo the bosses after their attacks if you're skilled enough and have synergistic weapons, and if you aren't able to combo them you're able to play safe instead due to having longer range.The curse system in the game is a double edged sword, and a well designed one at that. Curses are inherently supposed to be bad for you, but most of them have some kind of upside that may actually end up helping you (especially with certain playstyles and loadouts). You're able to buy weapons, relics, or stats with gold or "corruption" (the in-game meter that determines when you get your next curse), which makes it a strategic choice for if you're going to save the gold for later or use it so you don't get another curse. While most curses are minor hindrances for the most part, the fifth and final curse you can get is one that is easily able to end your runs if you're not really careful due to it constantly draining your life over time until you're at 1HP. So it's a constant balancing act of how many curses you're willing to take versus playing it safer but having less/worse equipment/stats later down the line, luckily the game will allow you to remove one curse of your choice after beating any non-skippable boss to help mitigate the penalty of having a lot of corruption.Currently I have all but 4 achievements, and I may actually end up getting the rest of them. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Because of the following reasons, I don't recommend:1) The curse mechanic can really mess up your run really fast. There were multiple times where I've had a nice sets of items with properties that work well together and then here comes the curse to totally cancel out your setup. 2) Stamina bar. Dodging uses a stamina point and so does strong attacks. You see where I'm getting at with this? If you're a very offensive player then you're going to have a bad time. 1 stamina point left? Better choose your next move carefully.3) Before you fight the last boss, you HAVE TO gamble your gold away and if you don't have money, there goes your run. This is unavoidable because it's the only way to open the gate.If the above cons don't bother you, then by all means buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game. I highly recommend it.First off, the whole aesthetic is wonderful. The visuals and sounds are haunting and perfect for the atmosphere that they are going for. The folks who worked on this game are true artists.The gameplay is the real star though. Structurally, yes, it's similar to games like Hades. However, it play s absolutely nothing like it. The combat is significantly more deliberate, much closer to a souls game.I would love to write out paragraphs to try and convince you to give it a try, but I really think you should experience everything yourself. The discovery, failure, and finally mastery of all this game has to offer.That said, it's difficult. Punishing. Infuriating. If you don't want a challenge, be wary. This is the real deal. Until you wrap your head around things, it can even feel unfair. I promise you, it's not.And just know, the highs of victory will dwarf the many stings of defeat.

_childDocuments_.review: This game comes pretty close to being really good, but there are a couple glaring flaws that ruin it for me.  The worst offender is the way that they handle healing, which is to say barely at all.  The only location that healing fountains exist is immediately AFTER a boss.  Literally every other source of healing in the game is rng dependent.  They require either some healing per kill on weapons (this is by far the best, but completely unreliable), or requiring a specific item that requires specific setup to get healing - for example, killing enemies with traps, killing enemies that are on fire, etc.  It is not guaranteed that you will get any of these items, and also not guaranteed it will be feasible (or even possible) to meet their kill requirements.They have a ton of unlockable abilities covering all sorts of strategies, but only one that even mentions healing.  That one heals you for 50% after you kill a boss.  You know, the one point in the game where you are able to heal to full 100% guaranteed.   I must emphasize that this is the ONLY mechanic in the game that allows you to start the game with ANY form of guaranteed healing.  It requires an unlock, and it is completely redundant.  Beyond that, you get your after-boss fountain and whatever rng gives you, which is often little to nothing.There is a reason basically every game ever either gives you some sort of rest point or other means to heal between level start and boss.  Once you've mastered the game, healing may well be unimportant, but few people are going to have the patience to master something that leaves so little wiggle room to actually learn.  If you constantly have to start your boss fights at 10% health, you don't really get much of a chance to analyze their attacks or practice.This isn't helped by the fact that a lot of the rooms are just needlessly winding and tedious - long snaking corridors with traps guarding nothing, or sometimes just empty hallways for no apparent reason.  Sometimes there is a door guarding a new room that locks behind you once you pass.  Alternately, they have bridges or ledges you can jump across that crumble behind you, accomplishing the same purpose.  Then sometimes there will be a door that locks followed by a bridge that crumbles.  Why?  This is like intentionally throwing in a second load screen for the sole sake of making you wait longer.  It's pointless to the point of being disrespectful.  There are loads of hidden breakable walls with nothing behind them but a couple empty pots.  They pad these things out with traps sometimes, but once you've figured the traps out it's laughably easy to just roll through them, effectively making for more empty space.The next major issue is the map choices - or rather lack thereof.  Weapon tiles are just pointless, and boy do they love to litter the dungeon with them.  You get a weapon, usually the starting one will be fine, then you upgrade it as much as possible.  That is the winning strat, and it is obvious.  At weapon shrines, You have to pay absurd prices to get a new weapon, at which point you throw the old one away and get NOTHING for it and all the upgrades you put into it.  Like, once in a while you might happen upon one that is better enough to warrant the absurd cost, but this is rare enough that you would probably never go out of the way to actually waste a move going to one of these things, unless you have no choice.  Which will happen a lot, because they put these worthless spaces EVERYWHERE.There is an easy fix here for both issues: do away with the stupid weapon tiles.  Put a weapon shop in with the upgrade tiles, let them choose one or the other.  Then, put healing shrines where the old weapon shrines were.  You already have to pay a cost to visit the shrines (a move and corruption gain), they should be an available option.  Limit them to two drinks if you're worried about it.  Like, every other game on the planet has this one figured out.These are the deal-breaking issues for me.  Here are some more minor notes.- The corruption / curse system is neat, but definitely needs tuning.  The risk/reward on them is way out of sync with several.  For a couple curses (Headless Horseman comes to mind) they are so good that I will actively try to corrupt myself further to keep the curse from being removed when I kill a boss.  Others don't seem to have the 'power at a price' thing quite figured out in the most literal sense; one prevents some torches from being lit with literally zero upside.  The majority of them, however, are just about right.  This is a pretty cool mechanic, just needs a little polish.-The lighting system needs some work.  It's a neat idea, but +50% damage is waaaay too harsh when lighting is not guaranteed even if you are trying.  Too many (ie almost all) of the braziers can and will be destroyed by any random enemy attack, so even if you light them all it often doesn't accomplish anything; the enemies attacking you will immediately snuff them out, since you have to be next to them to light them.  Note that this usually destroys the light source, so you cannot just re-light it.   Make those things indestructible or nerf the damage hike, or both.  Right now the lighting system is at the point where it is too penalizing to ignore and too unreliable to use even if you put in significant effort.  It's detracting from fun significantly more than adding to tension.EDIT:  I put in a little more time and have to revise my review.  I found a number of bugs.  The worst offender is with the greed timer.  It completely doesn't work, dropping randomly when you evade or parry attacks with no apparent pattern.  You really notice it if you take the starting power that keeps it from dropping due to time.  I made it from the 2nd room to the first boss without taking a hit, and the timer dropped on me 6 separate times.  No damage taken, I made certain, it is just dysfunctional and cannot tell the difference between a dodge and a hit.  The curses are also worse than I thought.  Some of them outright lie to you in the description - the one that says some braziers cannot be lit actually makes them emit a light-consuming giant sphere of oblivion that douses your torch and protects enemies from fire.  A lot of them just seem too lazy to bother to try to keep the cool 'negative but with a potential positive' theme and just give a straight up disadvantage.  It's just more rng on top of the insufferable mountains of it all over this game.The trap-only rooms have to go.  The game's attempts at this adventure-exploration thing are misguided at best, and these mechanics only grow more tedious every run.  Some rooms have the monsters spawn all in waves in one big room.  These rooms are great; if that was the whole game, it would be much better.  The weapon rooms are even more laughably pointless and frequent at the higher difficulties.  These things should not be in the game.  Every time I was forced to go to one I just sighed inwardly and hated this game a little more.Curse of the Dead Gods routinely turns 15 to 20 minutes of content into a 45-minute run, with runs that can and will be completely ruined by bad rng.  I don't mean 'ruined' like 'aw, man, that was a close one, sucks that I got unlucky.'  I mean it like: 'wow, this stupid mechanic / bug / whatever just completely wasted a half hour of my life, and I had zero fun during it'. Dropping my score to 5.5 / 10.  If you haven't played Hades, play it instead.  If you HAVE played Hades, replay it instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Bow + Crit heal build OP as ♥♥♥♥, thanks for carrying my ass to the end of the game. Also, ♥♥♥♥ those lightning babies. You will understand my hatred towards them, once you face them yourself. Especially the elite version. With that said, A very solid roguelike, with 45-50 hours of gameplay/replay value in the current content, to reach the . A fine game by a smaller studio, for sure. A lot of love was put into this, and it shows. Hopefully there is more to come. Things I really liked: -Outstanding, beautiful visual style, oozing with milieu and monsters inspired by ancient Mayan/Aztec/native civilization folklore and architecture  -Combat feels turbo good, a ton of care was put into how it works, every cleared room feels highly rewarding, and going into a new fight is always, shockingly: fun.  -The progression feels very smooth, the game eases you in with smaller treks first that ramp up very organically into larger and longer treks into the temple, the more you overcome the previous ones.  -Very wide arsenal of different play-styles to choose from, no one will be left cold as to not being able to find the perfect weapon combination they want to get good with. I personally got married to the two handed bows.  -Every decision you make in your treks matter, every path you take shapes your current run in interesting ways, that you may have not taken into account when you started, inclining you to actually plan ahead and make up a strategy according to your desired outcome/fulfilling your plan for your build. -Soundtrack is great! Things I thought could use improvement: -The story narrative is almost absent, only exists in form of unlockable monster trivia which you gain by killing a set amount of each one. With the recent masterpiece of "Hades", this game would've greatly been improved by the same kind of narrative richness, but it doesn't remove any quality from the game though, just personally wish it would've been there, to some degree. -The overall amount of replayability and game-modes. What is present, is incredibly solid, but I wish there was way more, since the groundwork is so damn good. Will keep an eye out for future updates/DLC, for sure. Overall, I give Curse of the Dead Gods a solid 9/10, where the only shortcomings for me were the lack of narrative and the amount of content regarding to it being a roguelike game, as I'm used to getting hundreds of hours out of games like these, when done absolutely right. (IE. Isaac, RoR2.) The cons being solely based on how good the game is and basically just wanting more of it, won't be a major hit in any way to my rating. Get this game if you like the genre and having fun in general, you won't regret one second of it.  With love, -Antiswagtoby

_childDocuments_.review: The first 10-15 hours were fun. I spent the time learning, unlocking and progressing the available quests. And I want to recommend the game for that period of time.But then I realized that there are basically only 5 perks that matter and certain weapons outclass all others. And I found the game to be too hard for my taste. I spent 25 hours (out of 45 hours in game time) trying to beat the last couple quests before realizing that I stopped having fun a while ago. If you're a god gamer or enjoy finding tough challenges, then pick this one up and ignore my quibbles with difficulty. However, if you're in it for variety and replayability from a roguelike, I'd recommend going somewhere else.PRO:- Curse mechanic is a unique way to add challenge for engaging in risk-reward decisions- Light/darkness mechanic is clever and fun- Visuals are great- Does really well at building up from tutorial to full run- Has assist modeCON:- Several enemies have tells that make it difficult to distinguish between different attacks- Bosses have so much health that it feels like a slog instead of an intense fight- Clearly optimal choices leads to lack of variety long-term- Assist mode disables achievements permanently. I get this for invincibility mode, but for everything else it undermines the idea that the game is actually accessible.
