_childDocuments_.review: Very hard to put this game into a single genre really, but If you like crafting and building games it's great, if you like survival games it's pretty thrilling, and quite eye opening if you don't know much about our evolutionary struggle to become the masters of our environment...even if we have lost our way.You can play the game customised to make it as easy or as challenging as you like, but there's quite a lot of depth if you persevere, and later in the game the difficulty starts ramping when resource and people management becomes an important part.  Not sure if game designers meant it as another learning curve, bet as you progress you even start learning better ways to use your skills to streamline the tasks you have throughout the game.Just as an example(without giving too much away), simple jobs like tilling the soil will be more efficient when you find the balance of action input, speed, and rhythm.  This can be important at the beginning of the game because you don't have workers to do it for you and the sunlight fades fast, also the faster you get the jobs done, the quicker you can upgrade your skills and technology, meaning you can make better and sturdier items and buildings.My main playthrough was only customised to be 30 days per season instead of the standard 3 days, but even I have found this game a bit easy as the world is full of useful items that have been left for you to find, in fact, I urge you to travel the valley before you decide where to settle down.  There's some great scenery, challenging encounters, and plenty of areas that would make a great village to build out from.  There's even some side quests you can do for rewards, and you will need to do those quests if you want to grow your village into a city(by old standards)....And here's the only gripe I have with the game really, the missions at first are fun, but they are recurring so can become a little monotonous later in the game.  They also don't make a lot of sense, for instance, you'll go to the smithy in a settlement and he'll ask if you can go and mine some copper ore for him....only to realise just two buildings down, in the same village, he could buy some from the excavation shed trader.  Kinda kills the immersion when it's that laughably easy.I'll give you a little hint to help you in the very beginning, stone knives are the way to go, make as many as you can between settlements and you'll soon have a lot less worries on your plate.Enjoy a more simpler less stressful time, where nature still has a bit of an upper hand, where work was hard but more rewarding, and your destiny and dynasty are in you OWN hands. 😎👌

_childDocuments_.review: OK, so I obviously really like this game if I sunk this much time in it. I played it mostly when it was still in early access so I had incredibly high hopes for it and it gave me an experience you won't really find in other games. But I would have to agree with some of the other reviewers and say that once you get past the initial quests, find a wife, have a kid, build up your town, etc, you're left feeling quite hollow & empty. This game had an incredible amount of potential that it seems will just never be met. It would have been nice to at least have a sign naming my town and an actual location for it on the map. It seems quite silly to me to have a highly populated town, larger than any other, pretty much making it the capital of the Valley, to have it just be some random place in the woods. The quests and story line get quite repetitive & annoying on a replay and because of this I have a hard time finding any enjoyment in it because there is literally nothing left. I almost found myself the second & third time around ( I mostly did this to have better starting locations) wondering why the MC even cared about all of this stuff? I mostly just skipped it because I hated all of the NPC's, especially after knowing the truth. I just couldn't tolerate them at all. There was nothing redeemable about any of them IMO. I guess overall I just have to say that I can't not recommend this game. It's very unique and fun to play the first time around. I put over 240 hours into it so there is definitely something here to love. But it just set the player up to believe it could be so much more than it is. The game is far from finished, imo. There are still a lot of buildings that should really be upgraded to stone but they're not, as well as cobblestone roads. This is really just nit picking but it would be nice to have a uniform look to my town that I poured 50-60 or more hours into perfecting. Also, please for the love of all that is holy implement a way to increase build amounts without completing the main quest.

_childDocuments_.review: This game recaptures a good deal of the feeling of playing something like Minecraft for the first time. The building and survival elements all make good sense and the details of the gameplay like sounds, animations and other details are well designed and satisfying. The level of detail with the building, farming and even hunting makes those more entertaining to do than they might sound. Shooting accurately with a bow from long range is not trivial and perks actually impact your experience of the gameplay like shooting rather than just giving a numerical modifier. Animals will slow down when they are wounded so getting that first arrow hit before its alerted is important, and getting headshots actually makes a huge difference in terms of one or two hits to kill versus several.The quest system gives a bit of structure to learning the game without having an overbearing tutorial. Information is easily accessible but going through a playthrough or two slowly allows you to learn all the game systems. There is limited voice acting and sometimes cheesy dialogue but its not cringeworthy for sure.I think this game is very worth it, it seems like the devs have quite a bit of development left planned and the freedom of the open world makes this replayable.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game as a starting point. Has lots of potential to grow with new content and develop into all in one experience. I think I’d speak for a lot of people, I think there is a desire to have a game where you can start as character trying to survive, then develop into building a settlement, then move into management, building a kingdom, waging war. Some areas of improvement:* Balance out the economy a little more. Costs/decay/effort. * New story lines/consequences/quests. * As the settlement grows, more management option, less hands on. * Possibly of the access to other lands. At least quest interactions, trade, war, etc. * More buildings, recipes, items. * Introduction of conflict, war lets say at further stages of settlement development. * Defnsive structures / castle building. * City watch creation, army creation. * Ships. Overall, a great game. Hope it continues to be developed.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm loving it. Nice story telling; nice graphics; amusing dialogue; SO many different things to do; so many choices to be made. I perceive a long-term addiction to this game!This is like a blend between a typical FPS, a people simulator like The Sims, and a business simulation. It begins with you playing a pre-made character in a medieval setting with absolutely nothing but the clothes on your back, and a story-line to discover -- you have to do everything for yourself, and your first challenges are ones simply of survival. As the game progresses your role changes quite a bit, and if you prefer you can become mostly or entirely a builder and city manager rather than doing all the things you once had to do for yourself.Eventually, unless you enjoy improving aesthetics one reaches a state where (like with a successful Sims family) there is little need to DO anything, which might be improved with game expansions. Otherwise, the game can retain entertainment value by starting over and founding your city somewhere else on the map, an approach that would be even better with additional maps as DLC if necessary. I cannot comment at all about co-op play because I'm a loner, but I do note that co-op play is only available on a more functionally-limited map which caused me to abandon my progression with a custom character there and return to playing the original map with a necessary pre-made character. edit: 900 hours solo playtime recorded now, and I'm still loving this game. Many recommend playing with altered game settings (for example, unlimited weight, less animal HP, and longer seasons) but I don't -- I tried less HP and longer seasons, and I think those players are going to get bored much more quickly that way. I would like an ability to speed up time when playing solo, and more maps as functional in every way as the original Valley -- not functionally limited maps like Oxbow (charming, but functionally crippled as in being unable to retire as an NPC, and no regime changes in the kingdom, etc).

_childDocuments_.review: It's an early production, it kind of feels like a Kingdom Come: Deliverance Town Builder.  It's kind of slow paced, as you have to gather your resources to build different buildings around your settlement, but it feels rewarding when you accomplish them. You also have to run to town and back to your settlement, as there is no fast travel option, and I think this makes it more engaging, like you are really there.There are a bunch of quests you can do while interacting with some of the NPC's, but there is currently no speech from any of the them, so you will have to read the dialog right now. But the words pop up on the screen right away, and you don't have to wait for them to scroll, so you can skip it if your not interested it what they have to say.Currently they don't have much in the way of tutorials, so you have to figure out some stuff on your own, but they do have a lot of information you can read through in one of the menus. A lot of the basic stuff is kind of easy to figure out, like basic crafting of things( ex: stone axe, rabbit cage, etc. ), but the town management is a little confusing ( not knowing which buildings to build in the correct order, and which ones to assign the workers too at the beginning ).You can tell the developers are passionate with this project, and I definitely believe that it is worth showing the support to see where they take this in the future. I have high hopes they will continue to make it better as time goes on.
_childDocuments_.name: Medieval Dynasty

_childDocuments_.review: Once you hit the mid-game, you've pretty much seen it all.I really wish I could give a yes and no recommendation. Animals all act the same, either running directly at you to attack you, or running away from you in wide circles as you attack them. Wisents and bears stop being a challenge by the time you get to copper tier weapons. The fancier clothing can be completely ignored once you have anything warm enough to not take damage from the cold in winter. Building unlocks hit a point pretty quickly where everything is just more efficient versions of previous buildings. Story quests are ok, but nothing that'll blow you away, and random quests are all either "give me this many of this item" or "go kill this many of this type of animal." Stealing has no consequence, as Dynasty Reputation doesn't do anything.It's a really fun and relaxing game, but it needs some major goal to work towards, or some reasons to keep going to different areas on the map, and it definitely needs some additional tech unlocks to keep spicing things up (donkey riding isn't enough to save it). At the very least, they need to tone down the quest rewards and random roadside pickups that give out iron tier weapons when the player is still working on stone.Alternatively, if they wanted to go crazy, they could implement bandit/soldier raids, what with the war going on nearby. Something to put the town you're building at risk, give a reason to put up fences and walls, and shake up the combat from just hunting animals and getting casually chased by the most pathetic bandits in the world. Something that would require posting guards as an additional job, that would require an additional "Combat" skill for yourself and your other villagers, and would unlock new fortifications the farther down the tree you go (castles anyone?) and would give a reason to build stone buildings instead of just for the insulation. Something that would require supplying your people with weapons and armor on top of food and wood, and that would give you a reason to always be working towards gear upgrades and grinding out more supplies. And it would make for one hell of a personal story to fail and have the village ruined by these raids, and have to rebuild from nothing, but with all the tech unlocks and higher tier gear you have now to make it easier.I know this would probably require such an overhaul to the AI and to the loot systems that it's probably not feasible, but I do believe it would fix the major problem this game has of running out of ♥♥♥♥ to do by your 3rd or 4th year. If they ever make a Medieval Dynasty 2, though...
_childDocuments_.name: Medieval Dynasty

_childDocuments_.review: The game promises an ambitious rise from peasant to ruling dynasty, but has the depth of a puddle. Graphics are alright, sound is glitchy but serviceable.  Performance is alright but buggy.All in all, the game doesn't have enough "game" in it. The game is just not ready or close to achieving it's lofty claims. It's a glorified graphics demo. There is no gameplay depth to be found in either the menus or the game mechanics. Observe a few things I noticed just in 2 hours of gameplay which I felt tapped the entirety of the content currently in the game.-you can now change keybinds, thank you devs-you can't name your saves, they don't even have a thumbnail. They just go up 001, 002 etc-no customization of character-dwelling cannot be changed in any way, even to upgrade or move furniture-items cannot be repaired-half of the skills aren't even function-no vehicles, such as boats, wagons, etc-no mounts, fast travel or transport options for movement around the map-visited all villages and NPCs on the map, all 110 including the children. No more than 12 buildings per village not including sheds. No two story buildings. Not even a gate on any village, just some log palisades with no battlements or guards. Since half are women or children, you have around 50 men which isn't even enough to form a company of soldiers (80-200 men).-combat barely exists. There is no armor, no swords, nothing but basic spears and bows out in the world. There are no NPC enemies, just hostile animals like boars that run at you in a straight line. -NPCs are static. There are no classes for them to change into, like merchant, official or soldier. You can't build a kingdom with 110 peasants.-NPCs are invincible and aloof. They don't interact with the world at all. They endlessly swipe at the same wheat all day or stand around. I lead a pack of wolves, which is a threat in a quest, into a village since it has no guards or gates. The NPCs were ignored by the wolves which only chase the player in a straight line. You can't hurt NPCs either, tried with stabs, swings, arrows and spear throws.-NPC dialogue is as dull as a board. Same dialogue with every village lass on the entire map. Nice weather. Seen that noble? (I sure haven't). Working the fields is hard. Hunting tips? (it is annoying but hardly challenging). Besides the scripted quest dialogue, the villagers are pretty much identical.-stealing just reduces your "dynasty reputation" with no physical consequences-tavern doesn't sell drinks-the backstory cutscene has almost nothing to do with the game, no wars, no germanic kingdoms invade, no bandits, your uncle is dead and left you nothing. There isn't even a revenge plot for your lost family.-there is nothing beyond village life. No kings. No bandits. No wars. Just thatched houses and hand tended fields. You can't build anything meaningful beyond crafting stations. It's like fallout 4 base building but without the charm, world, and combat. -the world's items are the barest minimum the game needs to function:-2 herbs, one insta heals 10hp and one removes poison. They grow like weeds-2 grains, wheat and rye-1 drink, water. Die of disease now since you don't even boil it-4 kinds of fruit, none of which grow in the map-2 kinds of vegetable, carrot and cabbage. strange choice.-1 root vegetable, onion. No potatoes for you comrades....-ALL animals turn into the same 3 things, leather, fur and meat. Fox pelt? Fur. Boar meat? Same as a rabbit. The age old, respected and lucrative leather making trade? I'm sorry, did you say skin the boar?-ALL vendors have the same prices. They all suck too. 2 gold for some meat, a delicacy for peasants? The same 2 gold as 2 sticks or a random herb grabbed by the handful on the side of the road. The same in every single village and every NPC I checked on the entire map.-All vendors buy anything with a stock of 1000 gold. What rich peasants. -skill grind is incredibly slow. You have to kill tens of animals for one skill point in hunting. Three hundred herbs for one skill point in that tree. Farm 2-3 seasons for some farming XP to get one skill point. All to get a shovel. Even an idiot can make a shovel in 2-3 years, much less pay 50 gold to nowhere to gain the blueprint after reaching the correct tier.-tech is super slow just like skills (they are kinda tied together). It takes hunting 50 ish animals with spears just to unlock the basic bow at the hunting lodge tier, which is even worse than the spear. There is simply no path to becoming a dynasty ruling over a kingdom in the game. There isn't even a framework. All that exists currently is a barebones medieval styled survival game that isn't even hard. You can live on just picking up berries and shrooms. MY inventory has 300 berries and 154 shrooms, my house has hundreds more and this is just 3 days of walking to visit every single village. There are no command mechanics, no conquest systems, you can't even change an NPC's attire. The game is barely even functional as a survival game, there isn't any hint of a kingdom builder anywhere in this game. Even if I moved the entire population of the game (~110+player) into one spot, it would only rate as a small town, much less a kingdom, dukedom, viscounty, barony, etc. It'll take years for this game to even hope to live up to it's claims of working from peasant to dynasty. Don't buy it now, maybe 3-4 years in the future.TLDR: Game makes ambitious claims and has lofty aspirations but is only a simple decent looking peasant who doesn't have a clue on how to become a ruler.Will update as needed.

_childDocuments_.review: I currently consider Medieval Dynasty to be the best medieval life simulation and settlement building game I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. The game offers an impressive amount of content, has stunning graphics and a very relaxing soundtrack. Furthermore, it is notable for its efficient optimization, managing to run smoothly on my average computer even with graphics settings at maximum.One feature that I really appreciate about the game is the absence of any progressive bias. Character creation is limited to the basic aspects of men and women, without the unnecessary inclusion of options related to "gender" or "genitalia" (like Baldur's Gate, for example, unfortunately). This helps to preserve the game's medieval authenticity, without being influenced by modern political issues.Although Medieval Dynasty stood out in several aspects, there are some points that I consider could be improved:- Character customization: there could be more options to make the character unique. Many current games, including this one, only offer limited options like preset faces and colors, rather than a more flexible system like that found in Elden Ring that allows for detailed adjustments through various sliders. I would like to change the shape of my character's nose, length of hair and reduce the size of her bust, for example.- COOP Experience: It would be amazing if my character could share the same house with my partner's character and have children with him (we are female and male in the game too). Currently, each player needs to have their own house and can only romance NPCs, which somewhat limits immersion in the game.

This game keeps getting better with every update

_childDocuments_.review: 1. I like the game and will keep on playing it. All is written already about that part.2. Balancing could be betterOne negative review hit a good topic. You need to rush before winter and get things done; things done really takes a lot of time. So it needs better balance. I talk to ladies always in order to get diplomacy and relationships up - I need a wife. This will take years in present game play. However, I need also certain building for farming or fishing. That also will take a long time, and, and, I will not be able to spend it on finding a wife.So with the current balancing in the game I will play it for a very long time.3. Fast travel would be nice too. All that walking takes the fun out of the game.4. Polishing graphics: small deer run away with my gigantic wooden spear through them? _childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. The world looks very real, and it's very lovely. The game obviously is a niche game of crafting, making a village and working with NPC's. You can get married and have children (God save us). The needed hunting is real in a way, the animals suffer and cry out in pain. Some thing are very odd, to me. I'm using to other games where the NPC's don't sit around the camp fire in the pouring rain, but when they do they're talking, laughing and playing music, quite lively. These npcs are like zombies, frowning, sitting around the campfire in the rain when they have a house right next to them. But other than a few quirky oddities like that, it's pretty good. You can't terraform or land level so building is frustrating. But it's not really building as you have a prefab player owned structure that appears out of the air and you have to try and place it where the ground is level and not blocked by unknown objects. But it can be done. The interaction between you and your village mates is interesting in the way they work for you, but your conversation is very, very limited. The old "Warn the village of the wolf attack" is a stand by for these games, but I have to cringe because contrary to old wives tales wolves did not attack the village, ever. But hey we gotta have something to be afraid of. There are bandits now but I've yet to run into one. All in all, if you love this crafting/npc niche type game, it's a very beautiful world and I just love it. My 2 cents if they made it a tower defense type game as well, where you can recruit not only workers but village militia and arm them, and they gain in skill, and over time the enemy gets harder, now that would sell a million games. But no one cares what I think heh. A game similar to the  concept of Going Medieval (which I do not like), and the tower defense/destructible world of 7 Days to Die, with this beautiful a world is something I'd pay a lot for. It means a lot more and the player becomes much more invested in a game when it feels like it means something, and harvesting your crops and all is fine, but managing to do it before the bad guys show up and defending your NPC's, is a hell of a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: My negative review is highly dependent on the price. This game doesn't have what it takes to move from 15€ bracket to 30€. My example is the polish.Big/main part of the game is to build a village with villagers, but you do not get villagers to work and live there. They don't eat, they don't work, they don't hunt. They are there to represent progress bars.Their food need is solely a timer representing how often food dissapears from their storage. Most of their time, they just stand near their job site, staring into the distance. It's like a scene from a horror movie. I jump everytime I pass my hunting cabin with the huntress lifelessly standing behind it, staring..The lumberjack isn't even operating the only "machine" he has at his job site, not even talking about his conjuring of wood from thin air.Menus. I will probably get used to it, but they are so user unfriendly. I feel like when moving from one thing to another, the controls completely change. It's so bad, that to do every single key input, I have to keep an eye controls overlay to actually do what I mean to do. It's not helped by the fact that outside of menus, your action button is E, but in menus it switches to F, so you mean to interact with something and suddenly end up on a completely different tab of the menu, canceling whatever you did.Last example. Something about the UI or questing system confused me into thinking that the story quests are relevant to the game. They are not. But I spend my first two hours running from one side of the map to another, just to get paragraphs of story, that was written by a ten year old. Just to waste time before actually playing the game.In total I probably spend just over 2 hours actually playing the game, but even in that time, I feel I've seen everything the game has to offer. I hope I'm wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played long, I feel I have a pretty okay idea of the game. I wish I could put an in between of yes/no, as a city builder where you actually play as a villager I recommend, as a survival I could see this being pretty brutal, as a medieval game it does hit the spot with a touch of Skyrim in places, as a game with quests and NPCs that feel they should be interesting? ehhhh... lets say, I haven't grown bonds with any of the characters, really.I'd say buy this on discount if you can, I'm not sure I'd pay the full $35 for it if given the chance but with time it may grow into its tag. I will try my best to update my review as things change, but no promises.NPC dialog, being often borderline meme-worthy, with the writing not being the best, is probably my only real complaint about the game even though I don't entirely  mind when the NPCs aren't written the best, as theres moments the game doesn't take itself seriously in the quest-front. That said I have ran into a few quests where it feels as though there was genuine thought and a pretty decent effort at trying to make the quest feel interesting. Better writing or a dedicated writing team wouldn't hurt the game is ultimately how I feel. It also wouldn't hurt to have dialog options grey out if you've used them before, as it feels no real progress is made to learn about a non-romancable NPC or to have their thoughts about you change.I  to learn about the people of Oxbow, but so far all that is memorable about the NPCs is that the Castellan is not a pleasant person, and Segowin is a father-like surgeon that saved you from certain death. I assume if I play long enough, eventually all these characters will die, but I feel that should be an event and it should be interesting and compelling to learn how the families of the land change and grow.It'd also be nice if romancable NPC personalities were possibly improved, or getting to know them was improved. I do not feel attachment to any of the NPCs I've brought into my village as all of them feel somewhat same-y, with exception for one male NPC who has the "Rogue" personality that I have debates with myself if its a good idea to keep him around, maybe it wouldn't if he were able to do a bit more based off his personality than just his job, eat, drink, sleep and his job. I want other NPCs to make me keep mental notes about them like this rogue, but it'd also be cool to see NPCs act based off their personalities.But that may also just be purely out of sight for the game at its current stage, as this may just simply not be a priority, and I can see that as being fair as the dynasty system sounds like a fairly... extreme goal to undertake as a game? What they have so far is pretty decent, even if the writing could use a little help.That said, as is while it  make the game feel a bit cheaply made, I don't see NPC interaction as the make or break factor for enjoyment of this game. As a city builder, and even to an extent as a survival, I have been enjoying the game. Exploration is fun and even rewarding, and usually fairly dangerous. I enjoy the village design aspect of it, and getting things going feels really good. It makes me think of how Fallout 4's settlements feel like they should work.Combat is another thing I am iffy on but it does not entirely bother me. I feel combat will be difficult - especially against the likes of a bear or a pack of wolves, which by all means it probably should be - but a little bit for the wrong reasons. Fighting with say, a spear, feels somewhat jank - the only thing I can get to properly work is throwing spears, but trying to use the melee attack with a spear 9/10 refuses to actually work. There is crossbows and bows, but I feel when an animal is charging at you, these aren't fast enough, and your other options - axe, dagger - feels they do little damage to these creatures.I'm not much of a combat person so I don't get many run-ins with hostile creatures or people, but even still I would enjoy improvements to combat.Haven't entirely gone through the dynasty system as I still have yet to even choose an NPC to romance, but from what I read it just kinda works? Pregnancy in the game sounds fairly shallow for lack of better words - being just an icon and changing a few lines until the child is born for which 2 (months? years?) the mother (or father for pc+npc relationships, if player is a woman) will have their job changed to Mother/Father to take care of the child. I'm not completely certain yet how the dynasty system works in the co-op mode.There is a few things I hope to see, like more feminine-based attire , the ability to build large walls, hire guards that patrol, be able to hire bodyguards for while you're out and about, have bandit raids possibly or criminals, or better expansion on how pregnancy works in the game to make it more impactful as a system, and not just an icon. Maybe especially where players are concerned to add an extra challenge, such as pregnancy actually effecting stamina, and how much you can carry. Maybe even the famous pregnancy bump, so you can see how far along an NPC (or a fem model player) is.I believe this would also be a fun game to see modding in, allowing modders to add systems, cosmetics, or items that is out of the dev's ability due to time or scale of project.Overall, if you want interesting NPCs that you'll grow bonds with, I wouldn't say this is the game for you, in its current state as of writing this review. I'm not sure how the Valley's NPCs act, but at least in Oxbow they don't always feel particularly well written. As a city-builder, especially if you enjoyed Fallout 4's Settlements but wanted more out of it and enjoy Medieval as a setting, its pretty fun.The game is being rapidly updated from what I understand, a lot of information is currently outdated. So a lot could change in a very small amount of time, I am curious to see how this game grows. I know shields and armors seem to be on the way so that'll be fun.Kinda wish I could recommend this to my significant other to try out co-op properly, but I wouldn't say this is their kind of game. Same time could see them running around chasing bears with sticks and getting destroyed.

_childDocuments_.review: At 275 hrs, I feel like I've put enough time in to do a proper review.First off, this is an Early Access title.  Let's be real clear on that.  If you are expecting a fully finished, perfectly balanced game filled to the brim with features and lacking any bugs.... Do not play Early Access titles.  It should also be noted that, unlike many EA titles, the developers are hard at work adding new content and functionality as well as tweeking the existing mechanics to improve over all balance.  There are regular, if not exactly scheduled, updates, and the developers really appear to be listening to what people have to say about the game.Next, I would like to point out that this (at least imo) is NOT a survival game.  Yes, animals and falls can kill you.  You lose health from not eating or drinking.  But those are very small parts of this game.  This is a village building simulator with survival aspects.  The main focus is on building your village and taking care of the needs of your villagers.  Making sure they have shelter as well as the resources and manpower to produce fuel and food.  If you're interested in a man (or woman) alone against the elements type of game, this isn't it.Now...  Lets talk about those logs.  It has been mentioned more than once the whole cartoon tree into toothpick thing.  I agree that there needs to be some improvement on crafting materials, but since I've been playing there have already been some much needed overhauling of required materials for crafting.  Besides the developers clear willingness to do their best the improve these issues, I feel like people aren't paying attention to the visual aspects of the game.  In those old cartoons, they would take a mighty oak tree and turn it into a toothpick.  Birch and maple trees are not oak trees.  Spruces may be tall, but they're not exceptionally thick.  When you cut down a birch tree in the game, looking at the top portion, you're not getting more than 1 spear out of that.  And given that the game doesn't have saw mills and you're literally making spears by hand, how exactly would you divide up a larger trunk in order to make multiple spears?  A hammer or a shovel requires a log, because the sticks aren't thick enough to product the kind of material needed for the heads of those items.  And yes.... There's going to be a lot of logs in construction.  Generally, it's only 1 log per wall/roof segment unless you're actually building something out of logs like the higher tier buildings.  That's not ridiculous.  All of that being said, it certainly feels strange to pick up a tree trunk and turn it into a slender spear.  But given that a large pouch allows you to carry 4 additional logs, do you really want this aspect to be perfectly realistic?  Would you rather be carrying logs 1 or 2 at a time to a building location?  Let's all just accept that "log" in game means wood bigger than a "stick".The economy in the game is much improved from when I started playing, but don't expect things to move quickly.  If you need to make money, have your crafters producing goods worth selling then take those and any excess grain you have and sell it at the closest village.  Because... that's how things worked in medieval times.  I'll admit that there still needs to be some balancing done with pricing, but as I said, it's already much more realistic than when I started.  You use to be able to sell things like stones, sticks, and herbs for a coin apiece.  Making money was easy.  Just go out in a field and spend 10 minutes picking everything up, and BAM! 700 coins.  Crafted items now have pricing that greatly exceeds the materials they're made of which gives you a reason to spend more time making stone knives or axes or wicker baskets.Hunting in the game is a necessary evil, and sadly, one of the areas that really needs more work.  Spears are nearly pointless (no pun intended).  It's frustrating watching a doe run around at full speed with 5 of your spears piercing straight through her.  It gets better once you progress to a bow.  It only takes 2 head/neck shots to take down a deer with stone arrows, and only a single shot with the iron version.  They've added more pronounced weapon sway which adds more realistic difficulty.  I have not been able to tell what difference there is (if any) between the different types of bows.  Possibly a longer, straighter shot with the arrows, but the damage does not seem to change between the different styles.  I would really love to see a larger variety of animals and maybe color variants as well.  Maybe every rabbit doesn't have to be brown?  I realize this isn't Red Dead 2, but it would add some spice to the monotony of hunting.The biggest issue with the game right now (imo) is how it handles loading in mobs.  Both NPCs and animals.  It is not uncommon to see in the distance an animal fall out of the sky and then zip across the landscape to get to where it's suppose to be.  Because they all seem to drop out of the sky, you sometimes get Wisents stuck in trees or villagers on their roof.  This can be more than a little annoying when you can't get to an NPC to turn in a quest because he's just chilling out on the thatch of his hut.  But overall.... The game is fun and fully playable.  It needs better controller optimization, but I still manage to play with a controller just fine.  The graphics are really good, and the landscape feels like a real place you could be walking through.  I very much look forward to seeing what the developers bring to this game.  Again, if you want a fully finished, well polished game, then keep your eye on this, but wait to buy.  If you want to enjoy a good medieval village builder while content is still being added and adjusted, then absolutely give this game a try.EDIT:  I took a break from the game for a year or more and only recently came back to it.  There has been a TON of content added to the game.  As I wished for, there is now an abundant variety of wild life to hunt.  There are a multitude of new buildings and jobs for your villagers to do.  I never notice weird spawn behavior with the NPCs or mobs anymore.  This game now feels like a full game.  And the developers are STILL adding content and tweeking game mechanics.  I have been very impressed with the passion and devotion shown by this development team.STEAM DECK NOTE:  This game plays fine on Steam Deck.  The Steam Deck info states that the configuration can be hard to read and that the game doesn't automatically play is the Steam Deck's native resolution.  I didn't have any issues with the setup screens.  Perfectly readable.  And the game loaded automatically into the 1200x800 native resolution, so I figure this info is old news.  I would highly recommend changing the graphics preset from high to medium.  The game runs fine on high, but the Deck will get extremely hot and it devours your battery.  I could play maybe an hour on a full charge before hooking up an external battery charger or plugging in the Deck.  On the medium preset, it doesn't get nearly as hot, and I honestly can't tell much difference in the graphics quality aside from view distance.  The game seems to run at a much better frame rate on the medium preset as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Medieval Dynasty is a wonderful gem of a game.  The world itself is beautiful, the scenery alone makes it feel like you are truly traversing a land from long ago with rushing freshwater streams and rivers, rippling lakes, forests thick with trees and wildlife, majestic mountains, all surrounded by the songs and sounds of nature.  Most of my hours are in single player, enjoying all The Valley has to offer - the villagers and travellers you meet are alive and have a reasonable amount of dialog, but also a number of personalities and quirks that can be charming, annoying, or comical, depending on what you're looking for - the variety is welcome.  The building/crafting is interesting - I enjoy how the builds come to life slowly, and the style fits very well in a rustic, medieval setting.  The open landscape offers plenty of choice when it comes to settling down and building your own house - and eventually settlement - and you can choose how you want to interact with the settlement as you go along.  The gameplay can be customized well enough directly through the game menu to suit several different play styles in terms of skill progression and experience, difficulty, and combat/interactions.  Improvements keep on coming, even as the new map and co-op play is introduced, which encourages further engagement and new things to check out.  All in all, Medieval Dynasty is an incredibly enjoyable game for those who like to survive and thrive in a 'village management' and builder scenario that offers far more that just management and immerses you in a beautiful world full of adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is literally only missing one aspect. Co-Op. It is a masterpiece that serves to grieve my heart that I cannot share it with my friends. STILL, definitely worth the price, I would pay twice what this game is listed as even now after playing for over a day of my life collectively.It is a challenging story that you create full of hard work, loss, triumph and beauty. You are placed in this world and given a loose narrative that you can very easily relate with regardless of your path in life, it teaches you how to build a house and then you are pretty much on your own from there. Free to do the main story quests full of rich story or the interesting and engaging side quests or simply ignore them and do your own thing. You can create, and while not limitless in it's design aspect, it offers variety that flows so easily together with the other numerous models and the terrain. You can build a family of your own and one you can actually fight for. You can travel long distances, needing to camp to maintain your health prior to purchasing your first steed and braving the harsh climate to meet people and recruit them to your mission where they will become workers, but not simply workers, workers with their own personalities, traits, and opinions. All of this makes this world feel alive.This is what I call a "Semi-Casual" gaming experience. You will grind and work hard, but the work will be enjoyable and get easier as time goes on, eventually you will reach optional autonomy. It is a great game to get lost in. It is worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: While this is a surprisingly fun game to play, there are a few things the game could use to liven it up. This game unfortunately suffers from feeling a bit hollow at times.- New/and or random quest and story lines each time you play ( or enough to make it feel different every time you play). As of right now, trying to get back into this game can actually feel like a bit of a chore considering quest are really simple in all fairness and they're always the same. Wanting to re-build/start a new game is exciting until...well, you run into the same,  boring quest every time. You can argue that other games have the same quest on start up every single time but sadly with this game, they're just..not very memorable or fun....like, at all. Very dry, very quickly.- Improved writing overall for said quest and added character depth. Not having people to do voice work is fine BUT...dull dialog and story/no character depth IS a problem this game faces. Example? Let's romance this lady! Why? Idk but it's a part of the game. That's it. No other reason.- The game could use some overall attention to detail. All the homes/villages/buildings lack decorations or sense of...you know, people living in them. They have beds...and...you know, they have beds. lol. This sounds minor, however it really would give the game an even MORE inviting and realistic feel to it and would give another opportunity to show off individual characters (Oh! here's so and so's house with the yellow flowers out front) They're adding more content to the game which is great but I strongly feel they need to spend more time building upon what they currently have. What I mean is...Maybe give us, or existing homes at the very lest, a little bit of love! Where's the furniture? The bear skin rugs on the floors, fireplaces to keep warm and cabinets full of mysterious bottles?There's a tavern down the road...with no music, no dancing and no one is eating hot meals. They just sit there...looking into the void. There is a world here and it's fun to play in. But it ( needs! ) that little bit more of soul added to it.6.5/10, game feels seriously hallow/empty

_childDocuments_.review: A great game, with a great story and hours of game play(if you don't adjust time settings/technology gain). Medieval dynasty is a type of game that a lot of people have been wishing/waiting for. Whether you're into role playing and immersing yourself in a medieval world, becoming a 1000 something AD tycoon, or just wanting a slow and easy going game to play after work, You'll enjoy Medieval dynasty.As of right now the story is kind of short, but still worth it's short while. Far as game play goes, don't buy this if you're looking for a combat dense medieval RPG, the most you deal with is occasional bandits(later game) and the occasional wolf, boar, or bear, However; the combat mechanics in the game aren't terrible and I think they plan to add more combat as Toplitz and Render Cube released future plans, including more weapons, craftable armors/shields and family crests. Aside from combat, Medieval Dynasty is a flora and fauna dense valley, with tons of NPCs, sidequests, and tons of open land for you to build your farm, village, or city. With that being said, I'm sure you're aware Medieval Dynasty is still  a work in progress, and Toplitz\Render Cube are very active in their community, in which they go to a great extent keeping us updated, and listening to player wishes\bugs reports.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of it during early access, and it was great.I recently played again, and it is even better than it was.The growth of your village flows well unless you are trying to force it to grow too quickly and the game lets you do what you prefer outside of building (only your character can make new buildings) and selling stuff every now and then for the yearly taxes.You can do quests, go hunting, collect materials, help out in the various things that your villagers can do...The only thing that is still not quite right is pacing when transitionning between the mid game (where you automate most tasks and have a self-sustained village in most aspects) to the late game (where your village mostly stops growing and you enter the whole "dynasty" part where you raise the next generation).It used to be incredibly dull since you were left with next to nothing to do other than pass time.Now it's just slightly dull as you still have things to unlock in most trees and have a lot of decoration you can do, but it's still mostly about passing the seasons/years.If you enjoy decorating your village and all that then there is still quite a bit to do in that phase, but if you don't you end up wandering between the NPC villages to do the same old seasonal quests and sell inventories full of items over and over (because NPC vendors have a relatively low limit on how much money they have).Still one of the best games of the village building genre that I played, definitely helped by the RPG-style approach of having a character rather than being a god-like entity giving orders.

_childDocuments_.review: Survival with so much more. What a phenomenal gem with an amazing experience! Strategy. Skill. Survival. Crafting. Building. Conversation. Reputation. Quests. Buying/Selling. And most important, Village (Dynasty) Management. Fun? Yes! Challenging with Learning Curve? Absolutely! (but in a good way)Still Early Access and Need of Improvement? Of Course!Potential? No Doubt!Great Game? Totally!Worth It? For Sure!Been playing since the release and cannot stop. Still early access with some flaws and bugs but developers are active. Scenery is beautiful and the soundtrack accompanies the atmosphere. There are definite future wishes but the potential is there. Longer seasons as an option (I could see this at the start but later on in the years of the game not so much), inventory transport (definitely needed for transporting logs, rocks, etc.), faster travel (we need a horse which is a future update), improved weapons, player fishing, improved dialogue with potential voice acting, NPC villager improvement, quest line fixes, adjusting an unfinished structure placement. I truly look forward to the progress and cannot wait to see what comes next. Don’t quit on this game. Enjoy the ride!

_childDocuments_.review: This could've been great but it was never really finished. It has great ideas, they're just not executed well.It's disappointing because I enjoy the game, but the reality of "early access" titles just rears it's ugly head whenever I start enjoying it. -Lots of automation and a very enjoyable progression-Perk-based character building-Extensive decorations and customizables in homes/buildings-Some basic quests/storylines-Zero voice acting for dialogue. Anyone looking for a story or immersion of any kind don't even bother. NPC's greet when spoken to and that's it. Villagers never talk or interact with each other. They just wander like robots waiting for the player to do something with them.-Animation such as skinning are difficult to cancel. If you skin an animal and something else pops up to attack you half way through animation, RIP. Combat is clunky. You can just dodge bandits and take zero hits all game.-Very dry character development, with no opportunity for divergent character creation. The main quest will always require you to be a farmer in the beginning and work your way through the same setup.-Minimalist building diversity, every building looks virtually the same.-Survival mechanics deliver nothing novel. It's just the same "pick these items up to make tool x" and "watch your food/water timers -- I mean status bars." Oh and of course "everything fits in your pockets, as long as its less than xx kg"-No meaningful interactions with NPC's. Buildings/workers just fabricate resources out of thin air and require no strategy on placement (mine/fishing hut are few exceptions)-NPC AI is terrible. I built my town intentionally next to a canal for water, but they still need it in a bucket or they riot.-Quests are kind of repetitive and without real consequence.-The game economy is non-existent. There's no dynamic pricing, no supply and demand, everything just has a fixed price and you can sell anything to any vendor. Also, you NEED to have a vendor near your settlement otherwise you will be walking all game. I've made my fortune selling everything from cabbage soup to weapons all to the same seamstress near my town. Where she fabricates 1000+ coins every day is beyond me. I don't question, I just keep making soup.-There is no way you can convince anyone this is a simulator game so just add fast-traveling, seriously.I'd give it a solid 6.5/10. I wish they'd make it a complete game.

name: Tales From Off-Peak City Vol. 1
detailed_description: Just Updated About the Game Tales From Off-Peak City Vol. 1 is set in the same universe as both The Norwood Suite and Off-Peak , Cosmo D’s previous games. It’s a hazy Sunday morning on the corner of July Avenue and Yam Street. Caetano Grosso, a former saxophone player and longtime pizza-maker, is just getting his pizza oven warmed up. Orders are trickling in, and he needs someone to help with the deliveries. You sense an opportunity, but unbeknownst to him, what you’re really after is his old saxophone, and you’re going to get it one way or another. Your pursuit will set off a chain of events across the neighborhood, taking you deep into the hidden worlds and private lives of the people living there. Tales From Off-Peak City is a first-person adventure game series, all set on, around, and under a single street corner. Filled with memorable characters and the spaces they inhabit, the game provides an open-ended world full of secrets and hidden agendas. Building on the gameplay foundations of Off-Peak and The Norwood Suite, players will explore the streets and its surroundings, make pizzas, take photos, push buttons, open drawers they’re not supposed to, and lose themselves inside the atmospheric musical score that integrates itself directly into the game world. Volume 1: Caetano’s Slice is the first game of many in the anthology of Tales. While each ‘Volume’ is its own self-contained story and experience, taken together, they build towards the larger over-arching narrative of what’s really going on at the corner of July Avenue and Yam Street and what role you ultimately play in its fate.

_childDocuments_.review: I hope everyone here understands that surrealism is about much more than just mashing a bunch of weird ♥♥♥♥ together. Plenty of aspiring indie games wither away from a lack of unifying vision and a clear feel, while games like this thrive in the universe they create. Tales From Off-Peak City is the kind of surreal that works, the kind that you feel in the small crevices of your brain and hear echoing in bones you don’t know the names of. It’s weird because it can be and because it has to be, and even so it manages to tell a story that’s both utterly bizarre and oddly familiar in places. For a supposed anthology series, this is definitely a strong start out of the gate.You arrive at the city by boat, ferried by a commanding woman and a quiet man. A flood has washed away much of the neighborhood you’re landing at but that’s okay, because the pizzeria still stands and you need the saxophone hidden within. Caetano Grosso was once a master musician, but gave it all up to sling pies in this run-down borough. Your benefactors want his sax, and they’ve given you an in as the next delivery person for the shop. So begins your adventures on the corner of July and Yam, cooking pizzas, delivering meals, listening to the dark history of the city, and navigating pitfalls both metaphorical and physical on your way to securing the instrument.Tales From Off-Beat City is a first-person adventure game, with only a single button for all of your important interactions. You can pick up items, turn handles, and advance dialogue spoken at you all with left-click, and that’ll get you through all your deliveries and detective work. I won’t say too much about the structure of the game but you’ll generally be making pizzas to fill the orders that come in, delivering them and talking to the customer for a bit, then puzzling out what you can about your objective before moving on to the next delivery. The events that occur as you go about your odd business seem fixed, so don’t expect much in the way of choices or branching paths here, and the aforementioned puzzling is an extremely simple affair.That’s not to say this is a simple game, of course, only that the gameplay taking you through this fever-dream of a town is really secondary to the experience itself. Off-Peak City is a very different world from ours, filled with sentient buildings and giant dogs and still people with very relatable problems. The orders that come in will ask for pizzas that “consider beyond that which is in front of me”, leaving the actual recipe to your interpretations. Deliveries reveal all sorts of strangeness with the residents and also leave a profound impact upon them, and they also call down some attention that you’re probably not going to want. There are a lot of stories here to unearth, and while most of them are not particularly deep as stated there’s clearly a lot of symbolism here, and the central mystery of the pizzeria goes to some really neat places.Along the way you’ll find additional ingredients to add to your prep station, and I’m sure I don’t need to tell you that some of these are a bit outside the norm. You can also buy a camera with some spare cash and find different rolls of film for it, which give your photos all kinds of strange effects. Neither of these things are necessary for finishing the game, nor is teasing out stories from some of the side characters scattered around the neighborhood. But all these things help give the game additional depth and texture, and tease out the length to a cozy two hours or so. Judging from the achievements there are also special conversations you can get by being in the right places at the right times, and I can only imaging what oddities are shared if you can swing that.The main thing here is that the look and feel of Off-Peak City just work. It’s a surreal aesthetic with some genuine thought behind it, guiding the bizarre book titles on shelves and persistent cow imagery and lo-fi jazz pumping through speakers found in the strangest of places. It feels like playing through an old subversive 90s cartoon or falling into a modern art exhibit, and that feel dovetails nicely with the tale of loss and mistrust being told here. The experience is linear and won’t last you too long, but it’s absolutely worth it for the creativity on display. Tales From Off-Peak City is a compelling start for this surreal anthology, and begs many questions about what could lie ahead.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: This is a universe inspired in equal parts by David Lynch, Salvador Dali, Ornette Coleman and William Burroughs. Has climate change ravaged this world? What makes a building sentient? Is this a dream? Why is the pizza so good? Can you get the saxophone? The music! So much music!! This is a visual and audible feast. _childDocuments_.review: Tales from Off-Peak City is the third game in Cosmo D’s series, after Off-Peak itself, and The Norwood Suite. While playing both of those games isn’t necessary to enjoy this one, it is recommended, as there will be references to the characters in the previous games. (And, y’know, Off-Peak’s free.) At its core, Tales is a walking-and-talking game, exploring the surreal locale of the corner of July Avenue and Yam Street. Make pizza, take pictures, get caught up in about three different conspiracies.The first and obvious thing to talk about is the art style; it’s rough, unpolished, and it works so damn well. Textures are either rudimentary and smooth, or eerily realistic. Character models are just on the edge of uncanny valley that you can’t really place: is it the face? The proportions? You can see the textures stretch on some of the walls, yet the pizzas you cook would make your mouth water.Yet, it all comes together, all too well. One of Cosmo D’s main narrative motifs is being an outsider, entering a slice of locale you’re unfamiliar with, and the tossed salad of a graphics aesthetic conveys it amazingly. The streets, the buildings, the people, all things that are kind of familiar, but ultimately alien. But the things you’re familiar with: pizza, camera, instruments, all of these are beautifully modelled. They seem almost out of place, and for good reason -- so are you. While his previous games touched at this aesthetic, Tales of Off-Peak City has, so far, executed it the best, with its misshapen buildings and strange back alleys contrasting the homey feel of the pizza parlor around the corner.The walking’s good, how about the talking? Also grand, but perhaps not to everyone’s taste. Like Norwood Suite and Off-Peak, the game effectively has two kinds of dialogue; outright conversation and eavesdropping on ongoing ones. Once again, though, you’re a visitor. Talk will be on past events no one will elaborate on, persons and groups you’ll never meet outright. Everyone’s got their own story, but no one will tell you everything. At best, the questions asked are augmentable with the pizzas you deliver. There is a story, told upfront, but if you enjoy piecing together a bigger picture, this narrative will definitely be for you.Finally, the music. Some of Cosmo D’s best work. The soundtrack should probably be listened to in-tandem with the game, for each track to infuse itself with the locale, and vice versa. But, even if the game doesn’t entirely interest you, do give the OST a listen.Tales From Off-Peak City is, so far, Cosmo D’s best work, and it’s only the first in a series. The bizarre art style has found its groove, the world’s established enough that the characters are at their most memorable, and the tunes are sublime. Make pizza. Take pictures.And remember to tip your deliveryperson well.

_childDocuments_.review: There’s something off in Off-Peak.Buildings talk, babies with adult faces look eerily similar to their parents, and one apartment is home to a stock of brain matter, which you can then decorate your pizza with. All of it is so outlandish, yet this is exactly what makes the experience mesmerizing. In Off-Peak, there are no rules; every encounter, location or item is simply one of many strange, disparate ideas held by its creator, bundled together in one complete package. And somehow, it works.As I think about the game, I keep coming back to the word . When we dream, we spin up places and situations not wholly unlike what we expect from the real world, yet they typically come with some strange or even preposterous notion. This is what separates the dream from reality, keeping it from becoming too real.Despite its absurdity, the city of Off-Peak is also host to ordinary situations. There are struggling musicians still clinging on to their aspiration no matter how unrealistic it may seem, an infamous landlord with a bossy attitude, and a young man struggling with his student debt. These are all situations that we recognize from the real world, and they keep the city from spiraling into complete absurdism. Over the course of the game, creator Cosmo D manages to effortlessly combine these stories of the mundane with his fascinating imagination. Whereas the surreal attractions keep you going, the characters remind you that there is, in fact, an intention behind all this; it’s not just here to weird you out. This intention is up to interpretation, of course, and I think that’s why I’m excited to one day revisit the city: perhaps I will find a new meaning to its strangeness.  We never learn anything about our protagonist, but that’s beside the point. This is a story of a city and its inhabitants; the title, , is no coincidence. The player character is merely a gateway into this weird world, and you’re even asked to provide your name. Whether you choose a funny name or write your real one is up to you; I went with the latter, and it made the experience strangely personal. If I had to criticize this game for something, or at least highlight an aspect that could be better, it would be the gameplay. Talking to people and clicking on objects notwithstanding, the only mechanic of note is the pizza minigame. This revolves around decorating a pizza with various and often odd toppings, some of which you’ll have to find yourself. For a two-hour game, this is fine, but I would like to see the developer experiment with more forms of interactivity in the future. With the exception of the aforementioned activity, the gameplay exists to  you to the creativity; it doesn’t enhance it. One aspect that does, however, is the music. Like the game itself, the soundtrack defies description; it is jazzy but also features several unique elements, perfectly complementing the peculiar setting. In addition, every action has an instrumental sound effect associated with it, and to support the dialogue, musical nodes will mimic the cadence of speech. This adds a rhythm to the text that most games without voice acting lack.  Off-Peak is at once uncanny, repulsive and somewhat soothing. In the strange city, Cosmo D has crafted a setting that I doubt I’ll ever tire of, its streets and alleyways serving as portals into his brilliant imagination. If anything, I would like him to innovate on the gameplay front, but even if he has no intention to, I’m still excited to see more from him.  In an interview with Alphr about his then-upcoming game The Norwood Suite, he compared his games to long-form jazz pieces. If we’re going with that analogy, then this first volume of Tales From Off-Peak City is certainly one worth listening to.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first time playing a game from Cosmo D and after getting to go through this one I definitely want to go back and play the others. I had always heard Norwood was a strange almost Twins Peaks like game but I just never ended up getting a copy. Luckily despite not playing the previous two games set in the same world including the free one Off-Peak I still felt like for the most it wasn't taking away much from the experience except a few name drops and references. From what I can tell Cosmo D has found their surreal style and ran with it. In this strange game you are tasked with stealing a saxaphone from a former player/longtime pizza maker. You are possibly able to accomplish this by becoming a pizza delivery protege so that you may gain more information and find a way to it. The gameplay is pretty simple. You will deliver pizzas and discover strange streets around you mostly through interaction and some light puzzle solving. The music, world, dialogue, characters, and colors are eccentric and artful. Seeing as surreal stuff falls in stuff I enjoy very much there wasn't too many gripes I had with this one. I didn't experience any issues and everything ran smoothly. The small area contained in this game makes it pretty much great to explore every little nook and cranny. About the only issue I would say I have is just about the time I was really getting into the game; it was over. That's pretty much it.After playing this one you can bet I'll be trying to go back and get into the others at some point. This is vol. 1 and a self contained experience. It's likely that the next volume won't be out for at least a year; but the quality of the work here is worth the wait. If you're unsure if this your cup of tea I would highly recommend either trying the original first game in the world called Off-Peak or trying out the demo to either this or The Norwood Suite. _childDocuments_.review: For surreal adventure game designers on steam, "Cosmo D" stands above all the other games that are too short or simply puzzle-focused. This "Norwood" game series combine a wild spirit of jazz music into the gameplay. The adventure is a breathtaking dream-like experience. This story expands on the Norwood Suite, which I was privileged to test on my Linux OS. I highly recommend playing that game, and playing that game before this one. Try the no-cost game demo, and find out whether you are one of the rare gamers, who appreciates surreal storytelling.I explored the corner of Yam and July Street, on an Ubuntu Linux 20.10 desktop, with radeon mesa graphic drivers. I played with a keyboard-mouse and a gamepad controller. I had no technical issues. The game uses the Unity Game Engine, and it uses 3.4GBs of diskspace.

_childDocuments_.review: Tales From Off-Peak City is the third game in Cosmo D's 'Off Peak' series. If you've played either Off Peak or The Norwood Suite, you'll have some ideas about what to expect, but even so it has some tricks up its sleeve. The framing device this time has you delivering pizzas, and in this way you meet the residents of July Avenue and Yam Street, get embroiled in sinister goings-on, and try to steal a prized instrument.As before, the game's surrealism and its wacky plot are a smokescreen for a remarkably human story, and one it's hard not to get invested in. Cosmo D has created an incredibly rich cast of characters, and shows a deft hand for making you care about them, even though your reasons for being there are questionable.The music is an effortlessly cool blend of jazz and electronica, and while the visuals do a lot of the heavy lifting when it comes to establishing the game's atmosphere, the music and sound design really cement the sense of place. It is a joy to explore its bizarre spaces, like a museum of uncanniness that constantly surprises you.

_childDocuments_.review: Tales from off-peak city is a third installment of the series of games that take place in the Cosmo D universe. Just like in the  Cosmo D's other games it features a colorful cast of characters that oftentimes verge on nonsensicality but it nevers goes too far and so retains some relatability and feeling that you can piece together what is actually happening in the city - that it's not an Inland empire kind of unreachable avant-garde. This, i feel, motivates the player to explore this absurd, surreal and intriguing world. The basic gameplay loop didnt change much from the last two games. You search for an item, you talk to characters, you search for more items, you talk to characters.. and so it goes, though this time instead of searching you deliver items, pizzas to be specific. This gameplay loop generally isn't a bad thing - that is as long as the game keeps your attention and paces it's story well enough and... that's exactly what this game does. On top of that the game is pretty short so i feel like the player doesn't even have a chance to get bored.One of the the strongest parts of the game is it's soundtrack which plays to the absurd atmosphere of the city quite nicely as it through jazz highlights the colorful, variant and at times chaotic structure the game's world possess. Another is it's visual presentation and story which is definitely a step up from the last two games.Though in order to understand the story i feel like you at least need to play the Cosmo D's last game - Norwood Suite which is just as good, so probably play that one first. So in summary definitely try this game out, preferably both Norwood Suite and this one.

_childDocuments_.review: A surreal first-person walking simulator with an actual story, sort of.I've played a ton of games that attempt to imitate surrealist art, but nearly all of them focus entirely on the visual presentation, and completely neglect things like ambiance, gameplay, and story.  This game - along with all the other games by this developer - is different.  It not only  the visual presentation, but also has great music and actual story/dialogue.  Granted, the dialogue tends to be hard to understand, but that fits in perfectly with the theme of the game.The story is  one of those artsy interpretivist ones where nothing makes sense and any interpretation is valid.  The gameplay is minimal, but that's pretty common among all walking simulators.My only complaint is that the game ends too suddenly. At the end of the game, there are still unfulfilled orders you never get to complete; items at the shop which can't ever be bought; and tons of doors (even in the main buiding) which are never opened. It feels like they planned on making the game longer, but then picked an arbitrary point to stop and called it "Volume 1".However, aside from that, I really enjoyed this game. I love the absurd environments and situations this developer includes in their games, which are so completely different from any other game out there.  If you're looking for a game unique from anything you've ever played, definitely give this one a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: An extravagant sequel to the Off-Peak/Noorwood series. I can't get enough of the soundtrack, and the puzzle solving leaves me bewildered. 100% enjoyed this game and its atmospheric vibe & insane visuals we came to know and love in the Off-Peak & Noorwood Suite games. I picked this up as soon as it hit the Steam store and obsessively played it all morning.It was quite an experience building & delivering pizzas with questionable ingredients gathered from unpleasant environments and abrasive & undesirable personalities, that somehow resulted in generous monetary tips upon delivery, and in most instances in exchange for an acid-trip resemblant experience and pizza themed loading screen that provides you a key or other means of accessing new areas to progress further in the storyline.I found myself puzzled, excited, and sustained a substantial increase in chemical happiness following solving complex mysteries and obtaining new information subsequently resulting in advanced game-progression in an ethereal state of tranquility and bliss as I was rewarded with tremendous doses of seratonin while losing myself in the harmonious atmospheric soundtrack. Simultaneously following my spiritual journey, I found great victorious perceptions following incessant coddling and generation of bizarre grey matter & flamingo meat pizzas (with extra chocolate chips of course).If you enjoyed Off-Peak or The Noorwood Suite, this game will surpass any preconceived expectations and transcend your consciousness and gaming experience into the astral plane. Your third eye will likely open and grant you the soul-fulfilling answers your pursuit of identity and personality has always desired. From start  to end, game achievements and hungry citizens motivate your every action, as you are granted the vintage camera to document your every sight and dazzle each individual who stumbles upon your carefully crafted and mentally-scarring roll of film. You explore the depths of a city built from the very limbo between heaven and hell, influenced by the subconscious happenings of overwhelming LSD hallucinations stitched neatly into one fine package brought to you by Cosmo D Studios. The courteous artists and developers provide us the incredible experience of combining pizza, photography, mystery, romanticism, bereavement, as well as much sought after employment.Give this game a chance, you won't regret it, and in some ways you may even lose, or discover yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Tales From Off-Peak City Vol. 1

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a fan of the other Cosmo D games, but this one hooked me from the start.Ugly at first glance, it revealed its unique beauty as I played, and turned out to be one of the most photogenic games. I'd say its visuals are the same atonal to perfectly match the soundtrack.It looks like a one-time experience but in fact, it's got enough replayability.It shows an alternative world that decided to remain as atonal as it's been for a million years. It's weirdly synaesthetic, showing pizza making as music and pizza itself as a dance. I could tell much more but sadly it was too much text for me to fully follow the story.Anyways, it's what a modern game should be, and it's truly a piece of art.ACCESSIBILITY: I was quite comfortable playing this game - its weird aspects mostly seemed interesting to discover or even welcoming, almost never giving that 'horror' feeling. However, its atmosphere, style, or imagery might still be disturbing for some.
_childDocuments_.name: Tales From Off-Peak City Vol. 1

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun game with quirky dialogues and intriguing art.This seems to be the first opus in a series but the game tells a story on its own.At the beginning, we arrive in Off-Peak city and are tasked to steal a saxophone.From there, we infiltrate the place by getting hired by the local pizza joint, and we will have to prepare and deliver pizzas to progress in the story. Most of the gameplay consists of interacting with the different npcs in the game and listening (reading as the game has no voice over) to their stories and conversations.Showing npcs some items also trigger some extra dialogues, and some of the talks will change depending on what and how much we choose to put or not on the pizza we deliver.The least I can say is that reading the exchanges was quite fun. I also really liked the surrealist look of the different buildings (inside and outside) in the game. Sometimes, it was just so weird!If you enjoy reading and like surrealist art, I definitely recommend this game to you!
