_childDocuments_.review: Bookbound Brigade. It's a 2D side-scrolling platform-adventure made by Digital Tales and published by Intragames. And it is a hybrid that mixes various genre games. Platformer, Adventure, Puzzle, Action, Boss Battle, RPG, etc. In this game, you will adventure out with historical or literary heroes to save the literary world.You will team up with 8 heroes. You can experience the 16 skills these heroes have. These skills are related to the background and origin of each hero. And you play the game, directing them as a corps. This corps can transform into 4 special formations. Choosing the right lineup could be more effective when solving specific puzzles and battles.There are 5 themed worlds for you to explore. You will meet more than 50 historical or literary characters in this game. There are some interesting twists related to them. And there are also 40 monsters to threaten you, and fierce boss battles await you. The game is interesting overall, but not deep. The motifs are taken from the classic characters you are familiar with, but most of them just scratch the surface. Except for those things, the game experience itself was not bad.

name: Iridion II
detailed_description: More than a hundred years have passed since the Earth was attacked by the vicious IRIDION forces. Legend tells of a single brave SHN Fighter pilot who found his way to destroy the evil IRIDION mainframe. After this glorious victory, all remaining enemy ships disappeared from known space. Humans began to colonize the planet systems of the IRIDION home galaxy. Peace and freedom came back to mankind. The IRIDION menace was history. Until now. Within only one day, all communication with the human space outposts had been lost. The last transmissions made it clear that the IRIDION Empire had returned and have taken over all colonized systems. Planet Earth is too far away to send help in time. Again only a single, but powerfully equipped spaceship is within reach to stop the IRIDION forces before they can go on to attack the last remaining planet of human beings... Earth. FEATURES Travel through 5 huge galaxies containing 15 unique and challenging planets Encounter over 200 enemies and 30 boss enemies Collect power-ups to gain new weapons, increase fire power, refill energy Choose between Starter, Advanced and Ace pilot difficulty setting Virtual Reality Training - ingame tutorial which explains all of the strategies needed to be victorious. Soundtrack with more than 25 songs, a 'create-your-own-musical-theme' part, and a gallery for you to unlock. Remap controls to your liking with both keyboard and gamepad support Save your progress at any point in the game MODES OF PLAY Story Mode - fight against the IRIDION armada in 15 planets spread over 5 galaxies. Arcade Mode - replay levels you already cleared in story mode and hunt for high scores. (secrets and beam combos have been added in arcade mode to a make the high score hunt more interesting) Challenge Mode - Try to beat all 15 end bosses as fast as you can.

name: ITORAH
detailed_description: The Save the World Edition contains Itorah as well as the official Soundtrack and Artbook and is a great way to show appreciation for the developers, while simultaneously supporting a good cause. Assemble Entertainment will donate 10% of the proceeds for every sold Save the World Edition to Survival International in support of indigenous people around the globe! YOU ARE THE ONLY HUMAN LEFT IN A WORLD FULL OF MASKS Guide Itorah through a fantastic world inhabited by strange masked beings. Mankind has vanished and Itorah seems to be the last of her kind! To uncover her past she will have to pick up her loud-mouthed axe and fight her way through lush forests, dangerous temples, stormy cliffs and more hand-painted biomes. Their innocent quest for knowledge quickly turns into a mission to save this strange new world from its biggest threat: A mysterious plague that threatens to consume everything. Hand-Crafted Quality: Explore a beautifully realized world inspired by South and Central American landscapes, each lovingly hand-painted by the development team to breathe life into the world of Nahucan Fluid controls: Enjoy a staggering amount of animations that truly bring Itorah and her amazing range of abilities to life in the hands of players Good ol’ Fashioned Platforming: When she isn’t hacking and slashing her way across the landscape, Itorah will need to keep her jumping and dodging skills as sharp as her axe as she conquers progressively more difficult puzzles and platforming challenges Challenging bossfights: Face Nahucan's voracious fauna and imposing boss fights Unravel the Mystery: Is Itorah the only human left, and if so, what happened to everyone else? Get to the bottom of the mystery with plenty of exciting twists and turns along the way as the brave young warrior battles her way through lush forests, ancient temples, and more on her quest to save Nahucan Make Friends Along the Way: As the old saying goes, the “real treasure is the friends we make along the way”. Meet a bunch of odd, quirky characters who may or may not help Itorah on her quest Captivating sound design: ITORAHs lovingly crafted, dynamic soundtrack invites to lose yourself in the beauty of Nahucan

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often say much unless I'm saying a lot, but having recently completed this, I felt this game is much better than its score is currently reflecting. It makes me feel awkward for loving this haha. I'm seeing many mixed reviews with some recurring complaints, so I felt I'd leave a review of my own and touch upon some of those things. I did leave a more thorough review in the discussions, but as a warning, it's a bit poorly constructed and very long, so I'll try and do better here while still addressing everything.Itorah was a game I came across shortly before release when it was featured by one of the Steam events. I wishlisted it, purchased it upon release, and it sat for a very short while until I started, and then quickly finished, it. And, wow. Normally if things "somewhat interest me" I wait for a sale, but the gorgeous 2D art of a Meso-American theme, and the gameplay featured in the promotional material, attracted me. Upon finishing it, I feel it stuck the landing on the bits that attracted me to begin with.For the most part, it's exactly what it presents itself as. The art is, and I can't say this enough, gorgeous. The Meso-American setting and theme is refreshing. The gameplay is great, though you'll probably fall into one of two camps on that. You'll either love it for not being convoluted and weighed down by systems upon systems, and while it's simple, the ability progression is spot on, or you'll be bored by those same things because you want something more in-depth. I will mention that the difficulty seems slightly "back loaded" rather than consistent. The early game is natural, the mid-game feels flat in places, and the end picks up the slack and is relatively sharp. It's not awful, but it might make people have poor early-mid impressions. If it was developed with multiple difficulties, it'd go a long way in addressing this. Campfires which replenish your health and heals are generously place, and punishments for falling into death pits is too forgiving IMO. It's a bit "casual" but it's great at what it does. You can do what I did and forgo upgrades to see how far you can challenge yourself (just keep multiple saves if you do please, as backtracking is prevented in some spots and you don't want to almost "soft lock" yourself unless you can "get good" enough to pass a later spot with reduced stats). But, the possibility for challenge is there; it'd just be nice if there were separate difficulties to cater to those wanting even more challenge without alienating the casual players.The music isn't top notch throughout, and I'm a huge proponent that great audio propels a game even further, but it's not awful either. The dialogue isn't fully spoken but instead is what I'll call "grunts of Itorah-lish" (think "simlish"). One one hand, it adds to the idea that these characters are not speaking your language, but their own, but on the other, voice acting can add immersion. But voice acting costs money, so for the price I guess I get it. Again, the audio isn't awful, it just doesn't go all the way. The visual work does the heavy lifting.The story isn't the script from a classic JRPG game, but like the audio, it works and isn't bad at all. Most of the background is filled in through sequences from either the future or past which suggest something rather than directly stating it, but the direct story as you play is pretty straight-forward. By the end, you'll probably be feeling for many of the characters.I spent ~11 hours to complete it, being thorough, doing some back-tracking, and repeating some segments. FWIW, I neglected upgrading my character until late (see my comments above about difficulty, this may mean the mid portion being flat is more pronounced if you're upgrading as you should). There are two achievements for completing it within given time frames, one being 5 hours and the other being 10, so I'd say this is fair to call an 8 to 10 hour game on the first play for most people. Given the price, this seems fair.I had no issues with performance, crashes, or stuttering (on a 3700X and GTX 1060 system). One bug where I fell into a death pit and didn't die, and was stuck in it, unable to get out. Do I recommend this? Without hesitation, yes. I want more of it. But if you want something more convoluted or less casual, or if the two chase scenes are deal breakers (they weren't to me, a self admitted casual), this might not be something you are wowed by. Otherwise, I'd say it's worth it at full price, and an even easier recommendation on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I really looked forward to play this game, even if I knew little about it. It certainly looked gorgeous.Unfortunately, I didn't really enjoy my time with this game upon release. I've played it for two hours and refunded it. I'll gladly return to it if it ever gets patched or worked on, like the recent Death's Gambit.What I didn't liked about this game is quite simple. It's quite boring. In my two hours of playtime, I didn't felt compelled to keep going. There weren't any carrot on a stick that kept my interest sparked. The first part with the spiders was a very good intro, but the following segment into the first temple falls flat. There is little to no challenge early on and most levels are often just long stretches of going left or right while killing annoyingly trivial foes that you might as well just ignore entirely.You gather experience points to buff up your health or your stamina, and that's it. I would have liked to unlock new combos, combat moves or manoeuvre to break up the monotony of button mashing through the levels. I know you'll unlock some other moves later on, but these should be available MUCH sooner, especially for a metroidvania 2D adventure. It's crucial that you keep the player engaged at all time. I wasn't.There's a stamina bar that seems to be exclusively linked to your ability to dodge or sprint and to me, it felt a bit useless. Up until where I've played, there doesn't seem to be a need for the stamina bar in this game.To the devs : You guys have a promising future. Keep up the good work.Pros :- Great visual style- Very unique main weapon- Cast of colorful charactersCons :- Early levels consists of long streches with a few enemies in between- Combat and platforming feels off

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen that in recent years some releases are overshadowed, or swallowed up by a tide of other titles that, fortunately for some and unfortunately for others, are released around the same time. Itorah caught my attention on that aspect, because while its trailer convinced me without problems, I saw a dissonance between it and the reception in general, and I was intrigued to know why. And it’s that the game is presented to us as a Metroidvania, but one that lacks some of the most important aspects of the genre, in my opinion. There are almost no secrets, and the progression is very linear, since that magic of going back and exploring again some old areas, but with new abilities, is not as present. It's not a bad game, I enjoyed the experience, but it is true that I felt it was very bare-bones and sometimes monotonous, although it is adorned by some cool visuals that add their own weight to the game.The story is one of the most interesting parts of the game, for me. We follow Itorah, a young girl who wakes up in some sort of ancient temple after a long sleep, and encounters a mystical, talking axe on her way. Their mission will be to cooperate, fight against the corruption that is eating away at the lands of Nahucan.As we travel through the world and meet its inhabitants, we’ll gradually get deeper into the plot, seeing glimpses of the past of both Itorah and our talking tool, and learning about what has happened through Nahucan over time, culminating in a nice ending. It's a somewhat predictable narrative past a certain point, but I found it all very enjoyable.The visuals are the aspect that caught my attention the most, especially the character design. Itorah's animations feel super fluid, from running and attacking, to simply crouching or looking down from a platform. Her movements constantly amazed me, and were a big part of my enjoyment of the game. The NPCs also have their own neat designs, but only a handful have any animation related to their relevance. Enemies are varied to some extent, as some are quite repetitive in some areas, and bosses are what stand out most on the antagonist side. On the other hand, some environments and backgrounds look slightly less detailed, although this doesn't detract from the overall gameplay. The music is great, though!The gameplay is where I have the most mixed feelings. I felt that there is a very linear loop, which consists of reaching an area and advancing until you come across a fork; on one side you'll have the door to continue progressing, on the other the key to it, and that's it. This is repeated in almost all areas, sometimes there are more doors, some half-hidden chests and little else.Occasionally we’ll come across an abyss too long to jump over, or a wall too high to climb, hinting that we can return when we get new skills and continue exploring. But the reality is that, behind most of these obstacles there is nothing new hidden, they are just blocked off areas that we can't access until we get there by story progression. This detracts a lot from the exploration, makes the skills feel like just another key, so to speak, and is not at all rewarding.But the skills themselves were a lot of fun for me, along with the platforming parts. Even if the world was linear, my entertainment was going up as I unlocked new moves, as chaining them together can gain you more travel speed, and it looks very cool. Unfortunately, Itorah has a stamina bar, which prevented me from going crazy and reaching unstoppable platforming speeds; but hey, what I did manage to accomplish wasn't bad.In addition to the magical double jump and other ways to move, we’ll make use of our axe in several ways, both throwing it boomerang style, as well as performing downward attacks to bounce on some surfaces (similar to the beloved "pogo" of Hollow Knight). I'd like to say that the combat entertained me just as much as the platforming, but it just feels too monotonous and easy most of the time, especially when the enemies and environmental hazards don't do enough damage to be a bother. It's enough to just stand around mashing the attack button to deal with most of the monsters.The bosses, on the other hand, provide us with a bit more of a fun challenge, as each has its own mechanic, such as one that is only vulnerable to pogo attack damage. Adding their roles in the story itself, they are the part I enjoyed most about the combat, without a doubt. As a final point, I comment that there are some character upgrades, such as health and energy, too.In conclusion, Itorah is a game that perhaps falls short as far as Metroidvania is concerned, but a nice adventure nonetheless. Not presenting much of a challenge, it could be a good entry point into the genre, and it has a nice story with characters that I really liked, along with visuals that accompany well and a great soundtrack. Despite the ups and downs I experienced in terms of gameplay, I can say it's not a bad game, I enjoyed it and I don't regret it by any means, but I must admit I'll remember the disappointment more than anything else.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Great art design, great animations, decent combat, but as a metroidvania, ITORAH is a rather bad metroidvania. To put it simply, a metroidvania, other than a well-designed combat system and platforming, is all about exploring nooks and crannies of its world and getting loot after overcoming some challenges. But disappointingly, ITORAH's map is too linear in terms of exploration and nothing makes you want to explore for it is not rewarding. Yes, you do get upgrade materials, but most of them are literally on or near the path of progress, with just a few that requires you to backtrack or take a detour. And yes, you do get health and healing charge upgrades, but there is so little combat and challenging enemies that you rarely get low on health. Overall, ITORAH can be better off if it was made as a pure platformer than a metroidvania.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start off this review by saying that I've played a lot of 2d platformers over the years, from Castlevania to Megaman, Mario, Celeste and yes, Hollow Knight. These are mainly my initial thoughts, most of them I probably stand by, some might change. Itorah is the first game by Grimbart Tales and it shows. While the game is definitely a passion project through and through, from the vibrant and extremely detailed backdrops to the beautiful, hand drawn sprites, this is game is not for veterans. The combat is mimicking Hollow Knight (you're going to be reading Hollow Knight a lot from this point onwards); it's deceptively simple but slightly expands by letting the player figure out how to use each attack to their best, yet Hollow Knight does this extremely well by having each attack be extremely swift, allowing the player to quickly maneuver and dash around to dodge attacks. Itorah tries to do this but fails as most of the attacks feel a bit clunky and the attack patterns when swinging the hammer are weird, not consistent. The movement is awkward as well, jumps being weird to properly steer, the character getting stuck on enemies if you move too close. The controls are fine, what really surprises and slightly bothers me is the the addition of a stamina bar, which is not seen in any 2d platformer I've played, the closest comparison would be dark souls (don't forget bonfires also act as save points in Itorah) but only running and dodging consumes stamina, you can attack as many times as you want. These are most of my thoughts for now, while I do enjoy this game, it doesn't hold a candle to Hollow Knight which also was the very first game Team Cherry worked on and look how that turned out. I will recommend this game as the team has put a lot of love into this game, but I do not recommend it for anyone that has a lot of experience with multitudes of different 2d side scrolling platformers.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Metroidvania tag is misleading, it's just a linear platformer. It is decently challenging and fun, but you can certainly see that most of the effort was spent on post-production and art rather than the core gameplay. There is nothing to explore and nothing to collect, levels are way to large for whats in them, you have a stamina system that is unused, etc. etc. All core pieces are there for a good game, it just never shapes together into a working whole.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: The look of this game based on the previews paints a vivid adventure, but playing it is a totally different story. Combat is boring, with only a handful of enemy types that are recycled and made a little harder because of being infested by the plague. The movement is clunky, and swings are heavy and commit you to combat. It's just very choppy and overall not dynamic. Last boss is a complete joke, so you can imagine the difficulty up until that point. Story-wise the grunting and moaning of the various characters is how narration progresses. It's literally like they recorded only 1-2 words per character that just keep getting repeated with various inflections. The story is dull, progresses slowly and predictably through an agonizingly simple map that has practically no secrets and constant backtracking through previously mentioned boring mobs. Upgrades are limited to health and stamina, which honestly you don't even need considering how vanilla this is. Overall horrible game despite it's beautiful art and style.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Itorah is a hand drawn metroidvania inspired by gorgeous South American landscape.  This game looks fantastic visually, incorporates charming characters, and offers lots of unique biomes, but ultimately fails in creating engaging combat and lacks any sort of tension or challenge.  What's Good:-Itorah looks like a million bucks aesthetically.  It's safe to say that most players will really enjoy the visual presentation b/c it's top notch.  One of my favorite moments in the game was a sunset where the devs used lots of shading and different textures to visually show the shadows of the characters and landscape.  There are lots of lush green plant life and tons of rolling hills in this really beautiful South American landscape.-Movement is another highlight.  I suspect that the Ori series was used as inspiration for this game due to the environment and heavy focus on fast, fluid movement.  The movement isn't as dynamic here as it is in Ori, but it's still really solid.  Once you acquire all of your upgrades, you will be able to bounce and double jump all over the environment, which always feels great.-There is a ton of charm in this game.  You can tell how much love the devs put into this game.  The story although simple, is very likeable.  It's easy to become invested in the adorable characters that you meet throughout your journey.  -The soundtrack and sound design is also really solid and fits the theme of the game well.  It has a nice balance of upbeat, whimsical music to more intense, threatening sequences during chase scenes.Could Use Some Changes:-The biggest problem by far, is the lack of challenge or any form of tension from start to finish.  It's okay for a game to be more forgiving, but I think the devs played it too safe here.  Tension is a good thing.  Players want to overcome adversity and feel a sense of accomplishment when they complete a challenging section.  Within the first hour, I realized that no enemy posed a real threat b/c nothing does enough damage to place you near the danger zone.  I only died 2-3 times in my whole 8 hr playthrough, and all of those deaths were me just being careless b/c I felt invincible.  -The second biggest issue is that the combat never feels very engaging.  It's extremely simple and never really evolves.  You have an axe-like weapon that later on can be charged up to do more damage or can be thrown like a boomerang.  The problem is that every attack feels very slow and cumbersome.  Another issue is that there are tons of tiny cannon fodder that are hard to hit b/c of how slow your attack is and the exact placement you need to have in order to hit them.  Being that a majority of the game is spent attacking, this is a massive problem that combat never feels very fun.-Another issue is that Itorah never really offers anything new or innovative to the genre.  It plays it really safe.  This would have been fine if released in 2014 or 2015.  But in 2022, there are so many dynamic and challenging metroidvanias out there to compete w/.  If you are going to play it really safe mechanically, then you need to make up for it w/ a really well rounded and engaging experience.  Unfortunately, Itorah isn't able to do that.-The world of Itorah is never really that interesting to explore b/c it always marks on the map the next location to go to.  Even if it didn't, it would still be way too linear.  The sense of wonder and reward of exploring off the beaten path is never present here.  Even if you do try your best to go your own way, the secrets that you will find are never that interesting.  It's always one of three currencies and the rewards for trading in those currencies are never very exciting either.  Consensus:-Bottom Shelf Game (Tier 5 and makes up 10% of my reviews).  I feel bad writing this review, b/c I know that the devs really put a lot of love into this game. I have been following this game for about the last two years and have been eagerly awaiting it's release.  I was on the fence about whether I was going to recommend this game or not b/c I can see this being a decent option for casual gamers that are new to the genre.  However, there are some incredible games in this genre that I could recommend at a $20 price point.  Most players will 100% the game in less than 10 hrs, which was the icing on the cake for me to give this one a thumbs down.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: The game is absolutely gorgeous, but it fails to deliver a full Metroidvania experience. The gameplay is often just platforming or killing the same types of mobs, which often are just more annoying than anything.Farther in the game, the abilities come together, but the control of the character isn't very fluid, and downright frustrating at times.The requirement to hold down a key/button to do things that should be instantaneous is poor design. Lack of fast travel makes it very annoying to go back to the main hub.I really think this game could have been something special had they stuck to their theme, but really put in the quality of life Metroidvania things.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: I came into this expecting more of a metroidvania style platformer, so perhaps it's more of a misconception on my part.  If you are looking for a metroidvania style adventure, probably best to skip on this one.  It does feature many of the staples of a metroidvania including a map, classic upgrades like double jump, and a way to upgrade your health.  The problem is that the game is very linear in terms of where you can go at a given moment, which results in the game leading you around by the nose from one area to the next with a map marker with no room for deviation.The ability upgrades like wall jump and double jump do not feel rewarding because as you play through the stages, you never see anything that makes you think you should come back later.  There are no secret side paths that lead to upgrades, just traversing a mostly linear path doing some platforming it and fighting some enemies.   In fact, the only place you can upgrades for your health and stamina is in the town, and the lack of a fast travel system to get back there (or anywhere for that matter) keeps you on the rails even further.  In this regard, I would classify this game as more of a traditional platformer with some very very light metroidvania elements.  There are enemies and some bosses, but not a lot in terms of variety.  The standard enemies in general I feel take too many hits to kill, and don't offer much in return.  After an hour or so, I found myself just opting to run past all of them.  There is a stamina meter, but attacking does not drain it, so it's only true purpose is to limit the amount of time you can sprint, or the number of times you can roll to dodge.  The enemies and bosses seem to inflict very little damage and the player seems to get a very generous amount of life, so the odds of death are very low.  In the 3 1/2 hours I spent playing before tapping out, I never died or ever really felt like I was ever close to death even during the seldemly placed boss fight.There are a few other weird quirks.   The UI in particular seems to have some odd design choices in some places.  The save points are fairly frequently placed, and offer the option to quick save, or normal save.  I saw no difference between the 2 except that the quick save took 3 seconds and the normal save took much longer due to having to press and hold buttons to navigate the menu.  This begs the question why not just have the quick save since its much faster?  Also the option to delete a save while at a save point struck me as odd, as one would think this should only be on the title screen.It's not all bad though.  The visual style is quite nice.  The visual production on the environments and the character animations are quite well done.  The music is fairly decent as it sets the tone for the theme of the game as you explore ruins and the like.  If you are looking for a more traditional platforming experience that is fairly forgiving, this is a game that may very well appeal to you.  Metroidvania and less casual players will probably want to look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: It's so weird when the gameplay in the first five minutes of a game reveals a lack of understanding of the fundamentals of game design.So often it is impossible to tell the background from the foreground. There are mushrooms you can jump on and identical-looking mushrooms that are merely part of the background. The delineation between terrain and extraneous detail is often nonexistent.The game teaches you how to slide (holding right trigger and then down) before it teaches you how to just dash (right trigger), and the slide seems completely pointless and is introduced at a time where it serves no purpose.

_childDocuments_.review: Itorah is a game with a lot of heart but very unpolished. I'll be honest, I wanted to like this game but there's just a few too many flaws with the game to really allow me to give it my recommendation.Itorah makes its first mistake by claiming itself to be a Metroidvania. I'm not sure if the community has called it that or the developers but it is not a metroidvania. There is no real backtracking except for stat upgrades and there's no reason to go back to old areas unless you're trying to complete the game. Each zone isn't interconnected but its own separate area and you don't need to discover new abilities or switches to unlock a location in an earlier level. I wasted time when I first started playing going back to a previously beaten area with a new ability to try and discover organically where I was to go to next, mostly ignoring the map icon but quickly discovered that backtracking was actually discouraged by the lack of fast travel and by the fact the maps were extremely massive. Although the Overworld is rather large, it has little difference than levels. Each location is more similar to a Zelda dungeon than a Metroidvania zone. And the difference might seem subtle at first but its massive. New abilities are not used in old Zones to access new areas or even new zones, rather once you complete it with that dungeon's power up you given a quest marker and sent off to the next area. This makes the game far more linear than it looks, a stark contrast to the metroidvania games I'm obsessed with.As far as visual direction and sound direction, Itorah is a treat. The game is lovely and the characters, animations, music and attack and ambient sounds are all great! The visuals are really what drew me into the game. And for the most part I can't complain about them. I think the Artists absolutely should be proud of how the game looks. It has some fantastic set pieces I won't spoil for those who will still want to play the game after reading my review because I think seeing them for yourself will be wonderful. I DO however have a mild complaint. There are foreground pieces which block the view of your character and enemies which does lead to cheap damage. And if art design gets in the way of the gameplay, this is bad design. And its the first instance I'm talking about that is just bad design. The devs should use a fade mechanic here where its mostly transparent when you walk behind it, which they didn't do.The game is not polished mechanically. In the very first section of the game I ran into a Run ending bug. The key I needed to unlock a second door was used on a door I had already unlocked. Which meant I couldn't progress and I had to start over to a point before I had gotten both keys. This is something that should be fixed, but its not the only issue I ran into. I also encountered Frame drops and slowdowns in certain areas, especially with heavy rain. Certain button presses or joystick uses were fairly unresponsive and stiff to execute which really hurt my play through of the game.Now, my hands do cramp from time to time and the controls of the game being so unresponsive was a major issue. playing this game for an hour or more would cause cramps and other pain. While other games which are much harder than Itorah and require faster response time would not cause these cramps. Its because I was fighting the controls to progress rather than feeling that fluid motion of gameplay I know the game was aiming for. This lead me to putting the game down for days because it was just too physically painful to play.A minor gripe, but the last one I'll mention is interaction with NPCs and saving. The requirement of holding down a button to save or skip a cut scene was even more taxing on my hands. I would rather things be quick and snappy to this slower method. Double tap to skip and ask to override a save vs holding the button down would go a long way to improving this minor gripe. Although this might be preference, with the physical pain my hands were going through this became more noticeable.Overall, I can't recommend this game. I think the team behind it has a lot of heart and put a lot of love into the game. And what really kills my recommendation is the mechanical issues and bugs. I can look past that its not a metroidvania but the mechanical issues I've pointed out are something I can't look past. IF the devs fix these bugs and mechanical issues I'll revise my review with a recommendation because I do believe the game is charming. But for now, I'm afraid not.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Itorah, for the most part, is a game that does almost everything wrong.  Enemy variety is lacking, as you spend the first three hours fighting the same stuff.  Tiny crawler that takes two hits.  Flies that take one hit.  Spitting plants that take three hits.  Charging beasts?  Screw it, they take, like, eight hits and they run across the map.  I'm not going to chase them down for 5xp.And that's kind of where I discovered that there is nothing in this hand drawn but bland map that is worth me stopping.  I'm speedrunning the game on my first play through because every branching path has no rewards.  Every enemy is a slog that offers not incentive to fight.  There are no hidden paths.  Climb up to the top of a big room with hanging logs only to discover there was nothing up there.  The game is laughing at you for thinking there's anything in this world.  Just run as fast as you can.  The enemies do basically no damage, so who cares if you get hit on your way.  You'll lose 90% of your health in this game falling in pits, and holy god you'll fall in a lot of pits.The platforming mechanics in this game are STIFF.  I had to walk away for a minute because I kept missing the same dandelion, not because it was a tricky jump, but because double jumping out of a sprint jump is like steering a sedan on icy roads.  Even after falling in the same pit 20 times, I still wasn't hurting for health.  Oh, and platforming sections while being chased by a lovecraftian nightmare?  Prepare to be miserable.If we can talk briefly about the silent protagonist, I don't understand why we need a silent protagonist.  When you're a young woman and the last human in the world and can also absorb darkness powers, it might be more appropriate to give us a character.  Or motive.  It feels like our hero, who I'm assuming is named Itorah, is silent because other popular games in the genre have a silent protagonist, so this game needs one too.Which brings me to the end.  The developers wanted to make Ori, or Hollow Knight, or... Yoku's Island Express with it's whacky uncontrollable in the air movement, but I don't think they either stopped to think about what made those games great or why they made the choices they did.  Instead you get a hollow recreation wandering blind in the forest.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks great but plays infuriatingly and the story goes nowhere fast.There are always multiple jump puzzles before a checkpoint.Upgrades consist of more health or more heals, and have yet to come across anything to make the character stronger. Movement feels sluggish and the jump pads have magnetism that push your character away from them. This means you are going to miss a lot of jumps that you should have made from the magnetism of the jump pad pushing your character away or taking away the speed that you need to get through the puzzle.TLDR: The game play feels bad, you never feel like you're getting stronger and the story doesn't go anywhere.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very simple. It appears to be a metroidvania at heart, but there are no real puzzles or secrets to find. I only died once at the final boss due to lack of effort/interest. By the time I got to the end, I was very tired of it.The art style is fantastic and the music is glorious. I just wish it had a little more meat to those bones. If you are BAD at platformers or simply new to gaming, it'd be a good one for a beginner to start up with.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Itorah delivers a solid platforming adventure with a stunning presentation. Many of the mechanics are basic, from the leveling system and platforming. You gain abilities that increase your mobility options and earn items to increase your base stats such as health, stamina, and healing. It doesn't attempt to reinvent the wheel but instead sticks to what works in a platforming adventure, creative areas and lots of platforming challenges.The game is easy with a handful of recycled enemies that are constantly reused and Itorah can tank most damage. But I found the colorful and often breathtaking presentation, visual style, and animations to overshadow the basic combat and systems. The boss fights are inventive and the game ends with a solid conclusion. Overall if you're looking for a classic adventure that doesn't overstay its welcome you cannot go wrong with Itorah.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to unfortunately agree with many others here, the game is wonderfully made, however it makes the cardinal sin of just being kinda boring and slow paced. its beautiful and the artwork and animations are top notch, but the controls feel a bit clunky and stiff and combat is too simple and doesn't offer enough. _childDocuments_.review: This game annoys the hell out of me. The art is excellent, I'll say that right at the start. This game looks great, and narratively it seems like it might have some mildly interesting ideas going on.But all of that falls away in just how underbaked it is as a mechanical experience. The level design is fine, but your jumps carry just a bit too much of your ground momentum, with not quite enough ability to correct your airspeed once you're up, so your platforming intuition is near-worthless - and without a compelling alternative mechanical feel, like how La Mulana gives you air control only after the peak of your jump and is then built around jumps being highly committal. Stamina gauges are fine, but instead of actually balancing the system to create a compelling combat dynamic, the devs just exempted basic swings from interacting with the stamina gauge. I keep waiting for the game to open up like a proper metroidvania, but after four hours I'm pretty sure that's just not going to happen. It'll be tutorial tunnel all the way to the endgame. The mechanical flaws just eat away at the experience, and I'm left frustrated by my time with the game. I payed less than $5 for this, so I don't strictly *regret* the purchase and I don't feel the need to refund, but the juxtaposition between what this game clearly could be and what it actually is creates a much sharper dissatisfaction than I'd get from a game that was just bland or bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Been wanting to play this game for a while, it looks gorgeous, had so much potential but ultimately failed at delivering.The level design often gets you running around completely empty stages or a few pretty uninteresting enemies and it gets pretty boring pretty quickly. There's no real sense of progression with the character either, you're basically the same from start to finish, no new relevant abilities, no level/attribute/skill points system, nothing.It's just a very basic 2D platformer that looks nice.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Itorah is a graphically beautiful game. With its bright colors, the game looks simply fantastic and the characters with their fantasy language are also very lovingly made. Nevertheless, I cannot recommend the game.The first three hours of play time are almost too easy. Then the game suddenly becomes very difficult. Exploding crowns of thorns on flowers that you have to jump on, ice crystals that injure you, exploding petals that sail in the wind, enemies that trigger area bombardments, the coordination of jumps from elastic flowers that catapult you upwards after which you have to coordinate the exact landing point in a flash, aggressive owls that shoot rocket salvos at you, make progress very, very frustrating. And that's just some of the obstacles. Ultimately, you play sections over and over again until you finally reach the next campfire where you can save.As beautiful as the game is, it is annoying. In addition, the enemies are not particularly varied and distances to destinations are far.Sorry, no, unfortunately I cannot recommend Itorah. The game simply becomes too frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: This game is clearly a labour of love: everything is very beautiful, and I want to call the story well written for a metroidvania (there is not terribly much dialogue, but what there is is alright). Overall a good game, got all but one achievement (the true speedrun achievement) in my first playthrough within less than 10 hours - I guess cutscenes do not contribute to the ingame timer. A bit short, but does not overstay its welcome, so I guess the length is perfectly fine.And now to nitpick at the worst parts you can expect, in the order I come up with them:- The exploration part of the metroidvania experience is extremely linear. This includes the penultimate dungeon which sends you all over itself before you notice that oh, there was only one path after all.- There are some very minor graphical glitches in most areas. I am talking unfortunate cutoffs on corners, particularly noticeable around the edges of saw traps.- A lot of areas lock you out of reentering them after you beat them; reminds me a lot of Owlboy in that regard (surely, that is the only thing reminiscent of that game...).- The final movement skill (which you get in the penultimate dungeon) does not seem to be hard required until the final dungeon where you can and will get softlocked if you did not pick it up before - because you cannot backtrack and even if you could: the penultimate dungeon is one of those that makes it rather clear that you will not be able to reenter it. At least I managed to beat most of the penultimate dungeon before heading to where the powerup exists, and did not notice any points that would really require it - except for the room where you pick it up... which you can also leave without picking up the powerup.- Speaking of softlocks, do not walk too slowly into certain waterfalls, you may end up ducking which causes you to be unable to move.- One thing which I have noticed in other people's reviews: they seem to have issues with the pretty stiff controls. Which... yes, they are stiff, but like... you are not instantly welcomed to La Mulana when you fail a jump because of the controls or anything, if you catch my drift. I have had worse/stiffer controls in better games (such as La Mulana), so I am pretty ok with the controls here, but you have been... notified.- Another thing I had been warned about when checking if there are missable collectibles (which yeah, they certainly exist, since you get locked out of some areas during the story): If you intend to upgrade everything, you require tons of currency. It seems that this warning came from an earlier patch/build of the game - or the person giving out the warning just was really bad at finding money chests - but when I played through I found way more currency than I needed. I usually killed enemies the first time I encountered them or if they bothered me (and since you cannot spend currency in the final dungeon anymore, I let a lot of things live there), and I always grabbed the respawning chest in thicc-Marsupilami-girl's house that kept refilling after each major plot point. If you do feel the need to farm currency, your best bet is in the third major dungeon with the first encounter with two sentinels on a bridge. They give 360 each and there is a save point nearby - just farm, save, reload to respawn them, repeat until happiness by currency is achieved. To note: enemies stay dead while you are on the same map, they only respawn if you reload the area one way or another.- The game seems to be created in Unity which seems to have decided to  with their engine recently. So... sorry if you devs have to pay for a future reinstall if and when I either feel like playing the game again or go for the speedrun achievement.Yeah, the nitpicky things seem like a lot, but really are not that big a deal as far as I am concerned.To wrap it up: I want one of them thicc Marsupilamis as a pet now.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: THIS IS NOT A METROIDVANIAdespite what recommendations will say, this game is a linear platformer that gives you VERY FEW incremental skills and abilities at set and specific points. there are literally 4 upgrades: amount of health flasks, strength of health flasks, amount of health and amount of stamina. That's it. No weapon upgrades, or even different weapons. It's the same thing the entire game.The art style is beautiful...and that's all this game has going for it. The maps are way too large and empty, with very little in terms of enemies and enemy types. You find yourself running and running and running to get from one checkpoint to another, and the huge and empty map is just boring and uninterestingAction is repetitive, and you can get away with just tanking hits from enemies and environmental obstacles until you get to the next save point. The roll is useless and the stamina bar is tied to movement instead of attacks for whatever reason. In a soulslike, cool. But in a platformer? Stupid.Do not waste your time, even if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Itorah is a beautiful looking platformer, but it's nothing to write home about.Pros:-The hand-drawn art & animations are fantastic and I love how vibrant the environments look.-Soundtrack is pretty good.-A fair amount of save spots throughout the world.Cons:-The game starts out slow and takes a while to actually pick up.-Controls weren't as smooth as I would've liked and combat felt a bit awkward.-A lot of areas seem empty and when you do come across enemies, they aren't very engaging and most of the time you can just skip them.-There's no difficulty option and with the game being so forgiving, it just seems a little on the easy side.-Bosses weren't that fun to fight except for maybe a couple.I really wanted to like Itorah, unfortunately I found it kinda boring to be honest.Overall it's not a bad game, it's just not great either, and the visuals can only carry it so much.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: As others already pointed out, this game has little to offer past its looks and it ends up being boring.The platforming is bland, the levels are too long and yet offer no challenge because you can tank your way through most things except the final boss, the character movement is awkward... You can't even say it's geared toward kids because a kid would get bored before long at how repetitive it is. It's also very linear, and every movement upgrade "unlocks" the path right ahead of you.The story has some interesting bits but treads no new ground or treads no old ground better than it's been done before. The south american influences seem to only impact the visual design and the names, but that might be my ignorance speaking.You're probably better off replaying an old game you already have than give this a spin. Not recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Itorah was one I was very excited for when I first saw the art style and animations in the early trailers. Claims of it being a new metroidvania had me hyped too. What I got was only one of those things lol.Pros:The game looks great, the music I really loved and the animations are all really well done. The characters and enemy designs are nice and the world is big and pretty to look at. Beyond the design however left a lot to be desired.Cons: oh boy where do I begin. It feels like in every aspect of the gameplay they did something good but than ruined it in another area. Moving around the world is really fluid and fun... but than you come to a full stop when you swing the axe or fight. There's also this weird delay in between attacks and it all just felt very clunky. So many times I would press the attack button but than the attack won't come out fast enough and I would run into the enemy instead.The world too is very vibrant and nice to look at, but its also very empty and not much room for exploration. Looking back i'm not sure where i heard it was a metroidvania but it certainly isn't. Everything is quite linear and with clear indications of where to go next. There's no reason to backtrack as gaining abilities don't really open up new areas in old places you've been to already. Even in dungeons the few times you have a branching hallway one side is just a dead end a couple rooms in.Closing:Overall it is an ok platforming game but needs more polish imo. It's not terrible but many things keep it from being on the level of some other games out there already in the genre. Also no fast travel sucks because you are forced to run back and forth in this big ass empty land.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: Take a middle of the road SNES action platformer and crossed it with a modern 2-D walking simulator (with some very nice production) and you would get this game. It pretends to be a metroidvania (at least all that I experienced it) with some branching levels, but there is no reason gameplay wise. There are few secrets and none that matter. There are no puzzles or meaningful backtracking. Everything seems in service of padding out the game time. It's been a while since I played a game that felt this empty, purposeless and boring gameplay-wise, when the graphics and music are good as they are. It's not a bad game, but just unnecessarily bland and tedious. This might be a very good game for younger players looking to try something like this (although some of the bosses and scenes might be a bit too intense for very young players).

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this but with major caveats,if you are looking for a mechanically interesting game this is not it,it is too simple,too easy,and too linear,as metroidvania it is extremely linear so much that you do not need to ever go back to areas previously visited,the game does not even have a fast travel system because oncre you are done with an area there is no need to ever go back there,this is how linear the game is,it is also so easy that you stop paying attention because you can make numerous mistakes without any riski whatsoever leading to you zoning out of the gameplay because your brain is simply not engaged.You might ask then why am i recommending this game it is for the people that place big importance on atmosphere,the music and visuals of this game are great,the animations are smooth the game is very colorfull and the soundtrack is varied but generally sticks to atmospheric music that builds the tone of the places you visit very well.In conclusion it is a decent game,a bad metroidvania,a boring action platformer due to how easy it is,and also a very good experience of taking in the scenary and visuals of the game with good music on top,and honestly a forgettable story,how good this game is is entirely dependant on what you value in a game,so make of this what you will.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game that could have been great. Gorgeous visuals, nice music, and an interesting enough narrative to keep us going. _childDocuments_.review: There were some bits I had to get over, but overall, this was a good game. Low points first, then high points.LOW POINTS- Controls are just a LITTLE janky sometimes. Mostly it's fine, but platforming and the occasional boss can be a bit frustrating when you lose due to control issues rather than skill issues.- Levels involve a lot of running through empty spaces, making backtracking tedious if you miss something or want to farm money.- I only had to farm money at the end, but it was difficult. I needed over 1,000 shards, but most enemies dropped only 1–5 (except one that dropped 120? That seemed weird).- All the most interesting parts of the story are infodumped at the end. (Though at least by then I'm invested.)- It seems like it wants to be a Metroidvania, but the map lacks any useful Metroidvania features (like marking chests on the map or being able to view maps outside of the area you're in) except for a single quest objective marker.- There are a lot of NPCs around, and there's an achievement for talking to them all, but almost none of them have interesting dialogue outside of cutscenes.HIGH POINTS- The art is BEAUTIFUL.- With the exception of a couple of bosses, the game isn't difficult, so any jank in the controls isn't usually a problem.- So long as you go from objective to objective (and don't need to farm money), backtracking isn't a real issue.- The story is pretty cool (even though most of it's told at the end).- It's not difficult to find all the chests even without map features.Overall, I did enjoy it, and I would recommend it as a kind of quick, low-budget, almost-but-not-quite Metroidvania.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: (FYI, I think "Do not recommend" is too harsh, but I wouldn't recommend it either--not when there are better Metroidvanias out there)This is the kind of game that starts out kinda rough and gets progressively better as you progress.  I don't think the end was quite good enough to bump up my rating to a 7/10, but I appreciated the constant positive trajectory.  The game starts out feeling kind of like a basic Flash-based game with better art, but every level gets better and better and feels more like a proper game up to the finale.Itorah is billed as a Metroidvania but I do not think that is an appropriate label.  There is little to no backtracking, and few if any secrets to find.  The game is very linear and you won't be returning anywhere for pretty much any reason.The music is okay but there are a couple of good tunes.  Most of the dungeons had good musical themes.  The first dungeon was incredibly bland but the rest were interesting and the settings felt fresh.  It is clear that the game had an artistic vision even if it did not quite meet it.You can pogo stick enemies like in DuckTales and Shovel Knight, which was initially exciting but was never used to its potential.  It's your go-to attack to spam though, most enemies and bosses cannot respond to it.  You can cheese almost anything.I think the basic parts are there for a game that can overcome its limitations and be a memorable title.  There are plenty of games that might be lacking in some areas but overcome their flaws in other areas.  However, I think this game was really missing some characters.  It does try to have characters but they are all incredibly bland and one-note.  I think having more endearing and memorable characters would have been what the game needed.  In line with the positive trajectory of the game, the characters do get more interesting just toward the end--but by then the game is almost done.  They needed to be like that at the start of the game; I bet then by the  end they would have been great.Worth mentioning that this is a German game, not a Latin American game.  I love the Mesoamerican aesthetic and would probably take some influences from the region myself if I made a game (I'm from the US).  I liked every drop of Mesoamerica that I got in the game.  But if like me, you were excited to see a game built on ideas and mythos from Mesoamerican culture, just know that this not the authentic experience--it's European.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a review, these are my first impressions of the first 3 hours of the game.Video version for those who prefer the format:Itorah is a game standing on three pillars for its gameplay: Combat, Exploration, Platforming. The negative write-ups you're seeing on steam are indicative of combat and exploration. Exploration:This game is not a metroidvania, it does not have that iconic spiderweb level design to constantly reward exploration, it's instead a big, adventure-like game but unfortunately with very little in it. The game is separated up into two categories: dungeons and the overworld and while the overworld is big and the dungeons are more focused, you don't have many reasons to explore off the beaten path if you can because there just isn't much to find. Sub bosses, lore, new and interesting items or weapons, none of that is really here, which is unfortunate. Combat:The combat also isn't very engaging. It's just okay. You can dodge roll, you can smack enemies and the feedback for hitting stuff is actually satisfying. But you don't have anything in terms of combos or special moves to really entice you and even the controls themselves could use work. You can't dodge-cancel out of attacks for the more agile enemies and everything just feels a bit slower and clunkier when the combat is involved. Platforming:So as you can guess, the final pillar is where the game transforms and this is the sole reason I'm recommending it. For starters, the art direction compliments the platforming. You have ancient meso-american fantasy-esque temples that have fun dart traps, spike pits and disappearing/rotating platforms with chains, hooks and bounce platforms everywhere in between. The game thrives on being a gauntlet-driven platformer whereby instead of having a set of really challenging levels like Super Meat Boy where a level might take 30 seconds to beat but the reality is it'll take you 5 minutes because you keep dying, instead of that, you have longer, less difficult segments where enemies and hazards slowly chip away at your health. This does mean the game is less challenging, but to the point where I'd say the game is really comfy and relaxing due to its excellent soundtrack and art direction while still maintaining gameplay that is stimulating and ultimately fun. It helps that the controls are really good. Jumping feels great, platforms come at you frequently enough that you're not getting bored. I kept playing the game at one point wondering why, as the aforementioned exploration and combat weren't doing it very well, then it dawned on me that I was really enjoying the platforming above all else. I used the D-pad most of the game but the game is designed around the stick, my only problem is that sometimes inputs don't register as you'd expect when you rock the D-pad back and forth really quickly during a wall jumping segment, switch to the analog stick in these cases, I didn't have much of a problem while playing. The platforming is excellent and thankfully you can blitz through areas and avoid monsters (minus the bosses and a few points) to a degree where they don't negatively impact this aspect of the game. Conclusion and final thoughts:If you wanna get the game, check it out for its platforming and as a bonus it has some nice sound design, music and art direction, it does have a story, one of mystery, but it's not going to really hold your attention, at least for the first 3 hours of the game, but it seemed neat if not a bit simple (world-ending corruption, protagonist doesn't talk or say their own name, talking side-character weapon, you know, that kinda deal).I can very easily recommend the game for the platforming alone, but don't go into it expecting a metroidvania or a brawler, If you want that, go buy Dust: An Elysian Tale. But this game is still great as a 2D platformer with a solid art direction and atmospheric soundtrack.If you liked this write-up, we have more recommendations via our curator page:Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like Itorah but sadly, the only positive I can really find is the beautiful art style. The rest of the game is awfully uninspired and clunky:Combat is a tad too slow which makes it feel unresposive and trying to do any follow-up attacks after an initial hit always takes so long that it just feels bad. Despite this, the game never is even remotely challenging. Some enemies are truly annoying to fight, though, and feel like they’re only there to waste your time. It’s not fun. On top of that, there’s a fireplace after every short jumping section or a path of a few enemies to the point that the short „animation“ of the screen going black for maybe 2 seconds when saving gets annoying because you keep doing it so often that it seriously eats at your time.The world design is really poor. There’s a lot of splitting paths that end up in a locked door on one side and a tiny pathway to a key or new ability on the other and it feels like they just do that to waste your time because then you have to walk back that short corridor to unlock the door or smash that rock with your new ability or something. Additionally, after beating a zone, the game always makes you run back to the little village and out on the other side. It’s like everything is built so that you have to waste the most time just mindlessly running crisscross across the entire world to the other end of the map. Basically everything in this game wastes your time.And the bit of story doesn’t make up for any of it either as it’s pretty cookie cutter. Ultimately, I don’t suggest spending money on this game, not even for small kids as the clunky combat will make it seriously hard for them to play properly. If you really want it, maybe if it’s in a Steam sale at 66-75% off. Wouldn’t pay 10€ for this again.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this game is beautiful. Every scene and every character. No notes. 10/10We are given snippets of lore throughout the game, but the main back story is presented at the end. Well worth the wait.Progression is reasonably paced. Powerups are obtained without having to grind. Most upgrades are available as soon as you're able to shop for them. There are minor issues with character controls, namely in-air controllability. The only thing you can do is git gud and deal with it. After some powerups are obtained, controllability becomes markedly easier. My only real gripe with the game is a lack of fast travel. For the game to progress normally, it is almost unnecessary, but to go back if you missed something can be a slog. Another minor issue is that you can only view the map of the particular area you're in (an issue which is alleviated by a full game map found online).

_childDocuments_.review: Nice graphics, but ... buy if you feel patient.No fast travel, cardinal sin: if exploring means getting blocked and having to reload and/or painfully retrace your progress ...Example:  Could jump some iffy parts in one direction, got blocked, couldn´t jump in the other direction, reload and lose your time.Looong jumping stretches can turn into a chore, sometimes hit and miss (and miss again).Restricted map makes traveling to target locations a guesswork.Aiming the axe takes pressing 2 directions keys for oblique angles then shoot, otherwise up or to the sides were the choices 99% of the time, never could angle it as I wanted consistently.And the idiotic dragon chase, near impassable, had to use a paper marked fixed distance ruler against the screen, to finally .... finally pass, what an aggravating chore.And the strike a exploding barrel up a curved slope to destroy a metal wall.Simple strike till a barrel stops a couple meters or so near the curved slope: then a Charged strike will kick the barrel upwards, time it so it explodes near the wall. _childDocuments_.review: Itorah is not a difficult metroidvania, but it is a beautiful one. Every bit of the presentation layer of the game is made with love and a wild attention to detail; the layers of the background, the animations (especially during character interactions), the lighting effects and silhouettes, the music - I was delighted with all of the little details. Props to the bells. I was surprised how emotionally impacted I felt by the end of the game.If you tried Hollow Knight but felt that the combat was a bit too much, or that getting lost was a little annoying, this game might strike a nice balance for you. As for me, I did find myself wishing for a hard mode or NG+ with meatier fights and more complex platforming; the game feels so smooth and kinetic in the air by the end (as long as you don't try to change directions without a wall jump) that I was hoping for a place to push the limits of the platforming. Another thing that I wanted by the end: more. The animations between characters, the familiarity between the main character and the others when waking up from a rest, had me wishing for a longer adventure game with more narrative and dialog. Everyone is so characterful, and the animations express so much, that I just didn't want the story to stop. I thought Itorah would be a fun, cute ride. With its relatively easy difficulty, I never thought it would become one of my favorite Metroidvanias. I was delightfully surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: There were some good sections in the game, but in general I was bored with it, or outright hated it. Itorah is a really mediocre metroidvania:- it basically brings nothing original to the genre. All the moves you will use are as vanilla as it gets, even the order to achieve them. There were at least 3 instances when I seen a barrier or enough time passed and thought: "well, it should be the time I get double jump / slam / dash", and two rooms later I've got the powerup.- the stamina system is a VERY bad choice, when you won't give traversal abilities, not even teleportation between save points. Only sprinting and dodging/dashing use stamina, but those are the things you need the most fo getting from A to B quickly.- the only 3 thing you collect are crystals and 2limited upgrade materials. Killing mobs give you 1-5 crystals, which is laughable compared to the upgrade prices (goes up to 6000), and the fact that chests often give you 2000 crystals outright. The only enemies that give a good amount are the few wood golems which gives 120, an you will grind on them if you want all the upgrades. I got all the chests before the point of no return, but was still 3000 short, but I've read others were even 13-15k short. The crystals wouldn't even be necessary, since the upgrades are already using the two materials which are carefully placed on the map, but I guess the developer couldn't think up anything to make killing enemies worth your time even so slightly.- The game is mostly linear, maybe thats why the dev found no need for teleport between checkpoints. But this results that in order to actually use the things you collected, you need to backtrack to the village. I've already wrote about the very limited traversal options, but this is where it really hurts.- There is the obligatory ice/vulcan/forest/moving objects areas, flying mosquito enemies, spiders, slow crawlers, and the final area which combines parts of the previous biomes. 95% of the puzzle elements and enemies are tropes. - The enemies look cool, and there are even a few interesting ones (I really liked the frost dragons), but they share a common feature: they are annoying to beat down. First, there are really no incentive to do so (see before), secondly they are damage sponges. You can't really upgrade your offensive abilities, only learn a few moves of which only 2 makes the killing faster, and even so slightly. The basic trash mob takes 2 hits at the start of the game and at the end of the game. The charged hit is basically useless, since it does the same damage per time as regular hits, but easy to interrupt. After getting them, you'll basically use axe throw and slam to kill every enemies, even bosses.- the camera movement is ridiculous. Its a common feature in platformers and especially metroidvanias, so you can look up/down before jumping to your death. You can move the camera around 10% screen distance and it does it really slowly. Basically useless this way, and the lack of the feature hurts quite a few times.- the backgrounds are really pretty and well-made, but the characters in front of it really stand out, the contrast is too high. Also sometimes it is really hard to distinguish the backround, foreground and play area are hard to visually, which results failed jumps until you learn the area.- in the first half of the game, save points are so frequent that I didn't really understand why is even a healing/hp/save system in the game, especially when there is no falling damage and falling into bottomless pits / traps just takes a little hp and places you at the edge of the trap section. In the second half of the game they placed better, but since they are not used for anything besides saving/healing (e.g. fast travel), and the game is mostly linear, they could be replaced by simple cooldowns (every x second one of your healing crystals would replenish) and location triggered autosaves.- the cutscenes are really slow, boring, and presented with inaudible mumbling. It works in some games, but here it would be better to just leave the audio out. The mute protagonist really doesn't help this case either.- the incan/aztec setting would be interesting, but the game does basically nothing with it. Most of the characters are monsters/furries, and mixed with medieval/sci-fi setting elements. I would be interested in how these creatures took the place of humans, and what about the three living weapons in the game, but the story really doesn't provide lore about it.In summary, this could've been a really decent game with more polished gameplay and presentation, but it feels like a beta version  and doesn't worth the €20 full price. I'm sad for it since there were some really cool puzzles/sections and small details (like the villagers with an extra hand in the end of their tails, the talking axe and how Itorah use it to hook on objects).
_childDocuments_.name: ITORAH

_childDocuments_.review: - Short game can be beaten in less than 5 hours and generally takes around 7-8 if your taking your time- Very nice art style- Fun character design- Characters are very emotive for how limited the animation of the game is- Movement feels really good after the first hour or two- Beautiful artsy running segments - Lovely soundtrack- Story is entirely skippable without hindering any gameplay- Controller support- Itorah is pretty cute- Combat is a little clunky whether its the hitboxes being a little hit to make the swing comfortable or the lack to gravity and reaction the enemies take when getting hit it all feels a little disjointed- Limited SFX for characters making some characters a little grating to listen to- Story is a little forgettable even when paying close attention maybe just not my cup of tea- To 100% achievements requires a little bit of speed running with can be a pretty big turn off for some people- This one segment at the end of the game where you slide down an aqueduct, land on a drip leaf and have to jump on falling architecture should have at least one more segment stay as if you hit all the pillars you get soft locked. It's right before a save so it's not a huge deal but it was the only part in the game like this making it feel out of place.

_childDocuments_.review: PROS+The game looks gorgeous, amazing art style+The combat, once you get the hang of it, is super fun and engaging+The platforming sections offer a decent challenge+There is a lot of attention to detail, the game has a lot of charm +Mesoamerican inspired world looks gorgeous and feels quite unique.+The last section of the game offers quite a decent amount of challenge.CONS-While combat is fun, if you know what are you doing most of the game will offer no much of a challenge-Most side characters feel underutilised. -Progression is fine, but does not offer any room for player expression.-No secret ending :( Overall I think the game is more than recommended, the gameplay is fun, the length is decent and even though it could use a little more of challenge, (I felt I could tank a lot of the bosses without worrying too much about learning their mechanics) with a few self imposed handycaps (like no healing on bossfights) you can mitigate that feeling so I recommend you to do that if you feel the bosses are not too hard.

_childDocuments_.review: With about 5 hours under my belt, here's my take.The Good:* Controller inputs are well done & are buttery smooth and responsive. Tested on a couple different controllers both on stream and offline.* Graphics are incredible. The artwork is stunning and the depth of colors between the foreground and background are quite immersive. Developer made excellent use of lighting in many spots. Especially one part where you walk with a low sun in the sky. Trust me, you need to just sit there and take it in.* Music & sounds are great as well. Really fits.* Achievement for trying to kill a chicken. I like the humor they had with this.* Challenge is well-balanced, even the crazy jumping session they threw in.* Character animation is well done with the variations on how the character moves based on jumping, crouching or standing.The Rest:* Kind of wish they went over all of the controls in the little tutorial section, they missed explaining one of the attacks.* Cost might be a bit high for some people's taste.* One of the early cutscenes is a bit confusing; probably explained later in the game but it was weird.Honestly to say I was mind blown is appropriate. It's been awhile I was genuinely impressed with a game like this.For my taste, $19.99 is fair, but as I mentioned above it might be a bit high for some people.Go check out my VOD on Youtube and then decide if this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad but the weak points are too much for me to enjoy Itorah. First the highlights are the visuals. The scene where you're running with the sun in the background causing everything in the foreground to be a shadow is fantastic. Definitely a wow moment and I'm sure the game is filled with those.But, to get to those you have to slog through incredibly boring hallways that seem copy pasted. And the hallways are filled with some of the most boring monster encounters. It feels like there are 3 enemies in the game and you have to keep fighting them over and over. At some point I just started running past them. Fighting is sluggish with little feedback. So Itorah wasn't enjoyable to play. Even the bosses didn't provide excitement or a challenge. I would have taken either.Finally the story is fine and I'm a little curious where it's going to go. But it was a lot of running around without a lot of payoff. I was hoping to find out more about the world or the main character. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a sweet little metroidvania, but differs from the majority of the genre in two things. First of all, it is very lineair. There aren’t many areas that you can go to before you NEED to go there. And when you have already been there, you don’t have much reason to go back there, unless you just want to get some collectables. The second difference is that the game is very colorful and bright. Most of the time Metroidvanias get so dark and gloomy and often pixel art, but this one has vibrant colours and beautiful hand drawn graphics. Both of these differences I really welcome, so that’s why I gave it a go. The hand drawn graphics also come with some downsides. The most important one is that the controls are a bit janky. The animations also sometimes remind me of Flash game animations. Still the game is very beautiful at moments, and they make good use of lighting and layering. After a few upgrades you will get double jump, dash, a downwards attack (think of Scrooge Mcduck with his walking stick in the famous ducktales game) and an upwards attack. These attacks make the controls feel much better, but it does require you to hang on for a while. The story I just couldn’t be bothered with. Suddenly at the end some very emotional things may have happened, but I didn’t follow it from the start, so it didn’t make much sense to me. The gameplay was good, but I wish the attack was a little nicer. Often, I just avoided the enemies because I couldn’t be bothered to hack at them a couple of times. Being able to throw the axe really helped here, but it never became great. The game was, however, a little easier than many other metroidvania’s I have played. But this is sometimes welcome too! It took me about 10 hours to reach the end, while finding most upgrades. Graphics:	 7.5/10Sound & music:	 7.5/10Atmosphere:	 9/10Story:		 ididntfollowit/10Gameplay: 	7.5/10Replay-ability: 	6/10Overall: 	7.5/10
