_childDocuments_.review: This game and I go way back. Honestly, while you may see quite a few negative reviews, I'm going to be honest. I'm not looking for a major, fancy graphical update to this game or a change to the system within the game itself. Basically a remake. No, this is a remaster.Basically, they took what the game had, gave it a new coat of paint and slapped on a few new features for us to enjoy. That is what we got with this game. And let's be honest, the new features, especially STARTING with the Time Shifter, is a game changer.Yes, being able to turn off battles and even cheese your way through it are kind of....weak. But, hey, they're not absurd, and they're useful for grinding out items you need for crafting later in the game. Although others will argue about framerate, and other aspects, I will say, this is by far the best remaster of an old game I've seen. They just basically take it, clean it up where needed, slap a few small new features in for us, and release it again. It was cheap. 20$. And for what it is, an old PSX game. Yeah, it's perfect just the way it is. Fans of this game shouldn't go into it expecting some massive revelations and changes to the game as a whole. This is just a polished up re-release. It's basically Chrono Cross. It's getting a bit of love and attention, which it deserves even a little bit.Enjoy the game for what it is. Don't expect too much of it. For as much as I love this game, I understand it had faults and problems even now, I can see it. However, after playing it on Switch for a short while and on here as well. (Just enough to unlock the reviews) I can say that, Chrono Cross aged gracefully. Better than most games from the era. It's not perfect. It's kind of niche actually. The battle system is a bit unique though, which is what I like about it. As well as the bizarre story. I played it as a kid, didn't understand the story. Just enjoyed the game. Made it a challenge to unlock all the characters in a single run and do EVERYTHING possible.Now, I hope I'll be able to understand and appreciate the story of this game. So, don't have high expectations for it. But certainly give it the chance it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first played Chrono Trigger my perception of what a videogame could achieve changed forever. When I learned that a sequel of sorts existed on the PSX I wanted to turn back time simply to play it. By then, the PSX was long gone and I didn't know how to get a hold of it... until emulation came along. The first time I played Chrono Cross I could barely make it work on my PC and just managed to play a little over a couple of hours because part of the data was corrupted. I only managed to get a glimpse out of it, but remember really liking it, but try as I might, I couldn't get it to work. To sort of remediate that, I played a translation of Radical Dreamers for the SNES, but when I finished it only made me crave more and more the complete Chrono Cross experience. This all happened some 15 years ago or so. I had forgotten about this game when, all of a sudden, I see a remaster is on the works. I grow excited and buy it the moment it's available.There are things in this game I devoutly adore. The old JRPG vibe, the fantastic music, the blocky models, the beautiful backgrounds, the fixed camera angles... All of that just brings a smile to my face and is the reason why I reccomend this game. It is a very good game in its own right and for those, like me, who're eternally nostalgic for these kind of experiences, it's simply a treat.The "remaster" itself, however, is thoroughly dissapointing. None of the FMVs have been upscaled properly and even if you run it on native resolution, you get to play on a letterboxed square. Worst of all, the framerate is horrid, almost unplayable, and the screen tearing is dreadful. Thankfully, modders have been hard at work and have managed to mitigate some of these issues, but it's sad that a mutimillion dollar company can only provide a substandar product for a game that is, for all intents and purposes, a classic.  All in all, amazing game, terrible port. If you get it, go mod hunting for FPS fixes and upscaled videos. They're out there.

_childDocuments_.review: ETA: After the game was patched in the last year or so, I started it up to do another play through. It freezes constantly now sadly. One of my favorite games, but it's broken. Below is my original review before the issue: I haven't played this since it originally came out, and it's bringing back so many great memories. Excellent music, beautiful world, and interesting characters. I'm in the rare camp that actually enjoys this one more than the original--though I do recognize some of the original complaints/issues--the link between Trigger and Cross is vague (at best). While you can recruit TONS of party members (a favorite feature of mine in any RPG)--lots of the characters just don't have time to be fully developed, and I think this costs characterization of even those party members that you get no matter what. My least favorite thing about this game--the combat system--hasn't improved with time. PS1 JRPs seemed to think JRPG fans wanted more complex combat, and they decided to do this by, essentially, adding button presses to attack sequences. I think I wouldn't mind it so much in this game if the 90+% hit chance didn't miss about half the time. Still, it's a wonderful game, and while I hear there are lots of "issues" with it--I haven't encountered any.Edit: I did encounter some stuttering in one of the earlier game dungeons but nothing since. I changed the graphics setting from the new HD to "classic" and it fixed it for that portion of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10Chrono Cross is a fantastic JRPG that tried to do things differently and succeeded for the most part; a kind of direct sequel to Chrono Trigger, this port makes it easy for anyone interested in playing it to have access and benefit from a few QoL improvements. 9/10Just as with its predecessor, the music is simply superb. The main tracks especially are just calming, and can be enjoyed at any time, even if you don’t know anything about videogames. Perhaps the only improvement would be some sound effects, but that is obviously an understandable limitation that comes with a product made more than 20 years ago.  9/10Despite their age, they hold themselves quite well. The character designs are really solid, the elements in action are good, and even the cutscenes work flawlessly.  8/10The gameplay is really simple in essence, but I like that they tried something different with the element grid and stamina and it worked (though if they make a remake, I hope they do manage to update the systems and modify them more closer to recent titles). There are always plenty of ways to move the story forward and characters to choose from. One of the downsides may be the forge system which I am not particularly fond of, but it isn’t a detriment. 9/10Two reasons it isn’t a 10.First, while a “direct” sequel to Chrono Trigger, and building upon it, I feel like it could have been it’s own game with no references and maybe worked better. There was space to unify the two games more and create a more cohesive world.And second, characters. There are simply too many characters involved, and we get to know only a bit of everyone; some characters simply exist without space to actually know them. Starky, the alien is one, Turnip is also another random character. I would have preferred a reduced cast, or a longer game with each character having some time to shine, or even having to choose between characters in certain decisions and getting them to join, then exploring their stories more.

_childDocuments_.review: So I feel a little mix on this game. FirstPros-Good story and decent expansion for the world of Chrono Trigger-Pretty Faithful remaster, at least i didn't notice any changes story-wise-New game+ and continue+ (continue+ was an odd feature that allows you to apply non-key items, character, and stats to another save file)-slightly better graphics (I'm going to talk about it later)Cons-at times for seemingly no reason it runs like hot garbage-buggy (interaction breaks, have to step away from something and approach it again, sometimes the wrong character portrait appears in the window frame when they are conversing)-Music (I'm gonna go into this too)I have played this on PS1, Emulated, and now the remaster. When Chrono Cross originally came out I was really excited because I loved Chrono Trigger and really wanted to see how they could add on to such a masterpiece. At first I wasn't a huge fan but it grew on me and after a hour or two I really liked it but that was back when I was a teen and this is now. The graphic improvements that appeared advertised seemed wonderful with cleaner upgraded FMVs and smoother looking in game models I thought that SE finally knew what we wanted, a real remaster. Really the only improvement i see is the text that appears on screen isn't the eye strain it used to be and is pretty consistent across the board including the text the appears during conversation and FMVs. I will give it that the in game models and battle backgrounds are neater looking and also less eye strain. Music was disappointing as the start menu has the sound track and sounds awesome making me think that this would be the music that appears in game but the in game music doesn't sound like what is in the menu. I really wish that we had the choice to use that as an alternative track in game where available.So I looked around during my first play-through to see what other people were saying, I saw one of the first complaints was dialogue was changed. Personally I didn't notice so whatever the context of what was originally said seems to be similar and didn't bother me, just seems like an odd complaint.The other complaint I saw was that character models have been changed. A lot of people really hopped on this but really for me as a person who just enjoys the story, I didn't notice. I just have a feeling that people are being nit-picky for nit-picky sake.  I still enjoyed the game.As Far as remasters are concerned it isn't that bad, especially for SE which kinda surprised me. Unlike virtually every other Remaster I have played from them which feel like a cheap cash grab that somehow makes me feel like an idiot for getting (although in some cases they have gone back and did some patching). This one feels like that they actually made an effort. Now for the actual review. The game takes place 10 years after the events of Chrono Trigger, some events in Chrono Trigger get referenced but if you have never played Chrono Trigger I don't feel it'll ruin your experience. Chrono Cross has you play as Serge hopping between dimensions to unwrap a mystery involving pirates, aliens, extra dimensional beings, and dragons. Its mostly RPG but there are some puzzles. There is a branching story that when played to the fullest does have the same ending, but for me it's all about the journey. Certain choices only give you access to certain characters and in some cases allow you to skip major parts. There are 45 characters in total that can be collected and in New Game+/Continue+ near  the end of the game can be brought back in as long as you had them in a previous play-through and whatever story arcs they had can still be completed. The game does award you with exploration and experimenting. Exploration can get you characters, items, spells (elements in this game) and some character combinations give you access to more powerful duel or triple-tech abilities. Overall I think its worth the $20 if you are a fan, however if you are uncertain and can wait then wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Great game, bad port. Emulators run better than this. I'm only gonna talk about Chrono Cross because I hope that even Square Enix can't mess up a text adventure like Radical Dreamers.- Incredibly choppy framerate despite the game running at 60 fps consistently. I don't care if the whole game is at 30, but give me some consistency.- [Pretty nasty 4:3 box. No actual widescreen support.] Correction: you can get widescreen if you press Escape and play with the video settings. Under video, use Screen Type - Full. Obviously this stretches things out though.- Fast forward makes the game a bit faster in the overworld and during combat if you're okay with the framerate looking even worse. In emulators, fast forward buttons typically uncap the framerate (the uncap is usually how the speedup happens) so you don't run into this issue. Fast forward doesn't affect the starting and ending cinematics of battles, which is where I would have wanted the speedup the most.- Very unresponsive controls during battle. When an enemy attacks your ally in the middle of your own attack, the game takes a second to register that you were attacking previously and shows you the base combat menu for a second before changing to the attack choices for you. Every time this happens I get confused. In the PSX version this hiccup doesn't happen at all, or in any emulators I've used (epsxe and psxfin).- Weird clipping in certain sounds like navigating a menu. This doesn't happen in the game launch menu, only through the in game experience. Clipping happens in fast forward too but that's expected.- "New" graphics for text and character portraits look fine (if a little out of place) but the prerendered backgrounds are pretty ugly upscaled. Someone told me once when watching the trailer that the game really looks like it's not using AI upscaling, but if that's true, then whatever they used is worse.At 20 dollars USD, this is not as expensive as other titles, but buying a 9 dollar matinee ticket for a bad movie still leaves you feeling like you could have done better things with your time and money. I'd either wait for a patch to play both or for a 50% or greater sale to try just the Radical Dreamers portion.This port is radically terrible and emulation provides a better experience universally. I wish that Square Enix wouldn't make us choose between bad port or no port. I would love older Dragon Quest games to get Steam ports so I can have one platform to play all of them. I especially would love Dragon Quest 7, but not if it's gonna feel like this.Save money. Live better. Walmart.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short review, and I might extend it later when I have finished the game. I first played Chrono Cross when it first came out on PSOne some 22 years ago (yeah, I feel old), and it is just as I remember. Not sure if that is a good thing or not, but it is Chrono Cross; you will always either love the experience or not quite enjoy it. The tale of Serge and Kid has always been a slower-paced experience than Chrono Trigger. The game touches on themes of identity and feeling lost in an unforgiving world. I think these themes will land better in 2022 than in 2000. The story will take you across parallel worlds with differences, and I like these subtle changes while trying to piece together the vile machinations of Lynx as you try to defy fate. The story does have multiple branching paths where you can recruit a varied cast of colourful characters (up to 45 of them). This does help a fair bit with replayability. As for the latter half of the adventure, it does get a bit information-dumpy. This, I feel, is the greatest weakness of Chrono Cross as if you are not paying absolute attention in these moments you will be lost as to what is even happening. But, if you do pay attention, you will be cast away into a unique and unforgettable adventure. The gameplay is where I have the most issues. The combat system can sometimes feel very slow as you select between weaker attacks with a higher chance of hitting the target or stronger attacks that will likely miss. At the same time, handling that, you have to pay attention to elemental affinities and charge your element gauge and hit the enemy with high-powered magic attacks. The combat does have deeper mechanics, such as controlling the field’s element, status effects and summons. But for the most part, enemy encounters are not that difficult and do not yield many rewards. You’ll get gold and items to forge more powerful equipment, but Chrono Cross forgoes the traditional level-up system. Instead, you level up after boss encounters, and smaller enemies may give you small boosts to your total health and other stats. This can leave you feeling like standard mobs are more of a waste of time rather than something worthwhile. Overall, the game does have an incredible story and characters, but the gameplay loop could be a major turnoff for a number of players. But, if you’re willing to forgive these rough edges and embrace the unique tropical world and outstanding musical score, you are in for an unforgettable adventure. Now onto the part I think people are most curious about. I’ve read several people critiquing the game's performance, so I would like to address that. This is a PSOne game, so it will always have rough edges, like texture warping or some ugly models. Performance on my PC has been quite lovely. I’ve not had noticeable performance issues and enjoy the updates to the character models, and character portraits, and the music is of a higher quality than the PSONE. I’m disappointed with the pre-rendered backgrounds. They don’t look like that much of an improvement from the originals. I’m willing to forgive that as I can always swap to the classic backgrounds (but, unfortunately, lose some of the changes I do quite like). Compared to Chrono Trigger, these updates are not the most offensive I’ve seen, and I’m entirely okay with the work done with the game. Overall, I will come back to flesh out my review if there are any changes to my experience on the latter half of the game. But, right now, I’m pretty happy with the experience. For about $30CND, I’m satisfied with my purchase, and I think the PSOne original still goes for about $15-40CND, so it is not like I’m being gouged as far as price goes. If you want nicer pre-rendered backgrounds, I’m sure the modding community will have your back later, but I’m pretty satisfied for what I’ve played so far. My recommendation is if you want to re-experience Chrono Cross and can forgive the rough edges; I’d say give this a go. If you don’t think you want to be reminded of how antiquated PSOne RPGs can be, this might be better to remain a dream from a more radical time.

_childDocuments_.review: When I played chrono trigger - which I consider the best JRPG of the SNES era - I needed to play Chrono Cross and I am thankful for a steam release because I had no desire buying a PS1 just to play this.Pros- The strongest pro first: CC tells an unique story. I don't think any game before 1999 had parallel worlds as a topic and just as well as CT handled the topic of time traveling, CC handles the topic of parallel worlds. Plus, the game is very well connected to its predecessor - CC picks up, were CT left off. The story of CC could not be withouth CT. But there is also a con to this. It is a VERY complex story and without having played CT, some might not understand, what is actually going on and could be in a snit. So do urself a favor and play CT first. You surely won't regret it. - Fun battle system, altough I would not like any other game to have it. It's enough that this game has it. - Beautiful world. Thailand and the ocean serve as an inspiration for El Nido and they conversed very well. Surely a welcome change to medieval settings.- Great OST.Cons- CC was born in an era, in which many JRPGs thought that many characters make a good game (e.g. the Suikoden series). Well, if you have about 40 hallow characters, maybe 10 characters with attention to detail would have been the better solution. CT had 7 characters, each serving a meaningful purpose within the story. In CC there are 35 characters with very little purpose at all - or none at all like Turnip - yeah, a humanlike Turnip may join your party. And even in battle characters only differ in stats and a few skills. Even worse: There are better and worse character - so you can leave most characters out. - The pacing of the storytelling could have been better. There were flaws at times, hindering a smooth experience of this great story.- Getting strong spells and weapons is not fun and takes a lot of grinding. However, it is not necessary to do it in order to beat the game. The main reason to play this is a truly unique story. If you are a JRPG fan, there is no way for you not to play this masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good: Having a modern means of access to Chrono Cross and Radical Dreamers is always a good thing, but I cannot in good faith recommend this release. The Bad: My PS1, PS2, and PS3 can still run this game and have it look a lot better than this port. Screen tearing is a problem, and there is no VSync to help mitigate the problem. This could have been built from the bottom up to avoid a lot of these problems. A "Polygon Perfect" upscale of this and other PS1 era games, along the lines of the "Pixel Perfect" remakes of the older Final Fantasies, is what these older games deserve. The Ugly: The old FMVs look really bad on this release. Backgrounds and characters clash, making them stand out in a very garish way. I also do not like the font used for the "remake" version.

_childDocuments_.review: Chrono Cross probably understands Chrono Trigger more than Chrono Trigger fans understand Chrono Trigger. In terms of gameplay, it has some details that are maybe too different from Chrono Trigger (which is not necessarily bad) and it definitely has too many playable characters. But it shines with its wonderful music, world and story that shows a nostalgic broken world with broken people (and at its core, is a good story that became an RPG, not the other way around). Chrono Cross might not be the standard sequel to its predecessor and it does not even try to be that. Chrono Cross is a bittersweet love letter to Chrono Trigger that can be hard to read.

_childDocuments_.review: No until it gets fixed with a patch. TL;DR: Square needs to fix the 15 FPS or lower lag in battles, and encounter bugs (which actually made me restart the game and pick it up from an earlier save). A nice touch would be increasing it to 60 FPS. Frankly, an emulator of the PSOne version of the game actually runs more smoothly, though you lose the minor graphical updates that came with this edition of the game.For people who want the full read:After 3 to 4 hours of gameplay, I have some thoughts. First, let me say that I am a huge fan of this game. When it was released in 1999 it received very little love, but despite the hate, I was in love with the game. So none of my issues are with Chrono Cross the game.My issues are specifically with the remaster. Locked at 30 FPS, it jars horribly and visually on PC, and I don't understand why it wasn't upgraded to at least 60. Furthermore, it doesn't maintain 30 FPS. Going in to battles, it drops to 15 FPS or lower, to the point where fighting without the fast forward on during the battle sequence is absolutely painful. Input lags terribly, and feels painful, especially considering the stamina based combat system, requireing physical attacks to build up your magic power.Additionally, Chrono Cross suffers the same problems that FF8 Remastered suffers from. Cutscenes not upgraded, backdrops not upgraded. The characters look jarring against the backdrops that haven't been touched.Another huge issue I take is that they couldn't find a way to upscale this to a widescreen format. As the first remaster post FF Pixel Remaster collection, this just feels lazy, and a grab for cash. I would have expected Square to take longer with the remaster and do a proper upgrade and quality of life improvement to the game, like better FPS and widescreen capabilities, maybe do the same graphical remaster to the environment that they did to the character models.I have it, I'm happy enough with it, for no other reason than the fact that it is on PC finally, but I would suggest to wait on a purchase until they fix the FPS lag in battles, or add in the feature to obtain 60+ FPS. I know it is far too late to dream of a wide screen, Pixel Remaster treatment to the game, but they can at least fix these FPS issues.After thought: I have also noticed some bugs with encounters in the early stages of the game, specifcally Opassa Beach. I got cornered by a beach bum I couldn't walk around, and it never let me engage. This also happened with a komodo dragon after arriving at the opassa beach in Another World.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I enjoyed Chrono Cross very much when I was younger, I would absolutely not recommend getting the Steam version of the remaster. It persistently gives me a "not enough VRAM" warning and I cannot use it with the new font because the game will immediately crash back to the launch window. Even on Classic font, the game is extremely laggy due to the VRAM issues and still crashes often. I had initially thought the problem was my old laptop (although most ported/remastered 90's games didn't have a problem running on it) so I kept it in the library until I eventually got a new one. I tried installing it this week, and it has the exact same problems.Googling around told me I was not the only person with this issue, and I couldn't resolve it because my computer does not have an NVIDIA graphics card, and the recommended fix for Iris Xe failed to work. A 1999 game with a modern font and smoothed-out character models should not need a high-end graphics card to work, nor should it require players to spend extra time futzing around with the settings of their high-end graphics cards just to run. The game crashes every time I hit the second fight with Solt and Peppor, so I just can't play it anymore. I am seriously disappointed that, nearly a year later, Squenix has not released a fix for these issues. I'm certainly not going to be first out of the gate to buy any more "remasters" from them after the shoddy job they did with this one. Unfortunately I can't get a Steam refund because the time between initial purchase and getting my new laptop was greater than two weeks, but please be very wary if you buy this game and ask for a refund immediately if you get the VRAM warning.

_childDocuments_.review: Assuming you already enjoy Chrono Cross, this is basically a slam dunk purchase. This is a more than adequate port of the PlayStation game to PC. The quality of life features really helped me enjoy the game again in a way that time has not allowed in many years. The ability to speed up the game to reduce the length of battle animations, which are considerable, as well as the movement across the map really made the experience of not just playing the game, but replaying the game repeatedly much more enjoyable than it had been previously.The increased resolution and frame rate are always welcome too. The art style of the maps really don't suffer for the upscaling. The other cheats are also a nice addition when you're already multiple playthroughs in and already functionally invulnerable and just going through the motions to try and get everything.If you have never played Chrono Cross, your mileage may vary.. It's definitely a tremendously flawed game. However those problems, rather poetically, all originate in the year 1999 and they are what they are. We have no time gates to traverse to undo the many mistakes the game makes in design and narrative but there is, in my opinion a good game there despite them all. Especially if you enjoy Choose Your Own Adventure style games with narrative consequences for your choices and actions. If you've not played and understood Chrono Trigger, go play that first. If you love Chrono Trigger, there is no guarantee you will enjoy this game. You may hate it. But there is no way you will  love this game if you haven't enjoyed Chrono Trigger first.

_childDocuments_.review: Chrono Cross is a 'cult-classic' JRPG mostly known for being a rough-around-the-edges sequel to Chrono Trigger. It has a semi-unpolished plot, a large amount of half-hearted character development and is mostly driven by its Celtic-influenced soundtrack. Despite all this, it's still a good RPG on its own terms. Its unique battle system revolves around preparing and collecting powerful attacks. Some of these attacks, the summons in particular, aren't absolutely necessary to fighting enemies effectively, but capturing and unleashing them makes the late-game boss battles significantly easier. It's worth noting that 'capturing' the summon elements and setting up the appropriate 'field conditions' to use these summons on your enemies is the same obtuse "card game flu" that Final Fantasy 8, Final Fantasy 9 and Baten Kaitos caught. These games were clearly influenced by the mid 90s / early aughts trend of collectible-card games like Yu-Gi-Oh, the Pokemon TCG and Magic the Gathering.Chrono Cross is also dated by some of the cultural / historical trends in Japan at the time: specifically 'Visual kei' and the aftermath of the Plaza Accord agreement. The game's existential regret (which you'll see through the Marbule-'Nikki concert' subplot) and its obsession with 'entropy as an arrow of time', if you will, don't make a lot of sense without the historical context of what Japanese academics were calling a "Lost Decade" for the country. You might find it fitting that this sequel to a 'dream team' video game takes a less optimistic approach to the same time-travel story. It's easy to see Chrono Cross as a dilapitated imitation; a self-conscious and incomplete nostalgia for a better game. Chrono Cross will always have a niche appeal to a wider audience, but it is still enjoyable as a relic of the past.

_childDocuments_.review: How many games let you recruit a cyborg, a pirate, a cat-furry, a mutant mushroom-man (“Funguy”), and 40 other weirdos to save time itself? Well?!Chrono Cross is one of the best, weirdest, and most fun examples of the traditional Japanese RPG. An innovative battle system, mind-bending story, way too many colorful characters, and off-beat humor make this game one of the most memorable and unusual adventures on the PS1. This is a competent remaster that does justice to a game that was often overlooked back in the day.The game’s central conceit is two parallel worlds that you can traverse to uncover the mystery of why you’re alive in one world but deceased in the other. The overarching story is mind-bogglingly convoluted and hard to follow unless you’re familiar with the lore of this game’s predecessor, Chrono Trigger. However, the writing is excellent, and the story saves itself with an enormous cast of characters, each with compelling, distinct personalities. Some fade into the background after you recruit them, which is a shame, but the game’s overarching mystery is enough to keep you going even when things get confusing. The plot may not grab you, but the characters’ individual stories will. And with 44 to find and recruit, there’s bound to be someone you’ll love. The battle system is unusual but easy to pick up. Weak physical attacks chain into stronger, less accurate ones, which charge your magic attacks. Characters have unique abilities and can also draw from a pool of shared spells (“elements”). There’s a lot strategy involved in picking the right elements and characters, and experimenting with the system is a lot of fun. With such a large cast, you won’t get bored mixing and matching your team. And because several characters are mutually exclusive, you’ll have to beat the game at least three times to recruit everybody and experience everything the game has to offer. There’s definite value for money here, with the replay value through the roof. The game looks beautiful on PC (I played it on the Steam Deck with no issues), with colorful, hand drawn backgrounds and a tropical island theme. The game creates a unique, spellbinding atmosphere that draws you in and keeps you hooked.Chrono Cross is beautifully weird in the best possible way. This is a must have for any RPG fan.

_childDocuments_.review: A radically unique follow with a radically poor remaster.To be upfront, the game is getting an overall positive score based purely on the game itself with the quality of the remaster in the background. Following the success of Chrono Trigger and not much else, Chrono Cross is a divisive, occasionally misguided adventure that I still think comes out on top in the Chrono duology.The narrative and world is really what the game excels in, paced perfectly for the first 75% of the adventure, you see yourself hopping between different timelines to stop a nefarious talking humanoid cat. All the while grabbing party members left and right like Pokemon with a lot more work. The game's narrative is compelling, and the world vibrant with personality. It's a much weirder adventure than it's predecessor, but it's exactly that strangeness that I find more alluring than the original, though it does come at several faults.The most notable fault is the battle system and it's rewards, or lack thereof. You don't gain experience after each battle and instead, only level up during certain in-game milestones. This makes each moment in the game relatively balanced (it's still surprisingly easy), though that makes normal combat feel worthless. It doesn't help matters that the battles are more involved than a standard JRPG combat system. During boss fights it makes the system of increasing and decreasing elemental powers by their overall usage mixed with the limited actions more compelling, but droning during regular encounters. And the final act is a bit of a bit of a love it or hate it affair. Still, this uniqueness is what makes this game more captivating than Chrono Trigger for me, which excelled at what it was trying to be. That being the pinnacle of Super Nintendo JRPG design philosophies.Now, on the remaster: the frame rate is absolute garbage and the fact Square Enix is selling the game for what it is with a lack of any sale price in sight is frankly, stupid. Also, the added music being only available during the game selection menu, and it being random every time you boot it up is such an odd choice. As far as I know, there's no way to listen to them in any other way through the game. The remaster does add the ability to speed up combat at the start (a reward originally offered exclusively in NG+) which helps some of the repetitiveness of the game's combat. And of course, the remaster includes Radical Dreamers, a visual novel companion piece to Chrono Cross. It's really interesting to play through, with a lot of cool ideas interesting to see resurface in Chrono Cross. Though if you're not the biggest fan of the genre, I would recommend looking at a guide as it has multiple endings with specific stipulations. All in all, it's a great game with an awful remaster, standard for Square Enix I suppose. I recommend you play this game, but maybe not this version.

_childDocuments_.review: Chrono Cross is the controversial but still solid followup to Chrono Trigger, carrying on its thought-provoking themes and (kinda-sorta) story, though with a much different tone and overall feel.  The "Radical Dreamers Edition" is a rather strange remaster, though, as there are only the barest-minimum of improvements made over the original.  There are redrawn portraits for the characters (which look quite good), but the "high-resolution" backdrops just look like they were ran through an online upscaling tool, complete with awkward-looking smoothed edges that don't blend quite right..  The 3D models look almost identical to the originals, though with cleaner edges owing to the antialiasing; they even still have that PS1 "jitter" even when characters are standing still.  The FMVs still have the familiar graininess and artifacting that was present in their PS1 counterparts, so no real change there either.  Strangest of all, the framerate isn't improved at all from the PS1, with a lot of noticeable slowdown and frame-skipping during the bigger, flashier moves, and even fluctuating as you move around the maps.  Basically, it feels like you're just running the original version in a third-party emulator with some upscaling options on; the only notable difference being the few token enhancements common to other modern Square ports (like the ability to toggle encounters and autosaves).  You also start the game with the Time Shifter (a New Game + feature in the original), which lets you slow down or speed up the gameplay with the shoulder buttons.  On the upside, this version does include the "original draft" of Chrono Cross (Radical Dreamers, formerly exclusive to the Satellaview), so it's nice to own for that if nothing else.TL;DR: Good game, but not much of a "remaster".  There's a good reason they're only charging $20 for it.Update: You can now grab a 60 FPS/64-Bit EXE patch and a much better set of upscaled backgrounds and FMVs from Nexusmods.  There ya go!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm admittedly very biased and can enjoy this game even with a clunky port, which is what this is so far. It runs about the same it would on emulator a few years back, that is, decently enough to play, with some filtering that makes it look smoother at the cost of looking a bit blurry. Emulator mods CAN make it look sharper but the cost of *that* is a darker, dirtier image, which is just what happens when you over-enhance when there's just no information there to enhance. Some people don't mind that but I personally prefer it a but blurrier but retaining a better color accuracy, so the filtering in this port is just about right.My actual issue with this port, which I hope will be addressed with patching, is the very noticeable lack of v-sync. The screen tearing and shaking is constant and very annoying, even a little nauseating at times (on the main map, for instance). I didn't find any issues with the sound quality, no weird clicks and hisses (common issues with emulating this game), controls are responsive, analog and vibration work well. Also had no lagging, freezing or crashing issues (Ryzen 5 3600, 32 GB RAM, RTX 2070 8GB, 2 QHD monitors).All in all, like I said, I'm biased, I've been waiting for this port for years and having it handy on Steam rather than having to set up emulators is enough for me, so I do recommend it, but would say wait for a sale (especialmente pros BR, 90 conto é demais). Modders did wonders with FFIX on Steam, if something like Moguri pops up for this it'll be perfect.I just hope the syncing issue is addressed.

I tried using Radeon Chill to lock the frame rate to 30 in the vein hope that it'd at least make it more consistent, but it literally doesnt work and the game is still trying in vein to run at 60 and flip-flopping all over the place the entire time I play. Go online and order the original PS1 version, play it on the original hardware or a PS3 or emulate it, you will literally have a better experience and spend about ten dollars less. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not too deep into the game, but already the issues are pretty glaring for a "Remaster."First, I should start with the good things.  Like the original Chrono Cross, the game itself is still a great journey full of twists, turns and options.  The speed option is handy for getting through areas quickly, and the redone menu and character portraits are very nice.  The inclusion of radical dreamers is a nice touch, and can help tie a few loose connections in for those unfamiliar with it.  I took time to play it first, and it was an enjoyable little text adventure.But now I should touch upon the issues.  While the new character models look very nice there are still clipping issues with hair and other extremities despite being redone, plus they can feel out of place with what often looks to be untouched backgrounds and environments.  And while the backgrounds are true to the original, they simply look blurred and out of sync, losing details that should be there.  On top of that, the cinematic moments may even look worse than they did back in the day, as they appear to be ENTIRELY untouched.  Next of course is what many are bringing forth, the frame rate.  This was an issue I felt playing the game as a child, that it often could seem clunky, especially in battle.  The transition to battle and motions seem to almost stutter and lag, causing battle to feel slow.  While I have given this a thumbs down, at the price point it is still a good by, especially for any fans and curious newcomers.  But with that said, I desperately hope that patches are put into place to deal with some of the issues, and that modders can take on what SE was too lazy to do.  In all honestly, it feels like the team forgot the deadline and skipped half of their work for the sake of release, leaving the many present issues.

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game back in 2001.I rememer going to a game store with my dad and I saw the cover from this game hidden behind some FF and other RPGs. Even after many years, not playing it on the PS1 or any emulators, I still remembered all the characters, all the locations, the elements and the amazing soundtrack by Yasunori Mitsuda. When I saw that there would be a remake, I was instantly teleported to that same moment at the store, 20 years ago. I felt like a child. Like I was starting to discover this amazing world of games and everything that it had to offer. I started to tell all about it to my wife and she surprised me by buying it for my birthday.This is an amazing game. Everything about it makes your heart warm and your curiosity at full attention. Emotional moments, funny moments. This game has it all.Now, for the technical part of this release:I noticed a lot of people talking about the frames and the screen tear. And they're not lying. There really are some FPS drops and tears. But for me, personally, it didn't bother me that much. It kind of reminded me of how it would perform on the PS1 (FPS wise, not the tear). _childDocuments_.review: I find it difficult to judge something like Chrono Cross without being affected by nostalgia. This was one of the first games I truly loved growing up, so it's probably impossible for me to look at it from the perspective of someone interested in buying it without a similar experience. However, I can say with a good amount of confidence that this game does rise above being just another old game that's not worth a look anymore. To me, this game has it all. A great art style, amazing music, a fun and deep combat system, challenging bosses, a colorful world filled with interesting characters, and a story that can feel intriguing and daunting at one moment and then carefree and silly the next. I think that, even now, a new player could enjoy Chrono Cross as a solid JRPG. Do keep in mind though, that the game is over 20 years old at this point.As for the port/remaster/remake/whatever the proper term is: it could be a lot better. I noticed some annoying performance issues, and it was very disheartening. Although I do not believe that it should be a deal-breaker, if you are someone that values performance super highly it just might be. You can tweak settings and some have mentioned mods help, so there is that silver lining. I love Chrono Cross, so it's probably impossible for me to not recommend it, even with it's issues. Even after all this time and knowing everything there is to know about it, I still found playing it to be an incredibly charming and fun experience. If you're looking for an RPG to play and don't mind the age, I would definitely recommend it, especially if it's on sale. o/

_childDocuments_.review: I'm making this review having beaten the game. My experience has been... frustrating but mainly positive. I wish Steam had better options then just "Do you recommend this game?". Sure fine, fine go for it. Although you might have a better experience with an emulator. I only played this game on PS1 and now on PC through steam. Its still a good game and brought me back in time when I was 16 playing this game in a home I no longer live in with parents who are now so far away. I'm obviously biased by nostalgia. Now I would buy this game and enjoy because I'm me. However, for those of you who place frame rate issues as one of your deal breakers then I can't recommend it to you. Also there is a nasty "Insufficient VRAM" popup that I had to resolve which also resolved the game's tendency to crash on me. Another bad port from Square of a great game that was lost to time and memory.I completely missed out on a number of details or maybe I forgot since I haven't touched this game in a while. How to recruit certain characters; certain scenes; how to get certain items and elements. There is a lot to do and if you're not thoughtful or clever enough you will miss them on the first go-around. However this game was designed for multiple play-throughs to get the complete experience.I was never a big fan of the number of recruitable characters. 45 is insane and a waste because I only used certain setups. Chrono Trigger had the right idea with its characters. Quantity is not greater then or equal to quality. The characters need to be woven into the narrative but a lot of them here just feel like they are just there. Not a great way to tell a story or explore character arcs. It was a bad idea then and a bad idea to this day. Speaking of the story itself its insanely convoluted and opens itself up to more questions then it answers. However the important thing is you saved Schala from Chrono Trigger and that was important to Misato Kato for some reason... Oh well we all have our waifus and Chrono Cross has a number of them. The main question is does this game need to exist? No, not really. All it did narratively was re-invent Lavos and make Schala more important then she was in Trigger. The multiple timelines idea is neat but creates plot holes and if this was a larger series this would be an even bigger problem... I would go into more details but I don't want to turn this into 30 pages or more.The combat system is insanely exploitable with little to no grind required to progress. However you still want to grind for the raw materials and money to make your weapons and gear. That's basically what you're grinding for. Success or failure is dependant on your use and understanding of the element system. The game play is really unique and if you're confused look up explanations on Youtube or just play the game and learn through trial and error.A messy story with redundant characters combined with a dirty combat system still turned out to be a fun experience. Like I said, a frustrating but mainly positive experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I've beaten PS1 version of Chrono Cross twice many years ago, so I'm an old fan.The game is 10 out of 10 for its time. It's one of the best JRPGs for PS1.Its story and art direction is very good, and it's got one of the best video game soundtracks of all time.- I was hesitant to get this PC port because of the players who expressed their problems with it at the launch. Nearly a year later I had a fresh start by playing this officially patched version 1.0.1.0.- At first the game gave me a "Not enough VRAM" error but still managed to run in windowed mode, couldn't enable to run in fullscreen. During playing the game, hitting the Esc button opened up an additional options menu that let me enable to apply "Fullscreen" mode. Then the game got incredibly slow running.- Then I've turned off the "anti-aliasing mode" in that video options. That FIXED the whole PC port.- Now it runs very well. After turning off the anti-aliasing, I have no problem with this game.- I recommend this PC version. Its frame rates are good in my opinion. It's got cleaner font, the text is more readable. Also character portraits have retouched by the original artist. All the backgrounds and textures are higher quality than the PS1 version, and they more look like paintings. This is the definitive version in my opinion. Cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: Foolishly thought Square had started putting care into their remasters, after the Pixel Remasters were so enjoyable and mostly free of game-breaking bugs. But Chrono Cross did not get that care - game frequently just stops working, while the music will continue to play, and you'll have to use Task Manager to force close the game, losing progress quite often. This issue seems to frequently occur during text box cut scenes and less frequently during battles, but is always frustrating. I regret being outside the refund window or I'd request a refund and just play the OG playstation version instead. Sure the graphics are less pixelated in the remaster, but there's no quality of life improvements that I've noticed, so the games menus are still tedious to navigate and managing elements and equipment for more than your 3 active party members becomes insufferable after awhile, discouraging using your excessively growing roster of team members (same as in the original). If you've never played, avoid the broken remastered software and just play the OG Playstation version. If you played the original and want to experience the facelift, just anticipate game freezes and broken software, which is becoming a standard practice for Square releases

_childDocuments_.review: Chrono Cross is a weird game. While it is a direct sequel to Chrono Trigger, it looks, plays, and tells nothing like Chrono Trigger. From the large cast of characters you can recruit, to its one of a kind turn based battle system, to its completely nonsensical plot, there's no other RPG like it. Its aesthetics, beautiful hand drawn backgrounds and an OST that could well be one of the greatest of all time, is the highlight of the game.However, this review is not just about the game itself, but rather as of the time of this review the extremely poor and unoptimized remaster version of the game. Frames are extremely choppy, button prompts look way out of place, and a rather sharp font for the text are just the few problems the remaster has.

This + OBS basically runs at 95% on an i5 7600k, with only about 20% GPU usage between the two of them. Cross using about 5% of that. _childDocuments_.review: Reeeee where do I begin?This is my favorite game of all time and has been for a good many many years. The Chrono series is worth a look for anyone who's never played. I cannot speak for Trigger on Steam and will not here, but the Cross port on Steam is in my opinion worth it (now).

_childDocuments_.review: I hate giving nearly every release a negative review, but here we go again :-\Where to start?If you were hoping for anything uniquely different than emulating -- ban me for saying the naughty word, I dare you -- the original PS1 game, you will not find it. Achievements are the only thing the Steam release does that an emulator would not do better.Under the hood, things are ugly. The only part of the game that actually renders using D3D11 is the game's UI. They give plenty of high-res UI assets and an insanely high resolution font that won't even load on Intel GPUs (textures larger than 128 MiB are not required by Microsoft to work in compliant D3D11 drivers and of course that means Intel users get the shaft as usual), but there's zero hope of doing anything like a re-texture mod since the game isn't even rendered using a PC graphics API.Making matters worse, the actual render rate of the game is decoupled from the UI framerate. You can use all the monitoring software in the world and you're not going to get an accurate measure of the game's actual framerate or the severity of its stuttering and slow downs. I can't quantitatively measure any of that stuff, but I can tell you it -feels- wonky as hell with definite uneven frame pacing between each UI and game frame. I think the game's only saving grace is its price. $19.99 is just low enough that you might not care you could have bought the game used at a yard sale for less and had a better experience. Buy the game because you have never played it before, not because it's anything special.

_childDocuments_.review: (Updated 4/12: Added another longer video showing out of battle performance + misc additional thoughts)Despite the steam of negative reviews and comments, this is a very serviceable port of a great game - with a few caveats.Obvious, this is one of the big draws, right? A classic PS1 RPG released with minimal changes and upgraded graphics. The new character models are generally fantastic and faithful to their original counterparts. The portraits are equally good, but they do take some creative liberties and some portraits don't do the character justice. The font, of course, is much more modern and readable, and the UI is as clean as it gets.On the other hand, you might remember that the game uses pre-rendered backgrounds. The Radical Dreamers Edition took these and more or less AI upscaled them, but the results vary wildly. Some areas look gorgeous, others(for example, the zoomed-in world map when you're on foot) look almost water-colored, but more of a blurry mess. It's endearing in a way, but also does the game a disservice.There are also options to switch between screen modes - Normal, Full and Zoomed. Normal is typical 4:3 with borders, Full stretches the image across your entire screen(but isn't true widescreen support) and Zoomed lets you zoom in by a specified percentage, maintaining the 4:3 aspect ratio and using more of your screen, at the cost of potentially cutting off some elements. For those who prefer the original graphics, you can switch between them or the new ones in the launcher. You can't, however, use the original graphics with the new font or UI.There isn't much to say here, as nothing has really been changed. While the launcher shuffles between arranged versions of songs from the game, the game itself uses the same music you'll remember from the original. They've been remastered and touched up, but nothing has fundamentally changed about them.Again, nothing to really note here. You have immediate access to the ability to speed up or slow down the game, and as with other PC ports they've added in the option to turn off encounters or give your characters a "Battle Boost" - making them much harder to kill. An Auto-battle function was added as well. These features are entirely optional and can be ignored, and the game is otherwise the same.This is where a lot of complaints come in. Out of the digital box, the performance of the game isn't terribly good. You'll need to mess around with your GPU's control panel and force certain options(vsync, framerate caps, triple buffering, etc) that the game itself doesn't offer. Even with that, the game does still suffer from FPS drops, particularly in battles with more than a few enemies. Battles also tend to be plagued by a bit of input delay of varying severity. As with the framerate, it tends to worsen in fights with more enemies such as the Man-Of-War fight. Outside of battle the framerate is relatively stable, though there are some problem areas.Here's two short videos, one showing the performance across various areas of the game and the other showing the performance exclusively in battle:On the other hand, the above issues seem exclusive to the New graphics mode. Swapping to Classic mode provides a very faithful experience, with a much more stable framerate. The input delay in crowded battles is still a minor issue, but much less noticeable.Overall, it's a solid and entirely playable port, though I hope these issues(which appear to be present on consoles as well) are fixed in time. First-time players will not likely be as bothered about the performance as returning fans.

_childDocuments_.review: I had expectations cause I played Chrono Trigger and it was so good but when I played Cross reality kicked me in the face. You know the rule of thumb for movies, sequels tend to suck and this game is no exception. Lets take 'Chrono' out of the title and pretend it had nothing to do with Trigger and then this game would feel like it was decent! This is one of those games where you like it or you don't. I don't care whether the reader agrees or not. This is my opinion on this game so here goes.This game is mixed bag of berries meaning it has good, bad and an ugly side to it. Good side: - It has a great battle system and the ost to this game is top notch with the exception of the regular battle music.- Has in-game enabled cheats so you can cheese your way if you don't feel like doing it normally. This feeling kicked in for me after I beat it the first time. - Has a good story about two worlds where the main character is alive in one and died in the other which causes a paradox. Blah blah blah go play the game, I'm so tired of reading all that text that it has to offer. Bad side:- The 45 playable characters is way too much for an RPG because they don't have much back story and I didn't even remember half the names of them even after playing through this game four times. - This game has a lot of fans which have biased opinions. You make a comment and the internet explodes on your butt. Ugly side: - This game tells you what happened to some of the Chrono Trigger characters in the game but it's mainly focused on Serge and the Chrono Cross world. You do get to learn to what happens to some of the main cast of the previous game (Chrono Trigger) which was my favourite part of the story. But it's very limited and you don't get to learn much.  It's kind of hard to like call this game a sequel.   - This game doesn't hold your hand and gives you arrows on the ground to follow. You have to explore around a lot and that really a time waster. This feels like Dragon Quest 1 all over again. If you're like me who would like to finish a game in a timely manner, I would recommend using a guide. - The worst achievement in this game is collecting all the characters. This game is about 30-40 hours on the first play through.Difficulty: Medium because I barely died in the game without using cheats.For me at least: I felt bored at times. But the game did have its moments too. Notes for achievement hunting people like myself: - At minimum you have to complete this game 3x to get all the characters. - Make multiple save files because this game is so easy to miss stuff. - Expect to make a stupid mistake that will cost you hours of your time.I got all my achievements which took me 100 hours on the dot. Final Words: To me this game was like at least 5/10. But everyone has different preferences so it's possible that you the reader would like this game more than I did. Thanks for reading and wasting your time. Chris

_childDocuments_.review: A personal favorite of mine marred by poor management and support offered by Creative Business Unit IV and D4Enterprise - a begrudging thumbs up if I have ever given one before. Let's address the elephant in the room first, this game has had a very troubled release that is still plaguing players over a year later. Yes, the original source code for many PS1 era JRPGs (Chrono Cross included) has been lost and are either rebuilt from scratch or emulated - Chrono Cross is the latter. Being an emulation isn't inherently a bad thing, but this is a very poor version that can frankly be done better by users with their own emulators and plugins. Your ability to play this game, and to play it well, ends up relying on too many factors and it is frankly unacceptable. You can compare your specs with your fellow peers, even the software that you run that may or may not interfere with your ability to play this game, but you'll never be any closer to knowing whether or now your rig will be able to play this game with little-to-no issue. I was lucky enough to have little issue with the original release, and none so far with the patched version, but many are not so lucky. Just your fair warning. Doom and gloom out of the way, the game itself is still as enjoyable of an experience as it ever was. I know a lot of Chrono Trigger fans don't look favorably upon this game, claiming that it has little-or-no relation to Chrono Trigger, but they are simply wrong. The game actually has a lot of direct parallels and effects on Chrono Trigger, but many of them are based on supposition and implications. The game doesn't spoon food you a cohesive narrative that weaves the two together. You have to think for yourself and make your own inferences. If you are someone who enjoys doing that, then this game is a treasure trove of "what ifs" and implications that will have you thinking about how the games are related, but if you are looking for a more straight foward approach then you will not find it here. The only real gripe I have with the game is the ending. The shear amount of pontificating about the nature of humans versus nature is nauseating. I don't mind the trope of "humans bad, nature good, humans destroy nature" but this game is so heavy handed with it in the ending of the game, while simultaneously almost never addressing the issue in the game except for a couple segments related to the fairies and dwarves and how the people of El Nido affected them by their very presence and ways of life, but it was far too little for the disgusting, dogmatic rhetoric we get about how evil humankind is. Spare me. Still the overall plot, the lore building, the deep-diving into the implications of transcendentalism, nihilism, and the eternal battle of fate versus free-will, all make for a very compelling narrative that makes you sit back and really think. What would you do if you were dropped into this game? What do you actually think about your life now? Either that or you don't want to think about the game and begrudge it for not being Chrono Trigger 2.0 - your choice. tldr; Chrono Cross is still an exceptional game (albeit only to those who are okay with having to make inferences and enjoy a deep dive into the human psyche,) but marred by a horible port that still has unacceptable issues over a year later. Where is my "meh" review option, Steam?

_childDocuments_.review: As a teenager, I blew my whole paycheck from stocking shelves at the grocery store to buy this game new the day it came out.  Filling the shoes of Chrono Trigger was kind of an impossible task.  Where a dream team had made Chrono Trigger; Cross was dumped down the Squaresoft B Team while their top men were working on garbage like FF9 (sorry, not sorry; that game was a disappoinment).  And while most critics and most of my friends were joining in a chorus of "This is nothing like Chrono Trigger... its really confusing." I was absolutely loving this avant garde work of Japanese art that is really unlike anything else before or since.What shines above all else here is the atmosphere, the narrative, and the visual story-telling.  That is where the emphasis in this game is.  There is literally no grinding.  I'll say it again: There * is * literally * no * grinding!  You can dodge the monsters.  The levels all come from bosses/story progression.  And... get ready for this.... a classic JRPG with story choices and replayability.  There are like 50 characters but you can't have them all in the same play; and yes the story goes a little different depending on your choices.MY THOUGHTS ON THIS PORT:Having played and loved the original to death and back, I am totally fine with pretty much everything they did.  The AI did a nice job touching up the backgrounds, which to be very honest, were most of the time, a confusing mash of colors in the original.  The OG had some serious pixel hunting issues which are, if anything, greatly smoothed over by the AI retouch.  I wish they had spent more time on the character models, but there are soooo many characters.  Its a fine job.

_childDocuments_.review: An underrated overrated gem.Honestly, the worst parts of this JRPG really only come in the form of expectation. I know I'm in the minority, but I don't think that being wildly different from a predecessor makes a game bad. This game is not Chrono Trigger, and if anything, tried very hard not to be. Hating this game for not being CT is a real waste of energy.The core cast of characters you might get in tight-team JRPGs is replaced with an eclectic ensemble. By necessity, this widening of the spotlight reduces the depth of each character. That's fine, that's the game.The game is not about one hero, one team. It's about FATE, and everyone affected by it. It's not about Serge, it's about Arni, it's about Fort Dragonia, it's about the S.S. Zelbess.The world map is shrunk to one location, El Nido. The idea is to feel like everyone in El Nido has an effect on FATE, both the concept at large and, arguably, the main villain. This is very interesting to me. A whole "village" of whacky goofs and weirdos, all willing to put their necks on the line for their own future. This opposes a cliche: NPCs in this game are not living their lives completely unaware that you are saving the world. NPCs in this game will join you. NPCs in this game become playable. It's the story of El Nido, all who live there, and all who are affected by its FATE. I believe that, given infinite resources and time, every single character model in Chrono Cross would have been recruitable somehow, and you could confront FATE as any person who has ever been touched by its manipulations.The battle system is almost excellent. It innovates, for sure, but doesn't quite know how to stick the landing.I can already see how the battle system was designed. First, they wanted the final battle to end with the player casting magic in such a way that the order played a special melody. And second, they wanted anyone in El Nido to be able to show up for the fight. Cool! So how do we do that? Well, for starters, anyone should be able to show up and play this magic song to the final boss. Anyone should be able to cast the spells necessary to invoke the titular Chrono Cross. Me: Ah, but what if the player brings in characters who can't use some of that magic, like how Crono only knows Lightning spells?  Easy, we make magic into Elements that you can equip and use like items.  So we don't have items?  Well, we kind of do. Elements is the merging of Magic and Items. Instead of a small pocket of specific spells and a large pocket of renewable items, we'll have one medium pocket of both. Okay, then what about MP? Does each Element have its own MP cost?  No, that won't work. MP is gone. Instead, using Elements will cost a flat amount, and it will cost your time. My time!? Yes. We are also going to merge MP with the Speed stat. We'll call it Stamina. The more Stamina you spend, the longer it takes for another turn. This way anyone can cast any spell for the same amount, and thus be able to help set up the Chrono Cross. Alright, so let me get this straight: Elements = A merging of typical Magic and typical Inventory systems? Yes. Stamina = A merging of speed-based turn order and MP? Yes. So now we have a system that facilitates all our needs. We can a) end the final battle by casting magic in a way to perform a beautiful song, and b) be able to recruit anyone in the world by equipping them with maneuverable Elements! Neat. Are there any other cascading effects to such big changes? Well, some small ones. For starters, since technically anyone can now be recruitable, we have to get rid of the idea of individual levels. It just wouldn't make sense with the free-swap idea we're trying to push. If every character is the same level, they are equally viable. So instead, we're going to give the team itself a level, which we'll call the Star Level. It'll increase after every major fight. Okay, but then I won't get EXP after battle? Why should I fight? Well, if you aren't fighting for EXP to level up, the only real reason to engage in battle is for loot. What kinds of loot? Hmmm... money, Elements... but also, I suppose we ought to create a crafting system that requires basic materials. Otherwise, all the battles between bosses will feel like hurdles you're better off avoiding, rather than chances to grow. Ah, okay, that sounds tricky, but I'm sure we can pull it off! What matters is that if you pluck a turnip character out of the ground, or if you recruit a pink dog, or if you find a giant voodoo doll, the battle system itself fully supports your urge to toss that weirdo onto your team! Try them out! Isn't it neat how all of El Nido is excited to join in the fight against FATE!?Well, in some ways they did, and in some they didn't. I enjoy the puzzle-like effect of the battles, and I think the idea of a whole archipelago ensemble is really beautiful. But I do think there are some pieces that could make it more exciting. Honestly, manipulating the Field Effect in order to Trap a Summon is a neat challenge, and having more things like that which required Field setup would have been really interesting. Also, as much as the crafting system requires you to do small fights, the fights are so liberal with materials, and the crafting itself so uninteresting, that you never actually need to seek enemies out in that way. To truly have fun with the system, you pretty much need to work with the few character gimmicks that present challenge and pay-off. Sprigg's Doppelganger collection and Pip's evolution are genuinely neat things to juggle.I honestly wish more indie games would look at this system and try to revamp it for the modern age, rather than messing with Chrono Trigger's tired and outdated system. Maybe one day we'll get a Cross-alike. Maybe.Personally, I think Chrono Cross holds up. It may not be the best JRPG, especially with how liberally it changes formulas, but it's exactly this boldness and creativity that draws me to it. It has real heart. And even though it doesn't satisfy the modern anime obsession with a "small cast of lovable characters with recognizable trope personalities," it is the only game I can think of that feels like the whole world is just as invested in me saving it as I am, even if only for silly little reasons.Actually, maybe specifically *because* of all the silly little reasons.

_childDocuments_.review: *There is an update section notated by the asterisk at the end of this Review.I played the original top to bottom in and out.Here's my initial reception:The graphics are touched up and the detail on the models are seen with incredible clarity. A shame I don't have a 4k screen for it tbh. Some NPCs have improved Portraits and the original illustrations are kept for recruit-able memebers. They contrast quite a bit but it's more appreciated than repulsive.This is a matter of preference thoughCritics are saying the pre rendered backgrounds are upscaled through AI and it definitely shows. (Town of Arni, some of the ropes seem a bit smudged) This has been a problem in recent remasters and is definitely a strike against it imo.> The bigger issue is definitely the cinematics. Hoo boy, you can see better cinematics through YouTube. I don't know where and how they got their hands on these (probably a scratched master copy or something?) But it is bad bad. Compression artifacts everywhere. It almost hurts going from a cinematic into gameplay. I think I might try the rest of this game in Original graphic settings to see how it goes.But we have to look at this from a new player perspective as well. It's not a terrible port altogether imo. It's just that it falls short in graphical fidelity. There's not many games made like this anymore so it's a bit hard to find modern comparisons, but I think any small time studios looking to make a speedy remaster need to keep in mind that they should be seeking alternate sources and do bare minimum hands on touch ups to be re-hireable/respected.> Animations, idles, running, etc are all limited to the 29 ish FPS the game was originally in for the old CRT monitors and TVs of the era. This is good for anyone looking for the vanilla/virgin experience. It is a bit jarring to see it while the screen pans at 60+ though. My guess for an easy work around for the remaster teams is to perhaps retool these?I do hear about frame dips, but that kinda adds to the nostalgia factor imho. Although I would like a smooth experience. It's a remaster, so I would like to see it how should have been.The combat system ,its settings, and the balancing seem to be all intact with some graphical face lifts. The saturation and overall tone of the game is kept in its original essence along with its clowny bg music. lol Hopefully a mod will come around to help with replacing the battle  terms of music, it certainly sounds a lot less compressed, albeit they probably didn't need to do much work with Mitsuda's talents paired with better technology following shortly after Final Fantasy 7 when SquareEnix--then Squaresoft--first developed and published this. Sound is clean and readable among the tracks and keeps me in the world. Everything has cued consistently. Add-onsThe Radical Dreamers release is such a nice add-on. Its graphics are ported from the original SNES title from the Japan only release along with an official translation that had a proper voice through out much of the prose.> As far as other changes, the change to put the Time Shifter in the beginning is a nice touch for old fans and new fans to push through the longer waits of a PS1 era game, and the No Combat switch is actually nice if you want to circle back around and save time on maps. Think of how much you'd put the game down for missing some timed presses.> Story wise: I recommend you take your time and read. This game wants to hint to you and give you the full picture as it has faced some troubles over its original development. And with the Parallel Universes concept it pivots off of, it has more to say and should be appreciated on its own merit. Yes i know there is a soft spot for a lot of Chrono Trigger fans out there, but please appreciate this as a new story in a Universe than it is as a continuation of Crono and co. Consider the fact that the good ending still happened!Now: Should you expect so much from a 20USD purchase? I don't think so. But I am absolutely ecstatic this game has made its way back to us in 2022 as it's part of my all time favorites and comfort games. It could use a lot more input from fans, but it was faithfully remade. It could have been a half hearted remake, or an IP that was too big to fail. There are indeed valid critiques on the game, but I feel that this is an overall positive.Would Recommend the buy for nostalgics and retro gamers for sure.*REVIEW UPDATE*> I've put significantly more hours into this port and can tell that the combat is much smoother in frames. The cinematic parts are a bit more smoothed out albeit still not given the AI upscale treatment. I would like to give the studio working on this the benefit of the doubt in that they may wanted more artistic integrity over losing detail from the original through upscaling? It's a long reach, but not every decision is apparent nor clear.Pip has also been fixed, though I have not tested them myself. Nor have I done a play through to get a certain plot relevant cut scene during the first half of the game that I think is still a bit vague to trigger. Everything, in my opinion, works just like the way it was on the PS1 plus a cosmetic boost and some outside freebies.The game is in a stable state to boot up and run out the box. What would make this one of the best ports of all time in my opinion would be to add old concept art (NDA permitting) and developer commentary packaged into the extra content for fans. Maybe some Toriyama art on the side? A note to the consumer,Either way, this game is in a decent place. If we don't support older IPs and modern game designs that are more consumer friendly, we won't get what we want as a fanbase. Story, art and design are subjective unless unintentional on the producer's behalf, and criticism is here to build a product up, not take it down. Getting an accessible port is what will keep this IP afloat, but if we bash it too much, we are all losers when the IP is considered not valuable enough to maintain. Whether Cross or Trigger, I think we all love the Chrono series. Heck, Armored Core got a new installment. Anything is still possible. Cheers.

While you are in another world you are piecing together what exactly happened which honestly still makes no sense to me so im not even going to bother trying to explain it here.  Meanwhile in your home world you are still alive and can walk around freely. Some characters you can recruit in the home world and in the another world. what happened when there Doppelgangers colloid? You'd expect some type of thing where if they interact it would cause the end of the world and everything goes to hell..... Not here they get a long like there best friends ! There are sometimes certain things you have to trigger in home world to recruit a character from the another world or vise versa  which i think is really fun to try and figure out and sometimes have pretty amusing outcomes. Now the heart of where everyone gets confused mainly the battle system.  Theres is no levels ups in this game... well not really. You level up by gaining stars after a major boss fight. What this does is you are never over leveled or you are never under leveled. You are always at the exzact level you should be. So whats the point of regular battles? Sometimes absolutely nothing. Other times it's to still gain minor hp gains and very rarely other stat gains. So you should still participate in the battles. The complexing part of the battles is the element system. Each character has an element along with enemies and bosses. It's important to somewhat pay attention to these. red is week to blue green is week to yellow black is week to white ect. The field effect is where this comes in to play you want your elemental colour to be the most present on the field as it will give you the most benefit. the monsters try to get there colour on the field filled up. This of it as a strength modifier.Alright now that that is explained enough the reasons why i am giving this a thumbs down... Most people confuse frames per second with frame timing... the frame timing timing in this game is absolutely horrendous however it actually runs at 60 fps most of the time though not in the first area of the game for some reason...  The animation of every character on the field if they are doing anything else other then walking and or running. That animation will play out like stop motion and will be absolutely dreadful to look at most of the time.   Does this effect gameplay.... Sort of? Walking around and running around on the field it selves feels fun however sometimes when you get into battle because theres so much going on at times it feels like the game is struggling to keep up with whats going on. Again this isn't an fps issues it's a timing issue. I do hope they can patch it out some how and make the animations play out a whole lot better. I guess the plus is to this is it's at least playable unlike the final fantasy 8 remaster which i am still bitter about...
