_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, I would recommend Frozenheim but getting it on sale is ideal. The graphics are good, the aesthetic is gritty but pleasant. The sound is good; not award winning but not annoying either. The voice over for the campaigns is a little jarring given all your units sound like they are speaking in some Scandinavian dialect but then an american lady talks at you throughout the campaign. The game is fundamentally basic and easy. The base building is not deep: once you work out the core formula for not starving (3 fisheries and 2 farmhouses), you never have to worry again. No matter how big my base got, I never struggled for food. You do, however struggle for wood constantly and it is tedious to keep having to tell your lumberjacks to move to a new area.There is no multiplayer scene for this game because it is too simplistic. The skirmish against the AI is just not worth it because they are too easy to beat but the campaigns were, at least, enjoyable and the missions were different enough to have some variety. Once you have completed the campaigns the game is kidna over - hence - buy it on sale. Lastly, combat is very meh. Don't get this game for combat. Something Like Age of Empires II or even Ancestors Legacy will scratch that itch infinitely better than this. Enjoyable but forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the early access release, and while it is clearly early I have to say this game has a solid foundation, and the potential to be really cool.First off, I have to say I LOVE that the game is going for a more historical tone, rather than fantasy. Norse mythology inspired meda almost never get anything right anyway, and more often draws on popculture rather than the actual sagas.The controls are nice and the UI is easily readable, the graphics are gorgeous!Below are some points I think would help improve the game in future updates.What I would love to see are variations of models for the workers. Right now, they're all bald dudes. Where are the women? Also I would personally love to see the game go even further on the historical details, add historically accurate clothing and hairstyles, not only does it look (imo) better than the current popculture Norse aesthetic, it would actually make the game look more unique since NO other Viking themed games actually use designs inspired by archaeology.This game is going to attract history enthusiasts, LEAN INTO IT.Also, please make farming an early game activity. The Norse did not persist on fishing and hunting alone. Barley was by far their biggest food source, and they dressed in linnen and wool, not leather! I would love to herd sheep for wool to make winter clothes, and grow flax to make linnen for summer clothing. Dawn of Man has a similar system and it works great.Also, please change Druids to something else. Druids were celtic. A more appropriate word would be guþi (guthi) or völva.I absolutely recommend this game, early dev as it is. I think it has enormous potential, especially if it takes steps to appeal to the audience wanting a solid citybuilder that focuses on the historical reality of the actual Norse people and not fantasy tropes. There are already tons of options if that's what people want to play. You have the chance to make something original, and the type of game people like me have wanted to play for years.

_childDocuments_.review: some say it is like Dawn of Man, but alas Not! Here you control the guys directly like Age of Empires. All things have white borders when selected or moused over. Whether moused over or selected, they look identical. Breaks immersion. Not possible to turn white borders off. Also the units have colors, like teal, and there are glowing circles under them, or some shapes etc, glowing with player color. Looks horrible, cannot be turned off.The manning of the siege machine is like how it should have been in Age of Empires, but not what I was looking for from a Viking game. Also the siege machines had like 3 centimeter range. It was completely off putting to play the tutorial.The tutorial viking ships were bugged, it took like 5 minutes for them to fight it out, even then the enemy ship probably died of collision damage, as it was swimming "sideways" towards my ship and jamming it against the rocks, somehow it was the enemy that sunk though.The woods are full of "caches" but even if you micromanage your scouts to loot them, they wont disappear, but if you hover a mouse, the message will come (at a half second delay, always, cannot be sped up from options) that it is looted already.The zooms and the map movement with ASDW keys is slow, and it has an acceleration, it starts slowly and then accelerates a little. No options to remove the acceleration or to make it quick enough. Off putting.I refunded this after 44 minutes. What I was hoping for was a better Dawn of Man where you dont control any of the people, but set goals for them. This was like Age of Empires or some tacky mobile game where you "upgrade" your huts. The military units were not the same as the magical "workers" that come from nothing to clearcut those woods. I think the makers of this game lacked vision and made it into what they wanted Age of Empires to be.Not for me, perhaps of you like Age of Empires and "no range ("viking") siege machines", and if you like to "upgrade" things, this might be for you. But not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept and great visuals, but there are issues that arose.-Multiplayer being very unstable with more than 2 people. -When you lose, or if the host loses, you can't spectate and you can't move your camera, making it very boring waiting. -There isn't a scoreboard or timeline of the previous game.-There is problems with the spawns being unbalanced with people starting with and w/o animals to hunt.But the game has great ideas,.-Taking the exploration route for traveling, using your units to fight against other players while side by side in boats.-The Zoom features in this game make it more interesting when fighting animals, raiders, or other players. Would be nice to be able to zoom out more.-Clean and smart way of managing your village, showing unmanned buildings and empty resource points with big icons makes managing the economy quick. The buildings snap to feature is quite useful while still being able to free place your buildings as you wish, giving it a ascetic option while still being efficient.-Keeping you close to home with a build perimeter can be annoying, but it prevents hard rushes and keeps it more realistic in the sense that you're vikings and not settlers. Maybe an option of being able to build a secondary settlement that way you can gain map control for strategic purpose or economic purpose.7/10, won't continue to play till bugs with multiplayer are fixed.----Edit----Please add a scoreboard in game, and spectate and statistics at the end of game! It would make dying at least worth it to see what you can improve on!

_childDocuments_.review: Hello Im Skill Incarnate and Welcome to My Games Review Series.My reviews cover indie games that i have bought, had gifted to me and have been provided by developers for review.In this episode I am checking out the new Nordic Themed Realtime Strategy Game Frozenheim. This game is the breakout title by small indie development team Paranoid Interactive who also created Kainga - Seeds of Civilization and was published by my friends at Hyperstrange, who have released several hit indie games ive previously reviewed including Empty Shell, Postal Brain Damaged and Supplice.Frozenheim is a Real Time Strategy game set in the violent age of Vikings. The player controls the survivors of a small village that was razed by a rival viking tribe. Beset by greedy bandits, savage wild animals and armies of viking pillagers you find yourself stranded in a strange new land. You will need to re-establish a new village, gather resources to expand your territory and raise your own army to keep your new home safe. Your actions will determine whether you establish a Viking Tribe to stand the test of time, or whether your people are lost to the unforgiving world of FrozenheimFrozenheim has a fast pace and unrelenting difficulty. It will challenge your strategy skills to their limit. I recommend this game to fans of Real Time Strategy Games or those who enjoy games set in the Age of VikingsPlease note: All opinions in this video are my own. _childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately I have to leave a negative review, as the game is extremely unstable and laggy on an AMD GPU. My friends that I played with that have nvidia GPU's had no issues, but the game is clearly not optimized at all for any kind of AMD GPU. (I have a 5700 XT and a beefy system, so the issue wasn't lack of hardware)The game itself is actually really nice, it is relaxing and familiar, yet does things slightly different, just enough to give it all a fresh taste. I would like to purchase this game again in the future if they can improve the FPS and stability issues on AMD GPU based systems. I'd also like to note that the game actually had a lot more depth to it than I was expecting when I went into it, which was nice. It is truly unfortunate that I was facing problems with my FPS getting worse and worse as time went on, and having to run the game on lowest settings to keep it at a playable state towards the end of the game. The FPS just kept getting lower and lower, while GPU usage was low too, so there is clearly a lack of optimization for AMD GPU's sadly.Final verdict: Buy if you have an nvidia GPU, avoid for now if you have an AMD GPU. _childDocuments_.review: Calling Frozenheim a city builder is like calling Age of Empires or Warcraft 3 a city builder - just because you plop down buildings and there are resources to get and manage. The buildable area is pretty small, so you're not building a city, but rather a tiny settlement. Initial resource deposits will deplete quickly leaving many of the buildings obsolete, forcing you into trading.Calling Frozenheim an RTS is like calling Pharaoh or Grand Ages Rome an RTS - just because you can train troops and send them to fight the enemy. The units themselves come in Company of Heroes-esque squads of 5, are bland and unremarkable, there's no "tactical" to this combat but sending one cluster blob to fight another. Some game design decisions along with the graphics and the UI feel like Frostpunk copy in a Norse setting. The only original and somewhat interesting concept Frozenheim has is ship designer - you get to pick the parts for your ships influencing the stats and the cost. Overall it feels grindy, clunky, not enough tooltips, no quality of life, there are bugs (the pathfinding ones are especially annoying). The game is shallow, barely any content, right now it doesn't qualify neither as a city bulder, nor as a management/tycoon, nor an RTS. It's just small bits of everything put together. Feels like an alpha/proof of concept rather than an Early Access title.While the game has a degree of charm to it and shows some promise, I can't recommend it based on promise alone.

_childDocuments_.review: While i'm used to Early Access games and expect some level of error to them , this was very surprising. Firstly if you enjoyed Age of Empires when it was first released, go and buy that instead because the game mechanics were a hundred times better than this.Where do i even start?-The game is hugely lacking in the tutorial information, it does not explain how to assign villagers tasks among other things which leaves you to trial and error to find out.- The animations are bad, like really bad, like Rayman on PS1 bad. Every unit has 1 animation and it sucks.-Units are trained in groups of 2 and 5 warriors. If for example you have a group of 5 and 3 die, you cant add 3 back to that group to bring it back to 5, there's no way to merge at all. This leaves you in a situation where you're walking around with 6 groups with one guy in them each which clutters the bottom of your screen with markers for no reason.-Another issue arises when one of your buildings catches on fire and you're not told you need to have a well within AOE of any and all buildings with a villager assigned to it in order to put it out.-In the first mission of the Campaign i went to the enemy village (Which wasn't even a quarter of the size of my own) with 65 warriors. I could have easily wiped out their base but instead i was forced to retreat as per the storyline. I understand i shouldn't have been able to wipe out their village but i easily could have as there was no restriction like a unit cap.- The camera is horrible, I've played a lot of City Builders and RTS games since the late 90's and this has one of the absolute worst  cameras I've witnessed. The pan with WSAD is way too fast, hills do that awkward zoom thing to the screen like in Kenshi but worse and you cant adjust the angle pan up and down. What i mean by that is you cant change the camera so you're more on level with your units.- RTS - There basically isn't any beyond select your  units and double click enemies so they attack them.- City Building is very meh, i wouldn't say its bad but its not good either, its extremely generic.- The graphics are good, not great and are basically the only thing this game has going for it, which doesn't say much in all honesty.I've got loads of games in my Steam Library  and never once have i asked for a refund until now, this game is not fun but i'm not angry, just very disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: People seem to confuse Early Access with Full Release. 90% of the complaints I see in the negative reviews are facts that are openly admitted by the developers. All you need to do is click on Early Access and you can see their post with what's currently in the game, not in the game, and what they plan to add in the future, along with the fact that they plan on developing this game further heavily depending on community feedback. That in and of itself is a great commitment that most developers don't even do.The game:-The game itself is gorgeous, full 3D camera controls with the ability to zoom in (or out) a lot, gives you a lot of control over seeing the land how you want to. The graphics on it fully zoomed in are also much better than I expected for a day 1 EA release.-You can speed up or pause time-The building area is limited as far as how much you can build, but the area itself is large enough that by the time it's full, you have a realistic looking viking settlement. If they added the ability to create multiple settlements or even small outposts, I think that would go a long way to improving anyone's feelings of being cramped. -The building itself is very straightforward with a decent amount of buildings that I would expect to make up a viking settlement. -Resource management is pretty basic, which might be the most limiting feature of the single settlement area. You are able to respawn trees at will once you've found the correct runestone for it and built a temple, but when your ore & stone expires I'm not certain if there's an easy way of obtaining more outside of buying it at the market. If they added a runestone to respawn the stone/ore it would be an easy enough fix, or add outpost creation. -The combat is definitely not the same across all units, as I said you can move the camera very close in on your units and watch the different attack animations. The developers do plan (if you read their road map you'd already know this) on enhancing combat with multiple updates and have it be greatly impacted by community feedback. There are only 5 unit types currently but each one has it's own uses. Generally I raid with a party of 1 of each unit type, per longship. -Exploration is very robust for the one map I played, 3 maps available (in skirmish). You start with a scout unit (of 2 scouts) that you use to explore the map. I'd like to see the ability to click the minimap especially while holding down shift to assign auto exploring (as this is a pretty common rts feature) but you might miss out on hidden loot or random NPCs/quests if you weren't watching them the whole time. The map itself was made up of a major continent with multiple smaller islands that I had to send my units exploring via ship. Doesn't appear to be any danger in the ocean yet(aside from enemy ships), but I'm sure that's something they'll add.-Story, I haven't tried the campaign yet, specifically because the devs (in the road map!!) have stated that they've only added the first very basic missions to it. It's something that is likely being worked on (Early Access).As other people have stated, yes it's not a fully finished game, and as a rational human I don't expect a day 1 EA title to be fully finished. Therefore I recommend the game, and for the price, it's a better purchase than most fully released games. I'm excited for how this game is further developed.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to get enough hours in to give a fair review, and I'm still on the fence to be honest. As of now, I will recommend this game, but it definitely needs some work. Some things need to be polished a little more, others need some TLC and to be expanded upon.What I know it does well:-Graphics: well-done; for the most part the game looks wicked (aside from the pathing mechanic units make when walking the terrain; that looks kind of ridiculous, especially in snow)-Economy/resources: the economy is easy to grasp and understand and the resources to maintain that economy are straightforward; nothing really revolutionary in this regard-Ambience: for the most-part the ambience in the game is well done and immersive; however, there needs to be more ambient audio. More sounds of your village being alive, especially. It's very bland in that respect-Aesthetic: the overall aesthetic of the game brings a nice Viking feel to it and helps bring some immersionWhat I Know Needs Work:-Combat: easily the silliest part of the game. It's underwhelming and lacks any feeling of accomplishment or reward. The mechanics, I have no idea about. A group of 5 archers stand as great a chance of beating a group of Axemen in close combat...almost every time. This is ridiculous. More in-depth combat needs to be introduced: units weaknesses and strengths levied against others needs to be a factor, and if it already is, some tweaking needs to be done and it needs to be outlined in-game.-Movement: while I've seen some complaints about the AI pathing, I haven't seen any issues with this personally. However, a better system for formations needs to be put in place. Trying to fiddle with the move direction mechanic to find your desired formation in the EXACT desired spot is tedious at best, and useless at worst.All-in-all, as of now I will recommend this game on the hopes that it will continue to be developed and built upon, but should it not receive some TLC in key areas, this recommendation may change. It really feels pretty lacklustre in many departments, as if the bare minimum was done to get the game out for Early Access, but the potential is there, which I'm hoping means we can expect this to change as time progresses. It has the foundation to be a wicked RTS and city-builder, alike, but as of now, it misses the mark, in my opinion. I can't shake the feeling that it's just "dry". I will continue to play, but having a wide-open day the first time playing and getting bored after 3 hours wasn't a great sign.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave a thumb down, though I don't want to say that game is tragic. It might be fun for many players, it has many interesting things inside... but there are several important reasons why I don't like it.I don't like it, but it is not that I hate it. So I will start with good things within the game:- design of buildings is nice, I really appreciate those viking-like structures, it is something that we don't see very often, right?- nature - this may sound like a secondary thing, but maps are nice to look at - flowers, grass, I totally love how things look when the snow falls (take a look at paths during winter, great!)- I like some element of town management, for example: very simple workers placement (with alt - which also allows u to instantly see what is the situation with labour in all buildings)- some other details.And that is it regarding good stuff. Now, the negatives (devs: I'm sorry, I understand that it wasn't easy to make this game, nothing personal, really):- town management is something that almost not exist - it is so basic, so simplified that instead of town management I would call this game a base builder. You don't build buildings to have small town with people living there and being happy or whatever. You build to have more resources to build army. Just like in old Command and Conquer or Age of Empires - by the way, game is really similar to AoE in many aspects, and in my perspective it is not an advantage (if I wanted to play AoE I would buy AoE)- so... maybe the military stuff is better? You train several types of units, each comes in teams (5 people typically). After you have trained enough you just select all troops and send them to attack. Yes, it is that simple. Tactics? Not really. You don't have formations, even guys with shields gain some temporal benefits from shields but they can't fight in realistic wall of shields. Moreover: you have catapults. Yes, whenever I think about Vikings I imagine them using catapults... so fun ;-P. On the other hand, if you keep in mind that all your units create just random mob not capable of using tactics... then catapults don't change that much, right?- AI is not using any tactics as well, but to make things work and to make game challenging AI units are always better. If u attack with 5 men a 3 men unit, u will win but with heavy losses. If you attack 5 men unit with your three men unit... you will MAYBE kill one of enemies. Moreover pathfinding is terrible. In some cases when you use several units and make them attack single unit they attack one at a time, no matter how many times u click, they just don't want to use advantage- and because AI is cheating we see things that were normal back in 90's - as far as I understand AI doesn't need resources at all. They just spawn units. Because why not.- last but not least: campaign. Second mission killed me. Really. I got bored, since I don't expect from strategic game missions like: go to that building, talk to this guy, reach this point, so that enemy will attack your settlement ect. I'm walking around the map, looting old carts, killing wolves and repelling randomly spawning attackers. But wait: in one of the following missions I will be capable to use catapults. Cant wait? Not really.I think that we are way beyond the point where simple point and click base building games make sense. So, sorry, but this game has nothing to make me want more of it. And it is a shame... I really wanted to play this game, but obviously expected much, much more.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks good, works bad.--------------------------------------------Pro:World - it's pretty lively, the sound effects are good, wind, noises of trees etc, on graphic side I think it's good enough, some smaller extras (like moving in bush hides you etc).Buildings - Instead of just giving a few light it up, like in most games, here you can see the caracters working in the workplaces.Feeling - Like you really are in this fantasy environmentWorking - you actually need people to move things into warehouse, so you need to think about logistics too (other thing that you put a stock in warehouse in the top of the map can be used instantly at the bottom, but hey, that much magic is fair)--------------------------------------------Con:Ohhh boy, there are too many, mostly in the main part, the control.Dumb warriors - if you click in the fog of war, but there is a mountain or other not reachable part, they stop, dont even start to move. I know, pathfinding is a hella hard thing to code, but still. You give out a chain command to move there, but if the last one is unreachable, they dont even start to move, thanks. You need actively look at your troops and move them, so can't build in the meantime (or explore while you are under attack).Troops movement - in tight places (like gates) they most of the time dont like to go through. You click to go there, they show you the indicator to move aaaaaand... the stop. I swear I sometimes heard them saying 'F you' in the distance.Fights - if you can't click on the enemies, and just click move there, they most of the time runs trough the enemy while they make minced meat from your troops. Sometimes, when they need to go through gates or others, half of the team doesn't even start to move, blocking the other half of your units. Brilliant.Unit types - You would think, logically, the different type of units are better against different enemies. Like Spearmen are good against bear, or so. Well, nope. my axemen can kill a single bear easily while most of the mean in spear unit dies. same with shield warriors vs archers, archers with precision shot decimate the shield warriors (only exception, if they use shield wall, but never seen an AI using that).Buildings - Build a palisade to keep enemies out? did you place it properly? 90% of the time they run around it on mountain feet or near the water. If you put a gatehouse next to the water 100% they can move around it.--------------------------------------------All in all, not a bad game, enjoyable too, but in my opinion only for short period of time. There are too many exploits and bugs. If you don't mind leaving the game there after 5-8 hours and never start again, then it's a funny little game.

_childDocuments_.review: Its like if you took Frostpunk, Northgard, and Age of Empires, put them in a blender, then slowly poured out a nice tall glass of viking RTS while Wardruna plays in the background.Its really fun. Slow paced, but you can tell it is meant to feel that way, especially with the ambient music playing while you gradually build up your settlement. Its kind of tranquil in a way, as long as you don't find yourself starving in the winter.Visuals are top notch for an RTS. Zooming in shows really nice details on the units and especially the buildings. Once you start to have your settlement put together, its nice to zoom in and watch it all work while people go about pulling carts or hammering away at the blacksmith.The combat is a tad clunky. Animations aren't as fluid as Age of Empires, but its still satisfying when you are rushing into battle using your axeman's rage ability as the music picks up.For $20 (or $17 right after releasing from Early Access on sale) I think its absolutely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great - a viking-themed city builder with a degree of rts built in, a crowded field filled with other, genuinely great games, but Frozenheim establishes a unique identity and an aesthetically-pleasing look.City building is complimented by having some buildings grant adjacency bonuses, meaning that your city will often look somewhat logical based on trying to stack as many bonuses as possible - homes close together, a nearby well, healing and spiritual guidance - the end result is a nice looking little settlement.Your workers aren't idiots, and will basically go about their business with the mere assignation by you of them to whatever building you want them at, and older resource gathering buildings are not rendered irrelevant simply because you ran out of local resources, most gather buildings allow you to reassign workers to gather far from the building itself.Lots of cool things to do, and only a tiny amount of annoyance - this game is a great addition to an established genre.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 9.3/10  rts/city builder game and absolutely worth the price An amazing refresher for the RTS genre as a whole, and an absolute bargain for the price. The game is still in early access and only expected to be fully released within a year or so, taking that into consideration the game as it stands now is an unpolished gem that will over time start shining.The core of the game is focused on city building (so if your one of those AOE players that loved making your base look pretty this games for you), more so than most RTS games as rushing is a bit more difficult to pull off, this suits the game well since the actual graphics in game are gorgeous to look at. You will need a GTX 1070 or above if you really want to max settings and still play on 60 fps, with something like a GTX 1050 even on a medium/low graphics in game and with lots of units don't expect anything above 50 fps. off course theirs always the option of reducing the resolution scale if you want to play at 80 fps and experience the game as if your playing it cross eyed Besides city building the game is a solid RTS game, a variety of military units (and more to come), upgrades, ships and defensive structured. So if your looking for a proper RTS game like Warcraft or Starcraft the game wont disappoint, if your looking more for a casual city builder like Frospunk, again the game wont disappoint. It is a beautiful mix between the two.Bug wise in my 9 hours of playing iv some across 1 full blown fatal error and 1 what im assuming is a sync bug since i couldn't damage any buildings in multiplayer. Dont forget this is normal for a Early Access game and to be expected, but already the game works 100% 98% of the time, during development the rest will be ironed out.Not much else to add, the combat is satisfying, the changes season are beautiful and effect both production and unit efficiency. besides running out of food a few times there isn't really much danger in winter. more work could be done to add different effects or make winter more dangerous to units outside your base without heat etc...Controls are quit clunky atm, and my only real pet peeve . Camera likes to jump around the terrain occasionally and you need to babysit your units often as the tend to get lost in there path-finding. again nothing game breaking and something that will be ironed out over time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets some things right but gets more things wrong. As a big fan of RTS games and Viking themes, this game checks boxes for me. However due to very annoying and common bugs, a lack of content, terrible unit pathing and some design choices, it is a bit of a chore to play after the first few games. The bugs in particular are really obnoxious; while playing with a friend we've both had units fall through the map, I had a ship decide to control itself after my troops disembarked which stopped well out of reach, units can get stuck on villages you try to help, units regularly stop following whatever order they were given and stop moving completely (especially with groups). Once I set up a massive palisade wall to defend my coast, only to have a full ship of enemies land on the coast INSIDE my walls, completely ignoring all the defenses I had set up and nearly winning if not for my friend's troops coming. Unit pathing is awful both on land and at sea.The city building is really good, it's fun to build settlements; however you have a very limited space to do so and the only way to upgrade this space takes a lot of resources and barely extends your settlement's territory. You can make outposts (with an even smaller radius) but there's not much point to doing so other than to get resources, which is something I've never had serious issues with thanks to the Marketplace building. Building your city is essential as your population is used both for workers and for your army, if you go too much into either you'll fail most of the time. There's a good variety of buildings, most of which are tied to resource production and gathering. There's a few upgrade buildings which provide useful bonuses, but nothing particularly game changing. This is the best part of the game by far, I tend to enjoy the first 30 Minutes to an hour building up, but then get bored finishing.The combat really needs to be fine tuned. As it is, taking the Wolf upgrade tree is pretty much required and unit variation doesn't matter much. The troops are balanced well but the clear winners are Spearmen, Berserkers and Archers. Sadly group fights tend to just bunch up into a big mosh pit against the AI, so troop composition and positioning barely matters. Against players it's a bit more engaging but for the most part it's very simplistic both mechanically and visually.Exploring the map is usually pretty fun, for the first few games. Unfortunately there's very little reason to actually bother exploring as more than half the map is usually completely empty in regards to players. There are bear and wolf caves/packs (functionally the same), settlements that give a few quests, runestones that only seem useful if you build the temple which takes up a lot of space, resource loot spots, and the very important stone and bog iron deposits. Exploring with the Scout requires constant micromanagement to prevent them from dying, which is tough to do when juggling all the buildings. I have yet to see the AI create a single outpost, and have never really felt the need to make one myself. This leaves around 60% of the map (at least the 3 and 4 player ones) with absolutely nothing going on, since players spawn in the exact same place every game. Combing the whole map for stone and iron deposits is pointless when you can just use the marketplace to get what you need.Overall I can't recommend this game in it's current state, especially for the price it's at. It has a great deal of promise and I really hope the developers will work hard to make this game as good as it can be! The city building is great but it's not enough to carry the game, I'd like to see the exploration, combat and outpost building be improved. The bugs and pathing issues are the biggest issue by far, as it is currently they make a passable EA experience tedious. If it's fixed and gets a lot more content, this game could easily be placed among CoH or AoE, however in it's current state it's too rough and the content is too scarce. I look forward to seeing what the developers do in the future, and will gladly change this review to positive once the change is merited!

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend based mostly on the game's potential. As it is, it's... kind of worth buying? It looks fantastic and the gameplay is almost there, almost.    A few serious problems for an RTS, though. Pathing is a major issue here. My units keep getting stuck on corners and in tight spaces, or they just forget that they have orders to move at all. For instance, whenever I order my units to move any real distance, they often stop half-way there. There is the issue of non-traversable terrain that when clicked on, your units simply stop moving, but that's not what I'm talking about. They will sometimes just refuse to move if you tell them to go too far. If their path takes to many turns around cliffs, etc., they will get stuck on the corners of those cliffs as well.     Unit posture is also a problem. While building up my village and seeing to resources I set my units to defensive posture around my village. Enemy archers come up and start attacking my units, my units just stand there and die... Rage, my friends.     Further more, I send veteran axemen with upgraded gear to kill a unit of enemy archers and the archers darn near slaughter my axemen? Wut? A unit of 6 axes vs a unit of 4 archers and even if I've closed the distance in good shape, my axes are guaranteed to bleed off 3-4 guys. Standing toe to toe with archers, axes should obliterate every time. Why are they getting destroyed? And that's not the only balancing issue between units.     The music here is meh. Not that the music is bad, but it is not what you're going to want to listen to while playing as vikings. I found myself looking up viking playlists on youtube to maintain a more appropriate vibe for the game. Otherwise, you'll be listening to classical folk music and wondering why you can't get your blood up for a fight.    The graphics are awesome, but need further stabilization. Lighting needs to be worked on as well. I often had trouble hunting for resources in stormy weather.    The weather system is nice, but moves too fast. Each season lasts about 2 min? Tops. Not that it really seems to matter. Winter and storms never seemed to actually hinder me. Winter doesn't freeze water, either, opening avenues to attack or be attacked, which would be a nice addition to the game. Lose the ability to use your boats, but gain a land bridge.     All in all, I did have fun and I have high hopes for its future. Please devs, keep going. There's more to be said for this game, but I feel like I've said enough. It's $17, roughly $15 when I bought it. Is it worth it? Depends on how bad you want to play this kind of game. I give it a 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing RTS games since Warcraft: Orcs and Human, and I've never been as let down with a game as I have Frozenheim. The controls and movement are a bit syrupy, however I didn't try to adjust them during my playthrough so maybe it can be improved. The camera is bad, following the terrain in the worst ways possible, especially going over mountains. I'd also like the zoom to be further out. The AI is a bit dumb, getting stuck on terrain features, getting in traffic jams on bridges, and generally requiring lots of micromanagement. Combat seems very unbalanced. You can set your units up in formation like in Total War/Battle for Middle Earth, but once the fighting starts it turns into a puppy pile. Units have aggressive/defensive stances but they don't seem to have much effect. Casualties after only one engagement are usually high, and sometimes one half-dead enemy is somehow able to wipe half my army. With no way to reinforce depleted units, you'll have lots of understrength units running around getting themselves picked off. I'm still not sure how some buildings work; do the workers assigned to the Great Hall build, or move resources, or both? What's the point of building a warehouse in the first place? Hopefully these questions will be answered in the future. But worst of all, in its current state the campaign is only two levels long. I'd love to be able to recommend this game one day, but as of today, I say hold off on it. Play Northgard instead

_childDocuments_.review: There's the bones of a solid game here, what's there is fun and engaging, but it's just too little, too small in scope rn to recommend at full price. After 11 hours playing, and a lot of that spent with tinkering and experimenting, I just had the disappointing realization that I've seen everything this game has to offer. There's nothing new under the sun, here.  You can build a modest sized village, but beyond that it's just repetition and scaling up the same build over and over. Resource management is rather shallow and you'll only ever have a few industries in your town, with no real need to expand them beyond basic levels of production. The tech tree, while having some cool techs and buffs, is small, and can be fully queued up and upgraded in one go once you get your production off the ground, meaning there's a tendency to go from no tech to full tech pretty quickly. The same thing for weapons upgrades. But once you're fully teched there's not really anything different to do, your builds don't change and nothing particularly game changing is unlocked, you mainly just get buffed. Nice and all, but you quickly begin to realize that each game is just kind of repeating the same basic steps, and those steps don't take very long to complete, so the entire gameplay loop feels almost condensed or "abridged" in some sense. I guess this is an issue of both the amount of content, and just the overall pacing of how that content is spread out. Some things are indeed gated in game, so there is an attempt at creating a sense of progression, but the reality is it's just so easy to unlock everything relatively quickly that instead of an organic and engaging sense of progression it feels more like "warping" through stages of the game like so: you get your production set up all at once, your housing/population center all at once, you build your army all at once, you max your tech all at once, you scour the map, game over you win.  The AI also leaves a lot to be desired. On harder difficulties the AI will launch seaborne attacks and be more aggressive generally. This can pose a challenge in the early game if the AI is more established than you, but it's mostly easily dealt with with a couple towers and some town militia. It's usually easy to put off building your military until later in the game because of this, meaning you can play quite greedily and get your economy going strong even against very hard AI. Once your economy is humming, it's quite simple to sweep the map. The AI will mount only a token defense, and won't use any kinds of formations or tactics but will charge piecemeal against a line of Huscarls or Shield-Bearers with archer support. Once their army is defeated they'll spam militia which are easily dealt with and your army can rapidly destroy the AI town with impunity. True to form, the most threatening thing you will probably face is enemy towers, but they can also be overwhelmed quite quickly. All in all, it's probably unfair for me to say I've seen "everything" in 11 hours. There are indeed other game modes I can try out, and more campaign for me to do. But I do feel like I've seen the entire gameplay loop from start to finish several times over already, and it's hard to get too excited about just repeating this same overall strategy over and over again when it can be done so quickly and easily. These are just my impressions, and I don't mean to be overly negative. I don't regret my purchase, I got it on sale myself and have had fun with it, I just wish there was a lot more fun to be had out of this game right now. With active development and another year or two this game could turn into something much more satisfying, so I will stay tuned, but for now, that's my advice for prospective buyers as well. Don't write this game off, it's got potential and what's there is good, but just stay tuned and wait for more, it's still got a ways to go.

_childDocuments_.review: So having now completed the "Campaign" I can see just how early access this title is; unquestionably Frozenheim has Huge Potential, but I cannot review on speculation alone.Instead I will review what is available today (28/05/2021).There is a MP and skirmish mode that really do not interest me, but for now at least, this is probably where the majority of gameplay would come from as the campaign seems so short (Unless I have somehow missed a big section of the campaign?).o The Campaign doesn't really exist yet & what is called the "Campaign" should be renamed as Tutorial & Mission 1; with another tab saying Campaign coming soon, because they are both very short and very simple (even if it is your first time of playing).o Combat is far from deep ATM, requires much deeper controls and strategic balancing (right now it feels like an eye for an eye - superior numbers always win) and the audio is seriously lacking.o Audio overall needs much more attention; the music is incredible however.o Camera movement is often sharp and uncontrollable, especially when the game snaps to an event.o Having to double click on units a LOT & Ctrl + 1 doesn't seem to work sometimes?MASSIVE POTENTIAL and if you want to invest in the game for what you hope it will be in the end then Great!  That is what EA is designed for, but I always feel some sort of reward or discount should be applied for EA contributors as an incentive.I like the game a lot, it is beautiful but lacks depth & I shall def. be keeping an eye on development.  I do RECOMMEND today based on what what it currently offers combined with what I think and genuinely hope the game could eventually become....but YOU Must decide if the footage I have shown you and the review left here is enough to convince you that the game has a future.Thank you.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Without ANY prior knowledge of the game (intentional to highlight issues) I am overall mostly impressed, but certainly there are some areas in need of further attention.  As an EA game it shows great promise & a decent RTS Viking saga is a most welcome addition to my Library.o Graphically the environment it is breathtaking, the best looking RTS I can recall having ever played.o Again Graphically the buildings are incredible!o I love how paths are formed when buildings are being used.o Very reasonable price.o Units of men appear to be the identical same character, this I hope will change in time.o Units when moving are silent, no clanking, talking or general immersion audio yet exists.o Units in combat; again the audio is lacklustre, lot's more needed here and the battle cries are very weak.o UI/Mouse seemed to sometimes cause issues.o Fires start too quickly and too often, nor do they spread.  Would like to see more realistic.o Seasons appear to happen a little too quickly? Be nice if the pace was a little slower perhaps.o Tutorial lacks a bit of guidance (regarding gathering of resources especially).  Would like a little more help here.o Cutscenes for epic moments (gatekeeper & double-cross).

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend to RTS fans, interesting and engaging campaigns with a distinctly vikings atmosphere, which can be strongly felt at every step from the character models and buildings design to the storyline. Sometimes the game is quite challenging in terms of difficulty level, but it's manageable (a plus for me). The city builder elements also add an interesting flavour to the gameplay, the variety of resources and buildings means that the game is not too simple and requires moments to work out the right strategy to build a settlement. However, this is a big plus, at least for me - it makes the game enjoyable and at the perfectly balanced difficulty level.Also, a major positive is the developers' support of the game - quite regular updates, new content added and bug fixes, what more can you ask for. I recently returned to the game having previously played the version from before a couple of updates and you can really see the progress. Looking at the direction the game is taking, I will definitely keep following its development.There's something for everyone in this game, whether you're a fan of RTS, city builders or the atmosphere of Vikings and Scandinavia from the old times - I definitely recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this knowing full well it was promoted by the publisher in a state where everything was merely promises. At it's best, it's a very well executed tech demo. Limited glitches etc. At it's worst, it's a shadow of a much deeper and more meaningful game. I suspect the game was made with a very specific vertical slice in mind to get it to market and money. There is nothing deeper than what you see on the surface. The progression is incredibly limited, Survival mode is completely linear (enemy waves attacking from the same place over and over in a scaler fashion), No attempts to solve navmeshing issues. Limited units with no differentiating fighting, Generic discoverable settlement always return the same thing as loot. It's as if someone implemented all the cool features but only in their most basic form then polished the visuals and put it on the market. I support indies so I won't refund but this game is unlikely to get any deeper so I can't recommend it. I have put my 3-4 hours in.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: This is not a finished game, it's an early access do not buy this game or take my recomendation for valid if you are not ok with an unfinished experience.With that out of the way, what is Frozenheim?This game is an RTS game at it's core, you have your base building, you have your army, you lose if your main building is destroyed, you win if you destroy the enemy's. BASE BUILDINGYou have your main building, which generates a circle of influence around it. Within this circle you are able to place buildings for housing, resource gathering, resource processing, combat units production, walls and watchtowers. You cannot build outside this circle, and you cannot expand it either. Sounds bad? Yes. Is it? Not really, it's big enough for all the buildings you will need and it makes the camp look somewhat realistic, the downside is that it doesn't allow for a lot of creative or strategic building other than optimizing housing bonuses. The game forces you to bunch the houses together around some buildings for happiness bonuses which result in more people per house. Making your base the first couple of times it's fun, but on the long run I fear it will be something that will feel on rails and always pretty much the same.COMBATNowhere near the levels of the top RTS competitors, combat here is super simple. It's squad based, but warriors don't engage like on a typical squad based game where each will take on an enemy until numbers dwindle in someone's favor, they will all bunch up together making a biomass of axes, shields, and spears that just isn't right. Archers have friendly fire and they are not very smart about it, I found them useful only to shoot at buildings or other archers while the melee engage. Units have several stances for default, defensive and aggressive combat which only seem to affect their automatic engagement distance. You can also build boats to transport your units, but at the moment I found it's just more convenient to kill invaders and use their ships as all of them seem to randomly catch fire and be destroyed for no reason when not in use. That's pretty much it from me, it was a fun little game, it was crazy cheap and the 6 hours I played are already paid off for me. I reckon I will pour another 6 to 12 hours into it and move on..... unless they come with nice some surprises along the way to release date. Best wishes for the developers, the game looks great and it's fun to play, it just needs more complexity to really stand out.

_childDocuments_.review: I (like another reviewer) saw a particularly negative review early on and decided not to purchase this game on release. In the mean time it went on sale for 10% off, which made me rethink my initial hesitancy. That review was very harsh for an early access title, and (at least in some cases) factually inaccurate. That being said, it didn't entirely miss the mark. This is not a great game. Yet. It definitely has some potential, it's quite pretty, and the idea is there, but it needs some love as it stands (6/25/2021) which makes sense - it's very early in its early access period.Yeah this is not a city builder, sorry devs. At least not in the traditional understanding of that genre (thinking Banished, Foundation, etc). There is next to no progression in city development, very little struggle to balance competing needs (besides your army), and unlike every other city builder I've ever played there's a way to win (by destroying your enemy). I would write more, but like I said, it's just not a city builder. Yep. This is it. This is absolutely an RTS, and while it's  right now, I really like where this is headed. The strategy is reminiscent of some of the early RTS giants like Age of Empires or Starcraft, but with enough changes to make it stand firmly on its own. You're definitely building to make an army (come on, they're vikings, what else would they be doing, ), but the way fighting works is  different (back to that in a moment). Economy is handled at a more macro level, and interestingly seems to be very back burner in comparison to the other titles I've mentioned. It is not hard to make a relatively balanced economy that overproduces demand (at least in the games I've played so far, which have been against AI). Not much to say on this topic, I think the devs may want to rethink their economy in a major way if they want a challenging game in the future.Fighting is where the devs really seem to have placed their focus, and it's very different to most titles I've played. If anything, it's as if someone took Age of Empires unit production and dropped the Total War series' control mechanisms into it. It's very bare bones at the moment, but if they continue down the route they're on, it could be very, very cool. Right now there's only infantry and some ships, but I think there's more to come here.This is early. Very early. But the Total War style combat has some room to really shine with some more development. The bugs are all over the place, especially with pathfinding (something they've already addressed even before I played my first game, I shudder to think about what that must have been like -bugfix). The campaign is (to be a maybe a little harsh) borderline incoherent and only two episodes long. That's okay, there's totally time to build it out. AI is stupid, unless I've just been accidentally playing on super easy mode (very possible). The possibility for tactical play is there - like a line of infantry set to defense with a back line of archers, all placed in in a choke point. It does tend to fall apart a bit though in practice, and most of my encounters have devolved into mobs of formationless units charging the enemy. Hiding in ambush is a possibility that looks very cool, but I've been so far unable to actually accomplish.My best advice: try it. If you've ever wanted a game that blends Age of Empires with Total War (me jumping up and down raising my hand) this looks like it might be that. Eventually.

name: The Falconeer
detailed_description: Designed for Controller and Flightstick This game was designed as a ' Stick Flyer ', various keyboard and mouse options exist and might require some experimentation to get right. The FREE VR update only supports controller and flight stick , no wands, knuckles or Quest controllers. If you have a controller or flightstick, in general, it's recommended to use that. About the Game Soar through the skies aboard a majestic warbird, explore a stunning oceanic world and engage in epic aerial dogfights, in this BAFTA nominated air combat game from solo developer, Tomas Sala. You take on the role of Falconeer, a powerful airborne warrior traversing a vast oceanic world torn apart by generations of poisonous decisions and dissent. Throughout multiple campaigns, you will experience life from many different perspectives and loyalties as you embark on a journey of discovery, and solve the mystery of the Ursee, its people and history. Progress through perilous missions and side quests, wielding your lightning caster to protect ships against pirates, kraken and other threats. Dive through the deep ocean depths, soar above the clouds to do battle with giant crab cities or engage in furious dogfights against the mysterious Mancer Order that controls and regulates technology. TAKE TO THE SKIES Experience the free-flying escapism of flying a giant warbird across a stunning open world. EXPLORE AN INCREDIBLE UNIVERSE Discover a vast oceanic world filled with lost myths and breathtaking landscapes. FRENETIC AERIAL COMBAT Soar above the clouds and engage in spectacular aerial dogfights. RIVAL FACTIONS Join and support your faction, taking on missions that may change the fate of your comrades as well as your own. MULTIPLE CAMPAIGNS Experience life as a Falconeer from many different perspectives. UPGRADE YOUR MOUNT Survive and earn splinters to improve your gear and mount. FULLY VOICED An incredible voice cast brings to life the world within the Falconeer. SOUNDS OF THE URSEE Immerse yourself in the world of The Falconeer with an award-winning soundtrack. TOMAS SALA The Falconeer is the sole vision of maverick independent developer, Tomas Sala. 3D VR The Falconeer in VR expands the boundaries of the Great Ursee offering fully immersive views of the oceanic world.

_childDocuments_.review: After my original review (below), I received a response from the developer with a few pointers and suggestions for playing The Falconeer. Out of respect and appreciation for the effort made to reply to me, and as I have seen, many others, I felt I should give the game another chance, taking into account what had been said. It turned out to be worth it too!I spent quite a bit of time initially tweaking and fine-tuning the settings and controls. This time I stuck to what I know. I ignored the recommendation for a controller and went with the mouse and keyboard. There were more built-in control options than I had realised, including a few different options for mouse and keyboard. After taking the suggestion from the dev, I set the controls to “mouse control and aim”. I also altered a several of the key-binds, played around the sensitivity and changed the difficulty to easy. With there being such varied choices, it would probably be useful to force players to choose their preference upon starting the game/prologue. While I still wasn’t particularly comfortable with the controls, they were much better than what I had experienced previously, and after a couple more hours of playing, it began to feel more natural.I also took the advice of buying speed and agility mutagens at the start of chapter 1, instead of the better weapon that I previously went for. There was a definite improvement when it came to flying, both in and out of combat! The initial battles and missions were still more difficult than taking over a fort, so I think it could still benefit from some adjustments to balance that out, but the game was certainly more enjoyable this time around. As the game progressed, I levelled up, and bought better mutagens and birds, there was a huge difference, and battles became much more active and fun, although they started to become too easy on the easy difficulty compared to the initial battles, but I chalk that up to me having gotten used to the controls and enemy movements by that point.Again, I went with the advice given and mainly focussed on the story missions. This generally goes against my nature as I like to explore and experience side missions from the start, but I went back to those later in the game instead. The story turned out to be pretty great and worthwhile! I explored and discovered all locations, including completing the races. The races were both fun and infuriating (my fault).While my experience was greatly improved by heeding the advice of the developer, that’s not something that should be required. The game would benefit from making players more aware of certain aspects, perhaps by forcing them to choose their preferred difficulty and controls upon starting the game/prologue and including the upgrade system in the tutorial. I was ready to put The Falconeer back on the shelf due to how painfully slow it was, and from what I’ve seen, it’s been an issue for others too, so addressing it would likely help retain some players and allow them to experience the rest of the game, where it actually blossoms into something pretty great.With these points in mind, and having enjoyed this playthrough after heeding the advice of the developer, I’ve altered my rating/recommendation. I really enjoyed the game once I got into it, and I truly hope changes are made to make certain aspects clearer and the start of the first chapter more bearable for users. I almost missed out on, what turned out to be, a decent game because of that, and I’d hate to think others are too!The Falconeer looks like a beautiful, interesting and fun game from videos and images on Steam. The world looked open and rather stunning, the flying looked graceful both in and out of battle, and the battles looked like great aerial combat fun! Unfortunately, once I had played a little, I realised this is one of those games that looks better than it actually is.First of all, it says on Steam that a “Microsoft Xbox Controller for Windows® (or equivalent) is recommended”. This is echoed in a brief message when opening the game. What that actually means is you need a controller. I found The Falconeer unplayable with a mouse and keyboard. That was fine though. I would have changed to a controller anyway simply because it’s what the developers recommend for the best experience.I played through the prologue/tutorial first, to learn the basics. I wouldn’t say the controls or instructions were hugely intuitive, but they weren’t terrible either. After some practice, I felt I was getting the hang of things. Unfortunately, I had to repeat various parts of the tutorial over and over because if you do something wrong and fail, you start from the very beginning, rather than before the stage you failed on. This became pretty boring, but at least it meant I started the rest of the game feeling more capable. Not that the feeling lasted very long.You get to select between characters to play as, although I don’t really know if it has much impact on anything. The selection menus didn’t provide a great deal of information. Once in the game, the options aren’t much clearer either. Not a big deal though. I’m a little tired of hand-holding in games anyway and I quite enjoy finding things out for myself. I soon found the shop in the starting location and did a couple of side-quests/missions before going with what I imagine was the main quest.The world is really beautiful, I can’t deny that. It’s a shame the flight speed, at least to begin with, is painfully slow. Most of my time was spent flying over the ocean with little to do. I found myself bored and zoning out, not realising the wind had blown me off course, leaving me flying in the wrong direction and resulting in more boring flight time to get back on course. There are occasional storms, wind pockets and wind streams that help make things a little more interesting, but not enough to make it fun or appealing. Even with the missions, there’s just too much time spent flying over an empty world.I did a fair amount of exploring and a few side-quests, dying multiple times on even the most basic of tasks. I would generally put this down to me being a terrible gamer, but then I went and took over a base for the Imperium with ease, and I don’t imagine taking over a base should be easier than taking down one pirate. It makes me feel like there’s a lot of balancing to be done for the game to feel and flow better than it currently does. The combat feels somewhat similar to that of War Thunder’s aerial combat, but nowhere near as fun, action-packed, or balanced. Now I’ve seen both birds and planes fly, and while you can do some impressive manoeuvres in planes, I don’t think I’ve ever thought of a plane being more agile or manoeuvrable than a bird, but that’s what I see when I compare The Falconeer to War Thunder. Even if I wasn’t making a comparison, the combat in The Falconeer still seems too limited and imbalanced. Flying a warbird should be much more free and fun than it is.I would generally play a large portion of a game, or ideally complete it, prior to reviewing it, but I can’t see me playing The Falconeer again unless there are some big changes to the game. It may be that it improves later in the game, but I couldn’t put myself through the pain and boredom to make it that far. It’s a stunning world with great potential, but as it stands, I feel it should be in early access at best and with a smaller price tag. Considering it was mainly one person who created The Falconeer (as far as I’m aware), it’s a really great piece of work, but I can’t recommend it as a game.

_childDocuments_.review: You can view my initial impressions review & gameplay here: Yes, the dev brought VR support to this game as a free update. It's also currently on a 60% off sale. So it's an easy recommend for me. However, there's a couple of things you do need to know about the VR experience.First and foremost, this game isn't for everyone. It's an arcade aerial combat game that is mission system based. Secondly, and almost as important, motion controllers are NOT supported. Gamepad is recommended. I used an Xbox One gamepad and found it worked great.This is a VR port of a non-VR game, so don't expect a roomscale experience. It's basically the same game, with only a few minor adjustments for VR. This VR experience is about the 360 3D eye candy. You get a nice sense of flight in VR. Flight is actually pretty relaxing for the most part outside of combat with beautiful vistas. The skies & ocean are beautiful. This is a very nice art style for VR.I haven't played the game for long, it says for 3 hours, but the problem is that I played about half in non-VR and it's two different save files. The only big difference I noticed was the UI / menus were tailored for VR. Other than that it's basically the same experience from non-VR, except with the 360 3D eye candy.

_childDocuments_.review: ***First thoughts***If you're being charitable this game has: interesting amateur voice-acting, pleasantly sedate flying, combat which accurately represents turning towards the reticule that precisely precedes an enemy and shooting (at it), and the QoL addition of holding a button to warp near to home at the end of a mission.If you're being less charitable this game has: voice acting that is bad enough that turning down voice volume is the only way to cope, flying so slow that it's a chore, combat which is uninspired and a QoL addition which shows that the devs understand that the act of flying is not by itself fun to do... when it's a game about riding giant birds.[Edit: and sometimes the game realises that flying from one checkpoint to the next is tedious so it very subtly slides a 'hold A to go forward' message -- I'm paraphrasing there, but that's the gist of the text -- as an apology. Quick thought: would it not be better to make the flying enjoyable so that I want to do it? And how about a general 'hold A to play the game for me' prompt for when the game senses I might be bored?]***Second thoughts***Then one of your early missions is to carry a jar, hide in the valley carved into the very sea itself, and wait for the pirates to be destroyed. Then the plot advances based on an island no longer being leased to... whoever it is who has it, it's all silly fantasy names and I'm not bothered. Whether or not this is 'gritty and realistic' or 'quite dull' is up to you.I do try to appreciate that this is almost entirely the work of one person. If I were reviewing this for a large publication I would feel very much compelled to accentuate the positive to support this project. There really is something here to enjoy -- I don't hate it. But, speaking as a faceless Steam reviewer who will not impact sales of the game greatly, or so I believe -- there really are issues which downgrade this experience enough for me to, sadly, give it the thumbs down.***Third thoughts*** what if this game had more interesting mechanics? Perhaps you can shoot where you look, not just straight ahead, giving the player more to do. What if height played a part, so struggling for the aerial advantage (with some more thought to flying than up = lose energy, down = gain energy, energy = go very marginally faster) helped in fights? What if the game were asymmetrical in the sense that enemy birds just used their talons (and their height advantage to attack you), and you were special and one of the only birdy knights with a gun? This could set up much larger battles as you would have an advantage against 1, 2 or 3 enemies, but it would get very tense with a larger number. You'd have to be thinking about attacking ground and sea targets while also dealing with birds.Whereas what we have now is: fly, shoot, go past, turn around, fly, shoot. You know, like we've been doing since the 80s. And, with that, I'm considering uninstalling the game as, after 100 minutes, I've already seen everything it seems to have to give at least three times. In that sense I agree with these more considered reviews:WindowsCentral: "With The Falconeer being close to a dozen hours, it's very tragic that the back half feels more like more of a chore than a game."Forbes: "And yet, you might come away from The Falconeer feeling very little. Missions can be repetitive; long flights are often boring, and sometimes have no real consequence; dogfights often feel like a game of luck, and are an inevitability of most journeys; and you yearn for structure, undermined by the illusion of open-world mechanics."GamingBolt: "lack of checkpoints in missions means that you end up repeating a lot of the missions very often; mission design can get repetitive."The Guardian: "Too much time is spent journeying through empty space, and there are sparse additional distractions beyond the missions. For a place so rich in folkloric detail, it’s lacking in things to do."PCGamer: "Difficulty throughout the story is all over the place, with no smooth gradient."The Sixth Axis: "The Falconeer feels like a boring game of tag rather than an intense aerial dogfight. There’s a chance that I simply came into this expecting something different from the combat, but even as I grew to adjust to the way my bird moved and how I could attack, it never felt all that satisfying to down an enemy."And with Gaming Age: "The controls are kind of wonky — as enjoyable as it is to soar, the birds here aren’t exactly the most agile things in the world, so you spend a lot of time banking around and coming in for a new pass, and doing that over and over again until you finally shoot down all your enemies."***Will I give it another chance?***Maybe I'll stick around to see what a boss looks like, although I can't but help think that it's going to be circle around + shooting + choppy seas + lightning. Again.***I gave it another chance!***I got to a boss! I think! The chapter ended after it appeared? Is that right? I'm a bit concerned that, currently, only 7.0% of players have completed the Dunkle chapter (Chapter One).And then Chapter Two starts with an escort mission. I am disappointed.***Why this review is now finished***No more updates because I've removed this from my account. I'm overwhelmingly sure there's nothing left to experience. To sum up the reviews I've posted above: there doesn't feel like much to do, and you're unlikely to find all that there is to do very fun. When you're a bird pilot with a gun, and neither the flying nor the shooting feel all that great, why would you feel compelled to play this?

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting Panzer Dragoon, but this is halfway to Privateer.  It's a single flat open world that you can BASICALLY go anywhere in, although if you land during a mission you generally lose the mission.  You buy different gear from outposts, but you can only do that if you've got a trading permit, which you earn doing missions, or buying elsewhere.  You can't do trade runs, though.  If you accidentally kill a friendly, BAM, you're a pirate, and there's a token pirate mission chain and some pirate-only gear.  If you just play the missions in the default order, you will discover most of the world automatically.The worldbuilding is great and gives the same feeling of "this is a totally alien world with alien rules" that the first Dune novel gave.  The scenery and the music reinforce this.  The voice acting is "lowest-bidder" quality, except maybe for the Brixton guy at Duncle outpost.  If the VAs had displayed some passion in their acting, it would really have elevated things.The class/bird system is a bit weird.  Each new chapter, your money, experience, and weapons carry over -- but your bird is reset (including gear "in" the bird, but not "on" the bird).  This kinda makes sense narratively, but feels weirdly arbitrary gameplay-wise.The actual combat is somewhere between adequate and good.  I did barrel rolls accidentally WAY too often.  This made me give up on the time-trial "race" tracks (which were poorly explained).  Some way to Imelmann would be nice.  The Pugachev and stoop manouvres work well.  The XP(?) orbs on kills often spawn too far from the player, so I have to "chase" downed birds to catch them.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Ace Combat, Project Sylpheed and other flight-sim arcade games, the moment I saw this my mind went "Oh look, it's a Birb Ace Combat". Since it was free on Epic Games, I had to try it and... Got so hooked I bought the Warrior Edition on Steam.The Falconeer is a simple game: You are a giant falcon rider (you can also mount a kind of wyvern with the Edge of the World and The Hunter DLCs) flying missions for one of the three main factions: The Civillian Freehouses, The Northern Imperium and the Mancer Order. For that you'll be able to equip your bird with different weapons, ammo, magical items, mutagens to increase its stats and even buy new birds after beating certain challenges.I'll summarize its pros and cons, but there is a more in-depth reviews afterwardsPROS:-Beautiful world map with a very unique artstyle;-You can fly giant birds into air battles-Awesome soundtrack-Intense dogfighting-Decent amount of weapons and upgrades to combine and match your playstyle-Interesting story with the multiple factions and their motivationsCONS:-The world map feels like it could have used more complex design like cave systems, archways and buildings to use as cover and set up ambushes-Controls can feel a bit janky at times-Little variety of warbirds to choose from (only falcons and two types of dragon-like creatures which are DLC-only)-Some missions have a low threat level but the few enemies carry much stronger weapons (like the Freebooters manta rays)-Story ends leaving some questions unansweredGameplay is a mix of Star Fox 64 with open world mechanics, having a bit of RPG in the mix with a level system that increase the bird's stats as the player levels up. This can be achieved by taking on missions in settlements as you fly around the world, which will also yield money (called splinters). You can use the money to buy a series of gear and upgrades and even new birds. The thing here is that the game lacks variety of creatures to choose from. The wyverns are DLC-only and they're starter beasts, meaning they can be easily outclassed by the birds you can buy (especially the Sark-Spotter and the Ravenkin), while Mancers will have the weavers (another kind of wyvern) and freebooters will have the razorbeetles and the manta rays.Speaking of creatures you can send back to the Ursee along with their riders in a ball of fire, combat is something that can go from a simple one-on-one dogfight to massive air battles with a large number of units fighting at the same time. While controls are simple in comparison to a game like Ace Combat or Project Wingman, this doesn't mean it's simple or boring. When dogfighting, there can be a lot going on around you, so you'd better take care of one target quickly and move on to the next. Managing your stamina is paramount since the higher it is, the quicker your bird regens health. Trading altitude for stamina is a smart move. Problem is when there are lots of things flying and you collide with one of them. Your stamina is instantly depleted and that can be deadly. Your bird also takes a while to respond again, which can give your enemies a few free shots. Not only that, but the speed up button is the same as the roll button (and yes, you can DO THE BARREL ROLL like in Star Fox). You have to wait almost two seconds before pushing the stick to turn while accelerating, otherwise you'll roll and lose a lot of speed, not to mention you'll make sharp turns. In combat this can get you in a really bad position.Overall, it's a really fun game with a lot of potential. Made by a single person and yet achieving this much? The whole idea of playing a open-world, dogfighting RPG-like game was completely new to me and turns out to be one of my favorite games finished this year. Definetely needs a sequel with more warbirds, weapons, locations to explore, new factions... The sky is the limit.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write serious reviews, but I feel this game deserves one. It's a game about flying where you only indirectly control your craft, which happens to be a really cool giant falcon. Or it can be a pterosaur or a dragon.You're armed with various kinds of laser-like weapons and will dogfight against other flying opponents, ships, flying ships, giant things hard to categorize, and even flying fortresses. You will learn to line your shots while  managing your bird's energy and health, and you will feel really badass doing so. You, as in the person in relative control of the flying beast, are expandable. You will pick a new character at every new chapter, which you can, oddly, play in any order. Don't fret, everything important that you unlocked at any time stays unlocked (birds, locations, missions, upgrades, etc.), so you can restart a chapter with a new class at any point without losing any progression. It seems a bit weird at first glance, when every other game has convoluted unlock trees and grind, but this freedom is actually very enjoyable. The scenario is pretty elaborate, and more than serviceable, with a complex lore about factions and houses waging wars, forging alliances and betraying each other in an enigmatic world full of ancient secrets. It should be noted that EVERY line in the game gets voice acting, which is even pretty good !! My favorite until now is a drunk character that is pretty funny, as in an obvious imitation of someone grossly drunk.The side missions are pretty forgetable (mostly combat or escort missions) but they have the merit to exist as additionnal content. The game world also benefits from some escort mission that are diegetically integrated into it in the form of ships that will ask for assistance or mention that the waters are dangerous, and in general the world feels alive, with ships crossing trade routes, odd pirate encounters, and hostile factions, depending of the chapter.  However the game succesfully avoids the "theme park effect" that some open world games have by offering vast expanses of oceans to cross. it has in general a sort of eerie feel to it, especially in some areas like  which I found completely by chance and was a pretty amazing moment. It is somewhat "simple" on the technical side (low poly, limited texturing) but every piece fits together with the others really well, to create a beautiful world that feels a bit out of time, or rather "after the times" : it feels that civilisations have already ran their best course, and all is left is an endless ocean of lost knowledge.  From what we can gather from npc dialogue their life is hard, and conditions dire for most, which I feel is also conveyed through the somber tones of the cities and the sea. In general the color palette is beautitul, with surprisingly superb combinations of colors for the ocean (deep purple, cyan blue). YMMV, my screen has weird color balancing. If I'm not mistaken this game comes from a very small dev team, which can explain the quirkiness of the game sometimes. I feel that also contributes to its odd charm though, and it should be noted that performance is incredible (some AAA should take note) and is perfectly stable. I'm really interested to see this studio's next projects.
