_childDocuments_.review: Starting a new game will have you first choose a character. There are three options available to you, Aivar the Warrior, Katherine a Mage and Elisa a Paladin, I decided to play as Aivar, leader of the famous Hounds of War. There is also some background information on each of the characters to help you choose which one to choose. Each of the characters has their own talents and play style which can have an effect on how the game will unfold. In the Kingdom of Nostria, It's the Year 320 in the Age of prosperity, high in the cold Albian Highlands is Fort Crucis. You’re getting your early morning wakeup call from the guards in the fort's dungeons. You’ve been summoned by Warden Valbert and are to be escorted by the guards to his office. On the way the guard, Bastian chats abouts things that have changed over the last six months you’ve been incarcerated. There’s a rumour the kings on his last legs and that Montier and the Prince can’t agree on how to divide the power. Pestilence has struck Monpatris, the dead are arising from their graves all over Crown Lands. Although Bastian seems to think that Warden Valbert has good news for you. After collecting your belongings, you go and see Valbert who explains that he received a letter from Prince Adrian with orders to release you and send you to Marcella. The warden is to provide you with a horse, allocate you some guards, Quartermaster Aestan will supply you with a weapon. After making your way around the fort collecting your weapon, guards and even some fighting dogs, you head off on the road to Marcella.  Travelling the roads around the kingdom will have you visiting places, meeting characters and you will have enemies which you will have to combat. Before you enter combat, you are able to see some details on yours and the enemy’s units and their hero if they have one. Selecting a unit will give you some basic information on the size of the Unit, Weapon Damage and Armour. Selecting a unit and pressing “Y" will give you some more detailed information such as Critical Hit, Initiative, Leadership, Speed, Health, Rank, Skills and Morale Type.  After you’ve done, you can select to start the combat. This will open the battle screen, here you can see where abouts the enemy is and where your units are currently. You can place your units into positions which you feel is better or you can leave them where they stand before for starting, once you have decided your units positions you can start the battle. To move you select your unit and then move it a number of hexes depending on the unit and the number of moves it’s able to make. Moving to an adjacent hex to an enemy will allow you to perform a melee attack. However, any surviving unit members will be counterattacked, a unit can counterattack once per turn. Units also have Passive and Active Skills depending on the type of unit. As you’re the hero you also have the use of a Book of Magic, you can use this once per round.  Upon your victory in defeating all enemies you will be rewarded with some experience points, gold and may be some items such as mana, gems, magic scrolls. As well as your character levelling up, each of your units will increase in rank as they are victorious. You can heal any units which have taken damage in battle although if a unit loses all of its members, then that unit is dead and unavailable anymore.  As you travel you have a trusty steed which you can whistle and he’ll come running so that you can ride him throughout the kingdom when your “plates of meat” get tired. You will come across places where you will have to solve a puzzle in order to proceed. You meet new characters, some of which you can buy and sell to. Scattered around the place are hidden caches, barrel and chests which will contain some items, gold etcetera. These items can be sold to buy new weapons, armour and equipment.  The gold you collect can also be used to buy new units to replace those who have been killed. You are able to buy and create an army and have them in reserve, so that you can swap units in and out as you please. Not all units play well with each other, all unit types fall in to one of four Ideal categories, Power, Anarchy, Order and Finesse. These are the moral choices that you’ll make as your character grows. Order is the opposite of Anarchy, while Power is the opposite of Finesse. Some of the quests you have to complete can be completed in two different ways. This will decide your morals and which Talents you can unlock as your character progresses. Having units in your combat squad with different Ideals can have an effect on the squad. You could have four Order units which would give you a positive bonus, however adding an+ Anarchy unit will change the bonus and the moral of the squad. So, you will have to decide which units to use and which will work the best in your current situation. Near some places you can find some Altars, you can use these altars to fast travel to other altars that you have previously visited. This will allow you to go back and forth to collect certain units or something else which you cannot get from traders elsewhere. In the settings you’ll find options for Game – Subtitles (On/Off), Show Tutorial Tips (On/Off), Dynamic Battle Camera (On/Off), Font Size (Small, Medium, Large and Very Large), Subtitles and UI Language (English, Russian, French, German, Italian, Korean, Polish, Chinese, Spanish, Japanese and Czech) and Voiceover Language (English and Russian). Video - Brightness, Resolution, Display Mode, Resolution Scale, V-Sync, Anti-Aliasing, Texture Quality, Effects Quality, Shadow Quality, Post-Processing, Foliage Quality and Shader Quality. Sound - Master, Music, Sound Effects and Speech Volume Sliders. Controls - Invert Mouse X and Y Axis, Mouse Sensitivity (World), Camera Movement and Rotation Speed (Battle). Keyboard Shortcuts. Controller Settings. So far, I’ve enjoyed playing King’s Bounty II, I’ve only played as Aivar so far. The graphics are good, they aren‘t groundbreaking but good enough, running on Ultra I’ve had no problems so far. My only little gripe is that I’d like to run a little bit faster, especially in towns when your trusty steed can only walk. Positives  + Decent graphics+ Multiple characters and stories + Decision making + Steam cloud + Has achievements + Full controller support Negatives  - I found running a little too slow    -  No cards currently Raise an army, fight against formidable enemies over diverse terrain, unlock secrets, explore the vast world of Antara with multiple characters in the turn-based RPG game, King’s Bounty II 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Here are a few things I liked and disliked about the game:Likes:- The combat is well done (aside from one minor annoyance, see below) and the wide variety of units/magic/items/terrain means that you can employ many different strategies.- With 3 characters having unique personalities and classes, 4 ideologies with different associated talent tress, dozens of different units, several different gear sets, dozens of different spells and many quests that can be completed in different ways, there is a lot of replayability (I completed the game with all 3 characters and each playthrough definitely felt different).- The main quest line is alright, but I found many of the side quests quite enjoyable.  Definitely worth taking the time to do them all (which you will likely need for the xp anyway to continue the main quest).Dislikes:- My one big dislike about the combat is the line of sight for ranged attacks.  Far too often are ranged shots blocked by small inclines or tiny obstacles which should in no way prevent line of sight.- I found the music and voice acting to be quite mediocre.- While I enjoy exploration, the huge amount of "hidden" treasures just felt tedious.  The rewards for winning battles and completing quests felt very small and I felt required to search in every box, barrel, rock and tree to scavenge every bit of junk I could find to fund my army.  Even more as a caster where I also needed to find every bit of mana I could as well.  What made all the exploration even worse was how often my character would get stuck on every little change of height in the terrain or every little rock/root. Conclusion:I enjoyed that game quite a bit, but I'm a huge fan of tactical combat games.  If you enjoy tactical combat, you will likely enjoy KB2.  If you're new to tactical combat games or don't really enjoy them, there are definitely better choices out there.   Overall, I give KB2 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: As a King's Bounty fan, little bit disappointed.Here's all of my review!Quality - FREAKING amazing! It shows you how good the Unreal Engine really is! Every battle has their own Battle Ground, so it means you will not encounter the same style of fight, with each scenario you will have to think about strategy how you will execute the attack.Combat - Hard to adapt, because new features have been changed from old KB games, There is limit how many troops in one slot can exist, for low tier soldiers maximum can be 10, and each tier higher, less of a army size per troop slot... and also the battleground physics. Hills, enemy ranged can use ranged attacks on you, meanwhile you are trying to get on the same level as them, to use your ranged attacks.Story - Funky.... Seems like the thoughts were all over the place, not so many side missions, which is sad, because old KB game was created with 80% side missions. And the ending got me confused, because it had such a epic buildup and then just "Congratulations You Won" vibe....Skill Tree - Seems a little bit unbalanced, hard to adapt when you choose one path and some features do not benefit you.Decisions - While playing the game you will notice that there are mostly 2 decisions covered up by all skill tree path icons, Evil which is Anarchy and Good which is Power, Order, Finesse. Map - I <3 that they changed from old KB where if enemy spotted you it would attack, to the huge circle, where from distance you can see all the troops waiting for a fight.... The circle represents the battle ground. But overall.... at start i thought the map is huge, but playing it didn't feel that way after a while.... feels smaller than old KB game maps.Items - The one thing I noticed, that items/equipment in this KB game have less effect than in old ones, would be nice if item stats would change on difficulty you playing on, fun adventure for veterans, but little help boost for casual gamers.Exploring - The game from exploring view feels A LOT LIKE the Witcher 3, but I will not complain, I LOVED that game.Troops - While having fun fighting and trying to choose which soldier to use on battlefield I noticed that there are not so many different type of troops.... Each talent will have from 1 to 3 different troops per tier.... and the highest tier is 5... :(Troop Leveling Up - The soldier Level Up system is DOPE where they get better attack and health per RANK... max Rank LvL is 3... But while using bad troops you realize too late that there are not that many enemy's left in map to fully max out your recently obtained Red Dragon or Bone Dragon... :(Player Leveling Up - When I played, seemed all over the place, sometimes LvL'd up too fast and sometimes took forever to hit that sweet LvL Up!Dialogue - In the old KB games it was too much for me, had to skip a bunch, but in this one, not so much dialogue, felt like, it needs more.Hardest part about the game - It was exploring, it took too much of my time, to explore the whole map, because traveling is slow AF.... And Pay 2 Win.... When I purchased the game, I went all out, the best option, and it had Lord Edition, which gave some items and new troop, that was too OP for the beginning....Overall - I give this game 8.7/10.... The only thing I want is more Side Missions which would give more fun for exploring and achieving new lore for the game and more combat, so when I'm bored, I don't need to start a new game, but could go in "Arena" or something similar to fight until I get bored... And DLC'S :D!

_childDocuments_.review: I really dislike rating the game negative as obviously a lot of people put a lot of work in this. Anyway, the game is a big disappointment for me being a fan of the series in general and it deserve a negative review for the very many flaws it has.I played the game to the end, the tutorial was terrible, after that the game got a little better and raised my hopes somewhat but at some point you realise that the game is very much scripted and limits you in a lot of things - unseen in other King's Bounty games.The few really positive aspects:1. The graphics are ok at close range, decent for mid range and pretty beautiful for anything afar.2. The music and sounds do fit.3. A new approach to battles compared to old King's Bounty games (however, the approach fails imo).The many negative aspects:1. The tutorial is terrible. You have no idea why you start where you start, you are lead through a very linear map layout that lasts for several hours. It is boring, feels partly imbalanced and introduces features of the game in a bad way. It is a terrible introduction overall and for that way too long. Also at the end you face a character that will be part of the rest of the game... your character is familar to that one but you have zero idea why! (it is explained a few minutes after that though, but very poorly at that still - does feel very random).2. The game leaves you without any explanation on a lot of game mechanics, it does not allow you to rate certain values in the game, also a lot of mechanics/features are simply bad - examples to follow:2.1. This includes the fact that you have no idea how much of the limited mana ressource you can use throughout the game without running into issues (I can tell you that you can use as much mana as you like in battles, so long as you don't intend to level all skills to max. - which you really do not need to). 2.2. You feel like gold is very rare ressource and indeed, it is! If I wasn't used to playing old King's Bounty games and if I wasn't focusing on getting a very few losses, then I would have probably run out of gold at some point - at least if my intention was to buy/upgrade a lot of units to their maximum level... which you somewhat want to in order to unlock new skills.2.3. Units gain levels and unlock new skills. I did not really see any hint that they get new skills if you level them up? That is an important information I would say. You cannot see a preview of level 2 or level 3 units (unless you face them in battle) so you are left to discover this all for yourself. The level gaining of units itself is a poor mechanic as not all units that take part in a battle gain experience, rather units get experience if they kill units of an enemy squad. This said, a healer or buffer or even a taunting, hiding melee unit, will have bad chances at gaining level unless you use wait and defend on other units so you can get last hits on your healer units. This defeats the purpose of a game that focuses on using all units as good as possible in battle!2.4. Enemy units skip on several skills, especially the ones that gives them more movespeed and defense. That is a poor design choice, really.2.5. You have to gain reputation points for certain "ideals" before you can unlock certain skills. This in itself is no big issue but the amount of reputation points you need for each ideal is absolutely slow to gain at the start, which leaves you with rank 1 skills for a long time. You have no idea how many reputation points you can get in total so you do not know if you can distibute them.2.5.1. This has a very negative aspect if you want to go for the skills that one usually aims for in extensively long RPG's: Gold and EXP gain. Indeed, it will take your hours before you can unlock and skill all those skills and in the meantime you do not want to skill other skills because you need the skill points.2.5.1.1. Another issue with that is that you spend a huge amount of total skill points on EXP and Gold skills to maximum both EXP and Gold gain. For the gold part you are then bound to wait until you get the better merchant price before selling anything - this is just terribly bad. Those skills should be available to maximum efficiency quickly or be removed completely.2.6. The walk speed in town is terrible and makes you waste a lot of time, the same applies to walking around if not in town. You would have a horse to fix this but the horse is as slow as you in town (+ massive mounting time) and it cannot loot in open field. This will be fixed by the developers but it was a bad mechanic to put in in the first place.2.7. Your character cannot move in uneven terrain! He cannot cross a distance of even 2 mm uneven terrain! This is sooooooooo bad, honestly! Also you get stuck on stones and corners a plenty. Apparently the designers knew this, that is why you have some sort of debugging every 3 seconds or so when you are stuck on the terrain.2.8. The game does not leave you as much freedom as you would think. It is very very much scripted!2.8.1. Every battle field is unique but each of them is static. This means that the terrain is pre-defined as well as the enemy troops. You face battles where you play vs a lot of range units that can decimate your units quickly. In other battle you will face melee units that have super high initiate and that can reach you in their first turn. This said, the game forces you to use specific units and equipment for specifc battles. So be prepare to change units and equipment a lot!2.8.2. Hoping to use level 3 spells in combat early on, if you focus on specific spells? Forget about it! You need a lot of arcane knowledge (gained by lvl up or equipment) and thus level 3 spells will only be available to you for a very limited number of fights towards the end of the game. A similar logic applies to level 2 spells which can be quite decent if it comes to buffs/debuffs but you will have to level/gain equipment before you can even dream about using them. Most level 1 spells are pretty bad, really.2.8.3. Want to wander around the map and pick up items/loots/quests/shrines and the like? Maybe you are used to that from other King's Bounty games? Well, forget about it. All areas are blocked by certain enemies or quests that you cannot avoid. The best you sometimes have is that you can choose to go 1 of 3 routes first. But at the end you will be blocked by some badass fight before you can progress to the next bigger area.2.9. Remember the ideals you can go for? Be warned: You can max an ideal and put a number of points in the opposing ideal... however the game does in no way tell you that doing this will very likely lead you to not be able to gain one of the "grand four full sets" completed. What is it I am talking about? There is a merchant in the first bigger town selling 1 part of each of 4 big sets, price of 50k gold each. Obviously you are very exited about these and wonder how they affect your late game? Well well, if you do not follow 1 specific ideal throughout the whole game, then you will never know! Obviously the game does not explain this, you will only figure this out at the end of the game - what a shame for you!2.10. Leadership limits the amount of units you can have for a specific troop, e.g. you can only use 3 warhorses, 4 archers, 7 peasants, 2 healers etc. depending on how much leadership you have. This is common for strategy games, however it is not common that units are also limited by their base level. If you end up with 6k leadership, then you can hire a 5700 leadership dragon but you can only hire archers with a leadership of 2000 leadership for example.Writing-space ends here I fear. But I may add: I do not really understand the story (?!), the game ends with a cliff-hanger! Loot is completely useless, part of the developer videos are deceiving/wrong (you canNOT buy mana!), no difficulty setting for casual players, terrible puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: King's Bounty II is a turn-based strategy RPG developed by 1C Entertainment and published by Deep Silver. The game is set in a fantasy world and players take on the role of a leader of a squad of heroes and soldiers, with the ultimate goal of becoming the ruler of the land.The game's campaign is where the game truly shines, with an emotionally charged story filled with political intrigue, betrayal, and a diverse cast of characters. The player's journey is filled with difficult choices, and the story takes a few unexpected turns that left me heartbroken. The game also has a variety of side quests and activities to keep players busy, but the main story is where the game truly excels.The game's open-world setting is also immersive and well-designed, allowing players to explore the game's vast and detailed map, filled with diverse regions, cities, and enemies. The player can also interact with various NPCs, complete quests, and gather resources to upgrade their army. The game's visuals are also impressive, with detailed character models and beautifully rendered environments.The game's combat system is also noteworthy, offering a unique blend of turn-based strategy and RPG elements. Players can choose from three different classes of characters, each with their own unique abilities and strengths. Players also have the option to command their army in real-time during battles, allowing for more dynamic and engaging combat.The game's soundtrack is also noteworthy, with a sweeping and epic score that perfectly complements the game's fantasy setting. The game's voice acting is also well done, adding to the overall immersion of the game.In conclusion, King's Bounty II is an excellent game that offers a unique blend of turn-based strategy, RPG elements, and an emotionally charged story. Its detailed visuals, engaging combat, and well-designed open-world setting make it a must-play for fans of strategy RPGs. The game will take you on an emotional journey that will leave you heartbroken but at the same time, it's a game you won't forget

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: At the time of this review, I have completed the game 6 times (2 as Aivar, 3 as Katherine, 1 as Elisa) and exhausted most unit combinations. I recommend to read this in-depth review for anyone who does not want to get a slighted review from jaded fans of the old games. In short, do not listen to critics bashing this game for not being what the old KB used to be. The score of 6.5-7 in Metacritic *is* accurate, but it has been unfairly derided. The game has a fundamentally great tactical combat system, and most of the joys derive from you being able to play around with different hero classes and units combos. It is really enjoyable once you get the hang of it. But it is true that the exploration and RP aspects are not great; however, they are more than passable and you can definitely blitz through those and get to the fun parts.Onto the full review...----King's Bounty 2 - Unintentionally Roguelike Tactical RPLENGTHYour first experience will roughly range around 30-40 hours to complete the game, and any subsequent playthroughs will take 10-25 hours depending on how much time you invest into dialog/cutscenes. Most things are fairly static (fights, quests, item locations), and are pretty much the same for each playaround, although there are some random treasures that you get and artifacts/quest rewards that depend on your class... which is actually a good thing for subsequent playthroughs as you can just breeze through the RP side and focus on the battles.DIFFICULTYThere is technically no difficulty choice, and the game seriously ramps up in difficulty if you are unfamiliar with the game and the units; however, one could use the three starting characters as a "soft difficulty" choice as Aivar (little magic, lots of damage, slightly tougher early game) is the best starting character for the uninitiated, with Elisa being the middle ground option (easier mid game), and Katherine being the hard mode (lots of magic, low damage output, easy early game but tough later on). The class and skill system also prods you in certain directions, and if you do not go with those, you can end up being too weak and overwhelmed easily; but for the hardcore players, once you know how to play, you will feel the lack of difficulty choices and may want something more challenging.EXPLORATIONThis game technically needs to looked at through two lenses: the RP aspects (adventure map), and the combat. The RP aspects are, as most say, dated, and slow movement across the map without jumping (for narrative reasons) bog it down somewhat. Other issues include tons of clipping issues walking over rocks, treasure box icons hounding you long after you go away from the location and the lack of a sprint button that can become downright infuriating. However, a Witcher 2-like navigable world does add and not detract overall, and indicate that it is a step in the right direction and can only be improved upon. It may be a slow experience, but I appreciated its slower pace and eventually could breeze through the game in 12 hours; however, it can be a chore for those who do not go out of their way to complete every quest and find every treasure.COMBATThe combat is the cornerstone of this game. Laid out on a grid-based battlefield that takes place in the surrounding area of the adventure map, similar to Heroes of Might and Magic and Age of Wonders, it requires you to maneuver your units to make the most of the environment and defeat the enemy. I could rave for hours about this, but it is great and offers immense replayability with the various unit combinations of close combat units, flyers, ranged units and spellcasters. All units have their own experience they gain from battling and have two upgradable tiers (from 1 to 3) that improve their capabilities with each new tier. This can be a downside later in the game, as there is a preset amount of battles in the game, and you may not have time to max out your units, forcing you to stick with certain choices you made earlier in the game.THE ALIGNMENT SYSTEMThe gameplay is organised around a sort-of dual polar order-anarchy (read: lawful v chaotic) / power-finesse alignment system. All skills, units and quest choices are tied to this 4-direction system, for better and for worse. You make choices in quests which give you points and unlock better skills for that alignment, all the while units you use in your army clash or complement one another depending on how many alignments you mix. While it offers a pretty wide cast of units and skills to play around with, the alignment system also lacks INCREDIBLY in balance. Although there are achievements tied to maxing out alignment points, you will enjoy most mixing skills from different trees - however, there are pretty much must-haves you cannot miss out or certain unit combinations will be downright unplayable vs the stronger opponents (who can also get the same skills you do), later in the game.Patch note: At first, you could complete all quests however you wanted without your alignment impacting your choices, but since the latest patch, it has become more of a factor (high alignment may restrict you from choosing other options). That is not  a good thing for mixing and matching and feels restrictive (esp in the RP department), but can be worked around if you spread yourself out in the early game.UNIT BALANCEOne part of the game that is somewhat lacking is unit balance. While I love the army management, it does not feel like unit balance is fleshed out well to cater for those not willing to mix and match, esp early/late game. Certain subfactions within alignments are also much weaker than others, and if you want to stick with them through endgame, it can get really difficult unless you know what you are doing. Also, there is a cap to unit variety, and it feels like the game could have done with another 2-3 units per faction or alternative units (which weirdly is available as DLC on Nintendo store from what I have seen). TECH ASPECTSThe one key sticking problem in this game is its tech. Though the engine feels old and graphics can look quite dated, it still will strain your rig (running a 2070super+10700k OC on ultra I still get spots where it chugs, ESPECIALLY if you like to minimize your game and run something in the background). The game has a lot of tiny bugs that won't mar the experience overall but can be annoying, particularly if it forces an annoying reload when you get stuck. The game options can also feel a bit restrictive when it comes to key bindings. Ultimately, none of these tech issues broke the experience for me, and I quite enjoyed the European style visuals for what they were, but I can definitely see people thinking all of that ain't great.Patch note: A number of initial tech issues have been fixed and the game is much better than at launch; however, performance chugging still persists, so be wary.OVERALLWith all that said, as I mentioned previously, if you enjoy mixing and matching unit combinations and tactical grid-based combat, you will love what this game can offer, so long as you are OK with the overworld exploration. If you do not, it might get tedious, but it is well-worth persevering as combat progression feels great, and the two game parts do not detract too much from each other. For the RPers, it does feel a bit barebones, and the story threads do not come together that well in the endgame/feel abrupt, but this is a game that is best enjoyed while it lasts rather than focusing on its endgame. You can always treat it as a roguelite and not focus on finishing the game, but rather restart when you feel you've capped out, as the most fun I've had is the early-to-midgame progression trying to take down tough mobs with different unit combos. Overall, I would say that this game can be both seen as a flawed gem or at least a solid foundation for things to come in the future, and is definitely worth it, esp if you can snag a deal.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is only suitable for people with a deep love for the King's Bounty series and a whole lot of patience. In a lot of ways, the game's a procession of minor annoyances. You'll be walking slower than any other game I've played recently, and doing things like mounting or dismounting a horse takes three seconds each way. If you want to look at a unit's stats or even see what an ability does, you have to look at a whole new screen. Archers are mostly limited by line of sight, and what counts as an obstacle is difficult to predict just by looking at the terrain. Repositioning units before a battle can take upwards of 15 seconds just watching them animate, and there's no options to speed the animation up. This is a representative sample more than a complete list.If you put up with the annoyances there's a passable King's Bounty game under it (you'll start to find it around hour 6), though it doesn't do anything novel and it cuts a lot of fun mechanics from previous games. The combat is fine, though there's a bit less to do on each turn, and the game seems scared to give you interesting units and spells early. The world is more linear than usual and a bit on the empty side, particularly given how slow you travel through it. The production values are on the line between mediocre and poor. The writing is also on the kind of shabby side of decent. The writing wants to be a bit more mature than the cheek and whimsy of the old King's Bounty games, but "maturity" implies exploring interesting ideas, and this game kind of doesn't. The game locks your skill tree behind a morality system - order and anarchy being a grab bag of good versus evil and other random situations that really don't feel like a moral axis, and force versus finesse substituting for "just kill them" versus "do a puzzle and then kill them easier". The writing's at its worst when the morality system is in play, with the choices feeling forced and non-compelling - would you rather get food from the petty-minded farmers or the scummy bandit lord? Would you rather steal the quest item from the honest merchant or pay a really trivial amount of gold for it? You'll probably choose based on what skills you want, unless you've went far enough on one alignment that the game stops letting you choose at all.There's nothing horrible about the game, and it's not unfaithful as a sequel - it just doesn't have that much going on. If you'll buy anything based on the King's Bounty title, you don't need this review to talk you out of it. You might even have a decent time. If you're actually reading reviews to decide whether to buy this game, the answer is probably "no".

_childDocuments_.review: There are some bugs and some changes I don't like but overall this is a welcome addition to the King's Bounty games. This one is more of an RPG than in the past with multiple ways to solve quests. The way you solve quests gives you points in that category: Power, Finesse, Order, or Anarchy. These points are required to invest skill points in those trees meaning if your playstyle is for spells you find yourself deciding to solve quests the Finesse route to get more points into that skill tree. This is the first system I've seen where the way I play actually influences my character build. This might mean I want to immediately do an Anarchy playthrough after doing an Order playthrough just to take different options and try out different troops. That is also a negative. While undead used to give morale penalties to living troops now all troops are in one of the 4 categories and they all hate eachother. This means spending a bunch of stats into making them NOT hate eachother so you can use mixed forces. Meaning at the beginning, you pretty much have to pick one and have an army of just those troops.All in all, I'd recommend it. Fully voiced acted with so much to do. Not Skyrim Modded beautiful but interesting and varied environments that look great. Just watch out for the horse. I get stuck on it a lot...

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the previous King's Bounty games before, casually, and I honestly think this is a big step in the right direction. It isn't perfect, true, the characters look like animatronics, the horse is weird (controls the same way as the Borderlands car, you get used to it after a bit), the camera during battles is really bad, but the core King's Bounty formula evolved in a way that made it become way more accessible to a modern audience.The tactical gameplay is really satisfying, game progression feels rewarding, the world is beautiful to explore and your characters shows off the gear you equip. The story and side quest stories are average.I wish for a sequel, want to see more of this world. If I had to score it, 7 or 8/10.If it's on sale, and you like casual tactical gameplay, you should buy this.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fans of former KB titles (crossworlds, darkside) I have neutral opinion for this KB II, some things I like better here, some don't. But as a RPG and strategy fans, this is such a great game, I ended up completing the game 3 times with each characters to 100% completion. What I like:- The branching quests which led to different stories and consequences. Though it doesn't change the main plot, to see the different fate of NPCs due to our choices is quite satisfying and adds more replay values.- Pretty cool armor and troops designs.- Decent amount of troop variants each with different stats and skills. It's fun to try them all to create army compositions, the morale limitation is quite annoying though.- The combat is super fun if you like turn base strategy games, but it's not for everyone.- Super cheap!!!What I dislike:- Limiting unit stacks, if I remember correctly the only limitation to recruit units in the old KB is the protagonist leadership. Now it's further limited per-stack which is annoying and make the weak unit practically useless late game. There will be no Paladin with absurd number of archer/peasant for example which strength can rival higher tier unit, here we can only bring ten at most, very disappointing.- The map could be bigger (I miss the adventure through different islands or even realms from previous KB), and the terrain could be better, there are a lot of weird clippings that make my char stuck quite often.- Too many named trash, there is almost no excitement in opening chest/treasure since most of the content are sold-only trashes. They make the inventory unnecessarily clunky. Previous KB would offer various useful things to loot while exploring (even an army sometimes) - Unbalance difficulty, easy is too easy where normal(or hard) is quite punishing since there are very few stock of units and gold/enemies to farm, especially in early game, losing too much unit from battles can result a deadlock (except by loading early saves) since the road related to main plot usually guarded by strong enemies.Honestly it's sad to see such a bad review score, kinda reminds me to Trine 3 when that one get bad reviews after trying the 3D approach, resulting the next games going back into 2D. Hopefully that won't be the case for this, since I have good experience here. Though I'm pessimistic that there will be any continuation at all for KB II in current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this at $10, but I can't recommend it even at that price point.  I went into this understanding it wasn't like the prior King's Bounty games, so i was OK with that change.  However, the new game really doesn't do anything well and does several things very poorly.* Voice acting is atrocious.  I played Katharine the mage, and she was arrogant and condescending no matter who she was talking to and in what situation.  I get her background, but it was over the top.  And the rest of the voice acting was very poor.* Graphics are good - for a game released 10 years ago.  The facial designs were very repetitive and the animations were wooden.  Not a huge deal, except you have a lot of cut scenes so are seeing this a lot in the game.* Travel is terrible.  There are travel waypoints and you get a horse, but there is still a lot of walking for every quest, and the horse travel is wonky, esp in tight areas.  And once the horse gets to town, it travels at walking speed anyway.* The talent trees weren't bad, but they were pretty shallow and you locked yourself out of some of them based on the decisions you made.  I get this from a RP perspective, but you are forced to play a certain way if you want to max out any of the trees.  In other words, the roleplaying is chosen for you once you decide which way you want to go.* The battles are the best part of the game.  There is strategy, they look good, and it's satisfying when you win.  However, there are just too few of them.   When there is an achievement because you won 70 battles, you know it's not a big part of the game (I'd argue it should be the biggest part).* The ending was jarring and abrupt - the story was difficult to follow at times due to everyone looking the same and it also didn't translate over to English very well at times.I know it's not an AAA title and I got it on sale, but I was still expecting more.  And what I was expecting should not have been too difficult to do.  If you buy, do so when it's a deep sale, but do not have too high of expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: King's Bounty II (KB) represents a turn-based tactical game with light RPG elements, developed by the company 1C Entertainment and published by the company Prime Matter. Previous titles of the series are KB (1990), KB: The Legend (2008), KB: Armored Princess (2009), KB: Crossworlds (2010), KB: Warriors of the North (2012), and KB: Dark Side (2014).+ The balance between exploring the world of Nostria and regular battlefield encounters is well maintained. Especially the sophisticated terrain layouts offer more tactical possibilities during battles. Nevertheless, here are some improvements I would like to see implemented in the future: terrain with bonuses or handicaps. In addition, spells that put obstacles on the cells.+ Units gain experience. Their appearance changes, statistics increase, and sometimes they even acquire new abilities. Pretty cool. Alas, they level up too fast. Furthermore, the variety of units within each of the four factions is not big enough.o The Scryer’s challenges are misplaced. This game is about freedom of choice in regards of army setup, yet the opposite is achieved with that side quest.- The following features should have been integrated before the game’s release: auto-resolve battle and speed up options. And they are still missing! Can you imagine how bored I felt during my third playthrough watching all those lengthy unit animations over and over again?- I miss the following aspects established in prior instalments: rage box, pet dragon, mates to marry aka. eye candy, unique bosses, and various neutral units that kick ass. That aside, what happened to demons? Haven’t seen a single one in all of Nostria so far. And before I forget; where are my vampires? As the leader of undead forces I feel incomplete without them. I demand blood suckers… and spiders!The game shifts the former formula towards a new direction, where exploration, NPC encounters, and storytelling are more dominant and elaborated in comparison with its former titles. Personally, I welcome this change.On the other hand, I miss a couple of features from the predecessors as already mentioned in the pros & cons. The combination of both aspects has split the community, resulting in an overall mixed review score.Recommended for curious adventurers with an open mind set.Estimated time for 100% completion: +100 hoursSingleplayer achievements: 49Multiplayer achievements: none

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a few prior King's Bounty games (Legend, Armored Princess, Crossworlds, and Warriors of the North) and I certainly remember enjoying those games; especially overcoming them on Impossible difficulty using all the tools the game provides.  I went into this iteration of the game with some expectations of having a hard difficulty that can be overcome.  But I was very disappointed.First off, the smaller battle maps, while looking pretty (and the concept of fighting using the over-world's terrain is novel), drastically reduce the player's capability to do anything but smash armies into each other head-on.  In earlier King's Bounty games, melee units would typically need 2-4 turns to walk across the map, giving ranged units a chance to pick them off.  And ranged units would have a distance penalty, making it much less effective for ranged units to target each other from across the field.  Earlier games also gave you the ability to spawn obstacles or traps to further stall armies from clashing.  In those earlier games, you could have an army significantly smaller and weaker than your opponent and still squeak through with a perfect victory (losing no units).In contrast, King's Bounty II has you enter melee combat within the first turn of combat.  Ranged units are immediately stuck in melee combat unless you completely surround them with units.  And this also means you can't leverage tactics.  You simply need to have more units, stronger units, or faster units (with strong spells).  There's barely anything you can do to overcome an enemy with stronger units than you.  Secondly, the way morale is implemented can swing battles far too wildly.  Basically for every 1 point of morale, a unit has a 10% chance of receiving a second turn after their first.  A unit that randomly gets a second turn can attack the same target twice, often meaning an attack with no consequences (each unit can only counterattack once per turn).  King's Bounty has always been a game that heavily advantages the first strike (since attacking first kills some number of the enemy, making their counterattack weaker).  And having occasional double-first-strikes just makes some battles a coin toss (you win if you get extra turns, you lose if the enemy does).Next, the limited stack sizes (tier 1 units can go up to 10 units; some higher tier units only allow 3 units per stack) means that lower tier units quickly become worthless.  There's no concept of having expendable arrow fodder.  I think the limit was added since units can also gain ranks as you use them.  But if you reach maximum rank with one unit type, you might not want to switch to a (momentarily weaker) new unit that needs ranking up.Overall, I appreciated the higher production value of this game, but I didn't like the simplified/constrained strategic aspects of the game.  The most enjoyable aspect was the lack of crashing.  Older King's Bounty games are crashy bugfests, but I got through this one without a hitch.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first review, but I felt I have to write this because of my disappointment.This game would be a decent title, if it were not a sequel to the Kings Bounty franchise. Even as a spin off, but thats not the case. This game is called King's Bounty 2 but it has so many things missing from the series. First of all: this game offers ZERO replay value. There are no random armies to fight with. Thats right, every fight will be the same regardless of your playthrough. There are no random items on the map except the junk which literally have no use other than selling them. No random armies to choose from: you will get the same units from the same vendors every game.Remember when you found the thorn's crown and you changed your strategy and army because of it? Or the dragon amulet that let you get more dragons? Well forgot about that in this game. There is only basic items in this game offering only minor stat boosts to your army and changing non of the mechanics. Morale mechanics got changed to basicaly RNGing every fight: if you have the same type of units you get a chance to get a second round and thats it.The only reason I started a new game was to try a new class. But after awhile I realised I'm doing the same thing all over again and I gave up on it. This is the first game of the series that managed to bore me, so there is something new they accomplished I guess...This game is just a pale imitation of the series, theres only a few units and a lot of the races are entirely missing... There are no Orcs, no Elves, no Lizardmen, no Vikings, no Demons... Only humans, some dwarves, the undead and some animals remain, and they introduced a new, non-playable race to fight against and thats it.This is not a Kings Bounty game, if you expect anything from the old series in this title, you will get dissapointed. Especially with this price range, this game worth nowhere near its full price with its 2010 graphics...

_childDocuments_.review: Usually I don't write reviews but in this case I feel like this game is underappreciated.Pro:- Scratches my itch for a Heroes of Might and Magic like experience- I like the choices possible and how the world changes around those- I really like turn based combat and trying different builds both which can be done ample in this game- A bugfree product! I am so used to bugs all over the place that I really enjoyed that I didn't encounter a bug in all of the 105 hours i played. No crash, no glitches, just playing the game without fiddling with settings or looking for a workaround- There are so few games of this kind around, and I'd love to see another entry of the seriesCon: -  After three playthroughs with the different classes, the campaign feels a bit confined. There are several gates bound by story and there are not that many different routes to explore- Though the balancing is ok in overall, some builds are way harder to pull off than others- I would have preferred some way to adjust the difficulty as some battles are a breeze, others really tough- Bigger armies please. The limit to 5 stacks only and also the small size of the stacks makes me miss the big stacks possible in other titles of this type. It would also allow for more diversity in army composition as some units are just not viable at allIn overall, I really enjoyed my time with this game. It for sure is not for everybody but I liked the presentation and the look and feel of the different fractions. The new 3d presentation of the overworld travel felt weird at first, but if you just imagine that you are looking top down on your kings bounty map but with more immersion than it feels fine. So if you liked Kings Bounty or Heroes of Might and Magic (I love both a lot), give this a spin. And don't put it on the price tag, in terms of enjoyment I got out of my money it was one of my better buys this year.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Kings Bounty series, this was certainly a bit of a departure from the old format.Positives- The core combat loop is really fun and engaging.- The magic schools offer a good variety of options to suit what you want to do.- Unit designs are fun and give different play-stylesNegatives- Expiration is a crawl- there is no sprint button, and your horse will walk slowly in towns. But for some reason holding down shift slows you to a walk (which is used for one side quest in the entire game, so why it exists I have no idea).- Lack of proper balance, Finesse is incredibly strong with the 28 point perk. Double casting magic trivializes even late game encounters. I beat the final boss without losing a single casualty. - Moving through the game can be frustrating when you hit literal road-blocks and don't necessarily know what you have to do to open them (usually just advancing the MSQ).- Voice acting is all over the place. Some of it is fine, some is just bad.- Game ends on a weird cliffhanger of sorts. Pretty unsatisfying.Overall, I would recommend this game on sale, I would not recommend it at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game. In fact I still aim to play it through at least once.But if you use the name of an established and beloved series you have to compare against the rest of that series.While the graphics and soundtrack are beautiful.. the game mechanics have undergone a number of changes for the worse.There are fewer and less varied battles and traveling/searching the overworld takes much longer now.. which is an utterly stupid design decision for a turn based strategy game.There is a lot less unit variety. The "rage" mechanic as an alternative to spellcasting has been dropped completely with no replacement whatsoever.Spellcasting has become a lot worse, as Mana is a finite resource (similar to gold) now. You also can only summon 1 additional troop regardless of type.. this makes the already weaker mage class just much less fun to play.Learning higher tier skills is now tied to 4 ideals that you only gain by story decisions.. meaning the decisions are already made for you if you want to learn a specific route of skills.. in which case they feel utterly pointless to begin with.All in all.. the game should have been so much better but is very flawed by horrible design decsion and a clunky UI.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: This is an incredibly boring game, made with lack of budget and an even bigger lack of talent. Graphics are dull, story is uninspired, music is forgettable, combat is full of bad game design choices, puzzles are so trivial that they don’t deserve to be called puzzles, and exploration is tedious and tiresome. STAY AWAY FROM THIS GAME, it isn’t worth your time. Longer version:I loved the predecessor of this game, “King’s Bounty: The Legend”, made by Katauri. It had an amazing soundtrack you fall in love with from the very first note, a bright, colorful cartoonish style, very deep and interesting combat system, and a decent plot. I’ve finished both “The legend” and “Crossroads” (its sequel) several times, and was overjoyed when King's Bounty 2 was announced. However, the more I watched the game development, the less excited I was - at some point it became obvious that King’s Bounty 2 authors are making a completely different game of the same genre, and are using the “King’s Bounty” franchise name to make the game noticeable. None of the things that made “King’s Bounty: The Legend” a great game were in the sequel. I still decided to give it a try. After about an hour I knew that I’ll refund the game, but decided to play for at least two hours, to give this game a chance, thinking that maybe it will change my mind.. After 90 minutes I was so bored that I couldn’t even force myself to play the game any longer. I’m dead serious. The voice acting is “meh”, from the sound of it, most lines were “one try only” thing. The models and graphics look like the game was made in 2005. Story is as cliche as it can get, and to top it off, it takes itself so seriously, it makes you cringe. You are a prisoner, who is liberated because a prophecy foretold that you will save a kingdom from a magic evil force. Ugh.The overall style is "realistic-ish medieval", so there's a lot of brown everywhere, very dull. Music is forgotten the very moment you stop hearing about it, if not earlier. There are “puzzle” bits in the game, but all of them are either “use three thingies in the right order”, or “put a thing on a thing right next to it”. There's zero satisfaction from completing these. Walking is slow and boring, horse riding feels awkward and the horse itself is glitchy. The combat has several interesting new things that are soiled by a bad game design. For an example - when you have a pack of 5 archers, there are 5 actual models on the hex, not just one unit and a number nearby, that’s cool. But the thing is that you won’t ever see that, because to effectively view the battlefield, you have to zoom out and none of these details will be noticable. Even worse - most of the units look very alike, it's hard to tell the difference between a dog and a wolf, or between an archer and a pikeman. What's worse - there's not a lot of combat. Encounters are rare and all of them are scripted.From what I've gathered, this game has 10 times less content compared to Katauri games, and it costs 10 times as much.So, this isn’t just a terrible sequel, it’s also a very poor game that doesn’t bring you any fun. If you like to play a good turn based strategy, buy “King’s Bounty: The Legend”, it’s old, but you will never be able to tell that, because it plays beautifully even today.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm absolutely not a fan of the first game and dlcs/stand alone, even if I have all of them, I didn't play them that much. I had no particular expectations towards KB2 so this review is nothing more than a honest review. The first KB is a topdown tactical rpg while the sequel is a "3D over the shoulder" game.  I'm not sure KB2 benefits a lot from the new POV because it makes the navigation very tedious. The character/skills/inventory panels are basically in a beta state.Sound design is really bad, the musics are scarce to a point it hurts immersion. No music or crowd noises in a crowded throne room, the same in cities, missing sounds while trading, etc...Gameplay wise, the battlefield has visibility problems and you'll often make unwanted moves after having selected the wrong units, since no visible panel of clicked unit is displayed on the hud.Another annoying thing: you can find legendary equipements in stores... Some legendary stuff were available to purchase in one of the first store I visited. Ridiculous. Legendary equipements and weapons should only be dispatched and available in the game through bosses rewards and world loots at a very low drop rate.  This is rpg "one o one". The result is something that is very clunky in every way and seems very old, even if the graphics can sometimes look nice, thanks to good use of shaders. Shortly said, the production value and level of workmanship does not justify the €50 pricetag. and like always nowadays, a publisher released an unfinished game.I will advise you to wait for patches that fix the problems that should have been fixed before the release or maybe a deep sale because in its state, King's Bounty 2 really doesn't worth its price.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed whole campaign with Elisa, below is some thought comparing to the original KB series.1. Rank on individual unit. Rank exp is gained through combat and rank up provides slight increase in unit stats and unlock new skill on certain rank. Max rank is three.2. Ideals replace Faction concept. Simplify impact on unit morale.3. Unlimited reserve unit space which save hassle in placing reserve units here and there in KB series.4. Travel stone allow quick travel to certain place in the map.5. Obstacles and high ground/low land do provide slight challenge in combat.6. Max unit cap. Recruitment no longer solely depend on leadership capacity. Lowest tier units tend to cap at max 10 units whereas highest tier units cap at 3/2/1.7. Trials to test on player's strategy skill. 8. Heal feature at the end of combat. This feature allow refill back unit with the cost of game currency. However, not sure why it doesn't work always. I noticed it will not heal the same unit which had unit killed in two consequence combat.1. Secondary non-mana "spellbook" (eg. Rage in KB-TL). Involvement of hero now only serves as a spell caster and attribute buffer. Lack of a more unique way to support the squad in battle.2. Boss monster fight.3. Hostile unit now remain at static location and will not chase hero around to pick a fight.4. Item upgrade by beating its guardian.5. Companion feature (eg. wife in KB-TL) to have additional specialized buff. I believed this is replaced by introducing additional equipment type for the hero.6. Ability to cast lower level learnt spell. Since in KB2, hero arcane knowledge not only affect which spell can be learnt, but also which spell can be cast during combat. If player switch to another set of equipment which lower the arcane knowledge as a result, some learnt spell can no longer be used as it can only cast on its learnt level.IMO, KB2 is telling an interesting saga. Player need to choose side on various occasion which give impact on your characters Talents build and item gain (certain legendary set equipment is rewarded differently vary from your choice). The gameplay pace is considered short (if ignore how slow player travel in the map) for this one (seem like more DLC/expansion is expected to complete the story on another map). Apart from minor glitches on the graphic and no significant different on army size over three different hero classes, this game is recommended for player who enjoy strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often feel that I have not received my moneys worth. This game however has done just that.I love mixed genre games , they are usually full of unique interesting and fun ideas filled with passion from the devs. Kings bounty 2 was an easy sale for me , it advertised both Strategy mechanics + Role playing , Both genres which I love.The game begins with huge amounts of potential and world building . The first area , the game feels great as you learn your place in it and the new game mechanics. I cannot fault this stage of the game. It has some deadpan facial animations , but I looked past it , as the game has charm in other areas.Onto the second area , the game continues at a good fun pace , at this time I cannot fully understand all the bad reviews.Suddenly about 15-20 hours in you start feeling a weird ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the back of your head , on further inspection the game starts to show many flaws , this is where ill explain them.- Dead pan animation and weird lip sync. Normally this can be overlooked in some games where the game is mechanic heavy. However in kings bounty 2 , it is integral to its new roots in the rpg genre , after about 20 quests you start to feel disconnected with your character and have no attachment to it whatsoever.- Story. I actually have no real idea what the main quest is or what are the side quests , no sense of importance or urgency or even feeling towards the characters in the world.- Lack of unit variety. On the surface it looks very complex and seems to have a huge variety of units. However in further inspection you begin to see many units are the same such as the mounted units from each of the ideals with only slight variations of usable skills. Furthermore you quickly advance to the end of the tier system just 15-25 hours in. Meaning there is no longer anymore excitement of what new units you can potential unlock and see.- Lack of army size. This is very subjective but the size of the army being limited to 5 units feels limiting and is quite hard to form strategic plans based around just 5 units that can only use 1-3 skills once per battle ( most battles last only 1-4 rounds) It also kind of deflates the selling point of being a general/hero commanding an army , it feels more like a series of skirmishes than actual battles.- lack of depth in skill trees and RPG mechanicsThe rpg systems in this game are very thin. You have 4 very uninspired skill trees that force you to delve into one or two skill trees through choices in the quests , which gives the whole game no grey area in choices. The gearing system is also very light and is just a series of stat buffs to your army with no real unique affixes or suffixes.Below I will go over some pros of the game.- World building.The game has great world building from the get go , it filled me with the same feelings i had when first starting fable for the first time , I can see the devs really tried to inject life and love into this fantasy world and it really shows in the graphic design an level design , its so full of charm.- Side quests and quests in generalThe side content in this game actually all feel very fine tuned , there's no busy work and each quest seems uniquely crafted. Honestly did not expect this level of quests from a mixed genre game like this , these are what kept me playing for as long as I did.ConclusionAt the end of all of this I was left with a feeling of "why don't i just play an actual top tier rpg like divinity/pillars of eternity"and then the comparison wrung true. In pillars for example you have a party of up to 6 characters which can be seen in this game as your army , the only difference being in pillars they actually have fleshed out deep character customisation (skill trees/gearing/levelling) and huge backstories. On top of this they also have many more skills/abilities and magic to use. Its kind of strange in a way that i felt i had more of an army in a sole RPG like pillars then i ever did in kings bounty 2. You also have the added bonus of actually being able to fight with your avatar and enjoy the RPG's well written stories.In essence Kings bounty 2 tries to fire on multiple cylinders but fails at almost all of them. Its average , and that's the problem , when there are games that are far superior in the rpg side and games that are far superior in the strategy side, it leaves gamer's with a feeling that they just want to play those games instead.My score 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Worst sequel of all time.  Rather than improving on tactics, strategy and army management, which was really what KB I was all about and why we loved it so much, KB II tries to go a completely different direction and manages to do so in such a horrific way that it takes the joy out of playing a game like KB in the first place.  I've played for over 3 hours and I think I fought about 4-5 battles that all lasted less than 3 minutes - the rest of the time I've been meaninglessly (and very slowly) running around the map looking for hidden stashes and listening to linear conversations in AI-like voices.  If I want to play an open-world RPG, I'll play one of the many that are out there, and when I'm playing KB, I want to play KB, but it looks like KB II simply doesn't want to let me.It would still be playable if the open-world experience was enjoyable, but seriously, the developers should at least play their games before releasing them, as even a brief play-through of the game would reveal the many discomforting technical aspects of the game that must be improved.  I can't help but think that this game is just a rip-off of the many loyal KB fans that have been eagerly awaiting this game for many years (and would pay any amount of money and would not be discouraged by any negative review like this).

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to start with a few changes that I believe can be easily implemented. 1: Allow us to fast travel to unlocked waypoints from anywhere instead of having to travel back to one we've already unlocked.2: Give us more camera control, both in battles and on overworld. Battles - let us look at the field from above. Overworld - just let us zoom out some.3: Give us difficulty options, even if something as small as on Easy all enemy troops have XP lv 1, and on hard all enemy troops are XP Lv 3 and Normal is somewhere inbetween.4: In battles, let us decide what side our unit attacks the enemy from based on what side of the hex we're pointing at.5: Give us something to differentiate our saves. Let us name our saves? List the character we're playing as on that file? Show a preview of our army? SOMETHING.6: Improved mouse/keyboard controls. A lot of times, something feels like it should be able to be done with the mouse, but can't, for example, moving troops between active army and the reserve in the army tab. Or have the option to auto-hide tool-tips when mouse cursor leaves the item/troop.7: Let us zoom out on the map more.8: Improved movement speed in the overworld. Character just feels slow.Some deeper design flaws that I don't expect changes to, but perhaps in future installments.1: Don't limit our armies beyond the Leadership. This makes so many troops useless later in the game when you can only use 1/2 of less of your leadership in a stack.2: Don't try and make every wild encounter a forced encounter. Yea, we need some fights we cant avoid, but at least let some fights be ones we can decide to fight or not without making us deal with a 5 minute trip around the world to avoid.  3: This ties in to point 2, but put more small encounters around the map, ones that you don't feel forced to fightSome of the things I like.1: Arcing damage on archers.2: Terrain blocking ranged attacks.3: The decision system.4: The world as a whole.5: The army factions (Power, Order, Finesse, Anarchy)As of writing this review, I have 23 hours in KB2, over 200 hours in the previous installments, and hundreds of hours in HOMM3. As I continue, I may edit this with more suggested or desired changes, more things I like, and I may update to a recommend, but as it is, I cant recommend unless you already know you enjoy this game for its genre.

_childDocuments_.review: (Just a heads up - I never played the original King's Bounty games.)I have not yet completed the game, but all the negative reviews lead me to writing the review after 10 or so hours...As a new player coming into the franchise I have to say I really enjoy my time with the game.For me it's not typical to sink that much time (only 10hrs so far) into a game, since work and life take over pretty much my whole day. But this game kept me interested and I actually look forward to half an hour of playtime a day. It's fun for what it is, definitely not without its bugs but if you like taking your time and don't mind a bit of hit or miss voice acting the game can shine.Is it worth the prize they ask for? Eh - maybe more like 35 - 40 bucks. Some bugs, slow-ish movement and not up to date graphics are what might bring the prize down for some people. I'm actually happy with the 50 bucks I paid for what it's worth. I assume you can sink more than 40hrs into this one - branching narrative, different units and so on might even merrit another playthrough. (Don't know, since I'm not even close to being done with the story)Graphics: So this is definitely not your perfect next gen eyecatcher, but it is quite beautiful at times. Textures could use a bit  of work but all in all with different environments the graphics are good and I enjoy them.Gameplay: You play one of three characters with different "skills" and go through the semi open world in third person. battles take place in a turn based matter of fashion - so you walk into the battles just like in most JRPGs. The environment in which the battles are situated in the overworld are actually present in the turn based battle map - so height advantages, rocks, boulders, cliffs blocking sight and paths, are all there and even visible before starting the fight, so you could potentially plan ahead. One thing is odd though - there's no difficulty selection, you play what you get and sometimes it involves some trial and error (especially the quests with pre made armies). The game is definitely not easy, sometimes it takes changing your troops and rearranging your equipment for specific fights. You've got different damage types, different troop alignments (mixing those together can result in moral loss), different troop variants, melee and ranged units, magic units and spells. Mixing all this together is super fun and enjoyable. Troops can be leveled up - if they die you have to buy them again, but they're leveled up - so potentially you can end up without gold and no troops if you screw up multiple times super badly. Story: So far it's pretty interesting, side quests are enjoyable with different possibilities on how to solve them. Got some good laughs out of some of them. The main story itself seems like a convoluted who betrays who and who is you're friend or enemy sorta thing - no clue on what's going on at the moment. But I'm interested in finding out more.If you are a fan of turn based RPGs this on is probably a hidden gem fo you - rough around the edges, but not so rough, you can't see its beauty.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally think this is a good core King's Bounty game (with a disclaimer). It has an interesting story, good quality battles, good graphics, good creatures and good RPG elements which are fit for King's Bounty. The concepts are sound too.However, there is much room for further improvement, and if the game is abandoned then the game can only be recommended at discount sales, despite having a fairly solid conceptual core.The main problem with KB2 is that it was seemingly cut and is only including two map areas (the first is just a tutorial and small). If it had progressed longer to different lands with the story widened and with additional different races such as elves and orcs then the game would have been a solid 10/10 in the KB series. As it is currently it is 7/10 but could reach 10 with new and improved content.Improvements for KB2 DLCs and expansions could include refined rules for the talent trees, additional talent branches such as Nature and Specializations. Also a new character based on the Anarchy path (Necromancer or Blackguard) could be added. Nature path would also have a character such as a Ranger or Druid. Voiced lines could be limited to just keep the current ones if that is what is needed to get production costs down.The Specialization path would be a variable path tied to character progress based on reaching a certain number talent power points in the talent circle. A character would at such a point be able to unlock one speciality path (which would replace the middle talent with its own strengths and perhaps also the way the character looks). The talent screen would then also have a second page for special talent powers. Creatures like Giants, Hydras, Manticores, Titans, Ogres, Genies, Minotaurs, demonic forces and others from the HOMM universe would be welcome additions as well. New lands would include more human centered lands such as Artisania, Rigern and such. Non-human lands would be dwarven, elven, orc, undead and demonic lands. A larger focus on making these lands more fantasy inspired would be important. Crown Lands is fine as is (for a human land) but the new lands should be fantasy immersed to reflect the fantasy creatures living there. Higher level/stronger creatures withing the level system, spells and items should be dispersed around this bigger world. There is inflation on all those aspects (plus inflation of XP points) in the Crown Lands currently (due to cutting out all other lands and their stories from KB2). Introducing castle sieges would be a fun feature too (like in HOMM).

Most of the time you have to steer your blandly scripted "character" through a game world that looks dowdy at best. The fights are okayish, but to my mind are lacking in comparison to the original series. The quests are linear and boring, no trace of the original humor.  The "puzzles" are pretty much cringeworthy.For the time being I can't bring myself to waste more time. the game is absolutely no fun at the moment and a great disappointment .  I am not kidding when I advise you to not pay more than 10 Euro for it at a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. I personally like the lively atmosphere in the game where you can hear NPC conversations here and there when you passing by. World is reasonably compact and you can find new quest waiting for you just around the corner. It certainly does not feel empty. As for strategic aspect of the game I play as paladin which is considered the easiest class in the game. I’ve got quickly spoiled by easy victories early in the game when everything just works because you have bigger troupes, but was punished later on seeing my cavalry completely wiped out by flamethrowers because my units had no fire resistance. And to make things worse merchants were sold out and despite winning the fight I could not replenish lost units. The lesson learned. Playing strategically pays off. There is enough room to employ different strategies you can think of. You have to analyze first whom you are going to fight and act accordingly.

_childDocuments_.review: This game needs a lot more work:1)  Its a poorly optimized for PC and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ console port. UI and controls are extremly frustrating and immersion braking for PC. 2) Far too many inconsistencies and poor dialog choices...I am cringing at every second line spoken. Again, the immersion  suffers heavily. 3) I like the idea of 1st Person, 3d exploration, but the execution is very poorly implemented by 1C. It is a chore to walk around and I avoid using the horse, because its just horrible console movement. To fill the void between fights, 1C just fills the world with hidden loot and its just tedious and non consequential. In the original KB it was fun to explore and it felt like you were always up to something and had a purpose. There was always something around the next corner, even if it was just like "Uhh that looks interesting, lets go there".  In KBII you have to stick to the predefined path and there is often nothing to do but walk and walk and walk to get to the next quest point or find your way back to a merchant. The teleporter stones help but do not remove the empty world feeling or meaningless walk distances.4) Battle and tactics. Here as well its a step back from the original KB. The battlefield is too small and does not leave room for great tactics. There are far too many troops that can reach you in the first turn and attack. Those with high initiative and walk distance have the upper hand, as they can always attack in the first turn. There is often no positioning possible for a good defense or a setup a situation where high initiative troops have to spend at least 2 turns to reach you. The small troop sizes and small battlefield does not help that you are suppose to feel like a general with an army behind you. Please 1C, seperate the annyoing console handling from the PC version. It is far too immersion killing and frustrating to guide your character.

_childDocuments_.review: The game needs a few fixes before I'd consider leaving a positive review, and my two main issues are the game's UI, as well as the character's speed when traveling/exploring. It has other flaws as well, but these two should be possible to fix at least.The UI is pretty clunky in general, and if you want to buy for instance a single wolf for your army reserves, you may need to tap the A key 50+ times since it starts at the maximum you can afford, and there's no easy or fast way of adjusting the amount.The default jogging speed of the character is really slow, and there's no way of going faster other than riding your horse. The problem is that the horse is  slow in towns, and mounting/dismounting takes more time than it should, which is an inconvenience if you find any loot on your way since you can't pick it up while riding.With the problems out of the way, I'll share my thoughts about some of the game's aspects below.The combat is more or less what you'r expect from a KB game, however there's a much bigger focus on story and exploration, with the combat basically taking a back seat. This isn't what I want from a KB game, but it's certainly better than nothing, and I can still appreciate the game for what it is.The graphics are in my opinion fine, and the scenery is for the most part really nice. There is unfortunately quite a bit of pop-in though, and the animations aren't always great.The dialogue is certainly nothing to write home about, generic fantasy stuff basically,  but the voice acting is even worse. I'm playing as the male warrior (Aivar), and his voice just conveys boredom through and through. The other voice actors are pretty hit and miss, and the music is mostly very ambient.Other than that I've had the game crash once so far (when I tried to fast travel), which made me lose about an hour of progress, but that's my bad for not saving more often. I wish the game had quicksave though, that would have saved me that one hour most likely.All things considered it's a pretty fun game, it just has a lot of flaws, and in its current state I wouldn't recommend it.
