_childDocuments_.review: Well, well, well...TLDR: Good, but not meeting (my) expectations (hardcore King's Bounty-Fan here). So I looked very much forward to another King's Bounty game. I had several hundreds of hours put in the old ones, having played every single one of them, most more than just once and all on impossible. I like the challenge. This one felt, easier at times, then harder at times (though as a mage I restricted using the spellbook much or at all until later in the game - which made it far harder than needed). Overall it is easier than the predecessors.1. Personally I really liked the new graphic style. The world looks great and I only run into very few graphical bugs as such (though small ones I don't even care about). 2. The length of the game is alright. It's not far too long, but not too short for the paid price either. 3. The new take on the army system has its pros. I felt it was a fresh approach, which gave the game FAR more customizability. It felt far more realistic, too. Seeing only 1 to max 10 troops in every regiment. 4. They at least tried to get the humour and slightly the music right, which sadly they most of the time failed at (in my humble opinion). 5. It was far more "realistic" than any of the games before. 6. The combat places were beautifully crafted and had a nice tactical useability. 7. Voice acting was superb AND everything was voice acted. Even three different heroes with different dialogs, which was great and gave the game a little bit more replayability.8. Item and RPG-System was great. I like the way, you can choose your own moral compass and the way you play and which units you want to use.  9. The story was more than okay. I didn't understand all the hate on this one. I have witnessed far worse. 10. You can save pretty much, whenever you want. I love this. 1. First and utmost the soundtrack. Guys, King's Bounty has had ! And with this title they failed miserably. There are some tracks, which are good. Especially at the end (credit songs are nice... at least that). I even went back to the old KB soundtrack to listen to it from while to while. This won't happen with this one. This is the worst and saddest part of this game for me. Yeah, you may have tried to get more realism or lower the creation cost of the game, but you lost so many emotions, so much flair, just a lot of epicness for real. 2. It was too easy for my personal taste. No impossible mode felt sad, however Hardmode IS hard. 3. I didn't like, I had to complete it three times, to gain all achievements. It was somewhat time consuming. 4. Several bugs and like three crashes. Which weren't too bad. It could have been more polished though.5. The way my horse stands. Like wtf. It looks like it's legs are breaking. I felt pain, watching my poor horse stand. (Sometimes it bugged into walls, doors, people and stuff, too). AND it was sooooo slow to ride it in town. 6. Slow. Your char moves slow too. No sprint option. It's not too big of a deal for me though. In the beginning it was annoying, until I got used to it. 7. There should be a DLC or another successor. I kinda doubt, they will release anything like that in the near future. Overall I had a lot of fun and a mostly good time. Therefore the good review. If you like games like Ages of Wonder or Heroes of Might and Magic, you may want to give this title a try.

_childDocuments_.review: As of time of writing this review, the game is being review-bombed by fake haters, 0.2-0.4 hours of "playtime" and claiming how they know how the game plays out. A lot of misinformation. Let me debunk and make a proper review from somebody who actually played/streamed game enough already (10+ hours, I had press access), and also hardcore fan of KB series, from all the way to DOS 1990 game to all Katauri Interactive ones, beating them all on Impossible No Losses. First of all, we, hardcore fans of KB, already seen previews, screenshots, videos about KB II before release and all dev explainations of their choices. If you don't agree with their third person RPG experiment, why are you even bothered with the game, buying, writing negative reviews, refunding etc . You had plenty of time to just realise it's not for you and just skip it.Let's move on to actual KB II analysis. Game performance for Day 1 release is pretty exceptional for AAA these days. Had 0 crashes, FPS issues. My rig is pretty clean and powerful so that might contribute to this, but trust me, as a streamer, I experienced plenty of games with FPS issues where they shouldn't be, especially with good hardware. Some people are saying they have crashes so I guess it varies, most likely will be hotfixed anyway. When buying this game, you should have a clear understanding that you will not get "2021 quality open world adventure RPG" in the King's Bounty world/franchise. Non-combat stuff graphically looks like something from 2012 at best, meanwhile, the actual reason for fun and enjoyment of this game are TBS hex-based combats, you will love them if you are a fan, these days we rarely get any TBS games to begin with. Even in the indie scene. Oh, and by the way, all the reviews calling this game indie, it's just laughable.One of the biggest issues I have is controls. They are made for consoles. First couple hours I was "fighting" controls as a keyboard/mouse user. Spacebar for "OK" (wtf), a lot of hotkeys are required instead of mouse clicks, even during battle, you cannot click Wait/Defend/Skills icons with the mouse, you will click on Hex instead and move your unit. You cannot rebind, which is unfortunate for such a game. No Quicksave/Quickload. Horse controls are janky, especially with reverse movement. Horse is honestly not needed, most of the time you will be spending scouting the map for loot in tight spaces, and on horse you cannot do anything but ride it, no NPC talking, no clicking on loot/puzzles. The game could benefit from "sprint" on MC, but unfortunately it's not present, the run speed is pretty slow and that's the best you will get. Annoying part is that mouse is pretty much feels like afterthought, you want to click things with it, and while some things are clickable with mouse, but you might get punished with missclicks or just menu micromanagement issues. Currently, the best way of handling/coping with some of these issues is memorizing most hotkeys the game have and stick to keyboard. Rebindable keys for PC game is a must have in 2021, also for a franchise that's pretty much build exclusively for PC.Lore/story/puzzles/and in general, the entire 3D 3rd person shell of RPG that this game has is mediocre and I recommend you don't focus your attention to it.Instead, look forward to King's Bounty gameplay, classes, perks, level ups, magic book, ranks on armies stacks, army management, and of course, the best part of the game - combat, and all the systems/mechanics connected to it. While the game starts pretty slow and boring for experienced players, it gets pretty exciting later on. First couple battles are played on very small maps so you don't really have too much strategy/cover/highground plays and enemies can reach you in turn 1, so you have the illusion that this might be the entire game like this, but no, it gets better. Like I mentioned, cover, highground and other mechanics start to appear, bigger maps and more complicated battle scenarios for which you need careful planning.Some of the army management/recruit mechanics are slightly different/more casual/easier compared to previous KB games, for example you can lose any amount of units in stack, just as long the stack survives with just 1 unit after victory, you can literally pay money to instantly heal the whole stack to full. This saves the time of backtracking/teleporting, but at the same time, some units have limited quantities in some vendors, so if you keep paying for healing after battles, you will never really have issues of running out of units in stack. Oh, and yes, there is fast travel in this game.Speaking of other different mechanics, you have unlimited reserves in KB II inside of you, you can also hire above your total leadership of the same unit in reverse, so if you have extra money you can save time on backtracking again. Loot in the game is savescummable, even gear from important chests can be manipulated (warrior vs mage gear).For the extra fun, just like the good old times in previous KB games by Katauri Interactive, with Impossible/No Losses, try to play the battles without any unit loss (no healing post battle). This is actually really hard in this game, there are no difficulty settings and game have less fights in general, and each battle is a huge stationary choke point block in world map that prevents further access to other areas/game's content until you beat it. Once you run out of optional quests/areas, you have to push for the main quest to progress, and because the battle maps are generally smaller, and game is obviously designed with this mindset of just bashing unit stacks into unit stacks, exhausting their retaliation and just ganging up, but in the process you guarantee lose something if not a lot of units or even stacks. It's very clear once you reach the final battle in the first area of the game, it's a hero battle which is warrior type, and pretty much everything will guarantee to kill at least 1 unit of your stacks, good luck with no losses. I had so much fun trying to figure out how to win it (with Mage, obviously you want to play with spellbook/magic MC if you have any hope of trying out No Loss playthrough). The game suddenly becomes a complicated battle puzzle instead of just mindless bashing units into units and winning without little-to-no effort because the game is balanced like that and then you press the "pay-to-heal stacks) button. Which is what I expect most people will experience which is a shame. Later parts in the game have complicated battles where you have to read into passives/actives, plan your army composition, take advantage of map, covers, spells, your gear/perks you get, buffs, debuffs. This is exactly what makes King's Bounty II a fun game.For fans of KB again, you will find a lot of similar units, their signature abilities/passives, like Griffins having infinite counter-attacks, a lot of references to HoMM / KB ideas/traits, basically, a lot of tiny moments/discoveries that you will appreciate, that devs took time and effort to research into it and add to KB II.English voice acting is a bit lackluster. Russian one as expected, above average (it's a russian game after all) and would be my recommendation if you are bilingual. Soundtrack is pretty nice and chill to listen to. Nothing too crazy and memorable. Battle music is where it's hype, I like these little touches like when you do an attack during battle, the music tracks get more intense for the short duration and then it returns to "normal".I obviously haven't finished the game and can update this review later. Also I suspect some patches will be deployed to fix some of the common outrage from the community.I would give this game 7/10 as most 1C games these days deserved that. They are nothing grand or masterpiece level, but just above average to enjoy it by many factors. Remember, this game is made with a different dev team, not Katauri Interactive and you knew it.

_childDocuments_.review: I just beat this game:  From where Kings Bounty was, to where it went to with this iteration, I think it's a $10 game and a complete mistep of direction and execution.  Ascension to the Throne, a $2 game with terrible graphics, is the same type of game but more enjoyable.  Pros:    -The battlefields IMO are actually better and more strategic than previous King's Bounties  -Some of the spells and units are interesting, and the battles can be challenging at times  -Some of the castles and buildings in the main towns are pretty, as are the views from some of the terracesCons:   -80% of the time is spent jogging everywhere, 5% is watching cutscenes, 10% is waiting for your units to execute their painfully slow spells/attacks, 3% is selling inventory and hiring units, and 2% (at most) is actually the fun strategic decision making of where to move troops, who to attack, and what spells to cast.     -The previous fun of hunting for treasure in KB?  Gone.  Instead it's a chore.  All of the treasure highlights random objects throughout the world, which you jog back and for to.  Missed one?  Don't worry, it shows up on your Map too.  And the treasure?  Useless trash you spend time re-selling.  No hope for any cool armor or anything useful.  -No difficulty setting.  Two or three fights seemed challenging, and the rest were too easy.  -Worried about preserving troops?  Don't be in KB2.  At the end of the battle you can pay to bring them all back.  Previous KB's forced you into trying different troop combinations, but KB2 never really does.  -Leadership is worthless in this game b/c units are capped.  Have enough leadership to hire 5 Griffins?  Sorry, that unit is 3 of 3.  Once you get past level 18 or so (and I was level 30 when I beat the game), you have more leadership than you'll ever need.  -Open world so it is interactive, right?  I didn't expect this to by Skyrim, but very little of this world is interactive, and it feels like a cheap skin over cold inanimate objects.   -Spending your money to obtain an Armor set for it's bonus?  Don't bother.  I tried for the Sanguine mage set, only to find out I had no chance at the Gloves b/c I sided with Finesse in one of my quest options.  Finesse is the mage route btw.  Apparently if I had sided with Order then I would have gotten the gloves, and there was no other way to obtain the gloves.  The game doesn't tell you the rewards of the various options you face.  -The UI is terrible for a PC player and is an enormous step back from other King Bounty games.  There is no hovering over of skills, or comparing gear.  It is incredibly clunky, and one of the first things you notice.  -Did you enjoy Rage, spouses, kid bonuses, unique gear, and different climates?  Gone, they aren't in KB2.  -The puzzles in this game are meant for 1st graders.  And after "solving" them your character will shout "I DID IT!!"  -Instead of reading text in KB and feeling like it's your character, you are left listening to someone who isn't like you.  I played as the paladin and she was a complete hypocrite.  "Stealing is bad Mr. Knight", and then she goes and robs farmer's chests and graves.  -The cutscenes stink.  The writing, the acting, and especially the awkward 2010 graphic characters who sway back and forth.  Almost every character has the exact same face, just with a different hat, or if you're lucky a beard lol.  -Bugs:  My tabula quest bugged out and was impossible to finish.  And multiple units have a bug where if you use their special attack (crossbowmen for example), then there is a 10 second wait period afterwards.Ultimately, the game is less engaging, less strategic, less enjoyable, with a 90% time waste (see above) than any of the previous King's Bounties (and I include the Sega version which I've beaten 2 or 3 times).  There wasn't one time where I wanted "just one more battle" to advance the map or storyline, whereas that happened all of the time in previous KBsMy recommendation to the developer for the future of KB - get back to the old model, enhance the graphics, come up with some new units, hire a good story writer, and you'll be able to charge $50 easily.

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings, I have 783 hours on all the previous KB games (380 in the legend).I paid full price for this 2, but I can not recommend it, specially if you are not a fan.The legend was truly a legend, in its size and innovations. Had a better plot and was light hearted.This one is so short that feels incomplete (Trine 3D vibes). Unlike the first one that you explored many lands and worlds, everything transpires in your backyard for this adventure (2 if you count the intro snow smaller map).The plot is kinda common place and not engaging. Maybe because when they tried to make it more "real" they created a word full of a**holes. I am worried about the life view of the developers, hope they can have more hope for the world and humankind. Or maybe they were just trying to copy and cash the doom n gloom of the Witcher and similars that sells crap reality. It is so bad that the Order and Anarchy paths in the game feels like two flavours of anarchy. Instead of king Mark the Wise, we get grown up Joffrey Baratheon.By the time you get to the level 5 army the game ends kinda abruptly and you feel like you wanted more battles to use your army. Actually, for a strategic battle game, this one is very short of battles.Too much time is spent wandering around (too many already complained of the speed, so I am not even going there) collecting trash. And I am not being harsh! There is actually a button that reads "Sell all trash".I get and see they spent great care creating a nice world, but after the first time/hours we just care about the game dynamics. Plus, they didn't have the resources to make a Skyrim, so the worlds feels nice and you want to explore for trash, but you can't even cross a small ditch, or Jump over a knee tall fence. So much for realism..

_childDocuments_.review: I can not recommend this game, especially for a full price.On the bright side, +the music, +and graphics as a whole are good, making some +atmosphere.But I was unable to find more pros, although there is a tonn of cons:-The gameplay was changed alot comparing to the predecessors, but it was not an upgrade-The writing, the dialogues, the quests, those are all dull, boring, not interesting at all,you would see the same kind of FedEx quests, on top of the "gameplay mechanic" of going back and forth through the map after most level ups to recruit more troops. And also on top of the fact that you are additionally slowed down in towns, as a game design decision. As if the character was moving fast by default...-Map was not made careful enough, you can sometimes see below the textures, go where you should not be able to go, flowers can grow from the stone and go even more inside the stone due to the wind...-Alot of parts were not implemented and balanced properly. Every (I mean literally) woman who would give you a quest is the SAME face woman, only the clothes and hair would change, but...Really?-Game design is not the best, let put it this way. Its not very player friendly, alot of bottlenecks for the player, and made in such a way, that you are forced to play a "lockpicking" battle game of going through all available battles first, so you could find something you could win without loosing alot of money.-Speaking of money, another bad game decision, half of the game is the Death stranding, but withouth a charm of it, its just a hobo simulator where you would have to go back and forth through each and every corner, bush, tree, hill, bridge, stone, alike looking mage hiding spots...To find 384 coins and a few trash items. You are forced to do it if you want to have enough money. Funnily enough, your character does not have a home, so...-Glitches. Not game crashing or breaking, but inconvenient? There are alot, you can be stuck at the ground, stuck at the door, stuck in your horse...Speaking of the horse - it has the worst controls of any game I ever played. Not cool.-Boring. There is simply nothing to do at that game. No secrets, or interesting characters, no place for imagination, no proper side quests (which you are forced to do btw), no side activities or minigames, nothing....The jokes in the game are mostly not even funny. Maybe cause the game itself is a kind of joke.-Horrible UI. Bad AI.For example it is very hard to understand and see that some traders would have new troops after you finish some quests. Not only that but overall UI is bad, and horrible at times, like in the battle, to see the effects applied to your troup you have to press additional button, open the big window and then look at one of the corners and hover over the effect to see it. It looks bad, and it IS bad. and AI, it simply triggers your zones of control freely, sometimes doing some very dumb stuff.-Main gameplay feature.Battles. They are repetitive, boring, not too much diversity, and your ass is locked behing your quests decisions to one, or two unit types. I mean not hard locked, but good luck with taking different troops hating each other at once. The troops themselves do not look very different. They are just copying and mirroring each other, like if there are human archers, there are skeleton archers? What is the difference? Just first are alive, the second are dead, but that does not change much. In predecessor games the units were bright, interesting, different and changing, you were like a collector in a way. In this game, however...What you get is what you get, play with those 5 squads of your choice, like them or not, respec of your character costs 10k (after the first respec) and also buying a whole roster of units would hit your wallet hard. I mean, if there is only 1 engaging gameplay feature - at least make it good. But no, it is not good, it just meh, you can play it, maybe you would enjoy it, but the chances are not great.-Gameplay. It does not feel like a Kings bounty, more like a cheap battle sim, one who tries to copy HoMM or KB, but fails at it. It is simply not interesting, and the only reason I have played this is abscence of anything else to play. I was also charmed by how bad it is for a game with that price, and 0 updates. There were just a few, then the devs just forgot about this game. Half-baked, playable, but not enjoyable, this one is. A nice lesson for every gamer out there - do not trust the devs word, especially for pre-orders. And especially the Fulqrum guys. If there is nothing to be paid for - do not pay for it.Btw I could not finish the game and left it finished for around 50%

_childDocuments_.review: King's Bounty II is an RPG with turn-based combat on hex tiles. The game gets a lot of negative reviews mostly from 2008's King's Bounty: The Legend players. The main reason being that this game has a lot more story and exploration as opposed to going from battle to battle with some text in-between. This isn't false as the game has less battles and more walking/story but I didn't mind that. Also the music of the 2008 King's Bounty was really good, this game has super basic music that doesn't even play half of the time.I had a lot of fun exploring the world & doing the quests, it is nothing new or special but it is exactly what I expected: Eurojank fantasy RPG. The game also looks pretty good with vibrant colours and inviting fantasy environments. The gameworld feels alive enough with NPCs walking around and the outcome of quests can change certain areas or have NPCs move somewhere else etc. Performance was really decent. Could play it on max settings on a 1080Ti at 1440p.I do recommend installing a mod (changing a variable) that greatly increases the players movement speed though, otherwise you end up with a lot of wasted time just running from point A to point B and back; At default the player character moves too slowly (the developers just increased the movement speed with a patch, but I already finished the game with the modded speed).The battles are really enjoyable once you get to know the mechanics. This will take some time given the user interface is pretty bad. Tooltips are lacking information, mouse-control is only so-so and certain status effects aren't very clear but you'll figure it out (this might improve with patches).There is quite a lot to play around with during battles including spells and different terrain mechanics etc. Balancing is also done well, there is no difficulty setting but the battles are fun and the special challenge encounters can be really difficult in a good way.Overall I would recommend this game if you're looking for a basic RPG with a focus on its combat (the battles). If you're not too sure then I would suggest buying this when it is on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It's kinda different from the previous KB games in some respects, but still similiar in its core gameplay - you gather an army and develop your character to beat the enemy, that's about it really.The game is not flawless for sure, here are some of the issues:1) Some character models are very often reused 2) Some animations are kinda stiff 3) Minor balance issues - some units are too strong, other seem too weak; same goes with some of the units' abilities4) Many 'puzzles' as in 'activate the crystals in the correct order' are often reused 5) The dialogues begin and end very abruptly, some dialogues also feel really weird (meaning their content) 6) The audio is also sometimes dissynched with the subs7) The ambient music occasionally bugs out.8) The horse physics succ a big one, you can barely control it and it often bugs out too.  - these are the ones that I personally noticed; they can be easily patched out though, which is what I hope for. Now, to be somewhat objective I gotta also list the things I liked:1) The world feels alive, the atmosphere in the game is really great2) The music is nice and fitting3) The whole role-playing system implemented in the game is good - that one is debatable though - in this game you have an alignment system, which consists of 'order, anarchy, power and finesse' - you earn some points in one of these in almost every quest and your build pretty much depends on it, since you need certain amount of points in each of the alignments to unlock associated skills.The problem with this system is that you might have to roleplay a character (if you're into that) you don't really like, all cuz you want to take an approach during the quest, say, that encourages power all the while playing as a mage. In other words, the game might force you to make decisions you wouldn't have made otherwise unless you needed those alignment points. 4) Replayability - there are numerous quests in which you have to make a decision on what actions to take; your decision then brings you points in some of the alignments listed above, depending on the way you chose (there are always only two opposite ways though, e.g. order and anacrhy or power and finess). This, coupled with the fact that there are 3 playable characters makes for a good replayability imo.5) Quests are numerous and widespread, albeit not always terribly imaginative (there are some good-ol' fetch quests too). 6) The models in the game look good.No game is perfect though, and KB2 is still very much worth a try.What is really important though is that the devs haven't abandoned the game, they keep releasing updates and from what I understand there're major patches coming some time in the future (which should be expected tbh, but is sadly not always a norm nowadays).Overall I would abosultely recommend KB 2  - it is a worthy successor to the previous entries in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I own and played all the older games, you can check my profile  Pay no attention to the review score, BUY IT, it is unique enough to at least you give it a try, if you like it just a little, you have to try the older games, they are all great/good (except for The dark side). The strategy part alone is going to be a lot of fun. Yeah, this is not the original game, I get it, but still feels like a KB game. Let me dive deeper.The combat is great, amazing turn base strategic RPG, arenas are unique, there are 4 "factions", I recommend using 2 at max per playthrough, the graphics are simple but good and you don't play this game for story... so the game is not garbage! As a matter of fact, I would say this is a A maybe AA game with a small budget very well used.It's only 40 hours long, short for a KB game, and the game ends abruptly, hope the devs release some DLC since there is plenty to dig here.The biggest complaint you will read in the negative review herer are: THIS IS NOT THE OLD KB therefore - > TRRASH. Well, it is indeed NOT KB 1, it is a new game, treat like it and give it a chance, it feels like a game which drew inspiration from it and  that is OK to me. However, there are some really issues I should address here.Difficult spike:  by the mid game, you wil face an extremely powerful mandatory enemy, which might make players give up, since there's a limited amount of XP to farm and the resources are scarce, in normal it was hard as hell and on Hard was nearly impossible.Classes: No matter the class you pick in the begining, you can access all skills and spells. The Devs should have make them more unique, giving access to exclusive/extra talents according to the class, would help the replay value.Mana: This one is HUGE. Mana is a currency! A resource like gold, super weird decision by the Devs, as someone who always play as Mage/Paladin, that was a disappointment to be honest. But I should make it clear, it is totally possible to beat the game with mana to spare (I did it on hard mode with the sorceress, you just have to pick a few spells and commit to them. By the way, Blade of death is broken, made the fights trivial by the end of the game casting twice per turn).Stats: there are only 3, and 2 are for casters, so if you don't play as a mage, just soak everything in Warfare. We should get at least another one, one for leadership, every X points increase the max number of units to 33% at max, which brings me to the next topic.Leadership: THERE IS A MAX NUMBER OF UNIT. Like? Why? Really? units of tier 1 and 2 are useless by the end of the game, and this happens due the cap number of every unit, you can have 2000 leadership or 5000, you still can only recruit 10 soldiers... That being said, everyone will end the game with the same tier 4/5 units per faction.Map: only 2 and one is the tutorial... come on... I was expecting at least one for each classic KB faction, elves and demons at least. On the other hand the map is blooming with quests, so evey inch is being used. However... I have to say this: loot is only gold and items for selling (more gold) there are too few equipments among them.All in all, there is plenty of room to improvement, this is not a 10/10 game, even so the game is solid, a mandatory buy to SRPG fans, I wish there were more fights and units, maybe respawn the enemies after the mid game story fight or bring back the items with levels, optional ways to add more content, since the battleground are beautiful and well made, sadly, many of them arre only used once...To the devs, bring me the DLC, I am craving for more KB, if you need to go back to the old games engine I don't care, we play this for the combat/strategy and huge content. Congratulations for the good game.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been a great disappointment.Don't get me wrong - yes, as a fan of the KB and Armored princess, I hate the over-the-shoulder view, but that's not the reason I don't like the game. It's because the game is simply bad.If you decide to create a realistic-looking AAA game in the 2020s, the graphics shouldn't look like it's from 2010. Even the main character I was playing for (the peasant girl) has a rigid face, her lips are weirdly overlapping with teeth when she speaks, her muscle movements create a feeling of watching a rubber manequine. When I was attacking a bear I had to click it to find out what it actually was. It looked more like a wierdly shaped lion.The dialogues are boring and often really unnatural.Skeleton: "Thanks for helping me defeating the evil power. Now I will become a necromancer and build my own army of ghouls."Hero: "Ok, I just hope you will not become evil as the evil power was."---end of quest---If this was an indie game, I'd give it a thumbs up. _childDocuments_.review: Not only is this game an ineffably boring walking simulator with inconsistent, flawed mechanics and boring side quests, but it also decided to break down on the last straight towards the end (literally with 95% of side quests complete) with random Unreal Engine crashes shortly after fights or during loading screens. So in the final phase I had to plow through the hardest fights multiple times because the game just felt like it wasn't the day to finish it. It seems that the only idea the devs had to sell the game was to differentiate it from the Behemoth that the Heroes of Might and Magic series has become and develop a dull third-person experience they could sell on consoles. It doesn't have much more to offer than a pretty diorama of a world, with tons of exclamation marks, giving you boring fetch quests that have you running from one side of the map to the other, with occasional encounters. Even if the main storyline is not the worst, it gets watered down by the amount of meaningless, boring side stories.Don't buy it, even if it's dirt cheap (it gets discounted on every possible occasion), don't waste your time with this half-baked product.

_childDocuments_.review: Offering a fresh take on the fantasy series, King’s Bounty 2 expands upon its tactical turn-based battles to offer players a truly immersive RPG experience that adds weight to their every decision, whether leading an army into battle against unliving horrors, or building relations with local townsfolk. Experience a rich world that blends realism and fantasy, filled with compelling stories, memorable characters and moral choices aplenty. Taking on the mantle of one of three heroes – each with their own unique story – players embark on a non-linear, open-world adventure across a detailed and densely-packed fantasy landscape. Split into two distinct phases, players traverse the realm from a third-person perspective, picking up quests, exploring the wilderness, and getting to know the people they meet. When conflict arises, however, the perspective shifts to tactical, turn-based combat. Players must then make smart use of their units as they fight to win. Set in the vast realms of Antara, a great danger has arisen. A mysterious blight has descended upon its furthest reaches, corrupting the land and all who live there. Refugees from the affected regions have begun arriving in the kingdom of Nostria, putting food and resources in short supply. Once living souls, blight-distorted creatures now roam the countryside leaving chaos and destruction in their wake. The land itself fights for survival, giving your decisions greater weight than ever before. How will you forge Antara’s future?
_childDocuments_.name: King's Bounty II

name: Unpacking
detailed_description: Unpacking is a zen game about the familiar experience of pulling possessions out of boxes and fitting them into a new home. Part block-fitting puzzle, part home decoration, you are invited to create a satisfying living space while learning clues about the life you’re unpacking. Over the course of eight house moves, you are given a chance to experience a sense of intimacy with a character you never see and a story you’re never told. Features Unpack a home — from a single bedroom to an entire house Meditative gameplay with no timers, meters or scores Explore domestic environments with all their nooks and crannies while you stack plates, hang towels, and arrange bookshelves Discover a character's story through the items that come with her to each new home (and the items that get left behind) Soundtrack by BAFTA award-winning composer and audio director Jeff van Dyck

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is a cute little game in which you follow the protagonist of the game through different stages of their life starting in their kids bedroom and help them decorate their home through out these times. The game is divided in different chapters, named after the year in which the specific chapter takes place.The game tells alot of its story visually, you get to know the protagonist through different visual clues which the game is giving you. For example that they like gaming or that they were doing cosplay at some point in their life. Those and many more little details make Unpscking so great in its visual story telling. The game does ALOT OF things right but there are a few smaller things that annoyed me personally ~ for example that you can only place some items in dpecific places/areas around the house. Or that even tho there is technically enough room, you can't place a smaller item next to other items. That mostly happened to me with pots or pans. But maybe the point that some items can only be in specific areas  around the house or room is also part of the visual narrative of the game, who knows? Overall I can wholeheartedly recommend the game to people who like cute, cozy and chill games or just people who want to play something relaxing after a long day. Due to its short playtime you could probably finish it in one sitting if you wanted to, but i'd personally recommend that you take your time with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Unpacking

_childDocuments_.review: Such a cozy and addictive game! I love the pixel art. There's a lot of cute details, like items that keep showing up, and fun hidden achievements. There's also a subtle and interesting story playing out in the background, which invites you to infer things about the main character without ever explicitly stating them. Mechanically, I really like that the game lets you stack things and put stuff where it logically should go. You can put the toothbrush in a cup! That's cool! There are times when it seems like something should fit somewhere and the game won't let you place it, but that's a very minor concern for me. The ONLY negative thing I have to say about this game is that it is a little short for the price. I got it on sale which was perfect. I can see myself playing this game again later though. Since there's no one right way to unpack everything, it's not like a puzzle game that's not fun anymore after you know the solution. So I do recommend Unpacking if like me you like organizing, but wish there was some way to do it in a video game instead of cleaning your own house.
_childDocuments_.name: Unpacking

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a cute and unique game, with one very big issue. The length. It´s just way too little gameplay for the price. ✔️ Wholesome story, super cute✔️ Nice graphics✔️ Lovely soundtrack✔️ Way too short✔️ The price✔️ No real replayability✔️ Leaves you feeling robbed of a true ending✔️ No future updates plannedI finished the game in one sitting, 2,5 hours. I was hooked.I really enjoyed figuring out what was going on in her life by finding the subtle hints while unpacking. It´s one of the most relaxing games I´ve ever played, and the pixel graphics are super cute. But when I got to the ending (which arrived very unexpectedly), it left me so disappointed. To me, it felt like the game ended in the middle of the story. I was expecting to follow the main character throughout life, but instead it felt like it ended when her life was just about to truly begin. It feels unfinished. But sadly not, after doing some research it was clear that the devs wont extend the game further. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most fun, relaxing puzzle games I've played in years! Admittedly, I'm not hugely into puzzles, but if I can find more games like this, I very well might become a fan of the genre!General praise aside, let's get down to the nitty-gritty: What makes this game so simple, so (comparatively) short, and yet so good? In a word, 'Ludonarrative'--that is, the way the gameplay supports the story, or in this case, the way it *tells* the story. The only text in the game is a single sentence or so at the end of each 'chapter', when you're done unpacking and take a picture of your preferred room to put in your photo album (every room in every chapter has different text, by the way, and they're all really fun and relatable, so I'd recommend reading them all if you're into that).So, since the game is so text-light, the bulk of the storytelling is done by environmental design and gameplay, and this is executed immaculately. First, a quick mechanics review just so we're all on the same page: The game starts you out with a single room to decorate (a very 90's-kid room, appropriately enough) and introduces the basic mechanics immediately: Start opening boxes and grabbing items with left click, rotate items with the right click, and put 'em where you feel like it should go. Once you've emptied all the boxes, then any item that's somewhere it shouldn't be (such as in the wrong room, or on the floor when it should be on a shelf) glows red to let you know that it needs to be moved. And that's pretty much everything you need to know! The simplicity of the mechanics allows for a significant amount of creative freedom (within reason), and just as importantly lets you take in the scene without being distracted by the cognitive load of trying to parse a million little gameplay bells and whistles.Alright, now to the meat of the thing: How does all this come together to tell a story? Well, first and foremost, you're not just moving colored squares on top of other colored squares. You're unpacking toys and dishes and pillows and electronics and all the other little things that tell you who someone is--you're essentially taking a visual tour through the main character's life and helping her put it all in place. You never see her face, but by the second chapter, you know her well enough to start recognizing her favorite stuffed pig and her art supplies, and this process continues until almost every item you unpack is laden with meaning. You get to handle her computer and sort her socks (Not to spoil anything, but I've never before realized the predictive power of a single rainbow-colored sock), and you start seeing all the little changes wrought by time, all the bits and pieces of life that we pick up or leave behind along the way, from the steady upgrades her computer receives to the new hobbies she acquires.While the red-outline-system mentioned above can very occasionally be frustrating if you really have no idea what an item is or where it goes, it generally encourages you to put things away in places that make sense, rather than throwing everything onto the floor and calling it a day, which is great because it encourages you to interact with the environment and find creative ways to make things fit, without being so restrictive that it completely stifles your ability to make the place your own--I'm a naturally precise person with a real love of organizing things, so I began by sorting everything into distinct categories and gave every category of item its own drawer/area, color- and style-coded as much as possible. And yet, the longer the game went on, the more I started to feel free to mess things up a bit more and embrace the freedom that the main character herself was experiencing. In other words, I was roleplaying, without a word being spoken or a person so much as entering a room.The primary caveat to the above is that one chapter in particular is *intentionally* designed to make it hard to find space for all your things unless you're willing to do some serious reorganizing of the stuff that's already there, which is ultimately more trouble than it's worth (which is fantastic ludonarrative metaphor/foreshadowing, by the by).Speaking of that chapter, it's brilliantly done because in the chapter immediately prior, you were living with roommates who had already set up a lot of their own stuff which you couldn't move. So as soon as you arrive at this new place and can move most things around again, it immediately clues you into the fact that something about the relationship is different here--but it's also obvious from the visual design of everything around you contrasted with your own stuff that you don't really belong, even if you're hopeful that you might be able to make it work.That chapter then sets the tone for the next (which is brilliantly aided by the music chosen for each chapter) which then further feeds into the chapter after that to create a renewed sense of excitement when the music and scenery changes yet again, and so on and so on until the end of the game.Lastly, we've arrived at the section I like to call "OMG The Sound Design!" You should absolutely play with the sound on, because it adds *so much* character to practically everything! Every item has a different sound depending on what surface you put it down on, and it all makes perfect sense given the material, weight and shape of the item and the surface. Every place you live has its own exterior soundscape, from highway traffic to the occasional take-off of a plane to the laughter of neighborhood children, and it blends perfectly with the feeling of the interior, which itself is packed with satisfying noises, from the 'tac' of a glass on a countertop to the 'swoosh' of a drawer (or the muted 'clang' of a metal cabinet door swinging open, in some cases).I apologize for the rambling nature of this review, but I honestly could go on for even longer if the mood struck me, and am refraining from doing so only so that I can say the following: Seriously y'all, experience this game for yourself! It's well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through this game 3x now so I've updated my review...---{ Graphics }---Absolutely adorable! I love the retro 90s aesthetic of this game. It reminds me of the life sim games I enjoyed in my youth. ---{ Gameplay & Story }---This game is a very calm, no-stress simple puzzle game. You're unpacking boxes and trying to put things in the rooms where they belong, following through the story line of the packer's life. There are some items that are required to go in specific rooms/places but, for the most part, the game allows you to freely place and decorate your rooms however you'd like. You're playing as a female illustrator/artist, following her journey...- Unpacking her childhood room in a new home (1997) - Unpacking her first college apartment (2004) - Unpacking her items into her post-grad shared apartment, a space that's already cramped with the possessions of her messy roommates (2007) - Unpacking her items into the city apartment of her boyfriend, a space where you can move things around but find there's really not enough room for you when you realize you can't put up one of your most prized possessions (2010)- Unpacking her downsized possessions post-break up into your move back into her childhood home (2012)- Unpacking her new life into a small apartment of her own (2013)- Unpacking a few new boxes of things into the same small apartment with items she accumulated from living overseas for work (2017)- Unpacking into a new home, with her family (2018)This game is something you can easily play through while you're sipping on a cup of coffee/tea in the morning/evening. I've done so 3x already and still find enjoyment in this game. It's the perfect cozy game when you need to just take your mind off things and play a game that isn't stressful and doesn't have rigorous game play.---{ Audio }---Calm, relaxing music. There are some moments where you can interact with items (such as the boomboxes, toys, computer, etc) that make music and noise, which I enjoyed.---{ Audience }---I think the target audience best fit for this particular game is adult women, especially millennial women who grew up through the 90s-early 00s. That being said, this game can definitely be played and enjoyed by anyone! I would buy this for yourself if you're an 80s/90s/00s young girlie. If your girlfriend or daughter is just getting into gaming or isn't into typical time-intensive rpg games (yet), this game would make an excellent gift and introductory game for them. ---{ Difficulty }---Very easy to learn.---{ Game Time }---Approximately 1 to 2.5 hours, depending on what your goal is. If you just want to "unpack" as quickly as possible, game time will be closer to 45 minutes to 1 hour (not recommended). If you want to take your time, get to explore the little quirks of the character you're playing as exploring her rooms and possessions and focus on decorating, then game time is closer to 2+ hours. ---{ Price }---Honestly, worth every penny but I would recommend waiting for it to go on sale, simply because there's really only a couple hours of game play.---{ Recommendations If You Liked This Game }---If you played through this game and enjoyed it, I highly recommend Assemble With Care (also available on Steam). It's another simple puzzle game that's got a similar feel to Unpacking. I highly recommend both, equally.---{ Overall Impression }---***WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD*** I ADORE the story line of this game. Going from moving into your own room as a child, to moving into your college dorm, to living with roommates as a new grad, to trying to fit yourself into your boyfriend's apartment, moving back in with your parents when that relationship fails, moving into your very own place, moving into a home with your family - it's the story of a typical Millennial  that I think can resonate with a lot of people. It's the little details that I really enjoyed in this game. The mismatched plates, bowls, and cups in your first apartment, realizing there's no where to put your diploma when you move in with your partner (as someone who lived with an emotionally abusive person once upon a time, that part especially got me right in the feels), the little D&D figure that follows you around and doesn't get painted until you move into your own place and rediscover yourself, the postcards that show the people you've gained/lost throughout your life, the little souvenir trinkets that are collected throughout your journey, and (of course) the stuffed pig that slowly gets torn apart and stitched back together, eventually finding it's new home in your child's nursery. It's a very sweet story line and I really appreciated the beauty of it. The biggest downside and only major criticism I have of this game is that it's too short. I truly wish it was longer!!! I hope they create an expansion to this or provide an update with more content (such as her journey further into adulthood or maybe a variation where you see her husband or child's life unfold... I mean "unpack").

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is not really a puzzle game, it's just an exercise in participatory environmental storytelling. It tells its story via the items you unpack and how you see your life circumstances change, and invites questions about the person's life as they go from child all the way into adulthood.I didn't really care for it. I'm not going to say it's bad because it lacked certain specific kinds of game elements - I'm evaluating it on what it is and not what it's not - but I just don't think it executed what it was trying to do very well or particularly artfully. The questions it invites and the inferences you draw are pretty basic; the game tries to tug on your heartstrings, but it does so with all the subtlety of a dog tied to a knife and loosed in a balloon factory. Often it feels like it's showing you things and nudging you repeatedly with a, "Look, isn't that sad? Isn't this sweet? Look, remember this item from the first place you lived? Don't YOU have something like that you've held onto in your own life? Doesn't that just make you feel nostalgic?" There is no real subtlety here. I think people rave about this game because they're not used to encountering this as a means of storytelling, so the *novelty* of it is really enticing to them, but the game does not actually make use of this novelty in a skillful way.It's also $20 when full price, which is outrageous for a 3.5 hour game, let alone one that isn't especially good.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most magical and satisfying game experiences I've had. If this type of game appeals to you at all, it's 100% worth full price in my opinion.The art is stunning, the music is lovely, and the storytelling is perfect - parts of it subtle, parts of it less so, with plenty of little details for you to discover yourself. Gameplay is very satisfying, and the game isn't nearly as picky about where you place things as some other reviews made me think it might be. There are so many thoughtful details here that make the experience much more wonderful - from how possessions change over the years, to the game remembering your placement of some things between levels. I enjoyed every minute of my gameplay and plan to replay this game more than once.I just want to close out this review by saying - I get that taste in games is subjective and that this extremely laidback gameplay isn't for everyone. But I don't agree with the reviews that say the short length of a single playthrough means this game is overpriced, or that you should only buy it on sale. Firstly, the game can easily take you 5-6 hours on a first playthrough depending on how quickly you organize things/how much time you spend reorganizing as you unpack. Secondly - for me, $20 is a pretty great deal for 5-6 hours of genuine enjoyment that I can re-experience any time I want to. It's cheaper than a trip to the movies. If you have $20 to spend on a game, if this game seems appealing to you at all - it's definitely worth that $20.Outstanding job to Witchbeam, and I'm so looking forward to experiencing this game again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very cute and well executed. It is very much a STORY game, and it takes as much time as it needs to tell the story. If you are looking for something like The Room or tetris then go play those, this game was not made to be slammed through to get to the tougher challenges, it takes the natural progression of the story. It definitely is made to appeal to people but not every type of gamer. Seeing as this game was not made on the base of RPGMaker or anything like that and was made by a team, I think the price is just fine. If the normal price is uncomfortable then wait for a sale. Also, this is the story of someone's life, not your own, so you don't control how the relationships and places you end up go. The story is sweet and charming, and I love it because it is telling the story through places and objects.The graphics are well done, the gameplay of being able to change direction of the object and place. As well as having the ability to stack books or put them next to one another, clothes and towels can be on racks or neatly folded, making it so that there are different options for how the player can sort things. When there are objects in the wrong spot they are outlined in red, and it is not overly hard figuring out where the thing goes. There were several times when I moved an object somewhat randomly until I found the spot for it, but it did not feel like I was being railroaded or anything.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is a puzzle game that tells the story by way of, well, unpacking. Not only is the art attractive, but the gameplay is simple enough that you can grasp the concept fairly quickly: Make sure everything is in its proper place.Don't let that fool you though. Once multiple rooms start coming into the picture, things can get chaotic. You'll likely have to shuffle things around just to get everything to fit. But it never feels frustrating or impossible to figure out, which I love.The story itself follows a woman as she grows up and lives her life. I won't go into detail about the story itself, but it's a genuinely relatable and hopeful one that kept me from putting it down from the moment I started it to the moment I had to take a break. I honestly found myself tearing up when I could identify with the character, and I found myself smiling and laughing when things from earlier levels made an appearance.If puzzles that tell a story are your kind of thing, then pick this up. It's worth the price, and I would love to see more games like it. You can eaily finish it in a day if you have the time to kill, and the number of easter eggs and hidden secrets scattered here and there makes it worth replaying levels later on.TLDR - This game is good. Buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy decorating houses on The Sims, you'll enjoy Unpacking.  It's offers about 4 hours of play per playthrough, but the replayability-level is really up to you.  If you'd enjoy decorating the same rooms again and again in different ways (I do) or finding wacky places to put things, you'll enjoy this game.  You can also try "DARK STAR MODE", which is where you make sure everything is in the "wrong" spot.  It's harder than you think - when you have massive clutter, it's easy to miss a shoe that you think is wrong but the game says is right!  Anyway, you can make some challenges for yourself or run through it once and be done with it, but I enjoyed the game and find myself coming back to it at least every other month.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the pixel-style and the relaxing music. However, after realizing that, no matter in which direction or layout I arranged the items, it didn't really matter, and that the only thing required to pass the levels was to place the items in the area specified by the game, although initially, I enjoyed decorating according to my taste, gradually I lost the interest and motivation and just wanted to quickly place everything to complete the levels. Of course, clearing a level is not easy; the further you go, the more your patience is tested, but at least there is unlimited space for trial and error, and the sound effect upon clearing levels is healing, making all the previous frustrations worthwhile. As for the story, it's only a few lines of text. However, you can infer quite a few details from the items themselves.Finally, I hope there can be an option that enables displaying the name of each item. It will be great to clear up a lot of confusion like 'what exactly is this thing?', and this feature can even make the game a great tool for learning these words in many foreign languages.

The story that you piece together through the levels is super cute and has some hidden secrets. Truly the essence of a cozy game. However, my biggest issue with the game is that it is far too short. I took my time, replayed levels, went through some with my partner, and still I'm at only 4 hours of play time. For $20, that is not enough. I had my fingers crossed for more content. But, the creator, Wren, has stated back in December that they are done with the game and will not be adding more content. If you can, grab it on sale and it'll be very worth it. But, I cannot recommend a game that I feel needs more. I truly hope they change their mind and add content in the future but in its current state, its lacking.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly cute and fun game. You play along a girl who goes through her life unpacking her life in several house moves. I love organizing so this was a fun game for me LOL. It's very satisfying to complete a level after you place all the objects correctly and you can take your time to complete each level. I absolutely love that you can really think carefully about where to place each item depending on in the character's living situation. I believe that the photo mode could have used some extra work as it felt a bit empty that it was just made to save pictures to your computer, would have liked it to be a part of the gameplay more. I also think that some of the items were tough to place in some instances, for example the picture frame didn't make sense to place under a bed when you didn't have space on the walls when it could have easily gone almost anywhere such as in her closet. I'd say my other only gripe about the game is that it could be slightly lower priced due to the amount of content that it offers but it's very close to a good price point. You can expect around 5-10 hours of gametime depending on your playstyle either fast, or casually and return to previous levels to 100% the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been going through some really difficult things in my personal life and have been looking for a game to help me unwind and relax. I have a habit of sorting and organizing my own home when I'm having difficulties, this typically results in me spending a lot of money. This game gave me the stimulation I needed of rearranging and organizing a space without the need to buy a bunch of new things to assist. The music is very calming and the graphics are very enjoyable. I do hope they release more stories in the future so that we can come back and play again.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is a slow, lazy, kind of game. A gentle puzzler which tasks you with emptying your packing boxes upon moving into a new home. Each home has a set of rooms, from a couple in the beginning to quite a lot at the end, containing boxes. Your task is to work through each item in turn, placing them where they should go until the box is empty and you move onto the next. Once you've done this for every room you can skip to the next level.  At the basic level it's that simple.  Obviously with it being a puzzle game there is some logic to be applied. Should the toaster go in the cupboard? Do DVDs live under the bed? But on the whole it's gently. At the end of placing items, the game marks up incorrect ones with a red border so you can instantly tell what's in the wrong place. Then it's just trial and error until everything goes where it should. If that's are there was to this though then it wouldn't be the success it is. No, it's the subtle storytelling that goes along with it that makes this special. Each home completed comes with a little tale from the protagonist that clues you into where they are at that time of their life. It can become quite touching, and when you see little items crop up again and again or indeed disappear forever it can be affecting, which is a big achievement for a relatively small puzzle game. It looks charming too, lovely pastel shades and well defined, recognisable objects. The soundtrack is spot on as well, it sits in the background but has enough about it to add charm rather than be blandly irritating.Bonus marks for it running really well and adapting very well to the Steam Deck. You can move objects with the thumbstick and shift room to room with the shoulder buttons. I had a very nice time playing it on there.

_childDocuments_.review: Here is the explanation; (No Spoliers)   Most of the bad comments are about the short playtime. Even though that's true, it depends mostly on you. There are no rules, no set challenges, you can just rush through and finish it within 2 hours, easy.   However, if you like immersive stories, and I really do mean immersive, if you want to experience a game almost as real as real life, and experience it truly from another person's eyes, YOU'RE GOING TO LOVE IT!At first you don't notice it. As you'll progress along, the game slowly starts to make sense. But you need to play it like real life, not like a game. Like if you've moved to a new house,  where would you put the kettle in the kitchen? What do you reach at the first thing in the morning? Do you have an order when you're doing laundry?You start by putting things the way you're used to irl, but that will change if you pay attention. That's the challengeing part. and you'll love the game for it.SPOILER PART !!!!  Thank you Devs for letting me on in this journey  !!!!! tfr

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is a cute eagle view game where you slowly unpack boxes of a character who continues to move throughout their life. Thats so cool!"-"Thats it? I was hoping there would be another part to the story or a new story..."This game is super beginner player friendly, it has easy controls and from what I know it is on numerous platforms. Even if you are just starting to get into video games, this game is such a good start and so addicting!The game play mainly consists of you taking things out of boxes and moving between rooms to do so. You can sort, organise and move things to your liking. Though some things you may not be able to put places if it does not make to much sense to put them there. The graphics are an adorable style that compliment the game play completely. I am very upset that there is no more stories in the game and the developers have stated that they do not intend to add more, hopefully that will change. But for 20 dollars, 5 hours isnt to to bad for play-ability. I just don't know if it was really worth spending my money on. If you are going to get it, get it while its on sale :) (Well, just get every game on sale.)Overall this game is super fun and beautiful with an amazing story. Though I really wish there was more too it, so if you are not someone who likes to replay games, and you need more then 2.5 hours of content I would say that this game is not for you and to continue your search for a different game. _childDocuments_.review: I thought I would be unloading someone's possessions into a home, decorating, and learning this person's life story, instead I was unloading someone's junk over and over. I never got a sense of a story, just a few bits of this person's life. A brush, a family picture, and toilet paper, these are indeed items a person owns. An easel, a twenty-sided die, and a yoga mat, these items tell something about the person.Every time I got into a new level I would find a familiar item and say "You're stilling holding on to this junk?", look for the appropriate place for that item, can't find any space for it, throw it wherever it fits, move to the next level and the repeat. There are so many levels and too many rooms that don't matter. There's no story behind unpacking the same five towels, a set of forks, and ten pairs of socks, in every level.Unpacking this junk has bored and annoyed me to the point of hating whoever this person is. Going through memories, piecing together a story, and solving a sorting puzzle is fun. Going through the same junk six times over and trying to fit it in specific areas with all the other junk, is not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: It's such a simple relaxing game, with puzzle aspects, a story, fun little hidden achievements, wonderful music, and all about unpacking the life of one person throughout different phases and times in their life. _childDocuments_.name: Unpacking

_childDocuments_.review: A short, sweet game told through the rooms and boxes of stuff of a faceless protagonist as (ostensibly) she grows up, moves out, and moves on. There is very little explicit storytelling, but each set of rooms tells a lot through the objects both present and waiting to be unpacked.As much is told by the possessions that are carried across sets as are the ones that disappear. It's not like the story is very deep and rich -- in fact, it's quite straightforward -- but having you, the player, make decisions on what to put where allows you to inhabit the persona of the unseen protagonist. Some changes across stages with regards to the acceptability of where to put certain items reveals the changes in the character's circumstances.Mechanically, it's very simple, relying on "common sense" as to what goes where in the house, but there's a decent amount of freedom within those limitations. The one complaint is that sometimes it's hard to tell exactly what something is (is it a bath towel or a kitchen towel? Could this possibly be a fridge magnet?), but I wouldn't go as far as to call it frustrating.All in all, a relaxing and yet touching reflection on our possessions and the stories they can tell. If you've got a few hours to spare, I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Unpacking

_childDocuments_.review: It's an extremely relaxing game with a beautiful unspoken underlying story line. i'm not really one to play video games much but this one I can see myself coming back to many times, while the story line and general arrangements stay the same, you can change the look each time and the game even offers an option where you can free play without the puzzle aspect! It is also really wonderful to see some LGBTQ+ representation as well as the other diverse content. Overall this game is a wonderfully made piece of work with a great soundtrack (Don't get me started on the unique sounds of each objects, they made the timelapse even more satisfying.) that's peaceful to listen to. I will definitely be recommending this for others!! Thank you so much for creating this experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Similar to , roughly 100% of people’s initial reactions to the gameplay of  will include the word “chore,” and just like with , it’s very hard to explain why it doesn’t entirely deserve that label. Even harder, in fact, because  is an incredibly pure experience. To wit, you unpack household items and put them in the correct places. That’s it. ’s engagement came from charm, progression, and personalization, and while  has those to some degree, its true specialty is something the other franchise lacks: story. The story itself is mundane as it gets – normal millennial lives a normal millennial life, basically – but the way it’s told is a masterclass of environmental narrative and characterization. Its protagonist is more realistic and well-rounded than most others despite being unseen and unheard.The game’s microscopic focus allows it to do this – you’d never notice the little details if you had something more important to do – but that’s a double-edged sword. The “chore” spectre is always looming, particularly behind repeated tasks that don’t really change or communicate much. And the more you get into the actual act of unpacking, the more you’ll get annoyed when every book won’t fit on a single shelf or when you can’t stack and arrange things the way you want. You kind of  to get into the act of unpacking, too, because everything else is designed to be as broadly appealing and unremarkable as possible to minimize distraction. With all that in mind, I don’t feel right giving  a universal recommendation, but it’s a unique product that will be completely engrossing to a specific type of person.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a saying among game developers, that ideas are worthless, because implementation is everything.  Unpacking is possibly the best example of this old saying that I've ever seen.  It starts with what sounds like a terrible idea - moving into a new place and unpacking all the boxes - and turns it into something compelling, emotional and beautiful.  The game in Unpacking - the entire game - involves taking items out of cardboard boxes and then arranging them in your new home.  But a few very smart design decisions are what make this excruciatingly mundane premise work so well.  Unlike other "home making" games like House Flipper or The Sims, Unpacking doesn't use 3D graphics, instead opting for a fixed isometric perspective and lovely pixel art graphics.  The satisfying way objects snap into place, or snap together, makes the whole process enjoyable.  You can stack plates together and then move the whole stack with one click.  Clothing automatically attaches to hangers or folds itself up in a way that feels almost magical.  Books automatically stand up, or shift over to make room on the shelf when a new one arrives.  Every click on the cardboard boxes reveals a new item, like a tiny surprise each time.  Manipulating the objects in this game is so pleasurable, it's slightly addictive.  Even the cardboard boxes fold themselves up and disappear with a satisfying swoosh when they're empty.  The audio is absolutely perfect.  There's an amazing amount of attention to detail that went into rendering the various clicks, clunks and thumps that punctuate the movements of all the household items and bring the little world to life.I suppose my biggest problem with Unpacking is that I just wish there was more to it, but adding anything more would have probably ruined it.  It has such a singular focus I can't really imagine anyone wanting to play this for dozens of hours.  But for a few hours, it's a gentle delight.The icing on Unpacking's pixelated cake is a storyline which is a marvel of subtlety.  By examining and placing every single one of the unseen protagonist's belongings, we learn - without words - an amazing amount about her life.  Her hobbies, her job, her relationships, even her health - all of this manifests itself in some really clever and nuanced ways.  It's one of the best achievements in storytelling I've ever seen in a video game.  And yet, I still feel like the storyline is a bit of a missed opportunity.  I was hoping Unpacking would deal with some of the difficult questions that come with ageing:  should I move to a smaller place?  Is it time to get rid of my childhood possessions?  If my partner dies, should I keep any of their stuff?  And when I die, who's going to deal with the mess I've left behind?But rather than deal with any of those (admittedly sad) issues, it simply ends - rather abruptly - when the protagonist reaches middle age, suggesting a "happily ever after" from this point forward.  And that's fine, I suppose.  I can understand why they would want to end the game on an optimistic note.  But had the game attempted to deal with those deeper issues, I think the emotional impact would've been fairly breathtaking.  In any case, I think I can give Unpacking a cautious recommendation.  It's certainly not for everyone, and I would definitely wait for a sale, unless you're comfortable spending $20 on a four hour game.  But for those few hours, it was one of the most unique and memorable experiences I've ever had with a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a gorgeous game that does what games as a medium can do uniquely - makes you feel and discover a story through inputs and actions. Unpacking is about exactly what it sounds like: unpacking your stuff in a series of places as your character moves through life. But the developers had an intuitive understanding of the ways in which this universal experience can tell us such specific things about a person. What items travel through a person's whole life and which fall away as the years pass tell us about a person's priorities and the direction of their growth, while the places they move to mark major life milestones. I'm pretty sure I've made every one of these moves, from going off to college to navigating space with roommates to coming home again, until eventually you find the right path and take decisive steps forward. Mechanics like whether you can move another person's possessions when you're moving into their space (roommates: no, boyfriend: yes) are a clever way to change the mechanics of the puzzles while alluding to the way it truly feels to inhabit others' spaces - and to have one all our own. It was emotional and satisfying to see this unnamed character taking new paths in life and finally moving from cramped spaces where things had to be shoved into every nook and cranny to larger abodes where she had more room to breathe. Our homes - and our possessions - are ultimately what constitutes our lives, and the intimate exploration of one person's stuff was a moving and joyful experience.
