_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished playing the game. I beat it in about 5 hours would have finished it a bit sooner if it hadn't been for getting caught up on one level due to my sheer stubborness.Let's get the one and only negative I have about the game out of the way... Simply due to the length of the game I would say that you should not buy this game at it's full price. I know the devs probably put a TON of work into this game, but the length makes it so that, when compared to other games with just as good of a story with similar price points, I can't recommend this game at the $20 price point. If you can I'd say grab it at a sale for about $15. For some that might still be stretching it but I'd say that had I spent $15 on this game I would have personally felt happy with it. I did get the game for less than that on Humble during a sale, but $15 would have been good with me.Now getting those only two negatives (price and length) out of the way let's move on the part where I compliment the game non-stop.First and foremost let's talk story. This game... has an amazing little story. Is it complex? Yes and no. The game takes on telling it's story in an incredibly unique way. Almost strictly through objects and moving boxes. There is a sparse amount of dialogue seen only when you take a picture of a room at the end of a level and see what our MC writes in her album under it (tip: you can back out of the album and take a pic of each room before moving on to get the dialogue for each room). Everything else in the game is just told through this womans possessions. By placing some of the same objects over and over... and sometimes when you notice an item missing. Like when I placed her cookie jar for the last time and the next level it was no longer there. Implying that this cookie jar that had been with her for so long had finally broken. You can gather the current state of her life based on the condition of some objects, such as her Bard mini and the stuffed pig. Then sometimes it's the placement of items... based on the items around the place she is currently living... or when the game forces you to place something a certain place. The reason I could have finished the game sooner was in the level when she moves in with a boyfriend and I was looking for a place to put a certain object (no spoilers) and I realized... there was only two places I could put it. I put it in one of the two places.... knowing full well that the game would make me choose the one I really didn't want to pick. Sure enough the level ended and I spent a solid additional 20 minutes REFUSING to continue as I desperately looked for ANYWHERE else I could put it. The same thing occurred in that level with a few other objects, that I was thankfully successful in finding far more suitable places for (by my standards) though not ideal. That one object though. I was so angry that I was just saying "No no no no no" to the screen enough that my kid was like "Mama? Why are you saying no?"The placement of things can mean a lot in this game if you can pick up on the subtle stuff being told here. Though even the stuff that isn't subtle just kinda adds up to an overall story of this womans life. Again. You place some of the same items over and over again to the point that you become very aware of when suddenly one isn't there or when it's condition changes.You see the things she's forced to give up and the things she fights for.You'll also notice when suddenly you are placing an item over and over that you weren't before. Like when I realized I had placed heating patches, a cane, and meds several times and I'm like "Oh! She has back problems now. I wonder if it's from being hunched over a desk a lot?"It is a wordless and really amazing way to tell a story. There was never a moment when I didn't realize what was going on in this womans life because her stuff made it so plain to understand. If you're the kind of person who doesn't get attached to objects and place meaning on them than this game might not be for you. If you are though... you'll enjoy this game.That damn pig man... I had a stuffed animal I was attached to as a kid that went missing when I was like 13 and I was distraught over it. I never got it back, but I did have another plush that I eventually got that has gone with me on every move I've ever made and always will. My son has a stuffed boa constrictor that goes to bed with him every night. So I get it and when anything happened with that stuffed pig it was a pang in the heart.This game made me cry.... TWICE. Once during actual game play and once during the credits. Kudos to whoever wrote that ending song it put a sad smile on my face and I loved it.So now that I'm done talking about how amazing the story telling is in this game. What about gameplay?I think I covered it pretty well on accident while discussing the story, but if you didn't catch it. The game play is very simple. Unpack the boxes and put stuff away. You follow our MC to different locations in her life and you open boxes and find places for her things. You can *generally* place anything anywhere. With exceptions being that a toothbrush goes in the bathroom, a coffee grinder goes in the kitchen, etc. As well as when the placement of something is impactful to the story and must go a specific place at which point you must figure out where it goes. It's a very zen and chill "puzzle" game. Though the puzzles aren't really puzzles for me. I very easily knew where everything should go. There were only a few items that tripped me up mostly because I couldn't identify WHAT they were supposed to be. Such as a pair of brown headphones that I assumed were able to go just about anywhere. Then I realized they must be sound reducing or sleep headphones because the only place where the game didn't tell me to move it was when I put them by the bed.And by telling you to move something I mean an item will have a red outline around it to let you know "Hey, move this thing". It's nothing intrusive to the game play.Last thing I'll talk about the art. I adore it. It's some really well done pixel art and I loved the designs of almost everything. The only time I didn't was, again, when there were things I couldn't identify. One of my favorite things though is the covers of books, games, and dvds. I couldn't peg everything but I noticed some things and it put a smile on my face. Like I'm not 100% sure but I'm pretty sure I that two of the games she has are Animal Crossing and Pheonix Wright. In the blue rays I spotted Jaws and a few other movies. My favorite though, and I might be wrong, is I'm pretty sure that for much of the game she brings the entire Eragon series around with her. Again, might be wrong, but there was a set of book she almost always has that just look like the Eragon series to me. I LOVE stuff like that. It made it fun to sit there and look at the covers of things for a second. Even if it wasn't a identifable series or anything and put stuff together. Like if it was clearly an artbook I'd make sure they all went together.I treated unpacking her house the way I would mine.To wrap up.Unpacking is a short and sweet and wonderful experience for those who want to chill and are able to read into subtle story telling. If you tend to see things at face value than you may not get as much out of the story as I did. If you go by the $1 per hour rule on game prices this game DEFINITELY isn't for you because this game comes out to way more than that. I again recommend pick it up when it's around $15 (though even then it doesn't hit the $1 per hour of entertainment unless you plan on playing the game through multiple times).

The pixel artstyle is wonderful as well, with some very intricate details in the items.The underlying story is very sweet as well, and the things you pull out of the boxes give hints at the life of who you play as, as wel as reoccurring items they take with them through their life.All in all, highly recommended if you need something chill to play!The only small downside I've noticed is that some items can be hard to discern if you're unfamiliar with them, albeit for cultural reasons or simply not recognizing it immediately. _childDocuments_.review: If you haven't already, buy this game.   It's beautiful and very thoughtful It's the chillest, coziest game ever.  Also, if you like the Stardew Valley style chiptune music, then you should also check out this game.On a side note, I was a little creeped-out (in an awesome way) how much my actual life resembles that of the "main character".  I grew up Jewish, was a pre-teen in the late 90's,  was always into art (drawing, painting, sculpting, baking, digital art), into Sailormoon, cosplay, DnD, had a bunch of game consoles, lots of stuffed animals (even still), and well, basically the list goes on and on. _childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential and it's extremely fun to play.  However, there are sadly two big points for me that make this game not worth the money. 1) It's length. 3 hours in and the game is finished. A 3 hour game for 15 quid is just not worth it in my opinion. Even if there was some sort of sandbox mode - but nope. Once you've finished the game you can create another save file and do the exact same thing again. And the worst part is, it's just over the time limit for me to refund.2) Some of the items in the game are poorly designed, therefore I had no idea what they were or where they went. If you place an item in the wrong area, once you have unpacked everything, they will flash red. However, it doesn't tell you what it is or even what room it belongs to, so when you have multiple rooms it's a bit of a chore going through each one to figure out where an unknown item goes.The story line is nice and it is pretty and relaxing with nice music too - but the length of the game really lets it down and it is definitely not worth the full amount.

The art style is so cute, the music is adorable and it is just such a cute game that tells a story in a different way than the norm.It is a short game, you'll probably play through it within a few hours (it took me 3.4hrs) but it is super relaxing and I will probably play through it again!It is on the pricier side compared to the contents but I think what a lot of people are forgetting is that this IS an indie game. It wasn't made by a huge business corporation, it was made by a small team of developers and artists. And imo as an artist, it is so so worth the price of a mere $20. (Also, as a small side-note, as an South-East Asian, I absolutely loved the incorporation of household Asian cooking supplies like the fish sauce! _childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun game. It is mostly relaxing and the puzzle elements does surprisingly fit into this type of game hand in hand. The only thing is that some items you come across is less then clear what they're suppose to be, which has led me frustratingly trying to figure out where it goes on multiple occasions.I love the aesthetic they went for - it's unique and overall visually pleasing. Also thanks to artstyle; I'm confident that even a potato could run this game without any objections.The Audio is also a plus, with every item having an appropriate yet satisfying sound when you plob then down! The music is the perfect accompaniment to the visuals and really does help giving the "zen" atmosphere the game is trying to achieve. My only complaint is the gap between when a given track ends, and when it start again, and at first it was a bit jarring as I expected it to seemlessly loop.But overall, it's a fun, short (sub 5-hour), addictive game! The problems I've outlined is me nitpicking essentially, and overall doesn't detract to the experience the game gives. I'm not sure it's a £16 experience, but I would recommend this game when it's on sale if you liked some of the other "zen" simulators that has popped up recently! =)

_childDocuments_.review: I can agree with other users that the game is fairly overpriced. THOUGH I really enjoyed the game. Honestly, i just spent 3 hours finishing it and added more hours replaying the game. It's a great relaxing game, and as for someone who likes chill puzzles, this was perfect. _childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is alright. It's a simple, chill game, though occasionally I was annoyed at the game not accepting certain item placements, or at times I didn't even understand what the item is supposed to be, so I didn't know where to put it.Still, the game is extremely short and has very little replay value. There are no custom levels, level editor, or really anything to keep you going once you beat the game. The game takes around 3 hours to complete, and then a bit more to get the last few achievements you missed (if any). The game is very simple, from its gameplay to graphics to music, and with how little content it has, I can not recommend it at full price. Maybe on 90% off. Or whatever 3 hours of simplistic gameplay is worth to you.I reckon this game appeals to certain people who find the process of organising and finding the right place for everything very rewarding and relaxing by itself. For everyone else, I would avoid, as there really isn't much of a game here, or much of a story.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is some of the best indirect storytelling I've ever seen in a game.The careful attention to detail as you navigate the protagonist's series of moves communicates volumes—all by showing which items remain, which disappear, and which change over time. This is also a game about love, happiness, and contentment, all communicated through the medium of having (and not having) the right amount of space for the objects that accompany us through life.This is a short experience (perhaps 3 hours of gameplay), so if you want more hours for your buck, I suggest you wait until it's on sale to pick it up. If you only care about the quality of the experience, this game will easily earn a place on your shelf.

Things don't have to be EXACTLY in the correct area, but after you've unboxed every box any items that are placed in a wrong place will 'blink'. The achievement list was also easy, nothing overly complicated, but this was a game you can just get lost in with the unpacking and sorting. _childDocuments_.review: I want to say for the record, while I recommend this game for being a cute, relaxing, satisfying experience, I would NOT recommend getting it at full price. I played through the entire game in one sitting, clocking in 3.8 hours and at least 45 minutes of that if not more was me pausing the game to do some stuff around the house before I forgot. So realistically this is 2 to 3 hours of gameplay depending on how detail oriented you want to be. To me, twenty bucks is pretty expensive for such little playtime. I got it on sale for $10 and even then I feel like I may have overpaid a little. There's only something like 8 levels, the achievements are all locked and they end up being dumb stuff like putting up a poster you find in the room. Definitely an easy game to 100% if one cares enough (I don't). There's no real replay value unless you want to see how many different arrangements you can do or something. It was fun while I played it, the gameplay is addictive, but there's not a whole lot of content. So keep that in mind if you're thinking about buying. Realistically I think this game should have a base price of $7.99 instead of $19.99.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is an exceptional storytelling game that takes the phrase "show, don't tell" to the nth degree. You are never explicitly told anything about the life of the character you play as, and are instead left to infer everything for yourself as you perform the titular activity of unpacking boxes in various stages of your character's life; represented by the different houses/apartments they've moved to throughout the years, stylised in in delightfully intricate and stunningly beautiful pixel art. You learn not just surface-level details about the character you're playing as (hygiene products showing your character is female, art supplies and gaming consoles suggesting hobbies, etc.) but also events that unfold throughout the years. Photos once heartfully displayed become shoved into the back of drawers, a degree once proudly hung gets shoved under a bed; moments like these paint such a vivid narrative picture without ever presenting you with a written or verbal story beat, instead using the ingeniously rudimentary core gameplay mechanic of "yes, this object can be placed there" and "no, that object cannot" to guide you in drawing your own conclusions on the significance that each box of unpacked mementos has. While listed as a puzzle game, I find Unpacking to not exactly meet that label, but I'm glad for it because getting frustrated by puzzles would ultimately just detract from how rich and involved the story unfolding before you can be enjoyed. Maybe that's just me though and there are people that are legitimately puzzled and stumped by the task of where in a house a bottle of shampoo should be placed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game will probably seem boring -- even pointless -- to some because it is literally unpacking stuff and putting the items into the correct spots in the correct rooms. No action, no horror, no drama, no dialogue, no....real story. However, for someone like me who suffers from OCD and absolutely LOVES to organize things, and as someone who also has problems with anxiety, this game is so relaxing and fun. It's sort of like a puzzle game since you don't always know where to fit everything and where certain things need to go. You have to experiment a little bit and see what works. It's not a difficult puzzle game but it's entertaining and easy-going. No time limit, so you can take as much time as you like.There isn't a very detailed story but if you pay attention, you do get little but important details about the protagonist who is presumed to be female. You follow her from childhood to adulthood as a mother, and the decor and the size of the homes increases as the years pass (and as she makes more and more money at her job). You can get a general sense of what she does for a living, and while it's all very cute and sweet, I don't see anything wrong with a light-hearted story. Not everything has to be angst-ridden or dramatic.The graphics are very charming, very colorful, and the rooms all look great. There are plenty of items to work with, including the reoccurring Mr Pigs (the plush pig who is in every "level"), Beetle Bard (a pet beetle the protagonist has for a little while), and the ever-growing chicken army. It was fun to see a new baby chick plush pop up in each level.And for the record, no, the plush pig has no name nor does the beetle. I just game them names for fun.The game lasts for quite a while, so it won't be a 1-2 hour experience. It could take several hours and time flies by as you continue to progress. The only flaw I can find with this game is that the music loops, but before it restarts, there's a long silence. It's kind of awkward and it made me wonder at first if the music for each "level" only lasts so long before ending completely. But, no, it loops with that weird silence between each interval. Overall, I love this game and I would definitely play a sequel. This game really calmed me down, which is saying something because I have been stressed out to the max lately.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this review by saying that while I do not recommend it at full price, I still think it’s a good game and that you should get it on sale. I don’t take my decision to say this lightly, but after much deliberation I feel that this is the most honest way to reflect my feelings about the game. Unpacking is a self described zen puzzle game that is part block-fitting puzzle and part home decoration and from the start it’s obvious that it’s jam packed full of love. It’s a charming game; with a wonderful artstyle, calm yet immersive sound design and an incredible attention to detail as it uses the game’s puzzle elements as a means to tell a story. The game focuses on one woman’s life as she grows up and moves from place to place, allowing the player to learn more about her as they unpack and organise her belongings. However, that said, it is a very short game that lacks replayability. A single playthrough will take the average player around two and half hours to complete over the course of 8 levels. I tried to play this game through twice, once on puzzle mode and the second time without that mode on to complete all of the achievements but it really doesn’t have much else to offer outside of that initial playthrough. I’ve been waiting for this game to come out since I first played the demo and I won’t lie that my own expectations of the game are muddling my feelings about the final product and it’s price. However, if I hadn’t had any expectations of the game to begin with, I likely wouldn’t have bought it at full price upon release either. Put frankly, at £15.49 I was expecting more. I think if this game were even five pounds cheaper than it actually is, I probably wouldn’t have any complaints about what I paid for. At the end of the day it is still a good game, but comparing it to other cheaper games that in my opinion tell richer stories and provide more content such as Stardew Valley or What Remains of Edith Finch it feels overpriced. Perhaps this is unfair and this should lead into a discussion about what video games are really worth and how we can properly compensate the people behind these creations but as it stands currently this train of thought soured my opinion of the game somewhat. I talked about this game with a few of my friends and family members after I played it, especially with those that I knew the game would appeal to and those who had it waiting on their wish lists prior to its release and they each individually decided that they would wait to get it on sale. I’d like to add that during those conversations I deliberately used impartial language to describe the game’s content so I could gage an outside opinion on the topic as I was still deciding on how to feel about it at the time so I’d like to think I didn’t influence anyone’s decision at the time and that it is just a honest reflection of what they think the game is worth. It really is a good game but I also think it still has a lot of potential left to unpack. For example, I would have loved to have gone through a series of different characters' lives, getting to know each one over the course of several different homes instead of focusing on just one person, as while it was intriguing it’s method of storytelling doesn’t leave a lot of room to get personally invested. Story wise as well, I feel that it ends a little too soon on a sweet but somewhat underwhelming note.  However, you may feel differently and if you wish to buy it at full price after reading a few more reviews then I fully encourage you to do so. TLDR: I think the game itself is fine but I don’t think it’s worth £15.49.

I think this story-telling is so creative because you get a sense of who this character is and what's happening in their life without a single line of dialogue or any cutscenes.While I really appreciate this game, I think this price point is a bit high for the amount of gameplay and levels the game has to offer. I got the game half-price and played the game twice over (once the regular way with each item in their spot to get gold stars, and once in the "secret" way to get all dark stars), and I think even at that discounted price the game should've been longer. They could've included a few more homes, or having a completely different character and their storyline, which I think could be really interesting since one of my favourite aspects of this game is the creative storytelling.Overall, I recommend checking out the game but only if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is one of those chill, relaxing games that will totally put you in comfort as you experience it. Over the course of several time periods, you have to unpack boxes of your possessions as the protagonist lives their life from childhood to adulthood. The gameplay really helps facilitate your creativity in where to put your possessions as you unpack. It can seem a bit overwhelming with the amount of items at first, but the game has a feature where it will not let you place things in improper places, which helps a lot with the quality of life aspect. From there on, you can engage with the relaxing zen you will feel as you move things around and see what looks best to you. Unpacking is a great case of "show, don't tell." With the items that you unpack, you get the understanding that it's the life journey of this woman who's the protagonist. It starts off with childhood with childhood-themed things then evolves into adult things to unpack. You get the sense of this woman's accomplishments, struggles, and more just from the items that you unpack and the process of settings things down. An actually strong sense of storytelling with no words at all. Unpacking is a game well worth the price tag and you playing through it. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is a relaxing game about unpacking boxes and arranging the items in their owner’s new home.  The standout feature of the game for me was the environmental storytelling.  The items that are brought or not brought to each new house tell us something about this person’s life.  If you play with the mild puzzle elements turned on, the placement of the objects can convey something of their living arrangements.  I didn’t use the accessibility options myself, but I did appreciate they were there, especially if you want to go back and arrange the rooms how  would want them to be.  The sounds used when clicking everything in place add to the very satisfying organisational experience.The pixel art aesthetic is very pleasing to look at, and the objects are appropriately detailed and identifiable to avoid confusion.  In the case of books, for example, there is a level of visual co-ordination to show which books belong to a set, and if inclined you can group them together. Each item feels highly considered and contributes to the notion that these items belong to a real person, rather than blank default items. For a short game like this, there are some fun achievements involved, each one with a sticker reward in-game.  The sticker names give clues as to what interaction may trigger the achievement, though I think finding them by accident and figuring out what to do can be equally appealing.   Unfortunately, outside of this, the game may not offer a lot of replay value.  I could justify the price for myself, I think the game is well-crafted and an enjoyable experience, however as a direct cost/hours of game play, this is definitely on the pricier side.   I finished the game in about 4 hours. I recommend this game for a chill, slow-paced organisational experience, the opposite of actually moving house.
_childDocuments_.name: Unpacking

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very cute, and I love how the "story" is up to the players' interpretations. I love how you can see time pass in little details such as plushies and stuffed animals becoming more aged over the years. I also enjoyed how a lot of the furniture was kept over the years by the player's character.While the first couple of years were relaxing and fun to play, the later years got very frustrating as I unpacked the house as I would in real life, only to tell me that the roll of paper towels doesn't belong on the left side of the sink, but on the right side, or the nail clippers can't go in the drawer, they HAVE to be on the sink. It doesn't necessarily make sense and can make the experience unnecessarily frustrating. Lastly, some of the objects were nearly impossible to distinguish what they were because they're so tiny.Regardless though, this was a cute little game and I enjoyed most of it! 8/10 :)

_childDocuments_.review: Before getting into the review, I want you to take a look around you. Bask in your scenery. Admire the stack of papers sitting on your desk, or your childhood photos decorating your shelf. Perhaps you even have a few souvenirs around your office or room that you can look at. Now, instead of just looking at it, really think about the object. Analyze it. Pick it up if you must. And now, answer me this: what memories come to mind when you think about said object?The truth is, we are surrounded by our own history. Everything we own has a story to tell. Sometimes, it’s not very interesting, but most often, it is significant. Now picture an entire game where you explore this concept, learning the story behind a whole life just from a person’s belongings. That is the premise behind Unpacking, and I think it’s safe to say that the game does a wonderful job at achieving it with , which will be the focus of this review as it’s easily this game’s strongest asset (at least in my opinion). Now time to get into it, as there’s lots to unpack (heh)!—------------------“Part block-fitting puzzle, part home decoration, you are invited to create a satisfying living space while learning clues about the life you’re unpacking”. This is part of the description taken directly from Unpacking’s steam page, and it is pretty much as accurate at describing the experience as a single sentence can possibly be.Your task in this game is simple: unpacking the unnamed main character’s belongings after she moves to a different place. To accomplish that,  At the end of a “level”, items that are outside of a proper location (for example, if you decide that the floor in front of the toilet is a great location for your toothbrush) are marked with a blinking red outline. You then have to move stuff around and find space for the object in the correct location. This is the “puzzle” element that was mentioned, but it can be outright skipped if you so desire via an option in the menu that lets you put objects anywhere. , making it easier to conclude the sometimes herculean task of unpacking an entire life. While the presentation is charming and the gameplay is engaging, that is  For example: sometimes, you won’t have any idea what an object is. This results in you having no idea of where the “proper” place for said object would be, which then results in mindless clicking around until it stops blinking red.Furthermore, the whole system of indicating that you’re trying to put something in the wrong place can be flawed. As an example, think of a common drying dish rack. Would you ever consider putting one on top of a fridge? For me, that makes absolutely no sense. Despite that, the game accepted the top of the fridge as a valid location. Honestly though, in a way, these issues happen due to the  The household objects I can’t recognize are actual objects… They just might not be part of my culture, or it might even just be me not knowing them. The whole reason why they’re there is due to the  But the attention to detail does not stop there. From items that change with each move (such as a mousepad that has a lot of wear after a few moves, and is eventually replaced) and doors being unable to close if a drawer is open, indicated by the door banging against the drawer… this game has it all. But above all else, this game’s attention to detail manifests in its incredible way to tell a tale.  With every move, you get to see the year you’re now at. With that, you can get an idea of what life stage the person is. And after you beat every level, you get a lovely photo album with the main character’s thoughts written right under the photo. You can even go back to a complete level, retake the picture in another room and get a different text. All of these elements feed us the story in a direct and unremarkable manner, sure, but what maybe goes unnoticed by some is the fact that this direct exposition is only a support for the true manner in which the game tells its tale: the household objects. Picture yourself witnessing this situation: someone just moved into their new girlfriend’s house, and during the move, decided to bring a picture of their grandma. It is an item of incredible importance, and they love it… except when they get to the small apartment, there is no room for the picture to be displayed. The person isn’t even allowed to move their girlfriend’s items. And so, the photo ends in a closet. What can you infer about the relationship? I’d say for example that it’s not a very healthy relationship if one party is unwilling to accommodate the other’s most important needs and possessions. Can we, as observers, be sure that’s the case? Nope! But that’s okay. Not everything in life needs confirmation.The example I gave above is not part of the game, but there are plenty of situations that are similar in their concept. If you were to unpack, for example, a piano, you would know your character is into music. Get a magic kit out of the box, and you can infer she’s probably the type to do magic tricks to impress friends. The list goes on, but the gist of it is:  You discover her hobbies, her degree in university, the trajectory her life took, her religion or lack thereof, her career choice, her trip destinations, some of the companies she keeps, her medical history… At the end of the day, is this game worth it, especially at full price? I would say so, but mostly due to the fact that it truly is a  However, the game is also very short (3.5 hours or so), so if you are one to equate the duration of the game to its monetary value, waiting for a sale might be needed. But for me, it was worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a sucker for calming, scenic, somewhat emotional games so it's difficult for my opinion to not be a biased one but I have to be realistic about this game despite how sentimental it makes me.This game is lovely, from aesthetics to how therapeutic the gameplay is. The storyline is wonderfully subtle and emotional in a way that isn't trying too hard and feels very organic. This is a very loveable game for the right audience <3In terms of constructive criticism it would've been nice to have access to a new set of rooms to unpack and a new narrative once finished with the main one. I was anticipating the new journey I'd get to play through now that the first one was over and I was left feeling unsatisfied. This development would obviously be difficult and require a lot of attention to detail but I think it would be worthwhile and something I'd like to see added in the future update.As for the story I've just played through though, it truly was a fantastic experience. I'm looking forward to what the developer has to offer in the future, be that an update to this game or new games entirely.Realistically, Unpacking isn't for everyone. If you're looking for something intense, some sort of challenging puzzle game or a complex narrative this may not be for you. The main motivation here truly seems to be aesthetics, relaxation and a subtle emotional bond towards our character.Overall I'd give the game a 7/10, but if we're given more stories to play through in the future I could see it being up to a 9/10 personally. TL;DR: don't play this if you're looking for excitement or difficulty, play it if you like pretty things or are somewhat mentally ill

_childDocuments_.review: How is it that games can be so effective at making menial tasks fun? It will never cease to astound me that there’s an entire flourishing genre of basic labor simulators, where people will pay money for the privilege of driving a bus or chopping down trees. It’s a testament to the developers, I suppose, that they can so effectively gamify work that most people desperately avoid in their everyday lives. That mastery is nowhere more apparent than in the gentle visuals and tactile joys of Unpacking, a lovely little title that simulates the absolute worst parts of moving. The fact that I can even load this game up a few months after unpacking my own new place is evidence of that.Unpacking takes you on a journey through eight residences as the subject of the story first moves into them. In each locale, you’ll have a selection of rooms rendered in absolutely gorgeous pixel art, blighted by moving boxes that must be, well, unpacked. A whole host of items will come spewing forth from these boxes, from clothes to cutlery, plushies to pills. It’s your job to find a place for each of these, such that the rooms may become a home of at least controlled chaos. Once everything is suitably put away, the game awards you fanfare to let you know your task is done, and that you might move on to the next milestone in this person’s life.It’s a simple premise with equally simple mechanics. Clicking on a box retrieves an item from it, right-clicking rotates it, and moving it around the room affords you a wide array of context-sensitive locations to place it. The first hint of real genius here is how clever that context sensitivity is. You’re not limited to lining up postcards in a drawer or books on a shelf. As you sweep items around the room, you’ll find you can fold and stack clothes, pin up or roll up posters, keep toothbrushes in cups, and so much more. This is key because it turns what would be a charming task simulator into a journey of discovery to see how few limits you have on where you can place things.Once you realize how open the game is in this sense, that’s when the real brilliance shines through. The eight scenes that you are tasked with unpacking are not all the same, and some play with those placement mechanics in interesting and logical ways. This all serves the story, which you might have been surprised at me mentioning earlier, given that this is a game exclusively about taking things out of things and putting them on or inside things. Unpacking tells a moving, nuanced story without need of a single word of text, because it does it entirely through context and the environment. You’re sure to notice the items that keep showing up as you move from place to place, as well as conspicuous absences from your belongings. New items can tell stories all on their own, simply from the point in the game where they first appear.The real wow moment for me was about halfway through the game, where there was a story beat told not by an item, but by the space I had in which to place it. That might sound odd but when I realized what was happening, it hit me harder than so many RPGs or text-heavy adventures ever have. You’ve surely heard the old aphorism “show, don’t tell”, and to me this is the absolute pinnacle of that guidance being heeded. Unpacking does so, so much with just a collection of rooms and items, supported expertly by lush graphics and a moving soundtrack. It’s warm and inviting and meaningful, and so many games with so much loftier ambitions have missed that mark that this game nails.If it seems like I’m gushing too much over a 3-hour game, that’s because I don’t remember the last time a 3-hour game brought me so much joy. It’s the day after and I’m still running through all the things I did in my head, wondering if I missed any additional significance in a mug or hand towel. There’s a collection of hidden achievements (they exist as adorable stickers in-game) that are awarded for doing specific things while unpacking, and I only got about half of them on a single playthrough, so I’m definitely thinking about going back for those. But even without that extra incentive, I wouldn’t trade my time in Unpacking for anything.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

I'd say it's a very cool and special experience that they've created here, its just not that fun as an overall game. Indie lovers will adore it for its concept, but those looking to "game" might be better served elsewhere.Rating: 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Original click-and-drag puzzle game uncovering stages of one person's life through the act of unpacking their possession (as you move-in to new places).(+) Original idea(+) Art style coherent across the whole game(+) Levels are narratively connected and the narrative also inherently defines the level's goals (fitting all your possessions within a small space; trying to fit your things with others' who live there with you; etc.)(+) The designers attention to describe personalities via the items they own(-) The potential of the game is much bigger than what you'll experience(-) A little bit too simple(-) The space and placement restrictions feel rather frustrating than challenging(-) The narrative is too passive, you don't affect the story/outcome whatsoever. The player could use a lot more agency as in, e.g. deciding every level between 10 things to throw away from the characters life and deciding (for the character) which new things to buy or even where to move (setting the direction of their life/the story).(-) The gameplay focus is too binary, requiring you only to fit the things in pre-defined space. Apart from fail/success state, there's no evaluation on how you did aesthetically, how much space you saved, how much sense your layout makes (e.g. are all the gadgets accessible?)

_childDocuments_.review: I'd been anticipating this game all year, checking damn-near daily on twitter for updates or more screenshots after having the chance to play the demo, I knew this game was going to be something special. My beloved dog, Lily, who'd been with me for 16 years and going strong, had a surgery scheduled the day before Unpacking was set to release, a surgery meant to extend and ease her life. This seemed like a ideal situation, I could pull my laptop up next to her and hang out as she recovered.Unfortunately, the surgery proved too much, and Lily drew her last breath in my arms while I lay helpless. It's uncertain the exact cause of death, but the surgery was set to prolong her life. It instilled hopes and dreams and in an instant I watched them do limp, then stiff. Never to be.I didn't get the chance to play Unpacking the second it released as I had intended to do for so long. I didn't have much drive to do anything but mourn and weep. I finally got the chance to play the game, while unpacking the contents of these cute cardboard boxes I also began unpacking my own memories. Each objects in-game reminding me of a real-life parallel, with many reminding me of my precious Lily. It was cathartic, it was an experience filled with joy and sorrow. I remembered things I'd entirely forgotten, and was able to forget about the one thing I desperately wanted to.Unpacking is a fantastic game, a beautiful story, a humble package laced with nostalgia and discovery. I wish I could play through it again for the first time, it's a shame I beat the thing (aside from all the stickers) in about 6 hours, and while I don't think I'm ready to go through everything that'll come with playing through this game for me again yet, I look forward to the day I revisit these cute cardboard boxes and stuffed chickies (and that one knife)

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful ride of a game. The simple premise followed by game play that satisfies my OCD was such a treat. _childDocuments_.review: Unpacking is a puzzle game about unpacking boxes and placing things logically.The game is very well made and while there are no set story, you can interpret your own. The music is super relaxing and while it's not super creative, each tracks are good. The art style is super cute and there are a great variety of items and furniture, even if I think some of the items are re-used way too much. I would say a solid 25% of the items are re-used over each levels.I love how the game is quite lenient on where you can place objects, but while it allows you for quite some freedom, I think some of the items could have more valid spots. I don't see why some stuffed animals can be set on the ground while some of them can't. Also why can you not keep a mug on your table, etc. The furniture could've also been slightly bigger, as the biggest areas to store pans and pots barely holds 2 of them. I could have done a much neater job if the storage was made slightly bigger, but without trying super hard to make everything tidy it did look rather messy once I finished the level. I couldn't make out some of the items due to the pixel art style, so that's also something to note.The game is also definitely way too short for the listed price! $20 for 3.2 hours of gameplay is not worth it for any games ever. Yes the game is relaxing, wholesome and well polished, but there's no replayability once it's over... unless you want to re-reorganize everything over and over...Overall, worth to get on sale because it is very short. Do note that it's a puzzle game despite it's appearance, as the items have only a few valid spots!

_childDocuments_.review: I watched a YouTube play-through of this game (By Seri!PixelBiologist) and just knew I had to buy and play it. I had high expectations for the game, and after playing through it once, my expectations were more than met. There were so many cute little things you notice as you go through the story, the twists and turns-- everything was absolutely amazing. I completed the game in just two days because of how excited I was to play it! The hidden achievements are so cute, and I love that it doesn't list out what they are or how to get them so you have to find them yourself! I will definitely play through the game again in the future. The credits at the end of the game even made me cry! It's not hard to make me cry, but this game deserves sentimental and surreal tears from everyone that plays it! I hope you make an Unpacking 2 or Unpacking Continued in the future! Perhaps for the future life stages. I won't say too much so that I don't spoil the game for anyone who reads this review, but I know I along with many others would love more to play using this storyline and these characters. <3

_childDocuments_.review: I've been on the verge of tears while playing this, and that's a good thing. This game is extremely sweet and cute, and it's kept my interest for hours. I'm autistic, and it's hard to keep my interest in most games that I play, but Unpacking is one of them that immediately engrossed me. Despite the others who say this game isn't worth the $20, I wholeheartedly disagree. There are infinite ways to design spaces, and that is what excites me. Puzzling together a room is so worth it when you see the whole thing come together. And as an artist, I can say that this gives me many, MANY ideas on rooms and backgrounds.I believe I'm almost finished with the game, and I'll come back once I'm done to finish this review off properly.Update: My heart is so warm and full of joy. Unpacking truly is an experience worth the money, and it can be completed in around 4 to 5 hours. 8 houses, and I'm almost in tears. I'll eventually go back and replay the game to get all of the achievements, but for now, I need to cry from joy. This game is the best I've played this year.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the demo I was really looking forward to this game's release, bought it the day it came out--am not disappointed!It's so satisfying putting things in the right places and organizing them, and the developers did a great job not just giving the rooms a sense of place and time but also of showing characters' personalities really well through the places they live in alone. When a picture on a wall is enough to make me dislike or like a character I never see, whose name is never shown, who I only interact with via moving things around in an apartment--that's really good.I love the attention to detail, the little wear and tear and the ways you can stack things and the little noises... all very good.Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the most relaxing things I've ever experienced. It is brilliant in every way. Art, music, sound effects, story, game play, etc is all perfect. _childDocuments_.review: As of right now, the game isn't worth 40 dollars...Pros:- The fact you can pick rifles and calibers separate from each other is super cool. It's unique and actually a lot of fun.- The guns look amazing, the lighting and detailing is really pleasing to look at.- You can choose what the dot on your scope looks like. In general the customization of everything involving the player is awesome.- Environments look pretty enough to pass, they could use a little work, but they are good for now.- Most animal models look alright, but I'll address my biggest issue with them in the cons..- The download size isn't too big, so people who don't have good internet won't wait for a week to download.Cons:- The animal's fur is way too thick and patchy.. They look manged and beat up, I personally think that if it was way shorter and actually covering the body instead of just spots, it would work fantastic. The elk antlers really need work, they don't look like they are trying to catch meteors out of the sky. - Gun sounds are really lacking, they look great but they sound like little .22 rifles.- There are only 3 scope options when it comes to magnification and model.. it would be really nice to have a few higher magnification scopes and the ability to choose what your scope looks like. ( example being: multiple 3x/4x/6x scope models)- The dogs look kinda creepy to be honest lol, they just don't look natural at all.- There need to be more maps (though if the developers stay with this project, I am sure they will add more. So this isn't a permanent con hopefully)- First day dlc looks kinda sketchy, makes the devs look like they are grabbing for money.In all brutal honesty it needs a ton of work, but it has SO much potential to be a fantastic game. If you aren't concerned with money, I would give it a serious try. As for the cons, I think they are pretty easily fixable.  I would hold off on judging the game super hard as of now since its's still pretty new in the market. I think a price tag of 20 bucks would draw a lot more people into the game, and would be a lot more suiting for what is in the game right now.To Neopica, PLEASE do not give up on this game. You have a game that has so much potential that it's dripping from the screen. People are calling out for a good hunting game outside of The Hunter, you have a chance to answer their calls. I personally am excited to see how you guys take this, and I know a lot of other people are too.

_childDocuments_.review: As with most of my reviews, the TL;DR and final verdict will be at the bottom.It is a bit strange for someone who loves animals, to go ahead and buy a game where you shoot animals, but I found a unique sense of peace wandering through the forest tracking animals, the water in the distance, the wind howling through the trees and a bird in the distance collectively brought the forest to life. I come from a family of hunters, but I myself never found joy in taking the life of an animal for sport, or tradition. But I enjoyed the wilderness, tracking an animal only to feel the joy of eventually having your patience pay off. So I decided I would get a hunting sim, but which one would fit the bill?I browsed through steam and found two hunting games that stood out, theHunter: Call Of The Wild and Hunting Simulator 2. I started comparing the two, looking at price, DLC and overall steam reviews. Although I felt wary of HS2 at the beginning due to it's mixed review, so I decided to take the time and read through some of the reviews, to get an idea of what exactly is hated and what is loved. But no review could give me a clear indication, it was either all bad or all good, there were no honest in between reviews, so I took the risk as  I found that overall it gave me the best value for money. I was glad I did, so in the hopes that my review could shine a proper light on the game for anyone considering to buy HS2 as well, I decided to point out everything good and bad.Being a hunting simulation game, HS2 really doesn’t have a story that other games would have,except for the newly added Ranger Mode. The hunting simulations of the current generation have mostly neglected this aspect altogether, the only semblance of a story comes in the beginning via a short tutorial which is understandable, you are after all hunting. While the tutorial was fine for myself as the controls really weren't that difficult to find out. This tutorial is very basic, as it just touches on the minimal controls needed to play the game. For further information, the player will have to consult the bookshelf (i.e. the Wiki section) in the lodge. Without discovering or knowing about this section, the tutorial may not be extensive enough for first-time players of the genre.After selecting a male or female character, a narrator guides you the player, as you learn to search for tracks, utilise your hunting dog, go on a short hunt, and claim your kill. Afterwards, you are taken to “the lodge” where you will prepare for your first hunt without any guidance. You start in the lodge with 5,000 credits, which can be used to purchase scents, calls, and clothing, but most importantly, animal licenses. These licenses range in price, but are necessary to hunt every species at each location. There are three regions: Colorado, Texas, and Europe, with each location having two subregions.Having to purchase these licenses felt like a good inclusion to me, as it added to the simulation experience. It forces the you to strategize and plan your hunts ahead of time. I was frustrated at times when I would come across a fox or Moose with no tag to hunt them, but I had only myself to blame. Ultimately, this feature puts more decision-making on the player and was enriching to the overall experience, even if it was aggravating at times.Once all of this is decided, you must pick where it is you want to hunt and head out into the wilderness. You start out at a cabin (there’s one at each map) and from there, you can go anywhere and hunt anyway you like. You can use your dog to track animals, track animals yourself, or find a stand to call an animal in with the use of scent lures and callers. The dogs are the newest addition to the series and there are three different breeds, all with different functions, that can be purchased. The dogs can be commanded to do different things based on their breed. Beagles are used to track or flush animals by means of barking, this will make certain animals "freeze" for a few seconds while with birds swimming in water, it will cause them to fly. Labrador Retrievers are used to return downed animals be it from water or from afar although I primarily use it for hunting birds on water. German Shorthaired Pointers will point at smaller game that is hard for the hunter to see, they also have a "flush" ability which will cause animals hiding in bushes to run or fly.Your dog’s expertise, drive, and stamina will improve the more that you utilise your dog. As your dog’s skills increase, the better they are at identifying animals, not giving up on searching for animals or just getting lost, and having better stamina to track or retrieve. While the latter two breeds seemed to be helpful all the time, there were times where I was able to follow tracks more accurately and quicker than my Beagle. I also didn't like the fact that my beagle would at times be the cause of me losing "game". While utilising the dogs takes some patience, it is still an amazing feature that improves the quality of the game overall.When it came to equipment I found myself sticking to a large calibre rifle for hunting big game, and either a crossbow or another rifle with smaller calibre rounds for the smaller game. I never really found myself relying on scents or "scent killers", instead I just wandered around at walking speed searching for animals. I believe that using lures could improve the speed at which I find animals, but at the end of the day I got the game for the experience that nature provides and the joy of hunting and tracking my prey.When it comes to sound, Nacon did an absolutely amazing job, nature really comes to life and when I would hear a wolf or deer in the distance I would immediately start tracking the sound. Visually there are some slight variations, at times I would have a smooth experience, while sometimes I would have random texture drops or frame rate changes. By texture drops I mean that if I looked sideways too fast textures would vanish for a brief moment before coming back. As for gunplay there really isn't much to say here, sometimes I would find it difficult to land a shot while at other times I would kill an animal from 300M+, it was never the same experience which could at times be frustrating, but it wasn't too much that I hated the game for it. Overall I truly enjoy Hunting Simulator 2, warts and all. I feel as though the money I spent on HS2 wasn't wasted, and that at the end of the day what I wanted was exactly what I received. Hunting animals never felt like a chore as some of the negative comments would have you believe, at first I was extremely sceptical to buy HS2 because of all the negative reviews, but in the end I am very happy that I went through with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun so far. It's different enough from Call of the Wild since (1) you have dogs to help you hunt, (2) it focuses more on "stalking" as opposed to ambushing, (3) the use of hunting licences, and (4) the practical implementation of hunting ethics. My main complaint is that you need to claim your animals in your cabin on the map before you exit the map and return to your lodge: if you forget to claim your animals in the map-cabin before returning to the lodge you could loose hours of progress. The game should not allow you to return to the lodge if you haven't claimed an animal. Other than that I have no significant complaints so far.Edit 211205: there are a few more issues I have come across since writing the above;1) there are too few animal tracks on the ground for you to discover and track2) there are too few animals overall in the game, especially in the Colorado map3) the above two issues means it is very difficult to make progress, as you can walk around for 60 minutes until you find an animal, and unless you kill it directly you can easily spend another 60+ minutes tracking the blood trails (which does not match the level of injury at all)4) the Beagle is pointless outside of bird and rabbit hunting since after running for 20 meters it always has to stop and pause, which makes the process of catching a wounded deer very irritating, a bigger starting dog would have been more appropriate

_childDocuments_.review: ForewordAs a preface, I want to say that I enjoy hunting games and know a thing or two about hunting in real life. I've spent a significant amount of time in COTW and hunted a lot in RDR 2. I'll be honest, I bought this game solely because it features SAKO and Beretta firearms, which I'm a huge fan of. The screenshots looked decent, and the dreaded IGN review painted a pretty picture. There are also a few paid videos of the game on YouTube by some relatively popular content creators, so if you take the time, you'll get a good look at the game and its mechanics. But what I want to get into is...The Devil is in the DetailLong story short, it's just plain lazy. The environments are large enough, but they lack variety. While in COTW you'll come across landmarks and unique locations that are memorable and interesting, this game offers you the bare minimum. Here's a mountain forest with a river and a few lakes; here's a meadow with some ponds, etc. It's as unimaginative and uninspired as possible. The weather system is really weird. There's a precise "forecast" for each biome, and if it rains there, it'll rain the entire time you're there. There's no day/night cycle.The weapons are a big disappointment. Selective ejection? Forget it. The barrels don't even have bores in them. That shotgun would've exploded in your face. Metal textures and controls look like they're wet, even when it's dry. No matter what caliber you select, the magazine capacity and receiver size remain the same. Iron sights are completely unusable. The in-game reticle stays on even when you mount, and it doesn't line up with the actual sights. The scopes are atrocious—just a jumbled mess of random parts glued together with no thought put into it. The mounts look extremely ugly, especially where the rings meet the base, and to make things worse, the scopes are mounted half a meter forward for one ridiculous reason: so you can see the scope on your gun in first-person view. It's absurd. This is supposed to be a hunting game aimed at gun enthusiasts, yet it insults their intelligence with the worst excuse for scopes and mounts in existence. Variable zoom hasn't even been invented in this game. Night vision and thermals? Also omitted. This is baffling given the obvious sponsorships from big brands like Bushnell, who specialize in optics. They included specific models of binoculars and rangefinders, but not a single real-life scope. Go figure.But wait, there's more. Every ejected casing sounds like a shotgun shell falling on a concrete floor. Enjoy your rifles! This is cringeworthy. What's the point of making a hunting game if you clearly don't care about the subject? I have no idea. And I'm just getting started.The wildlife is also lazily implemented. Animations are hilarious and destroy immersion if you look at them for too long. Some animals move in perfect sync, which is amusing but unrealistic. Red deer look nothing like their real-life counterparts, which is especially annoying for me because they're one of my favorite examples of European wildlife. The fur quality would've been passable for a game made 5 or 6 years ago, but for such a recent title, it leaves a lot to be desired. Traces of bodily functions are scarce compared to COTW, which is ridiculous. Besides tracks and poop, there's urine, food leftovers, and bitten vegetation, with multiple states of freshness, which is cool—except when you find half-eaten corn on top of a mountain in the Colorado wilderness.Callers work 100% of the time on every animal in range. Just spam them while running, and you'll get responses. Then wait a bit, and the animal will come straight to you, stopping for a split second occasionally. It's a guaranteed perfect shot. If you're in a stand, you'll have to try hard to mess it up. The dog mechanics are poorly explained, requiring a Dark Souls-like approach where you need to read to learn that one dog retrieves birds and the other points. Everything else regarding tracking requires trial and error.In their promotional video, the developers promised you'd see predators hunting. I never saw that, though maybe I'm just unlucky. But from what I've gathered, this is the worst animal behavior I've seen in a hunting game. The only good thing I can say about the wildlife is that they vary in age and size. That's it.ConclusionI obviously don't recommend this game. As mentioned in other reviews, this game has a lot of potential, but it's wasted due to the developers' laziness and lack of attention to detail. The main issue is that the developers abandoned improvements and switched to creating paid DLCs, which are terrible. Just read the reviews for the Warden DLC. I only bought the Bears and Berettas DLC and feel silly for doing so. The Berettas have their bores welded shut, and the bears are just as bare as the other animals (pun intended).If you made it through my rambling—thank you sincerely. I hope this helps you make the right decision.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; The game needs a lot of work. not worth the price the devs are asking. Should only be a $10-15 game. In its current state, the game looks and feels like a late 2000's hunting game with slightly better graphics.The option to choose the caliber of a gun is cool, having real guns in the game is cool and nothing is locked behind a slow grindy progression or leveling system. Thats it, thats the only things I like about the game.Not enough animal variation, every "mature" moose, elk or deer I shot was the exact same models as the last. Animals don't bleed out half of the time so you have to shoot it more times than you need to which results in a fine.Tracking is really bad and you NEED to use the dogs. If you're on the hunt for a moose, you need to get the dog to search for signs of an animal and hope its moose tracks that it finds.Gun sounds are lame and weak, they pretty much all sound like some kind of .22 caliber gun (about as loud as smacking two pieces of wood blocks together)The lighting and colours are kind of bad, it's ok but most of the time its hard to see animals moving through grass or bushes.Limited ammo during hunts unless you have a sporting gun which hold more reserve ammo, you can refill ammo at the cabin but that's a waste of time.Scopes NEED more zoom levels and variable zoom, the mil dots serve no purpose unless you're taking 5km shots and only at that distance will the bullet drop reach the 2nd line on your crosshair.The graphics need to be redone, as I already said its hard to see animals walking through grass or bushes, especially smaller game. Animal models look cheap and there is no variation in their models so they all look the same depending on their age. The first Mature animal you get feels rewarding but after that it feels boring, there's no excitement in finding another Elk or Moose because you already shot it before. The animals all share the same behavior, there are no herds. With "the other game" if you track and call out a whitetail deer, the buck will usually be cautious and stick to the tree line and send out the doe's, with Hunting Sim 2, the most animals I would find is 2 animals paired together and they're usually just automated robots that are walking in a straight line until you use a caller and then they walk in a straight line towards you.

_childDocuments_.review: where to start with this one.....i'll get rid of the negativity to begin with.... aiming first person with a compound bow is completely broken it works ok when in 3rd person but its miles off in first... rabbit species are practically nonexistent, I haven't seen sight nor sound of any rabbit species excluding snowshoe hares....pheasants and turkey hunting are back to front you should be calling turkeys in and hunting pheasants.. turkeys are made of paper i shot one at 160m with the shotgun and it died instantly yet a duck at 10m can take 3 or 4 shots and a good old 250 credit fine per extra shot to boot. sika deer look ridiculous, i think the animal designer needs to google an image search of a sika deer. if you run and are out of stamina you can still aim and hold your breath meanwhile your character is gasping for air. Duck and goose calls are pointless the duck blinds are idiotic in placement. animal paths are predictable. I mean afternoon hunt pawnee meadows for mountain lion fast travel to the SW tent go west  and TADA a mountain lion waiting to be shot for a handy 3000 credits (best way to get all guns and gear FYI). mature animals just appear too often and don't give any incentive to hunt for bigger game animals(very counter intuitive). whats the point of having a shotgun bead if you have to aim with that ridiculous circle crosshair? have the devs ever looked through a rifle scope? because your eyeball doesnt zoom in to see nothing but reticle... a bit of detail int he scopes would be a nice touch you know like parallax  or even the circular shape of looking through the optic. the ammo cap idea is idiotic i mean who goes duck hunting with 18 shells? and while im mentioning ducks again REMOVE THE STUPID FINE FOR SHOOTING AN ANIMAL MORE THAN TWICE. no way of telling what a big animal is in the lodge. over under shotguns seem to be more powerful.... (here is a quick lesson in how guns work... a 12g over under and semi auto and pump shooting the same shell and the same length of barrel and the same choke wont have any major variation in shot speed etc but the DAMAGE WILL REMAIN THE SAME, its a 12g they should all be the same on the damage scale. chokes and barrel length affect range but that's it.... this is the same for every other firearm. I've played it giving the benefit of the doubt for 30 hours and I've played the game to the point of being done and nothing else to do(but hunt rabbits that I'm sure don't exist in game). this is the furthest thing for a simulator, big game hunter 95 was more of a simulator and it was a heap of garbage. having got the negativity out of the way here is some light at the end of the tunnel. the lodge is awesome in general, i mean i like the idea of choosing your loadout etc. the dogs work really well for their intended purposes. lighting in game is beautiful but i guess that is due to the use of the unreal engine. the idea of tags is good but they need to be more expensive.  desert maps and the Colorado forest map are perfect sized for hunting but jeez the others need to be increased 10 fold.. but they all look great.overall is it disappointing YES, is it better than HS1, Yes. would i recommend it ... not so much there are better games out there that offer a much more in depth hunting experience... we hunters don't need to have replica IRL firearms to make us play a hunting game... maybe you should focus on game play over ensuring your character can use a branded gun or bow.the ball was in your court to bring something new to the hunting gaming community; unfortunately you fell WAYYYYYYYYYYYYY short of giving us something to keep us interested. better luck next time i suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of potential but it's not well executed. The UI is horrible, the dog is cool but takes a while before he becomes useful and the main thing for me is that the guns don't feel great.In "Call of the Wild "or "Receiver 2" we have great feeling ballistics at a much lower price point than this. The gun feel in this game is tech demo level at best, and it makes for an unsatisfying experience.Let me compare it to the .30-06 in COTW. When you pull that trigger, the gun cracks in your hands and bucks up to point at the sky. It feels good. You also get visual confirmation that your shot landed from the animation on the animal.In this game you get a slight popping noise and next to no animation to confirm that your shot was any good. It just feels a bit naff really. It could've done with another 6 months of development to further refine it.Refunded.

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be named "Get Fined!"You would be fined for everything that the developers don't like. A deer that you hit doesn't die and drags you around entire the map for 2 hours already, but you don't have more time to play today? You're fined!You bagged all the animals, but need to leave urgently, and can't travel to the cabin before exiting the game? Fined!You shot a goose on the fly, it felt in a middle of a knee deep puddle, but you don't have a retriever dog? Fined! No, you can't make your feet wet to pick a bird, but you can cross waist deep rocky rivers, that's allowed.Two shots were not enough to drop an animal in it's tracks, and you pull the trigger once more? Once you're in the game, just prepare to get fined whatever you do, and spend many hours buying what you missed.Besides that...- Elk cows sound like bulls.- No slugs or buckshot for shotguns. Birdshot only.- No clock in the game, how much it's until the sunset?- Ducks and geese take off and land like VTOL planes. Come on guys, send your developers to the nearest pond where they could see how the birds really fly!- Animals can ignore you running nearby, but flee when you raise a rifle in a tower 150 m away.- Markers on the map are huge. Any marker you put there covers area maybe 50x50 m or even more. Overall model of markers is much much weaker than you'd find in most popular free hunting mobile apps IRL.- It's so much blood in tracks of a wounded animal that it's more sometimes than a total weight of the animal.- Urine of animals is shown as puddles that are never absorbed in a soil.With all that above, the game is a total disappointment. _childDocuments_.review: Even if we ignore the fact that this is a 2020 game, it is still worse than a 2015 game. It appears like all the work and time are put into collecting ideas only. Everything from the environment to sounds or gameplay; looks like a total failure. The first thing you need in a hunting game is the surroundings because you will spend most of the time waiting patiently for a hunt. But traversing on the map was just awful and felt like a punishment. Flora and fauna, looks like unpolished mesh rendering. Terrible audio sections; environment audio sounds like a busy subway, not at all close to the beauty of nature. Walking on grass resonates more like stepping on wet polythene trash. You might think that maybe the game lacks in visuals or sound only, but NO! It is a disaster. The map looks straight out of a kid’s game. If you somehow identified an animal from the same color contrast and got a kill, you might get excited to see which organs you hit and how was the bullet impact. But your excitement will collapse after seeing a second-grade quality kill review infographics showing animal organs as blocks. No bullet hit trajectory, just a red block showing which organ got hit. You start the game and select your character from the two options. Then a tutorial describes mandatory aspects of the game, ranging from tracking footprints, hunting structures, how map/waypoint works, tracking the hunt with the most and only important part of the game; our dog/companion. At the start, you will get a beagle, and you can name your good buddy whatever you want, pretty basic tutorial covering all the key points. Then you visit your lounge, which is hands-down the most pleasant and only polished aspect of the game. It’s surprisingly well-crafted and filled with do-able interactive segments, like a store to buy hunting licenses, clothing, gears, and equipment. All the weaponry have official names, and you will recognize them instantly if hunting is your real hobby. The list moves forward with the option to buy different breed companions, configure loadout, and visit the shooting range. The shooting range was well built but was a kind of boring.  The first problem/drawback starts here, during the time of item purchases, most of the people will buy random items that look good and end up spending all their money, as it’s not mentioned anywhere that you don’t own any primary equipment and need to buy from scratch. That results in people buying different companions, all licenses of a single location, or some clothing apparel and end up going to hunt with incomplete gear. Either a tutorial for a lounge or a pre-made loadout can solve this problem. You can choose 6 different locations, grouped into three geographical areas. But they all have the same color contrast and hardly any wow factor.The Graphics section is a total failure, no cap. Poor rendering and color scheme ruins the fun of being in the wilderness for a hunting session. Not at all expected from a 2020 game, as several advancements already done in the field of game designing. Rocks look like a lump of mud placed randomly into the map. Bad rendering of trees and grass makes it look dull. Animals look like a potato sack quality. All this comparison is based upon the cost that the game is asking. Overall, they are ok-ish, but with high value, there come big expectations. The effect of fog was somewhat pretty and enhancing the lining of the horizon. Tracks are nearly impossible to spot. Blood looks like red acrylic paint. Dog animations are great, and their behavior is well worked upon too. All the graphic work in the interior designing of cabins, hunting structures, lounge, and shooting range deserves appreciation.Just one word to describe it–Awful. The environment and stomping sounds are just horrible. Animal sounds are somewhat okay, but the callers are loud and weird. In the name of environmental sounds, it was just loud noise and birds chirping. Narrations were good, along with dog interaction sounds.Decrease environment volume. When you reach the lounge and about to enter store purchases, only buy 243 calibers as most of the hunt can be done with the default 270. Select one region and only buy licenses that support 243 and 270 caliber. Don’t purchase a new companion, clothing, or anything at the start. It will take some time to train your canine companion, so don’t get frustrated. It uses tents for fast travel, so more the better. Hunting an animal and not bagging it will cause a penalty. Trails are too hard to spot, so it’s better to enable trail indicators.Each dog breed has certain traits, pointers will point an animal, while retrievers will retrieve your hunts. But you will need to train them to be more efficient. Don’t purchase, not worth it. Guns DLC are not useful and somewhat buggy. Stick to the default gear present in the game. Not recommended even on sale.  Dogs are probably the center of attraction for this game. Overall, a lot of good ideas, but it was not much fun and feels unpolished. Maybe in the coming future, new updates will push the game sales and fix the negative ratings. But right now, it’s nowhere near the asking price and not logical to recommend.The other title in this genre, “theHunter: Call of the Wild™” is a lot more polished game with realistic aesthetics. If you want to read a review about it, you can easily follow up on this link.Rating: 5/10
