_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I've finally finished every achievement (play time 29 hours, for you achievement hunters) and can officially say that I can't recommend this game. Let's start with the positives: -  I love the variety of trees in each landscape. It is obvious that the artists did not skimp on assets, and the color palettes are lovely as well! -  Trying to tastefully arrange furniture in the limited space while maximizing room score is challenging, especially as higher value functional furniture needed in late game takes up more space, but it's a good challenge, especially going back to earlier hotels and trying to upgrade them to the highest level.And.....those are the best things. For me however, the list of complaints is much bigger.-  I view myself as an average player, not trying any crazy speedrun glitches. But i still ran into several issues that caused me grief. None of them were game breaking or caused me to lose progress, but all of them were annoying. Here are a few examples:     * Items refusing to place. I had to restart the game once to get this fixed, though other times, it resolved itself after exiting from the UI build menu and then re-entering.     * The escape key randomly stopped allowing me to exit out of menus. 90% of the time, I used it to exit from the build menu. Sometimes though, it just wouldn't work.     * Recipes can be bought multiple times (unlike other one use items) if you don't close the shop after every individual purchase. They can only be used once, and cannot be sold or trashed, so they can just take up permanent inventory space.     * Visual glitch after character introductions and image flashbacks - these happen in the middle of dialogue, then clunkily makes you repeat the dialogue from before the cutscene, and it looks..... off..... when transitioning between these.     * The most annoying bug for me is the AUTO set-up button on cooking does not function if you load the page while something else is 'cooking', even after the previous item finishes cooking. Every time the timer finishes, i have to back out of and reload the next recipe i want in order to get the AUTO set up button to work was incredibly annoying. It happens  time and should have been fixed at this point in the full release.     * Visual glitch in loading the Guest Booking UI - if you click out to the 'Cabins' menu, then open any other cabin's booking UI (which you will do when booking up all your hotels in a row in late game), the booking menu shows the previous subpage highlighted, though you always open up on the first one. This is a small issue, and apparently a common unity menu error, but it is confusing. I often though that i was on the second subpage but was actually on the first. Just annoying enough. -  You can sleep the night after 21:00, but you have to wait until then. A lot of game progression is locked behind completing quests, and several of the quests are locked behind waiting for several days to pass (such as getting several 5 star reviews, or booking several of one type of guest). In the mid game, this isn't *too* bad, as you will have many quests running simultaneously, but at the beginning and end game, it's very frustrating. You can't get to new areas to explore, even though you've basically finished the management/decorating part for that section. At the end of the game, i just had to wait through the days, as i had done everything else possible and just needed time to pass.-  All items are assigned to price value in your inventory.....which is useless, as there is no place to sell them. There is limited storage and inventory space, but no way to get rid of unwanted items. This becomes a major problem when paired with the ability to buy multiple of the same recipe, which cannot be used. You could functionally soft lock your game this way, if you wanted. -  For example:     * Item pick ups can be dismissed by pressing E     * Dialogue can only be progessed by pressing Space     * Dialogue  can only be selected by Mouse, not Arrow keys + Space     * The Tutorial pop up, which does not pause time or take priority, need to be dismissed by Mouse.      * All UI menus can be dismissed by pressing Escape (unless it glitches)     * Random story progession pop ups  pause time and take priority, and need to be dismissed by Mouse, not Escape, which works for all other priority UI.-  to a few locations, making some tasks very arduous. There is a loading screen between every location, and it's frustrating to have to walk through multiple areas and their loading screens JUST to get to the bus stop to fast travel to another area with a loading screen.-  Don't even get me started. When I saw the cooking UI at first, I was pleased by how unique it is! And it is: using action cards to follow a recipe, and adding ingredients to each action. It's very cool! But it's also very frustrating to use in a way that could be easily fixed. Examples:      * There is a set timer for every recipe. It's 15 seconds long - not long enough to leave and do a different task around your hotel, slightly too long to just wait through. I figured that I would just set up my next recipe during this period..... but the cooking menu  until the timer finishes! All you can do is  at your next recipe until the timer finishes.     * The AUTO set-up button sounds great, but you need to exit and re-enter the recipe to get it to work if you pick the recipe while a prior recipe is cooking. annoying bug.      * The AUTO set-up only stocks enough ingredients to make one of each recipe. You then have to manually drag in more of each ingredient to set up multiples. This half defeats the purpose of the AUTO set up button.      * After making a recipe, extra items sort incorrectly back into your inventory. Thankfully there is an auto sort inventory button. -  - I get that this is aesthetic for places such as 'Darkgrove', but it is hard to navigate without turning my computer brightness up a ton (and then getting blinded when i open a menu).-  It's pretty lo-fi and fades in the background easily, which is nice at first, but there is so little variety that it felt lacking pretty quickly. At night, there is no music and it is very eerie. - Unless the character has a new quest for you (rare), then there is only one piece of dialogue per character.-  I started skipping through their conversations, as the player character of Hank the bear boils down to 'I'm stupid! Whaaa?', and Fin the shark just spews out corporate jargon. - , such as the ability to drag items between inventory and chest, or for items to auto-sort when moving between storage. You have to click the item from a chest, then scroll down all the way through your inventory to an empty space to place is. It could be much easier.There are too many bugs and quality of life issues for me to recommend this game to anyone. It's nice to look at, but for an adventure game, your exploration is limited, and for a management sim, there is surprisingly little to manage once the hotel is built. At it's best, Bear and Breakfast is a decorating simulator with limited decorations (why can't i put couches in my lobby? there are no general use chairs!), quests, and gathering materials.

_childDocuments_.review: I would of liked to give this game a positive review due to the fact that its adorable and a fun little way to pass the time with building and keeping your guests happy. _childDocuments_.review: This game could be really cool, but sadly through a significant number of bad choices the experience is really really bad.After playing for nearly an hour, all I have done is read dialogue and get stuck because the games' tutorial is so poorly structured that you will actively get stuck when playing the game. The player shouldn't be able to get stuck in the tutorial, ever, the tutorial is the safe space, where failure is shown, but never punished.Additionally, narrative is a layer on top of a fun gameplay loop. If I have to rely on the narrative pulling players through the gameplay, there is something seriously wrong. Stardew Valley knows this (one of the inspirations according to the devs), so i am curious, and a little disappointed that the devs weren't able to replicate this for their own game.

_childDocuments_.review: Is Bear and Breakfast fun? Generally yes, but in the lategame, it gets very tedious to do anything. _childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: Are you a cozy gamer? Have you seen everyone talking about this game and playing it in videos? Do you think it's the next best thing in comforting games that give you endless opportunities and hours of fun?Welp, sorry, but this isn't that game. It's super enjoyable, at times, and very cute. There are some things about this game that are great, especially when there are tasks within your control, but outside of that the game feels rushed by developers and lacking some seriously important traits of a good cozy game.Number one, there are countless impassable objects. Everywhere you walk there are trees, logs, stones, water formations, etc. that you can't traverse. It's a big pain, as they add nothing to the game other than annoyance. Sure, there are a few that block you from areas you aren't supposed to go to yet, but those make sense. The rest? Just something that seems like a bad decision on the developer's part.Second, this is a cozy game that, at times, requires you to walk away and leave the game running for a few hours. You will get to points where the quests you need to complete are out of your control. You can't just go to sleep at any time (like Stardew) and there's nothing you can do but wait. I don't know about anyone else, but when I play a cozy game it's because I'm anxious and need an escape, not a window of time and then another stressor I have to come back to.Third, and maybe most important, this game is stressful. As you level up, the items you need all seem to require the same materials. These materials are far and few between, and you'll constantly feel like you're behind. This is, in my opinion, a big issue in the design of the game. You shouldn't need the exact same items for every craft at one level. It literally makes the game impossible once you reach a certain point (without, as I said earlier, walking away for a while).Honestly, and this is an honest review from someone who just loves games, this game had a ton of potential to be better. It's fun, it's cute, but it isn't well made and thought out. Genuinely, Cult of the Lamb has better crafting and tool plans than this game. I'd still recommend it, but very cautiously. K thx.

_childDocuments_.review: Some graphical bugs but overall a really good game that will only get better with updates. _childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The grind to play this game is overwhelming, and the story is charming but flat with story beats that don't belong. The characters are funny, witty, and sometimes complicated, but were overall the only reason I kept playing, which does not make for a game.The game was a gift, and I DID enjoy playing, but this game is absolutely not for people who cannot stand grinding. You spend much of your game running among the areas, hitting up every spawn point for materials, then crafting for an almost never-ending slew of increasing needs until the VERY END when they start to provide you with managerial furniture that actually help you in a significant way which allows you more freedom.In a way, giving you these furniture items as a reward at the end is a satisfying 'thank you' for playing the game for me, but when progressing the story has to be balanced against a heavy load of...:1. Managing 5 locations with increasing needs such as raising comfort levels (attributed to select furniture), decorative influence (also only select furniture), hygiene needs, heating needs, food needs, and entertainment needs that your guests increase demand over time.2. Gathering up materials  to craft the aforementioned items, of which are heavily RNG related, by meandering through maps that aren't easy to navigate.3. Satisfying enough guests to keep a steady flow of money in order to buy things you can't find naturally in the environment or buy things to make travelling easier; harder to please guests give you more money which means you can't skirt by on the minimum forever.4. Gathering trash to get decorative items, of which is the worst grind of all....it almost becomes a chore to play. After a while, I honestly went and downloaded a cheat menu mod to help make things fun, which truly is a shame, as there is clearly so much love into this game that I have longed to play it since I saw its trailers! As for the story, I won't go too far into it, but there's elements that just seem... thrown in. They don't fit well. This coupled with the fact I didn't know where the main story ended and the 'epilogue' began left a worse taste in my mouth. In its current state, the only people I could recommend this to are players who are beyond patient, and are happy with what I would say is close to an MMO style grind for progress for a solo player game.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, it is relaxing and cute resource management game where you are a bear named Hank. Your job is to build hotels to attract humans and make money while learning about the stories of the people/animals of the valley. My favorite parts were seeing the cute art when learning more about characters and organizing the rooms in my hotels. If you are like me and heightened expectations give you the heebie jeebies, I encourage you to actually do the management quests and not leave them until the end because the rewards for them give you so many quality of life changing tools. I would not recommend this game if you do not like resource management games or games where you have to walk around to do things because this game requires that. I personally like those things so I had lots of fun.There are only two things I would change about this game if I could. 1) For quests that require a certain amount of things to happen I wish there was a counter keeping track of how many more you had to do (eg: 10/50). The second thing I would change is cooking, the recipes are not in alphabetical order or by food points, or by anything else I can tell. I wish there was a way to organize them or search within them, it would make cooking in the game a lot more fun and less stressful. Overall, it is one of my favorite games and I hope to see more from these devs in the future.P.S. Sending Ioana healing wishes and lots of loves to the team <3
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: (24 Hours in) I love the game so far. Its cute, plenty to do, and I enjoy the simple build mode.But: Too much talking and no option to skip. You have to spam the space bar to skip through each individual sentence. Literally.Day time feels really short. I often get stuck and can't really see even when it's "day time"Mission Progression is confusing: One of the main story quests is NPCs asking for food. However it's food that I don't have the ingredients to. Example: Julie asks for a recipe that involves cheese early on. It's not clear how or where to find cheese. I still have not figured out how to get ingredients even though I have progressed in the game far enough to have level 7+ recipes. Help? I have talked to everyone on the map possible and it feels like something is not in orderThe game depends on the decoration score, which you can improve by buying items with trash you pick up from your guests. But trash is barely dropped and as far as I know there is no other way to get it yet. The only reason I have stopped playing is because of the issues, but It's still a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game.This is a cozy, and hilarious, property management sim game. You're handed properties, 1 at a time, to build rooms of and manage booking guests, matching rooms with their tastes and providing for them if needed (bathroom facilities, food, etc. - though the game eases you into those mechanics). You go at your pace, there's no penalty for say, not sleeping a night away.This has awesome dialogue, the characters' personalities shine.I'm starting into the fourth area, and much of the game so far is resource gathering, clearing out areas of trash/valuables, building up/decorating the properties, booking guests, providing for them, optimizing.Some things get automated as time goes on, so getting overwhelmed by managing so many properties at once is minimized.I was just starting to struggle with inventory management a little when I unlocked a way to expand it, YAY.Note, there is no combat or relationship/dating mechanic.The cons - the day/night cycle moves fast. The game only seems to pause when you're in build mode to edit your properties, or when you go into the main menu for the game. it moves as you're reading the tutorial, and it moves as you're in dialogue. a lot of the feedback page is filled with people requesting more pauses or the day/night cycle to change, so hopefully that won't be a permanent complaint, but for now, time passes too quick.That's basically the only complaint, so far. and that's overall a pretty minor irritation for me, though I also see it as an accessibility issue (I read quickly, not everyone does, YMMV).EDIT:  I'll also add, there's room for improvement with the UI. I could see a lot of potential for quality of life changes, stuff that'd improve efficiency.Anyway, 100% recommend. If you're into cozy management sims like Stardew Valley, Animal Crossing, or Spiritfarer, you're bound to enjoy this too.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully chill and cute game about being a bear running a B&B.Even if I'm only a little way into the game I am very much enjoying this chill management-esque sim.The characters are wonderful and full of personality and although there is a niggling worry that this may turn into a more management heavy game, I don't think that's what the Devs have planned as the game feel very relaxed as I have been able to go at my own pace.The start might be a tad slow paced, but I wonder if that is due more to many modern games being more frenetic in comparison and these Devs seem to be really aiming for a very relaxing, chill game with a cute aesthetic .Overall a wonderful little game that is well worth a play. Very much recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't had any interest in gaming for about 2 months, this game eased me back into it.It's cozy, there's plenty to do and it's not your typical mindless grinding like I expected it to be. the characters are funny and I've been enjoying it a lot. _childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: If you really enjoy building rooms, decorating them, Gathering Resources and managing guests expectations then this is your ideal game. Resort Manager Simulator and running errands for NPCs is 95% of the game. Tips: Having more rooms early on lets you book more guests and earn more coins; however as guests expectations for a resort increase, you'll need more space to fit the upgrades. Once I got to the last resorts (6th,7th & 8th) I did a complete remodel of the first 5 resorts to increase the size of rooms-in order to complete all quests. Also, anytime you're in A24, go to the junkyard and gather the scrap; trust me, it's the only things that couldn't spawn fast enough for how much copper and iron plates are used to craft furniture.If you expect much in way of storytelling, you'll be sorely disappointed for the time spent vs. the payoff. You have to get through many quests before anything resembling a story is presented and then it sorta implies that it's made-up leaving you wondering what the truth is. That would be enticing, except it doesn't lead you to clues to piece together what happened (like a mystery would). More like you talk to some characters a couple times during each quest (while managing several resorts), hunt down some object, ingredient or fix up a building until you've done enough grinding to progress the 'story' because it's never clear which quests will. It goes from hardly fleshing out the world (NPCs don't have anything different to say except when they give you something to do for them) to introducing...'larger than life characters' to explain this important event. And then it just ends. I sadly wasn't satisfied and feel quite cheated on the mystery aspect. The bread-crumb pacing was so spaced out between the grinding that it all felt hollow. I would've liked to see them pursue the other mystery clearly going on with Finn; sadly his involvement in anything also just ends, with no answers. *sigh* I wanted to enjoy this, it sounded great. I even finished all the quests just to see if it would give me something more but no. I can't recommend this game; save yourself the great disappointment if you want a game to invest in.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute and cozy game about running various bed and breakfasts in a small secluded part of the world. The game starts out a little slow, but eventually there is always something to do and improve. All of the characters are charming and fun to interact with. The devs have been active and have fixed many of the initial bugs that I encountered. If you are looking for something chill to play that gives you good vibes, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I'd recommend Bear & Breakfast, but not for the reason I would usually do for a management game.Basically, I found myself really enjoying the story - firstly, it was a nice surprise to have something that was properly interesting and genuinely funny and touching in a genre that doesn't usually even bother with story, but also it went to some quite unexpected places.However, I'm a little more torn on the core hotel-building mechanics of the game.It's functional (occasionally guests bugged out and got stuck for no apparent reason was the only bug I had) and it's reasonably extensive; however, I found it quite repetitive.  While you do have multiple types of rooms to build, a lot of them use the same basic approach (like area of effect) so it doesn't really change things up that much.  A good example of the problem is that you have to put a minimum set of items into each room to make it meet the requirement for that type of room, but there's no options around that - you can't create just a toilet, it has to have a bath and sink too.  Or you can't have a combined cinema and museum.  And high level rooms require so many items I ended up cramming things in with little regard for layout and decor, especially in the smaller places.It could also have done with a few more quality of life features (e.g., the ability to filter and sort things in the shops). And for a game with some environmental messages it was weird that you had no way to sell items back to shops or recycle them - you just have to trash things you don't want/need and then they magically  disappear. [edit: recycling has just been added to the game.]There was also an odd balance to resources availability where almost everything is so abundant it can re-spawn before you've been fully round the map and you have to throw a lot of it away, and then a handful of things that are very rare/expensive and create a sudden roadblock.  They did tweak some of these, to be fair, but towards the end I was sleeping multiple days away just to get cash and it just made it feel a bit pointless.But I'm being harsh - I did enjoy the game and I would freely admit I did rush through the story and it really shouldn't be played like that.  It's supposed to be a chill game and you should play it focusing more on developing each location properly, rather than just hitting the minimum requirement so you can get to the next bit of the story like I did.I'm really hoping there's either a DLC or sequel - I felt there were quite a lot of dangling threads that could be picked up (some of the NPC stories don't really get resolved as such) and I'd love to play more.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: This game is addictive! If you enjoy a task based game where you can collect items, cook, decorate, build, and improve your buildings this game is fantastic. There is plenty of story, the characters are very cute, and it's very immersive. The only cons is there is no system for selling back or breaking down items you build which seems like such a waste and some of the cooking tasks and where to find ingredients is not very intuitive. A quick search on google fixes those. All in all I would highly recommend this game to someone who likes cozy games to unwind. It's provided me many hours of stress relief and enjoyment.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, but it's not an exceptionally good game. If you enjoy low-energy resource management and foraging, this is a good way to scratch that itch for a little while. The story and the structure, however, is a bit lacking. The majority of the plot is backloaded, meaning you'll be about 30 hours in before you get anything beyond vague implications, and then you'll get an entire plot's worth of revelations for questions you didn't even know you were supposed to be asking dumped on you at once. The worldbuilding and characters are all promising and interesting, but there's not much to it beyond interesting concepts. You are given best friends who you more or less immediately stop talking to, and stop having anything beyond their one mandatory line to say, you cannot make friends or progress any sort of relationship or story with these otherwise very interesting characters, and it makes the whole game feel a bit underbaked and lopsided. Ideally, the story would be spread throughout the story progression, and the questions planted early and given time to grow. It's not a bad game! The story, when you get there, is interesting, but not quite enough to make up for the time it takes to reach it if you don't already enjoy the resource and hotel management simulation. If you do like resource and hotel management simulation, absolutely, give it a shot, you will probably have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games I really wanted to like (and in some aspects did), but it's too rough in places where it really counts.tl;dr: The story is too weak to make it interesting, the management tools are too weak to make this a simulation and the controls with the Deck are abysmal. It's very pretty though.The good:- great art style and animations- they came up with very unique places, props and characters- tood sound design and musicThe bad:- playing this with a controller almost broke me; drilling down into menus, moving items in the inventor, etc. is extremely tedious; sometimes you wonder if they really tested this; this is meant to be played with keyboard and mouse, not on a Steam Deck :-(- there are weather effects (quite dizzying at times) and they are not cropped out when you are inside a building; that makes it actually hard to do things in there because you can barely see;- the cooking mechanics are punishing and an absolute catastrophy on the Deck; I found out way too late that I could outsource this to Julia if prioritize some quests for her;- the story and lore is pretty lame and I don't know how it should relate to the actual gameplay; I didn't care for it and the "conclusion" of the main quest at all;- no satisfying end at all- it's not a business simulation either as it doesn't have the depth nor does it give you the tools; if you want to see graphs and reports this is not for you;- the building mechanics are mediocre, but they really crumble when you want to remodel and optimise your resorts

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral review. :/ I'm going to play this a bit more to see if it gets better late game, but judging from the early game content, it feels really slow. I really wanted to like this game because of the art style and how endearing Hank is, but I can't seem to dismiss the issues I'm facing with the progression of the early game. To keep it simple, my main issues are:1. You can skip the night by sleeping through it BUT only when it's midnight. Some of the quests are time-locked so you end up just standing there during the night after gathering materials across different maps. You need to wait for the guests to leave after a certain amount of days--which wouldn't be a problem if there was a time-skip button, or make the sleep through the night button functional once the sky becomes dark and not wait until it is midnight. Feels like an idle game.2. This might be my fault, but I was misled by the preview/trailer. I thought it would be more sim-driven compared to story-driven.. so it feels very stagnant at the moment.3. While walking around is not usually an issue, it... feels incredibly slow, once again. I'm used to playing casual sim games (SDV, RF4, Harvest Moon, ACNH, etc.) so I have no inherent negative feelings towards walking around to explore. However, in B&B the early game exploring makes me feel like I'm wandering around with no purpose WHILE walking slowly. I am forced to wait until the next zone opens up after I finish a quest. Wish there was a sprint button somewhere.I will try to update my review as I continue playing the game, but for now it gets a 5/10. I was not expecting to idle for that long (or at all, actually) in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★☆☆ - 2.5 out of 5 StarsAs much as I want to be able to recommend this game, I find that I just cannot.I've played through the majority of the game now and have found myself wishing several times that it were over already, and that's never a good sign.First off, the game devs really were not upfront with what this game really is and it feels deceitful. From the trailer and description, you think you're going into a game where you run a singular B&B and you upgrade it overtime, which sounds amazing. But when you get into the game, you find out your bear is going to open SEVERAL B&Bs, motels and resorts, each one bigger than the last, and that you have to run around managing them all, never really getting the chance to connect with any of them. Why weren't they upfront with that? The description literally says,  Not a great start.- The art is adorable, truly. It's beautiful and satisfying to look at. The artists are talented and it looks AAA.- A few of the characters who help you are super helpful once you unlock what they do (Wade & Julia).- Some of the dialogue made me laugh out loud and I love the bear's emotions during conversations.- Most of the NPCs you meet are super cute.- The bear's personality is adorable- Most of the items in the game are cute- The devs updated for Christmas and left the items in the game and they are so cute, especially in the winter area- Fast travel is nice and makes sense- I love the different areas you can visit- The NPCs you meet are only in your life for a short amount of time. You meet two of the bear's friends in the beginning and I haven't seen them since I opened the first B&B. Why even have them in the game? They seemed to serve no purpose.- You have to run several B&Bs in different areas instead of one B&B that you get to upgrade and make your own.- The game isn't balanced; some of it (getting supplies for upgrading) is way too easy and other parts (cooking) way too hard or they take too long.- You can build the rooms yourself and add items to it, but you have to upgrade the items in order to maintain the "score" your customers have, and those scores force you to add more and more and more to the room, resulting in it looking SO cluttered and horrible. The rooms end up looking like an episode of hoarders.- You can put things in front of doorways or in customer's ways without realizing you are; the game lets you. Then you have to spend time looking at your cluttered rooms, trying to figure out where the item is they can't get by.- Customers walk through walls or refuse to use items. One room you have to build in order to progress in one area is a movie theater and I have tried EVERYTHING to get the customers to use it. They won't touch it.- There's an incredibly beautiful snowy area which was my favorite and the customers walk around outside in blinding snow in shorts and a tank top. Holy immersion breaking, Batman.- The music is just....no. I hated the music so much, I turned it off and literally played Stardew Valley and Undertale music on Spotify.- Cooking is awful. They made it a sort of weird card thing? But the worst part is that it takes FOREVER, and it doesn't make sense. How do I only get one bowl of soup from making tomato soup? Who only makes one bowl? Is it one of those single serve to-go soups?- There's an NPC you can get to help book customers and he doesn't even book them by their stats, resulting in unhappy customers, and he's SUPPOSED to work that way. Why? I didn't even bother using him, as useful as he could be. Why make him so useless?- Instead of getting money back for decorative items you no longer need, you have to throw them away. That is just SO frustrating. - The place where you buy decorative items is a mess when you're late game. It's hard to find the items (needs a way to categorize) and you can't tell how big the item is until you've bought it and tried to place it, so a lot of times you waste your money.I was really looking forward to this game and now I'm just really disappointed. I think I would recommend the game if you're playing very casually and understand going in that you're going to be running around to different areas, taking care of multiple hotels. But if you're thinking this is like Stardew Valley or want something with real heart, this isn't it. In the end, for all the clutter, it still feels empty.TLDR: Nah, bro. Go play Stardew for the 3rd time.Edit: I went back and finished the game. Still 2.5 stars. This had such potential, but it's really disappointing. I hope the dev keeps trying, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I have now 100% completed this game. More strongly do not recommend. This game has an identity crisis. Gameplay is blatantly front loaded. Around the 5-10 hour mark you can feel when game testing stopped. Progression is unintuitive and unsatisfying. There is a serious lack of variety in things that make gameplay enjoyable, like rating based decor for the rooms. And there is a gobsmacking amount of complexity in things that don't matter, like the meals (because the guests do not care about the variety of meals). The actual management sim elements of this game are weak. There isn't even a way to track your day to day profitability unless you wrote it down on a piece of paper yourself. What the hell. Every room looks the same because the only way to meet guest objectives is to use the same furniture. The shop interfaces don't update when you make a purchase. So you can purchase the same 1 use item (like a blueprint) multiple times, then be stuck with the copies in your inventory. There is no sell mechanic in this game at all, so the only thing you can do with items that you no longer want is throw them out (if you can figure out where the trash function is. Good luck on that one). Did you click that single recipe purchase more than once? Too bad. No take backs. The approach to inventory in this game is infuriating and the only container you can build in the game opens at the bottom. So you have to scroll UP to see how much space you have or what is in the container. It is maddening. For building furniture and objects, there are 2 filters to navigate through the blueprints you acquire, and 99.9% of the blueprints appear in one of those filters. It is ridiculous. Building anything on a 2nd level is buggy as hell. The whole building mechanic is very restrictive because every single item in the game is tied to a specific room. A room which must be built in an entirely closed in space. Did you think it would be nice to put a few tables on your veranda for the outdoor dinner crowd? No ♥♥♥♥ you all dining must take place within the enclosed dining room area. If you stick with this game long enough to automate the management of your B&Bs, it stops being a management game and turns ENTIRELY into a tedious story narrative where the gameplay mechanics you just spent 15 hours grinding through don't even come up. The characters talk way too much about stupid ♥♥♥♥. Sometimes when you finish dialogue you'll get a little quest auto added so you can see your next steps. And sometimes you don't - and there is no way to track the conversations you had or repeat what was said if you missed something. So have fun with that too. I didn't come here for sad animal stories. I came here to simulate running a small business as a bear. I don't know what this game is. But it isn't any of the things I bought it for.

_childDocuments_.review: I think one of the other reviewers had a good point, the developer should look to tailor the quests and progression for each inn to fit the character of the zone. It works decently and I like the CTRL+Click improvement to move things between inventory. The issue remains that it can be tough to meet the demands of picky guests without cramming the room with a bunch of random furniture. But they are making progress.

_childDocuments_.review: - it's missing some pretty basic sim-game features (can only skip time from 9pm to 8am, can't sell/recycle crafted items to get money or resources back, drop rates on some of the crafting items are not great - better after the 1.1.1 patch, but everything still feels like a slog.  - You never really get to the point where you can fully automate everything and just let it run in the background - best you get is 'mostly automated, but still checking back every twenty minutes' while doing other stuff, because it's expensive and some of the automations aren't really cost effective. - the ending to the main "build a lodge" plot seems to be basically "hah ha, ur dumb and have participated in capitalism"- they drop hints all along about 'hey, there's something creepy here in the woods", and nothing really comes of it until you've beaten the main plot, which took me about 30 hours of Mostly Idle play.   When the Spooky Woods plot thread finally resolves, it's still pretty underwhelming.  [note - review was originally written for the games's 1.0 release.  The devs have since patched the nail drop rate and moved time skip up from midnight to 9pm, and adjusted some of the employee costs - all of these help, but don't change the fact that it's still a slog through. I've updated parts of the above to account for the changes.]Overall, the game is split between being a text based adventure that has a promising story but doesn't fully flesh it out, and a hotel management sim, and doing both of those things poorly.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start with that the game still has some issues. I clipped out of the map, got stuck in loading screens, and got stuck in building mode. All where I had to restart the game in order to fix the issue.Having said that, the game itself is very pretty and relaxing. The art style is very pleasant to look at and the core gameplay is simple but fun. You manage a couple of inns all with slightly different traits and upkeep types. You can really let your creativity flow with the layout of the building and the decorating of those rooms.Downside is that the game is pretty badly paced. There will be moments you are running around, doing and collecting 101 things, and the next you will have to just.. Wait 10 in game days. There are some side quests that can entertain you in the meanwhile, but for most you will need to have certain blueprints unlocked or progress made. So end game is a lot of waiting around.It would seem the game was very well play tested for the first 2 inns, and after that it becomes a bit.. Wonky. Even tho with all it flaws, I enjoyed the game a lot. Just be aware that it is not a perfect game. Especially not nearing the 'end game'.I'd give it a 6.5/10. Not bad. Good core gameplay. Pretty visuals. Some bugs. Bad pacing.

_childDocuments_.review: Cozy, warm, nice. A great choice for fans of Stardev Valley, Traveller's Rest, and similar titles. Don't get discouraged by the intro; it's a bit long and boring, but then the good stuff begins. Building, arranging rooms, cooking... that's the good part of the game.Unfortunately, similarly to the intro, the general plotline is boring. _childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, cozy game with a lot of humor and that perfect edge of something dark and mysterious lurking at the seams without subverting the genre. What could be better than playing a regular, old, actual bear who somehow gets tangled up in running property management? (Seriously, if you're not wearing clothes, people scream and run away from you, because you're just a bear. It's awesome.)My two complaints: Does the game fall prey to the all-too-common issue of having to choose between the style you actually like versus the style that is worth more points? Yes. Yes it does. But all the items more or less fall into "log cabin chic" anyway, so it's not as onerous as tends to be in other games.And, there's an end game quest where I couldn't find the location I needed to go to due to the entrance being tucked away in the very top right hand corner of the location, hidden behind the HUD, so I never noticed it in the first place when I was exploring, let alone subsequently when I was scrubbing each map trying to figure out where the heck I was supposed to go.But do I recommend the game? Yeah. It's a lot of fun, and very entertaining. My recommendation? Take it slowly. Don't rush to unlock the next location, make sure you're totally happy with the rooms an accommodations you have before pressing on. Work to retroactively improve before moving on after unlocking new stuff. It can be a little overwhelming if you just assume you can do it all at once and push really hard to unlock everything all at once. Not that I know from experience or anything (nervous laughter).
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking for a good sim management game so I was excited when I saw this title.  The art style and animations are charming.  That's about the only component that I enjoyed so far.The quest-gating of content is suffocating and completely stifles any creativity or exploration elements.  The game punishes you for getting too far ahead in some quests by completely ignoring whatever progress you've already made.  This means you're either stuck standing around waiting for the day to pass so you can finally make your character sleep to pass the time until your guests leave reviews, OR you just get stuck.  An example would be quests like "build a 2-star bedroom" that I think requires you to place upgraded beds.  If you already placed upgraded beds, there are no better bed blueprints than what you already have and you're out of space to build more bedrooms... you're SOL.  Very frustrating.I should have quit 2 hours ago so I could at least get a refund.  I only stuck around hoping that unlocking more content might alleviate the monotony of the pacing.  I was very disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is a good decorating game, but not the greatest management game. Most of your time spent in this game is gathering resources and constantly re-decorating your Inns. At the same time, you can't really choose how to decorate since the best way to get your Inn score up is to use one set of furniture. This game is very simple, if you want something very chill and laid back, this game is for you. Don't really expect much story or much interaction with the other characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

_childDocuments_.review: Bear and Breakfast is a laid-back management adventure game where you play as a well-meaning bear trying to run a B+B in the woods. Hank and his friends find an abandoned shack and, equipped with their teenage ingenuity, turn it into a money-making bed and breakfast scheme for unsuspecting tourists. As your business expands so do the mysteries of the forest, and Hank soon finds himself uncovering a plot deeper than the wilderness itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Bear and Breakfast

name: Filament
detailed_description: ALSO BY THE PUBLISHER ALSO BE THE DEVELOPER Buzz 'Filament's a wonderful puzzler, and it's also wonderfully maddening' Eurogamer 'Space-age fantasy, a cosy puzzle game, a narrative-driven adventure – any one of these descriptions fits a part of what Filament is, and the result is tantamount to genius.' PCGamesN 'Hard. Filament is hard . So hard, in fact, that it took me somewhere in the ballpark of a week to beat the demo. Filament is also very good . So good, in fact, that I willingly spent that week wracking my mushy brain over a few dozen puzzles.' PC Invasion 70 'When a game is built around a single style of puzzle, it had better be good. Filament is that kind of game.' Shack News 8/10 'It is beautiful, both visually and audibly. I couldn't really give a suggestion on how to make this game any better.' The Digital Fix 'Filament does one style of maze puzzle but performs it exceedingly well' WCCFTech Marmalade Edition Make your mission loadout complete with the digital deluxe package - The Marmalade Edition ! Includes the base game plus: The stunning original game soundtrack featuring all the tracks from Filament. DELUXE EDITION EXCLUSIVE: Marmalade's Sketchbook which will give the artistic insight of the eponymous crew member, including sketches of actual in-game puzzles and objects from around the Filament Corporation ship. About the Game The truth is out there. Somewhere. Board The Alabaster, one of The Filament Corporation’s flagship research vessels, and try to wrestle control back from a mysterious complication which left the ship locked down and the crew missing. With only the help of Juniper, the ships stricken pilot, face fiendishly difficult puzzles that will push you to the limit in a bid to uncover what happened to the crew and why they disappeared. A single-player game with complex, yet ultra-addictive puzzles, challenge yourself to board the Alabaster, then challenge yourself to leave. Freely explore the ship, solving over 300 challenging and varied puzzles. Approach them at your leisure, in (almost) any order you like. As you survey the ship and solve puzzles, you will be in constant contact with Juniper. Learn more about her, her crew, and what happened as she opens up to you. Search crew logs, messages, records, as well as personal items and knick-knacks found around the ship on your quest for the truth as to what has happened aboard The Alabaster. Learn who the crew were, and maybe in doing so, find out why they left.

_childDocuments_.review: Filament is a puzzle game that feels like it took a lot of inspiration from "The Witness": It features a huge amount of puzzles which are all based on the same mechanic (laying a single cable around a number of pillars to activate them and unlock the exit), but provide lots of different variations within this mechanic (e.g. pillars that must not be touched, pillars that must be touched several times, pillars that change the color of your cable while others can only be activated with a specific color, etc.). These puzzles are placed in a small sort-of open world, so you'll usually have about a dozen of different puzzles available to you at any time. If you get stuck on one, there are always others to try your hand on before you return with perhaps some new ideas.Like "The WItness", the game does not hold your hand. It does not explicitly tell you how the puzzle mechanics work, instead it gives you enough puzzles to deduce the mechanics on your own. Personally I like this approach a lot, since it gives me a sense of discovery and of gradual understanding of complex systems that otherwise wouldn't be possible. However, if you're a player who prefers explicit instructions, keep in mind that this game was designed for a different audience.The puzzles can be quite tricky and although there are usually just a few elements in each puzzle room, the high amount of possible moves and interdependencies makes it hard to brute-force them. You usually have to really understand what you're doing. Some of the solutions can be quite tricky to find, though it does get easier once you develop some general strategies. I didn't find it _too_ difficult to solve all the puzzles without help, but some of them _did_ require many attempts and upwards of 30 minutes. If you're (like me) a persistent player who likes to develop their own strategies in a puzzle game, this game's puzzles can provide a proper challenge and an amazing, ultimately very satisfying experience. If you struggle with some of the puzzles, there are online walkthroughs for all of them, as well as a new in-game help system that I can't talk about as it has been added after my playthrough. I'd recommend to be careful with walkthroughs because if you use them just to "skip" a puzzle without properly understanding it, then you're actually making it harder for yourself to solve further puzzles which may build on the respective mechanic and expand it.Filament is not _only_ a puzzle game though, it also features an interesting, well-told story. Solving puzzles unlocks more than 100 log entries and occasional voice-overs that gradually unravel the multi-layered stories of a six-person crew on an exploration mission in space, who are confronted with a strange and potentially dangerous mystery. The way how the game presents a SciFi story about space exploration, but focuses on the interactions of characters that feel very human, reminded me a lot of "Tacoma".The game's presentation is pretty good considering that this is mostly the work of a three-person team. Every room in the spaceship looks unique, and most feature lots of details that are not only interesting to look at, but may also open up a whole new layer of dozens of _additional_ puzzles. Technically, games like "The Witness" or "The Talos Principle" have much higher production values, but Filament used its (probably much lower) budget exceptionally well. It's noteworthy though that this is a third-person game from an angled top-down perspective, so for some players it might not feel quite as immersive as a first-person puzzler. It's "world" is also much smaller than those of the other games I mentioned.Personally I had a _lot_ of fun with Filament, and I'd rank it together with "The Witness" and "The Talos Principle" among my favorite puzzle games of all time. In addition to the high quality (and staggering number) of puzzles, it also features a more detailed and interesting story than games of this genre usually have. And while smaller in the scope of its "world", it makes up for that with beautiful and diverse environments, as well as an incredible attention to detail.Conclusion: If you like challenging puzzles with innovative mechanics in a game that expects you to experiment with the mechanics (rather than holding your hand), don't pass this one up. I rarely write "glowing" reviews since I'm a terrible nitpicker who always finds _something_ to criticize, but this game deserves one.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: So I don't like giving thumbs down as this is clearly a well-made game. But the main issue I have is that I have not managed to find any strategy to think my way through the puzzles. Maybe I'm too dumb to figure it out, maybe I missed something, but for me lots of trial-and-error is the only approach that ever worked for most puzzles. The inability to develop strategies and think puzzles through means in the end it's just a lot of trial-and-error, and when I solve a puzzle I don't feel smart, I just feel I got lucky after trying 20 different combinations. YMMV.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: If you are here for just the puzzles, you will be very very satisfied. That was me initially. "Challenging", they say. "Best", "Satisfying", these words caught me hook, line and sinker. BUT, aside from the puzzles, there are even more SECRETS lying around in plain sight. "Bonuses" I would put it as. Those are even MORE exciting to discover!If you have read all up till here, please don't waste anymore time and just BUY this game and support the dev.Potentially the best buy this year. Definitely up for some Steam award!

_childDocuments_.review: Don't usually bother writing Steam reviews, but after 40 hours of slugging away at this, I have to recommend it. Maddeningly difficult, but absolutely worth it.The puzzles in this game are essentially mazes, where you have to lay a wire that touches every pole in each puzzle without crossing itself. Some of the negative reviews talk about trial and error gameplay, and there is a little bit of that, especially as you figure out how new puzzle mechanics work. But after a while, the game's logic starts to click. You realise how the wire divides the room, meaning you have to leave yourself routes for later in each puzzle. You realise how you can use a pole as a turning point so long as you take the narrowest angles around it first, meaning that you have to grab THIS pole before you grab THAT pole... The game isn't (primarily) based on guesswork - it's just very very difficult!The narrative side of Filament is really strong, too. You're trying to free a woman named Juniper trapped in the cockpit of a recently-abandoned spaceship - but you can find the email logs of Juniper and her crewmates by entering codes scattered around the ship, and thus learn what she's not telling you. The environmental storytelling is especially brilliant. Too often game designers think that environmental storytelling means graffiti artists writing personal essays in block capitals on their living room walls, but Filament gets it right. It puts a simple thing in the wrong place, and lets you put together the devastating details for yourself. Difficult to give a good example without spoilers, but when you beat the game, it's worth coming back to explore the ship one more time, just to slap your head at everything that was hiding in plain sight.The Witness comparisons are apt - Filament shares the same total dedication to a core concept, the same high difficulty, and the same learning-by-doing approach to teaching the player (not to mention the same secret-hiding sensibility). If you like (or want to like) The Witness but its faux-Zen attitude drives you up the wall, Filament will suit you.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I was suggested this game since I'm a huge fan of The Witness. While I can appreciate that this is fairly well-made and has a somewhat engaging story that is uncovered as you progress, the puzzles themselves are simply not very fun. Once you understand the rules for each type of puzzle it doesn't really feel like each progressive one teaches you anything new. They just become increasingly complicated so that you aren't so much figuring them out logically but are engaging in tedious periods of trial and error. The fact that you can't solve the puzzles in the overhead ("Focus") view also seems to add to the difficulty (in a rather cheap way). Many of the puzzles would be somewhat easier if you could see the entirety of the puzzle while solving instead of working your way toward the end only to find that one requirement early in the solution has been nullified by a slight angle change in the filament brought on by a latter part of the (incorrect) solution. In an overview you would see this immediately and just rewind rather than realizing very late in the solution that you were wasting your time all along. I love logic puzzles, but this just leaves me feeling more like I'm fighting the interface and just "brute forcing" much of the times.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This wasn't for me. The biggest problem for me is the unpredictability of the wire mechanic. Since you can't actually know how the line will stretch before you do it you basically have to do every possible solution over and over again until one works - you can't just ponder an idea and go "nah, that won't work", which wasn't very fun for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry, I can't recommend this. I want to like it, and I keep coming back to it, but it just frustrates me and I need to move on.  It's difficult and I can't seem to find any knack for getting better, and I'm lacking the will to push forward knowing I'll never finish this game even struggling with beginner series of puzzles.  There's so much love and care put into this game that I want to like it, but I just get frustrated playing it and get little sense of accomplishment in solutions.  The environments are great, the voice acting is well done.  There are main puzzles and side-quest puzzles to unlock a somewhat interesting story.  But in the end I can't stand coming back to the puzzles and trying one more combination/permutation of a failed solution.  Even when I find a solution I'm not sure why, it's feel like I'm just trying different things until something works - and if I had to redo the same puzzle tomorrow I'd probably struggle through it again. I'm going to force myself to delete the game so I can move onto something else.  I do wish I could like it though.  I normally should like this style of game, but I think this is for hardcore puzzle players only.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: TO ANY THE WITNESS FANS:Nothing this game does is inherently bad. Good graphics, good soundtrack, fun and varied environments... But in terms of puzzles, this game probably is pretty far from what you are looking for:This isn't a game of learning, this is a game of trail and error. This isn't a game of "AHA" moments. The only exception to this is a certain small section of other puzzles.It's true this game has a similar concept and structure to The Witness. You have one simple way of "inputting" puzzles, in this case wrapping wires around pillars in a specific order. There are multiple types of pillars, each having their own rules. The big difference with The Witness though, is that in Filament there isn't much development in terms of expanding or combining the game rules. This is more of an almost meditative experience where you semi-mindlessly try brute-forcing wire wrapping combinations.Many of the puzzles are pretty hard and can take a long time to solve, but not in the way of them being hard to grasp or figure out. No real "Eureka" moments, just systematically progressing through multiple dozens of pillars until you worked out a combination that works. After having played to about 50% completion, all puzzles really started to feel like a chore, even with all the different puzzle concepts. Near the endgame you'll get a few very complex puzzles, but these as well are just a chore to progress through.Now, this game has a hidden section of deeper puzzles, which are a lot more fun to figure out. Unfortunately the length of that section wouldn't really justify buying this game for...The game also has a plot, but it honestly was just very confusing, and the ending was.... unique...? (read, bad)Looks like a solid game on paper, but unfortunately isn't.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzles feel more trial and error than skill based sadly. Opening puzzles were good and communicated the rules well, however as puzzles become more complex there are so many possible paths that are sabotaged very close to the solution in ways that are extremely difficult to foresee.There is an obvious comparison to The Witness, however in that game you can usually apply the rules as you go to complete puzzles. I really wanted to like this but didn't find much satisfaction in the more difficult puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: The best puzzle game of the year.Nice background story, You are an astronaut who investigate abandoned spaceship and try to find out what happend.The spaceship is huge and very detailed. The  graphics are very good , beautiful surroundings everywhere, the music is really relaxing.All puzzles look similar , you control a robot to connect those pillars with filament. The puzzles have different themes, so you wont get bored. All puzzles are well designed. About 1/3 of those puzzles are very challenging, you have to think for a while. And another 1/3 of those puzzles are quite difficult and complex, you can easliy stuck for hours. This game will definitely make you question your own intelligence. According to the developers, the total amount of the puzzles are 300. I have played more than 42 hours and I only solved all puzzles on 3 floors, not even start the puzzles on the bridge, and there are a lot of puzzles there, and they are so far the difficult puzzles I have ever seen.If you got stuck, you can check my walkthrough videoUpdate:  all bridge puzzles solutions :

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I ultimately could not enjoy it. I found the puzzles to be difficult, and not in a fun way. Perhaps I just need to "git gud", but I think there is still a problem with the puzzle design. The puzzles have an enormous possibility space, since there are thousands of ways to weave your threat through each level's pillars. This is not a problem on its own; the problem is that finding the correct path is more like searching for a needle in a haystack than reasoning logically about a problem. If you are going to have very complicated puzzles, you need to give players a way to get traction. For example, if there is a way a puzzle can decompose into smaller sub-problems, then the player can make progress by solving the smaller parts. This rarely happens in Filament, since the wire can often connect pillars which range across the whole play area. Another way to make good puzzles is to teach the player certain "tricks" via intro puzzles, and then later have complex puzzles which are built around using these tricks in progressively more complicated ways. I do not feel that Filament does this well.Everything else about Filament is either great or acceptable. The space station atmosphere is mysterious and interesting, the lore is engaging, the voice acting is... fine... and the meta-puzzles and exploration seem like they would be cool. But the core puzzle solving is not enjoyable enough to support the rest.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I very much wanted to like this game. Many have compared it to the Talos Principle, which is one of my favorite games of the last decade, and I'm a big fan of puzzle games in general. But Filament is just... tedious. There's no real strategy as far as I can tell, just trial and error. And while I do feel a rush after completing one of the puzzles, it's short-lived because in the end it seemed like nothing but luck and persistence got me there. Maybe I'm too dumb to get it or my mind doesn't work the way that Filament rewards, but this game is just not fun for me. Nice soundtrack, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Despite some of the things I'm about to say, Filament shares a lot of similarities with The Witness, the biggest ones being the variety of different mechanics and the fact it teaches you new things by letting you solve very simple puzzles and gradually ramping up the difficulty. (And they do get very hard). Due to the nature of the mechanics some puzzles felt like I was just brute forcing them.The game also has some interesting side content in the form of environmental puzzles that you solve in computer terminals and they range from being pretty fun to just downright bonkers complexity.When solving the computer terminal puzzles you’ll receive lore pieces in the form of text messages, but the problem is that there is an insane amount of them (mostly being just fluff) and the terminals are excruciatingly slow and uncomfortable to navigate their bad UI.Besides the messages there's also the main story being told through the companion character that talks to you throughout the game. But I have to say after finishing the game I have absolutely zero idea about what the story was about.On the technical side I encountered some bugs like the cable getting stuck on things, the robot completely separating from the cable and sometimes just inconsistent behavior when wrapping around certain angles leading to you being able to solve puzzles in ways I think were unintended. Also when zooming out you can’t move your character and when using a controller there aren't any button icons which seems like a very basic thing to have.On the artsy side the game looks beautiful and features a pleasant soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great puzzle game at a more than reasonable price point. I need to keep updating this review because even at 30+ hours it's still going strong and remains very satisfying to play. I have been actively streaming it for a few friends and everyone gets really captivated by the ambience and mechanics. Everyone just gets really involved and just wants to join in. I don't review games on steam very often but I felt this game really deserves the extra attention. The depth is absolutely impressive and there's just so much game here.  The aesthetics and music are great and I can really just lose myself in playing it. The calming nature of the game makes it so I don't mind spending lots of time stumped on a puzzle. I think the level design has been great so far. I have enjoyed the various methods it has mixed up puzzles in clever ways and kept the challenge level high. I've had tons of "aha" moments where finding a solution feels like a great accomplishment.People will compare it to the witness, which it absolutely matches in depth with lots of extra hidden objectives to complete. I feel comfortable saying it's even better just because of it having more of a total package. There's more story here and the way its told is pretty organic and well done. Everything that's hidden is in plain sight, while still not so obvious that most will be challenged. The deeper intricacies of the Witness seemed beyond most players. I feel like the secrets of this game are far more achievable without any hand holding.  If you're the type to enjoy puzzle games I feel like you can't go wrong. Absolutely give this game a chance because you won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Difficulty : 4/5 (Very Hard)Global : 3.5/5 (Very Good)First, Filament is a VERY long game. It's not your average little puzzle game.Second, it's also VERY hard you're warned.It features lots of various puzzles and mechanics that are nearly impossible (or at least very hard) to anticipate. You have to try things and deduce while doing the puzzles but they are not unfair unless you're not even trying to think and just hope it's gonna solve by itself.The difficulty is progressive for each mechanic with the first puzzles acting as tutorials and the last ones being very hard (but the ship is free to explore so you can just leave and go back later on a puzzle if it's too hard).And there are also "environmental" puzzles hidden in the ship like in The Witness but harder which are a nice bonus.Apart from that the visuals are really good and the way the story is told is original with several twists. The end could have been explained better though.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is interesting, and the puzzles are challenging. However, the puzzles themselves aren't that satisfying to solve.One thing I like about other puzzle games is being able to put down a hard puzzle and randomly solve it outside of the game. This has almost none of that. The puzzle layouts and solutions are very long so it's hard to keep in your head. Also, some pathing is a bit finnicky so you actually do need to try out the path in game to see if it could work.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing puzzle with a lot of content and challenges. You're on aboard a ship and have to explore and investigate what happens to it while solving the various puzzles that are around. The puzzles are based around yourself within a room being connected to a cable and have to touch these tiles and make it out of the room. It starts off rather simple as you learn the ropes as to how the game is structured but does get quite difficult indeed, like there being different colours, the tiles moving or even just the layout of the room to solve. It does become a 5head game as the game gets much more complicated and various aspects are added to the puzzles. Though it is nice that there is really an order to do them in. I went on to explore the ship and you can go ahead to do some harder ones if you wish earlier as you have access to them. The visuals looks great with the top down view and the details within the ship, as well as your little astronauts running around looks very cute. The audio/soundtracks is also quite pleasant as it has a soothing tone of music playing and solving the puzzles. Along the content of the puzzles, there are also plenty of bonuses to look out for such as various items, records and messages which adds richness to the story. Overall, it absolutely is a great puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are hard for sure, but somehow manage to give nearly zero feeling of reward for finding the solution, since it's largely brute-forcing stuff.The accompanying "story" doesn't tie in to the puzzles, or bring anything useful to the game. Instead the spaceship set that relates to the story just makes it tedious to go between the different available puzzle levels.UI is very low-contrast, and why is it not possible to move around while in the directly-overhead view?One thing to note: if you actually enjoyed this game and found it satisfying, you might like to consider a career in PCB layout which will present you with all the same maddening routing challenges, with the added benefit of actually achieving something tangible when you find the solution.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sad to say I don't like Filament, but I'm not sure it is worth a thumbs down.I'm a big fan of masyu puzzles, and Filament reminds me of them, if about ten times as complex.  I wouldn't mind that, except that as other reviewers have noted, Filament has three "flaws":- The puzzles aren't on any kind of organized grid, so you can't look for familiar patterns of node types and utilize learned strategies.  Filament comes down to trial and error.- The puzzles are huge, even from early on in the game.  Solving them is time-consuming, and often frustrating because you can never see the whole puzzle on the screen at one time.- The puzzles have to be solved in one linear unbroken attempt.  This is the biggest difference between Filament and masyu, in my opinion -- masyu puzzles can be solved in chunks and the loop connected later, but in Filament, if you solve the entire puzzle except for one node, you have to unravel the entire loop and start again.Filament is HARD, and it is not easy to say whether it is challenging (good) or difficult (bad).  It is almost certainly some of both, and at the end of the day, while I am impressed with the puzzle design and mechanics, I don't enjoy playing Filament.  Solving puzzles gives a sense of relief, not success, and that is a shame.There's a story (and a starship you walk around) stringing the puzzles together, but mostly it feels like it gets in the way of the gameplay.  Unlike in Tacoma, which has a very similar narrative setup, I wasn't made to care particularly about any of the characters described in the logs, and the one person who speaks to you introduces themself by insulting you.  Interesting choice on the part of the devs.In summary: buy this one because you enjoy squeezing your brain through a straw.  It's not for me, but it was a near enough miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this to play on the Steam Deck since it is "Verified" but there is a graphical issue that I was unable to resolve, so on my stock Deck I was unable to play it.On a technical level the puzzles are sound; they have the logical elements and progressive mechanics of a good minimalist puzzler, but I definitely see what people are talking about with the guess and check especially at later levels. There are so many options and no logic to anticipate the solution and the stages are dark so you kind of are just wandering around until something works, you can't look at the puzzle from the start and puzzle it out. There are parts where I can see the wire clipping into the wall that I thought would have invalidated the solution, or anticipated an opening big enough to walk through but it's too small to pass when I get there even though it looks like I should squeeze through. Many elements feel like you've had to thread the needle to find a piece of the puzzle, and the solution is sometimes layered several of those thread the needle moments so it can get a bit rediculous to find the solution since there are no hints and you're quite literally left in the dark. There are puzzle elements as red herrings in some levels that are not required for the solution which already has many elements to focus on. There should be a hint system of some sort, at least to tell you if you're on the right path or not, like after some time or earning a hint somehow the bot points backward if you've got it wrong or confirms that you're good, so you can at least guess and check partially through a puzzle instead of having to get the exact permutation of each choice perfect to pass every level.The dialogue isn't for me either and wandering around to find the next set of puzzles also gets annoying towards the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a total win. Yes, you want to pick it up. There are not many games I would recommend as wholeheartedly as I do this one!I've had a lot of experience with these types of games, having played Portal, Portal 2, The Talos Principle, The Witness, The Turing Test, Steamroll, Lightmatter, Q.U.B.E, The Swapper, Chromagun, The Spectrum Retreat, MIND: Path to Thalmos, Etherborn, Polarity, Magrunner: Dark Pulse, and Relicta so I feel like I can speak with some leverage in the this particular niche (which happens to be my favorite!)There is a great range in quality of puzzle games, but this is high at the top. The puzzles are challenging, satisfying, head scratching, and fun. If you want a game to rush through, this is NOT the one. There have been times already, only 3 hours in, where I have had to sit and try different possibilities of a puzzle thinking how could it possibly be solved only to realize that some particular combination (or idea) evaded me because I missed something I could do! They all seem so simple until you try and solve them! Already with the few different elements or additions to the main puzzle idea I have encountered to make things more challenging I have been impressed with. The game doesn't explicitly tell you what to do, but instead lets you discover it on your own as you go. I have seen games where this idea is frankly terrible, and games where it is totally great, and this is on the latter end because the learning curve is set right. The game looks to be very long, based on how long it has taken me to get to where I am at and the map shown, and I am extremely excited about this, because it scratches the puzzle solving itch I have and makes me want more of the game and the story itself!The exploration of the ship has proved useful and interesting. Hidden away are  There are terminals you interact with to listen to audio, read emails, and learn more about the ship, and in that way it reminds me of the Talos Principle. You can also find collectibles if you search the ship. Your surroundings matter. I will admit that the art style of your character is not the greatest, but that's really neither here nor there.The art of the game is simple, but visually appealing. The colors of filament add some chromatic flair! When I first started playing, I immediately noticed was the beautiful, peaceful, addictive music. It's really something special.EDIT: I'm nearing the end now, and I have one negative comment...the bridge puzzles are completely outrageous (and there are a lot of them). They are way too difficult and some of them seem to introduce things that you have seen little to none of before which is completely unfair in my opinion. Lastly, I have to talk about the price. I got this game on sale for less than $10. This game is definitely, in my humble opinion, a steal for $10. I would definitely say it could have a $30-$40 price tag and still be worth it, because all of the right elements are there to make this game worth that.Honestly, this is a real breath of fresh air in the puzzle game industry that I didn't know I needed, but am so glad I discovered. Pick it up. Now.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fine game with challenging puzzles, but it lacks any real eureka moments, more often being rewarded for persistence rather than guile.  Most every level comes down to trial-and-error, and there's no good way to visualize if a cable will be taut enough around to register a pillar or if your bot can squeeze through a tight space.Or maybe I'm just dumb.  Game is a little too cerebral and slow for me, just missing element that makes me feel clever and motivated to tackle the larger puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I sort of can't recommend this one but this may be a me problem; I think I maybe don't have the fundamental mindspace that makes this game more intuitive.Filament very clearly compares to the Witness but I feel the latter does a much better job of easing you into each new mechanic and weaves them together in a gradual enough way to give a fulfilling sense of progression.  Filament has several similar setups where it'll show you a new thing in its simplest form, provide you a few more incrementally complex examples, but then has a tendency to immediately jump into an extreme of complexity; very frequently found myself coming across new puzzle sets where the first 4 stages are a breeze and then I'd hit a wall at the fifth.  And often times I'd stumble into the more complex solutions by chance through trial and error and come out the other end frustrated that I don't really feel like I'd learned anything new to carry over to other puzzles.  The experience feels very inadequately balanced to me; if it's intended to mirror the Witness' sense of discovery and progression this is a real hard miss for me, if the intention was straight difficulty then it's certainly a success.The visual design and voice acting aren't really to my taste either and the music seems wonderfully calibrated to amplify my frustration but again these are all definitely me problems.
