Not done with it yet, still hoping something clicks somewhere but I can't really personally recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Very, very good (and BIG) puzzle game that's essentially based around pathfinding, similar to The Witness. Uhh. It's very similar to The Witness in a lot of ways. Single interconnected map to explore, puzzles that exist mostly separate of the map, a story that's mostly told through collectible log entries (though there is a voiceover that will go through large chunks of the narration, albeit slower than you'll make discoveries yourself), puzzles based around a single puzzle base but with various mechanics, a non-100% but still relatively high requirement for accessing the endgame, the endgame being primarily remixes of other puzzle types (and in this case also not requiring 100% completion of all endgame puzzles), environmental puzzles that exist besides the main puzzles that are still related to the main puzzle mechanic (albeit, annoyingly, here you have to run all the way back to a terminal to solve the environmental puzzles, and a few of them are vague/confusing... and like who the hell would ever figure out that cryptography puzzle on their own, I'll freely admit to looking up the solution to that one and hints for a few others). Anyways it's not as good as The Witness (or as seamlessly designed) but it does approach that quality.Now then, the puzzles. There's a lot of different puzzle mechanics (somewhere around 15?) and generally three sets of 5 puzzles to go through for each. Which feels like too many, honestly, considering that most every mechanic gets remixed later in the game too. I feel like three sets of 3 or 4 could've made the same point, especially when later puzzles in each set only get more complicated in terms of # of moves and can get a bit tedious sometimes. There's also a few puzzle mechanics that I just did not end up liking at all - the wrapping puzzles and arches puzzles are probably my least favorites in that regard. But like... aside from a small handful of times I had to look up a hint (usually just the first steps, half the time which I was already doing but wasn't confident about) the puzzles are fun to complete and can get pretty dang challenging. I think my single favorite puzzle in the game was Colouredscreens 3, what a beautiful puzzle that is, danggg). The bridge puzzles also maybe had a few too many varieties, some of them felt a bit samey for sure. And that Riser puzzle is kind of just... dumb. Loved the glitch and dice puzzle though, very unique ones for the game. A general issue I did have with the puzzles is that often it felt like the devs really, really wanted to force you into the one single correct solution, despite the solution-space approaching infinite due to the free movement of the game (as opposed to The Witness' grid-based system where the solution-space is much narrower). It's super not fun to have a solution that almost works except you can't quite fit through a gap between a pillar and your rope and it turns out the solution is either 1. one move different or 2. something else entirely and you have no way of really knowing which. This happens a lot and it can be kinda frustrating especially when it feels like your solution makes sense and is really clever but it turns out to not be what the game specifically wants. Really though... the vast majority of puzzles (and the environmental puzzles) are fun to solve and can get kind of addicting with how many puzzles there are (even if, again, I think the same amount of cleverness could've been condenses to a smaller number of puzzles without hurting the game). As for the story... it's very frontloaded, since from the logs you can get pretty much the entire end-to-end narrative, barring maybe two plot points and the ending sequence, before you've even left the first floor. And it is interesting to dig through the logs and read the crew's interactions, learn their personalities, etc. though by the time you're seeing the same huge log for the 4th, 5th, 6th etc. time towards the end of the game it does lose its luster. The ending also... doesn't really explain the mysteries of the story, which is definitely really unsatisfying. The corrupted logs also mostly don't... have much to them except irrelevant flavor text and lore and again some of them are neat but most of them just kinda seem to be there to fill a quota. I dunno. TL;DR the plot is intriguing at first but doesn't end up feeling satisfying by the end.Overall I did enjoy this game a lot even if I do have a list of issues with it. Not perfect puzzle design and maybe too many puzzles, a bit of a messy narrative, but like... it's all intriguing, fun, original, creative, clever etc. and I absolutely don't regret getting into it, was a very good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Usually puzzle games are right up my alley and I love space themes with piece-it-together narratives, so I went in to Filament thinking this would be a great fit; sadly it has been a big disappointment.The puzzles are very challenging but not in a fun way. Normally puzzles, even difficult ones, have a systematic approach that lets you solve them piecemeal (e.g. a sudoku puzzle can be solved one square at a time, without guessing future moves) but Filament requires a huge amount of backtracking without a good way of marking "solved" portions of the puzzles. You can make a realization that a certain section requires a particular line-segment but there's no ingame mechanism to mark that for future reference. Some of the puzzles have very open-ended areas that can lead to frustrating false "ah ha!" moments; it's easy to waste 10 minutes on a dead end solution.Sadly the hint system isn't much help either. The red & green markers aren't self-explanatory and the 2-hint limit is harsh. The hints also seem to disappear with no way to get them back later. Disabling the achievement seems like a reasonable way to encourage players to not use hints - having a 2 hint limit seems unnecessary.A really big annoyance is that the game won't let you move in "focus" mode. It's really great to be able to see the whole field at once, but for no good reason it won't let you navigate from that birds-eye-view. So you end up constantly flipping back and forth between modes. There's nothing art-wise in the puzzles that really deserves a close up view.The space station world is aesthetically beautiful and I'm sure the story is great for those that get through the puzzles. Sadly I don't think I'll get to experience it as the game is just too frustrating to play right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Game's gorgeous, really good music and art. Unfortunately the puzzle-solving experience isn't great. It's clearly inspired by classics in the genre such as The Witness, The Talos Principle, and The Swapper, but while it took the best lessons of aesthetics from them, it didn't succeed in replicating one key thing that all those had: an economy of puzzling. The solving experience often feels arbitrary, I don't really "learn" anything beyond a few basic rules for each puzzle type. You can't "pick up on principles" the way you do those games so It's fundamentally a game of trial and error and ultimately that's not what I play puzzle games for.(Part of the issue is that the puzzles are often too large, with too many extra elements beyond a central concept. This was one of Talos's bigger problems, and it's a pity it's replicated here. The puzzle designing would have done well to take after something like Stephen's Sausage Roll instead.)
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Filament is a challenging, addicting puzzle game with a unique gimmick. You are a space man aboard a ship whose previous inhabitants suffered a catastrophic project failure. It is your job to figure out what happened, and to do so you must unlock 'Anchor' structures built around the ship. Anchors that are connected to each other share the same theme. There are 15 themes.  To solve each puzzle you must activate pylons scattered throughout the room by pulling a line tethered to you around the pylons so that the line contatcs the pylon.  The tricky part, and what makes this game challenging at times, is that the lines cannot cross.  The story is laid out for you in a similar fashion to The Talos Principle in that once you solve a set of puzzles you are given a short lore dump and an access code that unlocks more conversations the mysteriously vanished crew members had on the computer's communication system.There is a good amount of puzzles without it feeling bloated and overlong, however the spike in difficulty and complexity between the puzzles can be a bit too much at times.  Overall I feel this is a puzzle game that is well worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like endless trial-and-error and brute-forcing, rather than figuring out the solutions using clues and reasoning like the way puzzle games are typically designed to play. Reasoning does work sometimes like figuring out most prominent paths around a local formation, but that's all I can do. Most of the time I was doing trial-and-error here and there. This game might be "challenging" from some sense but really is not fun to play. If brute-forcing is the intended way to play, I'd deploy an algorithm rather than doing myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: So much of this game is good, but there are a few intentional quality of life omissions that I just don't understand.1) There's an overhead view for the puzzles, but the character movement gets locked for no reason.2) Puzzle movement speed is slow.3) Puzzles don't follow a predictable grid, meaning that it's always a gamble whether a diagonal line will touch a corner, or if the bot will be able to squeeze between something later.The game is already hard, and these points make it so much less predictable and solvable without just wandering around and trying out combinations. I much prefer the puzzles that are smaller and easier to predict, even when they can be just as difficult as the larger puzzles.I really love the storytelling and the spaceship. And frankly I'd be happy to swap the review to a positive if the devs unlock movement during the overhead view!
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I don’t like this game, maybe I am just too dumb for it, but it's neither fun nor that interesting, at first it seems like an interesting concept but it's the same over and over again and most of the time it's just guessing or/and trial and error, also I found the hints not that helpful but I’ll credit where credit is due, the atmosphere of the game is pretty charming
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Adding my commendatory support for this game, though I have not finished it. I intend to. The puzzles are similar in spirit to The Witness, but the game is less frustrating in certain ways. In particular, puzzles don't transgress the mechanics, as The Witness's environmental puzzles did. Nor are puzzles made mechanically, rather than intellectually, frustrating, as many of the inside-the-mountain puzzles were in The Witness (e.g., sound-based puzzles, puzzle screens for color-related puzzles strobing with other colors to make it more difficult to decipher the true colors). The game is superior to The Talos Principle, apparently another standard of comparison, many of whose puzzles felt like chores because, while solutions became evident in principle, they felt felt like a waste of time to execute. To me, it feels like Talos has less puzzle variety but more environmental variety than Filament. Others have noted correctly that Filament's puzzles involve a lot of trial-and-error: one usually cannot, just by looking, figure out a winning route. But to me, The Witness and Stephen's Sausage Roll similarly required repeated experimentation. I would not call this 'brute-forcing,' which suggests mindless probing; it is rather like a kind of skillful permutation. Often I will start a puzzle by experimenting with a few paths, after which I gain some sense of the order in which certain parts of the puzzle have to be approached. ("Either this or that pylon is first; this other pylon has to be left close to the end; I will likely have to travel back and forth between these two sections in order to hit these pylons at the right angles; I will have to loop through here more than once," etc.)Filament's sci-fi narrative, so far, is more interesting than both of its competitors, as unlike them, its writers do not reach at philosophical themes beyond their province. Where The Witness and The Talos Principle were obnoxious and embarrassingly pretentious, Filament has so far been serviceable.Rewards for puzzle-solving, apart from more puzzles, are more narrative-focused in Filament. In The Witness and Talos, the rewards are more exploration-focused (new environments, opened passages, bits of puerile philosophy). But Filament has some exploration too.Filament also has a fairly developed layer of meta-puzzles (puzzles in/about the ship and crew) that may hold your interest, but the anchor-and-string puzzles are its meat and potatoes. And they are hearty!Two significant criticisms. First, angles and openings are important to the puzzles: create a path that is too narrow, and you will not be able to loop back through or touch the right pylon. But there is no obvious way to tell whether, e.g., an angle is too narrow, apart from trying to fit through. A few times, I thought I would fit through an opening; but when I finally came to it, I did not, and had to abandon the solution I had been pursuing. My second main criticism is that the puzzle difficulty, even within puzzle sets, does not seem to scale orderly. A few times, I found a middle puzzle in a set quite challenging, but breezed through the remainder. But perhaps the difficulty will vary considerably from person to person. Less significantly, while the game reveals roughly where 'secrets' objects are -- these help to solve the meta-puzzles -- there is a little button-spamming to find them. There should be an option simply to highlight them, as few people enjoy looking for objects.If the puzzles look like fun, they are, and the content is extensive for the price; I do not think I am even halfway through. I wholeheartedly recommend Filament to puzzle-solving fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Filament is a bittersweet puzzle game with challenging line-based logic puzzles.  The puzzles are presented in a 3-D plane and the player must use a series of robots connected to the wall to wrap around pillars in the correct manner to solve the puzzle and unlock the door.  Completing a series of puzzles reveals more of the story through emails from the crew and Juniper reminiscing over the intercom.The rules of puzzles are taught through the use of simple rooms, where players are able to experiment and deduce the rules of each section before moving ahead to the complex puzzles.  I found this to be very effective, and create a sense of accomplishment, as if the rules themselves were a puzzle to solve too.  Controlling the robots in order to solve the puzzle feels smooth, especially when using the run option (Which is toggled on/off by pressing Shift, I found this to not be clearly defined in the game).  Backtracking and resetting options are quick allowing for quick reattempts of sections or entire puzzles, as there is inevitably some trial and error.  There is some frustration when the robot looks like it should fit through a gap or it doesn’t, or the angle of a filament is slightly different than anticipated, but it is part of the puzzle to find a solution that works.  The games visuals are simple but effective, presenting key information within the puzzles, and in the spaceship over-world.  The puzzle rooms themselves are kept very simple, with the robot, cable, and pillars all conveying exactly what they need to the player – most notably whether a pillar is active or inactive, and clues as to how to activate them.  The spaceship is where story elements unfold, and it more crowded, full of rooms, and details that bring this world to life.  It sets the atmosphere and tone throughout the game, and it is easy to believe that a crew lived and worked on this ship.  Secret puzzles can be found, and input into the computers in the over-world.  However, some are ridiculously hard to figure out, and I will admit I used a guide for that final achievement.  I found the story to be compelling, all the characters of the crew felt very human,  though it was not the focal point of the game experience. What kept me coming back to the game was the desire to solve each puzzle, and the sense of accomplishment that came with each solved room.  I recommend the game specifically if the style of puzzle appeals to you, and you're up for a challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Plenty of challenging puzzles, very reminiscent of The Witness. If you get stuck, there's always other paths you can try. When you need a break, exploring the ship and getting to know the crew through their email exchanges is a nice way to unwind your brain. An excellent experience so far, and I've only scratched the surface.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, great. Plot, so so with a lot of room for interpretation. Gameplay, nauseating and tedious. Puzzles, see below.A game that doesn't understand the difference between obscurity and a good puzzle. The number of combinations for puzzles goes well into the thousands and so often a puzzle will reject a solution because of some minor deviation that's acceptable in one context, but not in another. Gaps too small. Wires pulled barely off of their triggers or into a fail trigger. A significant number of the puzzles I "cheated" by just darting through the door when moving more slowly would disconnect something and stop me.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Im really disappointed in the game since i had high expectations because of recommendations for this game. It is simply not a puzzle game its just straight try and try again untill you find the solution kind of game hence i dont think i should waste my time in this "puzzle" game. Furthermore the game doesn't even contain wide variety of music to compensate it has only one music and it keeps playing forever. I just don't get how this game got good reviews
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Game is so close to getting it right, but fails in the most critical ways and I cannot recommend this game to others.  If the devs could incorporate a way of testing ideas or being able to work from other angles in a detached way then this game would be solid.  The missing pieces are hard to imagine without seeing it first hand.  Over looking some of the other smaller issues is easy like sound and delayed response times, but the inability to narrow the puzzles down to help better solves them is well game breaking blocking all progress and halting any enjoyment that could be felt to the point even getting the solution feel hollow and uneventful.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard game to recommend. The concept seems simple enough, but then the mechanics become oddly complex. It can become incredibly addicting, then the puzzles become more and more complex to the point of annoyance. Some of the final puzzles were so obtuse that I had to use a walk-through. Out of all the people who have downloaded the game, only 8 percent have actually completed it. While I did manage to figure out most of the puzzles on my own, it took hours and I can understand why people would simply give up. If you really want a puzzle challenge, then I would recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: When I play a puzzle game, I want to feel the satisfaction of solving the puzzles, but I didn't get that with this game.  It came down to trial and error rather than logic and reasoning.  Also thrown in is a mystery which is slowly revealed through crew logs you get access to from solving puzzles.  By the time I accessed the ship's bridge, I found the puzzles so tedious, I used a guide to finish the rest.  I was hoping the mystery had a satisfying end, but instead I found it too open-ended and anti-climatic.  There were a couple things I liked, mainly the art style and the environmental puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a game!  I just finished the whole thing after 45+ hours.  I've played many puzzle games and I think it's a really balanced game.  Challenging, but doable.  I know I've seen a lot of reviews with people saying it's too bloody hard, etc, but I really do think it's the perfect difficulty.  I got "really stumped" a few times (and by stumped I'm saying spending more than 1 hour on a single puzzle), but with persistence I made it all the way through and it was a great feeling.  The devs did a great job introducing mechanics with no instructions and allowed the player to experiment and learn.  All with great story telling behind it all.  Overall, I'd call this "the best puzzle game you're not playing" this year.  Really cool.  Also, is there any place where people are discussing the ending?  My mind was blown :)
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the game is really good, it feels a little bare but some of that void is filled in with extra areas and conversations you undercover; I enjoy that there is minimal tutorial because those can get in the way a lot of the time when a simple puzzle can demonstrate it. The biggest issue I see the game facing is the difficulty spikes; in a lot of the modules you have five puzzles you must solve, the first three to four are solved easily, within seconds in some cases, but then find I would myself stuck on the fifth puzzle for minutes to maybe an hour. It is really flustering to have simple puzzles and then run into one that feels impossible, it ruins the flow and experience. I really enjoy having a difficult puzzle when I am expecting one, they are very fun to work through but to hit a one suddenly in a group of puzzles that I solve in seconds really makes me want to close the game out of anger; the difficulty is suitable but the consistency is the issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately the fundamental puzzle solving gameplay is flawed in Filament. You don't have enough information when beginning a puzzle to make sound decisions. Whether one path works or another will often be determined by just a few degrees of angle that can be imperceptible on visual inspection. This leads to a lot of guess and check gameplay. Sometimes many minutes of puzzle solving can reveal everything you've done so far leads to a total dead end. It doesn't make for fun or satisfying gameplay.Another review characterized this as a "maze game". That is Filament's heart and therein lies the problem: mazes aren't fun. You just try a path at random and it either works or it doesn't. "Oh I guess I should have gone left instead of right back there" is not an inspiring moment of puzzle solution.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Overall progression and the kind of puzzle mechanics introduced seem very inspired by The Witness. Instead of a grid you find yourself in a free space where you can draw your lines however it physically fits. Which is one of its weaknesses because it's never clear in advance whether or not you fit through a small gap before trying. Or if you're capable of pulling a line and leaving a large enough gap so you can still squeeze through later. Calls for a fair amount of trial and error, but it's still line-drawing puzzles at core. And to my surprise, you eventually do manage to wrap (HAH) your head around how to approach these kind of puzzles, making it generally much more methodical as to how you solve new ones. The difficulty curve was just very steep in the beginning, but leveled out more later on.Very subjective of course, but I found a fairly large gap in the quality of the puzzles. Some requiring a genuinely logical approach, and some being nothing but brute force (Pad, and Constellation Wrapping puzzles can go ♥♥♥♥ themselves in particular). And not being able to move while in overhead view is bad design, especially for larger puzzles. Also you can actually run (L3 on controller), wish they would have explained that somewhere.There's a pretty intriguing mystery story, but putting the pieces together just completely depends on yourself. Unless you're thorough with unlocking and reading logs and emails, you probably won't see the whole picture and may be left disappointed or confused.As for the music, I quickly found it to get very repetitive and annoying. Disabled it for the majority of my playthrough.Bottom line is, I felt like I was engaging my brain in a new way, and for that purpose most of the puzzles were enjoyable. But if it's this or The Witness, I recommend starting with the latter. The Witness just has a much higher level of consistent quality, and you'll be able to gauge better if you're even into this type of open puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: actually just a worse version of The Witnesspuzzles tend to just get larger and more complex without getting more interestingnew mechanics add little variation to how puzzles should be approached. as a result, puzzles feel very sameymany annoying quality of life things. why can I rewind but not move in focus mode? why is "sprinting" so slow? why is focus mode toggled per bot? why isn't there a terminal in every room, or a portable terminal? why does it take 5 seconds to open the terminal? why can't I rewind in the terminal? why is scrolling in the terminal so slow?story was alright
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Reviews overpromised on The Witness-like, but it's nowhere near.I can't tell if this game isn't that fun, or if failed expectation ruined it for me but I'm not enjoying it.If I were to assume the former, this game lacks the 'eureka' feeling when solving puzzles.That feeling isn't achieved by finding the answer, but by understanding the mechanics that lead to it. And there's no room for that in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: If you like one or more of the following: challenging puzzle games, codebreaking, well-written stories, fantastic chill soundtrack, secret hunting or beans, Filament is a game for you. While the tasks might seem daunting at first, soon you will have a notepad beside you to jot down series of letters and numbers to aid you in solving puzzles, and you will never look at a tangled phone charger cord the same way again. Try the free demo to see if you like it! Come to the discord if you're stuck, we will provide you with free cryptic clues!After solving every single secret puzzle, I can report they're fantastically designed. There's a few that rely on a bit of real-life knowledge but it's never arbitrary, logical steps and rules will always provide a solution.If you're colourblind, I have good news for you - while there are colour-mixing puzzles, there is a colourblind mode in the setting that overlays symbols on top of colours as an alternative.If you suffer from tone deafness, there is no pitch/note/tune puzzles that seem to be inexplicably present in every other puzzle game. I know I always had to look up solutions for those and I'm happy they were omitted in Filament.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Not terrible, but not good enough to recommend either - so my recommendation/review assumes you're paying full price, it might be worth it on deep sale (75%+) for the puzzle elements if that's your thing. Played partially on Epic so add about 5 hours to playtime recorded by Steam.To summarise the game, it revolves around solving puzzles using coloured filaments and environmental clues; the closest comparison I would make is to 'The Witness' and in particular the line style puzzles within it. However, the puzzles are not as engaging and feel a lot less polished - 'The Witness' encourages the player to understand and find the rules of each situation organically, whereas Filament seems far more geared to methodical solving, and eventually in later puzzles just brute forcing through rather than elegant solutions or clues. The story element is not very interesting either, and is extremely disjointed in the way its presented to the player. You are also constrained by poor design decisions such as not being able to easily review outside clues whilst mid-puzzle (so you end up using a notepad to sketch out), and awkward camera views to force difficulty increases (you have an optional top-down view, but can't move/complete puzzles in this) which really detract from the experience. I've decided to retire the game halfway through largely for this - the puzzles become an annoying and repetitive drag as the game progresses, and feel like trying to pad out the experience rather than adding to it. Perhaps a better story or more engaging puzzle environment would compensate enough to overlook the other part of the package, but this falls short.Also FYI for anyone playing on steam deck - it runs decently, but with fairly annoying artefacts/flickers on default settings; changing this to Proton GE fixed the issue completely, and its very playable in this config. Be aware that switching between these might affect your save games, so ideally use Proton GE from the beginning.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Before starting this game, I said to myself, "let's just play for 30 minutes and see how good it is." Two hours later at midnight, I said to myself, "hot dang this game is actually really deep! I'm not sure if I can finish this!"Two hours later at 2 am, I said to myself, "one... more... puzzle..."Which must mean that Filament is pretty good!It's everything I liked about The Witness, but with a much more upfront story, lore, world building, and most of all a treasure trove of audio and text logs to read over between puzzles (though many of them are hidden away behind rather devious environmental clues). They aren't necessary in the slightest, but it really helped me immerse myself in the game in a way that most puzzle games completely fail at.The music and visuals are also 10/10. Bought the soundtrack too so I could listen to it on my own time.If I had to live the rest of my life on a space station like this, I would probably be quite content.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply fantastic. The puzzles are both difficult and creative with many variants that keep the many levels new and interesting. I played through the demo and fell in love instantly, but with the full game that has come out I am even more impressed. There is so much more content than I ever could have guessed but what really sells me on this game is the art. The art is somehow so detailed with every room having so much depth that makes this ship feel like it was truly lived in. I hope that you will make the fantastic decision of buying this game and exploring all of the depth of this game as I do as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Peaceful space. Hard puzzles. A beautiful ship. Harder puzzles. An intriguing crew. And even harder puzzles.Don't know how a game can be so infuriating as you fail and fail and fail . . . and fail again yet so relaxing as the soft sounds of the cosmos lulls you into a state of complete serenity. Truly an oxymoron of a game but worth every penny. Even if I stopped right now after 4 hours of play, I've thoroughly enjoyed every minute of playtime and it was money well spent (got it on sale but I'd definitely pay full price for it).30 HOUR UPDATE: I was not prepared for the space expedition I had just embarked on when I wrote the first part of this review. The puzzles were intricate, complex, and exceedingly satisfying once solved and I was thoroughly enjoying the snippets of dialogue from the faceless narrator for the first 15 hours. Then I discovered the riveting story which was hidden beneath a puzzle of its own, albeit a simple one. I have almost completed the game and I still have so many questions. Will this entire mission be a failure or a breakthrough revelation? Stay tuned . . .100% UPDATE: This is the first game I've ever fully completed (achievements and all) which speaks volumes about how much I was enthralled by this universe of puzzles.As I progressed through the last group of puzzles, they became significantly more difficult as they combined multiple aspects of previous ones. The solutions became more and more vague and I stopped enjoying them as much as at the beginning; I was able to refrain from looking up any answers save for one set of puzzles that fully stumped me and another set I thought was quite dull. As for the story, despite a mountain of suspense built throughout the game, the ending was anticlimactic and I didn't feel like I really got answers to almost any of the questions I had about the crew and the ship.TLDR: Awesome puzzles. Good story-line but falls short at the end. If you LOVE puzzles you will love Filament :D
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best puzzle games I have played in A LONG time, For those who play many puzzle games, this is very similar to The Witness, In the sense that every puzzle works around the same base concept, for Filament this is using your little Robot within the puzzles to draw cables around pillars. For the game there Is no set order for any of the puzzles other then the typical groupings of 3 found among the ship which consist of a same style of puzzle, Later on you will find puzzles that will use the knowledge you have learned from 2 or 3 previous puzzles together in 1 which I absolutely loved. If that wasn't enough there is a narration throughout the game pushing a story line aswell as many collectables to give insight into the story and some mysteries, There are plenty of secrets hidden too and i havent found all myself but plan to. For this price £15 or £17 for marmalade edition which includes this games wonderous soundtrack which is another amazing part of this game, It is an absolute steal for anyone interested in puzzle games and those who like to push their minds to the limit which this game will surely do.I could not recommend this game more as this has gotten my first ever review of a game and I couldn't think of a game more deserving then this to have it. I hope more will come from the developers cause this was a joy to play
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like Filament. It looks great, there's a mystery in the story that intrigued me, and some of the puzzles are fun and challenging. Overall, though, the puzzles are inconsistent, with some sets being really easy all the way through, some being just challenging enough that if you figure out the logic you can solve them, and some of them that don't seem to make sense in how they respond to my attempts to figure out how they work. After about 5 hours I got tired of the third kind and gave up.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with challenging puzzles. However, as somebody who heavily suffers from 3D motion sickness, the seemingly benign 3D views in this game made me feel nauseous. Wish the developers could add an option to solve puzzles from a top-down perspective -- like the one we have when pressing Tab, but also allowing player movements.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo and it was amazing, and I was very happy to see it launch. Gonna be honest this game angers me in the best way, because the puzzles look so simple and yet take me so long to complete! I'm not great at puzzle games but I want to finish this one because of the amazing art style and calming atmosphere, I don't know the extent of the story but It sounds pretty fun!TL:DR - Good game hurts my brain
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Man, that's a lot of puzzles. I didn't get to clearing them all, but I did clear a reasonable amount of them on my own. Some of them can actually be ridiculously challenging, exceeding what you would expect from what SEEMS like a simple puzzle game. What surprises me isn't really how hard they are to solve, but really how hard they are to think up. Once you think one idea has been used up and you've mastered a type of puzzle they come up with a bunch of different ways to get you to rethink everything. With great variety comes a few frustrating puzzles but that's just a part of any game, really. If you like to think, this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend for people who love casual atmospheric puzzle games. The more complex puzzles require lots of trial-and-error and patience rather than logic. Great soundtrack.Good:1. The music is relaxing and enjoyable2. The graphics, art style, and story are great3. Many puzzles are quite clever4. Wide variety of puzzles all using the same core gameplay mechanic5. Lots of Easter eggsBad:1. Very little sense of completion because there's no progress tracking2. There's no map so you end up wandering around the ship aimlessly3. Some core puzzle concepts are explained poorly or not at all4. Level of difficulty across puzzles seems random (earlier puzzles are often harder than later ones)5. Too many puzzles rely on obfuscation (hiding information), guess-and-check, and intuition rather than logic6. Later puzzles have so many possible permutations that it becomes a huge time sink7. Some solutions require pixel perfect precisionOverall, it was enjoyable, but I felt it was too long and complicated.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: There are many very good negative reviews pointing many of the flawed aspects of the game (quality of life thins, puzzle mechanics, etc) but I will add just one that I did not found elsewhere:The game is mainly split into two different tipes of puzzles. One of them is the main puzzles. These are the ones with fundamental mechanical flaws that make (the hardest of them) more of a backtracking exercise than a logical problem. The thing here is that if you do all of them and learn everything there is to learn, you would still find yourself having a comparable work in a 2nd playthrough (lets say in another year or so...). That to me is very bad, and the inverse is what makes a game like The Witness (with only a handful of these bad puzzles), for instance, a masterpiece.The other kind of puzzle I found out to be very logical (albeit having some kind of arbitrary logic testiness to them sometimes) and rewarding to find scattered in the map (the first kind is obviously stacked someplaces, these ones are kind of hidden from plain view).The fundamental problem that I want to highlight is that the story follows the completion of the  set of puzzles, while the second one just unlock tiny bits of almost useless chit-chat information about the world that seems to be **entirely unnecessary** to the completion of the game.So, in the end, I was having a lot of fun doing the completely unnecessary things and was just doing chores in order to advance the story until I hit the point I just didn't care anymore.As I said, this title is very close to being a really good game, but the way it is right now, is more like a chore than a delight.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Bad puzzle game.Puzzle should be intuitive. This game is not. Wires IRL can be stretch when we push or squeeze objects between gap. But this game treat those wires as hard walls. Furthermore, the playable character in the game also can't jump over / crouch under existing wires. It's so annoying counter-intuitive.Puzzle should be clear of logic. This game is not. Mainly this happen because of the design that's rely on continuous 2D coordinate (unlike other games that's play on square/hexagonal grid). The downside of this coordinate system is that there are infinitely possible positions to consider. No, not on the developer's programming side. But on the player's cognitive side. Say, if the puzzle require a wire from A to B with angle of 37 degree. How the heck we human can figure that out with the exact number? Keep in mind that there are other possible positions that yield very similar results, but fail to solve the problem, like a wire from C to B with angle of 40 degree. This design discourage planning since players will not know if the plan is right or not until actually try it out. (not to mention that when the plan is slightly wrong, there is no way to "fix" just some part of the plan. the player practically need to restart the whole level. what the fun with this approach?)Puzzle should gives a revelation. This game is not. This issue continue from the continuous 2D coordinate design, magnified by the  concept -- the developer carefully craft each level with a preferable "revelation" way to solve it: change the way to tackle the succeeding puzzles. But now we have infinitely many feasible solutions to play-test, it is unavoidable that unintended solutions pop up everywhere. These unintended solution are super complex (instead of a simple a-ha solution, which I think this game already fail to make even the preferred way simple in the first place), they not only ruin the fun of the game, but also hide away crucial information on how to tackle the puzzle in the future. So what, how the developer tackle this problem? They just fiddle their levels with bits and bobs. Evidently, you can see weird wall of different length here and there as a part of iteration to prevent players solve it unintended way (go see images in community's walkthrough). So ugly to the eye. (...and to be honest, I don't think the developer really craft the puzzle with revelation approach in the first place. instead, I think they just throw in noises and traps just to pad the hardness of their puzzle. so solve any of them was never felt eureka.)-- unlike mechanics IRL that keep people safe such as combination lock that only the owner know the right number --should be  to play. This game is not. Take a look at Wordle, everyone loves that game despite they sometimes fail to solve today's puzzle. This game, however, is a chore of unending trial-and-error with practically no strategy. What the fun (and fair) with this puzzle design?Actually, the sign that this game so proudly present itself as a  puzzle game, as seen in the promo video, hints that it has a very high potential to be a  puzzle. Because if you aim to produce a hard puzzle, just throw in a 6-digit combination lock. That's hard. Since there are one million possibilities for the player to consider, and that's take ages. A  puzzle design may throw 6-digit combination lock to the player as well, but they will leave breadcrumb trails along the way to reduce the possibility down to just one exact solution. And guess what? The game never bothered to spare us even a tiny bit of bread.Avoid this game at all cost.By the way, good luck playing this game at 4:3 aspect ratio, because THE crucial information will be only seen on 16:9 screen 😡😡😡
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game, so it gets a thumbs up. However, I'd like to manage some expectations. Playing it, it's hard not to draw comparisons to The Witness, but this is not that. The presentation is more straightforward and compartmentalized, and there's little in the way of the puzzles and solutions impacting the environment you find them in. This is fine, because I think this is more meant to be the sort of thing you play casually, one puzzle at a time.If I had any real complaint, it's that the "advanced" puzzles in any given area don't make me feel clever for solving them. They're just larger, rather than more sophisticated, so it ends up feeling more like I've just moved a pile of sand one grain at a time.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: At first I quit , then I picked it up again and played 25 hours more , and now I announce that I have quit again. This time maybe for good. I simply cannot solve the bridge puzzles and do not want to teeter on a guide for no reason to get a 100% that will then be meaningless as I didn't solve it myself.As for the game , I think there are a lot of positives , the puzzles are of increasing difficulty. Sometimes incredible difficulty but most of the main game ones are not without logic and precedent , making for some really fantastic and mind boggling solutions that make you think you are literally the smartest person to ever exist. This feeling is constant but so is the anger when non-completion stands in your way. Luckily I don't think in any instance you have to solve EVERY puzzle to progress but its a puzzle game , so , why would you not?If you're stubborn and impatient you may find yourself here , in a similar situation. You may be able to solve ALL with time and patience but those are two things you do not have much of. I appreciate this game for breaking the idea that puzzle games are all cozy , laidback and basically easy games. This is HARD , and I am not ashamed to admit that I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ struggled and I am upset that I have to quit here. But the game is no longer more fun than it is frustrating. This is of no detriment to the game but I will have to stop , and move on to a game I can actually beat. This review is a positive one , to all that beat it , congrats?
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics are pretty enough.Story is... well I mean there's a story there, so that's okay I guess? Most of it is told through the medium of the ship's logs, so if you're happy to read a novella in between puzzles then good for you, I prefer stories that show, don't tell.The puzzles themselves though?I've never once felt a sense of achievement when finishing a puzzle. The vast majority of the time I've felt like I've kind of intuitively bumbled through them, and when that hasn't worked it's felt like a brute force exercise.This game doesn't leave you feeling clever when you smash it on the first attempt, it leaves you feeling lucky.It doesn't leave you feeling clever when you finally get it on the 100th attempt either, because you've just thrown poop at a wall until it sticks.There are also minor issues with not clearly providing the player with sufficient information about what a particular move will do until you do it. Whether there is just enough gap to backtrack between a pillar and the filament or whether it's just a tiny bit too tight is entirely down to trial and error. Which happens in a lot of the puzzles.Most puzzle games give you that dopamine hit to just go one more puzzle until suddenly it's 4am and you have made a grave mistake in not going to sleep. This one doesn't.Probably the most telling thing about why this is a frustrating example of the genre is that people can offer you solutions to individual puzzles, but not a method that you can apply to solve them yourself.The closest someone got was a post talking about some archaic graphing maths, which might be useful to a maths nerd, but to us mere mortals might as well be glyphs on papyrus.I cannot recommend this game. I doubt I will ever finish this game.Save yourself the time and frustration on what is essentially a poor idea for a puzzle game which has been beautifully executed.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with many challenging puzzles wrapped with good cohherent background story. Some puzzles were a speccially challenging, requiring some calculations on the paper. Amaizing creativity from the creators. Exelent relaxing accompaining music. Various puzzle combinations were especially attractive. Sincerely thanksful to the developers of the game. Hope to see more products in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing.  Puzzle games don't usually hold me for very long.  They're either too hard or too easy.  This one is definitely on the hard end of the scale, but there's something soothing to it where I can spend hours working on the same puzzle without getting frustrated.  The great sound track probably helps with this.  It's beyond soothing.The puzzles do use some of the same tricks repeatedly, so once you figure those out some that are probably supposed to be quite difficult suddenly become much easier.  The thing that surprised me the most was the story line.  I usually hate when games force you to find hidden unlocks to figure out what the story actually is, but in this case it really works.  No spoilers, but the atmosphere does a great job of combining that soothing mentioned earlier with a clear sense of wrongness that you can't quite place your finger on.  The unlocked stories just build that emotional dischord and when you think you've figured out the surprise plot twist, you unlock another set of messages and discover that's not all there is to it.I haven't recommended a game this whole heartedly in a very long time.  Well done and money well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Chill puzzle game whose core mechanic is pulling a thread between pylons, with a rich set of rule variations throughout the game. It can get difficult (so far my max is one hour stuck on a single puzzle, damn you pad-3-5), but:- The music is pretty good, and doesn't really get old even if there are basically only a handful of music loops throughout the game.- For the main (square) puzzles: there is no hidden information, everything is plainly visible on the puzzle plane. Each rule variation is brought up progressively and it never gets confusing.- There are frequent rewards in the form of bits of story through monologues and text messages. I liked the tone of it all, but I can imagine some people will have a hard time getting into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite long, making it absolutely worth its money. The puzzles are difficult, but they constantly introduce variety, so it doesn't get boring. There are always new skills you have to apply to what is fundamentally the same puzzle throughout the game. The main story Juniper tells you is so excellently paced within the game, and the game does such a good job of giving so much personality to characters you never get to see. Overall great game, would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: It's not an easy game and the puzzles require a lot of back and forth trial and error. It's not easy to tell if you are close to a solution or doing it all wrong, making it frustrating a lot of the time. Still rewarding and a good mix of puzzle mechanics for variety.After 49 hours I've finished the game and gotten all achievements for it. The game really rewards you if you get to the end, with some really colorful, fun and creative puzzles that you will love, because by that point you have gone through the selection process as the kind of person who would enjoy solving these puzzles, because you already did all the previous puzzles required to get there. What I'm trying to say, the game is good, but understandably not for everyone. Also, there are delightful corrupted log messages to collect. I did use a guide for the hardest of these, just to see what was up with some of them. Really good and fun stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I should love this game, and for the most part I did enjoy it up until the point where I gave up and used a walkthrough. The thing is that the puzzles eventually get way too hard, and solving them requires brute force rather than logic. Also, a couple of puzzles are a bit buggy and I probably wouldn't have been able to solve them without the walkthrough explaining that the puzzles are buggy.While I don't recommend this game, I don't regret buying it. I enjoyed solving the puzzles that could be solved without brute force, and the environmental puzzles were a lot of fun to figure out.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just one of a kind - as someone who enjoyed the Witness and other challenging puzzle games, this is easily my favorite puzzle game ever. It tells a really interesting story that you piece together through logs, journals, and hints onboard the ship. If you like a compelling story, playing through this game to its extent will probably be your goal. However, you certainly do not need to 100% this game to enjoy it - it's a really innovative approach to puzzle games and the strategic building on previous concepts as you progress the game is a great way of keeping the gameplay feeling fresh (and sometimes frustrating). I highly recommend if you enjoy puzzle games of any kind - a game with this much content and thought into its production is a bargain at the usual $17, but an absolute steal at the current $10.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles and story telling in this game are tremendous. As far as story, you're being lead along by recorded logs and a narrator, and it feels extremely real and almost cozy learning all the story beats. As for the puzzles, there's one basic principle; You're a little robot man with a tether, wrap yourself around things and exit the room. It sounds simple, but the game manages to give you many new puzzle styles that it never feels stale. Until...the ending. The final puzzles of the game are galaxy brain puzzles that only friggin Magnus Carlson could 4D chess the solution of, and they're permutations of puzzle systems you've seen before. It feels like a huge hurdle to put right before the ending of the story of the game. If they were bonus levels or B-sides I'd feel better about it, but having to beat them to see the conclusion is a bit harsh. Finally, and mild spoilers ahead, once you do beat those quantum entanglement thesis puzzles, the story wrap up is a bit light. It's an ending everyone can debate ad nausem, but it's unsatisfying that a lot of the extremely cool mystery that's brought up throughout your time on the alabaster is for naught. Luckily, the puzzles and journey up to the ending are more than great enough that this is an easy recommendation to anyone who enjoys puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game gave me such a good first impression that I had to post a review after having barely started. The puzzle design is both devious and brilliant so far and the game is gorgeous. I'll update this when I finish the game but seriously, if you're an expert puzzler out of brain fuel, you have no excuse not to buy this right now.--EDIT--I beat the game. Crud, that went south. Ending is too pretentious for anyone to understand the meaning of as far as I can tell and they added a hint system? Really? Seriously, you advertise the game for its difficulty (which disappointed me a bit - not a single puzzle I did took me over an hour) and then you add hints because people are babies and aren't finishing your game. Still a relatively minor gripe with a game that is otherwise well made. Half point off for plot bait and switch that didn't really work in my opinion, full point off for adding hints. (Half point off for the instruction puzzles, absolute frustration engine).8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Filament goes straight into the hall of fame, together with puzzle games like The Talos Principle, The Witness, The Room, Portal and Q.U.B.E. It's one of those that when you finish it, you want another game on the same level and you search Steam for it. If you're in that phase, go for Filament, even full price, it's worth it.I'm 21 hours in it (not just by being stuck, by the way) and I completed like 60%.STORYYou enter a three-stories, abandoned space station. The only presence on board is Juniper, stuck in the command room. She will be the narrator, telling what happenened after completing each puzzle section.PUZZLESTo fix the spaceship, you need to fix the Anchors by solving puzzles.As in The Witness, puzzles are based on a single mechanism: guiding a biped bot, you draw and stretch a cable to light up some pillars. Then, each section adds its own variation, resulting in a great variety of puzzles.Each section has fifteen levels divided in three groups. The first group is usually a sort of tutorial for the new mechanism, then you're on your own.The good thing is that you can't almost get stuck because you can roam the ship freely right after clearing the entrance (first tutorial), so if you get stuck on a puzzle you can still go somewhere else.COLLECTIBLES AND SECRETSThe other half of fun in Filament is finding PC access codes. There are some terminals scattered around the ship, by which you can access e-mails and logs from the ship crew during the weeks preceding... whatever happened (I don't know yet). In order to access e-mails, you need access codes in the form of cards you can collect after puzzles or around the ship. The access codes work same as the main puzzles: you need to draw a line to touch some dots in a 4x4 square. This way, you can integrate the story told by Juniper with first-hand information (and, in the meantime, give some rest to your brain).Aside from e-mail codes, which are straightforward, you can also collect some other cards (gift cards, playing cards, apparently random stuff) which actually contain secret codes requiring a bit more thinking to be cracked. Not only that, secret codes are also present around the ship itself... you may want to look carefully around!Everything you collect is organised in two inventories accessible when on a terminal (very useful). Terminals also feature a map of the ship, indicating the locations of Anchors (the main puzzles) and even the presence of collectibles and/or secret codes in each room. This is a great help, especially considering that sometimes collecting cards is a bit of a pixel hunting (and this is my only negative comment on the whole game).CONCLUSIONIf you're looking hard for some well-made, long-lasting puzzle adventure game, stop looking and buy Filament now.EDIT:After 43 hours of playing and near the end of the game, I must add that some of the environmental / secret puzzles are... well... just too much. It's ok if they have you scracth your head for a while, maybe even look for information outside the game, but some of them are:- unfairly difficult (es. the cryosleep room secret code and the subsequent one; the resistors code)- poorly designed (es. the light puzzle in the staircase... how can you guess height from such a perspective?)- misleading (the paintings in the crew hallway and the cardboard boxes on the first floor... you can't use a 4x4 grid identical to that of the codes in a different way, that's just confusing)Besides, I hate when I crack a code, but I can't solve it right because of something that wasn't clear (es. the starting point of the cards binary code on the table on the second floor; the ID cards code... I thought the third letter in Juniper's card was an O, not a D)My opinion on Filament is still: go buy it now! But... it's not perfect, let's say.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful puzzles of varying difficulty, that I guarantee other players will find difficult in different ways. I got the game for my friend and it was interesting seeing how we'd have different solutions for the same puzzle, or one would have issues with a puzzle the other wouldn't. I really recommend it, the atmosphere is also perfect, the way the music integrates with the puzzles, and a few certain key areas..
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game.  Brilliant puzzles and it certainly makes you think.  You enter the different rooms and each of the rooms have puzzles to solve,  it definitely gets your brain working and there IS a solution, but what is it? The feeling of euphoria when I finally solve it.  The setting is just beautiful, with so much detail and a soothing music track to help you solve those lovely puzzles. Cannot find anything I don't like about this game.  Happy solving.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Fair warning; I've been heavily engrossed in this game since launch, and I've been spending time with the community. It probably isn't an issue, but I may have some positive bias because of that.Filament is very good, you should get it.People have been making comparisons to The Witness and, while those aren't unfair, Filaments puzzles look messy -- they feel more jury-rigged and untidy than The Witness's perfect solutions. There is still a strict, tight logic, often with only one correct answer, and my goodness you have to put work in to get some of them because *they are hard puzzles*... but the feeling is different. So you're not getting a clone, here.Not to mention that unlike the Witness, Filament has a story, rather than just a vibe, and I hope you'll enjoy it as much as I did. For me, Filament's lore, character writing and plot are the best I've seen in a game in a long time. But they also don't steal the spotlight from the puzzles until later in the game, perhaps when you're ready.The music is fine but not really to my tastes; I think I would have enjoyed something that fit the 80s aesthetic a bit more, and Filament's biggest let down is it's sound design. Many aspects of the game are missing sound cues, either in the form of generic blips and bloops, or tangible bumps and friction, as well as a general sense of atmosphere. That being said, it doesn't make a noticeable impact on the game; just lacks an extra level of polish.Filament could be a sleeper, and that would be a shame. It's genuinely worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Only 10 hours in (w/ plenty more to go) and I'm of the opinion that this is the first puzzle game that gives The Witness a run for it's money.  I know that claim is going to raise some eyebrows, but I said what I said.  In a word, Filament is brilliant.  Brilliantly designed and beautifully executed.Edit:  Oh yea! I forgot to come back and update after completion.  The above stands.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another game I really want to recommend and yet I can't. The concept of stringing a wire around levels is interesting. The game introduces new game elements at a steady pace to keep things interesting. I enjoyed the first couple of dozen puzzles but then the flaws of the game became apparent.As others have pointed out, the puzzle solving is mostly a case of trial and error. The difficulty ramps up fairly quickly as well. What makes the trial and error aspect particularly frustrating is the game display - you wander around levels that are quite large, so trying out solutions takes ages. Worse, you often can't see the whole level. I think I would have enjoyed this game more if the levels were all single screen and you used the mouse to string the filament around.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I mostly bought this game for the puzzles. They do not disappoint. A simple premise for them with many interesting variations that keep the game fresh. It can get quite challenging though, but still feels very doable. There are also many environmental puzzles that are very fun to find and solve. I didn't expect to get so hooked on the story, I was almost ready to skip it to just focus on the puzzles but it was so intriguing and so well written I couldn't do it. The messages and logs in the computers may seem boring, but they are concise and entertaining. The mystery was well done and kept me guessing through out the game. Last but not least, the soundtrack is amazing. Overall, it's a great game that I highly recommend to anyone who enjoys puzzle games or a good story. If you liked The Witness or The Talos Principle, this is surely up there with them.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: It was good fun for 10 hours but after a while the whole process of trial and error gets old, and although bringing in a new gimmick freshens things up a bit, the freshness is lost by the time you have completed 2 anchors of that type. The environmental puzzles were fun, though not all of the ones I found were very intuitive, like in The Witness. The story didn't feel intriguing. The story is progressed via card codes you gain by completing each anchor. In principle this sounds good, but in practice it's irritating. You get the codes in mixed order, and singular pieces don't give enough context to make reading them satisfying. On other hand reading 6 entries for single week doesn't feel very satisfying either, since you have lots of redundant messages between the members. Sometimes there are differences between these messages, as crew member has privately commented the message to another, and since these are hard to distinguish without opening the message, you end up opening them all anyway just to make sure. Each crew member also has their personal log / diary they write things up during the week, but these often feel very out of context, even after reading all the messages for the week. There is also the monologue provided by Juniper when you complete anchor, or stumble upon a story point, but these are generally just idle rambling.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: The game has now added a hint system that goes a long way to figuring out some of the more complicated puzzles without immediately spoiling the solution. It alleviates most of the frustration with the problems mentioned below, especially in some of the later puzzles while still retaining the difficulty. There is no reason for me not to recommend the game now. Good job, developers! (Note: enabling hints disables the achievement for solving all puzzles)Original Review:This game tries to be The Witness, but doesn't quite get there. The puzzle mechanics (wrap ropes around pillars to light them up) are clever, with some levels being super easy - but then others requiring loads of trial&error until you find the right path by sheer luck. Like The Witness, it slowly expands on the base puzzle mechanic. Some of the introduced mechanics do make for some good logical puzzles, while others make the trial&error worse. It is like a grab bag of puzzles of all kinds of quality, from fun to slightly frustrating. It *does* mostly work, but the times it doesn't are annoying.However, exploring the spaceship is kinda fun, the story and voice acting are fantastic and it is atmospheric enough to want to keep playing. The puzzles vary and can be hit or miss, but the game has an undeniable pull to it and the main mechanic is clever. And let's face it: there are just not enough atmospheric exploration puzzlers like this and the game definitely succeeds in this regard.I would recommend it to puzzles fans like me, but I would try out the demo first.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I can only recommend this game if you are REALLY REALLY into puzzle games. It is extremely repetitive, and quite long.The game is competently made (save for occasional bug where the line from robot just stops following you, requiring you to reset the puzzle) and the music is nice, but it just isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Filament is a narrative puzzler set aboard the spaceship Alabaster. The spaceship itself has three levels, all featuring puzzles of varying difficulty. Scattered around the ship are various consoles which you can 'plug' in to and attempt its puzzles. When you do this, you take control of a bulb (hence the 'filament' title) connected to a wire and have to navigate around a series of pillars and get to the exit. It sounds simple, and sometimes is, but you'll come to a puzzle that will confound you. Each puzzle area has three consoles, most featuring 5 puzzles. Once you complete these, you can move on to the second of the three consoles. Complete all three, you'll get an achievement, but, more importantly, a huge sense of satisfaction. The beauty of this game, like 'The Witness', is that you can approach the puzzle areas in any order. Each set of three consoles features a different gimmick, which adds variety. For example in one area, you are able to take control of more than one bulb. As you wander the Alabaster, you uncover the mysteries of the missing crew members. There are lots of notes/emails to read, and there is a surprising amount of dialogue for a single character on an empty ship. 'Filament' is beautiful, features serene music and is such a relaxing way to pass the time. Totally recommended for anyone who likes clever puzzlers.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a puzzle game enthusiast and I liked this the-witness-like a lot.I understand the complaints about too much trial-and-error though. But it's just some of the puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: Filament is pretty good. Some have praised it for how tricky it can be... BUT I think many are blinded by the fact they are being thrown to a setting where in most instances you are even told whats going on. The objective or challenge changes quite a bit in Filament. One moment you will be wrapping around certain pillars in order, rapping around pillars to light up certain other pillars, making certain pillars certain colors, following a line in which you cant wrap around on pillar to a particular other pillar blah blah blah. A lot of this can be dumbed down and explained from the beginning. Others, are too vague. It feels unfair and annoying not knowing certain principles when trying to figure out a puzzle. Its like playing a game and not being told or understanding the rules. This is where Filament mostly falls hard for me, except for one other thing I will mention next.Repetition and trial and error. Most seek a mental challenge, maybe at best, an intuitive experience. Take portal for instance, Portal is brilliant because it creates scenarios where you look around the environment and think: How can I accomplish this? You will look around for instance in many ways, how can I bounce here to put a portal here, how can I get to this point where I don't walk through this field and lose my portals, how do I bring a cube here, how can I catch this here, how can I take out these guns. It actually makes you think smart, sometimes fast in a situation and even testing your intelligence. Filament is not doing that, one could argue it comes to tastes when it comes to puzzle games. A good horror game to me is one that sets tension and fear through environment for instance, not something that jump scares you for a 5 second jump in your chair. Filament doesn't do it for me, I was hoping that things would be done a bit different, sadly do I see this game is mostly the type of puzzle game that is trial and error. It doesn't really matter if you are a glowing brain genius, or not. You will fail you will have to try again, you will have to find the route. In a few of these they are quite good, in a few of these... Its trial and error, nothing more. It doesn't make you feel good, you find OH I CAN SLIP THROUGH THIS SMALL SPACE or... I CANT SLIP THROUGH THIS SMALL SPACE!!! This is what breaks if for me. This will be one of those rare actions where I give something a good review for a not recommended. It doesn't do that type of puzzle game for me. It also, I think arguably in general is flawed for that reason, even if you like that type of game, it still has mechanics and environments that need better explaining or better made that you don't feel like you just have to see how the environment reacts to your little raps and turns.7/10 - I couldn't give it any lower, what is here is a game that kind of did deserve those rewards it received, but also struggles to hold good explanations, principles and follows a formula of trial and error.

_childDocuments_.review: is a lovely “little” puzzle game that I have to give a thumbs down for its sheer difficulty, more on this later, but first let’s start with the good:You pick up the distress call of a stranded spaceship and proceed to reconnect the modules that are not working to get access to more of the spaceship as a voice of a woman in the intercom gives bits and pieces of what life aboard the vessel was like before everything went to hell.When repairing the ship, you control a little robot carrying a filament, hence the name, who has to wrap what I guess it’s a power cable around rectangular pillars.Later puzzles will feature their spin on this formula, for example have multiple character with a certain color flipping certain switches, or gates you must pass through multiple times without touching their sides, and so on, but the core remains the same, wrap the filament around a pillar.The draw certainly comes from the space lo-fi ambience and the fairly unique mechanic to connect stuff with a string the way this game does it, but unfortunately that’s about it and the problems are too big to ignore.Difficulty.I think everyone saw this coming.I love me some good headscratcher, but I have to be both invested in the game, the progression of difficulty has to be smooth and especially I have to feel like I’m not just inputting random numbers in a safe one combination after the other.I’ll explain:While you just have to wrap your filament around all the pillars it’s the how you do it that is the problem, the filament restricts your own movement, and the vast majority of pillars have something attached to them in a way that bars you from approaching them in any order you want, but at the same time there’s no rhyme or reason to where are you supposed to start or let alone end.I really feels like the devs made a puzzle, solved it once, and then made these “add-ons” to make it impossible to solve it in any other way.Besides that, while the puzzles have this neat aesthetic to them, they have no connection to the narrative, imagine if yyou are playing a detective game and the vast majority of the time is spent doing white jigsaw puzzles.On a third and final point the writing feels very... millennial?Which isn’t a bad thing per se, but I mean... lady, you are stranded in a failing spaceship, maybe making fun of your rescuer and nonchalantly blabbing about how a guy once made a steak isn’t going to improve the situation.The pricetag is good for the kind of piece of art this is, even better on sale, but I’m still not going to recommend this, while the vibe is purely subjective it’s a bit more objective that the puzzles are frustrating for their trial-and-error nature.
