_childDocuments_.review: At a high level, there are two basic kinds of puzzle games: Trolly kinds and Thinking kinds. Trolly kinds use gimmicks to ramp up the difficulty, usually lazily. An example of this would be The Witness. Aside from being a steaming pile of literal ♥♥♥♥, the Witness is a trolly kind of puzzle game that depends on visual gimmicks (like hiding portions of the puzzle, making it difficult to look at, having it a different level...etc...) to give it an illusion difficulty (). Once you brute force your way past said gimmicks, the trolly kind of puzzle games dissipate like a hissing mephitis into the wind with little to no return for you wasting your time on it.Then there are the Thinking kind of puzzle games. A good example is the Zachtronics library. Here, the rules need to be discerned, but they allow for creative solutions to the puzzles. Filament falls somewhere between the two. It's not entirely trolly, but it also lacks the depth to allow for truly creative solutions. What is not like, however, is The Witness, and it is certainly not (the protestations of other reviewers below notwithstanding)  The Witness; and anyone saying so is the kind of person who leases a Lexus and then says they own a "luxury" vehicle. No, you don't, you pay the bank for an overpriced Toyota that you thought was flashy and you should feel bad about it. While the basic puzzles are in the same vein as "The Witness", Filament distinguishes itself in the execution.There is an actual story in Filament. Contrasted with the Twitter philosophy of The Witness, Filamnet's story actually instills in the player a desire to see the game through and to find out what happened to the characters. More importantly, the conclusion of the story (while somewhat tropey) isn't insulting to the intelligence of the player. This is especially true when compared against the conclusion to The Witness which only appeals to people who frequent r/philosophy and have a Nikola Tesla poster on their wall next to a picture of the spaghetti monster from "the oatmeal" because they think it's "so profound".And while there were some eyerolly/cringy parts of the story (espc in the logs), on balance, it contributed to the game instead of contributing to the regret of purchasing the game.The basic idea in this game consists of a series of rooms that each have a set of pillars that must all be lit up (sometimes in a particular sequence) in order to progress through the levels. The way you light up said pillars is by controlling a character (sometimes more than one) that extrudes a "filament" (hence the name) from behind it.The challenge comes from two mechanics:A) you can't cross an already laid out filamentB) you have to discern the rules for the particular level you're one to properly light up the pillars. From these two basics, you get a plethora of unique puzzles. These puzzles belong to groups that each have their own special mechanic in B that distinguish them from other puzzle groupings. Thus, this game is not a W key kind of game, it is a difficult game. There's little to no hand holding, no cheats, no difficulty settings, no parents calling the school demanding a grade change, no Dean of Student Affairs you can run to because someone in another country said something you found offensive. Just you and the game, which is to say, just you versus yourself; and since narcissism prevents any self-reflection or improvement, Filament is the kind of game that GenZ is lethally allergic to, making it a "GenZ repellent". And Filament is a gym sock in the trunk of your 1998 Honda Civic under the summer sun while you're browsing CDs at the stripmall levels of GenZ repellent.Since it is a difficult game, you can expect to sink some time into it. Generally speaking, each puzzle grouping is presented in 3 groupings of 5 individual puzzle "rooms" with increasing difficulty (created by pillar number/layout and being mindful of element A) as you work through them. All told there are something like 300 individual puzzle rooms which gives you about 20 unique puzzle mechanics to deal with (300/15 and 15 is the number of puzzle rooms per each mechanic).Some of the mechanics are, obviously, going to be harder than others, but most of them are not trolly. An explicit exception to this is the grouping where the mechanic is a visual obstruction - it's just lazy and mistakes obfuscation for challenge.The remaining puzzle mechanics are quite enjoyable, but they require that you forgo immediate gratification (hence the game being GenZ repellent) and take some time to figure out element B. Once you do that, it's generally a quick path to the solution across all 3 groupings. Over the course of the game you can expect to spend anywhere from 30 minutes to an hour or two clearing all 3 groupings for any one particular mechanic. Since the underlying type of puzzle here is "order of operation" there  some tedious trial and error along the way, but it's not game breaking (if you are finding it so or think that brute force is the only way - as people in the reviews have complained about - then you've misunderstood the underlying mechanic to some degree). So you can expect to spend about 10-15 hours to beat the game, a little longer if you're going for 100% puzzle completion.  And that's it. Most of the challenge and thinking will come from element B, most of the trolly times will come from element A, with an honorable mention to the game not adequately telegraphing when your character can and can't squeeze through an opening.As a side note: do yourself a favor and don't try to beat this game in one or two sittings, you'll end up banging your ♥♥♥♥ against a wall and hating the game for it. A system that I found worked well is turning on the game, leaving it on during the day and chipping away at it bit by bit - if you're not on a roll - over the course of the day. It's a nice break.Overall, the game hits all the boxes for price, plot, and puzzles. Is it the best of these types of games? No, but its price point of 16$ feels fair and definitely makes it a must add if you like these types of games. Also, the voice actress nails it, one of the best I've heard.

_childDocuments_.review: is a puzzle adventure game that's set in a spaceship that is mysteriously devoid of its crew... that is until you hear a voice through the walkie-talkie on the floor. It seems like this is probably the last surviving member of the crew aboard the ship and she needs your help! As you play, you'll reveal the story whether through the one-sided conversation with the surviving crew member or reading through messages and logs of various other missing crew members on the computer.----------------------------Filament only contains 1 type of puzzle that involves dragging around an apparently endless cord from its outlet (it works much like a coiled extension cord) to power up various pillars and opening the door. The catch here, however, is that the cord can't intersect with itself and you only have a single cord to use. Now, the puzzles here start off easy enough, but that difficulty really ramps up pretty quickly. In fact, I daresay that the "Difficult" label for this game is very fitting. I reckon about 25% of the puzzles can be very difficult mainly because the solution turns out to be very complicated, while another 25% is difficult mainly because you'll need to do a lot of thinking, whether it is to figure out what the puzzle wants you to do (before you even start solving it) or to find out which pillars you should power up first in order to be able to solve the puzzle.Although I've noticed that there are more than one way to solve certain puzzles, there are actually no "extra" pillars in this game, so in some way, it's like trying to put together a random IKEA furniture without the instructions - just when you thought you've assembled everything perfectly, you found a bunch of screws and some other pieces that you've completely missed, and now, you'll have to start all over. This is definitely a game a more hardcore or experienced puzzler would greatly enjoy. For average puzzlers like myself, I would love to learn more about the story but I just can't spend hours trying to possibly figure out the solution to a single puzzle - by the way, note that spending hours on a puzzle doesn't mean you'll eventually solve it. It would be nice to have a hint system that I can tap into whenever I need a little nudge in the right direction. + Gorgeous visuals and the voice acting's really great too! + Challenging and very unique puzzles+ Excellent storytelling - I'm utterly hooked! + Considering the hours you might need to put in to solve the puzzles yourself, the cost is definitely worth the playtime and the experience.- No hand-holding - you're expect to figure out how new elements of the puzzles you encounter works and that might take quite a while, and this brings me to my second point...- No hints either. This is a con for a midcore gamer with average puzzling skills like me. Personally, I prefer story-driven puzzle games, especially the ones that are labelled as "difficult", to have a bit of a hint available that I can tap into when I need it just so I can finish the story.- A glitch? At one point in my plyathrough, I reset a puzzle to start over and the screen kind of froze for a minute (the game's not responsive to any of the keys I've pressed, including Esc) while the music continues to play in the background. However, the game seems to fix itself and didn't crash as I'd expect :PDespite having so-so puzzling skills, I still enjoy a good challenge now and then, and boy... Filament doesn't only hit the mark on the head, it definitely went for the home run! I've greatly enjoyed solving the puzzles that I've managed to solve but I'm quite disappointed to find out that there aren't any hints that I can rely on if I've really hit a dead end and could use a lifeline, and hence, I might not be able to finish the story.So, to sum up, I would highly recommend this game to hardcore and veteran puzzle solvers, but for average ones, you might want to wait a while for some puzzle guides to be available before buying.
