_childDocuments_.review: Filament is a game with an exceedingly simple premise which blossoms into a plethora of puzzles ranging from mildly tricky to fiendishly difficult. And also some lovely music and a nice stylized art style.In Filament you explore a spaceship where the crew have gone mysteriously missing, with the puzzles being encryption devices you need to decrypt to unlock more of the various crewmembers' logs and figure out what happened. In the puzzles, you control a little robot who spools out an infinite length of cable, and the goal is to wrap the cable around various pillars such that every pillar is touched at least once. However—very importantly—you can't cross the cable you've already laid down.That's the basic premise. As you progress in the game, you start running into a number of tricky variations on this simple theme. Some puzzles give you more than one robot which need to be controlled. Others require you to wrap pillars in the right order, or to run the cable over pads on the floor in addition to wrapping the pillars, or to mix colors correctly in order to proceed. And on and on, unfolding in a kaleidescopic riot of different takes on the underlying mechanism.The game is also chock full of secrets. You'll start to notice them in the environment as you go on, and they offer tantalizing clues to the Filament universe. (My favorite was the tray of seedlings I picked up which contained a password in their arrangement.) This adds a sort of meta-puzzle to the game, though as far as I know (I still haven't finished it) they're entirely optional.I can't neglect to mention the music and art style in this game. You can get a feel for the art style in the screenshots, where you can see the clean, stylized look the game has going. It works very well, in my opinion. I'm also quite partial to the music, which is calming and unobtrusive. If you're like me, you're going to be hearing it for hours, but I haven't tired of it yet (in fact I got the Marmalade Edition to get access to the soundtrack, and I'm glad I did).All in all, Filament is in some ways the closest thing I've played to Portal since Portal 2. Both games have a single, simple central mechanic which they then use in increasingly more tricky and interesting ways to serve up some puzzles which will really get your gray matter humming. The ability to roam freely about the ship and try all the different types of puzzles from immediately after the opening also helps prevent the feeling of being stuck, as you can just go somewhere else and try a different puzzle. I can't recommend this game highly enough if you're looking for a good cerebral workout.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.Basically, you are in space doing a bunch of puzzles to unlock doors so your gamer girl gf can get out of the locked room before she dies of starvation.The game is rightfully so compared to The Witness, and I will be comparing them too. The entire game is free roam, puzzles are in batches, and each section takes the original concept of the puzzle and changes one thing drastically;The puzzle involves you in a 2D(/kind of 3D) box room carrying an infinite-length cord. The cord touching a pillar will power that pillar, and when all pillars are powered up the door opens so you may finish the puzzle.Those 4 things stay consistent. The cords, pillars, box-room and door will remain familiar but each section (which you can access at almost any time) introduces new mechanics exclusive to those sections. All similar to The Witness.One thing that The Witness definitely did better is that all the sections were much more recognizable and memorable. The environment was more colorful and interesting, meanwhile in this game there's more character building and world building. The space station is still interesting and your gamer girl gf will sometimes phone in some details to make you more interested in each area, which I admire about the game. There's a handful of details and lore in Filament that I know The Witness lacked, so it may just be different strokes for different folks. Personally, I skip most of the extra reading in this game but if you're more into the narrative, that should be twice as much reason to pick up this game.The puzzle difficulty is no joke, certainly on par with The Witness. The Witness does a MUCH better job using 3D for certain sections, but this game makes up for it with more increasingly difficult puzzles and each section having a mechanic unique to that section. If you're still not convinced then be smarter than I was and try the demo. It should definitely be the last thing to help you make your choice. This game is safely in my top 5 favorite puzzle games of all time, and I'm not even close to finishing. I've spent so much time playing for only owning this game for about a day.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Great value, best puzzler I've played in a long time. The base puzzle model seems basic at first but progresses through a significant number of variations, and there's a lot of meta-puzzle plot drivers hidden throughout the game. Making it as much an interactive scavenger hunt as a straight-up puzzle-solver. Appreciating the soundtrack, occasional graphics hiccups, it's missing a tiny bit of polish but willing to forgive that for the fact it's sucking me straight in. The pick-up-and-play aspect is great as you can bail halfway through a series of linked puzzles but still return later if you figure it out. This really helps as you jump around the game, sometimes inspiration from a completely different variation on the theme will inspire you, to find that the puzzle you were stuck on is really straightforward. Honestly it's worth full price and is a serious value at the current discount. If you're on lockdown this will give you an itch worth scratching.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun for those puzzle connoisseurs. If you get stuck at a puzzle, move on to a different one and come back later. Don't spend too long on a puzzle you're stuck on. It can seriously give you brain fart. Not kidding. I got stuck on a puzzle for more than an hour and it seriously gave me a headache that night.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Its a fun puzzler with similarities to Witness in which the World is open and you can decide what puzzle you take on next. The puzzles themselves are tricky sometimes, but for me the right kind of difficult.The story is interesting and is very well narrated. So im hooked, even if im not that far into the game yet. Defenitely will keep playing and its already worth its full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest, the core puzzle mechanic is not my favourite. Some of the "sub-areas" make great use of it, delivering fun, thoughtful puzzles; others can start to feel like a slog through trial and error. And while the game does allow you the freedom to pick which sub-area you confront, there's no skipping puzzles: you'll have to complete every single one in the sub-area, in order, to unlock the next bit of content. As a result, in mid- to late-game you can easily get stuck in a loop of forcing yourself to slog through one frustrating puzzle here, one frustrating puzzle there, while the plot just stands still because you aren't actually completing any sub-areas.Even so, it's hard for me to give this game a bad review. The real selling point for me is the atmosphere, the story and the meta-puzzles. The space station is big, colourful and lived in, with a lot of variety, and the ever-present planet looming in the background is so gorgeous I find myself sometimes just finding a window to look out of. It all helps alleviate some of the frustration I mentioned -- if you're in a rut, you can take some downtime to explore and maybe find some secrets. So overall, not the greatest game I've ever played, but a solidly enjoyable one.
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: Variety of the puzzles, with different rules, but same principle, so far, makes for a lot of time to be killed... It takes a bit of thought, and concentration, since even minor changes make them last longer... You also need to keep eyes open, as there are clues to be found, on how to get to the next room.If you like the demo, You are like to love the game
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game. Intuitive, deep, thought provoking and worthy of causing the occasional wall head-butt. Highly recommend if curiosity and puzzle is your thing...and even if it is not your thing it's beautifully made with a sound track that keeps you sane. Buy it anyway.So...I have now play a lot more of this game and I still stick to my original review although I would now advise a few extra helpful things to have available:1) Coffee2) Paper and pen3) some kind of anti-rage drug
_childDocuments_.name: Filament

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely incredible puzzle game. It is worth noting that the difficulty spikes pretty quickly - this should probably not be your first foray into the genre - but solving the puzzles is immensely rewarding. There is almost always multiple puzzles available to you, so if you're stuck on one, you can jump into any of the others, which means the chances of you hitting a progression "brick wall" are slim to none.The narrative unfolding through dialogue, logs and messages is intriguing, and paints a brilliant picture of the world of Filament.I am loving it so far, and am looking forward to many more hours spent in this world!

name: ENCODYA
detailed_description: The Save the World Edition includes ENCODYA, the official ENCODYA soundtrack, a lovingly designed artbook, wallpapers and a Making of Video. In addition, Assemble Entertainment donates 10% of the revenues of this edition to the children's charity Plan International . This is the best option for all those who would like to support the work of the developer of ENCODYA even more and do something good at the same time. Neo Berlin 2062. Tina – a nine-year-old orphan – lives with SAM-53 – her big clumsy robot guardian – in a rooftop makeshift shelter in Neo-Berlin, a dark megalopolis controlled by corporations. Tina is an urban jungle kid, who has learned to live alone, scavenging from city dumpsters and eking out a living from scraps. Her funny robot is always with her, programmed to protect her no matter what. One day, the little girl discovers that her father left her an important mission: to finish his plan to save the world from grayness! Tina and SAM embark on an incredible adventure across different realities full of bizarre robotic creatures and grotesque human beings. Through puzzles and exciting dialogues, they’ll find out the true meaning of being alive. About Encodya The sweetness and creativity of Studio Ghibli, the setting and atmosphere of Blade Runner and the humor and game style of Monkey Island: these are the ingredients that inspired ENCODYA, a point-and-click adventure game set in a dystopian future. Explore the dark cyberpunk world of ENCODYA in 2.5D with 2 playable characters. Over 34+ non-player characters bring the world of ENCODYA to life and provide a varied and exciting story. Your journey will take you to more than 100 locations where there is a lot to explore and discover. Special, randomly generated puzzles provide a unique gaming experience and present you with great challenges. The cinematic cutscenes and the futuristic art and sound design brings the story of ENCODYA alive. The original soundtrack, especially created for ENCODYA, makes the exciting, crackling atmosphere even more tangible. Professional dubbing actors lend their voices to the characters 'If you enjoy good looking point and click puzzlers, especially if they make you scratch your head along with an interesting story - ENCODYA seems like a good choice.' - Gamingonlinux 'Chaosmonger Studio has delivered a wonderful game with Encodya.' - Gamesunit 'Nice, imaginative and a bit gloomy point-and-click game with heart.' 80/100 - Senses 'A very well achieved Cyberpunk setting.'80/100 - PC Indie Master Race 'The game manages to combine the dark setting with the wit and lightness familiar from titles like Monkey Island.' 80/100 - Levelup Chip DE 'Pixar does cyberpunk. // If you’re a lover of classic adventure games, Encodya is worthy of your time.' 74/100 - Fullsync 'You just have to like the big robot and the little orphan!' 70/100 - 4Players 'Excellent aesthetics cyberpunk point 'n' click adventure, with a nice story and beautiful characters, which leaves a bittersweet taste in the end.' 70/100 - Ragequit GR[/list]

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but I'm afraid I can't quite recommend it. Pros:- lovely art and environments- some decent puzzles- characters are fleshed out, and the two-character system is nice- good QoL features: map, fast-walking, reminder of tasksCons:- some pretty bad puzzles (pixel hunts, a quiz where there's no way to know the answers and you have to start over every time you get one wrong - lampshading it doesn't make it better)- a shallow, contrived and often nonsensical plot - the overall message is reasonable but there are many jarring things like the incompetence of the villain, people helping you out for no real reason or interacting with you in ways that don't make sense- standard adventure game issues: multiple items that could solve a similar problem, but only one works; you know what you need to get or say but you can't do it till you unlock something else first; puzzle solutions that seem to just make no sense (to get a lever, I need to break the thing the lever triggers? a random dialogue line will get you an item?)Overall it's a good effort and will kill some time but it was often frustrating and I didn't feel like I gained much value from going through the narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: ENCODYA

_childDocuments_.review: Solid cyberpunk Point & Click with modern age graphics. A breeze of fresh air, and a recommend for most P&C lovers! Tina is an almost ten years old orphan living on a rooftop in Neo-Berlin, together with her guardian robot SAM-53 (2053 is the year Tina is born). Her father disappeared a long time ago, and that led to her mother getting addicted to the VR cyberspace that hooks the mass of the population. This eventually killed her, leaving Tina alone in this grim world. Luckily she still has her betrusted SAM, because many orphans that live on the street lost their guardian. The following events happen in the first chapter.  You control both Tina and SAM. SAM works best when talking to other robots or tech nerds, while Tina has most of the action since she's the leader. They have both unique tasks, in most cases the characters will tell that a certain job is better suited for the other. The game has modern techniques for player comfort, such as double click to make Tina run. The game doesn't get very complicated, although Tina carries a lot of junk around, it's mostly clear what needs to be done. The visuals are generally nice, but it uses 2D textures, works sublime in the city, but not so much in the forest, so that part looks a bit worse. Also the game has a blue/green-ish tint over it. I guess that makes it more cyberpunk? It does help to grimmen the mood. I'm not sure if I like it...The game recommends a GTX 1060 or better GPU. This is quite demanding, and a bit too high in my opinion. I've played this on a 1070 and gotten 300 fps average on the best settings. The need for a 1060 isn't that high, even with lower details it will look fine. The game could use a framerate limiter, because it's totally unnecessary to push the computer beyond 100fps. The music is clearly inspired by Vangelis's soundtrack of Blade Runner. It remains atmospheric, good eighties synthesizer tunes. The voice acting is decent. One of the achievements is beating the game in 3,5 hours. I really don't understand the reasoning of why to add such an achievement to a Point & Click... You can 100% it in 1 run, which I'm very happy about. By adding a timer to a run they essentially encourage to not explore and rush their creation? Either that or forcing a second playthrough? Is there a hidden layer that can be only seen a second time when you play really really fast? Are they entering next year's SGDQ and the competition will be fierce? No of course not! Speedruns have no place in P&C! This is slightly frustrating for me since the speedrun is impossible for me due to an illness. I can't double click, there is no autorun, so my Tina can't run. And oh boy she takes her time to walk to the next screen, which I don't mind, gives me time to admire the scenery. Now there are other ways for people like me to acquire such achievements, all of them require a lot of and aren't shortcuts. I tried looking for a savegame, but since most people are able to accomplish this by playing, it's not really an issue. So I approached the developer. Surely they considered the accessibility of their game, I thought. But no, they refused to assist, and directed me to the community. They don't feel part of their own game's community? It feels like an elitist approach... In the end i will get it through one of my friends who'll play it one day. I just hoped to get it before reviewing, but I don't want to put off this review any longer. When I want to play a game, I try to do as little research as possible. Even most trailers spoil at least part of the story. When I started Encodya, I knew next to nothing about it. The game starts with a very peculiar message, something like: all likeliness of the characters with real life are pure coincidence. That's a weird statement to make prominent at the start? And soon i discovered the intent of this message. Neo-Berlin has an evil mayor with the name 'Rumpf', who happens to be fat and have a blond hairdo. I can appreciate humour or caricatures greatly and frankly have no personal moral boundary of receiving humour. We write stories based on our experiences and our perspectives. Unless the names are created by a random names generator, and the character models via a similar process, the statement can't be true. Saying that something is coincidence doesn't make it a fact! I'd like to reiterate that I am fine with portraying Donald Trump and Bill Gates (and probably more people) in stereotypes. I am not fine with the way the developers respond on the forum against people on the forum with questions! They keep hammering that it's coincidence, that Rumpf in German means hull (now THAT sounds like coincidence!), and that people should play the game before commenting. Well, I played the game, Rumpf looks like a caricature of Trump and I think it's funny. I enjoyed Encodya a lot! It's so refreshing to play a P&C with modern graphics! Most scenes are beautiful, and the sound/music is good as well. I have a little bit problems with the writing, or to say it better: reviewing the writing. There are a lot of holes in the story. I don't mean 'how can a child live on a rooftop?', but major plotholes. I will list those at the end hidden. The game doesn't seem to make a choice between serious and comical. At one hand you have a very serious story with heavy cyberpunky themes like slavery and addiction, and at the other end you have the laughable cutscenes with Rumpf! An unfortunate mix. If you value story first and foremost, this game might not be for you. A lot of criticism for a game I genuinely like. I had to think for weeks about this one. 80/100Plotholes:- Neo-Berlin suggests a colony, or just Berlin? If so, why Neo?

_childDocuments_.review: Encodya is a beautifully crafted point-and-click adventure in the classic style of Broken Sword or Syberia. It has lovely artwork, solid voice-acting and a heroic quest. You play as two characters - an orphan child (Tina) and her robot guardian (SAM) in a dystopian future that is threatened by greed/power. If you are a fan of traditional point-and-click adventures, then you are very likely to enjoy this game. However, Encodya includes those facets of this genre that tend to become tedious for this gamer. Multiple locations to explore, many NPCs to repeatedly chat with, errands to run, excessive inventory, and very obtuse 'find and use' puzzle solutions. To simplify things a bit, the game uses maps for 'fast travel' and each chapter is self contained (so no backtracking once a segment is completed). There is also a hint system but using this is apt to cost you a couple of achievements.Speaking of achievements, completionists should know that there is a 'speed run' required for 100% - a development decision that (in my opinion) makes absolutely no sense for a game based on narrative and thoughtful exploration. Other achievements are story-driven or relate to finding easter-egg secrets (many of which will make you smile).Prepare to do a lot of back-tracking as dialogs and actions required for story progression tend to involve NPCs across locations. Also prepare to do a lot of pixel scanning, as actionable items are not always obvious.  In some cases, specific dialog choices are required for story advancement which can leave you in an extended loop until you figure out the magic combination.  To mitigate this slightly, you can play in 'easy' mode and gain access to both hints and a key to highlight hot spots.All in all, my time in Encodya was a pleasure and I could not help but have feelings for Tina and SAM. I admit that I grew weary of 'try this' and 'try that' with a plethora of weird objects in my inventory. If your experience is similar, there is a very helpful text guide available in the Steam ForumI recommend this to patient gamers who are fans of traditional point-and-click games that have a story with a heart!
_childDocuments_.name: ENCODYA

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are good, the constant rain and relaxing background music are atmospheric - and that's about all I can recommend. Is it horrible? No.You're going back and forth from places, in classic Point & Click Adventure-style, but so frequently for so little it becomes burdensome and boring. You have to try both characters to get different characters to say/do things, but with no common sense about why a character might respond differently to one than the other. No mini games/puzzles.$25?? Wait until it's under $10 if anything. I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: ENCODYA

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? The game is a polished point and click adventure, with mostly object-orientated puzzles and multiple-choice dialogues. Some items are a bit hard to find, and some objects have to be used in a very... creative way. You play Tina, an orphaned nine year old girl living on the street in a dystopian version of Berlin in the near future. By your side is your pet robot, and you can switch between the two characters to use their respective abilities. What starts like a normal day for Tina, where she needs to find food for herself and robot oil for her buddy and also plans to repair the leaky plastic roof of her shelter, soon changes to an adventure that will change the future of the whole city.While the setting is dystopian, with a corrupt mayor governing the city and most people addicted to cyberspace, the game is not dark and depressing. It is colorful, Tina and her robot are always cheerful, the inhabitants are mostly friendly and the streets are clean. The city is a bit empty, though. Only few robots, inhabitants or vehicles populate the streets.The visual presentation is top-notch, you can double click on an exit to immideately leave the room or press space to see all hotspots. Using the inventory or operating with the environment is very straightforward and hassle-free. The voice acting is professionally done, loading times are short. There are two difficulty settings, you can either play without hints or play an easier version with hints enabled.Loveable point and click adventure in the tradition of the old Lucas Arts classics.
_childDocuments_.name: ENCODYA

_childDocuments_.review: The worst of the 80s is back.Alone. Didn't bring the good along.First thing first, this is barely a Point n' Click adventure.Rather a mere Hidden Objects game.An extreme downgrade from solving puzzles to slowly and constantly scanning every screen with your mouse.A severe issue that tanked many sales and was resolved in Antiquity with the innovation called the Hot Spots key.Which doesn't exist here.You'd think it extremely hard to screw up the interface in a genre having the simplest of them all, and countless examples to remind you how it's done right, but with so many amateurs cosplaying as software engineers, you'd be wrong.What's worse, the devs were warned of this blatant flaw pre-release. Their answer ? "No, we like it that way." So it's incompetence coupled with ego. Here is a clue that shouldn't need to be written, Narcissus: if you are the sole target audience of your scribbles, don't ask money for them.I'm not exaggerating the pixel hunting aggro.It wouldn't be one if, like in games that can dispense with the Hot Spots key, hit boxes were large and their sprites fairly obvious.Here we have tiny buttons hopelessly drowned into the middle of hyper-detailed high resolution landscapes.Scrollable landscapes, of course, otherwise you might have a speckle of a chance at actual gameplay, and we wouldn't want that, would we ?Statistically, there was no way such a high level of UI ineptitude wouldn't manifest into other aspects.Hence the redundant action wheels, the loss of item acquisition after each inventory action, the sedated walk to specific spots before scenery descriptions, the useless dual-character gimmick, the giant robot sprite obfuscating large portions of landscapes, etc.The tedium is extreme.You need to scan manually for all interactibles; then forever remember where they are.There's no more log/journal than there is visual clarity.Enjoy the full rescans if you ever take a break.To make matters worse yet, many landscapes are open at once (which also creates backtracking, through scrollables,) while the inventory quickly fills up with garbage.Solutions disregard intuition. They rely on the bad ole try-all-on-all trope. With poor to no feedback, therefore this approach never prompts amusement.The feedback on inventory use is made of 1 generic sentence; subpar in this era; desolate.All positives lie on the world-building and the presentation.Those received much love and work.For example, some good time you can have is spent idling in a street, people-watching.Dialogue and delivery are of quality, engaging enough.Humour, however, is absent; no offset to the tedium.Encodya ends up in the tiny list of Pn'Cs that I drop unfinished.Dropped very early on in this case.I'd rather put my own effort on discovering the lore than on tunnel-visioning the cursor before grinding the sloppy inventory.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was first introduced to , I was drawn to its art and graphics. The mixture of detailed ligne claire art style and water colours to depict the cyberpunk setting of Neo-Berlin in 2062 is really appealing. The visual contrasts between the main characters, the nine-year-old Tina and her robot guardian/caregiver SAM-53, reminded me of Mei and Totoro from Hayao Miyazaki’s . SAM-53’s design was also reminiscent of the robots featured in Miyazaki’s .Sadly, that’s pretty much everything I’ve enjoyed about . This game’s story, puzzle design, and gameplay are so trite, unpolished, boring, absurd, and dated that I got tired of and frustrated with it half way through. 9 hours of playing time felt like 18. I couldn’t wait for this game to end so that I could move on to something else.The story of  is monotonous. Nothing significant happens in the prologue and in the first two of five chapters that captured my full attention. By the third chapter, the purpose of your adventure is still not fully clear. Tina questioned why she had to wait until she’s 10 years old to find out the purpose of her mission, and I agreed with her sentiment. The logic behind the motivations and actions of some characters are so ill-defined and ridiculous that I just can’t get invested in the adventure.The writers’ attempt at fourth-wall-breaking humour also falls flat, in part due to there being too much of it. Their commentary on the juxtaposition of societal collapse and high tech is also skin-deep. They proposed that cyberspace is a problem: it is addictive, rips family apart, and is a type of mind control. Fair enough, but their response to this issue is a different cyberspace that snaps you back to the real world. It’s ironic that this game, along with the director’s previous works in this Neo-Berlin universe, came to be because of online fundraising via Kickstarter. If it weren’t for cyberspace, the directors’ vision might have never been realized.The game starts off by declaring that it is “not meant to criticize or support a political view, party or person. But it is meant to comment on powerful private or public institutions controlling our lives through media.” Aside from the game NOT doing that by the end, the writers also didn’t have the courage to take a stance in their belief. This was reflected in their poor attempt at satire – it was superficial, and had no relation to the theme. The most fascinating aspect of the game is Tina and SAM-53’s relationship, which would have been a great thing to explore. Yet, it was merely glossed over and delivered little emotional impact in the end. When writing this review, I learned that  is a spin-off of a short film called , which also featured Tina and SAM-53 as main characters. Was I supposed to have seen it beforehand? If so, it would have been nice for me to know before I started the game. If not, then Tina and SAM-53 were simply under, if not poorly, written.Many supporting characters you can interact with exist to give you items or quests, but not enrich the game world. The beautifully designed setting of Neo-Berlin would have benefitted from detailed descriptions of its environment, history and people. Yet, remnants of the Brandenburg Gate only had a brief note, generically designed cyberspace junkies provide no response, and locations stay empty unless you need to find someone there. It’s clear that the game’s director and co-writer is more of a visual artist than a wordsmith.Then there are the puzzles, which are mostly fetch quests. Obtuse clues, backtracking, and pixel-hunting are plenty. The puzzles are arbitrary, forced, and needlessly convoluted even for in-game logic. For one puzzle, you need to find a missing person. The game has you run to different places, getting this and doing that. A more elegant solution exists in the game world, if only the writers would depict the supporting characters as more than just quest givers. A more fully realized, more realistically written character would do more to help a desperate, homeless nine-year-old than to ask her to run errands around the city at night.The puzzles also didn’t take advantage of Tina and SAM-53’s partnership. They are limited to Tina is small, and SAM-53 is tall and strong; Tina can’t operate complex machines, and SAM-53 can; Tina can talk to all people, but not all robots, and SAM-53 can speak robot language, but not all people are willing to talk to him. Basically, anything that a typical adventure game protagonist can do is now divided among the two. Aside from one puzzle, there isn’t much opportunity for Tina and SAM-53 to coordinate efforts to solve problems. What a shame!The part that made  truly unbearable, however, was the adventuring. Tina walks slowly, and SAM-53 even slower. For characters who are racing against time to complete tasks, they saunter everywhere. Running is done in what should have been normal walking speed. Worse, crucial objects are often too small to detect, blended into the background too well, and/or are easily obscured by SAM-53. If you play in Hard Mode as I did, the ability to highlight interactive elements is removed. This makes the game extra frustrating, especially when the solution to your puzzle literally looks like other scraps on the floor. may be visually captivating, but underneath is an adventure game with a boring story, nonsensical premise, illogical and dated puzzle designs, as well as unpolished gameplay. The tale that the writers wanted to tell would have been better served if this were a short film, and not a game. The game’s initial message ended with the advice for us to “unplug from cyberspace from time to time, and have fun out there too!” If ’s quality had anything to do with their recommendation, I’d say the developers had succeeded in getting me away from this game as fast as I could, so I could do something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Very difficult impressions and instant regret that Steam still does not provide an opportunity to leave neutral reviews. The cyberpunk adventure in 2062 for some reason mentally gravitates towards 2021 rather than the world of the future. A 9-year-old girl and her robot travel in search of food and new secrets, along the way helping various strangers, each of whom has their own problems. I will say right away that despite all my naivety and straightforwardness, I really liked the story told by the writers. Yes, she is rather superficial about the acute topics of the collision of reality and virtuality, the dimming of the lights of humanity in the world of endlessly shining neon signs, but in the relationship between the girl and the robot there is that correct soulfulness that disposes to herself, and the ending of the game is very appropriate. The only thing that looks strange is the so often repeated breaking of the 4th wall (why?) And the presence of such a powerful political platform and views in a 9-year-old girl, as if she is immediately ready to go to the debates at the presidential elections of the student club of debaters.Visually, the game looks great, reminded me of the bright style of games from Péndulo Studios, in some places the picture looks like a high-budget animated cartoon. Everything also sounds quite competent, the music is quite consistent with the semantic content of the game. All this is on one side of the scales, but on the other side with a huge weight lies the main "BUT" of this game - the inventory. It always seemed to me that all people who create such specific games as point-and-click quests are big fans of the genre and have played many games of the past, knowing its laws. It's like an axiom for me. Inventory for games of the genre is almost a fundamental thing, sometimes even the plot is not as important as the correct interaction of the player and objects. Here, in addition to the great non-obviousness in the use of objects, there is a terrible pile of garbage in the inventory. Not only are the things that you used and which will never come in handy, for some reason, are not removed from the backpack, there is also a large number of items in the game that will never be used at all, but are simply collected into inventory for ... For the final jokes in the credits? And this dubious decision just makes it incredibly difficult to interact with the world, stretching the gameplay in the wrong direction.The game may be imperfect in certain gameplay solutions, but it definitely deserves its chance with its soulfulness and atmosphere. You should try it yourself, and then make a verdict.

_childDocuments_.review: Production values (i.e. art work, setting, writing, voice acting, etc.) is passable, but the puzzle design is rather frustrating. I'm going to focus the rest of the review on discussing some of the puzzles, so MINOR SPOILERS for some puzzles below.The game features a built-in hint system where you can ask your robot companion on advice on what to do next, but the advice the robot gives is generally useless, as the robot is likely to just tell you that you need to solve the puzzle you're currently facing. For example, there's a point in the game where you'll see a puddle with an electrified wire going into it, and some objects on the other side of the puddle. From this, you can probably figure out that you should do something about the electrified wire so that you can cross the puddle and reach the objects on the other side. Let's say you try every verb ("look", "use", etc.) on the wire, every verb on the puddle, every object in your inventory on the wire, and every object in your inventory on the puddle, and you haven't had any luck. About ready to give up, you ask your robot companion for a hint. The robot merely tells you that you should find some object to use on the wire. Utterly useless. A more useful hint would have been something along the lines of "Did you check the abandoned store?"Later on in the game, you'll encounter an apartment building with several apartments. You need to enter one of them, but you don't know which one. You might at first try interacting with some of them, but your robot companion will say he "doesn't want to disturb the residents", which implies that we need more information rather than just randomly knocking on every door and bothering people. So you go around the world trying to figure out how you'll find information on which apartment you're supposed to enter, and eventually you might give up and ask for another hint. The robot tells you that you should just try every apartment, brute forcing the solution. Unbelievable. So you go through every apartment, ringing every doorbell. A lot of them have no answer. A couple of them have an NPC answer asking who is it, and your only choices are joke responses like "I'm selling these matches" or "You've won the lottery!" or "It's the police! Open up!" None of them allow you to actually ask the person on the other side if you can come in and look around because you're looking for the apartment your dad used to live in. So now you're stuck.If you go to a walkthrough online, it turns out that you're supposed to choose one of the joke answers, and pick a specific set of responses to get this particular resident let you in. Even though I've told you the essence of the solution to the puzzle, you don't know which joke answer is right answer to pick, so even with this guidance, you would still need to go to every door, talk to every resident, and try every possible dialog option."Puzzles" which simply require you try every possible combination is uninteresting and is more busy-work than actual puzzle solving.

_childDocuments_.review: Should be just my kind of game. Pure point-n-click and set in the future... I want to love it, but there are too many annoying things. You have the perfect tool for something - but have to collect some nonsense to solve it instead... 'barriers' that could be overcome by simply walking round... but you can't. I hate PnCs where you use a tool for a puzzle - lose the tool - then need the same tool for the next thing... Encodya has the opposite problem - you end up carrying a lot of stuff you never need.By stage 4 and 5 the 'puzzles' feel increasingly contrived... wait till you have to get strawberries, if you don't find that ridiculous... well.It's got some good elements, solid voice acting, likeable characters, a good aesthetic - but they're not enough to make up for the flaws.If you've run out of PnC games, and it's on sale, maybe give it a go - it's 5 out of 10 - so not trash. But it's not great either.

_childDocuments_.review: ENCODYA~~~~~~~~~There’s a new Indie clicker in town . . . ENCODYA is turning out to be a blast with an excellent combination of mystery-adventure and well-scripted narration set in a cyberpunk fantasy world. At the beginning, I struggled a bit with the game’s settings and its twist on the point and click genre. But slowly I started to appreciate the game more and more as I kept playing. The game’s main focus is to push the players further down a rabbit hole until the story starts to come clean, solving multiple puzzles and hurdles while doing so. Plot: Neo Berlin 2062. The world has changed a lot over the years, and is being controlled by corporations. You play as nine-year-old orphan Tina, who lives in a makeshift shelter on a rooftop with a nine-year-old nanny robot, in Neo Berlin. Growing up as an orphan made her both tough and an expert in survival in this jungle of a metropolis. Tina has learned to live alone, scavenging from city dumpsters and eking out a living from scraps. Her trusty robot SAM-53 is always with her, programmed to protect her no matter what.After another dull day of survival, she comes back to her shelter to find that it’s been ruined and searched.  After checking a surveillance robot, she finds out that for some reason the mayor is after her. SAM-53 discovers that Tina’s father left her a message saying that he wants her to fulfill his final mission; a mission to save the world from grayness! Now Tina and SAM embark on an incredible adventure across different realities full of bizarre robotic creatures and grotesque human beings. Through puzzles and exciting dialogues, they’ll find out the true meaning of being alive. Gameplay: Complimenting the incredible storyline of ENCODYA is its unique twist on point and click style gameplay. The game from the get-go encourages the players to explore and interact with items, structures, NPC’s, and all the elements in the game. As you progress through your daily task list, more and more story of the city unfolds in front of you. In the beginning, I was thrown a bit off guard with the game’s point and click style of gameplay. Also the way in which different items, scattered throughout the world, can be combined and used in multiple scenarios.I must say ENCODYA did a great job at this, using items that you have picked up from around the city to solve rather difficult day-to-day issues and puzzles. And all this plays through some simple gameplay machines, such as using Left click to walk and double Left to run. The left mouse button plays an important role throughout the game; you are meant to you the left button to perform five key functions throughout the game - Use, Look, Pull, Talk, Pick. All of these functions play out seamlessly through the gameplay to help Tina and SAM-53 to perform various tasks. You can select between SAM and Tina on the go with the tab key or left button click on their respective icons. For the most part, you can use Tina or SAM with any issues all over the city, but while interacting with specific NPC’s and doing specific tasks, only one or the other can be used. For example, you cannot use SAM while interacting with exposed electrical wiring, or Tina while interacting with Robot. Well, you can use them, but for these types of specific scenarios, they won’t be able to interact properly or at all. The city is divided into multiple areas and all of them can be explored after they are unlocked or show up on the map.  To visit these places all you have to do is click M or click on the map icon and select the desired area.It’s best to get familiar with each area the first time you visit and collect as many items as you can spot, as you might need to come back to finish a task that you have had to leave for the time being,  or perhaps because you were missing some items. You might need to go back and forth to finish one task or to interact with an NPC and get all of the necessary information out of them.Inventory system; ENCODYA features a simple yet effective inventory system by simply hitting I or the mouse scroll. Both Tina and SAM-53 have access to the same inventory and can interact, combine, and inspect the items at any given time. Narration: ENCODYA features some of the most well-scripted and well-performed narrations I have encountered this year. The style of the dialogue and the way they have been performed suits the theme of the game just perfectly. World design: ENCODYA’s world design is absolutely marvelous. From the slums, to the alleyways, it’s neon cyberpunk city centers each feel unique and yet familiar at the same time. Each area has its own unique charm, and the night city is just amazing, with it’s stunning lighting theme and rain effects. Music and sound effects: Well-selected background music, which fits the game's theme just fine. The devs did a great job with the sound effects; very well put-together and implemented, especially the raindrops and thunder effects. Positives: + Interesting story + Well put-together narration + Beautiful world design + Meet interesting characters throughout the game+ Simple and effective gameplay + Well put-together background music and sound effects + Interesting puzzles, simple yet effective+ Video tutorial Negatives: - Minor performance issues here and there- Momentary game freeze - NPC interacting system can be improvedTina and SAM will go to any lengths to fulfill Tina’s father’s last mission – to save the world from endless grayness. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: I feel very meh about this game. The GoodI enjoyed the general art style, it reminded me of old 3d animation.I liked the relationship of Sam and TinaThe MehIntractable items were hard to differentiate on screen from the background and felt like a pixel hunt at times. There was a claim that pressing/holding the space bar will light up those items, but it never worked for me. What I assume are translation issues, there was a part that suggested finding a secret word located on a big door. The answer to the puzzle was actually on an art carving over a gateway. The ram was a bit unfair to find, as it is not labelled on the shelf it is placed on and Sam is able to just take it from a shop with no issues from the owner, which made no sense. The plot was rather boring up to that point and did not spark my interest to find out what the ultimate secret was.The BadThe long note at the very beginning of the game stating that the company believe in no stereotypes, but will use stereotype to push the plot forward *right* before displaying an overtly racist caricature of a Japanese man is really gross. His name is Chef Hayao, they gave him buck teeth, and  a very exaggerated accent/pronunciation. Solving puzzles felt impossible at times as some solutions did not make sense. When looking for clothing Tina noted that a shirt was too big even though they were living on the street in a tent, layers are layers and she would likely grow into the shirt. _childDocuments_.review: An impressive looking but mediocre adventure game which struggles to tell its story at any kind of pace.  The graphics are great with an atmospheric setting, full 3D scenes and models and cartoon style cut scenes, and the voice acting is good, although Tina’s dialogue is inconsistent with her age.  The story however is far too childish, with everyone you meet too helpful and nice and the pacing is awful.  The puzzles are all fetch quests, involving a lot of back and forth and pixel hunting and the solutions are too precise even for adventure game logic, with things only being usable once you know you need them and only a single specific item will work, even if plenty of other things should do the job.The lead pair of characters have a good relationship and having two playable protagonists makes for a good dynamic, although not having any co-operative puzzles seems like a missed opportunity.  As for the other characters, there’s something off about them – apart from being stereotypes, they serve little function, much like a lot of the scenes, apart from adding to the setting.  The constant loading screens between scenes is frustrating as is the way the characters clip through each other and the lead villain’s incompetence defies belief, but none of this is a deal breaker.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game!  The story was engaging, funny, moving and kept my interest throughout.  I enjoyed the voice overs and music very much.  The puzzles were fair and at the right level of challenge, not too hard or easy.Unless you are a masochist, like me, I would recommend playing on easy mode first.  I played on hard mode without a hot spot indicator or hints and though hints weren’t necessary for me, some of the items and hot spots were small and very easy to miss and was the reason I got stuck now and again.The only thing I wish was different was the inventory interface.  I wish examining was a right-click and using an item was a simple drag motion instead of clicking to get to the icons for looking/using.  But that’s a small issue and shouldn’t be a deal breaker.My play time was about 13 hours and I thought the game was just wonderful.  It was well worth my time and the price.  I recommend this game for adventure lovers.

_childDocuments_.review: Encodya has us delve into a cyberpunk world, with all the similar world-building elements that are common in cyberpunk settings, but delivered in a more family-friendly manner. We play as two characters - a 9-year old Tina, and her nanny robot SAM-53, both living on the streets. After an encoded message from Tina's missing dad, Tina and SAM decide to set out on a mission that he's given them, all in a while the greedy city mayor is on their heels. The story is generally decent and main characters are charming and fun to follow, although don't expect big twists or a lot of tension as the tone is generally mild and family-friendly. The gameplay is a classic point-and-click that has us interact with the environments, talk to NPCs, and solve puzzles to make progress in the plot. The plot is linear and there are no story choices to make. Most puzzles are quite decent and logical, although a few could keep you stuck for a while. The game's easy mode allows you to get hints from SAM if you're stuck, although the hints might not necessarily help you with the exact issue you're stuck on.Since we play as both characters, we can swap between them at will at any time. Some interactions with NPCs and environment are different for Tina and SAM. For example, SAM is more suited to talking to robot NPCs, whom Tina does not understand, while on the other hand some people won't speak to SAM as they're not comfortable talking to a machine, so you'd want to use Tina when talking to them. SAM can lift heavier objects that Tina can't, but Tina can do things requiring use of small spaces or fine movements.The environments visuals are stunning and beautiful, especially the atmospheric cyberpunk urban areas full of neon signs, rain, and people wearing headsets and plugged into cyberspace. Voice acting is nice and suitable for the tone of the game, and music is ok.Generally, a nice point and click game. Nothing major to criticise. Story and gameplay are decent, but not extraordinary. Difficulty of puzzles is fine and satisfying for the most part, aside from a handful of examples. Full price is a little high, in my opinion, so recommended on a discount. Suited for younger audiences and those looking for a classic point and click experience.For a more in-depth review, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying that I am a big fan of point and click adventure games, my recent reviews of the Leisure Suit Larry games will tell you that a well written game with great puzzles will give you endless fun, so when I was asked to review Encodya (Stupid name I know), I jumped at the chance.Let's go over the plot quickly, set in the year 2062 and based on the short film "Robot will protect you",  you play as Tina, a 9-year-old orphan girl, and her guardian robot Sam 53.You live in a shelter on a roof top. Dystopian future, robots, you get the idea, you have seen it a thousand times before.As you play the game you are given daily tasks, to start with they are things like fix the shelter, get edible food, and so on. The graphics are stunning, the voice acting is decent. All in all it looks and sounds great.So far so good. In pretty much all point and click games, when you are on a screen you will press a button and that will highlight everything you can interact with. In Encodya this is done with the Space Bar, however it doesn't really highlight clearly anything, maybe something will lighten slightly in colour, and that is it, and it will often only be something that you can directly pick up, nothing else is highlighted, so you will end up scanning the entire screen slowly trying to find things, this is beyond frustrating.You will soon get stuck, luckily there is built in hints, but to access them you have to take control of Tina and then speak to Sam, you then have to go through annoying dialog EVERY SINGLE TIME to get to the question you want to ask to get the hint on. And then the hint you get is next to useless. What this leaves you doing is getting even more frustrated, endlessly walking around and trying a process of elimination with regards to things in your inventory, hoping that two things match up that may help you figure something else. Unfortunately, this tedious game-play will just either leave you thinking "what's the point, this is no fun", or just simply watching a walk-through video on YouTube and copying that. Which basically makes playing the game pointless.How to fix this. 1. Hints system needs to be a simple question mark on the side of the screen, one click help.2. The help itself needs to actually help you, not tell you things you already know.I wanted to enjoy this game, but there is just nothing in it to make me want to come back and finish it. I am left feeling indifferent, which is such a shame as clearly a lot of work has gone into the game, but the control system is annoying, the Robot gets in the way when you are trying to see something, and although you can control him and move him, it is just another thing to wind you up.The GoodThe game is beautiful, a lot of work has gone into it, and I really appreciate the hard work.The BadThe game is poorly designed, controls are slow, and you end up wasting too much time clicking through to get to what you want. Things need to be instant. It is 2062! SPEED THINGS UP!OverallWith a better control system, and maybe making the robot tiny so he doesn't get in the way, and a much improved hint system, this game could be great. It is one of those annoying occasions where everything that annoys me, is so very close to being done right, but then these little things all add up, and just drove me mad.I rate this game 5/10 I will let it go through a few updates and then give it another try as I am sure they will fix these things and the game will improve 100%

_childDocuments_.review: I can't like this game. It was too painful for me to play. I am a big fan of point-and-click puzzle games, so I thought I would like this one given it's highish rating. However, after beginning to play, I started having doubts. From the very beginning I was having to blunt force some of the "puzzles". A little bit is a given in these types of games, but at the very start I would think good game design would initiate some basic intuitiveness in the puzzles. After completing the starting area, I noticed that some items from my inventory had disappeared. These were items that I hadn't used yet and the realization that this game gave me completely pointless items fairly similar to ones I possessed as red herring irked me. However, it had a fairly good rating so I continued to give it a chance. I continue to play through a couple of more sections, but then I hit my frustration limit and I cannot continue. If you're going to play this game. Prepare for a pixel hunt. The hit boxes for clickable items are generally very small. The artwork is also hostile to finding items. There are plenty of things that seem like items that are just set pieces and some items blend in to an insane degree. Also sometimes you might think you tried to check an area only to find out 30 min later you just didn't quite hit the right spot on the screen for the spot you were aiming for. Prepare yourself to have to blunt force your way through spots. While some puzzle parts make sense, and you will find yourself solving the puzzle before the designer thought you would, others are so dang specific and nonsensical that you will find yourself trying every combination and every interaction possible. That combined with items and spots that end up having nothing to do with the game progression, and have no visible differentiation as the set pieces they are, will make your game-play a frustrating experience.Or prepare yourself a guide, if you want to avoid all that, but still "play" the game. Some of the other reviewers seemed to enjoy the story, although I didn't. I mean I did feel it had promise. The art seemed pretty good to me, though the humans went a little bit to uncanny valley for my liking. The plot had promise, but I was seeing some holes and it just didn't grab me enough to put up with the game-play. And the voice acting was honestly terrible. I mean it was impressive how much they had in it, but what I heard sounded like most people were just reciting words off a sheet.I will say I didn't get very far, so maaaybbeee it will get better later on, but I'm not willing to continue to find out.

_childDocuments_.review: My first "date" with Encodya was thanks to the free demo the devs had released some weeks before the full game was still to come out. It was one of those excitingly old-school adventures with lots of item manipulations.The main characters, little tiny Tina and her nanny-robot, are, at least for me, well-drawn and quite interesting to follow. However, I feel like we were left missing a lot of both our main personages' characters: the reasoning behind their actions was sometimes left ungrounded. This, however, didn't obstruct me from following or getting immersed in the game.This is a very linear game, so keep it in mind if you ever get stuck - the chances are you're missing something ridiculously elementary close to your last valuable action or development. The game atmosphere is a massive benefit for me - a few locations, but they were well-developed and looked realistic for the characters' universe.User experience-wise, I had some optimisation issues in the cutscenes, but they disappeared after I played around with the settings a bit. VSynch is something you should look at first and foremost if you experience such abnormalities.One negative development since the demo:I adored two aspects of the demo: the mixture of fantasy and cyberpunk that was using Whispered World-like character designs and Primordia-like environmental elements (of course, we also had the most-have Blade Runner aspects that every cyberpunk project "needs") and the inventory and item functionalities. The fact that we had to switch between the two characters to use features of the game adequately made absolute sense. Unfortunately, the latter was removed when the full game came out. Guess not everyone thinks that if you have two playable characters, you need to have a reason to have *two* of them. Otherwise, it's just annoying, which was while playing the full game - I just kept playing with one character until I was 100% obliged to use another in a conversation or action. Still, it had already lost the novelty of multiple character interactions for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like tedious pixel-hunting and hidden-object "secrets" in your "serious" non-casual adventures?Do you enjoy moon logic almost as bad as in the adventures from 90s?Are you exited about the idea of making a story with social conflict and politics, but for kids, yet sold like it's a serious game?Does yet another "cyberpunk" game that has nothing to do with cyberpunk as a genre besides being "sci-fi" and with "cyber" slapped over random stuff spike your interest?Then Encodya might be just for you!But assuming you are a normal person - skip that masterpiece of german (probably?) game developmentP.S. Oh, just 6 hours? Well, it felt like 20 hours, I was almost going to complain that it's too long. Well, no, it's just too bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Would recommend only if you buy it on discount. The puzzles were often frustrating, with lots of pixel hunting and trial and error when combining random pieces from your inventory, and I ended up just using a walkthrough for a good portion of the game. Visuals and soundtrack were top-notch however, and I wish they sold the soundtrack as a separate item since I'd buy that immediately (though it can be found on Spotify as well, but I'd prefer to support the artist). By the end of it I found myself wishing this was just a chill exploration game in the vein of Stardew Valley, since the city of Neo Berlin seemed to have a lot of thought put into its development and I would've liked to learn more about it than I was able to here.

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Well designed cyberpunk world with lots of details. It feels alive as vehicles and characters constantly passing by.- Great aesthetics. Gorgeous cartoonish 3d graphics.- Good, chill, atmospheric music through the entire game.- Voice acting is really good.- The main characters are adorable and they have some nice and smooth animations. The relation between them is so sweet.- There are some good jokes here and there with references to older video games. The collectibles are funny too.- Controlling two characters is interesting and gives an extra depth. Sometimes you have to use Tina and others Sam in order to proceed.- With double click you can run or instantly change screen. There is also a map for quick travel. Good additions. I am so bored of watching slow walking animation in most of the point and click adventures.- The hint system is well build and will discreetly help you if you are stuck.The bad- Puzzles are simplistic and uninspiring. _childDocuments_.review: ENCODYA is a point-and-click adventure game from first-time developer Nicola Piovesan, who has previously been successful an accomplished filmmaker and director.  The story is loosely based on his 2019 short film, Robot Will Protect You.Set 40 years in the future, in the cyberpunk dystopia Neo-Berlin, an increasing number of cyberspace junkies wander around like zombies with their cumbersome headsets, wasting away.  Tina, a homeless 9-year-old orphan, lost her mother to this cyberspace illness, and has been scraping out a living on the streets with her unfailingly loyal government-issue nanny bot, Sam.  One day, Sam suddenly becomes the target of a citywide manhunt, and the pair soon learns that Sam contains secret data left behind by the father that Tina never knew she had.  Tina embarks on her father's mission to locate the secret cyberworld of ENCODYA as government goons follow her every step of the way.ENCODYA is a massive success on all aesthetic fronts.  Visually, ENCODYA is unbelievable.  The game is gorgeous and evokes a very Ghibli vibe.  All of the environments are bursting with life and color.  The character models are pretty, even for minor NPCs, and the animation is smooth.  The game's soundtrack is also gorgeous and largely made up of these ambient orchestrations that feel firmly in touch with the game's cyberpunk genre.  Finally, the voice performances are strong, most notably Lizzie Freeman as Tina and Sean Weiland as Ren.Tonally, ENCODYA is kind of all over the map, and the more dramatic bits are far more effective than the funny ones.  The overall story of the game is quite a serious one, the overall themes of family and living in the moment are more appropriate for a serious game than a comedy.  I think the rooftop scene very early in where Tina learns of her overall mission is the best in the game, I felt my eyes watering a bit with the emotional performance.  Even when nothing dramatic is happening, the overall feeling of being small and lost in a big city is sobering.While I kind of wished the game stuck with that more mature tone, ENCODYA wasn't all serious.  Many of the characters you meet, including the main villain, are walking cartoons - from a self-absorbed social media influencer, to a stereotypically Japanese chef.  There are some strangely out-of-place fourth-wall breaks, and a solid handful of adventure game in-references.  There are also 10 specifically tracked easter eggs that are a little harder to find.  While this was fun, I don't feel it was necessary, and in some ways it felt like the game was kind of pulling its punches.  Towards the climax of the story, right when we should be getting the juiciest bits of plot, there's a random sidequest to gather ingredients for a picnic, and the final confrontation, because the bad guy is such a clown, just doesn't quite punch as hard as it could.I think that the puzzles in ENCODYA overall work well enough, although consensus seems to be that they are a mixed bag.  Early patches made one or two of the pixel-huntier issues I had on my first playthrough much more manageable, so this is no longer an issue you should experience.  With that said, you can expect a number of very genre-typical roadblocks and solutions.   There is a lot of back and forth, and I got stuck a couple of times.  When I finally figured out how to unstick myself, some of the solutions did have me rolling my eyes just a little bit.  I did play on hard mode, which eliminates the hint system and adds complexities to a few of the puzzles, but an easy mode is available as well.Overall, ENCODYA is a very good adventure game, and I am glad to have backed it.  The environments are so pretty and the main characters are so likable that I do foresee myself coming back to this and replaying it in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: is a really charming Point & Click adventure game in a cyberpunk dystopian world. The game is expansive with its locations well-designed characters and puzzles and show plenty of polish through its artistic touches, music, and also the voice-acted dialogue. Tina lives with her robot SAM-53 in the futuristic year 2062, when most people are addicted to cyberspace. Tina spends her days scavenging and living off of scraps, and SAM is always there to protect her. Their lives change when Tina discovers the important mission left behind by her father, to save the world. This is a traditional Point & Click adventure with a rather large world, featuring over 100 locations. You will choose between 2 difficulties in the beginning. There's Easy mode, which allows you to get hints and you can use spacebar to highlight things that you can pick up. It will not highlight all objects that you can interact with. The other difficulty does not give hints and does not allow for the revelation of pick-up items with spacebar. I did have to use a decent number of hints to get to where I am right now.The game features 5 chapters in total, with an elaborate story of finding out what it means to be alive. There are many NPCs that you interact with, and you will come across well-acted dialogues and scenes. The story progression in this game is really nice to follow.As most Point & Click adventures go, after you pick things up,  you will be able to interact with or combine items in your inventory to get a new item. You will be able to choose items from your inventory to interact with the other objects/people in the game.There is a manual save and an autosave function.The puzzles here can be a bit tough. Luckily I found the developers to be very kind and helpful whenever I felt to be really stuck.The game has a map for fast travel as well. The map is nicely made and you will likely be using it many times.The graphics are really great for this game. You can feel that darkness within this futuristic cyberpunk world.  The appearances of the characters, especially the main characters, are very well-made.The music is quite nice to listen to, and the voice-acted dialogue are excellent too.The game can be fully played with a mouse (and a keyboard).The price is around €25, which is something you would expect for a high-quality Point & Click adventure game. The launch sale of 20% off is pretty nice.This game is really great. I am somewhere in the middle of the story as of writing this review. I am enjoying the story progression as well as the puzzles. The nice artwork, music, and voice overs are nice touches to make this game really shine.When I was stuck a few times, I also reached out to the development team for assistance. Fortunately I was able to get the help I needed to keep going.I can fully recommend this game!

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game for free in exchange for my willingness to create content around it, which I'll be putting on my youtube after I edit the recordings. However, there was no expectation for me to provide a positive review in this agreement. So believe me or don't, that's your choice. But I enjoyed this game! I have an odd relationship with puzzle games like this, and that's usually that I get frustrated and cheat a lot with guides. Not so much on this one! I don't know if I got lucky or if the game was just so well designed to make navigation through the puzzles not so obscure.... The only warning I want to give is that this game has both subtle and not so subtle commentary on social / political / life views. You might not agree with the commentary, or you might. But of course, this game is entirely fictional and any likenesses to real life places or people is totally coincidental. I'm excited to see what else comes from those who made Encodya.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Encodya.The art is just phenomenal, creating an interesting world with beautiful settings and interesting characters. It makes any quirks here or there completely tolerable, because it's just... SO pretty.The voice acting of the main characters in particular is great, and the attention paid to quickly revealed character back stories and the later follow-ups is really nice. By the end, you feel like everything has been neatly tied in a bow.The story and gameplay are good. While it  at times feel a little bit like a *shudder* hidden object game in places, the settings are so beautiful (like I said), that it doesn't really piss me off too much. The initial story is just about survival as a street kid, so while it doesn't feel pressingly urgent, it does allow us to see why Neo Berlin isn't very nice. The pace increases and we start interacting with (even) more interesting characters after that first act.I appreciated the attention to detail of having two protagonists, switching back and forth as per their respective limitations and skills. I also loved how while many characters had a preference for talking to one of the pair over the other, there were occasions when a character would chat to both, but say or do something specific when interacting with one rather than the other - that kept things interesting.The puzzle design was very much like classic adventure games of old - with some classic puzzles, and a fair bit of picking up strange objects, working out why later, and combining things in unpredictable ways to solve puzzles. These had me stumped at times, and I resorted to a video walkthrough to help with the tough parts. i didn't use the in-game hint system, which probably would have helped, too.The one negative thing I'd say in relation to the puzzle design and the above is... Sometimes I just didn't see really obvious things. It wasn't so much that I didn't know how to solve a puzzle, but I frequently didn't see a given exit, or a particular object I should have picked up. There was the option to use space to highlight objects in the scene, but unfortunately, it only highlights things you can collect - not things you can interact with or exits. It was also not possible to use this on hard mode. However, most adventure games these days DO have a hot point reveal key option. While I get that the dev probably WANTED some pixel hunting going on, just like in the olden days, having a standard hot point reveal option that revealed ALL the interactive parts in a scene would have negated my need to scrutinise video walkthroughs to find some goopy substance or capacitor I'd missed. These are minor quibbles, though, for someone who plays for the story, the escapism, the art, and the experience - when all these are fulfilled very well. The game itself is extraordinarily well made - pretty stunning for the dev's first big project, afaik. The graphics, like I said, just blew me away. The story is also great, really uplifting and non-stressful - exactly what we all need in 2021. The at times very calm pace was actually quite welcome.The story is a great one. And maybe it's my hormones, but the ending even made me shed a tear. (Probably was my hormones, but that still doesn't mean it's nothing!) I'm glad to have been a Kickstarter backer for this one. Money well invested.Well done, Nicola! I look forward to seeing your next project!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A poorly designed point n click that’s just not worth it. It isn’t even unnoteworthy enough to be faithfully generic, and hasn’t managed to get a single thing right. Encodya is a bland and generic cyberpunk dystopia 1/5 cross (Mega City/Cyberspace) running indie story beats 1 and 8 (Child and Protector and stop the corruption). It’s a terrible Point’n’Click (PnC) adventure which manages to hit almost every genre branch on the way down. The game lacks any real character of its own, has no twists, and so it’s quite easy to jump into. We are Tina and SAM-53, we are a homeless orphan living in Neo-Berlin. A city so desperate for citizens it gives robots to parents to help with childcare, but then doesn’t look after the children at all. It’s in that comicbooky Borderlands art style and is voiced in English by someone who sounds like a 40 year old who’s only experience with children in the last three decades has been against their will, pretending to have the vim and vigour of a 9 year old.So let’s decodeya this failure. Generally speaking I’d say this game really isn’t worth your time or money. The only thing I’m glad about, and this is a MAJOR spoiler, is that I guess if you’re really not fussy, wouldn’t know a good story if it jumped up and bit your nose off, or will clap like a seal for the pretty pictures, then this might be for you.As a story, it fails. As a PnC adventure game, it fails. As a talking point, it fails. As art, well art is subjective, so it succeeds there, and it has its animation moments…But no, I don’t recommend it. with reviews by genre. _childDocuments_.review: Encodya is a decent adventure game. The art design was the best part for me, it felt like playing a cartoon. The storyline is the usual cyberpunk fare. If you like cyberpunk you'll probably enjoy it, although it really doesn't cover any new ground. The puzzles aren't great. About half of them are sensible and don't feel like chores, but there are also several tedious fetch quests thrown in. Aside from one really obscure clue in part 4, the main reason I played with a walkthrough was to get past the dismal pixel hunting. I wish in retrospect I'd played it on "easy" instead of "hard", if only to get access to the reveal hotspots button. There's not really an excuse for locking that out of an adventure game made in 2021 - if you're not going to give clues to the player about where the objects are, then hiding them in the background isn't "hard" mode, it's just "waste of time" mode. Still, despite the sometimes-frustrating puzzles, it's a well-produced game and fun enough to be worth buying if you like point'n'click adventures.

_childDocuments_.review: Driven by a naively lighthearted plot filled with good intentions, ENCODYA has an honest, kind heart at its base, a generally pleasant art style and enjoyable soundtrack. Nice animation details. It demonstrates an authentic passion for the genre, and undoubtedly a lot of talent despite numerous shortcomings.Dialogues often break the 4th wall to remind the player this is a point-and-click game. The future is entirely built out of tech from the early 80s and late 90s to purposefully serve nostalgic affection for the adventuring golden age. Everything feels out of time in 2062 with CRT monitors, 3½-inch disks, VHS tapes, brick phones and period car models (now flying). The game contains 10 hidden secrets in the form of optional interactions that often pay homage to the same sentiment.Occasionally interesting though shallow characters are often hurt by awkwardly delivered voice overs. Bad guys are stormtroopers. Antagonist politician Rumpf is not a parody of another well-known blonde-haired buffoon. Long overdue reunions feel careless and underwhelming. Abundantly stereotypical ethnic representations also appear lifted from decades gone.Various plot elements feel nonsensical, such as when Sam urges Tina to eat something while in cyberspace, though as a whole most interactions and puzzles remain fair.Switching between Tina and Sam at will announces a clever alliance to solve more complex puzzles, but more often than not ends up duplicating observations, with minor differences between the two characters. Sam is so huge he often gets in the way of conversations or hotspots when playing as Tina. Tina's youthful cleverness is rarely explored as both characters can perform most actions interchangeably. They both take forever to reach the other end of most screens with their staggeringly slow walking speed.The game offers two difficulty levels. Hit space bar in easy mode to reveal occasional items that may otherwise appear insignificant. Where most modern adventure games conveniently expose all hotspots, ENCODYA opts to highlight only select items.Other conveniences are absent, like immediate inventory access on mouseover, using an item with a single click and trying out various combinations without having to reselect the item every time, backing out of conversation trees without having to repeat the entire exchange to try alternate selections, etc.There are too many red herrings and random pick-ups here, a celebrated accomplishment in the end credits. Once an object has served its purpose, it is often not removed from the cluttered inventory until the next chapter. A few useless items annoyingly pervade the entire duration.Neon-lit Neo Berlin looks more like Tokyo. The real ENCODYA itself isn't particularly spectacular, where fresh bread is obtained via mechanical dispensers, and the world is nothing but haphazard vegetation and broken machines.I will be looking forward to more titles from this developer with the hope that their next effort will better utilize their abilities into crafting a more cohesive product, with refined interactions, better dialogues and voice over, and a more engaging story.
