_childDocuments_.review: If you really need to play a game, you might as well play a good one. For example this one.Vasilisa is a young baba dwelling with her grandfather Egor the moujik, who teaches her to become a witch and to fight or tame demons to bring back her fiancé from hell. As you see, it is not a mundane story.A "meget russisk" story, but the game is enjoyable and not too difficult. It is not boringThere are fights where you assemble cards to form a spell and you make moral choices in dialogs.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Get ready to get your reading comprehension skills on!In this game, it is all about the story and how well you are able to apply yourself as a Koldun (Witch)Though this game will probably not be one of the best games you'll ever play from your library; what it will be is a lot different than most of the other games you'll have and play.  As noted earlier, many of the dialogues and texts may be tested upon you again and will earn you extra experience points for getting it right.  The fun part is reading through your texts to try and get the answer right.  There are some choices within the game that will be based on earlier dialogues that have not been recorded in your book.  If you put this game down for a bit and then pick it back up after a few days then you might forget something and make the game a bit tougher for you. Battles are usually fairly easy except when fighting bosses with a lot of hp.   Puzzle battles are the worst idea in this game as it renders your whole build worthless.  I get that they were probably trying to make battles a bit more unique and different but losing a few times until you understand it, isn't very fun.  Although this game is a bit of a deckbuilder, arranging your black book seems awkward and difficult at first.  I wasn't sure how to fix up my book until much later in the game.  Cards you receive as rewards are magically inserted into your deck and there's really nothing you can do.   Again it wasn't until much later that you realize you can make a separate deck and then eureka that's how you can make a different deck. TLDR: Story based game with interesting mechanics but lots of dialogue and weird deckbuilding system.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a mix of a visual novel and card deck building game. It also has some RPG elements - decisions that influence on future events and sub-RPG elements - gear and level advancement.- Visual novel part is represented by a story infused with an old russian folclore. It is well made(as for a visual novel genre) and also has incredibly good voice acting(original language).- Card deck building part is also well made. Different cards are given to the player over the game course along with new enemies that encourage the player to use them. There also some puzzle card rounds where the deck is predefined for a special enemy set.- RPG part is surprisingly good for a visual novel. There are a lot of choices in game that will have a cut-off content as a consequence. Player also may chose between different ways of completing an encounter.Although the game is far from perfection. - It is still a visual novel. - It has stylish, but below medicore graphics, which sometimes is just out of place(but most of the time is ok).- It has a poor movement system and even worse - sometimes movement system is a part of a gameplay.- It has no resource balance.upd: changed to "Not recommended" due to notification feed abuse. _childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: A narrative deckbuilding game where you play a witch from Slavic folklore who helps and torments nearby villages while trying to unseal a black book of magic so that she  can bring back her beloved from hell. The story is great as is the foundation in folklore, and the fact that you can be a good witch or a jerkass witch or somewhere in between. Unfortunately, the game overstays its welcome with a lengthy and repetitive campaign. The deckbuilding aspect of the game is neat, but once you have a solid deck that works for you there is no point in changing it. New cards and mechanics are introduced, but generally all you're doing is swapping out existing cards in your deck for slightly upgraded cards. So the fights become very repetitive as you use the same cards against the same monsters over and over. It's a shame because the game starts very strong, but over time it becomes the same thing over and over.

_childDocuments_.review: 30.1h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. Yes (~40 achievements). No. is an RPG card-battler game set in Russia, telling the story of witchcraft and the local demons. You'll play as a witch in ancient times who will use your spells to curse people.- Create your deck based on certain builds- Minor story branching based on your choices- 3+1 endings- Story can be hard to follow, especially with the hard-to-remember names- Saving is only done at the beginning of each areaIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650Despite focusing on demons, the visuals in  aren't scary at all. All characters are deformed with most details left out. That being said, 2D portraits are still used on the characters to give a clearer expression while talking. tells its story similar to a choose-your-adventure game: a narrator will tell what happened poetically and explain the options that you can choose from. These dialogues are empty most of the time and don't matter to the story as a whole—it can be tiring to read them all if you like to focus on the battle aspect. Luckily, the same style isn't used for the main story. The dialogue will be done between some characters with them exchanging words in a conversation.I like the story's theme. It tells about the Russian culture and the local demons. As someone who is not familiar with it, I found it to be interesting to read. However, most of the names can be hard to remember, and it was hard to keep up with the story because of it sometimes. Luckily, the story isn't that hard to read—it mostly focuses on the activity you need to do in the chapter. The same can't be said for the extra information in the game, though. Some of the stories explain things too fast, making it hard to figure out what actually happened. What I enjoyed about the game was the choose-your-adventure part. You can choose any option that you want and the result will change based on your choice. Sometimes, the reward will come in the future, although it mostly comes right away. The decision that you did for the characters might decide their fate too, whether they are the protagonist or just a random NPC you met along the way.The gameplay is divided into two parts: the choose-your-adventure section and the battle section. The first one lets you explore some areas and choose between some options. Some might lead to battle, others might grant you something. There is also a chance that you won't get anything, even.The other unique aspect that the game has lies in the sin mechanic. You have a certain number of sins which will change based on your action. At the end of the day, this will determine the ending that you get. You can build a deck out of 13 cards at a minimum. New cards can be obtained after buying one from a merchant or finishing a battle. Each chapter will unlock a new set of cards, mostly stronger than the current one. You might even have to rebuild your deck using the new additions to finish the enemies.Enemies can be tough sometimes. They might inflict status ailments on you or attack with a huge damage. At first, it's not that noticeable since the enemies are weak, but they'll later give you issues if you don't deal with them properly since they will have higher damage and HP. Some battles will be in the form of battle-puzzles. You will have a set number of cards that are predetermined in your hand. The goal is to finish the battle in the predetermined amount of turns. It helps you to get familiar with other cards and build while giving your brain some work at the same time. Sometimes, it can take a while to figure out the solution, although the game also offers an option to skip any battle if you fail it three times.You can play Durak. It's a card game where you have to expend all of your cards before the enemy. I didn't know how to play it, and the tutorial didn't help much. Sometimes, I couldn't use a card even though it was in the same number as the one on the table. Sometimes I can't even use all of my cards with the same number to attack. It was confusing and I could only win by luck.I finished the game in 30.1h in the normal difficulty. There are four endings, with one being similar to the other. I finished the game on the borderline between the good and bad ending, then loaded my save after finishing the game to see the other endings. The game isn't hard—there is a difficulty option if you need it too.The game only saves right at the beginning of a new area. If you do something when you are in the area, that progress won't be saved. Also, it might not be obvious that you can hover the orange text in the dialogues for simple explanations of the Russian terms. Lastly, some texts might be hard to read due to the clash with the background.You are playing  for the experience. The story is mediocre, but it is a unique one with a focus on Russian culture. The card-building section is also enjoyable—the different builds are quite apparent, and with some enemies having resistance to a certain build, you are bound to try out a different one. It's a fun game if you enjoy both card-battling and choose-your-adventure kind of game.

But I ended enjoying the story, characters and the incredible research and documentary work the team has pulled to make the setting so interesting and informative.Russian mythology is not really well known (I knew a few demons thanks to SMT), so ending this game knowing more about it and even the culture from that time is something the team should be proud of. _childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth your time and money. It is an excellent game with a few minor quality of life issues.The Good: It is a very accessible game. The story and mechanics are well built. The music is incredible, and the setting, lore, and atmosphere all respect and honor to the culture of the people it portrays. The gambling mini-game Durak is incredibly fun, and I probably sunk about a quarter of my game time into just playing that.The Bad: The English voice acting is not great. I ended up changing the dialogue to russian, cause it sounds better. The mechanical interaction is not always as good as it could be. The game has trouble tracking what the output of damage and guard will be when you actually run the turn. It also does not convey some information about mechanics or item effects very well, but that may be a translation issue. Also, it does not tell you specifically what killed you when you die. This is mainly an issue in the roguelike mode, where you don't get to redo battles. At one point, three cycles into a run, I died immediately upon hitting the send button. I have no idea what killed me, and no idea how I could have avoided it. That's a huge turn off in a game like this. The good far outweighs the bad, and you might not even notice the things I complain about. I would say, to hold off on picking up the DLC until you're sure you will want to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend playing Black Book? Yes, absolutely. I was very positively surprised by it and couldn't help myself from 'binge-playing' through it over the course of 4 way too long evenings.If you want some additional thoughts:I should probably first drop the info that I am not a huge card game player. Like not at all. So I can't really compare this game to any others of its kind and the only thing I can say regarding this aspect of the game is that I - after a few 'starting difficulties' - enjoyed almost all card battles in the game, even the puzzle ones with the exception of one I think.The art style is probably not everyone's cup of tea but - with the exception of how some 3D character models look from the front maybe - I loved it. In combination with the great soundtrack and voice acting (Russian, srsly instead of complaining about the English one or whatever just take the dive and select the Russian voices - the subtitles are solid and it enhances the experience by a lot if you ask me) it creates a great atmosphere that on its own would make the game worthwhile to me.There are some clear flaws like having to click through all the dialogue before a battle should you want to restart it - which sadly you can find yourself forced to do if you try to play certain card combinations, which is another con I guess, although - again - I have no idea how other card based games handle this. Depending on the enemy some styles of play can be ridiculously broken (at the very least on normal difficulty, have to try harder ones at some point;  ). Sometimes it can also be rather frustrating not knowing what dialogue options exactly mean/make you do, I think there's some room for improvement.It's also great that you "have to" collect some knowledge about the mythology/history of the region and just the setting - which is a great plus in itself, can't stress how much I loved the atmosphere - through dialogues and the encyclopedia (could need some better organisation feature(?) though).Sorry for my ramblings but if they help someone pick up this game and enjoy it as much as I did/do it should be worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: This was a tough choice, but there's too many bad design decisions to make it worth it for me.The progression is very slow, and the game often unloads too much tutorial info at once. The conversations can be a bit repetitive and overlong. I kept wanting to get to the next mission or battle quicker.The exploration is fine, but it's often unclear what a choice will mean when selected. Characters often ask questions to which you do not know the answer, resulting in unwanted sins or losing out on XP. Choices about approaching enemies have no way to determine what will work or what will put the player at a disadvantage. Card abilities are not explained clearly, and so on.The writing is a bit wordy, which wouldn't matter except every single line is voiced. The voice acting is fine, but I keep clicking through and interrupting the voiceovers trying to get to more gameplay.The card game is pretty simple. It's usually not hard to figure out the best play each turn depending on what the enemy will do next turn. Having that foreknowledge means that the card mechanics need to be much more interactive to maintain interest. I like some of the effects, though, it's just not enough.If the game had been a little more card-battler and a little less visual novel (and a bit faster overall), it'd be an easy recommendation. The annoyances just overwhelm the good parts, which is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolutely lovely game. It has its downsides (the low-poly visuals are clunky, although this is somewhat balanced out by inventive direction), but the lore/story is superb, and the card-based gameplay is surprisingly solid for a story-driven game. Hard recommend.Don't be fooled by the description though. It's not an RPG — it's a choice-and-consequence adventure game that allows for some freedom, but generally is relatively linear.Still, it's a must-play for any players interested in traditional Russian mythology, that it explores on a level unusually deep for video games. Folktale logic mixes heathen beliefs with Christianity and good with evil, confusing saints with powerful spirits and making morality grey in a distinctly unique way.Imps are people with personality, and they're not evil by choice — it's just that their nature makes them incapable of doing good. They're eager to work, but the work they do always ends up being harmful. As a witch, you must take imps into your service, but they're demanding more work, so you have to send them off to curse people and destroy crops. Does that make you good or evil? The answer is both — you *are* the source of evil in the local lands, but you're also the person who thus obtains the power to make a difference and help people. It's an extremely compelling status, explored deeply by the game.And so it makes a lot of sense that diplomacy, winning in cards (normal cards, a la gwint), solving verbal riddles, and fights become interchangeable methods of dealing with demons. They're not really your enemies; and folktale logic often values trickery and cunning more than sheer power. The relationship between humans and imps is half-symbiosis, half cruel game, but it's hardly a war.This duality is oddly mirrored by the game's narrative that mixes a fictional story with actual folktales as written down by folklorists — and with scientific commentary on myhtology and folk beliefs. The game both shows and analyzes mythic archetypes, and none of that is done in a heavy-handed info-dump-y way, as the tidbits are short and relevant to the story. It's surprisingly informative without breaking immersion.And that, I think, is what sells the game for me the most.I'm not sure how well it translates in the international version, and I played in Russian. While the linguistic stylization is not perfect, it's still extremely compelling, with characters using dialectisms that deepen the immersion. I think it's a must-play for anyone who cares and is interested in the Russian culture.Do play it. It's worth it.(Not to mention the amount of content is quite impressive for an indie!)P. S. And yes, while the idea isn't exactly new, I still get the chills whenever anyone explores the idea that the XXth century was forged in hell, because it was.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to take a minute and recommend Black Book.It is a card-game RPG hybrid adventure game (yeah, its all those) available on Steam. It will also eventually be available on Switch (maybe already?) and I think Playstation.Its just under $30, so that's fairly low for a newly released game. I've played about 15 hours so far and I'm quite hooked. Plot: You are a witch who is trying to break the seven seals on a powerful artifact of evil (the Black Book) so that you can free your husband/fiancée from Hell and return him to life (he apparently committed suicide and so was not buried on consecrated ground therefore Hell).Over the course of the game you use your powers as a newly minted witch (magic user who has made a pact with the devil to gain power) and a knower (someone who is well versed in folk lore and generally clever). You also attain and must make use of demonic familiars known as "chorts". Each of these is unique in personality and stats, kinda like PokeMon (if PokeMon liked torturing children, setting houses on fire, or pushing old women off cliffs). These chorts need to be kept busy on tasks (that are evil, like causing strife in a family, or stealing food from the poor) or they vent their boredom on you (causing you to suffer combat penalties specific to the chort). Since these tasks are evil, you earn sins for sending the chorts to do them, but they provide a decent reward. You can also help people with problems of a spiritual nature through various means.Each night in the game there is a specific task that you have to complete, and several other optional tasks you are informed exist. You then have the option of making new spell pages, then set out to start the night. There is a simple map and you progress through a map of locations with a few branches. You can always go back to complete other side branches until you complete your main task. Once the main task is done you go home and the next night starts. Locations have various encounters, from combat, to puzzles, to choices (do a bad thing to get a reward and increase your sin value, sacrifice a thing of value to do a good deed, etc). There are also occasional merchants for spell pages, herbs, and equipable items. Combat: Combat is very simple, but very engaging. You and your opponent(s) have life totals. If you reach 0 you lose, if all opponents reach 0 you win. You always go first, and you know what each opponent is going to do each turn before you choose your actions. You don't know their future turns, but you can still plan out each turn easily. You have approximately twice as many cards as you can use each turn and need to choose which ones you want to use. Cards (called spell pages) have no cost to use. Each turn you can choose to use herbs (consumable items), and cast a single spell. That spell is composed of multiple spell pages of two general categories "orders" and "keys" when you start out each spell has two order slots and one key slot. You eventually get up to three order and two key slots (so 5 cards). You also have spells that linger for multiple rounds and are added as an extra card to each of those rounds, and very expensive and rare spells called "gestures" that don't count towards your  limit, so even in the early game its not impossible to have a spell made up of 5-7 words (there is an achievement for 13 pages in a single spell, so you can do at least that many). Each page goes off as a separate part of the spell (for example, shield self, attack enemy 1, heal self, then bestow a negative condition on enemy 2).Spells are available in two colors white and black. Black pages deal damage and bestow negative conditions on the enemy. White pages reduce the damage you take for that turn, heal you, or bestow positive condition on you. Several spells also gain additional effects for each spell of the same color, so using 6 black pages in the same spell for example might see two of those pages getting a HUGE boost. Most of the time you want to mix white and black (just so you can avoid damage while still hurting your enemy), but every so often you either desperately need to defend and heal yourself for large amounts, or your enemy is not going to be attacking directly so you can make a huge damage combo.There is also a traditional card game you can play to win money and sometimes defeat foes you challenge. Its kinda like hearts. You have a trump suit and try to beat your opponent and leave them with cards when you run out. Its kinda fun, but thankfully it largely optional, as its less fun than the combat.Leveling Up: There are about 25-30 skills. You get one skill point each time you level up. Each skill grants one specific bonus. The more boring ones give you a bonus to damage or defense. Others change how many cards you get to choose from each round, let you send your chorts on harmless tasks (instead of suffocating babies you can get them to dig holes with a feather or carry water with a sieve), meaning they don't do evil and you don't need to be tormented by them for a time. There are also skills that let you equip or use extra items or provide an improvement to your income.Setting and Art: The game is set in Russia in a fictional version of the 1800s. People believe in various demons and spirits and have lots of superstition, but also believe in Christ and Heaven and Hell. The voice acting is ok. The game has songs you can find and relisten to (they are impressive if you like Russian choruses). The art style is kinda like a minimalist graphic novel, with decent dynamic elements (plants move in the wind, birds fly overhead, buildings creak, etc). The spell pages look like hand drawn medieval playing cards. All refences in the game appear to be authentic Russian folk lore mixed with Russian Orthadox Christianity. There are 7 tiers of cards (one for each of the seals you unlock in the Black Book as you progress in the plot) and I have managed to find each of the first tier of cards. I'm looking forward to seeing the rest as there are apparently several new mechanics in the combat that I have yet to see (higher tiers of cards). The game takes approx 20-30 hours per playthrough and three endings (two of which you can get with a single play through), that means about 40-70 hours of play is possible. Getting the different endings is based on various levels of sin, so will require a different play experience to unlock the 'good' and 'bad' ending.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements and have this game in their backlog (minor spoilers ahead). Black Book is an adventure, roguelike game that uses a low-polygon game engine, but despite this limitation it as some beautiful scenarios and effects.  It explores in great detail Permian, Finno-Ugric and Slavic mythology and lore,  and how some of this primitive lore blended with the later introduced Orthodox Christianism, through the story about a young sorceress and her personal quest. The way you play the game will also affect the game ending.The exploration is based on a map system where you move through one location to the other, triggering combat encounters, random events or small explorable areas that have story or side story related NPCs and/or vendors that sell herbs, items or cards.The combat system is turn-based and uses cards (spell pages), of two types, that have several different effects like dealing damage, shield you, buff yourself and debuff enemies, and you need to put them together to form a complete spell, before you can pass the turn. As you progress and unlock new cards and items, you can create some very destructive spells and powerful synergies that will make you nearly unbeatable, especially if you’re already a card game veteran.   50 Achievements, some are obtained just by playing the game.  Around 26 hours, mostly on my own, but with some trial and error to get some answers right. Checking a guide while playing will reduce this time. Easy, for a card game veteran, but the start might be a bit hard because you depend on the cards you draw and in the beginning the card pool is very limited. But after that and in the last chapters, you’ll go through regular monsters like butter. Guides are available too. Normal. I think the game should be enjoyed with as little spoiling as possible, but to avoid having to do a second playthrough you should keep at least a saved game at the beginning of each chapter. Also, visit every location, answer the lore questions right (even if you have to reload), complete all side-quests and keep your sins below 100 until the last chapter. The amount of detail when it comes to lore is impressive and you’ll surely learn a lot. The main story will keep you engaged and the main characters are likable and interesting. The card battle part of the game is similar to other games like slay the spire, but in the end you’ll be so powerful that even the final bosses won’t be much of a challenge, if you change your deck to counter their deck’s strong points and strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game! Amazing art, music, and story. I'm usually not a fan of card based games, but this one is exceptional. Outside of that it's really great, would highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game and a wonderful experience overall. Stylish, enchanting, sometimes though-provoking, and full of interesting lore.Black Book is remarkable enough that this is my first Steam review even though I've played about a hundred different games on here.It immersed me in a world filled with demons as a fact-of-life. The story was engaging, and I felt I had enough agency to act as I wanted in the given situations.I liked the battles: the system is reasonably simple, with some subtlety. Putting together some zagovars (a hand of "cards") could be a little tricky but bring a satisfying sense of power as you deny opponents and build power into a final wu-pah! There are some "puzzle battles" with fixed decks and one (or few) solution(s) -- at first I was put-off because this sidesteps character development  death is likely because it's a process of learning through failure. Once I accepted that dying and redoing the battle was normal I was more at ease with it, though I'd prefer if you could reasonably play cautiously without dying.I played on Linux via Proton, and it worked perfectly.I only set the English voiceovers for a short time, but they seemed decent. I played most of the game with Russian voice and English subtitle for a but more immersion into the culture, and started to pick out some words.About 60 hours for a slow person (me) doing one playthough with nearly every side-branch, reading all the lore, and experimenting with different "decks" of pages.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game 10/10I've been waiting for this to come out since its demo last year. I didn't follow many of the news until its was fully released. First thing I can say is that it's definitely worth the money. It took me 24hrs to beat the game fully, but that's due to me being a completionist and taking every side quest and listening to the lore. The story is good and you play through the game almost like a visual novel with the narrator speaking about every area you visit. It ties in Russian mythology which is very interesting to read and collect as you play. The music is beautiful and along with the mythology you also can pickup new songs during side-quests to listen to again. Of course i can't understand what the music is about but the Russian chants are soothing to the ear. The game-play is your standard turn based card game, all with visual effects for each type of card. You play through the story and collect all different types of ways to damage, protect, and buff/debuff yourself and the enemies. What was interesting is sometimes the enemies would adapt to my deck. I got stuck on a poison enemy and changed my deck to fight again only for this certain enemy to play a card that took away my resistance that he didn't use in the battle before. I thought that was an intimidating detail. Auto save happens whenever you visit a new area, if you want only positive outcomes to your interaction with characters then quicksave is your friend. This was a fantastic game for me to pickup and play when I wasn't busy and I highly recommend to those who play these kinds of turn based games.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically, this is Slay the Spire clone set in a XIX century Russia and with a singleplayer story. Other than that, the concept is pretty similar. You collect cards to weave spells and kill evil with them.The story is rather long (20+ hours), but if that's not enough, there's endless mode which is almost exactly likle Slay the Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful game. The card game itself is engaging (the boss battles in particular are fun challenges), but what's uniquely fantastic is how the writing, story, and the gameplay itself immerse you in the brilliantly researched folklore and history. Carefully recalling snippets of folk wisdom (like wearing your clothes inside out to resist a forest spirit's trickery), exercising judgment, and correctly solving riddles, are just as important as slinging spells.It really feels like you're learning to be the town witch - steeped in sin or otherwise. Unlike many "karma" style morality charts, the sin mechanic really feels right for the setting. Playing as a good Christian witch, I would sometimes pick up sin unintentionally, but what else can a poor sinner do? Playing as a menacing hag, ruining my neighbor's crops and such, I quickly felt buried by the weight of my past, and with no hope for salvation I plunged deeper.The animation and voice acting are uneven, but at the worst it's charming and it's often eerie, monumental, or heartbreaking. My only gripe would be that the drawings of the characters during the talking portions lack the spark that the rest of the game has, but it's minor.Anyway, I highly recommend Black Book if you're looking to get lost in that good weird Slavic folklore, with a very solid deckbuilder at its core.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game. It strikes a lovely balance between whimsical, melancholic, and mysterious. An atmospheric treat full of little surprises. Explains the lore beautifully; I'm a Slavic mythology enthusiast, but you wouldn't have to be to play this and understand what's happening.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're interested in Slavic myths and folklore, this is your game. To me, however, getting through all the dialog feels like a slog. Particularly confusing is the distinction between demons and chorts, if there is one. The voice acting is pretty good. The exploration and combat is much more interesting. The mechanics of the cards seem a bit tangled, and lead to too many symbols on the screen, I think. The cards sometimes cover your companion's ability. I think it would be cool if the companions acted on their own, giving them more of their own agency. I think its a bit harsh to have no retreat option - it would be cool if you could retreat with some kind of penalty. The ability to take chorts as your companion would be cool too (I'm early in the game, but it seems like they just go around the map cursing npcs offscreen while you adventure) - perhaps they would prevent retreat, as they are supposed to be a blessing and a curse. They mostly seem like curses. I look forward to seeing how/if they change as the game progresses. Vasya's got good animations, but her walking and running is slow, and its strange that she only does it in the final area of the map. After a fight, she just stands in her combat animation. This game has some rough edges, but overall, it's interesting and enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally I didn't care about the game mechanics. Card games are not for me, issues I have with them were present where my hand was dealt with cards I could not do anything with, I'm not a good authority to judge how deep were the mechanics of slay the spire-like games, all I can say is that there are builds, and there's room for experimentation and the system did not feel offensive to me for most of the game.The more important thing for me is the game world, story, and else. I played many games and observed many more that tried to take on Slavic/Eastern European themes and I can honestly say that so far this might be the best Cultural Product that entered the market from any of the eastern European countries. It's rich in style and takes a fantastical take on the culture of Imperial Rural Russia without delving into over-the-top edginess cynical portrayals (I'm Looking at you majority of Polish Devs) and just want to portray the culture from the POV of quite interesting professional occupation that existed. If anybody wants to learn about the basics of old Russian culture, and have a game to boot, then it's the best position you can find on the market right now. The story is a mixed bag. Early to mid-game, its strong, themes are strong, and the story keeps itself low-profile tackling personal yet engaging events surrounding the goal of the village witch trying to get her boyfriend out of the hell. Narrow Scope, charming, good characters, and it goes downhill once you approach the end game. Characters start having motivations that don't fit in with the rest of the atmosphere and theme of the game (Chortocracy, my lord), twists that feel cheap and break characters, some heavy-handed motives of upcoming WW2 events, and the scope of the story increases to be reality defining. Despite problems with the story, and game genre not being up to my liking I feel that for themes alone and most of the story is most definitely worth checking out, just maybe not finishing it. And if by chance you'll enjoy the mechanics themselves then devs just released DLC that will satisfy your hunger for a proper roguelike formula.

_childDocuments_.review: I came across the prototype for the game (demo I guess?) about a year ago and really wanted to play the full game, fast forward to a few days ago, I see this game, think it looks interesting and buy it and realize it was that same game!The game's pretty long, so you get your money's worth, and it's really fun. I wouldn't know, that is one area that I have 0 knowledge in.I really love the game and while the game is almost perfect in every sense, there are some minor inconveniences that I wish to point out.First of all, Slavic languages are my big weakness and while the game gives you an option to hover over some terms highlighted orange to find out what they mean, it's not available in all dialogues - and the game, while it has an encyclopaedia, lacks a dictionary. _childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to assess. I like that it offers insight into mythology which is rarely explored, at least in English-language literature. I had a bit of taste of Slavic mythology through the Witcher and World of Watches book series, but Black Book offers a lot more depth and historical context. It also has a quite interesting card game at its heart. There is room for varied strategies through the different mechanics of particular cards.There are some caveats to these positives. The quality of the English translation and voice acting is inconsistent. A lot of it is surprisingly well done, but there are some clunky lines and oddly pronounced words which are jarring. A few times I wasn’t sure of a decision I was making as I didn’t fully understand what had led up to it. While the card game is enjoyable, it does not compel the player to consider alternative strategies and vary their deck as much as it should – most battles are very straightforward, and even the bosses have an obvious strategy to beat. This is fine until the very end of the game where there is a massive difficulty spike, which greater difficulty and variety in the build-up may have alleviated somewhat. The game at least is very generous in allowing battles to be skipped, but that made for a bit of a hollow ending.It’s also a surprisingly long game. It is not a matter of simple padding – there is dialogue at almost every step, and the battles tend to be quick – but it can become a bit wearing by the end.Overall I think it is different and interesting enough that it is well worth a shot; just prepare for a long haul and a tough final stage.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black Book is a near-masterpiece.“I give it a 9.5” – IGNBlack Book is a narrative card-battling/deck-building game based in Russian Slavic folklore. You play Vasilisa, a young woman whose lover has died. She seeks to break all seven seals of the black book in order to make a wish to bring him back, as legend tells she can. I spent 43 hours completing the game.• Black Book does a great job of presenting Slavic folklore to the player. The proper Russian words are used for many elements: the zagavor, the izba, chorts, rusalka, banya; these are words I’ll remember, and it was good for the developers to stay true to the roots. I never felt like I was confused by the usage of these words, or traditions that were evident on-screen. It was clear that the developers spent a lot of time researching lore and mythology.• Black Book isn’t the type of game for the player to skip dialogue. You’re often presented with questions and riddles that test your knowledge of the mythology, and everything they’ll ask has been delivered to you prior. The book contains entries for anything you’ve learned, given as you learned them. I read every entry; the ones in the final chapter are some you don’t want to miss.• The game is surprisingly long. I typically trust How Long To Beat and go by the completionists’ reported times. I played on hard difficulty and typically took my time, exploring “every nook and cranny” as I always do. I clocked in over 8 hours more than the other completionists.• But there’s good reason to replay: while you will get the same linear journey each time, the details of how you played are important. Which characters were by your side, who’s alive and not, who shows up later at a bonfire; the game never lets you forget that your actions had consequences, both good and bad.• Black Book delivers. It’s fair to say in gaming, I’ve gotten used to being unable to sock it to some jerk boss, or conceivably unconquerable foe, with the game handling their demise in some other way. In Black Book, you’re always given the chance to say: nah, your deal sucks, not compromising, time to die. The player’s reward is a tough boss battle that also fits thematically with the boss; all I will say is Chapter 7’s bosses were some of the more memorable boss fights I’ve had in years. They were entirely optional and allowed me to skip a short set of trials.• The ending also delivered. I’ll admit by 35 hours my interest was starting to wane, but I was absolutely hooked with the end sequence of chapter 6 and beyond.• It keeps itself fresh, introducing periodically introducing new mechanics both via new cards, and in-battle mechanics such as koldun and puzzle fights.• Durak was a miss for me; I appreciate that they wanted to include a card game from their culture, but the rules were confusing and I found it to be more of a distraction in an already long game. It didn’t have the up-front enjoyment of Witcher 3’s Gwent. It actually subtracted from the experience because there are items and skills built to allow you to cheat in it.• I didn’t feel connected to the lover at all. He was clearly a plot device, despite a short segment where we experience Vasilisa’s pain of losing him once again, where she reaffirms her dedication to him. Honestly, I thought Alexander was a fine chap and would have liked to spend eternity with him.• Often enough, the (excellent) narrator and words on screen don’t match up. You can tell the English-speaking voice actors offered some direction upon delivery of their lines. It was a bit distracting, but my understanding is the game is best played in Russian and the writing was solid enough that I could forgive it.• There’s an investigation segment which could have been done better. It was slightly buggy and a little hard to follow. My pick wasn’t even an option in the end, and the person I least expected was it. This was a system constraint; they just needed a better system for this chapter.• Money became irrelevant around the 4th chapter. As a completionist, it’s not uncommon for me to accrue resources and become overpowered, but I felt like some end-game gold sinks would have been warranted. I was disappointed that in the final dramatic chapter, no new items were offered (that I could tell).• Damage calculation could have been done better. The game requires you to calculate accurate damage any time you’re doing AoE because it sums that AoE damage. This is a common complaint with the game and I’m not sure how they released a battle-focused DLC without addressing this!• Chort management seemed annoying; I ended up going for a sinless playthrough, so I didn’t have to assign them constantly, but I can imagine how annoying it would have been to do so.All in all, I would still say it was nearly a masterpiece. It achieved what it set out to do, imperfectly in small ways, but it was everything it had to be. The Russian voice acting cast is about three times the size of the English one, and I can only assume the story was delivered better in proper Russian. I would recommend any Russian gamer to play it, and if you like the good points I described, give it a shot on sale. I personally got it through a Humble Bundle.

_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: it's really quite a charming little gamesome thoughts after ~18 hours: overall really fun, engaging game that treats its source material with love and respect. a mixture of a point-and-click adventure game and a deckbuilderat current playtime, combat system is still engaging and feels rewarding to come up with different combos and decks. playing on normal, i win most of the time quite handedly but there have been some battles i've had to reload and some which i've had to construct new decks to defeat. the system is rather opaque and not well explained, I can only suggest to experiment with different card effects and see what they do firsthand, which is half the fun anyways Battle Puzzles are a treat: use a premade deck and defeat an opponent within a certain number of turns. they feel like solving Tsumego or a Chess puzzle and also deepen your understanding of the game mechanicsthe story features a colorful cast of characters and issues, again with love and respect for the Slavic folklore and history it draws fromthe text translations sometimes don't match the voiceovers and all suffer from a lack of editing by an English-speaking professionalthe game suffers from several QoL issues, this is my biggest gripe- e.g. there's no clear ordering to the encyclopedia, or search function, so going through entries to find relevant information is a pain- e.g. there's no "history" function during combat which makes it more difficult to learn things like card interactions and order of operations- e.g. the chort management component requires a lot of repetitive clicking, could do with at least a "Finish All" button for jobsall of these are relatively minor, and I still heartily recommend this game
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a surprisingly good find and really fun to play on relaxing nights. It's a pretty interesting card battler with a fair amount of customization, so the gameplay is pretty fun. It can start to get repetitive eventually but it's really easy to swap up your deck and try something else out if you've found something that's getting old.It's absolutely FULL of really interesting lore and characters, the storytelling in between the card aspects of the game really had me hooked. There's a neat system where actually paying attention to dialogue can help you out with knowledge challenges that give you extra stuff or XP through dialogue so I found myself paying a lot of extra attention to actually try and learn these different creatures and spirits and how they interact with the local folk.If you're into deckbuilders and cool cultural lore definitely give this one a shot. It's long enough that it's worth it at full price but on sale you really can't go wrong.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Such a beautiful game.I first stumbled upon this game in May 2020 when the devs released the demo and I have been waiting for this game since, checking the release date at least once every week.The game is basically a turn based card game at its core, during the duels you fight against demons using your spells which are stored in your Blackbook (deck). This part is straightforward enough - the best part of this game is the story and the lore. The graphic style is beautiful too. I don't want to say too much, but if you like dueling card games and a bit intrigued about the story you are in for a treat. Hopefully this game will be very successful so we can see more games from Morteshka.One thing I want to tell the devs though, even though the voice actors do a really great job the perfect English accent they have is a bit unimmersive for a story set in Russian heartlands in late 1800s. I wouldn't call this "bad" of course, just mentioning.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent. Enough story events to keep the world lively, just enough combat in between to keep it fresh. Some people have complained about the puzzle battles--I never really had trouble with them. They're challenging, but I never found them to be impossible.Yes, the voice acting in English is a little weak. Yes, there are inconsistencies in the translation. Yes, the knowledge events seem to rely on information that hasn't been presented to the player. However, I found all of these things to be minor enough to not affect my enjoyment of the game.Above all, the greatest value of the game is presenting--in a very interesting and informative manner--a folkloric tradition not often seen out of its home territory. More than just Slavic mythology, Black Book is heavily based on Permian folklore and legends. I found the encyclopedia entries and the bailichkas (folk tales) absolutely engrossing and the game is almost worth it for that alone.I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in adventure games, witches, and deck builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black book is an underrated game with how little its following is online. The narrative is fun and enjoyable if you're not particularly attached to the modern interpretation of Christianity. The card game feels well balanced so far (though I definitely looked up a guide or two). A lot of guides talk about problems with the card game that appear to be fixed in the current game!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black Book is one of the best story driven RPGs I think I have played recently. Normally I have a hard time sticking with these really long story games but Black Book is one I could not stop playing.And I think that all comes down to the fact that it takes the card based deckbuilding gameplay from games like Slay the Spire and puts them in this super fascinating story that is based on Slavic myths. And I have absolutely no experience with Slavic and Russian myths and folklore and I think that’s one of the main reasons this game absolutely enticed me. And this is going to be a very non spoiler review, and in fact I am only actually going to be showing gameplay from the first couple of hours because I definitely want you to play this game on your own.But the game starts out with you learning how to become a witch from your grandpa because your fiance apparently committed suicide. And according to slavic religion those that commit suicide are destined to go to hell. So you go through this entire process to become a witch and end up with this Black Book that contains all your spells and Zagavors. And you apparently need to break open all the seals the book contains in order to be able to get a single wish that you will use to bring your fiance back from the dead. And so the story obviously has crazy twists and turns and can actually get pretty freaking dark at times but it always is super well paced and keeps things interesting.And throughout the game you will find new spells to put in your black book and you can customize your actuall deck. So the majority of my playthough I had a type of deck that was super aggressive and relied on playing multiple of the same type of card each turn.There seemed to be several different types of decks you could build though from block builds, to poison builds, and more. And some of the bosses you end up fighting later in the game require you to actually change up your deck as they might counter the deck that you’ve been running up to that point.And the game obviously being a super story based game has a ton of dialogue but it, like a lot of RPGs gives you a incredible amount of freedom in how you want to play the game. You can choose to fight people, monsters, and demons as soon as you see them or you can try to first talk to them. You will also have to make moral decisions that will raise your sin meter up or down and it actually has very satisfying and impactful consequences near the end of the game which I love but obviously won't spoil in this video.You also are constantly leveling up to get new skills though the skills are a bit on the more boring side I am not going to lie but I do think the game is better for having them.You’ll also have to juggle several different chorts which are pretty much demons that work for you and if you dont want to send them to torment other people they will stay with you giving you debuffs like poisoning you at the start of each turn or lowering your maximum health.There's tons of different passive items you can find in the game as well that help compliment the strategies you are trying to do either with your deck, your personality, or even a card game that can be played throughout the game. I can’t speak much on the card game because I avoided most of it in my playthrough.Also in the game you are constantly finding little poems, excerpts, stories, and even music that all are based on actual slavid myths and folklore. And so I truly felt like I was just absorbing tons of information on a culture that I had no exposure to and I think a game that can do that is amazing. I never read all the little secret things you can find in these type of RPGS but I have to say I read almost every piece of extra content the game gave me because I was so into the atmosphere and theme of the game. Also the game itself was just so freaking pretty to look at. It has a very distinct artstyle that really matches up with the folklore and the voice acting I thought was actually incredible besides a couple of random small side characters here and there.And so the game overall took me 25 hours to complete and I loved every minute of it. As you get further and further in the game you get more and more interesting cards, the story starts to really ramp up and didn’t feel predictable at all at least for me, and the ending of the game was absolutely perfect and I felt like I was really rewarded for trying to do good, as I was going for a good ending the entire time.I think this is a game that you absolutely need to try out if you either are interested in really good story games especially ones on unique culture like the slavic myths this game is based on but also if you are a deckbuilding fan. I know a lot of people myself are huge fans of roguelike deckbuilders like Slay the Spire and this is the first ever major story based deckbuilding game I have ever played and it really makes me want more games like this.Also this game just recently released a $5 DLC that adds an entire new roguelite mode the game! So after you beat the game or technically before that if you want you can play the entire game in this really awesome roguelite way that mimics games like Slay the Spire while still having all the charm of the original game. And I think that’s the perfect thing this game could use to give it more replayability and it just makes so much sense since the gameplay of this game so closely resembles deck building roguelites.And if you liked this review then follow my for more stuff like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely worth a playthrough, if only for the interesting Permian/Finno-Ugraic/Russian/... mythology and lore that is solidly baked into the story.Sadly, the voice-acting is quite uneven. The main storyteller and the female protagonist are very well-voiced in English, but the other character may at times pronounce certain words in baffling ways that take you out of the story for a few seconds there. At least it did for me.The combat system is well done and there are quite a few ways to build a deck: focusing on cursing, wasting, swiping or straight up offense, these are all possible as you level up and gain more cards. The only downside is that you have no clue what the skillset is of a particular area's "boss", so it's possible that you'll have to reload from an autosave file from 15 minutes ago...
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game!The story and characters are well written, and the deck-building-card battle game play is simple but fun.The story is presented in a visual novel style way with light environmental exploration, which I think works well.There is just enough combat to keep things interesting and each battle doesn't overstay its welcome.The world building is well done and I think anyone that likes dark fairy-tales and folklore would really enjoy game's setting.The 3D art is simple low-poly, nothing crazy but effective in conveying the visuals and atmosphere.On the other hand, I find the hand-drawn art of the character closeups during conversations a bit amateurish and I think it doesn't mesh with the style of the 3D environment all that well.The voice acting can be a bit rough sometimes too, but the game is fully voice-acted and in English so that's really nice.Overall, none of these two issues ruin the game. I got used to them fairly quickly and was able to see pass these minor flaws and enjoy the good story and fun gameplay.If you like slavic folklore, witches, and simple deck-building mechanics, you should give this game a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: 7 hours in on the first day. Coming from other card battlers like STS, Monster Train, Griftlands, and Across the Obelisk, I'm very impressed.The game has a campaign and level system, like Tainted Grail or Obelisk. But the story is just so much better. The game and dialogue are immersive and wonderfully done for the genre. It doesn't have the challenge of STS or MT, sure. And it doesn't seem like it has the endless replay-ability those games might offer after campaign completion. But the events for the campaign aren't repetitive at all and its a thoroughly enjoyable game overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: My personal Game of the Year. I have a tendency to be pretty distracted when gaming and move quickly between games, with an overall low completion rate. Black Book held me- the story is wonderful, the folklore is absolutely incredible, and I was obsessed. The game is deep and rewarding, the graphics are simple but beautiful, and the soundtrack is moving. I am not skilled at breaking down all the fine details of the things that made this game one of the best I've had the pleasure of playing, but I can find no flaw. If you enjoy deckbuilders and top-tier storytelling, it's an unsurpassable experience. I took my time on a single playthrough, I'll play it again when I've given it some time.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: - The character portraits are pretty rudimentary but nice in their own way. The backgrounds are pretty nice though- I would have liked a little more variety in the enemy designs. The bosses are pretty well done, though- The music is a pretty interesting blend of folk songs. I like how you can actually collect music as you progress through the story- The English voice acting is a bit amateurish and inconsistent, but that's okay. I just wish the pronunciation of various words and names was consistent across the board- The basic thrust of the story is simple and sad. Your lover has died, and you're trying to become a witch so you can make a bargain with the devil to bring him back to life- In order to do so, you have to use the titular Black Book to unlock a set of seals and proceed to hell to make your wish- All along the way, you'll learn a lot about eastern European folklore and the ways in which it interacted with Christianity. There's some fairly interesting cultural education in this game- It's a card battler RPG that eschews the usual rogue-like trappings of so many similar games. I have to be honest, that makes it a little refreshing- Unfortunately, that leads you to lean on maybe one or two different deck constructions for the whole game unless you hit a boss that requires you to switch things up. I just ran a curse deck for about 3/4 of the game that trivialized most encounters- When you are forced to switch things up, you better hope you have some money on hand. You'll probably have to buy cards while you're at your home base or from a vendor to switch to something more viable- Although it is indeed not a rogue-like, you'll often have mini-events in different areas you travel to that kinda feel similar to games in that genre. You'll have options to fight, try to weasel your way out of a fight, gain information, run away, etc.- Although an interesting concept that taught me a bit about a world folklore that I didn't know much about, I never really found myself having fun. Maybe card games aren't for me- Worked well on the Steam Deck. It's an easy game to pick up and put down- . If you love card games but want a cohesive story, this is a decent game to try. The card battles don't do anything innovative or fancy. A solid if unimpressive game
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: The voice acting is very good and there is many text. I really enjoy the atmosphere and the take on this culture.Edit: After finishing it: It was very nice. The atmosphere is lovely, but doesn't rely heavily on graphics. The story is coherent and you see many characters along the whole story. The take on folklore is very refreshing. The characters live between orthodox christianity, old beliefs and an emerging modern world. At the end, some mechanics are visually buggy. Cards are not removed from your hand when they are played (only after your turn) and sometimes I could not choose a minion as a target in fights with unusual patterns. If you equiop identical items, only one of them will give the stat on the first turn, it will work correct after the second turn. It shows correct, but calculates wrong. The rainy background was nearly too much for my graphics card. One puzzle was too much for me, but you skip can it. Overall I recomend this game if you like card games an a good story.

You have chorts which you cannot get rid of, they create sin and when idle they mess up your stats. Also I cannot freely manage the deck. Shouldn't the card deck game be about building the deck and experimenting with various combinations? Money system where you have to pay for each card added to book (wtf?) just kills it for me. _childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me scared of going into the woods. All this folklor hits me deep inside, and seeing it so masterfully crafted as a narrative experience is just stunning. Voice acting sends shivers down my spine, the plot is with clever twists, tips and trivia about the world captivates you. Some imagery still comes up to me even after one year from playing this game. And how some characters has developed throughout the story? Oh my... I just wish I could play Black Book even more, but it's just way too easy even on hard difficulty. Seeing all the decisions you could take like battle\no battle ones seem useless when you can bruteforce every encounter. And there are so many of them you get kind of bored. Even gimmick boss battles took almost no deck changing from my side to beat them. You should feel as a powerful witch as your journey progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: In the end, I'm feeling pretty neutral about the game. The premise was promising and I really wanted to like it more than I did.I love a good supernatural story with demons and folklore! But as other reviewers mentioned: some of it is hard to make sense of. The hints at times act as if the knowledge is so obvious, .Also, the voice acting is lacking and the mispronunciation of words is irksome to me. Still, I'd recommend it, because I liked the story and the combat system.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, The WITCH without the ER!This game is pure epicness. The gameplay is awesome, the voice acting amazing and it has very interesting folk songs and mythology. I'm a huge fan of folklore from all kinds of cultures, specially one that’s famous for its drunks, so this game had me ticking all my boxes.It has a really good story too and depicts the whole slavic mythology really well. The atmosphere is so good, it makes you feel like you are inside an old russian fairy tale (without all the starving and vodka of course).It’s also one of the very few games that l've seen actually conceptually justify playing cards in combat. Deck building is what makes this game awesome, especially in Endless Battles. There's a lot of leeway in terms of building decks but generally you want to focus on 1 or 2 buffs/debuffs.There’s obvious passion by the creators, would definitely recommend it to anyone who loves story-driven games. It’s the kind of indie game that makes me forget about soulless AAA games. Black Book is a very underrated game and it really deserves more attention.7/10,  and F**k Putin
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Russian player here.The game is great as far as deckbuilding games go. The card part is solid, the story is nice (although the final twist is too obviously foreshadowed, which you will certainly notice if you pay any attention to dialogues and encyclopedia), the voice acting in Russian is good, but sometimes actors pronounce words incorrectly by stressing the wrong syllable (if you play in English, this might not be the case). Character models are simplistic and I hope they will get an upgrade in the sequel. I'd also be grateful if the game gave an opportunity to rebind the book after a failed combat (currently you can swap pages in and out, but can't buy additional pages like you can during an intermission) as some enemies require a certain type of spells to be used (the ghoul in the hunter's cabin was, in my opinion, the most difficult enemy in the game and I had to reload an earlier save to buy additional cards to be able to beat him).Otherwise the game is nice and you should play it if you like card games and/or interested in russian folklore.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Game is super engaging and the lore is fascinating.  It's obvious that a lot of love and effort went into this.  The only real criticism I would have is that the camera can be somewhat annoying to use.  Fortunately, the amount of areas we have to explore are relatively few but that was the most frustrating aspect.  Brush up on your arithmetic skills before you play :)
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: It is incredible, how much of Russian/Permian authors managed to stuff into this game. Much of it lore can be seen and experienced in today's video games and other entertainment genres quite often, but usually its portrayed in much more modern outlook The game instead goes back with to the roots. Black Book is not about killing cool looking monsters as it is a trend today for modern games. No. Player can really see and feel, that authors' intention wasn't just give them great game to play, but also to educate them. I learned so much while experienced great story. Although the way it unfolded throughout the game, the events were a bit too convenient and simple. It still provided a great experience though.  it's also not the best, but it is good enough to keep you entertained. I am not too keen on deck-building myself, but even though, by the last third of the game, I already had my ultimate deck and wasn't interested in new cards or any changes to its. So if you are a person not enjoying this aspect of the game too much, do not worry, you should be able to build something powerful quite easily. On the other hand if are kind of person who enjoys that very much, there is also enough new cards through the game to keep you occupied.  Artistically, this low-poly style is not really my cup of coffee, but they still managed to utilize it excellently, creating amazing scenes. Combined with draw styled conversations, its fine. I wasn't tired of looking at it often managed to amaze me.  It's a shame authors did not utilize folklore songs more often. You only get to hear the song when you pick it up, you can't even play it in the background. For the most part its just ambient music.  It's great that they managed to fully voice act the game, but go for the Russian one. The English voice acting is kind of weird more often than not. Overall amazing experience. Thank you MorteshAmazing deck-building story driven game full of Russian/Permian lore. ka.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: In the strongest possible terms I recommend The Black Book on every front. Its quirky characters and engrossing story can take many different directions and react meaningfully to your decisions; its card-based gameplay has a heavy emphasis on gimmick fights and status effects that feel closer to Final Fantasy than to a roguelite; its soundtrack is breathtakingly ornate; its graphics are atmospheric and moody and dazzling; its deep-dive into the intricacies of Russian steppe culture both historical and modern are amazing to see brought to life. I have but two very minor complaints: occasionally a line of text is either not translated, or awkwardly translated; and sometimes fights will bushwhack you with unforeseen mechanics that you have to reload to adjust your deck around.One sentence summary: indie Witcher 3, without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: [UPDATE 2]For those who wonder about the time it will take you for a complete run:I have just completed the game after about 31 hours of total playtime, and I have done all but 2 optional quests/locations, while following the Path of Ultimate Evil (i.e. got the most evil ending, and what an ending that was!).While the english speakers aren't actually native english speakers and sadly fairly frequently mispronounce even very easy words, the story is well worth it to put up with that, especially if you, like me, yearn for games that allow you to be properly Evil, more than just a dumb, vulgar brute, but downright nefarious, cruel, and above all: intelligent.[UPDATE!]The devs have replied to my thread on the Steam forum and have already issued a Patch that allows you to skip these Puzzle Battles after having failed them 3 times in a row.Due to the excellent dev behaviour and the phantastic speed with which a Patch was released, I will now update my review to "YES, I recommend this game".After having played the demo, I was in love with this game.The artstyle, but especially the thick athmosphere this game manages to create through sound and music alone are truly wonderful, and the story, so far, also seems well-written.**BUT**What the demo never told me, and what you can only find out after about 4-6 hours of gameplay, i.e. well outside the refund window (coincidence... I think not), suddenly this game drops mandatory "Puzzle Battles" on you out of nowhere, which block story progression.You **have** to solve these "Puzzle" Battles to be allowed to continue with the story, and you get zero help, no hints, nothing... this is as pure a trial & error gameplay mechanic as it is a bad one.Depending on the battle, you only get 2 or 3 turns to finish the enemies off, but you can neither use your own Deck which you've built around your combat strategy and equipment, nor can you actually enjoy the benefits of your hard-won equipment either.That means you suddenly, with no reason or explanation provided, are forced to play with a pre-set deck, and you just gotta figure out the one, singular solution to the encounter, when before you always had multiple ways of solving encounters... Don't get me wrong, Puzzle Battles could be a fun optional thing for players who want to be challenged, sure... but making them mandatory out of nowhere and locking story progression behind these tedious trial & error annoyances is really, really bad game design!Especially since you can't even just restart the battle... you have to reload the Autosave that has you redo the entire scene from the start, since you first entered that location.This really feels like the worst kind of filler mechanic, mandatory only for the perfunctory reason of artificially inflating playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awsome.....I cant put it any other way...It seamlessly blends pagan mysticism, christian orthodoxy and time period accurate storytelling to create a compelling tale. _childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to give this game a thumbs-up but can't. It's great to see a game that shows off legends and folklore of a region and culture that's not normally covered. This is translated into dialogue, interactions, location design, everything you do in the game. Graphics are nice, all dialogue is voiced. There is lots of reading, lore, dialogue to go through if you fancy, and battles are skippable. So far so good if you fancy a narrative-rich game.Combat is standard card-based (with a restriction on how many cards of a given type can be played in a turn) and that's where the game loses some of it's shine. Combat seems dead easy (except a few challenge battles) and boring, animations are nice first time around but are painfully slow after a while even at fastest speed. So combat feels like a chore rather than a fun part of the game.The downvote is because I got bored with the game already and won't be finishing it. I unlocked 2 of 7 seals and was halfway to next. I just can't imagine slogging through the rest of the game. Each battle and each chapter is the same - go down the map, get the same random events, use the same cards to clear each battle, rinse and repeat. Story and setting was enough to carry me this far but no more.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game.The story progression is more or less linear; organized around days with one main objective, one or more optional objectives, and to move forward you click on points in a map and make choices for each one, sometimes uncovering more options. It's nice, as it lets you really focus and immerse yourself into the story. The narration is very descriptive, so you can really get into the setting if that's the sort of thing you like.The card game is entertaining, there are several different strategies you can pick to keep yourself healthy (shields? regen? vampirism? curse?) while doing enough damage to win (bless? waste?) and between cards that allow for exponential stacking of status effects, cards that modify other cards or the flow of the game itself, cards that allow you to attack with your shield or with the enemy statuses, there is plenty of depth and variety to play around. The game is divided in 7 chapters, and in each one you unlock new possible strategies and interactions,. It is certainly possible to optimize your way into steamrolling everyone relatively early though, some may like that and some may wish more of a challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: My grandmother came from a clan of Staraver that lived in western Russia. A lot of the stories and themes of this game remind me of her and all the little rituals she taught me to keep my home safe. I'm very thankful that this studio made a game that let me relive such positive memories of my childhood.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: The deck-building gameplay is a bit basic and easy to overwhelm with broken builds, but the game itself is captivating and just dripping with atmosphere. It's clearly a labor of love, and I could feel it just as strongly in the first hour of the game as in the 30th.It is worth noting that the fights are not the main focus of the game - the story and characters are. If you come into this expect deep combat a-la Slay the Spire, you will be disappointed; but if you play this to be immersed in the strange and rich world of Russian provincial folklore, you're in for a true delight.Bonus: the Russian voice acting is some of the best I have seen in any media, including movies and other triple A games. The people working on this game had an absolute blast and you can tell.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so this is a strange one. The writing is... well, "poor" would be generous. It's very badly localized and the voice acting is so heavily accented and clumsy is sounds as if it was done by the game developers themselves. That being said, this game is fun. And I mean really fun. I'm the first person to put down a book or game because of bad writing, so it's saying a lot that I sunk 20+ hours into this one DESPITE it's terribly writing.The deckbuilding is fluid, unique, and addictive. It's not a rogue-like deckbuilder, so you don't have to worry about losing your deck and starting over. And also in spite of its terrible writing, there's a great tooltip system that lets you hover over any highlighted word to learn about it, and because the game is HEAVY on Russian mythology/folklore, practically everything is highlighted. I actually learned A TON about Russian folklore from this and I found it all fascinating. Those skills have even translated to the real-world!So, if you're like me and writing matter a lot to you, you might be put off by this game's first hour. However. If you turn off the sound on the dialogue (the acting is really irredeemably bad) and focus on the gameplay, you're going to find yourself loving this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Tedious. We've all bought this game for the setting, and it's great, just needed to be twice as short. Card mechanics are shallow and the missions you have to do before you get to your main objective quickly become a chore. What's worse, is that in this exercise of wasting our time somebody had decided to also add inventory, skills, and object collection. I've wanted to like this game, but its bore stops me from playing it any more.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:1 Good story. Last couple of chapters fall off a little bit but it’s still pretty good2 kick ass witch/19th century Russia lore. The way the game uses historical mythology and lore is reminiscent of Gabriel Knight, Quest for Glory or even Kingdom Come: Deliverance. 3 JESUS AND HIS TROOPS. The voice acting in this game is actually really bad, but its mostly bad in a really amusing way. The game will teach you how to take the lord’s name in vain like a late 19th century Russian miller4 The game seems very reactive to the choices you make in resolving issues5. Magic in this game is pretty badass. The game captures the ‘magic’ of magic really well. You’ll run around feeling like a wizard detectiveCons:1 The card game starts off pretty simplistic and there's no randomization in subsequent playthroughs. The card game exists more as a mechanic to facilitate the rest of the game rather than being the primary draw of the game. It does get pretty complex as the game goes on, but this isn't monster train or slay the spire. If you’re familiar with card games max that difficulty out. By the end of the game, you’ll be dumpstering almost everything but you’ll be in it for the story at that point. Other:The game Is a good 25-30 hours long.
