_childDocuments_.review: This game is jampacked with Slavic lore that you will recognize if you have played the Witcher game series. It's weird to call this game grounded since it's all about magic, but everything is understand in a very confident way. It's "grounded" in the way that folk magic feels more "real" and less flashy than a Final Fantasy game, the same way Ip Man movies are in comparison to other Kung Fu movies.I respect a lot how this game does not hold your hand and expects you to study the lore given to you about demons aka chorts to progress through the game. Also the card combat system is extremely rich and well designed. I can tell a lot of love was put into it with the number of mechanics and ways to win a battle. This especially becomes apparent during boss fights. Bosses will have a lot more health and buffs that common enemies do not have. I admit, at first I thought boss fights were a result of bad design since I kept dying, but I realized I was being forced to actually think about my deck building since I wasn't before. I also LOVED the battle puzzles where you have a set hand with a set number of turns and have to figure out how to win in that number of turns. Being an indie game though, I do want to warn folks about some flaws that I hope are patched soon to help the game do well. The most annoying issue was loading save files. If you save in the middle of a conversation in an area, the save doesn't register that, you are almost forced to start the entire area over. Thankfully, every area is not long at all, but it's pretty annoying to have to skip over an intro scene that I already finished. It adds up, especially with this game being about 35 hours long despite being an indie game. I'm not sure if this was a design decision to prevent save scumming but I think it could have been implemented in a more clear way if so. The other main issue I've found consistently annoying are interaction/collision detection issues as well as subpar voice acting for the most part. Don't believe anyone that says it's good. They don't know what they are talking about. I almost think they could have done better without it.All that being said, I couldn't put this game down. Which is very hard to make me do nowadays. I highly recommend this if this sounds even remotely interesting to you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been a fascinating journey into Eastern European folklore! While I didn't appreciate the set up, becoming a witch to rescue a loved from hell, the game itself has been brilliant fun, the card battling is not super complex but provides sufficient opportunities to employ different strategies and can be incredibly challenging. The RPG elements are there and choices have important outcomes for the story.Warning - the voicing of the characters is not great, but not game breaking either.

_childDocuments_.review: If you get this on sale, it's worth a look. It can be a bit repetitive, though. For the majority of the game, you can get away with using only two deck types, and those two types will make the game trivial, even on the hardest difficulty. The developer should have forced you to be more creative with deck building. The save system is a bit odd. For instance, you can talk to the NPCs, save the game, but when you load that save, you have to talk to them all again. It saves at the beginning of the encounter, not at the end, so the only way to save the game properly is to save it at the next location.You can play the game to sin or not sin. If you play it to not sin, you can pretty much ignore the entire chort management system altogether. My play through ended with 0 sin.The developers really needed better play testing. There were many dialogues that didn't match the subtitles. There were also several voice lines that repeated multiple times. There were several dialogues that were much longer than the actual text on the screen. These are rather important "bugs" considering the game is mostly a story based game.If you played the Witcher series or read the books, you'll recognize some the terms this game uses.

_childDocuments_.review: *Black Book* combines Slavic folklore with a dark, immersive RPG experience where players embody Vasilisa, a young sorceress diving into the supernatural to uncover secrets and wield dark magic. Its unique deck-building mechanics blend with adventure, making for a richly atmospheric journey. Players explore an eerie, rural landscape while engaging in card-based battles that reflect Vasilisa’s spellcasting abilities. With a range of cards representing spells and curses, the deck-building mechanics add depth to the combat system, requiring strategic planning to balance offense and defense. Rooted in Russian mythology, *Black Book* is filled with rich lore and dark fairy-tale elements. The storyline follows Vasilisa as she confronts demons, bargains with spirits, and unlocks forbidden magic, all while navigating a beautifully haunting world. The story effectively pulls players into its mysterious world, with choices that affect the narrative. The game features a visually distinct, hand-drawn style that captures the haunting beauty of its Slavic setting. The ambient music and sound effects heighten the game’s atmosphere, blending seamlessly with the game’s eerie, supernatural undertones. *Black Book* is a unique adventure for fans of mythology and strategy, blending card-based combat with a rich, folklore-inspired narrative. Its captivating story and atmospheric setting make it a standout in the indie RPG genre.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good card game with some neat lore, but also with a lot of bad decisions tacked on.There's a morality system, but the choices are often poorly explained and the negative choices are far more negative than the positive choices are positive.  For example, trying to take a knife away from a killer results in a fight, and that's 50 sin.  Saving someone's life, which comes up a lot, is worth negative 0 to 1 sin.  You need less than 100 sin to get the good ending, so a couple of misunderstanding and you're locked out of that.It's quite possible to walk into a boss fight with no way to injure the boss, due to how many things they make bosses immune to.  Needing a very specific deck to be able to fight at all is poor design.The game features a lot of trivia, and I think the expectation is that the answer is in the notes you find.  But very often it isn't.Managing chorts is just annoying.The voice acting is bad enough to be funny.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: "Black Book" is a stylised and narration-heavy deckbuilding RPG revolving around a young witch in a rural 19th-century russia that gets her hands on an sealed artifact and pacts with the devil himself to release her bethrothed from the clutches of death.It is a great and lengthy experience and has an exceptionally well made worldbuilding of dark east-european/russian-folklore: A world full of superstition teeming with antagonising mythology and shaken by political unrest and modern ideas alike. It really checks all the marks in that regard and the atmosphere is further carried by using the original mythical-folklore-vocabulary.The simple and stylised look (in the graphics and animation) and the artwork (of the cards and UI) fits great, you really feel like a burdened knower having seen the veil between how things seem doubling down in the superstitious meta-narrative! Unfortunately the game is quite easy (even in the hardest difficulty, where you only have to change your deck on some puzzly boss fights). Also some fights in this explorative gameplay feel redundant because of power scaling; furthermore some passages can drag a little. Nonetheless a great and dark title with a great and story to be experienced if you have the time and don't mind some minor gameplay-hiccups.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite good, and a worthy "spiritual sequel" (in more ways than one) to The Mooseman, albeit in a completely different gaming genre.The good:- Pretty good story, with good use of drama, tension, and payoff- Although I feel they could have found a better solution for the character portraits, the graphics are otherwise quite good and really come into their own on the final level (the skyline in particular - the "sun" there looks like a black hole, quite appropriately). Some parts even revisit the trippy tribal grafitti from The Mooseman, a nice surprise.- Good battle music and a selection of Permian folk music you that opens up your horizons- Provides an educational introduction to some "Slavic" folklore, although as others have noted, it's not so much Slavic as more of a mix of Christian/Slavic/Finno-Ugric "paganism" that was specific to the Perm region in Russia. The game also goes out of its way to highlight the links and continuity between this set of beliefs and the earlier "pagan" beliefs that were more fully explored in The Mooseman.The bad:- The English voice acting is simply horrendous. Nevermind the cringe inflections, the ridiculous and inappropriate accents at times, the flaws in direction... the worse part is that sometimes the diction is so poor that it's hard to make any sense of the dialogue at all. Turning on subtitles is a must.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not usually fond of deck-building games, but the Black Book makes it very easy to learn, but still with enough depth to build powerful combos based on the complex synergy of different cards and effects. There are only two suits, damage, shield along with some buffs and debuffs, but you'll be surprised with the variety of tactics you can bring to life with that. Story-wise game based on gloomy but rich cultural mix still present in northern russian regions in the middle XIX centered on the witchdoctor girl's quest for saving her lover's soul (who just said Senua's Sacrifice?). The story is not completely linear, there are a lot of sidequests to defend folk from demons and monsters, and a lot of obstacles could be dealt with without a fight (I surely have heard someone saying Witcher). Also there are no white and black situations, even the hero is actually a warlock: you can choose the dark side and help her to become a real evil sorceress or suffer from unemployed demons, but keep your soul unstaing. Or anything in between. For the people who really want to learn about the world, there are a lot of lore entries (which sometimes bring hints for dialogue options) and even recreated folk-songs of the middle of XIX century. Also, there is a talent tree, consumables, salvaging, equipable items and so on, and so on, You even have a card game inside your cart game. To be honest, I never expected the game so complex and prolonged - you can expect at least 20 hours of gameplay for main storyline and up to 30 more to complete all side-quests - by the way, you can't usually complete a sidequest if you opted to skip in and to on: completing the main quest of the day (well. night) will end the day, and all unexplored events and unfinished sidequests will vanish. The visuals are quite simplistic, primitive even, but nice work with camera and light effects makes it somewhat scenic (an underwater realm of drowned dead for example) - if you’ve played Kentucky Route Zero, which also has a gloomy and mystical atmosphere, you'll find the Black Book very much alike sometimes. Tl:dr - lore-rich story-based RPG with deck-building combat. Must have for anyone not allergic to any of the components.P.S.For people who can't stand card games it's fine too - easy difficulty allows you to skip the CCG part for good.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this way more than I thought I would because the game's fairytale-like story set among Slavic mythologies pulled me in. The game is a mix of choose your own adventure book and deck builder, but the highlight is the storytelling which is handled through a series of small, satisfying chapters put into an epic journey. There are some minor blemishes in the UI, translation, voice acting, and clunky point-and-click adventure interactions, but it's not enough to drag down the fun. All of the basic mechanics are fairly light but never feel like they overstay their welcome or try to be difficult, and the core deck builder game is just deep enough to make collecting cards and deck building fun.Don't mind some of the jank, the game wants you to have fun and rewards you.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're just starting this game, I highly recommend that you turn on English subs and change the audio to Russian. I appreciate the effort put in by the English dubbers (who I think are the same ones doing the Russian version), but the accent and the mispronounced words can throw you off. Besides, the acting is just so much better in the actors' native tongue. The only other thing that's not good is the camera and how it pans. Sometimes, you have to make your character run to the edge of the screen and when the camera zooms out or moves around to show you where she's going, it can get disorienting. I got trapped in a house for about 30 seconds trying to get out of this loop.Other than that, it's an amazing game. I love it. I love the background stories, Russian folklore. You may read about this game being text-heavy. Don't let it discourage you because it's worth it reading everything.

I used my one non curse card to slowly whittle down the enemy and as many herbs as I could. But the card game is really just the means to the end. The story and voice acting by the main characters are excellent. I was drawn in by Vasilisa's struggles and the Slavic folktales. Give this a try, take your time and play durak.

_childDocuments_.review: Great Game! The strongest parts are Stories and overall atmosphere of it. Choices mater here, thou it is not always clear what consequences you would have. There is main plot line that will take you straight to Hell, but there are will be plenty of interesting characters and stories on a way there.Atmosphere is dark, but also very homey (probably because i am from Urals and darkness of fir tree forest feels very comforting). Visuals are actually very simple and prehistoric (like 90s 3D) but together with book art create an outstanding dark atmosphere. Music and local folk songs add a lot to it. Game play has two parts. Quest adventure part where you walk around talk to people, gathering clues, and conduct an investigation.Fighting part is a deck building, turn based combat. It could be challenging, but gets better after you realize  that smaller deck is an easier one.Game in general is diving deep into Uralic folk tales. This probably the best game about Urals (it is the only game about Urals). It shows great knowledge of local customs, songs and stories. Listen to the Russian voice over and you will hear realistic local accents and local words. They even use the word Basko in correct way!This game is a real gem if you are interested in Urals or Russian culture in general, but also just a good story if you are not.

_childDocuments_.review: Another living proof of how much the inner content of the game is more important than its obvious technical characteristics. "Black book", with the exception of additional illustrations and static arts, looks extremely modest, and sometimes even bad, you have to be honest to the end. But the game is so amazing that you don't pay attention to it at all, because the local world is something very special, and the whirlpool of events literally captures you. In this case, Slavic mythology becomes the most important thread by which all the components are held together, because the work on the study of the facts and (more importantly) the interesting implementation of these facts into the gameplay has been done simply monstrous. Moreover, it is in terms of incredible work with Slavic mythology that the game is the real spiritual heir to the first Witcher. The misadventures of the girl Vasilisa, who lost her fiancé, but is ready to go down to Hell for the sake of his return, unfold in the setting of dense Russian forests, various evil spirits, outlandish mixtures of peoples, beliefs and superstitions. It is noticeable that the development of characters for screenwriters is not just empty words, but a dogma that must be followed, thanks to which you believe in everything that happens. Battles with dark creatures are realized through a card system, variable and effective in its basis. The multitude of options for building decks, gradually opening new cards and opportunities for tactical maneuvers, all of which are fun throughout the game. I spent 27 hours in it and I can confidently say that this is the purest 27 hours of gameplay you can imagine. No time-wasting grind, no story fillers - just 27 hours of quality main storyline, great side quests, battles and fun exploration. The game does not hesitate to be varied, throwing surprises at you even at the last stages. Here you have puzzles, and gambling games, and detective investigations of the crimes of the dark forces, but you can at least sit on a bench and listen to Russian folk songs. Tasks can be solved in various ways, the player is very gently pushed to study the constantly updated local encyclopedia, which you do with pleasure. A huge number of different stories, some fascinating facts from Slavic mythology, are presented so elegantly and subtly that you absorb them like a sponge. And that's not to mention the fact that the main story itself is built cinematically and extremely professionally, the two plot twists were like a blow in the stomach. The voice acting from professional actors is impeccable, local dialects are also preserved; you can also hear the difference in language among representatives of various social classes, national groups. The composer generally deserves a separate mug of foamy kvass, everything sounds as if we are really in the appropriate entourage.This kind of adventure is rare. Adventures with such thoughtfulness and fantastic inspiration of the creators passed on to the player are even more serious rarities. A pure gem that I recommend to everyone, this kind of work must be rewarded with the love of the players.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me tell you about the Black Book. It starts with those very words from the Book of Revelation, and tells a tale of a young woman, Vasilisa was her name. She had a young man she was to be married to, but he died in suspicious circumstances, and was buried beyond the church's walls, condemned to eternal torment once forty days have passed. Vasilisa, cunning as she was, she would have none of that. So she went and took on the forbidden powers of the unclean spirits, under the mentorship of Old Egor, a warlock in his own right, and set on the way through the Perm gubernia to reclaim her beloved's soul.And a small Russian-based studio called "Morteshka" made a game about her.As literal and metaphoric crossroads play a major symbolic role in the game, Black Book itself is a crossroad - a crossroad between entertainment, history, and the human condition. It delves into the spiritual world of the late 19th century, of the rural people of Tsarist Russia once you leave Moscow about a thousand (give or take) kilometers towards the north-east, where Orthodox Christianity lives side by side with the pagan beliefs and fables of the indigenous people; where people know, revere, and fear both Jesus Christ and the spirits of the wild, and those of home.The powers Vasilisa has learned, however, do not come without a price. Seeing the world as it is, she is now at risk, and should she use her powers for selfish impulses and bringing ruin, the judgment on her soul will not be merciful at all. Should she resist the temptation and use her powers for the good of the Christian souls she encounters instead of cursing and extorting them, who knows, she might even be deemed worthy of redeeming her beloved's soul. I can't really tell you, you need to read the story to its end yourself.On her travels, Vasilisa will encounter many people, peasant and noble alike, with their own crosses to bear, which she can choose to help them with, or leave them to their ends. Her mission remains to break the seven seals of the Black Book, and she can only do so by chasing after and dealing with the more powerful demons of the Eastern-Slavic world. To do so, the Book itself will help her. As her powers grow, new incantations of myth are added to it, and in reading them, she can protect herself and her allies while raining doom on those who stand in her way. The combat plays in a turn-based dynamic, and page synergies will be an important part of defeating the more difficult opponents.The visual journey through the Perm gubernia leaves something to be desired - as long as the characters are facing away from the screen, the entire composition is brilliantly conveying the atmosphere of the time and place; but facing towards the screen, there's a bit of an "uncanny" element to them. Conversations and battles, however, are beautifully animated and executed, and adding the subtle yet powerful soundtrack and sound effects of the Black Book, they will not get old very soon.The localization is slightly off at times, my personal recommendation - if you require English to get through the game -  is to play with Russian audio and English subtitles. There have been some control and balancing issues that the folks from Morteshka were quick to patch, and the game is getting a lot of real-time support and community involvement from the developers, which is a big plus.All in all, Black Book is a welcome break from "shiny awesome" mythology where the stories and lore only serve the main plot and its protagonist; this is a well-researched and down-to-Earth world; the developers went as far as consulting anthropology experts and archives (maps, history, and all) to create an experience that brings you so close to the every-day (every-night, more like!) life of the peasants of the remote Russian settlements, you could almost start trying to figure out whether there's a  tending to your own stove at home, even today.So go ahead, step in and explore the crossroad where the barriers between the worlds get thin, and where truly fascinating stories can be told. Maybe, you yourself will tell the story of the Black Book to your grandchildren, as if you saw it with your very eyes...
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent setting, fun and engaging gameplay.  The story is fairly good, and the mechanics between conversations, using the in-game encyclopedia to provide the necessary background information to solve problems, and inventory management with herbs and items is engaging and well-designed. Strategy, and adjusting your strategy, is required for success in battles.The music is decent and appropriate.  The voice-acting in English is...tolerable, but not good, and it doesn't always match the typed dialogue and that's quite distracting--enough that I'd like to see that cleaned up in a future version or patch (possibly by having changes to the visible text on screen to match what the voice actors say).  Some of the minor characters sound pretty awful and the voice acting and text mismatch were the only flaw I found with the game that bothered by.Took me over fifty hours to complete the game, crashed once in that whole time, and some may desire a second playthrough.   8 of 10 would be creeped out by the swan with teeth in the basement again.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: So far the game is great. It's simple, but quite enjoyable. The core gameplay loop involves moving along the map to deal with "rooms" where you have a random event. The event could be a battle, a test of wit, a puzzle, or a shop. You have quests to finish, completing the main one will end the day. There is an element of resource management with your devils, mostly choosing whether or not to send them on jobs earning you money, but also accruing "sins" which impact your ending. If you keep them at home you won't get a sin, but will suffer damage.  The combat is turn based and relies on deck building. Not much to really discuss here, all you need to know is it works and is not dissimilar to other games in the deck-building genre.The puzzles/riddles do have some minor problems in my opinion. Overall they do a good job of providing you with the answers in game using the encyclopedia, but I have run into several where there was no answer hidden in the lore. Maybe I missed them somewhere, but I don't believe so. I also encountered a riddle that straight up relied on outside knowledge, thankfully I knew the answer but still. Games should never expect the player to have some external knowledge. All tools required to accomplish a task should be provided in game. Again, these problems are rare and they do provide a hint system. The "morality" decisions also have some problems. Occasionally it's not quite clear what is the "good choice", For example, I get a quest to explore an area. I did it, but got a sin for it. Most of the time it's perfectly logical, don't steal the old mans money, so don't allow it to dissuade you.My favorite part is the great accumulation of Slavic lore and it's integration into gameplay. Most of the riddles/puzzles are based on the folklore in game. I loved admonishing a character because she didn't properly store her silverware, so a demon punished her.  I admit I'm no expert but I'm enjoying what I've read so far.The art style is great, and the score lovely. Voice acting is stellar, at least the Russian track, and suits the characters well. Only compliant in this realm is the character models, in game not the drawn ones, look a bit too "bright". The blocky/cartoonish style takes away from the gloomy atmosphere of the surroundings. It fits the demons, ghosts, monsters, etc, but something about the human models just doesn't work for me.Ultimately, it's a great game and I recommend it enthusiastically.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Intriguing start but story and combat gets boring/repetitive over time. Go to one place, fight demons, go to another - make a choice and repeat. Graphics is also very basic for a game of this standard. Upside though is that choices do matter and they come back to bite you on the ass - which is good! Culturally, it's so interesting to learn about the slavic folklore and how it is intertwined.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing visual style and storytelling. The catalyst for the protagonist's journey and its denouement are less compelling than the journey itself, but that's kind of the point. I seriously envy anyone starting Black Book for the first time—it's a fantastic experience, highly recommended if you enjoy story-driven games of any kind, especially with history and/or folklore added to the mix.The game's one major flaw, imho, is that in the last quarter of the game, you can become OP, so it is primarily your patience that is challenged when you whittle down the last bosses' HP, even on the hardest difficulty. But hey, at least the bosses always look cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: cool lore and atmosphere. was expecting to get tired of the combat system more quickly, but surprisingly it wasn't the case. maybe more opportunity for exploring the environment would've been nice, but at the same time that generally just makes me feel like i have to explore EVERYTHING before i can move on with the main story, and make little to no actual progress in the game lol. so i guess the more linear approach this game has is actually helpful for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Great graphics and story-rich, but a too slow-paced for my interest. Games that throw you into a lore breakdown before letting you mess around with the mechanics immediately make me feel disconnected. The story is unique for a card battler, but the voice acting is not great at all. The pacing, cut scenes, and voices that don't quite match their characters made this game feel more like a chore than anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Good game with multiple endings and a Fallout-like epilogue. Well made. Do not be fooled by the graphics, it is the game's style. It works well with the game as a whole.Awesome thematic game. You learn alot about the slavic myths and legends.Good but limited deck builder.One or two areas where you control the Vasilia but there is no point controling her since there is only one option. I suggest removing those and put a cutscene instead... including the ending where you walk towards a tree. Very pointless.Aside from that, I have nothing negative to say about this game. :)Buy it if you like thematic games.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Russian folklore, somber dark aesthetic, card/turn based battling. The game starts promising and has some fun elements but it failed to pull me in or build any momentum. Actual time playing the game is probably closer to 4-5 hours after trying to get into it a few times, It didn't hold my attention so it was abandoned for more engaging media.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. I'm always interested in learning cultures that differ from my own, and I felt like I was allowed a unique glimpse into this world of the past. I enjoyed learning to play Durak during the regular game play. It took me 77 hours to complete one story line and I'm seriously tempted to play this again for a different outcome. This was my first card collecting game and I found the turn taking relaxing.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: This is a turn-based, deck building game based on slavic folklore. The events take place in the early 1900s countryside Russia where mythical creatures (both malevolent and benevolent) live amidst humans. MC's name is Vasilisa and she's on a mission to save her husband who died by mysterious circumstances and supposedly his soul went to hell. Vasilisa, under the guidance of her grandfather is now on a mission to break the 7 seals of the Black Book (an ancient and powerful artifact that grants any wish to anyone powerful enough to break all of the seals, or so the legend goes). Some of the environments felt unique and the combat music is very engaging.To me at least, the russian voice acting wasn't half bad so I just kept that on for the vibes. English voice acting is okay too. It was a blessing for me that I could go to the settings and speed up the cast animation speed because the game already drags on for far too long, seeing the same slow *zagovor* animation over and over again wouldn't have helped. Since MC is a sorceress, a knower, we get knowledge checked all the time in dialogues and get bonus xp if the player answers right. The player doesn't have to know much beforehand, all the info that they need is gathered across the game and kept as readable pages for future reference. This contributes a good amount to lore and immersion.The player has white pages (for defensive purposes) and black pages (for attacking). A spell per turn is composed of orders and keys. Even on normal difficulty the jump from one chapter to another felt inconsistent at times, because now I'd stomp a boss/ the chapter demons and as soon as I got into a new chapter, until I updated my spells I was the one getting stomped. For better or for worse it's impossible to get softlocked because you can skip any battle and get all of the rewards if you lose the said battle 4 times in a row. Certain book builds such as curse/ waste stacking feel way too powerful/ universal so I rarely ever changed the strategy.  Throughout your journey you'll gather powerful demons under your command. They need to be put to work else they'll torment MC and grant her debuffs. The demons' tasks are also the main source of sin income, which counts for the game ending (there's 3 main endings).There's also a pseudo-card game within the main card game (wild) but besides Steam achievements there's not much use for it, later in the game I got so many coins that I didn't need to bet on cards for even more coins.The mobs/ bosses seemed quite hellbent on what their fighting strategy was and me, as the player, didn't need a full bound book of pages. This assured that my hand was always decent/ the cards that I needed were dropping most turns. I'd recommend it at a sale or in a bundle. The game overstays its welcome, the normal battles get repetitive, the story sometimes gets dragged on too much between the important moments. The husband actually almost gets forgotten until the end . Unless you want to reload some savefiles for achievement completion/ start a new high sin / low sin playthrough, I don't see a lot of replayability coming from this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: It is a shame. The cultural and historical aspects of this game are fantastic. Ethnic songs are super cool too. BUT in some levels it is impossible to play because of bugs. Your character cannot go where it suppose to, she was constantly stuck half way. Levels weren't properly tested( I dropped it in the end because i was so tired of this bugs. unfortunatly, will have to watch the rest of the game on youtube.I hope that developers will do something about it
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, well crafted setting & story development. Perfect for someones first card game. Simple mechanics but slowly getting more complex which allow you to be creative with your builds.If you're playing this after enjoying other card games such as Slay the Spire, Monster Train or even Hearthstone make sure you turn up the difficulty above the recommended setting. This is not a rogue-like. Be aware that this game spends a lot of time setting up the environment, a simple "You gained 1 herb" with no choice action can take over a minute in dialogue explaining how.Worth the pick up, just make sure you know what you're going in to!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black Book = Slay The Spire on steroids + an actual story + Gwent + Fable.Very fresh game that doesn't feel unfamiliar at the slightest. Theme & lore is awesome.If you're a card game pro, you may want to start on the hardest difficulty. You can change difficulties mid-game.I've only reached the first Battle-puzzle. It took me a good number of tries, but it's definitely solvable. I'm glad I wasn't able to find the answer online lol (I looked.)
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely LOVE this game. After playing Inscryption, I was left with a card-battling itch I just couldn't scratch... Except this really did it for me. Not only did I get hours and hours of amazing and complex card battling, I also learned quite a bit of Russian lore and demonology/Eastern Orthodoxy. I really didn't expect the story to be all that great going into it, but I was happily surprised by the exceptional content of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I've always avoided card building games, as whenever I watched a friend play one it seemed exceedingly complicated to make cards jive with each other. Merge? Collaborate? Mesh? There's a technical term I'm forgetting.      Either strategy card games aren't as complex as I'd feared, or "Black Book" is exceptionally clear about how their cards work with each other. Even as I settled into my chosen strategy, I could see how certain other decks could be built around different mechanics. I had a great deal of fun tweaking my deck as I gained new cards, and even when an enemy I fought had immunity to my main technique, it added a new kind of challenge to still make my deck succeed.     The core story is...fine. As the game page says, Vasilisa's fiance dies, and you use your titular Black Book to go get him back. Depending on how cruel of a witch you are I assume your ending changes, but I often forgot what Vasilisa's supposedly main goal was. I felt neither sadness nor joy at the ending I received.     What I *did* get a lot of enjoyment from was finding all the pieces of real world lore and mythos that the game is full of. I loved that, not only do you get quick paragraphs of text, but you can see those beliefs shaping the world you walk through. You even get rewarded for finding and reading the lore you collect, as Vasilisa's correct advising of people gains you bonus experience.     I don't know if this is a game I'll play again immediately, but I've already recommended it to some of my more strategy minded friends. Definitely got my money's worth out of "Black Book."
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I'm usually not a fan of games with card-based combat but Black Book has such phenomenal writing and storytelling that I couldn't help but enjoy it. Coming up with combat strategies and trying to balance sins and good deeds was so fun and I now have a little notebook I've filled with notes just from this game. One thing to note is that if you are American like me, you may want to do a little googling on some Slavic folktales and superstitions to help with some of the decisionmaking, but it's not too hard to pick up! I really recommend this game to anyone who likes a good story and strategic combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Strangely cozy. This game made me invested in slavic folklore mid gameplay and surprise me with how much respect he treated the christian influences in his approach.  The soundtrack, story and the gloomy atmosphere of this game are really good too and the gameplay - whether it's choice-and-consequence or card battle - is solid and fun. Good game, better played at night.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: A decent card battler RPG in a world of Slavic myths. The best parts to me were the bits of folklore and folksongs you could collect along the way, it was a nice way to get to know slavic mythology a little. On the other hand the game is quite rough around the edges. The demon animations and player camera movement felt quite clunky and the card battles started to get a bit repetitive after a while (which to me usually isn't the case with card games). Strong theme, decent gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: This game is wonderful, the cultural exploration and information is a delight, the core loop of game mechanics themselves are for the most part very tight and fun (3d exploration is a bit janky but that aspect in general is such a small part of the game that it doesn't matter). Music, story, characters are all fun and enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: The deckbuilding and combat are satisfying, the story is good, and the translation into English is excellent. The extremely detailed portrait of 19th century Russian folk belief is fascinating, and the fact that the game often asks you to think like a koldun makes it an integral part of gameplay rather than just a menu of interesting stories. This is an impressive and absorbing game.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Mythology as well as history, highly intricare strategic combat, a deeply satisfying gameplay loop, stellar voice acting, an engaging plot. Themes of power and powerlessness, the old and the new, sacrifice and sin are fantasically well implemented. Also, you're rewarded for reading the lore because it has a proper gameplay purpose? I loathe reading in games, but here it feel not just necessary, but *satisfying*. It borders on diegetic, how the game lets you engage with the lore so you can make sure the main character is making the right choices.Not to mention that while the storyline doesn't pretend to be anything but linear, the player seems to literally always have *at least* two ways to approach any given encounter - which also ties into the themes. This game has some really tight, deliberate design choices at its foundation.Yeah, the 3D animation looks like crap, but that's literally the least interesting part of this game. Screw the polygon count - if they had wasted their budget on animation, the game wouldn't have been this good.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the interesting deep lore and story, which I generally like, I'm going to have to give this a thumbs down for execution. The game tries a bit too hard to give people a crash course in slavic mythology and makes game progression depend too heavily on it. You don't always get the clues you need to answer questions.The game is also terribly unbalanced and buggy. Unless you happen to get lucky with cards you get, you can get completely and irreparably stuck with a bad deck that will have you be unable to progress past certain bosses that will just stomp you over and over. Some text for the bad English voice acting isn't translated, and the first "puzzle battle" was unwinnable without any indication why (once losing 1 HP it was instant game over, no explanation) regardless of difficulty setting, at which point I gave up. A real pity as it's got a lot of heart and effort poured into it, but as it is I don't think I'll ever see most of the game as I got stuck in chapter 2 with no way forward.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much a toss-up for whether to recommend or not.The deckbuilding part of the game is very basic and while fine, can get a little tedious (might just be salty as right at the end a boss turned up that was just flat out immune to my build and I had no way of rebuilding in any meaningful way).I did very much enjoy the setting and Slavic folklore foundation to the story. That alone made it worth playing, but you probably won't get much out of the game if that aspect isn't particularly appealing to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game's atmosphere!  It's great, you just plunge right into childhood fairy tales, if you're Slav (especially Russian, as the setting takes place pretty far east from Moscow).The writing, if you have Russian text and voice over, is amazing!The card system is decent, as well as RPGish things like inventory, skill trees, etc.My only gripe is puzzle fights. Seriously, somehow the game makes it hard to calculate and understand exactly how much damage is going to be applied, which effects will wear off etc. I don't know why, it's just hard, and probably not only for me. And the puzzle fights are the fights designed to be won by a very very specific order and combination of cards. The idea behind puzzles might have been be great, but the implementation just gives me headache, honestly. :(UPDATE: After a few hours more - writing, visuals, story are still great! But also one more thing that maddens me...DEVELOPERS - Please give us a way to control chort if you get one during a quest. Otherwise the player might be screwed.I have no clue how to predict when (at which progression level) you get one more chort, or which one will it be (are chort effects random?)The thing is, you can't do anything with this chort - cant send him on a task, can't nullify his effect. For me this was a chort that nullifies any Bless (or how is it called in English, idk) effect on me. And he appeared right before a tough fight with a big ass fish. I'd kick that fish ass with Bless, but without it - can only try and shuffle your deck appropriately...
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Very immersive game, super instructive about - forgive me for I know this is not accurate - "Russian" culture. The card-battling part is nothing fairly original and not disappointing either. At some level, card-based combat is card-based combat so if you know the 'genre' you won't find innovating. But again, is good fun if you like it. Overall the lore is great and the 'choices matter' is also fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: The game is quite wonderful; interesting story and game mechanics, and a compelling sneak peek to the culture, mythology and history of an ethnic group in the Russian territory.There was a bit of difficulty to properly get in to the game. You frequently have to/get to make choices during the story, which are pretty difficult to guess correctly even with hints and rigorous reading of the game's encyclopedia. The first act of the story one can quite easily get through, but during the second act there is quite a steep rise in difficulty level; I had to start a new game since I just could not win a certain mini-boss with my mediocre deck and poor choice of level-up skills. But with some practice/knowledge on the game mechanics, the second try is so far going well.The game definitely has it's challenges (which in a sense makes the game even more interesting), but it also has a lot of charm; the voice acting, the theme, and the cast of characters is great, and it's sometimes really difficult to stop playing and go to bed.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Received this game as a gift through Humble Bundle. I didn't expect much and card battles are not my favorite but I quickly grew to like the playstyle. The lore is fun, the characters are cute or appropriately annoying, and I like the battle style. It's somewhat "choose-your-own-adventure" because you get optional tasks and get to make decisions based on gaining or losing sin. The item buffs are neat, although I wish I would have noticed the GAIN sin note below the first experience gaining item I got. Currently about 3/4 through the game and enjoying the story and character intricacies. I would definitely recommend to people who like games with a story or people interested in learning about card battles (its a good starter game). In my opinion, it's a bit overpriced, but I got it for free so I can't complain!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Having finished my first playthrough today, I can absolutely recommend this. The atmosphere is amazing, the core gameplay loop is really fun and regularly eased up by some surprising extra mechanics (solving a murder mystery) or riddles. The choices you make along the way matter and make it feel very impactful.The music is so amazing that I bought the soundtrack after 3 hours.The puzzle battles are fairly diffiult - It's very good that after 2 tries the game allows you to pass them (and you still get the reward for beating them!)The game also rewards you for actually reading dialog and encyclopedic information - whjile still giving you an option to continue if you didn't do that properly.Overall, a very cool experience - I'll let it lie for a bit and then go for a full evil playthrough, I think.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: It's interesting more of an experience than a game.  Being a true red-blooded American I don't really get all this Eastern Europe/Slavic folklore and references.  The game explains what they are (once) but them keeps referencing them and it's hard to keep track of what a Bannik, or a Leshy, or Domovoy are.The combat system is a card-battle type where the rules aren't ever quite fully explained in detail.  I'd recommend turning the difficulty down to low.  There are a few puzzle battles where you are given specific cards and are expected to use them in a certain order to win; but these can be skipped.There's attack, defend, but then waste, and curse, and hold and it never quite comes together in an understandable way.The voice acting is excellent, the narrative is compelling (if you can relate to Eastern European folklore) and your choices feel like they have impact.Right now I'm about 3 chapters in and i'm sort of struggling with a desire to finish it, I'm enjoying the game - but not understanding it.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy games where you gradually build up a collection of cards throughout the game without them being reset on each run and this game achieved that very successfully, with an interesting array of impactful and varied cards.The story was engaging and well-told.The fights were pretty easy on Hard (Koldunya) difficulty. I would probably recommend Hardest (Nightmare) difficulty to others and even then I don't think it would be too hard. The toughest fight is probably the first boss. From the second seal, you get some cards that make surviving much simpler.I'd recommend this game for anyone looking for a fun card game with a lot of atmosphere.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Downsides- after 35 hours in this absolutely majestic game, I've found myself wanting to make another run for the high sin ending. The game is wonderful, one of the better detective style games I've played, the atmosphere it builds is top-notch. It does everything it sets out to well, and then some.Upside- I have switched my milling-around addiction from solitaire to durak.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, a real gem of Russian gamedev. Nice to see that not all talented developers have been sucked into making some grindathon crap for Mail.ru!I am not typically into CCGs and I bought this because of the folklore, which I always found interesting. Russian folklore is very unique due to being a cocktail of many different ethnicities and cultures, but unfortunately much of it has been destroyed by the Orthodox church and then by communists. Furthermore, a lot of the documentation was written on bark which is not a very durable material. As a result this kind of information is rarely available in an "easy to consume" format. However, if you do bother to learn some of it, I think this game proves what fertile ground it is for building game worlds. Black Book really nails the atmosphere and I have to give special praise for the fantastically written dialogue that captures several dialects, as well as old Russian speech and the difference between peasant speech and that of educated people at the end of 19th century. This was also an interesting time when technology started to find it's way to the villagers, which too was played out cleverly in this game. Unfortunately you can't quite appreciate the brilliant writing if you don't know Russian as the English translation practically erases all the nuances of different dialects. Nevertheless, it's a good translation and you will still be able to enjoy the game's very well-written and paced plot with it. Voice work is also excellent in both Russian and English, though at times in the Russian VO, I could tell the actors got confused by the pre-revolution dialect and didn't quite match the intended tonality.As for gameplay - I think it was fun. As much as any CCG is for me. The cards are very well designed, they enable a lot of viable and varied builds, and the further you progress the more complex and powerful card effects you can unlock. However the deck building has many QoL issues - for example you can't empty your deck fully to rebuild it, you can't view all cards in one list (have to switch sections), the thumbnails are way too big and the previews are too big also, you can't restart the battle to change the deck without dying first and there are a lot of situations where your current build simply doesn't work against certain enemies.If I had to pick an actual problem with the game, I'd say it's the graphics. Especially the character portraits. It's clear from other art in the trailers and in the game's portrait gallery in one of the levels, that the game's artists can draw well. However when it comes to the most important portraits - the dialogue portraits, I feel that they've slacked off. The protagonist herself, especially, looks kinda ugly, the lack of proper shadows make her different-colored eyes look like she has strabismus.Overall Black Book is a really good game with fun gameplay, good story, interesting world and a good value (the full game + all side-quests takes 40+ of quality hours to complete). And if you are also intersted in Russian folklore it's pretty much the only such product on the market. 100% recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: i've never played a deck-building game before but i loved this one.the story is fun and engaging, and the world-building is fantastic. the slavic folklore drives the story in a meangingful way, and the folk songs were beautiful. you can tell that this game has been made with lots of love, definitely recommend. sidenote: i hate gwent but i enjoyed durak. i also played in russian with english text, which is the best way to play if you don't speak russian.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black Book is a turn based card game set in a fantasy version of eastern Europe where people living in small towns are tormented by demons and curses. The player character, Vasilisa, is a witch who is on a quest to break the seals on a magical book, in order to gain the power to resurrect her dead fiancée.•	Gameplay structure is similar to Thronebreaker (the Witcher 3/Gwent spin off). The story takes around 26 hours to play through, and if you die you can simply retry that fight. (Its not a Slay The Spire style roguelite).•	The Black Book contains lots of spells, which you’ll play like cards to either attack, defend, or apply/remove status effects from yourself or the demons you’ll have to fight against.•	Combat is turn based, and at the start of each turn the book will randomly draw some cards into your hand. You can see what action each enemy intends to take on their turn, and then you’ll decide which cards to play.•	Unlike other deckbuilders, cards have no energy cost and are all free to play, however they’re limited by type. Every card is either an “order” or a “key”, and you’re allowed to play a certain number of each type per turn.•	Cards are also coloured, with black cards harming enemies and white cards protecting Vasilisa. Some cards become more powerful when you play other cards of the same colour on the same turn, which adds another tactical layer when choosing which cards to play.•	You can add more spells to the book after winning fights, or buy them from a merchant. Every spell you learn during the game will stay in the book, but you can add or remove them from your active deck at any time outside combat, which lets you easily adjust your tactics while maintaining an efficient deck.•	Status cards have a big impact on combat tactics. There are lots of different statuses which can either be stacked up to deal massive damage, restore health, increase attack or defence, cause you to lose health when playing cards, prevent you from playing all cards of a specific colour, and more. Many enemies have abilities to either buff themselves or debuff the player, and boss fights in particular often turn into a status war where you’re constantly applying and removing from each other.•	The story takes place over several days, and each day your map will show a few locations where you can progress the main quest, do optional side quests, and have other encounters with civilians or demons. Sometimes you’ll have a choice about how to deal with the situation which could reward you with XP or gold.•	As you explore you’ll also find useful items. Herbs are consumables which can be used during combat, while relics can be equipped to gain passive bonuses.•	As you gain XP and level up you can unlock abilities which increase card attack/defence values, and allow you to draw more cards, play more cards, and use more items, each turn.•	Story is the weakest part of the game. Dialogue is often strange, and although I understood the important events, I sometimes felt like it lost something in translation.•	You can get a good or bad ending depending on how many sin points you earn during the game. Some quest choices will add or remove sins. Also there are a few demons who work for Vasilisa, and every day you have to send them out to do tasks, which usually involves cursing people. This gives you sins (and some gold), but if you don’t give these demons a task, they give you penalties during combat. When levelling up you can unlock some abilities which increase or reduce sin points gained from demon tasks.•	I didn’t really like Vasilisa’s character. In particular there are so many scenes where she criticises other characters for doing bad things, but somehow its okay for her to send an army of demons to curse people every day.•	Voice acting for all characters is poor. Some scenes are described by a narrator, whose voice acting is okay.Black Book has good, tactical combat which should be enjoyed by fans of turn based card games, but the story quality is low. Buy on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I had my fun with this niche card base strategy game dedicated to checking you if you pay attention to the Slavic folktales that you can read and, of course, how much you can 'break' the rules to your favor. And the story isn't half bad: A young witch named Vasilisa (which in Greeks means Queen interestingly) wants to find the titular Black Book so she can bring back to life her lost love.Unfortunately after a few hours it gets a little bit boring and the VERY low polygon graphics of the characters aren't appealing to me to draw my attention. Especially when you see their animations.The positives I liked are the story which I mentioned, the variety of the quests which are very faithful to the obscure world of Slavic witchcraft, some specific characters you meet are delightful hearing them (I love the freaking cat demon) and the atmosphere is great.So despite my decision to stop playing, I am very sure if you love a little bit more strategy card games, it will keep you a lot more busy than me.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not very hard once you know which cards are powerful and how to do as much damage as possible. I recommend starting with the 2nd or even 3rd difficulty. The story is pretty long, you probably won't be able to finish the whole campaign in a day.The main selling point of the game for me is the lore. It depicts Slavic culture, specifically how the introduction of Eastern Orthodoxy and technology mixed with traditional Slavic folklore to create a unique worldview. There are some riddles which require you to look in the notes you gather, which is a nice way of mixing gameplay and trivia (of course you can also make a lucky guess).

_childDocuments_.review: Feels extremely unfocused.I was given an overwhelming number of choices to make, and meanwhile the game is trying to tell an emotional story, *and* teach a lot of Russian culture (leaving a lot of native words untranslated). _childDocuments_.review: Pros:+ Deep lore+ Great music+ Good storytellingCons:- Fairly simple/exploitable card battles- A bit too long in the tooth, especially if you tend to go after all side quests.If you enjoy games that are dripping with lore and folklore, then this game is definitely worth the price of admission. The card battle system is fairly exploitable, and new cards unlocked in each chapter tend to be incremental, yet optional upgrades.  Normal mode is fairly easy, so if you are really into engaging card battles then you should probably play on a harder difficulty setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Due to not being able to access my gaming PC for the time being, I decided to double dip Black Book on Switch. Luckily it was on sale there too (I buy all my games on sale, don't you?). For the limited time I played it on PC I didn't really experience any technical issues with it. The Switch version however does have some annoying, albeit mostly non game breaking issues, but I will disregard them for this review, because it's supposed to be a review of the Steam version. So going forward just take it as a given that I'm unable to provide my judgement of its technical aspects.My, my, my, where do I even begin with this one? Let's being at the beginning, shall we? My first PC game ever was a Russian space game called Parkan (the manual told me it means "boomerang" in some unspecified language). After having my early childhood occupied mostly by my slick Atari 1200XL with a collection of Chinese bootleg tapes (yes, tapes) labeled "MIKROSOFT", and a bootleg Chinese Sega Mega Drive, Parkan was truly an almost religious experience. Never before a game I played offered me so much freedom, so much sense of adventure, exploration and mystery as Parkan did. It was made by Russians in 3 years time and was released in 1997, just by the time I got my first proper personal computer.Since then I started getting more and more familiar with both Western and Eastern games, with such radiant examples as the original Fallout duology (the only good Fallout games, sorry, not sorry) with its deep story. And almost its cosmic opposite in all the right ways: Tales of Destiny 2. Amazing games, very dear and near to my heart.I never forgot Russian games since Parkan though. I loved the others with all my heart, but a special place in it was always reserved for Russian games, and over the years I still remember them very fondly. Parkan, Vangers, the Space Rangers duology, Perimeter, The King's Bounty remake... And then, the dark ages of Russian game development came. King's Bounty is almost 15 years ago now, and since then I haven't played a single good Russian game that didn't awkwardly try to hide its Russian identity (oh, hi, Beholder!).The Black Book on the contrary, wears its identity on its sleeve. I learned a lot about the old faith Perm folklore from it, even being vaguely familiar with it through sheer osmosis. It did for the lack of the better word to "Russian" myths, what the Witcher did to Polish ones. There's so much love and care put into the game it really shows, it really is remarkable. So to explain why there's a special place in my heart for Russian it's this: heart. Russian games are hit or miss like no other, when they miss they miss catastrophically up to a point of putting an entire industry into the mobile dungeon. When they hit, they hit spectacularly, that very few games from other countries can compete with. That's why there's so few Russian games that are mediocre (wink, Partisans).Okay, enough with all this sentimentality. You didn't come here for my life's story. The game's great. You'll love it if you're interested in interesting folklore and other anthropological findings. You'll adore it if you like a very well written story with complex characters and an almost Shakespearean evolution of events. If you're into deck builders you might be disappointed however. It's not that the combat system is not interesting, on the contrary, but it is undone by one thing and one thing only: a complete disregard for anything resembling balance.By the time you get two cards: The Evil Eye and The Sea's Depths you might as well just throw every other card in your inventory into a trash bin. Normally the former is a defensive spell which lowers an opponent's attack. So far so good; right? It stacks. Okay. It stacks infinitely as long as you apply it every turn. That would be bad enough on its own, because obviously as a defensive move it's already broken like that. The only damage that can be done to you at this point is indirect; such as let's say poison.Okay, so we have a busted defense spell. Guess what the second card in this arrangement does? It's offensive, doing indirect damage (meaning it goes through shields) by a factor of three of the applied Evil Eye status. And to add insult to injury you can stack a bunch of items that augment that effect by a significant amount. Congratulations, you broke the game almost completely, except for one boss that has immunity to Evil Eye (the only enemy in the entire game!).Coincidentally that same boss is the perfect example of the absolute clown balance working against you. It took me three hours to figure out how to kill it. Without spoiling the story. You basically need to disregard shields. Max out healing. Convert damage done to you to a damage buff and keep it balanced because said boss also gets a bonus damage for every status point you get. And yes, it stacks, oh how it stacks. It can kill you in one hit with full health if you get too buffed. Getting the taste of your own medicine ain't pretty, it really hurts. By the way, this method is just another one to break the game, albeit more risky than my preferred one, because there's always a chance of running out of max HP.This is all a complete shame, because I was enjoying combat much more when it wasn't broken. It forces you into this dance of defense and attack and everything inbetween. One truly genius idea they had for it is that unlike a lot of things in the game, defense normally doesn't stack. It dissipates at the end of the turn, meaning hunkering down is not really an option. It's far more advantageous to have just as much defense as you need or even take a small hit in order to afford more offense. I wish the rest of the game would be like that, but having found the optimal fool proof strategy that works 99% of the time, why bother at all?Beyond the deck building and combat you get to do mostly graphic novel stuff. Send your demons out to either torment peasants or do meaningless work like trying to catch the sunset in a bottle. Talk to your companions, who by the way have special abilities that recharge after an X amount of turns (yes, there are ways to shorten that amount). Do quests for the common clay of the old East. Wander to the market to get trinkets and herbs. Another thing I noted as something pretty incredible is that the map system if you think about it, is really quite pointless on the surface. However it gives the world space due to how it's constructed. I keep forgetting that I'm mostly playing a graphic novel here because I can feel Vasilisa's travels. It does backfire though when used indoors sometimes, because obviously there's a disconnect between what is supposed to be an entire region and a small house. I wish they'd drop it there in all honesty.The graphics works very well being quite lowfi. It's very much reminiscent of original Alone in the Dark and Ecstatica. It works for the game exceptionally well. It certainly has these Russian Gothic horror elements in the lieu of Nikolai Gogol and his The Viy. The art style in general is very beautiful, ranging from the impeccably rendered character portraits to the mood setting lighting and particle effects.The music is great, but the voice acting steals the show, especially the narrator. Out of curiosity I played a bit of it in English and it's refreshing to hear a genuine Russian accent in a game for once. I think the same actors did both versions. Vasilisa definitely did, and she actually does an excellent job in either. I would recommend the original Russian dub however. For two reasons. The first one is that the English narrator with his impossible to pinpoint accent sucks. He has nothing on the Russian narrator, just hands down. And the second is that I really recommend a more authentic experience.Buy this game, buy it for your friends, buy it for your loved ones, buy it for anyone who'd like to play it. It is that good. A game like that comes once a decade.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:-You'll learn a lot of interesting stuff about Russian folklore and Eastern Orthodox Christianity-Nearly every line is voice acted in a somewhat goofy but charming manner-The 2d art for characters and cards is nice-The story is fun to followThe bad:-the entire card battling systemReally, almost every element of the card battling system is deeply flawed. To start, you can adjust the deck as you please with a huge degree of freedom. Between missions you can purchase any number of cards from a large pool to add to your collection. After setting off on a mission, you're still free to slot cards in and out as you desire, even being able to whittle the deck down to 13 cards. This leads to super streamlined, boring decks that do the same thing very consistently.The cards themselves are not particularly interesting in how they function, and the ones with more unique abilities often have tooltips which are very unclear and confusing (perhaps due to translation issues?).There is no system for energy or mana like in most card games, instead you simply get to play a set number of type A cards and a set number of type B cards each turn. This really simplifies the decision making process each turn in a bad way, since basically every card of the same type has an equal cost associated with it.You can't even see your draw and discard piles. Truthfully I'm not even sure if the game uses such a system or if you essentially reshuffle and draw at the start of each turn (not that this would be any better). This is completely ridiculous and massively undermines tactical play. I cannot think of a single reason not to make the player aware of what their potential draws are.Overall I'm torn. I got this game from the humble deckbuilding bundle and this was not at all what I expected. If you're like me and primarily interested in tactical gameplay and strategic deckbuilding, you probably wont like the game. Despite that, it's clear that a lot of effort was put into this game, and everything outside the card battles holds up quite well. I can't really bring myself to give an indie game like that a thumbs down, even if those elements aren't enough to keep me personally playing beyond the few hours I have. Think of it like an old school JRPG with intriguing characters and story but bland/crappy turn based combat.TL;DR: if the setting and characters look interesting to you, and you're willing to sit through some uninteresting but easy card battles, give this game a go.

_childDocuments_.review: GEORGE THE FATHER!!!Visual Novel + Turn Based strategy.You play as a young Witch who plans to open all the seals of the Black Book in order to revive your husband.In order to open the seals you need to meet a variety of demons, some of which you have to fight, some of which you have the choice to help and some of which you can accept into your service.But be wary, these chorts are still evil and will plague you if you dont send them on missions to cause suffering.Will you use your witchcraft for the good of the people or will you use it for your own gain?How many sins will you commit?Will you help those asking for your aid even if they ask you to curse someone?Short Note: If you dont like reading, dont play this game (due to its visual novel nature).If you love getting tons of information and immersing yourself in this mythological world go for it.Its definately worth it if you are into dark fantasy.

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10A story about a new witch trying to bring back her beloved from hell. It relies heavily on folklore to be effective. My main gripe is that while the game is entertaining, and fun, it just didn’t catch my attention.  6/10It’s good, but nothing memorable. 5/10I’d say it doesn’t really stand out as good or bad. 6.5/10Choosing your spells or pages in the book, ordering them, and creating combos is fun. However, that’s as much gameplay as there is, you can add some equipment and some herbs you can use, plus levelling (but that is as simple as it sounds). However, there are a lot of unpolished aspects of the gameplay that end up turning it more into a hassle. 7/10Interesting, good way to delve into folklore, and also play a character that is more morally grey than others. However, it simply isn't as engaging as I would have liked.

_childDocuments_.review: An endearing and surprisingly educational RPG. Learn about slavic folklore, kill monsters, and maybe make your little corner of the Russian Empire a better place. Or not, choices matter does give you some options to truly do some Mass Effect Renegade stuff.If all you want is the story, easy mode is, in fact, very very easy. with proper use of equipment, most fights can end by simply clicking go and letting your blessings and damage dealing artifacts do the killing instantly. _childDocuments_.review: Fun game so far. The gameplay is pretty solid, the history titbits well researched. The animations aren't anything to write home about, the story is just ok but serviceable, the characters aren't that interesting to me. I'd prefer to have the card game without the main story (just keep the encounters and the narration and the lore descriptions). There was also another optional card game which was completely unnecessary in my opinion but they don't force you to play it. Buy it when it's on sale to have some fun with the cards.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game with an engaging journey into its in-depth world. "Black Book" has a creative art style that lets its story come alive with the cheeky, and sometimes even horrific events. Some small shortcomings with the voice acting pop up every now and again, but with subtitles on screen, this issue is minor. Black Book's linear storytelling is shrouded with dread, lending to the magic, which is rooted in an extremely rich culture. The game respects a varied level of understandings of it though, adding easy to pick up and remember words that are highlighted with translations for ease of flow. All in all, it's very easy to get lost in this wonderfully spooky game.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this on my wishlist forever. I finally went for it on sale. 10/10 would pay more. This game is truly inspired and amazing. The art feels just right, the rich story and content are a wonderful experience so far.Absolutely delightful. Would recommend if you enjoy reading and really digging into a story. Beware though, if you're looking for the card based combat but are not a reader, pass. This one is all about the stories.

_childDocuments_.review: If your looking for a choices matter RPG game, turn back. The questions asked are just quiz questions from the lore, if you get it right you get XP. When you get it wrong you just get told it's wrong & no XP. Your decisions don't affect the story to a noticeable level, so can't recommend if that's what you are looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is pretty straightforward. Your husband died and you're trying to bring him back no matter what. Throughout the game, you are given choices that can change the outcome of the scene. You can fight your way or use your knowledge to defuse the situation without combat. I like the Mythology of the game but the story isn't anything to sing about so far.The reason why I bought this game is because of the Card system. It is very mixed for me. Can be addictive and fun but quite easy to master, especially for expects in the genre. I wasn't expecting Inscryption or Monster Train levels of complexity and depth. But a little more polish is needed. No different play style is a big turn-off for me. All you need to do is balance your  and , and you're unchallenged for most of the game with a few exception.I cannot recommend this game for its gameplay and graphic. Maybe I'll recommend the plot if you like Slavic mythology. The story is interesting enough and it's mostly the reason why I'm continuing this game till the finale.
