_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely FANTASTIC deckbuilder. It's a shame I didn't learn about it earlier.Don't go in expecting Slay the Spire or any of the other roguelike card games, though. This is more akin to Thronebreaker; a strictly linear RPG with deckbuilding/card combat, and it does it very well.The similarities don't end there either. Like the world of The Witcher, this game uses a lot of old Russian/Easter European folklore to tell its story. However, Black Book takes it much further by making these old beliefs the central tenet of its themes. Rather than being in a fantastical world with monsters designed like ones from folklore, you are instead in the real world, only with the twist that all of these archaic ideas are real and true. Its setting is hyper specific to a region in Russia where old pagan folklore and the new beliefs of Christianity first met and melded into one at the turn of the 19th century.Because of this, I learned SO MUCH about this region and its customs. It provided a really fascinating look at the history and religion of the area while simultaneously being a great strategic deckbuilder. The game even provides its research studies in the credits! It also has some real bangin traditional folk music sung by a choir local to the area the game is set in as well as fantastic Russian voice acting. I can't comment on the English voice acting because it seemed only right to play it in Russian.The only cons I could give are that it feels longer than it needs to be (30+ hours for one play through doing all optional tasks along the way) and the difficulty really drops by the last third. By the end I was making decks that trivialized the vast majority of combats, including bosses, on the normal difficulty setting. But that was some of the fun, theorycrafting new decks as I unlocked cards and seeing what crazy OP ♥♥♥♥ I could create.All in all it definitely joins the roster of the best deckbuilders out today.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It is a good deck builder that differentiates itself plainly from the titans of the genre (because it's a campaign, which changes the dynamics *enormously*), and it's the rare cultural project that's very effective at showcasing the culture it wants everyone to learn about. I'm learning a whole lot about a fascinatingly synchretistic religious milieu in which Orthodox Christian saints interact with demons some of whom happen to be gods. You banish devils with the sign of the cross, but when your character walks into a building and says "I don't detect any evil spirits here," she says it not with relief but with a little contempt, because anybody who's anybody employs numerous evil spirits. In a single combat turn, you're likely to invoke invoke St. George, the god that personifies the Ocean, and Antichrist, and more importantly, the game invites you into a vibrant spiritual world in which everyone agrees that this is normal. It's genuinely a thrilling way to encounter a religious tradition you don't know (I say as a religious historian). The gameplay is probably 60:40 events, sim elements, and story beats : card stuff. This is a campaign with a persistent deck that you can add to and subtract from at any time, which is already a huge departure from the genre. (It reminds me, in some ways, of the 90s Magic the Gathering PC game.) This starts out very simple and ratchets up in complexity after a gentle introductory chapter, after which the game encourages (and in some cases virtually requires) you to build bespoke decks for major fights. The card pool gets deep fast, and there's a ton of space for optimization. (It reminds me of Monster Sanctuary in that way, although this doesn't get as overwhelming.) The combat mechanics themselves are fresh, but still intuitive. It's a tempo-based game, so instead of energy or mana, each turn, you can play a certain number of cards across two types: Orders, your work-horse cards that do damage and add block and impart statuses; and Keys, smaller, more specialized effects that are nonetheless critical to your survival. In addition, you have two colors (Black/Pagan-Demonic and White/Orthodox) that generally benefit from being played with cards of the same color. So if you have space for two orders and one key on your turn, do you play your black key to boost the damage that your black orders are doing, or do you use the white key that will give you a ton of block eventually, to set yourself up for the next turn? At the same time, your hand of cards is persistent and you draw to a full hand with a specific ratio of orders to keys each turn. Unused cards sit in your hand, maybe taking up space from cards you'd like to draw, maybe being held in reserve for the perfect moment (frequently both). This opens up all kinds of interesting design space, because a card that lets you play an extra key next turn will also free up space in your hand to let you draw an extra key two turns from now. (I will say that the combat isn't necessarily *hard*. But that's because free, ad-hoc deck building moves the decisive gameplay into the time before the fight, and it's more like you're doing a puzzle to prepare. You do still get some nail-biters, but the fights are less tense because you're just watching your demonic Rube Goldberg machine go off. As is usually the case, there are a couple of overarching strategies that predominate, and I suspect you can get through the game only interacting with a couple of mechanics. If you have already guessed that  you have clearly played a deck builder before. There's enough weird stuff in the card pool that you can change your strategy to keep it fresh for yourself, but the game won't make you do that very often.)  But most importantly, the story is just, like, really good. You are dropped into a moral universe that the developers expect you to misunderstand, and you blunder around roleplaying as a character who only *kind of* understands how the world works. When you mess up (or "mess up") you get castigated by characters who think they understand how the world works, because they answer to the great spirits who act like they know how the world works, but also acknowledge that, look, nobody knows how any of this stuff works. You-the-player-character are a knower because you can see the demons that serve as the universe's hidden causes, and in a completely different way you-the-player are a knower because you can see the game mechanics down to their precise quantitative nature; you know the weight of the sins Vasilisa has committed, because to you it is an integer. But you're also a knower because you're from the 21st century, and you have the phenomenal power to go to Wikipedia and look up what a Rusalka is; in certain ways your knowledge of the past's future is a gameplay element. The two yous mutually strengthen one another and grow together into an entity that *actually* knows how stuff works. Just about every plot point emerges from this single tension of what it means to "know" whether it's knowing a ritual or a spell or a truth. It's just brilliant. Some things that are not quite caveats: - I keep seeing it listed under Roguelite/kes, and I'm a little more than halfway through the story without seeing any evidence of that. I assume it's just because they're listing it as "Spire-like" for marketing purposes, but the better tag would be "procedural." Again, I prefer this to another roguelite, and you'll probably appreciate it if you play a lot of deck builders! - The English translation is good *but* one of the mechanics tests your ability to use the lore to deduce what's going to happen next, and some of these are truly obscured in translation. (Example: You're answering multiple choice questions trying to work out what demon you're looking for, and two of the four options are "Mermaid" and "Rusyalka" which is a Slavic mermaid. And I believe the correct answer turned out to be "Mermaid.") I addressed this to my 100% complete satisfaction by save-scumming in the instances where I felt that something unfair happened. - You'll frequently have to walk around little adventure areas to look for things; if you try to use the mouse, you will discover that Vasilisa's pathfinding is very bad. You will have a better time if you use the arrow keys or WASD to move her.Ed. Ignore my play time vis-a-vis the "halfway in" comment. A whole lot of that is from leaving it up running while making dinner or whatever. I think a more realistic number would be ~20 hours to get to Chapter 5/7 (although the length of a given chapter does vary, and obviously I don't know how long the last 2+ are).

_childDocuments_.review: ✔️ Wonderful Slavic folklore mood.✔️ Engaging narration, with a lot of interesting characters, places to visit, and curious interactions.✔️ Great deckbuilding system, with progressive unlocking of cards and increase in complexity allowing the player to never be overwhelmed, while offering a rather rich pool of mechanics to toy with.✔️ Fair challenge difficulty, I never found myself blocked anywhere.✔️ Creative and beautiful art direction, based on an association of low poly 3D and traditional 2D art.💭 Only 3 deck slots, I wish I could have built more decks simultaneously, and linked equipment presets to each deck.💭 The save system is a bit weird, making you restart the whole encounter you saved at. Not a big issue once you understand how it works, but still.❌ Some glitches when you make cards interact in certain ways late in the game. Specifically the card that allows you to add Firm 1 to all your board interacts weirdly both with burnt cards and cards that aren't played on board and take effect immediately. Nothing too bad, and nothing I've seen earlier than the last act, but still pretty annoying.Definitely a big recommendation :)

Some subtitles were in wrong language, some mechanics don't seem to work as intended sometimes, subtitles don't often match VA, I had a weird issue in a late boss battle where during a cutscene the game said I lost and then after it said I won, and it crashed to desktop once. _childDocuments_.review: As a Slay of the Spire player, I came for a card game. What I got instead was an amazing RPG deeply anchored in folklore and legends from some russian area in the 1800s.The gameplay still needs to be tweaked, there's very little danger in hard mode.But as a rpg, it's one of the best I've ever played. _childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black Book is a great adventure/RPG game set in a rare setting of 19th century Urals - where in towns life is almost as we know it today, yet in villages it is still almost unchanged from medieval times (think Steampunk but in real world). You play as a young witch on a quest to resurrect her deceased boyfriend. The story itself is pretty epic, with everything from mage battles to difficult witcher-like investigations, and your choices (even minor ones) do matter here.Lore, music, characters, side quests - is top class a well. I especially like how consequences of some seemingly minor choices in side quests pop up much-much later in a very unexpected fashion sometimes and even directly affecting main story. I STRONGLY recommend you play with Russian VO and English subs. They did pretty decent English VO, but Russian one is iconic and much more fitting - since they speak Old Russian mostly, and the tones of Old-Russian-villagefolk-dialect will get to you the atmosphere if you can't fully understand tham (luckily you can set subtitles in settings to be English and VO to be Russian)The combat system is good, BUT - companion side quest "puzzle" battles - it is just UGGGH, please devs if you read this just remove them and/or replace with regular battles, they alone generate 99% of the negative reviews for your game.The 2 key things about combat here:1) This is not a game of potion-gulpers. Resource management is key2) Some enemies are tricky. "Just do the damage" deck will not always be helpful, so prepare accordinglyOnce you get this - combat here is fun, challenging and rewarding. Overall: Definitely a worthy buy for anyone interested in a quality RPG/choices-driven action. And must buy for anyone who loves slavic/finno-ugric lore (Thea, The Witcher, etc). 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games that choices matter with a rich story, then this is the game for you.   I wish they can make more narrative games like this that have a battle scenario.   It makes the game much more intriguing and you become involved in plot of the story.   In addition, you can be a good witch or an evil witch based on your decisions.   Grab this game now while it is on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A bulky game with far too much story when it is executed this poorly. It has a mountain of exposition before you can begin any kind of gameplay. Now I love story but not when it is shoved down your throat, let the story visually and elegantly tell itself through the game itself not cutscene after cutscene and poorly performed dialogue. Gameplay is simply not strong. It's basic, it doesn't present new mechanics or even standard complexity mechanics. Expect a damage defend system and maybe 3 extras for the bulk of the gameplay. 80% of combat will consist of damage and defend still. A long bulky process to access a game that doesn't deliver on any kind of skill expression.some stuff looks pretty doe
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Having completed a playthrough of the main story, I would definitely recommend this game to people who are interested in folklore and worldbuilding. You don't see a lot of slavic folklore in the western world, and this provides fascinating insight into that subject as you regularly collect folktales and encylopedia entries that give you more information.The story itself is also interesting. You follow a young woman who is attempting to use the power of The Black Book to bring her dead lover back to life. In order to do so, she needs to break seven seals on the book. This story is about her trying to break those seals and the friends, enemies, and adventures she encounters along the way. You use the book to cast spells via a card battling system in which you select a certain number of cards to play each turn against an enemy. There are a variety of effects and cards that you unlock as you progress, but I found that except for a few cases you could pretty much use the same deck everywhere. Overall though, still a fun battle system.The length is also pretty good. You'll see I have about 20 hours on the game, which represents one playthrough in which I attempted to do everything (I still missed some things, not sure if I will go back and try to get them). However, there are a multitude of options at each encounter and it is even possible to bypass many (maybe all?) bosses depending on the choices you make. There are also different endings depending on your choices as well.I did find a few bugs here and there (one is that the icons at the top of the screen do not cycle in order on a controller, the last two are reversed, which is odd but minor once you're used to it), but overall it's an enjoyable card battler made with a lot of heart and unique in its material. If you enjoy story and card battler type games, you'll definitely enjoy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game with an amazing story. I love the fact that I can just reload my save over and over to fill that itch to see everything without restarting from the beginning of the level. Thought I'd just skip past all the many folklore the game throws at you but many of the riddles and right answers require you to at least get the gist of it, was annoying at first but I found myself wanting to read each and every one of them once I get a new one, it really made me feel like I'm the Koldun that just knows all these things like the back of your hand, makes it feel quite rewarding when you already know the answer just by reading a few lines. Great game, buy it, do it, wait for a sale if you must, but do it.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game from Humble Bundle... it may change some later in the game, but the first couple hours don't provide a lot of "strategy" for a turn-based "card" style game, and it doesn't really hold my attention enough to get to the point where it might. There is a LOT of dialogue and throwing around a bunch of foreign terms, and then the game will start "quizzing" you on things. Seems aimed at a younger audience in some places (asks "what are 3 kinds of dates?", not even a real riddle and not something anyone over the age of 12 would have difficulty answering), but thematically and with the volume of reading it seems aimed at a more adult audience... the battles are sporadic and not very challenging, even with the game's poor attempt at explaining things and using jargon to refer to things to make it seem more "complex" than it actually is. Game seems to continually suffer from an identity crisis, after the above issues it also has sections where the player controls the character in a 3D environment, but it's so limited and out of place compared to the rest of the game being point and click navigation that it doesn't flow well or just seems unnecessary (although you can still click but half the time you have to watch the character slowly move around to do so). If you're looking for a high level/high difficulty strategy game, I don't recommend this one... it's more of a choice-based visual novel with RNG-decided-actions battles.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros : - Very immersive- Underrepresented mythos - Enjoyable storyCons : - Buggy. Movement, where it is possible, can be quite difficult in some areas, and at best counterintuitive. "Restart Battle" will not fully reset some states, in such a way that you can unexpectedly lose puzzle battles if you have forfeited early after noticing a mistake. Some dialogues lines were forgotten in translation and are still in russian. - Some features of the game are poorly distributed along its length, such as battle puzzles . Page creation makes book merchants rather obselete. Items are a hit-or-miss, either making your deck rely on abundant usage of items, or forget about them entirely , until you meet that one boss who was designed specifically against your deck type which makes you spam items .TLDR : Is it enjoyable ? Yes, but it lacks polish Is it unique ? In terms of storytelling, yes.Is it worth it ? Not at this price. There are better indie games that cost half what this game costs . _childDocuments_.review: Black Book is a pretty fun card-based combat game with an intriguing narrative.I don't get to see Finno-Ugric mythology all that often in games and I've been waiting on this for a long time since backing it on Kickstarter. I'm myself of Eryzan origin and it's always interesting to read about old tales. I like that a lot of the older words are defined by hovering over them. And you actually get rewarded for reading up on the in-game lore. I'm looking forward to uncovering more about the game's world as I progress further.The combat sections have a simplistic look, yet are deeper than at first glance. The cards can interact with each other in interesting ways across multiple turns. There's general attack/defense cards, but there's also all sorts of status effects and delayed gratification types. I would highly recommend Black Book for anyone interested in old stories and myth, especially beyond the typical Western European sort you usually come across in games. And for those looking for a solid card-based combat game.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Black Book is great and feels fresh in many ways. I give it a solid 9 for unique and rich Russian folk experience. It reconnected me with some of the russian folk heritage I grew up with in my village.Strangely, my biggest takeaway is that if the folk and christian stuff were all real, the world would have been bleak and hopeless place with mad and cruel God on a throne enforcing his inhuman laws.Considering how little the development team was, this is beyond impressive. The art style, the music and the plot are very good, except for one twist with grandfather that didn't make much sense.Binged this game for several nights across last two weeks. It feels pretty long and engrosses you in its atmosphere.The magic, the folklore demons and the bosses are weird and detailed in just the way I expected. Kudos to Gogol i guess. There's a good variety of strange mythical creatures that are depicted very differently than in most fantasy games.Magic looks proper, like an unholy and powerful force, thanks to colorful animations.I'm really stunned by how artists managed to get away with low-poly graphics while creating strong atmosphere and pleasant experience.Combat system sucks however - it seems overcomplicated and underdeveloped, far too easy to exploit, so fights quickly become tedious and free of any risk. Griftlands made it right, this game totally didn't.Originally I went with Curse-based deck, but it turns out Blessing + Pray buff items + Damage All or Multi Attack cards wreck EVERYTHING (except for the damage-immune, for those we have the Curse).Demon management is a fun idea of self-managed difficulty, but it doesn't influence the ending enough and is not that configurable. Some of the knowledge checks are impossible to guess even after reading the folk texts.Still, these feel minor, as story and art kept me engaged. Again, 9/10, will remember this experience for a long time

_childDocuments_.review: I wish for a neutral recommendation option here.   I see the other reviews vary a lot, and it looks natural considering the game is fairly mislabeled.   It is more "visual novel" than anything else.  So the fit for you will probably depend on how much you like to go through the story.    IMO it is nice with great voice acting and music.    But anyone may find it not engaging or just taking way too long.   The RPG element is so light barely worth mentioning.  You take some choices but they only impact a local resource or battle gain most time, and for the long term a single counter of sins.    not what we usually label RPG.The other major label if card better.  What is indeed a major mechanism here, but if you look for StS style game, you'll be disappointed likely.  Just for the fact that between battles you spend lot of time in the narrative.     Beyond that it is fine: you have a number of mechanisms for the cards,  a skill development system and items that boost various effects.   At some battles it used "puzzles" instead of your  deck that is good.    I'm playing on the default level and find it fairly easy this far (at maybe 40% of the game).   But I'm a veteran in the genre, novices who have no idea how to build a deck, keep it close to minimum and how to use the consumables and ally well may struggle.  The interface has some annoying elements, like cards picks after battle are dumped into the deck instead of the pool, so you must immediately go and pull them.    Also the save system is always saving the start of the "chapter", so at the most natural save points you'll re-do a ton of conversation after "continue".   TLDR; it's a mixed bag, do your research on personal fit

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played anything like this, and I'm usually not into turn-based games, but I genuinely enjoy this one. It's actually several games in one: Two different card games (one you play to fight demons and the other you play for fun at your 'home'), an exploration game to walk around different scenes to find objects and clues, a demon management game, and a knowledge/quiz game, among other little things. You unlock lore as you progress through the story, which you'll need to answer questions correctly and earn knowledge points or currency. While this could easily become tedious, the lore is not only intriguing, but it's written succinctly, so you're not spending hours reading text on screen (each 'encyclopedia entry' is only 1-3 paragraphs max). As others have said, the voice acting (especially the scene narrator!), soundtrack, and atmosphere make this game really immersive.The only two things I'm disliking are saving and collecting items. It's really unclear what saving actually does: Every time I've saved the game, when I've reloaded I ended up several steps prior to where I saved, and I end up repeating large chunks of the game for fear of missing the inventory you collect along the way. And you can only find herbs in the wild at specific scenes where you can click and explore, which seem few and far between, and given that the only other way to get herbs is to buy them for expensive prices, it makes them quite scarce. I suppose that helps make the gameplay challenging, but I wish I had more scenes to explore and find things on my own.The game is quite unforgiving if you make a mistake, or make any selection really. Some scenes allow you to click every option and hear all the dialogue, while others will lock out other options based on what you've chosen, and there's no way to tell when you can browse all options or will get locked into one. While that can be annoying, it also helps the game feel more grounded and the stakes higher: You truly need to live with the choices you make.I don't currently understand what sending my chorts on errands does other than accrue sins on me, but maybe I'm still early in the game.Definitely recommend as a fun Halloween game, or a way to explore folklore and legends in an immersive way.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is relaxing to play with a controller and sit back and enjoy the story. It's a beautiful game with an incredible art style and soundtrack and a very interesting mix of mechanics that just seem to work together, oddly enough. The most prominent gameplay aspect is the battles with demons in which you have to think about spells and their effects on you and your enemies, items that you can use on yourself, and herbs that give you temporary effects in a way that resembles any tabletop cardgame like gwent along with effect builds reminiscent of the binding of Isaac  You move along a map from location to location where on each stopping point you're faced with an event narrated to you like a DnD master would. This is the majority of the game; just sitting back and making decisions and then fighting against demons, unlocking more powerful spells as the story progresses. there are other mechanics but I'm not going to spoil them. I can definitely see myself playing multiple runs just to make different decisions and see what happens.CONS - Aspects of the game aren't described very well and there's even one whole feature that you can bypass altogether without anything negative happening as a result which almost makes it... redundant. Some of the spell descriptions are awful. and I mean I had to google the definition of 'cantillation' just to understand  one of the spells. I shouldn't need to do that and it's annoying. When you have to answer questions you're just going to have to guess. The answer is either really obvious or not at all and the hints don't help in those situations. At first I thought It was my fault for not reading the encyclopedia logs properly and remembering little bits of information which would have been a cool mechanic to actually get me to read every bit of information i find lest it come up in a question that i need to answer correctly. But no, a character will ask me a question and throw in a random word that just so happens to be highlighted in orange and I will not know what it means because its either Russian in how it sounds or it's made up and there is no clue on earth that is going to help me understand which demon is what in relation to that orange word ect... If you play this game you'll know what I mean when you experience this. I wish I could load my save when I actually saved, as in after i went through all the dialogue, instead of it loading up back at the Izba (house) after the morning cutscene with me needing to go through all that dialogue AGAIN....One last minor nitpick... I wish the dialogue written on the screen was the same as the damn dialogue that was spoken. and its not just cutting out little words here and there to make the dialogue more manageable to read its changing entire sentences around. One bit even said on the screen about "going north because its warmer up there" but what was spoken was "going south because its warmer down there" its just irritating because i like to read the dialogue as i hear it or sometimes just want to read it quicker than it is spoken and it throws me off when it is so drastically different. with all that said though am I having fun? YES. It this a fun concept of a game? YES. Am I probably going to play it again but do an evil route like in undertale? YESSSSS and i cant wait to do that.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a good story, and a solid card battler to boot. It's not a roguelike since the campaign is quiet long, especially if you chase every sidequest and long (a very good experience all around). The characters are great, I can't get enough of that bald redhead peasant who always sound lost and apprehensive. The guy is perfect meme material (someone please cameo him popping into the middle of a fight in some other card battler). I tried all of the cards, some of them are pretty good and become completely op without even any artefacts (access to curse and sea depth makes the game very easy). Overall the pacing was perfect and the focus of folklore roots provide insight into the fantasy genre we have today that are based around eastern european culture. I recommend this game to card battler and deck builder gamers 8/10 would play the sequel if it ever comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: I understand why Steam only has a "recommend" v.s. "not recommend" primary review option as increased granularity would only results in huge subjectivity between reviewers as opposed to better accuracy.  Still this is a case where I wish I had more options as my experience with the Black Book is definitely net positive, but nowhere near so as much as other games I have given "recommend" reviews to previously.  I.e. this game definitely needs to get something better than a "not recommend" but it also feels a bit disingenuous to give it the same "recommend" that I have given to truly stellar games I have reviewed previously.This is a *VERY* indy game, and all aspects of it feel indy for better or worse.  If you are someone who needs triple A polish, and can’t stand a bit of jankiness, you should skip this.  It has both an indy-game's individual love, unique perspective, freshness, and approach that can't be found in a triple A game, and also some of the worst of an indy-game's jankiness and complete lack of polish including poor play design choice, sometimes in the worst possible way as I’ll get to later.The good is that Black Book feels fresh and is clearly a labor of love from its creators.  While I have played games that contain basically all of the individual aspects of this one independently, the compositing of features and individual touch and tweaks for this one are unique and fresh.  The deck build playing doesn't have the glorious and frenetic action quality that many of the best such games, like Slay the Spire or Tainted Grail do, but it is still interesting in its own right and has its own features and approaches that are novel (to me), compelling, and engaging even at the slower and lower pace found In Black Book.The story, setting, and characters are different enough to be interesting and engaging enough despite their ... its hard to say … non-exceptionalness maybe?  The story's shockingly mundaneness, in spite of itself, in its take on all its content both tempers its excitement and yet also gives it a fresh unique feel that it couldn't possibly have otherwise.  I have never seen so many people so completely complacent and almost bored that their whole lives are completely saturated with the often uncontrolled antics of the minions of hell.  I found that off-putting and it downplays the excitement of demons and hell lose on Earth.  But at the same time there is something undeniably fresh about being a demon wrangler that occasionally visits hell, and yet having that setup somehow feel like being a mere local plumber.  The game makes you feel like your witchy demon wrangling is a useful job that people do appreciate, but somehow it is nothing special or exciting in any way and everyone whole calls on your services also secretly pities you because you have to metaphorically touch other people’s turds on occasion when a metaphorical pipe bursts -- the real reason people are thankful you have the job and not them.  At the meta level I found this to be a really funny experience.The voice acting is ... interesting to say the least.  Its not great voice acting, but it still adds a lot to the game especially the pronunciation of all the Slavic Occult words.  That is actually very net enriching to the game-feel despite some of the lack-luster voice acting work as far as conveyance and emotional consistency.  Thus, the voice acting is overall a net positive to the game even though it is rather weak in many parts.The game's biggest most frustrating weakness is its in-area maneuverability and navigation.  You will be stuck in a scene with a fixed angle camera, and some jankie combination of maneuvering around with clicking on dots and using the keyboard to fumble around in such a way to maneuver to a new view hopefully with more/new dots to click on -- especially by fumbling blindly and awkwardly toward the camera in a "blind luck hope for the best" way.  This is by far the weakest part of the game, and it is the only part of the game that I would say has fundamentally bad design that cannot be forgiven.  There is enough good elsewhere in the Black Book to grudgingly accept this aspect of it, but this is indeed bad and must be called out as such.Overall: a net positive indy game experience.  Its strength lies in the obvious personal love and individual and personal touches its creators put into it, its story, and its characters.  IMHO such touches are sufficient to overcome a good deal of its jankiness and even flat-out bad design on in-area play-style.  This game is definitely not for everyone, but it is something tasty, exotic, and indy-home-baked-with-love for those in the mood for such things.

_childDocuments_.review: No spoilers! I am absolutely loving this game so far, but I wanted to write up what the gameplay is like! I was hesitant because I am not into "deck building" games but I was enticed by the premise. I'm soooo glad I gave it a shot because it really doesn't FEEL like a "deck building" game to me because everything else in the game is so rich, and they made the deck-based combat extremely fun. I'm five hours in and not close to finishing the game yet. Below, I'll summarise the Premise, Gameplay, Combat, and Progression.* Your lover died and people claim he killed himself but you don't believe it. Because suicide is a mortal sin he was buried outside the cemetery ie not in hallowed ground, which means his soul went directly to hell.You become a witch to try to pull him out of hell.* The game explores a lot of northern Russian folklore and makes it extremely interesting and fun to engage with* As a witch you can see demons that other people can't see or hear, and you're considered a "knower," so people come to you with gifts and offerings to ask you questions or to solve their problems* It reminds me a lot of The Witcher in the sense of getting quests to deal with spirits/demons/etc and resolve problems, sometimes creatively* The atmosphere is done so well. I love the themes, the folklore, the writing, and the artwork!* A large proportion of it is having conversations RPG style. Relatively slow paced.* Each night starts at your grandpa's izba (traditional countryside dwelling) having conversations with him & with villagers who come to visit you for help* Then you set out on the road and it feels very much like playing D&D or a choose-your-own-adventure story. It's not open world. You select a place to go on the map and then there's a narrator who explains what happens & options for your actions. There are random encounters, puzzles/riddles, fairs/peddlers e.t.c.  One location each night is the required one that you're on your way to & that one has more of a physical space you can walk around in and interact with stuff.* I didn't think I'd like card based gameplay because it's never appealed to me. But this game makes it super fun.* It's turn-based combat where you cast "zagovors" which are comprised of a selection of cards from your Black Book. You can manage the available deck and select from a (random?) subset of them in combat.The cards interact with each other in ways that make this really fun and satisfying, like amplifying each other * The difficulty escalates in a fun way and critical fights are genuinely difficult* There's also "battle puzzles" that give you a special selection of cards and you have to defeat the enemies in limited moves. These are challenging but very fun and satisfying and really push you to learn how the cards work in a very natural way.* The story progresses each night* You gain knowledge points from correctly answering/ helping people since you're a Knower. There's usually a lot of context clues + there's a hint mechanic* There's a skill tree & leveling up* There's your demon minions (chorts) who can go out and do jobs* There's a "sin" mechanic from doing evil deeds like cursing people (which some villagers will ask you to do and you can choose whether or not to agree)* You can buy, find, or win additional cards for your black book

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that I find myself in disagreement on an Overwhelmingly Positive indie darling.I haven't experienced any of the crashes earlier negative reviews have mentioned; the game has run flawlessly. The game is dripping with charm, truly unique and well researched atmosphere, and has some creative mechanics to boot (running dual decks simultaneously, with Orders and Keys, is pretty clever). The fundamental problem that's just brutally beat down my enthusiasm for the game is that it's just too slow.The loading times between steps on your route are too long. Conversations take too long. Combat takes way, way too long; I've cranked the text and animation speed up to the max, but to no avail. Encounters on your journey are all unique and handcrafted rather than procedurally generated, but so many of them none the less feel just like filler.Part of it may be that I opted for 'normal' difficulty, as I generally do for playthroughs on new games, but have found it far too easy. That there's no tension or challenge to the combat encounters makes them feel all the more like a chore to get through. I'd really wanted to like this title, but a chore really does describe what it feels like, and I've been forcing myself to go through it for several hours now. The ending still seems remote, as there really is quite a lot of game here, but I'm not sure it's in me to finish it.If the Slavic folklore and atmosphere really resonates with you, I feel like this title could absolutely still be worthwhile, but purely on its basis as a game, I find this a pretty weak entry in the field of RPG card battlers.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: So far (completing Act 1), the cardplay is fine, but nothing special. I will edit my review if it improves as the game goes on. Puzzle fights are cool and make you work with the game's mechanics.DO YOURSELF A FAVOR: Switch the audio to the native Russian while having English subtitles on. The english dub is HORRENDOUS (and sometimes even blatantly incorrect) and almost made me stop playing the game before I found out you could have it changed.The graphics during dialogue scenes are good; the graphics at any other time feel downright lazy.The sheer amount of Slavic/Russian folklore in this game is worth it enough to play if you're interested. I would recommend the game, but only if you can get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with unique setting based on Slavic myths. Game is really wholesome and made with much care and love for characters. Devs worked with great source materials and myths here are much more pagan and old than known from modern remakes of Russian folklore tales. Good voice-over for Russian game and without much overacting. It is actually big problem in many Russian games that voice over is a bit off. Battles gameplay are diverse enough but it seems there is a few strategies that work best for battles. Fun part is to find them and encounter situations when they won't work. If seems game is a bit on easy side. Exploration scenes are short and I really like short quiz-like scenes. I think story here is most worthy of praise. Most choices and consequences are really well made, characters are nice and diverse, dialogues are really great in Russian.  All and all it is a masterpiece in its own kind and definitely worth a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow... I just... Wow (Contains spoilers)I finished the game today, I love stories and songs, and this is the best game I have ever played so far, Can't wait to play it again!Such a terrifying world Vasya lives in, because the narrator mostly adresses the player, you often forget that Vasilisa is the one going through all of this at the player's whim, that you are seeing the world through her eyes, the moment when she finally breaks down in the middle of the game, falls on her knees on that golden field and cries her heart out, no one to comfort her, no one to listen to her sorrow but the grave of her beloved, my heart broke, and I realized that we're telling her story, that the world she lives in is very real for her, all of her sorrows, all of her pain, to carry them alone, only the player to witness, and it saddened me that I couldn't comfort her.I love that there is no black and white here, but infinite shades of grey, not everyone is 100% good or bad, Alexander, who seemed just another character turned villian then hero for a noble cause, Old Egor, who seemed my lovely grandpa, had the most terrifying reveal ever!I also undererstimated how far the impact of my actions would reach, being reminded of stuff I did at the very beginning of the game, good thing I went or the happy ending or I wouldn't had passed the trials of hell!I kinda shipped her and Alexander, wished somewhat of an ending where, if Vasya couldn't get her beloved back, she and Al could have joined forces for the people in Russia, then something would flourish between them, at least a good friendship, seeing that he would be the only one that knew the torments of being Kolduns, but I teared up when I saw her reunited back with her lover anyways!Also that two elbow-ed thing in the forest scared the life outta me!!!! TTwTT I thought I would be stuck forever fighting that monster in the forest! oMG, And the toothy swan! I was like- Eh!?!?! Is this a joke from the developers at such crucial point of the game!?!?! But Pierre proved to be a lovely character, no matter how short his time was!Also I have a bit of a complain with Vasya's movement, specially during the 'sneak around' from the giant spider, she kept moving around too much and I died one too many times for my sanity, also she gets stuck on invisible walls and the camera plays against you when you are herb hunting, it get's kinda fixed if you lower the settings, though.Anyway! It's was an honor to get the demo and then the whole game, the wait was worth it! (Also, I think the developer's name's are hidden at the grave yards? Spooky!) Thank you so, so much for this amazing piece of art!!! I love talking to my coworkers and friends about it and they seem preyy hyped with just the concept! Keep doing what you do guys, kudos to all the love and hard work poured into this amazing journey, I can't get enough of it! Kisses!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I don't play many games, but this one really caught my attention. I played about a year ago, and I have to say it was the best game I had ever played. The visuals look really pretty and the story itself was really engaging and unique. I have never seen another game use Slavic mythology, but the way Black Book used it was absolutely amazing. It is a key component and driving force of the story and is explored in such a way that is interesting and educational to some extent, but not excessive or to the point where it gets boring. Overall, I loved the game and am thinking of playing it in full again to see the other ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: It is very hard for me to recommend this. Imagine playing slay the spire and for each mob node, you have to go through non-story dialogue with vague choices. Some lands you in battle, some deducts life, some locks you out, over and over again. When you reach an elite node, then you get some proper story progression. Even if you save scum hoping to view the outcome of other dialogues, the save checkpoints in weird parts of the map so you might end up having to replay several nodes just to reach where you saved. Halfway through, I was already skipping so much dialogue it felt like a hassle. The story didn't really pick up until towards the end where in one scene you actually saw the power as the black book holder. Otherwise you just get tossed around.I liked how each chapter has a theme around the deck unlocks but otherwise you can pretty much beat the game if you have experience with other deckbuilders. The gimmick fights are annoying as it doesn't really help you learn new mechanics most of the time either.Sometimes you get to move your character around but it is very janky. This game is too ambitious for its own good, too much dialogue where it is unnecessary, 3d character movement that could be replaced with 2d world/sprites and a bloody stealth mission where you hit a game over while struggling with the controls. It could have been gold.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: There's not much I can say that wouldn't have already been said by someone else in the reviews from the gameplay standpoint. It's on the easier side of card-games and once you find a deck that destroys there's not really much of an incentive to seek out other options unless you're reaaaaaally curious to try them.However the general story and the folklore that it's based around is pretty darn good. If you've played Witcher 3 and enjoyed the folklore-inspired monsters and the contracts that involved them, you will get a similar if not more in-depth experience and explanation of slavic folklore demons, monsters and the deals that surround them. I would really like to not spoil the story, which struggles in the prologue, but once you get past that point it really picks up.The art-style is not the best, but not the worst either, the models sometimes takes me out of the immersion and I do get a laugh out of the beady-eyed character models. Though I must say the landscapes and buildings are well-done. Some of the demons have interesting (in a good way) designs too.Also, if you speak or understand atleast a speck of Russian, use Russian audio, way better voice acting.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't really think anything of this game, just wanted to give it a quick try as it was one of the games I bought in a humble bundle. But, it exceeded all expecations, a fun and different gameplay with a quite captivating story. And, there is actually quite a lot of gameplay, I thought I could finish it in a couple of hours, but I was happy to learn that my assumption was incorrect.Can definitely recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Great game: interesting story, good music, lots of interesting historical and cultural information about an area most people don't ever really think about. And of course, the deckbuilding aspect, which is pretty good. Deckbuilding isn't a great mechanic for a game designed for one long play through, but it manages it fairly admirably. The only issue is that, since it's not a roguelike so your deck isn't based on your run, it can get a bit stagnant once you find a build that works for you. There are lots of new options presented fairly regularly though so there's a lot of space for experimentation, if you want more variety.One warning: The text translation is a little rough (I don't know about the VO as I have been using the Russian VO), it was pretty obviously done by a Russian or Russians who know English very well but are not professional translators, so there are a lot of kinda wonky things with missing articles, extra articles, incorrect prepositions or just weird grammar in general. It's never to the point that it is undecipherable, but if that's the kind of thing that bothers you, prepare to be bothered if you still get the game anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I accidentally saw Vasilisa's 3D face in the beginning of the game and was laughing a lot. However, after playing a bit longer I understood that I don't really care how some of the graphics look like: the great and dark athmosphere of this game swallowed me up. The world looks alive and is complemetnted by music and sounds that are very suitable for it. You don't feel bored when you meet new enemies - in fact, the longer you play the more interesting it is to set your Black Book's spells to be able to fight stronger demons.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with the other reviews that this game is more about the experience. The unique setting and the way you need to learn certain words and the interesting characters immerse you more than many games if you allow yourself to drift into it. I also enjoyed the visuals and the music. I've played a fair number of card tactic games and this one does a decent job of keeping it interesting with new cards and possible combinations although after I decided on what I wanted to do with my deck the battles did get a tad grindy towards the end. You could change up your deck more to keep the battles fresh and you probably need to on harder difficulties. I only tried normal. I'm not sure I will play it through again, perhaps. I'm fine with my decision to be queen of hell. Ha!
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: It's interesting mechanically and story-wise, but I got fed up with the "puzzle battles" which are limited-turn battles with a specific hand. These battles seem impossible to win, and after you lose a few times the game will prompt you to skip the battle whenever you retry it. It's really frustrating and the game just doesn't have any standout aspects that make up for this.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: English translation could be better, and some subtitles were untranslated. Key terms and concepts (such as "firm") need to be explained more clearly. Movement using mouse is awkward compared to gamepad. Finally, the game could have been a little bit longer (they could have padded it out). That said, this is a fun and worthwhile game, especially if you are interested in Slavic folklore. If you are not, you WILL be, once you play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a masterpiece. My playthrough was 32 hours and even in the game's last few chapters I continued to see new environments and characters. Most games cut corners in this area as budget concerns get bigger in the last phase of development, but this game keeps its momentum through the whole experience. The story goes VERY deep in to Russian folklore, which is great since most media will at most do yet another presentation of Baba Yaga and that's as deep as it gets. Difficulty gets a little weird in the mid game where you encounter enemies who do a ton of damage on the first turn before you can get a strong defense going, and in the late game you have so many powerful tools that enemies stand no chance unless they're gimmicky, but you can change difficulty between combats and there are cheats that the developers posted in the discussion boards if you need more than that.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished it and..... my heart....... my girl Vasilisa.....................I would give it an 8/10 almost entirely for the story, the Slavic lore and the gameplay. The story is rich with the Slavic mythology it draws upon and it's clear that the creative team really adores the culture. Plot-wise it's a slow-burn of an adventure that starts off relatively relaxed and climaxes at the end in a whirlwind of revelations. (it will hurt you.)The gameplay is card-based, where you assemble individual cards (pages) into a spell of three or more pages. It's a simple system but there's endless variety with the various builds you can assemble and combining various effects to throw out combos. It's surprisingly addictive but one problem is that you never know what kind of cards the next enemy will need you to use, so at several points I had to load an earlier save and rebuild my deck. My major gripe is with the visuals and the voice-acting. I only heard the English voice-acting so I can't speak for the Russian audio, but the characters tend to sound very much alike and they get boring to listen to very fast. The narration tends to be very slow so it was always a dilemma as to whether to skip or keep listening just to be a completionist. The 2D visuals are pretty in a Gothic sort of way but the 3D modelling is rather simplistic. The other major issue I had was with the difficulty of some of the battles.  It got so bad at points, even on Normal difficulty, that I had to cop out and skip some of the battles (the game does let you skip after three failed tries, fortunately). I dunno maybe it's just me being incompetent but I do feel that several of the battles could do with rebalancing.So, overall, 8/10. Definitely worth the price, it's quite a long game and a must-play for people who like games based on folklore and mythology.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best experiences I've had with an indie game in a long time. It's been a over a week since finishing it and when I'm playing other new games I got I'm bored and wishing I could find another game of this quality.What sets Black Book apart from any other game out there is the incredibly fascinating and unique world it takes place in. The supernatural mythology of late 19th century Russia was never something I would have thought I would be interested in but once immersed I absolutely loved exploring every corner of the game, learning as much as I could about this incredibly detailed snapshot of history.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it. Think of it as an easier narrative-oriented Slay the Spire. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a higher rating, but I really didn't enjoy a lot of elements. _childDocuments_.review: Black Book is a richly atmospheric blend of Visual Novel-style storytelling and Turn-Based Deckbuilding combat.Gameplay-wise, it is solid, entertaining and strategic. The deck building itself is not particularly intricate, but works well within the game's framework, with a decent amount of possible synergies.There are essentially two types of "cards" - pages from the title's own Black Book - Orders and Keys. Each turn you compose a Zagovor - a spell - out of these pages. The number of pages you may use depends on unlocked skills and equipped items and is different between Orders and Keys.Combat variety and challenge are mantained through the introduction of diverse enemies and the progressive unlocking of new pages, companions, items, and skills.The game's main draw is its narrative, though. Its representation of the intertwining mythology of Komi-Permian Folklore and Russian Orthodox Christianity makes for compelling material, and the characters and stories that arise from it are beautifully fleshed out. Every line is voiced, both in English and in Russian - which was my particular choice.The game's chapters are comprised of several nights, each with a single main objective and one or more optional tasks. Each night has several locations to visit: essentially little visual novel-style scenarios, with interesting decision-making, which may or may not result in combat. Some of these scenarios allow you to walk around and interact with people and the environment, often in order to collect clues for a puzzle or riddle.Many of the game's challenges also ask that you read through its Onomasticon: an in-game collection of Bailichkas - short supernatural folk tales - and codex entries. Entries are unlocked as the story progresses, and as rewards for exploring the world and inquiring its inhabitants.There are a few odd translation quirks and I found a couple of completely untranslated lines - literally a couple, as in two - but this in no way marred the excellent experience of playing through Black Book's compelling story.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: Going to recommend this one for anybody who's a fan of:- dark fantasy - heavy narrative- historical / international settings- turn-based RPGs- card-battlersThe world as a whole is dark, your powers are dark, and you can really lean into or away from it. I enjoyed the adventure's low-poly art balanced with deep writing, and don't feel much on the market really compares story-wise. All of the supporting characters were worth the time and filled the world with personality. As far as the combat goes, it has a steep learning curve and levels out by mid-game. If you're doing EVERY fight it might get repetitive, but they do offer alternative solutions to most situations.  The only component of the game I didn't like was managing chorts, it was annoying even with the right perks/equipment. TL;DR: They could charge double and it'd still be worth it.subs > dubs 100%

_childDocuments_.review: I was interested in this game because Russian/Slavic folklore is an area of mythology that I've never really delved into. I also enjoy deck building games and RPGs, so there was a good chance this game would be my cup of tea. While it's a bit slow to start, and the voice acting is a bit strange (I think most if not all the actors probably do not speak English as their primary language EDIT: I've just realized I can change the audio to Russian and it is CLEARLY the same actors which is super cool!), this game REALLY presents Russian folklore in a much bigger, detailed story than I had anticipated. It almost feels like a learning experience, which for me adds an extra element of entertainment. As far as the gameplay, I found it to be quite fun. Whenever I reached a difficulty spike in combat, the game gives you a chance to modify your deck and try again, which I was always able to figure out how to change it to allow me to win the battle. Other game mechanics that include side quests, a card game, and a sin counter, among other things, keeps things interesting. I would definitely call this a hidden gem!

_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I took 2 semesters of Russian culture in college. This game half-taught me more in the first hour.It's already not for me. Slow, story heavy and game play light. The cards are not interesting (mind you very early) and more importantly I suspect they won't become substantially better.The bigger issue is that the game doesn't even cater well to it's actual target: The lore keeping novel reading historian by fireside. It drops references to myths as though you were already familiar with them or leaves short stories, some with depth others hardly explaining anything at all. And the voice acting is...sub par. If this were a humble indie game at a humble indie price of $10-12 I'd be more understanding. Maybe a bit more because time are rough right now. But this is pretty inexcusable.TLDR creators definitely lean a certain way that I don't and that's okay. Then they tried to design and market to an entirely different audience instead of sticking to their natural inclinations. I really can't say this game had potential because I didn't find anything about it to praise but I do feel it could have been better had they kept true.

_childDocuments_.review: I am enjoying this game so far.  Slavic mythology is a breath of fresh air.  Reading the lore helps make choices and has a pay-off in game.  This game is constructed in a way that provides a light challenge without insulting your intelligence or making it feel like a chore. The card game mechanics are interesting and enjoyable.  Black Book scratches the itch for a classic RPG adventure feel in a simple yet satisfying way.  The setting is doing a lot for me. Fantasy games can be so predictable and boring, no matter how much you like the setting. It is so refreshing to have a game break the mold and apply tried and true game design techniques in an unfamiliar setting. I find the story itself is compelling because of its novelty. You play a witch in a world that doesn't view witches in a way I typically get in other games.  Everything in the game is following a set of rules set in a reality I don't have an inherent familiarity with. This heightens immersion and enjoyment for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Book

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing on Nightmare difficulty and as a veteran to the deckbuilding genre, I have been pretty dang underwhelmed. Boss fights are solid, but the in between stuff I can basically finish with my eyes closed, they're so easy. I gamed the system by abusing the early game fair and getting a ton of money from Daruk and getting good gear from the start. Vampirism is OP. It's really unfortunate that you have to play the same like 5 enemy types over and over and over across the first chapter of the game, which is WAY too long. Brings me to my next problem...Exploration is horribly boring. You repeat the same backdrops over all the maps, getting yet another pointless dialogue about a dead rando NPC, some demon, or other useless event. Because you need to hit every single location in order to grow properly, you basically start to see the pattern early on and it becomes quite tedious. Even mashing the mouse to skip all the dialogue, I can't bear it. It feels like extra bs I have to deal with to get to the fight, whereas with any other deckbuilder, I just get right to it. No fuss. The story itself, when you get to the main missions, starts really strong. The fight with the first demon and then dipping into hell is quite enjoyable. I haven't finished the final boss of act 1 yet, but everything leading up to it has been a CHORE. I just don't care about any of these characters or their boring stories and lives. The slavic names are impossibly hard for my uncultured mind to read or repeat, so I just outright ignore them and replace them with "unimportant NPC #x". The graphics seem like they'll be enjoyable at first but then come across as a bit amateur and way too cartoony for the setting. I'm supposed to be battle demons and traversing hell, not hanging out in a poorly animated, darker version of Adventure Time. I notice so many animation issues and ugly character art choices. I mean, good lord, the main character's face looks like a stick figure and her eyes are pointing up beyond anyone she's talking to.There is a game that does this game's entire concept 1000000x better and it's called Tainted Grail. Literally every aspect of it is done with vast superiority. The graphics are dark and gritty, the magic is more like proper runic magic, the story is thought provoking, terrifying, and engaging, and the combat mechanics are extremely varied, uniquely interesting, and always challenging without being unfair.I feel like anyone who rated this game high is just a novice in this genre and if you are, that's fine. You probably will find enjoyment out of this. I really really liked the book concept in combat (instead of mana, like every other game), but literally every other aspect has sapped every ounce of fun out of the game. I'm going to finish act 1 and see how I feel, but after the time I put in, I just feel cheated and lied to by the Steam userbase.
