_childDocuments_.review: I honestly wanted to like this game. The idea of a multiplayer dating sim is genuinely enjoyable – but this specific game seems to take every possible chance to make an otherwise potentially fun experience into a miserable slog, ESPECIALLY for people playing online.First of all, and I think this is the most objectively awful thing about this game: if you are playing online and one of your friends is on an internet connection that is anything less than 100% absolutely concrete stable with NO hiccups whatsoever, I understand netcode is a difficult thing to implement, and I think it was admirable for the dev team to attempt it, but the fact that there are no save points as a failsafe for less than stellar connections is baffling to me.On a more personal note, if you respect yourself, avoid this game completely. As a gay man myself, I was honestly excited to try a dating sim that allowed me to be gay. Sure, the two humanoid male characters you can choose from seem to have been drawn from the same base and have the same exact body shape (and the other one is a “funny robot” which is really more of a kick to the face than anything, given that all of the female characters are still humanoid with varied bodies), but whatever.At this point I literally can’t be picky, there’s basically nothing out there for me in regards to dating sims. But I would have rather just avoided this game entirely than having hope, which isn’t to say I was expecting anything serious. Just anything at all would have been nice.This game is very strange to me in that even though you are able to choose your pronouns, your sexuality is pre-determined and cannot be changed. That is to say, you are assumed to want to ♥♥♥♥ absolutely everything in this game regardless of gender. That means that if you’re gay, lesbian, or even straight you’re just kind of screwed in terms of representation.The game, from what I could tell with its honestly garbage writing (more on this later) seems to want to be as inclusive as possible, even to the point of feeling condescending, but locks you into this forced sexuality with no remorse, reminding you of how hot you find women almost every other line despite what you may think in real life.That’s a surefire way to pull me the hell out of a game’s writing, even if it’s not trying to be serious. I’ve played visual novels for straight guys that don’t feel the need to remind me that women are hot to the extent this game does. And yet “LGBTQ+” is the second tag for this game.Sure, you can be a guy and date a guy. But you also desperately want to ♥♥♥♥ everything else, so I honestly don’t find it any different from playing games for straight men or straight women. My sexuality is still misrepresented in the end.That’s not to say I was expecting to get legitimately attached to any of the characters in this game. The art style is subpar by my standards, with the art direction falling fully down the “women are curvy, and men are only made of squares and rectangles” hole. It’s not for me at all, but I understand that’s a very subjective opinion, and I can tell that there is some visual polish here.However, even if I did find any of the characters attractive, I would absolutely be turned away by the writing. Each character has a single trait, and I do truly mean a single trait. The witch girl is a witch, that’s her personality. The buff girl is strong, that’s her personality. The skeleton guy is vain, the demon guy is an arsonist, etc.Calling these characters even two dimensional would be a stretch. Their one trait seems to be the basis for every single line of dialogue they have. It’s bizarre as the dialogue tends to stretch onwards for uncomfortable amounts of time (odd decision for a multiplayer game) yet manages to say absolutely nothing because it largely consists of each character repeating their sole trait.My first interaction with the buff woman (who I was assigned to despite not being interested in women) was almost entirely her talking about how she wanted to beat up capitalism. For paragraphs on end. Oh, that reminds me…Outside of the character writing (if you can call it that), the game seems to pride itself on what I can only generously call a “Tumblrpoisoned sub-Netflix Original” style of writing. The game advertises itself as having “unapologetic writing”, which in this case means it will absolutely beat you over the head with amazingly hot political takes such as “capitalism bad”. How brave, how unapologetic. What a hot take I’ve never heard before. Thank god it repeats it ad nauseum for minutes on end, otherwise I don’t think I’d be able to understand it.The game treats you (and the characters themselves, for that matter) as if you are a brainless child with no actual takes on the world you live in, having to hammer its milquetoast messages into your head through constant repetition. A bizarre contrast to the amount of seemingly “adult” content in the game, such as the word ♥♥♥♥ and repeated mentions of sex.It becomes tiring almost immediately, and slowly turns very awkward as you have to stop and wonder if these allegedly adult characters are acting like preteens on purpose, or if the writing is truly that bad.I am not saying this game needs to take itself seriously. The core concept of the game is very silly, and I understand that. It’s a party game after all! But the game seems so utterly desperate to make you laugh that it’s just embarrassing. When it’s not serving you childlike “horny” dialogue or repeating a pathetically meek political stance (sorry, I mean unapologetic), it’s relying on outdated memes and corny internet jokes.There was an unbelievably long segment of the game wherein Bill Murray appears as a character – that’s the joke. You’re supposed to find just that one thing funny, for literal paragraphs of dialogue. It went on for so long that all I could think about was how ashamed I was to be subjecting my friends to this. It wasn’t even so bad or so absurd that it was funny, it was just really sad to think that whoever wrote this section of the game probably thought it was the funniest thing ever.I don’t think I’ve ever had my friends seem this joyless before in any game. It’s an awful thing to subject others to, but I have to imagine that playing it alone is maybe one of the most crushingly depressing experiences one could have since the game is so empty otherwise.As a side note, I would like to mention the music. Music is a core component of almost every game, after all. This game seems to have exactly one surf rock track (or at least multiple tracks that sound unbelievably similar). For the entire game. It’s infuriating. My friends and I had to mute it entirely halfway through as we felt like we were losing our grip on reality. I am amazed that a game was able to be sold like this on top of the lack of care for the online mode.I love dating sims and visual novels. I’ve even played other multiplayer dating sims before and had a great time. Games like this are not at all representative of the genre. It’s very sad to me that an otherwise cute idea is completely wasted on cheap jokes and disrespect towards individual sexualities.I could see a lot of potential in this game if it had a completely new writing team and a simple save system. But as it is it’s just very, very sad. A disingenuous bundle of outdated humor to slowly unpack in front of your friends – until somebody disconnects, of course!TL;DR: The online aspect of this game is fundamentally broken, and the writing is unfathomably bad and outdated. Try something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Camp is everything you'd want from a sequel to Monster Prom. There are more characters to go on fun hi-jinks with, including some returning favourites and bit-parts elevated to main event status. My personal favourite is Joy, a world-saving witch who played an occasional role in the first game, and now returns to go on dates with you and get distracted by saving the world from her evil exes. Dahlia, a hench demon queen who strives to be the best at everything, especially conquering her enemies, is another highlight.The art remains a high point of the game, and every run now culminates in a lovely animated sequence set to a cracking piece of music that further cemented my attachment to this group of weirdos. Once again, the game is great to play with friends, or just by yourself, as you seek out the many, many secret endings. My only advice would be that the suggested timings for game lengths are very short, so allow yourself at least two hours if playing a long game with 2 people, and probably more to be safe.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: You are better off just playing the first one if you already haven't.Oh boy, where should I start. Ok, I absolutely love the first game. But I have to say that Mon camp is not nearly as good and it's kind of sad, since I was really looking forward to this. You are better off just playing the first one.Them cons:- The game locks you with one character for the rest of the game, when in the first one you could change if you didn't like the options the game recommended. Now if you get stuck with one you don't like, you have to either suck it up or restart.- The cast is very weak compared to the og cast. 3 of the dateables have very similar personalities, all of them being very aggressive and stabby. It makes the game a bit bland since the first cast was such a mixed bunch.- So much unnecessary text and dialogue oh my god. Trim it a bit so people have the patience to actually read it out loud with friends and actually concentrate. There must be a way to make it shorter yet still comical. Now it just feels like a wall of text for a "haha random" factor.- Just a personal preference, but the game is so much hornier in a tasteless way than the first one. I don't mind raunchy humor and jokes but I feel like they overdid it here a bit.- The game launched as bit of a too much early access to me. No gallery etc. Some features are still not ready and stuff. They could have honed this more before publishing, I'm sure the fans wouldn't have minded.Let's end up positive (Pros) :- The drinks system is fun and refereshing. I really digged that.- The old main cast characters are still gold. So far I've had the most fun playing Damien's route. His interactions and dialogue just felt most like the good old mon prom. But at the moment I think his interactions are also still missing voice lines which made them feel empty.- Milo.- More side characters and some of them are actually really good like Counselor Flodge. I will update this review if the game ends up getting some major updates that change my stance here. But we'll see, since my biggest issues at the moment are in the long boring dialogue and the main cast they chose to go with.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy games with vibrant and diverse characters, great stories, the ability to never experience the same exact play through twice, and campy (figuratively and literally) humor, then you will absolutely adore Monster Camp! It's a great paced game with amazing comedic timing and plenty of relevant references. You'll always be on the edge of your seat trying to figure out what's coming next! I think the best part is that you don't have to have played the original to enjoy Monster Camp either (though I highly recommend it!). A lot of sequels rely on previous attachments to characters from the original game, but the characters from Monster Camp are endearing all on their own! On my first run I got Dahlia and was initially disappointed, not because of her but because I secretly wanted Damien (who doesn't?!). By the end of week 2, however, I was totally in love with her. Dahlia, please crack my head between your thighs I am BEGGING YOU. Absolutely in love with this game. I fell in love with Monster Prom because of the fun art, great music, and incredible dialogue. I wasn't sure they could top themselves, but they definitely did. 3 cheers to the amazing developers, writers, artists, voice actors, and everyone else who worked on this game. Hope you all pour yourselves a drink to celebrate! I wish I had more time to explore it before work, because I know It'll be the ONLY thing I think about. Can't wait to see more of the characters. I feel like I got a lot of solo Dahlia scenes compared to the number of solo scenes I got with other characters in original Monster Prom game. Until then, time to start working on my fan fiction!PS: I feel like you'd be the type to accept smut as a resume for writers, so if you need any new writers, hit me up ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Without any spoilers since this game is so new, I can say that if you enjoyed Monster Prom, you're going to LOVE Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp. The basic formula is the same--you're in a place (camp) for a set period of time/encounters and you're trying to woo a love interest to join you for a romantic night of star gazing. Two differences between the first game and the sequel--your initial stats are controlled by what you pack and there is a nightly drink that might change your stats/game play instead of Val's store. I was sad that it seems maybe not all of our previous love interests attend camp with us. But there are plenty of other characters and cameos! Also, successfully watched the stars with Damien on my first play-through (after he punched a bear and we ran (romantically) for two miles...clearly)! _childDocuments_.review: Monster Camp is more of what made Monster Prom fun, but with some alterations. There are changes that make things feel a little different (such as the campfire events instead of lunchtime, the drink events instead of weekends, and choosing items at the start of the game for your stats). I definitely recommend playing the first game and getting several of the secret endings before playing this game, as there are lots of references to events in the first game, so if you start with this game, you might feel a bit lost for some of the context.I want to start by saying I do enjoy this game, and would recommend it to friends who I think would appreciate the humor and style of gameplay this game provides. I will be honest in my feelings of this game compared to the first title though.The writing that made Monster Prom appealing is present in this game, although I personally felt it was missing a little bit of the charm of the first game. The addition of many new characters in this game is such a plus, while expanding on characters who had minor roles in the the first game. There are several references in this game that made me laugh, but a few of characters feel a bit one dimensional. I enjoy that there are location specific events, and some characters have enough variation to make them good, while others felt a little too obsessive or focused on one reference for me to say that I actually like them (Batniss comes to mind specifically). I find it a little sad that only 2 of the previous games romanceable characters return to those roles (Damien and Calculestor). I know that there are plans to focus on other characters in the future titles (such as Scott and Polly being featured in Monster Roadtrip) but I did miss them as main options in this game. A possible reason for me missing their presence in those roles is that I find some of the options in this game to be a bit obsessive in certain areas. Aaravi, even though I play a lot of RPG's so her references were fun to me, Dahlia and Milo all felt a bit consumed on one thing, which seemed to drag them down a bit in my opinion. With such a focus on multiple playthroughs, I found myself wanting to get to know the aspects of the characters of the first game more than this one. I do have more playtime on the first game than this one, so maybe my opinions on some things will change as I play more, but all in all, I think this is a good game if you enjoyed the first.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Monster Prom! Again! But that's high praise. Managing to reach the same heights of amusement factor as the original is still quite a feat. The game does unfortunately seem to drive you toward a particular character as your date option (for stargazing rather than prom this time) right from the get-go based on some of your setup decisions. While I don't really mind this, as I'm personally down to experience all the various storylines and scenarios, it is something I can imagine frustrating players who had a particular character in mind to woo, or aren't interested in the one they were "assigned". Especially for a relationship/date sim game, it's kind of a perplexing design choice. But it's really my only complaint! The humor is not exactly high-brow or subtle, but it still routinely gets hard belly laughs from me. If you've played Monster Prom and enjoyed it, I feel very confident in recommending this. If you haven't, and the aforementioned complaint isn't a dealbreaker, then I'd say anyone who appreciates rowdy bisexual disaster comedy is also in for a good time. _childDocuments_.review: An absolute blast. Everything is turned up higher than the first game - pop culture references, sexual innuendo (or outright thirst), shock humor, social commentary, side character usage, and overall quality. A short list of my personal pros and cons:CONS1. Some of the aforementioned social commentary is EXTREMELY heavy-handed and blatant, to the point where the joke becomes awkward. I'm not saying you shouldn't take shots at world economics or politics or anything like that, but when you can barely go one full rotation in a 4-player game without an evil Capitalist caricature popping up and reminding you he's trying to bulldoze Camp Spooky, his character loses the sharp wit and charm it initially held.2. Holy ♥♥♥♥ is it long. I cannot overstate that this game will be something you should sit down and set aside time to play (at least if you like to read the lines aloud, which is how me and my friends play) - a four-player FULL game says it should take about 200 minutes (a bit over 3 hours) but my first FULL game took nearly four, and that's with us rushing towards the end. This isn't a bad thing intrinsically, but some of the jokes or scenes go on too long or could simply be condensed for ease; some of them, however, really benefit from being longer. Just come in expecting to sit down and enjoy, not to quick play a round.PROS:1. God, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ jokes, you know? Amazing. So many of them hit it out of the park that my friends and I, who I was initially a bit anxious about bringing to play with me, had to regularly stop to giggle at particular jokes or characters. And on the topic of jokes, there're even settings to filter out some problematic content if some things put you off (like drug/alcohol references, references to the first game, etc)! If you're up to it, however, I'd recommend trying all of the content the game has to offer; there's nothing like some of the out-of-left-field humor this game can bring.2. Aaravi is a main RO. That's literally it. That's worth buying this game for.3. The new Campfire/Drinking mechanics are well implemented and fun. By the time we finished, things were an absolute beautiful mess when it came to our stats, our romances, all of it.4. Nothing is sacred when it comes to content. I don't want to spoil anything... but just be aware, things can get surprisingly chaotic. Be wild. Take risks. You'll love it.5. The art has improved! Not that the first game's art was BAD, of course, but the style remains distinct and lovable while also being refined and given a fresh coat of color. Every character looks good, every venue is memorable, and the overview map of camp is pleasant to look at.6. All the new characters! There are oh-so-many! So very many of them are fun and memorable and show up frequently but not overbearingly so (except one Mr. P, who I firmly believe has TOO many events with his intrusion)! They are funny, they have flair, and they'll keep you interested in when - or if - they'll come back! 7. New ROs! Milo is a blast. Still doesn't outshine my adoration for certain other options, but they've got their own unique niche and don't fade into the sideline at all. I'm quite fond of them, in fact, and their writing is snappy enough that I'll certainly be looking to them for future playthroughs. Hex, Aaravi's new shoulder-warmer, is also phenomenal - they are a wonderful addition to an already well-made and fun-to-interact-with character, and their interactions made me genuinely smile both at how cute AND horrid they could be to eachother. 8. Final one, and this is less about the game, and more about the Devs. I was a somewhat higher-tiered backer for Monster Camp, and all through development, they've been very inclusive and willing to talk about the ideas both they and other backers had for the game. In the end, Monster Camp is a labor of love from a passionate community from all over the world, whose main uniting factor is being horny for fictional monsters. You can tell that Beautiful Glitch put their heart and soul into Monster Camp, and that they sincerely hope it succeeds - not just to get that paper, but to see their vision fulfilled and their fans rewarded. I'm already on the edge of my seat for whatever they work on next, because I know it'll be good.So, that all covered... Why are you still reading this?! Go buy it! You'll love it, I promise - and if you need friends to play with, I'm sure myself or someone else out in that vastness that is the Internet would be happy to join you. <4EDIT: After seeing the comment from Beautiful Glitch, and having spoken a bit in the MonsterProm Discord, I'd like to rescind my initial complaint that some NPCs 'show up too much' - there's actually a game mechanic which promotes storyline consistency where if you see an NPC once they are more likely to show up again, which, while I wasn't fond of the one in my initial complaint, is an overall great idea and a positive addition to the game. Rock on, Beautiful Glitch!

It takes the style of Monster Prom to a new setting and improves on a lot of the mechanics that were there from the start. The online takes a step up in this game and rather than a shop this game uses drinks at the end of a week to give boosts to stats and unlocks secret endings. A campfire replaces the lunch time and is also at the end of the week rather than the middle like in Monster Prom. This change keeps the game interesting. New characters are highlighted as main love interests as well. My favorite mechanic is the inclusion of special events that are basically like mini secret endings that add a lot of replay value. Overall I feel that Monster Prom is better, If you loved the first game you'll love this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review is more for my benefit than others, this is a very simple sequel question if you like monster prom youll like monster camp. That said theres a handful of changes that ill or good really made me take notice. First off monster proms core loop, picking not the right answers but the ones matching your stats is really not intuitive, and while there is a tutorial in this game, you have to buy it. This game expects you to play through it a ton of times which is fine, which leads to a bad exhaustion problem. Trying to see the strongest writing, all in the secret endings, the majority of the event writing all blurs together and you begin to just sorta skim and not enjoy. The music is solid but after a couple rounds youre definitely going to mute it and play something else for your sanity. This games a bisexuals delight, but occasionally as a lesbian its a bummer that to get all the secret girl endings, you have to play the boys, which is fine, but I don't play vns to kiss men, far too homosexual for that. You can still get it with pure luck and i prefer the more predictable drink system for these secret endings, but ultimately it still means you got to see content you don't care about to get a bit of fun stuff you do. Now I still recommend it after all that purely because, the writings ultimately good. Its funny, often more wholesome than you expect which provides a lot of help to its overly zanny tone, and when the secret endings to extra hard you can sometimes just be gut punched with just how extra something small might be.That all said... by the end of my 18 hours many of which was just spent trying to unlock the pizza girl ending  I enjoyed the game, but still wonder if my time wouldn't have been better spent elsewhere? _childDocuments_.review: It's not terrible, it's got some funny moments and the artwork remains phenomenal, but while playing it I just couldn't shake the impression that I was playing a moderately worse version of the first one. My biggest gripe is that the character development seems more stunted than it did in the first game (I suspect because they used a lot of the same characters and it's hard to continue character development in a sequel when it was done so well in the original), making it harder to feel connected with the characters. The humor is still there, a bit of it at least, but they dipped a little bit further into the realm of absurdity than they did in the first one, a too much so in my opinion. The events are also consistently longer, which drew out the jokes in a way I rarely felt was worth it. They also leaned pretty heavily on the first game for a lot of the events, and while you can change the settings so that it leaves out those references, I seems like I'm given the choice to play what feels like half a game, or what is literally half a game. They also got rid of the polariods for achieving victory for each main/love interest pairing, which was something I really enjoyed in the first game and felt like a nice way to imply that their stories continued beyond the credits screen (I know they're just bits in a chip, but give me my happy little fantasy). They didn't do a bad job at this game, I just can't think of a reason why I would suggest playing this game instead of playing (or even just re-playing) the first one.(I'll still probably buy the third one. I enjoyed Monster Prom 1 just that much)

_childDocuments_.review: It almost hurts to give the thumbs down here, as I loved the original game and I appreciate the warmth and good spirit of both the developers and the community they've helped create.  My thumb is tilted downward ever-so-slightly.  Also, note that I only play this game with three other people; I never play it solo.  That will be relevant to a number of my criticisms here and may not apply to a solo run.Anyhow...I don't precisely remember how, but the original Monster Prom became a meme in my gaming group, presumably because it has a funny title and we didn't know anything more than that.  Then we ended up playing it together as a lark, and ended up loving it.  It was charming, unique and frequently hilarious in a black comedy kind of way.  We got a lot of unexpected mileage out of it, and gobbled up the DLC, too.  Needless to say, this sequel was a no-brainer buy as well, but unfortunately, it fell well short of our expectations, and after four or five runs, it fell out of our game rotation.  Why is that?  Well, I'm glad you asked.Gameplay-wise, everything is generally improved this time around.  (Which is an odd thing to say in a negative review for a video game, but here we are.)  Loading up your backpack with funny items is a much more interesting and flexible way to set your starting stats than answering a few quiz questions.  And the dreaded Wealth stat is gone entirely, eliminating Library grinds just to buy random knick-knacks to see the variant storylines.  This is a darn good thing.  The campfire has replaced the cafeteria, and it offers a few more ways to interact with the monsters, and even the other players.  Best of all is the cocktail hour, where the adorable Juan mixes up drinks that can have significant effects on statistics, gameplay, and even the interface.  This is all great stuff.Unfortunately, this is a visual novel, so gameplay can only take you so far.  It's the writing and characters that really matter, and Monster Camp falls well short of its predecessor here.  It's not a total train wreck or anything - we had some genuine laughs as we played - but the drop-off is very noticeable.The first issue is the monsters you can romance.  If you've played all of the content in Monster Prom, literally every monster you can date in Monster Camp is a repeat except for Milo.  (And Milo is basically Liam but 300% more fabulous.)  The monsters being fairly one-dimensional was a common critique of the original, prompting a number of updates that added bonus stories to flesh them out more.  With that in mind, bringing old characters back to do variations on the same jokes as before was a mistake.  Damien is still METAL and punches things, Joy is still a Buffy/Charmed hero trapped in monster hell, Dahlia is still Damien but somehow louder, etc.  There really should have been six new monsters here, with possible secret endings to date the classic characters as fan service.  I'm sure there are dozens of other students at Spooky High that we never got to meet; this would have been the perfect chance.The real issue, however, is the editing, or lack thereof.  Turns drag on MUCH longer in this game, with far more writing per encounter than in Monster Prom.  This issue began to manifest in the Second Term DLC for that game, and it's only gotten worse.  The writing isn't bad, per se, there's just way too much of it.  Brevity is the soul of wit, after all, and taking a funny encounter and making it longer isn't to anyone's benefit.  The writer(s) are talented, but pacing is of crucial importance in any written endeavor, and doubly so if that endeavor is a multiplayer game and people are waiting ten minutes to take their turn.  Monster Prom was tightly-written, and encounters went just long enough to have a setup and payoff and keep things moving and lively.  Turns in Monster Camp just feel bloated in comparison, and a legitimately funny scene can get run into the ground long after the gag has landed.  Honestly, this game is one devoted editor with a chainsaw away from being a great sequel.Production-wise, well, it's a visual novel.  I like the art style here and the sporadic voice-acting is perfectly fine.  The usual Monster Prom surf rock bops in the background; solo players will likely want to supply their own music after a few runs to stay sane.  Playing cooperatively is easy as heck and the game never crashed or glitched on us.If they make another Monster X game (and I hope they do), I personally recommend a whole new cast and a tighter rein on the word count.  There are some talented and likable people at the wheel of this franchise, and they've definitely got more great games in them.  I look forward to playing them.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the original Monster Prom- this is more of the same but with a number of incredibly refreshing quality-of-life updates to the formula. Such as the ability to lock in your date from the start, three options for the length of the game, and the ability to remove many triggers in the options if you so choose. This has the same fantastic writing, hundreds of hours of content, and loveable characters in excess- The cast including two old fan faves and four characters new and old that that have previosly on had one romanceable path. While I definately miss Scott and Vera being on the roster- there are already several confirmed sequels/spinoffs with them in mind. While certain features like the Gallery still have to be implemented- the team is constantly updating the game in response to fan feedback and features and balancing will come soon. This game is amazing now, will only improve with time, and has enough content to justify a pricetag much larger than it has. If a rougelike competitive datling sim sond like something you'd like to check out- do it!

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Camp in a nutshell is about enjoying the story, admiring the whacky, graphic-novel style artwork, and building up your stats over the course of the summer to make sure you have enough points to win over your monster and secure a date to the meteor shower. The dialogue features a great deal of vulgarity, and it’s certainly not meant for the eyes of children. It’s outrageous and hilarious, and the scenarios are just as over-the-top as you would expect. It’s all about savoring the journey, and for most fans of this genre, there is a lot to appreciate.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey you. Yes, you! St.Valentine's suck for you? You either going to celebrate it with your left hand or just play a Mafia/Gangster game to reenact the St.Valentine's Day Massacre? Well fear no longer!Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp is there to fill that void that is still getting damped with Kung-Flu. A simple "visual novel" that looks that it's a dime a dozen in the graveyard of "w a n k e r" games, but that's where your wrong. This fine crafted game is actually well written, choices in the gameplay actually matter and pretty good punk music that gets a good mood going. Choose 1 of 4 (or 8 if you buy the DLC) demons and go out and try and get a lass or lad that you want to end up as your summer soulmate. Or just do it to get a summer fling. Or just enjoy summer by yourself. See if I care. But if your not a sad w a n k e r, you can play through smartly, learn more about each of the characters. The writing is pretty d a m n good and not cringy, a complete 180 from Life Is Tumbl- I mean Life Is Strange. Each character and situation is unique. The beauty is that the game is full of choices and each time you start it up, it always plays diffrently with the scenes all Randomly Generated to the point it is what I can describe is "handcrafted". Think of a Visual Novel version of the Director from L4D 1&2. I may not be a fan of these kinds of games, but d a m n it's b l o o d y fun and worth it on sale. It is also fun when you play on multiplayer with friends. Seeing each of you is stuck with and how you all react to who's the biggest simp.If you got some Dosh to burn, instead of being a tier 3 simp on a ethot's Twitch, buy this and go back again and again to a nice selection of Lasses and Lads. Dahlia is best Tomboy Demon GF!!! Now back to drinking more booze and plugging away with a Tommy Gun.Happy St Valentines Day.

_childDocuments_.review: Kickstarter BackerI came into this game a little burned out. Monster Prom was great, the DLC was fairly good, but a lot of time had gone by and replaying that game just didn't have the magic anymore. I honestly thought that this would be at best more of the same. It was not. The writing feels so much sharper then it was. THey play out scenes for more, (admittedly occasionally going overlong) but the dialouge and the action is always entertaining. The characters are more diverse across teh board-4 out of 6 characters are here for the first time as main Romantic Interests, and the two that were in the past game have both grown-in particular Damien. His character has evolved a fair bit since Monster Prom, making him a lot more engaging and fun to interact with and see get into shenanigans. The money system is gone, and the store has been replaced by a more dynamic bar. The store before frankly got routine-you grabbed it for a special ending or if you wanted to use Money to beef up a stat with a standard item. Here the new drinks system is really dynamic, either in skill or gamble mode. its fun to press your luck and aim for certain drinks. Also just a /bunch/ more side characters? We're seeing them more often doing things and interacting in ways and just more bit players running around. a lot more opportunities to find new favorites, and there are a /lot/ more outfits also for our main characters. Things that woudl've just been described in text before are now getting outfit changes. Someone starts a business for Anger or hosts a fake awards ceremony? Suddenly they're in a suit. A very good boy goes to infiltrate the enemy with jello tools? Yes he will be having a custom sprite wearing a jello beard! This game is a work of love and its breathing new life into the series. Super excited to see what comes next. Everything feels /way/ more on point and dynamic. I've had events now where the romantic intersts /initiate/ and are the ones to come flirt with your character. How cool is that?

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp is not a game, it's a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure e-book that's been dumped on Steam masquerading as a game.  The vast majority of this E-book is just a lot of clicking through badly written dialogue that would never have been accepted or published in print, which poses the question, "How did something this badly written end up on Steam?".To answer that question: When someone hoping to become an author is unable to get published in print, they spend $100 and dump their high school fan-fiction onto Steam, under the guise of a game.This particular E-Book/CYOA does have some "stats", numbers added to create the illusion of gameplay, but these numbers are less meaningful than the stats in an old Fighting Fantasy novel, and have little bearing on the various E-book endings this visual novel provides.  Nobody finished reading a Steve Jackson Fighting Fantasy book and said "Boy, what a great game I just played!".  Because books aren't games.  And neither is this.This E-book is yet another rehash in the monster dating E-book series from the same completely unpublishable authors.  There's no value either as literature or as a video game here. The E-book is a picture book, of course, the writing is so bad that the author felt the need to try maintain the interest of readers with bright colourful pictures.   The artwork here is terrible, it's a hodge-podge of amateurish "My First Wacom Tablet" style drawings used instead professional looking game assets.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget to arrange someone who can create graphical assets properly, or lack of talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low, enough on its own to deter gamers.There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this E-book will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.Visual novels/e-books are tedious at best... imagine the best novel you ever read, be that Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy or 2001: A Space Odyssey or Twilight (if you have terrible taste in literature), but then translate that to a format where the words dribble out and you have to click your mouse every time you wanted to read the next sentence, instead of just turning the pages. You'd think it was garbage.Now imagine that experience, but with much worse writing (because if these guys could write professionally, they'd be published authors and this would be on shelves in bookstores, and they wouldn't have to pay Valve $100 to self-publish this on Steam), and you have your average Steam e-book.You can get better quality books and comics for free online or from public libraries, or from bookstores for a fraction of the price of this "game".  Steam isn't a comic book store, neither is it Netflix, it's for games.  Your gaming rig is not a Kindle.  It's impossible for me to recommend things to PC gamers that aren't really games.You're forced to sign a highly questionable yet legally unenforceable End User License Agreement.  This agreement includes questionable (and possibly law breaching) privacy requirements that no gamer should ever have to engage in.  Developers must learn they are here to serve gamers, not control them.  I had my cat walk over the keyboard while the EULA was displaying, which fixed that problem for me.As mentioned, this E-Book behaves as spyware and collects "telemetry" and personally identifying information.  There is no apparent way to prevent this hostile and sinister privacy invasion.  The developers will make the unverifiable claim that this data isn't personally identifying, of course that's BS as they're collecting IPs and all kinds of other information about gamers, when combined with other profiling data this can 100% identify an individual.  They say it's for "QA" purposes but there's no guarantee they're not profiling you or selling your data to third parties as they spy on you.  Should you trust them?  Of course not... if they had any concerns about user safety and privacy,   There's simply no reason to trust them and gamers should avoid this E-Book because of this unacceptable privacy invasion.To quote part of the toxic privacy policy: So you can see the developers toxic, harmful intention is very clear here.  Be warned. I'm sure Orwell would have had conniptions if he knew that books in the future would actively spy on their readers.  Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp has the completely unrealistic cash grab price of $12 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the E-Book, coupled with the unrealistic price, and the unethical embedded spyware, this is impossible to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Ugh god, I've only done like three playthroughs and I'm already in love with this game. The sense of humor is in the same vein as with Monster Prom, but with a lot more riffs and fandom jokes. So far, my favorite joke has been the character of Batniss, which is basically a small bat character who carries a quiver of arrows and is hilariously devious. All of the love interests are fun, too, with the same or similar personalities with the exception of character arc and developments. Milo is my new favorite love interest character, as he's really sweet and funny. The events and dialogue options are as silly and ridiculous as ever. Overall, it's just a completely gorgeous game and you can really tell that Beautiful Glitch really upped the ante with this one. The character art is phenomenal as always, but in the end credits sequence, they actually animated some of the scenes with the monsters. It's absolutely gorgeous to behold and the music is awesome, as always. My only real gripe about the game is the minigame with the drinks at the camp bar. Juan the Small Magical Latino Cat doesn't explain the gameplay very well, only the concept of what you're going for, so you're kind of left floundering and trying to figure out what the rules and controls are. But, on the bright side, if you don't like competing against the bots in that minigame, you can just choose the gamble option and either choose the drink Juan gives you or the mystery box--so even with the troublesome minigame, it's still possible to get drinks that way. It's not even that big of a gripe, and considering the rest of the game's content, I'd say the pros definitely outweigh the cons. Obviously, the bugs will be worked out of the game in time, but one bug I noticed was after certain events where I had to press my enter key, my mouse cursor would separate from the game's stylized one and have my normal cursor laying over top of it. To be fair, I had that problem with the original MonProm so it may be a bug with my computer specifically, but it's just a little annoying. It usually goes away on its own after a while, but I just wanted to bring it up in case the developers aren't aware of it.Final takeaway: if you love trashy humor with lots of sex- and drug-based jokes, then this is the game for you. It's offbeat, terrible, and murder-rife at times, but it never stops acknowledging that its humor is, in fact, not supposed to be normal. If you liked Monster Prom, you'll adore Monster Camp.

_childDocuments_.review: PROS: Listen. I laughed my ass off. I went slack jawed and uttered "oh my gooood" at some of the GORGEOUS, GORGEOUS art, I listened to my friend SQUEAL SHARPLY IN MY EAR whenever she saw a character who's design she was smitten with, I laughed my ass off a whole lot more, and then I surprisingly went "AWWWWWW???" when the game got weirdly deep and moving at times???It's basically Monster Prom turned up to 11. A fantastic mix of old characters and old mechanics with new characters and brand new mechanics, better writing, better jokes, better art, and more of everything you loved.Me and my friend were blown away that the main 6 love interests are only a small percentage of this game's large and lovely cast.If you haven't played Monster Prom: You don't HAVE to do that to enjoy this, in the same sense that you don't HAVE to watch season 1 of a sitcom to enjoy Season 4 of it - It'll still be a blast, but obviously it'll be MORE of a blast if you get the callbacks and jokes from the previous "season".This game works %400 times better in multiplayer - And if you don't have anyone in your day-to-day you feel comfortable swooning over cartoon monsters with, worry not! The game has a very active discord community with rooms specifically for finding matches.This game promotes things like gender inclusivity, letting players choose their own pronouns (and even having a player character that is canonically genderqueer in one of the DLCs) and generally promotes a very liberal left wing agenda that I (and statistically speaking, you) either identify with or find relatable enough from my peers to make for enjoyable comedy fodder.Also, unsurprisingly there's a bunch of secret endings and paths.Also, Milo's character design is, in itself, a big pro for this game.I wholeheartedly recommend this.CONS:Okay it's bad enough Monster Prom didn't have a save feature but why does THIS not have one either??? It's so frustrating playing a game with someone for SEVERAL HOURS (the "estimated play time" is never even close to accurate) and1. Not being able to stop halfway through when you suddenly get tired or someone has to go - because you know you can't save2. Having the game crash, or your internet to go out for like 2 seconds and BAM, game over, man.Every game has bugs, especially new ones, and it'd be forgivable, but the fact there is no save feature turns every potentially minor issue into a much bigger one. Please, a save feature in the next game!Having said all that, bottom line is still: Excellent game. Funny, fun, moving, surprising, and I can't WAIT for future content from this series even though I'm not even done with this installment yet!

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes I fail at every choice and get turned down. Sometimes I succed at every choice and still get turned down. I kinda got the feeling I got the dating skills of a fridge. The game agrees.Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp is a comedy dating sim. More inclined towards comedy rather than a dating sim.You have a couple rounds (in the short mode 6 activties, 2 campfires and 2 drinks) to get your partner to agree to go to the meteor shower with you. During the activitie rounds you are given strange and funny choices. And, if you do it right, there are multiple stories you can follow over multiple activities. You can only follow one story per run so there is a high replayabilty. To spice it up there are drinking rounds, where you can battle for a drink. The drink can have many effects on you and other players, it can change stats, add boosts, add nerfs or even change your character. It is chaotic and fun.During your run you are introduced to way more characters than the 6 datables. Each of them stranger than the last. The artstyle of the characters is nice and has gotten even better than the style from Monster Prom while still staying true to the original style.One downside of the game is that you get a single question at the start of the game. That question then binds you to a certain character you are now basicly locked with for the run. You don't 'really' get to pick yourself.Still the game is very enjoyable. With 300+ event, 1000+ outcomes and 25 secret endings you can play plenty of rounds before it starts to feel repetitive.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★☆Funny, witty, unpredictable monster romancing with awesome artwork and a lot of customisation. The humour in this game can be dirty, sometimes gross and generally what you'd expect from crude teens, but it definitely works. You will go from giving your pubic hair to make a potion, to crushing capitalism with a hat store.  If some of the more extreme humour isn't for you, or you come to the game for a good time and don't want to be bullied by characters or you don't want references to the first game since you haven't got it (yet), you can turn it all off in the settings! Make the game you will have fun with. The graphics are awesome. The style is fun and bright, and scenery is real pretty too. All the characters have unique expressions and cards. Free DLC! You can purchase some alternative costumes for the characters (and play as a fridge) with in-game currency. There is a lot to the game. With each play-through you'll find new plots, new characters and new endings. This might be a personal take, but I do wish there was some sort of skip. Perhaps a way to skip dialogue or plots the user has already used for those that have been playing for a while. When they said they had an online feature, I was hoping there would be a way to just join lobbies online but alas... The Blood Mary drink is a thing. A really fun game to play and look at, that has tons of replay value and can end friendships in the best of ways.  Well worth the price. If anything, it is arguably under-priced.  Being rejected, loving a demon and uncovering a Mer-King conspiracy has never been so fun.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I loved Monster Prom. I didn't sink that many hours into it, but it's a fun game with lots of cute monsters to smooch, what's not to love? Well, MonProm had its issues, with a TON of over the top drug/alcohol references and senseless violence that definitely crossed the line from funny to just uncomfortable, one of the love interests was literally a genocidal princess(Sorry Miranda, no matter how cute you are, the revolution is coming for your head), and sometimes it just missed the mark.MonCamp is /chill/. It's essentially the same game in terms of mechanics, with a delightful few twists here and there, tons of random events, secret endings, and cute stories. But it's all a little more... relaxed, out at the camp. Much more in line with the content from Monster Prom's first DLC, Second Term, than the edgier parts of MonProm's original release. It's still irreverent, violent, and yes there's drugs and alcohol, what summer camp is complete without them, but you're also given the option to filter content, although some of the warnings are unfortunately vague(/one category is just "Horrible People")The new love interests are actually mostly secondary characters from MonProm, so there's some delightful consistency and we get to see their characters fleshed out, plus Milo the Death Reaper is an all new addition for MonCamp and... whew. Wow. Yes. Helllllll yes.On my first playthrough I got a secret ending for Aaravi and the ending card was the Witcher Bathtub Pose(you know the one,) so really 10/10 great game can't wait to play with my friends

_childDocuments_.review: this is simply one of the best games I've played in this wild ride of a year. I've fallen in love with basically every single one of the characters (especially Milo) and that goes for my friends too. The gameplay is amazingly fun, the jokes hit basically every time and the small references to Monster Prom sprinkled throughout make it so much more endearing to me. I just love everything about this game. And don't get me started on the credits. They quickly became one of my favorite moments in my gaming life. The song. The animation. The references to events in the game. It's just perfect. This is also a point on Monster Prom, but as a non-binary person, I love how LGBTQ+ inclusive this game is. The amount of representation and casual handling of it I simply adore. The option of choosing they/them pronouns also falls under this category. I'm just very happy as we enbys are rarely represented, even though it's getting better. Sorry for the detour but representation in the video game industry is a very important aspect to me, ans this game (and Monster Prom) just do(es) it perfectly. Another thing i wanna praise the team for is the game customization. While mods aren't really available (yet) like in Monster Prom, the fact that you can enable and disable some potentially triggering content is very thoughtful and nice to see, even if I don't particularly use it. Overall, an amazing game that, if this is your type of humor, artstyle or just genre, I highly recommend. Tbh i just recommend it to everyone. 11/10, simply inncredible.

_childDocuments_.review: short and sweet: Monster Prom 3 is just a better game in every regard. a bit elaborated: my major issues are with the writing beats (often too graphic even with adjusted settings), and with the ineffective content notes (they didn't improve my playing experience really at all). I get it's a game about a bunch of monsters, but I wish I could play through even a single game without cringing. in the almost 14 hours I played this game I cringed at least once every single run. definitely worth spending your money elsewhere if you're a sensitive creature like me LOL
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp

_childDocuments_.review: Love that most of the characters to date are new. They also added new side characters. I love that a couple of the monsters use they/them, and one of these you can try wooing. The ending credits are animated which was fun. Compared to most dating sims these games present a fun challenge when picking the right option.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It call it self monster camp, and that is exacly what it gives you. Lot of fun characters, looooot of fun events, and simply lot of improvements compered to first game.If you are playing solo, you MUST get the item that shows what stat is requaired for what choice, as it is really bad to fail that final event because you swear that choice is a bold stat check but nop it was a a fun stat check in disguise.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp

_childDocuments_.review: "Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp" brings you more of the world's best (and maybe only?) multiplayer dating sim; but in a way you've never expected! The sequel brings you into a new setup (summer camp) with new characters to romance, including old faces and new ones: Damien, Calculester, Milo, Dahlia, Joy and Aaravi. But that's not all, Monster Camp comes with twists here and there: from the campfire mechanics to a new stage full of magic mixed drinks.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Prom 2: Monster Camp

name: Murder by Numbers
detailed_description: Collector's Edition About the Game Solve Pixel Puzzles to find clues. Use those clues to interrogate witnesses. Work your way to the truth... ...and uncover the mystery of Murder by Numbers! Los Angeles, 1996. Honor Mizrahi was just an actress on a hit TV detective show. But when her boss ends up dead just minutes after he fires her, she finds herself starring in her own murder mystery. Teaming up with SCOUT, a reconnaissance robot thrown away after a mysterious incident, she sets out to clear her name - and a new detective duo is born! Investigate a range of murders across TV studios, glitzy award shows, drag clubs, and more - all set to an energetic soundtrack from famed composer Masakazu Sugimori (Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Ghost Trick and Viewtiful Joe). Uncover a dark conspiracy by interrogating a wild range of weird and wonderful characters, designed by the incomparable Hato Moa, creator of Hatoful Boyfriend. 90s fashions! Upbeat jams! Sass dialled up to 100! Questionable jokes! Drag queens! All that and more awaits... in Murder by Numbers!
